Kuhn's paradigms explain why dissident alternatives like Atkins talk past the dominant school (Atkins and Agatston are cardiologists, not dieticians), and the 2002–2004 studies showing improved lipids on more fat figure as the kind of surprise that precedes paradigm change. His verdict: neither trusting nor resisting experts is foolish; 'human knowledge is too important to be left to experts.'
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 21 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Womack tests whether Atkins counts as a Kuhnian paradigm shift, using the Ptolemaic-to-Copernican transition as the model: paradigms define which problems matter, normal science accumulates anomalies, and crisis ends in a new paradigm. Measured against the dieting paradigm's own goals, Atkins flunks — its short-term wins fade by twelve months in the JAMA comparison with the Ornish, Zone, and Weight Watchers diets, with 30–50 percent dropout — so the dieting paradigm itself, which treats obesity as an individual plate problem, is the thing in crisis. Her proposed replacement shifts from the individual to the 'toxic food environment': sidewalks, zoning, food advertising rules, and the French Paradox as the existence proof.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 16 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Bruce Reichenbach recounts the failure of the Enlightenment quest for certainty from Descartes and Locke through Kant to the positivists, and argues that Lewis's Narnia instead models knowing as perspectival (the Stable door whose inside is bigger than its outside), value-laden (the Dwarfs' self-chosen dark paradigm that turns Aslan's feast into refuse and violets into stable litter), and personal (Lucy's unarguable knowledge that she has seen Aslan in Prince Caspian, read through Michael Polanyi's tacit knowledge). Kuhn's competing paradigms frame theism versus atheism, James's will to believe opens the chapter, and Plantinga's defeaters keep personal knowledge from collapsing into mere subjectivity.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 101 "Wittgenstein Ultimate Bullshit Detector—or Bullshitter" — Fuller argues that mastering a discipline converts critics into loyal insiders — Thomas Kuhn's 'normal science' enshrines the tendency, cognitive dissonance explains it, and Blaise Pascal's wager is the general model of betting on a way of life that makes you receptive to its confirming signs. Against this he sets the Protestant tradition of Luther's conscience, 'playing it by ear', which like the Sophists concedes that reality rarely yields yes-or-no answers — the gap we fill being bullshit — and he frames the dispute as realism versus antirealism, reading Frankfurt's On Bullshit as an ad hominem attack on antirealists. He then re-examines Frankfurt's star witness: Wittgenstein's rebuke of Fania Pascal for saying she felt 'like a dog that has been run over' now looks like a spectacular lack of imagination, since evolutionary psychology, being forged at that very moment, has been narrowing the human-animal mental gap ever since.
- **The Beatles and Philosophy - Nothing You Can Think that Can't Be Thunk**, ch. 10 "CHAPTER 3 “LOOKING FOR THE INNER HEAT”" — The chapter reads Dylan's self-becoming as a chain of identity-emulations and overcomings — Hank Williams, Woody Guthrie, Ramblin' Jack Elliott — with Jon Pankake's folk-police critique and the Mike Seeger epiphany acting as Kuhnian anomalies that force a paradigm shift from folksinger to songwriter, each gatekeeper playing the 'Hegelian negative' Dylan needed. It argues Dylan fused folk, beat poetry, and rock and roll into an 'archaic revival' of mythic, enchanted consciousness against modern rationalization, rejecting the Sartrean/beat existentialism of a meaningless world in favor of co-creating meaning, and treating authenticity as the refusal of fixed identity (the Zimmerman-to-Dylan renaming, 'I'm gonna get me a new Bob Dylan'). The Newsweek exposé, Irwin Silber's open letter, and Johnny Cash's guitar-gift blessing stage his passage from 'King of Folk' to electric rock, with the little-known 1962 cut of Presley's 'That's All Right' showing that going electric was a return home — folk having been, in Dylan's words, 'just an interruption.'
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 18 "Vertigo and Epistemological Vertigo" — Flory reads Vertigo as an epistemological parable: Scottie's 'hardheaded Scot' method, collecting facts and deducing from universal principles, fails three times (the step-stool 'cure' for his acrophobia, explaining away Madeleine's 'possession' with the horse statue, forcing Judy up the bell tower for confirmation), delivering an implicit critique of Vienna Circle positivism in the manner of Carnap and Ayer. Against Scottie, the chapter mobilizes Kuhn's theory-laden facts, Aristotle's point that human conduct resists codification by exceptionless laws, and Hume's 'slave of the passions,' with Descartes's automata and Chalmers's philosophical zombies framing the problem of other minds. Midge, who knows people emotionally as well as factually, models the alternative: philosophers who fear 'epistemological vertigo' should give up epistemological training wheels and accept that minds, especially emotions, escape law-like rules.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 11 "Thematic Synchronicity" — Jones asks what the famous Dark Side of the Rainbow synchronization (album plus The Wizard of Oz, started on the third MGM lion roar) could mean given that the band denies designing it. He catalogs vivid syncs ('Time''s chimes as Miss Gulch bicycles past, 'Money''s cash register entering Munchkinland, 'Us and Them''s 'black and blue' over the Witch and Dorothy), then rejects both the Waters-conspiracy model and Jung's acausal 'synchronicity' as pseudoscience, proposing instead Conrad's apophenia and Kuhn's point that suspecting patterns others miss is the lifeblood of discovery. His resolution is 'thematic synchronicity': both works stage the struggle between security and transcendence, Dorothy's 'Over the Rainbow' against 'Eclipse''s 'all you touch and all you see is all your life will ever be,' so the coincidences feel objective because they are subjectively real to everyone.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 29 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Surveys the philosophy of science through Breaking Bad: Walt's authority trades on the trusted white-coat stereotype (Jesse's 'you're supposed to be a scientist', Tuco's CPR demand), while the chapter traces how modern science distinguished itself from alchemy via Kuhn's structure of scientific revolutions and Lakatos's research programmes, and how Feyerabend and the Traditional Knowledge movement challenge Western science's monopoly - echoed in Jesse's chili powder and the ingenious 'shake-and-bake' method. Walt and Jesse's quarrel over method resolves into an apprentice-master reconciliation ('you're an artist'), mirroring science's own shifting self-image. Ellul's grim prediction that technology, once embraced, cannot be made humane explains the ending: remission comes too late, and Walt may as well try to un-invent a weapon of mass destruction.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 31 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — John Huss asks whether Andy Serkis deserved an Oscar nomination for playing Caesar through performance capture, and argues that 'What is acting?' is a Socratic-style definitional question (like stumping Euthyphro on piety) of the sort Wittgenstein diagnosed as a language confusion, since the definition of movie acting is in flux. Using the seeing-as debate, Kuhnian theory-ladenness of observation versus Fodor's Muller-Lyer point that belief does not dictate sight, he explains why animators and fans see such different things in the identical raw footage. He concludes, with James Franco, that acting is an emergent ensemble property of actors reacting to one another on a shared stage, which performance capture enables rather than threatens, and a coda notes PETA's hope that CG performers will end the use of animal actors.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 17 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Cole Bowman explains the human-Formic war through Donald Davidson's critique of the idea of a self-contained conceptual scheme: the buggers' inability to grasp 'father,' 'individual,' or human sentience looks like complete untranslatability, yet Ender donning the bugger mask and the hive-queen's philotic contact show, via Davidson's principle of charity, that translation and a new shared scheme are possible. Kuhn's incommensurable paradigms and Feyerabend's account of how new theories eliminate old meanings frame how both species discard their prior concepts once Ender becomes the single point where the two schemes meet.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 26 "The Devil and Philosophy" — The Bocks use the courtroom frame of The Exorcism of Emily Rose to ask whether anyone could be justified in believing in demon possession, since the same seizures, polyglot voices, and levitations read differently under naturalism and supernaturalism. Kuhn's paradigms explain why neither worldview abandons ship at anomalies, and they weigh Wiebe's 'finite spirits as theoretical entities,' Hume's miracles argument (with Levine's Red Sea thought experiment as rebuttal), and the Cartesian ghost-in-the-machine premise that possession would require. Testing even a Men in Black alien hypothesis against the religiously specific phenomena, they conclude that a witnessed case like Emily's could rationally justify belief in possession.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 26 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Russ Hamer takes Mac's 'Science Is a Liar Sometimes' defense - Aristotle, Galileo, and Newton each proved his predecessor 'a bitch' - and his claim that believing in evolution takes as much faith as belief in God, and answers with philosophy of science. Popper's falsificationism explains why Mac's 'I won't change my mind... regardless of the facts' is the essence of the non-scientific: only theories risking precise, falsifiable predictions (Einstein's light deflection) count as science, unlike vague astrology or Charlie's cherry-picked evidence that the Waitress will love him. Kuhn's distinction of normal and revolutionary science explains why past failures never discredited science - falsifications within a paradigm are tuning, and the Gang's group-configuration trials in 'The Gang Solves the Gas Crisis' are normal science at its best - so revisability is science's strength, not a reason to fear looking like a science bitch.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 33 "20. The Intersection of Science and Philosophy, the Seediest Corner in Ankh-Morpork" — A comic sprint through Western thought anchored in the Science of Discworld books, the chapter runs from Aristotle—whose geocentric four-element physics, it notes, fits Discworld better than Roundworld, and whose condemnations of usury it digresses over—through Descartes's cogito and mind-body dualism, Ryle's 'ghost in the machine,' behaviorism, identity theory, eliminative materialism, and functionalism's brain-as-computer picture, to show how philosophy of mind advances by each theory picking on its predecessor. Newton's occult-seeming gravity, later overturned by Einstein, illustrates the chapter's real thesis drawn from Pratchett's 'Lies-to-Wizards': neither science nor philosophy erects a timeless edifice of facts, since 'every so often, you have to unlearn what you thought you already knew,' while Diogenes and the Cynics supply the model of philosophy done in the common tongue that Pratchett shares.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 28 "16. The Pleasure of the Twist" — Scales maps the experience of a TZ twist onto Kuhn's Structure of Scientific Revolutions: planted anomalies (Nan Adams' 'things are a little wrong,' Jana's missing childhood photographs, the Kanamits' ominous 'simply trust us') accumulate until the ending makes viewers, like scientists in a revolution, 'come to live in a different world' — rejecting cumulative growth and theory-neutral observation along the way. He then explains the pleasure through Kuhn's theory-ladenness experiments with anomalous playing cards and Churchland's connectionist prototypes: at 'It's a cookbook!' the Kanamits' deeds are suddenly re-categorized from helping behavior to livestock, triggering the same dopamine jolt as getting a joke.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 29 "17. You’ve Never Seen a Miracle" — Andrew Kuzma reads the film's religious texture from Sapper's Graham Greene novel to Wallace as a Gnostic Demiurge — a lesser creator-god — whose 'angels', like biblical ones, possess the free will to rebel, which is exactly what Luv does when she lies to Wallace about Joshi's death. The mystery child imports the whole miraculous-birth and chosen-one tradition, from Rachel's opened womb to Joi's 'born, not made' echoing the Nicene Creed's 'begotten'. But K is not the chosen one, and via 'Galatians Syndrome' the chapter applies Paul's paradigm shift in Galatians — faith, not flesh, makes one Abraham's heir; 'no longer Jew or Greek, slave or free' — to show birth never mattered: K, Joi, and Sapper become human by believing, choosing, and dying for the right cause.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 25 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Reads the 'Sad Sack' photograph, which Wayne Jarvis sees as Iraqi WMD bunkers and Barry Zuckerkorn sees as Tobias's testicles, through the Duhem-Quine thesis of underdetermination and Kuhn's theory-ladenness of observation: the dominant 'George Sr. the traitor' paradigm dictates what is seen and nearly mobilizes Buster for war, while Barry's rival theory creates a crisis that only the omniscient narrator resolves. Kuhn's five criteria for theory choice (accuracy, consistency, scope, simplicity, fruitfulness) are applied to the rival 'theories', and George Michael's failed eye exam dramatizes the skeptical moment when no lens lets you see clearly, showing knowledge is a social and political position.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 18 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Jones explains the Leonard–Leslie breakup ('Tell me, Leonard, how would we raise the children?') as a genuine clash of research commitments: string theory with its demanded extra dimensions versus Leslie's loop quantum gravity. Along the way he uses Popper's falsifiability and Kuhn's paradigms — the 1998 dark-energy discovery as falsification at work, Sheldon's alien-parasite hypothesis as paradigm-protecting refusal to accept that Amy is aroused by Zack — and the Dirac-to-Anderson antimatter story alongside Sheldon's North Pole monopole expedition to weigh theoretical against experimental science. Leonard emerges as the Feynman-style skeptic ('At best you can say, hey, my idea has internal logical consistency'), which is exactly what Leslie cannot forgive.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 18 "Of Science, Sorcery, and Philosophy" — The chapter reads Strange's conversion from neurosurgeon to sorcerer as a Kuhnian paradigm shift: his medical materialism is 'normal science' puzzle-solving that keeps resisting anomalies (Pangborn's impossible recovery, the astral projection, the multiverse tour) until Kamar-Taj offers a rival paradigm with its own exemplars, which he can only adopt by learning 'knowledge how' through tedious practice. It explains incommensurability through Strange's inability to rationally persuade his old medical colleagues, then contrasts Kuhn with Popper's falsificationism, Feyerabend's 'anything goes' anarchism (sorcery once looked as disreputable as early heliocentrism), and Lakatos's progressive versus degenerating research programs to ask whether sorcery could count as a science in Strange's world.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 17 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Cole Bowman explains the three Formic invasions as failures between 'conceptual schemes,' deploying Davidson's 'On the Very Idea of a Conceptual Scheme' — translatability, the principle of charity, and the closet analogy — alongside Kuhn's incommensurable paradigms and Feyerabend's account of how new theories eliminate old meanings. Ender donning the bugger mask in Peter's game and his final philotic bond with the hive-queen show the two schemes touching at a single shared point, making Ender 'the metal in between' who begins translating between human and Formic worlds.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 30 "It’s Life in the Solar System, Jim, But Not as We Know It" — Uses MacIntyre's demand for self-knowledge — awareness of the social and political currents that shape one's beliefs — to diagnose the Martian Congressional Republic's exceptionalism (Lopez berating 'short-sighted and selfish' Earthers from the Donnager) and to chart Bobbie Draper's redemption arc: refusing to fire first on Ganymede, refusing to bear false witness after the hearings, protecting Holden at the Ring Station, defecting to Avasarala, and finally rescuing Naomi. It maps MCR culture onto American space culture — Kennedy's Rice speech, the Mars Society and National Space Society founding statements, Zubrin's Case for Mars, and Patricia Limerick's and Linda Billings's critique of the 'conquering the space frontier' metaphor, with Carnap's frameworks and Kuhn's incommensurability explaining how metaphors hide alternatives — and argues the MCR never acquires self-knowledge, a failure that ends in its alliance with Marco Inaros and the move to Laconia, while Draper's willingness to update her beliefs shows what philosophy asks of real spaceflight advocates.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 22 "NOTES" — Asks how to tell genuine science from pseudoscience using Chandra Suresh's rejected Activating Evolution theory, Sheldrake's morphic fields, alchemy, and Behe's intelligent design. Kuhn's picture of normal science, anomalies, and revolutions explains why Suresh would need a full-blown crisis in evolutionary theory — such as people actually flying — before the community accepts him, and why time rather than mockery settles a theory's fate. Ockham's razor condemns the unnecessary organizing principles in both Sheldrake's and Suresh's theories, and intelligent design is exposed as bad method because, like creationism, it was devised to protect a prior commitment from disconfirming fossil and cosmological evidence.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 12 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Johnson uses 'Go God Go's' future of 2546—where Dawkins-style atheism has become a warring religion and otter scientists intone 'Oh my Science!'—to ask whether science and religion genuinely conflict and whether New Atheism is itself a faith. Applying abduction and the four criteria of adequacy, he argues the embellished-story hypothesis beats miracle claims about Jesus (whose legend grew Gospel by Gospel), Sathya Sai Baba, Joseph Smith, and Xenu, that Mr(s). Garrison's 'you can't disprove God' and the show's sarcasm commit an appeal to ignorance, and that Stan's water-into-wine scene with Jesus shows how easily people are fooled. He allows Kuhnian theory change in science but rejects James's will-to-believe for existence claims—the moon whale Willzyx needs evidence—and concludes Parker and Stone are unfair to Dawkins: ending religion would not end violence, but it would remove the easiest justification for it, and some answers are simply true even when unknown.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 28 "16. The Pleasure of the Twist" — Scales argues that Twilight Zone twist endings are miniature Kuhnian paradigm shifts: anomalous clues accumulate ('things are a little wrong' in 'The Hitch-Hiker,' Jana's mismatched photographs, the Kanamits' book title), then the ending forces a wholesale reinterpretation in which we 'come to live in a different world,' as when 'To Serve Man' turns benevolence into livestock. Extending Kuhn's theory-ladenness with Paul Churchland's connectionist prototypes, he explains the pleasure of the twist as the brain's reward for suddenly re-categorizing a whole story under a new prototype. The show's twist toolkit, he adds, seeded later works from Planet of the Apes to The Sixth Sense.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 42 "The Doctor Dances" — Alexander Bertland uses Vico, Cassirer, and Horkheimer and Adorno to argue Doctor Who refuses to simply side with science over myth. Vico shows myth as world-constructing ritual that binds community and carries moral wisdom ('Snakedance's' Snakedance defeats the Mara; 'Meglos' shows myth's danger), while Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment argues science is itself a limiting, mythical framework: the Doctor's insistence that 'fixed points' in time cannot be changed ('The Fires of Pompeii,' 'The Waters of Mars') reflects his own self-constructed scientific paradigm, not real necessity. The Doctor lives well by humbly balancing myth and science.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 24 "14. Beyond Loyalty and Disloyalty" — Bartolo Alegre uses Seldon's trial claim that 'scientific truth is beyond loyalty and disloyalty' to ask whether even formal sciences like logic can be biased. Against Bogdanov's and Lenin's Marxist idea of a 'proletarian logic,' he shows that logical principles (non-contradiction, explosion) have been revised by paraconsistent logicians on purely mathematical grounds, using Hardin's symbolic-logic decoding of the Anacreon message and Orwell's doublethink as illustrations. Drawing on Popper's rejection of uninformative contradictions, Kuhn's sociological account of scientific change, and Lakatos's rational reconstruction, he argues science transcends individual scientists' loyalties only through a diverse, competing community of experts, as when Hummin's loyalty to humanity pushed Seldon to make psychohistory practical.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 28 "16. The Pleasure of the Twist" — Scales argues that Twilight Zone twist endings mirror Kuhn's account of scientific revolutions: seeded anomalies accumulate until a 'paradigm shift' makes us reinterpret everything, as in 'To Serve Man' ('It's a cookbook!'), 'The Lateness of the Hour,' and 'The Hitch-Hiker.' He ties Kuhn's theory-ladenness of observation (the anomalous playing-card experiment) to Paul Churchland's connectionist, prototype-based bottom-up neurophilosophy, concluding the pleasure of the twist is the dopamine reward for deploying a new prototype—the same jolt we get from a joke or a genuine insight.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 83 "78. The Witness as Philosophy How Knowledge Is Constructed" — Cuddy asks what epistemology Blow built into The Witness's frustrating puzzles and its windmill videos (Burke, Feynman, Moriarty, Spira, Gangaji). He rejects the sophistic/Protagorean 'knowledge depends on the observer' reading (most puzzles have objective, inductive-and-deductive solutions, e.g. the yellow-glass bunker) and the strict scientific realism of the Burke video defended by Putnam's no-miracles argument. Using Plato's cave and the aporia of Socrates' Meno (the puzzle's 'ah-ha' epiphanies), and Kuhn's incommensurable paradigm shifts (the game's 'hard left turns' forcing players to overhaul their understanding), he concludes the game argues that true knowledge is attainable, individually and collectively, though reached by a nonlinear, paradigm-shifting route rather than pure realism or relativism.

### Anything Goes (epistemological anarchism)

Epistemological anarchism is the provocative position advanced by Paul Feyerabend, summarized in his slogan 'anything goes,' that there is no single fixed method or set of rules to which all good science must conform. Drawing on the history of science, Feyerabend argued that major advances often occurred precisely because researchers broke prevailing methodological norms, and that rigid prescriptions would have stifled progress. The phrase is less a positive rule than a rejection of universal method, defending theoretical pluralism and the freedom of inquiry against attempts to impose one privileged standard of rationality.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 16 "Pals" — Madeline Muntersbjorn uses Season Four's Initiative-versus-Scoobies conflict to dissolve the Science Wars: Professor Walsh's secret, unfalsifiable Project 314 makes her Karl Popper's bad scientist, while Buffy's gang embodies Feyerabend's pluralism and Peirce-and-James pragmatism — Buffyverse rules are probabilistic rather than deterministic, and the gang welcomes anyone willing to ask questions and do research. Her three ideals — pluralism, pragmatism, pals — culminate in 'Primeval,' where the combo-Buffy enjoining spell (Willow's spirit, Xander's heart, Giles's mind, Buffy's hand) literally enacts James's meliorism: the world may be saved if each agent does their level best, together. Walsh dies alone because she has no pals; Buffy saves the world 'a lot' because she does.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 29 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Surveys the philosophy of science through Breaking Bad: Walt's authority trades on the trusted white-coat stereotype (Jesse's 'you're supposed to be a scientist', Tuco's CPR demand), while the chapter traces how modern science distinguished itself from alchemy via Kuhn's structure of scientific revolutions and Lakatos's research programmes, and how Feyerabend and the Traditional Knowledge movement challenge Western science's monopoly - echoed in Jesse's chili powder and the ingenious 'shake-and-bake' method. Walt and Jesse's quarrel over method resolves into an apprentice-master reconciliation ('you're an artist'), mirroring science's own shifting self-image. Ellul's grim prediction that technology, once embraced, cannot be made humane explains the ending: remission comes too late, and Walt may as well try to un-invent a weapon of mass destruction.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 28 "16. Why Scott Adams Is Stupid" — Miori audits Adams's science talk through epistemology: warrant for belief, empiricism versus rationalism, Wittgenstein's demand for unambiguous clarity, and Clifford's epistemic responsibility, that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence, which condemns sampling television news while blogging on climate science. Popper's falsifiability, learned from Einstein's willingness to be refuted against Freud's confirmation-seeking, exposes Adams's double standard in waving confirmation bias at critics while crediting his own predictions, and Feyerabend's epistemological anarchism is the view Adams most resembles, except that Feyerabend took responsibility and retracted. Cipolla's Basic Laws of Human Stupidity (the stupid person causes losses to both self and others) frames the closing charge: Adams suggests and retreats, sells product, and shirks the epistemic duty that experts in climate science and medicine shoulder.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 18 "Of Science, Sorcery, and Philosophy" — The chapter reads Strange's conversion from neurosurgeon to sorcerer as a Kuhnian paradigm shift: his medical materialism is 'normal science' puzzle-solving that keeps resisting anomalies (Pangborn's impossible recovery, the astral projection, the multiverse tour) until Kamar-Taj offers a rival paradigm with its own exemplars, which he can only adopt by learning 'knowledge how' through tedious practice. It explains incommensurability through Strange's inability to rationally persuade his old medical colleagues, then contrasts Kuhn with Popper's falsificationism, Feyerabend's 'anything goes' anarchism (sorcery once looked as disreputable as early heliocentrism), and Lakatos's progressive versus degenerating research programs to ask whether sorcery could count as a science in Strange's world.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 17 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Cole Bowman explains the three Formic invasions as failures between 'conceptual schemes,' deploying Davidson's 'On the Very Idea of a Conceptual Scheme' — translatability, the principle of charity, and the closet analogy — alongside Kuhn's incommensurable paradigms and Feyerabend's account of how new theories eliminate old meanings. Ender donning the bugger mask in Peter's game and his final philotic bond with the hive-queen show the two schemes touching at a single shared point, making Ender 'the metal in between' who begins translating between human and Formic worlds.

### On Bullshit

In his essay On Bullshit, Harry Frankfurt offered a philosophical analysis of a familiar but under-theorized form of speech, arguing that the bullshitter differs fundamentally from the liar. A liar knows the truth and deliberately asserts its opposite, thereby still respecting truth as the thing to be evaded, whereas the bullshitter simply does not care whether what he says is true or false and speaks only to serve some other purpose, such as impressing an audience. Frankfurt concluded that this indifference to truth makes bullshit a greater enemy of truth than lying is. The essay is a compact case study in conceptual analysis applied to a phenomenon of everyday communication and public life.

- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 23 "Poker and Philosophy" — Huss tests four models of bluffing on one K-9 all-in: it is not lying, because everyone at the table expects deception, so the victim is never Frankfurt's 'twice deceived' (and Kant's argument that lying fails where everyone lies applies); it is not bullshit, because Frankfurt's bullshitter ignores the facts a poker player cannot afford to ignore; it is not pure acceptance in Jonathan Cohen's sense, since bluffing adds deception to acting-as-if; and it is not full self-deception, since nobody can make themselves believe that 2+2=5 or that 4-7 offsuit is pocket aces. Good bluffing is an art blending all four: deceiving about hand and beliefs, prying attention away from your cards, acting as if, and trying — and necessarily failing — to fool yourself.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 5 "Bullshit and Philosophy" — First part of the editors' introduction, recounting how Harry Frankfurt's slim On Bullshit, after two decades circulating only among academic moral philosophers, spent twenty-six weeks on the New York Times bestseller list and outsold any commercial philosophy book. Reisch and Hardcastle treat the book's popularity as a puzzle worth explaining: a technical exercise in conceptual analysis struck a public nerve. The chapter uses Frankfurt's own definition of bullshit as indifference to truth as the anchor for everything that follows.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 6 "Bullshit and Philosophy" — The editors answer why On Bullshit hit a nerve using Jon Stewart's Daily Show interview with Frankfurt, where the audience laughed at the claim that the bullshitter does not care whether what he says is true. The unspoken elephant in the room was the Iraq war: the claims about weapons of mass destruction, remote-controlled delivery devices, and 9/11 complicity turned out, in the editors' words, to be best described by that word. They argue readers embraced the book as 'bullshit without tears,' a cushion of humor letting them approach the war's deceptions abstractly rather than face the disturbing political questions directly.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 7 "Bullshit and Philosophy" — 'The Year in Bullshit' catalogues the fraud climate surrounding the book's success: James Frey's fabricated memoir A Million Little Pieces exposed on Oprah, the wholly invented author J.T. Leroy, product placement and paid word-of-mouth advertising blurring the line between ads and ordinary conversation, and scientific fraud in pharmaceutical and federal research. It invokes Karl Popper's claim that science deserves respect precisely because it falsifies its own claims, presenting headlines about fabricated results as that ideal fading. Frank Rich's verdict that 'such distinctions have long since washed away in much of our public life' supplies the chapter's explanation of the book's appeal as cultural despair.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 8 "Bullshit and Philosophy" — 'The Dream of a Bullshit-Free Culture' argues Frankfurt revives a centuries-old philosophical tradition: Socrates searching for genuinely wise people rather than purveyors of hearsay, Descartes' Meditations discarding every belief short of certainty, and Hume's forkcondemning divinity-school metaphysics that contains neither abstract nor experimental reasoning to the flames. The twentieth-century apotheosis is the Vienna Circle, whose Rudolf Carnap dissected Heidegger's 'Das Nichts selbst nichtet' as mere appearance of meaning, calling metaphysicians 'musicians without musical ability'. The editors cast Frankfurt as the latest carrier of this Enlightenment anti-bullshit torch, with the book's popularity reconnecting seminar-room philosophy to the marketplace and voting booth.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 9 "I - To Shoot the Bull" — The Part I introduction, 'How This Book Came to Be,' explains what the volume is and is not: not a bullshit-detector manual but discussions and criticisms of Frankfurt's essay, including what it means to propose a theory of bullshit or articulate the structure of a concept. It previews each contributor: Kimbrough on why we let bullshit slide, Preti's use of G.E. Moore as a bullshit-free exemplar, Reisch's two-conversations account, Taylor on cognitive foibles, Bernal on personality pathology, and the Part II definitional debate between Frankfurt and G.A. Cohen's 'unclarifiable unclarity'. It frames philosophy itself as one of our best defenses against bullshit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 11 "Tolerable Bullshit" — Scott Kimbrough opens his essay with his six-year-old daughter shouting through a window that the house painter's smoking is unhealthy, and William Ian Miller's Faking It dictum that truth is seldom a defense. He takes up the puzzle Frankfurt left as an 'exercise for the reader': why our attitude toward bullshit is more benign than toward lying, even though Frankfurt defines bullshit as indifference to how things really are and therefore the greater enemy of truth. The chapter promises to solve the puzzle Frankfurt posed but never attempted.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 12 "Intolerable Bullshit" — Applying Frankfurt's definition strictly, Kimbrough argues much of civility is bullshit: coerced childhood apologies are 'humiliation rituals' where truth is the last thing wanted, politeness is benign hypocrisy that saves people pain, and the Super Bowl ad or the silly communist-professors editorial is valued as entertainment. We also tolerate PR and advertising bullshit out of respect for the ends served, from Exxon's green image to spin by teachers and military recruiters. His answer to Frankfurt's puzzle: we sympathize with bullshitters doing their jobs and contemptuously dismiss their victims as suckers who deserve their fate.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 13 "Bullshit and Self-Deception" — Kimbrough turns to when bullshit becomes intolerable: the philosophy-slam regulars' dismissive 'That's bullshit,' the girlfriend's indictment in The Black Eyed Peas' 'Shut Up,' and the boss's team-builder rationalization for passing you over for a promotion. He leans on Orwell's 'Politics and the English Language' and Nineteen Eighty-Four to show political euphemism ('collateral damage,' 'smart bomb') as the language of power, tolerated because repeating spin is easy and going along with bullshit is going along with power. The chapter closes on the danger of politicians believing their own bullshit, setting up the self-deception question of how one person can play both bullshitter and dupe.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 14 "Blameless Bullshit" — Kimbrough resolves the self-deception paradox using Alfred Mele's Self Deception Unmasked: like the cuckolded husband who masks evidence of infidelity, the self-deceiver biases evidence-gathering rather than playing deceiver and dupe at once. Since Mele shows unintentional motivated belief is common (94% of professors rate themselves above average), bullshit like the entrenched prejudice that 'smart boys are smarter than smart girls' can arise without intent, which is G.A. Cohen's opening against Frankfurt's process-centered definition. Against Cohen's output-centered alternative, the conservative-talk-radio fan who builds his own conclusions on cherry-picked propaganda shows a product can be perfectly clear yet still bullshit, produced through self-deception.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 15 "Bullshit and Truth" — Kimbrough defends calling alchemy bullshit even though Isaac Newton pursued it blamelessly: the charge's function is to excuse us from taking hopeless methods seriously, not to insult the theorist. His killer analogy sorts cases: the intentional bullshitter is the murderer, the self-deceived talk-radio fan the negligent driver who kills while reading, and Newton the blameless driver beside whom the pedestrian darts, with the pejorative resting on the method or theory rather than the person. This methodology shift lets him keep Frankfurt's insight that how bullshit is produced matters while conceding Cohen's point that it can be unintentional, though he admits even philosophy's status may never be settled.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 16 "Chapter 2 - A Defense of Common Sense" — Concluding his essay, Kimbrough observes people call bullshit whenever their values are threatened, so the bottom-line businessman dismisses ethics talk and investigations of his dodgy accounting as bureaucratic bullshit, and the linguist may dismiss armchair conceptual analysis itself. He rejects a subjective definition of bullshit as whatever provokes disdain, endorsing Frankfurt's anti-subjectivist closer that 'sincerity itself is bullshit,' and concludes bullshit must be recognized and restricted to justifiable uses rather than eradicated. He closes with Orwell's advice from 'Politics and the English Language': simplify your English so that a stupid remark's stupidity is obvious even to yourself.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 17 "The Truth Matters" — Consuelo Preti lays out Frankfurt's indifference-to-truth account and G.A. Cohen's academic bullshit as disregard for meaning, then argues both leave out bullshit's third element: the audience it needs. Bullshit, she says, sells us on our own estimation of what matters, from the Dior handbag to the guy bullshitting his way into bed or tenure. Reviewing the James Frey affair and Oprah's initial claim that truth was irrelevant because the story inspired, she proposes G.E. Moore's uncompromising commitment to truth and meaning as the model for resisting bullshit in the street and the seminar room.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 18 "“What Exactly Do You Mean ”" — Preti dissects l'affaire Frey: if Frey intended to palm off invented events as memory, he lied and his publishers committed fraud, but if they did not care either way, it was bullshit, and what exposed the menace was Oprah's own avowal that it did not matter whether the story was true. She argues inspiration tied to an assumed true story is sabotaged by discovering it false, so Oprah's retraction ('I left the impression that the truth does not matter') shows bullshit nearly turned even her head. The strategy she draws is to turn bullshit's need to be believed against itself, and for an exemplar of resolute caring about truth she reaches to G.E. Moore.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 19 "Let’s Stop Bullshitting Ourselves" — Preti builds the Moore exemplar from biography: with Russell and Wittgenstein at Cambridge, Moore founded analytic philosophy, demolished Absolute Idealism in the 1899 'The Nature of Judgment,' and wrote Principia Ethica, which the Bloomsbury group treated as their religion. Russell's autobiography joke about the only lie Moore ever told and Woolf's 'tenacity of a bulldog' portrait of his passion for truth set up Keynes's description of Moore's method, 'What exactly do you mean?'. The key episode is Moore's public apology for losing patience with a question he took to be merely vexatious, showing that what Moore could not tolerate was precisely bullshit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 20 "Chapter 3 - The Pragmatics of Bullshit, Intelligently Designed" — Preti's conclusion deploys Moore's 'A Defence of Common Sense' against philosophers who answer 'Do you believe the earth has existed for many years past?' with 'It all depends on what you mean,' a view Moore called as profoundly mistaken as any can be. She extracts a practical anti-bullshit strategy: dogged Moorean insistence on clarity, since bullshit's scorn for truth must stay masked and needs us to be less inquisitive. Her 'paradox of bullshit' is that truth and meaning do not matter to bullshit but bullshit must make itself matter to us, so caring about the truth-false distinction puts it on a short leash.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 21 "The Example of Intelligent Design" — George Reisch opens his essay with Frankfurt's unsolved puzzle: if bullshitters are more dangerous to truth than liars, they should be punished more, yet we are more tolerant of them, a puzzle Frankfurt admitted on radio he really does not understand. He diagnoses the puzzle as a symptom that Frankfurt's definition took a wrong turn. The remedy requires distinguishing the semantic from the pragmatic analysis of language, and the new definition it yields will both cover Frankfurt's own examples and explain our tolerance of bullshit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 22 "A Definition of Bullshit—New and Improved!" — Reisch offers the Intelligent Design movement as a paradigm of bullshit Frankfurt could not have used in the 1980s: like advertisers and politicians, ID urgently needs public approval ('teach the controversy') and is trying to get away with something. He traces ID's descent from constitutionally defeated creation science through Philip Johnson's Darwin on Trial, showing how Johnson speaks of evidence and naturalism to scientists while telling evangelical audiences that the real enemy is cultural modernism's tolerance of promiscuity and atheism. Judge Jones's Kitzmiller ruling that ID is 'a mere re-labeling of creationism' confirms what the bullshit was covering.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 23 "The Truth in Bullshit" — If ID is bullshit, Reisch argues, Frankfurt's definition fails, because Johnson and his followers are not indifferent to truth; they are devoted to other, rotten truths about modernism and even to elevating regard for truth in the culture. Frankfurt's error was writing of 'the truth' as a single unitary thing everyone but the bullshitter agrees on, when our beliefs about how things really are are diverse and contradictory. Bullshitters conceal a commitment to other truths and an agenda inspired by them, since revealing those truths would be embarrassing, unpersuasive, or, as with ID, unconstitutional.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 24 "The Truth about Semantics" — Even Frankfurt's bull-session example (with its Animal House atom-of-a-fingernail bit) shows relaxed talk serving other truths: self-image, reputation, and whether the apple of one's eye is impressed. Detergent slogans and politicians' rolled-up sleeves likewise run two conversations at once, one overt (clean clothes, policy) and one concealed (self-image, likeability), each resting on truths the bullshitter takes quite seriously. Reisch's definition follows: bullshit is the orchestration of at least two engagements between bullshitter and bullshitee, one concealed within or downplayed alongside the other, so indifference to truth is absent or only partly in play.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 25 "Solving Frankfurt’s Puzzle, or, Baseball, Hot Dogs, Apple Pie, and Bullshit" — Reisch explains Frankfurt's blind spot through the historical neglect of pragmatics: even Carnap took for granted that any complete theory of language must include how language is used in context, yet analytic philosophy came to favor semantics, as the Cambridge Dictionary's twenty-six semantics entries against seven pragmatic ones attest. Since bullshit's essence lies in using speech to hidden purposes, it is an essentially pragmatic, not semantic, phenomenon, which also shows the Frankfurt-Cohen debate (truth versus meaning) is narrow. From the recipient's side, bullshit works best when its two coordinated concerns seem maximally unconnected, as when a science-education advocate turns out to be an evangelical in disguise.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 26 "The Case for Purism about Bullshit" — The pragmatic definition dissolves Frankfurt's puzzle: the liar sins against the semantics of truth, while the bullshitter sins against pragmatics, disguising the effect his speech is designed to have (advancing science education) behind another (promoting evangelical Christianity). We can safely ignore bullshit, as with the coworker's Darwin rants, because without a gullible audience it has no effect, unlike the lie about whether the office milk has soured. Reisch adds that Stephen Meyer's post-Kitzmiller defiance, Willy Loman's optimism, the robber in Dog Day Afternoon, and Mamet's Glengary Glen Ross salesmen show why we even sympathize with bullshitters clinging to their creations, and that our tolerance extends to the pluralism of beliefs bullshit exploits.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 27 "Chapter 4 - Bullshit and the Foibles of the Human Mind, or What the Masters of" — Reisch concludes that on the pragmatic definition there is less bullshit than 'Bullshit!'-slinging suggests: your partner announcing the relationship is over and a White House claim about an oil-rich nation eager for democracy are merely true or false announcements, not bullshit. Real bullshit is the partner engineering a blame-free breakup through talk of feeling smothered, or the claim that a dictator possesses nuclear weapons about to be used. He closes by comparing bullshit to a poem or symphony: a specific, artfully layered creation intelligently designed for pragmatic effect, which our casual use of the word obscures to the bullshitter's advantage.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 28 "Some Cognitive Foibles of the Human Mind" — Kenneth Taylor opens his essay on the debased stew of bullshit, propaganda, and spin in public discourse, arguing that in an open public square the bullshitting arts must become highly refined, whereas a totalitarian state can afford crude bludgeoning, and that the marketplace of ideas has not spontaneously driven out bad discourse. His central claim: purveyors cannot sell what we do not buy, so the fault lies partly in ourselves, in built-in architectural foibles of the mind that make it permanently susceptible to manipulation. bullshit works best when we do not recognize it, and susceptibility to comforting falsehood is rooted in the mind's very architecture.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 29 "Reclaiming the Public Square" — Taylor illustrates the mind's foibles with the Iraq war beliefs that held a vice-grip on believers long after disconfirming evidence, explained by confirmation bias and information cocoons like Fox News and talk radio. He walks through the classic framing experiments, the avian-flu programs that are identical when described as '2,000 saved' or '4,000 die,' showing how politicians Smith and Jones exploit framing to jointly mislead voters, and the Wason selection task, where subjects fail on abstract cards but succeed when reframed as bartender cheater-detection. Citing Stephen Pinker on evolved, domain-specific modules, he concludes that whoever controls the frame may control all, which is exactly the leverage the masters of the dark arts exploit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 30 "Chapter 5 - Bullshit and Personality" — Taylor draws the hopeful and bleak conclusions: our minds are fine instruments for hunter-gatherer information environments, but the modern mismatch between savannah-designed cognition and deliberately framed misinformation explains why bull, spin, and propaganda abound. The masters of the dark arts are now astute students of cognitive foibles and wield means of persuasion with unprecedented reach. His two-front response is education that instills suspicion of comforting falsehoods and the habit of re-framing, plus widening access to the means of public representation now monopolized by a self-serving elite, because 'only those who seek more than bullshit can drive it out.'
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 31 "Does the Bullshitter Pay Attention to the Truth" — Sara Bernal distinguishes public, interpersonal, and private bullshit (bullshitting oneself) and argues that in an era rich in public bullshit like the Iraq war, private bullshit should not be overlooked, since it is at the core of personality disorders. Departing rapidly from Frankfurt, she rejects his claim that bullshit is essentially unconnected to a concern with truth, proposing instead that core cases of bullshit have a stronger connection to truth than Frankfurt allows. Applying her revised analysis to personality disorders will, she claims, explain why their core features produce social difficulties.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 32 "Two Modes of Bullshit" — Against Frankfurt's picture of the bullshitter who pays no attention to truth at all, Bernal argues the typical bullshitter is strongly connected to truth via a desire to obscure a specific part of it, conscious or not. Her prototype is the undergraduate who, knowing she has nothing thoughtful to say on an assigned essay, throws up a screen of verbiage, sometimes with malice aforethought, sometimes through a barely conscious motive to get an undeserved A. Unlike the liar she never denies the hidden truth directly but works indirectly, through pompous tone, reluctance to get to the point, and windiness, or simply by distracting the audience.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 35 "Bullshit and Personality Disorders" — Bernal gives the Bush administration's yellowcake-from-Niger and Saddam-9/11 red herrings as distraction bullshit concealing the antecedent intention to invade Iraq, then states five features of her two-part conception: the bullshitter must attend to the one 'target' truth she wants to hide, bullshit shades into lying as awareness increases, unconscious motives do the work, non-verbal means suffice (the Newport ads), and self-bullshitting is a species of self-deception. Split-brain patients who confabulate 'that funny machine' to explain unaccountable giggling at a picture shown only to the right hemisphere ground the claim that unconscious motives are respectable neuroscience. Her account, unlike Frankfurt's, applies in psychiatry.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 37 "Some Examples of Bullshit in Personality Disorders" — The essay defines personality disorder via DSM-IV as an enduring, inflexible pattern deviating from cultural expectations, and catalogs the ten disorders in three clusters: the erratic (antisocial, with the Enron crew and glib con artists as textbook cases; borderline; histrionic, from the undergrad who visits professors' office hours to talk about herself; narcissistic), the anxious (avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive), and the eccentric (schizoid, schizotypal, paranoid). The clue to where bullshit lurks: wherever the afflicted is out of touch with some key aspect of reality or where her stock behavior leads others to false beliefs. The disorders' rigidity makes life 'a bad one-act play that repeats again and again.'
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 38 "Bullshit and Philosophy" — The essay works through the disorders case by case: the antisocial's glib charm implicates 'I am not a nasty piece of work' without saying it, the borderline's suicidal gestures implicate 'life without you is not worth living' that her contempt belies, the histrionic's shallow opinions and sexual provocativeness implant false impressions of depth, and the compensating narcissist's charade of superiority hides a dimly glimpsed core of low self-esteem. Self-directed bullshit follows: the fanatic paranoid's superhero fantasies deny that she is not extraordinary, the phobic avoidant displaces anxiety onto elevators and dogs, the self-deserting avoidant escapes into fantasy, dependents distract themselves from doubts about their caregiver, and the obsessive-compulsive buries big-picture anxiety in rules and lists.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 39 "Perfect Partners Bullshit and Distorted Social Perceptions" — Surveying the catalog, the essay finds bullshit strategems that are first-rank symptoms in eight of ten disorders, quoting Frankfurt's 'each of us contributes his share' to observe that pathological personalities are notably generous contributors. Bullshitting is notably absent from the eccentric cluster: the schizoid's flat affect removes the pain-avoidance motive, and schizoids and schizotypals lack the mindreading facility successful bullshit requires. Other-bullshitting (mostly falsehood-implicating) marks the erratic cluster, self-bullshitting (mostly distraction) the anxious, and the essay closes by stressing that the disordered person is afflicted, her bullshit a personal tragedy as well as an infliction.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 40 "The Threat Posed by Bullshit" — The essay's final section argues distorted social perception and bullshit are perfect partners that reinforce each other: the paranoiac imagining insults, the histrionic inhabiting a world of admirers, and the borderline seeing abandonment everywhere each see less of social reality, supplying more 'easy targets' to obscure without the sting of conscience that aware deception provokes. The compensating narcissist's glimmering of her charade and the self-deserting avoidant's glimmering of her escape show how dim awareness eases bullshitting. The street runs both ways, since hiding parts of social truth from yourself further impairs your perception, so some disorder bullshit is causally downstream of distortion while self-bullshitting deepens it.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 41 "Chapter 6 - Performing Bullshit and the Post-Sincere Condition" — Concluding an essay on personality disorders, this chapter argues that pathological personalities (the antisocial, borderline, dependent, paranoiac) are especially good bullshitters and that their bullshit and distorted perceptions are what wreck their social relationships, since good relationships thrive on truth as much as on truthfulness. Against Frankfurt's claim that bullshit is the greater enemy of truth because indulging it erodes attention to reality, the author counters that the bullshitter does track truth at some level; bullshit's distinctive danger is that, unlike lying, it can be unconscious, so the sting of conscience never checks the habit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 43 "Shitty Attitudes On the Use and Misuse of Bullshit in Life" — This mini-essay opens by parodying a puffing university mission statement, aspiring to be 'one of the world's best philosophy essays' in the UBC mold. It then sets the agenda: Frankfurt left unanswered why our attitude toward bullshit is generally more benign than our attitude toward lying, and never considered bullshit's rhetorical uses and misuses - the two gaps the rest of the essay fills.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 44 "Bullshit as a Condition of Life" — Reworking Frankfurt's Fania Pascal anecdote (Wittgenstein's disgusted 'You don't know what a dog that has been run over feels like'), the chapter argues that the bullshit that earns the retort 'That's bullshit!' is speech whose truth is irrelevant and which aims to evoke a positive attitude toward the speaker - hypochondriac pain complaints, boilerplate about graduate training in grant proposals, praise of the Dean to pass a hiring motion. It separates this from bullshit-as-entertainment and from courtesy conventions like thanking the gift-giving aunt, concluding against Frankfurt that pretentiousness is constitutive of at least this central kind of bullshit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 45 "The World as Will to Bullshit" — This section answers Frankfurt's exercise about benignity: bullshit is 'dishonesty without tears' because whole genres - grant proposals, Fourth of July oratory, letters of reference - generically require performative values everyone knows count for nothing, like compulsory figures in figure skating. Rejecting free-riding as the origin of bullshit genres (bullshit letters get found out), it explains the reference letter instead by its multiple interested audiences: the writer must satisfy the student, the admissions committee, and her own conscience at once, and only the right dose of bullshit accomplishes that.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 46 "Overcoming Overwhelming Bullshit" — The chapter indicts an expanding class of 'performative bullshit': the video-store service pledge and the UBC mission statement, where a commitment is treated as fulfilled in the very act of being made, so no complaint can even be lodged. George W. Bush's fabricated WMD case for the Iraq war shows the political version - an argument counts as good simply because it was offered as the reason, and when the intelligence proved false another reason was fabricated. In such a world sincerity, irony, and even cynicism become impossible, since only pseudo-motives remain, lacking even sincere self-interest.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 47 "Chapter 7 - The Importance of Being Earnest A Pragmatic Approach to Bullshitting" — Closing the essay, this section argues the bullshit world is inherently stable rather than unstable: the administrator whose whole professional being is appending mission-talk to whatever the university already does is its emblem. The one live remedy is the Jon Stewart gambit - The Daily Show's openly fake news outperforming 'serious' sources, showing by self-consciously flouting the conventions of truth-telling what those conventions were for - and beyond that, actually taking a mission statement seriously enough to rethink higher education's values rather than settle, undeserving, for bullshit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 48 "Two Tauroscatological Schools" — De Waal's opening salvo: Frankfurt analyzed the concept of bullshit by ordinary language, but the interesting question is the intention with which bullshitting is produced. He announces a contrast between bullshitting and genuine inquiry, and blames bullshit's prevalence partly on a lost confidence that figuring out how things really are is possible or worthwhile.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 49 "The Epistemic Imperative" — Building on G.A. Cohen's split of bullshit thinking into a structuralist school (bullshit is an intrinsic feature of products, e.g. texts unclarifiably unclear whatever the author intended) and an intentionalist school (Frankfurt: bullshit is the act done with indifference to truth), the chapter defends intentionalism against the 'insight problem'. The sham astrologer whose Tarot-based celebrity-death prediction happens to come true, and Perry's undergraduates who aced an exam they bullshitted, show that a claim stays bullshit until someone not bullshitting has affirmed it and thereby transformed it into knowledge - just as one person's trash is another's treasure without the chair itself changing.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 50 "The Problem with Bullshitting" — Against the bullshitter the chapter recruits Peirce: genuine inquiry is defined not by method or results but by the attitude of truly wanting true answers, so homicide detectives, philologists, and car mechanics all count as scientists in this sense. Bullshitting is a free-rider riding the bus of real inquiry - even the bullshitter wants his doctor not to bullshit - and the chapter formulates an epistemic imperative: proceed on the hope that there is a true answer and act from the desire to find it, with fallibilism, not skepticism, the viable stance (the passenger who can occupy any vacant seat cannot occupy them all).
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 51 "So Why Bullshit" — Violations of the epistemic imperative are sorted into Peirce's 'sham reasoning' (the creationist who reasons only to prop up a fixed conclusion), Haack's 'fake reasoning' (corporate-funded research, vote-seeking politicians, the temporary-insanity plea), and the skeptic's premature 'we'll never know' - none of which is bullshitting, which is precisely not caring about truth, like the sales clerk praising shoes at random. Even philosophy can slide into bullshitting when, per Rorty, it becomes 'carrying on the conversation' with truth as what your peers let you get away with; and brainstorming differs from a bull session because brainstormers actually want to discover something.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 52 "II - The Bull by the Horns" — Why do people bullshit? Because liberal democracy, heir to the Cartesian rejection of authority and the Enlightenment's think-for-yourself ideal, expects instant opinions on everything from people detached enough that nothing they say makes a difference; and because a failed search for certainty breeds prophylactic pessimism about inquiry itself. The cure is earnestness - scientists take colleagues' results on trust - though the chapter concedes defensible cases: the formulaic 'It's nice to see you!' as fake reasoning for civility, and friends horsing around for fun.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 55 "2 Two Species of Bullshit" — Cohen's autobiographical preface: his youthful struggle with Althusserian French Marxism of the 1960s - interpellation, contradiction and overdetermination - taught him that writings attracting reverent attention can still be bullshit, a lesson sealed when his Marxist discussion group took the name Non-Bullshit Marxism Group, 'Marxism without the shit of the bull'. He also diagnoses the psychology (cognitive dissonance reduction plus adaptive preference formation) by which readers of rebarbative texts overvalue the banal sense they finally extract.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 56 "3 Bullshit and Lying" — Via the OED's two entries, the chapter finds that 'bullshit' denotes two different things: nonsense or rubbish (output-centered - the shit wears the trousers) and insincere talk (producer-centered - the bull wears the trousers, Frankfurt's kind). Frankfurt's fault is not error but generality: he cast his account of one flower as the 'essence' of the whole garden, ignoring the academically more significant kind that is defined without any reference to a producer's state of mind.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 57 "4 Bullshit as Unclarifiable Unclarity" — Cohen's main critique: Frankfurt identifies the liar by his goal (misleading about reality) but the bullshitter only at the level of tactic (indifference to the truth of what he says), leaving the bullshitter no distinctive goal - so advertisers and politicians, Frankfurt's own paradigm bullshitters, actually pursue the liar's goal and their bullshitting and lying coincide. Freud's favorite Pinsk/Minsk joke shows tactic and goal can come apart (deceiving by telling the truth), and the Fourth of July orator, contra Frankfurt, might care very much that the audience believe things about the Founding Fathers.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 58 "5 Bullshit as Product and Bullshit as Process" — Cohen's positive account: bullshit is a feature of texts, paradigmatically 'unclarifiable unclarity' - discourse that cannot be rendered clear without ceasing to be a version of what was said, which is why the way to defend Hegel or Heidegger is to show their texts make sense, not that they cared about truth. A sufficient test is the negation sign: if adding or subtracting it makes no difference to plausibility, as with Sokal's hoax physics, the text is bullshit - though suggestively valuable poetry is spared. 'Bullshitter' then splits into a dispositional reading and an aim reading, only the latter of which always bullshits when producing bullshit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 59 "Chapter 9 - The Unity of Bullshit" — Cohen concludes that because bullshit can be emitted innocently - even by honest acolytes - the Sokal-style struggle against academic bullshit must target the visible product rather than the producer's hidden intentions, lest innocent traffickers be slandered as insincere or deliberately obscure. Fun as it is to write 'bullshit' over and over in an academic article, the bullshitter/bullshit distinction matters because the justice of the polemic depends on it.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 60 "No Bullshit, Please, We’re Austrian" — Hardcastle proposes to settle the Frankfurt-Cohen quarrel by adding logical positivism to the mix: the Vienna Circle's war on metaphysics was the 1920s-30s' great anti-bullshit program, and both Frankfurt's negligence-of-truth and Cohen's unclarifiable unclarity have precedents in it. Laura Penny's Your Call Is Important to Us supplies the moral heat ('when you fuck with English, you are money-changing in my temple'), while the summary of both positions - the liar needs the truth, the bullshitter does not give a hoot - sets up the Carnap chapters.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 61 "A Little Carnap in Everyone" — Carnap's 'Overcoming Metaphysics through Logical Analysis of Language' supplies the unification: his verificationism renders the invented word 'teavy' meaningless for the same reason Cohen's texts are unclarifiably unclear, while Heidegger's 'The nothing noths' exemplifies the pseudo-sentence whose utterance expresses disregard for meaning - Frankfurt-style bullshitting. The 'toovy' example drives the point home: once a term's synonymy with 'quadrangular' is fixed, professing a further hidden meaning reveals a speaker who never intended to convey information at all.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 62 "The Unity of Bullshit" — Meaning, for Carnap, is bearing the right deductive relations to other claims - exactly Cohen's insight that clarity is relational, so that 'clarifying' an unclarifiable text mangles it into something unrecognizable. Carnap's diagnosis of why metaphysics flourishes - metaphysicians express a general attitude toward life (Lebenseinstellung), better expressed through art, and mistake it for a state of affairs - explains bullshit's ubiquity and tolerance; but the metaphysician who knows he says nothing, like Heidegger after Carnap called him on it, is Frankfurt's bullshitter pure and simple.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 63 "Chapter 10 - Raising the Tone Definition, Bullshit, and the Definition of Bullshit" — The unification: Frankfurt's intentionalist bull and Cohen's structuralist shit are two sides of one thing, since a language amenable to misuse meets the bullshitter's ends halfway. The response is gun control for language - not Carnap's ideal language, but shared responsibility for English in our presence, from writing letters to casting votes - ending with Otto Neurath's anti-pseudorationalist insistence that the world's shape reflects our own choices rather than reasons beyond our control: it really is up to us.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 65 "A Caricature History of Semantics" — The chapter christens Frankfurt's innovation 'semantic negligence' on the legal model: the deceptive bullshitter has a duty of care to truth and breaches it without intending the resulting deception, which is why lying (intentional) is more culpable, yet bullshit more insidious because it degrades the commitment to truth on which public discourse depends. Terry Pratchett's characters who applaud 'any man who can tell an outrageous whopper with a gleam in his eye' mark the complicit bull session - bullshit deceives only when it escapes the session and masquerades as ordinary assertion.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 67 "Broadening the Analysis" — Stevenson's persuasive definition - changing a term's descriptive meaning while keeping its emotive force - is restated in Fregean terms as changing sense or reference while representing tone as fixed, yielding a sixteen-fold table of definitional moves (PD, PQD, and beyond). Semantic negligence then grades PDs: the aphoristic 'Conservatism is true socialism' deceives no one, but the definer who hides an argument inside a definition gains rhetorical advantage while risking that his audience endorses conclusions they were never given a fair chance to appraise - analogous to bullshit rather than lying.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 70 "Bullshit and Philosophy" — Flew's No-True-Scotsman Move - retreating from 'No Scotsman takes sugar with his porridge' to 'No true Scotsman...' when Hamish MacTavish of Inverness falsifies it - is analyzed as a redefinition that converts a bold, falsifiable claim into a vacuous necessary truth. Because the two statements look and sound alike, confusing them (from carelessness as easily as deceit) is semantic negligence, and pressing on as if the original claim still stood is classic Frankfurt bullshit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 77 "Chapter 11 - Different Kinds and Aspects of Bullshit" — Closing chapter 10's circle: Frankfurt's definition of 'bullshit' is itself a persuasive definition of case d - it changes the term's sense and reference while keeping the pejorative tone, as the well-meant 'Help is on its way' to the critically injured shows. Because Frankfurt argues explicitly for his departures from conventional usage, his definition is semantically diligent rather than negligent, though Cohen's complaint that it omits academic bullshit remains to be answered - with which Chapter 11 opens.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 78 "Harry Frankfurt on Bullshit" — Maes and Schaubroeck open on the bookstore irony: Frankfurt's slim bestseller On Bullshit shelved beside Chakra Balancing Kit, The Hidden Messages in Water Crystals, and Astrology: A Cosmic Science - almost as if placed there to illustrate the very bullshit Frankfurt diagnosed as the most salient feature of our culture. They then introduce Cohen's admiring complaint that Frankfurt examined 'just one flower in the lush garden of bullshit', teeing up the academic kind Cohen will define.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 79 "A Different Take on Bullshit" — A faithful reconstruction of Frankfurt: the bullshitter is a slovenly craftsman whose laxity concerns truth rather than detail - spin doctors control every tiny thing except whether what they say is true. The bull session shows indifference alone is not enough, since bullshit adds the pretence that hides that indifference (the Fourth of July orator misrepresents his own state of mind, not American history), whence Frankfurt's conclusion that bullshit is the greater enemy of truth - and the announcement that all three claims (unconcern, concealment, blameworthiness) will be contested.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 80 "A Different Kind of Bullshit" — The Pascal anecdote returns to undermine Frankfurt: Wittgenstein's disgust at 'I feel just like a dog that has been run over' involves no fakery, so pretence is not an essential ingredient of bullshit - mere indifference to truth suffices, as the hypothetical politician who openly stops caring would show. Bullshit emerges as often benign: Ishiguro's butler Stevens in The Remains of the Day comes to see bantering as 'the key to human warmth', Nagel's polite 'How nice to see you!' is convention-governed and no deception, and Wilde's epigrams - nearly all bullshit - explain why our attitude toward bullshit is softer than toward lying.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 81 "III - It’s All Around Us" — Cohen's product-based kind (unclarifiable unclarity, probed by the negation-sign test) is summarized, and the chapter asks whether Frankfurt-bullshit and Cohen-bullshit exhaust the lush garden. They do not: pseudoscience like astrology, chakra balancing, and bogus healing is a third, damaging kind - its practitioners sincerely believe (failing Frankfurt's indifference test) and predict specifically and clearly (failing Cohen's unclarity test) - so insensitivity to evidence and fallacious reasoning must be central to its analysis, better to be vaguely right than precisely wrong.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 83 "Bullshitting and Lying in Politics" — Opening Mark Evans's Chapter 12: Frankfurt's claim that democracy especially breeds bullshit, since it charges every citizen with having opinions about everything - the 'Frankfurt thesis' that citizens do not care about truth. It is contrasted with the 'cynicism thesis' (citizens do not care about politics, out of well-founded disillusion with a system that fails to deliver), and both are framed by the objection as old as Plato that political understanding is an expertise we cannot all share - theses argued about, not against, democracy.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 84 "The Myth of the ‘Well-Informed’ Citizen" — Mark Evans opens the book's political section by insisting that politicians mostly produce bullshit rather than lies in Frankfurt's strict sense: lying requires knowing and concealing the truth, while the Bush administration's WMD case for invading Iraq shows truth-indifference, with post-hoc 'rejustifications' (humanitarian intervention, democratisation, Saddam-9/11 hints) spun as needed. Using G.A. Cohen's distinction between aim-bullshitters and disposition-bullshitters, it reads Winston Smith's routinized rewriting of The Times in Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four as falsehood that slides from lying into bullshit, since the Party aims to destroy the very true/false distinction. Totalitarian regimes (Havel's 'living in truth') thus embed themselves not in a web of lies but in a morass of bullshit insulated from any possibly refuting facts.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 85 "‘Dumbing-Up’ Some Distortions of Democratic Equality" — Evans argues that democratic citizens do their own share of Frankfurt-bullshitting about politics: because electoral democracy cannot admit how complex politics really is, it institutionalizes the fictional ideal of the 'well-informed' citizen, obliging voters to hold over-simplified views and politicians to pander to them. Campaigning forces candidates into dodges like the 'politics of distraction' and the empty promise to be 'a different sort of politician', producing 'Governor Schwarzenegger Syndrome' and opening space for dangerous demagogues and fundamentalisms. Following Churchill, the chapter concludes that this citizen-side bullshit vindicates the cynicism thesis only partially and gives no reason to reject democracy as 'the worst form of government except for all the others'.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 86 "Philosophy versus Bullshit" — The chapter claims that 'equal respect' in modern democracies has been distorted into a 'dumbing-up' relativism — 'I'm valid, you're valid' — which conflates the equal right to voice opinions with their equal intellectual merit and so leaves nothing that counts as bullshit. It illustrates this through the 'democratization of expertise' and management-speak ('downsizing', 'mission statements'), which mimics profundity while evading awkward facts, and it tests and rejects the quasi-Nietzschean ressentiment story of timid citizens dragging discourse down to a common denominator. To get the full measure of the phenomenon it expands Frankfurt's and Cohen's typologies into seven kinds of bullshit, adding clarifiable unclarity, plain rubbish, irretrievable speculation, pretension, and evasion.
