- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 21 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Lance Belluomini tests Card's creed that 'good or evil exist entirely in human motive' against Aquinas' Doctrine of Double Effect and Frankfurt's second-order intentions, arguing Ender's killings of Stilson and Bonzo fail double-effect proportionality because he intends excessive, fear-inducing harm to deter future attackers. He allows that Ender bears only partial responsibility for the xenocide since he could not know the 'simulation' was real, but concludes that, contrary to the Speakers for the Dead doctrine, Ender is not the blameless moral exemplar Card makes of him.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 23 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Danielle Wylie uses Aristotle's conditions for voluntary action - control and knowledge - to argue Ender's planetary strike is one of his 'mixed cases' made under coercion and factual ignorance, so praise and blame attach elsewhere: Graff and Rackham, who foresaw the attack and could easily have stopped it, meet both conditions through culpable omission. Borrowing Rachels' Smith-and-Jones drowning case to show moral responsibility can exist without causal responsibility, she ends with Ender's non-blameworthy 'taking responsibility' as Speaker for the Dead.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 20 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Jim Berti opens with a dream-fable in which the Devil tempts him with a bank-robbing 'quick fix' for his house-buying cash crunch, then reads the Rolling Stones' 'Sympathy for the Devil' as the Devil's resume of history's atrocities - Anastasia, the Blitzkrieg, the Kennedys - where he supplies the lighter fluid but never strikes the match. The chapter argues we give God too much credit and the Devil too much blame while omitting ourselves: the Devil is the 'drug dealer of sin,' peddling the seven deadly sins as shortcuts like Rocky IV's steroids, and only effortful virtue refuses them. As the song says, 'it was you and me.'
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 13 "Girls and Philosophy" — McCrossin asks whether Adam's Season Two finale run across Brooklyn to break down the door of a dangerously unraveling Hannah ('I was always here') is heroic, set against Hannah's 'You don't need to be like a hero' chair-and-mattress scene and Adam's 'I don't want to help... I was doing it because I love you' quarrel. He argues an act is heroic - being an 'Extraordinary Samaritan' like Wesley Autrey, the Subway Samaritan, unlike the trained Sullenberger - only when done on purpose to help, not from obligation, training, or love's compulsion, testing the point with Batman's motives. Since Adam insists no one ever does anything from a want to help, his rescue's heroic status is left genuinely open.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 23 "Girls and Philosophy" — Mahon and Walker rebrand the seven deadly sins for Girls: Self-Absorption as Augustine's 'love of one's own excellence' (Hannah pitching her e-book at her editor's funeral, calling her grandmother 'the old Flo Job... sluttin' around'), Entitlement for Hannah's 'voice of my generation' demands and Marnie's rage at Charlie's success, and Sleeping Around as the John Paul II point about reducing a person to an object of gratification - Adam's fantasy sex with Hannah and his degradation of Natalia. Envy (Hannah on Tally's tragedy), gluttony in drug-fueled relapses (Aquinas's five ways), flakiness as Kant's indolent free-rider who needs others but never helps (Jessa missing her own abortion), and Senecan irritability (Jessa spitting at the Bushwick party, Ray's hatreds, Shoshanna's 'whiny nothings' outburst) complete the survey - redeemed by the girls' stubborn friendship.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 9 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Karavitis argues Finn's 'Finn-losophy' is a metaphysics that prefers magic over Princess Bubblegum's science, and that this choice shapes his ethics: magic is the 'easy way out' requiring no understanding (Jake's stretching, the Glasses of Nerdicon), while science demands observation, experiment, and falsifiable ideas—'reality is the ultimate spell-checker.' Because magic promises instant gratification, Finn rushes into danger ('Wizard,' 'Donny,' the Goblin Kingdom) behind an inflexible hero code, and his altruism misfires, as the never-ending prize-winning battles of the 'Mystery Train' episode illustrate. The chapter concludes that your view of how the world works—magical or scientific—determines whether you can grow ethically at all.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 14 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — McCrossin asks why Finn and Jake forgive Marceline although she tries to kill Jake, evicts them twice, drains Princess Bubblegum, and never shows remorse. Jake's change of heart ('my fear was based on ignorance') comes from witnessing her father Hunson Abadeer's cruelty and her abandoned childhood, so her bad acts flow from causes outside her control rather than pure choice. The chapter presses the remaining problem: we normally forgive the penitent offender, not the unrepentant one, and Marceline—unlike the moping vampires of Twilight, Underworld, and True Blood—never regrets, leaving readers to decide whether understanding without remorse can ground trust and friendship.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 31 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter diagnoses Raylan with Aristotle's akrasia (lack of self-restraint): Art's 'lost cause' lecture, Arlo's boast that he has never shot anyone, and Boyd's 'you wake up in the morning pretending that you are not the bad guy' all charge him with acting on passion against his own calculations - sleeping with witness Ava, resuming adultery with Winona when her ring comes off. Because Raylan feels regret, the Aristotelian mark of the unselfrestrained person who knows his condition, he is curable and lacks self-restraint by habit rather than nature (Nicky Augustine's limo verdict: 'it's not who you are'). The chapter reads Raylan's signature move - forcing men to draw first so their deaths count as justified - as a perversion of justice by an akratic who is not wicked, and the series arc as his slow acquisition of self-restraint.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 11 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Mahon reads Jobs's 'reality distortion field'—the phrase Apple engineer Bud Tribble borrowed from the illusion-casting Talosians of Star Trek's 'The Cage' and 'The Menagerie'—through the ethics of deception. He argues that unlike the Talosians' non-consensual illusions (trapping Captain Pike to breed slaves), Jobs mostly changed people's beliefs about what was possible rather than deceiving them, often believed his own claims (even about his cancer), and sometimes freed people from false beliefs as the 1984 'Big Brother' Macintosh ad dramatized, so the field that produced the 'insanely great' Stevenotes, the impossible Macintosh schedule, and Dilbert's Dogbert parody needed little moral justification—and made Jobs's revolutionized industries possible.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 22 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Ethan Chambers asks whether we should pardon the Gang, arguing with Hume that their vices have a 'causal story' as rigid as physical law: Charlie's glue-sniffing, racism, and inability to connect trace to a Christmas Day childhood of squalor and Uncle Jack's abuse; Mac was bullied as 'Ronnie the Rat' for trying to be good and never once saw virtue pay in Philadelphia; Dennis, shaped by Frank's cruel parenting, claims and shows he cannot feel feelings, so Humean sympathy - the key moral sense - is simply beyond his reach; and Frank's 'donkey brains' asylum childhood or outright insanity directly undermines his responsibility. Knowing these psychological causes, sympathy (Hume's word for empathy) replaces blame: we blame the builders, not the house, and the chapter closes by urging compassionate rehabilitation over the show's never-ending circle of punishment and revenge.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 21 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Cherry uses Vee's season-two grooming of Taystee, Poussey, Nicky, Cindy, and Crazy Eyes to test philosophers' accounts of manipulation (covert influence, non-rational persuasion, targeting weaknesses, misleading truthfully). She shows Vee's skill is not virtue, since manipulation threatens autonomy by imposing a will the victim would not endorse (Kantian personhood denied) and employs dishonesty, predatoriness, disrespect, and laziness, with Machiavellian ends. The defense she prescribes is Socratic: reject purely emotional persuasion like the sophists' flattery, and live the examined life by checking premises and motives before being played.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 9 "Magnetic North" — Siler answers the Twelfth Doctor's question 'Am I a good man?' from 'Into the Dalek' by arguing that goodness is the Doctor's 'magnetic north'—the stable moral orientation his regenerations bend back toward, the force that drove him from Gallifrey's corrupt Time Lords. He concedes a dark side, from the would-be caveman killing of 'An Unearthly Child' to the 'Time Lord Victorious' arrogance of 'The Waters of Mars,' but insists character must be judged over a whole life, including the Doctor's effect on companions like Jo Grant, Leela, Ace, and Rose, whom he teaches 'a better way of livin' your life.' Clara's closing verdict—that he tries to be good and 'that's probably the point'—caps the claim that a settled direction of character, not perfection, makes him a good man.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 35 "20. The Doctor Lies" — McCain distinguishes lying (directly asserting what you believe false to make another believe it) from mere deception - the Sixth Doctor feeding Jamie false information for Sontaran Stike to overhear in 'The Two Doctors' deceives without lying - then asks whether the Doctor can lie to himself, answering that incarnations can lie to later selves (the Eleventh's suspicious 'I have absolutely no idea' about the children on Gallifrey in 'The Day of the Doctor') but a current self cannot. The stakes are moral: against Kant's and Augustine's absolute prohibition of lying, Plato's Republic and Sidgwick's Methods of Ethics defend noble lies, and Robert C. Solomon's view of self-deception as coping with the unbearable suggests that if the Doctor did engineer himself to forget the Time War genocide - as Ten and Wilf did to Donna in 'Journey's End' - it might be a good man's forgivable way of going on.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 38 "23. Failing and Forgiving in the Name of the Doctor" — Hoffman reads the Doctor's banishment of the War Doctor ('Doctor no more,' his actions 'not done in the name of the Doctor') as a failure of self-forgiveness driven by what Jeffrie Murphy calls the moral hatred of self and Robin Dillon the 'self-as-feared,' rather than mere guilt over the genocide of Gallifrey. Drawing on the self-forgiveness literature (Blustein, Griswold, Westlund), he argues that 'The Day of the Doctor' shows forgiveness neither excuses nor extinguishes blame: the Tenth and Eleventh Doctors forgive their past self by recognizing he shared their Doctorly motives and was forced into an impossible choice. Clara's outsider faith ('be a doctor') supplies the third-party affirmation that dissolves the identity-destroying dilemma and frees the Doctor to find the third option that saves Gallifrey.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 23 "12. The Courage of Selflessness" — Pless argues that courage and selflessness are not the opposed traits of Dauntless and Abnegation but one and the same virtue: any properly selfless act requires moral courage, any truly courageous act requires sacrifice so that others may prosper, and both depend on an outside party in need and on overriding the instinct of self-preservation. Because a rewarded sacrifice becomes social capital - the lunch-giving and bullet-catching examples - neither virtue can be institutionalized: Abnegation's legalistic rules and Marcus's publicly displayed selflessness destroy selflessness by removing choice, and Eric's fear-eradicating initiation produces glory and cruelty instead of courage, since fear connotes responsibility. Natalie and Andrew Prior's shared, gender-subverting sacrifices, and Tris stepping in to take Al's knives, show the single virtue of selfless courage chosen in the moment, culminating in a death that is an extension of her character rather than a surprise.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 15 "5. The Morality of Manners" — Dougherty argues that at Downton manners are not incidental etiquette but a central means of demonstrating moral character and respect. Matthew's shift from calling valeting 'a very silly occupation for a grown man' to valuing Molesley's role shows decorum tracking his growing respect; Branson's tweed suit at white-tie dinners and 'uniforms of oppression' display disrespect even where his politics are sound; Sir Richard's parting boorishness betrays a lack of moral character; and the Dowager Countess's polished barbs prove manners can serve as a mask for self-interest rather than virtue. The framework combines Nancy Sherman's 'aesthetic of character,' Aristotle's person of extraordinary virtue whose goodness must appear in particular ways, and Sarah Buss's idea that good manners constantly remind us that others are worthy of respect.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 18 "7. Psychopaths, Outlaws, and Us" — McClelland argues Lecter is neither psychopath nor sociopath, marshaling his empathic childhood (softening a bread crust for Mischa, polishing an eggplant because she loved purple, sensing Lady Murasaki's fatigue), his genuinely compassionate psychiatric work with Margot Verger, and his chess-master planning as evidence that both cognitive and emotional empathy operate normally - unlike Grutas, 'here's your real psychopath'. Reading Lecter's preternatural calm, mutism, and suppressed memories as PTSD and resilience after Mischa's death, and his fundamental project as the pursuit of autonomy (with Hirschman's exit-voice-loyalty framework explaining his contempt for declining institutions like the FBI), he reclassifies Lecter as an outlaw - one placed beyond the law's protection yet living inside civil society - who kills instrumentally the way evolutionary psychology says humans do, concluding that 'there is an outlaw in all of us'.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 19 "8. Consuming Homicidal Art" — McAteer uses Bullough's aesthetic distance to test whether the psychopath Hannibal can have genuine aesthetic experience, arguing against Maibom and Harold that egocentric pleasure in an artwork is compatible with aesthetic distancing - so a Lecter who loves Bach and Italian architecture (unlike Cleckley's unmoved psychopath and the Tooth Fairy's graceless 'performances') could really exist. But since psychopaths can value nothing as an end in itself - they treat persons and artworks merely as means - homicidal art like the Muralist's corpse cathedral and Hannibal's gourmet cannibalism is the logical extreme of Wildean aestheticism, proving Wittgenstein's 'Aesthetics and ethics are one' false; yet in homicidal art Hannibal's moral deficit becomes an aesthetic deficit too, because anyone who can see beauty in human bodies as mere material is over-distanced - the bodies, like any sculpture's material, matter.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 26 "13. An Aesthete par Excellence" — Holt argues that the key to Lecter is aestheticism: the Goldberg Variations scoring his nightstick killing of the Memphis guard is no camouflage, because art, cannibalism, murder and etiquette are all unified by aesthetic value prized apart from the good and the true. His 'ACME question' applies inference to the best explanation to show that a single hypothesis — the aesthetic — explains Art, Cannibalism, Murder and Etiquette together, with 'Discourtesy is unspeakably ugly to me' read as an aesthetic rather than a moral complaint. The final twist is that Lecter's psychopathic 'moral blindness' may enhance his powers of aesthetic discrimination the way literal blindness enhances hearing and touch.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 28 "11. I Ain’t No Hollaback Girl!" — Callens explains Carol's killing of Lizzie in "The Grove" through Kohlberg's stages of moral development, arguing Carol reasons at the post-conventional level (pre-apocalypse law and punishment no longer bind) while Rick, Hershel, and Daryl stay conventional, and then layers Maslow's hierarchy of needs on top: because survival needs are perpetually threatened, characters regress between stages, and only self-actualized Carol accepts reality and makes group-preserving choices like executing Lizzie and mercy-killing Karen and David. Gilligan's justice-versus-care critique supplies the gendered frame - Carol moves to the middle of the justice-care continuum, her diminished care (unlike Season Two's grief over Sophia) is what makes her post-conventional, and her non-lethal Terminus rescue contrasts with Rick's summary execution of Gareth.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 29 "12. They Just Want Me to Be Like Them" — Castro and Beisecker diagnose Lizzie's walker fixation as prolonged grief disorder: she displaces grief for her father onto the walker "Nick," denies final death ("They're just different"), and treats reanimation as a viable form of life she might join ("Maybe I should change"). They argue Carol's suppressive guardianship - the "look at the flowers" distraction and calling Lizzie weak and confused - aggravated the avoidance at the root of the disorder, so Lizzie's "transformation" of Mika was a misguided moral experiment rather than murder by a monster. The chapter contrasts Tyreese's affirming care ("You each do things your own way") as the guardianship that might have saved the girls, and notes Carol's refusal to let Lizzie reanimate denies her the dying-wish courtesy the group once granted Jim.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 31 "Walker Bite. Innocence in Shambles" — Yuen argues that childhood innocence is both an excusing condition - children like Lizzie lack the rational capacity to judge their own acts morally, which is why her killing of Mika shocks and why the audience half-excuses her - and a social arrangement that shields children from adult demands, one Carol deliberately ends by secretly teaching the kids knife skills. He then extends Lydia's comic line that "Childhood was always a myth brought about by the illusion of safety" to real-world child labor in impoverished countries, where innocence is a luxury families cannot afford, and closes by asking readers to ask how we could make innocence affordable for working children rather than simply denouncing sweatshops.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 32 "14. Carol Didn’t Care" — Yuen grants that executing Lizzie was not wrong but argues Carol fell short of a moral ideal by ignoring Lizzie's preferences, deploying R.M. Hare's move from Bentham's happiness-maximizing classic utilitarianism to preference utilitarianism - illustrated by the group refusing to let Eugene test Aaron's water in "Them." Since Lizzie prefers a reanimating death ("She didn't hurt her brain"), a heart shot like the group's courtesy to Jim would have maximized preference satisfaction without endangering anyone. He answers the objections that Lizzie is a child and that walkers are mindless: her attempts to reason and her coherent post-apocalyptic values (like generational value shifts on homosexuality via Aaron and Eric) deserve respect, and whether a walker would still be Lizzie matters less than that the preference is hers now.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 26 "13. The Shrieking Evils" — Piven argues that evil in the story runs from the overt villains to the beloved heroes: Humperdinck's rage at Westley is analyzed as malignant envy of true love, Rugen's torture as dispassionate sadistic curiosity, and Vizzini's pompous moralizing as narcissistic hypocrisy masking childhood shame and nightmares. He applies Hannah Arendt's banality of evil to Inigo and Fezzik, who soberly assault and abduct Buttercup, and then brands Westley - a pirate who admits he liked piracy and who slaps and strangles Buttercup to test her fidelity - as possibly the evilest character, likening his love-justified slaughter to the terrorist's logic. The point is that we adore these characters only by ignoring deeds we would condemn in real life.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 22 "9. What Fuckin’ Chance Does a Kid Have" — Joseph Westfall argues that Louis's parent-hating bits - the baby he doesn't know who 'might fuckin' hate Jews,' the four-year-old 'asshole,' 'I love her, but I wish she was never born' - voice the real ambivalence of parenthood while showing that children are developmentally incapable of responsibility, so parents must not blame kids for being kids. He contrasts Louis's unknowable, selfish infant with Augustine's doctrine that unbaptized babies are simply evil, and reads Louis's parenting maxim - 'you're not raising the kid in front of you, you're raising the grownup they're going to be' - through childhood as a state of becoming: Jizzanthapuss is on the road to Hitler thanks to his weak mother, and Louie berating little Jane realizes 'I'm her first asshole,' shaping the men she will later attract. Good parenting is keeping kids alive plus forming the future adult, which is why Louis denies his daughters cell phones (they prevent learning empathy face-to-face) and puts his daughter on the smelly city bus while his Mercedes waits.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 33 "17. Louis’s Little Believies" — Builds a three-part definition of moral failure—acting against one's own moral beliefs, freely chosen—and applies it to Louie's Infiniti bit, his stopping the country girl from helping the homeless man, and his refusal to give a soldier his first-class seat while feeling proud of merely considering it. The chapter concludes Louie acts unselfishly only when someone might judge him (the sheriff's kiss, the limousines for his daughter's stranded field trip), so without the threat of judgment his 'little believies' stay inert, and a world where such hypocrisy goes unremarked would lose the power of moral criticism altogether.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 34 "18. Believies are Not Motivaties" — Uses the 'believies' bit, the 'I think it's wrong to eat meat... I eat them all' confession, and 'of course, but maybe' to place Louis in the meta-ethics of moral motivation: he is a cognitivist and partial success theorist, but a Humean who treats beliefs as causally inert without desire and an externalist who denies a necessary link between moral judgment and motivation. That combination, the chapter argues, lets Louis sincerely judge and not be moved without incoherence—making the amoralist conceivable and avoiding 'the moral problem.'
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 22 "11. Can a Leopard Change Its Shorts" — Alloy asks whether Rincewind - the wizard who runs from Twoflower, the Dungeon Dimensions, and the Agatean Empire alike - is really a coward. Aristotle's doctrine of the mean frames cowardice as the deficiency of fear-regulation between foolhardy Cohen the Barbarian and true courage, with character traits describing, explaining, and predicting Rincewind's flight. But the situationist challenge - Harman's reading of the cookie, hurry, and obedience experiments - denies that character traits exist, and the replies available to the virtue ethicist (Miller's continence/incontinence distinction, Alfano's 'dodge') leave almost nobody with virtues or vices, so the chapter concludes Rincewind cannot be a coward: cowardice, like the leopard's shorts, was never there to begin with.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 30 "16. Is Sarah Manning Responsible for What She Does" — Uses the genetically identical Leda clones against genetic determinism: Helena seems excused and Cosima responsible despite identical genes, so upbringing must explain the difference. But appealing to background triggers Galen Strawson's Basic Argument — no one is ultimately responsible for who they are, so no one is ultimately responsible for what they do — which the authors escape through Peter Strawson's reactive attitudes (our disgust at Helena softening to pity once her abuse is known, our judgment of Donnie shifting from malice to gullibility) and John Martin Fischer's two conditions: an agent is responsible when she is responsive to reasons that would move well-adjusted rational people and takes ownership of the psychology that produces her action. Helena's Prolethean programming exempts her; Cosima, Alison, and a marginally reformed Sarah remain responsible for what they do.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 15 "6. Driven by Love to Go to War" — John Karavitis deploys Alain Badiou's account of love as a contingent encounter founding the 'Two scene'—seeing the world from the perspective of difference—to argue that Darrow and Eo were never truly in love: their glade conversation, his 'nobility of obedience' against her 'live for more,' was two monologues, and you cannot love a memory. He then diagnoses Darrow as a narcissist in Rousseau's sense of amour-propre—self-love turned vanity that lies to itself—whose quest serves to manage his shame at failing to protect Eo, citing Erich Fromm on narcissism's path to fascism and Aristotle on habituation into Gold ways. Only the Jackal's stone-table imprisonment shatters the narcissism ('Man is no island'), letting Darrow embrace agape, with Ovid's Echo and Narcissus and the haemanthus framing the trilogy as a warning against self-love.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 14 "3. Click Bait for Black Fish" — Porot reads Elliot through Berlin's positive liberty: people are enslaved to their lower selves - the 'daemons' of addiction and primal urge Elliot describes in 'eps1.3_da3m0ns.mp4' - and freedom requires a contract in which an external force holds you to your higher self. Elliot writes such contracts with Shayla over his drugs and imagines Mr. Robot as the paternalistic enforcer who pushes him off the pier when he breaks his word, while corporations run the reverse contract, 'hacking' people from within through addictive sugar, clickbait, and advertising. The black fish dream crystallizes this: everyone at the office devours the confined fish of reverse-contract slavery while Elliot alone eats Pop's pie - freedom through the father figure of Mr. Robot.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 26 "12. Why Angela Drops the Whistle" — Jones asks why Angela flees the Nuclear Regulatory Commission at the exact moment she could expose the Washington Township cover-up, and answers with the real world of whistleblowing: Chelsea Manning's thirty-five-year sentence shows the legal peril, and the Rasmussen poll branding Manning a traitor plus the Enron fallout show the court of public opinion demonizes whistleblowers. Tribal survival instincts make insiders punish anyone who drops the tribe's secrets, and coworkers must condemn the whistleblower to preserve their own self-worth against the mirror of their silence - so even a legally protected, morally sound Angela backs away.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 18 "7. And the Most Despicable Jessica Lange Character Is . ." — Ranks Jessica Lange's characters from least to most despicable using moral philosophy: Sister Jude earns credit for acting from duty (reporting the Nazi Dr. Arden at personal risk, Kant-style) and for genuinely feeling remorse; Elsa Mars partly honors the matriarchal obligations of care ethics but lacks Aristotle's habitual virtue and moderation, selling Bette and Dot to Dandy for fame; Constance Langdon abuses and effectively murders her disabled children; and Fiona Goode, motivated exclusively by youth, beauty, and power, murders her Supreme and torments Cordelia - never once acting out of concern for others.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 30 "18. Thoughtcrime or Feelingcrime" — Alba Montes Sánchez argues that the real crime in Oceania is not thoughtcrime but 'feelingcrime': Winston lands in the Ministry of Love only once he falls in love, because beliefs alone do not motivate action while emotions and loves do — the problem of akrasia that puzzled Aristotle, since Winston carries his proof of Party lies for eleven years without acting. Using Harry Frankfurt's account of love as an involuntary, non-utilitarian, rigidly focused, self-affirming concern that organizes a person's priorities, she explains why Julia is irreplaceable and why Room 101 must destroy Winston's deepest allegiance rather than just his opinions. Surveying theories of individuality from Locke's memory to recognition and narrative, she concludes that a stubborn residue of selfhood survives in what we love — which is why Ingsoc must make war on love itself.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 9 "1. Amy’s Self-Confidence and Self-Deprecation" — Argues that Schumer's self-deprecating and gallows humor succeeds when it models transcendence, connection, and acceptance, drawing on Freud's relief theory of laughter as a discharge of repressed energy. Atkinson reads the Trainwreck funeral scene where Amy turns on Aaron after her father's burial, plus the memoir's 'grape' and clam-chowder consent jokes, as gallows humor inviting audiences to laugh both at and with her. She contrasts the failing Snatched tapeworm and flirting scenes, which degrade Emily rather than showing her overcoming her circumstances, and frames the whole practice as humility rather than humiliation.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 20 "10. Multiple Murderer Emily Middleton" — Treats Snatched as a series of case studies in personal responsibility: who originated an action, who created the situation, and what was intended. Emily's non-refundable tickets and drunken night out are hers, but she did not kidnap herself, and the film's title card ('The kidnappers did bad stuff, too') lures viewers out of victim-blaming. Her shovel killing of Morgado's nephew and accidental spear-gun killing of his son are judged through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics III.2 on acts done in ignorance of circumstances, excusing the 'multiple murderer' while showing how perspective and intent shift blame.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 17 "6. Serena Joy, Miserable, Despicable" — Elsby refuses to see Serena Joy as a self-determined villain, arguing she annihilates her own freedom—negating her humanity in Beauvoir's sense—to become an empty vessel for Gilead's will. Working through Aristotle on coerced and 'mixed' actions and the bad-upbringing excuse, Sartre on freedom and responsibility in Being and Nothingness, and Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity, she asks how much blame an oppressed woman deserves who nonetheless helped build her own subjugation and holds June down during the Ceremony. The answer runs through bad faith: Serena deceives herself until raping June is no longer a necessary wrong but a good in itself, and the 'unwomen' logic echoes Boethius's claim that evildoers cease to be human—comprehensible, but still abhorrent.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 23 "11. Those Agonizing Choices" — Romanowski traces Chidi's indecision from the cowboy-boots lie through the rock-paper-scissors panic attack, arguing the show treats the agony of deciding as the universal human moral condition rather than a professor joke. 'The Trolley Problem' makes Foot's dilemma literal torture, and the show pointedly never gives the right answer, confirming Chidi's claim that there are no clean solutions to hard moral questions. Eleanor's Dancy-inspired particularism pitch in 'Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent' and Michael's 'I solved the Trolley Problem: you sacrifice yourself' moment, together with Chidi finally kissing Eleanor, show that acknowledging uncertainty is no excuse for inaction.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 36 "20. Moral Health Warning" — The moral philosopher Jonathan Dancy issues a warning against the show's premise that studying moral philosophy can make you a better person, the assumption behind Chidi's entire tutelage of Eleanor. What makes someone good is their motivation, and reading Kant and Scanlon is at best self-indulgent study that never redirects the will toward the right; indeed anyone genuinely motivated by the good would stop reading moral philosophy and go do good instead. He also contests the Kantian thought that only action done from a sense of duty earns moral credit: Douglas Wynegar's roses for his grandmother, given out of love, should count without any thought of obligation.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 38 "22. Professor Stomachache Needs Neuroscience" — Zebrowski brings Antonio Damasio's Somatic Marker Hypothesis to bear on Chidi's stomachaches: gut feelings built from a lifetime of social experience are essential decision-making shortcuts, not noise corrupting pure reason, as the tirelessly deliberating frontal-lobe patient shows. Chidi's failure is not brain damage but a refusal to trust his own somatic alarms while insisting ethics can be computed, exactly the mind-body split that Scanlon's contractualism, where morality is negotiated with other people, and Dewey's 'morals is education' both reject. Combined with Mark Johnson's moral imagination, this explains how the dead humans keep growing morally after death: bodies, relationships, and culture continue tuning their ethical instincts.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 39 "23. Like Boxing Gloves of Sadness" — Benko argues the show's deepest target is selfishness understood as inauthenticity: an over-investment in a self whose real motivations, Tahani's name-dropping, Chidi's moral filibustering, Jason's Acidcat fiasco, Eleanor's aggressive solitude, are hidden from the person herself. Drawing on Charles Guignon's account of authenticity, he shows that being true to yourself is not enough unless your self-expression enables others to become their authentic selves too, which is why Chidi's keeping of his promises across all 802 reboots is the show's moral core and why treating people as mere means fails on Kantian grounds. Eleanor's final willingness to lose Chidi rather than her better self demonstrates authenticity reoriented toward others, the show's answer to Schur's fourth-car-at-the-left-turn driver.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 22 "12. What about Della Street" — Birondo evaluates Della Street through moral psychology and Aristotelian virtue ethics: she is an excellent secretary in the role-specific sense (the Gregg shorthand that traps Robert Caddo's contradiction outside The Lonely Heiress crime scene) and supplies the 'woman's angle' the office needs, while Perry displays Aristotle's practical wisdom in court but a failure of recognition toward her, under-crediting her and kissing her for her 'feminine charms' upon her skullduggery in ways that today would be sexual harassment. The chapter also applies Aristotle on habituation through Mrs. Caddo's 'wildcat' tantrums hardening into character, and asks whether Della's team-playing beyond her duties is admirable, sad, or itself the product of mid-century sexism.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 26 "15. Judge Not, Lest You …" — Hooke uses Nietzsche, the 'pale criminal' of Thus Spoke Zarathustra and the 'valuating animal' of the Genealogy of Morals, to dissect our culture of judgment, in which judge, jury, spectators, and millions of readers assess the accused with an element of self-satisfaction (am I not better than the murderer?), even as Mason's plots ask us to imagine ourselves in the criminal's situation. Working through means/motive/opportunity in The Case of the Mischievous Doll (the client accused of killing her own disguised self) and The Case of the Angry Mourner (the telescope-wielding neighbors who missed the real killer husband), he ends with Mason's maxim that solving cases requires 'sympathy and tolerance for crime', seeing through others' eyes into the soul whose trace of madness Nietzsche says we cannot creep deep enough to find.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 10 "Olympic Tetherball A Final Lesson on Moral Frailty" — The chapter asks whether Kenneth the page is a Kantian rule absolutist who never makes exceptions, or an Aristotelian 'contextual absolutist' who sees that the right act depends on circumstances, as when he runs the Hill Witch ruse to scare Tracy into eating well. Jack's lifeboat hypothetical and rigged-elevator test bounce off Kenneth's refusal to believe in hypothetical situations, but Jack's gift of illegal cable exposes Kenneth's moral frailty when he enjoys the stolen channels. It concludes that Kenneth's gullibility, trust, and loyalty make his simple moral vision both admirable and easily corrupted, and that the real lesson is facing our failures with resolve rather than shame.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 10 "“Some People Have No More Sense Than a Baby!”" — Uses the White Queen's 'jam to-morrow and jam yesterday—but never jam to-day' to introduce Elijah Millgram's jam-yesterday-jam-tomorrow goods: jobs, parenting, and Utah hiking that feel drudging in every moment yet are remembered and anticipated as wonderful. Mark D. White brings in G. E. Moore's organic unity, illustrated by the Spice Girls' 'Wannabe', Wham!, and Led Zeppelin, to ask how a whole made entirely of bad parts can be good 'on the whole', then treats procrastination as akrasia (weakness of will) and endorses Millgram's remedy: manufacture short-term 'jam today' goals like graduation ceremonies and marked lookout points to motivate timely action.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 18 "Bending That Saves Life" — Flowers argues bloodbending is morally neutral: like Huu's plantbending ('The Swamp') and taijiquan's qinna joint locks, it is an advanced technique whose harm depends on the practitioner's intention, as Katara's gentle suppression of Hama ('The Puppetmaster') shows against her vengeful contortion of the Southern Raider. Waterbending's Taiji foundation, with the yin-yang harmony of Tui and La's circling koi and the Aikido/Aikijutsu contrast in applying kotegaeshi, grounds his conclusion from Yagyu Munenori's Heiho Kadensho: Hama practiced the sword that takes life, while Katara's compassionate bloodbending is 'bending that saves life'.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 33 "Becoming Good at Being Good" — Explains Zuko's cry 'Why am I so bad at being good?' through the gap between Christine Korsgaard's reflective practical identity (the self-conception under which you value your life) and Heidegger's being-in-the-world (who you are existentially engaged in being): Zuko can renounce his father and still accidentally burn Toph's feet because his rage and honor-seeking survive as residual dispositions shaping his perception and skills. The chapter tracks the arc from 'The Storm' (saving the crew despite himself) through the Appa-release metamorphosis fever, the relapse at the Crossroads of Destiny, and losing his rage-fueled firebending until the Sun Warriors re-teach him what fire is for. Aspiration (Agnes Callard) explains why deep change lags behind explicit commitment — becoming good at being good means rebuilding one's being-in-the-world, not just one's self-image.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 34 "Sometimes We Can Let Go" — Sets P.F. Strawson's blame-as-moral-anger picture against the Seneca/Buddhist case that anger is revenge-hungry poison, then reads ATLA as modeling ways to hold people responsible without toxic anger. Katara may stay angry at Yon Rha after 'The Southern Raiders' yet forgo revenge because he is incorrigible and not worth it, while forgiving Zuko on Lucy Allais's 'wiping the slate clean' logic since his villainy no longer reflects his character. Iroh's 'I was never angry; I was afraid that you had lost your way' and his tea with the mugger Tycho show blame being skipped entirely in favor of compassion, and Zuko's shift from hypocritical self-blame to self-compassion after confronting Ozai lets him take responsibility without self-destructive rage.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 18 "Bending That Saves Life" — Flowers argues bloodbending is morally neutral by locating it within waterbending's Taiji: its locking motions are qinna, the push-pull art whose harms scale with the practitioner, just as Aikido's kotegaeshi can be gradual or vicious depending on the wielder. Katara's painless suppression of Hama in 'The Puppetmaster' versus her violent contortion of the ship captain in 'The Southern Raiders' shows the technique itself carries no fixed evil, and plantbending's kinship with bloodbending reinforces the point. Yagyū Munenori's distinction between the sword that takes life and the sword that gives life supplies the verdict: Hama's bloodbending takes life, Katara's saves it, so it is people, not the art, that make bloodbending evil.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 31 "Opening Up Possibilities" — Argues, through Hilde Lindemann's relational account of personhood, that Zuko genuinely is all of the identities others hold him in (disappointing son, villain, ally) because being a person is a social practice of expression, recognition, and response. Aang's decision to hear Zuko out at the Western Air Temple, Iroh's stubborn refusal to accept Ozai's script for him (his anger itself recognizing Zuko as an agent capable of choosing otherwise), and Katara's historically-sensitive slow trust open up the possible future in which Zuko can become trustworthy, while the Earth Kingdom villagers' rejection of him in 'Zuko Alone' shows how weight of history and stereotype can shut possibility down. The chapter insists this is not letting wrongdoers off the hook: genuine apology, repair, and moral anger remain required (contrasting the Brock Turner case), but only a moral community that holds people in personhood makes redemption possible, so society should be arranged to give everyone the Iros and Aangs that Zuko was lucky to have.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 33 "Becoming Good at Being Good" — Argues that Zuko's cry 'Why am I so bad at being good?' after burning Toph shows that changing one's explicit self-conception (Korsgaard's practical identity, the description under which you value yourself) does not by itself change one's being-in-the-world (Heidegger): Zuko's perception, dispositions, and rage-fueled firebending still run on the residual identity of the banished prince seeking his father's approval. The chapter traces this friction through the series: releasing Appa triggers a metamorphosis fever, but he still sides with Azula at the Crossroads of Destiny; the regained 'honor' of Book Three leaves him empty ('I should be happy now, but I'm not'); and only after renouncing Ozai, apologizing to Toph, and re-learning fire from the Sun Warriors without rage do his conscious commitments and existential engagement begin to align, culminating in taking Azula's lightning for Katara. Aspiration, in Agnes Callard's sense, is thus a deep change in how one sees and feels, requiring retraining of bodily skills and practical perception, not just new stated values.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 34 "Sometimes We Can Let Go" — Sets the intuition that angry blame is how we hold people responsible (Strawson; Katara's useful fury at Pakku's sexism, Iroh's 'whatever you do to that spirit, I will unleash on you tenfold') against the Senecan and Buddhist verdict that anger is greedy for revenge, and reads ATLA as modeling ways to hold people responsible without toxic anger. In 'The Southern Raiders' Katara neither forgives Yon Rha nor kills him, showing that blame can be set down when expressing it is pointless, while she forgives Zuko in Lucy Allais's 'wiping the slate clean' sense because his past betrayal no longer speaks to his present character. Iroh's handling of the mugger in Ba Sing Se ('I was never angry; I was afraid that you had lost your way') models responding to the suffering behind wrongdoing with compassion instead of blame, and Zuko's self-anger is diagnosed as hypocritical self-blame whose antidote is self-compassion: acknowledging how he himself was hurt is what finally lets him take ownership of his wrongs.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 10 "Let there be an Ending!" — Southworth and Tallman ask why fans blame Hank Pym for Ultron's killings while never crediting Magneto for fathering two heroes, and answer with Aristotle's account of character formed by habitual imitation, renewed as 'moral exemplarism': praise and blame track exemplarship, not biology. Scott Lang earned credit because he actively taught Cassie right and wrong, making her the hero Stature; T'Chaka and stepmother Ramonda shaped T'Challa, while Heinrich Zemo's Nazi upbringing warped Helmut into the new Baron Zemo. The Avengers themselves—Cap's patient mentoring of Hawkeye, Stark hiring ex-con Scott Lang—function as moral exemplars for reformed villains, so the mentoring 'parents', not the siring ones, deserve the credit or blame.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 18 "Avengers Rehabilitate!" — Terjesen asks whether Cap's Kooky Quartet-style rehabilitation really works, pitting Aristotle's fixed-character virtue ethics against John Doris's situationist 'local traits' (backed by Milgram's experiments): Hawkeye succeeded because his regional traits—hotheadedness and a need for approval—were redirected to heroism, not erased, as when he cheats the Grandmaster to save the universe. Aristotle's continence-versus-virtue and vice-versus-incontinence distinctions explain why Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch keep backsliding, why Moonstone's true viciousness defeats rehabilitation while Songbird and MACH-1 reform. Against deterrence and retributivist theories of punishment, rehabilitation is defensible when applied early and to the unhardened—the Avengers Academy children and Young Avenger Patriot—so the Avengers can rehabilitate as well as avenge.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 4 "How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the ADAM" — Rose argues BioShock is not a cheap strawman of Ayn Rand but a use of her own philosophy-through-fiction method (Atlas Shrugged as the hidden utopia Rapture continues) to show what happens when an ideologue divides reason from emotion. Ryan, unlike the flawless John Galt, is a flawed human destroyed by his refusal to question and by sentiment (killed by the son he cannot shoot), while Fontaine wins by manipulating feelings and Tenenbaum's motherly attachment to the Little Sisters becomes her salvation. Drawing on Antonio Damasio's point that emotion filters options for practical reasoning, the chapter reads the save-or-harvest dilemma as proof that moral choices must include emotional response, concluding Randians should celebrate a game that warns against being blinded by ideology rather than against Objectivism itself.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 21 "This Is the End" — Muniz uses Dr. Steinman's surgical madness in the Medical Pavilion to test whether beauty and morality are entangled: Plato's Symposium makes beauty the value binding truth and goodness (Steinman's 'Goddess' of symmetry), Aristotle names order, symmetry, and definiteness the chief forms of beauty, and Keats's 'Beauty is truth' frames Steinman's descent into asymmetry-hating madness. Dewey's point that the young let the beautiful govern their behavior, plus the author's puppy-versus-rat classroom experiment, shows how the ugly get treated as morally worse, as in Steinman's 'moral obligation' to beautify. The Circus of Values vending machines frame the intrinsic-versus-extrinsic value distinction behind the Little Sister save-or-harvest dilemma, and the chapter concludes players must disentangle beauty from goodness and choose values for themselves.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 12 "Our First Gaze into the Black Mirror" — Collins and Boesch use Prime Minister Callow's coerced live sex act with a pig in The National Anthem to weigh conflicting moral obligations: the public's initial 72% Kantian refusal flips to an 86% utilitarian capitulation after the kidnapper's finger video, and the withheld revelation that Susannah was released half an hour early undermines any consequentialist justification of the act. A virtue-theory reading faults Callow's character for faking the rescue video and putting self-interest first, and the UKN media's Kantian compliance collapses once ratings are at stake. The closing section applies Martha Nussbaum's theory of disgust (contamination transferring disgust from blood and vomit to the spectacle-watchers themselves) to argue the episode's graphic imagery functions as a moral emotion condemning the audience's own obsession with spectacle.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 26 "The Future of Our “MASS Implant”" — Stripe's MASS implant in Men Against Fire, which makes targeted humans look like monstrous 'roaches,' literalizes the chapter's claim that dehumanizing language — chosen by Brooker after columnist Katie Hopkins called migrants 'cockroaches' — is the real-world technology that enables genocide, from the Armenian and Holocaust cases through Rwanda's Tutsis to the Rohingya. Wittgenstein's 'the limits of my language mean the limits of my world' grounds how propaganda deadens empathy, and Kelman-style accounts of excluded identity explain why the villagers hate but cannot kill while the implanted soldiers kill gleefully. Levinas's face of the Other explains the turn: once Stripe sees Catarina and Alec's faces, he cannot pull the trigger, and the chapter closes on our own MASS implant — Trump's 'animals,' the ascent-of-man studies, and the temptation to reset and forget.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 33 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Griffioen distinguishes two kinds of truthiness: believing what one prefers to be true (motivated epistemic irrationality) and justifying beliefs by gut feeling, using Colbert's premiere clips about Bush knowing Harriet Miers's heart and feeling that taking out Saddam was right. She models the first as wishful thinking and self-deception via a Samantha Bee/Jason Jones marital-fidelity example, works through the static and dynamic paradoxes of self-deception, rejects the Freudian divided-mind solution (imagined as Colbert debating himself in 'Formidable Opponent'), and defends an attention-directing account instead. Gut feelings justify only when they implicitly track facts, yielding her proposed fallacy argumentum Colberti ad ventrem.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 33 "“It's Been Handed Down from Goof to Goof to Goof, and Now, It's Yours, Son”" — Mentyka uses Goofy to test theories of the good life: Socratic intellectualism stumbles on uneducated-but-good Goofy, Kant's categorical imperative absurdly forbids handing Max the 'goof to goof' fishing pole (Goofy can't will it universal law), Mill's utilitarianism fails when Max's lukewarm reception makes the gift happiness-reducing, and Singer's extension to animals muddies Pluto the dog against Goofy the dog treated as a person. The chapter resolves with Scheler's claim that we first encounter values through moral exemplars — earnest, bumbling Goofy — not through rules or consequences, and a closing plea that philosophers narrate less like the smug 'How to...' narrator.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 8 "Of the Simple and Complex" — The editors' introduction argues that Downton's quaint domestic plots burst with universal moral and social meaning beneath their surface. Using the season 1 snuffbox incident, in which Thomas frames the innocent Bates for theft, it shows how the episode stages archetypal villainy and innocence akin to the universal figures of Plato's Republic and world mythology, so the 'simple' plot is morally clear rather than superficial. It then reads the hierarchy of Thomas, Bates, and Lord Grantham through Confucian propriety and Aristotelian justice, suggesting that justice partly consists in attention to 'greater and lesser,' something Western viewers raised on equality find foreign yet intriguing. Finally it insists that as concrete persons all three are morally mixed (Thomas takes a beating to spare Jimmy, Bates may have killed outside the law, Grantham is generous to tenants but cold to his daughters), and that this complexity is what rewards philosophical reflection, along with Hume's 'small morals' of etiquette.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 12 "3. Matthew’s Dark Side" — Wills deploys Georg Simmel's The Philosophy of Money, with its thesis that growing wealth corrodes individuality, to reread Matthew Crawley's courtship of Mary as corruption rather than romance: the man who vows Downton won't change him soon accepts Molesley's valeting, savors finding no grounds to challenge the entail, and returns to the fortune he claimed to renounce. He contrasts their 'relationship of convenience,' which conveniently solves the succession problem, with the penniless Anna and Bates courtship as the show's picture of love uncontaminated by money. The darker claim is that viewers are corrupted alongside Matthew, rooting for a marriage that serves the estate's economic structure, so the show indicts our own captivity to wealth.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 24 "12. Should We Really Care about the Crawleys" — Jones takes on the charge, voiced amid rising real-world inequality, that loving Downton seduces viewers into admiring hierarchy, and answers that the Crawleys deserve our care because they are human beings who share our bereavements (Mary's grief for Matthew, Cora's miscarriage, Edith's jilting) and because they use moments of cross-class contact well: Grantham paying for Mrs. Patmore's eye surgery, Violet throwing the flower contest at Isobel's urging, and the family's genuine embrace of Tom Branson. He reads the show as a manifesto for gradual social change through sympathetic contact rather than the Irish revolutionaries' arson, but ends with a serious objection: this philosophy makes ending oppression partly the duty of the oppressed, from Carson's 'foul' remark about Thomas's sexuality to today's super-rich, so more radical activism may still be required.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 10 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Merli argues from alignment role-play against Aristotelian virtue ethics: a morally decent player convincingly runs a vicious treacherous thief who frames others for murder, and a 'moral mediocrity' runs a genuinely good paladin, so the ability to judge what the virtuous agent would do is one thing and being virtuous another. This undermines the McDowell/Hursthouse/Jacobson line that only the virtuous, with habituated emotional responses, can 'see what to do' — the role-playing skill works off-line, without feeling the character's fear or sharing its motives, so right-action judgment does not require trained emotion. He adds that if the virtue ethicist retorts that non-virtuous players never really get it right, the contrast between guessing dice in a fist (verifiable success) and claiming to read auras (unverifiable) shows the retort makes virtue look fraudulent, and that role-playing, unlike reading Austen, demands active deliberation from another's point of view, exposing abilities literary examples miss.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 13 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Matthew Brophy argues the I.F. neutralizes Ender's moral agency by masquerading xenocide as child's play: Rackham's paradox that total empathy with the buggers forbids killing them (Sunzi's 'know your enemy') is solved by deception, Walzer's problem of dirty hands is shifted from the child to the politicians, and Milgram-style game framing plus Foot's trolley-problem 'moral distance' show how killing grows easier at a console. Against the innocent-pawn reading, Brophy ends by suggesting Ender was a willing pawn who let himself be deceived in order to save humanity.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 15 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Brendan Shea starts from Wittgenstein's point that 'game' resists any definition, then applies Bernard Suits' four-part analysis (prelusory goal, constitutive rules, lusory means, lusory attitude) to the battleroom contests and to the Giant's Drink as an 'open game' whose real goal is simply to keep playing. He argues games build Ender's skills and even his empathy — buggers and astronauts makes him take a bugger's perspective — but Battle School's 'winning is the only thing' attitude, which celebrates breaking the rules, trains brilliant commanders while corroding moral character.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 21 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Lance Belluomini tests Card's creed that 'good or evil exist entirely in human motive, and not at all in the act' against Aquinas's Doctrine of Double Effect, finding that Ender's self-defense killings of Stilson and Bonzo fail the proportionality condition — he intended to 'win all the next fights' — so he bears moral responsibility despite his tears. After weighing Frankfurt's second-order intentions as a way to keep Ender a good person who did bad things, he concludes with Anscombe's 'double-think about double effect' that Ender is deceived about his own intentions and is no moral exemplar.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 23 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Danielle Wylie applies Aristotle's conditions of voluntary action — control and knowledge, including his 'mixed' coerced cases like the wallet at gunpoint — to argue Ender's final attack was involuntary, since he believed he was throwing an unfair simulation to get himself thrown out, so his guilt is real but full blame is misplaced. Using Rachels's Smith and Jones drowning case she extends moral responsibility to omissions, showing Graff and Rackham foresaw the xenocide and could have stopped Ender, and closes with Ender's Speaker-for-the-Dead work as taking responsibility without being to blame.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 19 "The Upsides of Amos" — Diana Sofronieva asks whether Amos is evil and answers no — in some ways he is better than most. Drawing on psychopathy research (Blair's moral/conventional distinction), Glover's 'moral resources', and Damasio's somatic markers to explain both his emotional absence (cauterized by a Baltimore childhood where children were sold for sex) and his difficulty making choices ('I've been trying to make choices of my own lately, and I can't seem to make the right ones'), she distinguishes him from bloodthirsty killers like Murtry and from Cortázar, who surgically chose the emotionless life Amos wants to escape. Against Arendt's banality of evil, Amos is no thoughtless 'joiner': he holds an uncompromising inner code (family first, bullying punished), deliberately selects good people — Naomi, Anna, Holden — as his moral compass after verifying their reasons, and his honesty, loyalty, trust in competence, and selflessness make him paradoxically less capable of evil than nearly anyone else on the Roci.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 36 "20. Moral Health Warning" — A health warning from Jonathan Dancy himself: the show's premise that Chidi's lessons in Kant, Scanlon, and the Trolley Problem can make Eleanor better is false, because becoming good requires a change in motivation and intellectual study shapes motivation at most indirectly — and might attach to the wrong as easily as the right, since moral philosophy studies both. Worse, studying ethics looks like self-indulgence, time spent on Kant that could have gone to doing actual good. Against the Kantian thought that only acting from a sense of duty earns moral credit, Dancy argues that sympathetic love — Doug Wynegar bringing his grandmother roses simply for her sake — is enough, which undermines both Kant and Chidi's entire teaching project.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 10 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — White asks whether Sinestro's quip that Hal's mind is 'like a muscle unused for years' is a mere metaphor and argues willpower is a real, exercisable strength. Against the Humean desire-belief model, which cannot explain Tom Kalamaku fixing planes instead of browsing Facebook, he uses Searle's 'gaps' to locate an independent will that can choose against one's better judgment, and Kant's account of virtue as moral strength in fulfilling duty despite inclination. Holton and Baumeister's findings that self-control depletes and strengthens like a muscle fit the comics exactly: Ollie is exhausted by a single ring use in Rebirth, Hal sweats through moving a planet, and John Stewart must 'suppress my own terrors' to hold the Mosaic walls.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 16 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Darowski traces Hal's shifting motivations across fifty years: the Showcase #22 origin where honesty and fearlessness make heroism a simple vow, the selfish Parallax era after Coast City's destruction, the Spectre's atonement, and the guilt-driven Lantern of Rebirth. Plato's claim that knowing the good suffices for doing good would mean Hal never really chose heroism, but the chapter rejects it, since morality alone failed to stop Hal's turn to Parallax. Set against the darker post-Watchmen industry, it asks whether guilt-driven atonement is a nobler motive than simple duty and what standards we should hold heroes to.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 40 "Snape the Occlumens" — The section positions Snape as the third 'abandoned boy' beside Harry and Voldemort, a half-blood from an unhappy home for whom Hogwarts, as Harry observes, is where all three 'found home.' Voldemort chose power, selfishness, and a fragmented psyche while Harry opened his heart to friends and grew into integrity, and the section asks what makes this 'complicated amalgam of darkness and light,' Dumbledore's double agent and killer, tick.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 84 "How Revealing Are Our Choices" — The chapter builds on Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics account of choice (prohairesis) as 'deliberative desire' for things within our power and a better test of character than actions, then distinguishes three senses of choice. Internal-choice is Draco deciding but failing to kill Dumbledore; act-choice is Dumbledore's poor youthful choices; and motive-choice is captured by Kant's two shopkeepers who both refuse to cheat customers, one from fear of jail and one from honesty, so that only knowing the motive reveals the choice's moral worth.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 85 "Abilities" — The chapter argues motive-choices reveal character best: Hermione's rule-breaking for Dumbledore's Army does not make her a habitual rebel since character is habit, as Aristotle says, and Snape's apparently loyal Death Eater acts concealed his fidelity to Dumbledore and Lily, so bare acts mislead; Harry's decision to enter the Chamber to save Ginny, acted on despite the dangers, is genuinely revealing. But the wizarding world complicates self-knowledge: Harry's vision as Voldemort attacked Arthur Weasley, the implanted memory framing Morfin Gaunt for the Riddle murders, and the firewhiskey scenario of Imperius Curse, Polyjuice Potion, and memory charms can make it undecidable whether it was really you who chose, since the boundaries between self and other are thinner there.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 86 "How Revealing Are Our Abilities" — The chapter analyzes ability as a 'fuzzy concept': abilities are powers or capacities that come in degrees and vary with circumstance, like speaking seventy versus three hundred words of Mermish or conjuring a chipmunk Patronus only when relaxed. Choices, by contrast, are definite acts, Pettigrew's betrayal of Harry's parents and Harry's breakup with Ginny to protect her admit of no question, and this act-versus-capacity contrast explains why choices are the clearer self-revealers.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 87 "Beyond Choices Toward a Deeper Self-Understanding" — The chapter concedes Dumbledore's claim with qualifications: trivial, universal, unconscious, innate, or unrecognized abilities (Harry's Parseltongue before Sorcerer's Stone) reveal nothing, and the qualities Slytherin prized in Harry, resourcefulness, determination, and a certain disregard for rules, are morally neutral, since Voldemort's resourcefulness serves domination and immortality while Harry's saves his friends and fights tyranny. Yet abilities won only through hard work and self-sacrifice, and ethical capacities like empathy, prudence, and resilience do disclose character, so honest self-reflection about abilities matters too.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 88 "Unknown" — The chapter uses Gilderoy Lockhart as the failure case of self-knowledge by introspection: convinced he is a great Defense teacher and duelist, he cannot manage a cage of Cornish pixies, is floored by Snape's Expelliarmus, and removes all the bones from Harry's arm, because his rose-colored 'cognitive blinders' mean he looks but does not see. Bassham then previews four remedies for self-knowledge, each illustrated in the books: cultivate habitual self-examination, stay alert to irrational tendencies, get help from friends, and challenge yourself.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 90 "Unknown" — Against Aristotle's definition of humans as the 'rational animal,' the chapter catalogues wizarding irrationality, Percy's rule fetish, Malfoy's racism and classism, Ron's jealousy, Hagrid's blind affection for dangerous creatures, Fudge's closed-mindedness, and Luna's credulity, culminating in the wizards' blindness to house-elf slavery, excused because elves like Winky have been conditioned to find freedom shameful. Hermione's point that internalized oppression justifies nothing is one Harry finally absorbs, digging Dobby's grave with his own hands and writing 'Here lies Dobby, a Free Elf.'
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 91 "Unknown" — Because we each view life from our own 'personal mini-cam,' we can be too close to ourselves to see truly, so friends serve as honest mirrors in which we see ourselves as we really are. Hermione shows Harry his insensitivity to Cho, the trio helps Neville overcome his painful shyness, and Hagrid teaches Ron that friendship should not be wrecked by petty jealousy, while the friendless Dursleys, Lockhart, and Slughorn never progress in self-understanding.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 92 "The Ultimate Measure of a Person" — Quoting Lucretius, that in danger and peril 'the mask is torn off, the reality remains,' the chapter argues that ordinary behavior is stereotypical and only situations of challenge and adversity reveal what kind of person someone truly is. Harry and his friends pass repeated tests of courage, loyalty, intelligence, and resourcefulness and emerge humble but battle-tested heroes like Frodo's fellowship, with Ron's temporary abandonment in Deathly Hallows the instructive exception.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 37 "Notes" — Auxier asks who is morally worse, judging Frank and Claire by past deeds (Frank's murders of Zoe and Peter), future consequences (a president with the nuclear button), and the subjunctive (what each would do), while tracing Claire's lineage from Lady Macbeth and Elizabeth Urquhart, who assassinates Francis in the British series. Plato's and Aristotle's warning that democracy degenerates into tyranny frames the answer: Frank symbolizes the House, Claire the Senate, both coveting executive power, and Meechum - 'utterly loyal, utterly deadly' - is the military they seduce in the menage a trois and will underestimate. Niebuhr's 'moral mediocrity' of nations, from McCarthyism and the Joe Welch moment to mass incarceration, explains the verdict that neither individual is worse alone: 'they are far worse together,' and the union, not the person, has no decency.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 37 "Notes" — Asks who is morally worse by three standards-what each has done, is doing, and would do in the future subjunctive-and answers that Frank and Claire are far worse together, read symbolically as the US Constitution itself: Frank is the mercurial House, Claire the deliberate, more ambitious Senate, and Meechum the loyal military they seduce and underestimate at the republic's peril. Working from Plato's and Aristotle's claim that democracy declines into tyranny, Niebuhr's 'moral mediocrity' of nations, and the Welch-McCarthy 'have you no decency' moment, it asks whether a system that produced them is one 'we the people' deserve.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 14 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Andrew Shaffer imagines Capitol patrons at Caesar's Bar & Grill cheering the Quarter Quell bloodbath and asks what makes their enjoyment possible, answering with Schopenhauer's 'devilish' verdict on Schadenfreude as the mark of a worthless heart, Kant's calling it a 'diabolical' vice, and Nietzsche's account of another's misfortune as the social equalizer that appeases envy. He argues the spectators need dehumanization, from Effie's 'savages' rhetoric and the prep team's scrubbing to the wolf mutts wearing Glimmer's eyes, to enjoy innocent children dying, and that the star-crossed-lovers story humanizes the tributes enough to force the unprecedented double-victor rule change. The chapter closes by turning the diagnosis on us: readers thrill to the arena too, the whole trilogy arguably runs on Schadenfreude, and even Snow's execution is staged as a spectacle of righteous pleasure in a villain's death.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 17 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Abigail Mann argues that the Games only look like 'survival of the fittest': Darwinian natural selection runs on chance ('one slip in thousands') and explicitly rejects the social-Darwinist use of 'unfit' against the poor, while Darwin's Descent of Man explains the tributes' kindness through kin and group selection and an evolved moral sense, so Katniss's unhesitating volunteering for Prim is kin selection and Thresh's conflicted sparing of her shows conscience overriding self-preservation. She tests this against Kant, for whom only duty-motivated action is truly moral, which would make Thresh's inner struggle the more moral act and Katniss's instinctive sacrifice mere animal impulse, and against the egoism of Hobbes (giving to a beggar to relieve one's own distress) and Dawkins's selfish gene, answering with Hume and psychologist Daniel Batson that genuine altruism is real. Her coda: Katniss ultimately rejects Gale not only because his firebomb killed Prim but because it was engineered to trap and kill altruists, and her closing habit of listing 'every act of goodness' is the trilogy's verdict that simple kindness is not an illusion.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 15 "Does This Matter" — Garvin asks whether anything done in a dream can be right or wrong. He argues that in Inception's shared dreams ordinary ethics fully applies: the team really lies to Fischer (shared-dream communication is morally like waking communication), and the projections they mow down are, by a Turing-test-style argument, indistinguishable within the dream from persons — so either projections deserve rights or the dreamers can never know whom they are killing. For ordinary unshared dreams he engages Augustine's worry about nocturnal lust, concluding that mental acts like lust and lying are not excused by the dream state, though actions outside the dreamer's control are not blameworthy — dream wrongdoing being something to avoid repeating rather than to atone for.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 12 "The Guilt Never Goes Away" — Robichaud asks whether Iron Man can atone for Tony Stark's wrongs, using the Iron Monger's reprogrammed-suit example to distinguish causal from moral responsibility and to argue that omissions can be causes. Tony's negligence in running Stark Industries is blameworthy because his playboy ignorance was itself negligent (as with the Mandarin's willful ignorance), and via T. M. Scanlon's account of blame the families harmed by the illegal weapons sales are the ones most warranted in blaming him. Since 'I'm sorry' is not enough for wrongs this serious and Tony never submits to punishment, the chapter concludes that even his crusade as Iron Man to 'right the wrongs' — crushing Raza's group and collecting rogue weapons — may not yet warrant forgiveness.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 13 "The Hero’s Responsibility" — White defends Tony against blame for Captain America's assassination: spearheading registration in Civil War was a tragic dilemma, and Tony took the least bad option because 'if not me, who?' — telling Cap's corpse he sacrificed their friendship to save lives. Cap's death traces through Crossbones, the mind-controlled Sharon Carter, Dr. Faustus, and the Red Skull, not any direct act of Tony's; without foreseeability or wrongdoing, the chain of 'might haves' does not add up to responsibility, just as pushing someone out of a truck's path does not make you liable for the manhole they fall into. The motivation-centered lens of Kantian deontology and Aristotelian virtue ethics supports Tony (he gave up status, friends, and Cap himself), and living with tragic choices, as he does facing the Hulk, is itself heroic.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 14 "Drying Out" — Novy weighs the choice model against the disease model of Tony's alcoholism in 'Demon in a Bottle.' Frankfurt's principle that a person is not responsible for what he did only because he could not have done otherwise — tested by an imagined Dr. Doom brain-worm that would force Tony to drink — plus Plato's Protagoras claim that no one willingly chooses evil set up the puzzle of akrasia at the bottom of the bottle. Causal determinism would excuse Tony as a marionette, yet Mike Martin defines alcoholism as disordered agency and Jeffrey Smith pictures free will as an organ that disease can compromise, leaving Tony responsible for the first drink but not for the binges; sobriety is 'the drink or the dream' chosen one day at a time.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 22 "Amazing and Inspiring" — White explains Tony's drinking as weakness of will: Davidson's denial that akrasia is possible (Black Widow skipping Fury's spying order for a visit to Stark would have to have revised her judgment) is set against Searle's 'gaps,' where a person freely chooses against her all-things-considered judgment and nothing fills the gap. Frankfurt's wanton and second-order desires sharpen the picture — Tony wants a drink but does not want to want it, unlike the unreflective heroin addict — and volitionists like Wallace and Holton (the will as a muscle that Stane's orchestrated disasters exhaust) explain both his lapses and his daily resistance. If Searle is right, Tony's struggle with the bottle is not a defect of rationality but proof of it: akrasia is a symptom of freedom, which is what makes Iron Man amazing and inspiring.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 10 "NOTES" — Pierce argues that Lost's time travel runs on a fixed-time model in which nothing that happened can be undone, so the live question is ethical: Kate insists saving young Ben is still obligatory and Sayid remains responsible for shooting him, while Jack's plan to detonate Jughead at the Swan shows that trying to change the past can cause the very evil it targets, the Incident. Using Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity - future-tense truths made true by our own free choices - he shows that 'whatever happened, happened' does not abolish moral responsibility, applying the point to the Man in Black's causal-loop manipulation of Locke, Richard, and Ben. Desmond's consciousness travel in 'The Constant' is treated as the exception requiring hyper-time or alternate realities, and Pierce concludes that morality in time travel is simply ordinary morality, with Kate offering the most balanced view of the characters' choices.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 21 "Nonetheless, Don Can Be a Real Heel" — Terjesen asks whether Don is a good man, testing his mixed record (egalitarian instincts, loyalty to Mohawk Airlines, protecting Horace Jr., against habitual adultery and the stolen identity) through Aristotle's habituation, Plato's Protagoras unity-of-virtues theses, Hume's sensible knave, and John Doris's situationist attack on global character traits. The unity theses imply Don's vices undermine his virtues (affairs make him unavailable when Betty crashes; evasions about his past block honesty), and Doris's dime-in-the-payphone literature suggests even Don's reliability may be circumstance-bound, as with Pete's weddings-and-vacations-only philandering.
