They then unsettle moral judgment itself: utilitarianism would license the Slaver's Bay slaveholders, virtue ethics lacks action rules and cross-cultural agreement (charity is no Dothraki virtue), and Martin's POV narration gives direct access to Ned's inner life but only Varys's and Littlefinger's unreliable reports about Cersei - so our verdicts on her, like real-life judgments of others, rest on shaky evidence.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 10 "1 Acting Without Thinking The Sagacity of Indiana Jones" — Justin Kitchen rebuts the consequentialist charge (voiced by Big Bang Theory's Amy Farrah Fowler) that Indy plays no role in Raiders' outcome — the Nazis would have opened the Ark and died anyway — by shifting to virtue ethics: Indy's goodness lies in his character, not his consequences. His spontaneous 'I'm making this up as I go' decisions are read as Stoic sage-like action flowing from the two-stage moral education depicted in The Young Indiana Jones Chronicles, from Krishnamurti's lesson on death to Epictetus's 'winter training' in practice. The cardinal virtues as knowledge explain his instinctive courage (lifeboat, lead-lined refrigerator) and temperance (running past treasure), while his snake panic, his flash of greed at the Grail in Crusade, and his strained bonds with Marion and his father show he is a hero approaching but not yet attaining sagehood.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 11 "2 Does It Always Belong in a Museum" — Edwardo Pérez reconstructs the reasoning behind Indy's unargued mantra 'It belongs in a museum' via Bentham's principle of utility: museums maximize happiness because scholars and the public can study and enjoy artifacts for generations, unlike private collectors like Panama Hat. The same calculus explains his rule-breaking — he leaves the Mayapore Sankara Stone with the villagers ('It'd be another rock collecting dust' in a museum) because a flourishing village outweighs his fortune and glory, and he concedes the government's Area 51 warehouse may have been the utility-maximizing choice for the Ark after what it did to Belloq and Toht. Indy's apparent inconsistencies thus dissolve into case-by-case consequence weighing.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 32 "19 Meddling with (Almost) Incomprehensible Powers" — Argues that archaeology can never escape politics: Nazi relic plunder for the planned Führermuseum, French removals at Angkor Wat, the UNESCO 1970 convention, and Zahi Hawass's cultural nationalism versus James Cuno's 'encyclopedic museums' all determine what Indy — or any archaeologist — may legitimately do. Measured against Alison Wylie's stewardship principle, Indy emerges as a 'loot-and-scoot' adventurer whose 'it belongs in a museum' cosmopolitanism sits uneasily with national patrimony claims, and the chapter weighs backward-looking title-based versus forward-looking value-based approaches to the Golden Idol, the Sankara Stone he returns, and the Cross of Coronado. It closes by asking whether the living can wrong the dead and vanished cultures, and whether the government 'top men' warehousing the Ark were right after all.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 10 "So, That’s It No Solution" — Rieder argues Iron Man is the one 'realistic' superhero: nothing about him requires a different world, only incremental nanotech advances — precision engineering, miniaturized computing, and carbon nanotubes a hundred times stronger than steel — already pursued at MIT's Institute for Soldier Nanotechnologies. He then uses Iron Man as a nanoethics case study, pitting cost-benefit analysis (with David Schmidtz's proviso that it is necessary but not sufficient for right action) against the precautionary principle exemplified by Bill Joy's call for relinquishment, asking whether an Obadiah Stane selling 'Iron Armies' to the highest bidder is a risk we may not take even if it is improbable. He leans precautionary: we may be morally required to forgo the experiment because the world's population never consented to the risk.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 26 "The Office and Philosophy" — Johnson works through the standard objections to affirmative action using Scranton material: Ryan's paralysis before the all-Black management team in 'Traveling Salesmen' shows a single-race workforce is not intrinsically bad, while Michael's Chris Rock routine and his do-it-yourself slur exercise in 'Diversity Day' show that Dunder Mifflin meeting every quota does nothing about racism. A hypothetical about Dwight's grandfather refusing to hire Stanley's grandfather at the beet farm frames the compensation objection, answered by the 'cycle of poverty' account of the present effects of past discrimination. Finally, a fictitious hiring of guard Hank Tate over a better-qualified white candidate - justified, following Nagel, by the consequences of calming branch unrest - sets up the conclusion that education, not racially preferential hiring, would break minority poverty without discrimination, so affirmative action is ultimately unjustified.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 11 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — White analyzes Spider-Man's public unmasking in Civil War as a familiar ethical choice between the right and the good. Peter's promise to Tony Stark and obedience to the Superhuman Registration Act are deontological duties, explicated through Kant's test of universalizing the maxim of promise-breaking, while his worry for Aunt May and MJ pulls him toward consequentialist reasoning whose uncertainty, complexity, and incommensurability the chapter details. Aunt May's 'some things are worth the risk' speech tips Peter toward principle, but the Kingpin's sniper shoots her anyway, and Peter's hellish aftermath — ending in the Mephisto deal of 'One More Day' — shows both the tragedy of doing the right thing and the argument that when consequences are unknowable one should simply do what is right.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 27 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Defends South Park's anti-paternalism on both consequentialist and deontological grounds. 'Major Boobage' shows the futility of Gerald's cat ban meant to stop kids 'cheesing' — Kenny still gets high and Gerald himself relapses — while 'Medicinal Fried Chicken' shows how the KFC prohibition births a violent black market, with Cartman's $85 snack pushing him into the Colonel's Scarface-style drug war. On the deontological side, Mill's 'over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign', Locke's self-ownership, and Kantian respect for rational agents (via Nozick's inviolability, and the authors' autarchy-versus-autonomy distinction) ground the claim that coercion is wrong even when benevolent: 'Butt Out' has Kyle and Stan tell Rob Reiner that forcing others to quit smoking is fascism, while Big Tobacco's Kevin Harris wins their approval simply by informing and letting people choose.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 31 "Notes" — Applies Aristotle's three friendships to Trek: Ferengi Rules of Acquisition dealings and treaties as utility friendships, Bashir and O'Brien's darts and racquetball as friendship of pleasure, and virtuous friendship as requiring emotion, mutual goodwill, and irreplaceable intrinsic valuing - which emotionless Data fails at with Jenna D'Sora in "In Theory". The core argument, following Badhwar, is that consequentialism is logically and psychologically incompatible with virtuous friendship: Spock's "needs of the many" maxim and Data's "for the greater good" experimentation on Geordi in "Descent, Part II" show friends being treated as sacrificeable instruments, while the Kobayashi Maru cheat shows consequentialist reasoning blessing outcomes over means. Kirk's reversal - "the needs of the one outweigh the needs of the many" in The Search for Spock - and T'Pol's years caring for the amnesiac Archer in "Twilight" exemplify acting out of friendship rather than for any further goal.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 40 "The Last Jedi A New Hope" — Johnson defends The Last Jedi's Luke against the 'you ruined Luke' charge: his pacifism was set up when he threw away his lightsaber before Palpatine in Return of the Jedi, and his call to end the Jedi follows the lesson Hobbes and Locke drew from the English civil wars - since religious matters cannot be settled by reason, only by violence, Jedi and Sith factions fighting for political power yield only bloodshed like the Clone Wars and two Death Stars. Luke also seeks to destroy the Jedi texts out of guilt by association for the Order's failures, and to the end he remains a consequentialist pacifist, defeating Kylo on Crait through a nonviolent Force projection rather than a real duel. Far from betraying the character, this growth into proactive nonviolence - capped by Rey's yellow-bladed, mainly defensive style - makes Luke 'the ultimate Jedi' and the Resistance's new hope.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 24 "13. Time to Choose" — Goldberg and Gavaler read Superman's first-year Action Comics adventures (reforming the Blakely Mine owner, demolishing slums, buying back swindled stock) as consequentialism on Millian lines, and Batman's Detective Comics year (letting the Joker's victims die while 'the time isn't ripe', the batarang deflected by invisible glass) as a dark, vengeance-based cousin of Kant's duty ethics. Moral luck is the pivot — deontology ignores it, consequentialism is hostage to it — but Superman's powers cancel luck, and in the opening Luthor/Joker two-bomb scenario Superman defuses while Batman chases the villain, so the chapter rules Superman's 'super consequentialism' the superior code.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 25 "14. Who Watches the Justice League" — Judges the two heroes by negative consequentialism (attributed to Hume and Popper): the better hero is the one who best prevents future suffering, including suffering he might cause himself. Superman qualifies because he hands the League—Batman above all—the means to defeat him (as in Injustice) and kills himself with gold kryptonite after executing Mr. Mxyzptlk in 'What Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?', while Hume's reason-is-slave-of-the-passions reading explains the Zod neck-snap in Man of Steel as passion-driven necessity. Batman's countermeasures in 'Tower of Babel' and Justice League: Doom stop every Leaguer except Batman himself ('My failsafe is the Justice League'), an arrogance that loses him this round.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 21 "Notes" — White reconstructs the 'Sacrifice' storyline - Maxwell Lord mind-controlling Superman, telling lasso-bound Wonder Woman 'Kill me,' and her snapping his neck - and asks whether it was right. He argues Wonder Woman reasons as a threshold deontologist: her usual respect for life holds until the certain cost of letting Lord live (he would wield Superman to kill again) crosses the threshold where the consequentialist body-count argument takes over, and she was justified, so she would do it again. The contrast with Batman's refusal to kill the Joker shows his refusal is virtue-ethical self-definition ('I won't become them'), while Diana, regretting the necessity but feeling no remorse, is an Amazon warrior for whom lethal protection of lives is sometimes exactly the job.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 15 "Virtue and Violence Can a Good Football Player Be a Good Person" — Davison defends a 'Violence Principle'—intentionally causing violent harm known to be unnecessary for a greater good is wrong—and applies it to in-the-rules football hits like Jack Tatum on Darryl Stingley and Warren Sapp on Chad Clifton. Against a consequentialist defense of intimidation, he invokes Kant's requirement to treat persons as ends, not mere means, arguing players consent to accidental injury but not intentional harm. Citing the Socratic examination of the soul, he warns of moral danger to players who use excessive force and to fans who relish violence for its own sake.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 22 "A True MVP" — Kershnar analyzes what makes a football player valuable, arguing a player's value is his net benefit to his own team measured against a baseline. He compares three models—no-substitute, average/reasonable-substitute, and actual-substitute—using cases like Joe Montana backed by Steve Young and Emmitt Smith behind an all-pro line, and defends the actual-substitute model as the correct measure of value even though it yields counterintuitive results. He connects the account to a broader question of measuring a person's contribution to any organization or to the world.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 15 "Sixth Hole Virtue Ethics From Caddyshack to Better Golf" — McElreath tests three ethical theories against golf intuitions and argues virtue ethics wins. Consequentialism rightly judges a postal carrier's choice to work over golf but wrongly permits Judge Smails in Caddyshack to kick his ball when no bad consequences follow; Kantian ethics correctly condemns Smails's deceptive maxim as non-universalizable but mishandles the play-versus-work case. Virtue ethics, judging acts by what an ideally virtuous person would characteristically do, gets both right via the relevant virtues of justice and honesty, and he then applies benevolence, justice, and tolerance to argue golf should better treat women, minorities, disabled players (Casey Martin's cart), and homosexuals.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 6 "Not the Crime, but the Man Sherlock Holmes and Charles Augustus Milverton" — Rozema examines 'The Adventure of Charles Augustus Milverton,' in which Holmes burgles a blackmailer's house, feigns an engagement to the maid, and watches Milverton's murder without intervening. He argues that Kantian deontology (too abstract to judge rectification) and consequentialism (paralyzed by unpredictable outcomes) both fail to assess Holmes's acts, whereas Plato and Aristotle's virtue ethics fits: judging the man's character over the isolated act. Citing Plato's 'true falsehood' vs. 'falsehood in words' and Aristotle on voluntary acts and the storm-tossed captain jettisoning cargo, he concludes a virtuous person may rightly do what is normally forbidden against a vicious foe like Milverton.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 11 "Was it Morally Wrong to Kill Off Sherlock Holmes" — Terjesen asks whether Conan Doyle acted immorally in killing Holmes in 'The Final Problem,' framing it through property theory. He runs Locke's labor theory (illustrated via 'The Blue Carbuncle' gem), Proudhon and Marx's critiques, and both consequentialist and Kantian (respect-for-persons) justifications of intellectual property. He argues Conan Doyle's ownership of the iconic Holmes weakened as Paget, Gillette, Rathbone, and Dr. Joseph Bell co-authored the figure, so property rights alone can't justify the killing—but Conan Doyle's authorial dignity plus the narrative fitness of 'The Final Problem' and 'His Last Bow' make the send-off defensible.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 13 "Sherlock Holmes and the Ethics of Hyperspecialization" — Costello and Bassham critique Holmes's 'brain-attic' theory from 'A Study in Scarlet'—that the mind has fixed capacity and should hold only vocationally useful knowledge. Cognitive science (interference and schema theory) and the sociology of social/cultural capital show useless knowledge is often useful, as when Holmes trades boxing lore or reads cultural cues. They then argue for a duty of self-improvement grounded in consequentialism, Kantian and Rossian deontology, and virtue ethics (Aristotle, Aquinas, MacIntyre) plus Socratic care of the soul, concluding that Holmes—an omnivorous reader who quotes Goethe and Hafiz—doesn't practice what he preaches and took specialization too far.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 9 "The “Big-Little” Film and Philosophy Two Takes on Spielbergian Innocence" — Arms and Riley argue that Spielberg fuses spectacle with intimate 'broken family' drama, then use War of the Worlds, A.I., and Empire of the Sun to press the philosophical problem of special (agent-relative) obligations. They show that Ray's redemption (even murdering Ogilvy to protect Rachel), Gigolo Joe's protection of David, and John Graham's failure all turn on duties to the innocent that consequentialism's agent-neutral, greatest-good calculus cannot accommodate, formalizing the clash as a valid argument against consequentialism. They suggest Spielberg grounds these special obligations in the intrinsic worth of 'the Innocent.'
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 18 "8. Which Brother Is the Good One" — Browning contrasts the brothers' ethics: Dean is a consequentialist who judges hunts by outcomes ('the ends justify the means,' killing werewolf Madison or faith-healer Roy for the greater good), while Sam is a deontologist who treats lying, stealing, and killing as wrong in themselves. Tracking episodes like 'Bloodlust,' 'Croatoan,' and 'Fresh Blood,' he argues the murder-versus-kill distinction and the blurring line between human and monster show Dean's darker consequentialism is better suited to the Hunter's war, though both are driven to do good.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 10 "3. Can It Be Right to Defend the Guilty" — Cook tests whether lawyers may defend the legally and morally guilty against several ethical theories, anchored by Saul's contemplated lie at Lalo Salamanca's bail hearing (knowing Lalo murdered Fred Whalen). Kant's contradiction-in-conception makes lying to the court a perfect duty to refrain from, but Cook shows this looks too rigid via the invented 'Jemma' surgeon case; act and rule consequentialism (Bentham, Mill, Hooker) permit honest defenses while diverging on lies and mitigation. He argues Hume's sentimentalist virtue ethics best fits intuition: Saul's bail lie is wrong because motivated by self-interest rather than the procedural justice a virtuous advocate should feel.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 31 "20. Why Is Breaking Skateboarders’ Legs Wrong" — The chapter uses three characters to test three single-value moral theories: Chuck as a Kantian deontologist whose rigid loyalty to the categorical imperative and the 'sacred' law destroys his bond with Jimmy; Jimmy as a Mill-style consequentialist whose ends-justify-means scams (Sandpiper, the squat-cobbler film) let him decide what counts as good outcomes and cost him integrity, invoking Bernard Williams; and Mike as a Scanlonian contractualist who honors even immoral agreements like the Tuco hit. Through cases like the 'murderer at the door,' it argues each theory alone leads people to do wrong, so a moral life must combine outcomes, rules, and contracts.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 26 "15. Morality and Manipulation" — Kahn frames the Foundation series around personal autonomy, using Mill's image of humans as a growing tree rather than a machine 'built after a model' to condemn both coercion and manipulation. He shows Hari Seldon as a paradoxical champion of autonomy who nonetheless deceives his own followers about the fraudulent Encyclopedia Galactica and secretly forecloses their freedom of action via the Seldon Plan and Second Foundation—echoing the Mule's mind-control of Han Pritcher. He reads Salvor Hardin's maxim ('never let your sense of morals prevent you from doing what is right') as consequentialism that maximizes galaxy-wide autonomy, contrasts it with the deontology exemplified by Gaia/Bliss (who refuse to manipulate Trevize) and critics like Toran Darell and Branno, and leaves the reader to judge as Bliss urges Pelorat to think for himself.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 29 "“Who watches the watchmen ”" — Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as a would-be consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) whose plan to kill millions to end the Cold War exposes utilitarianism's neglect of rights and, via Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ends,' its dependence on an unknowable infinite future. Rorschach poses as a Kantian deontologist ('I shall not compromise') but Loftis shows his hypocrisy, black-and-white dichotomous thinking, and failure to respect persons betray Kant's categorical imperative. Loftis argues neither theory is truly held by either character; both are rationalizations of power, and the comic's real target, captured by 'Who watches the watchmen?', is authoritarianism itself.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 9 "What’s Wrong with Roland" — Greg Littmann asks why the Dark Tower judges Roland morally lacking for his sacrifices (his hawk David, Susan Delgado, letting Jake fall) and defends him on utilitarian grounds, invoking Bentham's greatest-happiness principle. He uses King's world as a series of thought experiments to test whether utilitarianism is too demanding—Susannah quitting the quest, self-sacrifice becoming compulsory, and the required sacrifice of innocents like the newborn Mordred or Jake when all universes hang in the balance. Littmann finds Roland 'innocent' because maximizing good can compel sacrificing innocents, but draws the real-world moral that being convinced you are doing right does not mean no innocents are being harmed.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 13 "Chapter 4 Huckleberry Finn’s Struggle between Sympathy and Moral Principle Reconsidered" — Michael Lyons defends the 'pedestal' of moral principles against Bennett's chapter 16 reading. He accepts that sympathy rightly saved Jim and that Edwards's principled cruelty and Himmler's suppressed sympathy show principles must be revisable, but rejects the stronger claim that sympathy should override conduct while leaving conflicting principles intact. Reconstructing Bennett's argument into 'stronger' and 'adjusted' versions, Lyons argues principles remain the best primary guide once corrected by sympathy, and that Twain shows Huck retaining a natural, humanity-grounded morality even after rejecting society's 'deformed conscience.' He prizes incorruptibility, sticking to correct principles, as the mark of the highest heroism Huck could aspire to.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 25 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Agnafors asks whether free soloing is morally permissible, opening with soloists dropping ice chips into his coffee cup to show soloing is not purely private. He tests Locke's natural rights to life and liberty (concluding no act is truly private since rescues, taxpayers, and grieving families are affected), Aristotle's virtue ethics (worrying that habitual risk-taking forms a reckless character), and Bentham and Mill's consequentialism (Bill's confidence-boosting solo of Nutcracker versus Derek Hersey's fatal fall). He concludes no universal answer exists, offering one rule: the soloist must carefully weigh all these considerations beforehand.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 29 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Naar and Masala defend the 'Secret Underground Internet Seduction Community' by grounding it in Darwinian sexual selection (the peacock's tail, mate value, women prioritizing status and men prioritizing youth/beauty) and an Aristotelian ideal of happiness as excellence: they read the community's aim of becoming a well-rounded seducer as cultivating virtue and social/emotional 'mating intelligence' that yields eudaimonic fulfillment. Against the Kantian objection that seduction training uses women merely as means, they offer a consequentialist and 'deflationist' reply that deception and manipulation already pervade ordinary courtship (makeup, lying about age), so raising one's mate value is morally neutral, and they extend the point to women's active and passive seduction strategies (Cleopatra, groupies).
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 10 "Who is Who" — Titled 'Exterminate!', the chapter analyzes evil in Doctor Who through Augustine's privation theory and Kant's 'radical evil,' distinguishing irrational evil (Light in 'Ghost Light,' the Daleks) from rational 'lesser evil' calculations (the Rani, mad scientists). It reads the Daleks as Nazi-analogue Others bred for racial purity, invokes Arendt's banality of evil and capacity to think for oneself (Rose challenging the ninth Doctor over the lone Dalek and the Delta wave), and cites Kierkegaard on losing oneself when one does evil alone.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 12 "Who is Who" — This chapter tests the Doctor's ethics against consequentialism and Kantian/Nagelian deontology, arguing both fail because his alien longevity and time-travelling relation to consequences resist algorithmic moral judgment ('School Reunion,' 'Attack of the Cybermen'). It proposes instead de Beauvoir's 'ethics of ambiguity' rooted in Romanticism and Sartrean radical freedom and bad faith (the student anecdote; Turlough refusing the Enlightenment diamond), casting the Doctor as a Promethean figure who liberates companions into risky self-perfection.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 29 "“Who watches the watchmen ”" — J. Robert Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as an apparent consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) who sacrifices millions of New Yorkers for the greater good, and Rorschach as an apparent deontologist ('I shall not compromise'), then argues neither is true to his stated theory. Utilitarianism is critiqued through Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ever ends' (the infinite future defeats the calculus) and its trouble grounding rights, while Rorschach's hypocritical, dichotomous, disrespect-for-persons stance is shown to be fascism, not Kant's categorical imperative (universalization and treating persons as ends). Loftis contends the deeper target is authoritarianism itself: the corrupt superheroes show that ethical theories are rationalizations of power, so no one should be entrusted with too much of it.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 11 "9. The Handmaid’s Tale as Philosophy Autonomy and Reproductive Freedom" — Robison-Greene argues that Gilead's core wrong is denying women autonomy, reducing them from Kantian moral agents to moral patients — walking incubators. She uses Frankfurt's theory of personhood (second-order desires and volitions about what we care about) to show how Gilead dismantles a woman's will by restricting first-order options, language, and critical thinking, so Offred's Scrabble tiles and forbidden reading become acts of reclaimed autonomy. She situates the Sons of Jacob's 'feminine function' ideology in Plato's Republic classes, Aristotle's natural slaves and History of Animals, Aquinas's natural-law subordination of women, and Malebranche's brain-fiber claims, contrasting Beauvoir's complicity of women and framing forced reproduction as the deontology-versus-consequentialism clash over whether species survival could ever justify treating women as mere means.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 53 "50. The Cabin in the Woods as Philosophy Cinematic Reflections on Ethical Complexity, Human Nature, and Worthw" — Kowalski argues Whedon and Goddard's The Cabin in the Woods stages a clash between classical utilitarianism and an ethics of care, and cinematically favors the latter. The Facility, sacrificing five campers to placate the Ancient Ones and save humanity, embodies Mill's greatest-happiness reasoning, but its callous celebration while Dana suffers on the dock undercuts that view. When the Director tells Dana she must kill her only remaining friend Marty to save the world, Dana's refusal is defended via Noddings's care ethics and Aristotle's claim that obligations track close personal relationships (special obligations), with Aristotle's Poetics catharsis and Plato's Leontius grounding the film's theory of worthwhile horror: 'people are more important than humanity.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 56 "53. Tarantino as Philosopher Vengeance – Unfettered, Uncensored, but Not Unjustified" — Johnson treats Tarantino's post-2000 filmography as an argument that vengeance is morally permissible when proportionate and directed at the genuinely guilty: Beatrix in Kill Bill, Shosanna in Inglourious Basterds, and Django all get celebrated revenge, while The Hateful Eight is used to distinguish vengeance from retribution and legal versus 'frontier' justice via Nozick's and Bacon's definitions. He rebuts common and historical objections—reading Plato's Gorgias as endorsing due punishment, arguing Spinoza's monism and Hobbes's and Locke's social-contract views do not forbid proportional revenge, and citing Nietzsche and Beauvoir's Eye for an Eye (her refusal to pardon the collaborator Brasillach) to conclude cost-free, proportional revenge can be justified though mercy remains praiseworthy.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 81 "76. The Last of Us as Moral Philosophy Teleological Particularism and Why Joel Is Not a Villain" — Horn takes The Last of Us as moral philosophy, arguing Joel is read as a villain only because players assume consequentialism or deontology. On Bentham/Mill's utilitarianism Joel fails to maximize utility by killing many to save Ellie; on Kant's categorical imperative his lying, stealing and killing are always impermissible. Horn instead defends 'teleological particularism' — an agent acts rightly when acting in conformity with a role, roles being socially constructed and variable — so Joel's role as Ellie's surrogate father (mirrored in his carrying her out as he carried Sarah, and the 'Future Days' lyric) obligates him to put her above humanity. On this view Joel's refusal to let the Fireflies kill Ellie, and his final lie, are morally permissible, not villainous.

### On Liberty

On Liberty is John Stuart Mill's 1859 essay defending individual freedom against the coercive power of the state and the pressure of majority opinion. Its central claim, the harm principle, is that society may restrain a person only to prevent harm to others, leaving self-regarding conduct free. Mill argues at length for freedom of thought and discussion, contending that even false opinions serve truth by testing it, and he warns against the stifling conformity he called the tyranny of the majority.

- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 52 "Where I Don’t Want to Be" — South reads Barbara's 'Where I don't want to be' monologue in Batgirl: Year One through Mill's On Liberty passage on people who ask not 'what do I prefer?' but 'what is usually done by persons of my station?' - the pressure to conform Barbara feels as a librarian with a denied police application and a father's expectations. He then argues neither utilitarianism nor Kantianism can guide such a life, since both exclude the question of what I want and who I am becoming; what Barbara needs - and we need - is to make our desires intelligible to ourselves and bridge the gap between who she is and who she wants to be ('Divine my own future... Not a page from someone else's book').
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 54 "There Is What Could Be" — Argues there is no single final 'best self' in the perfectionist quest: after the Joker shoots Barbara, Oracle: Year One has martial-arts teacher Richard Dragon ask 'Who are you?', and she emerges thinking 'I'm me — more me than I have ever been.' Against the conformity John Stuart Mill warned of, the chapter has Barbara leave Dick Grayson because he has 'managed to turn into Bruce' and keeps 'reminding me of what I once was' — the past acting as a retrograde exemplar and a Millian custom that blocks her next, still-unattained higher self.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 16 "Synthesis" — Elizabeth Brake asks what freedom Dylan's outlaw persona - refusing Maggie's Farm, possessive love, and conformity - actually wins, framing the answer with Berlin's two concepts of liberty. Dylan's negations look like Berlin's negative freedom, but Hegel's critique of the "freedom of the void" shows mere refusal ends in emptiness, so she reconstructs a Millian and Emersonian ideal of self-realization for which negative liberty is only the condition. "To live outside the law, you must be honest" supplies the synthesis: outside social law the free person answers to the Emersonian law of his own nature and to undistorted honesty with others, a more severe morality Dylan shares with Emerson and Nietzsche.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 10 "The Gathering of the Tribe Ironic Sacramentalism" — Horace Fairlamb argues the Grateful Dead were the Sixties' real revolutionary success: where the New Left failed by keeping confrontational politics, the Dead changed consciousness first, extending Mill's liberal 'experiments in living' into a whole alternative culture. He reads the total improvisation learned at the Acid Tests ('the form that follows chaos'), the band's leaderless 'functional anarchy' — Lesh: if anyone tried to take charge 'it would just dissolve in their hands' — and its flat business hierarchy with roadies as corporate presidents as a spontaneous order lived at the edge of chaos. The Deadhead community's ritual communitas, analyzed through Victor Turner's separation-liminality-reincorporation model, amounts to an 'ironic sacramentalism' that achieves what social contract from Hobbes (force), Locke (property), and Rawls (self-interest) cannot: unity that transcends difference while leaving it in place.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 15 "John Henry, the Steam-Engine, and Folsom Prisoners" — Mulnix pairs Cash with John Stuart Mill on the priority of quality of life over mere life: Mill's 1868 Parliament speech defends capital punishment as more humane than the "living tomb" of life imprisonment, and Cash agrees in the Folsom liner notes (the prisoner envying the cockroach that can leave) and in "The Mercy Seat," where the electric chair becomes both mercy and the throne of God. Mill's higher and lower pleasures, competent judges, and On Liberty's individuality illuminate Cash's gallery of fools, the "Folsom Prison Blues" narrator who shot a man just to watch him die, the mother-defying Billy Joe of "Don't Take Your Guns to Town," characters whose unreflective rebellion squanders rational freedom. John Henry, by contrast, exercised his higher faculties against the steam-engine and so died happy, proving the chapter's Millian thesis that freedom matters as a means to self-directed, deliberated happiness.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 13 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Fairweather casts the campaign against Pullman's books as Socrates's trial rerun (impiety plus corrupting the young) and asks whether legally protected speech can still be morally wrong, weighing Mill's On Liberty point that children lack the 'maturity of their faculties' against the charge that Pullman's 'killing God' rhetoric inflicts spiritual violence on young believers, by his own image of intercision. The answer comes through Nietzsche's Three Metamorphoses: Asriel, Will, and Lyra play the lion that slays the great 'thou shalt' of the Authority, but the lion's destruction is only the possibility of freedom, since full freedom is Nietzsche's child creating its own values rather than lapsing into nihilism or Sartrean bad faith. Pullman's Republic of Heaven, with its virtues of courage, compassion, love, kindness, and curiosity held in community, is a social ideal rather than a radically Nietzschean one, so the charge of corrupting young readers is deflated.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 35 "A Little bit of Messi for our Life" — The authors cast the contrast between disciplined European and improvisational South American football as Mill's struggle between liberty and authority: the coach's tactical orders are 'rules of opinion' the genius may defy, as Maradona did on his sixty-meter run to the Goal of the Century, while the harm principle marks the line at the 'rules of law' — FIFA's Laws of the Game. The Hand of God goal, which broke even a rule of law yet stood because 'a goal is scored when the referee says so', illustrates Searle's point that football's regulative capacity cannot guarantee its agreements, leaving a gap filled only by ethics and fair play. Following Wittgenstein's 'ethics and aesthetics are one and the same', they conclude that a bit of Messi-style rule-breaking — Messi replicated both Maradona goals in 2007 — is what makes football, and life, joyful and beautiful.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 28 "There’s Something Here that’s as Strong as Life" — Argues Rush's lyrics cohere as libertarianism: Rand's rational self-interest in 'Anthem' and 'Something for Nothing,' Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain argument and Hayek's knowledge problem behind '2112' and 'The Trees,' Mill's 'experiments in living' in 'Witch Hunt' and 'Nobody's Hero,' and market-enabled tolerance and cosmopolitanism in 'Heresy,' 'Territories,' and 'Tai Shan.' Like Cygnus resolving Apollo and Dionysus, libertarianism takes the best of left and right, with individualism the constant running through Peart's career.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 19 "The Ideal Candidate" — Nathan Zook uses the 'Royal Krabby' election from Vote for SpongeBob and the global-warming plot of SpongeBob Goes Green to weigh democracy. Mr. Krabs's rigged election, run only to sell patties, exemplifies C. Wright Mills's power elite manipulating the appearance of popular rule; Plato would bar Producer-class SpongeBob and Squidward from ruling and prefers educated Guardians, while Mill defends each citizen's liberty to choose and democracy's alliance with education (SpongeBob learns about global warming from Sandy). Aristotle's polity — citizens administering the state for the common interest — makes SpongeBob the ideal candidate because he saves Bikini Bottom without claiming power.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 29 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Fitzpatrick asks whether Klosterman's low-culture project (tribute bands, Toby Keith, the McNuggets diet) is mere titillation or genuinely valuable. Bentham's pushpin-versus-poetry hedonism matches Klosterman's rejection of 'guilty pleasures,' while Aristotle's eudaimonia — and Plato's forms, on which a tribute band is a copy of a copy of a copy — condemns a life of amusement. Mill resolves the question twice over: higher and lower pleasures justify ranking Klosterman's contemplative criticism above mere sensation, and On Liberty's free market of ideas shows that even false or partial low-culture claims (about Garth Brooks, Spurlock's Super Size Me) keep high culture's truths from decaying into unexamined dogma.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 24 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Takes apart Walt and Jesse's 'legalize it' excuse: Kantian autonomy would license adult drug choices, but knowingly self-harming meth use is a performative contradiction no rational adult can will, and Mill's utilitarianism condemns cooking because harms to all users must be weighed against one family's benefit. It reads the 'Cancer Man' revenge on Ken's BMW and the Tuco deal as proof that the meth world's criminality spreads like a cancer into Walt's ordinary life, and 'Gray Matter' as Greek tragedy - pride refusing Elliot's money when a way out existed. Against On Liberty's libertarian pull, it finally argues addicts forfeit full rational autonomy and so may be 'caged' by paternalistic law.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 33 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — A provocatively sympathetic application of On Liberty: Mill's harm principle protects Jesse's drug use from punishment, and Mill's celebration of individuality and 'experiments of living' makes Walt's cooking an 'individual spontaneity' valuable precisely because it defies custom - Marie's anti-pot panic and Hank's beer-and-Cub-cigar double standard illustrating the 'magical influence of custom' and democracy's drift toward 'collective mediocrity'. Mill's temperance-era remarks that intoxication 'is not a fit subject for legislative interference' are extended from use to manufacture. The chapter's thesis: even when Walt is wrong, mere nonconformity 'is itself a service', making Heisenberg an unlikely hero of liberty and human progress.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 10 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — Judith Andre uses the show's cases - Alicia's overnight prison visit to Peter for case information in 'Conjugal', snatching evidence before the police in 'Hi', Kalinda's inadmissible but coercive evidence in 'Heart', and Will's advice to use perjured testimony in 'Long Way Home' - to ask whether the profession's zealous advocacy actually serves justice. She explains the adversary system's two-level defense (each side's pursuit of victory supposedly forces truth out, mirroring sport) and its weaknesses: money decides outcomes, and no one in the courtroom is responsible for the truth, as the buried Childs tapes in 'Hybristophilia' show. Individual liberty against state power justifies criminal defense at most, and she endorses David Luban's sober conclusion that the system is justified yet 'cannot mandate lawyers to cut throats', with Alicia remaining the show's uneasy, unreconciled conscience.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 9 "Futurama and Philosophy" — In 'A Taste of Freedom,' Zoidberg eats Earth's flag Old Freebie on Freedom Day, is tried by Earth's Supreme Court, and his death sentence triggers a Decapodian invasion that enslaves Earth under the Mobile Oppression Palace. The chapter pits Mill's On Liberty defense of unpopular expression (mankind cannot silence a lone dissenter; unchallenged beliefs are mere 'true opinions' akin to prejudice) against Feinberg's offense principle, mapping the case onto Texas v. Johnson and the symbolic-speech line from Stromberg to Tinker. It ends with Zoidberg burning the flag 'to preserve the freedom it represents': liberty and majority will often conflict (doomsday devices, Proposition Infinity's robosexual marriage ban), so preserving freedom requires tolerating offensive expression.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 14 "5. The Truth Shall Make Ye Fret" — Watson uses The Truth - William de Worde's accidental invention of Ankh-Morpork's first newspaper and the plot to frame Lord Vetinari - to stage the three classic arguments for censorship: direct harm (character assassination 'works every day'), indirect harm (with MacKinnon's point that the speech of the dominant drowns out the subordinated, applied to speciesist insults at Koom Valley), and the false-beliefs argument. Against them stand the knowledge problem and the equality assumption: Mrs. Arcanum's deference to print, Vetinari's turtle-shaped-world joke, and the Montessori-Broca dispute show we never know in advance which beliefs are false, and any censor like Lord de Worde has his own agenda. Vetinari's verdict that 'free men pull in all kinds of directions' because 'pulling together is the aim of despotism' carries the chapter's Millian case that free speech is a horrible necessity.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 28 "16. Artistic Expression in the Land of the Free" — Argues that Hendrix's Woodstock 'Star-Spangled Banner' links political and artistic freedom: Mill's On Liberty — the harm principle, liberty of tastes and pursuits, and originality against the despotism of custom — both protects and celebrates the performance, since disliking it is no ground for suppressing it. Tolstoy's What Is Art? then supplies the aesthetic verdict: art is the infection of others by sincerely, particularly, and clearly felt emotion, so the anthem, like Picasso's Guernica, is great art expressing bad feelings about Vietnam — unlike José Feliciano's sincere-but-vague ballad or Roseanne Barr's failed joke.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 34 "22. A New Civil War" — Horn reads Marvel's Civil War as an allegory of post-9/11 America's Patriot Act debate over security versus liberty: Iron Man takes Hobbes's side, treating unregulated superhumans as the state of nature - a 'war of every man against every man' - that the Registration Act's social contract and punishment-backed rules must end, while Captain America takes Mill's On Liberty side, insisting full freedom for human nature must not be ceded to a government that will overreach, with Spider-Man torn between the two like the American citizen. Invoking Habermas's communicative action and deliberative democracy from Between Facts and Norms, he blames the two camps for talking past each other - Cap walling himself off while Tony keeps reaching out - and prescribes genuinely open dialogue as the only bridge that can marry security and liberty before the country devolves into its own civil war.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 14 "4. Non-State Enemies of Freedom" — Nash argues 1984 has been misread as a critique of state power alone; through Newspeak's silencing of thought (in the tradition Austin, MacKinnon, and Langton developed) it shows how any concentration of power oppresses via control of words, data, and information. Drawing on Goldstein's manual's debt to James Burnham's managerial revolution and Sheldon Wolin's 'inverted totalitarianism', she reads the non-centralized Oceania as a warning about non-state enemies: corporations, think tanks running the 'Tobacco Strategy', and global institutions peddling misleading poverty statistics. Popper, Arendt, and Berlin exemplify the state-focused liberalism she thinks blinded us to these horizontal threats, while the Newspeak appendix's past tense shows Orwell expected totalitarianism to be beatable through evidence and democracy.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 18 "After the Waldo Moment" — Littmann reads The Waldo Moment through Donald Trump — Waldo's 'knobber' and 'dickhead' taunts anticipate 'Little Marco' and 'Crooked Hillary' — to ask what is wrong with mockery and disrespect in democratic politics. Plato's Meno shows why true beliefs acquired by mockery rather than understanding are unstable and steerable toward any content, and ad hominem attacks substitute ridicule for engagement with arguments. Mill's On Liberty arguments against censorship and orthodoxy — we might be wrong, collision with error clarifies truth — show that refusing to engage opponents (as Waldo refuses Monroe) locks everyone in 'reality bubbles,' and the chapter concludes that letting anger and mockery replace reasoned engagement, as when Waldo's followers riot, sabotages democracy.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 12 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Littmann asks how a program built on mockery, falsehoods like Wyatt Cenac's Sarah Palin jokes and the 'santorum' coinage, can be a serious political voice, situating it in the tradition running from Aristophanes' roasting of Cleon and his distorting Clouds portrait of Socrates through Juvenal to Twain. He rejects Juvenal's hope that shame reforms the mocked (people do not listen to those who disrespect them) and argues mockery's real value is keeping issues like racism, war and Glenn Beck's rhetoric in public consciousness. Deploying Mill's On Liberty arguments against censorship, that silencing assumes infallibility and truth is sharpened by collision with error, he warns mockery works like censorship when audiences dismiss mocked views without consideration, the key difference being that Limbaugh demands to be taken seriously while Stewart bills himself as a comedian, and closes with Plato's Meno: opinions must be 'shackled' by understanding why they are true, not adopted because a comedy laughed at the alternative.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 30 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Vanderheiden treats America (The Book)'s textbook parody as serious democratic theory: its 'Democracy Inaction' diagnosis (a president chosen from a field of two, 99% incumbency, lobbyists as 'the white knights of democracy') tracks the thin versus thick democracy distinction and Benjamin Barber's deliberative democracy, with Putnam's social capital as the remedy for the satirized life cycle of national decline. The 'Dress the Supreme Court' gag, Senate color-by-numbers, and third-party graveyard expose representational exclusion, while the media chapter indicts conglomeration for killing the press's watchdog role, invoking Mill's marketplace of ideas. The Earth (The Book) postscript notes that social contracts were historically written without the assent of the women and minorities they subjugated.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 15 "“Cogs that Fit, that Cooperate by Design”" — Reads the government ban on Supers in The Incredibles through Locke's Letter Concerning Toleration and Mill's On Liberty, arguing the ban rests on the 'PREFER' principle — society's likings and dislikings as law — fed by perception management (Winston Deavor's suit-cameras PR campaign) rather than reasons, just as Locke diagnosed intolerance, not diversity of opinion, as the cause of civil strife. Mill's harm principle, illustrated by Elastigirl's 'drinking on duty' remark, should instead govern, so banning Supers' powers and pressuring Dash to suppress his speed ('Everyone's special, Dash' / 'Which is another way of saying no one is') is tyranny. Mr. Huph's 'cogs that fit, that cooperate by design' image of Insuricare shows the conformist cost: a society built on preference rather than reasons will never produce great thinkers.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 34 "Is Propaganda Permissible" — Manninen surveys Disney's WWII Donald Duck shorts (Donald's Decision, The New Spirit, Der Fuehrer's Face, Commando Duck) to argue propaganda is not only the enemy's tool and not always wrong. Hume's 'slave of the passions' explains why The Spirit of '43 works through the Thrifty-versus-Spendthrift slugfest rather than its implicit argument, and Mill's fallibility-corrigibility case for free expression gives even propaganda a seat in public discourse — though Mill's caveat against expression that instigates mischievous acts marks the real limit, which the contrast with the Axis's 'barefaced lies' (and the Yensid thought experiment) is meant to satisfy.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 25 "Notes" — The chapter asks whether Fallout's chems should be banned and answers no on Millian grounds: chem addiction harms only the user (and is trivially curable at any wasteland doctor, unlike Cait's Psycho addiction in Fallout 4, which shows what real addiction actually costs), so the New California Republic's firing squads for chem dealers and Caesar's Legion's crucifixion of the smuggler Anders violate the Harm Principle. Combat chem use is self-protection, drugging a Charisma check harms no one because NPCs act on their own programmed preferences, and paternalism fares no better in a wasteland where a failed speech check can get you killed. The analysis then extends to real-world performance-enhancing drugs: permissible for soldiers fighting a just war, but coercive in sports, where PED users force clean athletes to choose between their own health risks.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 12 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Don Fallis starts from Joffrey's lie about Arya and the butcher boy Mycah - which costs Mycah's life and Sansa's direwolf Lady's - to dissect lying versus other deception in Westeros: Catelyn accusing Tyrion is not lying because she believes it, Ned's coerced confession at the Great Sept is a real lie (Austin's duress excuse fails, as Thomas More's counterexample shows), and Ned's silence about Joffrey's parentage before the dying Robert is deception by withholding that he himself mistakes for lying. He asks whether lying is morally worse than misleading - Kant and Chisholm say yes, Williams and Scanlon no - testing breach of invited trust (Mirri Maz Duur's 'only death may pay for life'), responsibility-shifting to the audience ('That was a lie you told yourself'), and preserved autonomy (Kant's Groundwork, Mill's On Liberty). Finally, is it worse to lie to a king? Consequentialism explains the danger of misleading the powerful, oaths of fealty and divine right suggest a special duty, but Locke's demolition of divine right (seconded by Monty Python) leaves only the punishment, not the wrongdoing, greater.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 27 "The Office and Philosophy" — Nys asks whether political correctness is a genuine moral demand or mere verbal hygiene, using the British Office: Gareth's racist BMC joke, Brent aborting it when Oliver the Black coworker arrives, the 'wanking claw' impression, and the porn email with Brent's head pasted onto a woman's body. He argues words genuinely wound (Brent's 'sticks and stones' rehearsal collapses when Gareth reveals his cruel nicknames) but that offense is wrong as disrespect for human equality rather than as a feeling, an account filled out with Frankfurt's claim that our identity depends on what we care about, so the non-targeted can be offended too. After weighing Mill's defense of free discussion for social progress, the pornography debate (in which reduction to body parts is exactly what degrades, as Brent complains he was 'objectified'), and Marx's notion of ideology as a concealing set of ideas behind a 'white male' bias, he concludes that Brent's flaw is looking good rather than being good, and that PC language is rhetorical make-up over persisting inequality.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 11 "Robust Social Critique" — McGowan asks how SNL gets away with offensive material, from Larry David's concentration-camp monologue to the Chase-Pryor 'Word Association' and 'Nude Beach.' He argues censorship fails because offense is historically relative and slippery-slope prone, and that on Mill's On Liberty the harm principle never licenses suppressing speech SNL viewers can freely avoid, a point he sharpens with Feinberg's Volenti maxim and the offense principle. He closes by defending offensive comedy as robust social critique: Mill's fallibilist case that free speech drives human progress, with Baldwin's Trump and Tina Fey's Charlottesville bit as comedians speaking truth to power.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 14 "Live from Omaha" — Irwin argues that SNL's caricatures (Fey's Palin, Baldwin's Trump, Aristophanes' Socrates in the Clouds) misrepresent their targets and that learning politics from comedy traps viewers in ideological bubbles, since satire flatters rather than informs. He introduces the Ideological Turing Test, adapted from Turing's test: state your opponent's view so accurately and sympathetically that a neutral observer cannot tell it is not yours, and grounds the duty to learn the other side from its own partisans in Mill's On Liberty. The 2016 'Bubble' sketch passes the test, he says, but SNL's liberal bias (gentle Sanders, untouchable Obama) rarely challenges its audience, and a conservative 'Live from Omaha' alternative would just rebuild the bubble on the other side.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 16 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Koepsell surveys sixteen years of South Park blasphemy from 'Jesus vs. Santa' through 'Red Hot Catholic Love', 'Bloody Mary', the Scientology of 'Trapped in the Closet', and the censored Muhammad episodes 'Cartoon Wars' and '200'/'201', arguing that the show's equal-opportunity mockery is legitimate cultural criticism, not a sign of civilizational decline. Tracing the legal history from nineteenth-century blasphemy prosecutions through Cantwell v. Connecticut and Chaplinsky, he adopts Mill's On Liberty case that only free and open discussion of even the most sacred beliefs can shake out truth and keep opinion from becoming dead dogma. Comedy Central's black-screening of Muhammad while airing far coarser blasphemy was incoherent capitulation: nothing on the show is sacred, tolerance requires neither silence nor immunity from ridicule, and the Mormon Gary's 'suck my balls' sums the show's loving-but-mocking attitude.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 17 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Murtagh asks whether the Virgin Mary statue spraying menstrual blood on a cardinal and the pope in 'Bloody Mary' is morally wrong, and answers with a utilitarian weighing of blasphemous humor's consequences. On the negative side, offense to believers (with Cartman's sudden piety about Family Guy's Muhammad in 'Cartoon Wars Part I' articulating the utilitarian worry that millions watching intensifies the harm) and a possible desensitizing erosion of tolerance; on the positive side, pleasure and the show's power to provoke thought, as when Randy learns from Stan that his five sober days came from his own willpower, not 'divine ass blood'. Drawing on Mill's greatest happiness principle and On Liberty's defense of open discussion, he concludes blasphemous humor is morally justified when it is an important part of a presentation with significant social value, and wrong when used merely to piss people off or for profit.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 22 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Takes 'Douche and Turd' — Stan refusing to choose between Giant Douche and Turd Sandwich, Puff Daddy's gun-toting 'Vote or Die', and his banishment — plus the kindergarten tie in 'Trapper Keeper' (Flora's indecision, Rosie O'Donnell's recounts) to ask whether every vote counts in a two-party system. Through Locke, Stan's abstention becomes a withdrawal of consent to be governed by either mascot; through Mill, non-voting threatens the active participation that gives institutions legitimacy and wards off tyranny of the majority, even as the chapter catalogs real disincentives: the Electoral College's spectator states, the 2000 Florida debacle, and Commission rules excluding third parties like Nader. Habermas closes the chapter: the vote, read as positive liberty, is the paradigm of rights and inclusion in a community of equals.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 26 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Challenges the received libertarian message of 'Medicinal Fried Chicken' — Randy giving himself testicular cancer for a marijuana prescription, Cartman bootlegging KFC in a Scarface parody after Colorado bans fast food — by pressing Mill's liberty principle on what 'harm' means: Mr. Garrison's plot to murder the Queer Eye cast is immediate harm, but the S&M Mr. Slave displays to schoolchildren in 'The Death Camp of Tolerance' is only indirect, psychologically mediated harm Mill cannot clearly handle. Addiction then undermines Mill's assumption of sovereign tastes: corporations can shape desire without coercing anyone, so the libertarian 'omnicompetent individual' is a myth. Mead's intersubjectivity (Randy smoking pot before Officer Barbrady, blind to how Jimbo sees him) grounds the constructive claim that selves are socially formed, and the shark-tank defecation and Prisoner's Dilemma examples show why collective harms need rules and regulation.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 12 "Basketball Purists" — Kretchmar defends a 'modified purist' view that team-oriented, fundamentals-based basketball is generally better than the individualist modernist game, offering three arguments. The functionalist argument borrows Searle's account of constitutive rules to say ten-person interactive complexity makes a richer, more durable 'test' (like chess vs. tic-tac-toe); the variety argument uses Mill's On Liberty to warn that market pressures homogenize basketball toward football; and the communitarian argument uses MacIntyre's notion of a 'practice' with internal goods to show ESPN Streetball's isolated one-on-one feats erode basketball as a cooperative practice.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 19 "Fevered Desires and Interracial Intimacies in Jungle Fever" — Sundstrom uses Jungle Fever to dismantle the taboo (white and black versions) against interracial intimacy, treating Flipper and Angie's affair and the War Council's objections as a debate about black solidarity, loyalty, and self-hatred. He answers the War Council by invoking Mill's On Liberty and the tyranny of public opinion to defend sexual autonomy, and argues that demanding partners for political solidarity reduces them to props (objectification). He reads the psychoanalytic charge that interracial love is 'fevered' racial pathology as derived from Fanon's Black Skin, White Masks but ultimately baseless, and criticizes Lee for a puritanical ending that hides Orin and Paulie while exposing Flipper and Drew, failing to show interracial love as ordinary.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — Steve Benton reads Burton's Sleepy Hollow as a meditation on rationality and anti-intellectualism, contrasting it with Washington Irving's original where brainy Ichabod is run out of town. Burton's Ichabod, a rationalist constable, prevails only after tempering his faith in science with emotion, intuition, and the spirit world associated with his mother and Katrina—the paper-disk toy (bird/cage) symbolizing how head and heart must spin together. Benton maps the film's models of rationality onto Plato's philosopher-king and distrust of the mob and Hobbes's war of all against all (Burton's corrupt New York and Sleepy Hollow) versus the collaborative, democratic reason of Locke, Mill's On Liberty, and Dewey, invoking Aristotle and Nussbaum on emotion's role in practical wisdom; he leaves open whether the film is transgressive or a conventional 'woman heals cold rational man' Hollywood tale.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 11 "4. Better Call the DEA" — White uses Better Call Saul's cartel world—the 'Bagman' shootout, Mike's account of Philadelphia police corruption, Tuco's meth-driven violence—to frame the ethics of the U.S. War on Drugs, tracing its racist origins and drawing a sustained analogy to alcohol Prohibition. She marshals Mill's harm principle from On Liberty to argue adults may choose their own risks absent harm to others, making criminalization inconsistent given legal alcohol. She then fairly lays out the pro-War case (Bennett on deterrence, the Robins Vietnam-heroin study, Mill's own bar on selling oneself into slavery applied to addiction) before favoring decriminalization on the Portugal model.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 20 "10. Some Dark Genie" — Calef asks whether Bourdain's choice to become a heroin addict could be rational and responsible, using Mill's On Liberty and Harm Principle (including the voluntary-slavery exception) to argue addiction is reversible and can minimize suffering when alternatives are bleak. He then reads Bourdain's self-destructive drives — the drunk cliff-driving 'death trip' — through Freud's death drive (Thanatos) and Schopenhauer's pessimism, concluding the 'dark genie' was partly disease-like and thus not wholly blameworthy.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 12 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann defends political mockery as an ancient tradition (Aristophanes, Juvenal, Twain) but warns, using J.S. Mill's On Liberty, that if viewers let The Daily Show's jokes substitute for reasoned judgment the effect is like censorship, silencing ideas that must be heard to be understood. He cites Mill's arguments against silencing discussion and Plato's Meno on shackling true opinion with reasons, arguing that Stewart's virtue over Limbaugh is that he bills himself as comedy ('the show that leads into me is puppets making crank phone calls') and never presents mockery as a replacement for informed citizenship.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 30 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Vanderheiden reads America (The Book) as a work of democratic theory dressed as textbook parody, arguing its satire is a 'rhetoric of challenge' enacting deliberative democracy. He contrasts 'thin' (merely electoral) with 'thick' participatory democracy using Putnam's social capital and Barber's strong democracy, and invokes J.S. Mill's 'marketplace of ideas' and On Liberty to indict media conglomeration for killing the press's watchdog role. He reads the companion Earth (The Book) through social-contract theory (Hobbes-style), noting its jab that contractual authority historically required the assent of subjugated groups it never obtained.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 26 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Dromm and Salter analyze Persuasion by distinguishing persuasion (rational, argument-based belief change), influence (nonrational, resting on a person's charisma or status, as Lady Russell has over the Elliots), and 'overpersuasion.' Against Captain Wentworth's view that persuadability is a vice and firmness of mind a virtue (his hazelnut analogy, Louisa Musgrove's fatal fall from the Cobb), they adapt Mill's On Liberty: just as free discussion lets a society exchange error for truth and gain confidence in true beliefs, a persuadable person is happier and epistemically better off. They add that Anne broke the engagement from a sense of duty, not fickleness, and it is her own persuasion that finally reunites her with Wentworth.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 19 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Tait Szabo defends the guiltless consumption of pornography using Mill's Harm Principle from On Liberty: harmless conduct, even if deemed immoral, should not be censored. Classifying porn into erotica, sexist, dominance, and violent types (excluding child porn and snuff as clearly prohibitable), he rebuts the arguments that porn is prostitution (citing California v. Freeman), that loveless sex is wrong, that porn non-rationally causes or conditions violence against women, and the anti-porn feminist claim that it eroticizes patriarchal subordination. Each argument, he holds, either lacks causal evidence or would equally condemn romance novels, sexist jokes, and Cinderella — so under Mill, censorship is unjustified.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 25 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Miles argues that the popular 'porn is free speech applied to sex' defense (Wendy McElroy, Nadine Strossen) fails, using the contrast of Cohen's 'Fuck the Draft' jacket versus a hypothetical 'Schmoen' having public sex to express an opinion. He holds that political and religious speech persuade at a distance whereas public pornography coerces by making the unwilling audience actually perform the act of looking, so treating boobs like bumper stickers would be illiberal. The reasoning leans on a Millian harm/liberty framework: expression that merely offends is protected, but expression that forces others into an act crosses a line, so porn must be defended on privacy/autonomy grounds rather than as free speech.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 36 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — In this interview, dominatrix-director Mz. Berlin answers the classic moral objections to porn from inside the industry: she rebuts objectification by insisting she chooses to be 'a commodity' and that choice makes it permissible, rejects the rape-myth/harm claim by citing declining rape rates and comparing porn to violent TV, and grounds BDSM's legitimacy entirely on INFORMED CONSENT, contrasting her voluntary waterboarding with her real torture abroad. Endorsing a strongly Millian self-ownership view ('my body is my own commodity'), she extends consent to selling kidneys, assisted suicide, and even display of her corpse, while drawing hard limits at sex with children, animals, or the dead where genuine informed consent is impossible. She also frames femdom porn as subverting male hegemony and normalizing fluid gender roles.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 20 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Yim argues that clothing is a primary vehicle for autonomy, authenticity, and moral solidarity. Drawing on Mill's *On Liberty* and 'experiments in living,' he treats a teenager testing modest-vs-expressive dress against her mother, and 'Fashion Freaks' patterns for wheelchair users, as cases where wardrobe choice actualizes self-determination. He then reads dress as an emblem of communal solidarity and critique — the 1968 Smith/Carlos Olympic salute, the Israeli Kibbutz and Amish plain dress (with Rumspringa as a test of authenticity), gang colors, hippie androgyny, vegan 'cruelty-free' clothing, gay Levi's 501s, and Lubna Hussein's trouser trial in Sudan — concluding 'we are what we wear.'
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 29 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Musselman, Frohardt, and Lynch defend adult cannabis use through Mill's Harm Principle, using the hypothetical 'Patrick the pot smoker'—a professional who grows and smokes moderately on Friday nights—to argue that competent adults' self-regarding conduct is their own affair and does not violate the 'distinct and assignable obligations' Mill owes to family. They marshal health data (no lung-cancer link, negligible secondhand exposure, neuroprotective effects) to rebut the harm-to-others claim, and invoke Mill's higher intellectual pleasures plus the Michael-Phelps case to argue prohibition wastes resources better spent on the greater harms of alcohol and tobacco.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 23 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Scott reads three landmark climbs as expressions of the tension between individual freedom and community standards. He casts John Bachar's bold, ground-up, run-out Bachar-Yerian and its self-mastery ethic as a partial embodiment of Nietzsche's Übermensch and will to power, and Alan Watts' rule-breaking sport route To Bolt or Not to Be as an exercise of Mill's On Liberty defense of originality and diversity that benefits the whole community. Against both thinkers' negative view of community, he uses Charles Taylor's 'horizon of significance' to argue that Sonnie Trotter's The Path gains its meaning only through dialogue with the climbing community and its traditions.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 24 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Felipe Carvalho frames a friend 'Toby's' worry – tattoos are forever, so should one be impulsive or cautious? – as a problem about bodily freedom versus irreversible change. He rejects the hedonist position (seize the day, regret is just part of freedom) as too simple and the Millian position (drawing on Mill's On Liberty argument that one cannot freely alienate one's freedom, as in selling oneself into slavery) as too precautionary, noting his friend's happy irreversible ear surgery. He proposes a 'middle path' learned from the tattoo community: a complex interplay of motif, the tattooist-as-artist, and the body-as-canvas that lets permanence guide more principled choices – so no 'I Love Becky' tattoos.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 32 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Woods asks whether the claim 'tattooing is immoral' can be defended, taking Adolf Loos's 1908 'Ornament and Crime' (tattooed free men are latent criminals or degenerate aristocrats) as his provocation. He rejects Loos's equation of tattooing with murder, since tattooing is voluntary and self-regarding, but resists the liberal 'sovereign self' reply drawn from Mill's On Liberty by arguing autonomy and the body are relational, not absolute, so a person's self-regarding choices remain open to reasoned challenge and even regulation. He proposes regret evidence in informed consent and an age-25 minimum, concluding tattooing is a matter of both taste and morality.
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 22 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — The essay argues that soaring tuition drives college students into sexual self-commodification—egg-selling ('Pay your tuition with eggs'), craigslist/backpage escorting, and dorm-porn webcam sites like VoyeurDorm and CocoDorm—and reads these cases through Kant's second formulation, condemning them as treating oneself and others as mere means rather than ends of intrinsic dignity. It applies Marx's notion of false consciousness to Natalie Dylan's virginity auction and Ashley Dupré's 'empowerment' claims, comparing them to women choosing high heels as internalized oppression. It uses Rousseau's Social Contract and Mill's On Liberty to argue that prostitution is a form of illegitimate 'voluntary slavery' because one cannot rightly alienate one's own inalienable freedom, and contrasts coerced cases (Helena in Singapore, Rosie Reid's traumatic auctioned deflowering, John Gechter's porn suspension from a Christian college) with less-coerced ones to argue moral concern should track the degree of circumstantial coercion.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 30 "28. South Park as Philosophy Blasphemy, Mockery, and (Absolute ) Freedom of Speech" — The chapter argues, via the 'Cartoon Wars,' '200,' and '201' episodes, that South Park makes five arguments about free speech and evaluates each. Johnson defends the claims that catering to terrorist threats breeds more terrorism and that mockery is 'all or nothing,' but rejects South Park's implied case for absolute free speech: using Mill's On Liberty and harm principle he shows the 'marketplace of ideas' fails (citing 8kun and Fox News), and using Popper's paradox of tolerance he argues intolerance cannot itself be tolerated. He proposes a middle-ground 'PC Principle' where society, not the state, curbs harmful speech through deplatforming and public shaming while distinguishing tolerance from acceptance.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 69 "65. Louis CK as Philosopher The King and His Fall" — Marra Henrigillis first shows CK as 'philosopher king of comedy'—his cell-phone/'forever empty' bit echoing Buddhist and Stoic teaching on sitting with suffering, his 'why?' bit echoing Quine on not ontologizing, his 'So Did The Fat Lady' episode exposing how society denies fat women full humanity—then uses his 2017 misconduct scandal to stage competing verdicts: the feminist case for banning him (rape culture, power dynamics), Plato on censoring vicious art, Mill's four-part defense of free expression and Nozick's free-market/entitlement view against cancellation, and Aristotle's virtue ethics (character judged over a whole life) plus Pompa's prison-education view that no one is only their worst act.

### The Problem of Evil

The problem of evil is the challenge of reconciling the existence of a God who is all-powerful, all-knowing, and wholly good with the reality of suffering and wrongdoing in the world. In its logical form it alleges an outright contradiction between such a God and any evil at all, while its evidential form argues that the sheer amount and distribution of suffering makes God's existence unlikely. Responses, known as theodicies, appeal to free will, soul-making, or the limits of human understanding to explain why a good God might permit evil.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 26 "Against Fascism" — Neal King argues the Buffyverse is proto-fascist: Buffy kills demons and vampires on sight within a race-like hierarchy, tempered only by an Augustinian split between natural and moral evil (soulless vampires cannot choose otherwise; soul-bearing humans like Faith, Willow, and Warren can repent), she derives authority from an ancient calling rather than democracy, and the graduation battle of 'Graduation Day, Part Two' stages citizenship forged in mass combat. He imagines a fascist Buffyverse of 'brownskirt' death squads and concludes only the show's secrecy prevents full fascism, finally recommending that the racism be dropped but the ritual sacrifice of evildoers kept — with Willow's flaying of Warren as the model.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 29 "No Big Win" — Reads sacrifice, salvation, and redemption in the Buffyverse as secular myth: vampires manifest the shadow-side of the human (Liam's resentment becomes Angelus, William's repressed romanticism becomes Spike's rebellion), and the contrast between soulless Spike's genuine moral growth through love of Buffy and human Xander's arrested development shows redemption is measured by 'what have you done with what you've been given.' The Purpose of Evil section argues good and evil must stay in balance because without evil there is no free choice and hence no redemption, and Angel's 'no big win' epiphany — no grand plan, only lessening suffering one kindness at a time — locates life's meaning in the journey of becoming rather than final victory.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 21 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Scott Davison asks whether Tolkien's world is Manichean - two equal forces of Good and Evil - and answers no: the Ring is not 'altogether evil' in itself but animated by Sauron's infused will, and nothing, not even Sauron, is totally evil, since 'nothing is evil in the beginning'. Developing Augustine's account, he shows evil as parasitic privation - Ringwraiths wear robes 'to give shape to their nothingness', the Eye is 'a window into nothing' - and traces evil to inordinate desire: Sam stays content with his garden while Boromir, Saruman, Denethor, and Sauron reach for more than their place allows. Evil unmakes itself (Saruman dies by Wormtongue's knife), and because goodness is the world's default, there is always hope of overcoming it.
