They unpack Screwtape's tactics as textbook fallacies: jargon like 'religious phase' working as a red herring, dismissing Christianity out of boredom as a non sequitur, the 'Historical Point of View' as the chronological snobbery that cuts generations off from the past, and the endless loop of pride about one's humility as an infinite regress that paralyzes thought. Because reason is, for Lewis, the road toward Heaven, the Devil's highway to Hell is built entirely of bad logic.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 33 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Timothy P. Jackson argues Cohen is the closest thing today to a Biblical prophet - a 'strong poet' in Harold Bloom's sense, wearing a coat of many colors drawn from Judaism, Christianity, Buddhism, Taoism, and Sufism, sustained by an 'epistemic humility' that lives between dogmatism and doubt. Cohen leads Christian texts back to their Hebraic origins, critiques every arrogant nationalism including Israel (Book of Mercy, psalm 27), and gave his Tel Aviv concert profits to Israeli-Palestinian reconciliation. Jackson reads Cohen's equanimity at his business manager's embezzlement trial as forgiveness overcoming resentment, weighs his hesed/agape-style unconditional love against his failures in erotic love, and ends with Cohen's reticence about personal immortality - a prophet for the living.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 7 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Robert Arp's introduction explains that Homeland's jihadist material (Nazir, Hamid, Brody, 9/11) drew him in and previews the book's philosophizing with a sample argument: whether morality needs God. He argues jihadists ground ethics in Allah's commands, but since faith defies rational proof, competing conceptions of God conflict, and scripture (Abraham and Isaac, the Flood, the Egyptian firstborn, the genocide commands in 1 Samuel and Hosea) has God commanding atrocities, either the terrorists' God is evil or morality is better grounded in reason without God. The dilemma he poses - a good God would not command 9/11, so the command conception or God's goodness must go - is the Euthyphro structure applied to terrorism.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 15 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter asks whether Boyd's survival of Raylan's bullet in the premiere was a genuine sign from God: the atheist invokes Ockham's Razor and the promise of a naturalistic explanation, while the theist replies that a world-creating God would act through the laws of nature, making such explanations neutral rather than negative evidence. It then applies William James's pragmatist standard from his study of mystical experience - judge the sign by the fruits of the Spirit (Galatians' love, joy, peace, self-control) it bears - to Boyd's prison ministry, his urging Raylan to forgive Arlo, and his meth-lab crusade. Despite Boyd's eventual apostasy after Bo murders his congregation, the author concludes he passes James's test, since faith is a maintained journey that can be lost, and the born-again Boyd still struggles - like Jacob becoming Israel - rather than scheming coldly.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 16 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter reads preacher Billy St. Cyr's snake-handling through Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: like Abraham, Billy performs the absurd double movement - fully resigning himself to dying by rattlesnake while believing he will be spared - which is why Boyd Crowder, who abandoned faith for Hegel's objective rational certainty, can neither buy him out nor understand him. Kierkegaard's teleological suspension of the ethical explains why Billy and Abraham may set obedience to God above self-preservation and social morality, while Boyd's showdown in 'Truth and Consequences', where he hands Billy an un-milked rattlesnake, exposes that Billy's certainty has curdled into the hubris de Silentio warns against, so Billy is no Abraham. De Silentio's three marks - love, humility, no desire to instruct others - separate genuine faith from cult leaders and violent extremists.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 35 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Ketcham's invented chronicle sends Dracula and a village rabbi to 1194 Cairo to interrogate Maimonides: can resurrection - one of the thirteen principles of faith - apply to a soulless undead being, and is his blood-drinking a divinely imposed penance? Maimonides answers from the Guide for the Perplexed and the Letter on Resurrection, offering that intelligence is the essence of the soul yet judging the Count a likely trickster, while Dracula presses that no scientific evidence of dust becoming flesh exists. The diarist closes with the heretical worry that Maimonidean resurrection - no food, drink, or sex - might itself be a kind of undeath.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 35 "21. God-Talk at the Abbey" — Samuel Lumpenhouwer takes the Abbey's religious silences - Anna's 'we'll only fall out,' Alfred's baffled 'What?' at transubstantiation, and the Catholic baptism fight over baby Sybbie - and brings in Aquinas to make God-talk possible. Reason alone can know that God exists (the argument from design through final causes like the candle flame, carefully distinguished from Paley's watchmaker), revelation grasped by faith tells us God is personal, and human words reach God only analogically, as when Matthew calls God 'Father' at Lavinia's grave, or by way of negation. Against Carson's 'it is not our place to reason why' about Sybil's death, the chapter insists that mystery limits rather than excuses reason, ending with Aquinas's 'straw' and the Abbey's three attitudes: confident belief, searching doubt, and keep-it-private spirituality.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 12 "1. Reading the Signs" — Di Bernardo reads the religious language of The Walking Dead as sustained irony - a 'doubleness of sense' - arguing that the walkers, churches, and signs comment critically on faith rather than endorse it. He tracks the church scenes (the Southern Baptist church of 2.1 'What Lies Ahead' with its timed bells and sitting-dead congregation, Gabriel's Saint Sarah's where Maggie answers that it is 'just four walls and a roof'), the ambiguous 'sanctuary' and Terminus signs, and the comic-book Jesus (Paul Monroe) as a machine-gun savior, concluding that the scriptural promise of eternal life through consuming flesh and blood yields only undead life. Against Epicurus's consolation that death is nothing to us, and in the shadow of Nietzsche's madman announcing the death of God, the chapter warns against investing absolute trust in any signs - religious or secular - a warning capped by Rick biting out Joe's throat as his own 'day of reckoning.'
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 28 "15. It Would Take a Miracle!" — Barkman and Käärid ask whether Miracle Max's revival of 'mostly dead' Westley is a miracle, staging David Hume - for whom a violation of natural law is never more credible than mistaken or lying testimony, so Hume in Florin would call Max a deceiver and Inigo and Fezzik barbarous dupes - against C.S. Lewis, for whom a miracle is a new, unpredictable element introduced into nature rather than a violation of it. They add puzzles neither philosopher addresses: whether Westley was truly dead, whether a 'rotten miracle' would still count, and why Max's miracles seem to require 'unshattered' confidence, concluding that Florin's miracles are person-dependent in a way Hume's skepticism and Lewis's supernaturalism both miss.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 29 "14. Louis C.K.’s God" — Argues Louis's God material is a negativistic, immanent critique of religion in Adorno's sense of 'damaged human life': the 'God' episode's crucifixion doctor who makes young Louie hammer a nail shows faith wrecking children with guilt until his mother's skeptical 'malarkey' speech and donuts rescue him. His SNL 'did you look in the downstairs bathroom?' bit becomes an evidentialist ethics of belief aimed at over-certain atheists, his 'shitty girlfriend' Abraham bit and body/food/shopping jokes illustrate Tillich's functionalist test of what we treat with ultimate concern (echoing David Foster Wallace's 'everybody worships'), and the chapter closes that comedy here works like Ignatian Catholic reflection, keeping faith and doubt together.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 30 "15. God Started in 1983" — Uses the SNL bit of a God who has been standing in a room since 1983 to argue Louis is an 'apathetic agnostic': he cannot know whether God exists, lambastes atheists who claim certainty, and thinks the question barely matters for our lives. The chapter weighs Pascal's Wager against Epicurus's four-part cure ('Don't fear god, don't worry about death'), faults Louis's 'downstairs bathroom' bit for putting the burden of proof on atheists, reads the 'Heaven' glory-hole sketch through Clifford's ethics of belief as a rejection of faith without evidence, and ends with Louie's mother's line that you have to be good to people whether or not God is watching.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 32 "18. Gods and Beetles" — Cooper takes Jaime's challenge to Catelyn - 'if your gods are real and just, why is the world so full of injustice?' - as the problem of evil and tests three Westerosi theologies. Melisandre's Manichean divine patronage fails by Augustine's argument that evil is no rival substance but a corruption in the creature; Ockham's voluntarism, symbolized by cousin Orson smashing beetles while Tyrion watches in dread, is rebuffed by Suarez and by Tyrion's own 'why are all the gods such vicious c--ts?'; and the humanist free-will defense in Catelyn's reply ('evil exists because of men like you'), rooted in Augustine and developed by Plantinga, answers Jaime but leaves Ivan Karamazov's problem of suffering children - met only by existential responses like Dorne's 'we don't hurt little girls.'
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 16 "4. Is it God or the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown" — Using It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown (1966), the chapter asks whether belief without evidence can be rational, contrasting the classic evidentialist view (rational beliefs must be basic or derived from basics, in the tradition of Locke and Hume) with Alvin Plantinga's properly basic beliefs and a virtue theory of rational belief built on Aristotle-style intellectual virtues like humility, courage, and charity. Linus fails on every account - he insulates himself from counterevidence ('If you really are a fake, don't tell me'), lets the belief cost him friends and trick-or-treating, and never updates after the Pumpkin's no-show - while Sally's pumpkin-patch vigil shows rationality as a balance of evidence, value, and risk. The upshot: God-belief formed responsibly within a trusting community can be rational in a way Linus's solitary, evidence-dodging Pumpkin faith cannot.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 25 "11. The Sincerity of St. Linus" — The chapter argues Linus confuses sincere faith with indubitable certainty: on the Thomistic model (faith as chosen propositional belief held with knowledge-like certainty, between opinion and knowledge), his fateful slip into 'if the Great Pumpkin comes' wrecks his faith, turning doubt into hypocrisy. Against this it deploys doxastic involuntarism - we cannot simply choose to believe, as his failed attempts to psych himself up ('I believed with every fiber of my being') show - and philosophers like Daniel Howard-Snyder who allow faith without belief: what Linus does, staying in the patch and risking hypothermia and ridicule while doubting, is faith as action in the face of doubt. Hence the closing paradox: where there is certainty there is no room for faith, and Linus's patch only became sincere once doubt crept in.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 11 "2. Deadpool the Dark Angel" — Christopher Ketcham playfully argues that Deadpool's fourth-wall escapes show he exists partly in dimensions we cannot experience, read through string theory's ten curled dimensions and Maimonides's ten realms of angels—beings of form without matter—in the Mishneh Torah. Since only God and angels traverse those hidden dimensions, Deadpool must be an angel, likely a dark one, whose shuttling between realms explains his vacillation between mercenary violence and saving souls. Ezekiel's chariot vision, the vengeful Hebrew Bible God, and massless dark matter are recruited as supporting evidence for this deadpan-earnest science-and-scripture argument.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 31 "20. There’s Only One God, Ma’am" — Holt takes Captain America's line 'There's only one God, ma'am' and asks how Christian monotheism survives in a universe where Thor, Odin and the One-above-all really exist, answering with henotheism - Moses's 'I am', Jacob's household idols, and the Living Tribunal as the merely representative 'biggest kid in the playground' of a supreme Creator whose 'only weapon is love'. He then deploys Hume's Natural History of Religion, where the ignorant multitude progress from polytheism to monotheism, to explain why Cap dismisses Asgardians as superstition Thor says is 'no stranger' than his Sunday churchgoing, while Hume's own trajectory - all religion as vulgar superstition - lands instead in the post-religious rationalism of Tony Stark's 'I prefer fact to fantasy' futurism, which the Goddess calls a soul imprisoned in the ice of rationalism.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 30 "16. Gotta Have Faith" — Winters asks what faith is when the Party risks burning and becoming demodog chow so Eleven can close the gate: after arguing via George Michael and the talisman-free tunnels that faith need not be religious, he tests Bishop's models of faith against 'The Gate' (the affective and secular hope models fit; the belief and trust models fail because everyone has seen the Mind Flayer's work on Will). Hume's account that causation is never observed, only habituated, explains the Party's hope that heat will drive the Mind Flayer from Will and that Christmas lights will reach him, and Kierkegaard's teleological suspension of the ethical and knight of faith frame Eleven's willingness to die against the absurd, since aligning her life with friendship's higher purpose is what makes it meaningful.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 31 "Damned If You Do, and Damned If You Don’t" — McHenry reads the re-imagined series as a holy-war allegory in which both sides weaponize religion, then asks whether that manipulation is ever moral. Adama's lie about Earth is Machiavellian statecraft (with Foucault's point that privileged knowledge holds power), yet defended as serving the greater good, while Roslin's Pythia-based campaign contrasts with Bush's faith-based fear politics. The Cylons emerge as evangelical fundamentalists whose conversion of Baltar through inner Number Six runs on fear, exactly what Madison's case for religious liberty forbids. The chapter concludes the show's own gods have sided with the Colonials.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 41 "So Say We All" — Berger deploys Bakhtin's dialogism to answer the 'GINO' charge: the re-imagined series is not a betrayal of Larson's show but a heteroglossic utterance in an ongoing conversation that already included the Book of Mormon, von Daniken's Chariots of the Gods, Greco-Roman myth, and later fanfic and blogs, with each version sourcing its sources' sources. The 2003 series is read as polyphonic about belief: skeptic Adama, devout Number Six, the messianic convert Baltar, and Dawkins/Hitchens-style atheist critiques of fundamentalism are all given equal voice. The show's value lies in inviting debate across the whole continuum of belief rather than preaching a position.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 20 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Barkman and Kowalski mine the Cooper household for science-and-religion lessons: Mary's 'Third-World demon' diagnosis of Raj raises religious diversity (exclusivism, inclusivism, pluralism), her 'But intelligently designed by a creator, right?' prompts an assessment of Behe's irreducible complexity against Darwinian counterexamples like the flagellum-turned-syringe and a warning against god-of-the-gaps reasoning. Her claim that 'all that science stuff comes from Jesus' occasions Plantinga's argument that Darwinian naturalism undermines trust in our cognitive faculties, plus origin-of-life and fine-tuning probability arguments, tempered by Kitcher's caution that such estimates rest on unknown background conditions. Van Inwagen on why Genesis need not teach literal science, and Locke's advice to proportion belief to evidence, frame the mutual education Mary and Sheldon owe each other.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 25 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Sirvent and Baker use Daily Show segments (Wyatt Cenac reporting from a Vegas-style heaven, Lewis Black on Jesus as a primary requirement, Stewart on Pat Robertson praying down the Supreme Court) to skewer politicians who claim God's endorsement, from Michele Bachmann's guaranteed Iowa 'miracle' to Glenn Beck's apocalyptic readings. Locke's critique of religious 'enthusiasm' explains why taking private intuition for divine direction breeds arrogant conviction immune to counterevidence, while Gadamer's hermeneutics shows that Beck and Robertson practice objectivist misreading of texts written in a culture two thousand years distant. The chapter closes with the demand for humility about claiming the mind of God.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 28 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Pigliucci reads the 'Evolution, Schmevolution' series (Helms's Dayton, Tennessee reenactment-town piece, Stewart's panel with ID proponent Dembski and the scrotum question) as one of the best media treatments of the creation-evolution controversy. Popper's falsificationism marks intelligent design as non-science, since Dembski's designer works outside testable law and miracles are, as Larson says, unrepeatable and unfalsifiable, while Stewart's bad-design jokes about the scrotum and Mayr's 99.99% extinction figure replay the problem of evil. A compressed tour of rationalism (Plato to Descartes's radical doubt) versus Hume's empiricism explains why science yields tentative conclusions, and the chapter ends that resolving the controversy, like Aristotle's eudaimonia, is a lifelong personal project.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 13 "Might God Be Hidden for Love's Sake" — Uses Hidden Mickeys — like the ambiguous log-and-dump-truck at the Once Upon a Toy store — to attack the first premise of Schellenberg's argument from divine hiddenness: just as an arrangement of shapes can be a deliberate Hidden Mickey or a decorative accident, so God's traces in the world can be genuinely ambiguous, letting a non-resistant non-believer rationally fail to believe. Mother Teresa's decades of felt abandonment and C. S. Lewis's 'door slammed in the face' from A Grief Observed frame the experiential problem, and the authors concede the disanalogy that we independently know agents run Disney but not that God exists. As a partial response they offer Lewis's Screwtape suggestion that 'He cannot ravish, He can only woo': God hides precisely so that love can be freely given.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 20 "Knock and the Door Will Be Opened… Eventually" — The chapter reads Strange pounding on Kamar-Taj's door as Kierkegaard's passionate collision with 'that which thought cannot think': the materialist surgeon hits the unknown as a frontier, takes offense at the Ancient One's talk of healing through belief, and can only proceed by surrendering intellectual control ('I control it by surrendering control?'). It applies Kierkegaard's two teachers from Philosophical Fragments: Pangborn is healed the Socratic way, recollecting a power already within him, while the Ancient One's astral knock-out and eviction of Strange acts like the god as teacher, forcing him to discover that he is untruth, until faith becomes 'controlling magic by surrendering to it.'
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 29 "Magic and Deep Magic" — The chapter argues that Strange's universe implicitly contains the Creator God of theism rather than just Marvel's gods: Aristotle's impersonal prime mover will not do because Strange needs a relatable source of an objective moral order, so Aquinas's all-good author of eternal, natural, and divine law supplies the framework. It reads three comics as evidence: Strange defeating Dracula by invoking the Tetragrammaton, the Sise-Neg saga where a sorcerer who attains godhood at the dawn of time learns to recreate the universe exactly as the first cause made it, and the World War Hulk story where summoning Zom shows the hubris of violating the moral order—closing with C.S. Lewis's 'deep magic' as cooperation with the created order versus dark magic's will to control it.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 35 "21. God-Talk at the Abbey" — Samuel Klumpenhouwer uses the Abbey's awkward silences about religion - Anna refusing to discuss it over dinner, Thomas showing off with 'transubstantiation' - to introduce Aquinas on how God can be known and talked about. Mary's wartime bedside prayer ('I'm not even sure that you're there') shows she wants not just proof of existence but a personal God, so the chapter distinguishes Aquinas's argument from design - carefully separated from Paley's divine-watchmaker version - from knowledge of God through revelation and faith. Aquinas's two indirect ways of speaking, analogy (Matthew calling God 'Father' at Lavinia's grave) and negation, explain why the 'God is good' sign over Charles Grigg's workhouse should trouble us, and why Carson's 'it is not our place to reason why' about Sybil's death overstates the mystery of God's otherness.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 21 "10 Fact, Truth, and Evidence A Lesson from Dr. Tyree" — Dean Kowalski stages an imagined dialogue between Indy and William E. Tyree — Harrison Ford's real Ripon College philosophy professor, whom Ford's own script rewrite placed 'right down the hall' — to show that 'archaeology is the search for fact, not truth' is self-defeating if truth is correspondence with reality. Tyree's epistemology primer (principles of evidence, inductive generalization, hypothesis testing like Indy's Sankara-stone glow prediction, and Ockham's Razor) explains Indy's resistance to the God hypothesis despite witnessing the Ark, the Grail's instant healing of Henry Sr., and the invisible bridge he crossed on guesswork rather than knowledge. The resolution: Indy practices methodological naturalism, keeping deeper truths out of archaeology, without being committed to metaphysical naturalism.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 22 "11 Indiana Jones and the Quest for Agnosticism What if All Stories Are True" — Robert Grant Price observes that in Indy's world every myth — the Ark, the Sankara Stones, the Grail, and in the comics and novels Atlantis, Merlin, Noah's Ark, and the Philosopher's Stone — turns out factually true, producing a surplus of evidence for mutually exclusive religions (the personal Christian Trinity versus non-personal Brahman). Against Derrida's deconstruction and the postmodern claim that no grand narrative captures truth, in Indy's world 'the squash ball always comes back' — yet he stays agnostic, telling Spalko 'There is always another explanation.' The chapter weighs his three exits: remain agnostic, take a leap of faith as he does stepping onto the invisible bridge, or read Percival and Galahad as symbolically rather than historically true.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 26 "Paradise Found" — Paul Brown maps The Minish Cap's Hyrule onto utopian theory: Plato's Republic classes reappear as royal family (guardians), castle guards (auxiliaries), and market traders (producers), but Hyrule improves on Plato with no slavery, fluid social boundaries (Princess Zelda wandering the festival unrecognized), and Mayor Hagen's local democracy. Aristotle's polis supplies the town's design — small enough for community, walled for defense, river-powered — while Kant's disinterested appreciation of the beautiful fits Miyamoto's 'miniature garden' of pastoral idyll. The spiritual dimension completes the utopia: the benevolent Picori/Minish are a God walking unseen among people, a fuzzy religion without prophet or persecution, so no leap of faith is even necessary.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 27 "NOTES" — Brett Chandler Patterson reads Lost through C. S. Lewis's Chronicles of Narnia as myth rather than allegory - the Lamp Post station and flight 316 (the Prince Caspian dedication page) wink at the source - with the island, like Narnia, a world of crisis and second chances entered by plane crash instead of wardrobe. Flashbacks of past failures (Kate the fugitive, Sayid the torturer, Charlie's addiction, Locke's kidney con) set up struggles for faith that he illuminates with H. Richard Niebuhr on faith as a center of value and revelation as communal, and with Levinas's claim that we become ourselves only through responsibility to the Other in community. The Jack-versus-Locke man-of-science/man-of-faith debate, Charlie's moth-cocoon trial, and Jacob and the Man in Black's black-and-white stone game map onto Aslan versus the White Witch, ending in redemption through the new community and Jack's sacrificial death.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 28 "NOTES" — Daniel Gallagher uses Aquinas to read Lost as a drama about mistaking finite goods for the ultimate good: Jack's hope in curing, Kate's in deceiving, Jin's in his father-in-law's employment, Locke's in Anthony Cooper, and the Virgin Mary statues full of heroin all instantiate Aquinas's approaching-Peter analogy, where we know only confusedly that someone (the perfect good) is coming toward us. Desmond's and Charlie's paralysis before the good is the sin of acedia, Rose's faith that the island itself healed her cancer is presumption, and her certainty that Bernard is alive illustrates Aquinas's claim - framed through Plato's episteme versus doxa - that faith sits midway between knowledge and opinion. The chapter closes on the harmony of faith and reason, from the Five Ways' first efficient cause to Eko's dying 'I ask for no forgiveness,' grounded in Augustine's restless heart that finds no peace until it rests in God.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 12 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Johnson uses 'Go God Go's' future of 2546—where Dawkins-style atheism has become a warring religion and otter scientists intone 'Oh my Science!'—to ask whether science and religion genuinely conflict and whether New Atheism is itself a faith. Applying abduction and the four criteria of adequacy, he argues the embellished-story hypothesis beats miracle claims about Jesus (whose legend grew Gospel by Gospel), Sathya Sai Baba, Joseph Smith, and Xenu, that Mr(s). Garrison's 'you can't disprove God' and the show's sarcasm commit an appeal to ignorance, and that Stan's water-into-wine scene with Jesus shows how easily people are fooled. He allows Kuhnian theory change in science but rejects James's will-to-believe for existence claims—the moon whale Willzyx needs evidence—and concludes Parker and Stone are unfair to Dawkins: ending religion would not end violence, but it would remove the easiest justification for it, and some answers are simply true even when unknown.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 13 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Dueck takes Stan's closing pluralism in 'Super Best Friends'—all religions have something valuable to teach, as the interfaith superheroes' combined powers defeat Blaine—and tests it against Hick's pluralism, exclusivism, and Rahner's inclusivist 'anonymous Christians', using 'Go God Go's warring atheist factions to show exclusivity is unavoidable even without God. Hume's miracle argument explains why Jesus's look-away water-into-wine trick convinces no one in the episode: testimony can never outweigh the laws of nature, so supernatural evidence resists natural evaluation. Popper's falsificationism warns that watering doctrines down to make religions compatible (the rabbit-pope of 'Fantastic Easter Special') leaves nothing to test, while James's will to believe and Plantinga's defense of exclusivism ground the conclusion that faith can be rationally justifiable where evidence runs out—beware the Blainetologists, but do not surrender ways of life that define us.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 42 "Notes" — Charts Star Trek's handling of secularization, from the "Roddenberry attitude" of Kirk confronting fifteen would-be gods to later series' complications, using Robert Audi's nine features of religion and Benedict Anderson's "imagined community" - the Yangs' sacred flag and worship-word "freedom" in "The Omega Glory" show an incoherent civic religion Kirk can correct. "Who Watches the Watchers" inverts the dynamic by making Picard an accidental god who refuses to found a religion among the proto-Vulcan Mintakans, while real-world creationism in schools and abstinence-only sex education supply the chapter's empirical moral arguments that faith-driven public policy fails on its own terms. DS9's Bajor arc - Vedek Winn boycotting Keiko's school, Sisko's defense of the faith that sustained Bajor through occupation, and Akorem's restoration of the D'jarra castes in "Accession", likened to Plato's Republic-class soul hierarchy - grounds the claim that infallible religious authority corrodes democratic equality, with Sisko as the Emissary who synthesizes faith and secular governance.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Lindenmuth reads Luke's endgame in Return of the Jedi as Kierkegaard's knight of faith, reversing Abraham's binding of Isaac: where Abraham raised the knife, Luke, pressed by Yoda and Obi-Wan to kill his father, throws his saber away. Jedi detachment ('train yourself to let go') is infinite resignation, and Han Solo's arc from self-interested smuggler to hero at Yavin traces Kierkegaard's aesthetic-to-ethical stages. Luke's double movement - resigning everything, his cause and his life, while trusting there is still good in Vader - suspends the ethical demand to kill and accomplishes what neither side thought possible: turning a Sith back to the light.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 40 "The Last Jedi A New Hope" — Johnson defends The Last Jedi's Luke against the 'you ruined Luke' charge: his pacifism was set up when he threw away his lightsaber before Palpatine in Return of the Jedi, and his call to end the Jedi follows the lesson Hobbes and Locke drew from the English civil wars - since religious matters cannot be settled by reason, only by violence, Jedi and Sith factions fighting for political power yield only bloodshed like the Clone Wars and two Death Stars. Luke also seeks to destroy the Jedi texts out of guilt by association for the Order's failures, and to the end he remains a consequentialist pacifist, defeating Kylo on Crait through a nonviolent Force projection rather than a real duel. Far from betraying the character, this growth into proactive nonviolence - capped by Rey's yellow-bladed, mainly defensive style - makes Luke 'the ultimate Jedi' and the Resistance's new hope.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 11 "Notes" — Baggett sets W. K. Clifford's evidentialism (the negligent shipowner; believing on insufficient evidence is a 'sin against mankind') against William James's precursive faith, which permits believing ahead of the evidence when an option is forced, live, momentous, and evidentially undecided. He applies this to Sam's taping over the Dubai Air logo as social-coordination faith, Richmond's belief that it can finally beat Everton, romantic risk-taking like Roy and Keeley's, and the marriage of belief with hard work (Ted's practice tirade, Nate's False Nine), ending with James and Pascal on how evidential ambiguity about God makes a passional step of faith rational.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 27 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Greeley argues the zombie embodies a specifically modern fear of losing our humanity: walkers are persons stripped of the potential Aristotle and Aquinas made the measure of human worth, which is why Rick uniquely eulogizes the walkers he puts down ('I'm sorry this happened to you'). Following Aries, he traces modern death anxiety to the split of faith from reason and reads the CDC arc ('TS-19') as science offering only a self-destruct quick death where Jacqui's 'wrath of God' guess at least offers meaning. Rousseau's claim that civilization corrupts explains the survivors' return to the woods, where pizza-deliverer Glenn's heroics and the 'kingpin' Guillermo protecting nursing-home patients show the apocalypse can bring out the best in us while the Bradbury's Sale storefront and trampled Walmart worker hint we were already the walking dead.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Held asks what a god is and which gods deserve worship, using Rachels's definition (all-powerful, perfectly good, perfectly wise) to show no DC deity - dying Zeus, cruel Darkseid, creation-unmaking Parallax - qualifies, and that mere power generates fear, not the moral authority that could ground worship-worthiness or a parent-like right to command. Against the Christian campaigner Darrel Keyes, who calls Wonder Woman's cults idolatrous, he notes her gods visibly exist while his God is both unprovable and, per the Anselmian concept problem, indescribable without ceasing to be supreme. The chapter ends by relocating worship on earth: since we need orienting values whether or not gods exist, 'we could do worse than submit to the loving authority' of the justice, care, and integrity Diana embodies - pray to 'yourself, your own strength and character.'
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 26 "Is the Gridiron Holy Ground" — Hamilton analyzes the fusion of football, patriotism, and religion (Friday Night Lights' Odessa, Super Bowl rituals) as Rousseau's 'civil religion' from the Social Contract—socially unifying but content-empty and anti-intellectual, keeping faith bifurcated from real life. Drawing on Augustine's account of virtue as 'rightly ordered love' and vice as disordered love, he argues football has been wrongly elevated above higher goods. He rejects Higgs's incompatibility thesis for a Christian worldview approach—exemplified by Tony Dungy, Lovie Smith, and Joe Ehrman's 'men for others'—that makes the gridiron holy ground.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Clayton distinguishes the philosophical problem of evil (Aquinas's deductive argument, its inductive/evidential successors, and Plantinga's free-will defense) from what Plantinga calls the pastoral problem — the personal crisis suffering brings. He argues Eastwood, as 'practical philosopher,' registers the philosophical problem visually in Mystic River (camera panning heavenward at Katie's murder, the intercut Communion) but pointedly refuses to resolve it. In Hereafter the tsunami, deaths, and the twins' loss are met not with theodicy but with a recurring pastoral pattern of listening, being present, and acting compassionately (Dr. Rousseau with Marie, George's reading of Marcus), religion offering no answers.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 26 "15. God Is Good (Chuck Not So Much)" — Graves contrasts the Judeo-Christian God of scripture with Chuck, arguing Chuck fails theodicy: he neither shares human suffering (as Jesus does) nor pursues justice for the oppressed (as Yahweh does in Psalm 82), and using evolution to create sapient life guarantees disease, war, and injustice that Paley's Natural Theology design argument cannot excuse. He reads Amara's wish to unwind creation as arguably 'good,' rejects the Winchesters' fallacy that Nephilim Jack must inherit Lucifer's evil (nature versus nurture), and diagnoses Chuck as a pathological narcissist paralleling despotic real-world leaders.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" — Jacoby uses Stan Marsh as the embodiment of W. K. Clifford's ethics of belief, that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence. Stan debunks TV psychic John Edward, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the one making extraordinary claims. Jacoby distinguishes evidential from prudential reasons, presents and criticizes Pascal's Wager (using 'Cartmanland' and the problem of undeserved suffering), and argues via Clifford that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken the mind and, as Stan tells Edward, slow 'the progress of all mankind.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 22 "Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy" — Johnson uses 'Cartmanland' to lay out the problem of evil: Kyle loses his faith when the wicked Cartman gains perfect happiness, giving a logical problem-of-moral-evil argument against God. Johnson shows why the story of Job and Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' fail, then explains the greater-good and free-will defenses (invoking Augustine that only free acts are good) and the residual problem of natural evils like Kyle's hemorrhoid. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by South Park's Jesus, that God permits both moral and natural evil so we develop character, while noting the surviving evidential problem of evil's sheer amount.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 23 "To Know … and Believe" — Gallagher uses Lost's Rose Henderson, who says 'I just know,' to expound Aquinas on faith and reason. Aquinas places faith midway between Plato's knowledge (epistêmê) and opinion (doxa) and distinguishes its material object (God) from its formal object (first truth). Gallagher explains that all knowledge begins in the senses, so God's existence is known only by demonstration (the five ways), while faith's fuller content requires grace. Rose's sins bracket the argument: Charlie's despair is acedia, while Rose's insistence that she 'knows' the island cured her is presumption, mistaking faith for scientific knowledge.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 25 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Sirvent and Baker use Stewart's mockery of politicians who claim a divine endorsement (Bachmann's certainty of a 'miracle,' Wyatt Cenac reporting from a Las Vegas-style heaven) to apply John Locke's critique of religious 'enthusiasm'—the arrogance of taking one's own intuitions for divine direction without weighing them against reason. They then deploy Gadamer's philosophical hermeneutics against the 'objectivism' of Glenn Beck and Pat Robertson, arguing that treating scripture as an unambiguous rulebook ignores how every reading is conditioned by culture and history.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 26 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — LoPresti uses the 'This Week in God' segments (the God Machine, Ed Helms's Hindu-vs-Mayan 'faith-off,' Colbert's inclusivist White House roast) to lay out three responses to religious diversity—exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism—and defends John Cobb's Whiteheadian process-metaphysics pluralism. He insists the distinct concepts of religions be respected rather than collapsed, citing Buddhist impermanence and no-Self and the South Asian Atman/Brahman as unique and non-reducible, and closes by reading the show's turn to political framing of religion through Marx's claim that religion is a mechanism for controlling the masses.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 27 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Johnson argues that Fox News's 'war on Christmas' is fabricated and that the real conflict is a centuries-long Christian war FOR Christmas—Constantine tacking Jesus's birth onto pagan late-December Saturnalia and solstice celebrations. Using Stewart's and Colbert's segments plus Kevin Bleyer-style history, he defends the separation of church and state (courthouse nativities and school Nativity plays as unconstitutional endorsements of Christianity), debunks David Barton's claims that Jefferson was a conservative Christian, and shows Jefferson the deist coining 'a wall of separation between church and state.'
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 4 "There Is No God in Desperation" — Sutton and Held use King's Desperation and its God-speaking boy David Carver to stage the problem of evil, opening with Hume's Epicurean dilemma and Rowe's and Draper's evidential arguments from superfluous suffering (Brian's coma, Pie's murder). They survey theistic replies as defenses (Augustine's evil-as-privation, skeptical-theism humility) and theodicies (Hick's soul-making 'God is refining,' the free-will theodicy, Aquinas on natural law preserving the whole), concluding with van Inwagen that we lack epistemic warrant to judge God. Held reframes evil as a human problem of suffering, and reads Marinville's arc through Kierkegaard's despair and Anselm's 'faith seeking understanding,' arguing the antidote to 'desperation' (unbelief) is a non-cognitive, affective faith that keeps investigating.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 16 "Chapter 6 The Gospel According to Mark (Twain)" — Craig Vasey reads Twain's Letters from the Earth, narrated by a skeptical Satan, as a defense of critical thinking rather than the ranting of a bitter old man. He unpacks Satan's mockery of a self-understanding in which God obsesses over and demands worship from humans, a sexless harp-playing Heaven, and the punishment of curious, ignorant Adam and Eve, echoing Hume's catalogue of suffering (the fly as 'divine ambassador'). Invoking Nietzsche on life-after-death as vengeance dressed as love, and Socrates' 'unexamined life,' Vasey argues Twain's real target is human gullibility and willful childishness, calling humanity to grow up, think, and take responsibility instead of scapegoating a celestial fantasy.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 30 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Morgan asks when it is wrong for fathers to impose their ideals on children, arguing that forcing activities (like violin practice) risks alienation because meaningful pursuits must be embraced 'from the inside.' Using Robert Noggle's Rawls-derived hierarchy of goods (basic, pre-primary, primary, secondary, specialized), he grants fathers may guide toward universal goods but rejects Noggle's claim that parents may impose a full religious worldview, favoring David Archard's weaker right to 'guide family life' while respecting the child's growing capacity to choose – permitting compelled practice of talents only in light of the child's emerging identity.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 13 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Austin uses the everyday sense that 'we need the bean' to introduce a metaphysical debate about whether we need God to ground ethics, framed through the fair-trade coffee case. He contrasts Erik Wielenberg, who treats necessary ethical truths (e.g., that unfair trade is wrong, that suffering is intrinsically evil) as brute 'furniture of the universe' and follows Kant in holding that we ought to be moral simply because it is our duty, with J. P. Moreland, who argues such objective moral values, our knowledge of them, and the normative pull of obligation fit a theistic worldview better than naturalism. The chapter presents God as the 'Necessary Ground of Being' behind moral reality without settling the dispute.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 8 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — In this foreword, historian Stephen Nissenbaum frames the book's central puzzle by asking the reader to picture Santa Claus kneeling in the Bethlehem manger and feeling why the image jars. He argues Christmas began as a fourth-century compromise: the Church Fathers fixed Jesus' birthday on December 25 to co-opt Saturnalia and the solstice and to refute Docetism (the claim Christ only 'seemed' to have a body) by giving him a human birthday. He traces how the resulting tension between piety and revelry led the Puritans to ban Christmas and how the secular, commercial Santa of Moore's 1823 poem came to dominate the American holiday, leaving the manger and the sleigh perpetually unreconciled.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 9 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Editor Scott Lowe's introduction surveys the volume, using the disputed origins of Christmas – the December date borrowed from Sol Invictus and Yule, the Christmas tree from Germanic custom, and a Santa descended from Odin, Thor and Krampus rather than any Christian saint – to show how little about the holiday is settled. It previews each contributor's argument, from Hume-based attacks on the virgin birth and Aiken's denial of a 'War on Christmas' to Foucauldian readings of Santa's surveillance, the ethics of the Santa lie, and atheist or Festivus alternatives, positioning the book as a set of philosophical debates over what Christmas actually means.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 12 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Theologian Victor Lyons defends the virgin birth against the Humean empiricist objection voiced by Dawkins, Hitchens and Harris. He marshals the creeds and Church Fathers (Ignatius, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Origen's reply to Celsus) and argues Matthew's and Luke's independent nativity narratives point to a pre-gospel tradition of the virginal conception. Against Hume's claim that a wise man proportions belief to evidence, Lyons contends experience is not an infallible guide and that ruling out the miraculous a priori is a circular limit on inquiry, casting Mary and Joseph as the first skeptics who nonetheless accepted an event outside natural experience.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 13 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Medievalist Todd Preston argues that 'Put Christ Back in Christmas' misreads the holiday, which in the English tradition was always a balance of Christian and non-Christian elements. He shows Augustine (in On Christian Doctrine) and Boethius (in the Consolation of Philosophy, guided by Lady Philosophy) licensed Christians to absorb useful pagan philosophy, and that this apologetic openness let King Alfred, Pope Gregory and St. Boniface repurpose rather than erase heathen practice – turning Thor's oak into the Christmas fir. Tracing the Old English 'Cristesmæsse', Yule/Jol and Modraniht, and the secular revelry of Sir Gawain that Wyclif condemned, he concludes an authentic Christmas keeps its pagan half.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 15 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Scott Aiken argues the conservative 'War on Christmas' pushed by Gibson and O'Reilly is illusory on both fronts: cultural Christianity has already won, and keeping nativity scenes out of public schools protects minority rights under the Establishment Clause rather than persecuting the majority. He then mounts a separate attack, claiming both Christmas myths are bad on their merits – the nativity (star that leads wise men, vanishing Magi, Joseph's pointless genealogy) promotes mere credulity rather than tested faith, while the Santa myth glorifies a slave-owning surveiller who makes goodness merely instrumental. He adds that teaching the false Santa story undercuts parents' testimonial authority to teach the gospel as true.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 16 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Guy Bennett-Hunter treats both the Santa story and the virginal conception as mythologies whose value lies in meaning, not literal fact, drawing on Barthes and Gadamer's dictum that a myth needs no verification outside itself. He deploys Hume on miracles and Russell's Teapot to argue it is no more rational to believe the sacred myth literally than the Santa one, then turns to Tillich's religious case: taking the virgin birth literally is idolatry that drags the ultimate God into the chain of cause and effect. He urges 'breaking' the myth – keeping its significance while dropping its literal truth – a ladder to be kicked away like Edmund Gosse's childhood test of idolatry.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 22 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Will Williams recounts the legend that St. Nicholas of Myra, the historical basis of Santa Claus, attended the Council of Nicaea (325) and punched the heretic Arius, who taught that the Son was created and not fully God ('there was a time when the Son was not'). Setting the fight to a parody of 'The Night Before Christmas', Williams explains via Athanasius why the divinity of Christ mattered – only if Jesus is truly God can his death secure salvation. He contrasts this fiercely theological bishop with the de-Christianized modern Santa, using the syncretism of 'Here Comes Santa Claus' to argue Nicholas would deplore what consumerist Christmas has become.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 30 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Tallman offers a naturalistic (atheist) justification for celebrating Christmas, arguing first that the holiday's date and rituals (December 25 solstice, Christmas trees, Odin-derived Santa) predate and are not exclusively Christian, so non-believers may find their own meaning in them. Drawing on George Santayana's and Steven Cahn's 'religious naturalism,' she argues rituals and moral communities give meaning without supernatural belief, so atheists engaging even overtly religious rites (like Westerners doing Hindu-rooted yoga) are not being disingenuous. She locates a secular 'spirit of Christmas' — giving, love, community — in It's a Wonderful Life, where humans, not God, save George Bailey, and closes on a Venn-diagram overlap of Christian and naturalist Christmases.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 31 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Mason, a developmental psychologist writing as a Pagan, narrates her decades-long religious journey through James Fowler's Stages of Faith model, using each stage to reinterpret Christmas. She recounts childhood confusion over carols and chimney-invading strangers, fundamentalist-Christian zeal (stage 3 group belonging, then stage-4 doubt as she 'crusaded' against pagan Christmas trees), Unitarian Universalist questioning, and finally Wiccan/Pagan practice centered on Hecate and the winter-solstice Wheel of the Year (rediscovering Christmas's pagan roots in holly, mistletoe, and Yule). Reaching Fowler's stage 5 'Conjunctive Faith,' she concludes Christmas is neither hers nor anyone's to own but a self-perpetuating commercial 'Hallmark' phenomenon she can now greet with equanimity.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 18 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Taliaferro and Le Gall's 'The Great Escape' weighs four philosophical objections to cannabis-induced altered states — falsehood (Plato's ban on poetry/theatre in the Republic), distortion of reason (Euripides' Bacchae, James on nitrous oxide), undermining of agency (the Sirens, De Quincey's opium), and loss of self-determination (the Stoic Epictetus on freedom) — then surveys Jewish, Christian and Islamic treatments of wine, coffee and hashish. They rebut the objections using Aristotle's cathartic defense of theatre and Locke's imagination-based account of freedom, concluding that if cannabis is no worse than wine the philosophical and religious case against it is not decisive.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 34 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Barkman, prompted by his wedding guests' shared discomfort with his best man's tattooed arms, sets out to dispel a 'Christian Confucian confusion' that reads piety as requiring a tattoo-free body. He shows Leviticus 19:28 and 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 condemn tattooing only where it signals allegiance to impure cults or misuse of the body, not tattooing in itself, and that Confucius's Hsiao King injunction against wounding the body one receives from one's parents was linked to tattoos only by Han Chinese racism against tattooed minorities. Citing General Yue Fei's mother inking loyalty on his back, he concludes ink can even be pious, though a child under a parent's legitimate authority owes obedience if forbidden it.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" — Henry Jacoby channels W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' through South Park's Stan Marsh, who debunks John Edward, holistic healers, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the believer and that faith is belief without evidence. The chapter distinguishes prudential from evidential reasons and dismantles Pascal's Wager using episodes like 'Cartmanland' (why would a good God torment nonbelievers?) and 'Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?' (which religion?). Stan's speech to Edward's audience frames uncritical belief as mental laziness that slows the progress of mankind.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 23 "To Know … and Believe" — Daniel Gallagher uses Lost's Rose, who insists 'I just know' her husband lives and the island cured her, to apply Aquinas's account of faith as 'mid-way between knowledge and opinion.' Drawing on Plato's episteme/doxa distinction and Aquinas's God/'first truth' conceptual distinction plus the five ways, he argues reason can demonstrate that God exists while faith (a grace) grasps what reason cannot. Rose exemplifies both the sin of presumption (mistaking faith for knowledge, treating the island as God's certain instrument) and, by contrast to Charlie's acedia, robust faith, so the chapter urges keeping faith and reason harmonized rather than conflated.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 21 "19. The Orville as Philosophy The Dangers of Religion" — The chapter argues that Seth MacFarlane's The Orville is a pointed critique of religion, especially when merged with political and military power. Through the warrior-god Avis worshipped by the Krill (read as stand-ins for militant evangelicals and Islamist jihadists) and the Moclans' patriarchal bigotry, it contends religion is portrayed as archaic and dangerous. It deploys Socrates's Euthyphro argument to reject divine command theory, contrasts the Krill's dogmatic certainty with the secular Union's self-correcting ethics, and invokes Buber's I–Thou to explain the 'de-souling' of outsiders, while defending Lockean separation of church and state against theocracy and theonomistic ethics.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 28 "26. Midnight Mass as Philosophy The Problems with Religion" — The chapter argues that Mike Flanagan's Midnight Mass, through its atheist surrogate Riley, mounts a cumulative case for atheism. Riley's 'campfire' theory naturalistically explains religion's origins; Riley and Dr. Gunning's refusal to call Leeza's healing a miracle enacts Hume's argument against testimony for miracles; Dr. Gunning's EPP explanation of the 'vampires' rebuts methodological naturalism. Sheriff Hassan's grief over his wife voices the problem of evil (Mackie) against the free-will defense (Plantinga), while Erin's dying monologue endorses a Humean/Buddhist no-self bundle theory over the soul. Johnson argues the series treats faith as an epistemic and moral vice and holy books as dangerously interpretable.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 31 "29. Frank Herbert’s Dune as Philosophy The Need to Think for Yourself" — Reading the Sci Fi Channel miniseries Frank Herbert's Dune and Children of Dune, Littmann argues the saga warns against letting leaders or religions think for us: Paul Atreides fakes being the Fremen Mahdi, wages a holy war, and founds a theocratic tyranny that Alia and Leto II carry to worse extremes. He sets Plato's Republic (the guardian class, the noble lie, rule by the wise) and Hobbes against pro-democracy thinkers—Locke's consent and natural rights, Mill's harm principle, Dewey's democracy—then cites Locke, Paine and Russell on religion's dangers, closing with W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' that one must not accept religious claims without sufficient evidence. The chapter reads Paul's dictatorship and the Bene Gesserit's engineered messiah as dramatizations of the historical abuses of concentrated and religious power.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 64 "61. God’s Not Dead as Philosophy Trying to Prove God Exists" — The chapter evaluates the arguments college freshman Josh delivers in God's Not Dead and finds them to fail while the film demonizes atheists via caricature and the Christian persecution complex. It rebuts the Kalam cosmological argument (traced to al-Ghazali) with vacuum fluctuations and a quantum-foam explanation, shows the Big Bang refutes rather than confirms Genesis, and uses Russell's teapot and Hume's evidence proportioning on the burden of proof. Against Josh's 'without God everything is permissible' it applies Plato's Euthyphro to sink divine command theory, answers the free-will defense to the problem of evil, and closes that the film's fideism makes knowledge impossible.

### The Collective Unconscious

The collective unconscious is Carl Jung's term for a deep stratum of the mind that lies beneath the personal unconscious and is shared by all human beings. Unlike Freud's unconscious of individually repressed memories, it consists of inherited structures—the archetypes—that predispose people to experience and imagine the world in recurring patterns. Jung offered it to explain why similar symbols and mythic themes appear across cultures with no historical contact, treating them as expressions of a common psychic inheritance rather than borrowed ideas.

- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 48 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Liz Stillwaggon Swan explains why crime dramas like Criminal Minds, CSI, and Bones are so watchable: Jung's shadow archetype and collective unconscious mean the Devil in human form on screen taps humanity's shared dark layer, while Aristotle's catharsis lets viewers experience pity and fear safely from the couch, identifying with characters like repulsed Garcia or intellectualizing Dr. Brennan. She adds the CSI effect - jurors with warped expectations of DNA and fingerprint work - and argues the shows satisfy a deep need to see devils like Bundy and Dahmer caught within a tidy forty-three minutes.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 31 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Callis reads the 1931 Lugosi film through Jung: Dracula is Mina's Shadow archetype and animus, embodying her repressed fear of sexuality and of the married life she claims to want, while the vampire's presence in every culture places him in the collective unconscious. Mina's arc - the Call to Adventure, crossing the threshold into Dracula's embrace, and 'resurrection' after his staking - becomes a Shero's Journey of confronting the shadow, with Dracula also playing the Shapeshifter archetype. The chapter ends doubting the happy ending, asking whether Mina defeated her shadow or merely surrendered her dreams of freedom.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 13 "4. How Possible Is the Impossible Girl" — Smith asks how one Clara can exist as Oswin the converted Dalek, a Victorian governess, and a present-day nanny, and answers with philosophy of mind: after the real Clara steps into the Doctor's timeline on Trenzalore, the 'echoes' are best understood as manifestations within the Doctor's own subconscious, read through Freud's dream interpretation and id-ego-superego (the echoes act as his conscience) and Jung's archetypes, collective unconscious, individuation, and synchronicity—her name meaning clarity, her red wardrobe marking the copies, and the leaf of 'The Rings of Akhaten' as the meaningful coincidence that produced her. Aristotle's Categories frames what Oswin still shares with humanity after Dalek conversion, and the soufflé-is-the-recipe line together with social-cognition research on multiple selves supports the conclusion that the Claras are metaphysically the same person despite different bodies and roles—making the 'Impossible Girl' possible.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 26 "15. Aladdin Sane or Cracked Actor" — Riches and Watson weigh two readings of Bowie's 'cracked actor': either his cut-up method and persona-blurring (Ziggy taking over, the family schizophrenia that killed Terry) blurred imagination into hallucination, a Cartesian dream-vs-waking doubt filtered through Bowie's Jungian 'crack in the sky,' archetypes, and collective unconscious; or he deliberately challenged the sanity/madness distinction, as Foucault's Madness and Civilization and antipsychiatrist Thomas Szasz did. On the second reading 'All the Madmen,' the androgyny of 'Queen Bitch' and 'Jean Genie,' and 'Oh You Pretty Things'' Homo Superior rebel against Aristotle's identification of humanity with rationality, winning everyone the freedom to be their unconventional selves.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 23 "10. Stranger Shadows" — Cornell reads the Upside Down as an externalized Jungian Shadow: the faceless Demogorgon, 'almost human but it wasn't,' embodies the archetypal shadow of the collective unconscious intruding into Hawkins, and the moral task is integrating it with the conscious ego. Will's possession by the Shadow Monster shows what Jung calls the ego identifying with an unintegrated shadow (his timidity leaving him overpowered), while El is the contrast: after her symbolic rebirth from the fleshy wall she faces absolute evil, acknowledges her own monstrous capacity to kill, and turns the shadow into heroism, ending at Nietzsche's 'becoming who she is.'
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 18 "The Illusion of Choice" — Kajtár argues BioShock Infinite is meta-fictional art: applying Dewey's Art as Experience, the whole journey from lighthouse to drowning is 'an experience', a unified aesthetic whole you live as Booker rather than a mere object of contemplation. The recurring lighthouse-man-city figures work as Jungian archetypes of the collective unconscious (extended to Campbell's hero's journey structuring Booker's departure, initiation, and return), and the Rapture cameo plus the ocean of lighthouses make the game a story about video game storytelling itself, where the constants are the fictional worlds players enter and the variables are sky or sea. The bird-or-cage choice that changes nothing, like Booker forgetting his 122 previous attempts, shows that rail-bounded interactivity does not disqualify the game from being art, and Levine's 'narrative legos' may one day unite story with real choice.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 15 "NOTES" — Baldwin argues the popular view of Bushido as a moral code (Nitobe, Star Wars, Kurosawa, Campbell's Jungian hero archetype) is historically wrong: by the Hagakure, Bushido is a death-ready 'mode of action' so morally neutral that even villains like Takezo Kensei or Sylar can practice it. He traces Hiro's evolution from comic-book and video-game hero-worship, through the Yaeko betrayal that turned Kensei into Adam Monroe, toward the fearless Future Hiro ideal of 'no-mind' readiness for death (echoing D.T. Suzuki's Zen reading). Because the Meiji reforms abolished the samurai class, Hiro can never literally be a samurai, only follow Bushido analogically, which lets him remain both superhero and samurai.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 18 "Day Residue" — Auxier reverse-engineers how Nolan's dream-sharing could work — sedatives aligning brainwaves like a laser, the electrical dream machine, nested electromagnetic fields — and argues each deeper level buys time at the cost of lucidity, with Limbo as 'psychosis of forgetting.' He explains the film through Susanne Langer's theory of mythic consciousness: dreams become communicable only when forced into narrative order, so dream architecture is the insertion of images that survive transformation into the subject's dispositions — hence Eames plants the pinwheel in the safe so Fischer believes he placed it himself, and the Mombasa elders represent a collective, pre-modern consciousness modern individuals have lost. The resolution of the baggage-claim puzzle (Fischer's calm) is that the inception removed a doubt rather than planting one: doubt spreads easily in modern minds, and Fischer touched the ancestral place where 'our fathers desire our happiness.'
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Addey analyzes the show's web of coincidences - Sawyer and Boone crossing paths in the Australian police station, Jack meeting Desmond in the hatch - and distinguishes genuine coincidence from divine providence, fatalism, and determinism. She applies Jung's theory of synchronicity to Locke's walkabout conviction that he was 'meant' to reach the island, then uses the birthday paradox, the law of truly large numbers, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability to show why viewers and conspiracy theorists overestimate the improbability of such connections. Finally she evaluates Jacob's candidacy experiment as flawed social science: the candidates' circumstantial ignorance, maintained by the Others' deceptions, undermines the free and morally responsible choices Jacob claims to be testing, which is why the curious Hurley deserved to become protector.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 28 "Notes" — Reads Star Trek's "final frontier" through the European encounter with American Indians: the Hobbesian war-of-all-against-all stereotype of the "bloodthirsty savage" and Rousseau's opposing noble savage frame "The Paradise Syndrome", whose wigwam-and-tepee set mixes tribes into a no-place utopia. The chapter uses Hegel-style staged histories to debunk Star Trek's warp/pre-warp developmental scale (Spock on the Organians in "Errand of Mercy") as metaphysical assumption rather than biology, and counterposes the Prime Directive's noninterference to indigenous self-sovereignty and the Haudenosaunee-style consent governance that inspired the Federation. Chakotay's vision quests, the medicine bundle, Wesley's habak experience with Lakanta the Traveler in "Journey's End", and the Medicine Wheel in "Cathexis" are then interpreted through Jung's archetypes and collective unconscious, with Kirk, Spock, McCoy, and Scotty as the four Jungian modes of consciousness.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 36 "Notes" — Maps Campbell's Hero's Journey onto Luke's arc in A New Hope (ordinary world, meeting the mentor, crossing the threshold, atonement with the 'Dark Father' Vader), then argues both Campbell and Lucas misunderstand myth: following Malinowski, myth is a living social charter and therefore ideology, so Star Wars' cosmic dualism, male-centered monomyth, and celebration of violence conceal political and commercial power. The chapter's closing turn - 'Star Wars(TM) is the real Empire and the fans its consumer-subjects,' with Reagan's SDI and an 'insurgents vs. Empire' reading of the Rebellion as illustrations - applies ideology-critique to the franchise itself.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 12 "4. A Muscle Car and a Mythic Quest" — Huntingford reads Sam and Dean as the Cowboy incarnation of Jung's universal Mythic Hero archetype, their Impala road-trip an odyssey of Campbell's monomyth and Jungian individuation confronting the 'shadow' (Amara as the Darkness). She uses Hegel to cast the brothers' alienation as the start of self-discovery toward absolute knowledge, Kierkegaard to praise their nonconformity over the crowd, and Sartre's 'hell is other people' and freedom-as-otherness to argue the Quest requires killing the false narrative self—Chuck the Trickster—to become free.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Briony Addey defines coincidence and distinguishes three theories the castaways might invoke to say events are 'meant to be' — divine providence, fatalism, and determinism — using Locke's belief in his walkabout destiny and Eloise Hawking's 'the universe course corrects' as fatalist cases. She introduces Jung's synchronicity and collective unconscious as an acausal explanation of meaningful coincidence, then debunks our intuitions with the birthday paradox, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability, before criticizing Jacob's deception 'experiment' on the candidates for failing standards of informed consent and culpable versus non-culpable ignorance.

### Fate and Foreknowledge

Fate and foreknowledge name a cluster of problems about whether the future's being settled or known in advance is compatible with human freedom. If events are fated to occur, or if an omniscient God already knows what a person will do, it can seem that the person could not have done otherwise, undermining genuine choice and moral responsibility. Philosophers from the Stoics and Boethius through medieval theologians and modern thinkers have proposed various resolutions: distinguishing foreknowledge from causation, arguing that God stands outside time so that knowledge does not precede the act, or holding that freedom requires only acting from one's own will rather than the ability to do otherwise. The debate remains central to discussions of divine providence, determinism, and the nature of free will.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 47 "Fate, Freedom, and Foreknowledge" — Schick opens with the Morpheus-Neo exchange on Fate ('I don't like the idea that I'm not in control of my life') and Cypher's 'You call this free?', arguing that whatever freedom the enslaved enjoy outside the Matrix may be equally illusory: if the Oracle's prophecies are true, the future is fixed, and then no one, not even Neo, is in control of his life. He poses the subversive question of whether Cypher's return to happy slavery was really a betrayal, and sets out to examine the natures of fate and freedom.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 50 "Unknown" — Schick parallels the film's Oracle with Delphi - tripod beside the oven's fumes, 'Know Thyself' inscribed at both shrines, the cigarette a wink at the priestesses' smoke - and recalls Alexander the Great's forced prophecy and Oedipus as emblems of belief in fate. He then introduces Richard Taylor's corrected fatalism, 'whatever happens is unavoidable' rather than events fated no matter what anyone does, and grants that given the Oracle's accuracy, fatalism is an eminently reasonable view to hold about the world of The Matrix.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 51 "Unknown" — Schick presses the Oracle's foreknowledge into the classic theological dilemma: if she knows Neo will knock over the vase - as she correctly foresaw that and the fates of Morpheus, Trinity, and Neo himself - then it must happen, and no one is free; the price of omniscience is freedom. He walks through Boethius's formulation of the incompatibility, Calvin's predestination of lives fixed like film frames, and the Aquinas-style rejoinder that omnipotence and omniscience extend only to the logically possible, leaving the Oracle's own noodle-baker - would you still have broken it if I hadn't said anything? - and the worry that even predictability by psychological law would doom free will.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 53 "Unknown" — The chapter argues that the Oracle's predictions come true not because the future is fixed but because they are self-fulfilling: her remark about the vase is what brings about its breaking ('would you still have broken it if I hadn't said anything?'), and Morpheus's 'she told you exactly what you needed to hear' shows she shapes rather than reads the future. On this reading the Oracle needs no real foreknowledge, only believers who trust that she knows the path. Only so can Neo be in control of his life in a world where 'anything, within the bounds of reason, is possible.'
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 79 "Unknown" — Locating the Matrix's power in the fear of death - Neo frozen on the ledge, then discovering in the jump program that he must 'let it all go... fear, doubt, and disbelief' - the chapter reads 'the body cannot live without the mind' as meaning that even outside the Matrix the body depends on the mind's beliefs. The Oracle's either/or prophecy embodies the postulates: Neo's Fate is fulfilled through free choice (his life for Morpheus's) and through faith in our own Potential, so the God or savior we postulate is finally revealed as an extension of ourselves as we transcend separateness, not a separate miracle-worker.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 80 "Unknown" — The chapter presents the subway confrontation as the film's turning point: defying the crew's iron rule that one runs from Agents, and Cypher's 'realistic' sneering, Neo freely accepts death to save Morpheus, overcoming the fundamental fear that grounds the Matrix's power in both worlds. The Oracle's 'next life' prophecy is then fulfilled to the letter when Trinity - 'I'm not afraid anymore... you can't be dead. Because I love you' - refuses to believe in death, and Neo returns in his next life as the One.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 28 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Thomas Hibbs reads the Quest's ending as providential: the Ring is destroyed against Frodo's own will at the Cracks of Doom, through Gollum, exactly as Gandalf hinted when he said Bilbo was 'meant' to find the Ring, 'and not by its maker'. Providence first appears as chance - Bilbo's arrival, Aragorn's landing at the Pelennor, Gandalf 'sent back' until his task is done - and is discerned only in hindsight as the epic's dramatic unity. Against the worry that providence cancels freedom, he uses Kant on duty and dignity (Frodo's 'I will take the Ring', Sam's 'I must see it through', set against Denethor ruling his 'own end'), while noting Tolkien rejects Kant's autonomy/heteronomy split, and with Augustine he treats evil as parasitic, able only to mar itself ('Oft evil will shall evil mar').
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 30 "Fallible Prophecies" — Credits Aristotle with first raising whether the future is fixed and builds a sevenfold taxonomy of how a Seer might access the future, from fallible sensory prediction like Trelawney's and Muggle weather reports, through glimpses of likely or possible futures as Dumbledore describes, to infallible access to a deterministic or actual future. The section then asks which kind Trelawney's two genuine prophecies are.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 31 "Self-Fulfilling Prophecies" — Reads Dumbledore's gloss on the prophecy, 'you are free to choose your way, quite free to turn your back on the prophecy', as treating even real prophecies as non-compelling, and argues the two true prophecies cannot be mere likelihoods because they are involuntary trances with a magical source. Trelawney's card-reading episodes in Half-Blood Prince, accurate while she is oblivious to Harry behind the statue and to the lightning-struck tower, hint at inconsistent unconscious access to the future.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 32 "Destiny" — Examines Dumbledore's suggestion that the first prophecy was self-fulfilling: it did not originally mean Harry rather than Neville, but Voldemort's choice of the half-blood he saw himself in marked Harry as his equal, and Snape's ejection from the interview left Voldemort ignorant of the risk that attacking Harry would transfer power to him. Invoking Alexander of Aphrodisias's discussion of the Oedipus prophecy, the section argues a genuine prophecy reveals rather than causes the future, so self-fulfillment cannot distinguish Trelawney's real predictions, since the prophecy never made Voldemort do anything.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 33 "A Rodent’s Destiny" — Takes Rowling's 2007 remark that there is 'no such thing as destiny' and maps the logical space it could occupy: compatibilist freedom within a predetermined course, libertarian freedom with a fixed future of true statements about what will happen, or an open future where claims about free choices are neither true nor false until made. The section asks whether Dumbledore means prophecies do not compel anyone or that their content is merely one of several possible futures.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 34 "Time Travel and Fixed Time" — Argues Trelawney's second prophecy, that the servant will break free and rejoin the Dark Lord that very night, was far too improbable to be a merely likely prediction given how easily Wormtail's escape could have failed. Likewise the chain running from the first prophecy through Wormtail becoming Secret-Keeper to Lily's protective sacrifice shows the 'real' prophecies need a stronger connection to the actual future than probability.
