- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 11 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Auxier, an Atkins dieter, argues the diet works for the reason Dewey gives in Human Nature and Conduct: habits built in calm moments are the bulwark against desire in crisis, and Atkins succeeds by reshaping which gratifications are habitually available — 'a steak for the black eye of desire.' He then transfers Atkins's physiology to thinking: television and advertising serve 'conceptual carbs,' packaged bundles of doubt, emotion, and readiness to act that bypass inquiry and leave the public 'intellectually diabetic' and ideological. Peirce's pragmatic maxim is translated into an eight-step mental exercise (worked through a parent's tattoo-or-piercing doubt about a teenage daughter), while Descartes's hyperbolic doubt is discarded in favor of pragmatism's 'genuine doubt.'
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 16 "(Positive) Violence of Self-Discipline" — Shusterman opens with Plato and Socrates' ancient quarrel against poetry - banning the artists from the Republic, much as rap is demonized today - and rejects Aristotle's catharsis strategy of quarantining art from life, applying pragmatist aesthetics (Dewey, James, and the Du Bois-Alain Locke lineage) to argue that rap's aesthetic violence of beat, scratch, and "Bring the Noise" is life-enhancing force, with reality rap's metaphysics of mix and flow against Plato's changeless Forms. Reading KRS-One's "Stop the Violence" movement born from Scott LaRock's killing, Guru's "Choice of Weapons" (a mic or a gun), and Jeru the Damaja's command to "kill in thyself", he concludes rap overcomes bad violence not by abolishing violence but by channeling it into lyrical battle and the positive violence of self-discipline.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 14 "U2 and Philosophy" — Soper tracks Bono's public identity work across three paradigms: pre-modern Irish-Catholic inheritance, including a Du Boisian 'double consciousness' of the colonized Irish; the modernist artist-as-visionary, where Nietzsche, Freud and Marx destabilize the self and the Shalom fellowship nearly ends the band; and the postmodern masks of the Fly, Mirrorball Man and MacPhisto on the Zoo TV media collage, read via Lacan for 'Mofo' and via Baudrillard's simulacra for the 'Even Better than the Real Thing' video with its wax Beatles and cyber-sex imagery. Lyotardian skepticism toward grand ideologies explains the band's refusal of fanaticism in 'Sunday Bloody Sunday' and 'Two Hearts Beat as One'. Soper concludes that Bono fuses all three into a 'Postmodern Christian Pragmatism' that keeps Christian conviction and debt-relief activism while adopting postmodern playfulness without collapsing into ironic detachment.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 24 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Abrams explains Peirce's three modes of inference (deduction proves, induction shows, abduction merely suggests) and reconstructs, abduction by abduction, Bond's rapid chain of guesses in The World Is Not Enough: from the odd smell and foam on his fingers to the urea-coated fertilizer bomb he unknowingly delivered, the shared motto 'there's no point living if you can't feel alive' exposing Elektra's alliance with Renard, and her guilty subject-changing. He also covers the negative art: Bond plants false clues with Q's gadgets (the fingerprint re-printer, the cloaked Vanquish) while villains like Carver recode reality by sinking the Devonshire to frame the Chinese, and both sides try to force each other into false abductions. Bond wins because his mind is more playful - Peirce's 'musement', Eco's creative abduction, and an encyclopedic education - making 007 the superior player in what is ultimately a game of chance and strategy.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 15 "Tough and Tender, The Dead Keep Truckin’" — Gary Ciocco traces a line from Emerson and James through Kerouac, Ginsberg, and Neal Cassady to the Grateful Dead: Emerson's nonconformist 'infinitude of man' and James's 'live options' and religious appetite for being 'more fully alive' become, in the Beats, the project of living life itself as art ('the only people for me are the mad ones'). He argues the Beats splintered because each chased an atomistic, individual epiphany — Kerouac swinging wholesale from tender- to tough-minded temperament — while the Dead turned the same Jamesian hunger into a shared communal religious experience, a 'kindler, gentler' scene that better achieves Aristotle's eudaimonia. Cassady, muse of On the Road and driver of the Pranksters' bus, literally connects the two movements, but the Dead's unity-in-diversity made them the evolution, not the echo, of the Beats.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 19 "“You Rationalize” Jackie Brown’s Pragmatism" — K. Silem Mohammad argues Jackie Brown is a study in aporia and Wittgensteinian aspect perception: Ray Nicolette's purple/white bag paralysis, Ordell's 'Is that Rutger Hauer?' mistake, Jackie on the LAX moving walkway, and 'Across 110th Street' turning diegetic all force a re-description of experience within particular language games. The thrice-repeated Del Amo money switch-off adds no information but displays the characters' differing aspects of one event. Against Ordell's mind-fucking 'logical chains', Jackie's 'that's what you do to go through with the shit you start, you rationalize' embodies a pragmatist view of reason as context-bound use, matched by Max's calmly uncertain 'I think I do. Good enough?'
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 8 "And the Good News Second" — Auxier tests Cornel West's four marks of prophetic thinking — discernment of who bears the social cost ('Ghost of Tom Joad,' 'Born in the U.S.A.'), empathy as human connection, self-critical tracking of hypocrisy, and audacious hope (the E Street concert as galvanizing the world-weary) — and finds Springsteen nearly unmatched, yet something is missing from reading 'The Rising' as prophecy. He stages the pragmatist debate between Rorty's poetic pragmatism (poets create the vocabularies democracy lives by), West's prophetic pragmatism, and Putnam's sober reasonableness, then uses Abraham Joshua Heschel to distinguish poet from prophet: inspiration versus revelation, gratitude versus dread, the seduction-and-coercion of the call he comically retells as Jonah in Asbury Park. A true prophet would sing, with Isaiah and Jeremiah, that even the 9/11 hijackers were the rod of America's own God against its greed — so Springsteen's 'The Rising' is lamentation, not prophecy.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 21 "Back from the Edge" — McKenna and Pratt use McDermott's 'Promethean self' and meliorism to answer the riddle of Nebraska's closer 'Reason to Believe': among the dead dog, the deserted bride and the groom left at the altar, 'still at the end of every hard earned day people find some reason to believe.' They trace Springsteen's shift from escape songs ('Born to Run,' 'Thunder Road') to life at the edge ('Badlands,' 'Darkness on the Edge of Town,' and the two midnight drivers of 'State Trooper' and 'Open All Night'), arguing meaning is made by cutting and connecting relations at the margins. Belief without evidence of salvation is legitimate hope but illegitimate certainty; the reason to believe is Jamesian meliorism — making things 'not perfect, simply better.'
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 22 "Hometown Security" — Keith reads 'My Hometown' — whitewashed windows, the textile mill closing, Bruce telling his son 'take a good look around' — through Putnam's Bowling Alone, Dewey's socially constituted self, and Mead, to argue that Bruce and Kate should recommit to their dying town rather than flee in the moving van. Leopold's 'two spiritual dangers in not owning a farm' and Berry's healthy community as ecosystem ground an 'enlightened localism' that avoids both the town's racist parochialism and rootless cosmopolitanism. Volunteering, local food, and town-meeting democracy are the hometown security the song's sadness calls for.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 35 "Finding Our Way" — Trudy Milburn applies Dewey's account of habit, impulse and inquiry to navigation in the series: Adama's 'I know the way to Earth' declaration starts an inquiry whose end-in-view is continuously reformulated as humans creatively combine scriptures, pulsars and constellations as signs. Roslin uses scripture at face value and other people's belief in it, which on Dewey's anti-foundationalist terms is legitimate map-making rather than piety. The Cylons, by contrast, treat their plan as God-given, cannot reinterpret signs for themselves (needing Baltar to locate Earth) and fall back on inherited habit, which is why, on Dewey's view, they are the ones who are lost.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 10 "Progress Is a Myth that Truly Makes Life Worthwhile" — Garnar contrasts the material practice of collecting CDs -- shelving some 1,500-2,000 discs by genre, the Rachels' Egon Schiele packaging, and Humean associations binding particular discs to memories like buying blue hair dye the day he got New Order's Lowlife -- with the iPod-era 'iPhenomenon' of buying songs piecemeal from iTunes. Using William James's question 'How is the practice real?' he rejects the real/virtual split, and reads the freedom of iMedia as a corollary of Marx and Engels's 'single, unconscionable freedom -- Free Trade': the solipsistic consumer never confronts the artist the way the album as artifact (Coltrane's My Favorite Things ending, he realizes, had to end with 'But Not for Me') forces him to. The body supposedly made unnecessary by 'iLiving' remains, with Foucault, a site of discipline -- eating disorders, outsourced assembly labor, e-waste -- so he keeps his iPod but defends a plurality of media and calls progress a myth.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 25 "iPublic" — Dewey takes the iPod's beauty seriously (Chris Breen's 'beautiful and intuitive' player, Donald Norman's user-centered design) and uses John Dewey's Art as Experience to ask whether iPod use can be a 'consummatory' experience that ends with us no longer the same person — hearing a bitter song as insight into the social conditions that produced it — rather than the contrived 'now' of fashion and hyper-accumulation, per Benjamin's remark that there is 'always a sense of the same in the new'. Mass production flattened the aristocratic high-culture/folk division and handed the power to define 'cool' to advertisers and the market. The pragmatist test is political: with iTunes DRM and single-user design quietly individualizing consumption (the ritual of buying the Public Enemy tape at the mall versus the frictionless one-click download), the iPod is beautiful exactly insofar as its experiences help form a public — an inclusive, participatory democratic community.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 22 "Wait, Did I Hit Pause Where’d the Remote Get to . ." — Seng takes up the fan phenomenon of syncing The Wizard of Oz with Pink Floyd's Dark Side of the Moon and tests the three explanations fans offer: authorial intent (rejected on Pink Floyd's own repeated denials), Jungian synchronicity (rejected as needlessly complex, with the L. Frank Baum coat worn by Frank Morgan as the test case), and pure fluke. He argues the symmetries (the cash-register intro of 'Money' as Dorothy enters Technicolor, 'The Great Gig in the Sky' over the cyclone) are neither objective nor mind-created reality, but meanings made by a third factor in the experience: the viewer whose perceptual habits, in Dewey's and Louise Rosenblatt's sense, supply interpretations like reading the color-splash as prosperity or as the cost of Dorothy's lost innocence. Dorothy's own longing for home becomes the emblem of how habit, not reasoning, governs what we perceive and like.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 5 "Jimmy Buffett, Cultural Infidel" — The editors argue Buffett is a philosopher despite his own denials, in the sense of Royce and Dewey: philosophy is critical reflection on living that returns to ordinary experience, and Buffett's songs, books, and concerts pass Dewey's test of rendering everyday predicaments 'more significant, more luminous, more fruitful.' They compare 'Margaritaville' to Plato's Republic — not equal in pedigree but equal in kind as occasions for philosophical practice — to defend meaning-making as a democratic practice open to Parrotheads, not just professors. Reading the album 'Changes in Latitudes, Changes in Attitudes' as a guide, they set Buffett's 'Porpoise Driven Life,' where purpose is found by sailing your own waters in the company of friends, against Rick Warren's revelation-based 'Purpose Driven Life.'
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 10 "“Trip Around the Sun”" — Phil Oliver pairs Buffett with William James: both hold that philosophy is 'not a technical matter' but each person's sense of what life deeply means, had in non-verbal moments of elevation as much as argued in words. The chapter's core is James's 'moral holiday' — a morally legitimate respite from care and struggle — naturalized in Buffett's 'License to Chill' and 'Trip Around the Sun' ('it's good to know it's out of my control'), joined by James's lightness about error from 'The Will to Believe' and Russell's and Dawkins's responses to cosmic annihilation. Against those who hear mere hedonism, Oliver insists Jamesian holidays are care-free but never care-less: like Thoreau's 'live deliberately' echoed in 'Growing Older But Not Up,' they renew us for the return to work, and James's ambivalence about alcohol in The Varieties of Religious Experience mirrors the risk of Buffett's frozen concoctions.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 19 "“Happily Ever After, Now and Then”" — Erin McKenna explains how a feminist can love Buffett by reading 'Fins' and 'Why Don't We Get Drunk (and Screw)' as critiques of predatory land sharks rather than endorsements, and 'Margaritaville' as a man admitting 'it's my own damn fault.' Against Rousseau's pliable helpmate ideal of woman she sets Wollstonecraft's Vindication — equal education and personhood for women — and Charlotte Perkins Gilman's pragmatist-feminist case that women's economic, physical, and mental dependence stunts everyone. Buffett's novels then pass the Gilman test: Desdemona, Trevor Kane, Cleopatra Highbourne, and Sophie are smart, independent women, and the male leads must reform their habits to earn them, aiming at Desdemona's 'happily ever after, now and then' instead of the fairy-tale ending.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 22 "Wonder Why We Ever Go Home" — Duke Richey maps Buffett's West — 'Ringling, Ringling,' the Rancho Deluxe soundtrack, Tully Mars — onto Josiah Royce's philosophy of community: only people who root in a place, face its history ('wise provincialism'), and sacrifice selfish desires for the whole can build Beloved Communities, a lesson enacted when cattle rustlers Jack and Cecil accept community sanction and find belonging working the Rancho Deluxe. Wallace Stegner's coral-reef metaphor from Angle of Repose supplies the image of communities built up millimeter by millimeter yet still vulnerable to pollution and over-fishing, with Royce's environmental regret (covering 'the wounds' of the landscape with gardens) anticipating the chapter's sustainability ethic. 'Wonder Why We Ever Go Home' thus asks what we really seek when we seek grace through community: not the nomadic Pickup Truck Death of every-man-for-himself, but cooperation that makes a society to match the scenery.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 23 "“Where Did All the Good Songs Go ”" — Scott Pratt answers whether 'Margaritaville' is art by rejecting object-based theories (Kivy's score-compliance, the abstract perfect performance, the unrecorded instance that vanishes) for Dewey's Art as Experience: art is 'an experience,' complete and self-sufficient, followed by a reflective, evaluative second phase. He reads 'Makin' Music for the Money' as moving from solitary self-interested music-making to a community of musicians, and the Port of Spain steel-drum rehearsal of 'King of Somewhere Hot' that carried forward into the Miami concert as Dewey's two phases in action. Buffett's fly-fishing stories — the lost blue marlin that became 'a story,' the released Long Island bass that 'replenished his saline psyche' — supply Haeckel's ecological model in which music, like fishing, is an organism-environment interaction, making songs 'homemade' eco-music that belongs to listeners in its own ecosystem.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 21 "L2Design, n00b Knowledge As Design" — Sean Duncan follows a Rogue-class forum thread — Dismalstrike's detailed redesign proposals, debated by other players and acknowledged by a rare Blizzard 'blue post' — to argue that everyday players act as informal designers co-constructing knowledge about the game. Drawing on Donald Schön's reflection-in-action, itself rooted in the pragmatism of Dewey, James, and Peirce, he rejects the idea that rational facts come first and practice second: knowing how to fix the Rogue class is built through playing, posting, iterating, and revising. Knowledge construction is design, and the stakes extend beyond gaming to how literacy, learning, and civic participation should be understood in a world where play and work blur.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 24 "Beyond Picasso and Ronaldo Living Artfully" — Elcombe asks whether Cristiano Ronaldo, transferred to Real Madrid for $131 million—more than Picasso's Garçon à la Pipe fetched at its record 2004 auction—can be an artist like Picasso. Traditional metaphysics built on Plato's perfect Forms and Aristotle's necessary-and-sufficient conditions locks Art in a special museum realm that soccer, as a purposive sport whose beauty is only a byproduct, can never enter, leaving the game merely 'beautiful', not Art. Dewey's Art as Experience reorients the question from what art is to what art does: artworks are consummations of experience, moments of 'thatness'—that meal, that storm, that Ronaldo free kick—that lift us out of the mundane while remaining within the game's durable rules and history (Ronaldo's artistry grows from Zidane, Maradona, Cruyff, Pelé). On this pragmatist view Ronaldo is an artist in the act, the six-year-old testing a new turn on the pitch lives artfully too, and soccer's artistry becomes groundwork for communication, democracy, and the good life—doing more real work than a painting almost no one ever sees.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 12 "The Jihadist Way of Life" — Argues the Fremen are 'shockingly American': their Spannungsbogen self-discipline, spiritual self-sufficiency, and endurance of hardship exemplify Emerson's self-reliance, while the jihad's aim of razing the rule of the Great Houses into relations of equals echoes Dewey's democracy as a way of life—faith in the potentialities of every human nature. The parallel runs through the 'American Taliban' John Walker Lindh and Paul's blind walk into the desert, both acting on values Americans prize. Herbert's remark that people surrender judgment to leaders 'wrapped in the myth fabric of society' grounds the pragmatist point that Fremen myth-making, like America's exceptionalist self-image, works—and Alia's 'my brother is pragmatic' seals it.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 133 "Keith Richards the Prophet" — The arrest becomes legal philosophy: since statutes like 'reckless driving' are general while conduct is specific, law requires the art of judgment. Against John Austin's positivism (law as the sovereign's command backed by sanction), it adopts Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.'s 'bad man' view — law is just the prediction of what courts will in fact do — making Richards a 'prophet' of consequences, as when the band declined to raise a giant inflatable phallus in San Antonio. It closes with pragmatist accounts, Holmes's law as the 'external deposit' of our moral life and Dewey's law rooted in custom and judicial behavior, explaining why the South's history of racism and sexual anxiety seeped into Arkansas law.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 134 "Judge Richards Presides" — The farcical Fordyce proceeding — a golf-drunk judge sipping bourbon hidden in his sock, a BBC interview mid-trial, and Richards himself pounding the gavel at the press conference ('Case closed') — confirms for the author that Holmes was right: law is prediction all the way down, at every level from the bad man to the judge. It concludes that the 'devil' of rock was a projection of white southern fear and repressed libido, externally deposited in law yet too indeterminate to predict, as the Stones' motorcade escape at 2 a.m. showed.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 25 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Brooks argues Klosterman is an unacknowledged heir of McLuhan's media ecology: his Fargo Rock City account of hair metal's rise through FM radio, metal magazines, and MTV's 'collective unconscious,' Britney Spears as a low-definition 'cool medium' everyone rebrands, and the 'singular club scene' as global village all do media-ecology work. But Brooks docks him fifteen percent for clinging to an authenticity fantasy — the Unabomber-essay claim that technology makes us 'never been less human' — which McLuhan's dictum that 'there is absolutely no inevitability as long as there is a willingness to contemplate what is happening' refutes. In Rorty's spirit of persuading by joshing rather than arguing, he challenges Klosterman to drop the ontology and turn his interpretive powers on real problems like compassion fatigue and Darfur.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 33 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Vannatta reads Klosterman's born-again pop culture — the Left Behind novels, Victory TV's Steven, Kurt Warner's Super Bowl, Jesus Camp — as living Puritan Calvinism: original sin (Klosterman's cruel third-graders), justification by faith alone, unmediated access to God ('every man was his own priest'), and predestination that leaves uncertain whether our actions matter in the divine equation. The chapter's pivot is truth versus peace: Puritan-born-again certainty sacrifices peace for antecedent truth, from the 1675 Massachusetts settlements to Robertson and Falwell on 9/11. Against this Vannatta sets the pragmatist alternative — truth as the outcome of communal inquiry in service of peaceful living — recasting God as the web of relationships and dissolving his own childhood camp's contradiction between 'I'm Third' and its cult of competition.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 11 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Ray Bossert reads American Gods as an allegory of American philosophy: like Gaiman's gods, American philosophers labor invisibly in the background while European publics canonize their thinkers, and Shadow's prison exchanges show the point, since Loki must beg him to read Herodotus ('It's cool') while Johnnie Larch's 'don't piss off people who work in airports' beats Shadow's abstract generalization in usefulness. Following Hickman's Deweyan instrumentalism, he argues the gods are survival tools humans craft from need and discard when obsolete, so Czernobog's hammer gives way to Media's television, Wednesday treats even his own son as an instrument, and the buffalo man's 'believe everything' is advice about keeping one's tools of survival working. The chapter ends on liberty: Shadow refuses to be a god because 'we don't need anyone to believe in us,' and in the Egyptian death trial he claims the most American reward, the freedom to choose his own afterlife.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 40 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Eugene Halton retells human history as the fable of Peirce's 'degenerate monkey': a neotenous, instinct-weak blunderer (Homo errans) whose gift for abductive guessing and attunement to the intelligence of the wild was inverted by agriculture and civilization into Narcissistic self-mirroring, anthropocentric religion, and the worship of the machine. The telepathic, rubber-masked mutants of Beneath the Planet of the Apes who worship the Alpha-Omega bomb ('I reveal my Inmost Self unto my God!') become a prophecy of our own screen-mediated, empathy-poor life, from Facebook to Botox, in Huxley's pleasure-conditioning rather than Orwell's pain. Against this, the chapter holds up Armando's Franciscan empathy for Caesar and the hope of a 'planet of the regenerate monkeys' re-attuned to the community of wild life.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 29 "Psych and Philosophy" — Amanda Lusky argues Shawn is a model pragmatist in the lineage of Peirce, James, and Dewey: he treats ideas as tools judged by consequences, is tough-minded about facts over theory (James's temperament distinction), and applies the pragmatic maxim from the squirrel-and-tree dispute to his loosely formed but working hunches. His co-operative inquiry with Gus and the SBPD - Gus's safe-cracking knowledge in 'Sixty Five Million Years Off,' passing Lassiter's polygraph in 'Shawn Rescues Darth Vader' - enacts Dewey's democratic community solving problems together, and the chapter reads his tolerance of Gus's paranormal leads ('The Devil's in the Details') as pragmatic openness that enriches Santa Barbara's democratic life.
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 24 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter compares Barney's 'True story' pronouncements with William James's pragmatism, using James's squirrel anecdote and the 'Zoo or False' monkey-mugging to ask when an evidentially undecidable dispute becomes a live practical question. Like James's pragmatic cases for free will and religious comfort, Barney's monkey story and the twenty-eight-year-old 'with some sun damage' are beliefs made true by their practical (mostly entertainment) value, then replaced like outdated theories when new evidence arrives, as James's consistency requirement demands. The divergence: the Barney Stinson (BS) theory of truth is self-serving, engineering unverifiable stories others cannot disprove, while James weighs what works for everyone's experience.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 15 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter asks whether Boyd's survival of Raylan's bullet in the premiere was a genuine sign from God: the atheist invokes Ockham's Razor and the promise of a naturalistic explanation, while the theist replies that a world-creating God would act through the laws of nature, making such explanations neutral rather than negative evidence. It then applies William James's pragmatist standard from his study of mystical experience - judge the sign by the fruits of the Spirit (Galatians' love, joy, peace, self-control) it bears - to Boyd's prison ministry, his urging Raylan to forgive Arlo, and his meth-lab crusade. Despite Boyd's eventual apostasy after Bo murders his congregation, the author concludes he passes James's test, since faith is a maintained journey that can be lost, and the born-again Boyd still struggles - like Jacob becoming Israel - rather than scheming coldly.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 29 "16. My Name Is—Hang on, What Was It Meant to Be Again Are You Sure Well, Okay Then . ." — Tim Jones argues the book is not really a love story but a warning about identity: against Descartes's transcendent self, the American pragmatists William James, Cooley, and Mead hold that the self is fluid and socially constituted, and Westley's serial reinvention (farm boy, Dread Pirate Roberts, Man in Black) - along with Mandy Patinkin's cathartic channeling of his father's death into Inigo - shows the freedom this mutability grants. The Goldman frame then exposes the danger: the fictionalized Goldman seizes Morgenstern's text, cuts its history, and rewrites it to his own ends, exactly as other people can seize our plastic identities and shape them for their interests rather than ours.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 20 "7. What Kind of Revolutionary Is Mr. Robot" — Ralston traces Mr. Robot's hacktivist philosophy to David Graeber's anarchism behind Occupy Wall Street and to Anonymous's 'moralfags' who hack for a higher cause (Project Chanology as the template for fsociety), then stages the Dewey-Trotsky debate on means and ends: Trotsky's 'Their Morals and Ours' lets the end justify any means, while Dewey's means-end continuum demands experimental, democratic means suited to the end. The verdict: Mr. Robot's ends are anarchist and his means pragmatist - he will frame Terry Colby and risk lives at Steel Mountain, but rejects means like actual slavery that would betray the movement's own ideal of liberation.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 21 "10. Play in the Real World" — Elizabeth Cooke reads Rogers's double movement, demystifying reality (the studio reveal in episode 1530, the otoscope that cannot see into minds) while insisting 'anything is possible in make-believe,' as pragmatist epistemology: rejecting Plato's two worlds and Cartesian doubt, Rogers agrees with Peirce's open-ended 'musement,' Santayana's play as a 'holiday' revealing truer selves, and James's malleable world that our creativity 'adds to.' Pretend, as when Daniel wonders if he is a mistake or children take others' perspectives in competition episodes, is how children actively learn what is most real, with George Herbert Mead explaining how perspective-taking builds the self.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 9 "Hope for the Future" — Applies Dewey's The Public and Its Problems to Alien and Aliens: the real villain is not the Xenomorph but a United Americas too weak to govern Weyland-Yutani, whose crude cost-benefit erasure of the Nostromo crew's interests shows a state that has lost the public's voice. Ash's arrogant 'perfect organism' objectivity, the appeal to blameworthy 'human nature,' and faith that big business runs everything illustrate Dewey's targets - Plato's static Forms, economic determinism, and rugged individualism - and since beliefs are habits of action (Peirce), the Company's deeds expose its professed principles as negligible fictions.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 35 "Finding Our Way" — Milburn uses Dewey's account of habit, impulse, and inquiry to explain how the humans navigate: Adama's blocked plans (the decommissioning) are reoriented into a new 'end-in-view' (Earth), and the fleet continuously reformulates its route from scriptures, star charts, pulsars, and the Tomb of Athena constellations as interchangeable signs. The Cylons by contrast cannot revise - Boomer's peace initiative gets her model boxed, and even Cavil's admissions of error lead back to the same path - because they locate their plan in God rather than in constructed, revisable inquiry, needing Baltar even to interpret the signs to Earth. On Deweyan grounds the chapter concludes the humans are never lost while the Cylons are.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 15 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — MacMullan argues Stewart is America's most effective public intellectual working in the pragmatist tradition Cornel West describes, philosophy as continuous cultural commentary 'explaining America to itself' rather than academia's ingrown self-talk (the failure Rorty diagnosed). He shows The Daily Show performing this role through irony and critical cultural memory: the Colbert exchange rewarding Karl Rove's Plame leak with 'Chief Justice', 'Victory Lapse' on Republican outrage at Obama's bin Laden ad versus Bush's Mission Accomplished carrier landing, 'Gitmo's World', and the 'Meet the Depressed' Magic Bullet blender takedown of Obama's unkept promises. Stewart's Deweyan faith in democracy as a way of life appears in the Rally to Restore Sanity, his genuine debates with guests like David Barton and Marco Rubio, his anger at CNBC's Cramer for burning the house down with our money, and the 9/11 Zadroga Bill segments that shamed Congress into passing the law.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 12 "The Jihadist Way of Life" — Argues that the Fremen, despite their supposed Zensunni faith (which it argues was never a liberation theology), are quintessentially American: Emersonian self-reliance appears as spiritual self-sufficiency and the Spannungsbogen self-imposed delay, while Dewey's democracy as a way of life surfaces in the jihad's aim of replacing master-slave relations with relative equals under Shai-Hulud. It cites Herbert's 'Dune Genesis' on myth-making as pragmatically valuable and reads Paul, who ends Dune Messiah walking blind into the desert 'where we walk without footprints', as kin to the 'American Taliban' John Walker Lindh, whose conversion and jihad were driven by the same self-reliant, spiritual, pragmatic values.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 29 "“What happens to us now ”" — Tests the moral limits of science against Dresden's defense of Eros ('hardly a rounding error', 'we become our own gods'): Descartes' evil demon explains why Holden can never verify the protomolecule-ghost Miller — or even the Roci's bulkhead — is real; Baconian induction and mastery of nature explain why Protogen feeds biomass to the protomolecule ('we can only learn by letting it learn'), though Bacon himself demanded knowledge be shared for universal good; Peirce's pragmatism explains how the Donnager infers stealth ships from their effects and why protomolecule victims count as no longer human; and Dewey's inseparability of means and ends indicts Fred Johnson's readiness to negotiate with Dresden. It culminates in Miller shooting Dresden — 'I killed him because he was making sense' — as the straightest critique of utilitarian calculation, concluding that when empathy is excised (Cortázar's stimulation) or ignored, even science aimed at saving humanity produces Eros, Project Caliban, and the Earth-Mars war.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Albert Spencer reads Fallout 4's synth crisis as a philosophy-of-mind allegory - Brotherhood dualism, Institute reductive physicalism, Railroad functionalism - which he grounds in the classical pragmatists: Peirce's sign-interpreting mind, James's stream of consciousness, and Dewey's interactive consciousness make personhood a matter of social participation rather than essence. Quests dramatize the stakes: 'Human Error' has Covenant's interrogation of Amelia Stockton enact Du Bois's double consciousness (self-understanding against a devaluing gaze, as with the tragic Phyllis Daily), the Sole Survivor of 'The Battle of Bunker Hill' and Far Harbor becomes Anzaldua's Nepantlera straddling the human/synth binary, and the Railroad's memory-wipe 'resets' reproduce the domination they fight by ignoring Crenshaw's intersectionality (the Feral Historian's case that the Railroad kills the selves it saves). Acadia, where DiMA murdered and replaced Captain Avery to preserve peace, becomes Jane Addams's test case of democracy as associated living - an imperfect, lying community that nonetheless offers the only future of shared synth-human personhood.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 13 "3. Sympathy for the Devils" — Argues, against Michael, that the Soul Squad still belongs in the Bad Place: drawing on William James's conditions for actions having moral worth (foreseeable consequences, no do-overs) and his meliorism about an unfinished, responsive universe, it shows the points system is contextualist (the tricycle fix worth +4.79 or +0.04; the two Dougs' rose gifts), but the afterlife simulation is a context where nothing the humans do is consequential or permanent, so their moral growth earns no points. Worse, their growth adds net unhappiness — Michael's suffering, the demon cast's misery, Judge Gen's distress — so becoming better ironically confirms they belong in the Bad Place. Only Michael, whose retirement is a real, irreversible consequence and whose sacrifices add genuine good, deserves the Good Place.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 21 "Putting One’s Mind into a Body" — Seng reads the 2008 film's crash-and-stabilizer flying lessons as philosophy of mind: at first the armor seems to confirm Descartes' dualism, with Stark the thinking substance piloting a mechanical body and Jarvis playing the pineal gland. But Stark smashing into the ceiling while learning to fly shows the embodied mind of Dewey and Merleau-Ponty — habits, spatial existence, and the imported home preferences that make the suit feel like his own skin, so that the repulsors whir closed when he stands down before the village gunmen. Dewey's view of intelligence as acting on estimates of a situation then explains Stark's growth from selfish playboy to sharable goods (beating the merely self-interested Stane), and Jarvis counts as Stark's mind made manifest in the suit.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 18 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Godwin reads Spider-Man 3's black-suit episode as a question about the self: with the symbiote amplifying his anger, is Peter still Peter? Against Hume's and the Buddha's bundle theories, on which the self is only an imagined aggregate of thoughts and feelings, and Reid's common-sense simple self, she advances the pragmatist 'social self' of Peirce, James, Dewey, and Mead, updated as Engel's biopsychosocial model: Peter's identity is a shifting web of biology, psyche, and relationships (Aunt May, MJ, Harry) expressed in actions and character. Eddie succumbs to the symbiote because, as Dewey says of the slave to his own blind desires, hatred constitutes who he is, while Peter's thicker web of good relations lets him shed the suit at the church bell.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 24 "“You Like Me because I'm a Scoundrel”" — Decker asks whether Han Solo can truly evade philosophy, opening with Aristotle's Protrepticus proof that one must do philosophy either way. Han's demystifying skepticism ('no mystical energy field controls my destiny,' 'That's not how the Force works!') is paired with Wittgenstein's Tractatus, which dismisses traditional philosophical questions as senseless and offers therapy for the philosophical itch, and with Montaigne's skepticism about book learning — though Han's orphan scrumrat education exposes the class privilege behind Montaigne's 'sweet pillow' of ignorance. His anti-authoritarianism is read through Emerson (via Cornel West) and Rorty's pragmatism as anti-authoritarianism: build philosophical reflections around political hopes rather than foundations, which is why the 'everyday people' of the Disney+ era, epitomized by the scoundrel, break the spell of the Skywalker grand narrative.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 29 "Philosophers Can't Jump" — Tim Elcombe uses Dewey's pragmatist account of lived experience to read the Hoosiers scene in Butler Fieldhouse: Coach Dale's tape measure shows time and space are durable constants (the basket is ten feet in Indianapolis too), yet the awestruck Huskers will live that same space in a radically new way, and Kant and Augustine frame the gap between clock time and lived time. He argues basketball is the most 'phenomenal' game because the ticking clock creates genuine drama (Reggie Miller's 1995 buzzer three, childhood 'buzzer beater' games) and the ten-foot basket builds a vertical dimension no other sport matches, answering Scott Kretchmar's defense of event-regulated baseball. Our cultural obsession with dunking - Michael Jordan's Nike ads, Teen Wolf, Like Mike, White Men Can't Jump - expresses the human fascination with briefly defying gravity, a 'moving image of eternity'.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 15 "Knockout! Killer’s Kiss, the Somatic, and Kubrick Kevin S. Decker" — Decker reads Killer's Kiss (and later 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) through Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology of the lived body ('I am my body'), recovering the somatic that Socrates and Plato's Phaedo denigrated. In Killer's Kiss the boxing match, the mannequin-warehouse fight where bodies become weapons, spatial camera work, and the theme of contingency foreground embodiment; 2001 makes viewers feel their own bodies in space, and A Clockwork Orange's Ludovico 'cure' rewires the body-mind. Drawing on pragmatists Shusterman and Sullivan and on Foucault's biopower, he argues the anonymous masked bodies of Eyes Wide Shut turn Merleau-Ponty's projective intentionality into domination rather than communication.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Decker reads Killer's Kiss (with 2001, A Clockwork Orange, and Eyes Wide Shut) to recover the philosophy of the body against the Socratic-Platonic-Cartesian denigration of the somatic. Using Merleau-Ponty's existential phenomenology ('I am my body') and pragmatists like Shusterman and Sullivan, he shows Kubrick's obsessive use of space, contingency, and the visceral - Davy's boxing match, the mannequin-warehouse fight, the weightless bodies of 2001, the Ludovico brainwashing of Alex, and the anonymous masked bodies of Eyes Wide Shut - to argue that subjectivity is corporeal and that anonymity of bodies can fund Foucauldian domination rather than liberation.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Abrams reads Kubrick's Lolita as a parody of Poe's Dupin detective story, arguing that Humbert Humbert's method is not deduction but Peirce's logic of abduction (guessing). Humbert is the 'resolvent' half of Poe's double-Dupin - all calculation and chess - and excels only at overcoded abductions (spotting a nymphet) while failing the creative, undercoded abductions needed to see that Clare Quilty, the 'creative' double, is manipulating him. Abrams maps the film onto Poe's game-analysis (chess vs. cards) and the myth of the labyrinth, with Quilty as the ever-changing Minotaur whom Nabokov and Kubrick use for authorial 'involution.'
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 24 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Sterritt 'schizoanalyzes' The Informant! by arguing that its lying protagonist Mark Whitacre, an ADM executive turned FBI informant, is a nut psychoanalysis cannot crack because he has no unconscious depth: his self is Deleuze and Guattari's rhizomatic, depthless flow of desire with 'nothing behind it' (echoing Warhol). He reads Mark's compulsive fabrication as deterritorialization against the corporation-as-psychopath, links the film to the Socratic unexamined life and to William James's open, flux-embracing empiricism (via Cassavetes), and interprets the climactic collision of Mark's voiceover and dialogue as the film itself intervening as the ultimate informant.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 9 "Mommas, Don't Let Your Babies Grow Up to Be Pragmatists" — Csaki argues that John Wayne became the ultimate cinematic cowboy because his characters embody classical American pragmatism. Using William James's squirrel-and-tree parable and Dewey's account of 'inquiry' transforming an indeterminate situation, he reads Rooster Cogburn's split-second raft decision and Wil Anderson's hiring of schoolboys in The Cowboys as pragmatic problem-solving from experience. He treats the 'code of the West' not as fixed absolutes but as rules applied pragmatically (Rooster shooting men in the back, the cowboys letting Long Hair be dragged to death), where truth is what can be assimilated, verified, and made to 'work.'
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 24 "Regeneration through Stories and Song The View from the Other Side of the West in Smoke Signals" — Richard Gilmore reads Smoke Signals—the first feature written, directed, and coproduced by Native Americans—against Slotkin's myth of regeneration through violence, arguing it offers regeneration through stories and song instead. Drawing on Wilshire's claim that pragmatism is 'aboriginal,' he links Emerson and Thoreau's transcendentalism and Peirce's 'law of mind' to Deloria's American Indian metaphysics and Hyde's gift economy: Arlene's fry-bread story and Thomas's storytelling repair broken relationships, and Victor's final act of forgiving his father (and withholding that Arnold caused the fatal fire) is read as the film's central gift, completing relationships that violence had severed.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 11 "2 Neil Young and Creativity" — Berger surveys Young's repeated claim that he does not intentionally compose but "receives" songs, comparing himself to a radio station or microphone and echoing Schubert's "I remember it." He illuminates this with C.S. Peirce's categories of firstness (feeling), secondness (reaction) and thirdness (thought/signs), arguing that Young's refusal to "judge" lyrics like "Tell Me Why" or "Cowgirl in the Sand" protects the originary feeling, and that songs communicate feeling through Peircean icons and metaphors rather than deliberate rational design.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 14 "5 Neil Young Lover of Sun, Moon and Cars" — Anderson traces Young's environmentalism from the hippie-romantic nature worship of "After the Gold Rush" and Greendale toward a pragmatic "middle way" that reconciles his love of nature with his love of cars and recording technology (the Lincvolt project, Storytone). Drawing on Thoreau, Muir and Leopold's land ethic while rejecting the fixed prescriptions of Singer and Regan, he presents Young as an experimentalist "meliorist" who owns his own complicity in CO2 abuse and urges informed, practical, self-aware action rather than utopian or deontological solutions.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 18 "9. Anthony Bourdain’s Inquiring Mind" — Anderson and Mauro trace Bourdain's growth from the dogmatic provocateur of Kitchen Confidential to a Peircean inquirer, using Peirce's 'The Fixation of Belief' and its four methods (tenacity, authority, a priori, inquiry). They argue Bourdain's tattooed motto 'I am certain of nothing,' his surprise and self-correction in Cambodia, Beirut, Saudi Arabia, and Haiti, and his pragmatic theory of evolving truth make him a model of the self-correcting inquiring life.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 15 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Terrance MacMullan argues Stewart is America's most effective public intellectual, reviving the engaged tradition of Emerson, William James, Dewey, and Du Bois against the isolation Rorty diagnosed in academics. Using Cornel West's account of pragmatism as 'explaining America to itself,' he reads segments like 'Victory Lapse,' the Karl Rove 'what honor' bit, and 'Gitmo's World' as pragmatist cultural criticism, and casts Stewart's 'Worst Responders' campaign for the 9/11 Zadroga Bill and his amicable debates with conservatives as embodying Dewey's democracy as a shared 'working faith' in people.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 34 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Decker asks whether 'Stephen Colbert' the persona is an 'existential ironist,' tracing irony from Socrates's Delphic-oracle-inspired questioning through Schlegel, Hegel (irony as freedom but an abdication of responsibility), and Kierkegaard (the ironist detached from and not taking community practices seriously). He reads Colbert's centerless self-redescription and Super PAC stunt via Rorty's 'ironist' and 'final vocabulary' (built from Nietzschean self-creation and Deweyan plasticity through language), then argues that truthiness is a dangerous subjectivism—and that Colbert, unlike a pure Rortian ironist, drops the mask to side with the powerless.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 14 "Neither Here, nor There, nor Anywhere" — Randall Auxier reads Green Eggs and Ham as a primer in Peircean pragmatism. The contrarian 'C' illustrates how thinking only begins when a problem interrupts action, and Peirce's distinction between 'genuine doubt' and settled belief-as-habit explains why C clings to 'I do not like them' without ever trying them. Auxier runs C's stubbornness through Peirce's four methods of fixing belief (Authority, A Priori, Tenacity, Science), arguing C relies on tenacity, and likens Sam-I-Am to Saint Monica pestering Augustine into genuine doubt, so that even after C eats the eggs he only knows they settled belief in one context.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 20 "Pragmatist Ethics with John Dewey, Horton, and the Lorax" — Alexander contrasts Dewey's reflective, character-centered ethics with utilitarianism and Kantian deontology using the Lorax and Horton. The Once-ler is cast as the shortsighted 'utilitarian' maximizing Thneed happiness while the Lorax, urging us to 'stop and think' about the whole ecosystem, is really a Deweyan practicing reflective morality and deliberation as 'dramatic rehearsal.' Horton's conscientious care for the Whos illustrates Dewey's 'Who Factor' and growth of character rather than cold rule-following, showing morality as the ongoing education of desire toward inclusive, shared ends.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 12 "MOTHERHOOD" — Sue Ellen Henry uses John Dewey's pragmatism, especially The Quest for Certainty and Democracy and Education, to diagnose her own 'quest for certainty' as a new mother mediating expert parenting books against her own instincts. She argues Dewey's rejection of the false dichotomy between knowledge and belief shows that a mother's home is her 'laboratory,' where experience is itself a form of knowledge; her La Leche League experience models Dewey's integrated, feedback-driven inquiry against the isolating authority of 'scientific motherhood' texts.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 32 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Holt argues that Seinfeld's Festivus, invented by Frank Costanza as an anti-consumerist 'holiday for the rest of us,' is grounded in American pragmatism: truth is 'whatever works,' malleable and tested by results. Because commercialized Christmas fails to deliver the altruism it demands, it 'does not work' and by pragmatist standards ceases to be true, so Costanza pragmatically forges a holiday that fits his needs. Holt reads Festivus's elements pragmatically — the maintenance-free aluminum pole as a bare functional symbol, the airing of grievances as a needed cathartic release from everyday restraint, the wrestling as self-perpetuating ritual — and warns that as Festivus merchandise spreads it will lose its practicality and, being no longer pragmatic, be discarded; he closes with a mock 'airing of grievances' against philosophers including Plato and Bertrand Russell.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 23 "GARDENING" — Shapiro argues that Frederick Law Olmsted's Central Park is a major artwork realizing a 'pragmatic picturesque,' and reads the English picturesque garden as a 'diagram' (in Foucault's and Deleuze's sense) of the glance—the roving, liberated look—explicitly contrasted with Bentham's Panopticon, the diagram of the objectifying gaze. Using Derrida's paradox of the frame, he shows the picturesque hides its boundary (the ha-ha) while Olmsted inverts the diagram, making the frame explicit and admitting the city so citizens meet in democratic 'gregarious' recognition—a Platonic argument (aesthetic education in the Republic) turned pragmatic in the climate of Peirce, James and Dewey. Christo and Jeanne-Claude's 'The Gates' distills the park's diagram as a gift of time.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 14 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — David Robles's 'The Seeker' argues that declining trust in Western absolutist religion drives people toward yoga as an experiential, self-directed spirituality. His central move is that Patanjali's Yoga Sutras rank direct perception above testimony and scripture — mirroring the scientific method — so yoga functions as a 'spiritual science' harmonious with empiricism, whereas established religion rests on second-hand revelation. He distinguishes 'spiritual' (personal, inspiration-based) from 'religious' (culturally binding dogma) and casts the American 'seeker' as building a better, results-oriented, pragmatic spirituality.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 13 "Who is Who" — On regeneration and personal identity, the chapter runs Doctor Who through Leibniz's law of identity and soul-based individuation, Locke's memory criterion of personhood, and Hume's bundle theory, testing them against multi-Doctor stories, the Ganger duplicates ('The Almost People'), 'The Girl Who Waited' (closest-continuer theory) and 'City of Death.' It then shifts to physicalism (the Morbius brain) and to a pragmatist, social theory of the self (James, Dewey, Mead's 'taking the attitude of the other,' Dennett's intentional stance), reading the reintegration of identity in 'The Doctor Dances.'
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 13 "NOTES" — Richard Shusterman defends the entertainment value of popular art from a pragmatist ('meliorist') stance, tracing entertainment's genealogy through Plato, Aristotle, Montaigne, Kant, Hegel, Nietzsche, Heidegger and Adorno—whose 'culture industry' opposes pleasure to cognition. Using rap (KRS-One's 'Edutainment', Public Enemy, Ice-T) and T.S. Eliot's 'superior amusement,' he argues knowledge and enjoyment are compatible. He rejects Hannah Arendt's contrast of imperishable art vs. life-serving entertainment, and critiques G.E. Moore's Principia Ethica 'method of absolute isolation' for intrinsic value, replacing it with a Deweyan transactional account in which even intrinsic values are relational and temporal.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 12 "10. Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood as Philosophy Children as Philosophers" — Baggett argues that Mister Rogers' Neighborhood was a profoundly philosophical show because it treated very young children as natural philosophers — curious, wonder-filled questioners — rather than mere proto-adults. He frames child-development theory through the rationalism/empiricism divide (Skinner's behaviorism descending from Locke's tabula rasa, Chomsky's innatism from Descartes) and champions Gareth Matthews's claim that children's 'romancing' is genuine philosophy adults should not condescend to. Rogers modeled Hadot's philosophy-as-a-way-of-life and James's and Rousseau's active learning; episodes on death (the goldfish), work, and make-believe invited the same wonder Aquinas and Hume brought to happiness and causation, treating children as members of Kant's kingdom of ends.

### Existence Precedes Essence

"Existence precedes essence" is Jean-Paul Sartre's slogan for the core of atheistic existentialism: there is no fixed human nature given in advance, so a person first exists and only afterward defines what they are through their choices. Unlike a manufactured object whose purpose is set before it is made, the human being arrives without a predetermined role and must create meaning and value through action. This places the full weight of self-definition, and hence responsibility, on the individual.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 16 "No Exit and The Vault Sartre and Seinfeld on the Inescapability of Others" — Jennifer McMahon defends the heretical reading of Sartre as a relational theorist of the self: in Being and Nothingness consciousness is a nothingness, not an essential ego, and only the Other - 'the Other accomplishes... to see ourselves as we are' - lets us grasp ourselves as objects. Seinfeld illustrates this better than Sartre's own suspicion of others: Jerry's identity exists only through his entanglement with George, Kramer, and Elaine (change them and you get a 'bizarro-Jerry'), and the finale's prison cell ('The Vault') replays No Exit's locked room with the trial's parade of wounded minor characters - except that Seinfeld's chattering foursome shows friendship as a positive, not hellish, dependency.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 90 "Unknown" — The chapter walks through Nausea as the ordinary-world twin of the red pill: Roquentin, an unremarkable 1930s historian, is unravelled by a beach pebble, a handshake like 'a fat white worm', a door-knob that seems to grab him back, and finally the chestnut tree's 'naked World' - discovering that existence is a gelatinous, unjustifiable 'messy suffering' and that the order, names, and values we take for reality are only a veneer consciousness projects onto an indeterminate whole. His nausea is the horror of authenticity before it becomes anything else, the price Neo pays for swallowing the pill.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 26 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Dallas Willard defends the film's excess of violence as its whole point: it visualizes human evil as beyond the remedies of education, law, or counseling (the route Plato and Aristotle tried), with Satan — the androgynous figure carrying the smug dwarf through the scourging crowd — explaining why only Christ's non-resistant embrace of the cross can break evil's grip. Against the passive reading of 'the Passion,' he argues Jesus 'played' his judges, deliberately laying down his life to inaugurate the kingdom of God. The argument leans on the hidden God (deus absconditus): God stays hidden, contra Sartre's 'no nature' self-creation and closer to Pico della Mirandola, so that we can freely make ourselves, which is also why demanding 'more evidence' misses what belief in God requires.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 14 "Sick of Love" — Krein and Levin read Dylan's portraits of fallen socialites in "Like a Rolling Stone," "Just Like a Woman," and "To Ramona" as critiques of bad faith - characters who hide from freedom and responsibility in consumerist status games, in Sartre's sense that existence precedes essence. But Beauvoir's Second Sex exposes the cost: the women Dylan praises ("Girl from the North Country," "One More Cup of Coffee") are praised precisely for staying in immanent, pastoral passivity, denied the transcendence that for Beauvoir constitutes full humanity. Borrowing Benjamin's and Buck-Morss's notion of modern "dreamworlds," they finally read Dylan's pastoral utopias as a counter-dreamworld spun after the collapse of the mass-utopian promise of consumer happiness.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 14 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Auxier uses the question 'Would Bruce Springsteen ride a Honda?' as an ontological probe: Honda embodies defensible middle-class values while a Harley is not primarily a machine but 'a decision about life and what makes it valuable', a suicide machine Jesus could have ridden into Jerusalem and whose absence would render Easy Rider meaningless even if Fonda rode some other Harley. His own boyhood purchase of a Honda XL 70 over the Harley Z90 becomes a lesson in Heideggerian honesty, since he knew he belonged on a Honda, while buyers who choose for appearances are consumed by das Man, the they-self that lives inauthentically through images and slogans. Using Husserl's method of imaginative variation on the question, he concludes that the Harley as cultural icon represents an existential decision and the life that follows from it.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 21 "A Nietzschean Conclusion" — Slowik argues the Pythons have a positive existentialist message: Kafka's bureaucratic insanity, where ordinary people beat helplessly against irrational rules, recurs in the 'Cheese Shop' and 'Dead Parrot' sketches, and Camus's Sisyphus lives on in the monotonous lives of Palin's city stockbroker and the accountant who dreams of lion taming — repetition without Sisyphus's defiance. The core claim is that Python endorses individual-centered existentialism: Brian's 'You've got to think for yourselves. You're all individuals!' is the troupe's rare direct statement of Sartre's 'existence precedes essence', confirmed by Cleese's and Palin's interviews about resisting those who tell you how to behave, a theme the chapter extends through Nietzsche's critique of moral tradition and organized Christianity. Sartrean bad faith explains Python's stereotyped characters — the aggressive policeman, the pepperpots, and Mr. Praline insisting 'I am not a loony!' while demanding a fish license for his halibut — while Arthur Pewtey's meek 'Right. Right.' and Ron Obvious's physical limits raise nature/nurture objections to Sartrean freedom. The 'Nietzschean Conclusion' is that Monty Python itself exemplifies will to power as 'giving style' to one's character, constantly overcoming its own formulas rather than repeating what succeeded.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 14 "Poker and Philosophy" — Sanders splits poker into two philosophical styles. The Rationalist — Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason, Pascal's domestication of chance into probability — plays like Sklansky, Chris Ferguson, and Howard Lederer, whose temptation is the paralysis of analysis; the Existentialist — Sartre's existence precedes essence, Camus' scorn for the absurd, Kierkegaard's leap of faith taken without decisive evidence — plays like Gus Hansen calling Antonio Esfandiari's $334,000 all-in re-raise with ten-high. A Russell-and-Popper-style regress of predictions (knowing a prediction changes its outcome) becomes the tournament 'hall of mirrors' of intentions read in Phil Ivey and Johnny Chan, and the chapter lands on Richard Taylor's existentialist point that meaning comes from committed doing, at the table as in life.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 15 "Poker and Philosophy" — Vernezze uses Dostoevsky to make gambling existential: Notes from Underground's insistence that will trumps reason ('what do I care for the laws of nature and arithmetic?') and The Gambler's portrait of the calculating gambler — who loses like everyone else and worships money with a 'German' soul — prefigure existentialism's three traits: lost confidence in reason, despair as part of the human condition, and the willed overcoming of absurdity (Camus' Sisyphus happy, Sartre's condemned freedom). Dostoevsky's own roulette addiction fuels the reading, with Amarillo Slim and Brunson's side bets as heirs. The Cincinnati Kid's climax clinches it: Lancey Howard 'making the wrong move at the right time' by chasing a straight flush proves poker's essence lies beyond reason — a truly Dostoevskean activity.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 19 "Identities, Selves, and Others" — Patterson uses Thornhill's being mistaken for the fictitious George Kaplan to test theories of personal identity: the body theory fails a CIA thought experiment in which a Kaplan double is slowly rebuilt from Thornhill's own replaced cells; Locke's memory theory fails on amnesia scenarios and circularity, since one cannot have memories of a self unless one already has a self; and Parfit's psychological continuity survives, with Thornhill drifting along a 'Psychological Spectrum' toward 'one hundred percent Kaplan' as he plays the spy. The chapter then turns existentialist: with Sartre, no essential nature fixes who Thornhill is, so he is totally responsible for the self his choices create, from 'Expedient Exaggerations' to risking death on Mount Rushmore. Charles Taylor's claim that a self exists only in dialogue with a community explains why Eve and others literally help make Thornhill into the person he becomes.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 27 "Lonesome Day" — Calef asks how fictional story-songs can teach: lyrics yield neither know-how nor know-that, since Plato's Theaetetus shows true belief is not knowledge (the 'Meeting Across the River' narrator's plan works only by luck). The answer is a third kind — knowing what something is like: 'The River' lets a comfortable listener inhabit Mary's husband's slide into a dry marriage, and 'Nebraska' lets us feel Starkweather's numb void, 'what it's like to have no soul.' Aristotle's Poetics (we delight in imitation because learning pleases; poetry is more philosophic than history because it speaks in universals) explains why sad songs satisfy us, and Sartre's universal human condition grounds the empathy that makes The Rising render 9/11 ('You're Missing,' 'Empty Sky') thinkable at a personal scale.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 11 "The Avatar Unparalleled Opportunities" — Cuddy asks how gamers relate to BSG videogame avatars — as an extension of the ego or a disposable other — using Freud's id/ego/superego to cast the avatar as a socially safe venue for reconciling forbidden desires (piloting a Cylon Raider) with the superego's demands. Against Rehak's claim that gamers simply drop the avatar when losing, he enlists Sartre: blaming the game or 'cheating' opponents is bad faith, a denial of the freedom to create one's own essence, with Lee's '33' debate about responsibility for the Olympic Carrier and Baltar's vacillation as in-show parallels. Sartre's facticity bounds the freedom — hard missions are fixed facts to deal with — so the gamer, like Adama's fleet, must take responsibility within limits.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 13 "Why I Can Play Zelda for Four Hours Straight" — Fellela reads Link's endless drudgery (slashing grass for rupees, collecting bottles, leaving the final Ganon fight at a 'permanent pause') through existentialism: Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' is dramatized in Ocarina of Time's opening, where Link must acquire sword, fairy, and skills to make himself the hero, and Nietzsche's 'God is dead' call to become gods is answered by Link restoring meaning to a hostile Hyrule. Camus' Sisyphus figures the repetitive world-saving quest as an absurd hero's owned task, and Frankl's logotherapy (meaning as the tension between what one is and what one should become) explains why humiliating menial tasks, in camp or in laundromats or in Zelda, become bearable and even meaningful. Link's fixed options even illustrate Frankl's point that freedom is the stance we take toward conditions, not freedom from them.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 15 "The Missionary" — Christopher Hoyt reads Buffett's escape from Catholicism as a case study in secular meaning-making after Nietzsche's death of God, taking the Mardi Gras ritual of Folly swatting Death out of town as Buffett's core spiritual attitude — interpreted the way Wittgenstein criticized Frazer, as an expression of our stance toward death rather than mere magic. Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' frames the post-1960s task of self-definition without God, while Marx's alienation explains what the persona of *Jimmy* refuses: the impersonal work and borrowed values that leave moderns living an alien narrative, like McGuane's character Skelton in Ninety-Two in the Shade. The twist is that *Jimmy*'s pop-culture vocabulary — Tully Mars built from Donovan's Reef and Slim Pickens, Bogart, the Brylcreem jingle — is itself authentic, and the 'semi-true story' of the myth tells deeper truths than a literal biography could, making Buffett something like a pop prophet for late modernity.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 10 "15" — Three 'Phase Four' essays. Moseley reads the Joker across Batman #1, The Killing Joke, The Dark Knight, A Death in the Family, and Dark Knight Returns as a 'moral monster' who knowingly does evil - and, following Anscombe and Scanlon's guise-of-the-good analysis, pursues aesthetic 'higher values' in a Camus-like affirmation of the absurd, embracing the irrationality Batman's rational moral order cannot fathom. Levin uses X-gene biology (Beast's explanation in Astonishing X-Men, genotype vs phenotype, M-Day) to strip Magneto's Homo sapiens superior claim of any genetic or phenotypic basis, then argues via the moral community of rational persons (Kant's criterion) that mutants and humans share one moral community, condemning both the Registration Act and mutant separatism. O'Neil's prose piece traces Harvey Dent from Calvinist certainty through the acid that scars him to cosmic doubt - quantum randomness, many worlds, Sartre's condemnation to freedom - until Nietzsche's amor fati lets him embrace duality and let the scarred two-headed coin decide good and evil.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 14 "True Selves Found or Made" — Theodore Schick reconstructs Aleister Crowley's philosophy of Thelema to explain Jimmy Page's devotion—Boleskine Manor, The Equinox bookstore, the Zoso sigil, 'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the law' etched in Led Zeppelin III's run-out groove—and reads 'Stairway to Heaven' stanza by stanza as an allegory of awakening to the True Will. He then dismantles the framework: no spell has ever worked under controlled conditions (post hoc fallacy), Sartre's existence precedes essence denies any divinely written True Will or human nature, and Schopenhauer (via Einstein) argues we can do what we want but cannot want what we want. Using second-order desires and autonomy, the chapter concludes that selves are made, not found—so even if a True Will existed, following a program we did not write would make us 'loyal plastic robots', not free.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 14 "Mr. Monk’s Greatness" — Lewis argues Monk is Nietzsche's Übermensch. Sketching Sartre's existence-precedes-essence through the contrast between the designed wipe and self-defining humans, the chapter claims Monk creates his own essence through choices — keeping the coffee table askew in memory of Trudy, 'dirtying' his house in 'Mr. Monk Makes a Friend,' drinking stream water in 'Mr. Monk Gets Cabin Fever' — and lives by self-prescribed values (hourly flossing, bagged tissues, relentless truth-seeking) that separate him from the herd of the Court of Public Opinion. The comparison with Stottlemeyer — Nietzsche's lookalike with the mustache, 'the quintessential man' of the herd — inverts the expected hierarchy: 'He was a yardstick for me, of both detection and character' ('Mr. Monk Goes to Mexico') shows the badge-carrying everyman is the inferior one. Monk therefore challenges the macho sci-fi stereotype of the superman: the Übermensch can be gentle and kind, fight for truth and a cleaner world, and still have room to improve ('What does not kill me makes me stronger').
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 39 "Manny" — Santaniello reads five nonconformist Red Sox through ethical theory. Ruth's sale to New York becomes a Kantian case: he tore up his signed three-year contract and demanded a trade while expecting others to keep promises, violating the categorical imperative on promise-keeping. Ted Williams's lifelong war with the 'Knights of the Keyboard' exemplifies existentialist authenticity ('It just wouldn't have been me' tipping his cap), Spaceman Bill Lee embodies Sartre's condemned freedom and existence precedes essence, Jim Rice's Hall of Fame delay is Aristotle's failure to hit the mean between silent deficiency on Boston's racism and excess toward reporters, and Manny's 'Gas is up and so am I' money grab shows Aristotle's point that wealth is an incomplete end pursued for the sake of something else.
- **Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_**, ch. 2 "index" — This file holds the book's front matter, Wittkower's introduction 'A Reply to facebook Critics', and the 'facebook Itself' essays. Wittkower answers critics of trivial status updates with Sartre's claim that lives have no given meaning (so their value is ours to create, from the inside), Hegel's argument that real freedom means choosing alongside others (against both Sunstein's 'Daily Me' echo chamber and the forced community of family and hometown), and Schopenhauer's microscope image from 'On the Vanity of Existence', concluding that we care about a friend's dinner update for the same reason we care about our own. James Grimmelmann's 'The Privacy Virus' rebuts the claim that Facebook users don't care about privacy by arguing they practice a contextual, Nissenbaum-style privacy (untagging keg-stand photos, the News Feed revolt, the Miss New Jersey blackmail), while Facebook's architecture breaks the 'know your audience' rule and recruits users into spreading violations like a virus. Graham Meikle reads wall posts and status updates as a convergence of personal messaging and broadcast media (citing the MI6 chief's wife's holiday photos and the Sunday Express's Dunblane survivors story), and Ian Bogost applies McLuhan's media ecology to Facebook as an 'extension of man': it enhances the directory and the yearbook, obsolesces the reunion and the secret, retrieves the small town and the soda shop, and reverses into campus life and high school.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 15 "Living the Absurd Life" — Krein asks why he has spent fifteen years on karate when pepper spray and avoidance would serve self-defense better, and answers with existentialism rather than Buddhism. Nietzsche's death of God and Sartre's claim that existence precedes essence leave life objectively meaningless, but the dojo supplies a self-contained standard for Sartrean transcendence (kata quality is judged within the art), trains the courage and clarity authenticity requires, and enforces excuse-free responsibility: in sparring you either score or you don't. Studying a traditional martial art is thus a heroic, 'act without hope' defiance of the absurd.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 15 "Let Your Heart Be the Anchor and the Beat of Your Own Song" — Berti reads Neil Peart's 1997-98 catastrophes (his daughter's car accident, his wife's cancer death) and the 55,000-mile Ghost Rider motorcycle exile through Sartrean existentialism: existence precedes essence, so with no God-given script Peart must author his own reactions, exactly as Sartre's student had to choose between mother and Resistance. The chapter tracks alienation ('I do not know who I am'), the duty to choose rather than lean on outside voices, and 'The Pass' as the voice telling a suicidal teenager to walk back from the razor's edge. Thoreau's Walden retreat supplies the model for the healing road, and Peart's own directives ('keep moving; kick your own ass, gently') enact 'Freewill' and 'Something for Nothing': we are the ones who choose, and the choice to live made all that followed (re-marriage, Vapor Trails, five more tours) possible.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 36 "Bad or Bad Faith" — Rebecca Steiner Goldner reads the show through Sartre's Being and Nothingness: Dexter's watching is the Look that crystallizes his victims into a fixed essence - Matt Chambers can never again reinvent himself in a new town - and the kill room stages the demanded shame and confession ('Look at what you did!'), echoing Sartre's caught peeping-Tom. She then argues Dexter's belief that he was born a killer, that his Dark Passenger leaves him no choice, is itself bad faith: existence precedes essence, and by Sartre's account even the reformed thief remains responsible for his past, as with Jeremy Downs and Dr. Meridian. We viewers root for Dexter because we see the freedom he denies - and love him because he never makes the authentic choice to abandon his murderous project.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 53 "What Does A Scanner See" — The chapter answers Arctor's question with Sartre: the gambler cannot observe his way out of deciding again, because consciousness is a nothingness with no determinate essence to be observed, so a scanner used to find yourself 'sees nothing', and Fred watching his own footage is bad faith, hiding from freedom behind presumed facts about himself. Butler then flips the bleakness into Sartre's optimism, reading Dick's 'I myself, I am not a character in this novel: I am the novel' as the author freely remaking his life through the book, his first written without amphetamines, after the break-in he suspected he had staged himself.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 147 "Chapter 23 - Lonely Wolves" — Travis Paterson's introduction reads A Scanner Darkly as Dick's most autobiographical novel and explains Arctor's disgust at the over-happy Brown Bear Lodge audience through Sartre's Nausea: Roquentin's discovery that existence is sheer contingency, that we are superfluous, vaguely alarmed beings who cannot define existence as necessity. Arctor never finds Roquentin's slender chance of acceptance, so the nausea curdles into addiction and the wolf parable, the magnificent lone wolf shot to protect the meager, over-fed animals, poses the chapter's question of why the sensitive outsider is the one sacrificed.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 116 "A Footloose Man" — Dick expounds Sartre's 'Existentialism Is a Humanism' through the essentialist picture — a God-given blueprint, like Keith's Bentley designed before manufacture — against Sartre's claim that we exist first and invent essences afterward, marriage and family included. Monogamy thus emerges as a human choice mandated by Western authority and imposed on conquered peoples, not an absolute ethic handed down from heaven, a freedom humans exercise even in dropping Deuteronomy's stoning rule. Keith, Mick and Simone discarded the inherited tradition of monogamy, while Charlie Watts chose to stick with it.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 25 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Robert Tally Jr. reads The Graveyard Book as 'spectral existentialism': Bod's climax, 'I'm Nobody Owens. That's who I am,' is Sartre's existence precedes essence made literal, a self made rather than found, and the climactic claiming of the name enacts the self-ownership of the nursery-rhyme pauper 'who nobody owns.'
