- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 16 "Is Oskar Schindler a Good Man" — Ebertz treats Schindler's List as a thought experiment on what makes a person good, judging Oskar Schindler against Kantian and virtue-ethical standards. On Kant he fails: many acts (lying, bribery, infidelity) violate the categorical imperative, and even his rescues spring from growing partial attachment to 'his Jews' rather than rational duty or a good will. On Aristotelian virtue ethics he only selectively exercises virtues, so is not fully 'good' either; Ebertz resolves the tension with a Principle of Moral Exemplarity, holding Schindler up as a flawed but genuine moral example whose care promotes human flourishing.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 23 "Allons-y into the Starry Heavens" — Donna Marie Smith uses the Doctor and Rose's separation in "Doomsday" and "Journey's End" to explicate Kantian deontology. After framing the Doctor's virtues via Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and distinguishing eros, philia, and agape (with Reinette illustrating chivalrous self-sacrifice), she argues that Kant's categorical imperative and the duty-versus-inclination conflict explain why the Doctor and Rose Kant be together: their love pulls toward partiality while duty to save humanity is what they ought to do, so acting for the greater good is precisely what forces their parting.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 9 "2. Don’t Go to Lawyers for Moral Guidance" — Ralston reads Jimmy McGill's slide into Saul Goodman as a study in moral decline, using Dewey's (and Bourdieu's) theory of habit to explain why a person capable of right action repeatedly chooses the wrong path—the pressures of criminal clients, Chuck's contempt, and HHM's rejection wear down his will as an ingrained disposition. He contrasts Kant's categorical imperative with mere 'imperatives of prudence' (rules of thumb for achieving any end), arguing Jimmy consistently follows the latter, as when he unhinges Chuck at the disbarment hearing to win. Invoking Hart's separability of law and morality and Singer on the ethicist's training, he concludes lawyers like Saul make poor moral guides.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 10 "3. Can It Be Right to Defend the Guilty" — Cook tests whether lawyers may defend the legally and morally guilty against several ethical theories, anchored by Saul's contemplated lie at Lalo Salamanca's bail hearing (knowing Lalo murdered Fred Whalen). Kant's contradiction-in-conception makes lying to the court a perfect duty to refrain from, but Cook shows this looks too rigid via the invented 'Jemma' surgeon case; act and rule consequentialism (Bentham, Mill, Hooker) permit honest defenses while diverging on lies and mitigation. He argues Hume's sentimentalist virtue ethics best fits intuition: Saul's bail lie is wrong because motivated by self-interest rather than the procedural justice a virtuous advocate should feel.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 31 "20. Why Is Breaking Skateboarders’ Legs Wrong" — The chapter uses three characters to test three single-value moral theories: Chuck as a Kantian deontologist whose rigid loyalty to the categorical imperative and the 'sacred' law destroys his bond with Jimmy; Jimmy as a Mill-style consequentialist whose ends-justify-means scams (Sandpiper, the squat-cobbler film) let him decide what counts as good outcomes and cost him integrity, invoking Bernard Williams; and Mike as a Scanlonian contractualist who honors even immoral agreements like the Tuco hit. Through cases like the 'murderer at the door,' it argues each theory alone leads people to do wrong, so a moral life must combine outcomes, rules, and contracts.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 23 "13. In Defense of Demerzel" — Nurkic asks whether Demerzel, the loyal robot of the Apple TV+ Foundation, violates Asimov's Laws of Robotics when she poisons Zephyr Halima and kills Cleon XIV (Brother Dawn). He argues she is governed not by the ordinary First/Second Laws but by a reprogrammed priority—Daneel's 'Zeroth Law' (protect humanity) narrowed to 'Cleon I's vision'—and then contends the Laws are incoherent when applied to real cases (Buridan's-donkey paralysis, the surgeon dilemma, ambiguity of 'human' and 'harm'). He closes by testing the Laws against Kant's categorical imperative (the lying/murderer-at-the-door case) and Bentham-style utilitarianism to show robot ethics cannot be reduced to fixed programmed codes.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 29 "“Who watches the watchmen ”" — Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as a would-be consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) whose plan to kill millions to end the Cold War exposes utilitarianism's neglect of rights and, via Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ends,' its dependence on an unknowable infinite future. Rorschach poses as a Kantian deontologist ('I shall not compromise') but Loftis shows his hypocrisy, black-and-white dichotomous thinking, and failure to respect persons betray Kant's categorical imperative. Loftis argues neither theory is truly held by either character; both are rationalizations of power, and the comic's real target, captured by 'Who watches the watchmen?', is authoritarianism itself.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 18 "What Would You Do If Your Mother Asked You A Brief Introduction to Ethics" — Jacob Held and Eric Wilson introduce ethics by first dispatching cultural and normative relativism (the Butter Battle Book's Yooks and Zooks, the Once-ler's 'we're each allowed our own opinion') as a cowardly refusal to judge, then present three theories through Seuss characters. Horton is the paragon of Kantian dignity ('a person's a person, no matter how small') and the categorical imperative, tested against lying in The Cat in the Hat. Thidwick the Big-Hearted Moose dramatizes Mill's utilitarianism and its sacrifice of the individual to the greatest happiness, while Thidwick, courage, and Life's 'Great Balancing Act' illustrate Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, virtue as habituated character, and eudaimonia.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 19 "Horton Hears You, Too! Seuss and Kant on Respecting Persons" — Kowalski reads Horton Hatches the Egg and Horton Hears a Who! through Kant's two formulations of the categorical imperative. Mayzie's lying promise to Horton fails the universal-law test just like Kant's lying-loan and tax-shirking (Jo-Jo) cases, while Horton's insistence that 'a person's a person, no matter how small' embodies the ends-in-themselves formula treating the Whos as ends with dignity, not things. The essay argues Horton's fidelity is heroic rather than strictly required, revising Kant's moral absolutism (the inquiring-murderer case) so that when duties conflict one should act to disrespect persons least.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 21 "The Grinch’s Change of Heart Whodunit" — Cunningham asks whether the Grinch's sudden metanoia is a matter of head or heart, staging a debate between Kant and Hume. A Kantian reading treats the change as reason reasserting the moral law after the Grinch's inclinations (envy, resentment) hijacked it, so he realizes stealing Christmas disrespects the Whos as ends in themselves. A Humean reading, favored by the author given that the Grinch's 'small heart grew three sizes,' treats it as a new sentiment of sympathy rather than a rational apprehension, invoking Hume's claim that reason is the slave of the passions.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 13 "MOTHERHOOD" — Amy Kind examines the pervasiveness of parents lying to children (her own 'Bad Dream Spray') against Augustine's and Kant's absolute prohibition of lying, Mill's utilitarian permissiveness, and Sissela Bok's principle of veracity. She applies Kant's categorical imperative and formula of humanity – treating persons never merely as means – to argue that because young children have not fully developed their rational natures, the Kantian wrong of lying is mitigated, while illustrating the debate with South Park's Kyle reading Descartes, A Few Good Men's 'you can't handle the truth,' and Seinfeld's George Costanza ('it's not a lie if you believe it').
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 17 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Brophy puts Showtime's Dexter Morgan on 'ethical trial' before the reader-as-jury, applying four tests. Utilitarianism approves because killing killers maximizes happiness (the Ticking Time Bomb analogy); Kant's categorical imperative and even Kant's own endorsement of executing murderers cast Dexter as a 'just executioner' applying a dark golden rule; virtue theory finds Dexter progressing toward moderation and flourishing as a 'warrior' in his social role; and Rawls's veil of ignorance suggests one would consent to Dexter patrolling one's neighborhood. Brophy concludes Dexter is morally excusable, perhaps praiseworthy.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 20 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Amper reads Dexter as a comic-book superhero (orphan origin, secret identity, alien nature, dark side) whose first-person narration makes viewers identify with him. She uses Sartre's waiter and bad faith to analyze Dexter's self-ironic role-playing and denial of his true self, and Freud's id/superego conflict (with Harry's Code channeling the id) to frame his murderous drive as basic human nature. She then tests his killing against Mill's utilitarianism and Kant's categorical imperative, finding the verdict genuinely ambivalent, and concludes the show's 'try your best' ethic reflects a dark view of human nature we cannot feel at peace with.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 24 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Brown and Tien build a 'Kantian Gate' from Kant's Formula of Universal Law: you should date only if you wouldn't mind your dates acting on your own dating maxim, which bars the manipulative, deceptive, or coercive dater while permitting many ends. For those who pass the gate, they recommend pursuing Csikszentmihalyi's 'flow' and the Zhuangzi's cultivated spontaneity, describing a two-part self-cultivation (purging debilitating social programming via 'forgetting' and xinzhai, then training to act in accord with the Dao) so one can 'be in the moment' and get truly lucky on a first date. They apply the seven elements of flow directly to dating conversation, eye contact, and feedback.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 12 "6. Hollow Man" — Rowlands reads Hollow Man as a retelling of Plato's Ring of Gyges, posing 'why be moral?' once the invisible Kevin Bacon can act without sanction. He rejects the religious answer and Hobbesian social-contract theory (both reduce morality to prudence/fear of punishment and leave those outside the contract unprotected), and Hume's fellow-feeling as mere causal explanation not justification. He examines Kant's Categorical Imperative reducing immorality to inconsistency but argues it cannot answer 'why should I be moral,' concluding the choice is arational self-definition, closing with Nietzsche's 'become what you are' and the deed at the bottom of morality.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — South reads Batman, Batgirl, and Catwoman comics through J. M. Bernstein's Adorno-derived account of the 'damaged life' lived under Weberian rationalization and the disenchantment of the world. The Joker's 'one bad day' in The Killing Joke embodies 'affective skepticism'—the split between rational universal norms and agent-specific motivation—while the debate between moral internalism and externalism (which he ties to Kant-style abstract justification) expresses the hurt of a disenchanted world where justifying and motivating reasons no longer converge. Barbara Gordon's 'because I can,' Bruce Wayne's vow, and Selina Kyle's turn toward 'basic human dignity' exemplify Bernstein's 'fugitive ethics,' fragile promises that restore authority outside juridico-legal channels and produce genuine happiness in damaged lives.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 29 "“Who watches the watchmen ”" — J. Robert Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as an apparent consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) who sacrifices millions of New Yorkers for the greater good, and Rorschach as an apparent deontologist ('I shall not compromise'), then argues neither is true to his stated theory. Utilitarianism is critiqued through Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ever ends' (the infinite future defeats the calculus) and its trouble grounding rights, while Rorschach's hypocritical, dichotomous, disrespect-for-persons stance is shown to be fascism, not Kant's categorical imperative (universalization and treating persons as ends). Loftis contends the deeper target is authoritarianism itself: the corrupt superheroes show that ethical theories are rationalizations of power, so no one should be entrusted with too much of it.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 3 "1. The Good Place as Philosophy Moral Adventures in the Afterlife" — Engels argues that NBC's The Good Place, though premised on a merit-based afterlife, actually argues morality should not be grounded in afterlife reward. When Eleanor, Chidi, Jason, and Tahani learn the point system and can no longer earn points, they form the 'Soul Squad' to be virtuous for virtue's sake, echoing Aristotle's telos and Kant's claim that acting from fear of hell is a heteronomous, non-moral motive. She reads the unfair points system (no human admitted in 521 years) through Rawls's Veil of Ignorance and shifts the show toward rehabilitative justice, and treats the Good Place residents' boredom via Bernard Williams's tedium-of-immortality argument, with Chidi's 'wave returns to the ocean' speech mapped onto Hindu atman/Brahman and moksha.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 10 "8. Breaking Bad as Philosophy The Moral Aesthetics of the Anti-hero’s Journey" — Koepsell reads Breaking Bad as a satirical epic whose antihero Walter White illustrates philosophy better than argument can. He casts Walt's pro/con list before killing Krazy-8 as an ad absurdum refutation of Bentham's hedonic calculus and a violation of Kant's categorical imperative (treating Krazy-8 as mere means), and shows Walt cultivating the Aristotelian vices — recklessness, intemperance, injustice — rather than virtues. Drawing on Sartre, he argues Walt lives in bad faith by becoming 'Heisenberg' for the look of the other (the 'say my name' scene), like Leone's Man with No Name, and that Camus's Sisyphus marks the happiness Walt refused. He concludes the show endorses Hume's emotivism: justice is an aesthetic felt experience, not a rule.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 46 "43. Ex Machina as Philosophy Mendacia Ex Machina (Lies from a Machine)" — Grinnell argues Ex Machina is fundamentally about lying, read through Kant's deontology. He frames Nathan's rigged Turing test on Ava against Glaucon's Ring of Gyges challenge and Kant's two formulations of the categorical imperative, deriving three 'wrinkles': lying is heteronomous programming rather than the autonomy Nathan seeks; the experiment is defensible only if Ava fails, since a genuine person may not be manipulated (Formula of Humanity); and the cascade of lies among Nathan, Caleb, and Ava vindicates Kant's absolute prohibition on lying. He uses Caleb's telling of Frank Jackson's Mary's Room and Searle's weak/strong AI distinction to question whether Ava's 'pleasure response' amounts to genuine consciousness or personhood.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 62 "59. Don’t Look Up as Philosophy Comets, Climate Change, and Why the Snacks Are Not Free" — The chapter argues Don't Look Up is less a film than a moral imperative: its comet is an allegory for climate change, and Randall Mindy's on-air breakdown presents Singer-style simple premises (the end of human life is bad; prevent bad things you can) that compel action. It uses Plato's knowledge-as-the-Good and 'blameworthy ignorance' to condemn the willfully ignorant (Kate's parents, the Orlean Bros) who act as if they know, and Kant's categorical imperative to condemn General Themes's 'free snacks' lie and to cast the moral as the rational. It defends the comet/climate analogy against critics and insists individual action is insufficient while collective government action is required.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 81 "76. The Last of Us as Moral Philosophy Teleological Particularism and Why Joel Is Not a Villain" — Horn takes The Last of Us as moral philosophy, arguing Joel is read as a villain only because players assume consequentialism or deontology. On Bentham/Mill's utilitarianism Joel fails to maximize utility by killing many to save Ellie; on Kant's categorical imperative his lying, stealing and killing are always impermissible. Horn instead defends 'teleological particularism' — an agent acts rightly when acting in conformity with a role, roles being socially constructed and variable — so Joel's role as Ellie's surrogate father (mirrored in his carrying her out as he carried Sarah, and the 'Future Days' lyric) obligates him to put her above humanity. On this view Joel's refusal to let the Fireflies kill Ellie, and his final lie, are morally permissible, not villainous.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 85 "80. Detroit Become Human as Philosophy Moral Reasoning Through Gameplay" — Engels and Evans argue that Detroit: Become Human stages moral reasoning through the interactive stories of the androids Connor, Kara, and Markus, whose 'deviant' awakening they read through Frankfurt's distinction between wantons and persons with second-order desires and through Kant's requirement of the ability to do otherwise. Scenes like Markus scavenging a pump regulator from a dying android, the blood-on-hands visualization after his speech, and Kara protecting Alice force players to weigh Kantian, utilitarian, virtue, and Gilligan-style care frameworks. Through Alice's reveal as an android and the grieving-widower scene, the game makes an implicit anti-speciesist argument (via Singer) that beings who can suffer are morally considerable, and that agency and responsibility emerge through suffering and struggle.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 93 "87. Frank Miller’s Batman as Philosophy “The World Only Makes Sense When You Force It To”" — Bein reads Frank Miller's Batman (chiefly The Dark Knight Returns and Year One) as rejecting the utilitarianism he ascribes to Superman—who would 'rightly' nuke a city to prevent two—in favor of a Nietzschean will to power, distinguished from mere force (Macht vs. Kraft), born of Miller's own mugging. The Joker problem is worked through Kant's categorical imperative, desert-based death penalty, and the slippery slope of denying moral standing to the insane. Bein then separates Miller's avowed libertarianism (Nozick's canteen/lifeguard thought experiments, the minimal state) from Bruce Wayne's coercive 'Bat-libertarianism,' and confronts the 'Frank Miller problem' of Holy Terror's Islamophobia against Miller's anti-corporate, anti-Reagan streak.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 100 "94. Yes, Roya and Philosophy The Art of Submission" — Goldberg, Gavaler, and Chavez use Trotman and Denich's Yes, Roya—where Roya dominates Joe and Wylie professionally (publishing under Joe's name) and sexually, all consensually—to ask how the three major Western ethical theories can accommodate consensual dominant/submissive relationships. They argue Aristotle's virtue ethics handles them via unequal friendships (submissives depending more, within a mean), Kant's Formula of Universal Law permits them once consent is built into the maxim (aligning with the Formula of Humanity), and Mill's utilitarianism sanctions them because justice and felt safety, grounded in consent, follow from the Greatest Happiness Principle.

### Class Struggle

Class struggle is Marx and Engels's claim, announced in the opening of The Communist Manifesto, that the history of society is a history of conflict between classes with opposing economic interests. In capitalism this conflict centers on the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production, and the proletariat, who must sell their labor to survive. Marx held that this antagonism is built into the structure of production itself and that it would ultimately drive revolutionary change, making class conflict the engine of historical development.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 109 "The Matrix , Marx, and the Coppertop’s Life" — Danahay and Rieder read the film as dramatizing Marx's account of the exploited worker, from UPS drivers with tracking devices to keystroke-counted data clerks, continuing the workplace surveillance Marx attacked. The pivotal scene is Morpheus's loading-program lesson: 'You've been living in a dream world' followed by 'Welcome to the desert of the real' and the definition of the Matrix as control that turns a human being into the Duracell battery he holds up—the 'coppertop' Switch earlier called Neo.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 110 "Unknown" — The chapter reads the pod power plant—naked humans stacked like workers in corporate cubicles—through the Communist Manifesto's enslaved factory masses and 'Wage-Labor and Capital's' claim that labor power is a commodity sold by the clock like sugar. Against readings of alienation as private feeling, it uses Morpheus's 'The Matrix is a system' speech to show Marx's point that alienation is produced by the system of social relations: workers see their own labor as a commodity and cannot recognize their connection to the capital they generate.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 30 "The Superhero As Liberal Reformer" — Jeffrey Pasley traces the show's radical surface — capitalism equated with vampirism (Anya's greed, Glory the über-consumer, the Master's blood factory in 'The Wish'), Big Bads tearing down dimensional barriers exactly as Marx's Communist Manifesto describes the bourgeoisie dissolving feudal ties into free trade, Buffy refusing to commodify slaying into wage labor, and Giles's Magic Box selling mystified junk at inflated margins — but concludes the heroes are not revolutionaries. In the comic-book lineage of Superman and Spider-Man, Buffy and Angel are liberal reformers bound by a superhero code against killing, so Giles must murder the innocent Ben precisely to preserve Buffy's heroic mercy; Angel's 'champions' speech in 'Deep Down' states the incrementalist creed.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 15 "Hip Hop and “This Makin’ Dollars Shit”" — Pittman argues the rap battle - UTFO's "Roxanne, Roxanne" answered by Roxanne Shanté's "Roxanne's Revenge", Run-D.M.C.'s "Sucker MC's", Jay-Z's "Takeover" versus Nas's "Ether" - is hip hop's enactment of Hegel's master-slave struggle for recognition, where self-consciousness proves itself only through an all-or-nothing contest ending in domination rather than destruction. Gangsta rap (N.W.A's "Gangsta Gangsta", Ice Cube's fantasy raid on the suburbs) radicalizes the battle into a collective demand that America recognize black urban conditions, and the chapter turns to Du Bois's race-centered and Marx's class-centered revisions of Hegel's history to read "this makin' dollars shit" - Wu-Tang's "C.R.E.A.M.", Talib Kweli on capitalism and crack, Mos Def's "The Rape Over" - as the dialectic's capture of the cipher by corporate beef.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 16 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Goldstein applies Hegel's thesis-antithesis-synthesis and Marx's more complex, multidimensional dialectic to the splits within biker culture: bar-room stare-downs as struggles for recognition, wrenchers versus trailers, RUBs versus working-class riders, helmet disputes, and one-percenters versus the rest. He traces the collapse of brotherhood (the clenched fist of solidarity giving way to the selective wave) to the commodification of the motorcycle during the Japanese invasion and to Harley's own yuppie-era Willie G. marketing, arguing via commodity fetishism that bikers misread economic forces between manufacturers as personal differences. His conclusion is that the seeds of unity lie within the divisions, and that Harley-Davidson Motor Co. will not save the culture, since its task is profit, not tradition.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 40 "Downsizing Dreams" — Michael Bray argues the American Office portrays the "salaried masses," a class that exists in denying class: Jim, Pam, and Michael's rationalized, meaningless paper work realizes Marx's account of surplus value and degraded labor (the "run-out-the-clock" truck unloading, Pam's tepid watercolors), while their self-image survives by distinguishing itself from warehouse and prison labor. Episodes like Michael's condo purchase and Pam's "dreams are just dreams" show characters secretly longing for downsizing to force a different life. Against the New Yorker's claim that the show ignores class, Bray reads its comedy as standing on the edge of naming its economic conditions, with Michael's failure to inhabit management-speak making him, via Walter Benjamin, a last glimpse of "authentic humanity."
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 9 "Quittin’ Time" — Michels surveys Marx (alienation, false consciousness, the Communist Manifesto's reduction of family to economics), Weber's Protestant work ethic, and Arendt's labor/work/action distinction, then reads Springsteen's whole career against them, from 'Factory' (the working life that 'takes his hearing' and leaves 'someone's gonna get hurt tonight') through 'Hungry Heart,' 'Mansion on the Hill,' and The Ghost of Tom Joad ('Youngstown,' 'Sinaloa Cowboys,' 'Straight Time'). The verdict: Springsteen is a man of the left but no Marxist — his characters struggle with their own restlessness and with each other rather than with class oppressors, the wealthy suffer their own bourgeois malaise, and work, however brutal, is no cause for revolution. Nor does he share Arendt's ideal: his realm of freedom is unapologetically middle-class — cruising in a cool car, hanging with friends, getting with your favorite girl, and always the radio.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 24 "It’s the Disappointing Stories that Sound True to Life" — Shipman argues that the re-imagined Cylons, having rebelled as slaves, recreated oppression inside their own society: the human-form Numbers rule over mute Centurions (voices literally bred out, like banning slave literacy), animalized Raiders, and dismissed 'insane' Hybrids, whose sentience ('Scar' shows strategy and self-preservation) the Numbers willfully deny. The division of labor echoes Marx's 'from each according to his ability,' but assignments are engineered by their makers, and the model-making program is eugenics rather than evolution — the series' own word 'evolved' is, he says, disingenuous. Hence the Numbers lose the moral superiority their victimhood earned, and the scriptural 'all of this has happened before' implies the subaltern models may rebel next.
- **Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_**, ch. 6 "index" — Scholz completes his 'playground and factory' argument: user translations, photos and profiles are unpaid digital labor locked inside a walled garden whose data trails are sold to marketers and governments, even as the same platform hosts a genuine power to act together. Morgan and Clulow frame activism with the Communist Manifesto's class struggle, staging fictional discussion-board posts from Engels, Luxemburg and Chomsky that update the proletariat into the internet-era 'iProles', then show Facebook's ease breeding slacktivism, from the '1,000,000 For Obama To Grow An Afro!' group dwarfing real causes to the platform itself banning a father's 'Justice for Francesca Bimpson' page. Muhr and Pedersen use Zizek's interpassivity to argue the Facebook profile is a surrogate self that enjoys, believes and mourns on our behalf, like canned laughter or a Tibetan prayer wheel, deferring the social duty to be authentic while the site quietly installs its own ideology of relentlessly interesting happiness.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 26 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Curry refuses to celebrate The Wire, arguing that Simon's class-based realism ('more about class than race') misrepresents Black urban life, and he contrasts it with Black film from New Jack City to Menace II Society where these issues were already explored. Reading scenes like Rawls's 'project nigger' murders no one cares about, Bunk shrugging at Stringer's unsolved killing, and McNulty telling Brianna that nobody will look into D'Angelo's death, he argues the show registers an indifference specific to Black life, not to the poor as such. Drawing on W.E.B. Du Bois's account of colonialism and the slave trade as the genesis of modern capital ('capital noir') and rejecting the intersectional race-class-gender frame as a 'discursive distraction', he demands a racial realism in Derrick Bell's sense: racism is permanent, the underclass is really an racialized undercaste, and the War on Drugs continues Jim Crow by other means.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 31 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Zizek reads The Wire as subject-realism, a city's collective self-staging (with Simon as its DJ-curator) of the class struggle between the two Americas, where postmodern institutions play the Olympian gods and the self-propelling abstraction of capital is the Lacanian Real running the show, a point he anchors in Marx's prosopopoeia of commodities and 'real abstraction'. Following Jameson he catalogues the show's utopian gestures woven into reality (Frank's dream of revitalizing the port, Colvin's Hamsterdam, Prezbo's dice-based math, Avon and Stringer's last drink, D'Angelo's family utopia), then argues the Major Crimes unit of McNulty, Freamon, Kima, and Omar is a proto-Communist conspiratorial collective whose honest individual resistance (from Snot Boogie to McNulty's firing) merely feeds the system's self-reproduction. Hence his provocation: the only radical step beyond Simon's social-democratic reformism is the strike of the 'inherent transgressors', withdrawing the resistance that keeps the system alive so that Fate itself, not just its victims, can be changed.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 34 "Psych and Philosophy" — Jeff Ewing applies Marx's critique of religion - the supernatural as ruling-class ideology, 'the opium of the people,' behind which priests and shamans hide real material processes and prop up hierarchy - to Shawn, who likewise masks his genuinely material observational talent as psychic gift to escape arrest in the pilot and keep access to SBPD cases. But the comparison inverts: unlike Marx's priests, Shawn serves ordinary people rather than the ruling class, and the chapter concludes he is better understood as an alienated worker - forced by a repressive state's threat of prosecution to sell a false product, defined by what he is not, and never credited for his true skill.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 18 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Fitzpatrick runs Marx's account of alienated labor from the 1844 Manuscripts through the novel: Victor's creature is the product of estranged labor, 'an alien object exercising power over him,' which he cannot name, comes to loathe, and which finally destroys him - the devaluation of the creator tracking the increasing value of the thing made, while workers become commodities producing commodities. The De Laceys' eviction in Branagh's Mary Shelley's Frankenstein and the Ingolstadt cholera riots stage class struggle at feudalism's end, and Victor's failure to self-actualize (to 'hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon... criticize after dinner') shows how capitalism turns science into 'a tool of our own destruction.' The chapter closes with 'Frankenstorm' climate change as the alienated externality par excellence - capitalists selling us the rope with which we hang ourselves.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 19 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Sexton reads the park as capitalist ideology in action, quoting Marx and Engels on the ruling class controlling the means of mental production: Hammond's flea circus is the illusion we agree not to see, and Nedry's sabotage shows what happens when workers are told their poverty is their own problem. He applies Veblen's leisure class to Gennaro, who judges the night-vision goggles valuable because they are expensive, and Marx's general law of capitalist accumulation to Hammond's squeezing of wages once every other cost is beyond his control. The dinosaurs themselves figure as the exploited working class, held not by ideology but by electric fences, and when the fence falls they seize the park.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 11 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter argues coal made Boyd Crowder possible: company scrip, Bloody Harlan's union-busting terror, black lung (Boyd's would-be assassin takes the bridge job because mining ruined his lungs), and Black Pike's mountaintop removal leave Harlan no viable work outside the mines, so crime is the rational alternative. It reads this through Hegel's 'rabble' from the Philosophy of Right - civil society is never wealthy enough to prevent an excess of poverty, and the rabble loses the honor of self-support - plus Marcuse's affluent-society critique of an existence that 'violently defends its own servitude'. Boyd's outlawry, which sets its own code above mere criminality, is a rebellion against being pushed into the rabble, and Hegel's remedy of emigration explains why leaving Harlan is the only escape, though the coal train hauls coal out while the people stay.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 33 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Karavitis fabricates a recovered 'Dracula's Journal' in which the Count retells Stoker's plot as rational self-interest: he owes no one anything, Lucy 'came to me of her own free will,' Van Helsing's crew are a 'craven collective' spouting 'from each according to his ability,' and only objective reality - not their subjective feelings - counts. He claims a fundamental right to pursue his own happiness, casting himself as the thinking individual crushed by proletarian herd morality. An editor's framing email makes the point explicit: Rand-style egoism could justify even Dracula, a 'manual for vampires' set against Marx's collectivism.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 36 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Sexton's mock FBI COMPIC file stages a Cold War reading of Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein: screenwriters Lees and Rinaldo remake Dracula as Marx's Das Kapital vampire - capital as dead labour sucking living labour - so blood-draining becomes profit-draining and 'This man belongs to me!' the capitalist's claim on his workers. A fictional Ayn Rand review for HUAC decodes the film as collectivist propaganda that slanders the businessman McDougal and dreams of a creature with 'no will of his own,' touching Marxian alienation along the way. A final note links screenwriter Robert Lees's blacklisting by Sterling Hayden and his real-life decapitation to Stoker's vampire-killing instructions.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 19 "9. Class Warfare in Chicago" — Canode reads the trilogy as a study in class warfare: the factionless are the invisible lower class kept poor as a warning, the factions the middle class distracted by initiation rankings and faction pride, and the Bureau the self-righteous upper class that created and manipulates the whole system. Marx's analysis structures the argument - the ruling class's specter now haunts the powerless, and 'from each according to his ability' shades into coerced harmony - while the American Dream rhetoric of Carter, Reagan, and Obama plays the aptitude test's role: an ideology of merit that converts structural limits into personal failure. The Bureau's genetic sorting of GP scientists above GD support staff mirrors how meritocracy blames the poor for their poverty, so Tris's verdict - the factions 'gave us the illusion of choice without actually giving us a choice' - indicts the US class system too.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 11 "2. I May Be a Socialist, But I’m Not a Lunatic" — Walderczak stages the Branson-Robert-Matthew triangle as socialism, aristocratic conservatism, and capitalism colliding over the estate's duty to its people. He tracks how Tom's Marx-flavored socialism - really closer to Owen's and Fourier's utopian cooperatism - evaporates once he marries Sybil and co-manages the land, the chauffeur 'Branson' becoming family-member 'Tom,' a case of David Harvey's capitalist pacification. Meanwhile Robert's noblesse oblige - secretly paying a tenant's overdue rent from private funds, ranting 'profits, profits, profits,' treating ownership as custodianship of the tenants - leaves the author asking who the real socialist is, and answering that Robert's conservatism has far more in common with socialist ideals than Tom's self-confessed politics ever did.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 13 "4. Finding One’s Place and Being Useful" — Karavitis argues that work, not social class, is Downton's real theme, sorting characters in a two-by-two matrix of class membership against acceptance or rejection of the existing social order. Those who accept their place stagnate - Violet ('We don't work,' 'What is a weekend?'), Robert the mismanaging custodian, the perpetually jobless Molesley - while those who reject it flourish: Isobel's drive to be 'useful,' Sybil's nursing ('I feel useful for the first time in my life'), Gwen's hidden typewriter, Alfred's Ritz training. He surveys Rousseau on work's role in inequality, Smith on the division of labor, and Marx on labor and ideology on the negative side, and Aristotle, Russell's 'In Praise of Idleness,' and Pieper on leisure and personal projects on the positive side, ending with the prediction that automation will soon give everyone the Crawley daughters' problem of what to do with a life without work.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 24 "12. Should We Really Care about the Crawleys" — Jones takes up the charge that loving Downton seduces viewers into admiring inequality, and answers that the Crawleys deserve our care because birth, not choice, gave them their position, so they should be judged only by what they do with it: Grantham paying for Mrs. Patmore's eye surgery, Violet throwing the flower contest after Isobel's challenge, the family gradually embracing Branson. He reads the show as a manifesto for social change through sympathetic contact between classes rather than Irish-style revolt - befriend the rich and their good nature will start to level the playing field. His own objection is that this makes change partly the responsibility of the less privileged, from Thomas being asked to soften Carson's homophobia to the poor being asked to be nice to the rich today.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 7 "Red Rising and Philosophy" — The editors' introduction argues that Red Rising grips because it mirrors our own world of class struggle, where a Gold-like elite lives in luxury on the backs of oppressed laborers kept distracted by games and propaganda. It traces Darrow's arc from resigning himself to death after Eo's execution, through his carving and campaign of destruction, to the discovery that friendship with Sevro, Mustang, Victra, and Ragnar—not revenge—is what actually pulls him out of life's mines. It closes by previewing the volume's questions: whether enhancement could doom humanity, whether Darrow is the same person after the carving, love versus vengeance, how society should be structured, and the meaning of life.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 9 "1. When Evolution Strikes Back" — Tim Jones argues the Golds misread Darwin: they take themselves to be the perfected endpoint of natural selection and use the Passage and Institute to 'help Nature along' by culling weaker Golds, justifying the subjugation of lower Colors—the same social-Darwinist logic Hitler and Stalin used to dress up atrocity. Using Darwin's own contrast between natural selection and man-made selective breeding, he shows the Institute is an artificial arena and the Golds' shaping of Reds and Pinks is self-serving husbandry, not nature's work. The twist is that the very traits the Golds bred into lowReds—Helldiver knuckles, miner's endurance, drill-floor courage—are what win Darrow the Institute, the Iron Rain, and the fight against the Jackal, so their manipulated evolution becomes the tool of their own extinction, just as Quicksilver's case against the static Color hierarchy implies.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 23 "11. The Iron Bank Will Have Its Due" — Ewing argues money is the real determinant of the Iron Throne: Lannister gold made Cersei queen, Tyrell grain and taxation bought Margaery's crown, Baelish's financing decided the Battle of the Bastards, and the Iron Bank disciplines kings. Reading Westeros as a late-feudal economy through Marx - smallfolk whose work and taxes support lords who 'reap where they never sowed,' a hierarchy held by coercion and fear as the High Sparrow tells Olenna ('You are the few, we are the many'), and money dissolving feudal bonds into a 'money aristocracy' - he predicts the throne will go not to dragons or White Walkers but to the capitalist-financier figure of Petyr Baelish.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 37 "23. A Chimichanga for the Mercenary Soul" — Through Gramsci's Prison Notebooks the chapter casts Deadpool as the 'Eternal Proletariat': the military superstructure (Weapon X) recruited him precisely because he was broke and class-positioned, and as a mercenary he has no capital, no upward mobility, and no exit from wage-killing. His hunger beyond money - the Bullseye payday that ends in him shooting himself, the dead shark's verdict 'what you are . . . is alone' - drives him toward the X-Men, read as a subaltern coalition of the marginalized like Gramsci's socialist parties. But as a non-mutant 'mutate' who cannot meet the hegemonic standard of heroism (the Hit-Monkey arc with Spider-Man, his bitter plea to Wolverine that 'at least they wanted you'), his only Gramscian options are coalition building or reshaping the X-Men's culture from inside.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 24 "10. If It Isn’t Justified Is It Still My Revolution" — Writing as a guilt-ridden fsociety member haunted by James Plouffe's on-air suicide, Altmann tests the 5/9 revolution against three theorists: Burke's conservatism condemns all revolution as destruction of social tradition (and fsociety's blackout chaos and Susan Jacobs's death seem to prove him right), while Marx's class struggle between E Corp's bourgeoisie and the indebted proletariat makes revolution the only exit from history's cycle. Kai Nielsen's condition - revolution is justified only when no other recourse exists - settles it: Angela's failed attempt to reform E Corp from within shows non-revolutionary change is impossible, so the author keeps fighting 'with a keyboard whose clacking is endless.'
- **The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed**, ch. 9 "1 Introduction" — Smith introduces his project of explaining the subordination of women and blacks philosophically and empirically by comparing the social contract liberalism of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau with Marxism, building on Carole Pateman's Sexual Contract and Charles Mills's Racial Contract/Contract and Domination, which show the classic contracts were male supremacist and white supremacist. He argues sexual and racial egalitarianism is about politics and power, cataloguing nine power bases women and blacks should acquire, and stresses that because family and state are historically connected (Aristotle's Politics, Hobbes's 'little kingdoms', Locke's conjugal society, Rousseau's family as the oldest society, Engels's 'first class oppression' of the female by the male), equality in marriage may be a precondition for equality in society. He defends Marxism against Mills's dismissal of it as moribund, endorses MacKinnon's linking of sexism and racism while arguing (with Linda LaRue and Du Bois) that the racial contract has been more tyrannical than the sexual contract, and closes with Walzer's definition of egalitarianism as a society free of domination.
- **The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed**, ch. 10 "2 Power and Politics" — The chapter traces politics from the classical ethics-fused view (Aristotle's Politics, where politics exists for the sake of the good life yet also supplies one of the first justifications of patriarchy and the public/private split) to the Machiavelli-Hobbes break where politics becomes simply the possession and exercise of power, adopting Bertrand Russell's claim that power is the fundamental concept of social science. It then builds the book's central instrument, a Weber-derived analysis of nine power bases (money, knowledge/technology/information, religion, morality, authority, charisma, size/solidarity, violence, status), contrasting the Marxian reading - money as ultimately determinative, the ruling ideas of each age as the ideas of the ruling class, religion as the opium of the people, the state as a committee for managing bourgeois affairs - with the liberal-Weberian reading in which no single base is decisive. It closes by showing that Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau and Marx divide over the morality of egalitarianism (Popper's Marx moved by moral impulse versus Locke's possessive individualism), and that power is domain-specific, inert until used, skill-dependent and always relative.
- **The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed**, ch. 15 "7 The Bourgeoisie and the Blacks" — The chapter sets business - the US bourgeoisie whose privileged position Charles Beard read into the Constitution and which survived the Jacksonian and New Deal challenges by breaking labor through Taft-Hartley, right-to-work laws and the PATCO lockout, its solidarity secured while worker solidarity was undercut by what Marx called the Achilles heel of racism - against blacks as the paradigmatic powerless, shut out of every power base since slavery, which the chapter treats with Baptist and Marx's 1846 letter as a totalitarian system of super-exploited, tortured labor that built American capitalism, its neo-slavery progeny (Blackmon) pauperizing the black community under Dred Scott's 'subordinate and inferior class of beings'. It then narrates black counter-power base by base: the abolitionist interracial coalition wielding charisma (Douglass, Nat Turner, John Brown), information, morality and religion; the NAACP era and King's fusion of charisma, church religion, Myrdal's An American Dilemma and televised nonviolent provocation against Bull Connor's violence, contested by Malcolm X, SNCC and the Black Panthers; and a post-civil-rights scorecard showing a wealth base 94.2 percent white, persistent education and media gaps, constrained black officials from mayors to the symbolic Obama presidency, and a captive but potentially leveraged black vote in a 'Sisyphean' struggle.
- **The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed**, ch. 16 "8 Conclusion" — The conclusion restates the book's method - centering political philosophy in a consciously normative, empirical study of power - around its two contrasts: the family as a natural, subordination-requiring institution in liberalism versus a property-rooted, historically determined one in Marxism, and the state as a freely agreed contract of all (Locke, hence no food stamps) versus what actually happened, a charter 'ordained and established by a small group of wealthy white men, meeting in secret' to protect their wealth, so that the state which created gender and racial inequality must now play an equally decisive role in undoing it. Reviewing the nine bases since the 1960s, it finds women have closed the knowledge gap and nearly completed Engels's liberation program except universal child-care and non-exploitative housework, against conservative marriage-movement scholars like the Lockean Yenor, while blacks still face a tripling wealth gap that only social democratic capitalism on the Danish model plus comprehensive reparations can close - the latter argued on the moral base of power, Congress's 2009 apology, and Bernard Boxill's Lockean inheritance argument for a decades-long 'Reparations Superfund' as the civil rights issue of the 21st century.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 13 "3. Why Don’t the Proles Just Take Over" — Littmann asks why Oceania's proles, 85 percent of the population who could 'blow the Party to pieces tomorrow morning', never revolt, answering with Winston's diagnosis: until they become conscious they will never rebel. The Party keeps them unconscious through its media monopoly, crimestop, doublethink, reality control, perpetual war hysteria, and a nationalist identity that cuts them off from the international proletariat. He maps each mechanism onto the modern US, where six corporations control about 90 percent of media, citizens tailor their own reality bubbles, opponents are assumed to argue in bad faith, and partisan 'nationalisms' block common cause, arguing that American political conflict is mostly over facts rather than values.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 23 "11. Forever the Wild One" — Anders grounds Petty's artistic freedom in Kant's Critique of Judgment: genius, the innate talent for original art freed from patron control, describes Petty's refusal to let commercial success measure his work. Singer's practical ethics supplies the frame for the $8.98 fight over Hard Promises, where Petty weighed outcomes for all affected, especially teenage fans, and threatened to withhold the masters or rename the album "Eight Ninety-Eight." Marx's worker-owner analysis maps the Shelter-to-MCA contract saga, in which Petty was sold like a piece of meat, countersued, hid the master tapes nightly, and filed for bankruptcy like a worker confronting the owners who pocket the value of the records he produced.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 42 "28. Replicants of California, Unite!" — Christopher Innes gives 2049 a Marxist class analysis: the replicants are an enslaved working class, the Wallace Corporation the ruling class owning the means of production, and the LAPD a state apparatus with 'relative autonomy' that really upholds the system — K is a slave who kills his own kind without seeing his class position. Applying the materialist (not idealist) dialectic and the Eighteenth Brumaire's lesson about conflicting ruling-class interests, he reads Wallace, Atari, and even Ana as factions with divergent interests. Freysa's 'we are our own masters' and 'we are building our own army' mark the replicants as class conscious, aware of their Marxian 'species being', with nothing to lose but their chains.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 35 "22. Won’t You Be My Comrade" — Christopher Innes runs Marx's critique of Hegel's idealism against Mister Rogers: the show treats problems (divorce, war, the Clemmons pool scene) ideally, as symbolic gestures rather than material change, much as Hegel's storybook individuals miss money's role. Measured against Capital's alienated worker, 'an appendage to the machine,' contrasted with the suitcase worker who 'knows her work,' and the Communist Manifesto's 'bourgeois socialist' who demands reform not liberation, Rogers emerges as a progressive bourgeois socialist whose make-believe may console children for, or subtly resist, their future exploitation.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 14 "Alien Nation" — Reads Alien as a film about alienation in Marx's fourfold sense from the 1844 Manuscripts: the crew is estranged from the product of its labor (the retrieved Xenomorph turns on them), from the labor process (Brett and Parker's bonus dispute, Dallas shilling for the Company that deems him disposable), from species-being (infantile dependence on Mother, whose Special Order 937 merely formalizes an expendability they already live), and from one another (they never unite against the Company or suspect Ash). In Aliens the Colonial Marines repeat the failure, while the coordinated alien 'nation' under its queen - possible victims of Engineer colonization - makes the humans look like the inferior species.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 14 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Applies Marx's fourfold alienation (from product, from labor, from species-being, from others) to Bluth capitalism: George Michael dips and sells bananas he cannot keep, Lupe cleans Lucille's home under duress, and classes divide the family from the people it exploits. George Sr.'s Boyfights tapes and Caged Wisdom show the capitalist commodifying his children and himself, Gob's figurehead presidency turns employees into resources, Lindsay is 'having without being', and Engels's property-based account of the nuclear family explains Tobias's repressed sexuality; the cure offered is democratic socialism, since within-system fixes only get more absurd.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 16 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Reads Bluth bourgeois identity through Marx's class vocabulary: consumption as status display (Lucille's furs, $6,300 suits), labor-as-leisure (Tobias's acting, Buster's cartography, Gob's illusions), and the observation that the family's real workers are children, women of color like Lupe, and a Roomba. Class is performed, as Tom Jane's homeless method acting and Lucille's 'poolside only' meltdown show, and the Bluths' narcissism (Lindsay's cause-shopping activism, the family's disgust at Buster's severed hand) is analyzed as a form of bourgeois privilege, while the family fails at the reinvestment that would make it a proper bourgeoisie.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 14 "A Specter Is Haunting the Bending World" — Lin argues the Bending World's supernatural inequality breaks Hobbes's condition that even the weakest can kill the strongest, the equality that motivates the social contract, so might-is-right is magnified: Ozai rules without bargaining while weak Earth Kings become Dai Li figureheads. Energybending's built-in 'moral self-destruct' needs no earthly accountability, resembling the divine right of kings rather than Arendt's insight that violence eradicates politics, and Aang wisely remains a passive guardian. The Avatar's reincarnation creates recurring power vacuums, and because bending is a non-redistributable endowment, the Equalist revolution haunts the Bending World like the specter of communism in the Communist Manifesto.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 14 "A Specter Is Haunting the Bending World" — Lin uses Hobbes's observation that in our world the weakest can kill the strongest, grounding the social contract, to show what breaks when supernatural power is wildly unequal: Fire Lord Ozai need not bargain with generals as Earth Kings must with the Dai Li, and the eclipse is the only equalizer. Energybending gets a 'moral self-destruct' that no real technology has, making Aang an unaccountable guardian closer to the divine right of kings than to naturalist politics, though his refusal of rule keeps politics alive in Arendt's sense. Like Marx and Engels's specter of communism, the 'specter of Equalism' outlives Amon, because bending is a non-redistributable, lethal endowment, so democracy in Republic City is structurally haunted.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 24 "It’s the Disappointing Stories that Sound True to Life" — Shipman argues the series first builds viewer sympathy for Cylons as rebel slaves (their monotheism and their New Caprica role as US-style occupiers make them 'more like the viewers than the humans'), then undercuts it: the Numbers rebuilt Cylon society as oppressors, breeding the voices out of Centurions, dismissing the Hybrids as mad, and breeding the sentient Raiders (Starbuck's discovery in 'Scar') into functional animals. The opening narration's claim that Cylons 'evolved' is disingenuous, since the model hierarchy was deliberately engineered, 'not evolution, but eugenics,' with Marx's 'from each according to his ability' division of labor as thin cover for literal class construction. The former slaves became slave-owners, fulfilling 'all of this has happened before': heroes of one story become villains of the next, inviting the muted models to rebel against the Numbers in turn.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 16 "Symbolism How We Create Meaning" — DeHaven and Hendrickson read Columbia through Marx's class struggle: Comstock and Fink form the bourgeoisie controlling the means of production (Finkton, Handyman conversions of injured workers), while religion as 'opiate of the masses', the deified Founders, kinetoscope propaganda, and the Raffle keep the Shantytown proletariat in check. The Vox Populi's revolt instantiates conflict theory's inevitable collapse, but the revolution loses its ideals, turns anarchistic, and becomes the new oppressor burning Columbia. Against Marx the chapter sets Spencer-style structural functionalism (Fink's lions-and-oxen ecology justifying the status quo) and Rawls's difference principle, asking whether Columbia's inequalities ever benefited the least advantaged; Booker's rejection of baptism-as-erasure of his past contrasts with Comstock's laundered sins.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 11 "2. I May Be a Socialist, But I’m Not a Lunatic" — Walderezak tracks Tom Branson's trajectory from Marxist-quoting socialist chauffeur to estate manager, arguing that the show quietly makes Robert, not Tom, the 'real socialist.' Robert's aristocratic conservatism is read as noblesse oblige (funding the hospital, the Downton Fair, and secretly paying a tenant's arrears), while Matthew's capitalist drive for 'investment, increasing productivity, and reducing waste' is presented as the profit-first ownership system that Marx and Fourier actually criticized. Tom's socialism, closer to the utopian visions of Robert Owen and Charles Fourier than to Marx's class struggle, dissolves as he assimilates into the family ('I haven't abandoned all of my socialism, although sometimes it feels like it'), a capitulation the chapter explains through David Harvey's 'capitalist pacification,' whereby capitalism absorbs all facets of society. The chapter concludes that Robert's treatment of ownership as a duty owed to tenants approaches the cooperative ideals of Fourier and Owen more than Tom's abandoned radicalism ever did.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 24 "12. Should We Really Care about the Crawleys" — Jones takes on the charge, voiced amid rising real-world inequality, that loving Downton seduces viewers into admiring hierarchy, and answers that the Crawleys deserve our care because they are human beings who share our bereavements (Mary's grief for Matthew, Cora's miscarriage, Edith's jilting) and because they use moments of cross-class contact well: Grantham paying for Mrs. Patmore's eye surgery, Violet throwing the flower contest at Isobel's urging, and the family's genuine embrace of Tom Branson. He reads the show as a manifesto for gradual social change through sympathetic contact rather than the Irish revolutionaries' arson, but ends with a serious objection: this philosophy makes ending oppression partly the duty of the oppressed, from Carson's 'foul' remark about Thomas's sexuality to today's super-rich, so more radical activism may still be required.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 33 "20. Masters and Servants and Soldiers" — Carl Sobocinski asks whether WWI caused Downton's social upheavals or merely accelerated trends already underway, using the philosopher of history's problem of separating change from continuity. The Boer War bond between Lord Grantham and his former army 'batman' Bates displays the constancy of noblesse oblige beneath the class system, while Thomas Barrow wielding authority over his social superiors at the convalescent home, Sybil's hands-on nursing, and the socialist chauffeur Branson marrying into the aristocracy show genuine change - though he argues most of it (mass recruiting, field commissions for commoners) enlarged pre-1914 trends. Closing with The Clash's 'Something about England,' he notes the same era that transformed the Crawleys' world left the servant class's life largely unchanged, with change ultimately coming out on top.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 25 "“I Want to Conquer the World”" — Uses Agamben's bios/zoē distinction (with Foucault on biopolitics and fragmented sovereignty, Hardt and Negri's 'Empire', Marx on surplus-value, and Rosa Luxemburg on unchecked capital) to read the Anderson Station massacre, Murtry shooting Coop on New Terra, and Protogen infecting 1.5 million Belters on Eros as reductions of Belter life to bare life that corporate sovereigns may kill without homicide. It then argues the instability capitalism creates births authoritarian sovereigns — Murtry's martial law, Inaros's Free Navy, Duarte's Laconia — whose followers (Chandra Wei, Cyn, Santiago Singh) display the 'total, unrestricted, unconditional loyalty' Arendt says totalitarian power demands, and closes with Foucault's warning that liberal government's security-for-freedom trade slides into the very corruption and oppression it was meant to prevent.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 20 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — Michel Beaulieu reads the series through Marx's materialist conception of history: the 'Proletariat Patrons' Movement' sign in FFIX's Alexandria, the job system as a class system, and Shinra dropping the Sector 7 plate on its own laboring class all instantiate class struggle, while Vaan's life in Rabanastre shows social existence determining consciousness. But he argues the heroes are not Marxist revolutionaries, since Cecil ends up King of Baron and the Light Warriors leave feudal structures intact, and the Moogles, the series' true proletarian serfs, never revolt, because no Final Fantasy world has yet matured to the stage where the Marxian transformation becomes possible.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Byron and Wood use Marx's claim that the modern state is 'a committee for managing the common affairs of the bourgeoisie' to read House of Cards: Raymond Tusk secretly dictates President Walker's policies, SanCorp buys influence over Frank through Claire's water-filters favor, and Frank's rise to the vice presidency is engineered by capitalists to protect their market interests. Even Frank's seemingly pro-worker America Works plan serves capital, since gutting Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid to subsidize $45,000 hiring costs boosts business profit, and the Dunbar-Walmart dispute shows the state arbitrating between conflicting capitalists rather than aiding workers. The chapter concludes that worker victories like a Dunbar minimum-wage win would only be the bourgeoisie losing a battle while winning the class war, confirming Frank's line that 'democracy is so overrated.'
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Argues that Marx's claim that the modern state is 'a committee for managing the common affairs of the bourgeoisie' explains House of Cards better than Frank's own power-over-money creed: Raymond Tusk and SanCorp dictate President Walker's policies and cost Frank the Secretary of State post, and even Frank's signature America Works jobs bill functions as a capitalist subsidy (government-paid wages, gutted entitlements), while the Dunbar-versus-Walmart fight over Medicaid shows the state arbitrating among capitalists. The authors conclude that even a worker victory like a Dunbar minimum-wage raise would only be a concession in an ongoing class conflict, so 'democracy is so overrated' because capital, not Frank, is really in charge of the White House.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 13 "Notes" — Thomas reads Bartertown's economy as embedded in social and political relations rather than a free market: the Underworld laborers versus Bartertown's elite stage Marx's class struggle, and the Aunty Entity–Master Blaster conflict runs through Hegel's thesis-antithesis-synthesis of capital versus labor. He treats the franchise as a post-peak-oil world, applies the tragedy of the commons and lifeboat ethics to water rationing and the Citadel's hierarchy, and counterposes Gandhi's cooperation, Adam Smith's invisible hand, and open-source-style collaboration. The conclusion: the Wasteland shows the failure of self-interest-based capitalism and the need for cooperative alternatives like direct democracy.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 21 "The Office and Philosophy" — Answers The New Yorker's claim that the American Office 'doesn't care about class' by reading it through Marx: capital's growth logic and surplus value explain the degraded office labor the show depicts (Stanley's 'run-out-the-clock type of situation' truck unloading, Pam's tepid watercolors, Roy's 'unloading trucks without meaning', Ryan's rejected assembly line), while the salaried masses' class position survives precisely as unnamable and denied - Michael's botched condo purchase, his fury at Ryan's business-school ambition, and Prison Martin's observation that office and prison are both 'doing the same thing every day'. Drawing on Kracauer, the chapter argues the show's comedy walks between distraction and awakening, and ends with Walter Benjamin's 'authentic humanity' located in the gap between professional and private life: Michael's failures make him an unwitting critique of the system that produced him.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 21 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Uses 'The Last of the Meheecans' to argue that Marx's account of labor-power needs race built into it: once Butters is mistaken for a Mexican immigrant 'Mantequilla', the couple who hit him hand him Windex and a leaf blower and he sings 'Work, Mexican, work', showing how racialization assigns his labor a demeaned value. The episode's conflicting stereotypes (lazy shiftless 'Meheecans' versus the hard-working backbone of service labor) and the mass 'Orgullo de Mantequilla' migration home reveal a super-exploited population. The author then recovers Marx's own writings on Polish and Irish liberation, American slavery, and Lincoln's reelection ('labor in the white skin cannot emancipate itself where in the black skin it is branded') to show that for Marx, racial and national domination were always obstacles to working-class freedom.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 23 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Reads '1%' — where Cartman's failed fitness test makes him the scapegoated one percent, and the school's 99% splinter into warring 83%, 30%, and 5% factions occupying the Red Robin (and its restroom) — through Rousseau's Social Contract on freedom and equality and the dismembered social body, showing how popular solidarity shatters into meaningless percentage tribes. 'Night of the Living Homeless' (the poor as zombies who 'feed on our change', Kyle's $20 spawning the swarm, the shotgun as the only remedy) dramatizes the dehumanizing social-Darwinist picture of the economic undead, and the underpants gnomes' business plan (Phase 1: Collect Underpants, Phase 2: ?, Phase 3: Profit) mocks CEOs who cannot say why they amass wealth. The chapter's own verdict: corporations as such are good (cars, computers, canned soup), and blame falls on the greedy individuals inside them, since death — Tolstoy's two meters of burial land — levels all players.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Jeff Ewing argues the Federation's moneyless, postscarcity economy is Marx's transitional stage on the way to classless communism: Picard's 'we've eliminated hunger, want, the need for possessions' and Troi's exchange with Samuel Clemens in 'Time's Arrow' mark Marx's shift from the realm of necessity to the realm of freedom. He reconstructs Marx and Engels on alienation, the division of labor, labor-tokens, and the withering state to dissolve the apparent anomalies—Federation credits, Quark's tab, the Chateau Picard vineyard—as survivals of transition rather than capitalism. Rom's 'workers of the world unite' in 'Bar Association' and the self-actualizing leisure of Enterprise crews complete the case.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 15 "“We Were Trained to Be Keepers of the Peace, not Soldiers”" — Shakibnia reads The Clone Wars through Cornel West's three dogmas threatening democracy — free-market fundamentalism, aggressive militarism, escalating authoritarianism — and Chomsky's critique of inequality: Senator Halle Burtoni is a deliberate Halliburton/Cheney nod, and the banking-deregulation vote in 'Heroes on Both Sides' mirrors the US military-industrial complex. He argues the Separatist people's movement ('Corporations do not rule us!') was justified in seeking self-determination, while 'Sabotage' shows the Jedi losing legitimacy by becoming 'military weapons' — underpaid Temple worker Jackar Bowmani's squalid housing indicts the Republic's class divide. Ahsoka's departure and her maxim that 'it's every citizen's duty to challenge their leaders' model the accountability movement (like Black Lives Matter) that the Jedi failed to be.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 15 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Canode reads 'It's a Terrible Life' as Marx's alienation of labor: Dean Smith's corporate existence at Sandover Bridge & Iron is Zachariah's ruse, and the American dream, like the promise that one more hunt will finally let the brothers quit, is the ideology that keeps workers laboring for owners who profit from them. Sam and Dean become the proletariat and the angels the owners of the means of production, and their refusal of Heaven's plan enacts the Communist Manifesto's line that the bourgeoisie has forged the weapons of its own destruction. The closing meta-turn applies the critique to the audience: fans who watch, buy DVDs, and attend conventions are the bourgeoisie whose demand keeps the Winchesters hunting.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 15 "NOTES" — Ewing reads Cameron as a Marxist: Cyberdyne's profit-driven reverse-engineering of the recovered Terminator arm, Dyson's alienated labor ('Don't ask'), and U.S. militarism absorbing Cyber Research Systems develop Skynet as capitalism's 'final contradiction,' in which the drive for destructive, labor-replacing technology converges with the profit motive to threaten humanity. Sarah and John are useful to the resistance only when they exit wage labor - waitress to warrior, ATM hacking instead of work - dramatizing Marx's claim that liberation requires transcending class positions. Yet technology itself is neutral and reclaimable: the reprogrammed T-101 learning 'I know now why you cry' shows even killing machines can be humanized for liberation, and the saga ends where Marx does - not interpreting the world but changing it.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 25 "Anarchism and the Beats" — Ed D'Angelo argues the Beats had a philosophy after all: a romantic bohemian anarchism that made poetry a means to a religious transformation of consciousness, with political change following consciousness rather than the reverse. He shows Ginsberg inverting Plato's rationalist hierarchy (grounding reason in imagination and the body) and reads Beat 'criminality' as a shamanic journey to the unconscious underworld, distinct from Mailer's macho 'White Negro' hipster. He traces their lineage through Greenwich Village bohemia, Proudhon/Bakunin/Kropotkin anarchism, and pacifist anarchists like Rexroth and Dellinger, arguing the Beats rejected Marxist materialism and class warfare, and that the movement was 'born' out of Rexroth's anarchist poetry circle at the 1955 Six Gallery reading of 'Howl.'
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 25 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Tait gives a Fredric Jameson-derived Marxist reading of Ocean's Eleven, treating Danny Ocean's heist crew as a utopian 'figure of collectivity' whose diverse, cross-class, pan-American membership recalls the WWII combat film and rallies against Terry Benedict as the polysemous 'monster' (Jameson's shark in Jaws) standing for globalized capital displacing nostalgic American Las Vegas. He argues the victimless heist allegorizes a competing value system in which love, solidarity, and friendship trump money, restaging class conflict from Asphalt Jungle, Rififi, and Big Deal on Madonna Street. The film's utopian happy ending imagines redistributing wealth and 'beating the house' within the very system of late capital it critiques.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 11 "Beyond Panopticism The Biopolitical Labor of Surveillance and War in Contemporary Film" — Gooch argues that the post-2005 surveillance film cycle moves 'beyond panopticism': Foucault's disciplinary gaze gives way to Deleuze's 'societies of control,' and the surveiling gaze becomes direct domination and a form of biopolitical labor (Hardt and Negri) rather than an impersonal structure. He reads the prestige dramas (Redacted, Stop-Loss, In the Valley of Elah, Lions for Lambs) as exposing the soldier's proletarianization and self-surveillance, and the thrillers/blockbusters (Déjà Vu, The Kingdom, Body of Lies, The Bourne Ultimatum, Eagle Eye, Burn after Reading) as staging a Marxist antagonism between living labor (the watching hero) and the fixed capital of surveillance technology. Using Deleuze's 'degraded time-image,' Kant's needed separation of subject and law, and Benjamin/Agamben's state of exception, he shows Eagle Eye inverting law and subject to justify preemptive war and turn biopolitical labor into the labor of subjection.
- **Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy**, ch. 8 "Screaming for Change" — The methods chapter, laying out ideological rhetorical criticism supplemented by Gramsci's theory of hegemony. It explains Gramsci's revision of Marx: society as a dynamic core/periphery equilibrium rather than a rigid base/superstructure, hegemony maintained by 'force plus consent,' and the 'organic intellectual' who pierces 'common sense' to offer 'good sense.' On this basis it justifies analyzing four albums (Sex Pistols' Never Mind the Bollocks, Bad Religion's Suffer, Refused's Shape of Punk to Come, NOFX's Wolves in Wolves' Clothing) as sites where the subaltern contest hegemonic culture.
- **Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy**, ch. 9 "Screaming for Change" — The core analysis, reading all four albums track by track through Gramsci and Marx. The Sex Pistols' 'God Save the Queen' and 'Anarchy in the UK' attack the monarchy and consumerism as false consciousness; Bad Religion's 'Suffer' and 'You Are (The Government)' cast the state as gatekeeper of 'common sense' and religion as social-Darwinist superstition; Refused's 'New Noise' and 'The Deadly Rhythm' explicitly ventriloquize Marx on the production line, alienation, and organized revolt; NOFX's 'USA-Holes' and 'The Man I Killed' target Bush-era imperialism. Kristiansen extracts a shared subaltern rhetoric of nonconformity, anti-authoritarianism, and breaking 'the chains of false consciousness.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 40 "Downsizing Dreams" — Michael Bray argues the American Office does register class - precisely as a 'salaried mass' whose identity lies in denying class difference. Through Marx's account of surplus value and the degradation of rationalized labor (Stanley's 'run-out-the-clock,' Pam's deadened art, Michael's condo as consumer coffin), the office workers are alienated and secretly long for downsizing that never frees them. Bray invokes Benjamin to suggest Michael Scott's gap-ridden failure to be professional or private embodies what little 'authentic humanity' capitalism leaves, standing on the edge of naming the class it never names.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 24 "Whose Egg Is It, Really Property Rights and Distributive Justice" — Cribbs treats the Horton-versus-Mayzie custody fight over the egg as a property-rights puzzle, applying Locke's labor-mixing theory (Horton's season of incubation versus Mayzie's laying and abandonment, plus squatter's rights) and its provisos against waste and taking more than 'enough and as good,' illustrated by the Once-ler and Hardin's tragedy of the commons. Adam Smith's invisible hand and the Wubble-chap's skilled labor defend market inequality, while Sylvester McBean's Sneetch exploitation, Yertle, and Marx's alienated proletariat motivate Rawls's veil of ignorance and distributive justice as a corrective to unregulated property rights.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 23 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Bane surveys fidelity criticism of film adaptation (McFarlane, and especially George Bluestone's Novels into Film) and applies a Marxist reading to the 1940 Pride and Prejudice. He shows how Bluestone praises the film as faithfully capturing Austen's 'aristocratic dance,' then argues a single altered line, Darcy's 'the middle classes at play,' injects a post-Marx notion of class struggle absent from Austen's Regency world of gentry versus nobility. Reading the Bennet-Lucas competition as proletarian striving and set against the 1940s Red Scare and HUAC blacklist, Bane concludes that adaptation lets Austen's ironic critique of class speak to new times, marking her a great author across eras.
