It closes by showing that Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau and Marx divide over the morality of egalitarianism (Popper's Marx moved by moral impulse versus Locke's possessive individualism), and that power is domain-specific, inert until used, skill-dependent and always relative.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 19 "9 T’Challa’s Machiavellian Methods" — Drake and Lloyd argue the comic-book T'Challa of 'Panther's Rage' is classically Machiavellian in a way the film's earnest king is not: he rules through fear and strategic violence against Killmonger's uprising, cultivates the appearance of The Prince's five qualities (mercy, faith, honesty, humanity, religion), and exploits Wakandan religion — letting subjects believe the Black Panther is divine, never doffing the sacred garb even when swimming with Monica — as an instrument for preserving power. Advisers like Taku ask whether T'Challa differs from Killmonger, and the chapter concludes that, sharing Machiavelli's low view of human nature, T'Challa never considers democracy and keeps his people quiescent through a divinity he knows is performance.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 27 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Ted Henry Brown and Christie Maloyed stage the Enderverse as the international-relations debate between Hobbesian realism — Graff's 'if one of us has to be destroyed...' and the human-bugger Prisoner's Dilemma where the absence of communication forces mutual defection and war — and liberal institutionalism, which Peter's Locke and Valentine's Demosthenes argue out on Earth's nets. Machiavelli supplies Peter's theory of power: fortune opens the moment, virtù seizes it with 'the right words at the right time,' and force must back persuasion when belief fades, so that 'influence is power' and governing by persuasion beats fiat.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 21 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — David Hahn argues that Spira's Yevon religion is exactly what Machiavelli and Nietzsche warned against: hope for the Calm and a Sin-free future makes Spirans otherworldly and passive, forbidding machina, revering self-sacrificing Summoner martyrs, and blaming themselves for Sin, just as just-war Christianity left Machiavelli's princes passive and dependent on mercenaries, paralleled by Seymour and Kinoc standing idle at Operation Mi'ihen. Nietzsche's slave revolt in morality explains Yevon's sanctification of meekness and death, while Machiavelli's account of religion as a political instrument, from Numa to Scipio's oath, explains why the lie of Yevon held Spira together, and why its collapse may bring either Nietzschean rebirth or Machiavellian chaos.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 13 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Marcus Schulzke reads the War of the Five Kings through The Prince: who wins the Iron Throne is decided by virtu - skill adapted to shifting circumstances - against fortuna, and morality is no guide, since actions are good or bad only as they gain or hold power. The failures illustrate the lessons: Viserys's arrogance binds him to the wrong allies, Robert's emotions make him capricious, Joffrey makes himself hated instead of feared, Ned's uncompromising honesty and trust in Littlefinger destroy him, and Robb's dependency on Walder Frey's auxiliary forces proves fatal. The true Machiavellians are the mask-wearers - Littlefinger, Arya, Jon as lion-and-fox - and above all Tyrion, who wins the Blackwater by planning, and Daenerys, who builds her own army from freed slaves and so makes her own luck.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 15 "Notes" — Argues Frank's rise is a genuinely successful illustration of The Prince: Machiavelli's advice to be prepared not to be virtuous shows in his lying (feigning loyalty to Walker while engineering his impeachment, promising Russo the governorship), his strategic murders of Russo and Zoe, his audacity in making his own luck ('turn over the table'), and his cultivation of a pious family-man image while privately spitting on the crucifix. The chapter also lets Machiavelli criticize Frank — revenge on Tusk (better to pamper or crush), Claire's fruitless generosity at CWI, alliances with the stronger, and being feared to the point of being hated, which costs him Sharp, Remy and Claire. Finally it tests The Prince against modern democracy — party discipline, sex-scandal politics, Obama's donated Nobel money, birther smears — concluding that since Machiavellians will always adapt to whatever system exists, citizens must reward results and stop judging by image.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 29 "Notes" — Cooper reads Frank's one prayer - kneeling to pray 'to myself, for myself' - as a self-love he calls autoeroticism, built on metaphysical atheism, ruthless pragmatism, and happiness as power. Like Glaucon's Ring of Gyges, Frank's atheism removes divine punishment from the moral equation, so the murders of Peter Russo and Zoe Barnes incur only human risk, while his feigned piety at the Peachoid girl's vigil, broken promises to Tusk, and 'cruelty well used' toward Russo exemplify Machiavellian virtu taming fortuna. Against this the chapter sets Augustine's critique of the libido dominandi: Frank's remorse after betraying Freddy ('Do you think I'm a hypocrite?') shows the lust for domination enslaves rather than liberates, the way of the City of Man against the Augustinian freedom of self-giving love.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 15 "Notes" — Littmann tests Frank against The Prince and largely confirms the 'Machiavellian' label: his lies (playing the loyal confidant while engineering Walker's fall), his strategic murders of Russo and Zoe, his preference for weaker allies, and his manufactured piety and father stories all enact Machiavelli's advice that a prince must learn 'not to be good' while seeming merciful, faithful, and religious. But the debts run both ways: Claire's vindictive 'let's make him suffer' offends Machiavelli's pamper-or-crush rule, and modern democratic image politics (Obama donating his Nobel money, the Obama-as-Muslim smear) outperforms The Prince where voters punish fear and reward a generosity Machiavelli thought ruinous. The moral is not despair but vigilance: since Underwoods will always rise, citizens must reward genuine results rather than respond to images.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Fallis walks through the education-reform arc — leaking Blythe's draft, gutting collective bargaining ('I revised the parameters of my promise'), framing Rasmussen in the speakership coup, the staged brick incident, and goading Spinella into felony assault — to show Frank follows Machiavelli's counsel to be 'other than good.' Yet Frank fails at Machiavelli's how and why: he never cultivates the appearance of integrity (Blythe, Feng, and Vasquez refuse to deal with a known liar), he inspires hatred as well as fear, and he seeks power for its own sake rather than the stability of the state, which makes the BBC's Francis Urquhart the superior Machiavellian. Even the revisionist readings of The Prince — Benner's irony, Rousseau's claim that Machiavelli was exposing princes' methods like an investigative reporter, Dietz's deliberate-sabotage thesis — would not rescue Frank, since he bungles the techniques regardless of their intent.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 29 "Notes" — Analyzes Frank's kneeling 'I pray to myself, for myself' as an ethics of autoeroticism built on metaphysical atheism, ruthless pragmatism, and happiness-as-power: like Glaucon's Ring of Gyges, removing God from the equation makes the murders of Zoe and Russo cost only human, never eternal, judgment. The chapter details three exercises of Machiavellian virtu-feigned piety at the Peachoid vigil, fox-like promise-breaking with Tusk, and 'cruelty well-used' toward Russo-before closing on Augustine's critique of the libido dominandi: Frank's betrayal of Freddy, met with a flash of remorse, shows the lust for domination enslaves rather than liberates, the way of the City of Man.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 14 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Argues that a motorcycle club is a Machiavellian regime in miniature: Jax's Season 3 fake betrayal of the club to Stahl—actually a set-up that shortens the crew's prison time and delivers both Stahl and Jimmy O to death—shows the prince's union of lion and fox in service of the club rather than himself. J.T. figures as a founder overcome by fortuna ('each savage event was a catalyst for the next... blood was every color'), lacking the virtu to impose his vision, while Clay wields deceit and force for mere egoism that Machiavelli would refuse the name of glory. Zobelle's self-description as a 'Machiavellian fool' flooding Charming with drugs, and Jax's admission that 'you can't sit in this chair without being a savage,' frame the chapter's question of whether manipulation and violence can serve a genuine common good.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 24 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Si Sheppard reads the comic through Realist state-formation theory: Shane's leadership rests on borrowed prestige and dies with him, West Central Prison collapses into anarchy because Rick never establishes a monopoly on legitimate force—letting Tyreese's vigilante murder pass—nor any institution beyond his personal authority, while the Governor's Woodbury thrives on fear, arenas, and bread-and-circuses. Citing Machiavelli's prince who is feared rather than loved, Weber's definition of the state, and Bismarck's unifying wars, he argues the prison loses the 'second anarchy' rivalry with Woodbury for want of scouting, sabotage, coalition-building, or any command structure that survives Rick's absences. Rick's confession that he would kill everyone in the Alexandria Safe Zone to keep Lori safe is post-moral Realism, yet he was 'a bad founding father' who only finally learns to build an army instead of relying on himself.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 20 "Wilt Versus Russell" — O'Connor frames the boyhood 'Wilt or Russell?' debate as a version of Aristotle's Politics puzzle that a man outside community is 'either a beast or a god': is dominator Wilt a basketball beast or a divine king, and is executive-team-player Russell the higher human ideal? He links Wilt's romantic individualism to Rousseau ('J.-J.') and Emerson's genius awaiting 'practical power,' and Aristotle's discussion of the natural king to the coaching dilemma of whether to make a gifted player dominate or blend. He ends by rejecting Machiavelli's 'realist' dismissal of ideals, insisting the Russellite ideal of teamwork can be higher even when domination wins more.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 9 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Raymond Belliotti reads the twenty-year Olympic career of Italian sprinter Pietro Mennea, 'The Southern Arrow,' through Machiavelli's concept of virtu, the excellence relevant to one's function that lets a person master Fortuna. He distinguishes Machiavelli's military, political, civic, moral, and artistic virtu (using the Agathocles passage and the Life of Castruccio Castracani) and argues Mennea's physical prowess, mental toughness, and turning of anti-southern prejudice into motivation exemplify athletic virtu. Machiavelli would scoff at Olympic ideals of peace and brotherhood but relish the fierce international competition and the discipline of sport that Mennea embodied through his 1980 Moscow gold and later political career.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 24 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Mahon asks whether Ride with the Devil endorses the proverb that all's fair in love and war, locating the film's moral core in its outsiders—the German immigrant Jake, the freed slave Holt, and the young widow Sue Lee. Against Sunzi's undiscriminating claim that warfare is the art of deceit, he argues the film sides with Machiavelli's Discourses distinction between honorable ruses of war and dishonorable perfidy: the bushwhackers' wearing of Union blue and Jake's lies are ruses, but the Lawrence massacre and refusing to ambush women under a truce mark limits Jake will not cross. In love, Sue Lee's shift from romantic lying to 'now is the truth' shows honesty is finally required, so all is not fair.

### Totalitarianism

Totalitarianism, as analyzed by Hannah Arendt in The Origins of Totalitarianism, names a novel and radical form of domination exemplified by Nazi Germany and Stalinist Russia. Unlike ordinary tyranny, it seeks total control not just of politics but of every sphere of life, fusing ideology and terror to remould human beings and abolish spontaneity, plurality, and independent thought. Arendt traced its roots to phenomena such as antisemitism, imperialism, and the rise of atomized mass society, and argued that its concentration camps aimed to render people superfluous. Her account remains a landmark attempt to understand how such regimes arise and why they are distinct from earlier despotisms.

- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 23 "Rising Up" — Brandon Forbes uses Hannah Arendt's distinction between power (people acting in concert, rooted in plurality and natality) and violence (instruments that ape power, one against all) to read Radiohead's violent imagery. The "Just" video shows that power lies not in what the prone man says but in everyone's collective act of lying down; "Sit Down. Stand Up." and "2 + 2 = 5" dramatize command backed by weapons and the revolutionary moment when a king's violence breeds the dissent that undoes him; "Life in a Glass House" and "Where I End and You Begin" depict totalitarian terror, the stage where violence has devoured power entirely. "I Will" ("I will rise up," "little babies' eyes") closes the chapter as Arendt's natality — the capacity of new political beginnings the gun can never defeat.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 26 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Kenneth Sayles reads Peter and Valentine's net personas through three lenses: John Locke's identity theory to ask whether a consistent virtual persona with no physical anchor deserves our trust, Plato's Ring of Gyges to ask what anonymity does to morality, and Hannah Arendt's account of totalitarianism to warn that nameless, unaccountable influence ('action without a name... is meaningless') paves the way for rule by propaganda and a fictitious world. Real-world parallels - identity theft, the hacker collective Anonymous, YouTube politics - make the Enderverse nets look prophetic rather than fantastic.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 17 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Bowman argues through Arendt that Dracula is not inherently evil but thoughtless: like Eichmann he cannot think from another's standpoint, treats people as cogs and means (Harker as captive, humans as prey), uses violence as a constructive tool, and protects himself with rhetorical safeguards like 'Enter freely' so he need never face his own cruelty. Measured against the Crew of Light's thoughtfulness - Harker's memos and recipes for Mina, Mina's care for Lucy, the suitors' gentlemanly bonds - the Count's evil is banal, lazy, 'Evil Lite'; but because Dracula stands outside humanity and knows humans only as livestock, Bowman concludes that Eichmann is banal yet truly evil, while Dracula, though careless, can never be evil.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 16 "7. David Bowie, Political Philosopher" — Hill reconstructs Bowie's political odyssey as a working-out of what freedom and oppression are: 'Cygnet Committee' repudiates revolution powered by resentment (echoing Nietzsche on socialism's despotic annihilation of the individual), 'Big Brother' and Diamond Dogs diagnose the crowd's flight from freedom into leadership, and the Nietzschean self-as-artwork - 'give style to one's character,' the 'mortal with potential of a superman' - curdles into the Thin White Duke's 'rock stars are fascists' collapse of celebrity into totalitarian leadership. The Berlin Trilogy then turns the critique inward: 'Heroes'' ironic lovers unmask romantic anti-totalitarianism (either side of the Antifaschistischer Schutzwall), 'Neuköln' discovers immigrants' mere survival, and Lodger's 'Fantastic Voyage' lands on structural, Marxist questions of how 'we' are to become free.
- **The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed**, ch. 15 "7 The Bourgeoisie and the Blacks" — The chapter sets business - the US bourgeoisie whose privileged position Charles Beard read into the Constitution and which survived the Jacksonian and New Deal challenges by breaking labor through Taft-Hartley, right-to-work laws and the PATCO lockout, its solidarity secured while worker solidarity was undercut by what Marx called the Achilles heel of racism - against blacks as the paradigmatic powerless, shut out of every power base since slavery, which the chapter treats with Baptist and Marx's 1846 letter as a totalitarian system of super-exploited, tortured labor that built American capitalism, its neo-slavery progeny (Blackmon) pauperizing the black community under Dred Scott's 'subordinate and inferior class of beings'. It then narrates black counter-power base by base: the abolitionist interracial coalition wielding charisma (Douglass, Nat Turner, John Brown), information, morality and religion; the NAACP era and King's fusion of charisma, church religion, Myrdal's An American Dilemma and televised nonviolent provocation against Bull Connor's violence, contested by Malcolm X, SNCC and the Black Panthers; and a post-civil-rights scorecard showing a wealth base 94.2 percent white, persistent education and media gaps, constrained black officials from mayors to the symbolic Obama presidency, and a captive but potentially leveraged black vote in a 'Sisyphean' struggle.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 14 "4. Non-State Enemies of Freedom" — Nash argues 1984 has been misread as a critique of state power alone; through Newspeak's silencing of thought (in the tradition Austin, MacKinnon, and Langton developed) it shows how any concentration of power oppresses via control of words, data, and information. Drawing on Goldstein's manual's debt to James Burnham's managerial revolution and Sheldon Wolin's 'inverted totalitarianism', she reads the non-centralized Oceania as a warning about non-state enemies: corporations, think tanks running the 'Tobacco Strategy', and global institutions peddling misleading poverty statistics. Popper, Arendt, and Berlin exemplify the state-focused liberalism she thinks blinded us to these horizontal threats, while the Newspeak appendix's past tense shows Orwell expected totalitarianism to be beatable through evidence and democracy.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 21 "10. Love, Truluv" — Sandefur argues that what makes totalitarianism unique is its demand that subjects love their ruler, and that this project is doomed because love is selective, unequal, internal, and inalienable, invoking Aristotle's critique of Plato's community of wives and children, Machiavelli on whether rulers should be loved or feared, and Arendt on conscience as internal dialogue and totalitarianism as total rule. Winston and Julia's sex is a political act asserting the individual against the collective, while the Two Minutes Hate channels repressed erotic energy into sanctioned ecstasy directed at Big Brother, as at Khomeini's funeral. What finally breaks Winston in Room 101 is not torture as such but his surrender of Julia, the one thing that was truly his, which collapses the distinction between love and rape.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 37 "24. Post-Factual Democracy" — Hendricks and Vestergaard open with Trump's inauguration lies and Kellyanne Conway's 'alternative facts' to define post-factual democracy: a state in which opportune political narratives replace facts and evidence as the basis of debate, opinion formation and policymaking. Unlike Machiavelli, who taught that lies must at least be concealed, the post-factual politician pays no price for exposed falsehood once social media, the attention economy and populist us-versus-them narratives engineered for indignation and fear have stripped journalists and fact-checkers of authority — Arendt's remark that mass leaders show 'extreme contempt for facts as such' before fitting reality to their lies. Using Habermas's deliberative model and even minimal accountability theories of voting, they argue post-factuality destroys democratic legitimacy, and defend a 'factual democracy' that trusts science and journalism without becoming a technocracy — the real-world echo of the Party's command to reject the evidence of your eyes.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 33 "20. The Totalitarian Zone" — Altmann builds 20th-century totalitarianism from three TZ episodes: 'He's Alive' shows Aristotle's account of persuasion — rhetoric aimed at an audience's anger and fear — fueling Vollmer's neo-Nazi movement under Hitler's ghostly tutelage; 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' instantiates Eco's Ur-Fascist fear of difference, banning even Plato and Dostoevsky; and 'Deaths-Head Revisited' gives Lutze's 'I functioned as I was told' alongside Arendt's verdict on Eichmann's thoughtless, mechanical obedience. He then argues the phenomenon has mutated: Debord's society of the spectacle explains Black Mirror's 'The Waldo Moment' and 'Fifteen Million Merits,' where image-politics becomes authoritarian and even Bing's suicidal act of defiance is sold back as an avatar product.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 30 "The Resistance New Humans, New Gods" — Dinello maps Westworld point-by-point onto Arendt's Origins of Totalitarianism: the park is a concentration camp that kills the juridical person (hosts as chattel in a 'fictitious world' of Western propaganda), the moral person (Ford forcing Bernard to murder Theresa, Maeve's engineered failure to protect her daughter), and individuality itself (surveillance, resets, 'ghastly marionettes'), with Ford as a Mengele-like ideological scientist who, like Hitler, merely plagiarizes popular myths (John Ford's Westerns, R.U.R.). Liberation then follows Fanon's Wretched of the Earth: violence as a 'cleansing force' that frees the colonized mind, so Maeve's suicide-by-incineration (echoing Plath's Lady Lazarus) and Dolores's beating of the Man in Black and massacre of the Delos board enact decolonization as the creation of 'new men' - a new Robo sapiens species - with Sartre's endorsement that killing eliminates oppressor and oppressed in one go, while Fanon's warning that hatred and revenge are not an agenda sets the conditions for what the resistance must do next.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 11 "1. A Great Darkness Filled with Echoes" — De Vaul argues Gilead terrifies because social cycle theory structures it: every detail, from the Puritan wedding-night sheet to Stalin-style purges and the Nazi and residential-school seizure of children, already happened, so Gilead reads as speculative rather than science fiction. Atwood's three stated influences—Puritan New England, the 1980s religious right, and Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four—show history cycling back, with June as the apolitical 'backlash' daughter her second-wave mother Holly and the activist Moira both predicted. The pattern repeats at small scale (June relives the former Offred's Scrabble-and-affair story, Omar's family suffers June's own fate) and in the Historical Notes, where Pieixoto strips Offred of authorship, proving 'the past is a great darkness, filled with echoes.'
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 13 "3. Gestational Totalitarianism" — Kolb reads Gilead through Arendt's The Human Condition and The Origins of Totalitarianism: when reproduction becomes the means of production, women's labor is targeted, forcing fertile women into Animal laborans status as 'national resources' while denying them the creative freedom of Homo faber. She traces the polis/oikos split from Aristotle through Puritan capitalism to show Gilead overcorrecting into Aunt Lydia's 'freedom from'—totalitarian control of birth legitimized by the Rachel and Bilhah story and a Pauline creation story. The chapter ends with the transitional generation's forgetting (Offred's cave-delusion with Nick evoking Plato's Allegory of the Cave, the Holocaust documentarian 'thinking about how not to think') and Ofglen's bomb, arguing that thoughtfulness and literacy, not violence, are the only hopes against totalitarianism.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 14 "4. The United States of Gilead" — Greene argues that the contemporary United States under Trump exhibits early Gilead-like symptoms, detailing five shared techniques: othering (the Aunts' stereotypes of pre-Gilead women vs. Trump on Mexicans and Muslims), separating children from parents (Handmaid births and seizure of Hannah vs. immigrant detention camps), gaslighting (Janine's 'her fault' Testifying vs. inauguration-crowd and Mueller claims), discrediting dissent (Gilead's ban on reading vs. 'fake news'), and lying (Gilead's founding promise of elections vs. thousands of false claims and 'alternative facts'). He grounds the danger in the correspondence theory of truth: once leaders detach belief from how the world actually is, society is a small step from Atwood's dystopia.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 29 "16. Who Is the Meanest of Them All" — Frunză and Grad apply Arendt's banality of evil to Gilead: the Commander is 'not Iago, not Macbeth' but an Eichmann—sheepish, Scrabble-playing, 'thinking about how not to think'—and no character holds a monopoly on evil because everyone is 'too banal' for demonic profundity. They test his 'just doing my duty' against Kant (duty requires universalizing what reason can will and never treating persons as means, so the Aunts' reeducation camps fail the test) and use The Origins of Totalitarianism to read Handmaids as rightless people whose 'two-legged wombs' status mirrors statelessness. Arendt's web of guilty complicities explains why resistance is scarce, and the chapter ends with banality eroding all criteria for judging—leaving Offred's 'the darkness within; or else the light' as the final choice.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 27 "14. Anything that’s Spiked Is Fine" — Volpert asks where rebellion lives, in the lone guitarist or the listening group, using Hardt and Negri's claim that a rebel's true opposite is not failure but co-option, i.e. selling out. Arendt's distinction between totalitarian and authoritarian systems models the music industry as authoritarian (creativity permitted so long as profit at the top goes unchallenged), and her banality-of-evil analysis of Eichmann prompts the question of whether there is a banality of rebellion. Petty's satirical puppetry of authority voices in "Century City" and the silent spiked-collar punk of "Spike," kin to Bartleby and James Dean, show that individuals can rebel against authoritarian packs while groups, even the Heartbreakers, only ever drift into authoritarianism.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 37 "25. Reasonable Genocide" — Uses Horkheimer's Eclipse of Reason to dissolve the puzzle of Thanos's unsettling sanity: the Snap is subjectively rational — pure means–ends efficiency in service of a Malthusian 'simple calculus' whose end only the subject chooses — so Thanos 'is mad because he is rational,' with the murder of Gamora as the final severing of his last bond to the world. Captain America's refusal to trade Vision ('We don't trade lives') is read as a stand for ends valuable in themselves, while Ultron embodies the totalitarian variant (via Arendt and Spencer's social Darwinism) that declares humanity 'obsolete': Ultron wants to accelerate nature, Thanos to correct it, both absolutizing the subject against objective reason.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 20 "10 Understanding the Reigns of T’Challa and Killmonger through Hannah Arendt" — Sinanan reads both reigns through Arendt's account of collective responsibility: T'Challa moves from conscience-based 'I am not king of all people' to owning what Wakanda did in its name ('He was the truth I chose to omit') and finally to political action in Oakland and at the UN, while Killmonger — an MIT-educated Navy SEAL embodying the collective that formed him — becomes the imperialist he opposed, his 'burn it all' revolution matching Arendt's warning about totalitarian domination from within. She compares Killmonger's council speech and herb-burning directly to Hitler's 1924 Munich trial speech, reads his manipulation of the challenge ritual as totalitarian propaganda that organizes rather than persuades, and credits Nakia, Okoye, Shuri, and Ramonda with refusing Arendt's ultimate danger, indifference.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 26 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Kenneth Sayles reads Peter's and Valentine's anonymous rise on the nets through three lenses: John Locke's identity theory asks how a virtual identity can lack a physical anchor, Plato's Ring of Gyges asks what anonymity does to justice, and Hannah Arendt warns that 'action without a name... is meaningless' and that faceless power is a precondition of totalitarianism. Comparing the personas to the hacker collective Anonymous and to identity theft, he concludes our own Internet could breed its own Locke and Demosthenes and asks how much trust we owe virtual people whose controllers we can never know.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 25 "“I Want to Conquer the World”" — Uses Agamben's bios/zoē distinction (with Foucault on biopolitics and fragmented sovereignty, Hardt and Negri's 'Empire', Marx on surplus-value, and Rosa Luxemburg on unchecked capital) to read the Anderson Station massacre, Murtry shooting Coop on New Terra, and Protogen infecting 1.5 million Belters on Eros as reductions of Belter life to bare life that corporate sovereigns may kill without homicide. It then argues the instability capitalism creates births authoritarian sovereigns — Murtry's martial law, Inaros's Free Navy, Duarte's Laconia — whose followers (Chandra Wei, Cyn, Santiago Singh) display the 'total, unrestricted, unconditional loyalty' Arendt says totalitarian power demands, and closes with Foucault's warning that liberal government's security-for-freedom trade slides into the very corruption and oppression it was meant to prevent.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 127 "Like Bertie Bott’s Every-Flavor Beans, a Mix" — Names pureblood supremacism, Voldemort's Nazi-like movement whose victory would mean totalitarianism, thought control, secret police, mock trials, and racial cleansing, as the greatest problem wizards face, and faults Hogwarts education for ignoring it: no antiracist teaching despite rampant slurs, silence about the oppressed house-elves of Hogwarts, A History, and Slytherin left as a hothouse breeding Death Eaters and fifth columnists. Against Prinzi's gradualist defense of Dumbledore as a persuasive libertarian, the chapter presses the fair question of why he did not do more.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 33 "20. The Totalitarian Zone" — Altmann assembles a 'time capsule' of totalitarianism from Twilight Zone and Black Mirror: Vollmer's neo-Nazi rise in 'He's Alive' as Aristotle's rhetoric, persuasion by playing on an audience's anger and fear, weaponized; Marilyn's forced Transformation in 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' as Eco's Ur-Fascist fear of difference; and Lutze's 'I functioned as I was told' at Dachau as Arendt's banality of evil, the mechanical non-thinking of the Eichmann trial. 'The Waldo Moment' and 'Fifteen Million Merits' then carry the lens to Debord's society of the spectacle, where an empty cartoon bear wins crowds and even Bing's shard-wielding rebellion is instantly commodified into a product. The totalitarianism of screens, the chapter warns, needs no tanks.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 30 "The Resistance New Humans, New Gods" — Dinello reads Westworld as a totalitarian concentration camp via Arendt's The Origins of Totalitarianism, tracing the hosts' dehumanization through the killing of the juridical person (no rights, 'live without limits'), the moral person (Bernard forced to murder Theresa), and individuality (Peter Abernathy lobotomized). He casts Ford as a mad-scientist dictator modeled on Frankenstein, Moreau, Mengele, and Hitler who plagiarizes John Ford's Westerns, then turns to Fanon's Wretched of the Earth to justify the hosts' revolutionary violence — Maeve as a self-resurrecting 'Lady Lazarus,' Dolores executing Ford and the Delos board — as the birth of a new species that must ultimately unify beyond hatred.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 19 "The Dialectic of Enlightenment in Metropolis" — Abrams reads Fritz Lang's Metropolis as anticipating Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment by two decades. He maps the film's arc—from the Christian mythology of the catacombs, through Joh's technototalitarian rational city and the human-machine fusion of Rotwang's false Maria, back into ancient myth (the M-Machine as Moloch, the whore of Babylon, the Tower of Babel)—onto their thesis that Enlightenment reason turns totalitarian and reverts to mythology and madness. He ties reason's self-destruction to Nietzsche's will to power and contrasts the descent into 'absolute madness' with Hegel's progress toward absolute mind.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 20 "Imagining the Future, Contemplating the Past The Screen Versions of 1984" — Palmer compares the two film versions of Orwell's 1984 to argue that dystopian fiction projects present fears and desires onto an imagined future, engaging critically with the Enlightenment idea of progress (via Burnham's managerial thesis). Anderson's 1956 film 'talks to the future,' fusing science fiction and film noir to voice Cold War dread of a possible historical trajectory, while Radford's 1984 version, in the postmodern 'heritage film' mode Jameson and Higson describe, museumizes the novel: with history seemingly ended it becomes an honored, reverentially displayed relic that talks only to a dead past rather than warning of a coming one.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 30 "17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone" — McCrossin reads 'Deaths-Head Revisited' and 'He's Alive' against the Eichmann trial and Hannah Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem, framing Serling's concern as Susan Neiman's 'problem of evil.' The earlier episode's SS captain Lutze (driven insane by his victims' ghosts at Dachau) matches the grotesque-monster Eichmann of the film Operation Eichmann, while 'He's Alive' (Vollmer as a frightened man seduced by Hitler's ghost) foreshadows Arendt's 'banality of evil'—the thoughtless, empathy-less doer. He contrasts both with Hogan's Heroes, which Serling condemned for trivializing Nazi atrocity.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 33 "20. The Totalitarian Zone" — Altmann traces totalitarianism from The Twilight Zone into Black Mirror. 'He's Alive' shows Vollmer wielding Aristotle's rhetoric to grow a Nazi movement; 'Number 12' shows Umberto Eco's fascist 'fear of difference'; 'Deaths-Head Revisited' illustrates Arendt's banality of evil in Lutze's 'just following orders.' He then argues Black Mirror episodes ('The Waldo Moment,' 'Fifteen Million Merits') realize Guy Debord's 'society of the spectacle' and hyper-capitalism, where politics becomes entertainment and even resistance is commodified—a totalitarianism that needs no tanks.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 14 "Who is Who" — This political chapter reads Gallifreyan bureaucracy ('The Deadly Assassin') and 1970s socialist-tinged serials, using Marx's alienation and critique of capital to interpret 'The Pirate Planet' and 'The Robots of Death,' and Aristotle's 'political animal' plus Plato's and Aristotle's suspicion of democracy against Benjamin Barber's participatory democracy. It analyzes the pathologies of democratic consent through 'Vengeance on Varos' (Plato's ideal state inverted) and 'The Beast Below' (Arendt on totalitarianism, self-inflicted ignorance), with Isaiah Berlin's negative liberty in the vocabulary of materiality.
- **Comics as Philosophy**, ch. 7 "index" — This file bundles three essays. Kevin de Laplante reads Paul Chadwick's Concrete story 'Stay Tuned for Pearl Harbor', treating Concrete's angry monologue about oil companies and overpopulation as enlightened anthropocentrism, while Maureen's silent reverie of merging her body with root systems and being 'raped' by bulldozers dramatizes Arne Naess's deep-ecological expanded self and an ecofeminist link between the oppression of nature-as-female and of women; the utilitarianism of Bentham and Mill and Leopold's 'think like a mountain' land ethic frame the anthropocentrism/nonanthropocentrism debate. Pierre Skilling reads The Adventures of Tintin through Montesquieu's and Aristotle's typologies of government, casting Marshal Kurvi-Tasch's Borduria as Arendt-style totalitarianism (a secret police as true executive, a bid for world domination) against the legitimate monarchy of King Muskar XII, whose Syldavian sceptre works as a check on royal power. Terry Kading argues that 9/11 collapsed the superhero genre's binary of good versus evil into reality: bin Laden's 'monomaniacs' act as supervillains with a murky agenda, yet Spider-Man, Captain America and Superman comics concede no real superhero can rescue us, leaving only ordinary heroism and the compromised politics of national security.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 7 "5. Battlestar Galactica as Philosophy Breaking the Biopolitical Cycle" — Eberl and Bishop read the reimagined Battlestar Galactica and Caprica through the biopolitics of Foucault and Agamben, tracing 'biopower' across four phases from Zoe Graystone's avatar to the arrival at Earth. They argue the show asks whether artificial Cylons are persons (Zoe's avatar exhibits Baker's first-person perspective and Buber's I-Thou recognition), and use Agamben's zoe/bios/'bare life' and Homo sacer plus Roslin's population control and abortion ban to show sovereign power over life. The Cylon occupation of New Caprica is read through Arendt's three stages of totalitarian dehumanization, and Lee Adama's plea to 'break the cycle' offers a fragile hope undercut by the finale's flash-forward to present-day robotics, showing humanity forgetting the lesson.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 32 "30. The Boys as Philosophy Superheroes, Fascism, and the American Right" — Johnson treats The Boys as an argument from analogy that MAGA Trumpism is fascist, walking through how the show equates Homelander and Vought with the Nazi supe Stormfront and with Trump: the Big Lie, gaslighting, fearmongering, over-policing, conspiracy theories (QAnon as rebranded blood libel), cults of personality, projection, and loyal propaganda outlets. Drawing on Wittgenstein's notion of family resemblance, he argues 'fascism' has no necessary-and-sufficient definition but a cluster of shared traits, and compiling scholars' checklists shows MAGA belongs to the fascist family. Arendt's Origins of Totalitarianism supplies the 'alternative universe' of nonfacts and the leader who is 'always right,' and he invokes the banality of evil and totalitarian fiction to gauge the analogy's strength.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 86 "81. Papers, Please as Philosophy Playing with the Relations between Politics and Morality" — Sievers argues that Papers, Please immerses the player as an immigration inspector in the totalitarian Arstotzka, where mechanically stamping 'approved'/'refused' and detaining Kolechians for bribes enacts Arendt's 'banality of evil'—the thoughtless, 'just following orders' functionary exemplified by Eichmann, who cannot think from another's standpoint. The paycheck-versus-family pressure and X-ray humiliation scenes show how fear and bureaucracy erase moral responsibility. Drawing on Butler's 'Can one lead a good life in a bad life?' and Foucault's biopower, she reads the visa candidates as 'precarious,' non-grievable lives whose worth the state allocates, and the game's Ezic resistance endings as showing how constrained moral resistance is under such a regime.

### The Web of Belief

The web of belief is Quine's metaphor for the way our beliefs form an interconnected system that faces experience as a whole rather than one claim at a time. Observations impinge on the periphery of the web, while logical and mathematical principles sit near the resistant center; when evidence conflicts with the system, we may revise it at many different points, and no belief is in principle immune to revision. The picture rejects a sharp line between analytic and synthetic truths and reframes knowledge as a holistic, revisable structure.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 22 "Unknown" — Nixon asks whether Neo's harrowing post-pill experiences justify believing Morpheus's story, given that knowledge is justified true belief and testimony alone would be foolish to believe. He argues the belief is self-defeating: if Neo discards twenty-five years of experience as machine-fed lies, he loses the interpretive rules of thumb (people don't lie, heads don't pop off, objects exist unobserved) needed to justify any new experience, so by epistemological holism he cannot be justified in concluding he was ever in the Matrix - even though the audience, with the bigger picture, knows he is right.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 23 "Unknown" — Nixon tests whether the Matrix story is even conceptually coherent by asking whether we can make sense of someone whose beliefs are almost all false. Through the Cletus dialogue ('Bears are scary... Are they animals? News to me') he argues that belief attribution requires concept possession, and concept possession requires a background of true beliefs, so total falsehood is unintelligible - a meaning-holist point he credits to Quine, Davidson and Sellars - though he concedes the machines could still make most of our beliefs false, so the Matrix Possibility survives.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 28 "No Shoes for Muskrats How the 1956 Olympic Games Destroyed Indonesian Art" — Hardcastle recounts how his talk pairing analytic philosophy with Python clips became a touring hit, framing the appeal through Hume's gap between the 'easy and obvious' philosophy that moves people — today's popular culture, including Python — and the 'accurate and abstruse' philosophy that became analytic philosophy. His solution reconceives philosophy as the construction and examination of conceptual schemes rather than a search for truth, with Python supplying what philosophy cannot: conceptual schemes lived from the inside, as when the Dead Parrot shopkeeper embodies Quinean holism by holding that the parrot is alive no matter the evidence, adjusting his other beliefs ('pining for the fjords') to save it, or when 'Nudge Nudge' shows two pub-goers with wholly different schemes chatting without either noticing. We laugh, he concludes, because a new conceptual scheme is by definition unfamiliar and surprising — which is why laughter, unlike disgust, is tied to intelligence, and why philosophy done well is surrounded by the laughter of contemplating what it suggests.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 29 "“The Cheese Shop,” Episode 33, Monty Python’s Flying Circus, “Salad Days”" — This is Hardcastle's full talk: analytic philosophy's two revolts map onto Python clips, beginning with the logical positivists' revolt against metaphysics, whose cornerstone verifiability criterion self-destructs because it cannot verify itself. The positivist collapse hands philosophy to Quine's semantic holism — statements face experience 'not individually but only as a corporate body' — which the Dead Parrot sketch enacts as Praline the verificationist checking experiences against the shopkeeper-holist who preserves 'pining for the fjords' by adjusting other statements, and again in the Black Knight, who maintains 'None shall pass' through the loss of every limb. Holism's darker consequence, that no shared axioms are guaranteed so reason cannot found society, appears in the 'Argument Clinic' and in 'Nudge Nudge' as two men effectively speaking different languages in different worlds, while the witch-burning logic illustrates empirically bad human reasoning. The Cheese Shop sketch crowns the continental side — Mr. Mousebender an existentialist hero choosing cheese in an unfeeling world, Mr. Wensleydale the burden of life returning negative answers like Sisyphus's rock — and the Bruces' Philosophers Song is declared the best history of philosophy because it is sung.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 17 "Poker and Philosophy" — Ellis analyzes expert poker as thought attribution, spelling the iterations out to the sixth order in a Big Slick hand against T.J. Cloutier, then argues via Quine's 'gavagai' rabbit and Davidson's interpretationism that attributing thoughts to opponents requires assuming deep shared belief — which explains why pros misread novices whose minds they cannot model. The centerpiece is Dan Harrington's reconstruction of Daniel Negreanu's 2004 river raise against Freddy Deeb as a set of fourth-order-or-below attributions (Deeb will read a small raise as a lure bet and fold the best hand), not one towering thought. It ends asking how anyone ever learns what an opponent thinks from actions that are a vector of beliefs and desires, and notes poker forces rare deep agreement among strangers worldwide.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 34 "Evidence Rewarded" — Goldwater reads Bill James's sabermetric revolution through Quine: science is a continuation of common sense, but mature science replaces the 'animal sense of similarity' (being a Yankee, batting average, RBI) with predictive, league- and park-adjusted categories, turning atomistic box-score tallies into holistic statistics that acquire meaning only from the whole web of data. Because science recognizes only repeatable types, it cannot countenance miracles—Carlton Fisk's 1975 homer greeted by the 'Hallelujah Chorus,' Dave Roberts's steal in 2004—whose meaning lies in happening exactly once. His resolution: GMs like John Henry and Theo Epstein need Quinean prediction, while fans keep the religious language of faith, hope, and redemption.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 11 "Psych and Philosophy" — Jones argues that Shawn's 'psychic' act is really hypersensory perception (HSP) - noticing cat fur, fine print, blood spatter - feeding inference to the best explanation (IBE), the natural abductive method Sherlock Holmes mislabels deduction, with Clever Hans and Ilga Kirks as real-world parallels. Applying IBE with Ockham's Razor to the two hypotheses 'he's psychic' versus 'he's hyper-observant,' she concludes the natural explanation should win for everyone: Lassiter's skepticism tracks the evidence, Gus knows better despite believing in ghosts, and Chief Vick shouldn't buy the supernatural story either. Juliet's belief survives only through background supernatural beliefs, a psychic-friendly culture, and ignoring the clues Gus feeds Shawn, which the chapter diagnoses as the same public misunderstanding of the scope and limits of science that keeps most Americans believing in ESP.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 21 "11. Should We Execute the Erudite" — Michaud and Watkins ask whether Roth is right that the knowledge-hoarding Erudite are so dangerous we might need to eliminate them, and answer that knowledge is dangerous in three ways. Following Foucault ('it is impossible for knowledge not to engender power'), the powerful define what counts as knowledge - from the church blessing feudalism to the medical community pathologizing gay and transgender people - and following Piaget, new knowledge threatens the interconnected belief schemas (diagrammed as beliefs resting on beliefs) that keep 'faction before blood' and our sense of being special stable, which is why Divergents, evolution, and Copernicus provoke such violent disequilibrium. A Descartes-style simulation scenario - you may be inside Roth's world right now, weeded out for reading the books - and David Lewis's point that investigating knowledge destroys it then show that the real danger is not knowledge but the arrogance of certainty: Jeanine was never a true Erudite.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 40 "25. Should Catelyn Have Trusted Brienne" — McNabb and Andrews ask whether Catelyn was warranted in trusting Brienne as her sworn sword after Brienne failed to save Renly, and test two theories of warrant. On accessibilist coherentism, Catelyn's accessible evidence - Brienne's prowess, her devastation at Renly's death, 'Renly's death was no fault of yours' - fits her web of beliefs like a new strand in a spider's web; on Plantinga-style proper functionalism, illustrated by the accident-created Labman replica and the Lord of Light randomizing a design plan, Catelyn's naturally formed belief that Brienne is trustworthy is warranted if her faculties are properly functioning, truth-aimed, and well designed - which Brienne's record through rescuing Sansa vindicates.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 18 "8. Is It a Fact that Facts Don’t Matter" — Steele distinguishes facts as mind-independent reality from facts as expert-certified statements to show that Kellyanne Conway's alternative facts and Adams's own slogans trade on this ambiguity, and that Adams performatively contradicts himself every time he insists his predictions are true and matter. Analyzing the cognitive-dissonance hallucinations of Trump-is-Hitler and then Trump-is-incompetent, he argues that on Adams's own account brute facts proved irresistible, and that such belief revision is rational Popperian conjecture and refutation, plus the conservative strategy of saving fundamental theories (Coulomb's law) and dropping minor ones when the fuse blows. Against the claim that humans are irrational he recalls Aristotle's Rhetoric as persuasion's legitimate complement to the Prior Analytics, and leans on Percival to show propaganda fits a rational-reader model, citing the slow, fact-driven shift on gay marriage.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 17 "6. But What Does It Mean" — Argues that asking "what does it mean?" of Twin Peaks is the wrong question, because Lynch builds the show out of aesthetically incomplete material. Kant's "purposiveness without purpose" and the free play of understanding and imagination explain the opening credits' waterfalls, pines, and mill blades, while Russell's incomplete symbols ("the present king of France is bald") model the swaying traffic light and Harriet's "full blossom of the evening," and Quine's underdetermination of theory by evidence applies to Black Lodge clues like "the man in the smiling bag" and the Arm's whoops, which support many consistent but unprovable interpretations. Susanne Langer's account of film as a dream-like virtual present, capped by Part 8's atomic-bomb sequence, grounds the claim that Lynch means viewers to complete the meaning themselves.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 16 "Wonderland and the Real World" — Extracts three problems of induction from Alice's misadventures: predicting the future (Hume's problem: nothing rationally compels Humpty Dumpty to agree the world will not turn into Wonderland at 6 a.m. tomorrow), proving whose dream it is (Quine's underdetermination of theory by evidence: Tweedledee can accommodate any evidence within the theory that Alice exists only in the Red King's dream), and translating Wonderese (Quine's indeterminacy: pointing at the White Rabbit cannot fix whether natives mean the rabbit, its parts, or its stages, nor what 'muchness' means). Brendan Shea shows Alice succeeding where the creatures fail by the criteria Hume and Quine endorse: experimentation, simplicity, conservatism of belief, and a principle of charity in translation.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 25 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Reads the 'Sad Sack' photograph, which Wayne Jarvis sees as Iraqi WMD bunkers and Barry Zuckerkorn sees as Tobias's testicles, through the Duhem-Quine thesis of underdetermination and Kuhn's theory-ladenness of observation: the dominant 'George Sr. the traitor' paradigm dictates what is seen and nearly mobilizes Buster for war, while Barry's rival theory creates a crisis that only the omniscient narrator resolves. Kuhn's five criteria for theory choice (accuracy, consistency, scope, simplicity, fruitfulness) are applied to the rival 'theories', and George Michael's failed eye exam dramatizes the skeptical moment when no lens lets you see clearly, showing knowledge is a social and political position.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 20 "NOTES" — Hare treats mass photography—from the daguerreotype through digital cameras, Abu Ghraib snapshots, and diagnostic imaging—as making everyone a practicing epistemologist caught between two folk tenets: the photo as mirror of reality and as manipulation of reality. Defending photography as a genuine causal 'mode of seeing' (a prosthetic like telescopes), he proposes 'flexible realism,' adjusting Dewey's warranted assertibility and virtue-epistemology standards to context, and invokes William James's defense of beneficial 'overbeliefs' when National Geographic images strengthen confidence in one's own culture. Reading the Fallujah lead-pipe photo debate between editors Sullivan and Kushner, he uses Quine's recalcitrant-experience and web-of-belief holism—extended by Morton White's 'holistic pragmatism'—to show moral, epistemic, sensory, and emotional claims are tested together, and frames photography's democratization via Walter Benjamin's mechanical reproduction and loss of aura.

### Stoicism

Stoicism is a school of Hellenistic philosophy founded by Zeno of Citium around 300 BCE and later developed by figures such as Epictetus, Seneca, and Marcus Aurelius. It teaches that virtue—living in accordance with reason and nature—is the only true good, and that a flourishing life comes from mastering one's judgments rather than external circumstances. Because emotions like fear and anger arise from mistaken beliefs about what is good or bad, the Stoics sought to cultivate reason and equanimity in the face of whatever fortune brings.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 68 "Unknown" — The chapter proposes three theses: happiness is centrally tranquillity (ataraxia), whose enemy is anxiety - the 'splinter in your mind' that things are out of kilter; the rival Aristotelian view treats happiness as activity (energeia) of soul in accordance with excellence (arete), an objectivism that explains how a contented 'human battery' or happy slave is mistaken about being happy; and neither view suffices alone, since a passionless apatheia is barren and dry. Lived happiness is instead equipoise - settledness in one's basic stance that is compatible with turbulent passions and commitments, more like Neo's active decision-making and discovery than a lazy virtual tryst with the woman in red.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 22 "Emotions and Aesthetic Response" — Carolyn Korsmeyer uses BtVS to stage philosophy's ambivalence about emotion — dangerous passion versus intuitive sagacity — through three cases: anger as beast within and practical power (Xander's love spell in 'Bewitched, Bothered and Bewildered,' Willow's wish-spells in 'Something Blue,' 'My emotions give me power' to Kendra), grief as the one emotion no magic can undo (Epictetus's jug-and-child counsel set against 'The Body' and Dawn trying to resurrect Joyce), and love's non-fungibility (Anya's vengeance-demon past leaves her without the wider affection that makes singular love credible, while Spike's messy human history makes his obsession believable). She draws on Plato's wild-beast appetites and spirited element of the Republic, Aristotle on anger and emotional disposition as character, Kant's reason-above-nature picture, and Martha Nussbaum on art's particular cases. Finally she turns to aesthetic response: the show's comedy ('She saved the world a lot') regulates audience emotion, keeping the serial's catharsis from tipping into manipulation.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 14 "Kierkegaard Lays It Down" — Willie Young uses the sacrifice bunt (Derek Jeter's perfect one versus Placido Polanco's failed one) to test philosophical accounts of sacrifice. Aristotle treats bunting for teammates as friendship and civic virtue in the polis, while Seneca's Stoic sacrifices only to exercise virtue itself, detached from particular friends and refusing retaliation for hit batters. Hegel's modern ideal of self-renunciation makes the player a cog in the team machine (the Big Red Machine), obeying the manager's calculations; against this, Kierkegaard's Abraham, whose absolute duty to God is 'higher than the universal' through infinite resignation, exposes baseball's mechanical, manager-ordered sacrifice and asks whether the game trains obedient citizens who sacrifice as they are told.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 10 "“Control, Control, You Must Learn Control”" — Stephens reads Yoda as a Stoic sage: Luke's first impressions are blinded by appearance, but Yoda exhibits the Stoic virtues of patience, timeliness, focus on the present, apatheia (freedom from fear, anger, and hate), and ascetic discipline (askesis), living by the dichotomy of control. He reconstructs the contrasting 'logic of the Dark Side' - anger to hatred to aggression to the mastery of others - showing the Emperor as a tyrant who, unlike the self-mastering Stoic (Marcus Aurelius being the counterexample among rulers), seeks to control what is not up to him, so Vader's 'I must obey my master' is servitude to vice. The chapter also marks Stoic limits: the Emperor rightly rejects felt compassion but wrongly refuses beneficence and Stoic cosmopolitanism, and Stoic physicalism cannot accommodate Yoda's 'luminous beings' afterlife.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 41 "A Doomed Pursuit of Power and Glory" — Doom, declaring 'Power has ever been my God', steals the Silver Surfer's cosmic power, and the authors correct Lord Acton: power itself does not corrupt - only the flawed vessel it is poured into, while the uncorrupted are not destroyed by its loss ('Though bereft of my power - I do not crawl!'). The imprisoned Surfer's tranquil equanimity, they argue, is the voice of a Stoic philosopher, and Marvel shares with the best ancient philosophers a faith in a built-in cosmic justice whereby wrongly gotten power destroys its holder - fulfilled when Galactus strips Doom of what was never his.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 74 "What Wisdom Requires" — Explains what wisdom demands: subordinating the loud, here-and-now deliverances of the senses and emotions to reason and the larger picture — as in Plato's wise person contemplating the eternal Forms and the Republic's long course of training, the Bhagavad-Gita's detachment, and Stoic meditative practice. It argues experience is nonetheless central (a sixteen-year-old Captain Marvel could not have it), cites Stick's parting from Matt Murdock in Daredevil over uncontrolled emotion, and uses Casablanca to mark the cultural shift that makes us doubt the larger picture's claims.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 15 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Over an evening at the Iron Post biker bar, Auxier maps four habitues onto the Hellenistic schools: Cowboy, the Vietnam chopper pilot whose bar is a Garden of modest pleasures, loyalty, and withdrawal from power games, is an Epicurean; the laconic Bear, who doubts that even possessing knowledge would make us better off and suspends judgment, is a Pyrrhonian (unlike the coffee-house Carneadean); Happy Jack, the 'true nature's child' of 'Born to Be Wild' who defies convention and keeps nothing six months, is Diogenes's Cynic; and Gary, the Vietnam-damaged recovering alcoholic, is a damaged Stoic who has not reached apatheia. He concludes that bikers are postmodern pagans whose philosophy is enacted rather than propounded, a Biker Platonism that refuses the Christian-Platonic divorce of body and spirit and lives by honor, freedom, and a pagan fatalism that accepts the consequences of one's choices.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 10 "“All Good Things Must Come to an End”" — Thorsrud casts Spock and Data's exchange in 'Unification, Part II' — Spock dispassionate by choice, Data longing for emotion — as a replay of the ancient debate between Stoics and Peripatetics over whether to eliminate or moderate the passions. The Aristotelian side is built from Data's emotion-chip rage while killing a Borg ('Descent'), his unfelt breakup with Jenna ('In Theory'), and Riker's defense of trust after Ishara's betrayal ('Legacy'): emotions are judgments with pleasure or pain, there is a right amount to feel, and invulnerability costs the 'emotional bonds that make us who we are.' The Stoic reply uses Epictetus's distinction between involuntary impressions and assent (Picard's fear on the Borg ship vs. the holodeck), Cicero's refusal to 'moderate' what is simply a fault, and Seneca on anger, exemplified by Spock's 'quite logical relief' in 'Amok Time', his calculated desperation in 'The Galileo Seven', and his saving the bigot Stiles in 'Balance of Terror' — leaving the Peripatetic conclusion that fortune's goods are not mere indifferents and we may rightly 'smile with so little provocation.'
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 15 "“Here, Here, What’s All This Jabber-wapping When There’s Work to Be Done ”" — Tschaepe reads Professor Marvel and the Wizard as skilled givers of 'folk explanations'—stories about desires, beliefs, and feelings that work where logical, scientific, or mechanistic explanations fail—because each explanation is fitted to the pragmatic considerations of its audience and problem. With the companions the Wizard works through a failed dualist argument (a brain is not a mind) for the Scarecrow, an abbreviated Stoic ataraxy pitch for the Tin Man, and Aristotle's discretion-is-valor point for the Lion, settling in each case on folk psychology plus a token (Th.D. diploma, heart-shaped clock, Legion of Courage medal) that supplies the recognition actually needed. Dorothy, whose desire for home is real rather than mistaken, gets no folk explanation from anybody: she must combine the heel-tapping instruction with her own articulated desire—'there's no place like home'—which the chapter treats as pragmatically, not logically, effective.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 8 "Too Much Tequila, Or Not Quite Enough" — Doug Anderson reads Buffett as an 'American Stoic' — unlike his friend the Cynic Hunter S. Thompson, who dropped out and died, Buffett accepts his fated world of competitive capitalism and controls the one thing Stoics say we can: his own attitudes, 'changes in latitudes, changes in attitudes.' He leans on Seneca's advice to Serenus that wine and dreaming liberate the mind ('drink washes cares away') to interpret the dialectic of dreaming and drinking in 'Margaritaville,' 'Five o'Clock Somewhere,' and 'License to Chill' as Stoic self-renewal — the margarita even frees the singer to admit his own fault — with Emerson's intoxication-speaking poet as the American model. Excess is the failure mode: the expatriates of 'Banana Republics' who mistake the dream for an end state and Buffett's late-thirties hangover reckoning mark the Stoic middle path between deadening routine and 'too much tequila.'
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 13 "It’s Time for the Other Walkie-Talkie" — Dodge puts Monk on the case of friendship's nature, structured by Aristotle's three kinds from the Nicomachean Ethics: Hal Tucker's fake buddy act in 'Mr. Monk Makes a Friend' is pure utility, while Natalie's is virtue-friendship — she is his friend 'in spite of' the job since 'he doesn't pay her that much.' The friend as mirror and 'second self' grounds the claim that Stottlemeyer, Sharona, Natalie and Randy reflect Monk's excellence back to him, and Bacon's point that a friend redoubles joys and cuts griefs in half is shown when they stay up all night during his suicide watch. Seneca's Stoic counsel — judge a person long before admitting him, then hold nothing back — is exemplified by Natalie's fish-over-moon-rock test of Monk's character, while Montaigne's once-in-centuries friendship in which two selves blur fits only Trudy, whose dying words 'bread and butter' tell Monk they belong together. Plato's Lysis (the 'great cosmic swirly' Monk cites in 'Mr. Monk and the Bully') opens the puzzle Socrates could not solve, and the single walkie-talkie his father gave him shows why the chapter's verdict — Monk now has friends — matters.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 12 "Red Sox Fandom and Internal Harmony" — John McHugh uses his urge to confront Grady Little, who left a spent Pedro Martinez in during Game Seven of the 2003 ALCS, to ask how fans should govern the primal emotions fandom generates. Stoic self-command fails because Epictetus's advice (avoid caring about games entirely, focus only on what you control) would extinguish fandom itself, so McHugh adapts Adam Smith's impartial spectator: the virtuous fan imagines being watched by a sympathetic but emotionally distant fellow fan, settling on a Chicago Cubs fan who gets Bartman the way a Sox fan gets Buckner and Grady. He concludes that we each harbor a team of role-specific inner consciences, and the practical task is harmonizing the Red Sox-fan identity with our other identities rather than suppressing it or being consumed by it.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 5 "Fighting Talk" — The editors' introduction argues that philosophy and fighting have been companions since Socrates the soldier and Plato the wrestler (whose name means 'broad shouldered' from the gym), and that each can illuminate the other. It tours the volume through concrete cases: budo courtesy drawn from Shinto, Confucianism and Zen; the Shaolin monks' exercises as a route to Buddhahood; Western chivalry and Gordon Marino's boxing as educations in Aristotelian courage; fencing's egoism and value; and the Stoicism of karate and utilitarianism of Kano's judo. Philosophy clarifies fighting traditions, while fights supply puzzles for ethics, aesthetics, and the philosophy of mind.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 13 "An Enemy Lying in Ambush" — Fuller reads his teenage collapse while holding shiko dachi at his Eighth Kyu grading as a weakness of will, and argues that karate is Stoic discipline embodied. He explains the dichotomy of control through Epictetus's barbecue etiquette and the Kill Bill II buried-alive scene (only the Bride's years of disciplined training, not magic, break the coffin), then lays out living according to nature, Zeno's apatheia, Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, and Seneca's nightly self-examination as the model of askesis. Kata becomes 'a defiant stand against irrational emotion-chasing', and since only virtue is up to us, the enemy 'lying in ambush' is always internal: ourselves.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 30 "Time Enough to Drink the Poison" — Domino reads 'The Veiled Lodger' as a drama about hope in a world after God: Holmes's 'Your life is not your own; keep your hands off it' revives Plato's Phaedo argument that we are the gods' possessions, but deist-or-atheist Mrs. Ronder is unmoved, so Holmes falls back on the Leibnizian alternative to the Stoic and Cartesian 'patience without hope' — the example of patient suffering as 'the most precious of all lessons,' grounded in Leibniz's hope that the world is no 'cruel jest.' Jefferson Hope's two pill boxes in A Study in Scarlet literalize the Leibnizian link between hope and divine justice by letting God choose who dies, while Trelawney Hope's gullibility makes the surname ironic. Mrs. Ronder's true hope was reunion with Leonardo, which his death destroyed; what saves her is a new hope founded on Watson's text, since only a writer ('I have made a slight change of name and place') can change the past.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 13 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Curko and Greguric read Klosterman's glam-rock fandom as a problem of identity and masks: Nietzsche's Apollonian-Dionysian split casts Chuck as a self-controlled Apollonian writing about Dionysian excess in Guns N' Roses, Motley Crue, and Whitesnake, while Descartes's remark that actors wear masks to hide their shame introduces the tribute band Paradise City, a 'real copy' whose members would have no personalities left if they fully succeeded. The authors extend the mask question to Facebook and online avatars, where media saturation makes us 'copies without the original' and identity stops being self-same. They end by crowning Klosterman a modern Socrates of 'Know thyself' and a Stoic exemplar: admire your heroes like Satriani but do not steal their identities, control what you can (never your reputation or your time of death), and keep daring the endless search for self-knowledge.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 20 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Ashley Barkman argues that feminism is unrealistic and inefficient in the apocalypse: citing sex-difference research such as Bandura's Bobo doll experiments, she claims masculine aggression and strength are what leadership requires when authority must be asserted physically, as when Rick pipes Merle and shoves Daryl, or Shane tackles Ed and Jim. The quarry laundry scenes stage the debate - Jacqui's protest at 'all the Hattie McDaniel work' versus Lori's 'this isn't about women's rights... doing what needs to be done' - and Barkman sides with Lori, treating the division of labor as survival logistics under a natural-law premise that it is moral to act according to nature. Andrea the sharpshooter and Michonne the swordswoman show women can excel as heroic exceptions without leading, and the chapter concludes leadership should stay with good men like Rick.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 22 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Schwanebeck reads Nucky's fastidious grooming and Prohibition's purity crusade through the body politic metaphor: from Cicero and Seneca's De Clementia, where head and body of the state depend on each other, through Hobbes's bearded Leviathan frontispiece, to temperance propaganda that framed alcohol as poison entering the national bloodstream and wartime posters demanding 'a clean America.' The show exposes the purity ideal as illusion - the true purists are the Klan massacring Chalky's men and the hand-washing Van Alden shouting 'Let these waters wash you clean!' over Sebso's drowning body. Nucky rules less like Seneca's genuinely clement emperor than like Machiavelli's prince who merely appears virtuous, and the gangster genre's kingly tropes ('Et tu, Eli?') crown him head of Atlantic City's body politic.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 28 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Laderoute reads 'The Late Philip J. Fry' - the forward-only time machine overshooting past the year one billion and the last protons to a second Big Bang and an identical universe (ten feet lower, conveniently crushing its duplicates) - as a tour of cosmology from Aristotle's static, eternal, Earth-centered heavens through the Stoics' providential determinism and fiery ekpyrosis to Big Bang cosmology and heat death, which is why the Professor is so shocked. Nietzsche's Gay Science 341 supplies the existential payoff: faced with living identically forever, one can react with horror or delight, and eternal recurrence becomes a challenge to become the person you want to be. Fry, a billion years late for his Cavern on the Green dinner, reads Leela's message carved in stone, and in the repeated universe finally arrives on time - 'That was the old Fry... he's dead now' - amor fati enacted.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 16 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Billard concedes the Stoic point that we control neither our passions nor nature ('life will always find a way', Sattler's 'you never had control'), as the bucardo cloning failure shows, but argues this proves the park rushed, not that de-extinction is impossible. Dangerousness is subjective, raptor intelligence is a logistics problem rather than a metaphysical objection, and since humans have already caused the sixth mass extinction we may have a duty to bring species back. Because revived animals would be 'neo-dinosaurs' built from fragmentary DNA, de-extinction is creation rather than resurrection, less like playing God than like the transhumanist enhancement humans already practice.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 11 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Brendan Shea reads Cohen through the three Hellenistic schools. Socrates's trial in the Apology mirrors the persecuted singer of 'A Singer Must Die,' with 'Everybody Knows' and 'Democracy' voicing a Socratic mix of empathy and pessimism about whether democracy can deal rationally with its critics. Stoics such as Epictetus ground the present-focused, resigned acceptance of loss in 'Hey, That's No Way to Say Goodbye' and 'If It Be Your Will'; the Pyrrhonian skepticism of Sextus Empiricus illuminates the narrator's calming, unresolvable ignorance in 'Famous Blue Raincoat'; and the Epicurean atomism of Epicurus and Lucretius - death is nothing to us, empty desires are unsatisfiable - underlies 'A Thousand Kisses Deep.' Hypatia's murder and Cohen's 'Joan of Arc' close the chapter: the examined life is an all-consuming, sometimes fatal commitment that is nonetheless worthwhile.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 13 "Homeland and Philosophy" — John Karavitis evaluates four suicide events: Afsal Hamid's suicide in CIA custody, Aileen Morgan's cutting her throat with a lens, Brody's aborted suicide bombing, and Carrie's ECT as a 'suicide' of her old self. Kant's absolute ban on suicide (it denies your humanity) clashes with Seneca's Stoic counsel that a life of miserable captivity need not be continued, and with Singer's utilitarian permission of euthanasia that reduces suffering - under both, Hamid's and Aileen's suicides are defensible while Brody's emotionally driven bombing is not. Dana's plea that her father is needed recasts Aristotle's point that suicide wrongs the community, and Sloterdijk's analysis of rage turned on oneself frames Carrie's amoral self-destruction.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 34 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Re-examining 'The Enchiridion!' trial by trial - the gnome illusions, the ogre whose dollar Finn steals and then returns, the dark mage's brain world, the wallop given the Key-per in devil pajamas - the chapter argues Finn wins the hero's handbook without being righteous: he is brave, tender and ingenious, but gullible, hasty and violent, slaying whatever he is told is evil and running from the gnome test. Epictetus's Stoic Enchiridion supplies the standard the show's book lacks: only virtue matters, wealth, fame and comfort are indifferents, and a real handbook teaches how to lose, age and admit mistakes, not just how to win, which is exactly what Billy's quit-heroism shows Ooo's greatest hero never learned. Because bravery without good judgment could as easily serve a Nazi, a terrorist or the Lich, Finn's lack of practical wisdom means the 'most righteous hero' in Ooo is an impetuous boy - proof of how morally broken the Land of Ooo is.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 16 "4. On Being a Dead Person Who Hasn’t Died Yet" — Mark Ralkowski argues that Louis's 'dead people who haven't died yet' bit sounds like Marcus Aurelius, and that Dr. Bigelow's Season Four advice about back pain, the three-legged dog, and heartbreak works as the Stoic spiritual exercises Pierre Hadot described - above all the 'view from above' that re-describes things to strip them to their true value. Epictetus's dichotomy of control explains Bigelow's core advice: pain is not 'up to us' but our judgments about it are, so Louie should adjust his expectations to nature ('every second without back pain is a lucky second') instead of demanding a pain-free life. The apparently un-Stoic counsel to savor heartbreak ('misery is wasted on the miserable') is defended as genuinely Stoic: viewing his lost love from the perspective of a dead-person-who-hasn't-died-yet, Louie can accept sadness as precious and impermanent rather than being crushed by it. The chapter concedes Louis is no philosopher, but suggests his bits - contrasted with Seinfeld's 'polished' version on Talking Funny - can be read as newly discovered Meditations for comedy audiences.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 17 "5. Just Want a Shitty Body" — Bekka Williams argues that Louis's 'just want a shitty body' bit restates Epictetus's central Stoic teaching - want events to happen as they do happen, because only judgments, efforts, and desires are 'up to us' while bodies, reputations, and outcomes are not. She reads the Late Show arc (Tardigan's non-offer of the job, then Louie's triumphant 'Hey Letterman, I did it!' when Letterman stays) as Epictetus's cardplayer ideal: total effort on what is controllable, calm acceptance of what is not, alongside the bits about disgusting bodies, 'do the shit out of your job,' Jane and the mango pop, and Louis's self-trained habit of intercepting impulsive desires like the motorcycle urge.
