- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 27 "16. You Made Me First" — The chapter argues that origin stories fix character: Batman, forged by watching his parents murdered (and in Burton's film by the Joker himself - 'You made me first'), is trapped by a past that sets his trajectory, since as Schopenhauer said we can do what we will but cannot will what we will. Kal-El's origin is instead an act of hope - his parents launch him into the universe believing the wildly unlikely - which the chapter reads through William James's will-to-believe, the same faith Bruce needs to jump the chasm unroped in The Dark Knight Rises. Because the past causes the future and 'I can do whatever I want' is not free will, Bruce can never escape his tragedy, while Superman's hopeful origin lets him believe, and make us believe, that we might yet fly.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 27 "13. Linus’s Wager" — The chapter stages a three-way debate over whether Linus may believe in the Great Pumpkin without evidence. Clifford's ethics of belief (the ship-owner whose wishful thinking sinks his ship) condemns Linus's sincerity-based wager; Pascal's Wager endorses it (forgoing one night of trick-or-treating costs nothing if the Pumpkin is fake and wins toys if he is real) but assumes a doxastic voluntarism we lack, since no one can make themselves believe for even a million-dollar reward. William James's 'The Will to Believe' gets the final word: if Linus's option is live, forced, and momentous with no decisive evidence either way, his leap of faith - like loving without guarantees - is morally justified whenever life would be greatly impoverished without it.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 29 "16. I Should Have Known It" — Watkins reads the later albums Mojo and Hypnotic Eye ("Power Drunk," "Burnt Out Town," "Playing Dumb," "Shadow People") through Clifford's ethics of belief: the powerful suppress their doubts like the unseaworthy shipowner and come to sincerely believe their own lies, while the overpowered hide behind the cliche that everyone is entitled to an opinion. Because belief formation is a doing inseparable from action, there is a moral obligation to hold beliefs to evidentiary standards, we should have known, and James's will-to-believe and fideist appeals (Tertullian, Pascal, Kierkegaard) offer no license for self-serving faith. Facing the evidence in front of us is the first step to telling the power-drunk it is the last time they are going to hurt us.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 13 "5. Greatness or Nothingness" — Courtland Lewis uses KISS's career gambles to compare theories of decision-making. After Tolstoy's twig-over-the-dragon allegory of mortal life, he tests W.K. Clifford's shipowner (never act without sufficient evidence) against KISS's counter-evidence bet on the Alive! live album, models the choice with Pascal's Wager, and uses the Prisoner's Dilemma to explain the flop of the four 1978 solo albums. He then argues William James's pragmatism — beliefs as rules for action, the living, forced, and momentous option that 'KISS is the best' — best explains why acting on the band's self-created narrative was authentic, with Nietzsche completing the picture: greatness requires leaping, living dangerously, tightrope-walking toward self-defined success.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 29 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Malloy examines Walter's incorrigible leaps — Bunny kidnapped herself on no evidence, the toe is a fake ('I can get you a toe by three o'clock'), the Big Lebowski can walk — through Clifford's ethics of belief (the ship-owner who sinks his passengers) and James's 'Will to Believe' reply with its living, forced, and momentous genuine options, applied to Walter's 'dabbled' pacifism and his preference for Nazism's ethos over nihilism's nothing. Walter's conversion to Judaism for Cynthia raises whether practice can will belief, tested via Pascal's wager and James's objection, and the verdict borrows Bernard Williams: we cannot choose beliefs, but Walter's reckless policy of dismissing counterevidence makes him 'not just an asshole, he is also wrong'.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 12 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Johnson uses 'Go God Go's' future of 2546—where Dawkins-style atheism has become a warring religion and otter scientists intone 'Oh my Science!'—to ask whether science and religion genuinely conflict and whether New Atheism is itself a faith. Applying abduction and the four criteria of adequacy, he argues the embellished-story hypothesis beats miracle claims about Jesus (whose legend grew Gospel by Gospel), Sathya Sai Baba, Joseph Smith, and Xenu, that Mr(s). Garrison's 'you can't disprove God' and the show's sarcasm commit an appeal to ignorance, and that Stan's water-into-wine scene with Jesus shows how easily people are fooled. He allows Kuhnian theory change in science but rejects James's will-to-believe for existence claims—the moon whale Willzyx needs evidence—and concludes Parker and Stone are unfair to Dawkins: ending religion would not end violence, but it would remove the easiest justification for it, and some answers are simply true even when unknown.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 13 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Dueck takes Stan's closing pluralism in 'Super Best Friends'—all religions have something valuable to teach, as the interfaith superheroes' combined powers defeat Blaine—and tests it against Hick's pluralism, exclusivism, and Rahner's inclusivist 'anonymous Christians', using 'Go God Go's warring atheist factions to show exclusivity is unavoidable even without God. Hume's miracle argument explains why Jesus's look-away water-into-wine trick convinces no one in the episode: testimony can never outweigh the laws of nature, so supernatural evidence resists natural evaluation. Popper's falsificationism warns that watering doctrines down to make religions compatible (the rabbit-pope of 'Fantastic Easter Special') leaves nothing to test, while James's will to believe and Plantinga's defense of exclusivism ground the conclusion that faith can be rationally justifiable where evidence runs out—beware the Blainetologists, but do not surrender ways of life that define us.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 27 "16. You Made Me First" — Starting from the Joker's 'You made me' / Batman's 'You made me first' exchange in Tim Burton's Batman, the chapter argues origin stories fix character: Bruce's witnessed trauma destines him to darkness (and we expect his death to match), while Kal-El is sent to Earth as an act of hope that the chapter reads through William James's will-to-believe—belief itself makes success possible, like Bruce's ropeless leap in The Dark Knight Rises. Against 'I can do whatever I want' free will it deploys Schopenhauer's 'we can do what we will, but we cannot will what we will': Bruce cannot will away his vengeance, and Red Son's Soviet-raised Superman shows biology and upbringing determining who Clark becomes. Superman still wins because his origin story permits the hope that Bruce's cannot.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 11 "Notes" — Baggett sets W. K. Clifford's evidentialism (the negligent shipowner; believing on insufficient evidence is a 'sin against mankind') against William James's precursive faith, which permits believing ahead of the evidence when an option is forced, live, momentous, and evidentially undecided. He applies this to Sam's taping over the Dubai Air logo as social-coordination faith, Richmond's belief that it can finally beat Everton, romantic risk-taking like Roy and Keeley's, and the marriage of belief with hard work (Ted's practice tirade, Nate's False Nine), ending with James and Pascal on how evidential ambiguity about God makes a passional step of faith rational.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica to explore knowledge as justified true belief. Adama's 'true lie' about knowing Earth's location makes Starbuck's belief in Earth a Gettier case, a justified true belief resting on false justification. He tests Adama's testimony against Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for spotting Cylons; memory deceives Boomer and Tigh) and Hume's skepticism about testimony versus Plantinga's defense of it. Finally, against Clifford's evidentialism he deploys William James's 'will to believe,' arguing that faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice that gives the Colonials purpose.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 18 "Time Belongs to the Tower" — Auxier frames King as 'Tolkien meets Poe' and reads the Dark Tower's temporalization through the literary and psychological experience of time. Drawing on Susanne Langer's 'virtual present' and Sartre's psychology of imagination, he argues readers surrender their real present to a novel's suspended time, which he links to William James's 'will to believe' rather than mere suspension of disbelief. He uses Kant's distinction between amazement (seeing the seemingly impossible) and admiration (accepting it) to explain the psychological cost time travelers like Jake Epping and Wesley Smith should pay, faulting King for keeping ordinary heroes sane while displacing the strain onto insane 'gatekeepers,' and concludes the Tower is 'real' as the way each person binds possibility to their own lived past, present, and future.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 6 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — In this Foreword, John Rousmaniere argues that sailing's 'numinous' moments — like his own experience of stillness on a becalmed ketch mid-Atlantic, when the skipper cut the engine and the crew felt suspended between sky and sea — are paths to genuine philosophical truths, not embarrassing flights of fancy. He enlists William James's 'Varieties of Religious Experience' and James's nautical metaphor for free will (the passenger who volunteers to take the helm) to argue that such mystical feelings can 'team up' with reason rather than opposing it. He insists mystery and craft must work together: piety is no substitute for seamanship (Shelley drowned in an unseaworthy boat), yet competence and numinous experience nurture each other.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 25 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Johnson argues that the Santa Claus lie is immoral and should be abandoned, giving three reasons: it is deceptive lying (Kant's absolute prohibition is too strong, but the lie lacks life-saving justification and functions as a Platonic 'noble lie' no more noble than a cult leader's); Santa robs parents of credit and warps children's moral development and trust, illustrated by anguished 'finding out' stories and Virginia O'Hanlon's letter; and it damages credulity, invoking Clifford's 'Ethics of Belief' against belief on insufficient evidence while James's 'Will to Believe' cannot rescue Santa since evidence against him is overwhelming. He recommends revealing the truth early, even via a Socratic-Method questioning game.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 14 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Roche's 'Seeing Snakes' attacks the psychedelicist claim (William James on nitrous oxide, Huxley's 'reducing valve,' Leary) that drugs including cannabis reveal reality-as-it-is. He deploys Russell's line that we 'can make no distinction between the man who eats little and sees heaven and the man who drinks much and sees snakes,' and a reliabilist demand that knowledge have a source proven reliable over independently verifiable cases, to argue drug 'revelations' are indistinguishable from delusion. Foucault is cited that drugs have 'nothing to do with truth and falsity,' and Nietzsche's Dionysian veil-of-Maya passage is used as an example of the mystical rhetoric he debunks.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 20 "NOTES" — Hare treats mass photography—from the daguerreotype through digital cameras, Abu Ghraib snapshots, and diagnostic imaging—as making everyone a practicing epistemologist caught between two folk tenets: the photo as mirror of reality and as manipulation of reality. Defending photography as a genuine causal 'mode of seeing' (a prosthetic like telescopes), he proposes 'flexible realism,' adjusting Dewey's warranted assertibility and virtue-epistemology standards to context, and invokes William James's defense of beneficial 'overbeliefs' when National Geographic images strengthen confidence in one's own culture. Reading the Fallujah lead-pipe photo debate between editors Sullivan and Kushner, he uses Quine's recalcitrant-experience and web-of-belief holism—extended by Morton White's 'holistic pragmatism'—to show moral, epistemic, sensory, and emotional claims are tested together, and frames photography's democratization via Walter Benjamin's mechanical reproduction and loss of aura.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Eric Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica's Adama, who lies that he knows Earth's location, to run the Gettier problem: Starbuck's true belief that Earth exists rests on a false justification (that Adama knows), so it is justified-true-belief without being knowledge. He tests testimony via Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for telling Cylons from humans) and the Hume/Locke/Plantinga debate over testimony's epistemic role. He closes with James's 'will to believe': faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice where agnosticism forfeits meaning, so belief without certainty can be reasonable.

### Democracy

Democracy is a form of political rule in which authority is grounded in the people, who govern themselves either directly or through elected representatives. Philosophical debate about democracy concerns not only procedures such as voting and majority rule but also the values it is meant to realize—political equality, liberty, and legitimacy through the consent of the governed. Thinkers disagree about its proper scope and limits: whether it is chiefly a method for making collective decisions, a way of protecting rights, or an ideal of shared self-rule, and how it should guard against both tyranny and the domination of minorities. These questions run from ancient Athens through modern liberal and participatory theories.

- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 22 "Our Big, Fat, Greek Democracy" — Eric Bronson reads the brawling 1977-78 'Bronx Zoo' Yankees (Steinbrenner firing Billy Martin five times, Martin dragging Reggie Jackson off the field in Fenway, Jackson's dugout charge and defiant bunt) as an argument that dissent is good for democracy. Through Alexis de Tocqueville's warnings about majority conformity and democratic leveling (Nietzsche's herd mentality), he argues America needs gadflies like Socrates condemned by Athens for 'creating tension' and MLK's nonviolent troublemakers, while Adam Smith's invisible hand shows the Yankees' internal self-interest and conflict still produced championships, unlike the harmonious 1979 'We Are Family' Pirates. Dysfunctional discord, like free speech, keeps teams and democracies from going stagnant.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 18 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Kurtz, the secular humanist, argues the film is a political weapon of the Religious Right (O'Reilly, Dobson, Gingrich) that presents fantasy as fact: Gibson claims fidelity to the Gospels while borrowing torture scenes such as the bridge plunge and the savage flogging from Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions, whitewashing the historical Pilate, and erasing that Jesus, Mary, and the disciples were themselves Jews. Applying historical criticism, he contends the Gospels are anonymous, second- and third-hand missionary propaganda written forty to seventy years after Jesus, shaped by the rivalry between rabbinic Judaism and Gentile-seeking Jewish Christianity and canonized politically at Nicaea under Constantine. He concludes by defending the freedom of inquiry, skeptical scrutiny of all sacred texts, and the First Amendment's separation of church and state against the film's power to inflame anti-Semitism and the American culture war.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 25 "Palpatine’s Legacy" — Decker reconstructs Palpatine's career as a case study in how democracies die: using Aristotle's definition of tyranny and the precedent of Pisistratus and Julius Caesar, he shows Palpatine manufacturing the Separatist threat so the Senate grants him emergency powers - a twist on Machiavelli's loved-versus-feared dictum in which playing the reluctant democrat is itself the means to absolute rule. The Attack of the Clones debate between Anakin ('Someone wise' should make people agree) and Padme becomes a clash between Leo Strauss's philosopher-king ideal of rule by the virtuous few and John Dewey's conception of democracy as a way of life trusting the intelligence of common people, with Rousseau's social contract framing the stakes. The chapter concludes that democratic ends require democratic means and that unaccountable 'watchers' - Straussian statesmen or Anakins - are exactly the path to Empire.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 83 "Bullshitting and Lying in Politics" — Opening Mark Evans's Chapter 12: Frankfurt's claim that democracy especially breeds bullshit, since it charges every citizen with having opinions about everything - the 'Frankfurt thesis' that citizens do not care about truth. It is contrasted with the 'cynicism thesis' (citizens do not care about politics, out of well-founded disillusion with a system that fails to deliver), and both are framed by the objection as old as Plato that political understanding is an expertise we cannot all share - theses argued about, not against, democracy.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 85 "‘Dumbing-Up’ Some Distortions of Democratic Equality" — Evans argues that democratic citizens do their own share of Frankfurt-bullshitting about politics: because electoral democracy cannot admit how complex politics really is, it institutionalizes the fictional ideal of the 'well-informed' citizen, obliging voters to hold over-simplified views and politicians to pander to them. Campaigning forces candidates into dodges like the 'politics of distraction' and the empty promise to be 'a different sort of politician', producing 'Governor Schwarzenegger Syndrome' and opening space for dangerous demagogues and fundamentalisms. Following Churchill, the chapter concludes that this citizen-side bullshit vindicates the cynicism thesis only partially and gives no reason to reject democracy as 'the worst form of government except for all the others'.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 86 "Philosophy versus Bullshit" — The chapter claims that 'equal respect' in modern democracies has been distorted into a 'dumbing-up' relativism — 'I'm valid, you're valid' — which conflates the equal right to voice opinions with their equal intellectual merit and so leaves nothing that counts as bullshit. It illustrates this through the 'democratization of expertise' and management-speak ('downsizing', 'mission statements'), which mimics profundity while evading awkward facts, and it tests and rejects the quasi-Nietzschean ressentiment story of timid citizens dragging discourse down to a common denominator. To get the full measure of the phenomenon it expands Frankfurt's and Cohen's typologies into seven kinds of bullshit, adding clarifiable unclarity, plain rubbish, irretrievable speculation, pretension, and evasion.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 22 "E Pluribus Unum" — Auxier frames Hitchcock's Lifeboat against Garrett Hardin's 'lifeboat ethics' essay, arguing the lifeboat converts political questions into ethical ones by stranding the survivors outside law and politics ('We're on our own here. We can make our own law'). The survivors are ethical pluralists - Rittenhouse lives for money, Kovac for equality, Constance for fame, Joe for God, MacKenzie for care - and their clinging to private versions of the Good lets Nazi captain Willy, whose only principle is survival, manipulate them all. Using Maslow's hierarchy of needs, Auxier shows the boat descending to bare survival, yet argues the mob killing of Willy when he hoards water is moral outrage rather than survival-driven, and that the final rescue scene replays the opening dispute with nobody having grown - a vindication of pluralistic democracy capable of unified action.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 13 "What Is Truth" — Lavaque-Manty and Mickey define populism by distinguishing its content from its discourse (via Michael Kazin), tracing the 1892 Populist Party platform and southern race-baiting demagogues like Vardaman and Huey Long, then locate Cash in that Dixie soil, his family rescued by the patronizing New Deal Dyess Colony that fed his populist distrust of elites. Cash's populism is anti-racist and pro-prisoner ("The Ballad of Ira Hayes," his empathy for convicts against tough-on-crime politics), his patriotism borders on kitsch ("Ragged Old Flag"), and "What Is Truth?" argues the young may be right, breaking with populist certainty about the obvious. The closing worry is the deep tension they pose with Locke's "the people be the judge" against democracy as "government by discussion": a Cash concert, like a mass rally, may stir people following rather than thinking, so populism's ring of truth is not yet truth.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 11 "Unity Born from Diversity" — Shook narrates the 1984 Born in the U.S.A. tour — George Will's 'Yankee Doodle Springsteen' column, Reagan's Hammonton speech, Springsteen's refusal to be either campaign's tool — and reads the song as the hopeless story of a Vietnam-generation man's living death (the refinery that won't hire him, the dead brother and the Saigon woman) mistaken by flag-waving crowds for a patriotic anthem. He then maps the song's possible meanings onto democracy's possible destinies: Carl Schmitt's friend–enemy politics of national homogeneity and permanent emergency, Schlesinger's assimilationist Disuniting of America, and liberal cosmopolitanism's citizens of the world. Dewey's The Public and Its Problems wins: democracy must intelligently manage rather than eliminate diversity, each citizen holding a double loyalty to subgroup and to the democratic 'great community,' so being born in the U.S.A. is a responsibility and pride is properly placed in democratic ideals.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 22 "Learning from Our Mistakes" — Tamplin defends democracy through the Baltar election: Roslin's attempted theft failed, the voters' bad choice produced the New Caprica occupation, and this is exactly what Plato and Aristotle predicted of democracy as the deviant rule of the many, contrasted with Aristotle's polity aimed at the common advantage and a virtue 'every city' must care for. A thought experiment — an infallible computer advising citizens on every choice — shows that following it would abolish democracy, whose value lies not in results but in Aristotle's freedom, 'living as one wants.' Only by being allowed to frak things up can citizens learn from their mistakes, the road Apollo points to in his 'Crossroads' trial speech about collective shame, which is why Baltar's acquittal is a good sign.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 30 "Walking the Tightrope" — Louis Melancon weighs the Fleet leadership's secrets and lies: Adama's 'blind squirrel' lie about Earth, classifying the fact that Cylons look human, Roslin's faked death of the baby Hera, and Tom Zarek's secret collaboration courts on New Caprica. Democratic duty is framed as a deontological obligation of transparency grounded in the governed's trust, while the leadership repeatedly defaults to consequentialist wartime exceptions. The chapter proposes a rule-of-thumb: secrecy is justified only to hide specific information from an external threat like the Cylons, never to protect the government from its own citizens, and each violation erodes the trust on which Colonial democracy's 'soul' depends.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 23 "13 - Don’t Talk to Me" — Pitt argues the iPod is 'pernicious' not because technology is intrinsically bad — a device is judged by the uses it is put to and their consequences — but because its consequences are antisocial: silent subways, 'brainsnatched' beach-walkers, and the silenced graduate corridor where loud philosophical argument used to live. Comparing the gadget to Huxley's soma (each user programs his own blissful isolation, going so far as to avoid domestic conflict by plugging back in), he contends social skills — argument, eye contact, advocacy for ideas — are what drive both technological innovation (even Steve Jobs had a co-inventor) and functioning democracy. Hence the earbud habituation summarized as 'Don't talk to me, I'm listening to MY music!' is, he claims, one of the final nails in the coffin of the social skills a civil, democratic society needs.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 20 "“Its Continuing Mission”" — Argues that Star Trek's real subject is Hegelian recognition: a society is worth living in when every member's claims count as reasons and their talents get developed. It reads 'The Measure of a Man' (Data winning legal personhood), 'The Outcast' (Riker defending the J'naii Soren), and DS9's 'Past Tense' Bell Riots as dramas of winning recognition, and maps the Romulan-Reman and Stratos-Troglyte hierarchies onto Hegel's master-slave dialectic, contrasting Descartes's solipsistic cogito with Hegel's claim that self-awareness needs another. Since recognition requires more than non-interference against Locke-style atomism, the Federation's appeal lies in positive liberties — education, open debate, guaranteed basic needs — even though the shows oddly skip elections and democratic politics, a tension the authors flag through Leonard Nimoy's praise of a world with 'no political agenda.'
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 13 "Leto’s Not So Golden Path" — Diagnoses the Duniverse's recurring collapse not, as Herbert's 'Dune Genesis' has it, in hero-worship, but in rule conducted entirely through strategic action—Habermas's term for goal-oriented, self-interested rationality—as when even the Atreides council discusses only the appearance of a constitution rather than its legitimacy. Physical stability enforced by threats never becomes normative stability: Corrino, Paul's jihad-empire, and Leto II's 3,500-year tyranny all fail because their subjects are never authors of the law, and Leto's return to Bene Gesserit-style breeding programs ignores humanity's deliberative potential. The proposed remedy is democracy—rule by the people—even against Alia's cry that 'Atreides power must never be marginalized by the chaos of democracy.'
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 19 "The Ideal Candidate" — Nathan Zook uses the 'Royal Krabby' election from Vote for SpongeBob and the global-warming plot of SpongeBob Goes Green to weigh democracy. Mr. Krabs's rigged election, run only to sell patties, exemplifies C. Wright Mills's power elite manipulating the appearance of popular rule; Plato would bar Producer-class SpongeBob and Squidward from ruling and prefers educated Guardians, while Mill defends each citizen's liberty to choose and democracy's alliance with education (SpongeBob learns about global warming from Sandy). Aristotle's polity — citizens administering the state for the common interest — makes SpongeBob the ideal candidate because he saves Bikini Bottom without claiming power.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 69 "Rule of the Wise" — Updates Plato's rule of the wise to the pre-cogs of 'Minority Report,' noting that Socrates' 'divine sign' made him a kind of pre-cog. It then argues expertise cannot be operationalized — self-proclaimed authorities from Sarah Palin to Barack Obama disagree, and there is no accepted test of who the experts are — closing with Plato's own comparison of voters to children choosing between the doctor's medicine and the confectioner's candy, which explains why the Founders added the Electoral College.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 70 "Spinning a Bottle" — Sets Solar Lottery's Bottle beside the Athenian kleroterion and Madison's fear of factions: because telepaths make any strategy predictable, the Bottle game is a pure game of chance like dice rather than poker. The random twitch that deposes Reese Verrick for Leon Cartwright illustrates the same logic behind Philips and Callenbach's A Citizen Legislature proposal to replace the House with a randomly selected 'portrait of the people in miniature.'
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 71 "Throwing the Rascals Out" — Uses Joseph Schumpeter's deflationary account of elections — no meaningful popular will, just marketplace competition ensuring rotation in office — to explain Herb Moore's claim in Solar Lottery that the Bottle's random twitch prevents dictators. Since no one can be sure of holding power, a lottery guarantees turnover at least as well as elections, though it introduces the mirror-image danger of simply selecting an incompetent.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 72 "Checks and Challenges" — Walks through Solar Lottery's two-part selection machinery — the random Bottle plus the Challenge, an officially appointed assassin who filters out incompetent Quizmasters like the psychotic Robin Pitt — comparing them to Athenian scrutiny of officials and impeachment. It also shows how the unk underclass selling its power cards concentrates any chance of office in the hands of the rich, undercutting the lottery's democratic justification, and asks whether surviving assassination predicts governing any better than winning elections does.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 73 "How Can Random Machinery Be Rational" — Answers Verrick's complaint that the Bottle is irrational by distinguishing tools, which are arational, from agents who act for reasons: a lottery is inappropriate for choosing a spouse or career but rational where unpredictability or impartiality is wanted. In Solar Lottery the assassins DeFalla and Keith Pellig randomize their courses against telepaths, just as draft and green-card lotteries ensure equal chances, so random rotation in office is a rational tool for stopping anyone from holding power too long.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 74 "Giving and Selling" — Takes Plato's warning that those who want to rule, like Verrick, will profit from office — true philosophers rule only under compulsion — into the question of whether power cards may be given away or sold. Since we permit donating organs and having sex but criminalize selling them, letting the rich buy up the unks' tickets destroys the equal-chance rationale, the realization that leads Cartwright to see the game as stacked, and that the chapter links to Lani Guinier's smeared electoral-reform proposals.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 23 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Sienkiewicz argues that Klosterman's LeBron James 'Decision' episode on Bill Simmons's B.S. Report modeled genuine public-sphere deliberation: where ESPN's Skip Bayless scored points over whether James looked remorseful, Klosterman proposed, via Tupac's 'Only God can judge me', that the televised announcement was a statement of confidence and a refusal to play the one-dimensional reality-TV role America demanded. The chapter lays out Habermas's eighteenth-century public sphere, its salons and 'public sphere of letters' where low-stakes aesthetic arguments (Mozart then, the Guns N' Roses tribute band Paradise City now) train disinterested rational debate, and concedes Habermas's golden age is idealized historical fiction much like a Klosterman hyperthetical. Though Habermas blames commercial media for corroding rational discourse, Sienkiewicz contends that long-form podcasts like The B.S. Report and Contexts give Klosterman's pop-culture arguments the time and independence the old salons had, so arguing about Billy Joel or Ace Frehley strengthens rather than absolves democratic culture.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 33 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — A provocatively sympathetic application of On Liberty: Mill's harm principle protects Jesse's drug use from punishment, and Mill's celebration of individuality and 'experiments of living' makes Walt's cooking an 'individual spontaneity' valuable precisely because it defies custom - Marie's anti-pot panic and Hank's beer-and-Cub-cigar double standard illustrating the 'magical influence of custom' and democracy's drift toward 'collective mediocrity'. Mill's temperance-era remarks that intoxication 'is not a fit subject for legislative interference' are extended from use to manufacture. The chapter's thesis: even when Walt is wrong, mere nonconformity 'is itself a service', making Heisenberg an unlikely hero of liberty and human progress.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 28 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Joseph Foy argues Jeopardy! quietly serves democracy: the breadth of its categories rewards exactly the well-rounded, informed citizenry that theorists from Tocqueville to Delli Carpini and Keeter think self-government needs, and it answers Plato's Republic worry that ordinary people are unfit to rule by showing experts and stay-at-home parents alike fluent across the board. Because civic knowledge correlates with defending First Amendment freedoms, and because the show inserts the glorification of knowledge into the public sphere while bar-trivia gatherings build Putnam-style social capital, playing along at home rehearses the habits and virtues of democratic citizenship.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 18 "8. Plato’s Chicago" — Littmann systematically maps Roth's Chicago onto Plato's Republic: like Marcus, Plato rejects democracy after Athens executed Socrates; both dissolve the family ('faction before blood' versus children raised in common and bred by state schedule); Erudite's IQ-selected leadership mirrors the rigorously trained philosopher-rulers, Dauntless the warrior class whose purely physical training Plato warns turns 'savage and harsh,' Abnegation's poverty the guardians's communism of property, and the factionless the powerless producers - with Plato's noble lie about the metals matching the Erudite's propaganda and serums as instruments of control. The shared flaw, he argues, is concentrated power without external checks, which corrupted Abnegation, corrupts every Dauntless leadership change, and would corrupt Plato's guardians too. The lesson is not to hand power to the least vicious but for democratic voters to confront their own ignorance - or end like Roth's America, in apocalyptic war.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 20 "10. Amity—Directly Democratic" — McCrossin identifies Amity's consensus circles as direct democracy - the people exercising government in person, against the republics of Abnegation, Candor, and Erudite and Dauntless's open oligarchy - and hears Tris's skepticism ('How do they get anything done?') and Tobias's admiration ('it makes them kind') echoing the 2011 public debate over Occupy Wall Street. Johanna Reyes acts as a facilitator who helps Amity's general will develop rather than articulating it, but when the planned attack on Erudite threatens innocents she leaves the faction rather than quietly mold its will, confirming Tris's worry about talk in the face of terrible deeds. Through Alexander Meiklejohn's absolutist reading of the First Amendment, the chapter then argues that New Chicago's self-government needs both uncompromisingly protected political speech and a direct-democratic dimension for working out what the common good actually is.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 24 "9. Anarchy, State, and Apocalypse" — Da Silva and McKendry test the political legitimacy of four post-apocalyptic governance types: the Claimers' anarchy that collapses into Joe adjudicating 'claims', the Governor's and Rick's dictatorships ('This is not a democracy anymore!'), the prison Council's representative democracy with the three questions as a quasi-constitution, and Terminus's quasi-theocratic cannibal creed ('You're the butcher or you're the cattle'). Using Hobbes's state of nature and war of all against all, hypothetical social contract, and the twin tests of power and morality, they judge even the benevolent Rick-tatorship unjust because concentrated power is fallible and unaccountable. They conclude, with Churchill, that the Council's imperfect democracy is the worst form of government except for all the others.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 15 "6. Who’s the Better Friend" — Bowman sorts Marvel relationships through Aristotle's three friendships: Ant-Man's starstruck alliance is friendship of pleasure, Obadiah Stane's partnership with Tony a toxic friendship of utility, and Steve's bond with Bucky a friendship of virtue that loves without reciprocity - making Cap better TO his friends, though saving Bucky endangers everyone else. Turning to Derrida's Politics of Friendship, where fraternity grounds democratic equality among all persons, he argues Tony's refusal to privilege any individual over mankind makes him better FOR his friends. The Civil War split thus replays the old tension between personal autonomy and responsibility to humanity, at the destructive scale only super-powered friends can achieve.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 34 "22. A New Civil War" — Horn reads Marvel's Civil War as an allegory of post-9/11 America's Patriot Act debate over security versus liberty: Iron Man takes Hobbes's side, treating unregulated superhumans as the state of nature - a 'war of every man against every man' - that the Registration Act's social contract and punishment-backed rules must end, while Captain America takes Mill's On Liberty side, insisting full freedom for human nature must not be ceded to a government that will overreach, with Spider-Man torn between the two like the American citizen. Invoking Habermas's communicative action and deliberative democracy from Between Facts and Norms, he blames the two camps for talking past each other - Cap walling himself off while Tony keeps reaching out - and prescribes genuinely open dialogue as the only bridge that can marry security and liberty before the country devolves into its own civil war.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 36 "24. Aftermath" — Faller argues Civil War is Marvel's meditation on the aftermath of 9/11 - the Raft as Guantanamo, Zemo's interrogation as the waterboarding debate - and on America's red-blue polarization, with Steve Rogers embodying the virtue of the Good and Tony Stark the virtue of Truth as the two values democracy constantly pits against each other. Turning to Athens, he reads Plato's Euthyphro - are the gods good because goodness is a standard above them, or because their power decrees whatever they do good? - as the exact dilemma splitting Democrats, who define truth by the good it does, from Republicans, who define good by conformity to law and constitutional process, the same democratic dynamic that voted to execute Socrates and, in the comics, leaves Captain America assassinated by a sniper on his way to trial. Transcending the dualism is modeled by Spider-Man's identity disclosure and Black Panther's renunciation of vengeance over Zemo.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 37 "24. Post-Factual Democracy" — Hendricks and Vestergaard open with Trump's inauguration lies and Kellyanne Conway's 'alternative facts' to define post-factual democracy: a state in which opportune political narratives replace facts and evidence as the basis of debate, opinion formation and policymaking. Unlike Machiavelli, who taught that lies must at least be concealed, the post-factual politician pays no price for exposed falsehood once social media, the attention economy and populist us-versus-them narratives engineered for indignation and fear have stripped journalists and fact-checkers of authority — Arendt's remark that mass leaders show 'extreme contempt for facts as such' before fitting reality to their lies. Using Habermas's deliberative model and even minimal accountability theories of voting, they argue post-factuality destroys democratic legitimacy, and defend a 'factual democracy' that trusts science and journalism without becoming a technocracy — the real-world echo of the Party's command to reject the evidence of your eyes.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 20 "10. Intelligence and Duh-mocracy" — Saunders uses Adams's induhviduals and a hundred-voter dilution example in which smart people's votes are swamped to stage the classic case against democracy: Plato's physician analogy against Athenian rule by the ignorant and his philosopher-kings, Jason Brennan's hobbits, hooligans, and Vulcans with voter licensing, Mill's plural votes for the demonstrably wise, and Nussbaum's claim that humanities education breeds empathetic democratic citizens. Each fix fails on Dilbert's own terms, since competence tests demean the labeled, the Pointy-Haired Boss would amass extra votes while Dilbert-grade engineers lack political judgment, Asok's degree would not help, and the more educated are demographically skewed toward men. He concludes that equal votes win as a pragmatic default and muses that workplaces, not polities, might be the truer target of democratization.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 34 "21. Mister Rogers’s Lesson for Democracy" — Matthew Ussia maps the Trolley's transition between Rogers's house and the Neighborhood of Make-Believe onto Habermas's public sphere: the first-week crisis, Lady Elaine's rearranging of the neighborhood, King Friday's barbed-wire wall and 'Down with the Changes!,' Chef Brockett's humiliation, shows fear collapsing the space where a democracy works through conflict. Like Habermas, who feared television debates would hijack real public talk (and contra Sartre's 'Hell is other people'), Rogers used puppets to say the unsayable, modeling the deliberative space privatized modern life threatens to close.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 22 "Learning from Our Mistakes" — Tamplin uses Baltar's landslide win on the New Caprica issue and Roslin's attempted election theft to argue democracy's guarantee of bad decisions is its saving feature: Plato and Aristotle ranked democracy among bad regimes because the many rule for private advantage rather than the common good, and Baltar's campaign of 'hope rather than truth' exploits exactly that weakness. A thought experiment about an oracle computer that always selects the best option shows that following it would abolish self-determination, the freedom to 'live as one wants' that democracy values above results. Only by choosing and frakking up (settling New Caprica, suffering the occupation, Apollo's shame speech at Baltar's trial) can citizens confront their role, learn from mistakes, and move toward Aristotle's polity aiming at virtue, making self-determination the mediating value between freedom and virtue.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 30 "Walking the Tightrope" — Melancon weighs the Fleet leadership's secrets and lies: Adama's false claim to know the way to Earth, concealing that Cylons look human, Roslin faking Hera's death and hiding the baby, and Zarek's secret collaboration courts on New Caprica. He argues that keeping secrets from the Cylons can be justified by the state's duty to protect, but the leadership repeatedly deceives the governed themselves, discarding the transparency democratic legitimacy requires. Deontological duty to the governed keeps losing to consequentialist reasoning, and the chapter asks what happens to Colonial democracy's 'soul' when trust between government and governed erodes.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 32 "Misunderestimated" — Muir argues the 1978 original was serious political allegory rather than Moore's 'popcorn': Adar's armistice with the Cylons stands in for Carter-era detente and the SALT treaties, and the sneak attack dramatizes hard-right fears of unilateral disarmament. Adama's 'preparedness' and Sire Uri's disarmament proposal map onto the 'Peace through Strength' doctrine that carried Reagan to power, and 'Experiment in Terra' repeats the lesson as Apollo tells Terra's politicians the opposite of war is slavery, not peace. The chapter notes Soviet Izvestia read it the same way, and that the original thereby fulfilled Moore's own criterion of relevant science fiction from the opposite end of the political spectrum, including Apollo's wartime argument that dissent weakens Colonial resolve.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 14 "Bird or Cage" — Elmore reads Columbia's founding through Carl Schmitt: Comstock's baptism Voxophone ('who is that man who lies submerged?') dramatizes how every legal order is founded from outside the law, and the city's identity is built on friend/enemy antagonisms, racial, class, and theocratic, against the 'Sodom below'. The Vox Populi's collapse into tyranny (Daisy Fitzroy threatening Fink's son) follows logically from an identity defined purely by opposition, while Columbia's dependence on Georgia's penal labor shows the friend group materially needs its enemy, making politics an endless war like the War on Terror. Schmitt's sovereign ('he who decides on the exception') and the tears' endless splitting of Booker and Elizabeth mirror the infinite regress of legitimate decision, leaving 'you can't lose if you don't play' as the bleak lesson, softened only by old Elizabeth's tear that lets Booker try again.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 18 "After the Waldo Moment" — Littmann reads The Waldo Moment through Donald Trump — Waldo's 'knobber' and 'dickhead' taunts anticipate 'Little Marco' and 'Crooked Hillary' — to ask what is wrong with mockery and disrespect in democratic politics. Plato's Meno shows why true beliefs acquired by mockery rather than understanding are unstable and steerable toward any content, and ad hominem attacks substitute ridicule for engagement with arguments. Mill's On Liberty arguments against censorship and orthodoxy — we might be wrong, collision with error clarifies truth — show that refusing to engage opponents (as Waldo refuses Monroe) locks everyone in 'reality bubbles,' and the chapter concludes that letting anger and mockery replace reasoned engagement, as when Waldo's followers riot, sabotages democracy.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 9 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Erion reads The Daily Show's sharpest bits as jokes that only work if the audience already grasps Neil Postman's thesis in Amusing Ourselves to Death that television's entertainment bias renders news irrational, irrelevant and incoherent, from hurricane-reporter parodies and 'The Less You Know' to news-style graphics like 'Mess O' Potamia'. He treats Stewart's 2004 Crossfire confrontation ('stop hurting America', 'you're doing theater, when you should be doing debate'), the 2009 Jim Cramer CNBC 'Brawl Street' interview after the financial crisis, and the 2011 Chris Wallace exchange as explicit versions of the same critique that TV's real bias is toward sensationalism, conflict and laziness rather than partisanship. He closes with the Rally to Restore Sanity and/or Fear's 'conflictinator' speech, noting Stewart is ultimately more optimistic than Postman that television could clarify rather than obfuscate.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 11 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Sotos locates The Daily Show within an emergent 'Fifth Estate', a watchdog for the failing Fourth Estate press, and recruits Arendt's actor/spectator distinction to defend Stewart's refusal of activism: like judge, journalist or comedian, the spectator withdraws from action yet gives events their meaning and voice in public conversation. She traces an American fake-news lineage from James and Benjamin Franklin's colonial papers (Silence Dogood, Polly Baker, the Vindex Patriae hoax) through Twain to Stewart, contrasting honest satire with Glenn Beck and Rush Limbaugh's 'fake fake news' and the repeal of the Fairness Doctrine. Juvenalian indignatio ( Stewart's somber 'Fuck you' to CNBC in the Clusterf#@k to the Poor House) and Horatian playfulness (Colbert's Super PAC saga) supply the ethos, and she reads the Rally to Restore Sanity as Aristophanic Old Comedy, complete with agon, parabasis ('A Moment of Sincerity') and a reconciliatory ending that makes 'We the People' exist.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 30 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Vanderheiden treats America (The Book)'s textbook parody as serious democratic theory: its 'Democracy Inaction' diagnosis (a president chosen from a field of two, 99% incumbency, lobbyists as 'the white knights of democracy') tracks the thin versus thick democracy distinction and Benjamin Barber's deliberative democracy, with Putnam's social capital as the remedy for the satirized life cycle of national decline. The 'Dress the Supreme Court' gag, Senate color-by-numbers, and third-party graveyard expose representational exclusion, while the media chapter indicts conglomeration for killing the press's watchdog role, invoking Mill's marketplace of ideas. The Earth (The Book) postscript notes that social contracts were historically written without the assent of the women and minorities they subjugated.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 31 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Sotos reads America (The Book)'s fake Jefferson foreword and Daily Show writer Kevin Bleyer's Me the People as anti-originalist satire aimed at Tea Party 'historical fundamentalism', Jill Lepore's 'anti-history' that literally cancels historical time and treats the Founders as infallible prophets. Jefferson's anti-originalist principle that 'the earth belongs to the living' and his call for a constitutional convention every generation anchor the book, dramatized in Bleyer's imaginary lunch with Justice Scalia (the originalist as Ahab) against Stephen Breyer's living constitutionalism. John Oliver's Morristown Tea Party interviews and the Beck-Hannity-O'Reilly nostalgia montage ('the best time in American history was when they were all six years old') show how altar-worship of the Framers abandons popular sovereignty.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 41 "“Look at This Stuff; Isn't It Neat ” disney and the Commodification of Political Values" — Dale and Foy tour the parks' political philosophy: Cinderella's Castle looming over Liberty Square embodies the contradiction between princess hierarchy and Lockean self-government, since Locke's Second Treatise grounds rule in consent and majority will, forbids special rights for rulers, and justifies revolution — the very ideals the 'Declaration salad' celebrates under a monarchy's silhouette. The Epcot World Showcase, judged through Kymlicka, Benhabib, and Taylor's recognition-based multiculturalism, reduces eleven cultures to a consumable menu, so that per Barber's 'McWorld' Disney sells pre-packaged 'freedom' and 'multiculturalism' as spectator values that reinforce rather than transform.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 13 "Leto’s Not So Golden Path" — Rejects Herbert's own explanation (hero-worship) for the repeated collapse of Duniverse empires, arguing instead that every ruler from Shaddam IV through Paul and Alia to Leto II governs purely through strategic action, authority enforced by coercion and sanctions, with no democratic legitimacy. Using Habermas's distinction between strategic and communicative action, it reads the Atreides council's evasion of the Landsraad constitution demand, Alia's cry that 'Atreides power must never be marginalized by the chaos of democracy', and Leto II's reliance on breeding programs and deterrence as failures to make the ruled into authors of the law, concluding that physical stability can only last when built on normative stability that democracy provides.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 23 "Notes" — Andrea Conque argues the adult-free ('Mungo-free') children of Little Lamplight are genuinely political: they socialize each other into distrust of grownups (mandatory exile at 16 to Big Town), elect mayors by secret popular vote - MacCready's punch against Princess was a coup made legitimate by subsequent election - and fill every office from doctor Lucy to teacher Joseph to Knock Knock, whose Vault Boy jokes 'keep the peace' against social isolation. Sherif's Robber's Cave experiment supplies the comparison: unlike the Eagles and Rattlers, Lamplighters avoid in-group conflict because the radiation-absorbing cave fungus and shared survival give them permanent superordinate goals, while Biwwy's high-damage 'wazer wifle' shows they deter oppression by being, not just posturing as, tough. Against MacCready's claim of 'pure anarchy', the chapter concludes Little Lamplight is the Capital Wasteland's most successful government - freer and better ordered than Megaton, Andale, Paradise Falls, or even the Republic of Dave.
- **The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire**, ch. 17 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" — The chapter reconstructs the real Swedish journalist behind Kalle Blomkvist: the 1950s reporter as the welfare state's mouthpiece alongside heroic police, the 1970s radical investigative journalist epitomized by Jan Guillou—whose exposure of the secret IB organization earned him a prison sentence and a revenge vindication, the direct template for Blomkvist—and the 1990s–2000s slide into 'sensation, scandal, and spectacle' around crime. It shows journalism decoupling from crime statistics—about a hundred killings a year in a country of 9.4 million, falling, yet alarmist coverage fueling tougher sentencing and the Nazi-rooted Sweden Democrats' entry into parliament—so the watchdog ideal of the muckraker who draws aside the veil on 'men who hate women and democracy' becomes a question: where have you gone, Kalle Blomkvist?
- **The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire**, ch. 24 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" — The chapter reads Salander's hacking beside Julian Assange's WikiLeaks: both are hard to classify as criminal or activist, and both live by the hacker ethic Stephen Levy codified—unlimited access, all information free, mistrust authority, judgment by skill—which later versions soften with privacy and social responsibility, matching 'Salander's Principles' (a bastard is always a bastard) and Assange's 'capable, generous men do not create victims; they nurture victims.' Through David Brin's Transparent Society it asks who watches the watchers—the police-camera city of the state or the citizen-accessible city—and argues for WikiLeaks-style reciprocal transparency that keeps the 'mighty' (governments, the Vanger Corporation, Wennerström) exposed while protecting whistleblower anonymity. Blomkvist's choices—suppressing the Vanger murders, encouraging Salander to steal Wennerström's files, planting disinformation—mark him as the journalist half of Larsson's new information-age hero pair.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Argues Frank is 'Hobbesian to the core': for him democracy is just the state of nature with elections, which is why it produces mediocre, fearful presidents like Walker (a Xanax-taking incumbent undone by a mere legislator) while a real sovereign like Frank — or the autocrat Petrov, with whom Frank shares cigars precisely because no common power enforces rules between them — gets things done. The chapter reads Frank's appetites (ribs at Freddy's, power over money against Remy and Tusk, contempt for sleep and death) through Hobbes' pleasure-and-pain psychology and his account of conflict arising when equals want the same thing, which finally drives Claire from the White House. Frank's church scenes ('I pray to myself, for myself') illustrate Hobbes' subordination of religion to civil power, the Kate Baldwin 'he is the tyrant' charge illustrates that a tyrant is only a king disliked, and the closing appeal is to Madison's Federalist 51: only the ambition of others can contain this one.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Argues the Underwoods' success is not far-fetched fiction but the structural outcome four critics of democracy predict. Plato's Republic supplies the spine: the kallipolis of philosopher-guardians decays through timocracy and oligarchy into democracy, whose love of freedom invites the tyrant — Peter Russo with his random desires is the democratic soul, Frank the tyrannical soul ruled by one illicit appetite, doomed to the fear and friendlessness Book 9 describes (which Season 3 delivers). Hobbes and Hegel then explain why monarchy may beat popular rule (the monarch's private interest aligns with the public's; the monarch lets a people will as one), and Marx reframes the whole show economically — SanCorp, Tusk and Feng as capitalists, the laid-off shipyard workers as proletariat, and AmWorks as self-interested politicians flirting with expropriation. Against all four, Mill's Considerations on Representative Government gives the democratic reply — elections force responsiveness, participation educates citizens — so the burden falls on viewers to keep elections fair, the press free, and checks on unscrupulous politicians effective.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 23 "Notes" — Sirvent and Diorio apply Foucault's panopticon (built on Bentham's prison design) to the show's web of watching: Frank manipulates Zoe through leaked stories, Doug keeps Rachel permanently locatable by phone, and Claire must demand the bug be removed from Michael Corrigan's Russian cell, showing watched subjects paralyzed by fear. Against Bauman and Lyon's 'liquid surveillance,' the chapter argues democracy is an anti-institutional force requiring free dissent and a press at arm's length from power, and that surveillance collapses the Greek public/private distinction so citizens fear punishment for questioning rulers. Frank's 'Nobody can hear you. Nobody cares about you' to Zoe captures how the surveillance state turns criticism into danger, leaving a society that is no longer a democracy.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 37 "Notes" — Auxier asks who is morally worse, judging Frank and Claire by past deeds (Frank's murders of Zoe and Peter), future consequences (a president with the nuclear button), and the subjunctive (what each would do), while tracing Claire's lineage from Lady Macbeth and Elizabeth Urquhart, who assassinates Francis in the British series. Plato's and Aristotle's warning that democracy degenerates into tyranny frames the answer: Frank symbolizes the House, Claire the Senate, both coveting executive power, and Meechum - 'utterly loyal, utterly deadly' - is the military they seduce in the menage a trois and will underestimate. Niebuhr's 'moral mediocrity' of nations, from McCarthyism and the Joe Welch moment to mass incarceration, explains the verdict that neither individual is worse alone: 'they are far worse together,' and the union, not the person, has no decency.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Michels reads Frank as 'Hobbesian to the core' and democracy as 'the state of nature with elections': Walker, Matthews, and Vasquez show that elections elevate mediocrities, while Frank's America Works and his FEMA/Stafford Act end-run around Congress display the energetic sovereign for whom 'a tyrant is only a king disliked.' Hobbes's pleasure-pain psychology of appetite and aversion explains the cast — Frank's ribs, PlayStation, and pure taste for power; Russo's indiscriminate addictions; Doug's serial ones — while Hobbes's competition for gain, fear, and glory structures the Tusk money-versus-power war whose casualties include Freddy. With Hobbes's subordination of religion to civil power, Frank's crucifix-spitting 'I pray to myself, for myself' caps the case that truth only obstructs sovereignty, leaving Madison's 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition' as the lone check.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Shea argues the Underwoods' rise is structurally guaranteed rather than far-fetched, surveying democracy's critics: Plato's Republic Books 8-9 has the kallipolis of philosopher-guardians decay through timocracy and oligarchy into democracy, where a 'protector'-tyrant like Frank exploits the drones and the people's love of freedom (Russo as the prototypical democratic soul, Tusk as the oligarch-in-fact), while the tyrant ends fear-ridden and friendless — precisely Frank's Season 3. Hobbes and Hegel then reverse the verdict, arguing monarchy aligns the ruler's private interest with the public good and lets a people will as one instead of a formless mass — the insight Tom Yates has about voters identifying with the Underwoods as people — and Marx reframes it economically: SanCorp, Tusk, and Feng are the capitalist structure, and Frank's AmWorks, entitlement cuts, and nationalization threats show self-interested politicians siding with a growing proletariat. Against all four, Mill's Considerations on Representative Government supplies the democratic reply — responsiveness, better information, and citizen participation mean an Underwood cannot last if we keep fair elections, a free press, and real checks.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 23 "Notes" — Uses Foucault's panopticon (built on Bentham's prison design) and Bauman's 'liquid surveillance' to read Frank's Washington as a surveillance society: Zoe's archived texts, Doug's inescapable tracking of Rachel, and the bugged cell where Claire visits Michael Corrigan all show how being watched destroys privacy and paralyzes dissent. It argues that democracy needs free spaces in which citizens can question power without later punishment, so the culture of fear Frank rules through-'you are a rock, you absorb nothing, you say nothing'-turns checks and balances into instruments of control even inside an elected government.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 37 "Notes" — Asks who is morally worse by three standards-what each has done, is doing, and would do in the future subjunctive-and answers that Frank and Claire are far worse together, read symbolically as the US Constitution itself: Frank is the mercurial House, Claire the deliberate, more ambitious Senate, and Meechum the loyal military they seduce and underestimate at the republic's peril. Working from Plato's and Aristotle's claim that democracy declines into tyranny, Niebuhr's 'moral mediocrity' of nations, and the Welch-McCarthy 'have you no decency' moment, it asks whether a system that produced them is one 'we the people' deserve.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 20 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Argues that South Park performs Popper's defense of the open society by ridiculing 'enemies' on both flanks: Cartman as a Glenn Beck-style ranter in 'Dances with Smurfs' and a xenophobic border agent in 'The Last of the Meheecans', versus liberal fanatics like Rob Reiner in 'Butt Out', Rosie O'Donnell's recount antics in 'Trapper Keeper', and Tom Cruise's litigious Scientology in 'Trapped in the Closet'. The show does not silence extremists but lets them speak and then mocks them, which the authors read through Popper's paradox of tolerance: tolerance cannot be extended to those who suppress criticism, as the Church of Scientology's pressure campaigns showed. A closing section links this to Jefferson's Virginia Bill for Establishing Religious Freedom — 'truth is great and will prevail if left to herself' — making free, offensive argument and dissent the lifeblood of democracy.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 22 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Takes 'Douche and Turd' — Stan refusing to choose between Giant Douche and Turd Sandwich, Puff Daddy's gun-toting 'Vote or Die', and his banishment — plus the kindergarten tie in 'Trapper Keeper' (Flora's indecision, Rosie O'Donnell's recounts) to ask whether every vote counts in a two-party system. Through Locke, Stan's abstention becomes a withdrawal of consent to be governed by either mascot; through Mill, non-voting threatens the active participation that gives institutions legitimacy and wards off tyranny of the majority, even as the chapter catalogs real disincentives: the Electoral College's spectator states, the 2000 Florida debacle, and Commission rules excluding third parties like Nader. Habermas closes the chapter: the vote, read as positive liberty, is the paradigm of rights and inclusion in a community of equals.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 42 "Notes" — Charts Star Trek's handling of secularization, from the "Roddenberry attitude" of Kirk confronting fifteen would-be gods to later series' complications, using Robert Audi's nine features of religion and Benedict Anderson's "imagined community" - the Yangs' sacred flag and worship-word "freedom" in "The Omega Glory" show an incoherent civic religion Kirk can correct. "Who Watches the Watchers" inverts the dynamic by making Picard an accidental god who refuses to found a religion among the proto-Vulcan Mintakans, while real-world creationism in schools and abstinence-only sex education supply the chapter's empirical moral arguments that faith-driven public policy fails on its own terms. DS9's Bajor arc - Vedek Winn boycotting Keiko's school, Sisko's defense of the faith that sustained Bajor through occupation, and Akorem's restoration of the D'jarra castes in "Accession", likened to Plato's Republic-class soul hierarchy - grounds the claim that infallible religious authority corrodes democratic equality, with Sisko as the Emissary who synthesizes faith and secular governance.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 15 "“We Were Trained to Be Keepers of the Peace, not Soldiers”" — Shakibnia reads The Clone Wars through Cornel West's three dogmas threatening democracy — free-market fundamentalism, aggressive militarism, escalating authoritarianism — and Chomsky's critique of inequality: Senator Halle Burtoni is a deliberate Halliburton/Cheney nod, and the banking-deregulation vote in 'Heroes on Both Sides' mirrors the US military-industrial complex. He argues the Separatist people's movement ('Corporations do not rule us!') was justified in seeking self-determination, while 'Sabotage' shows the Jedi losing legitimacy by becoming 'military weapons' — underpaid Temple worker Jackar Bowmani's squalid housing indicts the Republic's class divide. Ahsoka's departure and her maxim that 'it's every citizen's duty to challenge their leaders' model the accountability movement (like Black Lives Matter) that the Jedi failed to be.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — Paul A. Cantor argues that Mars Attacks! inverts the pro-government ideology of 1950s flying-saucer films (Earth vs. the Flying Saucers, Invaders from Mars, The Day the Earth Stood Still) in which scientific and military elites save a helpless public. Burton instead mocks Washington's vain, media-obsessed, multicultural establishment—Kessler, President Dale, the generals—who all fail, while Kansas 'trailer trash,' a Las Vegas boxer, and truant video-gaming kids improvise the defense; Slim Whitman's yodeling, not the state, defeats the Martians. Cantor reads the film through Tocqueville's Democracy in America on the self-organizing power of citizens' associations and the danger of soft despotism, and against Hobbes/The Day the Earth Stood Still's Leviathan solution, casting Burton as a Tocquevillian celebrant of ordinary Americans over their governing elite.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — Steve Benton reads Burton's Sleepy Hollow as a meditation on rationality and anti-intellectualism, contrasting it with Washington Irving's original where brainy Ichabod is run out of town. Burton's Ichabod, a rationalist constable, prevails only after tempering his faith in science with emotion, intuition, and the spirit world associated with his mother and Katrina—the paper-disk toy (bird/cage) symbolizing how head and heart must spin together. Benton maps the film's models of rationality onto Plato's philosopher-king and distrust of the mob and Hobbes's war of all against all (Burton's corrupt New York and Sleepy Hollow) versus the collaborative, democratic reason of Locke, Mill's On Liberty, and Dewey, invoking Aristotle and Nussbaum on emotion's role in practical wisdom; he leaves open whether the film is transgressive or a conventional 'woman heals cold rational man' Hollywood tale.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 30 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Vanderheiden reads America (The Book) as a work of democratic theory dressed as textbook parody, arguing its satire is a 'rhetoric of challenge' enacting deliberative democracy. He contrasts 'thin' (merely electoral) with 'thick' participatory democracy using Putnam's social capital and Barber's strong democracy, and invokes J.S. Mill's 'marketplace of ideas' and On Liberty to indict media conglomeration for killing the press's watchdog role. He reads the companion Earth (The Book) through social-contract theory (Hobbes-style), noting its jab that contractual authority historically required the assent of subjugated groups it never obtained.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 31 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Sotos uses America (The Book)'s fake Jefferson foreword and Kevin Bleyer's Me the People to attack constitutional 'originalism' and Tea Party 'historical fundamentalism' (per Jill Lepore), arguing the Framers were revolutionaries who intended a living, amendable document. She champions Jefferson's view that 'the earth belongs to the living' and every generation should refound its constitution, contrasts Justice Breyer's living-constitutionalist 'active liberty' with Scalia's originalism ('the Constitution is dead'), invokes Plato's Laws as thinking in similarly living terms, and uses John Oliver's Tea Party interviews to expose 'anti-history' that cancels historical time.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 14 "Who is Who" — This political chapter reads Gallifreyan bureaucracy ('The Deadly Assassin') and 1970s socialist-tinged serials, using Marx's alienation and critique of capital to interpret 'The Pirate Planet' and 'The Robots of Death,' and Aristotle's 'political animal' plus Plato's and Aristotle's suspicion of democracy against Benjamin Barber's participatory democracy. It analyzes the pathologies of democratic consent through 'Vengeance on Varos' (Plato's ideal state inverted) and 'The Beast Below' (Arendt on totalitarianism, self-inflicted ignorance), with Isaiah Berlin's negative liberty in the vocabulary of materiality.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 8 "6. Black Sails as Philosophy Pirates and Political Discourse" — Jones argues that Starz's Black Sails, a Treasure Island prequel set in the Golden Age of Piracy, dramatizes social contract theory as non-hypothetical practice. Captain Flint's drive to make Nassau a sovereign pirate commonwealth ('I am your king') channels Hobbes's state of nature and irrepressible sovereign, while his choice to settle Nassau and belief that people can thrive if left free channels Locke; his eventual plan to install Silver and Madi as liked-and-feared leaders synthesizes the two. Jones maps the pirates' familial bonds onto Rousseau and their responses to injustice (Vane's gallows speech, the maroon alliance) onto Rawls's Veil of Ignorance, and reads pirate 'articles' and deposable captains as radical democracy and equality, complicated by manipulation, slavery, and tolerance.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 18 "16. House of Cards as Philosophy Democracy on Trial" — The chapter uses the Underwoods' extra-electoral rise to autocracy in House of Cards to test Plato's and Hobbes's antidemocratic arguments. Frank and Claire exploit the exact weaknesses Plato's Republic diagnoses—Thrasymachus's 'justice is the advantage of the stronger,' the decay of oligarchy into freedom-loving democracy into tyranny, and Peter Russo as the disordered-soul 'democratic man' and 'drone.' It then invokes Hobbes's Leviathan, arguing the show's power-struggle resembles a state of nature and that Hobbes would welcome Claire's absolute rule as more predictable and less corrupt than democracy, before weighing modern defenses of democracy (Levitsky and Ziblatt, Locke, Mill, Rawls, Sen) against these critiques.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 29 "27. Squid Game as Philosophy The Myths of Democracy" — The chapter argues that Squid Game exposes five 'myths' of democracy by showing how its trappings mask control by the wealthy few. Using Aristotle's Politics and Nicomachean Ethics it attacks the myth of free choice (the players' consent is coerced by debt) and the failure to cultivate virtue and transparency (Gi-hun deceives Il-nam in the marble game); it uses Sen and Nussbaum's capability approach to deny genuine empowerment; and it applies Plato's Phaedo two-worlds doctrine to argue the game instantiates no true form of truth, beauty, goodness, or justice. Il-nam's tie-breaking vote and Player 111's advantages illustrate that equality is only superficial, leaving a Hobbesian war of all against all inside a democratic shell.

### Reason Is the Slave of the Passions

The claim that reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions expresses David Hume's view that reason alone cannot move us to act or set our ends. Reason, on his account, discovers facts and traces relations of ideas, but it is desires, feelings, and aversions that supply motivation; reason serves by finding the means to satisfy passions it does not itself generate. This sentimentalist position locates the springs of action and the foundations of morality in human feeling rather than in pure rationality.

- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 20 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Argues Simple Subjectivism ('right for Tony') fails as a reading of the show because it cannot make sense of genuine moral disagreement - Carmela and Tony's adultery battle in 'Whitecaps', Agent Ciccerone versus Tony on extortion - nor ground outrage at the killings of Pussy and the sobbing Matt Bevilaqua. Humean ethical subjectivism, grounded in a common human nature and the sentiment of sympathy (with Berkeley's pin example to explain vice as perception-dependent), fares better: it lets us condemn Tony while explaining his warped sympathy - grieving Pie-O-My more than his human victims - as the product of a mob upbringing that Melfi's alexithymia diagnosis in 'House Arrest' targets.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 18 "Vertigo and Epistemological Vertigo" — Flory reads Vertigo as an epistemological parable: Scottie's 'hardheaded Scot' method, collecting facts and deducing from universal principles, fails three times (the step-stool 'cure' for his acrophobia, explaining away Madeleine's 'possession' with the horse statue, forcing Judy up the bell tower for confirmation), delivering an implicit critique of Vienna Circle positivism in the manner of Carnap and Ayer. Against Scottie, the chapter mobilizes Kuhn's theory-laden facts, Aristotle's point that human conduct resists codification by exceptionless laws, and Hume's 'slave of the passions,' with Descartes's automata and Chalmers's philosophical zombies framing the problem of other minds. Midge, who knows people emotionally as well as factually, models the alternative: philosophers who fear 'epistemological vertigo' should give up epistemological training wheels and accept that minds, especially emotions, escape law-like rules.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 9 "What of Philosophical Relevance Is there in Tarantino’s Films" — Bruce Russell argues that Tarantino's films share a pattern—a cruel man's life goes awry, violence erupts, and glimpses of compassion appear, like Mr. White comforting the shot Mr. Orange—but that fiction can raise philosophical questions without justifying general philosophical theses. He uses the Pulp Fiction exchange over the bullets that missed Jules and Vincent to raise Hume's problem of miracles (divine intervention versus a 'freak occurrence'), and applies the accounts of Mill, Gibbard, Hare and Hume to show that even Vincent's twisted code—balcony drops for foot massages, execution for keying a car—counts as having a morality. His conclusion: the films raise, but never answer in depth, the questions of what a miracle is and what it is to have a morality.
