- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 22 "The Kick—Back to ‘Reality’" — Richardson and McWilliams read Inception as an 'existential heist film' by diving through four layers of meaning. At the layer of reality they use Descartes's dream skepticism and wax argument, Hume on belief as custom and cause-effect, and Goffman on being shocked between frames to argue the film makes touch — the fall that wakes, pain ('pain is in the mind'), Saito's wrong-textured polyester carpet, the broken totems (Cobb's top, Arthur's loaded die, Ariadne's holed chess piece) — the only semi-trustworthy sense, while Mal, who locks her totem in the dollhouse safe and picks the dream, replays the cave prisoner who chooses the shadows. The car-chase layer ('downwards is the only way forwards'), Saito's 'old man filled with regrets' limbo, and the pharmacy dreamers who 'come to be woken up' are read through existentialism (Beckett's Waiting for Godot, Jaspers on loneliness and nothingness) and Peirce on the continuity of consciousness, with Cobb cast as the ideological existentialist who chooses action and reality where Cypher in The Matrix and Vanilla Sky's David face the same choice. The chapter then treats the film's reflexivity — the team as screenwriter/producer/director, the Escher-esque Penrose stairs, cross-cut dream time à la Peckinpah — as a lesson in film theory, and finally reaches phenomenology: Cobb's angry projection of Mal shows the dream world displaying his subjective meanings, against Arthur's calm, orderly hotel mindscape.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 23 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Blackmon and Foresman ask what makes ghosts, spells, and holy water supernatural, rejecting definitions based on fiction, disbelief, or weirdness, and using Quine's point about the circularity of dictionary definitions to show lexicography cannot settle the question. Definitions keyed to current science or to the causal nexus fail because ghosts in Supernatural and in Hamlet causally interact, Bobby's ghost talks, moves objects, and possesses a maid, so the authors define the supernatural as what can on occasion transcend the world of material interaction. Descartes' interactionist substance dualism supplies the model: the cogito (even a djinn cannot make you falsely believe you exist), the pineal gland as the soul's point of causal contact, and a testable hypothesis that makes the supernatural scientifically investigable and implies that we, as spirits, are supernatural too.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Tests whether Rust's pessimism is a principled rationalist philosophy (Dienstag's view, versus Ligotti's temperament view) by mapping the Descartes-style rationalist and Hume-style empiricist opposition onto the partners: principled, deductive Rust versus impulse-driven Marty, including Rust's religion debate at the tent revival. It then reads the death of Sophia — Greek for wisdom, root of 'philosophy' — as symbolism suggesting Rust's pessimism stems from the death of wisdom rather than rational reflection, especially since Rust holds that the suffering of growing up is needed to become a pessimist. The finale's experience of Sophia's love is taken as a pure philosophical experience that collapses the reason/emotion distinction, so that pessimism belongs to both sides of the opposition at once.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 18 "Notes" — Reads Rust's 'dream inside a locked room' and 'everybody is nobody' monologues through the dream-argument and illusion-of-self traditions: the Upanishads and Advaita's atman/brahman, Vasubandhu's Buddhist non-self, Zhuangzi's butterfly dream, Plato's Theaetetus, and Descartes' dream doubt, plus Metzinger's self-model neuroscience. It diagnoses Rust as a neuro-nihilist in Metzinger's sense and defines his predicament with Nietzsche's nihilist, who judges the world as it is that it ought not to be, while noting Schopenhauer misread India's religions as pessimistic. Thompson argues nihilism is a deep insight gone awry — the self is not a thing but an enacted process like dancing — and reads Rust's final near-death experience of love as proof that transcendence of the dream of being a person is possible.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 21 "11. The Truth about Lying" — Fallis treats the Zone as a seminar in the philosophy of testimony: truth-tellers like Bob Wilson warning of a gremlin get dismissed as insane ('The Whole Truth' forces truth-telling as a curse), while convincing liars like Arch Hammer come to bad ends, so Kant's letter recommending reticence, saying true things but not the whole truth, looks like the best policy. On the receiving end, Descartes's malicious demon returns as aliens and devils ('To Serve Man,' 'The Howling Man,' 'Printer's Devil'), and Hume's advice to reject miracle-like testimony fails because in the Zone crazy stuff is often true. The chapter ends by endorsing Pascal's wager through 'The Big Tall Wish' and Jeff Myrtlebank's threat: believe the incredible witness just in case.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 27 "Kickstarting Inductive Inference" — Daniel Wilkenfeld analyzes Veronica's 'magic trick' in the 'One Angry Veronica' juryroom and her season-long bus-crash solution as Peter Lipton's inference to the best explanation: the hypothesis 'Beaver is a killer' wins by consilience (explaining the explosion, the dead rat, Curly Moran, even her chlamydia), simplicity, and completeness. But the criteria face Hume's problem of induction — why think the future will resemble the past, when yesterday's popular girl is today's pariah? — and Descartes's evil demon undermines even what Veronica 'sees,' since Curly Moran could fake a bus crash, leaving no non-circular justification for inferential habits none of us can live without. Following Nelson Goodman, Wilkenfeld concludes the demand for justification is misplaced: what matters is that Veronica reasons consistently, in the juryroom as at the cliff.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 3 "The Ethics of Pretending to Be a Cowboy" — Don Fallis uses Westworld to work out definitions of pretense and deception, testing successive accounts (acting-as-if, Austin's intend-to-deceive, Langland-Hassan's believe-P-is-false) against cases like guests playing cowboys, Ford passing off Bernard as human, and Maeve and Hector pretending to be deactivated. He adopts a Cartesian evil-demon model of deception but rejects the claim that deception must manipulate perceived evidence, arguing Ford's direct implanting of Teddy's Wyatt backstory still counts. He concludes, citing Kant on autonomy and Walzer on foreseen collateral harm, that staff who intend to deceive the hosts and even guests who foreseeably contribute to it act wrongly, since deceived hosts suffer real harm to their agency.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 12 "Inside the Helmet What Do Football Players Know" — Geivett uses football to illustrate epistemology, distinguishing factual (propositional) from competence (skill) knowledge through what running backs and quarterbacks must know and enact under split-second pressure, including 'football physics' vectors on a rollout pass. He treats the athlete's need to be mindful of knowledge amid stadium noise as a lesson in reliable belief, then critiques classroom skeptics who deploy Descartes's evil-demon and the brain-in-a-vat thought experiment, arguing mere logical possibility is no evidence for skepticism.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 22 "The Matrix, the Cave, and the Cogito" — Conard argues that The Matrix alludes to Plato's cave (the pod-bound humans mistaking the program for reality, Neo's painful ascent) and to Descartes' dream argument and evil-genius doubt (the singular consciousness generating the Matrix), but betrays their spirit by rejecting transcendence and the a priori. Because the film is 'Christianity without God'—Neo can only remake the shadow-world of the Matrix, not touch ultimate reality—it grounds knowledge in a subjective gut feeling ('being the One is just like being in love') rather than Descartes' intellectual intuition of God or Plato's rational grasp of the Forms, leaving no answer to whether life outside the Matrix is itself another illusion.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 8 "Sherlock's Reasoning Toolbox" — Pigliucci shows that Holmes's celebrated 'deduction' is really a mix of induction and abduction, contrasting Aristotelian syllogism and Cartesian rationalism (with its failed Cartesian circle) against the fallibility of real investigation. He walks through Hume's problem of induction (Russell's inductivist chicken), the Mill-Whewell 'great induction debate,' and Popper's falsificationism—qualified by the Neptune/Uranus episode where scientists shielded Newton. Using 'Thor Bridge' and 'The Three Students,' he concludes Holmes is a pragmatic scientist wielding a whole toolbox, since there is no single scientific method.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Rodriguez-Ruiz argues that Schizopolis and sex, lies, and videotape function as everyday 'thought experiments' about knowledge, contrasting them with Descartes's evil-genius and dream arguments and Dretske's disguised-zebra case. Fletcher must literally become his wife's lover's double to know she is cheating, and Ann pieces together John's affair from a stray earring, dramatizing how high the bar for knowledge of others is and how much depends on lucky accident. The trashcan-music scene stages the problem of induction and Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp. Soderbergh's boss's 'confirm nor deny' speech and Lester's preventable death show the films endorse a moderate skepticism that still affirms nature and power as real, rejecting full relativism and dogmatism.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 7 "“Do Not Forsake Me, Oh, My Darling” Loneliness and Solitude in Westerns" — Biderman argues that the western hero's solitude carries philosophical benefits, distinguishing being alone from feeling lonely (McCauley in Heat: 'I'm alone, I'm not lonely'). Epistemically he likens the silent, self-reliant hero (Kane in High Noon, Shane, Munny in Unforgiven, Blondie) to Descartes retreating into methodological doubt and solipsistic solitude to secure knowledge. Ethically he sets Aristotle's claim that man is a social animal (so the friendless hero cannot flourish) against Stoic detachment and Sartrean/existentialist authenticity, concluding the hero must be 'lone' because his heroism is inseparable from his chosen solitude.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 10 "Filmmaking and Philosophizing against the Grain of Theory Herzog and Wittgenstein" — Mihai Ometita pairs Herzog's anti-intellectualism with Wittgenstein's later philosophy, arguing that the obstinacy of Herzog's protagonists (Aguirre, Fitzcarraldo) and the dogmatism of Wittgenstein's interlocutors are two faces of an unbounded attachment to a single theory. Herzog's dictum 'An ape is an ape' echoes Wittgenstein's motto that everything is what it is, warning against forced metaphor (the smoking monkey in Echoes from a Somber Empire). Citing the Big Typescript and On Certainty, Ometita reads philosophy's difficulty as one of the will, and treats Aguirre's 'delirium' and Fitzcarraldo's 'dream' as quasi-nonsense that resists hasty diagnoses of madness; he invokes Descartes's window and Merleau-Ponty on film being perceived, not thought.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 3 "Introduction" — The editors' introduction surveys Nolan's oeuvre chronologically to argue that a recurring theme of self-destruction and unstable self-identity runs through every film. It reads Following's needy Young Man through Buber's I/Thou (existing fully only when a Thou acknowledges you) and Hegel's master/slave dependence between Cobb and his mark, casts Inception's spinning top as a version of Descartes's dream argument about telling the real from the constructed, and invokes Hobbes when the Joker introduces 'a little anarchy' into Gotham. It frames Doodlebug as Nolan's most Freudian film and Interstellar as uniting personal identity, moral choice, and epistemology in Cooper's self-sacrifice.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 6 "Spinning Tops and Brains in Vats" — This bundle of essays reads Memento and Inception as epistemology. Knepp uses Peirce's icon/index/symbol triad and Plato's Phaedrus critique of writing to show Leonard Shelby's tattoos and Polaroids give a false illusion of permanent truth (he tattoos Teddy as 'John G.' on purpose). Hoffman uses Kierkegaard's subjective truth to contrast Leonard, who lies to himself while pretending to gather objective 'facts', with Cobb, who takes a Kierkegaardian leap of faith and walks away from the spinning totem to embrace his children. Watson runs the Cartesian/Pyrrhonist dream argument against Inception's totems, arguing beliefs can be valuable via intellectual virtue even if unverifiable, and Lindenmuth pits Nozick's experience machine against Cobb's choice of real children over the dream-shade of Mal to argue reality matters more than pleasure.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 14 "6. The Foundations of Psychohistory" — Irish roots psychohistory in the seventeenth- and eighteenth-century clash between rationalism and empiricism over whether history can be a science. Descartes's mathematical, a priori method (which bred an 'anti-historical skepticism') is the ancestor of Seldon's dream of mathematizing human behavior, while Locke's empiricism and probabilistic knowledge inspired Gibbon's defense of historical evidence. Irish stages the Ancients-versus-Moderns debate through the Lord Dorwin / Salvor Hardin exchange over first-hand versus armchair scholarship, and contrasts Gibbon's moral, backward-looking history with Seldon's amoral, forward-looking prediction.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 14 "Skepticism Outside the Matrix" — Lawrence uses The Matrix to raise Cartesian skepticism: Neo's deception dramatizes Descartes's dream argument and evil demon, the computer-run Matrix being a technological version of the demon. He argues even Morpheus cannot be certain he has truly awakened ('the Matrix within the Matrix'), so the only certainty is Descartes's cogito. Drawing on Russell's 'Appearance and Reality,' he then argues that even setting aside Matrix scenarios, naive realism fails, since a chair's color, texture, solidity and shape are all perception-relative, leaving the external world's nature deeply uncertain.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 10 "2. Where Is the Twilight Zone" — Scalambrino argues the Twilight Zone is a televised expression of surrealist philosophy (Breton, Dalí) that provokes the Freudian 'uncanny.' He traces a line from Descartes—whose cogito and 'clear and distinct' rational mind produced the mind–body problem that lets surrealists destabilize waking reality—through psychoanalysis to Breton's 'point' where real and imagined cease to be contradictions. Episodes like 'A World of His Own' (automatic writing), 'The Mirror' (Dalí's paranoiac-critical method), 'Shadow Play,' 'The Shelter,' and 'The Lonely' unleash the imagination unbound by reason and provoke the uncanny in viewers.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 15 "McElligot’s Pool Epistemology (with Fish!)" — Ron Novy uses Marco's faith that unseen fish swim in McElligot's Pool to survey theories of knowledge as justified true belief. The farmer's empiricism and Marco's inference from a book frame a tour through Descartes's evil-genius doubt and skepticism, Locke's primary/secondary qualities (indirect realism), Berkeley's idealism ('to be is to be perceived'), and rationalist a priori knowledge, before turning to feminist epistemology (Schott, Kant's 'intuitions without concepts are blind,' Nietzsche on perspectival seeing) and Quine's naturalized epistemology to argue knowers are situated and the pool may indeed be 'bigger than you or I know.'
- **Food & Philosophy - Eat, Think, and Be Merry**, ch. 10 "Chapter 4" — Verene frames the two great cookbooks, Apicius's De Re Coquinaria and Artusi's La scienza in cucina, through a contrast between a 'Cartesian' and a 'Vichian' epistemology of cookery: Descartes' Discourse on Method, which discards custom for clear-and-distinct reasoning, is blamed for the restaurant chef's invented 'stacked food,' while Vico's New Science, which grounds knowledge in historical tradition, underwrites the trattoria and the home kitchen. Reading Apicius's garum and dormice and Artusi's health-and-economy motto (glossed via Aristotle's Economics as household management), he defends recipes as repeatable topoi like songs rather than one-off novelties. He closes by tying table manners to Rousseau's moeurs and to Socrates' claim in the Phaedo that speaking (and by extension cooking and eating) badly does harm to the soul.
- **Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low**, ch. 23 "BLUES" — Jesse Steinberg argues that doubt — a pervasive blues theme (B. B. King's 'nobody loves me but my momma,' Otis Spann's 'another mule kickin' in my stall,' Buddy Guy's 'I Smell a Rat') — supports Descartes's external-world skepticism, since knowledge would require ruling out the dreaming hypothesis. Against the 'I don't care' hedonistic reply he deploys Nozick's experience machine to show we value authentic reality over mere pleasant appearance, and he rejects contextualism as a solution. Endorsing Socrates' examined life, he settles for strong justification rather than certainty, reading Charley Patton's 'can't tell my future, can't tell my past' as the blues' honest coping with irreducible doubt.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 8 "Horror and the Idea of Everyday Life On Skeptical Threats in Psycho and The Birds" — Philip J. Nickel argues horror has an epistemological value structurally parallel to philosophical skepticism: it maliciously rips away the tacit 'cognitive trust' backing our everyday actions. In The Birds, the diner 'symposium' where Mrs. Bundy's confident science that birds cannot coordinate an attack is refuted moments later dramatizes a paranoid scenario we cannot rationally rule out. In Psycho, Marion Crane's isolation and misplaced trust in the seemingly normal Norman Bates enacts the skeptical premise that the ordinary person you rely on could murder you. Like Hume returning to backgammon, viewers can only resume everyday life, which Nickel says horror exposes as a necessary but insecure construction.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 8 "2. The Matrix" — Rowlands reads The Matrix as a vivid staging of Cartesian skepticism: Neo's pod-world is Descartes's dream and evil-demon conjectures (AI plays the demon) plus the modern brain-in-a-vat, showing we cannot be certain the external world exists. He uses the 'there is no air/muscles' and 'twin buildings' variant of Putnam's Twin Earth to argue we cannot even be certain which thoughts we think. The Hume-Nietzsche bundle critique undermines even the cogito, and the spoon-bending boy ('there is no spoon') illustrates Berkeley's idealism as the endpoint of skepticism about the physical world.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 8 "NOTES" — Carolyn Korsmeyer uses Aristotle's Poetics dictum that the 'probable impossible' beats the possible improbable to argue popular narrative can actually conduct philosophy, not merely illustrate it. Her central case is that the TV series Angel—the ensouled, guilt-cursed vampire who concludes 'if nothing we do matters, then all that matters is what we do'—independently arrives at the same existentialist position as Simone de Beauvoir's The Ethics of Ambiguity, with no textual borrowing. She contrasts The Matrix's dramatically sustained Cartesian dream-doubt against the 'improbable impossible' Dallas dream-season, showing why one is a philosophical vehicle and the other bankrupt.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 14 "Skepticism Outside the Matrix" — Matt Lawrence uses The Matrix to stage the skeptical problem, running Descartes's dream argument and evil-demon method of doubt (the Matrix as a technological demon) and even a 'Matrix within the Matrix' to show Morpheus cannot know he is awake. Descartes's cogito supplies the one certainty that survives radical deception. Lawrence then draws on Russell's analysis of the red chair to argue against naive realism: color, texture, solidity, and shape are appearances, so even setting aside the Matrix we cannot know the world in itself.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 4 "2. Twilight Zone as Philosophy 101" — Marinucci uses The Twilight Zone as a triple introduction to philosophy, the show, and the handbook, arguing that philosophy is defined not by necessary-and-sufficient conditions but by Wittgensteinian family resemblance and salient features (curiosity, depth, abstraction, controversy) learned through MacIntyre-style immersion in a practice. She reads episodes as thought experiments: the amnesiac astronaut in 'Where Is Everybody?' and living-doll/robot episodes echo Plato's cave and Descartes's Method of Doubt about appearance versus reality, Nagel's 'what is it like to be a bat?' frames the problem of other minds, and episodes like 'The Shelter' and 'It's a Good Life' dramatize the tension between egoism and altruism and social conformity, including feminist gaslighting in 'Twenty Two.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 34 "31. Inception as Philosophy Choose Your Dreams or Seek Reality" — Johnson uses Nolan's Inception—Cobb's dream-heists, the ambiguous spinning top, and the case that the whole film may be a dream—to test the moral Todd McGowan draws from it: that since we can't be sure what is real, we should abandon the quest for reality and choose the dream (his object of desire, his children) as Cobb does at the end. He evaluates six defenses of that moral, rejecting Descartes' skeptical dream/evil-demon problem (answered by abduction and by Plato's cave and Nozick's experience machine showing true belief is valuable), Baudrillard's denial of reality, Locke/Kant on the unknowable noumenal world, and Kierkegaard's leap of faith and Pascal's Wager, before softening it with Hume's return from skepticism to backgammon: entertain the doubt, then walk away when your children walk in.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 51 "48. The Matrix as Philosophy Understanding Knowledge, Belief, Choice, and Reality" — Perez reads the Matrix trilogy as a sustained argument about how choosing what to believe and 'know' shapes the reality we live in. He opens with Descartes' dream problem and cogito, contrasting Descartes' foundationalism with Rorty's anti-foundationalism to explain Cypher's choice to reject reality for the Matrix's certitude, and uses Searle's brute vs. institutional facts (the cookies, the steak, 'there is no spoon') to show social reality is constructed. Against the fatalism of the Oracle, Architect, and Merovingian, he argues nearly every character makes free choices, and resolves the tension via Hume's compatibilism — liberty requires necessity, and choices gain meaning only in response to causality — while noting agent-causation objections (Reid, O'Connor, Rowe) that make Neo's 'Because I choose to' significant. Gettier's justified-true-belief critique and Plato's Cave frame the knowledge and enlightenment themes.

### The Harm Principle

The harm principle, advanced by John Stuart Mill in On Liberty, holds that the only legitimate ground on which power may be exercised over an individual against their will is to prevent harm to others. On this view a person's own good, whether physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant for coercion, so conduct that affects only oneself lies beyond the rightful reach of law or social pressure. The principle marks out a protected sphere of individual liberty and has become a touchstone in debates over paternalism, free expression, and the limits of state authority.

- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 24 "Check Out Time" — McGrath and Tilahun ask whether hip hop is bad for women, setting protest and sex-positive tracks (Tupac's "Brenda's Got a Baby", Missy's "One Minute Man", Queen Latifah's "Ladies First", Ms. Dynamite) against endorsements of violence (N.W.A's "One Less Bitch", Snoop's "Can You Control Yo Ho?", 50 Cent's "P.I.M.P"). They apply Mill's harm principle - offend yes, harm no - Hume's counterfactual analysis of causation (the Derek Fisher shot case) to show that whether lyrics cause violence is an unsettled empirical question, Austin and Rae Langton's speech-act theory to argue rappers' cultural authority may let pimp lyrics subordinate women in a way pornography cannot, and Kant's kingdom of ends to charge misogynist lyrics with treating women as mere means.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 25 "Final Skit Paris’s Field Nigga Boogie" — Corlett evaluates the ethics of "bitch" and "nigga" in hip hop through Dave Chappelle's comedy, using the use-mention distinction and speaker intention to argue Chappelle's gender-neutral, affectionate, equivocating uses ("now that's a nigger who's one crazy nigger", the blind Black Klansman of "Frontline: Black KKK", "Reparations 2003") are racial rather than racist language. Invoking Mill's harm principle - words should be legally barred only when they harm, as with the KKK cross-burning example, not merely offend - he defends in-group reclamation, then extends the analysis to Paris's "Field Nigga Boogie" and "AWOL", whose epithets carry a progressive, Malcolm X-style challenge to unjust wars and state evil.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 10 "The Gathering of the Tribe Ironic Sacramentalism" — Horace Fairlamb argues the Grateful Dead were the Sixties' real revolutionary success: where the New Left failed by keeping confrontational politics, the Dead changed consciousness first, extending Mill's liberal 'experiments in living' into a whole alternative culture. He reads the total improvisation learned at the Acid Tests ('the form that follows chaos'), the band's leaderless 'functional anarchy' — Lesh: if anyone tried to take charge 'it would just dissolve in their hands' — and its flat business hierarchy with roadies as corporate presidents as a spontaneous order lived at the edge of chaos. The Deadhead community's ritual communitas, analyzed through Victor Turner's separation-liminality-reincorporation model, amounts to an 'ironic sacramentalism' that achieves what social contract from Hobbes (force), Locke (property), and Rawls (self-interest) cannot: unity that transcends difference while leaving it in place.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 17 "Mr. Rawls and the Decision Procedure" — Joseph Ulatowski uses Mr. Blonde's torture of Marvin to test theories of punishment. He argues Blonde is not a mere psychopath but a retributivist within his social code—punishing clerks who 'touched the alarm' and cops who violated Mill's harm principle—while distinguishing acting on a principle from merely acting in accordance with one, since Blonde acts from sadistic urges. After reviewing Kant's lex talionis and the utilitarian theory's flaws, he asks whether Hart and Sterba's Rawlsian 'retributivism as fairness', whose principles are chosen behind a veil of ignorance, could justify Blonde's actions, concluding Blonde could not by his own lights have done otherwise than punish.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 22 "The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly" — Johnson and Schmitz argue that Cash, through songs like 'San Quentin,' 'Jacob Green,' and his cover of 'The Mercy Seat,' championed reforming prisons from a retributive to a rehabilitative model and abolishing capital punishment (songs like 'Joe Bean' and 'Long Black Veil' center executed innocents). They defend Cash with Mill: Socrates shows vengeful retributive sentiment is immoral, Mill's harm principle says government may coerce only to prevent harm, so punishment should be justified only by future deterrence and rehabilitation. Since the death penalty's deterrent effect is empirically weak (California, Missouri-vs-Iowa murder rates) and wrongful convictions are common, Mill today would join Cash in calling for abolition.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 35 "A Little bit of Messi for our Life" — The authors cast the contrast between disciplined European and improvisational South American football as Mill's struggle between liberty and authority: the coach's tactical orders are 'rules of opinion' the genius may defy, as Maradona did on his sixty-meter run to the Goal of the Century, while the harm principle marks the line at the 'rules of law' — FIFA's Laws of the Game. The Hand of God goal, which broke even a rule of law yet stood because 'a goal is scored when the referee says so', illustrates Searle's point that football's regulative capacity cannot guarantee its agreements, leaving a gap filled only by ethics and fair play. Following Wittgenstein's 'ethics and aesthetics are one and the same', they conclude that a bit of Messi-style rule-breaking — Messi replicated both Maradona goals in 2007 — is what makes football, and life, joyful and beautiful.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 150 "The Problem with Drugs" — The closing section rebuts the communitarian defense of California's drug laws, noting there is more than one community and most people belong to several, then turns to Douglas Husak: moral rights exist to protect persons from majority interference, and the crusade against drugs is cultural hegemony. Cocaine, marijuana, and opiates were outlawed along racial lines (blacks, Mexicans, and Chinese respectively) while the ruling class's alcohol and tobacco remained 'autonomous choices,' suggesting the real problem with drugs is who uses them.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 11 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — A palliative-care bioethicist dissects the 'Gray Matter' family meeting, arguing Skyler's ambush coerces Walt's autonomy through an implied threat of emotional isolation, while Walt Jr.'s honest 'I'm pissed off!' and Marie's defense of his choice are non-coercive. The chapter frames the issue with Kant's ideal of choice free from emotion and circumstance and Mill's insistence that even self-destructive decisions are beyond legitimate coercion, and indicts doctors too for 'selling' futile treatment rather than admit mortality. The verdict: Walt accepted chemotherapy through 'autonomous beneficence' - a freely made sacrifice for his son - so Skyler's manipulation was unethical even though the decision it produced was genuinely his own.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 26 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Asks what exactly makes a meth cook a 'bad guy' and finds the line hard to draw: Walt forces no one to use, so like tobacco farmers and gun makers he merely enables self-harm - yet Saul's proposed prison shanking and Walt's order to murder Gale show culpable enabling without direct harm. Gale's libertarian purity argument ('they're getting exactly what they pay for') and Prohibition economics even suggest that on utilitarian grounds skilled cooks might do less harm than worse ones, though the industry as a whole remains indefensible. The chapter's moral center is Jane's death - Walt's monstrous 'standing by' - and the closeness effect that makes the personal Krazy-8 murder feel worse than the gas; it concludes the good-guy/bad-guy frame itself fuels the failed war on drugs.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 33 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — A provocatively sympathetic application of On Liberty: Mill's harm principle protects Jesse's drug use from punishment, and Mill's celebration of individuality and 'experiments of living' makes Walt's cooking an 'individual spontaneity' valuable precisely because it defies custom - Marie's anti-pot panic and Hank's beer-and-Cub-cigar double standard illustrating the 'magical influence of custom' and democracy's drift toward 'collective mediocrity'. Mill's temperance-era remarks that intoxication 'is not a fit subject for legislative interference' are extended from use to manufacture. The chapter's thesis: even when Walt is wrong, mere nonconformity 'is itself a service', making Heisenberg an unlikely hero of liberty and human progress.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 9 "Futurama and Philosophy" — In 'A Taste of Freedom,' Zoidberg eats Earth's flag Old Freebie on Freedom Day, is tried by Earth's Supreme Court, and his death sentence triggers a Decapodian invasion that enslaves Earth under the Mobile Oppression Palace. The chapter pits Mill's On Liberty defense of unpopular expression (mankind cannot silence a lone dissenter; unchallenged beliefs are mere 'true opinions' akin to prejudice) against Feinberg's offense principle, mapping the case onto Texas v. Johnson and the symbolic-speech line from Stromberg to Tinker. It ends with Zoidberg burning the flag 'to preserve the freedom it represents': liberty and majority will often conflict (doomsday devices, Proposition Infinity's robosexual marriage ban), so preserving freedom requires tolerating offensive expression.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 10 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Young tests Isaiah Berlin's distinction between negative liberty (absence of external interference) and positive liberty (rational self-government) on three episodes: Fry's super-Slurm compulsion in 'Fry and the Slurm Factory,' human Bender's lethal gluttony in 'Anthology of Interest II,' and the worms whose upgrades win Leela's love in 'Parasites Lost' - each agent is externally unobstructed yet not self-governing. Bender's jacking-on addiction and the Temple of Robotology's threat of Robot Hell in 'Hell Is Other Robots' illustrate Rousseau's 'forced to be free,' the coercion that Berlin warned has licensed totalitarian regimes. The chapter concludes Futurama takes no side, suggesting genuine freedom needs both positive and negative liberty.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 39 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Joe Slater builds a two-premise anti-natalist argument from Shelley's Paradise Lost epigraph ('Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay / To mould me man?'): since it is wrong to inflict harm on an autonomous being without consent, and every autonomous life inevitably contains harms, creating autonomous beings - Adam in the lab or a baby in the womb - is wrong. He answers the objection from Parfit's non-identity problem via the damaged-brain Adam case, and defends the Harm Premise with Mill's On Liberty: consent matters because autonomous agents must be free to harm themselves, as with the smoker, the drinker, and Frankenstein's stolen kidney. G.E. Moore's 'Moorean shift' and Benatar's genetic, social, and institutional pro-natal biases explain why we resist the conclusion, with a 'Super Adam' incapable of harm as the only escape.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 28 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann reads Graff and Ender as act utilitarians in John Stuart Mill's mold, drawing a detailed parallel between Ender's engineered Battle School childhood and James Mill's grueling raising of his son to be utilitarianism's champion, down to both boys' breakdowns. He argues that although the xenocide was a tragic wrong by Mill's own lights (the hive-queens' happiness counted too), the harm principle permits overriding individual liberty when humanity's survival is at stake - which is why Card's novel, unlike Crime and Punishment or 'The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas,' shows consequentialism at its most troubling rather than its most absurd.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 26 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Christian Cotton asks whether Carrie's clandestine surveillance of the Brody home, though illegal, is morally wrong, distinguishing legality from morality. Locke's state of nature grounds natural rights to life, liberty, property - and by extension privacy - that government exists to protect and that no national-security goal automatically overrides; Mill's utilitarianism would justify violating one family's privacy to prevent an attack, but Mill's own harm principle and 'tyranny of the majority' caution blocks it when Carrie has only a hunch. Kant's respect for persons as ends in themselves condemns Saul's blackmail of Judge Turner as using a man merely as means, so the Right constrains pursuit of the Good.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 21 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Framed by Dickens's Jacob Marley, Walker asks whether Jobs deserved his posthumous accolades despite giving far less to charity than Bill Gates, and tests him under three frameworks. Aristotle's virtue ethics acquits him (character is judged holistically, and charity sits near the golden mean of open-handedness rather than being a checklisted duty); Mill's utilitarianism acquits him (his innovations maximized happiness and he violated no Harm Principle—though abandoning daughter Lisa counts as a harm); and Singer's drowning-child argument condemns him as near-morally-bankrupt for selling luxury gadgets while children starve. Kant both convicts (charity is an imperfect duty under the categorical imperative) and saves Jobs: treating the affluent individual as an end in himself, never merely a means to the destitute, blocks Singer's demand for giving to marginal utility.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 14 "5. The Truth Shall Make Ye Fret" — Watson uses The Truth - William de Worde's accidental invention of Ankh-Morpork's first newspaper and the plot to frame Lord Vetinari - to stage the three classic arguments for censorship: direct harm (character assassination 'works every day'), indirect harm (with MacKinnon's point that the speech of the dominant drowns out the subordinated, applied to speciesist insults at Koom Valley), and the false-beliefs argument. Against them stand the knowledge problem and the equality assumption: Mrs. Arcanum's deference to print, Vetinari's turtle-shaped-world joke, and the Montessori-Broca dispute show we never know in advance which beliefs are false, and any censor like Lord de Worde has his own agenda. Vetinari's verdict that 'free men pull in all kinds of directions' because 'pulling together is the aim of despotism' carries the chapter's Millian case that free speech is a horrible necessity.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 21 "9. Variation under Ethics" — Weighs the clones' bodily autonomy against the special obligations they owe one another, since genetic sisters can harm each other as no strangers can: Helena's murder of Katja nearly pins a killing on Sarah, and Vic's drug-world drags danger into Alison's suburb. The chapter builds a clone-specific cousin of Kant's categorical imperative — "act only and always in a way that you would want your clone to act" — to argue that the clones' liberty may be legitimately more restricted than ours: Alison's public drunkenness endangers sisters who can be mistaken for her, clones arguably must stay in Clone Club and share medical information like Cosima's illness, and hard cases (Beth's suicide leaving cases dangling, the brain-cut-open Castor clone begging Helena to kill him) all turn on balancing autonomy against what we owe others.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 28 "16. Artistic Expression in the Land of the Free" — Argues that Hendrix's Woodstock 'Star-Spangled Banner' links political and artistic freedom: Mill's On Liberty — the harm principle, liberty of tastes and pursuits, and originality against the despotism of custom — both protects and celebrates the performance, since disliking it is no ground for suppressing it. Tolstoy's What Is Art? then supplies the aesthetic verdict: art is the infection of others by sincerely, particularly, and clearly felt emotion, so the anthem, like Picasso's Guernica, is great art expressing bad feelings about Vietnam — unlike José Feliciano's sincere-but-vague ballad or Roseanne Barr's failed joke.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 22 "A Black Mirror of Our Anxieties" — Nosedive's star ratings are read as a digital panopticon — Bentham's prison design generalized by Foucault's Discipline and Punish — with China's Zhima Credit and Social Credit Systems showing the 'future is already here.' Rousseau's general will and Plato's ship-of-state frame the tyranny-of-the-majority worry (Chester destroyed by an office mob, Lacie jailed for a wedding toast, post-truth tribalism), which Mill's harm principle rebuts: Lacie's rant harms no one and should not be punished. Sartre's 'look' and No Exit explain Lacie's staged cookie photo ('Heaven!') and her final liberating exchange of insults with her cellmate, while Goffman's masks ground the epistemological worry that digital profiles are performances we nonetheless trust, and Bourdieu's symbolic capital names what the scores actually measure.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 24 "Do We Attain Justice by Punishment" — Kenny's blackmail arc in Shut Up and Dance — the twist that reclassifies the sympathetic protagonist as a child-pornography offender — anchors an argument that the hackers' vigilantism cannot attain justice: their punishments are unannounced, disproportionate, aimed at merely moral wrongs (infidelity, racist emails), and exempt from the presumption of innocence and nulla poena sine lege that states replaced vendetta with. A distinction between natural-law and legal-positivist conceptions of justice shows why punishment belongs to the state alone. Against retribution ('a mere prison sentence is too good for Kenny'), Bentham's and Mill's utilitarianism — deterrence, incapacitation, and above all rehabilitation, capped by the harm principle — shows punishment should be no more than deterrence requires, making the hackers sadists rather than agents of justice.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 15 "“Cogs that Fit, that Cooperate by Design”" — Reads the government ban on Supers in The Incredibles through Locke's Letter Concerning Toleration and Mill's On Liberty, arguing the ban rests on the 'PREFER' principle — society's likings and dislikings as law — fed by perception management (Winston Deavor's suit-cameras PR campaign) rather than reasons, just as Locke diagnosed intolerance, not diversity of opinion, as the cause of civil strife. Mill's harm principle, illustrated by Elastigirl's 'drinking on duty' remark, should instead govern, so banning Supers' powers and pressuring Dash to suppress his speed ('Everyone's special, Dash' / 'Which is another way of saying no one is') is tyranny. Mr. Huph's 'cogs that fit, that cooperate by design' image of Insuricare shows the conformist cost: a society built on preference rather than reasons will never produce great thinkers.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 34 "Is Propaganda Permissible" — Manninen surveys Disney's WWII Donald Duck shorts (Donald's Decision, The New Spirit, Der Fuehrer's Face, Commando Duck) to argue propaganda is not only the enemy's tool and not always wrong. Hume's 'slave of the passions' explains why The Spirit of '43 works through the Thrifty-versus-Spendthrift slugfest rather than its implicit argument, and Mill's fallibility-corrigibility case for free expression gives even propaganda a seat in public discourse — though Mill's caveat against expression that instigates mischievous acts marks the real limit, which the contrast with the Axis's 'barefaced lies' (and the Yensid thought experiment) is meant to satisfy.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 28 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann defends Graff and Ender as act utilitarians in Mill's own image, noting that Mill's father raised him in calculated isolation and brutal study as a tool to reform humanity just as Graff engineers Ender, so both acted rightly given the stakes even though Mill's harm principle and his regard for animal suffering also condemn the xenocide itself. Against Crime and Punishment and 'The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas,' he argues Ender's Game shows consequences can genuinely justify breaking any moral rule when human extinction is on the table.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 25 "Notes" — The chapter asks whether Fallout's chems should be banned and answers no on Millian grounds: chem addiction harms only the user (and is trivially curable at any wasteland doctor, unlike Cait's Psycho addiction in Fallout 4, which shows what real addiction actually costs), so the New California Republic's firing squads for chem dealers and Caesar's Legion's crucifixion of the smuggler Anders violate the Harm Principle. Combat chem use is self-protection, drugging a Charisma check harms no one because NPCs act on their own programmed preferences, and paternalism fares no better in a wasteland where a failed speech check can get you killed. The analysis then extends to real-world performance-enhancing drugs: permissible for soldiers fighting a just war, but coercive in sports, where PED users force clean athletes to choose between their own health risks.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 24 "Notes" — Writing as a mechanic, Gordon argues Max embodies Plato's Republic: like the ship-of-state navigator, only someone who knows justice may rule, and the Myth of the Charioteer — reason holding the reins over spirit and appetite — explains why the Nightrider's unchecked spirit crashes while the cool-headed, deliberative Max endures. On punishment, Plato's rejection of retaliation (the unjust should be made just, not harmed) interrogates Max's execution of Johnny the Boy, while Polemarchus's 'render to each his due' frames the just-deserts debate. Mill's harm principle then justifies Max's force against the gangs once the state and its courts have vanished, leaving Max an administrator of street justice.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 27 "The Office and Philosophy" — Nys asks whether political correctness is a genuine moral demand or mere verbal hygiene, using the British Office: Gareth's racist BMC joke, Brent aborting it when Oliver the Black coworker arrives, the 'wanking claw' impression, and the porn email with Brent's head pasted onto a woman's body. He argues words genuinely wound (Brent's 'sticks and stones' rehearsal collapses when Gareth reveals his cruel nicknames) but that offense is wrong as disrespect for human equality rather than as a feeling, an account filled out with Frankfurt's claim that our identity depends on what we care about, so the non-targeted can be offended too. After weighing Mill's defense of free discussion for social progress, the pornography debate (in which reduction to body parts is exactly what degrades, as Brent complains he was 'objectified'), and Marx's notion of ideology as a concealing set of ideas behind a 'white male' bias, he concludes that Brent's flaw is looking good rather than being good, and that PC language is rhetorical make-up over persisting inequality.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 11 "Robust Social Critique" — McGowan asks how SNL gets away with offensive material, from Larry David's concentration-camp monologue to the Chase-Pryor 'Word Association' and 'Nude Beach.' He argues censorship fails because offense is historically relative and slippery-slope prone, and that on Mill's On Liberty the harm principle never licenses suppressing speech SNL viewers can freely avoid, a point he sharpens with Feinberg's Volenti maxim and the offense principle. He closes by defending offensive comedy as robust social critique: Mill's fallibilist case that free speech drives human progress, with Baldwin's Trump and Tina Fey's Charlottesville bit as comedians speaking truth to power.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 14 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Keeping asks what grounds the claim that great power brings great responsibility and answers through Good Samaritan ethics. Building on MacIntyre's account of human interdependence in family and community, and Mill's point that failing to aid can itself cause harm, he argues that Bad Samaritanism is a blameworthy harm-causing omission, so Spider-Man's rescues of strangers are obligatory negative duties rather than supererogatory favors. His vigilantism is excused because only he can stop supervillains, 'can implies ought' explains why his duties exceed ordinary people's, and his life-risking feats against the Sinister Six and Firelord still go beyond even what his enlarged duty demands.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 22 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Takes 'Douche and Turd' — Stan refusing to choose between Giant Douche and Turd Sandwich, Puff Daddy's gun-toting 'Vote or Die', and his banishment — plus the kindergarten tie in 'Trapper Keeper' (Flora's indecision, Rosie O'Donnell's recounts) to ask whether every vote counts in a two-party system. Through Locke, Stan's abstention becomes a withdrawal of consent to be governed by either mascot; through Mill, non-voting threatens the active participation that gives institutions legitimacy and wards off tyranny of the majority, even as the chapter catalogs real disincentives: the Electoral College's spectator states, the 2000 Florida debacle, and Commission rules excluding third parties like Nader. Habermas closes the chapter: the vote, read as positive liberty, is the paradigm of rights and inclusion in a community of equals.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 26 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Challenges the received libertarian message of 'Medicinal Fried Chicken' — Randy giving himself testicular cancer for a marijuana prescription, Cartman bootlegging KFC in a Scarface parody after Colorado bans fast food — by pressing Mill's liberty principle on what 'harm' means: Mr. Garrison's plot to murder the Queer Eye cast is immediate harm, but the S&M Mr. Slave displays to schoolchildren in 'The Death Camp of Tolerance' is only indirect, psychologically mediated harm Mill cannot clearly handle. Addiction then undermines Mill's assumption of sovereign tastes: corporations can shape desire without coercing anyone, so the libertarian 'omnicompetent individual' is a myth. Mead's intersubjectivity (Randy smoking pot before Officer Barbrady, blind to how Jimbo sees him) grounds the constructive claim that selves are socially formed, and the shark-tank defecation and Prisoner's Dilemma examples show why collective harms need rules and regulation.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 27 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Defends South Park's anti-paternalism on both consequentialist and deontological grounds. 'Major Boobage' shows the futility of Gerald's cat ban meant to stop kids 'cheesing' — Kenny still gets high and Gerald himself relapses — while 'Medicinal Fried Chicken' shows how the KFC prohibition births a violent black market, with Cartman's $85 snack pushing him into the Colonel's Scarface-style drug war. On the deontological side, Mill's 'over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign', Locke's self-ownership, and Kantian respect for rational agents (via Nozick's inviolability, and the authors' autarchy-versus-autonomy distinction) ground the claim that coercion is wrong even when benevolent: 'Butt Out' has Kyle and Stan tell Rob Reiner that forcing others to quit smoking is fascism, while Big Tobacco's Kevin Harris wins their approval simply by informing and letting people choose.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 29 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Uses 'Follow That Egg!' — Mrs. Garrison's jealous crusade to stop Mr. Slave marrying Big Gay Al, her two-daddy egg experiment where Stan and Kyle out-parent Cartman, and the governor's 'butt buddies' separate-but-equal compromise — to demolish the standard arguments against gay marriage (scripture, dictionary definition, procreation, tradition, harm to children, the slippery slope to polygamy and incest) as post-hoc rationalizations of disgust. Mill's harm principle and negative liberty supply the positive case: unlike under-age, incestuous, or polygamous marriage, gay marriage demonstrably harms no one, so no legitimate reason remains to ban it, and rights should never be put to a referendum anyway. The 'butt buddies' label fails because separate is never equal — marriage's social recognition, not just its 1,100 benefits, is what its defenders are denied.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 16 "What's so Bad about Performance-Enhancing Drugs" — Ryan evaluates three arguments that using performance-enhancing drugs is wrong, drawing on cases like Barry Bonds, Lyle Alzado, and Ben Johnson. The Against-the-Rules argument shows only that PED use breaks current rules, not that it should be banned; the Unfairness argument overgeneralizes, since sport is full of tolerated unfairness (better coaching, nutrition, natural gifts); and the Harm-and-Pressure argument turns on empirical facts and a paternalism-versus-autonomy debate about whether adults may choose the risk. She concludes no argument yet establishes that PEDs ought to be banned as inherently wrong.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Roberts argues that across Lee's 'Father Knows Best' trilogy (Pushing Hands, The Wedding Banquet, Eat Drink Man Woman) the clash between traditional Confucian values and Western modernity is best resolved by the virtue ethics of Confucius and Aristotle rather than by deontology or utilitarianism. Master Chu literally refusing to be pushed, the Gaos accepting Winston's homosexual relationship, and Chef Chu adapting to his daughters all require Aristotle's golden mean and habituated virtue, which accommodate special relationships and situations. Kant's categorical imperative (rejecting paternalism as treating persons as means) and Mill's harm principle are shown to be too rule-bound to reconcile tradition with modern individualism.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 10 "Beat U-topos or Taking Utopia on the Road The Case of Jack Kerouac" — Adamo argues Kerouac's 'On the Road' is a new kind of utopian text: because classical collective utopias (Plato's Republic through More) were judged by Berlin, Popper, and Arendt to slide into totalitarianism and to conflict with political liberalism's individualism, Kerouac relocates utopia from place to the individual life lived 'on the road' (u-topos = no-place). He reads Sal Paradise's disillusion with Dean Moriarty—who uses people up—versus his admiration for Mississippi Gene and the hobos as dramatizing J. S. Mill's harm principle, fused with the Buddhist vow to harm no living thing, radicalizing personal liberty as perpetual movement without injury to others.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 14 "Technology and Ethics in The Day the Earth Stood Still" — Skoble reads The Day the Earth Stood Still as an allegory about the ethics of force and technology. He argues Klaatu's ultimatum extends Mill's harm principle to the interplanetary level: societies may fight among themselves but not threaten others, so Gort's robot police enforce a right to peace that no one has a right to violate. He distinguishes the robots' narrow, non-paternalistic authority from Hobbes's absolute sovereign, defends the ultimatum as preemptive self-defense rather than a rights violation, and contrasts the film's trust in machines with the later technophobia of Colossus and The Terminator.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 11 "4. Better Call the DEA" — White uses Better Call Saul's cartel world—the 'Bagman' shootout, Mike's account of Philadelphia police corruption, Tuco's meth-driven violence—to frame the ethics of the U.S. War on Drugs, tracing its racist origins and drawing a sustained analogy to alcohol Prohibition. She marshals Mill's harm principle from On Liberty to argue adults may choose their own risks absent harm to others, making criminalization inconsistent given legal alcohol. She then fairly lays out the pro-War case (Bennett on deterrence, the Robins Vietnam-heroin study, Mill's own bar on selling oneself into slavery applied to addiction) before favoring decriminalization on the Portugal model.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 36 "23. Why Does Jimmy Get to Determine Chuck’s Healthcare" — The chapter uses Chuck's EHS to probe when paternalistic intervention against a competent person's will is justified. It argues Chuck is epistemically irrational (the hidden battery and electrified bed disprove his causal beliefs) yet notes, via Sharon Street and Nietzsche, that we all act on 'illogical' but coherent evaluative attitudes, so absurdity alone cannot license Dr. Cruz's push to commit him. Invoking Isaiah Berlin's warning against oppression in the name of someone's 'real self' and Mill-style concern for self-regarding choices, it finally uses Simone de Beauvoir to distinguish Jimmy's genuine devotion to Chuck from Chuck's controlling 'tyranny,' which shaped Jimmy's turn into Saul.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 20 "10. Some Dark Genie" — Calef asks whether Bourdain's choice to become a heroin addict could be rational and responsible, using Mill's On Liberty and Harm Principle (including the voluntary-slavery exception) to argue addiction is reversible and can minimize suffering when alternatives are bleak. He then reads Bourdain's self-destructive drives — the drunk cliff-driving 'death trip' — through Freud's death drive (Thanatos) and Schopenhauer's pessimism, concluding the 'dark genie' was partly disease-like and thus not wholly blameworthy.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 26 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Dromm and Salter analyze Persuasion by distinguishing persuasion (rational, argument-based belief change), influence (nonrational, resting on a person's charisma or status, as Lady Russell has over the Elliots), and 'overpersuasion.' Against Captain Wentworth's view that persuadability is a vice and firmness of mind a virtue (his hazelnut analogy, Louisa Musgrove's fatal fall from the Cobb), they adapt Mill's On Liberty: just as free discussion lets a society exchange error for truth and gain confidence in true beliefs, a persuadable person is happier and epistemically better off. They add that Anne broke the engagement from a sense of duty, not fickleness, and it is her own persuasion that finally reunites her with Wentworth.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 19 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Tait Szabo defends the guiltless consumption of pornography using Mill's Harm Principle from On Liberty: harmless conduct, even if deemed immoral, should not be censored. Classifying porn into erotica, sexist, dominance, and violent types (excluding child porn and snuff as clearly prohibitable), he rebuts the arguments that porn is prostitution (citing California v. Freeman), that loveless sex is wrong, that porn non-rationally causes or conditions violence against women, and the anti-porn feminist claim that it eroticizes patriarchal subordination. Each argument, he holds, either lacks causal evidence or would equally condemn romance novels, sexist jokes, and Cinderella — so under Mill, censorship is unjustified.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 23 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Jacob Held argues that US obscenity and anti-pornography law fails for indeterminacy. Tracing Roth v. United States (Brennan's 'prurient interest' standard) and Miller v. California's three-part 'serious value' test, he shows judges must act as aesthetes (Justice Stewart's 'I know it when I see it'; Scalia's doubt about objective artistic value), so the law gives no fair notice and lacks the form a rule of law requires. He then turns to MacKinnon and Dworkin's Indianapolis civil-rights ordinance defining porn as the 'subordination of women,' struck down in American Booksellers v. Hudnut, arguing its vague 'subordinating' criterion — read through Dworkin's jaded view of sex — would sweep in nearly all explicit material, per Douglas that 'censors are propelled by their own neuroses.'
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 25 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Miles argues that the popular 'porn is free speech applied to sex' defense (Wendy McElroy, Nadine Strossen) fails, using the contrast of Cohen's 'Fuck the Draft' jacket versus a hypothetical 'Schmoen' having public sex to express an opinion. He holds that political and religious speech persuade at a distance whereas public pornography coerces by making the unwilling audience actually perform the act of looking, so treating boobs like bumper stickers would be illiberal. The reasoning leans on a Millian harm/liberty framework: expression that merely offends is protected, but expression that forces others into an act crosses a line, so porn must be defended on privacy/autonomy grounds rather than as free speech.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 29 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Rose takes a paradigm plotless YouPorn-style clip and tests the four standard charges against porn—obscenity, coercion/exploitation, harm to women, and harm to society—arguing each either collapses into cultural relativism or applies equally to any aesthetic object. He answers the feminist (MacKinnon/Dworkin-style) claim that porn subordinates women by noting that unjustified hierarchical power distorts the self-understanding of dominator and dominated alike (comparing it to 50 Cent's 'P.I.M.P.' and blaxploitation), so the wrong is not gender-specific. His conclusion is that porn should not be treated as different in kind from other art but judged aesthetically and morally by whether it distorts equitable social relationships, locating the real problem in capitalist cultural production rather than in porn as such.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 36 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — In this interview, dominatrix-director Mz. Berlin answers the classic moral objections to porn from inside the industry: she rebuts objectification by insisting she chooses to be 'a commodity' and that choice makes it permissible, rejects the rape-myth/harm claim by citing declining rape rates and comparing porn to violent TV, and grounds BDSM's legitimacy entirely on INFORMED CONSENT, contrasting her voluntary waterboarding with her real torture abroad. Endorsing a strongly Millian self-ownership view ('my body is my own commodity'), she extends consent to selling kidneys, assisted suicide, and even display of her corpse, while drawing hard limits at sex with children, animals, or the dead where genuine informed consent is impossible. She also frames femdom porn as subverting male hegemony and normalizing fluid gender roles.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 23 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Jacquette argues that cannabis opens a 'creative inner space' of loosened associations but is skeptical it yields genuine, lasting insight, using Ginsberg's claim to have newly 'apprehended the structure' of jazz and classical music and the conjecture that Shakespeare's Sonnet 76 'invention in a noted weed' hints he wrote high. He treats the aesthetic case as a phenomenology problem: separating cannabis's real contribution to appreciation from mere buzz-glow. He then defends a right to get high by invoking the Declaration's 'pursuit of happiness' and a Mill-style principle that private, non-harming pleasure should not be criminalized.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 26 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Tahko surveys the empirical evidence on cannabis from the standpoint of the individual and of society, concluding that its health harms (respiratory illness, mild cognitive impairment, possible dependence, weak links to psychosis) pale beside those of alcohol and tobacco. He argues the gravest costs—legal risk, social isolation, contaminated black-market supply—are consequences of prohibition itself, not the drug. Endorsing public-health experts, he recommends abandoning elimination-based policy for a harm-reduction approach modeled on the Dutch coffee-shop system and Portuguese decriminalization.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 29 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Musselman, Frohardt, and Lynch defend adult cannabis use through Mill's Harm Principle, using the hypothetical 'Patrick the pot smoker'—a professional who grows and smokes moderately on Friday nights—to argue that competent adults' self-regarding conduct is their own affair and does not violate the 'distinct and assignable obligations' Mill owes to family. They marshal health data (no lung-cancer link, negligible secondhand exposure, neuroprotective effects) to rebut the harm-to-others claim, and invoke Mill's higher intellectual pleasures plus the Michael-Phelps case to argue prohibition wastes resources better spent on the greater harms of alcohol and tobacco.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 30 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Earleywine dissects the moral versus practical arguments over prohibition, attacking legal moralism—the drug-czar claim (Bennett, Wilson) that use is wrong simply because it is immoral—as circular, and noting that the law does not criminalize every immoral act (broken contracts, lying). He shows purported moral arguments collapse into utilitarian harm estimates that the data undercut, since use rates are essentially orthogonal to policy across Amsterdam, Australia, Portugal, and US states. He then weighs anti-prohibition rights arguments (religion, privacy in Ravin, property via Szasz, self-determination) and closes on proportionality: owning a harmless plant merits no punishment.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 31 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Miori, a palliative-care physician assistant and clinical bioethicist, separates personal ethics, professional ethics, and bioethics, then evaluates tattooing through Beauchamp and Childress's principles—especially autonomy (intention, understanding, freedom from outside influence) weighed against risk versus benefit. He concludes tattooing is bioethically fine because safer pigments and market forces reduced its disease risks and because autonomy makes 'to ink or not' the patient's own call, echoing a Millian liberty that one's choice not harming others is 'none of your beeswax.' He ends by defending the memorial tattoo as therapeutic 'memory remodeling' that gluing a positive event in place with pain can make good for you.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 32 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Woods asks whether the claim 'tattooing is immoral' can be defended, taking Adolf Loos's 1908 'Ornament and Crime' (tattooed free men are latent criminals or degenerate aristocrats) as his provocation. He rejects Loos's equation of tattooing with murder, since tattooing is voluntary and self-regarding, but resists the liberal 'sovereign self' reply drawn from Mill's On Liberty by arguing autonomy and the body are relational, not absolute, so a person's self-regarding choices remain open to reasoned challenge and even regulation. He proposes regret evidence in informed consent and an age-25 minimum, concluding tattooing is a matter of both taste and morality.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 28 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Waller interviews two retired California officers (Amarillas and Kos), framing their front-line experience through Aristotle's 'natural philosophy' of theorizing from observation. The conversation raises the killing-versus-letting-die distinction over a neglect case, uses a harm principle to weigh whether rape can be worse than murder, and sets early-twentieth-century verificationism against later philosophy of mind in debating whether serial-killer 'types' (thrill-seeker, mission, power/comfort killers) are meaningful if only behaviors are observable. Kos recounts her own multiple-murderer grandfather, and both officers close by warning how media fiction distorts the public's grasp of real, charming, camouflaged killers.
- **Comics as Philosophy**, ch. 5 "index" — This composite chapter opens with the volume's Introduction and then runs several essays. Jeff McLaughlin's 'What If?' reads DC's Crisis on Infinite Earths and Marvel's What If? series as literal illustrations of Leibniz's possible-worlds metaphysics: the multiverse of Earth-1, Earth-2 and the 3,000 doomed universes dramatizes counterfactuals and Leibniz's Theodicy argument (via the principle of sufficient reason) that God actualizes only the best of infinitely many possible worlds, with Descartes invoked on why a perfect God permits imperfection. Amy Kiste Nyberg's essay analyzes the 1954 Senate hearings on EC horror comics (Gaines's 'The Orphan') as an applied-ethics clash between publishers' free expression and protecting children, explicitly deploying Mill's On Liberty and harm principle to argue why the child-audience framing defeats the anti-censorship case. Stanford Carpenter's piece treats the Black Captain America (Truth: Red, White, and Black) as an epistemology-of-authorship problem.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 13 "11. Futurama as Philosophy Wisdom from the Ignorance of a Delivery Boy" — Lewis surveys how Futurama's satire raises philosophical questions without taking sides. 'Zoidberg's Freedom Lesson' pits Mill's harm principle and free speech against Feinberg's offense principle; the mutants' and robots' oppression is read through Foucault's disciplinary normalcy and Locke's and Rawls's social contracts (state of nature, veil of ignorance). 'The Problem with Popplers' stages Bentham's utilitarianism, a might-makes-right food-chain view, and an intelligence criterion that commits Singer's 'speciesism,' with sentimentality winning. 'The Late Philip J. Fry' and 'Free Will Hunting' dramatize determinism, Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, and Sartre's existentialist free will, while 'Godfellas' and 'A Clockwork Origin' probe the problem of evil, fine-tuning, and Occam's razor.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 30 "28. South Park as Philosophy Blasphemy, Mockery, and (Absolute ) Freedom of Speech" — The chapter argues, via the 'Cartoon Wars,' '200,' and '201' episodes, that South Park makes five arguments about free speech and evaluates each. Johnson defends the claims that catering to terrorist threats breeds more terrorism and that mockery is 'all or nothing,' but rejects South Park's implied case for absolute free speech: using Mill's On Liberty and harm principle he shows the 'marketplace of ideas' fails (citing 8kun and Fox News), and using Popper's paradox of tolerance he argues intolerance cannot itself be tolerated. He proposes a middle-ground 'PC Principle' where society, not the state, curbs harmful speech through deplatforming and public shaming while distinguishing tolerance from acceptance.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 31 "29. Frank Herbert’s Dune as Philosophy The Need to Think for Yourself" — Reading the Sci Fi Channel miniseries Frank Herbert's Dune and Children of Dune, Littmann argues the saga warns against letting leaders or religions think for us: Paul Atreides fakes being the Fremen Mahdi, wages a holy war, and founds a theocratic tyranny that Alia and Leto II carry to worse extremes. He sets Plato's Republic (the guardian class, the noble lie, rule by the wise) and Hobbes against pro-democracy thinkers—Locke's consent and natural rights, Mill's harm principle, Dewey's democracy—then cites Locke, Paine and Russell on religion's dangers, closing with W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' that one must not accept religious claims without sufficient evidence. The chapter reads Paul's dictatorship and the Bene Gesserit's engineered messiah as dramatizations of the historical abuses of concentrated and religious power.

## Thomas Kuhn

*1922–1996 · 26 chapters in the corpus.*

Thomas Kuhn (1922–1996) was an American historian and philosopher of science whose book The Structure of Scientific Revolutions transformed how scientific change is understood. He argued that science normally proceeds within a shared framework, or paradigm, of assumptions and exemplary problems, punctuated by revolutionary shifts in which one paradigm is replaced by another. His notions of paradigm and incommensurability challenged the idea of science as a steady, cumulative march toward truth and reshaped debate in the history and philosophy of science.

### Paradigm Shifts

A paradigm shift, a notion made central by Thomas Kuhn in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), is a fundamental change in the framework of assumptions, methods, and exemplary problems that guides a scientific community. Kuhn argued that science proceeds not by steady accumulation but through long periods of 'normal science' under a reigning paradigm, punctuated by crises when mounting anomalies force a revolutionary switch to a new one. Because rival paradigms can be 'incommensurable,' the transition involves a wholesale reorientation of how practitioners see the world, not merely the addition of new facts.

- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 19 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Steele starts from Orwell's worry that laypeople accept scientific consensus as unreflectively as tribesmen accept witch-doctors — sharpened by Lysenko and Nazi 'racial science' — and answers it with Popper's critical rationalism: since Hume's problem of induction bars proof from instances, we can only provisionally prefer theories that survive severe attempts at falsification, so trusting experts is reasonable exactly when their community tests rather than defends its theories. Kuhn's paradigms explain why dissident alternatives like Atkins talk past the dominant school (Atkins and Agatston are cardiologists, not dieticians), and the 2002–2004 studies showing improved lipids on more fat figure as the kind of surprise that precedes paradigm change. His verdict: neither trusting nor resisting experts is foolish; 'human knowledge is too important to be left to experts.'
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 21 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Womack tests whether Atkins counts as a Kuhnian paradigm shift, using the Ptolemaic-to-Copernican transition as the model: paradigms define which problems matter, normal science accumulates anomalies, and crisis ends in a new paradigm. Measured against the dieting paradigm's own goals, Atkins flunks — its short-term wins fade by twelve months in the JAMA comparison with the Ornish, Zone, and Weight Watchers diets, with 30–50 percent dropout — so the dieting paradigm itself, which treats obesity as an individual plate problem, is the thing in crisis. Her proposed replacement shifts from the individual to the 'toxic food environment': sidewalks, zoning, food advertising rules, and the French Paradox as the existence proof.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 16 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Bruce Reichenbach recounts the failure of the Enlightenment quest for certainty from Descartes and Locke through Kant to the positivists, and argues that Lewis's Narnia instead models knowing as perspectival (the Stable door whose inside is bigger than its outside), value-laden (the Dwarfs' self-chosen dark paradigm that turns Aslan's feast into refuse and violets into stable litter), and personal (Lucy's unarguable knowledge that she has seen Aslan in Prince Caspian, read through Michael Polanyi's tacit knowledge). Kuhn's competing paradigms frame theism versus atheism, James's will to believe opens the chapter, and Plantinga's defeaters keep personal knowledge from collapsing into mere subjectivity.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 101 "Wittgenstein Ultimate Bullshit Detector—or Bullshitter" — Fuller argues that mastering a discipline converts critics into loyal insiders — Thomas Kuhn's 'normal science' enshrines the tendency, cognitive dissonance explains it, and Blaise Pascal's wager is the general model of betting on a way of life that makes you receptive to its confirming signs. Against this he sets the Protestant tradition of Luther's conscience, 'playing it by ear', which like the Sophists concedes that reality rarely yields yes-or-no answers — the gap we fill being bullshit — and he frames the dispute as realism versus antirealism, reading Frankfurt's On Bullshit as an ad hominem attack on antirealists. He then re-examines Frankfurt's star witness: Wittgenstein's rebuke of Fania Pascal for saying she felt 'like a dog that has been run over' now looks like a spectacular lack of imagination, since evolutionary psychology, being forged at that very moment, has been narrowing the human-animal mental gap ever since.
- **The Beatles and Philosophy - Nothing You Can Think that Can't Be Thunk**, ch. 10 "CHAPTER 3 “LOOKING FOR THE INNER HEAT”" — The chapter reads Dylan's self-becoming as a chain of identity-emulations and overcomings — Hank Williams, Woody Guthrie, Ramblin' Jack Elliott — with Jon Pankake's folk-police critique and the Mike Seeger epiphany acting as Kuhnian anomalies that force a paradigm shift from folksinger to songwriter, each gatekeeper playing the 'Hegelian negative' Dylan needed.
