- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 21 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Kakko's 'Hallucinatory Terror' uses Fitz Hugh Ludlow's 1857 The Hasheesh Eater to ask 'How can these things be?' — the ontological status of hallucinations that neither exist nor fail to exist. He traces Ludlow's own reading from Locke's empiricism through Hume's skeptical worry that all perception may be hallucinatory with no verifiable external object, to Kant's Copernican turn: the phenomenal/noumenal distinction, synthetic a priori judgments, and space and time as pure forms of intuition. Kant's framework lets Kakko recast Ludlow's 'virtual change of worlds' as a literal, non-metaphorical restructuring of the intuitions conditioning experience.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 27 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Penrose subjects the 'soft drug / hard drug' distinction to conceptual analysis, arguing that—unlike genuinely graded soft-vs-hard eggs—it tracks no single real spectrum. He tests three candidate bases: phenomenological intensity of the high (incoherent, since 'comparable amounts' and interpersonal 'highness' can't be measured), addictiveness (fails, since the traditional distinction counts non-addictive LSD as 'hard'), and dangerousness (Nutt's Lancet study ranks cannabis as more dangerous than some 'hard' drugs, and the distinction trades on illicitly excluding legal alcohol and nicotine). He concludes drugs vary along many distinct property-lines, so the traditional binary is simply false.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 29 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Downes argues, against a Cartesian confidence in self-knowledge, that climbers do not have reliable access to their own internal states while climbing. Drawing on Nisbett and Wilson's sock experiment and dual-process 'new unconscious' psychology, he shows self-reports are often post-hoc confabulations: climbers who declare a wobbler 'felt easy,' claim to be 'not strong enough' on moves they later top-rope easily, or unknowingly dab or stand on the rope. He recommends leaning on external 'scaffolding' (partners, chalk marks, guidebooks) and the 'you're only as good as your last problem' rule to temper dangerous self-assessments, since overrating ability sits in a deceptively close possible world.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 14 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — David Robles's 'The Seeker' argues that declining trust in Western absolutist religion drives people toward yoga as an experiential, self-directed spirituality. His central move is that Patanjali's Yoga Sutras rank direct perception above testimony and scripture — mirroring the scientific method — so yoga functions as a 'spiritual science' harmonious with empiricism, whereas established religion rests on second-hand revelation. He distinguishes 'spiritual' (personal, inspiration-based) from 'religious' (culturally binding dogma) and casts the American 'seeker' as building a better, results-oriented, pragmatic spirituality.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 16 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Steve Jacobson's 'Standing on Your Head' asks whether an educated Westerner can reasonably believe 'yoga theory' (chakras, prana, kundalini, koshas) given that science has superseded ancient theories. He raises a 'standard objection' from the superior predictive power of science (invoking Hume's problem of induction), rejects weak replies, but argues via the epistemology of testimony that people with weak scientific grounds and strong critical testimony can rationally accept yoga theory. He concludes that even if no part of it is credible, abandoning it would leave yoga intact — 'yoga with fewer illusions.'
- **Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low**, ch. 23 "BLUES" — Jesse Steinberg argues that doubt — a pervasive blues theme (B. B. King's 'nobody loves me but my momma,' Otis Spann's 'another mule kickin' in my stall,' Buddy Guy's 'I Smell a Rat') — supports Descartes's external-world skepticism, since knowledge would require ruling out the dreaming hypothesis. Against the 'I don't care' hedonistic reply he deploys Nozick's experience machine to show we value authentic reality over mere pleasant appearance, and he rejects contextualism as a solution. Endorsing Socrates' examined life, he settles for strong justification rather than certainty, reading Charley Patton's 'can't tell my future, can't tell my past' as the blues' honest coping with irreducible doubt.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 8 "Horror and the Idea of Everyday Life On Skeptical Threats in Psycho and The Birds" — Philip J. Nickel argues horror has an epistemological value structurally parallel to philosophical skepticism: it maliciously rips away the tacit 'cognitive trust' backing our everyday actions. In The Birds, the diner 'symposium' where Mrs. Bundy's confident science that birds cannot coordinate an attack is refuted moments later dramatizes a paranoid scenario we cannot rationally rule out. In Psycho, Marion Crane's isolation and misplaced trust in the seemingly normal Norman Bates enacts the skeptical premise that the ordinary person you rely on could murder you. Like Hume returning to backgammon, viewers can only resume everyday life, which Nickel says horror exposes as a necessary but insecure construction.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 8 "2. The Matrix" — Rowlands reads The Matrix as a vivid staging of Cartesian skepticism: Neo's pod-world is Descartes's dream and evil-demon conjectures (AI plays the demon) plus the modern brain-in-a-vat, showing we cannot be certain the external world exists. He uses the 'there is no air/muscles' and 'twin buildings' variant of Putnam's Twin Earth to argue we cannot even be certain which thoughts we think. The Hume-Nietzsche bundle critique undermines even the cogito, and the spoon-bending boy ('there is no spoon') illustrates Berkeley's idealism as the endpoint of skepticism about the physical world.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 14 "Skepticism Outside the Matrix" — Matt Lawrence uses The Matrix to stage the skeptical problem, running Descartes's dream argument and evil-demon method of doubt (the Matrix as a technological demon) and even a 'Matrix within the Matrix' to show Morpheus cannot know he is awake. Descartes's cogito supplies the one certainty that survives radical deception. Lawrence then draws on Russell's analysis of the red chair to argue against naive realism: color, texture, solidity, and shape are appearances, so even setting aside the Matrix we cannot know the world in itself.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 25 "23. The X-Files as Philosophy Navigating the “Truth Out There”" — The chapter argues that Darin Morgan's X-Files episodes philosophize by critiquing the show's own 'the truth is out there' mantra from within. Through the conflicting hypnosis testimonies and identical camera blocking in 'Jose Chung's From Outer Space,' Morgan cinematically stages Nietzsche's perspectivism and the claim that 'truth is as subjective as reality'; through Clyde Bruckman and the doomed Ansel of 'Quagmire,' he mounts an anti-Socratic case that relentlessly pursuing truth (as Mulder does) is not worth the ruin it brings. Kowalski then rebuts Morgan using Descartes's cogito and inference-to-the-best-explanation to defend objective truth against radical skepticism, arguing subjectivism about truth is self-refuting.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 52 "49. A Serious Man as Philosophy The Elusiveness of Moral Knowledge" — Biderman reads the Coens' A Serious Man through Beauvoir's figure of the 'serious man' (from The Ethics of Ambiguity), the man who craves a single absolute value and blinds himself to moral complexity: physics professor Larry Gopnik, beset by divorce, a bribing student Clive, and Sy Ableman's death, seeks moral knowledge that would let him be such a man. The chapter argues Larry's quest fails across cognitivist, noncognitivist, and pluralist accounts of moral knowledge, showing moral knowledge to be elusive if not impossible. The film's Kafkaesque fables (the Dibbuk, the Goy's Teeth, Rabbi Nachtner's 'L'olam ha-ba', Schrodinger's cat, and the Binding of Isaac in Caravaggio's painting) all stage the absurd collapse of interpretation, echoing the Book of Job, which Maimonides read as a parable rather than history.

### Power/Knowledge

Power/knowledge is Michel Foucault's thesis that power and knowledge are not opposed but intimately bound together, each producing and reinforcing the other. Rather than treating knowledge as a neutral discovery of truth that stands apart from power, Foucault argues that systems of power generate the categories, institutions, and expertise through which certain claims count as knowledge, while knowledge in turn organizes and justifies the exercise of power. Fields such as medicine, psychiatry, and criminology, on this view, both study and help constitute their objects, defining what is normal, healthy, or deviant. The concept reframes truth as something produced within relations of power rather than existing prior to them.

- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 31 "Numbers as Players" — Bennett and Martin argue that the statistics baseball fans treat as objective truth embody far more chance and convention than fans realize. Statistical theory shows luck explains roughly half the spread in 2002 batting averages (Bonds's .370 versus Larry Walker; the 2003 Ramirez–Mueller race decided by one at bat), and Jim Albert's simulation of 1,000 seasons shows about four of five World Series are not won by the most talented team. Drawing on Thomas Kuhn's history of scientific quantification and Theodore Porter's Foucauldian point that numbers 'have agency' and exercise power, they show statistics also act on the game — shaping drafting, salaries, and Hall of Fame election — so Schroeder's stats to Charlie Brown are both indispensable and misleading.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 31 "After . . . Word!" — Marcyliena Morgan's afterword traces hip-hop battling to the philosophical houses and crews of Saturday kung-fu cinema (Wu-Tang's obsession included), reading hip hop's South Bronx birth through Victor Turner's ritual threshold state and defining "flow" as conscious movement within chaos to create balance and collective identity. The mantra represent-recognize-come correct, shout outs as a system of indexicality, and hip hop's counterpublic sphere function, she argues, to expose hegemony and contest Foucault's technologies of power - answering Cornel West's "ignoble paradox of modernity" - so that hip hop battles through the theoretical houses of Foucault, Bakhtin, Butler, Gramsci, and Habermas, where "there is no such thing as a dead philosopher - just one that has not been resurrected yet."
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 15 "Both Sides of Dylan and Politics" — Jordy Rocheleau reads Dylan's protest era ("The Lonesome Death of Hattie Carroll," "Hurricane," "Chimes of Freedom") as Enlightenment social criticism in Kant's and Mill's sense: reason can expose injustice and secure autonomy against majority tyranny. The post-protest Dylan ("My Back Pages," "Desolation Row," "It's Alright, Ma") turns postmodern - Lyotard's incredulity toward metanarratives, Derrida's ever-deferred meanings, and Foucault's power/knowledge, where ideals of freedom become instruments of domination. Yet Dylan keeps crying for justice ("Political World," "Dignity"), so the chapter concludes postmodern skepticism can only serve as a cautionary check within, not a replacement of, Enlightenment politics - the thief's line in "All Along the Watchtower" as commitment amid confusion.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 28 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Kieffner applies Foucault's deployment of sexuality to show how power centers constructed biker sexual stereotypes: the psychiatric profession behind Time's 1970 'Motorcycle Syndrome', the press that sexualized the Van Buren sisters and filled Easyriders with centerfolds, police 'gauntlets' that pull over bikes but not cars (and ask Raw Thunder's Char Zack if she is a lesbian), and even Harley-Davidson's own 'mystique' video deploying eroticism to sell bikes and HOG memberships. Following Foucault's rule of the tactical polyvalence of discourse, he ends with resistance within the same power structure: riders' rights organizations videotaping police encounters, and the tactical discourses of queer, lesbian, and female riders, from Evelyn Greenway's 1921 'Do it with a motorcycle' onward, who refuse the labels of sexual outlaw and gender traitor.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 19 "Urban Idiots Foucauldian and Pythonesque" — Using Foucault's Madness and Civilization, the chapter reads the Flying Circus sketch 'The Idiot in Society' and the 'Hermits' sketch as commentary on madness as a social construct that changes from the medieval tolerance of fools, through the Great Confinement, to modern psychiatric medicalization. Arthur Figgis, the village idiot, is nothing like Foucault's silenced asylum inmates: he speaks rationally to camera about the 'vital psycho-social service' idiots provide, deposits moss at the bank, and lectures in idiocy at the University of East Anglia — madmen who are integrated, have agency, and speak for themselves. The Pythons turn Foucault's picture upside down, since the visibly idiotic are socially integrated while the urban idiots in business suits are the ones confined behind asylum-like walls, and by making idiocy funny they restore the dialogue between reason and unreason that Foucault says the monologue of reason destroyed.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 31 "A Meditation on the Word" — Randall Auxier and Eileen Townsend fictionalize the history of philosophy as vampire predation in letters, emails, and IMs (1983-2009) between the 800-year-old Etienne Lavec - a student of Siger de Brabant who drained Thomas Aquinas over the Summa's Treatise on Angels, which wrote vampires out of existence - and Paulie, a freshman turned at Memphis State. Lavec recounts tasting Pico, Spinoza, Hegel, and the willing Kierkegaard, sparing Nietzsche who 'stole some of my ideas about free death', and contrasts vampire self-knowledge (embracing desire) with the Socratic beginning in affirmed ignorance. The centerpiece is Foucault: Lavec summarizes his genealogies of how institutions create the sick, the mad, the prisoner, and the pervert, fails to drain him, and is then haunted for decades by posthumous publications, taunting 'nietzsche26' emails, and finally a catacombs trap - power/knowledge that refuses to die. Lavec's embedded 'Meditation on the Word' recasts the Logos of John's Gospel so that vampires are the uncreated darkness at the boundary of the divine Word, pure self-grounding desire 'beyond good and evil', while the closing Twilight-era chats satirize Stephenie Meyer's sparkling, abstinent Edward as Foucauldian 'sin by words'.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 37 "Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!" — Jeremy Wisnewski's mock-manifesto uses Family Guy's cutaway gags and taboo jokes (Hitler sausage vendors, Petoria at the UN, Saddam and Khadafi bonding over Seinfeld) to stage postmodernism: Lyotard's "incredulity toward meta-narratives" and Baudrillard's claim that the real is no longer real, since our families are as televisual as the Griffins, who at least know they are cartoons. The danger is that joking about everything breeds cynical passivity, "liberating us from our causes." But Foucault, the 1968 activist and prison reformer, shows through power/knowledge that one can be postmodern and still fight locally, so the Griffins, and the show's satire of religion and politics, get to live.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 27 "Art, Madness, and Syd Barrett" — George Reisch reads The Wall through Foucault's Madness and Civilization: madness is not a brain lesion but a historical construction — Renaissance unreason, classical confinement, then Tuke's and Pinel's psychiatric regime in which the madman must know 'he is watched, judged, and condemned' until judgment is internalized — which explains why Pink imprisons himself brick by brick and asks at 'The Trial', 'Have I been guilty all this time?' The fascist worms and skinhead riots of 'Waiting for the Worms' are the same crusade for uniformity that drove Pink mad — Foucault's 'moral city' where 'virtue is an affair of the state' — so fascism and insanity are versions of each other, with Sartre's 'Hell is other people' from No Exit as the framing thought. Both the album ('Outside the Wall': 'the bleeding hearts and artists make their stand') and Foucault end by defending art as the last channel of unreason, and Reisch argues Syd Barrett's unanswerable absence was exactly that interrupting void powering 'Echoes', Dark Side, Wish You Were Here, and The Final Cut.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 26 "The Final Word That’s Right, I Said Preliminary Thoughts" — Patton starts from wildly disputed Springsteen interpretations — Reagan's 1984 campaign use of 'Born in the U.S.A.,' Flint protesters playing 'My Hometown' as civic pride, Kerry's 'No Surrender' — and asks whether any reading is better than another. He frames the issue as Socratic dialectic versus Gorgias-style rhetoric, passes through Augustine's polysemy (multiple intended levels of meaning, as in 'I'm on fire') to Nietzsche's claim that the text disappears beneath its interpretation, extended by Foucault (truth as an instrument of power) and Derridean deconstruction. His conclusion: authorial intent cannot settle meaning, but some readings ('Born in the U.S.A.' as pro-Reagan anthem) are non-starters, otherwise it is rhetoric all the way down and the sophists win.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 10 "Frak-tured Finality" — Booth argues that the 'Resistance' webisodes fracture BSG's narrative across television and Internet, forcing viewers to actively construct the story — Jammer's execution in 'Collaborators' and Duck's suicide bombing only make full sense if you pieced the webisodes together — and that this viewer-side fragmentation mirrors the characters' fractured identities. Drawing on Foucault's constructed self, Deleuze and Guattari's 'schizophrenia,' Goffman's performed roles, and Haraway's cyborg, he reads Baltar's 'Am I a Cylon?', Boomer's amnesia in 'Water,' Hera's human-Cylon hybridity, and Tigh's choice in 'Crossroads' to actively construct who he will be. The payoff: there is no central location for the self, the narrative, or Cylonhood — each becomes whole only through active construction.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 20 "Become a Work of Art!" — Dumitrica reads iPod customization (skins, colors, playlists) as a Foucauldian technology of the self: identity is not a stable inner core but something continually made, as when a Facebook user who loses her 80G black iPod feels 'empty'. Against Foucault's examples of ancient care of the self and Christian confessional self-renunciation, she argues the iPod embodies the modern disciplinary self: we survey our playlists against what friends will think, dividing practices split iPod owners from users of 'lame MP3 or CD-players', and social-science-style lifestyle classifications (hip-hop vs heavy metal) shape our choices. The chapter ends by urging Foucault's aesthetic escape from pre-packaged lifestyle models — treat the self as a work of art, like the author sharing holiday photos with her father instead of plunging into a self-enclosed sonic bubble.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 31 "A Meditation on the Word" — Randall Auxier and Eileen Townsend stage the chapter as fiction: letters, emails, IMs, and texts (1983-2009) between the ancient vampire Étienne Lavec and the newly turned Memphis student Paulie, through which shifting vampire pop culture — Anne Rice, Buffy, True Blood, and Twilight's sparkling, animal-only Cullens — is debated. Lavec's embedded 'Meditation on the Word' recasts the Johannine Logos so that vampires are pure desire, the uncreated darkness at the border of God's light, and his biography enacts the thesis: a Latin Averroist student of Siger de Brabant who drained Aquinas over the Summa's Treatise on Angels writing vampires out of existence, and a collector who hunted or interviewed Royce, Pico della Mirandola, Descartes, Spinoza, Hegel, Kierkegaard, and Nietzsche, whose 'free death' and 'beyond good and evil' he claims as stolen vampire ideas. The running gag and argument is Foucault, whose account of institutions (medicine, psychology, prison) creating their objects Lavec endorses as the order of desire, but who, half-undead after Lavec's failed bite and taunting him anonymously as 'nietzsche26', finally lures him into a trap in the Paris catacombs.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 16 "The Last Resort" — Petersen recounts fighting off a man who threatened to rape and kill her, and argues that karate, not feminist doctrine or therapy, made her a real feminist by rewiring her self-concept, fear responses and relationships. Against the Lara Croft fantasy she sets practical self-defense doctrine ('don't be there'; assertiveness, not aggression, with the bus pest), Australian, US and UN statistics on violence against women, and the Guthrie study of Chicago's feminist Thousand Waves dojo. She frames the transformation with Foucault's 'care of the self': karate's practices of the self give women power through knowledge, so that by black-belt time enduring harassment simply 'isn't who she is'.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 29 "Morgan or Moser" — Everitt Foster reads Dexter's first season through Foucault's History of Sexuality: the relationship with Rita, the comic attempt to 'reciprocate,' and the therapy sessions with Dr. Emmett Meridian all show the 'deployment of alliance' (kinship, family, blood) intersecting with the 'deployment of sexuality,' while the observer-observed 'spiral of power and pleasure' explains Dexter's watching as a power play - letting Rita have carnal knowledge of him would hand her control over his mask. Knowledge of his past (Joe Driscoll, Rudy's true identity) destabilizes the Morgan alliance, and the finale is Dexter's deliberate choice: he kills Brian and saves Debra ('You hurt her, you hurt me'), an act Foster identifies as Foucault's 'right of death' that affirms the identity Dexter Morgan over Dexter Moser.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 26 "Expansive Gameplay as Simulation" — Felan Parker coins 'expansive gameplay' for players adding optional rules inside Halo's fixed rules—speed runs, Pacifist and Zero Shots runs, the player-invented Zombie mode later made official as Infection, and Warthog jeep jumping over the Silent Cartographer archway. This mirrors Foucault's late ethics of aesthetic self-fashioning: within the constraints of Power-Knowledge, imposing personal optional rules makes existence a work of art, which Deleuze summarizes as rules 'at once ethical and aesthetic' inventing new possibilities of life. Parker tests three readings—expansive gameplay as metaphor for self-fashioning, as a genuine practice of freedom when players problematize Halo's militarist hero worship (the Pacifist Run), and finally as a simulation of rule-based systems letting players rehearse self-fashioning at a safe scale, with the gloomy alternative that it merely replaces real practices of freedom.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 58 "I Love You, My Artificial Construct" — Deckard registers an empathic 4.0 on the Voight-Kampff at the thought of retiring Luba Luft, and Resch's remark that including androids in our empathic range would leave us defenseless leads the chapter to Foucault's claim that true/real distinctions reduce to struggles for power. Bounty hunting is read as a reactionary humanism whose 'barrier' keeps humans and androids distinct because technology has otherwise made them indistinguishable — as Deckard's electric sheep, needing exactly the same care as the real one, and the electric toad ('the electric things have their lives, too') confirm.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 16 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Franklin Allaire uses Cliff Clavin's defiant 'Who are three people who've never been in my kitchen?' on Cheers to stage the fight between modern and postmodern theories of knowledge. He rehearses Plato's Theaetetus account of knowledge as justified true belief, Descartes's cogito, and Kant's thing-in-itself as modernity's quest for objective truth via universal intersubjective agreement, then argues through Foucault and Deleuze that Trebek and the judges are gatekeepers whose power controls the narrative - his Civil War renaming example ('What is the War of Northern Aggression?') shows many knowledges competing for one answer. On this view, Cliff's insistence that different questions can fit the same answer exposes the non-objectivity of Jeopardy!'s 'objective' knowledge, making the barfly a postmodern champion.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 35 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Eckstrand uses Foucault to explain the show's central pattern that 'our thing is part of the big thing': power is exercised rather than possessed, flowing through networks in every direction, so even pawn Wallace can have kingpins, captains, and prosecutors running around after him, and McNulty's fake serial killer shows how the police-Sun-politics network can be worked from below. The stat game and standardized tests are Foucauldian power/knowledge, producing a truth ('shining up shit and calling it gold') that hides systemic crime and poverty while punishing truth-tellers like Daniels and reformers like Colvin and Freamon, and its three tools of discipline, hierarchical observation, normalizing judgment, and examination, are visible from Comstat and the project-class window to the grand jury that tames the dockworkers' union. Even reform becomes part of the machine it targets (Templeton's Pulitzer chase), so the best hope is the constant accumulation of small victories by those who keep fighting.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 10 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Chad Timm applies Foucault's disciplinary power to the International Fleet: Graff sorts monitored children like 'formless clay,' watches them through a Battle School Panopticon of head monitors and battleroom observation, and uses constant testing and the normalizing gaze to make Ender his own overseer and construct the identity of a commander. He closes by mapping the same sort-examine-discipline circuit onto standardized testing and Race to the Top, noting Ender's flicker of resistance when the children finally see through the adults' game.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 36 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Jonathon O'Donnell reads DmC: Devil May Cry's Limbo City - demon-run banks, the Fox-News parody Raptor News, Virility soda - as the newest stage in the Devil's career. Tracing the shift from Dante's frozen, defeated Satan to Milton's active deceiver and the Black Mass's sacramental counterfeits, he argues the game's demons are both the hiders and the hidden: reality itself is the demonic lie, a counterfeit truth with nothing truer beneath it. When Dante and Vergil's WikiLeaks-style reveal frees humanity, what is unveiled is not God's order but just another contingent world, a secular tale of media institutions manufacturing 'truth' for a conforming public.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 20 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Stephenson and Waller start from disliking bland, marketable Piper and use Foucault's Discipline and Punish to argue that Litchfield is a microcosm of State power: arbitrary unwritten rules, counts, strip searches, and constant surveillance train prisoners into docile, compliant participants in capitalism, with specialist wardens, psychologists, and lawyers molding the abnormal into the normal. Prisoners specialize too (Red's kitchen, Nicky's ear, Vee's drugs) to survive, and specialization hides the surveillance. The show itself embodies the mechanism, making viewers aware they too live under the Panopticon, though deviants like Crazy Eyes and her standing pee keep open the possibility of refusing State values.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 9 "1. Drugging the Kids" — Seymour argues that the serums of Roth's world mirror the real-world medical control of young people: with no objective test, about 6.4 million American children are diagnosed with ADHD and medicated for diverging from adult-defined 'normal' behavior, just as Amity bakes peace serum into its bread and Dauntless uses simulation and truth serums on initiates. Tris's Divergence, and especially her failure to resist the peace serum because some part of her wanted to stop feeling, shows that the desire to conform is what makes chemical control work, while Tobias (re-running his own fear landscape) and Peter (erasing his own memory) model appropriating the serums as tools of self-control. Tris's resistance to the Bureau's memory serum then becomes a vicarious experience of power for young readers who face medication for their own 'divergence.'
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 21 "11. Should We Execute the Erudite" — Michaud and Watkins ask whether Roth is right that the knowledge-hoarding Erudite are so dangerous we might need to eliminate them, and answer that knowledge is dangerous in three ways. Following Foucault ('it is impossible for knowledge not to engender power'), the powerful define what counts as knowledge - from the church blessing feudalism to the medical community pathologizing gay and transgender people - and following Piaget, new knowledge threatens the interconnected belief schemas (diagrammed as beliefs resting on beliefs) that keep 'faction before blood' and our sense of being special stable, which is why Divergents, evolution, and Copernicus provoke such violent disequilibrium. A Descartes-style simulation scenario - you may be inside Roth's world right now, weeded out for reading the books - and David Lewis's point that investigating knowledge destroys it then show that the real danger is not knowledge but the arrogance of certainty: Jeanine was never a true Erudite.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 20 "9. Not Knowing Serial Killers with Hannibal Lecktor" — Davis reads Manhunter's Lecktor through agnotology - Robert Proctor's study of how ignorance is made - arguing that Lecktor runs a 'knowing game' with Will Graham, strategically withholding what he knows (the Pilgrim's lunar cycle, his fan mail from the Tooth Fairy) so that Graham must do his own dangerous 'field work' and risk becoming killer or bait, a playbook he delivers as an invented Rumsfeldian riff on known knowns and unknown unknowns. The same lens then exposes the real world: the FBI's post-Silence serial-killer panic (Jenkins's evidence that the BSU's statistics were false, capped by the USS Iowa profiling fiasco) as institutional ignorance-making that inflated the FBI's power, and Egger's 'less-dead' - marginalized victims like Kendall Francois's Poughkeepsie sex workers whom media footprints render invisible, 'the missing missing' - as the human cost of our fascination with a killer who never existed.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 23 "11. A Rare Gift" — Breikss reads the Hannibal-Will bond as Sedgwick-style homosociality filtered through gift theory: Mauss and Bataille explain how Hannibal's lavish dinner parties and mentorship function as gifts that assert dominance, overwhelming Will until his inner voice becomes Hannibal's. Girard's mimetic desire then maps the rivalry's escalation — Alana as the shared object, Will's proxy murder attempt via Matthew Brown, the killing of Randall Tier that merges the two men into the 'Willdigo', and Mason Verger as the scapegoat whose death would have purged the conflict. Foucault's reading of Bosch's 'Cutting the Stone' casts Will as the patient and Hannibal as the doctor 'far more insane than the patient', with Jack and Alana as unwitting accomplices in the psychiatric stripping of Will's life, while Bataille's Erotism frames the cannibal feasts as transgression that heightens rather than abolishes the taboo.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 10 "1. More Golems around Than You Might Think" — Using Feet of Clay and Witches Abroad, Froehlich argues we are all like golems: our behavior is driven by the 'words in our heads,' the texts that society and the powerful put there. Lyotard's metanarratives explain how Lily Weatherwax forces Genua to live out fairy-tale plots and how Dragon King of Arms rewrites Nobby's family tree to manufacture a king, while dwarfish gender norms keep Cheery Littlebottom trapped in a culturally imposed text. Freedom comes only when, like Dorfl after Carrot buys him his own receipt, a person rejects the imposed words and chooses words of the heart - 'words in the heart cannot be taken.'
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 27 "15. The Serious Monk’s Guide to Re-writing History" — Framed as a monkey monk-to-be telling four bored children the 'history' of four Discworld novels, the chapter argues that history is not a record of what happened but a constructed narrative: in Wyrd Sisters the Duchess commissions Hwel's play to rewrite the murder of the king, since 'the past is what people remember, and memories are words.' In Small Gods, Brutha's photographic memory of Ephebe's burning library shows that even perfect recollection is lost unless written down, while in Thief of Time the History Monks openly rebuild time as a patchwork after the Big Crash, and Susan watches historians 'rebuilt the image of the past to suit the eyesight of today.' Drawing on W. H. Walsh's idea of history as intelligible narrative, it concludes that history is performative—what people are told it is—and that we ourselves are the crowbar that opens the box of history from the inside.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 18 "6. Anti-Psychiatric Help 5¢—The Doctor is IN" — The chapter takes Lucy's five-cent psychiatry booth as a parody that vindicates the anti-psychiatry movement's three core criticisms: an abusive doctor-patient power relation (her insults, the threat of the stool, the football gag), ineffective or harmful treatment ('Snap out of it! Five cents, please'), and the impossibility of objective mental diagnosis (Thomas Szasz, the DSM's tangled history, Big Pharma's over-prescription). Foucault's History of Madness grounds the point that madness and psychiatric expertise are historically shifting social categories rather than neutral science. Lucy's accidental mindfulness-style advice and Charlie's 'existential depression' (Yalom's death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness) point toward alternatives, and the closing thought is that Charlie's willingness to voice his sadness destigmatizes getting help.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 23 "12. Only Deadpool Is Sane" — Chad William Timm argues Deadpool is not really insane but was made 'insane' by power: via Foucault's genealogy of madness, experts like Dr. Brighton (a robotic shell for Psycho Man) at Ravenscroft and Dr. Whitby at Crossmore, along with the courts that institutionalize him after the Hulk trial, run a knowledge/power nexus that labels, sorts, and disciplines him until he internalizes the madman identity ('I think I might actually be crazy'). Nineteenth-century psychiatry's invented link between crime and madness secured the experts' authority, and disciplinary power plus technologies of the self made Deadpool discipline himself. Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe's 'I can see through the bull##$%' and his fourth-wall awareness become resistance to these regimes of truth, and the chapter closes by turning Socrates's examined life on the reader: be careful whom you tell.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 18 "6. Who Has the Power" — Samuelson uses Foucault to dismantle Phillip Price's creed of being 'the most powerful person in the room': power is not a possession but an operation. Elliot's men in black and the FBI's surveillance are disciplinary power - Bentham's panopticon realized in Allsafe's cube farm and the internet itself - while Angela's fight over the Washington Township leak is a struggle with biopower that no sovereign can be punished for, and Whiterose's knowledge is power-knowledge that operates anonymously no matter who holds it. If Foucault is right, Price, Mr. Robot, and Zheng are mere conduits, and no one will ever be the most powerful person in the room.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 11 "1. Revolutionary from the Waist Down" — Storrie and Martin use Foucault's critique of the repressive hypothesis to argue that Winston is wrong to think sex is naturally subversive and the Party merely represses it. Power over sexuality is productive: the Soviet sexual revolution, Ceausescu's Decree 770 and its 'Decree Generation', Pornosec's pornography for pacifying proles, and tacitly tolerated prostitution all channel erotic energy into state power rather than simply forbid it. Reading O'Brien's torture of Winston as a sustained scene of rape and castration (following Cass Sunstein), they conclude that only understanding power's productive use of sex, as Julia does, makes effective resistance possible; it is Winston who turns out to be merely 'a revolutionary from the waist down'.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 25 "14. The Seduction of Winston Smith" — Mark Alfano reads the novel's ending ('He loved Big Brother') as a seduction story: following John Forrester, a seducer opens with 'I know what you're thinking', which O'Brien enacts when he voices Winston's unspoken thought under torture and demands not mere obedience but enthusiastic consent. Big Brother wins Winston over through four epistemic methods: total surveillance (telescreens, Thought Police, Parsons's own children), the Ministry of Truth's annihilation of records like the photograph of Jones, Aaronson and Rutherford, the destruction of self-trust in the 'how many fingers?' sessions, and the isolation of intimates until Winston betrays Julia. Alfano closes by mapping all four methods onto post-9/11 mass surveillance and Trump-era attacks on records, perception, and the press.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 22 "10. Babies and Pleasures" — Wesch uses Foucault's Discipline and Punish to explain how ordinary women so quickly served Gilead: power is exercised rather than possessed, so Offred enjoying the Guardians' frustration, the 'Her fault!' Testifying, and the Particicution show everyone wielding whatever power is within reach. Gilead is a panopticon in Bentham's sense—the Eyes, paired shopping, 'Under His Eye'—where unverifiable surveillance makes citizens their own overseers, while biopower sorts desirable from undesirable populations, 'making live' fertile Handmaids (shatterproof glass against suicide) and letting Unwomen and unbabies die in the Colonies. Resistance is Foucauldian too: Offred's remembered food, Moira's bathroom gossip, and sex with Nick are the 'bodies and pleasures' that counterattack the deployment of sexuality.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 34 "20. Under a Watchful Eye" — Timm gives a full Foucauldian reading: the Sons of Jacob's biblical 'knowledge' is a regime of truth produced by power (via the genealogical method Foucault took from Nietzsche), and Gilead rules less by sovereign violence (particicutions, the Wall) than by disciplinary power that defines, sorts, confines, and retrains—precisely the asylum-prison-school trajectory of Foucault's History of Madness and Discipline and Punish. The Red Center is that institution in miniature (Janine's 'Her fault, her fault'), the black vans with painted Eyes enact Bentham's Panopticon—power 'visible and unverifiable'—and biopower's medicalized control of women's reproductive bodies ties Gilead to Iowa's 2018 fetal heartbeat law. Offred's small refusals—her hidden name, the night that is 'mine,' the act of telling her tale—are the resistance Foucault always found inside disciplinary power.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 24 "11. Not from Around Here" — Zanin applies Foucault's Abnormal lectures, where a monster is a juridico-natural being violating both the laws of nature and of society, to the show: the Demogorgon and demodogs break biology and morality, while El and Eight are biologically abnormal (psionic) and law-breaking, making them Foucauldian monsters too, as Lucas's 'maybe she's the monster?' suggests. Monsters emerge wherever power/knowledge assemblages operate, hence Hawkins Lab's MK-Ultra-style experimentation conjuring the very Demogorgon it hunts, and the chapter extends monstrosity to human 'assholes' like Brenner, Lonnie, and Billy before concluding that knowing the monster, being a freak, is a virtue and a weapon against fear.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 29 "15. Abnormal Is the New Normal" — Berns, Foronda, and Zarate read the show anachronistically (via Didi-Huberman), arguing its millennial sensibilities deliberately clash with the 1980s setting to reveal that normalcy is a shifting social discourse rather than a natural fact: Joyce defends Will's possible sexuality like no 1980s mother would, Jonathan claims freakishness as a right, and audiences mourn plain, awkward Barb. Through Foucault's three figures from Abnormal, the monster (androgynous, tomboy-coded Eleven called 'freak'), the individual to be corrected (hippie Terry Ives, 'hysterical' Joyce, un-macho boys), and the masturbator (surveillance of the most intimate life), plus biopolitics and bullying as State-sanctioned discipline, they show the abnormal are the heroes: 'The X-Men are weirdos.'
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 18 "Death" — Reads Alien3's Fury 161 through impurity and contagion: Mary Douglas's 'matter out of place,' Foucault's confinement of the mad (the YY-chromosome inmates quarantined as social infection; Golic's fixation on the 'dragon' as Schopenhauer's madness of a fixed idea), Hegel and Schelling's philosophies of biology in which disease, decline, and death are necessary moments of life, and Plato's virtue-as-health of the soul. Ripley's fall into the molten lead embraces Schelling's 'indifference' of freedom and its enemy - she refuses Bishop's quack offer to 'deal with the malignancy' so Weyland-Yutani can never harvest the queen inside her.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 27 "The Buck Stops Here" — Argues that Earth King Kuei, not Grand Secretariat Long Feng, bears the real responsibility for Ba Sing Se's fall, because he willfully maintained ignorance of the war and of his own capital's poverty so he could enjoy palace privilege, playing with his bear Bosco and never once riding the monorail among his people. The city's ring walls work as architectural exclusion that keeps the lower ring's refugees out of elite sight, while the Dai Li's brainwashing ('there is no war in Ba Sing Se', Jet's reconditioning at Lake Laogai) actively manufactures the ignorance the King depends on. Drawing on Charles Mills's epistemology of ignorance and Fricker and Medina's work, the chapter reads Kuei's 'I can't believe I never knew' as epistemic ignorance retained because knowing would cost him his lifestyle, so the buck stops with the seemingly childlike king rather than the arch-villain behind the throne.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 36 "Silent Wounds" — Argues that the Fire Nation's empire, like the United States, was founded on genocide that national narratives erase: Sozin's extermination of the Air Nomads to remove the one check on his ambitions parallels manifest destiny and massacres of Indigenous peoples such as Sand Creek and the Wiyot killings at Tuluwat. The chapter shows erasure at work inside ATLA itself, as Gran Gran repeats Fire Nation propaganda by calling the Air Nomads 'extinct' rather than victims of genocide, and the refugees of the Northern Air Temple appropriate the annihilated people's home, identity, and sacred murals for a bathhouse. Aang's discovery of Gyatso's skeleton and his grief-block on the Avatar State are read as the 'silent wounds' of genocidal trauma, with the caveat that Guru Pathik's chakra cure is far simpler than the real, ongoing healing Indigenous communities require.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 22 "Can You Face the Bat" — Sarah Donovan and Nicholas Richardson use Nietzsche and Foucault to present Batman as a self-constructed identity: across Batman: Year One, Arkham Asylum, and The Dark Knight Returns, Bruce consciously builds the persona ('Yes, Father, I shall become a bat') rather than revealing a deeper true self. Foucault's constructed categories of normal and abnormal surface in Arkham Asylum's 'super-sane' Joker and the Alice in Wonderland parallels that put Batman's own sanity in question alongside Amadeus Arkham's madness. Nietzsche's will to power and eternal recurrence, via the shepherd biting the snake in Zarathustra, explain why Bruce can face the bat that others flee, becoming heroic where Arkham and Dr. Cavendish go insane.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 31 "Damned If You Do, and Damned If You Don’t" — McHenry reads the re-imagined series as a holy-war allegory in which both sides weaponize religion, then asks whether that manipulation is ever moral. Adama's lie about Earth is Machiavellian statecraft (with Foucault's point that privileged knowledge holds power), yet defended as serving the greater good, while Roslin's Pythia-based campaign contrasts with Bush's faith-based fear politics. The Cylons emerge as evangelical fundamentalists whose conversion of Baltar through inner Number Six runs on fear, exactly what Madison's case for religious liberty forbids. The chapter concludes the show's own gods have sided with the Colonials.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 10 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Chad Timm reads Battle School through Foucault's disciplinary power: monitors in the skull, sorting into armies, minute-by-minute schedules, and constant testing are the power/knowledge that constructs 'the soldier,' while the ever-possible observation of teachers and desks makes the school Bentham's Panopticon that trains students to police themselves. The proof of Ender's constructed identity is his singling out of Bean exactly as Graff singled him out on the shuttle, and Timm extends the lesson to standardized testing and Obama's 'Race to the Top.'
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 25 "“I Want to Conquer the World”" — Uses Agamben's bios/zoē distinction (with Foucault on biopolitics and fragmented sovereignty, Hardt and Negri's 'Empire', Marx on surplus-value, and Rosa Luxemburg on unchecked capital) to read the Anderson Station massacre, Murtry shooting Coop on New Terra, and Protogen infecting 1.5 million Belters on Eros as reductions of Belter life to bare life that corporate sovereigns may kill without homicide. It then argues the instability capitalism creates births authoritarian sovereigns — Murtry's martial law, Inaros's Free Navy, Duarte's Laconia — whose followers (Chandra Wei, Cyn, Santiago Singh) display the 'total, unrestricted, unconditional loyalty' Arendt says totalitarian power demands, and closes with Foucault's warning that liberal government's security-for-freedom trade slides into the very corruption and oppression it was meant to prevent.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 9 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — Kylie Prymus asks whether Kefka is truly mad, using Foucault's Madness and Civilization to argue that madness is a label society applies to dismiss what it cannot control, so players and heroes refute Kefka with the ad hominem 'you're crazy' rather than answering him. She then reads Kefka's 'monument to non-existence' through Nietzsche: his godlike discovery that existence has no justification echoes the death of God, our horror at him reflects slave morality's relabeling of noble strength as evil, and the heroes' appeal to purposes he lacks fails because existence is only a hypothetical imperative. Kefka ends up a failed Ubermensch who overthrows the gods but cannot overcome nihilism, leaving the World of Ruin heroes the genuinely Nietzschean task of creating meaning where none is given.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 34 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Applying Foucault's History of Madness, the chapter argues that sanity in Westeros is an act of naming by the powerful: Joffrey literally remakes the drunken Ser Dontos into a court fool, and 'Mad King' Aerys's brutality gets labeled madness while comparable violence by Jaime (throwing Bran from the window) and Robert (ordering Daenerys's assassination) counts as sane necessity. The power/knowledge nexus and the psychiatric fusion of crime with insanity explain how Robert's personal hatred of Rhaegar hides behind a medicalized diagnosis of Targaryen madness. The chapter then tracks Foucault's shift from sovereign to disciplinary power and technologies of the self: Dontos internalizes and performs his fool identity, Dany wonders 'perhaps I am mad' at Drogo's pyre, and Catelyn's freeing of Jaime is written off by Robb's bannermen as 'a mother's madness.'
- **The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire**, ch. 12 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" — The chapter uses Foucault to explain how Salander could leave school without a certificate yet master Fermat-class mathematics: schools 'cut' students into fabricated 'human kinds'—the problem-solving child and the at-risk child (Popkewitz's alchemy)—and under No Child Left Behind that sorting licenses surveillance and discipline of everything an at-risk student does. Lisbeth's case shows the machinery: her correct answer marked wrong from the textbook key, her Rubik's-cube brilliance ignored, her 381 days strapped to a bed under Teleborian's silhouette-like gaze recasting Bentham's Panopticon, and her subsequent guardianship extending the watch over her money and behavior. Because power 'produces reality,' the at-risk label becomes self-fulfilling, and Lisbeth's refusal to be disciplined—her silence, tattoos, and asocial style—only supplies fresh evidence for the label.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 31 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Van Dyke uses Foucault's account of discipline and 'docile bodies' (with Susan Bordo's feminist elaboration) to explain how the Capitol rules: citizens satiated with abundance channel their hungers into fashion, body modification, and self-surveillance, and this self-focused discipline trains their attention away from the injustices that sustain them — which is how the genuinely affectionate prep team can weep over Katniss yet love the Games. She shows that District 13 disciplines just as totally through rigid schedules, rations, and punishment (the prep team chained for taking bread), so neither Snow's hidden indulgence nor Coin's overt regimentation leaves room for autonomy. Cinna's styling of Katniss demonstrates the alternative: body modification as internally generated self-expression and resistance that helps Katniss become the Mockingjay rather than a docile body.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 23 "Notes" — Meyer reads the franchise through Foucault's Madness and Civilization: Max's terror of becoming a 'terminal crazy' replays madness-as-contagion, the great confinement of the mad alongside rabid animals recurs in Max's leashing and Humungus 'unleash[ing] my dogs of war,' and delirium as one step out of reason's furrow frames Johnny the Boy's 'I was sick!' plea. Applying the M'Naghten cognitive test and the wild-beast standard to Johnny the Boy, Blaster, Wez, and Nux, he concludes most followers can still tell right from wrong and remain responsible. The ultimate blame therefore falls on the cult leaders — Toecutter, Humungus, and Immortan Joe — who manufacture and exploit a shared psychosis.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 15 "“We Always Have Something To Do”" — Engels uses Foucault's Archaeology of Knowledge, authorities of delimination, and power/knowledge to show that SNL now produces rather than merely reports political truth, as when the Fey-Palin sketch shifted media blame for the Couric interview from the McCain campaign onto Palin herself. The 2016 sketches (McKinnon's Clinton as the inevitable winner, David's Sanders as a fringe idealist, Baldwin's Trump as a self-sabotaging loser) are read as discursive framings that confirmed and shaped mainstream narratives. Like Foucault's doctors defining madness, comedy writers now set the boundaries of political truth, which spotlighted sexist double standards but proved dangerous when SNL's detached writers misread working-class voters; following Foucault's 'everything is dangerous,' she concludes we always have something to do.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 21 "The Past Is Now History and The Hudsucker Proxy" — Coughlin argues The Hudsucker Proxy, far from being empty pastiche, is a postmodern meditation on history as a constructed text. Drawing on Linda Hutcheon he treats the film's parody of screwball comedy and Frank Capra as a 'value-problematizing' tool: Norville is a hollowed-out anti-Capra hero, and Moses stopping the clock and addressing the audience foregrounds the artificiality and 'telling' of all narratives. Foucault's claim that resistance uses power's own tools underwrites the reading that recycling dead styles and cultural memory (the J. Edgar Hoover quip, the array of intertexts) challenges the authority and singularity of historical representation.
- **The Philosophy of Horror**, ch. 11 "Monstrous motherhood" — The chapter argues that horror films about mothers are not static representations but Foucauldian sites where 'discourses of motherhood' are produced, policed and contested; using Foucault's account of bodies disciplined through power/knowledge, it treats films as cultural artefacts that both enforce and challenge norms of 'essential' and 'ideal' motherhood. It reworks Sarah Arnold's Lacanian 'Good Mother/Bad Mother' schema (the mother who sacrifices herself so the child enters the Symbolic and submits to the Law of the Father) alongside popularised Freudian mother-blame (the 'refrigerator mother', 'tell me about your mother') to read Psycho's Norma(n), the phallic mothers of The Killing Kind and The Brood, and the doomed single mothers of The Ring, Silent Hill and Triangle. It coins the 'monstrous-maternal' to argue that motherhood is framed as always-already monstrous because no woman can meet the impossible, shifting criteria of ideal motherhood, illustrated through Grace's Vivian/Madeline generational clash and Serial Mom's Beverly Sutphin.
- **The Philosophy of Horror**, ch. 12 "The ageing woman as (American) horror story" — The chapter theorises the 'abject barren body' — the menstruating, menopausal and post-menopausal woman — connecting menarche as an upswell of feminine power (Carrie's telekinesis, Ginger Snaps, The Witch's Thomasin) to menopause's cultural construction as loss and 'living decay'. Drawing on Mary Douglas and Kristeva on pollution and abjection, and on Deleuze and Guattari's 'becoming-woman' and bodies defined by capacities rather than fixed being, it argues that the female reproductive body is more often barren than fecund and that this state is another generative modality, not an absence. It reads the Western biomedical pathologisation of menopause (Wilson's Feminine Forever, HRT) as a Foucauldian disciplinary discourse, then tracks older women through Sunset Boulevard's Norma Desmond, the hagsploitation cycle (What Ever Happened to Baby Jane?, Strait-Jacket, Hush Hush Sweet Charlotte), and The Taking of Deborah Logan, concluding that Jessica Lange's American Horror Story roles offer the fullest, sexually frank rebuttal to the abjection and invisibility of the ageing woman.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 37 "Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!" — J. Jeremy Wisnewski stages a mock threat to 'kill' the Griffins to expose Family Guy as postmodernism incarnate. Its blizzard of equal-footing references (Hitler beside Scooby-Doo) illustrates Baudrillard's hyperreal where 'the real is no longer real,' and its relentless mockery of religion, war, and politics enacts Lyotard's incredulity toward meta-narratives. Worrying this breeds cynical conservatism, he rescues the show via Foucault's power/knowledge: like Foucault's activism, one can be incredulous toward grand stories yet still fight local battles - a little incredulity is exactly what we need.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 16 "On Beyond Modernity, or Conrad and a Postmodern Alphabet" — Jacob Held explains postmodernism as Lyotard's 'incredulity toward metanarratives' using On Beyond Zebra! Conrad's twenty-six-letter alphabet is the metanarrative that fixes what can be said and known, while the narrator's invented letters (Yuzz, Snee, Floob) show language expanding to present the unpresentable. Held casts Kant's three Critiques, phenomena/noumena, and his defining of the mind's 'alphabet' as the exemplary modern grand narrative Lyotard rejects, then turns to Foucault's Nietzschean genealogy, using You're Only Old Once! for the medicalization of life and (via a Beauvoir quotation) the claim that gender is a constructed mechanism of control that can be transgressed.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 11 "Propaganda and Pedagogy for Apt Pupils" — Potter and Cobb read Apt Pupil—the blackmail-driven 'teaching' relationship between the boy Todd Bowden and the fugitive Nazi Kurt Dussander—to argue that all effective teaching is propaganda: persuasion by nonrational means (ethos and pathos beyond logos). They analyze the shifting teacher-student dynamic through Foucault's Power/Knowledge, showing power as a fluid relational 'order' rather than a possession, with Russell's definition of power and Nietzsche's Genealogy on the pleasures of subordination explaining Dussander's relief in obeying. Citing Bernays and Chomsky, they contend Todd and Dussander's oppressive, sadism-soaked curriculum merely strips the artifice from ordinary schooling, which has always been a system of control—culminating in Todd's transformation into a killer.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 12 "The Shining ’s Overlook Hotel as Heterotopia" — Elizabeth Hornbeck analyzes King's Overlook Hotel through Foucault's 'Of Other Spaces,' arguing the hotel is a heterotopia—a socially produced space of crisis and deviance that juxtaposes and inverts normal relations, accumulating time as a 'chronic heterotopia' stuffed with its own ghosts and murders (Mrs. Massey, the Gradys, the 1921 photo). Cut off in winter, it strips away the norms of 'home' so Jack Torrance's inherited monsters (alcoholism, his father's abuse) can turn him from protector into a family-killer. She contrasts the maze-like Overlook with the panopticon of Grand Hotel and Bentham's surveillance-prison from Discipline and Punish, noting that King, unlike Foucault, treats transgression as horrific: the conservative horror genre restores the status quo only when Jack dies and the hotel burns.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 34 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Parkhill challenges Jenefsky and Miller's second-wave feminist reading of Penthouse 'girl–girl' pictorials (that they present lesbians as sexually available to naturalize heterosexuality) by arguing that what some straight men enjoy is their own ABSENCE from the scene. He deploys Butler's 'Imitation and Gender Insubordination' to show mock-lesbian-wedding drag can subvert rather than confirm heterosexual 'originality', Foucault's repressive hypothesis and productive power to argue the lesbian is a product of, not outside, patriarchal norms, and Lacan-derived 'projective identification' and feminine jouissance to explain the male viewer's libidinal investment in his own ego-erasure. He concludes both the 'conqueror' and the self-shattering 'jouissance-chasing' pleasures coexist, and that girl–girl porn is ethically no different from ordinary hetero porn since the consumer still assumes a right of access to women's bodies.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 35 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Through the narrative of 'Aisha', a feminist who is aroused by SM imagery she has been taught to disown, Khan attacks the censorship of SM pornography and its 'monkey see, monkey do' harm hypothesis (citing declining rape rates). She names three state-inflicted harms: physical violence (prison sentences in Guglielmi and R. v. Brown), phenomenological violence—using Husserl and Merleau-Ponty's embodied phenomenology to argue courts dismiss submissives' lived reality as 'worthless'—and epistemic violence, using Foucault's power/knowledge to show how the Supreme Court of Canada in Little Sisters overrode expert and practitioner testimony about coded SM meaning. She argues SM consent and pleasure are real knowledge that censorship, aligned with MacKinnon/Dworkin anti-porn feminism, coercively erases.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 21 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Hancuff and O'Connor read the song 'Santa Claus Is Coming to Town' and films like The Polar Express and Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town through Foucault's Discipline and Punish. Santa's all-seeing list-checking is a version of Bentham's Panopticon: children, watched but never seeing the watcher, internalize permanent visibility and discipline themselves. Invoking Foucault's Power/Knowledge and discursive practices, they argue the surveillance does not actually make children 'good for goodness' sake' – punishment is rarely delivered – but instead disciplines them into wish-lists and consumption, training them to be good consumers in late-capitalist culture, with Santa doubling as a corporate pitchman (Coke, Budweiser).
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 37 "Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!" — Wisnewski casts Family Guy as pure postmodernism: its cut-away collage of Hitler, Scooby-Doo, and Tiananmen makes everything equally real, illustrating Baudrillard's hyperreal ("the real is no longer real") and Lyotard's incredulity toward meta-narratives. Worried that such cynicism breeds conservative inaction, he turns to Foucault's power/knowledge to argue that one can be incredulous toward grand narratives yet still fight local battles — so Family Guy's mockery of religion and politics can be genuine critique, and the cartoon need not be killed.

### Problem of Induction

The problem of induction concerns whether we are ever justified in inferring from observed cases to unobserved ones, such as expecting the future to resemble the past. David Hume argued that such inferences rest on a presumption of the uniformity of nature that can be established neither by logic, since no contradiction follows from denying it, nor by experience, since that would already assume the very principle in question. He concluded that inductive expectation is grounded in habit and custom rather than rational demonstration, a skeptical result that continues to shape the philosophy of science.

- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 7 "The Force Is with You . . . but You’re Not a Jedi Yet" — The editors' introduction argues that beneath its action scenes Star Wars stages ageless philosophical questions through the Skywalkers' struggles with identity, truth, freedom, and tragedy, opening with 'I've got a bad feeling about this' as basic philosophical wonder and doubt. It playfully transposes classic problems onto the saga: an Euthyphro-style question of whether Jedi virtues are good because the Jedi appreciate them, Anselm's question whether Yoda is a master greater than which cannot be conceived, Augustine on whether Anakin can be chaste 'but just not yet,' Machiavelli on Palpatine's Empire, Descartes' mind-body question asked of C-3PO, Hume's problem of induction applied to whether the sun will rise on Alderaan, Nietzsche's abyss for Vader, and Sartre's hell for the Sith. It previews each contributor's chapter rather than settling any question, framing the volume as a Kessel Run for the brain.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 21 "“May The Force Be with You”" — Jones uses the Force's telekinesis (Luke's lightsaber flying to his hand, Yoda raising the X-wing) to probe the metaphysics of causation. Hume shows we never observe the necessary connection between cause and effect - only constant conjunction and habit - so Jedi mind-power is no more mysterious than gravity or magnetism; Leibniz's Monadology argues one substance cannot transfer properties to another, so 'how' any cause works is unintelligible; and Hume's problem of induction (will Tatooine's twin suns rise tomorrow? will Vader's officers always choke?) shows law-governed expectations cannot be non-circularly justified. Concurring with Russell that 'cause' is a relic, the chapter concludes the Force qualifies as a kind of cause precisely because our causal concept is too vague to exclude it - and plugs science fiction as a laboratory for sharpening concepts.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 16 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — O'Connell extracts Brillat-Savarin's 1825 anti-flour-and-starch regimen — clear soup without croutons, shun beer, rye over white bread — as a 'proto-Atkins' and reconstructs its real argument: farmers fatten livestock on starches, so by Humean 'species of Analogy' starches fatten humans, from which abstinence from floury foods is 'deduced.' Hume's Enquiry Section IX, 'Of the Reason of Animals,' supplies the philosophical audit, distinguishing relations of ideas from matters of fact and grading the animal-to-human analogical inference as probable at best. The chapter ends with Hume's fork turned on the diet-book shelf: any volume without experiential reasoning concerning matter of fact deserves the flames — 'nothing but sophistry and illusion.'
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 19 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Steele starts from Orwell's worry that laypeople accept scientific consensus as unreflectively as tribesmen accept witch-doctors — sharpened by Lysenko and Nazi 'racial science' — and answers it with Popper's critical rationalism: since Hume's problem of induction bars proof from instances, we can only provisionally prefer theories that survive severe attempts at falsification, so trusting experts is reasonable exactly when their community tests rather than defends its theories. Kuhn's paradigms explain why dissident alternatives like Atkins talk past the dominant school (Atkins and Agatston are cardiologists, not dieticians), and the 2002–2004 studies showing improved lipids on more fat figure as the kind of surprise that precedes paradigm change. His verdict: neither trusting nor resisting experts is foolish; 'human knowledge is too important to be left to experts.'
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 29 "Questioning Everything The Birds" — The Deavels argue that Hitchcock's suspense is fundamentally epistemological. In the social world, heroines in love - Constance in Spellbound, Lina in Suspicion, Rose in The Wrong Man - must weigh mounting evidence of their beloveds' guilt against the Aristotelian premise that character is consistent because virtue and vice are habits: Constance rightly bets that J.B.'s gentleness with her proves he is no murderer, Lina reasonably concludes Johnnie may poison her, and Rose survives only by inventing a persecutory 'they'. With The Birds the question widens to nature itself: Mrs. Bundy's ornithology assumes past bird behavior predicts future behavior, and the film's terror is Hume's worry that causal order may be an unfounded projection, leaving Mitch to stake his family's escape on the humble observed pattern that attacks come in waves.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 10 "Step Back" — Gallagher uses Monk's phobias to test Hume's claim that believing is itself a kind of feeling. The chapter asks whether a fear conflicting with a rational belief (Monk paralyzed by the possibly-on stove during a murder investigation) feels any different from a conflict between two fears ('Snakes trump heights' in 'Mr. Monk and the Very, Very Old Man') or two beliefs, and answers with Hume that beliefs are forceful-feeling representations — there is a 'what it's like' to believing the German shepherd is dangerous. On Hume's account the force of a belief comes from repetition of experience, which explains both why Monk's fears should fade (countless safely landed flights, millions of milk drinkers) and why they persist: his mind dwells repeatedly on the rare catastrophe, giving fearful representations extra force, as when his repeated experience that 'she's always cheating' makes him wrongly believe Brody's wife in 'Mr. Monk and the Bully.' The practical lesson is to step back and widen attention to all the possibilities, as Monk intermittently manages with the help of Natalie and Stottlemeyer.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 9 "Area Philosopher (Me!) Is Sick Of The Stupid Debate About Stupid" — Cuddy stages the generational-decline debate between Mark Bauerlein's The Dumbest Generation and Stephen Johnson's Everything Bad Is Good for You, showing that Onion stories can be marshaled for both sides: Aristophanes complaining that today's audiences 'just don't get me' vindicates the perennial declinist, while 'US Students Lead World in Detention' wryly supports Johnson's sleeper curve. Comparing Bauerlein to Aristophanes and the 'Our Dumb World' entry on Aristotle and Plato's schools closing, he concludes every era teems with idiots, so The Onion could have existed in any century. Because induction from earlier generations' failed predictions cannot settle whether Millennials really are dumber, he suspends judgment and toasts The Onion as the smartest perspective around.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 28 "Get Serious" — David Kyle Johnson takes Nietzsche's suggestion that God is slowly dying and reads The Onion's religion stories — the faith healer who loses a patient during a routine miracle, Kansas fundamentalists lobbying to overturn the Second Law of Thermodynamics, and 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' — as evidence of secularization. He splits blind faith (irrational belief despite evidence, as with Bush's 'Blind-Faith-Based Initiatives') from genuine faith as belief without sufficient evidence, arguing religion does science badly whenever it shields creationism from falsification. But science rests on unproven assumptions too, he shows via Hume's problem of induction, Descartes' skeptical problem, and Wittgenstein's charge that naming a 'strong nuclear force' explains no more than God pushing things down. Ockham's razor then decides for atheism — an unexplained universe is simpler than God plus a universe — though William James's will to believe leaves a door open for faith where evidence is impossible, qualified by Clifford's warning that beliefs likely to harm others are never permissible.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 22 "The Honorable, the Woman" — Mona Rocha and James Rocha charge that Holmes's 'deduction' is really Humean induction, and that his inductive shortcuts about women, tricking Mrs. Smith in The Sign of the Four, reading Mary Sutherland's pacing as a love affair, and dismissing Lady Frances Carfax as a 'stray chicken in a world of foxes', are hasty generalizations made dangerous by gender stereotype. Watson is worse: his 'experience of women... over many nations and three continents' reads Mary Morstan's soul off her face and grants full courtesy only to the beautiful intruder of 'The Solitary Cyclist', a feminist case study in objectification. Irene Adler's escape in 'A Scandal in Bohemia', disguising herself as a young man and outwitting the fire ruse, is Doyle's deliberate proof that treating women as a class fails, making her a proto-feminist decades before Poirot's Rossakoff or Spade's O'Shaughnessy.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 32 "Our Best Bet" — Terjesen argues Mycroft surpasses Sherlock because he truly grasps Hume's Problem of Induction: Sherlock's celebrated eliminations (the three key possibilities for Cadogan West in 'The Bruce-Partington Plans') and his newspaper-ad tests are inductive, Popperian conjecture-testing that can never confirm anything, while Goodman's 'grue' shows the same evidence always supports rival explanations. Watson's failed attempt in 'How Watson Learned the Trick,' the amateur reasoner's wrong solution in 'The Lost Special,' and Holmes's own 'Norbury' failure in 'The Yellow Face' prove that a correct method guarantees nothing. Mycroft, who 'would rather be considered wrong than take the trouble to prove himself right,' implicitly embraces Reichenbach's pragmatic justification — induction is simply our best bet — and therefore hunts longer for the facts that do not fit, acting only when England's fate is at stake.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 18 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Elsby argues Fry's 'brain thing' illuminates how humans form beliefs and adapt to misconceptions: Fry accepts swans as swan boats and deduces 'boat eggs,' romances the radiator woman from the radiator planet, and insists he is in the ruined New York of 4000 rather than L.A. - each time reasoning flawlessly from a false premise before readjusting when corrected. Using Aristotle's incidental perception (seeing the pale thing as Cleon's son), Hume's warning that grouping similar-but-non-identical objects breeds ambiguity, and Mom's grandiose misreading of Fry's anchovy purchase in 'A Fishful of Dollars,' the chapter traces how error enters at each step of identification and inference. The payoff: Fry differs from us only in degree, and our capacity to adapt to overturned assumptions might be inferior to his.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 16 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Michaud plays the 'David Hume' Card Wars deck against Princess Bubblegum's confidence in science: following Hume's problem of induction, every scientific law rests on observation and is only probabilistic—we never observe the necessary connection between cause and effect, whether in magnetism, Jake's hunger-induced jerkiness, or the first law of thermodynamics. Humans are pattern-makers who project causal order onto the world (seeing Gunter in clouds, blaming one bubblegum incident), while quantum physics reveals genuine randomness that Einstein hated. Ooo's residents, who watch Tree Trunks explode and simply move on, may grasp reality better than we do, because they never smuggle in stable, lawlike expectations that the show—and the universe—keep violating.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 13 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter turns Raylan's claim that shooting Tommy Bucks was 'justified' into a question of epistemic justification, expounding Plato's Meno definition of knowledge as justified true belief, Gettier's 1963 counterexamples (rebuilt with Boyd truly but luckily predicting that a marshal will be arrested), and the repairs of Goldman's no-false-causal-link condition and Harman's inference to the best explanation. It then grades the show's reasoners: Raylan knows the Crowes rather than Boyd killed Wade Messer, Boyd knows Cassie milks the revival snakes' venom, Art Mullen does not yet know Raylan helped Winona return the evidence-room money, and gut-feeling victims like Ellen May do not know what they saw. Against Humean skepticism about cause and effect it defends inductive, detective-style knowledge - Raylan can know who done it without courtroom proof.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 19 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Roger Hunt answers 'what do philosophers do?' through Dennis's seduction methodology. Frank embodies empiricism, leaving the comfort of principle for the messiness of the world as Hume did when he found no impression of causation, space, or time; Mac embodies rationalism, reasoning with total confidence from a principle he cannot doubt, as Descartes did from the cogito; and the dialectic of Socrates and Plato, questioning beliefs in dialogue to see what survives scrutiny, describes philosophy as it is actually practiced. Boethius's Consolation - the imprisoned author consoled by dialogues with Lady Philosophy - supplies the frame of philosophy as an encounter with a woman one pursues, and each D.E.N.N.I.S. step maps onto the craft: Demonstrating value to the problem, Engaging physically in its awkward grind, Nurturing dependence through thesis panic, Neglect and Inspiring hope on the road to the defense, then Separating entirely - 'be a sociopath about it.'
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 38 "18. Gruesome Walkers" — Yuen turns the walkers into a lesson on Hume's problem of induction: the pre-apocalyptic belief that the dead do not rise was justified by all past experience until Rick wakes to a world where they do, and Rick's distrust of Alexandria repeats the same inductive move from Woodbury, Terminus, and Grady - useful, Hume says, since custom compels us, but never knowledge.
