Russell's chicken illustrates the fatal surprise, and Goodman's grue (the pun of the title) shows the outbreak could be a future-swinging regularity like the seventeen-year cicadas, undermining even Jenner's experimental science. Popper's falsificationism is offered as the rescue - Shane's reanimation falsifies the "walkers make walkers" theory, leaving the "everyone is infected" theory corroborated but never known.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 38 "23. How Can We Know Anything in a World of Magic and Miracles" — Baldwin asks whether Westerosi characters can know anything inductive in a world without lawlike nature: seasons of unpredictable length, wargs in animal minds, Faceless Men changing faces, and resurrections by Thoros, Melisandre, and Qyburn. After laying out the Platonic justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge (those who saw the pyre are justified in believing Dany is the mother of dragons; those relying on rumor are not), he runs Hume's problem of induction - we never perceive causal connection, so no jar of wildfire must explode - against Reid's common-sense reply that reason and induction stand or fall together, concluding that Westeros gives its people special reasons for skepticism while we, lacking evidence of magical irregularity, are rational to trust everyday inductive belief.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 21 "8. For Hume the Ball Tolls!" — The chapter argues Charlie Brown's repeated falls for Lucy's football gag are failures of induction: given the history of the gag since 1951 (first with Violet, then Lucy's fake reasons each fall - a handshake, a contract, a hundred million dollars), he should draw the meta-level conclusion that she will always pull the ball away. It then tries Hume's problem of induction as his defense, but since that would cost him all knowledge of the external world (that Snoopy is a beagle, that Lucy is mean) and end in skepticism, Charlie - a student of his world, not a doubter of it - cannot take it. The verdict: he is not a blockhead but determined and committed, willing to lose every fall because kicking that ball would be worth it, as in the 1979 hospital strip where he finally gets his kick and still ends up on his back.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 10 "2. Persuade Me Once, Shame on You . ." — Greene dismantles both phases of Adams's case that Trump is a Master Persuader. The trait-list phase (opening with big demands, the Intentional Wrongness Persuasion Play, never apologizing, exuding confidence, recruiting the reciprocity instinct, and the talent stack) fails because doing what master persuaders do is not being one, by the Tom Brady versus Archie Manning point that we never define good quarterbacks by wins alone and by the Kantian thought that an act must be done for the right reason. The reality phase borrows Plato, Hume, and Kant to deny us access to an objective world, but the chapter replies that the experts' predictive failures illustrate Hume's problem of induction rather than proving there are no facts, notes Adams even misreads Plato, and observes that nothing links the Persuasion Filter's one success to Trump's skills rather than to a one-off political climate.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 30 "16. Gotta Have Faith" — Winters asks what faith is when the Party risks burning and becoming demodog chow so Eleven can close the gate: after arguing via George Michael and the talisman-free tunnels that faith need not be religious, he tests Bishop's models of faith against 'The Gate' (the affective and secular hope models fit; the belief and trust models fail because everyone has seen the Mind Flayer's work on Will). Hume's account that causation is never observed, only habituated, explains the Party's hope that heat will drive the Mind Flayer from Will and that Christmas lights will reach him, and Kierkegaard's teleological suspension of the ethical and knight of faith frame Eleven's willingness to die against the absurd, since aligning her life with friendship's higher purpose is what makes it meaningful.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 15 "6. The Facts Don’t Speak for Themselves" — Muyskens asks why Burger and Tragg's evidence keeps pointing at innocent people, answering with Hume's distinction between relations of ideas and matters of fact and the problem of induction: inferences from past experience are never guaranteed. In 'The Case of the Shapely Shadow' the prosecution's seven pieces of testimony against Janice Wainwright are reasonable but false, and only Mason, because he believes his client, presses to the water-records discovery that exposes Cole Troy; 'The Case of the Runaway Corpse' then shows Burger and Tragg settling on Myrna Davenport on flimsy, self-contradictory evidence and simply failing to investigate, while Mason withholds judgment, checks her account against documents and witnesses, and digs until justified true belief is achieved.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 16 "7. Beyond a Reasonable Doubt" — Jordan argues Mason's real superpower is logic rather than client selection or legal brilliance: since conviction requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt before a unanimous jury, and since by the problem of induction (traced from Sextus Empiricus's regression arguments through Hume) no accumulation of probabilities yields deductive certainty, the prosecution can never conclusively prove guilt while Mason need only exploit that structural gap, as in The Case of the Howling Dog's cab-driver and document evidence and the TV movie Perry Mason Returns where Della is the accused. He illustrates with modus ponens examples about Della and Hamilton Burger, contrasting sound deductive arguments with merely strong inductive ones like predicting Mason's next win.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 14 "“Consider Your Verdict!”" — Splits Wonderland's nonsense into the tolerable kind (strange but lawful regularities, like mushroom side-effects and walking the opposite way to reach the Red Queen, which Alice masters by experiment) and the intolerable kind (the creatures' eristic logic). Using Hume's fork of relations of ideas versus matters of fact, George Dunn and Brian McDonald argue Alice rightly concludes the pig-baby is merely an out-of-the-way matter of fact, while the White Queen's 'jam every other day: to-day isn't any other day' and the King's beheading of the bodiless Cheshire Cat repeat the Sophists' tricks from Plato's Euthydemus, which Socrates deflates from the standpoint of common sense and the examined life. The Knave's trial ('sentence first, verdict afterwards') lands on cable-news pundits who, like the show trials of Stalin, argue from predetermined conclusions.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 15 "The Lasting Legacy of Logic" — Treats Carroll the Oxford logician as a teacher hiding five lessons in Wonderland: watch your assumptions (the King infers the Knave's guilt from an unsigned letter), know what your words mean (Humpty Dumpty on 'glory'), don't confuse categories (the King's 'Nobody' and the Hatter's personified Time), don't switch subjects and predicates ('I mean what I say' versus 'I say what I mean'), and don't confuse necessary with sufficient conditions (Alice's Ada and Mabel arguments, with a hammer-and-egg illustration). David S. Brown grounds the lessons in Hume on causes discoverable only by experience, Aristotle's law of non-contradiction and categories, the Marx Brothers' 'Either he's dead or my watch has stopped', and Popper's point that a successful prediction cannot prove a hypothesis, only a failed one can refute it.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 16 "Wonderland and the Real World" — Extracts three problems of induction from Alice's misadventures: predicting the future (Hume's problem: nothing rationally compels Humpty Dumpty to agree the world will not turn into Wonderland at 6 a.m. tomorrow), proving whose dream it is (Quine's underdetermination of theory by evidence: Tweedledee can accommodate any evidence within the theory that Alice exists only in the Red King's dream), and translating Wonderese (Quine's indeterminacy: pointing at the White Rabbit cannot fix whether natives mean the rabbit, its parts, or its stages, nor what 'muchness' means). Brendan Shea shows Alice succeeding where the creatures fail by the criteria Hume and Quine endorse: experimentation, simplicity, conservatism of belief, and a principle of charity in translation.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 23 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Mackonis shows Sheldon is wrong about being wrong: Stuart's tomato counterexample ('it's very wrong to say it's a suspension bridge') refutes his claim that wrongness admits no gradation, and closeness to truth is cashed out with possible-worlds similarity — vegetable theory sits one small alteration from actuality, echoing Sheldon's own many-worlds refusal to dance in any of them. The Raj exchange ('So you were wrong' / 'I didn't say that') motivates many-valued logics in which degrees of truth let both be partly right, while the 'Cooper-Wrongness Paradox' argues that if Sheldon always knew when he was wrong, he could never know that he was wrong. Hume's problem of induction then shows his post-Toby confidence in his other beliefs can never be inductively verified, only sometimes falsified, and his French-sprinkled 'victory' over an exhausted Stuart is sheer logical fallacy.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 31 "APPENDIX - Who are Locke, Hume, and Rousseau The Losties’ Guide to Philosophers" — Scott Parker's appendix profiles the philosophers behind Lost's namesake characters: John Locke for the survivor (blank-slate empiricism, belief tempered by tolerance, The Reasonableness of Christianity), David Hume for Desmond (causation as habitual inference, with the button press as the image of induction, plus bundle-theory skepticism about the self), and Jean-Jacques Rousseau for Danielle ('man is naturally good, and only by institutions is he made bad,' private property as the root of inequality). It adds Jeremy Bentham (the alias on Locke's coffin), Kierkegaard via the Fear and Trembling Hurley finds under the Temple (Abraham's teleological suspension of the ethical and the leap of faith), Dogen on zazen, Edward Said for Sayid (Orientalism and the audience's own projected savagery onto the Others), and short lives of Kate Cooper Austin, Carlyle, Rutherford, Hugo Grotius, Bakunin, Ram Dass, Edmund Burke, Hawking, Minkowski, Faraday, C. S. Lewis, and Lennon.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 11 "Notes" — Adams pairs Anakin with Achilles to show how Palpatine's lesson that 'good is a point of view' - Nietzsche's claim that there are no moral facts, only interpretations - nearly destroys both heroes before a father's love pulls them back: Priam's tears before Achilles, Luke unmasking Vader. Against nihilism the chapter defends moral realism through Apollo's lion simile (compassion and respect are objective facts about what persons require) and Kant's self-critical inquiry, with the Jedi Council's twelve-way deliberation illustrating that some interpretations are better than others, beyond Hume's problem of induction. Both epics settle on a 'Pagan Golden Rule' - help your friends and harm your enemies, but never lose compassion for either.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 30 "Notes" — Asks whether Han Solo's 'hokey religions' dismissal of the Force is unreasonable given his evidence, answering no: Hume's argument against miracles explains why testimony of lightsaber tricks and mind tricks should not overturn Han's experience of consistent natural law, while Hume's problem of induction and custom/habit explain why both Han's 'luck' verdict and Obi-Wan's 'no such thing as luck' are habit-based generalizations. Peirce's fallibilism (backed by Putnam's 'fallibilism does not entail skepticism') lets Han and Obi-Wan each claim knowledge without certainty, echoing Obi-Wan's line that many truths depend greatly on our own point of view.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 27 "Kickstarting Inductive Inference" — Daniel Wilkenfeld analyzes Veronica's 'magic trick' in the 'One Angry Veronica' juryroom and her season-long bus-crash solution as Peter Lipton's inference to the best explanation: the hypothesis 'Beaver is a killer' wins by consilience (explaining the explosion, the dead rat, Curly Moran, even her chlamydia), simplicity, and completeness. But the criteria face Hume's problem of induction — why think the future will resemble the past, when yesterday's popular girl is today's pariah? — and Descartes's evil demon undermines even what Veronica 'sees,' since Curly Moran could fake a bus crash, leaving no non-circular justification for inferential habits none of us can live without. Following Nelson Goodman, Wilkenfeld concludes the demand for justification is misplaced: what matters is that Veronica reasons consistently, in the juryroom as at the cliff.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 28 "Feel the Big MO'" — Letson asks whether momentum in football is a real explanatory phenomenon, opening with the Bills' 1993 comeback over the Oilers. He notes momentum is invoked only for success and only for one team at a time, and struggles to separate it from the mere evidence of playing well, comparing it to 'talent.' Surveying psychological models (Taylor and Demick's momentum chain) and David Romer's fourth-down analysis denying momentum, he argues that even if a small momentum effect exists, its size relative to chance means appeals to it in any particular game are usually unjustified—like blaming one heart attack on smoking.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 8 "Sherlock's Reasoning Toolbox" — Pigliucci shows that Holmes's celebrated 'deduction' is really a mix of induction and abduction, contrasting Aristotelian syllogism and Cartesian rationalism (with its failed Cartesian circle) against the fallibility of real investigation. He walks through Hume's problem of induction (Russell's inductivist chicken), the Mill-Whewell 'great induction debate,' and Popper's falsificationism—qualified by the Neptune/Uranus episode where scientists shielded Newton. Using 'Thor Bridge' and 'The Three Students,' he concludes Holmes is a pragmatic scientist wielding a whole toolbox, since there is no single scientific method.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 12 "4. Demons, Game Shows, and Baguettes" — Wenmackers traces psychohistory's scientific lineage from Newtonian determinism through Laplace's demon, arguing Foundation stays within nineteenth-century limits by predicting only probabilities. She uses Newcomb's Paradox to capture the unease of living under a predicted Seldon Plan, Poincare's chaos and the three-body problem to show determinism need not mean predictability, and Poincare's baguette-fraud tale plus Quetelet's social physics and statistical mechanics to explain psychohistory's core assumption that mobs of billions behave lawfully even when individuals do not. She suggests Seldon's science was in some sense historically inevitable.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 22 "12. Raven Seldon Predicts Disaster" — Malloy argues psychohistory rests on induction and therefore inherits Hume's problem of induction: Seldon generalizes from Trantor's past to predict the Empire's fall, but nothing guarantees the future will resemble the past, and the Mule's unprecedented rise shows there is no deductive guarantee (the future-unlike-past idea is not self-contradictory). He tests Popper's falsificationism, under which psychohistory is science because it makes falsifiable predictions and can never be confirmed, then notes Popper leaves hypothesis-origin and post-failure revision inductive, and finally offers Reichenbach's pragmatic 'vindication' of induction, likening it to Hardin making do with the only tools at hand in a Seldon Crisis.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 11 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Jurgensen and Southworth apply Hume's argument against miracles to the virgin birth, treating it as a claimed violation of the natural law that virgins do not conceive. They attack the credibility of the only witnesses, Matthew and Luke, noting their third-hand sources (Mark, Q, L/M), their contradiction over whether Mary and Joseph were married, and the mistranslation of Isaiah's ambiguous 'almah' as the Greek 'parthenos' (literal virgin). Invoking Hume's four defects of miracle testimony and his maxim that no testimony suffices unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the event, they conclude a rational person must reject the Christmas miracle.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 21 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Kakko's 'Hallucinatory Terror' uses Fitz Hugh Ludlow's 1857 The Hasheesh Eater to ask 'How can these things be?' — the ontological status of hallucinations that neither exist nor fail to exist. He traces Ludlow's own reading from Locke's empiricism through Hume's skeptical worry that all perception may be hallucinatory with no verifiable external object, to Kant's Copernican turn: the phenomenal/noumenal distinction, synthetic a priori judgments, and space and time as pure forms of intuition. Kant's framework lets Kakko recast Ludlow's 'virtual change of worlds' as a literal, non-metaphorical restructuring of the intuitions conditioning experience.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 16 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Steve Jacobson's 'Standing on Your Head' asks whether an educated Westerner can reasonably believe 'yoga theory' (chakras, prana, kundalini, koshas) given that science has superseded ancient theories. He raises a 'standard objection' from the superior predictive power of science (invoking Hume's problem of induction), rejects weak replies, but argues via the epistemology of testimony that people with weak scientific grounds and strong critical testimony can rationally accept yoga theory. He concludes that even if no part of it is credible, abandoning it would leave yoga intact — 'yoga with fewer illusions.'
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 23 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Terjesen defines a 'real date' as a shared intention to try out romantic possibility, using Abelard's claim that intention (not behavior) determines the nature of an act to show that identical activities are or aren't dates depending on mutual intent. He then invokes Russell's argument-from-analogy account of knowing other minds to explain how daters 'mind-read' each other's intentions, and notes this yields only probable conclusions, generating an infinite regress ('I know that you know...') that only 'the Talk' resolves. He cites Hume's problem of induction as the deeper reason analogical inference can never be certain, and uses the Friends 'Mayor of the Friend Zone' gag and Ross and Rachel to argue the Friend Zone is a step toward, not a trap against, committed relationships.

### Pascal's Wager

Pascal's Wager is Blaise Pascal's argument that belief in God is the rational bet even under uncertainty about whether God exists. Reasoning that the matter cannot be settled by proof, Pascal frames it as a decision under risk: if one believes and God exists, the gain is infinite, while if God does not exist, the loss is slight; disbelief risks an infinite loss for a small worldly gain. Because an infinite potential reward outweighs any finite stake, he concludes that prudence favors wagering on faith, a move often regarded as an early piece of decision theory as much as theology.

- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 13 "Who Should Be Committed" — Thomas Senor argues that rooting for the perennially losing Cubs is rationally and morally on a par with religious commitment: genuine fandom, like faith, is loyalty that survives repeated disappointment (distinguished from the zealot's 'my team right or wrong' via the Portland Trailblazers' 'Jailblazers' era). Since beliefs and fan loyalties are not under direct voluntary control, he rereads Pascal's wager not as choosing to believe but as cultivating belief indirectly: attending Mass the way moving to Chicago and following the Cubs daily can make you a fan. The believer's epistemic optimism toward religious experience and the devout's second-order hope in dark times mirror the Cubs fan's springtime optimism, so neither Cubs fans nor the religious should be committed.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 37 "The Catholic in Spandex" — Weighing whether Matt Murdock can be a 'good Catholic', Morris catalogs his commandment-keeping and lapses, then argues his real safety net is his mother Maggie's faith: her intercessory prayer over his broken body in Born Again is the force behind his rebirth, on a communitarian view where one person's faith covers another. When Matt's crisis of faith comes in Kevin Smith's Guardian Devil, Maggie's peasant-and-knight fable delivers a version of Pascal's Wager - bet on God, since atheism risks infinite loss for finite gain - and his heart is calmed; Pascal's 'greatness and wretchedness of man' also echoes in Daredevil's own prayer about humanity's 'disparity of magnificence to actions'.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 15 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Steven Lovell reads the Green Witch's enchantment in The Silver Chair (the sun is only a copy of the lamp, Aslan only a bigger cat, Narnia a children's tale) as Lewis's staging of the Freudian critique of religion, and answers that similarity cannot tell copy from original, that the genetic fallacy vitiates arguing from a belief's origin, and that Aslan is 'not safe,' so Christianity is hardly wish-fulfillment (Augustine's restless heart and Pascal's God-shaped hole point the other way). Puddleglum's stamping out the fire and vow to live 'as like a Narnian as I can even if there isn't any Narnia' is defended through Pascal's Wager and James's 'The Will to Believe': the reality of Narnia is a live, forced, and momentous option that may legitimately be decided on passional grounds.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 12 "Getting Right with Brian (Just in Case)" — Reads Life of Brian through Nietzsche's madman: the crowd's laughter at Brian's market sermons ('consider the lilies... have the birds got jobs?') enacts the death of the cheerless, pathos-soaked God, with Brian as a sincere 'divine idiot' who escapes ressentiment by falling idiotically below the dialectic rather than rising above it as an Übermensch. Bergson's account of the comic — rigidity invisible to its bearer, 'as though wearing the ring of Gyges with reverse effect' — explains why the Pythons' straight men, British class consciousness, and the Roman/British empires ('Romani ite domum,' the centurion's Latin lesson) are funny, and why Britons and Romans can laugh at themselves while Americans cannot. Pivoting from Jorge's war on laughter in Eco's The Name of the Rose, the chapter closes with a Pascal's-wager parody: having laughed at Brian, you have already wagered your immortal soul on God being British — the sort of God who can take a joke.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 9 "Poker and Philosophy" — The editor's introduction stages poker and philosophy as twin crafts of risk: 'philosopher' was once slang for a card cheat, Socrates and Wild Bill Hickok both died for keeping villainous company, and the Buddha's six years to enlightenment are measured against the Birdcage Theater's eight-year poker game. It recruits Nietzsche's 'live dangerously' and Kierkegaard's leap of faith to defend the all-in as the only meaningful way to live, then traces probability from Cardano's Book on Games of Chance to Pascal's wager that believing in God is the smarter bet — the ancestor of today's pot-odds reasoning. Chris Ferguson's PhD, Annie Duke's psycholinguistics, and Jesse May's 'the trick to poker is mastering the luck — that's philosophy' set up the book's Texas Hold'em focus.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 101 "Wittgenstein Ultimate Bullshit Detector—or Bullshitter" — Fuller argues that mastering a discipline converts critics into loyal insiders — Thomas Kuhn's 'normal science' enshrines the tendency, cognitive dissonance explains it, and Blaise Pascal's wager is the general model of betting on a way of life that makes you receptive to its confirming signs. Against this he sets the Protestant tradition of Luther's conscience, 'playing it by ear', which like the Sophists concedes that reality rarely yields yes-or-no answers — the gap we fill being bullshit — and he frames the dispute as realism versus antirealism, reading Frankfurt's On Bullshit as an ad hominem attack on antirealists. He then re-examines Frankfurt's star witness: Wittgenstein's rebuke of Fania Pascal for saying she felt 'like a dog that has been run over' now looks like a spectacular lack of imagination, since evolutionary psychology, being forged at that very moment, has been narrowing the human-animal mental gap ever since.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 12 "Introduction" — Frames Part II's epistemology chapters. Jacoby's chapter uses Stan Marsh debunking TV psychic John Edward, holistic healers, and Mormon belief to teach the ethics of belief against Pascal's wager; Lawrence's uses The Matrix to pose the skeptical problem and Descartes' response; Silverman's uses Adama's lie about Earth in Battlestar Galactica to raise the Gettier problem and the Clifford–James dispute over believing without sufficient evidence.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" — Jacoby reads Stan Marsh as W.K. Clifford's ethics of belief in action: from 'All About the Mormons' ('you better have something to back it up') to 'The Biggest Douche in the Universe,' Stan insists the burden of proof lies with claimants and that faith used as a fallback is no evidence at all. 'Cartmanland' and the story of Job serve to criticize Pascal's Wager — a good God would not eternally torment the virtuous nonbeliever, and the Wager simply assumes its afterlife payoff — while the harms of Miss Information's holistic healers, David Blaine's cult suicide, and Scientology show Clifford was right that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken minds and, as Stan tells John Edward, slow down the progress of all mankind.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 24 "“You Have to Believe in Something”" — Eberl and Vines use Battlestar Galactica to weigh theism against atheism: Baltar's scientific rationalism meets Aquinas' five ways (the universe's ordered structure demands an unmoved, uncaused cause), Six's faith faces the problem of evil answered through Augustine on the perverse will and John Hick's soul-making (Starbuck's mother, 'your life is a testament to pain'), while Hume's faulty-architect analogy presses the atheist case. The chapter concludes with Russell's 'A Free Man's Worship': even in a Godless universe the Colonials find meaning in comradeship and humanity's survival — 'the gods shall lift those who lift each other.'
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 21 "Hedging Our Bets" — Kind asks whether humanoid Cylons have moral status, using Warren's stone-versus-child contrast to show that the Fleet's blender-and-toaster attitude (Roslin airlocking Leoben, Fisk's 'you can't rape a machine') rests on the unargued assumption that Cylons are mere machines. Singer's anti-speciesism grounds status in sentience (Gina's suffering, even Scar the Raider), while Regan's subject-of-a-life criteria are met by rational, self-aware Cylons; Helo's 'no human could do the things they've done' argument fails because humans commit equal evils, as the legal limits on punishing criminals show. Since we cannot rule Cylon status out, she closes with Pascal's Wager: treat them as morally considerable, because the asymmetry of error costs us our moral compass.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 14 "Questioning the Question" — Hartung takes Ross's snapping reply to Armitage's repeated 'Why are you helping me?' in Armitage the Third: Poly-Matrix as a misreading: she wants a practical reason for his choice, not theoretical evidence, and since no evidence can prove an android is a person, William James's 'Will to Believe' applies — Ross's belief in her moral standing is a live, forced, and momentous genuine option (suspending judgment means she is scrapped, and losing her means losing a possible life together), so his passions may legitimately decide. He contrasts this with evidentialist cases where suspending judgment is right (the shuttle company skipping inspection; Dr. Asakura's silicon-based-life hypothesis) and with Pascal's Wager, reading Mars's church-empty, hedonistic culture of sex-tourism Seconds as one that denies genuine options and so kills Thirds. The attached original screenplay 'Eye Am,' a sequel to Magnetic Rose, extends the theme as salvage officer Nadine Beckner is lured by the AI Eva/Sam impersonating her dead husband Heintz, with Schrodinger-style observer-affected reality deciding which version becomes real.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 18 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — Lisa McNulty asks what could oblige us to believe someone: Peter's lying fails Kant's Categorical Imperative (a world of universal liars makes lying impossible), while friendship explains Alicia's readiness to believe client Kenny Chatham even before the evidence does. The 'Death Zone' libel trial over an Everest death shows that one's position of power fixes whom one owes presumptive belief - a reader should side with Cardiff, a judge must presume Lambrose innocent - and Pascal's Wager supplies the method of 'behaving like a believer': withholding rumors, withholding conviction, and Alicia publicly playing the wife and sleeping with Peter in a bid to believe in her marriage again. She concludes Peter forfeited any right to be believed, so Alicia has no moral obligation to behave like a good wife.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 30 "15. God Started in 1983" — Uses the SNL bit of a God who has been standing in a room since 1983 to argue Louis is an 'apathetic agnostic': he cannot know whether God exists, lambastes atheists who claim certainty, and thinks the question barely matters for our lives. The chapter weighs Pascal's Wager against Epicurus's four-part cure ('Don't fear god, don't worry about death'), faults Louis's 'downstairs bathroom' bit for putting the burden of proof on atheists, reads the 'Heaven' glory-hole sketch through Clifford's ethics of belief as a rejection of faith without evidence, and ends with Louie's mother's line that you have to be good to people whether or not God is watching.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 27 "13. Linus’s Wager" — The chapter stages a three-way debate over whether Linus may believe in the Great Pumpkin without evidence. Clifford's ethics of belief (the ship-owner whose wishful thinking sinks his ship) condemns Linus's sincerity-based wager; Pascal's Wager endorses it (forgoing one night of trick-or-treating costs nothing if the Pumpkin is fake and wins toys if he is real) but assumes a doxastic voluntarism we lack, since no one can make themselves believe for even a million-dollar reward. William James's 'The Will to Believe' gets the final word: if Linus's option is live, forced, and momentous with no decisive evidence either way, his leap of faith - like loving without guarantees - is morally justified whenever life would be greatly impoverished without it.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 21 "11. The Truth about Lying" — Fallis reads the series through the philosophy of testimony: TZ relentlessly punishes both truth-tellers (Bob Wilson's gremlin warning and nine more episodes) and liars ('Hocus-Pocus and Frisby,' 'The Four of Us Are Dying'), while Kant's letter on reticence suggests the untried third option of keeping quiet. On the receiving side, Hume's rules for discounting witnesses and his argument that one should never believe miracle reports explain why the crew disbelieves the gremlin and why 'Printer's Devil's' Devil reasons like Hume, Descartes' malicious demon returns in the disguised devils of 'The Hunt' and 'The Howling Man,' and the chapter ends endorsing Pascal's Wager: 'The Last Rites of Jeff Myrtlebank' argues we should believe even crazy, lying testimony just in case it is true.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 19 "9. With Infinite Power Comes No Responsibility" — James Hart casts Tony Stark as a consequentialist and Steve Rogers as a deontologist, then argues Endgame's infinite stakes destroy Tony's morality through Nick Bostrom's 'infinitarian paralysis': in an infinite multiverse every act leaves the balance of happy and sad lives unchanged, as an infinite Stark orphanage rearranged Hilbert's-Hotel style shows, and even genocide becomes permissible so long as infinitely many remain alive. Tony's attempted fixes each fail: the causal approach collapses because reversing the Snap has infinite butterfly effects, expected value (credited to Frank Jackson) runs into Pascal's Mugging and an 'infinitarian trance' demanding suicidal bets on any chance of infinite value, and Bostrom's 'infinity shades' that filter tiny probabilities would blind Tony to the one-in-a-trillion time-heist chance he should take. The chapter concludes there is no consequentialist way to say when wagering lives on infinite stakes is ethical, and Iron Man should let Captain America lead.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 13 "5. Greatness or Nothingness" — Courtland Lewis uses KISS's career gambles to compare theories of decision-making. After Tolstoy's twig-over-the-dragon allegory of mortal life, he tests W.K. Clifford's shipowner (never act without sufficient evidence) against KISS's counter-evidence bet on the Alive! live album, models the choice with Pascal's Wager, and uses the Prisoner's Dilemma to explain the flop of the four 1978 solo albums. He then argues William James's pragmatism — beliefs as rules for action, the living, forced, and momentous option that 'KISS is the best' — best explains why acting on the band's self-created narrative was authentic, with Nietzsche completing the picture: greatness requires leaping, living dangerously, tightrope-walking toward self-defined success.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 21 "Hedging Our Bets" — Kind asks whether the Fleet's treatment of Cylons (Roslin airlocking Leoben, Fisk's 'you can't rape a machine,' Cally's killing of Boomer charged as mere discharging of a firearm) presupposes that Cylons lack the moral status Mary Anne Warren defines against the stone-versus-child contrast. Against species membership as a criterion she deploys Singer's anti-speciesism (sentience grounds equal consideration: Gina's torture, the Raider Scar) and Regan's subject-of-a-life, and against the 'no souls' argument she cites Descartes's animal automata and Turing's reply that an omnipotent God could give machines souls, as Leoben himself suggests to Adama. Since no criterion rules Cylons out with certainty, the chapter closes with a Pascal's Wager structure: under uncertainty, treat plausible moral-status-holders as having it, because denying it costs us our moral compass, answering Adama's 'why are we worth saving?'.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 29 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Malloy examines Walter's incorrigible leaps — Bunny kidnapped herself on no evidence, the toe is a fake ('I can get you a toe by three o'clock'), the Big Lebowski can walk — through Clifford's ethics of belief (the ship-owner who sinks his passengers) and James's 'Will to Believe' reply with its living, forced, and momentous genuine options, applied to Walter's 'dabbled' pacifism and his preference for Nazism's ethos over nihilism's nothing. Walter's conversion to Judaism for Cynthia raises whether practice can will belief, tested via Pascal's wager and James's objection, and the verdict borrows Bernard Williams: we cannot choose beliefs, but Walter's reckless policy of dismissing counterevidence makes him 'not just an asshole, he is also wrong'.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 16 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Eric Silverman argues Game of Thrones explodes the storybook link between virtue and worldly happiness: Ned, 'one man in ten thousand,' is betrayed and executed, so Plato's claim that the just person is happy must mean psychic order rather than material flourishing - reason ruling spirit and appetite - as with Bran, who flourishes as a greenseer though he will never walk again. Cersei is Plato's tyrant, her soul ruled by insatiable appetite and paranoia, so no external goods can ever satisfy her, while Aristotle's correction - virtue necessary but not sufficient for eudaimonia, which also needs health, friends, and good fortune - explains why both Ned (virtue without external goods) and Cersei (goods without virtue) end up unhappy. Finally he inverts Pascal's Wager: since playing the game of thrones risks total loss (torture, humiliation, death) for limited gain, and even winning hollows you out - Robert confesses he was 'never so alive as when I was winning this throne or so dead as now that I've won it' - only a fool would play.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 8 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Jacoby defends W.K. Clifford's ethics of belief—it is wrong to believe on insufficient evidence and the burden of proof falls on the claimant—through Stan's exposures of TV psychic John Edward ('The Biggest Douche in the Universe'), the Scientology of 'Trapped in the Closet', and the faith-based story of Joseph Smith in 'All About Mormons'. The centerpiece is a South Park-illustrated demolition of Pascal's Wager: Kyle's hemorrhoid-driven despair in 'Cartmanland' shows a perfectly good God would not eternally reward evil Cartman or torture honest nonbelievers, and 'Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?' shows the wagerer cannot even know which religion pays out. Stan's closing speech to Edward's frightened audience carries the moral: comforting lies weaken the mind and slow the progress of finding the real, amazing answers.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 14 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Johnson formalizes Kyle's crisis in 'Cartmanland'—evil Cartman inherits a million dollars and buys the amusement park while good Kyle suffers hemorrhoids and loses faith—as a valid argument from the logical problem of evil, then evaluates the town's theodicies against the philosophical ones. The Job story Kyle's parents read him fails like skeptical theism (it proves too much and ends in moral agnosticism), Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' mirrors Calvin's and Edwards's God-glorifying account, Stan's restored faith via Cartman's perfect misery is a greater-goods response, Augustine's free will defense purchases goodness at the price of God's control of prayers and elections and cannot explain natural evils, and Hick's soul-making theodicy founders on fawns, tsunamis, and Kenny's deaths. Pascal's Wager and Plantinga's divine sense are dismissed in turn: evil does not disprove God, but proportioning belief to evidence makes non-belief the rational stance.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 21 "11. The Truth about Lying" — Fallis treats the Zone as a seminar in the philosophy of testimony: truth-tellers like Bob Wilson warning of a gremlin get dismissed as insane ('The Whole Truth' forces truth-telling as a curse), while convincing liars like Arch Hammer come to bad ends, so Kant's letter recommending reticence, saying true things but not the whole truth, looks like the best policy. On the receiving end, Descartes's malicious demon returns as aliens and devils ('To Serve Man,' 'The Howling Man,' 'Printer's Devil'), and Hume's advice to reject miracle-like testimony fails because in the Zone crazy stuff is often true. The chapter ends by endorsing Pascal's wager through 'The Big Tall Wish' and Jeff Myrtlebank's threat: believe the incredible witness just in case.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — Richard Greene analyzes The King of Comedy's Rupert Pupkin, who kidnaps talk-show host Jerry Landers to force his way onto TV and emerges a celebrity, calling this the 'Pupkin gambit' (harming others and oneself to secure an overwhelming personal payoff). Distinguishing internalist accounts of rationality (Plato's well-ordered soul, Kant's universalizable maxims) from an externalist one, Greene argues the gambit is irrational for a sane agent like the financier Michael Milken but rational for Pupkin via a Pascal's-wager structure: because Pupkin is delusional, even imagined success satisfies his desire, so the wager has huge upside and no real downside for him. He also invokes ethical egoism to show unethical acts can still be assessed for self-interested rationality.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" — Jacoby uses Stan Marsh as the embodiment of W. K. Clifford's ethics of belief, that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence. Stan debunks TV psychic John Edward, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the one making extraordinary claims. Jacoby distinguishes evidential from prudential reasons, presents and criticizes Pascal's Wager (using 'Cartmanland' and the problem of undeserved suffering), and argues via Clifford that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken the mind and, as Stan tells Edward, slow 'the progress of all mankind.'
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 21 "11. The Truth about Lying" — Fallis treats the Twilight Zone as a workbook in the philosophy of testimony (the ethics and epistemology of communication). Truth-tellers get dismissed as insane ('Nightmare at 20,000 Feet') while liars come to bad ends even when believed ('The Four of Us Are Dying'); Kant's reticence offers a third option to truth-telling and lying. On receiving testimony, he uses Hume on evaluating witnesses and disbelieving reports of miracles, then argues the show endorses Pascal's Wager—believe crazy testimony just in case—citing 'The Last Rites of Jeff Myrtlebank' and 'Mr. Garrity and the Graves,' plus Descartes's deceiving demon for the show's alien and devil deceivers.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" — Henry Jacoby channels W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' through South Park's Stan Marsh, who debunks John Edward, holistic healers, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the believer and that faith is belief without evidence. The chapter distinguishes prudential from evidential reasons and dismantles Pascal's Wager using episodes like 'Cartmanland' (why would a good God torment nonbelievers?) and 'Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?' (which religion?). Stan's speech to Edward's audience frames uncritical belief as mental laziness that slows the progress of mankind.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 24 "“You Have to Believe in Something”" — Jason Eberl and Jennifer Vines use Battlestar Galactica's Baltar (skeptic) and Caprica Six/Roslin (believers) to debate God's existence, presenting Aquinas's five ways (unmoved mover, uncaused cause, governance) against a self-explaining big bang, and noting Baltar's self-serving faith resembles Pascal's Wager. They raise the problem of evil, answering with Augustine's free-will account of moral evil and Hick's soul-making theodicy (via Hume's faulty-architect analogy) for natural evil. Writing as a theist and an atheist, they argue meaning survives without God in human solidarity ('the gods shall lift those who lift each other'), and that faith and reason can share common ground.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 34 "31. Inception as Philosophy Choose Your Dreams or Seek Reality" — Johnson uses Nolan's Inception—Cobb's dream-heists, the ambiguous spinning top, and the case that the whole film may be a dream—to test the moral Todd McGowan draws from it: that since we can't be sure what is real, we should abandon the quest for reality and choose the dream (his object of desire, his children) as Cobb does at the end. He evaluates six defenses of that moral, rejecting Descartes' skeptical dream/evil-demon problem (answered by abduction and by Plato's cave and Nozick's experience machine showing true belief is valuable), Baudrillard's denial of reality, Locke/Kant on the unknowable noumenal world, and Kierkegaard's leap of faith and Pascal's Wager, before softening it with Hume's return from skepticism to backgammon: entertain the doubt, then walk away when your children walk in.

### On Bullshit

In his essay On Bullshit, Harry Frankfurt offered a philosophical analysis of a familiar but under-theorized form of speech, arguing that the bullshitter differs fundamentally from the liar. A liar knows the truth and deliberately asserts its opposite, thereby still respecting truth as the thing to be evaded, whereas the bullshitter simply does not care whether what he says is true or false and speaks only to serve some other purpose, such as impressing an audience. Frankfurt concluded that this indifference to truth makes bullshit a greater enemy of truth than lying is. The essay is a compact case study in conceptual analysis applied to a phenomenon of everyday communication and public life.

- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 23 "Poker and Philosophy" — Huss tests four models of bluffing on one K-9 all-in: it is not lying, because everyone at the table expects deception, so the victim is never Frankfurt's 'twice deceived' (and Kant's argument that lying fails where everyone lies applies); it is not bullshit, because Frankfurt's bullshitter ignores the facts a poker player cannot afford to ignore; it is not pure acceptance in Jonathan Cohen's sense, since bluffing adds deception to acting-as-if; and it is not full self-deception, since nobody can make themselves believe that 2+2=5 or that 4-7 offsuit is pocket aces. Good bluffing is an art blending all four: deceiving about hand and beliefs, prying attention away from your cards, acting as if, and trying — and necessarily failing — to fool yourself.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 5 "Bullshit and Philosophy" — First part of the editors' introduction, recounting how Harry Frankfurt's slim On Bullshit, after two decades circulating only among academic moral philosophers, spent twenty-six weeks on the New York Times bestseller list and outsold any commercial philosophy book. Reisch and Hardcastle treat the book's popularity as a puzzle worth explaining: a technical exercise in conceptual analysis struck a public nerve. The chapter uses Frankfurt's own definition of bullshit as indifference to truth as the anchor for everything that follows.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 6 "Bullshit and Philosophy" — The editors answer why On Bullshit hit a nerve using Jon Stewart's Daily Show interview with Frankfurt, where the audience laughed at the claim that the bullshitter does not care whether what he says is true. The unspoken elephant in the room was the Iraq war: the claims about weapons of mass destruction, remote-controlled delivery devices, and 9/11 complicity turned out, in the editors' words, to be best described by that word. They argue readers embraced the book as 'bullshit without tears,' a cushion of humor letting them approach the war's deceptions abstractly rather than face the disturbing political questions directly.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 7 "Bullshit and Philosophy" — 'The Year in Bullshit' catalogues the fraud climate surrounding the book's success: James Frey's fabricated memoir A Million Little Pieces exposed on Oprah, the wholly invented author J.T. Leroy, product placement and paid word-of-mouth advertising blurring the line between ads and ordinary conversation, and scientific fraud in pharmaceutical and federal research. It invokes Karl Popper's claim that science deserves respect precisely because it falsifies its own claims, presenting headlines about fabricated results as that ideal fading. Frank Rich's verdict that 'such distinctions have long since washed away in much of our public life' supplies the chapter's explanation of the book's appeal as cultural despair.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 8 "Bullshit and Philosophy" — 'The Dream of a Bullshit-Free Culture' argues Frankfurt revives a centuries-old philosophical tradition: Socrates searching for genuinely wise people rather than purveyors of hearsay, Descartes' Meditations discarding every belief short of certainty, and Hume's forkcondemning divinity-school metaphysics that contains neither abstract nor experimental reasoning to the flames. The twentieth-century apotheosis is the Vienna Circle, whose Rudolf Carnap dissected Heidegger's 'Das Nichts selbst nichtet' as mere appearance of meaning, calling metaphysicians 'musicians without musical ability'. The editors cast Frankfurt as the latest carrier of this Enlightenment anti-bullshit torch, with the book's popularity reconnecting seminar-room philosophy to the marketplace and voting booth.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 9 "I - To Shoot the Bull" — The Part I introduction, 'How This Book Came to Be,' explains what the volume is and is not: not a bullshit-detector manual but discussions and criticisms of Frankfurt's essay, including what it means to propose a theory of bullshit or articulate the structure of a concept. It previews each contributor: Kimbrough on why we let bullshit slide, Preti's use of G.E. Moore as a bullshit-free exemplar, Reisch's two-conversations account, Taylor on cognitive foibles, Bernal on personality pathology, and the Part II definitional debate between Frankfurt and G.A. Cohen's 'unclarifiable unclarity'. It frames philosophy itself as one of our best defenses against bullshit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 11 "Tolerable Bullshit" — Scott Kimbrough opens his essay with his six-year-old daughter shouting through a window that the house painter's smoking is unhealthy, and William Ian Miller's Faking It dictum that truth is seldom a defense. He takes up the puzzle Frankfurt left as an 'exercise for the reader': why our attitude toward bullshit is more benign than toward lying, even though Frankfurt defines bullshit as indifference to how things really are and therefore the greater enemy of truth. The chapter promises to solve the puzzle Frankfurt posed but never attempted.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 12 "Intolerable Bullshit" — Applying Frankfurt's definition strictly, Kimbrough argues much of civility is bullshit: coerced childhood apologies are 'humiliation rituals' where truth is the last thing wanted, politeness is benign hypocrisy that saves people pain, and the Super Bowl ad or the silly communist-professors editorial is valued as entertainment. We also tolerate PR and advertising bullshit out of respect for the ends served, from Exxon's green image to spin by teachers and military recruiters. His answer to Frankfurt's puzzle: we sympathize with bullshitters doing their jobs and contemptuously dismiss their victims as suckers who deserve their fate.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 13 "Bullshit and Self-Deception" — Kimbrough turns to when bullshit becomes intolerable: the philosophy-slam regulars' dismissive 'That's bullshit,' the girlfriend's indictment in The Black Eyed Peas' 'Shut Up,' and the boss's team-builder rationalization for passing you over for a promotion. He leans on Orwell's 'Politics and the English Language' and Nineteen Eighty-Four to show political euphemism ('collateral damage,' 'smart bomb') as the language of power, tolerated because repeating spin is easy and going along with bullshit is going along with power. The chapter closes on the danger of politicians believing their own bullshit, setting up the self-deception question of how one person can play both bullshitter and dupe.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 14 "Blameless Bullshit" — Kimbrough resolves the self-deception paradox using Alfred Mele's Self Deception Unmasked: like the cuckolded husband who masks evidence of infidelity, the self-deceiver biases evidence-gathering rather than playing deceiver and dupe at once. Since Mele shows unintentional motivated belief is common (94% of professors rate themselves above average), bullshit like the entrenched prejudice that 'smart boys are smarter than smart girls' can arise without intent, which is G.A. Cohen's opening against Frankfurt's process-centered definition. Against Cohen's output-centered alternative, the conservative-talk-radio fan who builds his own conclusions on cherry-picked propaganda shows a product can be perfectly clear yet still bullshit, produced through self-deception.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 15 "Bullshit and Truth" — Kimbrough defends calling alchemy bullshit even though Isaac Newton pursued it blamelessly: the charge's function is to excuse us from taking hopeless methods seriously, not to insult the theorist. His killer analogy sorts cases: the intentional bullshitter is the murderer, the self-deceived talk-radio fan the negligent driver who kills while reading, and Newton the blameless driver beside whom the pedestrian darts, with the pejorative resting on the method or theory rather than the person. This methodology shift lets him keep Frankfurt's insight that how bullshit is produced matters while conceding Cohen's point that it can be unintentional, though he admits even philosophy's status may never be settled.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 16 "Chapter 2 - A Defense of Common Sense" — Concluding his essay, Kimbrough observes people call bullshit whenever their values are threatened, so the bottom-line businessman dismisses ethics talk and investigations of his dodgy accounting as bureaucratic bullshit, and the linguist may dismiss armchair conceptual analysis itself. He rejects a subjective definition of bullshit as whatever provokes disdain, endorsing Frankfurt's anti-subjectivist closer that 'sincerity itself is bullshit,' and concludes bullshit must be recognized and restricted to justifiable uses rather than eradicated. He closes with Orwell's advice from 'Politics and the English Language': simplify your English so that a stupid remark's stupidity is obvious even to yourself.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 17 "The Truth Matters" — Consuelo Preti lays out Frankfurt's indifference-to-truth account and G.A. Cohen's academic bullshit as disregard for meaning, then argues both leave out bullshit's third element: the audience it needs. Bullshit, she says, sells us on our own estimation of what matters, from the Dior handbag to the guy bullshitting his way into bed or tenure. Reviewing the James Frey affair and Oprah's initial claim that truth was irrelevant because the story inspired, she proposes G.E. Moore's uncompromising commitment to truth and meaning as the model for resisting bullshit in the street and the seminar room.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 18 "“What Exactly Do You Mean ”" — Preti dissects l'affaire Frey: if Frey intended to palm off invented events as memory, he lied and his publishers committed fraud, but if they did not care either way, it was bullshit, and what exposed the menace was Oprah's own avowal that it did not matter whether the story was true. She argues inspiration tied to an assumed true story is sabotaged by discovering it false, so Oprah's retraction ('I left the impression that the truth does not matter') shows bullshit nearly turned even her head. The strategy she draws is to turn bullshit's need to be believed against itself, and for an exemplar of resolute caring about truth she reaches to G.E. Moore.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 19 "Let’s Stop Bullshitting Ourselves" — Preti builds the Moore exemplar from biography: with Russell and Wittgenstein at Cambridge, Moore founded analytic philosophy, demolished Absolute Idealism in the 1899 'The Nature of Judgment,' and wrote Principia Ethica, which the Bloomsbury group treated as their religion. Russell's autobiography joke about the only lie Moore ever told and Woolf's 'tenacity of a bulldog' portrait of his passion for truth set up Keynes's description of Moore's method, 'What exactly do you mean?'. The key episode is Moore's public apology for losing patience with a question he took to be merely vexatious, showing that what Moore could not tolerate was precisely bullshit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 20 "Chapter 3 - The Pragmatics of Bullshit, Intelligently Designed" — Preti's conclusion deploys Moore's 'A Defence of Common Sense' against philosophers who answer 'Do you believe the earth has existed for many years past?' with 'It all depends on what you mean,' a view Moore called as profoundly mistaken as any can be. She extracts a practical anti-bullshit strategy: dogged Moorean insistence on clarity, since bullshit's scorn for truth must stay masked and needs us to be less inquisitive. Her 'paradox of bullshit' is that truth and meaning do not matter to bullshit but bullshit must make itself matter to us, so caring about the truth-false distinction puts it on a short leash.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 21 "The Example of Intelligent Design" — George Reisch opens his essay with Frankfurt's unsolved puzzle: if bullshitters are more dangerous to truth than liars, they should be punished more, yet we are more tolerant of them, a puzzle Frankfurt admitted on radio he really does not understand. He diagnoses the puzzle as a symptom that Frankfurt's definition took a wrong turn. The remedy requires distinguishing the semantic from the pragmatic analysis of language, and the new definition it yields will both cover Frankfurt's own examples and explain our tolerance of bullshit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 22 "A Definition of Bullshit—New and Improved!" — Reisch offers the Intelligent Design movement as a paradigm of bullshit Frankfurt could not have used in the 1980s: like advertisers and politicians, ID urgently needs public approval ('teach the controversy') and is trying to get away with something. He traces ID's descent from constitutionally defeated creation science through Philip Johnson's Darwin on Trial, showing how Johnson speaks of evidence and naturalism to scientists while telling evangelical audiences that the real enemy is cultural modernism's tolerance of promiscuity and atheism. Judge Jones's Kitzmiller ruling that ID is 'a mere re-labeling of creationism' confirms what the bullshit was covering.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 23 "The Truth in Bullshit" — If ID is bullshit, Reisch argues, Frankfurt's definition fails, because Johnson and his followers are not indifferent to truth; they are devoted to other, rotten truths about modernism and even to elevating regard for truth in the culture. Frankfurt's error was writing of 'the truth' as a single unitary thing everyone but the bullshitter agrees on, when our beliefs about how things really are are diverse and contradictory. Bullshitters conceal a commitment to other truths and an agenda inspired by them, since revealing those truths would be embarrassing, unpersuasive, or, as with ID, unconstitutional.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 24 "The Truth about Semantics" — Even Frankfurt's bull-session example (with its Animal House atom-of-a-fingernail bit) shows relaxed talk serving other truths: self-image, reputation, and whether the apple of one's eye is impressed. Detergent slogans and politicians' rolled-up sleeves likewise run two conversations at once, one overt (clean clothes, policy) and one concealed (self-image, likeability), each resting on truths the bullshitter takes quite seriously. Reisch's definition follows: bullshit is the orchestration of at least two engagements between bullshitter and bullshitee, one concealed within or downplayed alongside the other, so indifference to truth is absent or only partly in play.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 25 "Solving Frankfurt’s Puzzle, or, Baseball, Hot Dogs, Apple Pie, and Bullshit" — Reisch explains Frankfurt's blind spot through the historical neglect of pragmatics: even Carnap took for granted that any complete theory of language must include how language is used in context, yet analytic philosophy came to favor semantics, as the Cambridge Dictionary's twenty-six semantics entries against seven pragmatic ones attest. Since bullshit's essence lies in using speech to hidden purposes, it is an essentially pragmatic, not semantic, phenomenon, which also shows the Frankfurt-Cohen debate (truth versus meaning) is narrow. From the recipient's side, bullshit works best when its two coordinated concerns seem maximally unconnected, as when a science-education advocate turns out to be an evangelical in disguise.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 26 "The Case for Purism about Bullshit" — The pragmatic definition dissolves Frankfurt's puzzle: the liar sins against the semantics of truth, while the bullshitter sins against pragmatics, disguising the effect his speech is designed to have (advancing science education) behind another (promoting evangelical Christianity). We can safely ignore bullshit, as with the coworker's Darwin rants, because without a gullible audience it has no effect, unlike the lie about whether the office milk has soured. Reisch adds that Stephen Meyer's post-Kitzmiller defiance, Willy Loman's optimism, the robber in Dog Day Afternoon, and Mamet's Glengary Glen Ross salesmen show why we even sympathize with bullshitters clinging to their creations, and that our tolerance extends to the pluralism of beliefs bullshit exploits.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 27 "Chapter 4 - Bullshit and the Foibles of the Human Mind, or What the Masters of" — Reisch concludes that on the pragmatic definition there is less bullshit than 'Bullshit!'-slinging suggests: your partner announcing the relationship is over and a White House claim about an oil-rich nation eager for democracy are merely true or false announcements, not bullshit. Real bullshit is the partner engineering a blame-free breakup through talk of feeling smothered, or the claim that a dictator possesses nuclear weapons about to be used. He closes by comparing bullshit to a poem or symphony: a specific, artfully layered creation intelligently designed for pragmatic effect, which our casual use of the word obscures to the bullshitter's advantage.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 28 "Some Cognitive Foibles of the Human Mind" — Kenneth Taylor opens his essay on the debased stew of bullshit, propaganda, and spin in public discourse, arguing that in an open public square the bullshitting arts must become highly refined, whereas a totalitarian state can afford crude bludgeoning, and that the marketplace of ideas has not spontaneously driven out bad discourse. His central claim: purveyors cannot sell what we do not buy, so the fault lies partly in ourselves, in built-in architectural foibles of the mind that make it permanently susceptible to manipulation. bullshit works best when we do not recognize it, and susceptibility to comforting falsehood is rooted in the mind's very architecture.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 29 "Reclaiming the Public Square" — Taylor illustrates the mind's foibles with the Iraq war beliefs that held a vice-grip on believers long after disconfirming evidence, explained by confirmation bias and information cocoons like Fox News and talk radio. He walks through the classic framing experiments, the avian-flu programs that are identical when described as '2,000 saved' or '4,000 die,' showing how politicians Smith and Jones exploit framing to jointly mislead voters, and the Wason selection task, where subjects fail on abstract cards but succeed when reframed as bartender cheater-detection. Citing Stephen Pinker on evolved, domain-specific modules, he concludes that whoever controls the frame may control all, which is exactly the leverage the masters of the dark arts exploit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 30 "Chapter 5 - Bullshit and Personality" — Taylor draws the hopeful and bleak conclusions: our minds are fine instruments for hunter-gatherer information environments, but the modern mismatch between savannah-designed cognition and deliberately framed misinformation explains why bull, spin, and propaganda abound. The masters of the dark arts are now astute students of cognitive foibles and wield means of persuasion with unprecedented reach. His two-front response is education that instills suspicion of comforting falsehoods and the habit of re-framing, plus widening access to the means of public representation now monopolized by a self-serving elite, because 'only those who seek more than bullshit can drive it out.'
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 31 "Does the Bullshitter Pay Attention to the Truth" — Sara Bernal distinguishes public, interpersonal, and private bullshit (bullshitting oneself) and argues that in an era rich in public bullshit like the Iraq war, private bullshit should not be overlooked, since it is at the core of personality disorders. Departing rapidly from Frankfurt, she rejects his claim that bullshit is essentially unconnected to a concern with truth, proposing instead that core cases of bullshit have a stronger connection to truth than Frankfurt allows. Applying her revised analysis to personality disorders will, she claims, explain why their core features produce social difficulties.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 32 "Two Modes of Bullshit" — Against Frankfurt's picture of the bullshitter who pays no attention to truth at all, Bernal argues the typical bullshitter is strongly connected to truth via a desire to obscure a specific part of it, conscious or not. Her prototype is the undergraduate who, knowing she has nothing thoughtful to say on an assigned essay, throws up a screen of verbiage, sometimes with malice aforethought, sometimes through a barely conscious motive to get an undeserved A. Unlike the liar she never denies the hidden truth directly but works indirectly, through pompous tone, reluctance to get to the point, and windiness, or simply by distracting the audience.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 35 "Bullshit and Personality Disorders" — Bernal gives the Bush administration's yellowcake-from-Niger and Saddam-9/11 red herrings as distraction bullshit concealing the antecedent intention to invade Iraq, then states five features of her two-part conception: the bullshitter must attend to the one 'target' truth she wants to hide, bullshit shades into lying as awareness increases, unconscious motives do the work, non-verbal means suffice (the Newport ads), and self-bullshitting is a species of self-deception. Split-brain patients who confabulate 'that funny machine' to explain unaccountable giggling at a picture shown only to the right hemisphere ground the claim that unconscious motives are respectable neuroscience. Her account, unlike Frankfurt's, applies in psychiatry.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 37 "Some Examples of Bullshit in Personality Disorders" — The essay defines personality disorder via DSM-IV as an enduring, inflexible pattern deviating from cultural expectations, and catalogs the ten disorders in three clusters: the erratic (antisocial, with the Enron crew and glib con artists as textbook cases; borderline; histrionic, from the undergrad who visits professors' office hours to talk about herself; narcissistic), the anxious (avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive), and the eccentric (schizoid, schizotypal, paranoid). The clue to where bullshit lurks: wherever the afflicted is out of touch with some key aspect of reality or where her stock behavior leads others to false beliefs. The disorders' rigidity makes life 'a bad one-act play that repeats again and again.'
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 38 "Bullshit and Philosophy" — The essay works through the disorders case by case: the antisocial's glib charm implicates 'I am not a nasty piece of work' without saying it, the borderline's suicidal gestures implicate 'life without you is not worth living' that her contempt belies, the histrionic's shallow opinions and sexual provocativeness implant false impressions of depth, and the compensating narcissist's charade of superiority hides a dimly glimpsed core of low self-esteem. Self-directed bullshit follows: the fanatic paranoid's superhero fantasies deny that she is not extraordinary, the phobic avoidant displaces anxiety onto elevators and dogs, the self-deserting avoidant escapes into fantasy, dependents distract themselves from doubts about their caregiver, and the obsessive-compulsive buries big-picture anxiety in rules and lists.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 39 "Perfect Partners Bullshit and Distorted Social Perceptions" — Surveying the catalog, the essay finds bullshit strategems that are first-rank symptoms in eight of ten disorders, quoting Frankfurt's 'each of us contributes his share' to observe that pathological personalities are notably generous contributors. Bullshitting is notably absent from the eccentric cluster: the schizoid's flat affect removes the pain-avoidance motive, and schizoids and schizotypals lack the mindreading facility successful bullshit requires. Other-bullshitting (mostly falsehood-implicating) marks the erratic cluster, self-bullshitting (mostly distraction) the anxious, and the essay closes by stressing that the disordered person is afflicted, her bullshit a personal tragedy as well as an infliction.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 40 "The Threat Posed by Bullshit" — The essay's final section argues distorted social perception and bullshit are perfect partners that reinforce each other: the paranoiac imagining insults, the histrionic inhabiting a world of admirers, and the borderline seeing abandonment everywhere each see less of social reality, supplying more 'easy targets' to obscure without the sting of conscience that aware deception provokes. The compensating narcissist's glimmering of her charade and the self-deserting avoidant's glimmering of her escape show how dim awareness eases bullshitting. The street runs both ways, since hiding parts of social truth from yourself further impairs your perception, so some disorder bullshit is causally downstream of distortion while self-bullshitting deepens it.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 41 "Chapter 6 - Performing Bullshit and the Post-Sincere Condition" — Concluding an essay on personality disorders, this chapter argues that pathological personalities (the antisocial, borderline, dependent, paranoiac) are especially good bullshitters and that their bullshit and distorted perceptions are what wreck their social relationships, since good relationships thrive on truth as much as on truthfulness. Against Frankfurt's claim that bullshit is the greater enemy of truth because indulging it erodes attention to reality, the author counters that the bullshitter does track truth at some level; bullshit's distinctive danger is that, unlike lying, it can be unconscious, so the sting of conscience never checks the habit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 43 "Shitty Attitudes On the Use and Misuse of Bullshit in Life" — This mini-essay opens by parodying a puffing university mission statement, aspiring to be 'one of the world's best philosophy essays' in the UBC mold. It then sets the agenda: Frankfurt left unanswered why our attitude toward bullshit is generally more benign than our attitude toward lying, and never considered bullshit's rhetorical uses and misuses - the two gaps the rest of the essay fills.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 44 "Bullshit as a Condition of Life" — Reworking Frankfurt's Fania Pascal anecdote (Wittgenstein's disgusted 'You don't know what a dog that has been run over feels like'), the chapter argues that the bullshit that earns the retort 'That's bullshit!' is speech whose truth is irrelevant and which aims to evoke a positive attitude toward the speaker - hypochondriac pain complaints, boilerplate about graduate training in grant proposals, praise of the Dean to pass a hiring motion. It separates this from bullshit-as-entertainment and from courtesy conventions like thanking the gift-giving aunt, concluding against Frankfurt that pretentiousness is constitutive of at least this central kind of bullshit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 45 "The World as Will to Bullshit" — This section answers Frankfurt's exercise about benignity: bullshit is 'dishonesty without tears' because whole genres - grant proposals, Fourth of July oratory, letters of reference - generically require performative values everyone knows count for nothing, like compulsory figures in figure skating. Rejecting free-riding as the origin of bullshit genres (bullshit letters get found out), it explains the reference letter instead by its multiple interested audiences: the writer must satisfy the student, the admissions committee, and her own conscience at once, and only the right dose of bullshit accomplishes that.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 46 "Overcoming Overwhelming Bullshit" — The chapter indicts an expanding class of 'performative bullshit': the video-store service pledge and the UBC mission statement, where a commitment is treated as fulfilled in the very act of being made, so no complaint can even be lodged. George W. Bush's fabricated WMD case for the Iraq war shows the political version - an argument counts as good simply because it was offered as the reason, and when the intelligence proved false another reason was fabricated. In such a world sincerity, irony, and even cynicism become impossible, since only pseudo-motives remain, lacking even sincere self-interest.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 47 "Chapter 7 - The Importance of Being Earnest A Pragmatic Approach to Bullshitting" — Closing the essay, this section argues the bullshit world is inherently stable rather than unstable: the administrator whose whole professional being is appending mission-talk to whatever the university already does is its emblem. The one live remedy is the Jon Stewart gambit - The Daily Show's openly fake news outperforming 'serious' sources, showing by self-consciously flouting the conventions of truth-telling what those conventions were for - and beyond that, actually taking a mission statement seriously enough to rethink higher education's values rather than settle, undeserving, for bullshit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 48 "Two Tauroscatological Schools" — De Waal's opening salvo: Frankfurt analyzed the concept of bullshit by ordinary language, but the interesting question is the intention with which bullshitting is produced. He announces a contrast between bullshitting and genuine inquiry, and blames bullshit's prevalence partly on a lost confidence that figuring out how things really are is possible or worthwhile.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 49 "The Epistemic Imperative" — Building on G.A. Cohen's split of bullshit thinking into a structuralist school (bullshit is an intrinsic feature of products, e.g. texts unclarifiably unclear whatever the author intended) and an intentionalist school (Frankfurt: bullshit is the act done with indifference to truth), the chapter defends intentionalism against the 'insight problem'. The sham astrologer whose Tarot-based celebrity-death prediction happens to come true, and Perry's undergraduates who aced an exam they bullshitted, show that a claim stays bullshit until someone not bullshitting has affirmed it and thereby transformed it into knowledge - just as one person's trash is another's treasure without the chair itself changing.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 50 "The Problem with Bullshitting" — Against the bullshitter the chapter recruits Peirce: genuine inquiry is defined not by method or results but by the attitude of truly wanting true answers, so homicide detectives, philologists, and car mechanics all count as scientists in this sense.
