Bullshitting is a free-rider riding the bus of real inquiry - even the bullshitter wants his doctor not to bullshit - and the chapter formulates an epistemic imperative: proceed on the hope that there is a true answer and act from the desire to find it, with fallibilism, not skepticism, the viable stance (the passenger who can occupy any vacant seat cannot occupy them all).
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 51 "So Why Bullshit" — Violations of the epistemic imperative are sorted into Peirce's 'sham reasoning' (the creationist who reasons only to prop up a fixed conclusion), Haack's 'fake reasoning' (corporate-funded research, vote-seeking politicians, the temporary-insanity plea), and the skeptic's premature 'we'll never know' - none of which is bullshitting, which is precisely not caring about truth, like the sales clerk praising shoes at random. Even philosophy can slide into bullshitting when, per Rorty, it becomes 'carrying on the conversation' with truth as what your peers let you get away with; and brainstorming differs from a bull session because brainstormers actually want to discover something.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 52 "II - The Bull by the Horns" — Why do people bullshit? Because liberal democracy, heir to the Cartesian rejection of authority and the Enlightenment's think-for-yourself ideal, expects instant opinions on everything from people detached enough that nothing they say makes a difference; and because a failed search for certainty breeds prophylactic pessimism about inquiry itself. The cure is earnestness - scientists take colleagues' results on trust - though the chapter concedes defensible cases: the formulaic 'It's nice to see you!' as fake reasoning for civility, and friends horsing around for fun.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 55 "2 Two Species of Bullshit" — Cohen's autobiographical preface: his youthful struggle with Althusserian French Marxism of the 1960s - interpellation, contradiction and overdetermination - taught him that writings attracting reverent attention can still be bullshit, a lesson sealed when his Marxist discussion group took the name Non-Bullshit Marxism Group, 'Marxism without the shit of the bull'. He also diagnoses the psychology (cognitive dissonance reduction plus adaptive preference formation) by which readers of rebarbative texts overvalue the banal sense they finally extract.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 56 "3 Bullshit and Lying" — Via the OED's two entries, the chapter finds that 'bullshit' denotes two different things: nonsense or rubbish (output-centered - the shit wears the trousers) and insincere talk (producer-centered - the bull wears the trousers, Frankfurt's kind). Frankfurt's fault is not error but generality: he cast his account of one flower as the 'essence' of the whole garden, ignoring the academically more significant kind that is defined without any reference to a producer's state of mind.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 57 "4 Bullshit as Unclarifiable Unclarity" — Cohen's main critique: Frankfurt identifies the liar by his goal (misleading about reality) but the bullshitter only at the level of tactic (indifference to the truth of what he says), leaving the bullshitter no distinctive goal - so advertisers and politicians, Frankfurt's own paradigm bullshitters, actually pursue the liar's goal and their bullshitting and lying coincide. Freud's favorite Pinsk/Minsk joke shows tactic and goal can come apart (deceiving by telling the truth), and the Fourth of July orator, contra Frankfurt, might care very much that the audience believe things about the Founding Fathers.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 58 "5 Bullshit as Product and Bullshit as Process" — Cohen's positive account: bullshit is a feature of texts, paradigmatically 'unclarifiable unclarity' - discourse that cannot be rendered clear without ceasing to be a version of what was said, which is why the way to defend Hegel or Heidegger is to show their texts make sense, not that they cared about truth. A sufficient test is the negation sign: if adding or subtracting it makes no difference to plausibility, as with Sokal's hoax physics, the text is bullshit - though suggestively valuable poetry is spared. 'Bullshitter' then splits into a dispositional reading and an aim reading, only the latter of which always bullshits when producing bullshit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 59 "Chapter 9 - The Unity of Bullshit" — Cohen concludes that because bullshit can be emitted innocently - even by honest acolytes - the Sokal-style struggle against academic bullshit must target the visible product rather than the producer's hidden intentions, lest innocent traffickers be slandered as insincere or deliberately obscure. Fun as it is to write 'bullshit' over and over in an academic article, the bullshitter/bullshit distinction matters because the justice of the polemic depends on it.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 60 "No Bullshit, Please, We’re Austrian" — Hardcastle proposes to settle the Frankfurt-Cohen quarrel by adding logical positivism to the mix: the Vienna Circle's war on metaphysics was the 1920s-30s' great anti-bullshit program, and both Frankfurt's negligence-of-truth and Cohen's unclarifiable unclarity have precedents in it. Laura Penny's Your Call Is Important to Us supplies the moral heat ('when you fuck with English, you are money-changing in my temple'), while the summary of both positions - the liar needs the truth, the bullshitter does not give a hoot - sets up the Carnap chapters.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 61 "A Little Carnap in Everyone" — Carnap's 'Overcoming Metaphysics through Logical Analysis of Language' supplies the unification: his verificationism renders the invented word 'teavy' meaningless for the same reason Cohen's texts are unclarifiably unclear, while Heidegger's 'The nothing noths' exemplifies the pseudo-sentence whose utterance expresses disregard for meaning - Frankfurt-style bullshitting. The 'toovy' example drives the point home: once a term's synonymy with 'quadrangular' is fixed, professing a further hidden meaning reveals a speaker who never intended to convey information at all.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 62 "The Unity of Bullshit" — Meaning, for Carnap, is bearing the right deductive relations to other claims - exactly Cohen's insight that clarity is relational, so that 'clarifying' an unclarifiable text mangles it into something unrecognizable. Carnap's diagnosis of why metaphysics flourishes - metaphysicians express a general attitude toward life (Lebenseinstellung), better expressed through art, and mistake it for a state of affairs - explains bullshit's ubiquity and tolerance; but the metaphysician who knows he says nothing, like Heidegger after Carnap called him on it, is Frankfurt's bullshitter pure and simple.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 63 "Chapter 10 - Raising the Tone Definition, Bullshit, and the Definition of Bullshit" — The unification: Frankfurt's intentionalist bull and Cohen's structuralist shit are two sides of one thing, since a language amenable to misuse meets the bullshitter's ends halfway. The response is gun control for language - not Carnap's ideal language, but shared responsibility for English in our presence, from writing letters to casting votes - ending with Otto Neurath's anti-pseudorationalist insistence that the world's shape reflects our own choices rather than reasons beyond our control: it really is up to us.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 65 "A Caricature History of Semantics" — The chapter christens Frankfurt's innovation 'semantic negligence' on the legal model: the deceptive bullshitter has a duty of care to truth and breaches it without intending the resulting deception, which is why lying (intentional) is more culpable, yet bullshit more insidious because it degrades the commitment to truth on which public discourse depends. Terry Pratchett's characters who applaud 'any man who can tell an outrageous whopper with a gleam in his eye' mark the complicit bull session - bullshit deceives only when it escapes the session and masquerades as ordinary assertion.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 67 "Broadening the Analysis" — Stevenson's persuasive definition - changing a term's descriptive meaning while keeping its emotive force - is restated in Fregean terms as changing sense or reference while representing tone as fixed, yielding a sixteen-fold table of definitional moves (PD, PQD, and beyond). Semantic negligence then grades PDs: the aphoristic 'Conservatism is true socialism' deceives no one, but the definer who hides an argument inside a definition gains rhetorical advantage while risking that his audience endorses conclusions they were never given a fair chance to appraise - analogous to bullshit rather than lying.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 70 "Bullshit and Philosophy" — Flew's No-True-Scotsman Move - retreating from 'No Scotsman takes sugar with his porridge' to 'No true Scotsman...' when Hamish MacTavish of Inverness falsifies it - is analyzed as a redefinition that converts a bold, falsifiable claim into a vacuous necessary truth. Because the two statements look and sound alike, confusing them (from carelessness as easily as deceit) is semantic negligence, and pressing on as if the original claim still stood is classic Frankfurt bullshit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 77 "Chapter 11 - Different Kinds and Aspects of Bullshit" — Closing chapter 10's circle: Frankfurt's definition of 'bullshit' is itself a persuasive definition of case d - it changes the term's sense and reference while keeping the pejorative tone, as the well-meant 'Help is on its way' to the critically injured shows. Because Frankfurt argues explicitly for his departures from conventional usage, his definition is semantically diligent rather than negligent, though Cohen's complaint that it omits academic bullshit remains to be answered - with which Chapter 11 opens.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 78 "Harry Frankfurt on Bullshit" — Maes and Schaubroeck open on the bookstore irony: Frankfurt's slim bestseller On Bullshit shelved beside Chakra Balancing Kit, The Hidden Messages in Water Crystals, and Astrology: A Cosmic Science - almost as if placed there to illustrate the very bullshit Frankfurt diagnosed as the most salient feature of our culture. They then introduce Cohen's admiring complaint that Frankfurt examined 'just one flower in the lush garden of bullshit', teeing up the academic kind Cohen will define.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 79 "A Different Take on Bullshit" — A faithful reconstruction of Frankfurt: the bullshitter is a slovenly craftsman whose laxity concerns truth rather than detail - spin doctors control every tiny thing except whether what they say is true. The bull session shows indifference alone is not enough, since bullshit adds the pretence that hides that indifference (the Fourth of July orator misrepresents his own state of mind, not American history), whence Frankfurt's conclusion that bullshit is the greater enemy of truth - and the announcement that all three claims (unconcern, concealment, blameworthiness) will be contested.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 80 "A Different Kind of Bullshit" — The Pascal anecdote returns to undermine Frankfurt: Wittgenstein's disgust at 'I feel just like a dog that has been run over' involves no fakery, so pretence is not an essential ingredient of bullshit - mere indifference to truth suffices, as the hypothetical politician who openly stops caring would show. Bullshit emerges as often benign: Ishiguro's butler Stevens in The Remains of the Day comes to see bantering as 'the key to human warmth', Nagel's polite 'How nice to see you!' is convention-governed and no deception, and Wilde's epigrams - nearly all bullshit - explain why our attitude toward bullshit is softer than toward lying.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 81 "III - It’s All Around Us" — Cohen's product-based kind (unclarifiable unclarity, probed by the negation-sign test) is summarized, and the chapter asks whether Frankfurt-bullshit and Cohen-bullshit exhaust the lush garden. They do not: pseudoscience like astrology, chakra balancing, and bogus healing is a third, damaging kind - its practitioners sincerely believe (failing Frankfurt's indifference test) and predict specifically and clearly (failing Cohen's unclarity test) - so insensitivity to evidence and fallacious reasoning must be central to its analysis, better to be vaguely right than precisely wrong.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 83 "Bullshitting and Lying in Politics" — Opening Mark Evans's Chapter 12: Frankfurt's claim that democracy especially breeds bullshit, since it charges every citizen with having opinions about everything - the 'Frankfurt thesis' that citizens do not care about truth. It is contrasted with the 'cynicism thesis' (citizens do not care about politics, out of well-founded disillusion with a system that fails to deliver), and both are framed by the objection as old as Plato that political understanding is an expertise we cannot all share - theses argued about, not against, democracy.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 84 "The Myth of the ‘Well-Informed’ Citizen" — Mark Evans opens the book's political section by insisting that politicians mostly produce bullshit rather than lies in Frankfurt's strict sense: lying requires knowing and concealing the truth, while the Bush administration's WMD case for invading Iraq shows truth-indifference, with post-hoc 'rejustifications' (humanitarian intervention, democratisation, Saddam-9/11 hints) spun as needed. Using G.A. Cohen's distinction between aim-bullshitters and disposition-bullshitters, it reads Winston Smith's routinized rewriting of The Times in Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four as falsehood that slides from lying into bullshit, since the Party aims to destroy the very true/false distinction. Totalitarian regimes (Havel's 'living in truth') thus embed themselves not in a web of lies but in a morass of bullshit insulated from any possibly refuting facts.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 85 "‘Dumbing-Up’ Some Distortions of Democratic Equality" — Evans argues that democratic citizens do their own share of Frankfurt-bullshitting about politics: because electoral democracy cannot admit how complex politics really is, it institutionalizes the fictional ideal of the 'well-informed' citizen, obliging voters to hold over-simplified views and politicians to pander to them. Campaigning forces candidates into dodges like the 'politics of distraction' and the empty promise to be 'a different sort of politician', producing 'Governor Schwarzenegger Syndrome' and opening space for dangerous demagogues and fundamentalisms. Following Churchill, the chapter concludes that this citizen-side bullshit vindicates the cynicism thesis only partially and gives no reason to reject democracy as 'the worst form of government except for all the others'.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 86 "Philosophy versus Bullshit" — The chapter claims that 'equal respect' in modern democracies has been distorted into a 'dumbing-up' relativism — 'I'm valid, you're valid' — which conflates the equal right to voice opinions with their equal intellectual merit and so leaves nothing that counts as bullshit. It illustrates this through the 'democratization of expertise' and management-speak ('downsizing', 'mission statements'), which mimics profundity while evading awkward facts, and it tests and rejects the quasi-Nietzschean ressentiment story of timid citizens dragging discourse down to a common denominator. To get the full measure of the phenomenon it expands Frankfurt's and Cohen's typologies into seven kinds of bullshit, adding clarifiable unclarity, plain rubbish, irretrievable speculation, pretension, and evasion.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 87 "Chapter 13 - Political Bullshit and the Stoic Story of Self" — Evans concludes that the antidote to political bullshit is a discursive culture trained in Socratic skills of self-examination — citizens taught to recognize how their own views may be imperfect and how to refine them — together with the analytic-philosophical style his Oxford tutor called 'a very good bullshit detector'. Experts may lead debates by their greater factual knowledge and critical acumen, but the debates must stay democratically inclusive rather than become an elite monopoly. Citing G.A. Cohen, he warns that too much fashionable philosophy disparages truth and so itself produces bullshit, and that using the ubiquity of bullshit to justify the cynicism thesis's crippling inertia would be potentially catastrophic.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 89 "Stories Shape Our Feelings" — Vanessa Neumann sets out a third strategy for analyzing bullshit, beside Frankfurt's agent-centered and G.A. Cohen's content-centered definitions: studying the mechanism of bullshit, the speaker-listener relation through which it works in political discourse. Bullshit need not be false — even true statements can be non-germane or obfuscatory — and it serves two purposes: depicting the speaker as desirable ('I'm one of you') and targeting groups ('they are different from us, so we should treat them like this'). Its key trick is moral language without moral commitment, as when a politician condemns a rival's corporate free trip without explaining why it is wrong, scoring points while preserving wiggle room for future favors of their own.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 91 "Chapter 14 - Bullshit at the Interface of Science and Policy Global Warming," — The chapter dissects 'we are waging a war on terror' word by word: the inclusive 'we' conscripts the listener, 'war' triggers unquestioning patriotism, and 'terror' — an emotion, rather than 'terrorists' or 'terrorism' — keeps the enemy suitably vague, a bogeyman Other to hunt. The phrase is bullshit not because fighting terrorism is wrong but because it replaces the thought and debate that democratic policy and military decisions require with fear management, and militant jihadists' 'God's will' rhetoric works the same way, never explaining how bombing or torturing the uninvolved will end fear. Both sides use bullshit to supply identity and purpose while evading genuine moral justification, which degrades our capacity to be moved by ideas.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 92 "Bullshit of the Isolated Fact" — Heather Douglas opens her chapter on science advice by framing the problem with Plato's parable of the stargazer as expert navigator for the ship of state in the Republic, tracing the debate from excluding pseudoscience through 'junk science' to 'politicized science'. She identifies two kinds of bullshit at the science-policy interface: true-but-misleading statements that exploit technical complexity to confuse the public about uncertainty, and appeals to a nonexistent universal standard of 'sound science' that actually smuggle in judgments about the consequences of error. Remedies include constant vigilance and reframing debates around the explicit weighing of evidence, uncertainty, and the risks of getting things wrong.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 93 "Bullshit of Universal Standards" — The chapter explains 'bullshit of the isolated fact' through the climate-change debate: skeptics like Robert Balling and Fred Singer repeatedly cited the 1940-1975 cooling trend as incompatible with human-caused warming while omitting the aerosol research — confirmed when models correctly predicted the cooling after Mt. Pinatubo's 1991 eruption — which shows sulfate scrubbing had been masking the greenhouse signal. Likewise the satellite-versus-ground temperature discrepancy, which skeptics took as disproof, dissolved once instrument errors were re-examined. Repeating an isolated fact after its debunking has been publicized in Science or National Academy reports is, with Frankfurt, to reveal oneself unconcerned with the truth — willing to spread bullshit to win.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 94 "Combatting the Two Kinds of Bullshit" — Douglas argues that 'universal standards bullshit' — the assumption that evidence must meet one threshold before it counts as scientific — comes from textbook schooling and has no warrant: there is no such standard, and we shouldn't want one. She shows how it distorts debate on all sides, from Bush administration uncertainty claims to Michael Gough's Popper-inspired insistence that climate models cannot be tested, and argues that whether evidence suffices always depends on the risks of error — the gas-gauge warning versus the bomb in your car. Genuine politicization (suppressing evidence, firing researchers) must be condemned, but deciding how much uncertainty is acceptable is an ineliminably political and ethical judgment.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 95 "Chapter 15 - Rhetoric Is Not Bullshit" — Douglas concludes that the two kinds of bullshit need different remedies. Isolated-fact bullshit — Fred Singer's commentaries resting on selective omission and emphasis — can only be met with vigilance, since the public forum must remain open and even its spreaders may not grasp the nature of their claims. Universal-standards bullshit, by contrast, can be permanently undermined once we recognize there are no such standards: asking instead about the strength of evidence and the risks of error, and getting used to expert disagreement, would deflate the persuasive power of a single isolated fact.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 96 "The Problem (and Politics) of Rhetoric" — David Tietge opens his defense of rhetoric with the aphorism that rhetoric isn't devious and untrustworthy — those are features reserved for language itself — and reports a semester-long count in which 156 of 157 media uses of 'rhetoric' were pejorative, the sole exception being George Carlin telling Jon Stewart that a comedian is essentially a rhetorician who unpacks how words mean. He traces rhetoric's decline from its honored place in the Trivium of the Seven Liberal Arts, notes the societal paradox that we condemn 'bullshit' yet richly reward lawyers, politicians, and advertising executives for producing it, and promises to dissolve the crude truth/falsity dichotomy that fuels the identification of rhetoric with bullshit.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 99 "Chapter 16 - Just Bullshit" — Tietge argues that postmodernism, far from denying objective reality, supplies a vocabulary for how language and interpretation shape small-t truths, and that rhetoric — Kenneth Burke's 'logology', words used to talk about words — is the discipline uniquely built to study this; hence rhetoric and bullshit are 'not even distant cousins'. He concedes Frankfurt's 'talk without knowing what he is talking about' catches genuine bullshit, like the student paper opener 'In today's society, there are many things that people have different and similar opinions about', and allows that 'salesman syndrome' rhetoric can be bullshit when its pitch is too transparent to persuade anyone. His remedy is to learn rhetoric — through hypothetical situations, deconstructing model essays, and keeping a commonplace book — since navigating the gray area between Truth and bullshit without understanding how language works leaves us to avoid the pitfalls by sheer chance.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 100 "Bullshit as a Call to Open-Mindedness" — Steve Fuller opens by asking whether bullshit detection coarsens the detector: Nietzsche and H.L. Mencken embraced the debunker's role (Mencken coining 'bunk'), while Ibsen's The Wild Duck and Hedda Gabler dramatize the need for a 'life lie', and detectors who find bullshit everywhere slide from nihilism into dogmatism. He re-reads bullshit as sophistry — the Sophists taught that securing your audience's belief is the only knowledge you need, against Socrates's attack and Plato's coining of 'rhetoric' to demonize them — and faults Frankfurt for calling the bullshitter 'indifferent' to truth when the accomplished bullshitter must be a keen student of what people tend to regard as true. The Sokal affair and Benjamin Franklin's 'economical with the truth' lead to his Kantian mapping of bullshitters (rationalists selecting among already-imaginable alternatives) against bullshit detectors (empiricists demanding evidence), which the scientific method will dialectically synthesize.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 101 "Wittgenstein Ultimate Bullshit Detector—or Bullshitter" — Fuller argues that mastering a discipline converts critics into loyal insiders — Thomas Kuhn's 'normal science' enshrines the tendency, cognitive dissonance explains it, and Blaise Pascal's wager is the general model of betting on a way of life that makes you receptive to its confirming signs. Against this he sets the Protestant tradition of Luther's conscience, 'playing it by ear', which like the Sophists concedes that reality rarely yields yes-or-no answers — the gap we fill being bullshit — and he frames the dispute as realism versus antirealism, reading Frankfurt's On Bullshit as an ad hominem attack on antirealists. He then re-examines Frankfurt's star witness: Wittgenstein's rebuke of Fania Pascal for saying she felt 'like a dog that has been run over' now looks like a spectacular lack of imagination, since evolutionary psychology, being forged at that very moment, has been narrowing the human-animal mental gap ever since.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 102 "Bullshit as Deferred Epistemic Gratification" — The chapter reverses Frankfurt's verdict: Wittgenstein may himself have been a grandmaster of bullshit who practiced 'ventriloquism', speaking through the authority of ordinary language and 'paradigm case' examples, and whose scolding of Fania Pascal strikes some readers today like a priest fussing over a parishioner's impure thoughts. His bullshit was backward-looking ('you already know this'), unlike the forward-looking promissory bullshit of Galileo, whose deferred vindication Paul Feyerabend used to argue that the Papal Inquisitors were originally justified in their skepticism. Ernest Gellner's ostracized diagnosis — that Wittgenstein fed off British class anxiety most clearly marked in language use — is resisted both because careers ride on his authority and because his erratic 'idiot savant' persona keeps bullshit from sticking to him.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 103 "The Scientific Method as a Search for the Justice in Bullshit" — Fuller portrays the bullshitter as the consummate hypocrite, bluffing from behind genuine uncertainty and exploiting the sophistic principle that controlling the moment of decision controls its outcome — calling the question when the balance of arguments favors you. Since we can rarely audit anyone's track record, epistemology leans on 'trust', 'witness' and 'testimony', read optimistically through Thomas Reid's divinely guaranteed common sense or, à la Kierkegaard, malignly as cowardly delegation of belief; either way 'reliability', which papers over the gap between evidence and belief, is itself a bullshit concept. He then analogizes the epistemic economy of evidence to the moral economy of sensation: as utilitarianism defers immediate gratification (taxation insuring against discounting our future selves), so the bullshitter's imperviousness to current evidence-weightings is prudence — an 'affirmative action' for weaker-evidenced positions that may prove the better bet in the fullness of time.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 104 "Our Distinguished Panel of Incomparable Geniuses" — Fuller's finale casts Francis Bacon's scientific method as an inquisitorial trial designed to manage bullshit: everyone may produce it, provided a third-party judge frames a 'crucial experiment' that decides between the parties — a vision only partially realized by the Royal Society and later positivism, and tempered by Karl Popper's open-society point that all may bullshit to their heart's content given agreement on how to clean up after it. He tests the model on the Lomborg affair (initially found 'scientifically dishonest', then acquitted on appeal because politicized research is the environmental norm), on Zola's J'Accuse and Galileo's vindication in Newton's Principia as productive bullshit, and on his own service as expert witness: McLean v. Arkansas cut through creationist and evolutionist bullshit with a neutral definition of science, while Kitzmiller v. Dover adopted a 'methodological naturalism' custom-built to exclude Intelligent Design — justice losing out to the side whose bullshit is piled higher and deeper.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 15 "Wishing and Dogmatism" — Matthew Pierlott argues Colbert the satirist conflates two things his character, Stephen, merges: truthiness (trusting gut and heart over external authorities like dictionaries) and bullshit in Frankfurt's exact sense - speech indifferent to truth, which Pierlott finds in Hillary Clinton's dismissal of economists on the gas-tax holiday and likens to Steve Careill's habitual pleasantries versus Jon Stewart's honesty and Stephen's lies. He defends gut and heart as evidence-bearing tools - knowing a candidate's 'heart' from character evidence (the Westmoreland Ten Commandments interview), gut intuitions as unconsciously processed experience, and choosing which of the two Cheneys (1994 quagmire prophet or 2003 liberators booster) to trust - so in an information-saturated democracy truthiness is a necessary part of any orientation toward truth. The real enemy is dogmatism, the 'Dark Side of Truthiness' that cuts off future evidence, while wishful thinking kept modest (optimism that people are honest) can even be beneficial, a Jamesian willing-to-believe.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 30 "18. Superman the Super Dick" — Modeled on Harry Frankfurt's analysis of 'bullshit,' the chapter defines a 'dick' as someone who willfully disregards others' needs, and argues Superman qualifies: he lets crimes proceed while he works at the Daily Planet or hunts vending-machine change, although the SuperBat storyline (Superman/Batman #53-56) shows a briefly super-powered Batman clearing every city's crime in a single night. Applying Peter Singer's famine-and-affluence argument - the penny that saves a life, the ten-cent polio vaccine - the chapter contends that saving at little or no cost to oneself is obligatory rather than supererogatory, so Superman's convenience-first choices make him a 'Super Dick.' Batman, who risks his mortal life seeking out strangers to save, does what he can and therefore escapes the charge.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 25 "Trust and Truth" — Kellen builds successive definitions of lying through ATLA cases: Aang's 'Bonzu Pippinpaddleopsicopolis' alias, non-linguistic disguises versus Toph's 'I'm blind!' mere misleading, brainwashed Jet whose false statements are not lies ('Lake Laogai'), and Azula's battleship metaphor ('The Beach'), arriving at Carson's warranting contexts to count the Dai Li's 'There is no war in Ba Sing Se' and Azula's '400-foot-tall purple platypus bear' as Sorensen's bald-faced lies told without intent to deceive. Frankfurt's bullshit explains Aunt Wu's fortunetelling, and the conclusion is political: bald-faced lies corrode the trust on which communities rest, so we must refuse to live in a real-world Ba Sing Se.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 25 "Trust and Truth" — Kellen builds successive definitions of lying from ATLA cases: Aang's invented Jin Wei and Wei Jin story in 'The Great Divide' is a plain lie, Toph's 'How could I possibly play? I'm blind!' merely misleads, brainwashed Jet's false statements are no lie because he believes them, and Azula's '400-foot-tall purple platypus bear' breaks the intent-to-deceive requirement. That prepares the diagnosis of Ba Sing Se: the pet-shop owner's 'That would be illegal' and the 'There is no war in Ba Sing Se' mantra are Sorensen's bald-faced lies, undisguised and not meant to deceive, countable as lies only via Carson's warranting contexts. Aunt Wu's fortunes illustrate Frankfurtian bullshit, indifference to truth, and the chapter closes on how such lies corrode the trust communities are built on.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 15 "Noble Lies, Noble Propaganda" — McKinnon distinguishes lying (asserting what you believe false) from Frankfurtian bullshit (indifference to truth) and argues Andrew Ryan's propaganda, from 'Is a man not entitled to the sweat of his brow?' to the smuggler scare, is closer to bullshit than lying: it aims at controlling citizens' behavior, not at fooling them about facts. Frankfurt's warning that habitual bullshitters lose the ability to discern truth is borne out by Ryan's own audio diary ('have I become so convinced by my own beliefs that I have stopped seeing the truth?'). Yet the chapter defends 'noble' warranted assertions: Ryan's nostalgia lie to Jack about family and friends is told so Jack will discover the truth of what he is, showing that some propaganda aimed at the hearer's truth is not morally problematic.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 20 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Blessing and Marren mine Stewart's two interviews with Harry Frankfurt to work out the lie/bullshit distinction: liars like Edwards, Weiner and Clinton know and care about the truth they distort, while bullshitters, from Travelodge PR stunts to subprime lenders, are indifferent to truth in service of selling, which is why Frankfurt calls bullshit the more corrosive force. They take up Stewart's Socratic questioning of whether political spin is a subset of bullshit, and answer that spinners, unlike bullshitters, must know the truth in order to color it, making spin closer to lying in attitude, tolerated because Spin Alley agrees not to call bullshit on it. Documenting the PR-ization of media (the Cardiff University study behind Flat Earth News, the Wall Street Journal press-release finding), they close with Frankfurt's On Truth sequel, that a society cannot survive without truth, with ridicule of the kind The Daily Show practices as the best defense.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 23 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Torosyan argues The Daily Show models the critical thinking and good-faith civic discourse that real politics and TV news lack, reading John Oliver's 'Civil Disservice' interview with Froma Harrop and Stewart's clips of Rumsfeld contradicting himself on WMDs as exposing bullshit in Frankfurt's sense: assertion indifferent to truth. Stewart's reframing of William Bennett's gay-marriage talking points (is the debate about marriage or about who counts as human?) and his self-effacing interviews with Ramesh Ponnuru enact Rousseau's social-contract ideal of what news owes the public against Machiavellian ends-justify-means manipulation. Gadamer supplies the demand that Bennett question his own horizons, Nietzsche's Apollonian-Dionysian account of tragedy frames the show's satire, and the Tao Te Ching's 'let yourself be partial' governs the whole chapter.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 17 "And in the End" — Irwin and addictions specialist Lombardo ask where comic inspiration comes from, using Socrates' discovery that poets do not know the meaning of their own work, Hume's account of creativity as recombining materials of experience, and Nietzsche's point that inspiration is really continuous production sifted by judgment, to explain why Belushi and Farley treated cocaine and alcohol as muses. They contrast Belushi's fatal 'I use drugs' hubris, which no one around him challenged, with Farley's genuine twelve-step recovery, three sober years, and relapses. Stuart Smalley's affirmations, which bullshit himself into feeling 'good enough,' spoof recovery culture's cliches while Farley's story shows what actual recovery demands, ending with the advice to look elsewhere for the muse.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 30 "18. Superman the Super Dick" — Borrowing Harry Frankfurt's move of philosophically defining a colloquial term (as Frankfurt did for 'bullshit'), it defines a 'dick' as someone who willfully disregards others' needs and argues Superman is one: the vending-machine thought experiment shows he could rescue a sinking school bus in less time than it takes Clark to buy a chocolate bar, so saving people at little or no cost to himself is obligatory, not supererogatory. Peter Singer's famine-and-affluence argument extends the same obligation to the affluent reader, while the SuperBat arc of Superman/Batman #53–56—in which Batman temporarily gains Superman's powers and empties every city's jails in one night—proves Superman could do vastly more than he does. Batman, who risks his mortal life and seeks out strangers to save, is 'not a dick' and wins the round.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Husmann and Kusko apply Frankfurt's On Bullshit distinction - the liar cares about truth while the bullshitter is indifferent to it - to argue Ted Lasso combats BS through correctness (accurately representing a shared world) before sincerity. Ted never fakes tactical knowledge and accepts hard truths like his divorce; the good guys (Sam's protest, Roy refusing a fake-injury ruse, Trent's fair profile) reject BS; Rupert is the show's virtuoso BS artist from the charity gala interruption to crashing the funeral; and Rebecca, Jamie, and Nate's arcs are measured as their movements up and down the BS spectrum.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Corne unpacks Vincent Hanna's tirade in Heat against his wife's ex-husband's 'dead-tech, postmodernistic, bullshit house.' He reads the smashing of the television and the headless sculpture through Bataille's Against Architecture (buildings as latent prisons of authority) and Jameson's diagnosis of postmodern depthlessness and the silence of affect. Using Hegel, Hugo and Ruskin on architecture's obligation to tell the truth, and especially Frankfurt's On Bullshit, Corne argues the house is 'bullshit' because it is indifferent to truth; Vincent's workaholism becomes a Frankfurtian discipline, and the film reflexively treats truth, authenticity and space as a problem.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 25 "15. Saul’s Bullshit’s Not All Good, Man" — Applying Harry Frankfurt's account of bullshit as speech that lacks proper concern for truth, the chapter reads Jimmy's reinstatement-hearing speech about Chuck as pure bullshit: every word he says is true, yet he says it only to win the panel over, as his 'Did you see those suckers?' aside reveals. It then argues Jimmy and Saul's bullshit is harmful on three fronts: it undermines the epistemic demands we owe to what we care about (Kim's ability to know Jimmy's real state), it corrupts the epistemic duties tied to social roles (the panelists as quasi-jurors), and it erodes general epistemic trust across society.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 20 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Kimberly Blessing and Joseph Marren build on Harry Frankfurt's two Daily Show appearances and On Bullshit to distinguish the liar (who respects and knows the truth) from the bullshitter (who is indifferent to it), then take up Stewart's own question of whether political spin is a subset of bullshit. Against Frankfurt they argue spin is closer to lying—spinners must know the truth to slant its significance—and trace the 'PR-ization of media' (Nick Davies's data, Travelodge, subprime lending) that fuels it, endorsing Frankfurt's and Stewart's remedy: ridicule bullshit and spin through satire because truth matters.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 13 "Socratic Seuss Intellectual Integrity and Truth-Orientation" — Matthew Pierlott casts Seuss as a Socratic gadfly for intellectual integrity, built on Frankfurt's distinction between the liar (who respects truth) and the bullshitter (who is indifferent to it). Sam-I-Am's reluctant friend in Green Eggs and Ham is 'bullshitting' to be left alone; the boasting rabbit and bear of 'The Big Brag' are humbled by a worm who plays Socrates as in Plato's Euthyphro; Horton Hatches the Egg and Mulberry Street show self-delusion (believing what we wish were true); and 'What Was I Scared Of?' shows fear distorting the interpretation of evidence, all mapped against Pierlott's five aspects of intellectual integrity.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 61 "58. Tom Sawyer as Philosopher Lying and Deception on the Mississippi" — The chapter treats Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer novels as applied epistemology, arguing lying is far broader and more varied than spoken falsehood. Using Augustine's intent-to-deceive definition it analyzes Tom whitewashing the fence, the blood oath about Injun Joe's murder, Huck's 'sacrifice lie' about smallpox, and disguises as 'showing the false' (mimicking, inventing, decoying) versus 'hiding the truth' (masking, repackaging, dazzling). It invokes Gettier's method of counterexamples as a parallel to Twain showing the traditional definition of lying is too narrow, and links Tom's gaslighting of Aunt Sally and evolutionary/self-deception to modern fake news and deepfakes.

### Authenticity

Authenticity, in Heidegger's sense, names a way of existing in which one takes ownership of one's own possibilities rather than drifting along in the anonymous patterns dictated by "the they." It is achieved not by escaping the social world but by resolutely owning one's finitude and choosing in light of it, as against the inauthentic tendency to lose oneself in conventional expectations. The term is descriptive rather than moralistic, marking a difference in how existence is enacted rather than a code of correct behavior.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 88 "Popping a Bitter Pill Existential Authenticity in The Matrix and Nausea" — The chapter frames Neo's red/blue choice as the existential choice between authenticity - honest awareness of a condition without inherent purpose or design - and inauthenticity, named as Sartre's bad faith, Camus's intellectual suicide, and Heidegger's 'levelling down of all possibilities'. It notes the irony that although existentialists praise authenticity, their literary portraits make authentic characters anxious, alienated, and near-mad while the inauthentic remain tranquil - raising the possibility that ignorance is bliss and the blue pill is wiser - before promising an argument, via The Matrix and Sartre's Nausea, for the red pill.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 89 "Unknown" — The chapter sets Neo and Cypher as the two poles of authenticity: Neo's unplugging is agony, like the prisoner dragged from Plato's cave - atrophied limbs, eyes that hurt because 'never used them before', and the cognitive shock of the 'desert of the real' - while Cypher, freed young and worn down by years of fear and gag-inducing goop, sells out the crew for a steak he knows does not exist: 'ignorance is bliss'. McMahon asks us to sympathize with Cypher, since in his place, facing perpetual annihilation, 'we too might opt for the illusion'.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 90 "Unknown" — The chapter walks through Nausea as the ordinary-world twin of the red pill: Roquentin, an unremarkable 1930s historian, is unravelled by a beach pebble, a handshake like 'a fat white worm', a door-knob that seems to grab him back, and finally the chestnut tree's 'naked World' - discovering that existence is a gelatinous, unjustifiable 'messy suffering' and that the order, names, and values we take for reality are only a veneer consciousness projects onto an indeterminate whole. His nausea is the horror of authenticity before it becomes anything else, the price Neo pays for swallowing the pill.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 91 "Unknown" — The chapter concedes authenticity's costs - the truths of death, suffering, and meaninglessness are hard to stomach, and inauthenticity is the social norm that makes the authentic person feel alienated and even mad (Roquentin's 'crazy loon category', The Matrix's 'hardware' people who fight unplugging) - but argues the red pill still wins. Inauthenticity never eradicates anxiety (the 'splinter in the mind'), only misattributes it to mundane causes like jobs and cars, and it costs freedom and genuinely informed choice; authenticity ends the flight from being and yields a serenity Roquentin finds when existence becomes 'a perfect free gift'.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 30 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Lenore Wright reads Sam and Frodo's Quest through the two journey motifs of Western philosophy: the journey out (Plato's cave, structuring Augustine's Confessions and Descartes' escape from the senses' deceptions) and the journey inward (the cogito, self-transformation, with Nussbaum's claim that literature gives philosophy a body). Frodo's steps out of the Shire-cave - selling Bag End, 'I will take the Ring, though I do not know the way' - create the Fellowship and its freedoms, while Boromir attains self-knowledge only at death's door and Gandalf, Aragorn, and Sam are remade by the road. Against classical heroes like Theseus and Odysseus, Sam and Frodo are modern pilgrims - Nietzschean Yea-sayers becoming who they are, with Heideggerian 'potentiality-for-Being' - whereas Sméagol and Saruman live inauthentically, defined by their pasts.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 23 "Inauthenticity and Fascism" — David Detmer treats Zelig, the mock-documentary 'chameleon man' who turns black, Chinese, fat, or a Nazi depending on his company, as a stark dramatization of personal identity and the existentialist critique of inauthenticity. After rejecting the memory, bodily-continuity, and immaterial-soul criteria of identity, the chapter takes the existentialist line, quoting Heidegger on Dasein's selfhood, that a self is its choices, projects, and commitments, so Zelig's chameleonism is self-estrangement motivated by fear and the craving to be liked. Politically, the chapter draws Allen's lesson that genocides happen not because millions go mad but because millions passively conform, made literal by Zelig appearing at a Hitler rally, and supports it with Asch's conformity experiments and Milgram's obedience studies.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 25 "Hope" — Jill Gordon reads Another Woman as a film about self-knowledge structured by Socrates' self-seeing eye from Plato's Alcibiades I: just as an eye sees itself only in another eye, the emotionally walled-off philosophy professor Marion Post finally sees her own repression by overhearing the 'other woman' Hope's therapy through a vent. Each of her relationships, with husband Ken, brother Paul, renounced lover Larry, stepdaughter Laura, and friend Claire, mirrors back truths ('she stands above people and evaluates them') that her self-deception refuses until her dream stages her own analysis and the final session describes her own life exactly. Counting the irrecoverable cost of her chances (Larry, the aborted child), the chapter closes with Rilke's 'Archaic Torso of Apollo', 'You must change your life', as the command Marion finally obeys, yielding a hard-won and still hopeful transformation.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 139 "The Approaching Battle" — Introduces the chapter's Heideggerian frame: authenticity comes from facing mortality rather than evading it, against the Epicurean advice to be unconcerned since death is merely the end of experience and so happens to no one; death's imminence forces us to define ourselves and not live half-asleep. Harry, death-marked since infancy, lives authentically where Voldemort lives inauthentically, with Plato's dictum that true philosophers make dying their profession as ancient corroboration.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 140 "King’s Cross Station" — Reads Harry's march into the Forbidden Forest as paradigmatic Heideggerian authenticity: knowing he must die to destroy the soul-fragment in him, his senses sharpen, gratitude wells up for what he never fully valued, and he accepts that he is not fetching his dead loved ones but joining them. The Godric's Hollow gravestone first strikes him as a Death Eater creed of defeating death, and Colin Creevey's return to battle at fourteen shows the same clear-eyed embrace of mortality.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 141 "Reap a Destiny" — Reads the King's Cross limbo through Heidegger's counsel to choose a hero from the past and gain insight through dialogue with them: Dumbledore appears not as a king of that place but as the humble penitent, confessing his youthful hunger for glory, and the way-station evokes purgatory. The flayed child beneath the bench shows Voldemort's soul beyond repair - his fear of death drove the very choices that now give him reason to fear it - and Tolkien's remark that The Lord of the Rings is really about 'death and the desire for deathlessness' (Sauron pouring his life-force into the One Ring) frames the motif.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 28 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Bruce Reichenbach reads the film's choreographed pas de deux as three distinct theories of atonement: the conquest dance with Satan in Gethsemane (crushing the serpent of Genesis 3:15, Satan's final scream) enacts the Christus victor view of the Church Fathers; Simon of Cyrene's reluctant co-bearing of the cross illustrates Abelard's moral-influence view, though Gibson shows resilient fortitude rather than the love Abelard's theory requires to transform Simon; and Mary's mirrored 'parallel dance' makes her a co-redemptrix sharing her son's agony. Against this he sets Heidegger — Jesus grasps his death with anticipatory resolve, thrownness, and the 'moment of vision' with Mary, but dies for the Other rather than to authenticate his own life — and faults the film for omitting Anselm's (and Swinburne's) substitutionary atonement entirely: no sin, repentance, reparation, or penance appears, unlike Maximilian Kolbe's real substitution at Auschwitz.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 19 "Only a Jedi Can Save Us Forgetting and Recollecting" — Abrams reads the saga through Heidegger's philosophy of technology: the lightsaber Luke learns to feel as an extension of his body is the authentic 'ready-to-hand,' while the Death Star - a massive mechanical eye that enfames Alderaan on its viewscreen before destroying it - embodies the 'present-at-hand' gaze of enframing that converts nature into standing reserve (clone and droid armies, stormtrooper armor). Yoda on Dagobah is perfect attunement, an authentic being-in-the-world who is 'at home' with being, and the Force parallels Heidegger's being: everywhere, easily forgotten. Anakin's slide - slave of Watto, severed hand replaced by cybernetics, final encasement in Vader's armor - is progressive enframing and forgetting of his own being, and Luke's 'the name of your true self... you've only forgotten' is the recollection of being by which the Jedi, not a god, saves us.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 131 "Switching Identities" — Maps Superman and Batman onto Plato and Aristotle — the otherworldly philosopher of the heavenly Good versus the this-worldly master of logic and applicable science — then argues that Bruce Wayne's years of intentional self-transformation may have swapped the mask, making Batman the core identity and Bruce the disguise. With Mark Waid, he sees Superman inwardly embracing his alien otherness as the path of authenticity, both cases yielding a fused "heterosis" of identities; Aristotle, Pascal and William James back the closing lesson that who we are is a matter of what we repeatedly do, so every mask may eventually become the face.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 20 "The Possibility of Authenticity The Life We Choose" — Gines reads hip hop's sexual imagery through Black feminist thought - Tupac's feud with C. Delores Tucker over "Wonder Why They Call U Bitch", Patricia Hill Collins's controlling images of the jezebel and welfare mother, bell hooks on the slave-rooted devaluation of Black womanhood, Nelly's "Tip Drill" video with a credit card swiped between a woman's buttocks, Jay-Z's "Big Pimpin'". Applying Sartre's keyhole gaze from Being and Nothingness and his Anti-Semite and Jew point about hierarchical societies, she argues the gaze under racism and sexism is non-reciprocal - women are seen without seeing - and that Lil' Kim's reversal of it reinforces rather than subverts the stereotypes; Butler's gender performativity then frames the closing Sartrean choice of authenticity or inauthenticity, Nas's "I Can" and "the life we choose."
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 11 "The Ends of Despair From “Things Have Changed” to “Love and Theft”" — Rick Furtak traces an existential arc through Dylan's later albums, reading Blood on the Tracks ("Tangled Up in Blue," "You're a Big Girl Now") as Camus's absurd divorce between a mind that cares and a world that has gone silent, and Heideggerian care as what the narrator loses in "Simple Twist of Fate." "Brownsville Girl" and "Most of the Time" embody Kierkegaard's knight of infinite resignation - hope abandoned but the precious past never forgotten - while "Not Dark Yet" and "Things Have Changed" mark the nadir of despair. On Love and Theft ("Mississippi," "Sugar Baby") the singer turns toward an absurd, Kierkegaardian faith that keeps caring and even loves without demanding that life make sense.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 14 "Sick of Love" — Krein and Levin read Dylan's portraits of fallen socialites in "Like a Rolling Stone," "Just Like a Woman," and "To Ramona" as critiques of bad faith - characters who hide from freedom and responsibility in consumerist status games, in Sartre's sense that existence precedes essence. But Beauvoir's Second Sex exposes the cost: the women Dylan praises ("Girl from the North Country," "One More Cup of Coffee") are praised precisely for staying in immanent, pastoral passivity, denied the transcendence that for Beauvoir constitutes full humanity. Borrowing Benjamin's and Buck-Morss's notion of modern "dreamworlds," they finally read Dylan's pastoral utopias as a counter-dreamworld spun after the collapse of the mass-utopian promise of consumer happiness.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 16 "Synthesis" — Elizabeth Brake asks what freedom Dylan's outlaw persona - refusing Maggie's Farm, possessive love, and conformity - actually wins, framing the answer with Berlin's two concepts of liberty. Dylan's negations look like Berlin's negative freedom, but Hegel's critique of the "freedom of the void" shows mere refusal ends in emptiness, so she reconstructs a Millian and Emersonian ideal of self-realization for which negative liberty is only the condition. "To live outside the law, you must be honest" supplies the synthesis: outside social law the free person answers to the Emersonian law of his own nature and to undistorted honesty with others, a more severe morality Dylan shares with Emerson and Nietzsche.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 14 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Auxier uses the question 'Would Bruce Springsteen ride a Honda?' as an ontological probe: Honda embodies defensible middle-class values while a Harley is not primarily a machine but 'a decision about life and what makes it valuable', a suicide machine Jesus could have ridden into Jerusalem and whose absence would render Easy Rider meaningless even if Fonda rode some other Harley. His own boyhood purchase of a Honda XL 70 over the Harley Z90 becomes a lesson in Heideggerian honesty, since he knew he belonged on a Honda, while buyers who choose for appearances are consumed by das Man, the they-self that lives inauthentically through images and slogans. Using Husserl's method of imaginative variation on the question, he concludes that the Harley as cultural icon represents an existential decision and the life that follows from it.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 18 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Responding to the Guggenheim's record-breaking 'The Art of the Motorcycle' show, Rollin argues that Dickie's institutional theory explains how motorcycles became art but not why people lined up, and offers three aesthetic lenses: Marinetti's Futurist celebration of machine speed, danger, and rebellion; Dewey's 'an experience', which every ride exemplifies, from his two-week trips with his son to the blown engine rescued by a ranch truck and the canned-spaghetti feast; and the Bauhaus doctrine that form follows function, making customized Harleys industrial sculpture that appreciates in value. He closes with Heidegger: riding's regular face-to-face with 'the possibility of the impossibility of one's being' is a call to authenticity and the final warrant for calling the motorcycle a fountain of aesthetic experience. American Indians revering Harleys as 'iron horses' illustrate the freedom and speed at the core of the bike's aesthetic pull.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 14 "U2 and Philosophy" — Soper tracks Bono's public identity work across three paradigms: pre-modern Irish-Catholic inheritance, including a Du Boisian 'double consciousness' of the colonized Irish; the modernist artist-as-visionary, where Nietzsche, Freud and Marx destabilize the self and the Shalom fellowship nearly ends the band; and the postmodern masks of the Fly, Mirrorball Man and MacPhisto on the Zoo TV media collage, read via Lacan for 'Mofo' and via Baudrillard's simulacra for the 'Even Better than the Real Thing' video with its wax Beatles and cyber-sex imagery. Lyotardian skepticism toward grand ideologies explains the band's refusal of fanaticism in 'Sunday Bloody Sunday' and 'Two Hearts Beat as One'. Soper concludes that Bono fuses all three into a 'Postmodern Christian Pragmatism' that keeps Christian conviction and debt-relief activism while adopting postmodern playfulness without collapsing into ironic detachment.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 19 "U2 and Philosophy" — Delancey asks why anyone should take moral and political cues from a rock band and answers via Heidegger: in a mediascape where a few corporations orchestrate what everyone hears, the mass tune is das Man ('Numb'), and adopting it is inauthenticity - so U2, who believe what they sing for their own reasons ('Mothers of the Disappeared' against the official line on Latin America), may be among the most authentic voices available. Plato's tripartite soul and Aristotle's golden mean supply the thesis that reason needs rightly trained passion: the righteous anger of 'Sunday Bloody Sunday' and 'Silver and Gold' and the resolve of 'Walk On' are practical wisdom in song, the emotions democracy requires. Against Plato's philosopher-king and his noble lies, Delancey argues utopia can only be fostered, not enforced - so in a democracy, if you want to change the world, you may have to sing to people.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 20 "U2 and Philosophy" — Benfell reads U2's apocalyptic songs through Heidegger rather than through eschatological doctrine: 'The Playboy Mansion' depicts fallenness in the 'they', a consumerist paradise with 'no time for sorrow' that lets us flee our own death, while the angel's fall in Wenders' films evoked by 'Stay' and the day-to-day constraints of 'Some Days Are Better than Others' illustrate thrownness, and 'Gone' existential guilt as an unpayable debt. A verse-by-verse reading of 'Until the End of the World' - the Judas-at-the-last-supper reading as one register - shows the speaker moving from 'passing time' and playing roles in the 'they' to anxious guiltiness and the call of conscience, reaching for the one whose resolute waiting models anticipatory resoluteness. The 'end of the world', he concludes, is the end of the speaker's own world: U2's apocalyptic imagery calls listeners to authentic, finite existence, not to prediction of last things.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 13 "Heil Heidegger Dracula’s Willing Executioners" — Adam Barrows reads Stoker's Dracula through Being and Time: the staking of Lucy is the liberation of a true humanity trapped in a deathless shell, and Dracula's endless, mirror-less, selfless existence is Heideggerian inauthenticity - the 'they' that tranquilizes the dying, Renfield's seduction repeating the neighbors' comforting, the refusal of being-toward-death - so vampire-hunting becomes a philosophical task of enforcing authentic, death-claiming being. The chapter then turns the critique on Heidegger himself: his Nazi membership and fundamental ontology's contempt for the everyday leave a gap for racial purity thinking, making Van Helsing's 'butcher work' look like the ritual expulsion of the inauthentic from ontological purity, and asking whether, in adaptation after adaptation, we are Dracula's willing executioners.
- **The Beatles and Philosophy - Nothing You Can Think that Can't Be Thunk**, ch. 8 "CHAPTER 1 “LET’S GET REAL, REAL GONE FOR A CHANGE”" — The chapter argues that Elvis's Sun recordings — the staged rupture in 'Milkcow Blues Boogie' ('That don't move me. Let's get real, real gone for a change') and the accidental 'acting the fool' emergence of 'That's All Right' — enacted an epistemological revolution: a leap out of modernity's rationalized, disembodied mode into repressed bodily affect, defining American cool as affective authenticity against Bill Haley's affected performativity. Elvis's immersion in a Black Memphis neighborhood and his emulation of Black performers made him a catalyst for racial-musical integration and the 'visceral empathy' that prepared desegregation, while the panic of critics (Sinatra, the Times, Congressman Celler) is reread via Hegel's 'tarrying with the negative' as the resistance Geist needs for its self-overcoming. Creative novelty is described with Whitehead's and William James's metaphors — the 'lure of feeling,' sudden phase transition, radical empiricism in what Elvis kept or dropped onstage — with his 'did it make me feel good' studio criterion and a Zen-like mushin statesmanship of loosing egoic control in the band.
- **The Beatles and Philosophy - Nothing You Can Think that Can't Be Thunk**, ch. 9 "CHAPTER 2 “A CREATIVE TENSION”" — The chapter traces the Beatles' rise as a case study in how novelty enters culture: Lennon and McCartney polarize into transgressive truth and melodic beauty, their 'creative tension' producing an emergent whole greater than either (the 'holding a mirror' songwriting method, their fused harmonies, the Decca audition versus Hamburg swings between commerce and authenticity). Hamburg is the underworld initiation where 'Mach Schau!' humiliation, absurdist humor read as Freudian catharsis, and Preludin-fueled marathon sets broke them out of English propriety into ecstatic physicality, before Epstein's suits and George Martin's harsh Abbey Road critique dragged the pendulum back toward rational professionalism. Against the Cartesian thesis that humanity is defined by the thinking mind ('I think, therefore I am'), the chapter reads 'Please Please Me,' Beatlemania's screaming crowds (citing Ehrenreich on female assertiveness and solidarity), and Rubber Soul as successive dialectical phase transitions integrating affect with intellect — a rock-and-roll answer to rationalized modernity, in James's wave-crest image of novelty flung ahead of history.
- **The Beatles and Philosophy - Nothing You Can Think that Can't Be Thunk**, ch. 10 "CHAPTER 3 “LOOKING FOR THE INNER HEAT”" — The chapter reads Dylan's self-becoming as a chain of identity-emulations and overcomings — Hank Williams, Woody Guthrie, Ramblin' Jack Elliott — with Jon Pankake's folk-police critique and the Mike Seeger epiphany acting as Kuhnian anomalies that force a paradigm shift from folksinger to songwriter, each gatekeeper playing the 'Hegelian negative' Dylan needed. It argues Dylan fused folk, beat poetry, and rock and roll into an 'archaic revival' of mythic, enchanted consciousness against modern rationalization, rejecting the Sartrean/beat existentialism of a meaningless world in favor of co-creating meaning, and treating authenticity as the refusal of fixed identity (the Zimmerman-to-Dylan renaming, 'I'm gonna get me a new Bob Dylan'). The Newsweek exposé, Irwin Silber's open letter, and Johnny Cash's guitar-gift blessing stage his passage from 'King of Folk' to electric rock, with the little-known 1962 cut of Presley's 'That's All Right' showing that going electric was a return home — folk having been, in Dylan's words, 'just an interruption.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 34 "Determinism and the Dark Knight" — David Hart uses Heidegger's Being and Time to explain Batman's dedication without reducing it to trauma-determined compulsion: Alfred's butler's-world illustrates being-in-the-world and the thrown-project, and Bruce's confrontation with death, culminating in the bleeding alley scene of Miller's Batman: Year One, is Angst, the recognition of finitude that strips ordinary meanings away. Seen this way, "I shall become a bat" is an authentic, responsible choice of a whole life rather than a mechanical effect of childhood trauma. Hart concludes that Heidegger's analysis dissolves the free will versus determinism debate, since Batman neither blindly follows causes nor chooses from nowhere.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 48 "Reap a Destiny" — Jonathan and Jerry Walls read Deathly Hallows philosophically: Harry's willing march into the Forbidden Forest is Heideggerian authenticity, confronting being-toward-death, while Voldemort's horcruxes and the maimed King's Cross stowaway are the inauthentic flight from mortality that ruins the soul. The afterlife scene raises the stakes of this life: by James's "sow a thought... reap a destiny," Aristotle's habituation, and Locke's memory-based identity, Voldemort's lifelong refusal of remorse fixes his character beyond repair, and Kant and Pascal supply reasons why belief in an afterlife transforms morality. Dumbledore's purgatory-like repentance, contrasted with Voldemort's fate, shows that our choices reap a destiny we must live with forever.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 6 "Previews and Opening Credits" — The editors' introduction argues that Hitchcock is a profound artist whose classic films are organized around ideas, citing Chabrol and Rohmer's claim that each film rests on a 'formal postulate,' so that philosophical issues arise directly from his cinematic motifs. It previews four features of Hitchcock's vision the volume will explore: an anti-utopian outlook on a fallen world perpetually at risk of chaos, an existentialist affirmation of self-definition through choice and commitment, a construal of spectatorship as flight from commitment and authenticity, and an anticipation of later thinking on the social roles of women. It closes with acknowledgments to the contributors, series editor Bill Irwin, and Open Court.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 15 "Bad Faith" — Lee reads the 'Breakdown' episode of Alfred Hitchcock Presents existentially: when the executive Callou coldly fires Humka and hangs up on his despair, he treats a person as a thing, Buber's 'I-It' pseudo-listening where Humka sought an 'I-Thou' dialogue with the godlike source of authority in his world. Heidegger's account of inauthenticity explains the mask of rational control behind which Callou hides, and Sartre's bad faith names the self-deception by which he pretends his godlike management of others is justifiable. Paralyzed and taken for a corpse after a car crash, Callou can be saved only when rational strategy fails and he finally weeps: the single tear reveals his caring nature, Jessie addresses him person-to-person, and, vulnerable before God and others, he becomes an authentic self, Hitchcock's pointed moral for bosses who give an employee the sack.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 31 "I’ll Get Up and Fly Away" — Ian Duckles and Eric Rubenstein use the community's losses of Pigpen and Jerry Garcia to ask whether death is bad, running Epicurus's argument that being dead is no experience and hence no harm, the tedium-of-immortality argument that eternal life would eventually exhaust every fundamental desire, and Socrates's Phaedo claim that death frees the soul to philosophize — which disturbingly implies Pigpen's early 'burn out' was the better fate. Their resolution is Heidegger: authentically confronting death as the end of all possibilities strips socially imposed values (consumerist 'keeping up with the Joneses') and frees us to create our own projects, so mortality itself is something to be grateful for. On this reading the Deadhead counterculture — rejecting 1950s suburban scripts for free love, psychedelics, and life on tour — lived Heideggerian authenticity, and it is better to fade away (like Garcia) than to burn out (like Pigpen).
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 7 "Does Johnny Rotten Still Hate Pink Floyd" — Reisch argues that Johnny Rotten's 'I hate Pink Floyd' T-shirt was a provocation aimed at the band everyone loved, since Pink Floyd was the exception to late-1970s corporate blandness rather than a symptom of it. Tracing the band from Syd Barrett's disintegration (the ever-changing 'Have You Got It Yet?', his unrecognizable 1975 walk-in at the Wish You Were Here sessions) through the Dark Side triumph and the Waters/Gilmour split, he contends that Pink Floyd 'was punk long before the Ramones and the Sex Pistols.' Where punk used two-minute power chords, Pink Floyd meticulously sharpened an ax to grind: 'Have a Cigar' and 'Welcome to the Machine' dissect the industry machine that cages and commodifies artists, and the whole project attacks the inauthenticity, alienation, and tragedy of modern life.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 14 "We Don’t Need No Indoctrination" — Detmer argues the four classic albums from Dark Side to The Wall form a unified meditation on alienation, from others, work, nature, and oneself, and reads Waters's stated 'political and philosophical' aims through the existentialists. 'Breathe''s rabbit digging one hole after another illustrates Marx's alienated labor (the worker 'only feels himself freely active in his animal functions'), echoed by Russell on industrialism's life against instinct and Camus on the day the 'why' arises; 'Time''s missed starting gun dramatizes our thrown condition and Heidegger's claim that only facing mortality head-on cures the inauthenticity of living as 'they' do, while Gilmour's improvised solos model the spontaneity such authenticity requires. 'Money' is a satire of greed confirmed by 'Dogs,' whose self-rationalizing climbers end 'dragged down by the stone,' and 'Us and Them' attacks artificial divisions (soldiers manipulated by map-movers, racism's 'black and blue,' the old man who dies 'for the want of the price of tea and a slice'). 'Another Brick in the Wall (Part 2)' indicts indoctrination, being told what to think, rather than education itself, making independent critical thought the road to the Sartrean autonomy and responsibility the chapter urges.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 8 "Authentic Cash" — Butler rehearses how the Johnny Cash persona was socially manufactured: Sam Phillips coined the name "Johnny Cash" for its rebellious marketing value, "Folsom Prison Blues" narrates a prison term Cash never served (and borrowed from Jimmie Rodgers and Gordon Jenkins), and the Man in Black image began as an accident of black shirts at a Memphis church performance. Against Jung's persona-as-mask and Dr. Phil's "authentic core self," and armed with George Herbert Mead's social theory of the self, he argues authenticity is not fidelity to a hidden inner essence but active engagement with the social processes shaping one's identity, the way paper money gains "cash value" through use. Cash invested the imposed persona with value by sincerely living it (for example, writing "Man in Black" to give the black clothes his own meaning), so the construct became genuinely his identity.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 18 "Reason to Believe When There’s None" — Couch takes a night drive through Springsteen's road songs guided by Karl Jaspers's 'ultimate situations' — death ('Wreck on the Highway,' the bottomless gorge under the cruise-controlled life), suffering (the never-ending badlands, shared in Tom Joad's ghost), struggle (violent like 'Johnny 99,' loving as the search for 'one clear moment of love and truth'), and guilt ('Everybody's got a secret, Sonny'; 'you learn to sleep at night with the price you pay'). Jaspers's Existenz-philosophy — built on Kierkegaard's inward self and Nietzsche's diagnosis of the herd, against Kant's optimism about knowledge — explains the songs' endless border-crossings as attempts to evade limits that cannot be evaded, and the fear that turns 'your God filled soul' to 'devils and dust.' The answer to how there's a 'Reason to Believe' is Jaspers's leap of philosophic (not religious) faith toward the unknowable Transcendent, chosen in complete freedom.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 29 "Epilogue" — Auxier's epilogue teaches readers to build playful 'ontologies' from the book's list of Springsteen's proper names — imagining Elvis's .44 Magnum ('Betsy') traveling from a Vegas evidence room into 'Johnny 99' and '57 Channels,' and asking 'Would Bruce ride a Honda?' He borrows Heidegger's idea that the answer already lives in the question, and uses das Man — the inauthentic 'they-self' that chooses by appearances — to contrast Harley riders who confront an existential decision with Honda's self-conserving middle-class pragmatism. The Harley as 'suicide machine' (like Captain America in Easy Rider, like Jesus's passion) embodies freedom and authenticity; Foucault's Borgesian Chinese encyclopedia reminds us that orders of things are conventional, so the ontology itself is one imaginative path among many.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 27 "If You Think that You’re Strong Enough . ." — Matthew Lampert argues that Radiohead's stock theme of "alienation" is exactly Heideggerian inauthenticity: das Man's platitudes made audible in "Fitter Happier," the falling into the world's "uninhibited hustle" of "Ripcord" and "Let Down," and the tranquility that hides both the problem and any exit. He traces the band's arc from the punk-romantic fix of "Anyone Can Play Guitar" (choose and win yourself, form a band) to a deeper diagnosis on The Bends and OK Computer, where Heidegger's Ge-stell and standing-reserve show that in a technological framework only further technological solutions to technological alienation are available. Following "Why Poets?" and Holderlin's question, he concludes that Kid A makes Radiohead the poets in a desolate time: by risking disappearance itself ("How to Disappear Completely," "Idioteque") and singing alienation in its fullness rather than offering false hope, they stare into the abyss where "the more brightly do the ways into the saving power begin to shine."
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 9 "Jimmy Buffett “Singer of Inordinate Tunes” and Heideggerian Troubadour" — Drew Dalton takes Buffett's claim that 'we don't just enjoy our escapism — we NEED it' as an admission that being itself is burdensome, overturning the Plato–Augustine–Leibniz consensus that it is good to be. Since 'Margaritaville is nowhere' — it is on no map and can never be reached — what we long for is not a better vacation but release from having to be at all, which is why even on holiday in Key West we still dream of escape. Heidegger's Being and Time supplies the framework: thrownness, being-toward-death, anxiety, and guilt reveal existence as a weight we never chose, so the escapist longing to be otherwise than ourselves is the 'inauthentic' flight Heidegger describes (without moral condemnation), and Levinas's On Escape confirms that 'it is precisely from all that is weighty in being that escaping sets forth.'
