- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 10 "Caring Dogs Watching Flying Pigs" — Croskery reads Animals as a beast fable in the tradition of Orwell's Animal Farm that opens with a thought experiment ('If you didn't care what happened to me / And I didn't care for you') and portrays a world without empathy across three corruptible institutions. 'Dogs' dramatizes a malfunctioning marketplace where Adam Smith's invisible-hand justification fails, since success requires lying to those you must trust and ends with the sad old man 'dragged down by the stone'; 'Pigs (3 Different Ones)' targets state corruption from Mary Whitehouse's censorship crusade to war-waging and regulatory capture; and 'Sheep' depicts Marxist false consciousness, the pastoral illusion hiding the slaughterhouse, capped by the Twenty-Third Psalm parody that 'converteth me to lamb cutlets.' The chapter concludes that libertarian, statist, and traditionalist errors each idolize one institution, and that Waters's closing 'Pigs on the Wing' points to the delicate balance of market, state, and community that political philosophy must strike.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 9 "Quittin’ Time" — Michels surveys Marx (alienation, false consciousness, the Communist Manifesto's reduction of family to economics), Weber's Protestant work ethic, and Arendt's labor/work/action distinction, then reads Springsteen's whole career against them, from 'Factory' (the working life that 'takes his hearing' and leaves 'someone's gonna get hurt tonight') through 'Hungry Heart,' 'Mansion on the Hill,' and The Ghost of Tom Joad ('Youngstown,' 'Sinaloa Cowboys,' 'Straight Time'). The verdict: Springsteen is a man of the left but no Marxist — his characters struggle with their own restlessness and with each other rather than with class oppressors, the wealthy suffer their own bourgeois malaise, and work, however brutal, is no cause for revolution. Nor does he share Arendt's ideal: his realm of freedom is unapologetically middle-class — cruising in a cool car, hanging with friends, getting with your favorite girl, and always the radio.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 32 "Ineptitude or Wickedness" — Durand begins from Hume's moral sentiments, the way first impressions (Miss Gulch, the farmer-actors, Professor Marvel) fix our judgments, and shows how Wicked delivers the new information that muddies them, relocating villainy from the green Witch to the green Wizard: an alien despot who scorns Oz's communal moral sense ('I am beyond that lisping childish recital of wrongs and rights'), stations an army of observation at the Witch's borders, and schemes to annex Munchkinland after Nessarose's fall. Marx's 'opium of the masses' frames the religion of Frex and Nessarose as the tool that first pacified, then repressed, the Munchkinlanders, while the Wizard's 'reunification' that is really annexation shows imperial ideology at work. Elphaba's own 'wickedness' comes out as habituated vengeance and an embraced reputation, so the title question is whether she is inept rather than evil, 'a bad witch, but not a wicked one,' and no worse than the Wizard who is merely 'a very bad wizard.'
- **Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_**, ch. 6 "index" — Scholz completes his 'playground and factory' argument: user translations, photos and profiles are unpaid digital labor locked inside a walled garden whose data trails are sold to marketers and governments, even as the same platform hosts a genuine power to act together. Morgan and Clulow frame activism with the Communist Manifesto's class struggle, staging fictional discussion-board posts from Engels, Luxemburg and Chomsky that update the proletariat into the internet-era 'iProles', then show Facebook's ease breeding slacktivism, from the '1,000,000 For Obama To Grow An Afro!' group dwarfing real causes to the platform itself banning a father's 'Justice for Francesca Bimpson' page. Muhr and Pedersen use Zizek's interpassivity to argue the Facebook profile is a surrogate self that enjoys, believes and mourns on our behalf, like canned laughter or a Tibetan prayer wheel, deferring the social duty to be authentic while the site quietly installs its own ideology of relentlessly interesting happiness.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 18 "An Island of Milk and Honey or Rock Bottom" — Shaun Young asks whether governmentless Bikini Bottom refutes political philosophy's claim that the good life needs a state: it is not the anarchism of Godwin and Kropotkin (police fines, health inspectors and the Fry Cooks Union constrain liberty), not Marx's communism (Krabs keeps exploiting SpongeBob, whose 'false consciousness' surfaces only briefly in 'Clams'), not the utopias of Plato, Bacon or More (Squidward and Plankton are miserable), and not Nozick's night-watchman state (SpongeBob is arrested for failing to invite police to his party). The lesson he draws: expect neither utopia nor Rock Bottom, because no single theory captures a real (or imaginary undersea) society.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 14 "Chapter 8 - The Case of the Dangerous Detective" — In a Platonic dialogue, Ronald Green and D.E. Wittkower argue the detective is dangerous because knowledge itself threatens a society's ideology: Oedipus's fatal investigation, the Athenian prosecution of Socrates and Anaxagoras, and Holmes's exposure that genteel Victorian society breeds the same crimes as the slums (while the hard-boiled PI shows official authority cannot deliver), with Aristotle's catharsis re-described as ideological enforcement that teaches audiences not to question social foundations. They then widen to Indian traditions: Vyasa dividing knowledge into the Vedas like an inverted Descartes, Krishna's two paths of inquiry in the Bhagavad Gita, and the Ramayana's dharma, where Rama's trial of Sita upholds cosmic order over truth, compared with the film Raavan, to ask whether ruling by an upheld lie is the greater danger.
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 18 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Zanelotti takes up the charge that Larry is a self-hating Jew, from whistling Wagner to 'The End,' where learning he is a gentile turns him into a churchgoing enthusiast who sings 'Go Tell It on the Mountain' and gives Richard Lewis his kidney. Sartre's bad faith diagnoses both poles: Larry denying his facticity by imagining he can simply shed his Jewish past and re-adopt it at will, and critics who demand he live up to an 'authentic' Jewish essence; Marx's false consciousness, meanwhile, explains the self-hating baldy who buys into the haired agenda. Using Ronald de Sousa's rejection of the 'Just Joking Defense'—we are accountable for laughter because we let ourselves become people who cannot restrain it—the chapter argues the show sets a comic frame that mocks bad faith rather than Judaism. Its deeper target, via Nietzsche's death of God, is the overenthusiastic meaning we manufacture when faith is 'curbed,' which is why Larry ridicules only public displays of religion, not belief itself.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 34 "Psych and Philosophy" — Jeff Ewing applies Marx's critique of religion - the supernatural as ruling-class ideology, 'the opium of the people,' behind which priests and shamans hide real material processes and prop up hierarchy - to Shawn, who likewise masks his genuinely material observational talent as psychic gift to escape arrest in the pilot and keep access to SBPD cases. But the comparison inverts: unlike Marx's priests, Shawn serves ordinary people rather than the ruling class, and the chapter concludes he is better understood as an alienated worker - forced by a repressive state's threat of prosecution to sell a false product, defined by what he is not, and never credited for his true skill.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 29 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Mellamphy uses Zizek's Violence to divide the show's bloodshed - Jimmy's hijacking shootout, Eli's wrench murder of O'Neill, Rosetti burning Sheriff Sickels alive - as subjective violence whose spectacle distracts from objective violence: symbolic (the Klan's racism, the language of the Muhammad caricature controversy) and systemic (the capitalism that keeps Nucky untouchable). Zizek's 'chocolate laxative' logic - ruthless exploitation masked by charity - captures 'I'm a philanthropist now' answered by 'You're a gangster. Plain and simple,' and the opening credits' shifting sea shows Nucky's dual roles merging. Critics who complain about gore see only subjective violence and miss the system that produces it, exactly as Zizek predicts, with Marx's self-enhancing circulation of capital as the unseen engine.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 19 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Sexton reads the park as capitalist ideology in action, quoting Marx and Engels on the ruling class controlling the means of mental production: Hammond's flea circus is the illusion we agree not to see, and Nedry's sabotage shows what happens when workers are told their poverty is their own problem. He applies Veblen's leisure class to Gennaro, who judges the night-vision goggles valuable because they are expensive, and Marx's general law of capitalist accumulation to Hammond's squeezing of wages once every other cost is beyond his control. The dinosaurs themselves figure as the exploited working class, held not by ideology but by electric fences, and when the fence falls they seize the park.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 19 "9. Class Warfare in Chicago" — Canode reads the trilogy as a study in class warfare: the factionless are the invisible lower class kept poor as a warning, the factions the middle class distracted by initiation rankings and faction pride, and the Bureau the self-righteous upper class that created and manipulates the whole system. Marx's analysis structures the argument - the ruling class's specter now haunts the powerless, and 'from each according to his ability' shades into coerced harmony - while the American Dream rhetoric of Carter, Reagan, and Obama plays the aptitude test's role: an ideology of merit that converts structural limits into personal failure. The Bureau's genetic sorting of GP scientists above GD support staff mirrors how meritocracy blames the poor for their poverty, so Tris's verdict - the factions 'gave us the illusion of choice without actually giving us a choice' - indicts the US class system too.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 13 "4. Finding One’s Place and Being Useful" — Karavitis argues that work, not social class, is Downton's real theme, sorting characters in a two-by-two matrix of class membership against acceptance or rejection of the existing social order. Those who accept their place stagnate - Violet ('We don't work,' 'What is a weekend?'), Robert the mismanaging custodian, the perpetually jobless Molesley - while those who reject it flourish: Isobel's drive to be 'useful,' Sybil's nursing ('I feel useful for the first time in my life'), Gwen's hidden typewriter, Alfred's Ritz training. He surveys Rousseau on work's role in inequality, Smith on the division of labor, and Marx on labor and ideology on the negative side, and Aristotle, Russell's 'In Praise of Idleness,' and Pieper on leisure and personal projects on the positive side, ending with the prediction that automation will soon give everyone the Crawley daughters' problem of what to do with a life without work.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 16 "7. What if Your Hero Is a Fascist" — Bruce Krajewski provocatively argues that Dick and his works promote fascism rather than warn against it, citing Dick's Exegesis confession that 'my real idol is Hitler' and his fascist epistemology on which what we believe becomes objective truth. Reading the opening credits' overlays (Nazi eagle on the American eagle, 'Edelweiss,' swastikas in Times Square ads) as capitalism colonizing the swastika, and noting the 'structuring absence' of the communists who actually fought fascism, he treats the show's success amid the alt-Right moment as evidence that Dick's projected fascist America is already arriving.
- **The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed**, ch. 10 "2 Power and Politics" — The chapter traces politics from the classical ethics-fused view (Aristotle's Politics, where politics exists for the sake of the good life yet also supplies one of the first justifications of patriarchy and the public/private split) to the Machiavelli-Hobbes break where politics becomes simply the possession and exercise of power, adopting Bertrand Russell's claim that power is the fundamental concept of social science. It then builds the book's central instrument, a Weber-derived analysis of nine power bases (money, knowledge/technology/information, religion, morality, authority, charisma, size/solidarity, violence, status), contrasting the Marxian reading - money as ultimately determinative, the ruling ideas of each age as the ideas of the ruling class, religion as the opium of the people, the state as a committee for managing bourgeois affairs - with the liberal-Weberian reading in which no single base is decisive. It closes by showing that Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau and Marx divide over the morality of egalitarianism (Popper's Marx moved by moral impulse versus Locke's possessive individualism), and that power is domain-specific, inert until used, skill-dependent and always relative.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 13 "3. Why Don’t the Proles Just Take Over" — Littmann asks why Oceania's proles, 85 percent of the population who could 'blow the Party to pieces tomorrow morning', never revolt, answering with Winston's diagnosis: until they become conscious they will never rebel. The Party keeps them unconscious through its media monopoly, crimestop, doublethink, reality control, perpetual war hysteria, and a nationalist identity that cuts them off from the international proletariat. He maps each mechanism onto the modern US, where six corporations control about 90 percent of media, citizens tailor their own reality bubbles, opponents are assumed to argue in bad faith, and partisan 'nationalisms' block common cause, arguing that American political conflict is mostly over facts rather than values.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 31 "19. Nineteen Eighty-Four’s Religion" — Crossley and Markou trace Orwell's ambivalence about religion — a lifelong atheist who loved the Church of England's liturgy — into the novel: Goldstein's book repeats the socialist critique of priests who 'softened by promises of compensation in an imaginary world beyond the grave' propped up hierarchy, yet the Party then occupies religion's vacant place itself, with O'Brien as 'priest of power', Goldstein as arch-heretic, and 'Thou art' replacing the old despotisms' 'Thou shalt not'. They argue Orwell thought a purer socialism needed the communal goods of religion, from the proles' fuzzy 'Christianness' to the radical Christian tradition of the Diggers and Levellers, and read Ingsoc as that utopian tradition betrayed. The novel's warning is therefore double: what fills the gap when religion dies, and how religion itself can be a blueprint for totalitarianism.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 32 "20. Wheat Can Become Rye!" — William Goodwin reads Syme as Orwell's portrait of the scientist who serves totalitarianism: the genuine intellectual integrity that Newspeak work requires — consciousness of what the language is for — is exactly why he must be vaporized, since 'orthodoxy is unconsciousness' and totalitarianism can tolerate only pseudo-inquiry, never real inquiry. The chapter sets this beside the Lysenko affair, where dialectical materialism and Stalin's favor overrode Mendelian genetics ('wheat can become rye') and purged Soviet biologists, and beside J.D. Bernal, whose scientism, vague Marxist euphemisms and proto-Newspeak made him a real-world Syme defending Lysenko and Stalin against his own interests. Goodwin extends the lesson to today's 'fake news' and 'junk science' politics: once ideology replaces inquiry with self-deception, the destruction of objective truth that Orwell feared becomes complete.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 18 "9. Girls Just Wanna Have Mediated Fun" — Applies Guy Debord's society of the spectacle to Inside Amy Schumer: relationships and self-image become 'mediated' by women's magazines and advertising, so Amy hides under the bed in 'Sex Prep' rather than be seen unretouched, a manufactured boy band dictates 'natural' beauty in 'Girl, You Don't Need Makeup', and 'Publicity Stunt' ends with thin arms in photos mattering more than the prom disaster. Celebrity culture, reality-TV breakups, and 'Sext Photographer' illustrate having and appearing displacing being, while the spectacle's alienation and false consciousness surface in 'Judging Strippers'. The verite 'Amy Goes Deep' interviews and end-of-episode bloopers puncture the spectacle with glimpses of the real.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 35 "22. Won’t You Be My Comrade" — Christopher Innes runs Marx's critique of Hegel's idealism against Mister Rogers: the show treats problems (divorce, war, the Clemmons pool scene) ideally, as symbolic gestures rather than material change, much as Hegel's storybook individuals miss money's role. Measured against Capital's alienated worker, 'an appendage to the machine,' contrasted with the suitcase worker who 'knows her work,' and the Communist Manifesto's 'bourgeois socialist' who demands reform not liberation, Rogers emerges as a progressive bourgeois socialist whose make-believe may console children for, or subtly resist, their future exploitation.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 11 "When Life Gives You Liz’s Lemons, Can You Make Lemonade" — Hinzmann reads Liz Lemon's workaholism through Marx and his successors: she gives NBC-Universal-Shinehardt her best years, but her alienation is social and existential rather than the classic alienated labor of the factory, since her creative job leaves her unable to connect with people or to choose love, as with Dennis and Floyd. Drawing on Adorno and the Frankfurt School, the chapter argues Liz cannot see her job as the problem because capitalist ideologies like meritocracy and free will make self-blame feel natural, and the 'Jackie Jormp-Jomp' fight-club episode shows even a life of leisure turns miserable without purpose. Freud's dictum that happiness requires work and love frames the diagnosis: Liz's work gives her life meaning precisely by shutting out everything else that could.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 16 "Symbolism How We Create Meaning" — DeHaven and Hendrickson read Columbia through Marx's class struggle: Comstock and Fink form the bourgeoisie controlling the means of production (Finkton, Handyman conversions of injured workers), while religion as 'opiate of the masses', the deified Founders, kinetoscope propaganda, and the Raffle keep the Shantytown proletariat in check. The Vox Populi's revolt instantiates conflict theory's inevitable collapse, but the revolution loses its ideals, turns anarchistic, and becomes the new oppressor burning Columbia. Against Marx the chapter sets Spencer-style structural functionalism (Fink's lions-and-oxen ecology justifying the status quo) and Rawls's difference principle, asking whether Columbia's inequalities ever benefited the least advantaged; Booker's rejection of baptism-as-erasure of his past contrasts with Comstock's laundered sins.
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 26 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — Erich Christiansen reads the supernatural imagery of the first two albums as the worldview of powerless working-class Birmingham men, applying Marx's claims that social being determines consciousness, that capitalists are "privileged and idle gods" over the worker, and that religion is simultaneously an expression of real suffering and its opiate. On this reading the figure in black of "Black Sabbath" personifies foremen and unseen bosses looming like factory smoke, "The Wizard" and the Lucifer-seducer of "N.I.B." answer the desperate worker's need for hands-on power when prayer fails, and "War Pigs"' Day of Judgment for the sorcerer-generals is itself the opium fantasy of workers who cannot deliver justice themselves, with "Wicked World" naming the whole system.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 26 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — LoPresti uses 'This Week in God' segments (Ed Helms refereeing a Hindu-versus-Mayan 'faith-off', Colbert's roast line that all religions are infinite paths to accepting Jesus, Rob Corddry's purification rituals and God Exchange stock ticker) to lay out exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism as responses to religious diversity. Inclusivism like Colbert's 'anonymous Christian' logic is exposed as intellectual imperialism that erases genuinely distinct teachings such as the Buddhist non-self and impermanence, while the chapter defends a deep pluralism against the relativism that makes 'all religions equally true' meaningless. Its eulogy for the God Machine borrows Marx's view of religion as an instrument of mass control to explain why religious humor now survives only through a political lens.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 13 "4. Finding One’s Place and Being Useful" — Karavitis argues that work, not social class, is Downton's real theme, sorting characters in a two-by-two matrix of class membership versus acceptance or rejection of the social order: the Dowager's 'we don't work' stagnation, Isobel and the Crawley sisters' redemptive projects, Molesley's grateful endurance, and the escapes of Gwen, Alfred, and Branson. The Anna scene, in which she answers her attacker Mr. Green with trained servant courtesy moments after the assault, shows how work 'becomes' us, while the alphabetical ordering of the opening credits suggests that only fulfilling work, not class position, matters. Rousseau, Adam Smith, and Marx frame the negative view of work (agriculture breeding inequality, the pin factory's deadening division of labor, wage exploitation and ideology), against which the chapter endorses Aristotle's pleasures of play and leisure, Russell's 'In Praise of Idleness,' and Pieper, predicting that automation will soon force everyone to confront what leisure is for.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 33 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Timm uses Bourdieu's forms of capital (economic, social, cultural) and habitus to explain why Panem needed no brute force for seventy-five years: District 12's school teaches the Hunger Games as normal, doles out history as 'what we owe the Capitol,' keeps districts ignorant of each other, and trains Seam children for the mines, so education reproduces inequality instead of curing it. Katniss and Gale's hunting and trading skills are only 'resistant cultural capital' — worthless to Capitol taste but a habitus of lawbreaking that made rebellion thinkable for them alone. Katniss's public defiance exposes the 'wavy squares' in the force field of taken-for-granted power, and the chapter likens her fate to Socrates, condemned by Athens's holders of capital yet igniting a revolution in values.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 20 "“Lost”" — Karen Gaffney argues that Lost exposes ideology as a pair of glasses you do not know you are wearing, using Louis Althusser's interpellation and his distinction between repressive state apparatuses (Sawyer's outdoor cage) and ideological ones (the fake heart-rate monitor that makes Sawyer police himself inside a figurative jail). She reads the Swan button ritual, Claire 'drinking Locke's Kool-Aid,' and Desmond's 'stuck in a bloody snow globe' speech as images of being trapped inside a socially constructed worldview, and notes the viewer is interpellated too by the fake-off-island openings of seasons 2 and 3. The chapter then tracks how the show builds and dismantles the ideology of otherness - Rousseau's 'run, hide, or die,' Ana Lucia calling the Others animals, the theatrical glue and fake beard, 'Others 101' Latin lessons - until the survivor/Other border dissolves when Jack and Hurley become Jacob's successors.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 27 "The Office and Philosophy" — Nys asks whether political correctness is a genuine moral demand or mere verbal hygiene, using the British Office: Gareth's racist BMC joke, Brent aborting it when Oliver the Black coworker arrives, the 'wanking claw' impression, and the porn email with Brent's head pasted onto a woman's body. He argues words genuinely wound (Brent's 'sticks and stones' rehearsal collapses when Gareth reveals his cruel nicknames) but that offense is wrong as disrespect for human equality rather than as a feeling, an account filled out with Frankfurt's claim that our identity depends on what we care about, so the non-targeted can be offended too. After weighing Mill's defense of free discussion for social progress, the pornography debate (in which reduction to body parts is exactly what degrades, as Brent complains he was 'objectified'), and Marx's notion of ideology as a concealing set of ideas behind a 'white male' bias, he concludes that Brent's flaw is looking good rather than being good, and that PC language is rhetorical make-up over persisting inequality.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 36 "Notes" — Maps Campbell's Hero's Journey onto Luke's arc in A New Hope (ordinary world, meeting the mentor, crossing the threshold, atonement with the 'Dark Father' Vader), then argues both Campbell and Lucas misunderstand myth: following Malinowski, myth is a living social charter and therefore ideology, so Star Wars' cosmic dualism, male-centered monomyth, and celebration of violence conceal political and commercial power. The chapter's closing turn - 'Star Wars(TM) is the real Empire and the fans its consumer-subjects,' with Reagan's SDI and an 'insurgents vs. Empire' reading of the Rebellion as illustrations - applies ideology-critique to the franchise itself.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 15 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Canode reads 'It's a Terrible Life' as Marx's alienation of labor: Dean Smith's corporate existence at Sandover Bridge & Iron is Zachariah's ruse, and the American dream, like the promise that one more hunt will finally let the brothers quit, is the ideology that keeps workers laboring for owners who profit from them. Sam and Dean become the proletariat and the angels the owners of the means of production, and their refusal of Heaven's plan enacts the Communist Manifesto's line that the bourgeoisie has forged the weapons of its own destruction. The closing meta-turn applies the critique to the audience: fans who watch, buy DVDs, and attend conventions are the bourgeoisie whose demand keeps the Winchesters hunting.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 14 "Notes" — Applies Slavoj Zizek's distinction between subjective violence (murders, assaults, what makes the news) and objective violence — symbolic and systemic, the catastrophic consequences of the smooth functioning of capitalism — to season two's Vinci, modeled on the really corrupt city of Vernon, California. It reads Velcoro's 'we get the world we deserve' line and Frank Semyon's 'papier-mache' water-stain monologue as revelations of systemic violence, with the stain marking how the past stares back at Bezzerides, Velcoro, and Woodrugh. Through Zizek's 'cynical ideology' (a West Side Story reading) and his account of fantasy, the chapter argues the show demands we target the system producing violence rather than treat its visible symptoms.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 17 "Notes" — Brake applies Zizek's distinction between symptom and fetish to Grant Morrison's treatment of Wonder Woman: in Final Crisis, making her Darkseid's masked, bondage-suited thrall is a symptomal reading that forces the repressed kinky truth of Marston's origin to the surface, while the industry's chant that she is a 'feminist icon' works as a fetish - a fetishistic disavowal letting misogynist comics practice continue ('they know very well what they are doing, but still, they are doing it'). He extends the analysis to Earth One, where Hippolyta's clay-birth story is the primordial lie founding the Amazon community, Diana herself being the fetish that lets her mother sustain a separatist utopia while raising a weapon against Man's World.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 19 "17_LaRocca_Chapter_016.html" — Elan Gamaker analyzes Ken Loach's Cathy Come Home and Ken Russell's London Moods and Shelagh Delaney's Salford as British social-realist 'documentary style,' arguing that agency (in the Marxist sense of free choice against structure) is progressively eroded from funder to filmmaker to subject to viewer. He shows how Grierson's neo-Hegelian faith in state institutions turned documentary into 'good propaganda' that alienates the underclass it claims to serve, so the form reproduces cultural hegemony and false consciousness. Loach's stylization and Russell's ambiguity strip the depicted subjects of voice, though Gamaker holds that a later viewer's shifting interpretation can partly restore agency.
- **Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy**, ch. 10 "Screaming for Change" — The conclusion, which synthesizes the analysis into a tentative unifying 'punk philosophy of deviance': individualism, DIY practice, perpetual questioning of authority, self-education to escape false consciousness, and rejection of tradition and structures of power. Explicitly Gramscian, it frames the punk as an 'organic intellectual' who converts hegemonic 'common sense' into 'good sense,' argues the philosophy transcends age, style, and geography (Graffin looks nothing like a 'punk'), and flags the study's small four-album sample as its chief limitation while calling for future work on non-Western and religious punk.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 17 "8. Between Cynicism and Faith" — Buhlert contrasts the Apple TV+ series' reverent treatment of religion (the sincere anti-science faith of Synnax, the elaborate Luminism whose 'walking the spiral' ritual seems to vindicate that clones lack souls) with Asimov's cynical originals, where religion is Marx's 'opium of the people'. She shows the fake religion of Scientism in 'The Mayors' and the hypocritical Askonian elders in 'The Traders' treat faith as an instrument of control, situates this within Golden Age SF (Leiber's Gather, Darkness!, de Camp's Lest Darkness Fall) and its techno-optimism, and speculates on why the showrunners omitted Scientism.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 20 "“Lost”" — Karen Gaffney reads Lost through Louis Althusser's account of ideology and interpellation, arguing the show repeatedly exposes how belief systems are socially constructed and taken for granted. She treats the survivors' compulsion to keep pushing the Dharma button, Sawyer's fake heart-rate device, and Claire's being made to 'drink Locke's Kool-Aid' as interpellation, and Desmond's 'stuck in a bloody snow globe' as a figure for being trapped inside an ideology. The category of 'the Others' is analyzed as the ideology of otherness, built up through Rousseau's and Ana Lucia's fear-driven 'us versus them' descriptions and then dismantled when survivors turn out to be Jacob's candidates and the Others become 'the good guys.'
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 26 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Hartmann argues the specialty-coffee 'third wave' (Stumptown, Intelligentsia, Counter Culture) could not exist without Starbucks, which taught consumers to pay for a boldly-roasted, ethically-branded, self-gifting aesthetic under neoliberalism. Drawing on Heidegger's thrownness and Gadamer's hermeneutical phenomenology, he punctures Nicholas Cho's claim that the third wave 'lets the coffee speak for itself': just as we perceive a chair as for-sitting through pre-given cultural meaning, cupping rituals actively build a coffee 'hermeneutic' that reshapes the drinker's very perception (the trained palate 'tastes' plantain and graham cracker). He likens this to ventriloquism—the coffee only 'speaks' because someone feeds it its lines—and uses Žižek's account of cynical ideology to expose the gap between fair-trade branding and reality.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 23 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Brophy prosecutes Santa for 'elfploitation,' treating the North Pole workshop like an overseas sweatshop (with Willy Wonka's Oompa-Loompahs and Rowling's house-elfs as parallels) and dismantling a Nozickian entitlement-theory defense: the elfs' 'consent' is coerced by their bleak alternatives, so absolute property rights fail just as Locke's desert water-hole owner must grant access. He diagnoses the elfs' apparent contentment as Marxian false consciousness, invokes Kant's humanity formula to condemn using rational elfs as mere means, and rejects the utilitarian 'greatest happiness' justification via Le Guin's Omelas and Rawls's veil of ignorance. He concludes with a call to boycott Christmas until Santa's labor practices become transparent.
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 22 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — The essay argues that soaring tuition drives college students into sexual self-commodification—egg-selling ('Pay your tuition with eggs'), craigslist/backpage escorting, and dorm-porn webcam sites like VoyeurDorm and CocoDorm—and reads these cases through Kant's second formulation, condemning them as treating oneself and others as mere means rather than ends of intrinsic dignity. It applies Marx's notion of false consciousness to Natalie Dylan's virginity auction and Ashley Dupré's 'empowerment' claims, comparing them to women choosing high heels as internalized oppression. It uses Rousseau's Social Contract and Mill's On Liberty to argue that prostitution is a form of illegitimate 'voluntary slavery' because one cannot rightly alienate one's own inalienable freedom, and contrasts coerced cases (Helena in Singapore, Rosie Reid's traumatic auctioned deflowering, John Gechter's porn suspension from a Christian college) with less-coerced ones to argue moral concern should track the degree of circumstantial coercion.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 14 "Ideological Formations of the Nuclear Family in The Hills Have Eyes" — Lorena Russell reads both versions of The Hills Have Eyes through Althusser's Repressive vs. Ideological State Apparatuses (building on Gramsci's hegemony) and Foucault's account of power as multivalent with resistance internal to it, defending nuanced ideological criticism against Carroll's caricature. The films pit the 'normal' Carter family against the mutant/feral family produced by U.S. nuclear testing, using Clover's 'urbanoia' and class/Indian-exploitation guilt, Freudian repression, and the mannequin ghost town to expose 'family values' as constructed ideology. The Carters' descent into the mutants' own violence (Doug and Brenda 'butching up') destabilizes the bourgeois family rather than reaffirming it.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 15 "Zombies of the World, Unite Class Struggle and Alienation in Land of the Dead" — John Lutz reads Romero's Land of the Dead as a sustained Marxist allegory: the walled Pittsburgh with Kaufman's luxury Fiddler's Green tower over the exploited poor stands for America and global capitalist imperialism. The zombies embody Marx's alienated, dehumanized workers and the exploited underdeveloped South, while cannibalism/consumption figures commodities as 'dead labor.' The Fiddler's Green ad and Cholo's doomed aspiration illustrate Althusserian ideology (false consciousness). Big Daddy leading the zombies to arm themselves and cross the river dramatizes the growth of revolutionary class consciousness, and the destruction of Kaufman and the Green stages a socialist revolution in which the exploited are the ruling class's 'grave-diggers.'
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 17 "From Domestic Nightmares to the Nightmare of History Uncanny Eruptions of Violence in King's and Kubrick's Ver" — Lutz argues that King's novel and Kubrick's film of The Shining both stage Freud's uncanny as the return of a repressed, corporeal past: the woman in Room 217 and Grady's ghosts, the father-mirroring of Jack, his abusive father, and Delbert Grady, and Danny's Tony double. He reads King as an 'inverted family romance' where the good replacement father is the Black cook Hallorann, then shows Kubrick widening domestic abuse into a Marxian nightmare of history: the Overlook built on an Indian burial ground, the Calumet cans, and Jack's craving to join the hotel's ghostly 'management' expose the racist, patriarchal, class violence founding American institutions. Jack's 'All work and no play' manuscript figures his entrapment in ideology and repetition.

### The Web of Belief

The web of belief is Quine's metaphor for the way our beliefs form an interconnected system that faces experience as a whole rather than one claim at a time. Observations impinge on the periphery of the web, while logical and mathematical principles sit near the resistant center; when evidence conflicts with the system, we may revise it at many different points, and no belief is in principle immune to revision. The picture rejects a sharp line between analytic and synthetic truths and reframes knowledge as a holistic, revisable structure.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 22 "Unknown" — Nixon asks whether Neo's harrowing post-pill experiences justify believing Morpheus's story, given that knowledge is justified true belief and testimony alone would be foolish to believe. He argues the belief is self-defeating: if Neo discards twenty-five years of experience as machine-fed lies, he loses the interpretive rules of thumb (people don't lie, heads don't pop off, objects exist unobserved) needed to justify any new experience, so by epistemological holism he cannot be justified in concluding he was ever in the Matrix - even though the audience, with the bigger picture, knows he is right.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 23 "Unknown" — Nixon tests whether the Matrix story is even conceptually coherent by asking whether we can make sense of someone whose beliefs are almost all false. Through the Cletus dialogue ('Bears are scary... Are they animals? News to me') he argues that belief attribution requires concept possession, and concept possession requires a background of true beliefs, so total falsehood is unintelligible - a meaning-holist point he credits to Quine, Davidson and Sellars - though he concedes the machines could still make most of our beliefs false, so the Matrix Possibility survives.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 28 "No Shoes for Muskrats How the 1956 Olympic Games Destroyed Indonesian Art" — Hardcastle recounts how his talk pairing analytic philosophy with Python clips became a touring hit, framing the appeal through Hume's gap between the 'easy and obvious' philosophy that moves people — today's popular culture, including Python — and the 'accurate and abstruse' philosophy that became analytic philosophy. His solution reconceives philosophy as the construction and examination of conceptual schemes rather than a search for truth, with Python supplying what philosophy cannot: conceptual schemes lived from the inside, as when the Dead Parrot shopkeeper embodies Quinean holism by holding that the parrot is alive no matter the evidence, adjusting his other beliefs ('pining for the fjords') to save it, or when 'Nudge Nudge' shows two pub-goers with wholly different schemes chatting without either noticing. We laugh, he concludes, because a new conceptual scheme is by definition unfamiliar and surprising — which is why laughter, unlike disgust, is tied to intelligence, and why philosophy done well is surrounded by the laughter of contemplating what it suggests.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 29 "“The Cheese Shop,” Episode 33, Monty Python’s Flying Circus, “Salad Days”" — This is Hardcastle's full talk: analytic philosophy's two revolts map onto Python clips, beginning with the logical positivists' revolt against metaphysics, whose cornerstone verifiability criterion self-destructs because it cannot verify itself. The positivist collapse hands philosophy to Quine's semantic holism — statements face experience 'not individually but only as a corporate body' — which the Dead Parrot sketch enacts as Praline the verificationist checking experiences against the shopkeeper-holist who preserves 'pining for the fjords' by adjusting other statements, and again in the Black Knight, who maintains 'None shall pass' through the loss of every limb. Holism's darker consequence, that no shared axioms are guaranteed so reason cannot found society, appears in the 'Argument Clinic' and in 'Nudge Nudge' as two men effectively speaking different languages in different worlds, while the witch-burning logic illustrates empirically bad human reasoning. The Cheese Shop sketch crowns the continental side — Mr. Mousebender an existentialist hero choosing cheese in an unfeeling world, Mr. Wensleydale the burden of life returning negative answers like Sisyphus's rock — and the Bruces' Philosophers Song is declared the best history of philosophy because it is sung.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 17 "Poker and Philosophy" — Ellis analyzes expert poker as thought attribution, spelling the iterations out to the sixth order in a Big Slick hand against T.J. Cloutier, then argues via Quine's 'gavagai' rabbit and Davidson's interpretationism that attributing thoughts to opponents requires assuming deep shared belief — which explains why pros misread novices whose minds they cannot model. The centerpiece is Dan Harrington's reconstruction of Daniel Negreanu's 2004 river raise against Freddy Deeb as a set of fourth-order-or-below attributions (Deeb will read a small raise as a lure bet and fold the best hand), not one towering thought. It ends asking how anyone ever learns what an opponent thinks from actions that are a vector of beliefs and desires, and notes poker forces rare deep agreement among strangers worldwide.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 34 "Evidence Rewarded" — Goldwater reads Bill James's sabermetric revolution through Quine: science is a continuation of common sense, but mature science replaces the 'animal sense of similarity' (being a Yankee, batting average, RBI) with predictive, league- and park-adjusted categories, turning atomistic box-score tallies into holistic statistics that acquire meaning only from the whole web of data. Because science recognizes only repeatable types, it cannot countenance miracles—Carlton Fisk's 1975 homer greeted by the 'Hallelujah Chorus,' Dave Roberts's steal in 2004—whose meaning lies in happening exactly once. His resolution: GMs like John Henry and Theo Epstein need Quinean prediction, while fans keep the religious language of faith, hope, and redemption.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 11 "Psych and Philosophy" — Jones argues that Shawn's 'psychic' act is really hypersensory perception (HSP) - noticing cat fur, fine print, blood spatter - feeding inference to the best explanation (IBE), the natural abductive method Sherlock Holmes mislabels deduction, with Clever Hans and Ilga Kirks as real-world parallels. Applying IBE with Ockham's Razor to the two hypotheses 'he's psychic' versus 'he's hyper-observant,' she concludes the natural explanation should win for everyone: Lassiter's skepticism tracks the evidence, Gus knows better despite believing in ghosts, and Chief Vick shouldn't buy the supernatural story either. Juliet's belief survives only through background supernatural beliefs, a psychic-friendly culture, and ignoring the clues Gus feeds Shawn, which the chapter diagnoses as the same public misunderstanding of the scope and limits of science that keeps most Americans believing in ESP.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 21 "11. Should We Execute the Erudite" — Michaud and Watkins ask whether Roth is right that the knowledge-hoarding Erudite are so dangerous we might need to eliminate them, and answer that knowledge is dangerous in three ways. Following Foucault ('it is impossible for knowledge not to engender power'), the powerful define what counts as knowledge - from the church blessing feudalism to the medical community pathologizing gay and transgender people - and following Piaget, new knowledge threatens the interconnected belief schemas (diagrammed as beliefs resting on beliefs) that keep 'faction before blood' and our sense of being special stable, which is why Divergents, evolution, and Copernicus provoke such violent disequilibrium. A Descartes-style simulation scenario - you may be inside Roth's world right now, weeded out for reading the books - and David Lewis's point that investigating knowledge destroys it then show that the real danger is not knowledge but the arrogance of certainty: Jeanine was never a true Erudite.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 40 "25. Should Catelyn Have Trusted Brienne" — McNabb and Andrews ask whether Catelyn was warranted in trusting Brienne as her sworn sword after Brienne failed to save Renly, and test two theories of warrant. On accessibilist coherentism, Catelyn's accessible evidence - Brienne's prowess, her devastation at Renly's death, 'Renly's death was no fault of yours' - fits her web of beliefs like a new strand in a spider's web; on Plantinga-style proper functionalism, illustrated by the accident-created Labman replica and the Lord of Light randomizing a design plan, Catelyn's naturally formed belief that Brienne is trustworthy is warranted if her faculties are properly functioning, truth-aimed, and well designed - which Brienne's record through rescuing Sansa vindicates.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 18 "8. Is It a Fact that Facts Don’t Matter" — Steele distinguishes facts as mind-independent reality from facts as expert-certified statements to show that Kellyanne Conway's alternative facts and Adams's own slogans trade on this ambiguity, and that Adams performatively contradicts himself every time he insists his predictions are true and matter. Analyzing the cognitive-dissonance hallucinations of Trump-is-Hitler and then Trump-is-incompetent, he argues that on Adams's own account brute facts proved irresistible, and that such belief revision is rational Popperian conjecture and refutation, plus the conservative strategy of saving fundamental theories (Coulomb's law) and dropping minor ones when the fuse blows. Against the claim that humans are irrational he recalls Aristotle's Rhetoric as persuasion's legitimate complement to the Prior Analytics, and leans on Percival to show propaganda fits a rational-reader model, citing the slow, fact-driven shift on gay marriage.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 17 "6. But What Does It Mean" — Argues that asking "what does it mean?" of Twin Peaks is the wrong question, because Lynch builds the show out of aesthetically incomplete material. Kant's "purposiveness without purpose" and the free play of understanding and imagination explain the opening credits' waterfalls, pines, and mill blades, while Russell's incomplete symbols ("the present king of France is bald") model the swaying traffic light and Harriet's "full blossom of the evening," and Quine's underdetermination of theory by evidence applies to Black Lodge clues like "the man in the smiling bag" and the Arm's whoops, which support many consistent but unprovable interpretations. Susanne Langer's account of film as a dream-like virtual present, capped by Part 8's atomic-bomb sequence, grounds the claim that Lynch means viewers to complete the meaning themselves.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 16 "Wonderland and the Real World" — Extracts three problems of induction from Alice's misadventures: predicting the future (Hume's problem: nothing rationally compels Humpty Dumpty to agree the world will not turn into Wonderland at 6 a.m. tomorrow), proving whose dream it is (Quine's underdetermination of theory by evidence: Tweedledee can accommodate any evidence within the theory that Alice exists only in the Red King's dream), and translating Wonderese (Quine's indeterminacy: pointing at the White Rabbit cannot fix whether natives mean the rabbit, its parts, or its stages, nor what 'muchness' means). Brendan Shea shows Alice succeeding where the creatures fail by the criteria Hume and Quine endorse: experimentation, simplicity, conservatism of belief, and a principle of charity in translation.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 25 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Reads the 'Sad Sack' photograph, which Wayne Jarvis sees as Iraqi WMD bunkers and Barry Zuckerkorn sees as Tobias's testicles, through the Duhem-Quine thesis of underdetermination and Kuhn's theory-ladenness of observation: the dominant 'George Sr. the traitor' paradigm dictates what is seen and nearly mobilizes Buster for war, while Barry's rival theory creates a crisis that only the omniscient narrator resolves. Kuhn's five criteria for theory choice (accuracy, consistency, scope, simplicity, fruitfulness) are applied to the rival 'theories', and George Michael's failed eye exam dramatizes the skeptical moment when no lens lets you see clearly, showing knowledge is a social and political position.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 20 "NOTES" — Hare treats mass photography—from the daguerreotype through digital cameras, Abu Ghraib snapshots, and diagnostic imaging—as making everyone a practicing epistemologist caught between two folk tenets: the photo as mirror of reality and as manipulation of reality. Defending photography as a genuine causal 'mode of seeing' (a prosthetic like telescopes), he proposes 'flexible realism,' adjusting Dewey's warranted assertibility and virtue-epistemology standards to context, and invokes William James's defense of beneficial 'overbeliefs' when National Geographic images strengthen confidence in one's own culture. Reading the Fallujah lead-pipe photo debate between editors Sullivan and Kushner, he uses Quine's recalcitrant-experience and web-of-belief holism—extended by Morton White's 'holistic pragmatism'—to show moral, epistemic, sensory, and emotional claims are tested together, and frames photography's democratization via Walter Benjamin's mechanical reproduction and loss of aura.

### Virtues, Practices and Traditions

Alasdair MacIntyre sought to revive an Aristotelian account of the virtues by embedding them in the concepts of a practice, the narrative unity of a human life, and a moral tradition. A practice is a cooperative human activity with internal goods, such as medicine or chess, and the virtues are the qualities that enable us to achieve those goods and to sustain the practices and communities that transmit them. On his view, a single life is intelligible as a quest for the good, and that quest is always carried out from within a historically extended tradition of inquiry rather than from a neutral standpoint. MacIntyre argued that modern moral discourse is fragmented precisely because it has lost this teleological and traditional framework.

- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 23 "America’s Game" — William Morgan answers Richard Rorty's charge that American pop culture breeds only militaristic chauvinism by pointing to baseball's moral self-story: played for love of the game (Whitman) rather than market value. Using MacIntyre's notion of a practice's internal goods, he argues baseball's excellences and fair play are shared, socially constructed goods that resist commodification; through Annette Baier's ethics of trust and Bernard Williams's 'one thought too many' (saving your wife because she is your wife), the home team extends familial trust into a public moral community. Hence the moral outrage of 'Say it ain't so, Joe' after the 1919 Black Sox scandal and 'Say It Ain't So Sammy' after Sosa's corked bat: fans demand that players justify themselves to the community whose common good the game embodies.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 38 "20b" — A paired political-philosophy debate over Alex Rodriguez's $252 million contract. Albert Duncan defends the salary as the just outcome of market forces: stars like Bonds, McGwire, and Sosa maximize fan satisfaction, pack stadiums (600,000 extra Cardinals tickets in 1998), and generate hundreds of millions for local economies. Joel Shuman, a self-described socialist, replies with Alasdair MacIntyre's notion of baseball as a 'practice' whose intrinsic goods belong to a traditioned community of players, coaches, and fans: when market ideology alienates fans, unbalances competition, and prices out small markets, money has stopped serving the human activity it was meant to be part of.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 26 "Goals for All Ages and All Occasions" — Opening with Camus's line that crushing truths perish from being acknowledged (and his Sisyphus, invoked to show the intrinsically interested player always wins), the authors force football to face its ugly side—divers, Pepe kicking Casquero on the ground, Catania's mooning free-kick screen, referee Pérez Burrull's robbery of Osasuna, the Heysel disaster, Bilardo pinning opponents and drugging Branco, FIFA's resistance to technology—analyzing it all with MacIntyre's account of social practices: football's constitutive rules and internal goods generate standards of excellence that cheating betrays for extrinsic rewards. Their positive ideal is the Greek Kalon, the noble-and-beautiful they field for Plato and Aristotle, exemplified when De Rossi confesses his handball goal against Messina or opponents return the ball after an injury stoppage—the beau geste uniting aesthetic grace and moral honor, as in the 4–4 Arsenal–Liverpool classic where 'neither side deserved to lose'. The ugly, they conclude, is exactly what lets the beautiful shine, as Eto'o floats over Scholes's tackle to assist a Messi goal.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 15 "An Eye for an Eye" — Mihaela Frunza and Anatolia Bessemer use MacIntyre's Whose Justice? Which Rationality? to frame Holmes's casual felonies, the disguised-clergyman trick on Irene Adler, freeing Captain Croker after staging a mock courtroom in 'The Abbey Grange', and compounding a felony with Isadora Klein in 'The Three Gables', as one tradition of justice among several with no neutral court of appeal. Against the police's letter-of-the-law tradition stand the criminals' own codes of retribution, above all Jefferson Hope in A Study in Scarlet letting 'the high God judge' between the poisoned and harmless pills, making Holmes and his prey mirror-image vigilantes who prefer restitution or chivalric acquittal to statutory punishment.
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 17 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Mudde and Piercey argue Curb depicts Nietzschean nihilism made humdrum: in Larry's world 'the highest values devalue themselves,' so Ted Danson's 'anonymous' donation is leaked for glory, a terrorist warning becomes leverage in a tiff with Mindy Reiser, and strangers judge everyone constantly because no one is a moral authority. The Platonic and Aristotelian answers to what 'the good' is have no purchase here; moral language survives only as a hollow shell, which is MacIntyre's 'simulacra of morality,' and his own remedy—rebuilding communities that give moral rules a point—fails because on Curb community is hell ('I'd rather have the thieves than the neighbors'). Since ought no longer implies can, the show is tragic, though the Tourettic chef's opening night in 'The Grand Opening,' where Larry leads a communal torrent of obscenities in solidarity, offers a fragile glimpse of doing a little good.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 18 "8. How Shitty Can a Hero Be" — Corey Horn maps the Deadpool movie onto Joseph Campbell's monomyth—ordinary world, call to adventure (the cancer diagnosis), refusal of the recruiter's offer, acceptance, and the ordeal of hunting Ajax—then asks whether a mercenary chasing reward can be a hero at all. MacIntyre's chess example distinguishes instrumental from intrinsic rewards of a practice, and Kant splits motivation into duty versus self-interested motives; since Wade hunts Ajax to recover his face and Vanessa, both thinkers would deny his journey is moral. Still, MacIntyre's allowance for migrating from instrumental to intrinsic motivation leaves Deadpool a hero-in-progress, already promising Colossus he will consider joining the X-Men.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 17 "7. How Captain America and Iron Man Embody America" — Altmann contrasts Tony's individualist cosmopolitanism - privatizing world peace, building Ultron alone - with Steve's community-rooted patriotism, the team player from war bonds through the Howling Commandos to Winter Soldier. Using Scruton's definition of patriotism as standing or falling together, MacIntyre's claim that morality grows only within a particular community, and Nussbaum's suggestion to be a patriot first and grow into a cosmopolitan, he concludes Cap's thoughtful patriotism is morally preferable while Tony's globe-saving individualism keeps backfiring. The best American would combine Tony's concern for the whole Earth with Steve's love of neighbor, so no civil war is needed.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 25 "14. After the Blackout" — Martin Muchall treats the offscreen Blackout as an emblem of the moral catastrophe diagnosed in MacIntyre's After Virtue: our moral vocabulary has shattered into emotivist hissing and clapping, with Roy's murder of Tyrell, his 'God of biomechanics', staging the death of God and the 'everything is permitted' that follows. Utilitarian pleasure and Kantian cold reason (Spock, who must tell the truth to the murderer at the door) have both failed, leaving neoliberal hypercapitalism — corporate psychopathy, the orphanage sweatshop, the Baseline as workplace performance review — as the real villain. Against this, K's ending models the Buddha: everything is impermanent, there is no self to defend, and his selfless, empathetic death points to a morality grounded in evolved and cultivable altruism.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 20 "Too Big to Function" — Terjesen argues Jack's combined title, Vice President of East Coast Television and Microwave Oven Programming, exhibits the corporate mentality: following Robert Jackall's Moral Mazes, credit flows up (Jack's Trivection oven) and blame flows down (Greenzo, the fireworks fiasco), so managers learn to avoid decisive action. Peter French's thesis that corporations are moral persons explains why GE runs fine with Don Geiss in a coma and Kathy Geiss playing with unicorns, so no one at the top needs to understand the businesses they oversee. MacIntyre's distinction between practices with internal goods and external rewards shows profit-thinking erasing comedy's internal good, turning TGS into 'pos-mens' and product integration, and Adam Smith's attack on distant, ignorant regulators is turned against conglomerate central management itself.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 28 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Interrogates Gob's catchphrase 'I've made a huge mistake': on Aristotle's account of hexis, the mean of truthfulness and proper pride, and justice as proportional distribution, Gob's prison-escape key stunt and 'Hermano' jealousy make him wicked rather than merely error-prone, since he lacks grasp of his own injustices. Hume's sentimentalist reply is that immorality is a nonrational moral sense refined only through experience, so mistakes could educate Gob, except he roofies away his one growth moment with Steve Holt (!). MacIntyre's practices (the Magician's Alliance versus non-practitioner Gob) and the narrative unity of character explain why a man who tells no coherent story of himself ends up with no wisdom.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 20 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Nicholas argues the film's supposed nihilists, Walter, and the Big Lebowski are all failed Nietzschean value-creators: Walter's arbitrary givings of value ('Donny was a good man... he was one of us') just enact nihilism, and the disabled achiever's money-and-plaques world mistakes symbols for value. He then uses Charles Taylor's three malaises of modernity — disenchantment, disengagement, atomism — to explain the Dude's world (even bowling stops mattering: 'Fuck the tournament'), and finds the way out in MacIntyre's notion of a practice: bowling's internal goods, standards of excellence, and community of giving and receiving tie the three friends to meanings outside themselves, resisting nihilism.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 30 "It’s Life in the Solar System, Jim, But Not as We Know It" — Uses MacIntyre's demand for self-knowledge — awareness of the social and political currents that shape one's beliefs — to diagnose the Martian Congressional Republic's exceptionalism (Lopez berating 'short-sighted and selfish' Earthers from the Donnager) and to chart Bobbie Draper's redemption arc: refusing to fire first on Ganymede, refusing to bear false witness after the hearings, protecting Holden at the Ring Station, defecting to Avasarala, and finally rescuing Naomi. It maps MCR culture onto American space culture — Kennedy's Rice speech, the Mars Society and National Space Society founding statements, Zubrin's Case for Mars, and Patricia Limerick's and Linda Billings's critique of the 'conquering the space frontier' metaphor, with Carnap's frameworks and Kuhn's incommensurability explaining how metaphors hide alternatives — and argues the MCR never acquires self-knowledge, a failure that ends in its alliance with Marco Inaros and the move to Laconia, while Draper's willingness to update her beliefs shows what philosophy asks of real spaceflight advocates.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Kuzma uses MacIntyre's After Virtue to argue the Wasteland is modern morality itself: a fragmentary rubble where, like Bartertown's cobbled-together vehicles, utilitarian and deontological fragments survive without the shared telos that gave them meaning. Immortan Joe's V8 cult imposes a false telos and embodies Nietzsche's will-to-power Übermensch, while Bartertown's rules express mere individualism without any vision of the good life. Max — 'haunted by those I could not protect' — can seek the good life only by joining Furiosa's community and embracing its telos, and the Green Place turns out to be not a place but a way of life, confirming MacIntyre's Aristotle over Nietzsche.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 22 "Reconciliation Doesn’t Come in a Bottle" — Elia reads Don through Camus's Clamence in The Fall, an establishment success shadowed by guilt and self-medication, while insisting Don is no existential hero: unlike Sisyphus or Meursault, Dick Whitman never lucidly chose his freedom, he merely fled his past by stealing dog tags in Korea. Using MacIntyre's After Virtue opposition between Nietzschean value-creation and Aristotelian tradition-embeddedness, the chapter argues Don lacks integrity, the virtue that justifies breaks in one's narrative by deeper commitments, which is why peace appears only when past and present reconcile: phoning Anna as 'Dick Whitman,' the ocean immersion, and the confession to Betty ('I can explain' / 'You're a very, very gifted story-teller'). His justice is real but thin, a merit-based accounting that works at the office (promoting Peggy on talent) yet fails Betty, the children, and Adam, and reconciliation, the title insists, doesn't come in a bottle.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 30 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Sanford argues, through the arc of the Raimi trilogy, that Peter becomes good by becoming the narrator of his own life. On Aristotle's Poetics — a story has a beginning, middle, and end, and art imitates life — and MacIntyre's claim that man is a 'story-telling animal' whose life is 'the unity of a narrative quest,' Peter's involuntary obligations (orphanhood, Uncle Ben's death, the spider bite, love for MJ) ground the voluntary ones, and his quest is to use his great powers responsibly. Tracking Aristotle's categories, Peter moves from incontinence (vengeance on Flint Marko, the jazz-club strut in Spider-Man 3) through continence to genuine virtue, and his practice of telling his own story — 'it's the choices that make us who we are' — models how we must get our own stories straight to flourish.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 4 "Allure of the West" — Nicholas Moll reads the Westworld park as a tabletop-style sandbox and LARP role-play experience with Ford as Game Master mediating guests' mediated 'illusion of choice.' Drawing on MacIntyre's narrative unity of a life and Bernard Williams's critique about the constraints of coherence, he argues guests author competing self-narratives to reach greater self-knowledge, as William discovers his capacity for ruthlessness and becomes the Man in Black. He contends violence functions as the rule-mediated engine of this 'gameful,' educative experience, and that Ford's transformative insight is aimed less at the guests than at the hosts who are engaged in the park's production.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 12 "Basketball Purists" — Kretchmar defends a 'modified purist' view that team-oriented, fundamentals-based basketball is generally better than the individualist modernist game, offering three arguments. The functionalist argument borrows Searle's account of constitutive rules to say ten-person interactive complexity makes a richer, more durable 'test' (like chess vs. tic-tac-toe); the variety argument uses Mill's On Liberty to warn that market pressures homogenize basketball toward football; and the communitarian argument uses MacIntyre's notion of a 'practice' with internal goods to show ESPN Streetball's isolated one-on-one feats erode basketball as a cooperative practice.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 17 "Love–Love A Fresh Start at Finding Value and Virtue in Tennis" — Tommy Valentini argues that because winning lies outside a player's control (he could never beat Nadal by simply choosing to), success in tennis should be redefined around what is controllable. Using Alasdair MacIntyre's After Virtue, he treats tennis as a MacIntyrean practice and distinguishes external goods (trophies, prize money, ranking—zero-sum, tied to winning) from internal goods (full effort, positive attitude, sportsmanship) that require the virtues of justice, honesty, and courage and are available to winner and loser alike. Drawing on Aristotelian justice ('giving each their due') and Randolph Feezell on the opponent as competitor-and-friend, he holds up Arthur Ashe's Stoic response to AIDS in Days of Grace as the exemplar of carrying tennis's internal goods into life in the face of an uncontrollable outcome, death.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 19 "Stabbing Seles Fans and Fair Play" — Opening with Gunther Parche's stabbing of Monica Seles to injure Steffi Graf's rival, the chapter argues that a win-at-all-costs mentality misunderstands sport's value. Using Suits's account of games (lusory goals, means, rules, attitude) and rejecting bare formalism for Simon's broad internalism, it grounds tennis's intrinsic worth in the difficulty of achievement, the level of the opponent, and MacIntyre's notion of a practice with internal goods. It reframes fair play as 'respect for the game,' classifies fans as partisan, purist, or ideally moderate partisan, and concludes that by eliminating Seles, Parche damaged not just her but Graf's legacy and tennis itself because he loved the game too little.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 10 "Charlie Kaufman, Screenwriter" — Evans reads Adaptation as a creation story: the character Charlie Kaufman must make a script 'out of nothing' rather than transcribe Susan Orlean's Orchid Thief, so the film enacts Deleuze's idea of the writer as fabulator who confronts the audience with the text as invention. She sets Charlie's Genesis-like 'beginning without end' against Donald and Robert McKee's Aristotelian, plot-driven Story where the ending justifies the means (glossing MacIntyre's 'stories are lived before they are told'). Naming the character after himself, she argues, marks the distance between imaginative making (poesis) and Orlean's realist journalism (mimesis).
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — The editors' introduction argues that Eastwood, though no academic, does 'practical philosophy' through his films as a craftsman who inherits and then revises genres (revising the Western in Unforgiven, rethinking rugged individualism in Million Dollar Baby and Gran Torino). Invoking MacIntyre's claim that we are only co-authors of interlocking narratives, it reads Eastwood's focus on decisive moral choices (Francesca's refusal to leave in Bridges of Madison County, Butch Haynes in A Perfect World) as a 'laboratory of moral psychology' echoing Aristotle's 'choice discriminates character.' It ties his concern with loss, justice, and Aristotelian friendship and flourishing (Grinnell on Million Dollar Baby) to a Socratic 'know thyself,' arguing his philosophizing is implicit and nonverbal rather than argued in words.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 22 "“A Homespun Murder Story” Film Noir and the Problem of Modernity in Fargo" — Abrams reads Fargo as a noir study of modernity via MacIntyre's After Virtue: humans are 'story-telling animals,' and the Enlightenment project (Descartes, Sartre) shredded the shared myth, leaving Cartesian monadic selves who float in a void as 'unscripted, anxious stutterers.' The whiteout blizzard becomes an ontological tabula rasa of Heraclitean flux where every conversation collapses (Jerry, Carl, Mike Yanagita, even Marge at the drive-thru). Abrams reads Marge as morally good but intellectually shallow—wrong to call the sublime, Kantian 'dynamically sublime' day 'beautiful'—and Grimsrud as the one who dimly 'sees' the modern abyss, so the film hands the deeper mystery of modernity's crime to the viewer.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 11 "Aristotle and MacIntyre on Justice in 25th Hour" — Conard uses Lee's 25th Hour to test Aristotle's claim that justice is inseparable from community and necessary for eudaimonia, and MacIntyre's charge that liberal individualist society lacks any common good. Comparing the greedy Wall Street broker Frank (an Aristotelian overreacher driven by pleonexia) with the drug dealer Monty (fairer, though convicted under unjust Rockefeller laws), he argues Monty is not unjust yet still cannot flourish in a fragmented New York. Monty's profane bathroom 'fuck you' soliloquy dramatizes the city's incommensurable values, while the post-9/11 fellow-feeling offers a fleeting glimpse of the shared good MacIntyre says modern society lacks.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 36 "One More Thing, Don’t Blink!" — Michelle Saint and Peter French explain why 'Blink' is horrifying despite the Weeping Angels being beautiful, not disgusting. Using Noël Carroll's fear-plus-disgust theory of art-horror as a foil, they draw on Frankfurt's account of caring and MacIntyre's narrative identity to argue the Angels destroy personhood: by hurling Kathy Nightingale out of her time and place they strip away everything she cares about and the narrative that constitutes her self. They then revise Carroll, proposing horror is fear plus impotence: the Angels weaponize the impossible task of not blinking, exposing our powerlessness to protect our own identity.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — LaRocca unpacks MacIntyre's After Virtue claim that Austen is 'the last great representative of the classical tradition of the virtues.' He traces MacIntyre's argument that Austen synthesizes Homeric social roles, Aristotelian practical wisdom (phronesis), and Christian humility, making constancy her master virtue (analogous to phronesis) and distinguishing genuine amiability from mere agreeableness (Knightley on Frank Churchill: 'amiable only in French'). He contrasts Austen's internal, teleological virtue with Franklin's utilitarian ledger, cites Ryle's 'gradal' Aristotelian reading of Austen's character vocabulary and C.S. Lewis on her Christian 'undeception,' and reads Fanny Price's charmless constancy as exemplary of virtue over charm.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 28 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Scott reads Dickens's A Christmas Carol through virtue theory, treating Scrooge's transformation as a lesson in the virtues of generosity and gratitude that constitute eudaimonia (human flourishing). Drawing on Niebuhr, he explains Scrooge's greed as an anxious, insecurity-driven quest for security through wealth that fails because flourishing depends on relationships, not money (the poor-but-happy Cratchits). He invokes MacIntyre's 'just generosity' and Aristotelian habituation to show virtues are cultivated through practice, and uses Charles Taylor's weak/strong evaluations to warn that Christmas consumerism threatens 'keeping Christmas' by reducing moral worth to preferences and purchases.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 25 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Joe Kraus argues Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings as a protest against modernism, the mood that 'all that is solid melts into air' and that the past no longer matters, voiced by Marx, Freud, and Nietzsche's 'God is dead.' Tolkien's heroes survive because they remember lore and tradition (Gandalf watching the Shire, Sam's book-learning at Cirith Ungol), while Saruman and Denethor embody modern despair: they misuse the palantir, lose faith in tradition, and can only try to destroy the present. Against Berman's claim that there is no escape from modernism, Kraus reads Middle-earth as a fantasy where clinging to tradition still yields real, tangible power and certainty.

### Ockham's Razor

Ockham's Razor is the methodological principle that, among competing explanations, one should not multiply entities or assumptions beyond necessity, so that the simpler account is to be preferred when it explains the evidence equally well. Named for the fourteenth-century logician William of Ockham, who favored parsimony in his rejection of superfluous metaphysical posits, it functions as a rule of theoretical economy rather than a proof of truth. It responds to the temptation to explain phenomena by inventing unobserved causes, urging that explanatory machinery be justified by what it actually accounts for.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 23 "Erotic Love and Friendship" — Maps Aristotle's three levels of friendship onto Buffy's three boyfriends: Riley is a utility friendship chosen for the rational goal of a 'normal' boyfriend (echoed by Warren's robot April and the Buffybot, which prove programmed perfection cannot be loved), Spike is a pleasure friendship driven by passion and danger that Buffy ends in 'As You Were,' and Angel is a complete friendship where each values the other for his own sake despite the gypsy curse. This lets the authors solve Aristotle's love paradox (is erotic love chosen or does it choose us?) by adding Augustine's and William of Ockham's third power of the soul, the will: an arational faculty that values the other as an end in himself, neither rationally chosen nor irrationally caused.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 28 "The Meta-Fear of Fear" — Noel Carroll traces Halloween's Undead imagery to the Celtic Samhain and its Catholic absorption into All Hallows' Eve, then asks the paradox: why do we take pleasure in images of the death that, as Heidegger says, is the deep source of Angst we spend our lives denying? He examines Ernest Jones's Freudian analysis - the vampire as wish-fulfillment disguising an incestuous desire, horror as the price the super-ego exacts - and rejects it as theoretically expensive, invoking the demand for simpler, more economical explanation. His own hypothesis is the 'meta-fear of fear': adolescent viewers (and aging ones) use horror films and the holiday's zombie costumes to test and master fear itself, with parody and Bergson's laughter as companion devices of emotional control - a folk remedy that needs no unconscious to work.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 27 "Emergentism Now Can Scotty Beam Us Up" — Tests three theories of mind against Spock's katra transfer in The Wrath of Khan and The Search for Spock and his mind melds with Kirk, the Horta, and Rock people. Descartes's divisibility argument backs the dualism the katra assumes, but the argument from parsimony (Ockham's razor), the problem of mental causation, and the conservation of energy weigh against it; Churchland's eliminative materialism plays by science's rules but runs into Nagel's 'what it is like' objection, dramatized by Geordi failing to describe anger to Data without circularity.
