- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 20 "Knock and the Door Will Be Opened… Eventually" — The chapter reads Strange pounding on Kamar-Taj's door as Kierkegaard's passionate collision with 'that which thought cannot think': the materialist surgeon hits the unknown as a frontier, takes offense at the Ancient One's talk of healing through belief, and can only proceed by surrendering intellectual control ('I control it by surrendering control?'). It applies Kierkegaard's two teachers from Philosophical Fragments: Pangborn is healed the Socratic way, recollecting a power already within him, while the Ancient One's astral knock-out and eviction of Strange acts like the god as teacher, forcing him to discover that he is untruth, until faith becomes 'controlling magic by surrendering to it.'
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 29 "Magic and Deep Magic" — The chapter argues that Strange's universe implicitly contains the Creator God of theism rather than just Marvel's gods: Aristotle's impersonal prime mover will not do because Strange needs a relatable source of an objective moral order, so Aquinas's all-good author of eternal, natural, and divine law supplies the framework. It reads three comics as evidence: Strange defeating Dracula by invoking the Tetragrammaton, the Sise-Neg saga where a sorcerer who attains godhood at the dawn of time learns to recreate the universe exactly as the first cause made it, and the World War Hulk story where summoning Zom shows the hubris of violating the moral order—closing with C.S. Lewis's 'deep magic' as cooperation with the created order versus dark magic's will to control it.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 35 "21. God-Talk at the Abbey" — Samuel Klumpenhouwer uses the Abbey's awkward silences about religion - Anna refusing to discuss it over dinner, Thomas showing off with 'transubstantiation' - to introduce Aquinas on how God can be known and talked about. Mary's wartime bedside prayer ('I'm not even sure that you're there') shows she wants not just proof of existence but a personal God, so the chapter distinguishes Aquinas's argument from design - carefully separated from Paley's divine-watchmaker version - from knowledge of God through revelation and faith. Aquinas's two indirect ways of speaking, analogy (Matthew calling God 'Father' at Lavinia's grave) and negation, explain why the 'God is good' sign over Charles Grigg's workhouse should trouble us, and why Carson's 'it is not our place to reason why' about Sybil's death overstates the mystery of God's otherness.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 21 "10 Fact, Truth, and Evidence A Lesson from Dr. Tyree" — Dean Kowalski stages an imagined dialogue between Indy and William E. Tyree — Harrison Ford's real Ripon College philosophy professor, whom Ford's own script rewrite placed 'right down the hall' — to show that 'archaeology is the search for fact, not truth' is self-defeating if truth is correspondence with reality. Tyree's epistemology primer (principles of evidence, inductive generalization, hypothesis testing like Indy's Sankara-stone glow prediction, and Ockham's Razor) explains Indy's resistance to the God hypothesis despite witnessing the Ark, the Grail's instant healing of Henry Sr., and the invisible bridge he crossed on guesswork rather than knowledge. The resolution: Indy practices methodological naturalism, keeping deeper truths out of archaeology, without being committed to metaphysical naturalism.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 22 "11 Indiana Jones and the Quest for Agnosticism What if All Stories Are True" — Robert Grant Price observes that in Indy's world every myth — the Ark, the Sankara Stones, the Grail, and in the comics and novels Atlantis, Merlin, Noah's Ark, and the Philosopher's Stone — turns out factually true, producing a surplus of evidence for mutually exclusive religions (the personal Christian Trinity versus non-personal Brahman). Against Derrida's deconstruction and the postmodern claim that no grand narrative captures truth, in Indy's world 'the squash ball always comes back' — yet he stays agnostic, telling Spalko 'There is always another explanation.' The chapter weighs his three exits: remain agnostic, take a leap of faith as he does stepping onto the invisible bridge, or read Percival and Galahad as symbolically rather than historically true.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 26 "Paradise Found" — Paul Brown maps The Minish Cap's Hyrule onto utopian theory: Plato's Republic classes reappear as royal family (guardians), castle guards (auxiliaries), and market traders (producers), but Hyrule improves on Plato with no slavery, fluid social boundaries (Princess Zelda wandering the festival unrecognized), and Mayor Hagen's local democracy. Aristotle's polis supplies the town's design — small enough for community, walled for defense, river-powered — while Kant's disinterested appreciation of the beautiful fits Miyamoto's 'miniature garden' of pastoral idyll. The spiritual dimension completes the utopia: the benevolent Picori/Minish are a God walking unseen among people, a fuzzy religion without prophet or persecution, so no leap of faith is even necessary.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 27 "NOTES" — Brett Chandler Patterson reads Lost through C. S. Lewis's Chronicles of Narnia as myth rather than allegory - the Lamp Post station and flight 316 (the Prince Caspian dedication page) wink at the source - with the island, like Narnia, a world of crisis and second chances entered by plane crash instead of wardrobe. Flashbacks of past failures (Kate the fugitive, Sayid the torturer, Charlie's addiction, Locke's kidney con) set up struggles for faith that he illuminates with H. Richard Niebuhr on faith as a center of value and revelation as communal, and with Levinas's claim that we become ourselves only through responsibility to the Other in community. The Jack-versus-Locke man-of-science/man-of-faith debate, Charlie's moth-cocoon trial, and Jacob and the Man in Black's black-and-white stone game map onto Aslan versus the White Witch, ending in redemption through the new community and Jack's sacrificial death.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 28 "NOTES" — Daniel Gallagher uses Aquinas to read Lost as a drama about mistaking finite goods for the ultimate good: Jack's hope in curing, Kate's in deceiving, Jin's in his father-in-law's employment, Locke's in Anthony Cooper, and the Virgin Mary statues full of heroin all instantiate Aquinas's approaching-Peter analogy, where we know only confusedly that someone (the perfect good) is coming toward us. Desmond's and Charlie's paralysis before the good is the sin of acedia, Rose's faith that the island itself healed her cancer is presumption, and her certainty that Bernard is alive illustrates Aquinas's claim - framed through Plato's episteme versus doxa - that faith sits midway between knowledge and opinion. The chapter closes on the harmony of faith and reason, from the Five Ways' first efficient cause to Eko's dying 'I ask for no forgiveness,' grounded in Augustine's restless heart that finds no peace until it rests in God.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 12 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Johnson uses 'Go God Go's' future of 2546—where Dawkins-style atheism has become a warring religion and otter scientists intone 'Oh my Science!'—to ask whether science and religion genuinely conflict and whether New Atheism is itself a faith. Applying abduction and the four criteria of adequacy, he argues the embellished-story hypothesis beats miracle claims about Jesus (whose legend grew Gospel by Gospel), Sathya Sai Baba, Joseph Smith, and Xenu, that Mr(s). Garrison's 'you can't disprove God' and the show's sarcasm commit an appeal to ignorance, and that Stan's water-into-wine scene with Jesus shows how easily people are fooled. He allows Kuhnian theory change in science but rejects James's will-to-believe for existence claims—the moon whale Willzyx needs evidence—and concludes Parker and Stone are unfair to Dawkins: ending religion would not end violence, but it would remove the easiest justification for it, and some answers are simply true even when unknown.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 13 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Dueck takes Stan's closing pluralism in 'Super Best Friends'—all religions have something valuable to teach, as the interfaith superheroes' combined powers defeat Blaine—and tests it against Hick's pluralism, exclusivism, and Rahner's inclusivist 'anonymous Christians', using 'Go God Go's warring atheist factions to show exclusivity is unavoidable even without God. Hume's miracle argument explains why Jesus's look-away water-into-wine trick convinces no one in the episode: testimony can never outweigh the laws of nature, so supernatural evidence resists natural evaluation. Popper's falsificationism warns that watering doctrines down to make religions compatible (the rabbit-pope of 'Fantastic Easter Special') leaves nothing to test, while James's will to believe and Plantinga's defense of exclusivism ground the conclusion that faith can be rationally justifiable where evidence runs out—beware the Blainetologists, but do not surrender ways of life that define us.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 42 "Notes" — Charts Star Trek's handling of secularization, from the "Roddenberry attitude" of Kirk confronting fifteen would-be gods to later series' complications, using Robert Audi's nine features of religion and Benedict Anderson's "imagined community" - the Yangs' sacred flag and worship-word "freedom" in "The Omega Glory" show an incoherent civic religion Kirk can correct. "Who Watches the Watchers" inverts the dynamic by making Picard an accidental god who refuses to found a religion among the proto-Vulcan Mintakans, while real-world creationism in schools and abstinence-only sex education supply the chapter's empirical moral arguments that faith-driven public policy fails on its own terms. DS9's Bajor arc - Vedek Winn boycotting Keiko's school, Sisko's defense of the faith that sustained Bajor through occupation, and Akorem's restoration of the D'jarra castes in "Accession", likened to Plato's Republic-class soul hierarchy - grounds the claim that infallible religious authority corrodes democratic equality, with Sisko as the Emissary who synthesizes faith and secular governance.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Lindenmuth reads Luke's endgame in Return of the Jedi as Kierkegaard's knight of faith, reversing Abraham's binding of Isaac: where Abraham raised the knife, Luke, pressed by Yoda and Obi-Wan to kill his father, throws his saber away. Jedi detachment ('train yourself to let go') is infinite resignation, and Han Solo's arc from self-interested smuggler to hero at Yavin traces Kierkegaard's aesthetic-to-ethical stages. Luke's double movement - resigning everything, his cause and his life, while trusting there is still good in Vader - suspends the ethical demand to kill and accomplishes what neither side thought possible: turning a Sith back to the light.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 40 "The Last Jedi A New Hope" — Johnson defends The Last Jedi's Luke against the 'you ruined Luke' charge: his pacifism was set up when he threw away his lightsaber before Palpatine in Return of the Jedi, and his call to end the Jedi follows the lesson Hobbes and Locke drew from the English civil wars - since religious matters cannot be settled by reason, only by violence, Jedi and Sith factions fighting for political power yield only bloodshed like the Clone Wars and two Death Stars. Luke also seeks to destroy the Jedi texts out of guilt by association for the Order's failures, and to the end he remains a consequentialist pacifist, defeating Kylo on Crait through a nonviolent Force projection rather than a real duel. Far from betraying the character, this growth into proactive nonviolence - capped by Rey's yellow-bladed, mainly defensive style - makes Luke 'the ultimate Jedi' and the Resistance's new hope.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 11 "Notes" — Baggett sets W. K. Clifford's evidentialism (the negligent shipowner; believing on insufficient evidence is a 'sin against mankind') against William James's precursive faith, which permits believing ahead of the evidence when an option is forced, live, momentous, and evidentially undecided. He applies this to Sam's taping over the Dubai Air logo as social-coordination faith, Richmond's belief that it can finally beat Everton, romantic risk-taking like Roy and Keeley's, and the marriage of belief with hard work (Ted's practice tirade, Nate's False Nine), ending with James and Pascal on how evidential ambiguity about God makes a passional step of faith rational.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 27 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Greeley argues the zombie embodies a specifically modern fear of losing our humanity: walkers are persons stripped of the potential Aristotle and Aquinas made the measure of human worth, which is why Rick uniquely eulogizes the walkers he puts down ('I'm sorry this happened to you'). Following Aries, he traces modern death anxiety to the split of faith from reason and reads the CDC arc ('TS-19') as science offering only a self-destruct quick death where Jacqui's 'wrath of God' guess at least offers meaning. Rousseau's claim that civilization corrupts explains the survivors' return to the woods, where pizza-deliverer Glenn's heroics and the 'kingpin' Guillermo protecting nursing-home patients show the apocalypse can bring out the best in us while the Bradbury's Sale storefront and trampled Walmart worker hint we were already the walking dead.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Held asks what a god is and which gods deserve worship, using Rachels's definition (all-powerful, perfectly good, perfectly wise) to show no DC deity - dying Zeus, cruel Darkseid, creation-unmaking Parallax - qualifies, and that mere power generates fear, not the moral authority that could ground worship-worthiness or a parent-like right to command. Against the Christian campaigner Darrel Keyes, who calls Wonder Woman's cults idolatrous, he notes her gods visibly exist while his God is both unprovable and, per the Anselmian concept problem, indescribable without ceasing to be supreme. The chapter ends by relocating worship on earth: since we need orienting values whether or not gods exist, 'we could do worse than submit to the loving authority' of the justice, care, and integrity Diana embodies - pray to 'yourself, your own strength and character.'
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 26 "Is the Gridiron Holy Ground" — Hamilton analyzes the fusion of football, patriotism, and religion (Friday Night Lights' Odessa, Super Bowl rituals) as Rousseau's 'civil religion' from the Social Contract—socially unifying but content-empty and anti-intellectual, keeping faith bifurcated from real life. Drawing on Augustine's account of virtue as 'rightly ordered love' and vice as disordered love, he argues football has been wrongly elevated above higher goods. He rejects Higgs's incompatibility thesis for a Christian worldview approach—exemplified by Tony Dungy, Lovie Smith, and Joe Ehrman's 'men for others'—that makes the gridiron holy ground.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Clayton distinguishes the philosophical problem of evil (Aquinas's deductive argument, its inductive/evidential successors, and Plantinga's free-will defense) from what Plantinga calls the pastoral problem — the personal crisis suffering brings. He argues Eastwood, as 'practical philosopher,' registers the philosophical problem visually in Mystic River (camera panning heavenward at Katie's murder, the intercut Communion) but pointedly refuses to resolve it. In Hereafter the tsunami, deaths, and the twins' loss are met not with theodicy but with a recurring pastoral pattern of listening, being present, and acting compassionately (Dr. Rousseau with Marie, George's reading of Marcus), religion offering no answers.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 26 "15. God Is Good (Chuck Not So Much)" — Graves contrasts the Judeo-Christian God of scripture with Chuck, arguing Chuck fails theodicy: he neither shares human suffering (as Jesus does) nor pursues justice for the oppressed (as Yahweh does in Psalm 82), and using evolution to create sapient life guarantees disease, war, and injustice that Paley's Natural Theology design argument cannot excuse. He reads Amara's wish to unwind creation as arguably 'good,' rejects the Winchesters' fallacy that Nephilim Jack must inherit Lucifer's evil (nature versus nurture), and diagnoses Chuck as a pathological narcissist paralleling despotic real-world leaders.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" — Jacoby uses Stan Marsh as the embodiment of W. K. Clifford's ethics of belief, that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence. Stan debunks TV psychic John Edward, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the one making extraordinary claims. Jacoby distinguishes evidential from prudential reasons, presents and criticizes Pascal's Wager (using 'Cartmanland' and the problem of undeserved suffering), and argues via Clifford that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken the mind and, as Stan tells Edward, slow 'the progress of all mankind.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 22 "Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy" — Johnson uses 'Cartmanland' to lay out the problem of evil: Kyle loses his faith when the wicked Cartman gains perfect happiness, giving a logical problem-of-moral-evil argument against God. Johnson shows why the story of Job and Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' fail, then explains the greater-good and free-will defenses (invoking Augustine that only free acts are good) and the residual problem of natural evils like Kyle's hemorrhoid. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by South Park's Jesus, that God permits both moral and natural evil so we develop character, while noting the surviving evidential problem of evil's sheer amount.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 23 "To Know … and Believe" — Gallagher uses Lost's Rose Henderson, who says 'I just know,' to expound Aquinas on faith and reason. Aquinas places faith midway between Plato's knowledge (epistêmê) and opinion (doxa) and distinguishes its material object (God) from its formal object (first truth). Gallagher explains that all knowledge begins in the senses, so God's existence is known only by demonstration (the five ways), while faith's fuller content requires grace. Rose's sins bracket the argument: Charlie's despair is acedia, while Rose's insistence that she 'knows' the island cured her is presumption, mistaking faith for scientific knowledge.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 25 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Sirvent and Baker use Stewart's mockery of politicians who claim a divine endorsement (Bachmann's certainty of a 'miracle,' Wyatt Cenac reporting from a Las Vegas-style heaven) to apply John Locke's critique of religious 'enthusiasm'—the arrogance of taking one's own intuitions for divine direction without weighing them against reason. They then deploy Gadamer's philosophical hermeneutics against the 'objectivism' of Glenn Beck and Pat Robertson, arguing that treating scripture as an unambiguous rulebook ignores how every reading is conditioned by culture and history.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 26 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — LoPresti uses the 'This Week in God' segments (the God Machine, Ed Helms's Hindu-vs-Mayan 'faith-off,' Colbert's inclusivist White House roast) to lay out three responses to religious diversity—exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism—and defends John Cobb's Whiteheadian process-metaphysics pluralism. He insists the distinct concepts of religions be respected rather than collapsed, citing Buddhist impermanence and no-Self and the South Asian Atman/Brahman as unique and non-reducible, and closes by reading the show's turn to political framing of religion through Marx's claim that religion is a mechanism for controlling the masses.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 27 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Johnson argues that Fox News's 'war on Christmas' is fabricated and that the real conflict is a centuries-long Christian war FOR Christmas—Constantine tacking Jesus's birth onto pagan late-December Saturnalia and solstice celebrations. Using Stewart's and Colbert's segments plus Kevin Bleyer-style history, he defends the separation of church and state (courthouse nativities and school Nativity plays as unconstitutional endorsements of Christianity), debunks David Barton's claims that Jefferson was a conservative Christian, and shows Jefferson the deist coining 'a wall of separation between church and state.'
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 4 "There Is No God in Desperation" — Sutton and Held use King's Desperation and its God-speaking boy David Carver to stage the problem of evil, opening with Hume's Epicurean dilemma and Rowe's and Draper's evidential arguments from superfluous suffering (Brian's coma, Pie's murder). They survey theistic replies as defenses (Augustine's evil-as-privation, skeptical-theism humility) and theodicies (Hick's soul-making 'God is refining,' the free-will theodicy, Aquinas on natural law preserving the whole), concluding with van Inwagen that we lack epistemic warrant to judge God. Held reframes evil as a human problem of suffering, and reads Marinville's arc through Kierkegaard's despair and Anselm's 'faith seeking understanding,' arguing the antidote to 'desperation' (unbelief) is a non-cognitive, affective faith that keeps investigating.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 16 "Chapter 6 The Gospel According to Mark (Twain)" — Craig Vasey reads Twain's Letters from the Earth, narrated by a skeptical Satan, as a defense of critical thinking rather than the ranting of a bitter old man. He unpacks Satan's mockery of a self-understanding in which God obsesses over and demands worship from humans, a sexless harp-playing Heaven, and the punishment of curious, ignorant Adam and Eve, echoing Hume's catalogue of suffering (the fly as 'divine ambassador'). Invoking Nietzsche on life-after-death as vengeance dressed as love, and Socrates' 'unexamined life,' Vasey argues Twain's real target is human gullibility and willful childishness, calling humanity to grow up, think, and take responsibility instead of scapegoating a celestial fantasy.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 30 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Morgan asks when it is wrong for fathers to impose their ideals on children, arguing that forcing activities (like violin practice) risks alienation because meaningful pursuits must be embraced 'from the inside.' Using Robert Noggle's Rawls-derived hierarchy of goods (basic, pre-primary, primary, secondary, specialized), he grants fathers may guide toward universal goods but rejects Noggle's claim that parents may impose a full religious worldview, favoring David Archard's weaker right to 'guide family life' while respecting the child's growing capacity to choose – permitting compelled practice of talents only in light of the child's emerging identity.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 13 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Austin uses the everyday sense that 'we need the bean' to introduce a metaphysical debate about whether we need God to ground ethics, framed through the fair-trade coffee case. He contrasts Erik Wielenberg, who treats necessary ethical truths (e.g., that unfair trade is wrong, that suffering is intrinsically evil) as brute 'furniture of the universe' and follows Kant in holding that we ought to be moral simply because it is our duty, with J. P. Moreland, who argues such objective moral values, our knowledge of them, and the normative pull of obligation fit a theistic worldview better than naturalism. The chapter presents God as the 'Necessary Ground of Being' behind moral reality without settling the dispute.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 8 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — In this foreword, historian Stephen Nissenbaum frames the book's central puzzle by asking the reader to picture Santa Claus kneeling in the Bethlehem manger and feeling why the image jars. He argues Christmas began as a fourth-century compromise: the Church Fathers fixed Jesus' birthday on December 25 to co-opt Saturnalia and the solstice and to refute Docetism (the claim Christ only 'seemed' to have a body) by giving him a human birthday. He traces how the resulting tension between piety and revelry led the Puritans to ban Christmas and how the secular, commercial Santa of Moore's 1823 poem came to dominate the American holiday, leaving the manger and the sleigh perpetually unreconciled.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 9 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Editor Scott Lowe's introduction surveys the volume, using the disputed origins of Christmas – the December date borrowed from Sol Invictus and Yule, the Christmas tree from Germanic custom, and a Santa descended from Odin, Thor and Krampus rather than any Christian saint – to show how little about the holiday is settled. It previews each contributor's argument, from Hume-based attacks on the virgin birth and Aiken's denial of a 'War on Christmas' to Foucauldian readings of Santa's surveillance, the ethics of the Santa lie, and atheist or Festivus alternatives, positioning the book as a set of philosophical debates over what Christmas actually means.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 12 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Theologian Victor Lyons defends the virgin birth against the Humean empiricist objection voiced by Dawkins, Hitchens and Harris. He marshals the creeds and Church Fathers (Ignatius, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Origen's reply to Celsus) and argues Matthew's and Luke's independent nativity narratives point to a pre-gospel tradition of the virginal conception. Against Hume's claim that a wise man proportions belief to evidence, Lyons contends experience is not an infallible guide and that ruling out the miraculous a priori is a circular limit on inquiry, casting Mary and Joseph as the first skeptics who nonetheless accepted an event outside natural experience.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 13 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Medievalist Todd Preston argues that 'Put Christ Back in Christmas' misreads the holiday, which in the English tradition was always a balance of Christian and non-Christian elements. He shows Augustine (in On Christian Doctrine) and Boethius (in the Consolation of Philosophy, guided by Lady Philosophy) licensed Christians to absorb useful pagan philosophy, and that this apologetic openness let King Alfred, Pope Gregory and St. Boniface repurpose rather than erase heathen practice – turning Thor's oak into the Christmas fir. Tracing the Old English 'Cristesmæsse', Yule/Jol and Modraniht, and the secular revelry of Sir Gawain that Wyclif condemned, he concludes an authentic Christmas keeps its pagan half.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 15 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Scott Aiken argues the conservative 'War on Christmas' pushed by Gibson and O'Reilly is illusory on both fronts: cultural Christianity has already won, and keeping nativity scenes out of public schools protects minority rights under the Establishment Clause rather than persecuting the majority. He then mounts a separate attack, claiming both Christmas myths are bad on their merits – the nativity (star that leads wise men, vanishing Magi, Joseph's pointless genealogy) promotes mere credulity rather than tested faith, while the Santa myth glorifies a slave-owning surveiller who makes goodness merely instrumental. He adds that teaching the false Santa story undercuts parents' testimonial authority to teach the gospel as true.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 16 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Guy Bennett-Hunter treats both the Santa story and the virginal conception as mythologies whose value lies in meaning, not literal fact, drawing on Barthes and Gadamer's dictum that a myth needs no verification outside itself. He deploys Hume on miracles and Russell's Teapot to argue it is no more rational to believe the sacred myth literally than the Santa one, then turns to Tillich's religious case: taking the virgin birth literally is idolatry that drags the ultimate God into the chain of cause and effect. He urges 'breaking' the myth – keeping its significance while dropping its literal truth – a ladder to be kicked away like Edmund Gosse's childhood test of idolatry.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 22 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Will Williams recounts the legend that St. Nicholas of Myra, the historical basis of Santa Claus, attended the Council of Nicaea (325) and punched the heretic Arius, who taught that the Son was created and not fully God ('there was a time when the Son was not'). Setting the fight to a parody of 'The Night Before Christmas', Williams explains via Athanasius why the divinity of Christ mattered – only if Jesus is truly God can his death secure salvation. He contrasts this fiercely theological bishop with the de-Christianized modern Santa, using the syncretism of 'Here Comes Santa Claus' to argue Nicholas would deplore what consumerist Christmas has become.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 30 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Tallman offers a naturalistic (atheist) justification for celebrating Christmas, arguing first that the holiday's date and rituals (December 25 solstice, Christmas trees, Odin-derived Santa) predate and are not exclusively Christian, so non-believers may find their own meaning in them. Drawing on George Santayana's and Steven Cahn's 'religious naturalism,' she argues rituals and moral communities give meaning without supernatural belief, so atheists engaging even overtly religious rites (like Westerners doing Hindu-rooted yoga) are not being disingenuous. She locates a secular 'spirit of Christmas' — giving, love, community — in It's a Wonderful Life, where humans, not God, save George Bailey, and closes on a Venn-diagram overlap of Christian and naturalist Christmases.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 31 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Mason, a developmental psychologist writing as a Pagan, narrates her decades-long religious journey through James Fowler's Stages of Faith model, using each stage to reinterpret Christmas. She recounts childhood confusion over carols and chimney-invading strangers, fundamentalist-Christian zeal (stage 3 group belonging, then stage-4 doubt as she 'crusaded' against pagan Christmas trees), Unitarian Universalist questioning, and finally Wiccan/Pagan practice centered on Hecate and the winter-solstice Wheel of the Year (rediscovering Christmas's pagan roots in holly, mistletoe, and Yule). Reaching Fowler's stage 5 'Conjunctive Faith,' she concludes Christmas is neither hers nor anyone's to own but a self-perpetuating commercial 'Hallmark' phenomenon she can now greet with equanimity.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 18 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Taliaferro and Le Gall's 'The Great Escape' weighs four philosophical objections to cannabis-induced altered states — falsehood (Plato's ban on poetry/theatre in the Republic), distortion of reason (Euripides' Bacchae, James on nitrous oxide), undermining of agency (the Sirens, De Quincey's opium), and loss of self-determination (the Stoic Epictetus on freedom) — then surveys Jewish, Christian and Islamic treatments of wine, coffee and hashish. They rebut the objections using Aristotle's cathartic defense of theatre and Locke's imagination-based account of freedom, concluding that if cannabis is no worse than wine the philosophical and religious case against it is not decisive.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 34 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Barkman, prompted by his wedding guests' shared discomfort with his best man's tattooed arms, sets out to dispel a 'Christian Confucian confusion' that reads piety as requiring a tattoo-free body. He shows Leviticus 19:28 and 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 condemn tattooing only where it signals allegiance to impure cults or misuse of the body, not tattooing in itself, and that Confucius's Hsiao King injunction against wounding the body one receives from one's parents was linked to tattoos only by Han Chinese racism against tattooed minorities. Citing General Yue Fei's mother inking loyalty on his back, he concludes ink can even be pious, though a child under a parent's legitimate authority owes obedience if forbidden it.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" — Henry Jacoby channels W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' through South Park's Stan Marsh, who debunks John Edward, holistic healers, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the believer and that faith is belief without evidence. The chapter distinguishes prudential from evidential reasons and dismantles Pascal's Wager using episodes like 'Cartmanland' (why would a good God torment nonbelievers?) and 'Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?' (which religion?). Stan's speech to Edward's audience frames uncritical belief as mental laziness that slows the progress of mankind.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 23 "To Know … and Believe" — Daniel Gallagher uses Lost's Rose, who insists 'I just know' her husband lives and the island cured her, to apply Aquinas's account of faith as 'mid-way between knowledge and opinion.' Drawing on Plato's episteme/doxa distinction and Aquinas's God/'first truth' conceptual distinction plus the five ways, he argues reason can demonstrate that God exists while faith (a grace) grasps what reason cannot. Rose exemplifies both the sin of presumption (mistaking faith for knowledge, treating the island as God's certain instrument) and, by contrast to Charlie's acedia, robust faith, so the chapter urges keeping faith and reason harmonized rather than conflated.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 21 "19. The Orville as Philosophy The Dangers of Religion" — The chapter argues that Seth MacFarlane's The Orville is a pointed critique of religion, especially when merged with political and military power. Through the warrior-god Avis worshipped by the Krill (read as stand-ins for militant evangelicals and Islamist jihadists) and the Moclans' patriarchal bigotry, it contends religion is portrayed as archaic and dangerous. It deploys Socrates's Euthyphro argument to reject divine command theory, contrasts the Krill's dogmatic certainty with the secular Union's self-correcting ethics, and invokes Buber's I–Thou to explain the 'de-souling' of outsiders, while defending Lockean separation of church and state against theocracy and theonomistic ethics.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 28 "26. Midnight Mass as Philosophy The Problems with Religion" — The chapter argues that Mike Flanagan's Midnight Mass, through its atheist surrogate Riley, mounts a cumulative case for atheism. Riley's 'campfire' theory naturalistically explains religion's origins; Riley and Dr. Gunning's refusal to call Leeza's healing a miracle enacts Hume's argument against testimony for miracles; Dr. Gunning's EPP explanation of the 'vampires' rebuts methodological naturalism. Sheriff Hassan's grief over his wife voices the problem of evil (Mackie) against the free-will defense (Plantinga), while Erin's dying monologue endorses a Humean/Buddhist no-self bundle theory over the soul. Johnson argues the series treats faith as an epistemic and moral vice and holy books as dangerously interpretable.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 31 "29. Frank Herbert’s Dune as Philosophy The Need to Think for Yourself" — Reading the Sci Fi Channel miniseries Frank Herbert's Dune and Children of Dune, Littmann argues the saga warns against letting leaders or religions think for us: Paul Atreides fakes being the Fremen Mahdi, wages a holy war, and founds a theocratic tyranny that Alia and Leto II carry to worse extremes. He sets Plato's Republic (the guardian class, the noble lie, rule by the wise) and Hobbes against pro-democracy thinkers—Locke's consent and natural rights, Mill's harm principle, Dewey's democracy—then cites Locke, Paine and Russell on religion's dangers, closing with W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' that one must not accept religious claims without sufficient evidence. The chapter reads Paul's dictatorship and the Bene Gesserit's engineered messiah as dramatizations of the historical abuses of concentrated and religious power.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 64 "61. God’s Not Dead as Philosophy Trying to Prove God Exists" — The chapter evaluates the arguments college freshman Josh delivers in God's Not Dead and finds them to fail while the film demonizes atheists via caricature and the Christian persecution complex. It rebuts the Kalam cosmological argument (traced to al-Ghazali) with vacuum fluctuations and a quantum-foam explanation, shows the Big Bang refutes rather than confirms Genesis, and uses Russell's teapot and Hume's evidence proportioning on the burden of proof. Against Josh's 'without God everything is permissible' it applies Plato's Euthyphro to sink divine command theory, answers the free-will defense to the problem of evil, and closes that the film's fideism makes knowledge impossible.

### Allegory of the Cave

The allegory of the cave, from Plato's Republic, imagines prisoners chained since birth so they see only shadows cast on a wall, mistaking these projections for reality. One prisoner is freed, painfully ascends to the sunlit world outside, and comes to understand that the shadows were mere images of true things. The story dramatizes Plato's distinction between the world of appearances and the world of the Forms, and it pictures education as a turning of the soul toward truth rather than a filling of it with facts. It also suggests why the enlightened person, returning to explain what they have seen, may be met with hostility.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 9 "The Fates of Socrates and Seinfeld" — William Irwin compares Jerry and Socrates: the 'Jerry problem' of whether the fictional Jerry is the real Jerry (complicated by Seinlanguage) mirrors the Socratic problem of separating Socrates from Plato's dialogues. Jerry, like Socrates the gadfly, provokes his circle with questions that hunt for essences - the black-and-white cookie, 'is soup a meal?' - and shares Socrates' irony (the 'War: What Is It Good For?' gag in 'The Marine Biologist' works exactly like Socratic shamming ignorance). But where Socrates died serenely per the Apology and Phaedo, Jerry is self-absorbed and ends the series convicted under the Good Samaritan law, doing his stand-up 'gadfly' routine for prison inmates - an examined life, but not an exemplary one.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 11 "Unknown" — Irwin reads Neo's unplugging as Plato's cave allegory restaged: the pod farms are the cave, the cables feeding the illusion are the chains, and Morpheus (named for the god of dreams) plays the liberator who drags the prisoner painfully into the light of 'the desert of the real'. He frames the 'prison for your mind' theme through figures who kept their minds free under captivity, notes that 'education' etymologically means 'leading out' as the prisoner is led out of the cave, and contrasts Neo, who would endure anything rather than return to illusion, with Cypher, who goes back to the shadows.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 12 "Unknown" — Irwin argues the cave story's real point is Plato's Theory of Forms: life inside the Matrix, like ordinary sensory life, is a realm of copies - sunsets, just acts, really good noodles - imitating Beauty, Justice and Goodness themselves. He reads 'there is no spoon' and Morpheus's 'no one can be told what the Matrix is' as Plato's claim that the Forms are grasped by intellect rather than senses, and explains Neo's amnesia and the film's deja vu through Plato's doctrine of recollection (anamnesis), with the soul beholding the Forms between incarnations.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 27 "Unknown" — Korsmeyer traces how the film deploys each sense: vision is both the channel of illusion and, as from Plato's cave onward, the metaphor for understanding ('Why do my eyes hurt?' 'You've never used them'); hearing serves surveillance and bodily invasion, from the centipede-like bug to the screaming 'WAKE UP!' and whispers that nearly touch; and smell marks corporeality, from Trinity's affectionate sniffing of the sleeping Neo to Agent Smith's disgust at human 'stink', which drives him to break protocol and remove his earpiece.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 31 "The Metaphysics of The Matrix" — Gracia and Sanford open with Neo and Trinity in the club and the question that drives the film, 'What is the Matrix?', mapping Neo's path out of the pod onto Plato's cave ascent while stressing the twist: what Neo finds is not the shining realm of Forms but a war-scarred desert, preferred only because it is true, and like Plato's escaped prisoner he returns to free the others. They state their three questions - what are appearance and reality, what separates them, and what properties belong to each - as the paradigmatically metaphysical questions the film poses.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 34 "Unknown" — The authors distinguish the two worlds twice over: by source, since everything in the Matrix issues from the AI machines' program while the real world's ultimate causes lie elsewhere; and by ontological status, since the unreal world depends entirely for its existence on real machines, electrical signals, and minds. They add that recognizing the difference requires a teacher - Morpheus playing to Neo's 'splinter in your mind', just as Plato's cave needs a first freed prisoner - though they file how we come to know this under epistemology rather than metaphysics.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 66 "Unknown" — The chapter reads the pod farms as Plato's cave from Republic VII: prisoners chained from birth who mistake projected images for reality and 'do not know that they are prisoners', insisting on the truth of their world. Morpheus, named for the god of dreams, is the liberator-expert who can rouse sleepers in the right sequence, and Neo's sense of not being sure he is awake parallels the prisoner's primeval recollections. With Plato, it argues that happiness is objective like health - one can say 'I am happy' and be wrong, as the battery-humans are - so true happiness and freedom depend on knowledge of what is real.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 89 "Unknown" — The chapter sets Neo and Cypher as the two poles of authenticity: Neo's unplugging is agony, like the prisoner dragged from Plato's cave - atrophied limbs, eyes that hurt because 'never used them before', and the cognitive shock of the 'desert of the real' - while Cypher, freed young and worn down by years of fear and gag-inducing goop, sells out the crew for a steak he knows does not exist: 'ignorance is bliss'. McMahon asks us to sympathize with Cypher, since in his place, facing perpetual annihilation, 'we too might opt for the illusion'.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 98 "Real Genre and Virtual Philosophy" — Knight and McKnight argue The Matrix must be read as a mixed-genre film: pure genres are 'a theorist's fiction', and the film's genre inheritance supplies the narrative roots of its philosophical thematics - Plato's cave from the Republic, Descartes's Dream Hypothesis from the Meditations, Nietzsche's Ubermensch, Zen Buddhism, and apocalyptic Christianity. Recognizing the genre mix explains both why the film raises questions about justified true belief in a virtual world, free will versus deterministic control, and appearance versus reality, and why it offers no philosophical answers, only genre ones.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 102 "Unknown" — The chapter argues that the film's philosophical allusions—students comparing the pod-bound humans to Plato's cave prisoners and Neo's bewilderment to Descartes's First Meditation dream hypothesis—are designed to generate suspense, anxiety, and horror rather than philosophical reflection. Because genre texts are centrifugal, pointing viewers to outside connections, and their pacing never lingers on themes, The Matrix can use philosophy only to trigger audience interest and never to argue for answers. Its conclusion is that the film is unquestionably real genre but only virtual philosophy.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 115 "Unknown" — Developing thesis one, the chapter shows Morpheus's question—'How would you know the difference between the dream world and the real world?'—restates Plato's cave dwellers mistaking shadows for things and Descartes's First Meditation progression from unreliable senses to dreaming to the malicious demon that makes every belief false. What is genuinely new is that computer simulation and brain science have made the once-outlandish demon scenario thinkable, so the film has made philosophy teachers' job easier: global skepticism no longer seems ridiculous, and maybe you are lying in a tub of goo right now.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 119 "The Matrix Or, The Two Sides of Perversion" — Žižek opens with the 'ideal spectator' beside him exclaiming 'so there is no reality!' and notes the film works as a Rorschach test in which Lacanians, Frankfurt School partisans, and New Agers all recognize themselves. He reframes Plato's cave: when the prisoners escape The Matrix's version of the cave, what they find outside is not the sunlit realm of the Good but the desolate 'desert of the real', and he asks whether the choice between reading the film as Capital colonizing subjectivity or as the virtual symbolic order as such is itself a false alternative.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 17 "Conquering the Inner Demon" — James Lawler casts Buffy as a contemporary allegory of Plato's cave-escaped philosopher and reads the show through Kant: the Slayer moves between a hellish lower world of instrumental appetite and an intelligible higher world of the soul, and Kant's Copernican revolution ('objects must conform to our knowledge') explains Marcie's invisibility in 'Out of Mind, Out of Sight' and the fear-made-flesh Master of 'Nightmares.' Kant's formula that every rational being exists as an end in himself grounds Buffy's duty in 'Anne' ('I am Buffy, the Vampire Slayer'), her rejection of Spike's chip as no substitute for a soul in 'Crush,' and her 'As You Were' admission that using Spike treats him as a mere means. Season Six explores 'too much heaven': Buffy's blissful death in 'The Gift' makes earthly life hell, and only conquering the inner demon — Willow's fear-driven dark magic defeated by Xander's yellow-crayon love in 'Grave' — restores the balance between heavens and hells.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 30 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Lenore Wright reads Sam and Frodo's Quest through the two journey motifs of Western philosophy: the journey out (Plato's cave, structuring Augustine's Confessions and Descartes' escape from the senses' deceptions) and the journey inward (the cogito, self-transformation, with Nussbaum's claim that literature gives philosophy a body). Frodo's steps out of the Shire-cave - selling Bag End, 'I will take the Ring, though I do not know the way' - create the Fellowship and its freedoms, while Boromir attains self-knowledge only at death's door and Gandalf, Aragorn, and Sam are remade by the road. Against classical heroes like Theseus and Odysseus, Sam and Frodo are modern pilgrims - Nietzschean Yea-sayers becoming who they are, with Heideggerian 'potentiality-for-Being' - whereas Sméagol and Saruman live inauthentically, defined by their pasts.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 35 "Last Pitch" — Reid argues that baseball and Socratic elenchus are both constructed to cultivate aretē, excellence. She maps four parallels onto concrete moments: both live off uncertainty (pre-game jitters, the 2001 Rivera–Gonzalez Series finish), both require risking failure (Ted Williams playing a doubleheader to protect his .400, Kirk Gibson's hobbling 1988 homer off Dennis Eckersley, Billy Beane's fear beside Lenny Dykstra), both demand active self-testing (Lou Gehrig retiring when complimented on a routine play), and both impose an obligation to return and challenge others — Plato's cave allegory, Socrates the gadfly, the aging champion who applauds the record-breaker. The Delphic oracle's riddle, that Socrates is wisest in knowing his ignorance, is the batter's-box humility every at-bat demands.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 105 "What Is Real" — Presents the two lines Rowling said she waited seventeen years to write: dying Harry, in the King's Cross limbo, asks Dumbledore whether their conversation is real or only 'inside my head', and Dumbledore answers that of course it is in his head but that does not make it unreal. The section frames this as the philosophical question of separating appearance from reality, cites A. J. Ayer's dismissal of his own near-death experience as hallucination, and introduces Plato's cave as the classic image of mistaking shadows for reality.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 14 "The Jedi Model" — Barad presents a handbook of Jedi virtue modeled on Plato's Republic: the Jedi are Plato's Guardians, trained through physical exercise and Socratic questioning to guard peace and justice. Aristotle's golden mean explains courage as the balance between Chewbacca's cowardly fear and Anakin's rash rush at Dooku, with Luke's decision to leave Dagobah counting as courage because it has just cause. Luke's Dagobah cave vision (Vader's mask opening to reveal his own face) is read as Plato's Cave allegory turned inward - self-knowledge of one's fear of becoming evil - while compassion and forgiveness, not forbidden attachment, complete the Jedi character. The chapter even defends Jedi mind tricks via Plato's noble lie (the myth of the metals) as manipulation of the weak-minded for the common good.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 24 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Wendy Hamblet asks whether Narnia feeds children a dangerous militaristic moral imaginary: Homeric warrior heroes, swarthy Calormene villains, voiceless animals excluded from moral concern, and battles that decide truth, in a lineage running from Plato's censorship of nursery stories through Descartes's modernity to Heidegger's seduction by Hitler's myths. On closer reading she finds Lewis undermining militarism: morally mixed characters, condemnation of aggression, despotism, and 'reasons of state,' and room only for just war and righteous self-defense. The finale is read through Plato's cave, as the Last Battle's worlds-within-worlds expose our political 'truths' as shadow-images that unscrupulous leaders manipulate when the god is absent.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 27 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Takes Digory's dying remark 'It's all in Plato' as the key to the Chronicles. It compares the Professor's guided questioning of Peter and Susan about Lucy's wardrobe testimony to the Socratic method, though noting he supplies evidential maxims rather than eliciting a virtue-definition as Socrates does with Cephalus on justice. It maps Underland in The Silver Chair onto the Allegory of the Cave (Rilian bound in his silver chair like the chained prisoners, the Green Witch's enchantment that denies any world beyond), observing that the Witch 'plays Aristotle' by ridiculing Aslan as an invented perfect Form, while Puddleglum's 'stand by the play-world' speech echoes Socrates's reply to Glaucon that the ideal pattern is none the worse for being unrealizable. Finally it reads the 'real Narnia' of The Last Battle ('world within world, Narnia within Narnia') as Christian Platonism, with the nested heavens even raising Plato's Third Man problem.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 23 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Harman argues the real heroes of Easy Rider are the two Harley-Davidsons: the exploding Captain America bike that drowns out its rider's corpse, the cocaine hidden in the gas tank like a prosthetic organ, and the obscured helmets and muffled dialogue reduce Fonda, Hopper, and Nicholson to 'stowaways and parasites' of their machines. He uses this reversal to attack Kant's Copernican Revolution, on which we could know only how Harleys appear to us and never the things in themselves, and to champion the Whitehead-Deleuze-Latour current in which genes, pickup trucks, bridges, and Harleys are autonomous actors no less than humans, against Plato's two-world heir of appearances and unknowable things. Billy and Captain America's 1960s transgression, he concludes, quietly ends in submission to the power, rhythm, and demands of their bikes.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 11 "U2 and Philosophy" — Dreyfus and Wrathall read U2's head/heart split through Kierkegaard's Sickness unto Death: the Christian-Platonic strategy of escaping the earthly (the sun-blindness of 'Staring at the Sun', the ascent of 'Gone') collapses into despair once both sides of the self prove essential, while 'The Playboy Mansion' and 'Discotheque' depict Kierkegaardian leveling and spiritlessness in consumer culture and 'Last Night on Earth' the aesthetic-sphere despair of living pure possibility. Pascal's contradictory great-and-miserable self and Augustine's two cities supply the tradition U2 inherits, and Nietzsche's 'nihilism' names what U2 calls 'pop'. They close by arguing that Bono's pseudonymous stage characters (the Fly, MacPhisto) do phenomenology just as Kierkegaard's pseudonyms do, and that U2's songs about something missing bear out despair's 'dialectic of eternity'.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 9 "Plato’s Cave Again" — Curran uses Shadow of a Doubt to teach epistemology: Charlie's claim to 'know' her uncle distinguishes knowledge by acquaintance from propositional knowledge as justified true belief, with the permanently stuck 'Til Two clock showing a true belief that is not knowledge because its warrant is unreliable. Coherence (Hegel, Blanshard), pragmatist (James, Dewey), and correspondence theories of truth are tested against the townspeople's false but convenient beliefs about Uncle Charlie, and only correspondence survives. Kant's absolute duty not to lie is weighed against Mill's act and rule utilitarianism for the detectives' deceptions, and a feminist care-ethics perspective assesses Charlie's shielding her mother from the truth. Plato's cave frames the cinema itself: film can deceive like shadows on a wall, yet the detectives' unused photograph shows the camera can also reveal truth, so movies help us face facts, at the price, as Charlie pays, of lost innocence.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 24 "Curtain Down" — Silberstein reads Rear Window as a self-reflexive film about film-watching: the shades rise like a curtain, the courtyard apartments play like frames on a filmstrip, and wheelchair-bound Jeff with his binoculars is the movie spectator - the courtyard is Plato's cave and we are the chained prisoners watching shadows (copies of copies of the forms). The chapter stages the Plato-versus-Aristotle debate over imitative art from Republic Book X and the Poetics, then argues the film vindicates both: Jeff's voyeurism breeds detachment and misjudgment (he misreads Lisa, Miss Torso, the composer and the newlyweds), yet the same watching awakens - the song 'Lisa' saves Miss Lonelyhearts from suicide, Thorwald is brought to justice, and Jeff and the audience leave the theater wiser about fantasy, boredom and their own lives.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 15 "Would You Help Me to Carry the Stone" — Weinstein argues critics who call Waters a gloomy misanthrope misread him: he is an existentialist whose work maps point for point onto Camus's absurd, the human demand for unity endlessly frustrated. Waters's imagery tracks Camus's: the sun (Plato's cave symbol of the good, and the light Sisyphus loved on earth) against the eclipsed moon of death and madness; the stone we secrete through failed communication ('the bad blood slows and turns to stone' in 'Dogs,' 'would you help me to carry the stone' in The Wall) against Sisyphus's rock; and Pink's Trial, condemned for 'showing feelings of an almost human nature,' replaying Meursault's condemnation for failing to cry at his mother's funeral. Since the institutions of home, school, military, and the music industry's machine block every genuine encounter, Waters's persistence in making art that mostly fails to communicate is itself the absurd revolt, so with Camus one must imagine Sisyphus happy, and Weinstein imagines Waters happy too.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 16 "Thinking Inside the Pod" — Condella reads the opening of Saturday Night Fever -- Tony Manero strutting to 'Stayin' Alive' while delivering a can of paint -- as the iPod condition in miniature: music that alters rather than captures reality, now dial-up-able for workouts ('Eye of the Tiger'), bus rides, and grocery runs. Through Heidegger he argues the iPod is calculative thinking incarnate, annihilating the time, silence, and solitude meditative thinking requires (the shower as last refuge), and deepening technological homelessness by flattening every place into whatever soundtrack we choose -- the Rhine dammed into a 'gigantic gasoline station,' the iPod pushing us 'pretty far down' in Plato's Cave, its very possibility prepared by Descartes's thinking thing. Yet his wife's yoga instructor chanting on a Bronx bus shows the iPod can also open meditative space, so what Heidegger demands is not Luddism but Gelassenheit, a free relationship to technology.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 19 "Youth and the Image" — Hickey argues the iPod is the 'iCon of a generation' because it is a Baudrillardian simulacrum of youth: like the Gulf War consumed as CNN fireworks or reality TV's fabricated 'real,' Apple's silhouette ads sell faceless dancers whose entire identity is the white device -- a 'symbolic cyborgism' read through Donna Haraway. The vernacular of iPodding, podcasting, and downloading forms what he calls, with Wittgenstein, a language game woven into the actions of the 'now' that authorizes this youthful, tech-savvy identity as natural, while the ads' imagery works like Platonic shadows in the caves of our desire. Still, citing Giddens's structure-agency negotiation and DeCerteau's consumer tactic of re-appropriating everyday images, he insists we are not brainwashed: we can switch off, refuse, or remake the images that 'tell us who we are.'
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 6 "Ex Astris, Scientia GEORGE A REISCH" — The editors' introduction takes Starfleet Academy's motto 'Ex Astris, Scientia' as its frame: Picard handing cadet Wesley Crusher a book by William James shows officers need philosophy, not just ship operations, and the starry-heavens motif runs from Thales and Plato's cave through Kant's 'moral law within and starry heavens above.' It surveys the book's Trek dilemmas (Picard and Dathon's alien language, Data's emotion chip, Khan's vengeance, Riker's Q powers) as 2,500-year-old philosophical problems, and argues Trek's optimism — Picard's 'the acquisition of wealth is no longer the driving force' — restates Aristotle's claim that all humans by nature desire to know. Like philosophy from Socrates on, Trek is presented as 'an entertaining, edifying preparation' for living by one's ideals, a life-education primer sealed with Roddenberry's advice to 'slip in a heavy idea or two.'
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 26 "Must I Repeat Myself" — Seng maps Dorothy's journey onto Plato's cave allegory: Kansas is the cave of shadows, Oz the painful ascent into light, and the crucial shared point is Socrates' demand that the freed prisoner go back down into the cave, which explains why Dorothy, once enlightened, must return to gray Kansas bearing self-knowledge. He surveys the film adaptations (1910, Semon's 1925, Eshbaugh's 1933, Fleming's 1939, Return to Oz, and The Wiz) to show that each rewrites 'home' as self-knowledge rather than a place, culminating in Glinda's The Wiz speech, 'If we know ourselves, we're always home, anywhere.' Kierkegaard's contrast between recollection and repetition then sorts the homecomings: Baum's Dorothy wills recollection of what was lost, while Diana Ross's Dorothy wills repetition, holding to her self amid change, which Seng says Kierkegaard regards as the equivalent of faith.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 20 "Colbert Is (the Tragedy and Comedy of) America, and So Are We" — Ralkowski asks whether Colbert is America's Socrates, comparing Colbert's ironic interviews (Caitlin Flanagan on feminism, Harvey Mansfield on manliness, Howard Dean's superdelegates, the ABC Stephanopoulos-Gibson debate) to Socrates' definitional refutations of Euthyphro and the Athenian elite. Like Socrates in Plato's cave allegory, Colbert is a shadow on the wall undermining truthiness from within, yet both fail: audiences laugh, guests collect the campaign-donation 'Colbert Bump,' and nothing changes, making America the self-satisfied one who is ignorant of its ignorance. Through Nehamas's contrast of Socratic and Platonic irony and the Symposium's demand that the greatest work read as both tragedy and comedy, the chapter concludes Colbert may be America's Plato — condemning and laughing at us like a Sisyphean liberator who knows we will not leave the cave.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 7 "4" — Four 'Phase One' essays. Dyer reads Mark Millar's Wanted through Plato's cave: Wesley Gibson escapes a pathetic life like the freed prisoner, but like Adolf Eichmann (via Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem) he murders his conscience, so the Fraternity's consequence-free world leaves him numb and unable to value anything - a descent deeper into the cave, ending in the banality of evil. Novy explains why henchmen betray using Aristotle's utility/pleasure/complete friendship distinction (Big Cheese, Henchmen Muenster and Feta): supervillain gangs are Hobbesian pirate crews with no enforcer, so a modus vivendi of self-interest collapses under interrogation and only Machiavellian fear secures loyalty. Foresman applies Goodman and Rawls's reflective equilibrium as a 'cheat' to rank Apocalypse, Magneto, Luthor, the Joker, and Bizarro, concluding the 'best of the worst' is judged on evil ends (or evil means, as with Magneto) and even on glorious failure. Arinder and Milton, in a staged descent-into-madness frame, diagnose mad science in Victor Frankenstein and Dr. Doom as science that denies value-laden theory choice - impossible because data underdetermine theory - breeding the hubris that dehumanizes the scientist.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 26 "You Can Discover More about a Person in an Hour of Play than in a Year of" — Tim Christopher weighs pseudonymity — multiple persistent in-game identities — against responsibility for what those identities do, opening with his accidental first 'honorable kill' and the real-world extremes of a stabbing over loud WoW and a murder over a borrowed virtual sword. Using the Tae Kwon Do mat as a model of the sacred gamespace, he argues that WoW's persistent world and anonymity invite misbehavior, yet since no one is kind in WoW out of fear of punishment, any kindness there may be kindness for its own sake — an honest character may be a better person than an honest player. Plato's Allegory of the Cave is his master image: players see only shadows (avatars) of the real people behind them and must remember the world outside the cave.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 33 "Cyborg Goddess" — Reads Ghost in the Shell as Donna Haraway's 'Cyborg Manifesto' made flesh: Major Kusanagi is built not born, has no sexuality or romance, and relegates male partners to sidekicks, enacting Haraway's post-gender cyborg that breaks the dualisms binding women to body, nature, and reproduction. The chapter traces the 'ghost' back through Koestler to Ryle's mockery of Descartes's mind-body dualism, reads the genderless, net-born Puppet Master as the Singularity of transhumanist philosophy, and interprets the Major–Puppet Master fusion — urged to 'come out of the shadows and into the light' in an explicit Plato's-cave gesture — as a posthuman, techno-spiritual 'Cyborg Goddess' that renders both gender and humanity obsolete.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 11 "He’s Got to Make His Own Mistakes" — Cole pits Plato against Walter Benjamin to vindicate the imitation of Rush: Plato's cave makes art a shadow twice removed from the Forms, and on that view a perfect copy is impossible and every cover degraded, while Peart's 'Limelight' calls the stage a 'gilded cage' that is 'just a prettified cave' yet, with 'we are merely players' (via Shakespeare), makes performing the way out rather than deeper in. Benjamin's translator essay, with its 'language forest' echo and 'pure language', shows how Rush's cover of 'Summertime Blues' on Feedback layers Blue Cheer and the Who into one perception, and how live variations of 'Witch Hunt' and the premature chord of 'Turn the Page' let error overtake and become the new original. The chapter exceeds Aristotle's principle of non-contradiction in 'pure language', where original, copy, and fan covers (Rock Band failures, the South Park 'Lil' Rush' flub, Rick Mercer's drum lesson) are fragments of one greater vessel, so errors are portals of discovery.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 12 "Guardian Training" — Roger Travis argues Plato would welcome Halo as guardian training: mimesis is really 'playing epic pretend,' and Halo, like the Homeric epics that were Athens' textbooks, trains players in a way of life. Plato's Republic Book 10 critique—the painted bed as copy of a copy of the Form of Bed—warns that playing Master Chief could let appetite rule, yet the Laws' admission that the ideal city's politeia is itself a mimesis turns the tables: the Republic is its own training simulation of philosophic pretend. Re-imagining the cave as prisoners tied to couches playing Super Mario Bros, he argues Halo's dutiful NPCs and waking-to-duty player (literal cryo-wakeups in Combat Evolved and Halo 3) make it philosophy in Plato's own sense, with Aristotle's catharsis leavening the verdict.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 7 "Happy Ending" — Wenmackers uses Inception's dream levels and its ambiguous spinning-top ending as a guided tour of skeptical philosophy, diagramming how dreams-within-dreams, kicks, Limbo and exponentially dilated dream time work. She tests the totem against Zhuangzi's butterfly and lucid-dreaming reality checks, then runs Plato's Cave and the eternal Forms, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine to ask whether Cobb's world - or ours - is real. Her conclusion is Socratic ('know that you know nothing'): subjective reality feels equally real on every level and the top level can never be known. She even argues that dream-time dilation means Cobb should not kill himself while in doubt, since real time barely passes, so a little philosophy rescues the happy ending.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 10 "The Power of Choice" — Rennett tests Cobb's choice to leave Limbo against Nozick's three reasons for refusing the experience machine: we want to actually do things (raise his real children, not loving projections), to be a certain kind of person (Yusuf's dream-den addicts are 'indeterminate blobs'), and to touch something deeper than a man-made world. He then recruits Berkeley's esse est percipi to explain Mal's sincerity - she perceives Limbo and remembers it, so for her it is real - and argues that shared dreams differ from private dreams and the experience machine because they leave waking traces, like Mal's bullet in Arthur's leg. The chapter ends by making reality a matter of choice: like the cave prisoners of Plato's allegory, each character believes a world, and Cobb's ignoring of the top is his choice to live in the world with his children.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 22 "The Kick—Back to ‘Reality’" — The authors read the film in descending layers: reality as an ideology of touch and unreliable sensory experience, framed by Descartes's wax thought experiment and dream argument, with the kick explained through Hume's account of belief as custom and the totems as broken game pieces marking broken people (Mal's choice of the dream echoing prisoners returning to Plato's cave). The heist is then read as an existentialist drama where Cobb's 'downwards is the only way forwards' rejects the passive waiting of Beckett's Waiting for Godot and the pharmacy dreamers, with Jaspers's analysis of solitude making Limbo a hell of lonely regret that only an encounter with another can end. The chapter then argues the film is reflexively about movies (the crew mirrors a film crew, the Penrose stairs expose cinema's flat illusions, crosscutting manufactures time) before ending on Descartes's unresolved doubt about whether the final reality deserves our trust.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 94 "Chapter 14 - Trauma of the Real" — Introduces Paul Livingston's part with Dick's confession that reading Plato in college convinced him the empirical world was not truly real, then retells the cave of Republic Book VII in detail: prisoners bound since birth watching shadows of puppets cast by a fire. The cave becomes the frame for Dick's fiction — the 'reality' our percept-systems report is a show of images, and the philosophical quest is the prisoner's turn toward the archetypal reality behind the scenes.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 95 "Breakthrough to the Real" — Details the disorienting breakthrough in which characters learn that they themselves are fakes: Rachael's distress at her implanted memories ('How can it not know what it is?'), Deckard's paper unicorn in the director's cut confirming his own replicant status, and Ragle Gumm's soft-drink stand dissolving into a slip of paper reading 'SOFT-DRINK STAND' in Time Out of Joint. Each case maps onto the freed cave prisoner's discovery, and the disorientation is pressed onto the viewer: how can I be sure my own life and memories are not a fabrication?
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 97 "Procession of Dummies" — Uses Dick's 1972 one-sentence definition ('Reality is that which, when you stop believing in it, doesn't go away') and his claim that absolute reality reveals itself only when our space-time categories collapse, arguing the definition fits Lacan's Real better than Plato's picture of looking away from the cave wall. Through Žižek's readings, Ragle Gumm's objects being literally replaced by their symbolic labels and Deckard's replicant recognition as a 'total loss of the hero's symbolic identity' show the traumatic Real first appearing precisely where symbolically constituted reality fails.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 48 "Out of the Cave" — Traces the light-versus-darkness metaphor tradition from Plato's cave and Socrates' unexamined life through medieval 'illumination' and the Enlightenment to St. Paul's glass darkly, then lets Nietzsche ('shadow is as needful as light') and Derrida's deconstruction of presence/absence oppositions overturn it. The Stones do the same work in song: 'Just as every cop is a criminal, and all the sinners saints' in 'Sympathy for the Devil,' with 'Here Comes the Sun' overturned by 'Paint It Black' and 'Let It Be' by 'Let It Bleed.'
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 15 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Rood unpacks Klosterman's 'This Is Emo' thesis that no woman will ever satisfy him: women love Lloyd Dobler rather than John Cusack, and everyone measures real relationships against Hollywood fake love (Coldplay songs, the Woody Allen Personality Type) until, as Klosterman puts it, real people actively trying to live like fake people are no less fake. He reads this through Sartre's cafe waiter and Butler's gender performativity to argue identity is learned performance, and through Plato's cave updated to a reclining-seat movie theater where we mistake projected shadows for real love. The deepest diagnosis is Baudrillard's hyperreal, glossed as a social-constructionist rerun of Kant's Copernican revolution, against which Rood's own objection lands: Klosterman covertly assumes a pure unmediated self that cannot exist, so the answer to fake love is not escape from mediation but self-control within it.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 12 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Richard Rosenbaum asks how Gaiman's gods, abstract concepts made flesh who live or die by human belief, could exist, starting from Plato's Forms (Odin as personified battle-wisdom, Media as media) and the Allegory of the Cave, which gives new meaning to a protagonist literally named Shadow. Finding Forms too independent to need believers, he upgrades the metaphysics with Leibniz's Monadology: if everything, bodies and ideas alike, is composed of perception-bearing monads, then shared beliefs can agglomerate, 'level up' into a soul, and become a living god walking around America. Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness, panprotopsychism, and the claim that information has interdependent physical and phenomenal aspects supply the final mechanism, so collective belief realized phenomenally must become physically embodied, in contrast to the dualism of Descartes that made mind-body interaction mysterious.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 23 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Rick Mayock stops a fictional Jeopardy! clock to apply Plato's divided line: most contestants, like the cave prisoners rewarded for predicting shadow sequences, trade in doxa - conjecture (eikasia) and belief (pistis) - while the Meno's slave boy shows how Socratic questioning ties true opinions down into knowledge. Winning requires only dianoia, hypothetical reasoning from hypotheses and definitions, never noesis, the dialectic that ascends to the eternal Forms; the Phaedo's example of perfect 'equality' shows why the 'Aha!' of recognition is re-cognition by an immortal soul already acquainted with the Forms. Watson, lacking such a soul, can clear a buzz threshold but never have an Aha! moment - it is Daedalus's statue, lifelike but sure to run away from the truth unless tied down.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 32 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Reitter reads the sewer mutants - banished underground, surviving on what the surface flushes, as in 'The Mutants Are Revolting' where Leela is deported without trial the moment Fry reveals she is not an alien - as philosophy's Other, illuminated by Plato's cave (surface dwellers fear and demonize what they have never seen) and Beauvoir's The Second Sex (Leela passes as an acceptable alien until exposed as a mutant). Mrs. Astor's United Mutant Scholarship Fund film, with its 'noble sewer mutants... uh, people, I guess,' is read alongside Said's Orientalism and racist charity imagery as a third face of Othering. The chapter then adds folklore theory: the mutants are a folk group with their own urban legends (alligators in the sewer, and the 'sub-urban legend' of sub-mutants), ballads like 'The Legend of El Chupanibre,' and freegan-style recycling ethics - a counterculture whose difference the dominant universe-view casts as monstrosity.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 24 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Arp uses King Worm's dream-within-dreams to pose the perception-reality problem: distinguishing perceiver, perceptions, and perceived, he maps the triad onto Plato's allegory of the cave, then contrasts epistemological and metaphysical realism (the fallen tree fort still makes sound waves unheard; Pythagoras discovered rather than invented his theorem) with idealism and antirealism, whose dead end is solipsism—Lumpy Space Princess locked in a private movie theater of perceptions. Hume's picture of the mind as a theater of successive perceptions and Berkeley's Hylas-and-Philonous worry that we are trapped inside perceptual reality give the skeptical threat its force. The chapter sides with Jake—'You gotta focus on what's real, man'—while conceding that after 'King Worm' Finn and Jake can never be certain they escaped the hypnotism.
