- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 10 "I Think, Therefore I Exist . . . I Think" — Johnson argues that the Platonic-Cartesian soul is refuted by neuroscience (Phineas Gage, Penfield's stimulation studies), and that Locke's memory criterion fails on Reid-style transitivity cases like DoctorDonna and on Bernard-Williams-inspired worry about the amnesiac John Smith, who would still dread the Family of Blood's torture. Parfit's causal-continuity criterion then wrongly makes the meta-crisis Doctor of 'Journey's End' identical with the Tenth, so Johnson defends a four-dimensionalist 'time worm' view on which the Doctors are stages of one person — before a final sorites-style argument (heaps, spin-offs like Torchwood) suggests that 'persons' may not exist at all.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 28 "Here They Are ... Ready to Outsit Eternity" — Argues that regeneration helps show life after death is logically possible: the successive Doctors (Fourth to Fifth in 'Logopolis') prove identity survives radical personality change, so a perfected heavenly Joe would still be Joe. Testing whether identity lies in body or memory, he contrasts John Smith in 'Human Nature' (same body, so same person) with the 'Journey's End' Doctor-clone whose replicated memories Rose rejects ('But he's not you'), favoring bodily continuity. This leaves the unavailability-of-atoms problem, which he solves with van Inwagen's theory that God removes and preserves our bodies at death like a divine cryonicist, echoing the Fourth Doctor's 'ready to outsit eternity' tribute in 'The Ark in Space'.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 29 "Love and Doctors" — Asks whether 'the Doctor' is a Kripkean rigid designator naming one individual or a non-rigid role filled by different people, using the Ninth Doctor's deathbed doubts and the Time Crash memory loop to settle on the rigid reading. He then deploys Locke's body/organism/person distinctions, Parfit's overlapping psychological-connectedness fix to Reid's transitivity objection (Sarah Jane across 1983-1996-2006), and the amnesia-prone regenerations and the Valeyard to show the organism survives regeneration while the person might not. Finally he argues that because DoctorTwo in 'Journey's End' shares all the Doctor's psychologically connected memories of Rose, fission makes them two persons with equal claim, so Rose gets the person she actually loved.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 36 "One More Thing, Don’t Blink!" — Uses Carroll's art-horror theory (monster = threat plus disgust) to ask why the Weeping Angels of 'Blink' terrify despite being beautiful, harmless-seeming statues. The answer: by dumping Kathy and Billy in the past they destroy identity itself, understood through Frankfurt's account of caring and MacIntyre's narrative identity, since everything a person cares about is tied to a time and place. Since the Angels provoke no disgust, the chapter revises Carroll: horror is fear plus impotence, and forcing victims to survive by not blinking makes viewers feel their powerlessness over their own bodies.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 20 "Long-Term Identity" — Asks whether the final Duncan Idaho ghola, whose serial memories wake during his encounter with Murbella, is the same person as the original who died holding off nineteen Sardaukar. It tests physical continuity, Locke's memory-based sameness of person (Hayt becomes Duncan only when the original's consciousness reawakens), Parfit's psychological connectedness with its redescription of identity as survival through quasi-memory, Schechtman's narrative self-constitution, Velleman's self-inventing characters, and four-dimensionalist 'space-time worms' on which Leto II's 3,500 years and the Duncans' gappy five millennia are single long selves. Herbert's moral: identity is not fixed—societies and technologies, from the Tleilaxu tanks to the Sisterhood's swift accommodation, keep redrawing what counts as the same person. Same Duncans, same person.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 22 "Get Out of My Mind!" — Runs Lady Jessica's spice-agony Other Memory through Locke's Essay: if a person is a 'thinking intelligent being' whose identity extends as far as her consciousness reaches, then Jessica—having received the memories of every Reverend Mother back to Raquella Berto-Anirul—must be identical with Raquella, and with Alia who shares the same memories, which is absurd. Thomas Reid's gallant officer is staged as Gurney Halleck, who remembers Rabban's whip but not his sister's eyes, breaking the transitivity of memory-based identity. The chapter closes with three modern paths—psychological continuity, Eric Olson's animalism, and Dennett's selves as 'centers of narrative gravity'—plus a Lockean coda defending the Abomination Alia as a person no fixed class of nature could exclude.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 14 "A Story in Search of a Narrator" — Brian Gregor reads Dexter through Charles Taylor's 'self-interpreting animal': Dexter's identity is not a fixed thing but comes into being through self-interpretation within an inescapable framework of value, so even his 'Am I good? Am I evil?' rebellion and the Nietzschean Übermensch reading fail to escape the deeper convictions about innocence, evil and desert that Harry's Code presupposes - as his guilt over the innocent Farrow shows. The chapter interprets Dexter's serial failures at being 'seen' - Harry's 'only one who really saw me', Brian's fraternal 'you can be yourself with me', Lila's probing, and Miguel Prado as Aristotle's friend, 'another self' - as Hegelian struggles for recognition that collapse because his real self can never come into the open. Finally, drawing on MacIntyre's narrative account of identity, it argues Dexter is literally a story in search of a narrator, whose selfhood persists through flashbacks, blood slides and noir-style voice-overs, and whose humanity shows in the need to have his account of himself heard and corrected by another.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 10 "Mastering the Chief" — Joyce Havstad asks which of the millions of player-instantiated Master Chiefs is real, and whether the flash-cloned John left behind on Eridanus II is the same boy. She runs the Ship of Theseus on the MJOLNIR armor—a technician rebuilds a second suit from every replaced piece—contrasting material with historical continuity, and adds Hobbes's reassembled-planks version. Locke's prince-and-cobbler memory criterion is reconstructed across John, John-117, and Master Chief, then broken by Reid's brave-officer objection, leaving psychological continuity as the best but imperfect criterion; the Flood's conversion of a Covenant soldier into a Combat Form shows identity lost once original sentience is gone.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 17 "Where Parfit Went Wrong" — Peter Ludlow and Chiara Repetti-Ludlow read Red vs. Blue as an intuition pump for personal identity, running through Locke's prince-and-cobbler, Bernard Williams's duplicated Guy Fawkes, Shoemaker's brain transplant, and Wiggins's split brain before aiming at Parfit. Project Freelancer's Director fractures the Alpha AI into fragments (Epsilon's memories, Omega's rage) recombined into the Meta, and they argue intuitions break against Parfit here: psychological continuity via small fractured pieces—unlike Parfit's fission into two substantial halves—does not secure the source's survival. Church's disembodied AI existence and the ever-present agent-AI voice (Agent Washington driven mad by Epsilon) illustrate Putnam's 'soul stuff' and the extended-mind hypothesis of Chalmers and Clark better than Chalmers waving his iPhone.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 19 "Surviving Fusion" — Amy Kind asks whether the Holmes who marries Laurie R. King's Mary Russell could still be Holmes, weighing Aristophanes' speech in Plato's Symposium (Zeus split the original spherical humans, and love seeks our lost half) against Derek Parfit's fusion case from Reasons and Persons, in which two people grow into one body, which we would all find horrifying. Against Nozick's account of love as becoming a 'we', Delaney's merger and Gaylin's 'fused identity', she deploys Marilyn Friedman's federation model, lovers as sovereign states forming a flexible third entity, to argue that Holmes and Russell's marriage survives because its fusion reshapes identity without obliterating it: his 'half a creature with two brains and four eyes' and her refusal of the nickname 'Zherlock Mary' show both lovers keeping separate selves.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 9 "Does the Top Fall Does It Matter in the End" — Andersen contends Inception goes one deeper than Descartes: where the dream argument threatened only the external world, inception threatens the autonomy of thought itself, since the 'core conception' that defines identity - Fischer's reading of his father's dying word 'disappointed' - can be implanted. Tracing Nolan's obsession with thought-manipulation through his earlier films (the manipulator Cobb of Following, Leonard's self-deception in Memento, the Joker's schemes), he shows inception as co-opting subjectivity. Against the Cartesian answer of doubting everything, the fates of Mal and Cobb in Limbo - where doubt, once planted, grows devastatingly, and where a totem cannot guard against self-deception - teach that the way back to reality is the leap of trust in others: only by opening himself to Ariadne, Miles and his children can Cobb turn away from the top and go home.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 36 "Chapter 05 - Just Who and How Many Do You Think You Are" — Feist opens with Dr. Wigan's autopsy of a man with half a brain and a full mind, moves through the split-brain experiments (the left hand writing 'PIPE' for a concealed pipe as the hemispheres autocomplete each other), and lands on Joseph Bogen's revived thesis that each of us has two minds that merely feel like one. He shows Dick threading Bogen's actual sentences mid-dialogue into A Scanner Darkly so the reader experiences a voice from nowhere, foreshadowing how Arctor's self explodes under the scramble suit, the Fred persona and Substance D into separate persons, Bob and Fred, who end up unsure who, and how many, they are.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 37 "The User Illusion" — The chapter interleaves a doctor's line-card quiz of Fred with Bogen and Wigan's claims that each cerebrum is 'a distinct and perfect whole as an organ of thought' and that our cherished 'inner conviction of Oneness' is mere opinion. Descartes supplies the target: a partless mind known directly and with certainty, external things known only indirectly through possibly misleading ideas, and Dick, we are told, flips this picture so the inside is messy and the outside clear.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 38 "In a Mirror, Darkly" — The chapter stages Arctor's bishop's-robe musing ('What is identity? Where does the act end?') against the classic puzzles: the Ship of Theseus with its two reassembled vessels, and the baby photos you share no cells with. Locke gives memory plus a unified 'thinking, intelligent being' with real unity; Hume bites the bullet, finding only perceptions in introspection, never a self, so the self's identity over time is a normal, inescapable delusion like a mountain's. All of it converges on Fred watching Bob and asking 'who am I? Which one of them is me?'
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 39 "You Don’t Always Get Along" — The chapter animates Hume's bundle as a 'little republic' of mental citizens without a universal citizen, staging a dialogue between Person-Hume, who cannot believe there is no self, and Philosopher-Hume, who counsels beer and billiards. It traces the view back to Plato's Republic: the tripartite soul (with Freud's id-ego-superego as a modern rerun), the example of desiring and refusing the same cold beer when you must collect your mother from the airport, and Leontius raging at his own eyes before the corpses, cross-chatter as civil strife among inner citizens, exactly what the doctors diagnose as Fred's symptom.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 44 "Follow the Psyche" — The chapter assembles Dick's survival-of-the-psyche cases: Agneta Rautavaara kept alive as a brain in a nutrient bath, Professor Thomas's conscious brain piloting a spaceship, the wub transferring into Captain Franco mid-execution, and the Rexorian consciousness in 'Human Is', then grounds the pattern in Locke's prince-and-cobbler and detached-little-finger thought experiments: 'consciousness makes personal identity.' Everything is codified as the Psyche Continuity Rule, to keep track of the person follow the psyche, with brains mattering only as convenient storage vessels.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 45 "The Perils of Rekall, Inc" — The chapter runs through three incompatible backstories for Total Recall's Quaid, Cohaagen's infiltration plot, Hauser's genuine defection and self-erasure, or a Rekall trip gone live, and shows that in all three no single psyche links the life stages, forcing a Body Continuity Rule and then a Combined Rule that follows the psyche when mental life is unified and the body when it is disjointed. Paycheck's Jennings, who starts referring to his earlier self in the third person, exposes the rule's weak joint: deciding when a mental life counts as sufficiently disjointed.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 46 "Gotta Have Soul" — The chapter tests a Soul Continuity Rule: the wub and Hauser survive because their souls do, though Locke himself denies the soul is the person, and Leibniz's King-of-China bargain, become the richest man if you forget everything, shows why, since it would amount to being annihilated while a King of China is created in your place. Kant's case of one mental life relayed across a chain of souls yields just one person, and the rule's practical failure is evidential: nothing could tell one soul with swapped psyches from swapped souls in the same body.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 47 "Future Selves and Imposters" — The chapter builds a counterexample from Imposter: suppose the same mind-transfer process makes the alien android an imposter in one story but the dying Olham's chosen future self in another, with identical bodily and mental continuity but opposite verdicts, so the Combined Rule fails. Intention cannot rescue the Soul Rule either, since in a government-forced transfer Olham would absurdly have to say 'I am dead over there across the room' if souls simply went where we wanted.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 48 "Selfless" — The chapter concedes that no rule, psyche, body, soul, or combined, accommodates all of Dick's transformations, and refuses to blame Dick for incoherence: his stories force our own conflicting intuitions about wubs, Quaids and downloaded minds into the open. Pessimist, optimist and skeptic each get a verdict, the skeptic's being the chapter's cliffhanger: if we are none of these things, maybe there are no enduring persons at all.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 49 "Is It Live or Is It Memorex" — The chapter supplies the missing detail, transfer versus copying: a 'snapshot' of Olham's brain imprinted on an android leaves Olham where he was, and frying the original destroys him rather than moving him, while the bank-transfer versus copying-money analogy and the question of one psyche imprinted on two androids show why the difference matters. Once the mechanics are filled in one way the alien android is a mere copy and Olham dies, filled in another way he survives bodiless, which restores the Psyche Rule pending a science of how psyches are realized in us.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 57 " . . You Ever Take That Test Yourself" — Rachael's question to Deckard at the piano ('you ever take that test yourself?') and Luba Luft's suggestion that a human Deckard was killed and replaced put the viewer in the same quandary about implanted memories. The Penfield mood organ lets humans dial numbered moods, so the empathy that supposedly separates humans from androids is itself artificially inducible, while Phil Resch's torment over whether he is an android — compared to Munch's 'The Scream' — shows the human/android line collapsing from inside.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 95 "Breakthrough to the Real" — Details the disorienting breakthrough in which characters learn that they themselves are fakes: Rachael's distress at her implanted memories ('How can it not know what it is?'), Deckard's paper unicorn in the director's cut confirming his own replicant status, and Ragle Gumm's soft-drink stand dissolving into a slip of paper reading 'SOFT-DRINK STAND' in Time Out of Joint. Each case maps onto the freed cave prisoner's discovery, and the disorientation is pressed onto the viewer: how can I be sure my own life and memories are not a fabrication?
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 101 "How Do We Get Deceived" — Catalogues the channels of deception: the senses (the nonexistent Martian canals, Quaid's fat-lady disguise and hologram watch, and the Adjustment Team literally remaking the world) and, more worrisomely, memory, with implanted pasts for Quaid, Rachael, and the Impostor replicant 'so that the Tyrell Corporation can control them better.' Real cognitive science backs the threat: Nader's reconsolidation experiments show memory is Read-Write rather than Read-Only, and 'lost-in-the-mall' interviews implant rich false memories without any drug at all.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 142 "Memory and the Brain-Butchers" — The section uses Quaid's Rekall-fabricated life, complete with false wedding memories and a false eight-year marriage, to challenge Locke's memory theory of personal identity: implants, together with ordinary forgetting, revision, and loss, show memory cannot be what makes you the same person from one day to the next. Kuato's line, 'A man is defined by his action, not his memory,' is offered as the alternative the following sections develop.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 143 "Owning Your Actions, Owning Your Past" — This section reconstructs the traditional view of free agency from Aristotle: an action is freely mine when it 'has its origin in the agent himself,' so owning an action means tracing its causal chain back to one's own decision. It explains Aristotle's picture of natures as internal sources of motion and decision as the distinctively human motion, then asks whether Quaid, following the suitcase, video, and clues Hauser pre-arranged, is picking up the chain of his own prior decision, and so becoming himself again.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 144 "Inpsychation and Chains of Will" — The section develops freedom as extending the will through tools and other people, via Nietzsche's 'inpsychation' and Emerson's conversion of fate into force: Cohaagen shuts off the air through Lori and Harry as Hitler invaded Poland through his soldiers. Locke's memory theory returns demoted to a useful tool rather than an identity-maker, and Nietzsche's Genealogy II.1 on the unbroken 'long chain of will' explains Hauser's masterpiece, planning around his own memory wipe so that Quaid, following the planted clues, re-inpsychates Hauser's decisions.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 145 "Quaid’s Problem—Mucky Origins" — This section complicates everything: two taped Hausers contradict each other, rebel hero or Cohaagen's 'bosom buddy,' so Quaid cannot settle who he is by tracing his origins. It then generalizes: in the scientific worldview of universal causation, from gravity to DNA inherited through chimps and sea squirts from the primeval muck, no one originates anything, a conclusion quoted at length from Baron d'Holbach's System of Nature, yet first-person deliberation still leaves Quaid feeling the weight of choice.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 146 "Freedom Without Origins" — The section rejects randomness as a foundation for freedom, quantum indeterminacy being Epicurus's swerve again, since actions tracing to random particle events are no more mine than law-determined ones, then turns to the ethical problem: if Hauser volunteered and Cohaagen's story is true, freedom-as-origination would require Quaid to become Hauser again, Mercedes included. Quaid's verdict ('The guy's a fucking asshole') shows freedom is also changing course to do what is right; as Lowe says in 'We Can Remember It for You Wholesale,' what defines us is 'not a memory but a desire,' and in breaking with his past Quaid decisively becomes free.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 13 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann asks whether 'you' survive a walker bite, testing bodily identity, behaviorism, and functionalism as theories of personal survival against Jenner's verdict that after death 'everything you ever were... gone'. His centerpiece adapts Daniel Dennett: survivors yoke walkers to plows and tanks, dangle meat to move them between positions labeled 1 and 0, and gradually build a rope-and-corpse computer functionally identical to a human brain - which behaviorism and functionalism must call conscious, yet which we can conceive as utterly dark inside. The lesson is that we cannot know whether any system, walker, animal, or AI, is conscious, so treatment of non-human systems may need to err on the side of caution.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 15 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Delfino and Taylor ask whether Morgan's zombified wife is still a person, which decides whether shooting her is murder. On the dominant Western view - Boethius's 'individual substance of a rational nature', Aquinas's image-of-God intellect, Kantian dignity against Singer's speciesism challenge - walkers lack intelligence and so are not persons, so Morgan should shoot. They then argue walkers are metaphysically impossible beings, square-circles: dead tissue that somehow sees, smells, and runs down prey without functioning organs, energy intake, or the reanimated neocortex that movement and sensation require. Zombies fascinate because they are projections of our fears - dead yet moving, an afterlife of horror - a Hamlet-like caught-between-being-and-nonbeing.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 18 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Dave Beisecker amplifies Noel Carroll's paradox of horror: why would anyone enjoy watching, let alone compete for, AMC's 'stagger-on role' as a repulsive walker? Curiosity fails as an answer, since by Nagel's bat argument no amount of staggering around a set tells us what it is like to be a zombie - and since zombification destroys memory, desire, and self-concern, we would not survive it as persons in any interesting sense anyway. His solution is that zombies are the endearing losers and clowns of the undead world: playing one is a way to celebrate our inner awkward nerd and laugh at universal human ineptitude, which is exactly why Kirkman's shambling walkers, unlike fast zombies or glamorous vampires, invite impersonation.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 13 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Silcox recalls his middle-school Paladin dying to eighty-three orcs while his friends held a memorial service, and asks whether grief for a player character is irrational. He tests Charles Taylor's narrative ethics—the thesis that we grasp our lives as unfolding stories—finding it challenged by Beckett's Godot, the novel-within-a-novel of Atonement, and Samantha Vice's warnings about story-shaped lives, and he notes leveling up and 4E's heroic PCs make characters story-like in ways ordinary lives are not. Ultimately PC death differs from real death because the campaign's story continues without the character, whereas death, as Nagel argues, cuts off our open-ended future; Silcox ends by recasting the self as a 'back-story' or metanarrative that enables storytelling, rejecting Descartes' claim that the power of imagination is inessential to our essence.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 23 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Monica Evans argues that D&D is identity play in which players explore who they are through characters they create, perform and try to keep alive, opening with Plutarch's Ship of Theseus to ask whether a character re-rolled under a new edition, or replayed by another player, is still 'the same' character. She tests theories of the player-character bond (Gee's virtual, real and projective identities; Fine and Worch's 'identity bubble') on Wil Wheaton's Avenger Aeofel, whose in-character oath made Wheaton split the party and lose him rather than metagame. Bartle's four player types and the bulette-knowledge example show how each player manages the line between what they know and what their character knows, in a shared fiction where a glorious failure can be better than winning.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 8 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Jeopardy! champion Ken Jennings argues that the silly answer-in-the-form-of-a-question conceit is the engine of the show's appeal, because it turns every topic, even Belgium, into a fractal of surprising factual connections rather than a dull definition. He defends the old-school internalization of facts in a Google age - champions are congenitally curious 'sponges' whose stored knowledge makes them better citizens and thinkers - and speculates that what we call the Self is largely the accumulation of facts in one's head. His philosophy of the show in a nutshell: do not just answer in the form of a question, live your life in the form of a question.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 32 "Psych and Philosophy" — Dena Hurst reads Shawn as the mythological trickster - the fool who fools fools - who brings disorder to order by overturning hierarchies (Henry's ring-in-the-box lesson in '9 Lives'), taunting Lassiter, and inventing Gus's nicknames, while using his convenient psychic act to surface clues when found and excuse blunders. She argues people buy the act because we crave patterns and motivated narratives (Alfred Mele's work on seeing what we want to see), and closes with Hume's and Dennett's view that the self is a loose narrative we star in: Shawn literally invents himself as psychic detective, an exaggeration of the identities we all construct.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 15 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Jenkins asks what makes Bender Bender when Leela still recognizes him as the walnut-panelled steam robot of 'Obsoletely Fabulous.' Scruffy's progressively repaired conference table stages the Ship of Theseus problem and the same body theory, while the Roboticon 'Soul Detector' (Fry sets it off, robots pass through) rules out Descartes' same soul theory for robots. Episodes from 'Anthology of Interest II' and 'The Honking' to 'The Prisoner of Benda' mind swap and Roberto's instant 1-X re-education support Locke's psychological continuity: Bender persists through an overlapping chain of memories and traits stored on his hard drive - 'Everything that is Bender is right here' - which is why an empathic, ascetic Bender ('The old Bender is gone') threatens his very identity.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 27 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Williams uses Hermes's slide from chest-harpoon to extendo-arm to Cylon eye to full robot body in 'The Six Million Dollar Mon' - until Zoidberg's 'Monster Mash' surgery restores his brain to Li'l Hermes - to ask what makes a person themselves under voluntary enhancement. The 'Ship of Planet Express' and the seven-year cell-replacement fact recast the Ship of Theseus, exposing our terror of upgrades as inconsistent with our constant physical change, while the therapeutic-versus-enhancement line (medical steroids vs doping, Aimee Mullins's blades) explains why Hermes's chosen upgrades disturb us. Cartesian interactionist dualism predicts Mecha-Hermes stays the same person, yet his personality shifts with his parts, so the chapter turns to physicalism and lands on functionalism: Hermes persists through each swap until the Roberto brain-chip replaces the brain that houses his memories and motivations.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 34 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Micic uses Fry's hundred-cups-of-coffee rescue in 'Three Hundred Big Boys' - a mysterious orange blur to onlookers while Fry calmly watches each cork pop - and the chronoton time skips of 'Time Keeps on Slippin'' as breaks in experience that Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit explains better than Descartes. Against the cogito's inference of a separate thinking 'I,' Hegel treats consciousness as the act of relating subject to object, whose ceaseless repetitions (here1, here2, here3...) we knit into the illusion of a unified self. The identical universes of 'The Late Philip J. Fry' (U1 = U2 = U3...) then model the same collapse of enumeration: the gaps in experience feel abnormal only because we never notice the constant gaps our own consciousness smooths over - including Nibbler's shadow in the pilot's cryogenics lab.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 26 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Lopez uses the monster - 'one man made out of many' - to stress-test personal identity: brain-swap and amnesia-torture thought experiments first drive us to identify with our memories (the memory-based psychological criterion) and then, when Victor offers to wipe memory before the pain experiments, with our bodies, yielding inconsistent answers. The monster's own testimony - waking confused, prodding fire like an infant, acquiring language by eavesdropping on Safie's lessons, and building his values from scratch out of Paradise Lost and the cottagers - shows he is a genuinely new person rather than whoever once owned his corpse-parts, since we would not say a memory-wiped torture victim ceases to exist. He concludes the monster satisfies the five listed personhood criteria (consciousness, reasoning, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness), with identity riding a continuing stream of consciousness running on a body that is, in the end, secondary 'hardware.'
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 32 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Michael Mendelson rereads James Whale's 1931 Frankenstein as a metaphysics of appearance versus reality: the seemingly monstrous creature killed Fritz only after Fritz tormented him with fire and the whip, killed Dr. Waldman while Waldman was trying to dissect him alive, and drowned Maria in innocent play, expecting her to float like the flowers they had been throwing. The 'criminal brain' was Fritz's accident and explains less than we assume, since the creature spares Henry's fiancée when she screams and faints. The real point is alterity: otherness is a relation, not a property, and individual and social identity are built by excluding an outside where monsters reside - so the horror was inside the well-ordered village all along, the monster is us, and we are its creators.
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 26 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter reads the show's storytelling as identity construction through Paul Ricoeur's narrative identity, built on Heidegger's insight that human being is fundamentally temporal: we live in memories and future possibilities, so 'damn you, past Ted!' collisions between selves are structural. Ricoeur's two times - linear cosmological time versus fragmented phenomenological time - explain the show's looped, goat-intruding storytelling, while Giddens's reflexive project of the self (dubbed 'reflexibility') and Turkle's new-media multiple windows explain our fragmented, self-designed identities. Goffman's dramaturgy completes the picture: Barney's womanizer persona is a Goffmanesque masquerade that collapses, the yips, when his first lover reveals the founding story was false.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 35 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Nicolas Michaud argues that when you go extinct you do not come back, dismantling our three hopes: the soul, cloning, and an essential self. Cloning a T. rex yields a new individual 'Rex' with her own perspective, not the original; the soul cannot both be beyond science's reach and record memories and move bodies; and he deploys Gilbert Ryle's view that 'soul' is a language mistake - a mind is just what a functioning brain does, the way 'Jurassic Park' is just buildings, dinosaurs, staff, and money working together, ceasing when the functioning stops. A Hammond stripped by Alzheimer's and atom-replacement of every memory, trait, and particle still gets called John Hammond, so there is no essence over time: we already die constantly and never notice, which is why a second extinction holds no fresh terror.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 60 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann asks whether the Devil could actually get you by testing theories of the afterlife against Hamlet's ghost, Freddy Krueger, the possessions of The Exorcist and Evil Dead, Paranormal Activity, Dante's Inferno, Marlowe's Doctor Faustus, and Doom. Substance dualism cannot explain how a non-physical soul moves so much as a finger; the view that you are your body founders on recycled grave matter and the primacy of the brain; and if you are a program running on your brain, the Devil could torture infinite copies of you in Hell - even re-running you there from Heaven - unless duplication means neither copy is really you.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 9 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Jason Iuliano asks whether the Brody who lied to Helen Walker about Tom Walker's death is the same person as the one who beat Walker, and whether 2011 Brody is responsible for 2003 Brody's acts. He contrasts the biological criterion (same human animal), the psychological criterion of overlapping memories and intentions (so Brody remembering his family remains the same person), and the narrative identity theory Carrie invokes in 'Q&A' when she says Nazir pulled Brody apart and put him back together as someone else. A Carrie thought experiment about ECT outcomes and a Nazir mind-swap of Brody's and Walker's psychologies argue that only narrative coherence captures whom we should praise, blame, and anticipate surviving.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 11 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Laszlo Kajtar uses Brody's Complex PTSD - torture, forced killing of Walker, intrusive nightmares attacking Jessica - to test theories of personal identity. Animalism says Brody is the same biological organism before and after captivity, while the psychological approach, sourced in Locke's memory criterion, traces continuity of beliefs, desires, and intentions and finds it disrupted by trauma and Nazir's brainwashing, which filled the hole trauma left after Issa's death. Kajtar argues both miss the first-personal 'sense of self': like many PTSD sufferers, Brody feels he is not the person he was, and 'It's like she doesn't know who I actually am now' shows identity shattered from the inside.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 29 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Frank Scalambrino probes Carrie's 'personality paradox' through the 'You can't change your soul!' / 'Yes you can' exchange. Aristotle's Metaphysics offers one pole: only generation and corruption are substantial change, so Carrie persists essentially as human however her mania, job, and loves shift. Hume's rejoinder - sameness of kind is not given in sense experience but added by interpretation - opens the question of whether Carrie's identity is determined by intrinsic factors (love, soul, truth) or extrinsic ones (the CIA's rules, religious affiliation), with Saul representing extrinsic determination and Carrie privileging the intrinsic, while Brody's conversion shows a soul can change and re-order which factors govern a self.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 28 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — The chapter asks whether Marceline has lost Simon Petrikov forever now that he is the Ice King, and tests every criterion of personal identity - body, memories, beliefs, personality, soul - finding each one either something that changes over time without ending a person (Finn survives losing his arm, Jake his fear of vampires) or something shared that then explains nothing. Borrowing Ryle's deflation of the soul as just the way the brain works - like Lemongrab renaming and remaking the Candy Kingdom, killing it without touching a single building - the author concludes Simon and the Ice King are two different people sharing one piece of machinery, like two operating systems on one computer. The dark payoff: bringing Simon back permanently would delete the Ice King, and by the same reasoning our own past selves are equally gone, a 'thousand deaths' a day that the chapter offers as Marceline's consolation, with Death's line 'you're gonna be the Ice King' as the haunting exception.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 24 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Richard Greene uses Dracula's transformations (man, bat, wolf, mist, and human-to-vampire) plus Vlad the Impaler's ordinary aging to pose the puzzle of persistence: the claims of consistency, change, and persistence cannot all be true together. He raises the justice objection to mereological essentialism (if any change made Vlad a new person, imprisoning him would punish someone else) and then tests endurantism (wholly present with time-indexed properties), perdurantism (temporal parts), and exdurantism (temporal counterparts) against the Count. He concludes endurantism best captures the intuition that one and the same guy was first human and later vampire.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 13 "4. How Possible Is the Impossible Girl" — Smith asks how one Clara can exist as Oswin the converted Dalek, a Victorian governess, and a present-day nanny, and answers with philosophy of mind: after the real Clara steps into the Doctor's timeline on Trenzalore, the 'echoes' are best understood as manifestations within the Doctor's own subconscious, read through Freud's dream interpretation and id-ego-superego (the echoes act as his conscience) and Jung's archetypes, collective unconscious, individuation, and synchronicity—her name meaning clarity, her red wardrobe marking the copies, and the leaf of 'The Rings of Akhaten' as the meaningful coincidence that produced her. Aristotle's Categories frames what Oswin still shares with humanity after Dalek conversion, and the soufflé-is-the-recipe line together with social-cognition research on multiple selves supports the conclusion that the Claras are metaphysically the same person despite different bodies and roles—making the 'Impossible Girl' possible.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 21 "10. One Good, Solid Hope—the Impossible Girl" — Elsby and Luzecky ask what stays constant across Clara's echoes and argue traditional identity theories fail her: Locke's memory-continuity and same-life account cannot apply because no echo remembers the others, and Plutarch's Ship of Theseus—invoked by the Doctor's broom speech in 'Deep Breath'—rules out bodily continuity, since the echoes have different bodies and minds. Their positive view is that Clara is less a particular than a universal, a 'recipe' or species whose instances share an essence ('the soufflé isn't the soufflé; the soufflé is the recipe'), with the modern-day Clara 'real' as the origin of the echoes. That essence, shown in climbing the ladder to the clouds in 'The Snowmen,' facing the parasite-god with the most important leaf in human history in 'The Rings of Akhaten,' stepping into the Doctor's torn timeline in 'The Name of the Doctor,' and persuading the Time Lords in 'The Time of the Doctor,' is hope itself.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 36 "21. Forgetting Is the Human Superpower" — Seymour reads the War-through-Eleventh Doctors through Freud's notion of Afterwardness (Nachtraeglichkeit) from Studies on Hysteria - memory is continually reforged as new information recontextualizes the past - so that learning Gallifrey was saved in 'The Day of the Doctor' changes not the Doctor but his memories of himself, turning penance into hope. She traces each Self constructed from Time War memory: Nine's guilt exploited by the Gelth and voiced in 'Boom Town' ('Only a killer would know that'), Ten's hubris once he forgets what he is capable of ('Time Lord Victorious' in 'The Waters of Mars'), and Eleven's danger when the memory fades and companions must remind him who he is ('A Town Called Mercy'). The chapter concludes the Doctor must keep the memory of his regret to keep being the Doctor - Clara's 'What you've always done. Be a doctor.'
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 38 "23. Failing and Forgiving in the Name of the Doctor" — Hoffman reads the Doctor's banishment of the War Doctor ('Doctor no more,' his actions 'not done in the name of the Doctor') as a failure of self-forgiveness driven by what Jeffrie Murphy calls the moral hatred of self and Robin Dillon the 'self-as-feared,' rather than mere guilt over the genocide of Gallifrey. Drawing on the self-forgiveness literature (Blustein, Griswold, Westlund), he argues that 'The Day of the Doctor' shows forgiveness neither excuses nor extinguishes blame: the Tenth and Eleventh Doctors forgive their past self by recognizing he shared their Doctorly motives and was forced into an impossible choice. Clara's outsider faith ('be a doctor') supplies the third-party affirmation that dissolves the identity-destroying dilemma and frees the Doctor to find the third option that saves Gallifrey.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 12 "4. Nietzsche’s Faction Test" — Mallalieu uses Nietzsche's slave morality, will to power, and Ubermensch to read Roth's social experiment: Abnegation's foot-washing, guilt-driven selflessness is slave morality, Amity's drugged peace makes them willing slaves, and Peter - cruel, self-promoting, guilt-ridden - is the most Nietzschean character, whose memory wipe is an attempt to forget his way out of slave morality. Even the heroes turn out Nietzschean when Tris and Tobias dose the Bureau with memory serum, since Nietzsche holds that the old values must be forgotten before new ones can be created. But the chapter concludes the price is too high: losing your values along with your memories means losing your identity ('I would rather be dead than empty'), so Nietzsche's imagined experiment, played out through the Bureau's tools, would be a world good only for the strong and cruel.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 27 "15. Memories. In the End, Is That All There Is" — David LaRocca tests Mr. Carson's claim that 'the business of life is the acquisition of memories. In the end, that's all there is' against the tradition of spatial memory metaphors and modern neuroscience. Downton itself becomes a memory palace - echoing Cicero, the Ad Herennium, and Augustine's 'court of memory' - whose characters defer endlessly to the past, while photographs (Tom with Sybil's image, Carson with Alice Neal's) act as sources and surrogates of memory in an age of acquisitional capitalism. Daniella Schiller's reconsolidation research, Nicholas Carr's Nietzsche-typewriter anecdote, and Langdon Winner's point that technologies reshape life show memories are malleable rather than collectible possessions, undermining Carson's model and any fixed memory-based account of personal identity.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 29 "12. They Just Want Me to Be Like Them" — Castro and Beisecker diagnose Lizzie's walker fixation as prolonged grief disorder: she displaces grief for her father onto the walker "Nick," denies final death ("They're just different"), and treats reanimation as a viable form of life she might join ("Maybe I should change"). They argue Carol's suppressive guardianship - the "look at the flowers" distraction and calling Lizzie weak and confused - aggravated the avoidance at the root of the disorder, so Lizzie's "transformation" of Mika was a misguided moral experiment rather than murder by a monster. The chapter contrasts Tyreese's affirming care ("You each do things your own way") as the guardianship that might have saved the girls, and notes Carol's refusal to let Lizzie reanimate denies her the dying-wish courtesy the group once granted Jim.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 32 "14. Carol Didn’t Care" — Yuen grants that executing Lizzie was not wrong but argues Carol fell short of a moral ideal by ignoring Lizzie's preferences, deploying R.M. Hare's move from Bentham's happiness-maximizing classic utilitarianism to preference utilitarianism - illustrated by the group refusing to let Eugene test Aaron's water in "Them." Since Lizzie prefers a reanimating death ("She didn't hurt her brain"), a heart shot like the group's courtesy to Jim would have maximized preference satisfaction without endangering anyone. He answers the objections that Lizzie is a child and that walkers are mindless: her attempts to reason and her coherent post-apocalyptic values (like generational value shifts on homosexuality via Aaron and Eric) deserve respect, and whether a walker would still be Lizzie matters less than that the preference is hers now.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 34 "15. My Zombie, My Self" — Greene asks what Walking Dead-type walkers are and answers with the Platonic method of definition learned from Socrates: place them in the genus undead (died but not at rest, neither alive nor dead) and differentiate them by differentia - corporeal, mindless, lacking superhuman or magical powers, still decomposing. Aristotle's hierarchy of life functions (nutrition, locomotion, reason) explains why walkers are not alive despite ambulating, and the standards of death (putrefaction, heart-lung, whole-brain, higher-brain) all certify that walkers are dead yet active. The chapter closes on personal identity - whether you survive becoming a zombie, as Carol's face at the barn and Carl's "she'll turn" about Lori presuppose - and admits the author chooses the self-interested reading that he could become his own zombie, for the sake of the scare.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 29 "16. My Name Is—Hang on, What Was It Meant to Be Again Are You Sure Well, Okay Then . ." — Tim Jones argues the book is not really a love story but a warning about identity: against Descartes's transcendent self, the American pragmatists William James, Cooley, and Mead hold that the self is fluid and socially constituted, and Westley's serial reinvention (farm boy, Dread Pirate Roberts, Man in Black) - along with Mandy Patinkin's cathartic channeling of his father's death into Inigo - shows the freedom this mutability grants. The Goldman frame then exposes the danger: the fictionalized Goldman seizes Morgenstern's text, cuts its history, and rewrites it to his own ends, exactly as other people can seize our plastic identities and shape them for their interests rather than ours.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 23 "12. Becoming Vetinari Personal Identity on the Discworld" — Pierce uses Moist von Lipwig's rehabilitation (Albert Spangler becomes Postmaster General), Cosmo Lavish's doomed project of literally becoming Vetinari, the Auditor Myria LeJean, Angua's transformations, the Librarian's orangutan body, Miss Level's two bodies, and duplicated Rincewind teleportation cases to test theories of personal identity. Locke's memory theory, patched by Leibniz into psychological continuity, collapses into circularity under false-memory cases like a wizard implanting Teatime's murders in Rincewind's mind, while bodily and brain-continuity views founder on Igor part-swaps, splitting hemispheres, and identical-twin-style fission. Leibniz's own soul view and Reid's treatment of identity as a primitive, unanalyzable fact get their due, and Hume's skepticism about any continuing self marks the chapter's conclusion that every available view exacts a price.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 25 "14. Being One’s Me (Witchy) Personal Identity on the Discworld" — The chapter reads Granny Weatherwax's analysis of Magrat—'you're your me'—through Locke's memory theory of personal identity, opening with Granny's broomstick, whose stick and bristles the dwarf engineers have replaced dozens of times yet which remains 'the same' broomstick, as a Theseus's-ship puzzle for witches. It stages Locke's view against the classic objections: Butler's circularity charge that memory presupposes identity, and fission worries raised by the duplicated Glods of Al-Ybi and by the mirror magic that splits Granny and Lilith among a billion reflections. Death's challenge to each witch to find 'the one that's real' in the mirror universe becomes the test case, and Granny's simply looking down at herself and saying 'This one' is offered as a vindication of a Butlerian, body-anchored and indefinable conception of personal identity.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 35 "22. Cocking a Snook at Death, and Getting Away with It Does the Personification of Death Make It Less Scary" — Asking whether Pratchett's personified Death makes mortality less scary, the chapter reads Reaper Man's claim that belief created Death—the moment a living thing grasped non-existence, Death came into being—as a co-arising of dualistic concepts, and surveys psychopomps from Thanatos and Azrael to Yama and even modern assisted-dying organizations. Windle Poons's several kinds of death in Reaper Man ground the distinctions between animalistic, mindistic, and personistic death, showing that whether someone counts as dead can turn on which conception of the person is doing the counting. The closing meditation on Pratchett's own posterior cortical atrophy and the documentary Choosing to Die argues that conceptualizing death in advance—in living wills and bedside conversations with loved ones—is what lets us meet 'THERE'S JUST ME' a little less afraid.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 17 "6. One Clone from Another" — Asks what metaphysically individuates one Leda clone from another, surveying the tradition: Aristotelian substances bearing properties, Plato's and Descartes's non-repeatable individual essences, Berkeley's and Hegel's soul-substances, Aquinas's matter-based view, Locke's memory-based personal identity (with its sleeping-copy and consciousness-download objections), and Hume's argument that substance is a meaningless idea. It then turns to the Buddhist framework — the Four Noble Truths, anatman (no eternal self), the five skandhas, and dependent origination, illustrated by Alison's soap-and-drug crates — before closing with Nishida Kitaro's logic of contradictory self-identity. Read through that lens, the clone dance party in Felix's loft shows each clone's moves are truly her own precisely because they incorporate and mirror her sisters': identity is relational, not intrinsic.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 18 "7. I Am and Am Not You" — Reads the opening scene phenomenologically: when Sarah sees her face on Beth, her identity does not merely change genetically but unravels generatively, since her birth, ancestry, and place in world-history are all thrown into question. Using Husserl's lived-body (the absolute "here" of experience), his static/genetic/generative levels of analysis, the homeworld/alienworld distinction (Clone Club solidifies its identity against the Castor "brothers," until Helena cradles the dying Rudy), and Husserl's co-originality of I and world, the chapter presents identity as intersubjective, constituted by shared projects like Sarah's fight for Kira and the Clone Club's tribe-rituals. Kierkegaard's "life must be lived forwards but understood backwards" is broadened: to understand identity we must look before our own birth and beyond our death, into the lifeworld we inherit and pass on.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 32 "A Brief History of Cloning" — A history of cloning in science and popular culture, from Driesch's 1885 sea-urchin split and the tadpole nuclear-transfer work of Briggs, King, and Gurdon, through Rorvik's In His Image hoax, to Dolly, Polly, Ditto and Neti, and Mitalipov's human embryonic stem cells. On the fiction side it tracks how early stories (Sleeper, Four Sided Triangle, The World of Null-A, Invasion of the Body Snatchers) assumed a clone is literally the same person as the original, with the same age, memories, and desires — a metaphysical mistake, since a clone is a new person whose own experiences make her someone else — while later work (The Boys from Brazil, Jurassic Park, The Island, Never Let Me Go, Moon) got the science roughly right and moved on to the ethics, exactly where Orphan Black, with its careful Leda and Castor biology, lands.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 7 "A Farewell to David Bowie" — The editor's farewell argues that Bowie's greatness lay in relentless transformation joined to honesty: unlike acts from Kiss to Miley Cyrus whose theatrics are mere spectacle 'in an Aristotelian sense,' Bowie's characters (Ziggy, the Thin White Duke, simulating fellatio with Mick Ronson) opened a discussion of gender and 'the multiple ways of being in the world.' Tracing the career from parents' fear of rock through the Eno-shaped Berlin trilogy's symbolist minimalism and the despised continuity of 'Changes,' it reads The Next Day as a defacement of 'Heroes' and Blackstar as a Mapplethorpe-like series of self-portraits made while unflinchingly facing death.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 11 "3. The Flux of It All" — Ammon asks whether anything persists beneath Bowie's serial personas, staging Parmenides's denial of change (with Zeno's paradoxes) and Descartes's melting wax against the Heraclitean flux of 'ch-ch-ch-changes.' Rejecting soul-substance views, he takes the empiricist line - Hume's introspection finds only particular perceptions, never a self - warns via the intentional fallacy (Manson's 'Helter Skelter,' Bloom's hawk) against letting Bowie's own pronouncements fix his songs' meanings, and tests 'meaning is use' on Bowie's calling rock stars fascists. Recurring undercurrents (dancing, apocalypse, distrust of authority) survive, but the conclusion is that Bowie's essence just is flux, 'the river we can't step into twice.'
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 13 "5. The One, the Only, Darrow" — Kevin McCain uses Darrow's transformations—Helldiver of Lykos, carved Gold lancer, Reaper of Mars—to ask what makes him numerically the same person, warming up with Plutarch's Ship of Theseus replayed on the Pax and the Quinn trading parts. Same-matter and animalist views (Eric Olson) struggle with Mickey's near-total carving and Darrow's restarted heart, and Locke's prince-and-cobbler example, run as a carver swapping Darrow's and the Jackal's psychologies, sinks all physical-continuity views. The simple memory theory breaks transitivity across Darrow's childhood, and Sydney Shoemaker's psychological-continuity fix then fails when a carver splits Darrow's brain into two surviving bodies—a fission case where both new Darrows continue him—while the soul view cannot be verified; the chapter ends with Trenton Merricks's suggestion that there may be no criteria of identity over time at all.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 20 "9. Is Headless Deadpool Still Deadpool" — Ben Fulman runs Deadpool's decapitations, the T-Ray personality split, and Evil Deadpool—his discarded body parts regenerating together in a dumpster—through the theories of personal identity: Locke's memory continuity, Reid's branching-memory 'Deadpool paradox', Chisholm's essential parts, the Ship of Theseus traced from Heraclitus to Plutarch, and later positions by Sider, Wiggins, Noonan, Grice, and Perry on overlapping memory chains and their circularity. Finding each account strained by Deadpool's cases, the chapter proposes that Deadpool stores his memories in the readers via the fourth wall. His identity over time is thus jointly sustained by the audience—a 'non-personal identity' that ends only when every reader has forgotten him.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 7 "Johnny—James—Buster—Jimmy—Jimi . . . How Many Jimis" — Editorial introduction tracing the successive identities of Johnny Allen Hendrix, James Marshall Hendrix, Jimmy James, and Jimi — from Seattle and the chitlin' circuit with the Isley Brothers and Little Richard to Chas Chandler's London — arguing there was no single Hendrix but a series of continual transformations. It dismisses a 'Hegelian unfolding of The Absolute' that would require true blues musicians to be born in the South, and speculates that the Jimi lost in 1970 was a would-be jazz-blues synthesizer, reading 'Rainy Day, Dream Away' and 'Still Raining, Still Dreaming' as evidence and invoking the rumored Miles Davis collaboration.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 23 "12. The Broken Pieces of Yesterday’s Life" — Uses the flood of posthumous Hendrix releases — the dismal Lonnie Youngblood eight-track, 380-plus albums, the PPX litigations — to ask what we owe the dead and what access we may claim, weighing Kafka and Max Brod, Nietzsche's sister, Harper Lee's Go Set a Watchman, and Kundera's Mirek. It rejects the framing of conflicting rights: against the Cartesian picture of a hidden self the authors deploy Wittgenstein's beetle in the box — 'the human body is the best picture of the human soul' — to show that no one can fully control their public self, leaving only prudential discernment about which recordings should shape our image of the artist.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 11 "1. What’s So Scary about Demonic Possession" — Using the Asylum possession arc - the boy who rips open the pig's heart, the demon exposing Sister Jude's hit-and-run secret and whispering 'You're Bloody Face' to Thredson, and Sister Mary Eunice's corruption - the chapter argues that possession stories terrify because they break our identity judgments through time, the same judgments on which moral responsibility, criminal punishment (the Manson family parole cases, Phineas Gage), trust, and personal safety depend. Descartes's mind-body union and psychological-continuity theories of identity explain why sameness of body can no longer guarantee sameness of person, and why we fear our own identity being erased next.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 13 "3. My Sister, My Self" — Staged as a remembered backstage conversation among Elsa's freak show performers, the chapter has conjoined twins Bette and Dot work through the Ship of Theseus, the psychological-continuity theory of identity and its coma and false-memory counterexamples, Quine's claim that persons are only convenient posits rather than real entities, split-brain cases suggesting one body can host two minds, and fission worries about what would happen if they were separated - to ask whether they are one person or two, concluding it is a genuine paradox with no agreed answer.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 30 "18. Thoughtcrime or Feelingcrime" — Alba Montes Sánchez argues that the real crime in Oceania is not thoughtcrime but 'feelingcrime': Winston lands in the Ministry of Love only once he falls in love, because beliefs alone do not motivate action while emotions and loves do — the problem of akrasia that puzzled Aristotle, since Winston carries his proof of Party lies for eleven years without acting. Using Harry Frankfurt's account of love as an involuntary, non-utilitarian, rigidly focused, self-affirming concern that organizes a person's priorities, she explains why Julia is irreplaceable and why Room 101 must destroy Winston's deepest allegiance rather than just his opinions. Surveying theories of individuality from Locke's memory to recognition and narrative, she concludes that a stubborn residue of selfhood survives in what we love — which is why Ingsoc must make war on love itself.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 16 "7. Loss of Memory, Loss of Me" — Lay tests Locke's memory theory against the series: Marsha in 'The After Hours' is only the mannequin-person again when she remembers being one, and David Gurney in 'Person or Persons Unknown' has lost his identity because his memories lack factivity — they correspond to no actual past. Reid's brave-officer chain and Parfit's psychological continuity from Reasons and Persons then let him handle the hard cases: Jana's fake 'memory tracks' in 'The Lateness of the Hour' can still constitute her identity as overlapping chains of mental states (severed by reprogramming into Nelda), while the post-Transformation girl of 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' has all of Marilyn's memories but not her beliefs, desires, or character — so Marilyn did not survive.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 19 "Part III Endless Forms Most Beautiful" — Muntersbjorn argues that freedom comes in kinds and degrees and that selves are social fictions sustained by others, building on Annette Baier's claims that we are 'second persons' whose self-consciousness and freedom grow out of childhood interaction and mutual cross-examination. She reads the hosts' selective ignoring ('that doesn't look like anything to me') as Baier's dangerous art of self-deception, and contrasts Descartes' solitary introspection (hats and coats that may cover automata) and Russell's analogy-based answer to the problem of other minds with the hosts' deliberately scripted interpersonal checks that keep them from questioning their reality. Plato's Meno statues of Daedalus (opinion 'fastened up' into knowledge) frame hosts as property whose freedom is a matter of degree, and the chapter closes that if artificial beings are ever to become persons they must be treated as second persons first - the Golden Rule applied to the park.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 21 "Memory, Imagination, and the Access for the Self Dolores and Maeve" — Trapero-Llobera reads Westworld as the culmination of Jonathan Nolan's Memento and Person of Interest projects, mapping seven nested 'observing systems' (Nolan, Sizemore, Stubbs and Elsie, Ford, the creators' personal stories, Maeve, and William as beta-tester) onto second-wave cybernetics (Foerster, Maturana, Varela, Hayles), where the observer participates in and constructs the observed world through feedback loops. She argues the show's hosts pass through Turing's imitation game (fake memories and personalities from textual repetition, as with Peter Abernathy's reveries), and that Dolores's and Maeve's breakdowns convert prosthetic memory into experienced, autopoietic memory reconstructed in a 'Bergsonian' backward movement that gives them agency and purpose. William's two-timeline transformation into the Man in Black figures the 'semiosis of virtuality' - the hyperreal where original and copy are indistinguishable - ending in a collective bicameral mind in which everyone, audience included, inhabits the god-creator Ford's dream.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 11 "1. The Genuine Article" — Written in the voice of a non-C-137 Rick, the chapter argues that whether the Beth at the end of 'The ABCs of Beth' is a clone doesn't matter, because our reverence for 'the genuine article' (like the original US Constitution) is romantic packaging, and a functional clone is as good as the original. It tests Robert Nozick's experience machine, whose three objections supposedly show we value genuine reality intrinsically, against Rick's pragmatism of believing what is useful, and reads 'The Wedding Squanchers' (Rick turning himself in to the Federation) as proof that his family is both instrumentally and intrinsically valuable to him. Your answer to the clone question, it concludes, is a Rorschach test revealing what you place intrinsic value on.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 12 "2. The Unimportance of Identity When You Have a Portal Gun" — The chapter argues Rick C-137 is already dead: the Brainalyzer body-hops in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption' and the Operation Phoenix swap in 'Big Trouble in Little Sanchez' copy psychological states rather than transfer a consciousness, so each post-transfer Rick is a new psychological clone, exactly as in Parfit's Teletransporter. Building from Locke's memory theory of personal identity to Parfit's claim that identity is not what matters, it reads the dimension-hop in 'Rick Potion #9', the Morty voucher, and the ambiguous clone Beth of 'The Rickchurian Mortydate' as the show itself endorsing psychological continuity over numerical identity. What matters is that someone carries on Rick's desires and relationships, so nobody noticed the protagonist's death.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 15 "5. Who’d Rick Kill Or, Who Killed Rick" — Framing Rick's massacre of the Council of Ricks in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption' as a crime-scene investigation, the chapter asks whether killing qualitatively identical Ricks is murder or suicide. It contrasts Leibniz's abstractionism (possible worlds as mere descriptions, pictured as the Palace of Fates in the Theodicy, allowing transworld identity via essential properties) with David Lewis's concretism/modal realism (all worlds really exist but are causally isolated, with world-bound individuals and counterpart theory instead of transworld identity). The show, it argues, is a modified concretism: portals let people interact across worlds, so Rick C-137 murdered distinct cosmic doppelgangers, not himself, as the interdimensional cable channels of 'Rixty Minutes' confirm.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 21 "9. To Err Is Human, to Forget … Sublime" — Huntingford contrasts Stranger Things with its blueprint, Stephen King's It: where It forces the Losers Club back to the traumatic truth of childhood, the show traffics in 'false nostalgia,' vicarious nostalgia for an Eighties that only existed on screen, supported by Loftus's false-memory experiments (the impossible Bugs Bunny, Stewart's Root Beer) and Will's anniversary effect and El's mother's broken record of 'breathe, sunflower, rainbow... 450.' Against this malleability she sets Locke's memory theory of personal identity from the Essay and Sacks's 'lost mariner,' warning that nostalgic self-deception can rewrite the self, yet concluding, with It's own ending, that since we cannot survive some horrors, the comforting lie of misremembered childhood is what we tune in for.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 25 "12. Who Is Will Byers" — Hammonds and Gordon use Mead's symbolic interactionism, in which the self emerges from interaction and stabilizes around 'identity anchors' others can expect, to unpack 'Zombie Boy': Mr. Clarke's Phineas Gage story frames Max's doubt that Will is still Will, Joyce's hovering and Will's fragile-child role co-constitute each other, and Will renegotiates a different identity with Jonathan ('Stop treating me like I'm gonna break'). During the Mind Flayer's possession, when Will screams that the creature is 'everywhere,' his family's stories of the toy truck and the crayon spaceship summon the kind, honest anchors of the old Will, showing identity as recognizable and stable yet ultimately negotiable, and that realizing and actualizing agency lets Will beat the role the monster assigned him.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 16 "7. More Human than Humans" — Rob O'Connor reads replicants through N. Katherine Hayles's posthumanism — persons as amalgams of biological and informational-technological systems — arguing Rachael's procreation shows the posthuman body bypassing its designed limits, while Joi is a posthuman of the opposite construction, a hologram transcending her limits through emotion. Memory and experience, even implanted ones (Batty's 'tears in rain', Deckard's unicorn dream, K's wooden horse, 'all the best memories are hers'), supply the existential context that defines the posthuman self. K's epiphany before the giant Joi advertisement reveals he is a tool of the capitalist system, and his choice to die for the right cause is how he takes charge of his own identity.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 25 "12. How the Fork Did I Get Here" — Tepley uses Eleanor waking in Michael's office to pose the problem of numerical personal identity: what makes the person in the chair the very same person who died seconds earlier on Earth? He eliminates the same-body theory, since bodies stay behind and lack spatiotemporal continuity, the same-mind theory of psychological continuity, which fails on the 802 reboots and implies the absurdity that two duplicates would both be Eleanor, and the same-soul theory, which offers no criteria for sameness. The 'Janet(s)' revelation that the humans are recomposed from 'essences' turns out to be Aristotelian-Thomistic hylomorphism, committing the show to a same-soul theory of identity it never defends.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 10 "2. KISStory and Kulture of the Hottest Band in the World" — Historian and lifelong fan Matt Alschbach argues that the history of KISS is the history of its fans: his police-officer father taking him to the 1979 San Diego show, schoolyard debates over Alive! versus Alive II, rubbing pencil shadings over the Double Platinum gatefold to guess the band's faces, and strangers' comments on his KISS T-shirts all show the band forging identity and community. He recounts how Alive! rescued Casablanca Records, how the 1983 MTV unmasking and 1996 remasking reinvented the brand for new generations, and how the KISS KRUISE, $50,000 Vault Experience, and Rock & Brews extend its cultural reach. The chapter's claim is that KISS fandom supplies camaraderie, family bonds, and life-meaning across generations.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 15 "6. The KISS Franchise" — Peter Finocchiaro takes Gene Simmons's and manager Doc McGhee's suggestions that KISS could become a franchise — new musicians stepping into the Demon and Starchild roles — and works out what band identity could mean. Using the Ship of Theseus, he distinguishes qualitative from numerical identity, invokes collective intentionality to explain how a band without a mind can perform intentional actions, and contrasts the 'originality connection' (being the actual founding members) with the 'continuity connection' (day-by-day chained succession), mirroring the bodily-versus-psychological debate about Gene Simmons's personal identity. His conclusion is that bands are governed by social rules fans collectively create — like the rules of basketball or musical genre — so in his imaginary two-KISS scenario, and for any future franchise, the fan base would decide which band is the real KISS rather than discovering a pre-existing fact.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 25 "Liz Lemon and High School The More Things Change, the More They Don’t" — Shores uses Jack's cookie jar collection and his fiftieth-birthday home movies in 'Apollo, Apollo', plus Liz's catastrophic high-school reunion in 'Reunion', to examine personal identity over time. Hume's bundle theory denies any self beyond a flux of perceptions, Whitehead offers three senses of a person over time, and Augustine locates past, present, and future in the mind as memory, sight, and expectation, which explains why Jack cannot recover his tenth-birthday joy by buying the Apollo Lunar Module toy yet feels 'like a kid' after laughing until he vomits. Ryle's 'elusiveness of I' and Rousseau on happiness as a fleeting state frame the conclusion that we continually reinterpret the past from the present, so the self is a stretched-out temporal continuity.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 7 "Introduction" — Frames the volume with Morpheus's red-pill speech in The Matrix, treating the rabbit-hole as our culture's portal of escape and asking how to make sense of what we find in Wonderland: hookah-smoking caterpillars, babies that turn into pigs, grins without cats, and trials where the sentence comes before the evidence. It takes Alice's 'Who in the world am I? Ah, that's the great puzzle!' as the book's guiding question, tying knowledge of who we are and can become to memory of who we have been, and previews chapters on the feminist Alice, the Red Queen and nuclear strategy, mushroom trips, and the connection between Alice, procrastination, and the Spice Girls.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 25 "From Backwards -Working Memory, or Working Backwards from Memory" — Treats the Caterpillar's 'Who are YOU?' and Alice's 'Who in the world am I? Ah, that's the great puzzle!' as the classic memory-and-identity problem, rallying Plato's wax tablet and Meno doctrine that learning is recollection, Locke's memory criterion of the same person, and Diderot's dialogue on how without memory there would be no connected self. Tyler Shores reads Alice's botched recitations as Bergson's impersonal habit-memory swamping personal memory, her name-forgetting in the wood through Nietzsche's Untimely Meditations on the necessity of forgetting, the Red King's dream as Freud's alienated memory, and the White Queen's memory that 'works both ways' as a thought experiment tying memory, time, and self together.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 21 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Sorts the Oscar/George Sr. twin confusion into the metaphysical, persistence, and evidential problems of personal identity, testing Aristotle's essential properties (why two actresses play one Marta, what makes each Richter brother distinct) and Descartes's immaterial soul (undermined by surrogate Larry, who stays Larry while Buster remotely operates him). Locke's memory criterion then explains why Oscar is not guilty of George's crimes and why Gob disowns what his forget-me-nows erased, before Thomas Reid's transitivity objection, staged through a lifetime of Gob's roofies, shows Locke committed to old Gob both being and not being young Gob.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 31 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Uses the show's narrator and structure (the chain of contingencies costing Buster his hand, 'now that's how you narrate a story') to argue that we impose narrative on life to make it meaningful, starting from Aristotle's Poetics requirement of beginning, middle, and end. George Sr.'s endlessly reinterpreted J. Walter Weatherman lessons show storytelling as moral choice among possible versions of events, Nietzsche's advice to learn from artists commends styling one's own life aesthetically, and Kierkegaard's 'life must be understood backwards but lived forwards' explains both self-narration and the show's rewatchable 'call forwards', ending on narrative as the sense-making abstraction by which we know ourselves.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 31 "Opening Up Possibilities" — Argues, through Hilde Lindemann's relational account of personhood, that Zuko genuinely is all of the identities others hold him in (disappointing son, villain, ally) because being a person is a social practice of expression, recognition, and response. Aang's decision to hear Zuko out at the Western Air Temple, Iroh's stubborn refusal to accept Ozai's script for him (his anger itself recognizing Zuko as an agent capable of choosing otherwise), and Katara's historically-sensitive slow trust open up the possible future in which Zuko can become trustworthy, while the Earth Kingdom villagers' rejection of him in 'Zuko Alone' shows how weight of history and stereotype can shut possibility down. The chapter insists this is not letting wrongdoers off the hook: genuine apology, repair, and moral anger remain required (contrasting the Brock Turner case), but only a moral community that holds people in personhood makes redemption possible, so society should be arranged to give everyone the Iros and Aangs that Zuko was lucky to have.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 12 "Are you the Next Goliath" — Nelson tests body theory and psychology theory of personal identity on Avengers cases—a Rogers/Pym body swap in the spirit of Locke's prince-and-cobbler experiment, and a Pym brain-hemisphere duplication puzzle—before proposing a distinct 'mantle theory' of superhero identity requiring an appropriate heroic role plus legitimate pedigree, like intellectual property. Legitimacy explains how John Walker (appointed by a government commission) and Bucky Barnes (endorsed by Stark and then Rogers) each really were Captain America. The same theory rules Pym can wear only one of Ant-Man, Giant-Man, Goliath, Yellowjacket, and the Wasp at a time—confirmed by Clint Barton snapping his bow in half when he shed Hawkeye to become the new Goliath.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 9 "Retelling Our Stories" — Milsky applies the narrative theory of personal identity drawn from Paul Ricoeur and Alasdair MacIntyre (we are the story we emplot about ourselves) to the two Sharons: Boomer's discovery that she is a sleeper Cylon is a 'factual disruption' of her self-story (she shoots Adama because her human narrative cannot cohere), while Athena's love for Helo is a 'disruption of belief' that rewrites her values about humans.
