Rachael, Weeping for Her Children" — Bonnie McLean maps Baudrillard's four-stage precession of simulacra onto the women of 2049: Joshi anchors reality, implanted memories distort it, Joi is representation masking the absence of reality, and the eye-color-wrong reconstructed Rachael is a simulacrum of a simulacrum bearing no relation to reality. Read this way, the film lionizes birth — Wallace kissing the replicant he has just disemboweled, her blood running down her legs — while stripping every woman of agency in service of K's quest, a dynamic the chapter links to pro-life politics and DACA-era savior narratives. Only by removing K from the narrative, she shows, does the women's erasure become visible.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 10 "1. RuPaul Is a Better Warhol" — Volpert maps Baudrillard's four levels of simulacra onto Drag Race's 'realness': faithful copies (Trinity the Tuck's tucking tutorial, the Season 10 Cher challenge), distorted copies (Sasha Velour and Eureka's nerve, double wig reveals), simulations masking an absent reality (Vanjie's nonsense-word meme, Valentina replacing the judges' verdict with her own fantasy), and the pure hyperreal (Bob the Drag Queen as a queen made entirely by the show, BenDeLaCrème's self-elimination as uniqueness with no referent). She then argues RuPaul is a better Warhol because Warhol merely produced superstars like Candy Darling, Holly Woodlawn and Jackie Curtis, profiting while they died unmourned, whereas Ru could compete in her own challenges and returns love to her girls. Realness, she concludes with Ru's Billboard interview and the Season 3 'Pop Art Ball', is always a wink: the facade talking about facade.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 13 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Bean reads both fake-news shows through Baudrillard's account of a media age with 'more and more information and less and less meaning': mainstream news is already simulation, and Colbert is 'a walking talking simulacrum', more O'Reilly than O'Reilly, whose five-deep receding portrait series and 'The Wørd' graphics (the abstinence-education 'Gateway Hug' bit) stage signs that refer only to themselves. Stewart, broadcasting from a simulacrum of a simulacrum, a television news studio, instead punctures the hyperreal: translating Obama's 'audacity of hope' convention speech into 'calibration of expectations' and rendering Laura Ingraham's dismissal of the party platform in Valley Girl vocal fry. Adapting Baudrillard's fake-holdup thought experiment into an 'organize a fake news broadcast' test, she argues the shows fall into the real precisely because they report on and stage simulation, anchoring audiences against media's 'communication without a response'.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 39 "Hey Goofy! Somebody Just Slipped My Culture a Mickey…" — Schuchardt argues Disney's real product is 'getting you in there' — colonizing the geography of the imagination: Pirates of the Caribbean is read as an allegory of corporate globalization, White Wilderness fabricated the lemming-suicide myth, and the parks' visual containment keeps visitors inside a world with 'more reality than nature' (Eco's hyperreality, in Baudrillard's territory). He claims Disney built this on Jung's archetypes via Joseph Campbell's Hero's Journey under the mantra 'We Create the Mythology of the Future,' so that media consolidation (the Fox merger shrinking six conglomerates to five) narrows the Overton Window and Disney's manufactured mythology displaces Christianity as the reigning worldview.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 23 "An Old Man, Filled with Regret . ." — Matthew Brophy argues the film's plot makes most sense if it is an addicted gamer's MMORPG session: Cobb is an avatar, his corporate pursuers are named COBOL after the old programming language, dream 'architects' mirror world-designers like Second Life's Furia Freeloader with her Escher Relativity House, and Mal is a 'gamer's widow' whose in-game suicide deleted her character so she could return to the real family Cobb abandoned. Using the 'egocentric predicament' that no one can access another's mind, he suggests shared dreaming can only really happen on servers, and via Borges's map that covered the empire and Baudrillard's claim that the simulacrum outlives the real he reads Second Life replicas (the virtual Texas A&M campus) as the preferred level of reality decaying the actual one. He then deploys Bostrom's simulation argument — we may already be conscious simulations — and casts Yusuf's basement dreamers, Xiao Yi's Warcraft suicide, and WoW-neglect cases as modern Lotus-Eaters, concluding that the ending is a 'long con': the real inception planted in Cobb the belief that his game is real, so he will one day wake 'an old man, filled with regret, waiting to die alone.'
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 24 "Architecture and the Dream Machine" — Thorsten Botz-Bornstein argues that Inception presents dreams neither as divine messages nor as stylized fantasy but as hackable programs, making the film itself a 'thinking machine' in Jean Epstein's sense — a 'robot brain' whose synchronized kicks, Piaf countdown, and phone-number safes 'think' the different layers of time instead of reproducing a reality, with slow motion as cognition rather than dream-sign (against Bazin). He reads inception as Dawkins's meme theory given a psychoanalytic vertical dimension: the idea is implanted deep in the subconscious (Fischer's relation to his father), can grow autonomously 'like a cancer' as Mal's did, and subconscious projections converge 'like white blood cells' as in Solaris. The chapter then traces how the computer era — hypertext, Second Life, media-absorbed realities like Baudrillard's 9/11 — reshaped cinematic dreams and architecture, so that Ariadne's 'pure creation,' Cobb's Limbo dystopia, and Dubai's empty speculative towers all become the 'gilded dreamworlds' of an ephemeralized, hacker-ready built world — the dream machine as allegory of the globalized world, with atomized grains of reality echoing Democritus via Epstein and Benjamin's account of cinema bursting the prison of the everyday.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 25 "Notes" — Lueth maps Baudrillard's four stages of the image from Simulacra and Simulation onto LEGO history. Early basic-brick town sets reflect a profound reality; the late-1980s shift to cops-and-robbers conflict play masks and denatures it — prison-striped convicts presuppose a justice system that never appears in the sets; sky-fi MOCs like the Savoia S.21 from Porco Rosso, which borrows a real WWII-era designation for a fictional plane, mask the absence of reality; and ApocaLEGO — MOCs riffing endlessly on Metro 2033, Fallout, The Walking Dead, and each other — is the pure simulacrum, images referring only to images with no real-world counterpart to check against (via Borges' 'Tlon, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius'). If Baudrillard is right that images now precede reality, ApocaLEGO is, culturally, literally building the apocalypse.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Boardman reads Miniland USA at LEGOLAND California and Florida as the nation itself rendered a 'Fan Developed Theme': an archipelago of tourist destinations — NYC, Washington DC, Las Vegas, New Orleans, 'New England' — connected not by geography but by the visitor's body performing a simulated cross-country tour that skips the flyover states entirely, with Bachelard's Poetics of Space on miniaturization and Debord's spectacle (footnoted) framing the effect. The California Freedom Tower reproduces a rejected architectural design, a literal Baudrillardian simulacrum, a copy for which no original exists, while Florida's version simply deletes Lower Manhattan and swaps Coke for Pepsi per sponsorship deals. Comparing the two parks' itineraries shows that 'America' here is constructed from circulating tourist imagery and corporate logistics — Carlsbad itself erased from its own park's map.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 23 "The Office and Philosophy" — Uses Baudrillard's three orders of simulacra to read the UK office: Neil Godwin embodies the first order where the boss's signs reflect real virtue (Aristotle's practical wisdom), Gareth's health-and-safety training of Donna - which degenerates into interrogation about her sex life - is the second order where virtuous signs mask desire, and David Brent is the third-order hyperreal, his management-speak ('team individuality', 'mutual likewise reciprocated', the 'rape' role-play outburst) signs with no referent masking that he is not a boss at all. The chapter's sting is that laughing at Brent we tacitly endorse the 'real' managerial system that produces Neil and redundancies, while Gareth - who models himself on Brent and pushes his codes to suicidal extremes ('will there ever be a boy born who can swim faster than a shark?') - instantiates Baudrillard's fatal strategy, a system carrying the seeds of its own destruction.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 36 "The Office and Philosophy" — Written as a fake email thread among University of Scranton faculty, the appendix has junior professor Joe Kraus propose reading the town through Baudrillard's simulacrum - the 'Scranton Welcomes You' sign from the credits becoming real for him only as a TV image - while senior colleagues tutor him through the history of representation theory. Stephen deploys Plato's Ion (Socrates' magnet-and-iron chain of imitation, with Ion's Brent-like obliviousness) and Aristotle on mimesis, pity, fear, and catharsis to explain the show's tragicomic discomfort, while Maria adds the Antiochene, Alexandrian, and Augustinian fourfold senses of scripture applied to Scranton; Michael Friedman contributes a Chekhovian reading of Pam's bird eulogy as subtext about Michael's fear of dying alone. The thread itself mirrors an Office plotline as the senior faculty quietly decide to cut the untenured Joe out of the project.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 31 "Live From New York" — Perez sorts SNL's realities using Plato's cave and Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation: Kate McKinnon's Bieber Calvin Klein ad is a first-phase reflection, Natalie Portman's raps a masking second phase, Ferrell's commodified Bush a second-order copy, and Maya Rudolph's Donatella Versace a third-phase simulacrum with no reality behind it that Versace herself protested. The Church Lady's 2016 Update appearance and the Palin-meets-Palin and Hillary-at-the-bar sketches show characters substituting for the real, while the May 2018 cold open where the real Stormy Daniels tells Baldwin's Trump 'a storm's a-comin',' live-tweeted by @nbcsnl, achieves Baudrillard's hyperreality where fiction and reality are abolished as distinct. Studio 8H becomes a Plato's cave viewers willingly re-enter each Saturday to glimpse the real through simulation.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Culver explains Sarah Connor's harshness through Girard's Violence and the Sacred: like any warrior she is 'stained' by contact with violence and needs purification rites before reentering society, but her society refuses to recognize her as a warrior, so her cleansing becomes psychiatric wards, nine aliases, and fugitive life - measured against the true machine Cameron, whose 'inefficient' coldness throws Sarah's residual humanity into relief. She then applies Baudrillard's hyperreal: the Connors must prove a future nobody else sees while destroying every trace of the Terminators (lowering the T-101 into the steel), a simulation where a T-1000 wears a 'To Protect and Serve' uniform and law and order themselves may be simulated. The upshot is that Sarah's failures at conventional motherhood are those of a warrior-mother raising John inside a war only she experiences, staining him too (he kills Sarkasian) to give him a future.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 30 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Sharpe analyzes the Olympics as an aestheticized 'spectacle' (Debord, after Marx's commodity analysis) whose real product is the shareable 'Olympic moment.' Reading Kant's Critique of Judgment through Terry Eagleton, he argues the games trade on the sensus communis Kant finds in the judgment 'this is beautiful', an intimated universal harmony among humans that mirrors the ancient Olympic ekecheiria (truce). He links Beijing 2008's simulated fireworks and lip-synced girl to Baudrillard's simulacra, and uses Benjamin's 'Work of Art' essay, Riefenstahl's Olympia and Hegel's account of Greek sculpture to show how the Nazis' 1936 Games weaponized this aesthetic power, warning the spectacle serves both good and evil.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 20 "Living a Part Synecdoche, New York, Metaphor, and the Problem of Skepticism" — Deming argues that Caden Cotard's attempt to build a full-scale replica of New York inside a warehouse enacts a skepticism toward the givenness of life—the belief that reality can be denied and remade as art. Drawing on Cavell's claim that film is 'a moving image of skepticism' and Heidegger on world, earth, and dwelling, he shows the play traps Caden rather than freeing him: to represent the world is to be flung outside it. He invokes Wittgenstein's image of language as an ancient city one can never step outside of, and Baudrillard's simulacra (Caden even considers titling the play 'Simulacrum'), to explain why the literal doubling fails to yield the 'true self' Caden seeks.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 12 "Deceit, Desire, and Dark Comedy Postmodern Dead Ends in Blood Simple" — Woolfolk argues that Blood Simple is 'resolutely postmodern': it recycles noir motifs as Jamesonian pastiche but, unlike classic noir (Double Indemnity, Detour), offers no modernist critique of capitalist civilization and no saving metanarrative, leaving only a profane comic present. He reads the three men who go 'simple'—Ray, Marty, Visser—through Girard's triangular desire, driven by unchecked, mutually imitated passions with no external mediating authority, while Visser's sidewalk individualism supplies a minimal social philosophy. Crucially the film's world is ruled by chance, not fate (the pistol's three bullets, Abby's lucky single shot), so Abby's clueless 'health' and survival affirm postmodern contingency rather than any critique of late modernity.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 21 "The Past Is Now History and The Hudsucker Proxy" — Coughlin argues The Hudsucker Proxy, far from being empty pastiche, is a postmodern meditation on history as a constructed text. Drawing on Linda Hutcheon he treats the film's parody of screwball comedy and Frank Capra as a 'value-problematizing' tool: Norville is a hollowed-out anti-Capra hero, and Moses stopping the clock and addressing the audience foregrounds the artificiality and 'telling' of all narratives. Foucault's claim that resistance uses power's own tools underwrites the reading that recycling dead styles and cultural memory (the J. Edgar Hoover quip, the array of intertexts) challenges the authority and singularity of historical representation.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 33 "19. A Pataphysical Cherry Pie" — Pagnoni Berns, Aguilar, and Veteri argue Twin Peaks stages metaphysics—a dual reality of a physical world and an unknowable superimposed one—drawing on Descartes' dualism and Gustav Fechner's animistic day/night double aspect (souls of plants, the Log Lady's log). They then claim its real philosophy is Alfred Jarry's pataphysics, the science of imaginary solutions to real problems: Cooper solves crimes not by deduction but by absurd means—smelling trees, throwing rocks at a bottle while naming suspects, reading dreams—superimposing another plane on ours (echoing Baudrillard), so Twin Peaks is 'metaphysics with humor.'
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 23 "The Shining and Anti-Nostalgia Postmodern Notions of History R. Barton Palmer" — Palmer reads The Shining as a postmodern anti-nostalgia film using Fredric Jameson's account of late-capitalist culture as a depthless perpetual present that can only cannibalize the past as pastiche. He argues Kubrick invokes the ghost-story and nostalgia-film conventions of 1970s Hollywood only to reject them: Jack Torrance's endlessly retyped 'All work and no play' and his entrapment between the empty present and the 1921 ballroom photo dramatize the failing artist 'adrift in a kind of weightlessness,' echoing Baudrillard's post-deconstruction art that can only play with the pieces. The Citizen Kane homage that closes the film deliberately refuses the explanation its model provided.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Paulus and Adriaensens argue that Mann's 'stylized realism' is best understood not as neobaroque spectacle but as mannerism: a self-conscious, image-conscious cinema in tension between classicism and anti-classicism. Reading Mann's green-screen shooting on Heat, the hyperreal night look of Collateral and the ultra-sharp digital of Public Enemies through Deleuze's letter to Daney on cinematic mannerism, they cast Mann as a Coppola-like 'bridge-builder' who offers a pedagogy of the image and gains Nietzsche's 'powers of the false.' Baudrillard's account of Apocalypse Now as excess of means and simulation frames the immersive spectacle Mann resists in favor of realism.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Wildermuth argues that Mann dramatizes a postmodern critique of law in which justice itself becomes a commodity, drawing on Baudrillard's hyperreal and simulation, Marxist legal theory (Pashukanis's 'organized class terror'), and critical legal studies. In The Last of the Mohicans the British social contract with the colonial militia is exposed as a cover for imperial hierarchy; in Crime Story's 'Abrams for the Defense' and Miami Vice's Lao Li, and in Collateral's hit man Vincent, contracts and legalism deconstruct into simulated justice that serves the top of the economic order, so resistance is possible only locally and temporarily.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Corne unpacks Vincent Hanna's tirade in Heat against his wife's ex-husband's 'dead-tech, postmodernistic, bullshit house.' He reads the smashing of the television and the headless sculpture through Bataille's Against Architecture (buildings as latent prisons of authority) and Jameson's diagnosis of postmodern depthlessness and the silence of affect. Using Hegel, Hugo and Ruskin on architecture's obligation to tell the truth, and especially Frankfurt's On Bullshit, Corne argues the house is 'bullshit' because it is indifferent to truth; Vincent's workaholism becomes a Frankfurtian discipline, and the film reflexively treats truth, authenticity and space as a problem.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 21 "Disenchantment and Rebellion in Alphaville" — Woolfolk reads Godard's Alphaville as an imagination of spiritual disaster: the Alpha 60 computer's reduction of time to divisible units suppresses the Bergsonian durée and fundamental self, and the city's architecture of 'nonplaces' embodies Weber's disenchantment and the Frankfurt School's culture-industry critique. Following Charles Taylor, he argues disenchantment opens a new heroic framework of facing an indifferent universe with lucidity, in which Lemmy Caution—a postmodern pastiche of noir dandies—rebels through an aestheticized eroticism and Éluard's surrealist poetry, achieving a Weberian 'this-worldly salvation' of art and love that succeeds where Orwell's Julia and Huxley's Savage fail.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Palmer reads The Shining through Fredric Jameson's account of postmodernity as a 'perpetual present' that has lost its past and can only cannibalize it as pastiche and nostalgia film. He argues Kubrick's film enacts an 'anti-nostalgia' that invokes the nostalgic impulse—Jack Torrance's wish to escape an empty present into the Overlook's endless 1921 party—only to destroy him with it, refusing the genre's happy-ending wish-fulfillment. Drawing on Baudrillard's image of art 'adrift in a kind of weightlessness' merely 'playing with the pieces,' he casts Jack, endlessly typing 'All work and no play,' as the failed postmodern artist trapped between times, reduced to pointless Nietzschean ressentiment, with the film's Nietzschean death-of-God flux underlying its refusal of stable meaning.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — The editors' introduction surveys the volume and frames Soderbergh as a maker of 'philosophical cinema' whose films engage epistemology, metaphysics, and ethics. It previews the essays' claims: that sex, lies, and videotape and Schizopolis stage epistemological questions of truth, evidence, and skepticism; that The Underneath and The Limey use Bergson's durée to explore time and self-understanding; that Traffic tests Kant's ethics against Sartrean individual decision; and that Solaris recasts memory and authenticity via Augustine and Baudrillard's simulacra. It positions Soderbergh within Indiewood filmmaking after Welles as a self-reflexive artist.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — de Waard argues that The Good German embodies Soderbergh's 'neo-meta' philosophy of history as polyphonic mediation, staged by Levi's line about a camera that turns the image upside-down to set it right. Shooting with 1940s-era equipment and pastiching Casablanca, The Third Man, Chinatown, and Schindler's List, the film presents not history's progression but 'history as time,' a simultaneity of broken mirrors. Reworking Benjamin's angel-of-history thesis, de Waard claims images of the present threaten to reappear ad infinitum, and contrasts Soderbergh's cold, morally relativist tale of American war-criminal whitewashing (Lena's confession that she betrayed twelve Jews) with Spielberg's emotionally manipulative Holocaust spectacle, invoking Eco on Casablanca as 'movies' itself.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Ritzer reads Kafka through Deleuze (and Guattari), Jameson, Barthes, and Lacan as a self-reflexive, schizophrenic pastiche. The film's shift from black-and-white to color as Kafka enters the castle is analyzed via Deleuze's 'colour-image' and Barthes on color as artifice, using color's sensual materiality rather than realism. Its dense allusions to Wiene, Murnau, Lang, Welles's The Trial, and German expressionism make it, in Jameson's terms, a postmodern pastiche marking the waning of historicity, while Lacanian schizophrenia (the breakdown of the signifying chain) models Kafka's paranoia about power structures controlling the individual. Ritzer finally argues the film approaches Deleuze and Guattari's 'minor cinema,' deterritorializing classical Hollywood's realism through intensity and the supremacy of sign over referent.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 29 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Moses reads Solaris through Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation, arguing the sentient planet is a 'dream factory' that reproduces Kelvin's dreamed Rheya as facsimiles with no original, literalizing hyperreality and the precession of simulacra. He treats Soderbergh's remake-of-a-remake status and the final scene, where Kelvin and Rheya speak directly into the camera as Solaris implodes, as pure cinema collapsing reality and representation, life and death, in Baudrillard's 'end of history' implosion. Moses extends the reading to unnatural reproduction (Baudrillard's clone/matrix, the aborted child), pervasive surveillance and monitors, and post-9/11 affects of terror, nostalgia, and melancholia, concluding the film offers no escape from postmodernity, only a way deeper in.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — LaRocca argues Burton's 'Ed Wood' (1994) is a metafilm that, via Baudrillard's simulacra and Plato's cave/dialectic, transforms how we watch Wood's 'bad' films. He casts Wood as a cave-dweller and naive literalist who conflates representation with reality ('film equals life,' 'that was perfect'), while Burton is the Platonic dialectician who posits two worlds and provokes thought. He distinguishes two interacting metafilm types—biographical simulacrum (a hyperreal Ed Wood with no original, per Baudrillard's 'artificial resurrection') and mimetic reenactment (loyal remakes of Wood's films)—so that Martin Landau's Lugosi and Parker-as-Fuller's non-acting reveal the emotional 'affect without illusion' latent in Wood's work.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 6 "Introduction War Films and the Ineffability of War" — LaRocca argues that a war film can never be war itself but only a mediated, post-facto fabrication, and reads the camera and the gun as twinned instruments ('point and shoot' becoming digital 'point and click' in Skyfall). He mobilizes Baudrillard's claim that the Gulf War 'did not take place' to describe war video games and CGI spectacle (Avatar, Call of Duty) as hyperreal simulacra, and Freud's 'Why War?' letter and death instinct to explain the compulsive proliferation of war representation. Foucault ('peace is a coded war'), Heraclitus ('war is father of all'), and Isaiah Berlin's plurality of incompatible values frame war's ineffability and perpetuity, while Cavell's ontology of film grounds the viewer's 'mechanically assured' helplessness before on-screen dying bodies.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 10 "Lenses into War Digital Vérité in Iraq War Films" — Peebles defends the 'digital vérité' of Iraq War films (Stop-Loss, In the Valley of Elah, The Battle for Haditha, Redacted, Standard Operating Procedure) against Garrett Stewart's charge that grainy embedded footage elides critique, arguing instead that the multiplying lenses close the distance between soldier and viewer to build empathy. She invokes Baudrillard's 'the Gulf War did not take place' to show how CNN's video-game-like distance erased the common soldier, which the up-close soldier-shot cell-phone image corrects. Reading Hank Deerfield's reconstruction of his son's fatal Humvee incident in Elah and Errol Morris's reframing of the Abu Ghraib photos in Standard Operating Procedure, she argues each frame is 'both an aperture and a restriction,' and that these tragedies are inherently antiwar.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 15 "The Violated Body Affective Experience and Somatic Intensity in Zero Dark Thirty" — Burgoyne argues that Kathryn Bigelow's Zero Dark Thirty places the violated body at the center of its rendering of the War on Terror, using somatic intensity and affective experience against Steven Shaviro's reading of the film as pure, affect-draining proceduralism. He traces Maya's arc from witness to coercive agent through the torture of Ammar, the Goya-like montage of interrogation videos, and the suicide-bomb killing of her friend Jessica, mapping the film onto Sarah Cole's poles of disenchanted violence (the raw, exposed flesh of the interrogations) and enchanted violence (the technologically choreographed, almost magical SEAL raid on Abbottabad, likened to Baudrillardian simulated combat). The closing unzipping of bin Laden's body bag deflates any triumph into embodied ambiguity.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 13 "Fake News and Ecstatic Truths" — Kyle Novak uses Herzog's fabricated Pascal epigraph in Lessons of Darkness to distinguish 'ecstatic truth' from Trump-era 'alternative facts,' arguing that unlike Kellyanne Conway's deception, Herzog openly reveals his inventions to deepen an artistic experience. Rejecting Russell's correspondence theory of truth, Novak turns to Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation and The Gulf War Did Not Take Place to show how media create norms and a hyperreality independent of facts, then to Nietzsche's 'On Truth and Lies' (truth as agreed-upon metaphor) and Deleuze's affirmation of life as a non-relativist standard, concluding that Lessons of Darkness is 'sparse on facts but full of truths' that penetrate deeper than CNN footage.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 3 "01_LaRocca_Chapter_000.html" — LaRocca's introduction frames the whole volume through Plato's ancient 'quarrel between philosophy and poetry' and his critique of mimesis (Republic Book X), arguing that documentary film is just another kind of poetic imitation whose truth-claims deserve philosophical scrutiny. Drawing on Cavell's 'film was as if made for philosophy,' Kiarostami's 'cinema is nothing but fakery,' Herzog's 'ecstatic truth,' and Flaherty's 'sometimes you have to lie to tell the truth,' he shows how documentary blurs fiction/nonfiction and courts fabrication. He reads the digital turn (Manovich, Rodowick) as pushing cinema toward Baudrillard's hyperreal simulacra, images that no longer index reality but simulate it.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 13 "11_LaRocca_Chapter_010.html" — Pederson and Zimmermann analyze Vincent Grenier's 'avant-doc' videos (Color Study: Slaterville New York, Watercolor: Fall Creek, Les Chaises, Armoire) as interventions in the philosophy of documentary landscape. They read his flattened tableau shots and digitally manipulated color fields against the Hudson River School and Ansel Adams's transcendentalist (Emersonian/Thoreauvian) American sublime, invoking Timothy Murray's Heideggerian poiesis of habitats and Baudrillard's simulation/simulacra to argue Grenier replaces representation of nature with simulation—e.g., the pigeon reacting to its mirror image in Armoire—dissolving the divide between the natural and the technological.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 34 "32_LaRocca_Chapter_031.html" — LaRocca argues that Casey Affleck's I'm Still Here, in which Joaquin Phoenix faked a drug-addled retirement and hip-hop career, is best understood as a 'hoax-verite' whose collapse of the boundary between real and represented turns it into a Baudrillardian simulacrum and hyperreal artifact, a documentary of images 'without an original referent.' Against Noel Carroll's account of documentary as a film of presumptive assertion and Plantinga's assertive stance, LaRocca shows how Affleck exploited audience faith (staged home movies, the David Letterman 'beat down') so that the film's metaphysical, epistemic and ethical status transformed once the fraud was confirmed. He invokes Hegel's remarks on abstract individuality and compares the case to Herzog's 'ecstatic truth,' Roth's and Kaufman's metafiction, to argue the deception paradoxically discloses deeper truths about what documentary is.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 15 "6. How the Hell Are We Supposed to Kill an Idea" — Simsek reads the 'Hell House' tulpa—a monster made real by mass belief on the HellHoundsLair website—as a philosophical challenge about the power of ideas and how one 'kills' an idea, which the brothers can only attempt by seeding a counter-belief. She invokes Socrates' call in the Republic to censor the arts that shape moral character, and the Streisand Effect, to argue that internet-amplified ideas (memes, conspiracy theories, gender and racial norms) take on autonomous, hard-to-kill life much as fandom overrides creators' intent.
- **Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy**, ch. 7 "Screaming for Change" — A literature review that critiques three prior scholarly frames for punk. It rejects Hebdige and the Birmingham CCCS reading of punk as mere subcultural 'resistance through style' (bricolage that only rearranges commodities and so is easily co-opted by the hegemony), then critiques postmodern 'authenticity' accounts drawing on Baudrillard and Lyotard, where the collapse of grand narratives leaves punks policing who is a 'real' punk versus a 'poseur.' Kristiansen argues all these approaches rob punk of complexity and proposes instead that punk is a philosophical/ideological system that produces the style, not the reverse.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 24 "13. Anthony Bourdain’s Antisocial Ethics" — Kitchen and Scalambrino build Bourdain's 'ethics for travelers' around his tagline 'Be a traveler, not a tourist,' arguing he preferred authentic community over abstract, Capitalist-conditioned society. Using Guy Debord's Society of the Spectacle to characterize the tourist's 'corporate commodified darkness' and Kierkegaard's dictum about contemplating death daily, they show through the Bhutan and Lebanon episodes how Bourdain's food-based humanism values lived communal reality over consuming others' experiences as banal spectacle.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 37 "Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!" — J. Jeremy Wisnewski stages a mock threat to 'kill' the Griffins to expose Family Guy as postmodernism incarnate. Its blizzard of equal-footing references (Hitler beside Scooby-Doo) illustrates Baudrillard's hyperreal where 'the real is no longer real,' and its relentless mockery of religion, war, and politics enacts Lyotard's incredulity toward meta-narratives. Worrying this breeds cynical conservatism, he rescues the show via Foucault's power/knowledge: like Foucault's activism, one can be incredulous toward grand stories yet still fight local battles - a little incredulity is exactly what we need.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 13 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Kellie Bean reads Colbert and Stewart through Jean Baudrillard's simulacra and the hyperreal, arguing that mainstream news has become an image unmoored from reality. Colbert is a 'walking talking simulacrum' who out-O'Reillys O'Reilly (the portrait-within-a-portrait, 'The Word' segments like 'Gateway Hug'), enacting news as pure sign; Stewart, broadcasting from a simulacrum of a news studio, instead punctures the hyperreal to expose the real, parsing Obama's convention rhetoric and Laura Ingraham's platform dodge. The 'Best F#@king News Team Ever' slogan lays bare the empty hyperbole of 'Fair and Balanced,' re-anchoring the audience to meaning.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 33 "20. The Totalitarian Zone" — Altmann traces totalitarianism from The Twilight Zone into Black Mirror. 'He's Alive' shows Vollmer wielding Aristotle's rhetoric to grow a Nazi movement; 'Number 12' shows Umberto Eco's fascist 'fear of difference'; 'Deaths-Head Revisited' illustrates Arendt's banality of evil in Lutze's 'just following orders.' He then argues Black Mirror episodes ('The Waldo Moment,' 'Fifteen Million Merits') realize Guy Debord's 'society of the spectacle' and hyper-capitalism, where politics becomes entertainment and even resistance is commodified—a totalitarianism that needs no tanks.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 31 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Koppedrayer analyzes the modern North American 'traditional' and 'primitive' bowhunting movement—the Traditional Bowyer's Bible, magazines like Primitive Archer, and gatherings like ETAR—where crafting a selfbow from a single wood stave and hunting under a 'fair chase' ethic promise an authentic, unencumbered, 'really real' experience against high-tech compound bows. Drawing on Arjun Appadurai's 'synchronic warehouse of cultural scenarios,' she argues the past functions as a reproducible resource yielding a hyperreal authenticity, and that bowmakers describe the self-made bow as an embodiment of the maker's own substance and a spiritual link to earlier hunters.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 32 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Brophy warns of a coming 'pornographic singularity' when veridical, immersive, interactive, unbounded virtual reality (extrapolated from Second Life, Rapelay, and Sony's brain-stimulation patent) makes hypersex and hyper-romance supplant real intimacy. He uses Baudrillard's hyperreal/simulacra to explain how airbrushed models and 'pornbots' render real women 'just bad porn', invokes Nozick's experience machine as literally realized, and argues that utilitarianism and Kant's humanity formula fail to condemn using pornbots, so only Aristotelian virtue theory locates the wrong—the user malfunctions and cannot flourish as escalating deviance (furries, age-play, rape games) conditions vice. His bleak prophecy is that unbounded virtual desire will corrode families and community.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 17 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Thorsten Botz-Bornstein argues contemporary female tattoos have lost their one-dimensional identifying function and instead create a new 'tattoo space.' He dismantles the paradoxical 'savage/civilized' and 'nature/purity' schemes (drawing on Baudrillard on the smooth, made-up female body-screen that reflects male desire) and Loos' 'ornament and crime' verdict on women's tattoos. He proposes that female tattoos have 'become graffiti' – a Bergsonian spatial 'center of action' and 'skinscape' that disperses meaning horizontally rather than branding an identity, recuperating the female body as a political body against commercialized post-political bodies.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 27 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Lee argues that tattooing is a performative 'practice of writing' whose meaning always exceeds its origin, comparing Holocaust survivor Tova Friedman's Auschwitz number 'A27633' with the Suicide Girl Jaylin's chosen feminist ink. Drawing on Judith Butler's account of the body as a site of inscription and counter-inscription, and Walter Benjamin's 'Critique of Violence' distinguishing law-making from law-preserving force, she claims Friedman's tattoo resists the Nazi law itself while Jaylin's only satirizes heteropatriarchy. She then invokes Baudrillard's 'ecstasy of communication' and the obscene to show tattooing can desubjectify by dissolving the embodied self into pornographic information.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 12 "Making Their Presence Known TV's Ghost-Hunter Phenomenon in a “Post-” World" — Jessica O'Hara argues TV ghost-hunter shows (Ghost Hunters, Paranormal State, A Haunting) stage classic philosophical problems in a postmodern key. Their reliance on technology to escape 'fallible senses' echoes Descartes's Meditations, while Husserl's intentionality raises whether clients' dysfunction makes them perceive the normal as paranormal (or invites the demonic). Baudrillard's simulation/hyperreal troubles whether a 'simulated' haunting differs from a real one; Plantinga's free-will defense frames their treatment of the problem of evil. Following Lyotard she reads the shows' micro-narratives and bricolage as postmodern, and via Derrida's Spectres of Marx casts ghost-hunting as post-9/11 mourning and the pursuit of justice, offering a Burkean/Kantian sublime.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 37 "Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!" — Wisnewski casts Family Guy as pure postmodernism: its cut-away collage of Hitler, Scooby-Doo, and Tiananmen makes everything equally real, illustrating Baudrillard's hyperreal ("the real is no longer real") and Lyotard's incredulity toward meta-narratives. Worried that such cynicism breeds conservative inaction, he turns to Foucault's power/knowledge to argue that one can be incredulous toward grand narratives yet still fight local battles — so Family Guy's mockery of religion and politics can be genuine critique, and the cartoon need not be killed.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 88 "83. Disco Elysium as Philosophy Solipsism, Existentialism, and Simulacra" — Khamis reads Disco Elysium's 'Pale'—a property-less substance said to be decaying human thought that consumes reality—through three idealisms. The phasmid's warning that the world might vanish if humans stop thinking it evokes Berkeley's subjective idealism (esse est percipi) but without God as guarantor, leaving Harry in existential dread. The Pale as human-produced 'second nature' laid over 'first nature' evokes Kant's and Schelling's transcendental idealism, while the Pale as decaying signs without signification—like the vacuous dockworker 'sheriffs'—matches Baudrillard's hyperreality and simulacra, where information proliferates as meaning collapses, paralleling the amnesiac Harry's own loss and remaking of self.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 90 "85. Persona 5 Royal as Philosophy Unmasking (Persona)l Identity and Reality" — Lopez and Marquez use Persona 5 Royal's Phantom Thieves to explore Schechtman's 'characterization' question of personal identity ('Who am I?') via three bases: qualia (the privately felt sense of self expressed when Ryuji names himself a 'troublemaker' and Morgana insists he is 'NOT a cat'), Wittgensteinian hinge propositions, and language-games in which identity and 'justice' get their meaning through use. Ryle and Wittgenstein's behaviorist worries about private language are set against Nagel's bat and Chalmers's qualia. The Maruki arc—offering a pain-free false utopia and Sumire living as her dead twin Kasumi—poses whether Bentham's utilitarianism, James's pragmatism, or Baudrillard's hyperreality could justify a blissful simulacrum, which the game's 'true ending' rejects for painful reality.

### Allegory of the Cave

The allegory of the cave, from Plato's Republic, imagines prisoners chained since birth so they see only shadows cast on a wall, mistaking these projections for reality. One prisoner is freed, painfully ascends to the sunlit world outside, and comes to understand that the shadows were mere images of true things. The story dramatizes Plato's distinction between the world of appearances and the world of the Forms, and it pictures education as a turning of the soul toward truth rather than a filling of it with facts. It also suggests why the enlightened person, returning to explain what they have seen, may be met with hostility.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 9 "The Fates of Socrates and Seinfeld" — William Irwin compares Jerry and Socrates: the 'Jerry problem' of whether the fictional Jerry is the real Jerry (complicated by Seinlanguage) mirrors the Socratic problem of separating Socrates from Plato's dialogues. Jerry, like Socrates the gadfly, provokes his circle with questions that hunt for essences - the black-and-white cookie, 'is soup a meal?' - and shares Socrates' irony (the 'War: What Is It Good For?' gag in 'The Marine Biologist' works exactly like Socratic shamming ignorance). But where Socrates died serenely per the Apology and Phaedo, Jerry is self-absorbed and ends the series convicted under the Good Samaritan law, doing his stand-up 'gadfly' routine for prison inmates - an examined life, but not an exemplary one.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 11 "Unknown" — Irwin reads Neo's unplugging as Plato's cave allegory restaged: the pod farms are the cave, the cables feeding the illusion are the chains, and Morpheus (named for the god of dreams) plays the liberator who drags the prisoner painfully into the light of 'the desert of the real'. He frames the 'prison for your mind' theme through figures who kept their minds free under captivity, notes that 'education' etymologically means 'leading out' as the prisoner is led out of the cave, and contrasts Neo, who would endure anything rather than return to illusion, with Cypher, who goes back to the shadows.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 12 "Unknown" — Irwin argues the cave story's real point is Plato's Theory of Forms: life inside the Matrix, like ordinary sensory life, is a realm of copies - sunsets, just acts, really good noodles - imitating Beauty, Justice and Goodness themselves. He reads 'there is no spoon' and Morpheus's 'no one can be told what the Matrix is' as Plato's claim that the Forms are grasped by intellect rather than senses, and explains Neo's amnesia and the film's deja vu through Plato's doctrine of recollection (anamnesis), with the soul beholding the Forms between incarnations.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 27 "Unknown" — Korsmeyer traces how the film deploys each sense: vision is both the channel of illusion and, as from Plato's cave onward, the metaphor for understanding ('Why do my eyes hurt?' 'You've never used them'); hearing serves surveillance and bodily invasion, from the centipede-like bug to the screaming 'WAKE UP!' and whispers that nearly touch; and smell marks corporeality, from Trinity's affectionate sniffing of the sleeping Neo to Agent Smith's disgust at human 'stink', which drives him to break protocol and remove his earpiece.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 31 "The Metaphysics of The Matrix" — Gracia and Sanford open with Neo and Trinity in the club and the question that drives the film, 'What is the Matrix?', mapping Neo's path out of the pod onto Plato's cave ascent while stressing the twist: what Neo finds is not the shining realm of Forms but a war-scarred desert, preferred only because it is true, and like Plato's escaped prisoner he returns to free the others. They state their three questions - what are appearance and reality, what separates them, and what properties belong to each - as the paradigmatically metaphysical questions the film poses.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 34 "Unknown" — The authors distinguish the two worlds twice over: by source, since everything in the Matrix issues from the AI machines' program while the real world's ultimate causes lie elsewhere; and by ontological status, since the unreal world depends entirely for its existence on real machines, electrical signals, and minds. They add that recognizing the difference requires a teacher - Morpheus playing to Neo's 'splinter in your mind', just as Plato's cave needs a first freed prisoner - though they file how we come to know this under epistemology rather than metaphysics.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 66 "Unknown" — The chapter reads the pod farms as Plato's cave from Republic VII: prisoners chained from birth who mistake projected images for reality and 'do not know that they are prisoners', insisting on the truth of their world. Morpheus, named for the god of dreams, is the liberator-expert who can rouse sleepers in the right sequence, and Neo's sense of not being sure he is awake parallels the prisoner's primeval recollections. With Plato, it argues that happiness is objective like health - one can say 'I am happy' and be wrong, as the battery-humans are - so true happiness and freedom depend on knowledge of what is real.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 89 "Unknown" — The chapter sets Neo and Cypher as the two poles of authenticity: Neo's unplugging is agony, like the prisoner dragged from Plato's cave - atrophied limbs, eyes that hurt because 'never used them before', and the cognitive shock of the 'desert of the real' - while Cypher, freed young and worn down by years of fear and gag-inducing goop, sells out the crew for a steak he knows does not exist: 'ignorance is bliss'. McMahon asks us to sympathize with Cypher, since in his place, facing perpetual annihilation, 'we too might opt for the illusion'.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 98 "Real Genre and Virtual Philosophy" — Knight and McKnight argue The Matrix must be read as a mixed-genre film: pure genres are 'a theorist's fiction', and the film's genre inheritance supplies the narrative roots of its philosophical thematics - Plato's cave from the Republic, Descartes's Dream Hypothesis from the Meditations, Nietzsche's Ubermensch, Zen Buddhism, and apocalyptic Christianity. Recognizing the genre mix explains both why the film raises questions about justified true belief in a virtual world, free will versus deterministic control, and appearance versus reality, and why it offers no philosophical answers, only genre ones.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 102 "Unknown" — The chapter argues that the film's philosophical allusions—students comparing the pod-bound humans to Plato's cave prisoners and Neo's bewilderment to Descartes's First Meditation dream hypothesis—are designed to generate suspense, anxiety, and horror rather than philosophical reflection. Because genre texts are centrifugal, pointing viewers to outside connections, and their pacing never lingers on themes, The Matrix can use philosophy only to trigger audience interest and never to argue for answers. Its conclusion is that the film is unquestionably real genre but only virtual philosophy.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 115 "Unknown" — Developing thesis one, the chapter shows Morpheus's question—'How would you know the difference between the dream world and the real world?'—restates Plato's cave dwellers mistaking shadows for things and Descartes's First Meditation progression from unreliable senses to dreaming to the malicious demon that makes every belief false. What is genuinely new is that computer simulation and brain science have made the once-outlandish demon scenario thinkable, so the film has made philosophy teachers' job easier: global skepticism no longer seems ridiculous, and maybe you are lying in a tub of goo right now.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 119 "The Matrix Or, The Two Sides of Perversion" — Žižek opens with the 'ideal spectator' beside him exclaiming 'so there is no reality!' and notes the film works as a Rorschach test in which Lacanians, Frankfurt School partisans, and New Agers all recognize themselves. He reframes Plato's cave: when the prisoners escape The Matrix's version of the cave, what they find outside is not the sunlit realm of the Good but the desolate 'desert of the real', and he asks whether the choice between reading the film as Capital colonizing subjectivity or as the virtual symbolic order as such is itself a false alternative.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 17 "Conquering the Inner Demon" — James Lawler casts Buffy as a contemporary allegory of Plato's cave-escaped philosopher and reads the show through Kant: the Slayer moves between a hellish lower world of instrumental appetite and an intelligible higher world of the soul, and Kant's Copernican revolution ('objects must conform to our knowledge') explains Marcie's invisibility in 'Out of Mind, Out of Sight' and the fear-made-flesh Master of 'Nightmares.' Kant's formula that every rational being exists as an end in himself grounds Buffy's duty in 'Anne' ('I am Buffy, the Vampire Slayer'), her rejection of Spike's chip as no substitute for a soul in 'Crush,' and her 'As You Were' admission that using Spike treats him as a mere means. Season Six explores 'too much heaven': Buffy's blissful death in 'The Gift' makes earthly life hell, and only conquering the inner demon — Willow's fear-driven dark magic defeated by Xander's yellow-crayon love in 'Grave' — restores the balance between heavens and hells.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 30 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Lenore Wright reads Sam and Frodo's Quest through the two journey motifs of Western philosophy: the journey out (Plato's cave, structuring Augustine's Confessions and Descartes' escape from the senses' deceptions) and the journey inward (the cogito, self-transformation, with Nussbaum's claim that literature gives philosophy a body). Frodo's steps out of the Shire-cave - selling Bag End, 'I will take the Ring, though I do not know the way' - create the Fellowship and its freedoms, while Boromir attains self-knowledge only at death's door and Gandalf, Aragorn, and Sam are remade by the road. Against classical heroes like Theseus and Odysseus, Sam and Frodo are modern pilgrims - Nietzschean Yea-sayers becoming who they are, with Heideggerian 'potentiality-for-Being' - whereas Sméagol and Saruman live inauthentically, defined by their pasts.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 35 "Last Pitch" — Reid argues that baseball and Socratic elenchus are both constructed to cultivate aretē, excellence. She maps four parallels onto concrete moments: both live off uncertainty (pre-game jitters, the 2001 Rivera–Gonzalez Series finish), both require risking failure (Ted Williams playing a doubleheader to protect his .400, Kirk Gibson's hobbling 1988 homer off Dennis Eckersley, Billy Beane's fear beside Lenny Dykstra), both demand active self-testing (Lou Gehrig retiring when complimented on a routine play), and both impose an obligation to return and challenge others — Plato's cave allegory, Socrates the gadfly, the aging champion who applauds the record-breaker. The Delphic oracle's riddle, that Socrates is wisest in knowing his ignorance, is the batter's-box humility every at-bat demands.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 105 "What Is Real" — Presents the two lines Rowling said she waited seventeen years to write: dying Harry, in the King's Cross limbo, asks Dumbledore whether their conversation is real or only 'inside my head', and Dumbledore answers that of course it is in his head but that does not make it unreal. The section frames this as the philosophical question of separating appearance from reality, cites A. J. Ayer's dismissal of his own near-death experience as hallucination, and introduces Plato's cave as the classic image of mistaking shadows for reality.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 14 "The Jedi Model" — Barad presents a handbook of Jedi virtue modeled on Plato's Republic: the Jedi are Plato's Guardians, trained through physical exercise and Socratic questioning to guard peace and justice. Aristotle's golden mean explains courage as the balance between Chewbacca's cowardly fear and Anakin's rash rush at Dooku, with Luke's decision to leave Dagobah counting as courage because it has just cause. Luke's Dagobah cave vision (Vader's mask opening to reveal his own face) is read as Plato's Cave allegory turned inward - self-knowledge of one's fear of becoming evil - while compassion and forgiveness, not forbidden attachment, complete the Jedi character. The chapter even defends Jedi mind tricks via Plato's noble lie (the myth of the metals) as manipulation of the weak-minded for the common good.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 24 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Wendy Hamblet asks whether Narnia feeds children a dangerous militaristic moral imaginary: Homeric warrior heroes, swarthy Calormene villains, voiceless animals excluded from moral concern, and battles that decide truth, in a lineage running from Plato's censorship of nursery stories through Descartes's modernity to Heidegger's seduction by Hitler's myths. On closer reading she finds Lewis undermining militarism: morally mixed characters, condemnation of aggression, despotism, and 'reasons of state,' and room only for just war and righteous self-defense. The finale is read through Plato's cave, as the Last Battle's worlds-within-worlds expose our political 'truths' as shadow-images that unscrupulous leaders manipulate when the god is absent.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 27 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Takes Digory's dying remark 'It's all in Plato' as the key to the Chronicles. It compares the Professor's guided questioning of Peter and Susan about Lucy's wardrobe testimony to the Socratic method, though noting he supplies evidential maxims rather than eliciting a virtue-definition as Socrates does with Cephalus on justice. It maps Underland in The Silver Chair onto the Allegory of the Cave (Rilian bound in his silver chair like the chained prisoners, the Green Witch's enchantment that denies any world beyond), observing that the Witch 'plays Aristotle' by ridiculing Aslan as an invented perfect Form, while Puddleglum's 'stand by the play-world' speech echoes Socrates's reply to Glaucon that the ideal pattern is none the worse for being unrealizable. Finally it reads the 'real Narnia' of The Last Battle ('world within world, Narnia within Narnia') as Christian Platonism, with the nested heavens even raising Plato's Third Man problem.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 23 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Harman argues the real heroes of Easy Rider are the two Harley-Davidsons: the exploding Captain America bike that drowns out its rider's corpse, the cocaine hidden in the gas tank like a prosthetic organ, and the obscured helmets and muffled dialogue reduce Fonda, Hopper, and Nicholson to 'stowaways and parasites' of their machines. He uses this reversal to attack Kant's Copernican Revolution, on which we could know only how Harleys appear to us and never the things in themselves, and to champion the Whitehead-Deleuze-Latour current in which genes, pickup trucks, bridges, and Harleys are autonomous actors no less than humans, against Plato's two-world heir of appearances and unknowable things. Billy and Captain America's 1960s transgression, he concludes, quietly ends in submission to the power, rhythm, and demands of their bikes.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 11 "U2 and Philosophy" — Dreyfus and Wrathall read U2's head/heart split through Kierkegaard's Sickness unto Death: the Christian-Platonic strategy of escaping the earthly (the sun-blindness of 'Staring at the Sun', the ascent of 'Gone') collapses into despair once both sides of the self prove essential, while 'The Playboy Mansion' and 'Discotheque' depict Kierkegaardian leveling and spiritlessness in consumer culture and 'Last Night on Earth' the aesthetic-sphere despair of living pure possibility. Pascal's contradictory great-and-miserable self and Augustine's two cities supply the tradition U2 inherits, and Nietzsche's 'nihilism' names what U2 calls 'pop'. They close by arguing that Bono's pseudonymous stage characters (the Fly, MacPhisto) do phenomenology just as Kierkegaard's pseudonyms do, and that U2's songs about something missing bear out despair's 'dialectic of eternity'.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 9 "Plato’s Cave Again" — Curran uses Shadow of a Doubt to teach epistemology: Charlie's claim to 'know' her uncle distinguishes knowledge by acquaintance from propositional knowledge as justified true belief, with the permanently stuck 'Til Two clock showing a true belief that is not knowledge because its warrant is unreliable. Coherence (Hegel, Blanshard), pragmatist (James, Dewey), and correspondence theories of truth are tested against the townspeople's false but convenient beliefs about Uncle Charlie, and only correspondence survives. Kant's absolute duty not to lie is weighed against Mill's act and rule utilitarianism for the detectives' deceptions, and a feminist care-ethics perspective assesses Charlie's shielding her mother from the truth. Plato's cave frames the cinema itself: film can deceive like shadows on a wall, yet the detectives' unused photograph shows the camera can also reveal truth, so movies help us face facts, at the price, as Charlie pays, of lost innocence.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 24 "Curtain Down" — Silberstein reads Rear Window as a self-reflexive film about film-watching: the shades rise like a curtain, the courtyard apartments play like frames on a filmstrip, and wheelchair-bound Jeff with his binoculars is the movie spectator - the courtyard is Plato's cave and we are the chained prisoners watching shadows (copies of copies of the forms). The chapter stages the Plato-versus-Aristotle debate over imitative art from Republic Book X and the Poetics, then argues the film vindicates both: Jeff's voyeurism breeds detachment and misjudgment (he misreads Lisa, Miss Torso, the composer and the newlyweds), yet the same watching awakens - the song 'Lisa' saves Miss Lonelyhearts from suicide, Thorwald is brought to justice, and Jeff and the audience leave the theater wiser about fantasy, boredom and their own lives.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 15 "Would You Help Me to Carry the Stone" — Weinstein argues critics who call Waters a gloomy misanthrope misread him: he is an existentialist whose work maps point for point onto Camus's absurd, the human demand for unity endlessly frustrated. Waters's imagery tracks Camus's: the sun (Plato's cave symbol of the good, and the light Sisyphus loved on earth) against the eclipsed moon of death and madness; the stone we secrete through failed communication ('the bad blood slows and turns to stone' in 'Dogs,' 'would you help me to carry the stone' in The Wall) against Sisyphus's rock; and Pink's Trial, condemned for 'showing feelings of an almost human nature,' replaying Meursault's condemnation for failing to cry at his mother's funeral. Since the institutions of home, school, military, and the music industry's machine block every genuine encounter, Waters's persistence in making art that mostly fails to communicate is itself the absurd revolt, so with Camus one must imagine Sisyphus happy, and Weinstein imagines Waters happy too.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 16 "Thinking Inside the Pod" — Condella reads the opening of Saturday Night Fever -- Tony Manero strutting to 'Stayin' Alive' while delivering a can of paint -- as the iPod condition in miniature: music that alters rather than captures reality, now dial-up-able for workouts ('Eye of the Tiger'), bus rides, and grocery runs. Through Heidegger he argues the iPod is calculative thinking incarnate, annihilating the time, silence, and solitude meditative thinking requires (the shower as last refuge), and deepening technological homelessness by flattening every place into whatever soundtrack we choose -- the Rhine dammed into a 'gigantic gasoline station,' the iPod pushing us 'pretty far down' in Plato's Cave, its very possibility prepared by Descartes's thinking thing. Yet his wife's yoga instructor chanting on a Bronx bus shows the iPod can also open meditative space, so what Heidegger demands is not Luddism but Gelassenheit, a free relationship to technology.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 19 "Youth and the Image" — Hickey argues the iPod is the 'iCon of a generation' because it is a Baudrillardian simulacrum of youth: like the Gulf War consumed as CNN fireworks or reality TV's fabricated 'real,' Apple's silhouette ads sell faceless dancers whose entire identity is the white device -- a 'symbolic cyborgism' read through Donna Haraway. The vernacular of iPodding, podcasting, and downloading forms what he calls, with Wittgenstein, a language game woven into the actions of the 'now' that authorizes this youthful, tech-savvy identity as natural, while the ads' imagery works like Platonic shadows in the caves of our desire. Still, citing Giddens's structure-agency negotiation and DeCerteau's consumer tactic of re-appropriating everyday images, he insists we are not brainwashed: we can switch off, refuse, or remake the images that 'tell us who we are.'
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 6 "Ex Astris, Scientia GEORGE A REISCH" — The editors' introduction takes Starfleet Academy's motto 'Ex Astris, Scientia' as its frame: Picard handing cadet Wesley Crusher a book by William James shows officers need philosophy, not just ship operations, and the starry-heavens motif runs from Thales and Plato's cave through Kant's 'moral law within and starry heavens above.' It surveys the book's Trek dilemmas (Picard and Dathon's alien language, Data's emotion chip, Khan's vengeance, Riker's Q powers) as 2,500-year-old philosophical problems, and argues Trek's optimism — Picard's 'the acquisition of wealth is no longer the driving force' — restates Aristotle's claim that all humans by nature desire to know. Like philosophy from Socrates on, Trek is presented as 'an entertaining, edifying preparation' for living by one's ideals, a life-education primer sealed with Roddenberry's advice to 'slip in a heavy idea or two.'
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 26 "Must I Repeat Myself" — Seng maps Dorothy's journey onto Plato's cave allegory: Kansas is the cave of shadows, Oz the painful ascent into light, and the crucial shared point is Socrates' demand that the freed prisoner go back down into the cave, which explains why Dorothy, once enlightened, must return to gray Kansas bearing self-knowledge. He surveys the film adaptations (1910, Semon's 1925, Eshbaugh's 1933, Fleming's 1939, Return to Oz, and The Wiz) to show that each rewrites 'home' as self-knowledge rather than a place, culminating in Glinda's The Wiz speech, 'If we know ourselves, we're always home, anywhere.' Kierkegaard's contrast between recollection and repetition then sorts the homecomings: Baum's Dorothy wills recollection of what was lost, while Diana Ross's Dorothy wills repetition, holding to her self amid change, which Seng says Kierkegaard regards as the equivalent of faith.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 20 "Colbert Is (the Tragedy and Comedy of) America, and So Are We" — Ralkowski asks whether Colbert is America's Socrates, comparing Colbert's ironic interviews (Caitlin Flanagan on feminism, Harvey Mansfield on manliness, Howard Dean's superdelegates, the ABC Stephanopoulos-Gibson debate) to Socrates' definitional refutations of Euthyphro and the Athenian elite. Like Socrates in Plato's cave allegory, Colbert is a shadow on the wall undermining truthiness from within, yet both fail: audiences laugh, guests collect the campaign-donation 'Colbert Bump,' and nothing changes, making America the self-satisfied one who is ignorant of its ignorance. Through Nehamas's contrast of Socratic and Platonic irony and the Symposium's demand that the greatest work read as both tragedy and comedy, the chapter concludes Colbert may be America's Plato — condemning and laughing at us like a Sisyphean liberator who knows we will not leave the cave.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 7 "4" — Four 'Phase One' essays. Dyer reads Mark Millar's Wanted through Plato's cave: Wesley Gibson escapes a pathetic life like the freed prisoner, but like Adolf Eichmann (via Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem) he murders his conscience, so the Fraternity's consequence-free world leaves him numb and unable to value anything - a descent deeper into the cave, ending in the banality of evil. Novy explains why henchmen betray using Aristotle's utility/pleasure/complete friendship distinction (Big Cheese, Henchmen Muenster and Feta): supervillain gangs are Hobbesian pirate crews with no enforcer, so a modus vivendi of self-interest collapses under interrogation and only Machiavellian fear secures loyalty. Foresman applies Goodman and Rawls's reflective equilibrium as a 'cheat' to rank Apocalypse, Magneto, Luthor, the Joker, and Bizarro, concluding the 'best of the worst' is judged on evil ends (or evil means, as with Magneto) and even on glorious failure. Arinder and Milton, in a staged descent-into-madness frame, diagnose mad science in Victor Frankenstein and Dr. Doom as science that denies value-laden theory choice - impossible because data underdetermine theory - breeding the hubris that dehumanizes the scientist.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 26 "You Can Discover More about a Person in an Hour of Play than in a Year of" — Tim Christopher weighs pseudonymity — multiple persistent in-game identities — against responsibility for what those identities do, opening with his accidental first 'honorable kill' and the real-world extremes of a stabbing over loud WoW and a murder over a borrowed virtual sword. Using the Tae Kwon Do mat as a model of the sacred gamespace, he argues that WoW's persistent world and anonymity invite misbehavior, yet since no one is kind in WoW out of fear of punishment, any kindness there may be kindness for its own sake — an honest character may be a better person than an honest player. Plato's Allegory of the Cave is his master image: players see only shadows (avatars) of the real people behind them and must remember the world outside the cave.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 33 "Cyborg Goddess" — Reads Ghost in the Shell as Donna Haraway's 'Cyborg Manifesto' made flesh: Major Kusanagi is built not born, has no sexuality or romance, and relegates male partners to sidekicks, enacting Haraway's post-gender cyborg that breaks the dualisms binding women to body, nature, and reproduction. The chapter traces the 'ghost' back through Koestler to Ryle's mockery of Descartes's mind-body dualism, reads the genderless, net-born Puppet Master as the Singularity of transhumanist philosophy, and interprets the Major–Puppet Master fusion — urged to 'come out of the shadows and into the light' in an explicit Plato's-cave gesture — as a posthuman, techno-spiritual 'Cyborg Goddess' that renders both gender and humanity obsolete.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 11 "He’s Got to Make His Own Mistakes" — Cole pits Plato against Walter Benjamin to vindicate the imitation of Rush: Plato's cave makes art a shadow twice removed from the Forms, and on that view a perfect copy is impossible and every cover degraded, while Peart's 'Limelight' calls the stage a 'gilded cage' that is 'just a prettified cave' yet, with 'we are merely players' (via Shakespeare), makes performing the way out rather than deeper in. Benjamin's translator essay, with its 'language forest' echo and 'pure language', shows how Rush's cover of 'Summertime Blues' on Feedback layers Blue Cheer and the Who into one perception, and how live variations of 'Witch Hunt' and the premature chord of 'Turn the Page' let error overtake and become the new original. The chapter exceeds Aristotle's principle of non-contradiction in 'pure language', where original, copy, and fan covers (Rock Band failures, the South Park 'Lil' Rush' flub, Rick Mercer's drum lesson) are fragments of one greater vessel, so errors are portals of discovery.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 12 "Guardian Training" — Roger Travis argues Plato would welcome Halo as guardian training: mimesis is really 'playing epic pretend,' and Halo, like the Homeric epics that were Athens' textbooks, trains players in a way of life. Plato's Republic Book 10 critique—the painted bed as copy of a copy of the Form of Bed—warns that playing Master Chief could let appetite rule, yet the Laws' admission that the ideal city's politeia is itself a mimesis turns the tables: the Republic is its own training simulation of philosophic pretend. Re-imagining the cave as prisoners tied to couches playing Super Mario Bros, he argues Halo's dutiful NPCs and waking-to-duty player (literal cryo-wakeups in Combat Evolved and Halo 3) make it philosophy in Plato's own sense, with Aristotle's catharsis leavening the verdict.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 7 "Happy Ending" — Wenmackers uses Inception's dream levels and its ambiguous spinning-top ending as a guided tour of skeptical philosophy, diagramming how dreams-within-dreams, kicks, Limbo and exponentially dilated dream time work. She tests the totem against Zhuangzi's butterfly and lucid-dreaming reality checks, then runs Plato's Cave and the eternal Forms, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine to ask whether Cobb's world - or ours - is real. Her conclusion is Socratic ('know that you know nothing'): subjective reality feels equally real on every level and the top level can never be known. She even argues that dream-time dilation means Cobb should not kill himself while in doubt, since real time barely passes, so a little philosophy rescues the happy ending.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 10 "The Power of Choice" — Rennett tests Cobb's choice to leave Limbo against Nozick's three reasons for refusing the experience machine: we want to actually do things (raise his real children, not loving projections), to be a certain kind of person (Yusuf's dream-den addicts are 'indeterminate blobs'), and to touch something deeper than a man-made world. He then recruits Berkeley's esse est percipi to explain Mal's sincerity - she perceives Limbo and remembers it, so for her it is real - and argues that shared dreams differ from private dreams and the experience machine because they leave waking traces, like Mal's bullet in Arthur's leg. The chapter ends by making reality a matter of choice: like the cave prisoners of Plato's allegory, each character believes a world, and Cobb's ignoring of the top is his choice to live in the world with his children.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 22 "The Kick—Back to ‘Reality’" — The authors read the film in descending layers: reality as an ideology of touch and unreliable sensory experience, framed by Descartes's wax thought experiment and dream argument, with the kick explained through Hume's account of belief as custom and the totems as broken game pieces marking broken people (Mal's choice of the dream echoing prisoners returning to Plato's cave). The heist is then read as an existentialist drama where Cobb's 'downwards is the only way forwards' rejects the passive waiting of Beckett's Waiting for Godot and the pharmacy dreamers, with Jaspers's analysis of solitude making Limbo a hell of lonely regret that only an encounter with another can end. The chapter then argues the film is reflexively about movies (the crew mirrors a film crew, the Penrose stairs expose cinema's flat illusions, crosscutting manufactures time) before ending on Descartes's unresolved doubt about whether the final reality deserves our trust.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 94 "Chapter 14 - Trauma of the Real" — Introduces Paul Livingston's part with Dick's confession that reading Plato in college convinced him the empirical world was not truly real, then retells the cave of Republic Book VII in detail: prisoners bound since birth watching shadows of puppets cast by a fire. The cave becomes the frame for Dick's fiction — the 'reality' our percept-systems report is a show of images, and the philosophical quest is the prisoner's turn toward the archetypal reality behind the scenes.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 95 "Breakthrough to the Real" — Details the disorienting breakthrough in which characters learn that they themselves are fakes: Rachael's distress at her implanted memories ('How can it not know what it is?'), Deckard's paper unicorn in the director's cut confirming his own replicant status, and Ragle Gumm's soft-drink stand dissolving into a slip of paper reading 'SOFT-DRINK STAND' in Time Out of Joint. Each case maps onto the freed cave prisoner's discovery, and the disorientation is pressed onto the viewer: how can I be sure my own life and memories are not a fabrication?
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 97 "Procession of Dummies" — Uses Dick's 1972 one-sentence definition ('Reality is that which, when you stop believing in it, doesn't go away') and his claim that absolute reality reveals itself only when our space-time categories collapse, arguing the definition fits Lacan's Real better than Plato's picture of looking away from the cave wall. Through Žižek's readings, Ragle Gumm's objects being literally replaced by their symbolic labels and Deckard's replicant recognition as a 'total loss of the hero's symbolic identity' show the traumatic Real first appearing precisely where symbolically constituted reality fails.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 48 "Out of the Cave" — Traces the light-versus-darkness metaphor tradition from Plato's cave and Socrates' unexamined life through medieval 'illumination' and the Enlightenment to St. Paul's glass darkly, then lets Nietzsche ('shadow is as needful as light') and Derrida's deconstruction of presence/absence oppositions overturn it. The Stones do the same work in song: 'Just as every cop is a criminal, and all the sinners saints' in 'Sympathy for the Devil,' with 'Here Comes the Sun' overturned by 'Paint It Black' and 'Let It Be' by 'Let It Bleed.'
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 15 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Rood unpacks Klosterman's 'This Is Emo' thesis that no woman will ever satisfy him: women love Lloyd Dobler rather than John Cusack, and everyone measures real relationships against Hollywood fake love (Coldplay songs, the Woody Allen Personality Type) until, as Klosterman puts it, real people actively trying to live like fake people are no less fake. He reads this through Sartre's cafe waiter and Butler's gender performativity to argue identity is learned performance, and through Plato's cave updated to a reclining-seat movie theater where we mistake projected shadows for real love. The deepest diagnosis is Baudrillard's hyperreal, glossed as a social-constructionist rerun of Kant's Copernican revolution, against which Rood's own objection lands: Klosterman covertly assumes a pure unmediated self that cannot exist, so the answer to fake love is not escape from mediation but self-control within it.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 12 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Richard Rosenbaum asks how Gaiman's gods, abstract concepts made flesh who live or die by human belief, could exist, starting from Plato's Forms (Odin as personified battle-wisdom, Media as media) and the Allegory of the Cave, which gives new meaning to a protagonist literally named Shadow. Finding Forms too independent to need believers, he upgrades the metaphysics with Leibniz's Monadology: if everything, bodies and ideas alike, is composed of perception-bearing monads, then shared beliefs can agglomerate, 'level up' into a soul, and become a living god walking around America.
