Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness, panprotopsychism, and the claim that information has interdependent physical and phenomenal aspects supply the final mechanism, so collective belief realized phenomenally must become physically embodied, in contrast to the dualism of Descartes that made mind-body interaction mysterious.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 23 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Rick Mayock stops a fictional Jeopardy! clock to apply Plato's divided line: most contestants, like the cave prisoners rewarded for predicting shadow sequences, trade in doxa - conjecture (eikasia) and belief (pistis) - while the Meno's slave boy shows how Socratic questioning ties true opinions down into knowledge. Winning requires only dianoia, hypothetical reasoning from hypotheses and definitions, never noesis, the dialectic that ascends to the eternal Forms; the Phaedo's example of perfect 'equality' shows why the 'Aha!' of recognition is re-cognition by an immortal soul already acquainted with the Forms. Watson, lacking such a soul, can clear a buzz threshold but never have an Aha! moment - it is Daedalus's statue, lifelike but sure to run away from the truth unless tied down.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 32 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Reitter reads the sewer mutants - banished underground, surviving on what the surface flushes, as in 'The Mutants Are Revolting' where Leela is deported without trial the moment Fry reveals she is not an alien - as philosophy's Other, illuminated by Plato's cave (surface dwellers fear and demonize what they have never seen) and Beauvoir's The Second Sex (Leela passes as an acceptable alien until exposed as a mutant). Mrs. Astor's United Mutant Scholarship Fund film, with its 'noble sewer mutants... uh, people, I guess,' is read alongside Said's Orientalism and racist charity imagery as a third face of Othering. The chapter then adds folklore theory: the mutants are a folk group with their own urban legends (alligators in the sewer, and the 'sub-urban legend' of sub-mutants), ballads like 'The Legend of El Chupanibre,' and freegan-style recycling ethics - a counterculture whose difference the dominant universe-view casts as monstrosity.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 24 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Arp uses King Worm's dream-within-dreams to pose the perception-reality problem: distinguishing perceiver, perceptions, and perceived, he maps the triad onto Plato's allegory of the cave, then contrasts epistemological and metaphysical realism (the fallen tree fort still makes sound waves unheard; Pythagoras discovered rather than invented his theorem) with idealism and antirealism, whose dead end is solipsism—Lumpy Space Princess locked in a private movie theater of perceptions. Hume's picture of the mind as a theater of successive perceptions and Berkeley's Hylas-and-Philonous worry that we are trapped inside perceptual reality give the skeptical threat its force. The chapter sides with Jake—'You gotta focus on what's real, man'—while conceding that after 'King Worm' Finn and Jake can never be certain they escaped the hypnotism.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 23 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Wolfe asks what makes Stoker's mustachioed Count, Lugosi's, Dell Comics' science-hero Dracula, The Electric Company's malt-drinker, Blade's Drake, and Hotel Transylvania's overprotective dad all 'Dracula'. Plato's theory of Forms promises a shared ideal essence, but comparing particulars (origins from Vlad Tepes to Judas Iscariot, blood-drinking vs vanilla malts) finds no common thread, his 'Allegory of Dracula's Dungeon' recasts the cave to suggest Dracula may be only a shadow of some other Form like 'the undead', and the Republic's condemnation of art as imitation of imitation implies a fictional character may have no Form at all. Wolfe's own answer: the ideal Dracula is an outsider, an aristocrat, and a feeder on others, with everything else up for grabs.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 7 "Choose!" — The editor's introduction argues that Roth's series does not just contain philosophy but actually does it, proposing hypotheses about virtue, social order, evil, and forgiveness and testing them for consistency. It casts Tris as a Socratic figure who retraces the Allegory of the Cave: she starts 'chained' inside the cave of Chicago's faction system, climbs out to discover the faction life is a lie, and is tortured and eventually killed for the truth she tries to bring back, just as the cave-dwellers would kill the returning prisoner. The introduction closes by insisting the series is really about choice - that wisdom, unlike knowledge, must be lived, that self-reflection and even self-doubt are the hallmark of the wise, and that when life offers no options, like Tris and the factionless, you have to create your own.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 10 "2. Peculiar!" — Ketcham reads the faction system as the Bureau's behavioral-correction experiment after a eugenics disaster, and compares the Bureau to the Tuskegee syphilis study: subjects who never gave informed consent, were denied treatment, and were treated as expendable because 'the experiment must continue at all costs.' He maps W.E.B. Du Bois's 'twoness' - double consciousness - onto Tris, who thrives in Dauntless yet belongs to no faction, and onto Tobias, whose identity collapses when he learns he tests as merely Dauntless. Closing with Gramsci, he argues Chicagoans have bought into the oppressor's story about genes and factions, so they need an organic intellectual to lead them out of the cave, and proposes Freire's praxis as the unfinished sequel.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 25 "14. You Have to Be Good before You Can Be Smart" — The Bocks argue that the Erudite pairing of ignorance with knowledge is morally loaded: with Linda Zagzebski's and James Montmarquet's virtue epistemology, high-end knowledge requires intellectual virtues like the courage to test your beliefs publicly, so you really do have to be good before you can be smart. The Erudite manifesto's curriculum omits the humanities that open the mind, and its IQ-only leadership test fails Plato's requirement that philosopher kings love wisdom itself and, like the freed cave-prisoner, return to benefit society - which is why Jeanine, driven by lust for power and concealment of the truth beyond the fence, is 'a poor example of a philosopher king.' Both the Erudite and the Bureau reason as consequentialists ('Knowledge is power... power to do good') to justify slaughtering Abnegation and experimenting on unconsenting Chicagoans, when the pursuit of knowledge must be constrained by informed consent and human dignity.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 36 "19. The Playful Thought Experiments of Louis C.K" — Argues Louis's bits function as playful philosophical thought experiments in Ernst Mach's and Tamar Gendler's sense: the white-people time machine, sitting 'in a chair in the sky,' and the 'Indians' naming skit are make-believe scenarios that reconfigure our frames and draw out truths we already knew, just as Plato's cave and Nathan's parable to King David do. Pairing the cognitive 'Aha!' with the mirthful 'Ha-ha' (via Hurley, Dennett, and Adams's Inside Jokes) makes his humor an error-detection reward loop that takes audiences to upsetting territory and makes them glad they went.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 35 "22. Unmasking the World and Its Heroes" — Mapping both heroes onto Plato's cave, the chapter argues each must first see past shadows: Bruce abandons revenge on Joe Chill to change Gotham's whole idea of justice, its citizens climb out of apathy when the Dark Knight ferries refuse the Joker's detonators, and Clark needs Jonathan Kent ('It's not to score touchdowns') and Jor-El to learn what his powers are for. Socrates' Apology supplies the mask's rationale - the just man must lead a private life to survive, so secret identities protect loved ones from Luthor's kryptonite stabbing and FBI kidnapping - and Plato's warning that the returned cave-escapee would be killed explains why the heroes must lead by hope rather than force. The oracle story's lesson that wisdom is knowing that you know nothing grounds the close: anyone can be a hero, as Batman tells Gordon about the coat around a boy's shoulders.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 19 "9. Pierce’s Republic" — Randall Jensen maps the Society onto Plato's Republic (Brown has said he drew on it): the Color hierarchy parallels the Myth of the Metals' gold, silver, and bronze souls, the Golds' scorn for Demokracy echoes Book VIII's account of degeneration into tyranny, and Leto's 'We are Plato's philosopher kings' claims a mantle Plato himself doubted anyone could ever fill. Darrow's story is the Allegory of the Cave run from below—a Helldiver literally raised in a mine, blinded by surface light, whose return to a shrunken, grayer garden mirrors the philosopher's homecoming—except Plato never imagined the prisoner carved into a Gold. The Noble Lie survives as the terraforming myth fed to lowReds while the surface has been habitable for centuries, and the chapter weighs Darrow's gospel ('we choose who we are') against Plato's caveats: you can choose who to be only within limits, if you are lucky and greatly helped.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 21 "9. Varys’s Riddle—Where Does Power Come From" — Iuliano uses Varys's riddle - king, priest, and rich man each bidding the same sellsword to kill the others - and 'power resides where men believe it resides' to stage a contest between John Austin's command theory of law (sovereign orders backed by force) and H.L.A. Hart's The Concept of Law, where authority rests on social acceptance. Cersei's 'power is power' scene with Littlefinger shows obedience that is mere coercion - Hart's gunman, being obliged rather than obligated - making the Lannisters gunmen writ large; the Hound's walkout on Joffrey exposes the illusion collapsing, and Plato's cave explains why Westerosi smallfolk prefer the comforting shadow to the truth that would free them.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 9 "1. Juliana in Plato’s Cave" — Dennis Weiss argues the Amazon series is really about television and screened images: Juliana screening the Grasshopper newsreel in her basement replays Plato's Cave, except that the projected images, not the 'real' world of Nazi America, are what offer her 'a way out.' Following her from transfixed belief to doubt (calling the final film 'a nightmare' and choosing to trust Joe over the reel), and reading the show's media surfaces (Nazi commercials, 'Edelweiss,' the Riefenstahl comparison, Tagomi's cross-world vision), the chapter uses media thinkers like McLuhan, Meyrowitz, and Don Ihde to describe learning to see with 'compound vision' in a placeless, image-saturated culture.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 20 "10. Hendrix Out of the Cave" — Scores 'Are You Experienced?' and 'Purple Haze' against the Allegory of the Cave: the backwards guitar and reversed cymbals are the painful, clumsy ascent from shadows toward the Form of the Good, with Hendrix as the initiator who must first drag the prisoner violently and then gently — 'come on across to me... we'll hold hands.' 'Purple Haze' becomes the midway delirium between cave and sun ('don't know if I'm coming up or down,' 'scuse me while I kiss the sky'), and the chapter concludes that the psychedelia is philosophical — consciousness opened by liberation from received opinion, not by LSD — warning the freed prisoner not to remain a pale copy of Plato or Hendrix.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 29 "17. The Cry of Love" — Reads Hendrix as a romantic idealist on a Platonic-Neoplatonic arc: 'Room Full of Mirrors' shatters the cave wall and its projections toward The One, whose presence is pursued through eros with the veiled Beloved of Plotinus — the semi-divine feminine of 'Little Wing,' 'One Rainy Wish,' and 'Angel.' Hegel's Zeitgeist and world-spirit then frame the planned First Rays of the New Rising Sun as music meant to carry humanity's collective evolution, with Hendrix as Hegel's 'spiritual workman' and self-described messenger ('I am only a messenger and you are a Sheep in the process of evolution').
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 13 "3. Gestational Totalitarianism" — Kolb reads Gilead through Arendt's The Human Condition and The Origins of Totalitarianism: when reproduction becomes the means of production, women's labor is targeted, forcing fertile women into Animal laborans status as 'national resources' while denying them the creative freedom of Homo faber. She traces the polis/oikos split from Aristotle through Puritan capitalism to show Gilead overcorrecting into Aunt Lydia's 'freedom from'—totalitarian control of birth legitimized by the Rachel and Bilhah story and a Pauline creation story. The chapter ends with the transitional generation's forgetting (Offred's cave-delusion with Nick evoking Plato's Allegory of the Cave, the Holocaust documentarian 'thinking about how not to think') and Ofglen's bomb, arguing that thoughtfulness and literacy, not violence, are the only hopes against totalitarianism.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 32 "18. Smoke and Mirrors in Gilead" — St. Martin structures Gilead with Plato's Republic: Thrasymachus's 'justice is the advantage of the stronger' is the Sons of Jacob's operating principle (the Wall, the cattle prods, 'removing the damaged ones' from the ambassador's reception), and Glaucon's claim that it is best to do injustice without paying the penalty describes Commanders, while Handmaids suffer injustice with no revenge. She maps Socrates's division of labor onto Gilead's color-coded castes (Handmaids, Marthas, Aunts, Wives), then uses Glaucon's mocking 'city of sows' to show Gilead betraying even that model, since the regime exists to keep men powerful rather than babies alive—baby Charlotte recovers only when reunited with Janine. Serena's awakening after Eden's execution is an emergence from the cave, and the chapter closes that justice must be chosen for its own sake, with biases checked.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 13 "3. The M. Night Sh-imulation Hypothesis" — The chapter runs Bostrom's simulation argument against 'M. Night Shaym-Aliens!', where the Zigerions trap Rick in simulations-within-simulations to steal his concentrated dark matter formula, and reads their cheap shortcuts ('My man!' NPCs, human music, Jerry's Appley award) as the glitches and shadow-people Bostrom predicts. It presses the epistemological problem that any evidence for the simulation equally supports its denial, an underdetermination that devastates the theory, and traces the lineage of 'the real world isn't real' through Plato's summoners and allegory of the cave, Descartes's dream doubt, and Paley's design analogy (Morty as the beautiful machine), ending with the microverse battery of 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy': this is the universe we live in, so get used to it.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 8 "On Philosophers and Drag Queens" — The editors' introduction argues that Drag Race is an unexplored philosophical playground because it builds on marginalized black and Latinx queer herstory and because RuPaul, whose creed of love and self-improvement makes her a philosopher in her own right, has made the show her magnum opus. It invokes Plato's cave to explain why philosophers crave the 'untucked' version of everything RuPaul shows on stage. Its central move is a virtue-ethics reading of the show's judging: Ru's demand that a queen first be fierce, and through fierceness achieve charisma, uniqueness, nerve and talent, mirrors Aristotle's question of what makes a good person, with fierceness playing the role phronesis plays in securing the other virtues. Comparing queens like Silky Nutmeg Ganache, Jinkx Monsoon, Yara Sofia and Sharon Needles, it poses 'what makes a good drag queen?' as a live philosophical problem.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 24 "The Danger of Thinking “Science Is Whatever We Want It to Be”; or, the" — Barkman reads the 30 Rock cast as prisoners who prefer delusion, using Plato's allegory of the cave and the Upanishadic scheme of samsara, karma, maya, and moksha, in which Atman is realized as one with Brahman, as twin diagnoses. Drew's 'bubble' of good looks, Liz's false memory of being a harmless nerd in 'Reunion' and her belief she can have it all, Jack's pride about his terrible sketch ideas, Kenneth's unexamined dogma ('I can't handle the truth!'), Jenna's age-hiding, and Tracy's white myths about diabetes and Colorado all illustrate ignorance of reality that costs happiness. The Hindu-Platonic lesson is that knowledge of reality, not Dr. Spaceman's 'science is whatever we want it to be', is the route to happiness, because ignorance is not bliss.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 19 "Perceptions Are Fine, but Dull Reality Is Still Better" — Distinguishes perceiver, perceptions, and perceived external objects to ask whether Alice, or anyone, can get beyond her perceptions to a mind-independent world, entering through Robert Arp's own painkiller hallucination of stones that were really Jell-O. The chapter sets epistemological idealism and metaphysical antirealism (the movie-theater-in-the-mind picture, traced to Plato's cave and Berkeley's suggestion that we are trapped inside perceptual reality) against the epistemological and metaphysical realism it finds in Alice and Carroll: fossilized ferns, dodo birds, and the Pythagorean theorem are discovered rather than invented, and at story's end everything rightly changes 'to dull reality'.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 9 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Tests Socrates' claim (via Plato's Apology and the Myth of the Cave) that the self-examined life is the happiest against the Bluths: Michael, the one who escapes the cave in the pilot (learning at the boat party that his father is a criminal and he was never getting partnership), turns out chronically miserable, while self-deceivers Gob, Lindsay, and Tobias are mostly content. The chapter concludes that Bertrand Russell's Conquest of Happiness fits better: reflection makes sinners (George Michael's self-loathing over Maeby), narcissists (Michael's need to be seen as good), and megalomaniacs (Kitty) unhappy, so the unexamined life is not a huge mistake, though moderate examination still pays.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 9 "Just How Dark are the Dark Avengers" — Donovan and Richardson read Osborn's Dark Avengers through the Republic: Osborn is a modern Thrasymachus for whom justice is merely the advantage of the stronger, managing Bullseye's murder of Lindy and the team's image exactly as Glaucon's ring of Gyges predicts—villains like Moonstone, Daken, and Venom appearing good while doing injustice. Captain America, who tells Stark 'who made you the moral compass of us?', embodies the Socratic belief in a justice beyond human advantage, backed by the Forms and the allegory of the cave. Ms. Marvel, Noh-Varr, and Ares choose being just over appearing just, defecting or dying (Ares torn in half during the Siege) rather than serve Osborn's fraud.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 25 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Drawing on fieldwork and surveys at the 2011 Tampa Lebowski Fest, Dufort and Lemire-Cadieux use Kierkegaard's Concept of Irony and indirect communication — contrasted with Plato's condemnation of mimesis in the cave and Aristotle's rehabiliation of it — to explain why Achievers who dress as rugs, memorize lines, and re-watch the film dozens of times find no objective message to decode. Kierkegaardian irony leaves each receiver to dig out a subjective existential truth through self-reflection and repetition, so that fans repeating the Dude's message become part of the irony itself: being an 'Achiever' achieves nothing objective and something deeply personal ('don't pee on other people's rugs').
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 10 "Pretending to Talk about It" — Travis claims everyone misses the point of both Plato's cave and BioShock, and reads the post-assassination self-destruct sequence as the game's cave moment: though you may roam Ryan's office shooting walls ('active inaction', like the escaped prisoner contemplating the form of the Good), the sequence will not resolve until you insert the item, exposing 'a man chooses, a slave obeys' as hollow. The harvest-versus-save equivalence (Tenenbaum's gifts cancel the ADAM loss) is likewise a stroke of genius, not a flaw, because it shows in-game 'ethical choices' are as meaningless as the prisoners' shadow-naming contests. Since both cave and game run on mimesis, playing pretend, the way forward is to 'pretend to talk about it': performing philosophy through play as Plato's dialogues stage Socrates.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 38 "25 Fear of a Black Museum Black Existentialism" — Charles Peterson reads the museum scene through Black existentialism and Africana phenomenology: colonial museums freeze African existence in an 'archaic amber' of aesthetic purity, and Killmonger's reclaiming of the mask and questioning of the curator perform a truth-telling that breaks the museum's performance of dominance. Du Bois's double-consciousness explains Killmonger's inseparable Wakandan-and-American two-ness (extended to Nakia and the War Dogs), while Paget Henry's contrast of the DuBoisian subject who oscillates between two 'We's' with Hegel's recognition-seeking subject explains why T'Chaka chooses Wakanda and abandons N'Jobu, and Plato's cave frames Killmonger as dragging Wakanda's comfortable council toward truths 'some truths are too much to bear.' The chapter concludes that Killmonger fails because wearing the mask he embraced negrification rather than shedding it, whereas T'Challa matures from a Hegelian into a DuBoisian subject by opening Wakanda to the world.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 29 "Happily Ever After" — The chapter maps the Beast's enchanted castle onto Plato's cave: the spellbound household, dimming in the decaying West Wing, are prisoners whose human capacities are suppressed, and Belle is the missing cause that breaks the chains Plato never explains. Using Diotima's teaching from the Symposium that beauty compels love, it reads the Beast's curse as externalizing his indifference to beauty, so that the staircase dance, his freeing of Belle, and Belle's 'I love you' trace Diotima's ladder from outward to inward beauty — the light that releases the prisoner.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Dal Barco maps Lucy's arc in the Amazon series onto Plato's cave stage by stage: Vault 33's fake sky, curated history lessons, and Vault-Tec-managed information are the shadow-puppet show, her first step into the sun after Hank's abduction by Moldaver is the freed prisoner's blinding ascent, the hidden hospital vault tempts her (and Maximus, who wants to stay) like the return to the cave, and the truth - her father helped orchestrate the nuclear war, her mother is now a ghoul - plays the role the sun and the Good play in the Republic. Plato's claim that only the educated philosopher who has seen beyond the cave should govern (Republic 496a, 519a-d) explains why Lucy, unlike the frightened Norm or the tempted Maximus, goes back out into the wastes: she is becoming the philosopher-ruler whose hard-won knowledge enables Moldaver to restore power to the surface and begin a civilization no longer built on shadows. The chapter answers its own question - yes, it was worth leaving the vault for the truth.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 28 "Notes" — Tracing Fallout's own censorship history — the GURPS licensing cancellation threat, the invisibility of child NPCs in the European release, the moral panic after Columbine — the chapter asks whether it is wrong to simulate evil, framing the issue with Morgan Luck's gamer's dilemma. Plato's cave and the Forms ground the 'media impacts morals' worry: games are shadows of shadows whose simulated vice accumulates 'a large evil in our souls', which is also why Lucy's Vault upbringing leaves her underprepared for the wasteland's emotions. Against this, Aristotle's catharsis and Schulzke's claim that Fallout trains phronesis support depicting wrongdoing as practice for moral judgment, so the chapter concludes the right wrongs to depict are whichever maximize the simulation of choice, with Braun's player-controlled Tranquility Lane simulation as the dystopian counter-model.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 106 "Going Mental" — Opens the Just in Your Head? essay by taking Dumbledore's reply to Harry (of course it is happening inside your head, but why should that mean it is not real?) as a live metaphysical and epistemological question about appearance versus reality, noting that even A. J. Ayer dismissed his own near-death experience as hallucination. It retells Plato's cave allegory and reads Harry and Dumbledore's descent into the creepy cave in Half-Blood Prince, plus Harry's worry that the King's Cross dialogue was just a shadow on the wall, as a modern image of prisoners mistaking appearances for reality.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 6 "introd.xhtml" — The editors' introduction frames The Hobbit as Plato's Allegory of the Cave retold 'there and back again': like the freed prisoner, Bilbo leaves his comfortable hole, has his eyes opened by a frightening journey, and returns 'queer' to neighbors who cannot accept that life offers more than order and routine. It lists the book's guiding questions - whether adventures are worth missing dinner, whether food and song outrank gold, whether powerful technology can be trusted or must be destroyed, and the duties of friends - as the essays' shared agenda.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 7 "Happy Ending" — Wenmackers uses the spinning-top ending — Cobb reuniting with his children while the top wobbles off-screen — to run a guided tour of skeptical philosophy through the film's dream mechanics (totems, kicks, Limbo, exponential dream-time). She diagrams and compares Zhuangzi's butterfly, Plato's Cave and theory of Forms, Socratic know-that-you-know-nothing, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine, arguing that Inception does to its viewers what Plato's Cave was meant to do: make us doubt our own level of reality, so that Nolan himself performs inception on the audience. Her resolution is subjectivist — from inside, every level feels equally real, so like Cobb you should turn away from the top and make the best of wherever you are, which even rescues the happy ending since dream-time runs faster than real time.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 10 "The Power of Choice" — Rennett stages Ariadne's 'who would want to be stuck in a dream for ten years?' against Nozick's experience machine: Nozick's three reasons for staying unplugged (doing rather than merely experiencing, being a determinate person, contact with a reality deeper than human construction) map onto Cobb's reasons for leaving Limbo — he wants to actually raise his children, be a good father, and love children who can love him back rather than projections. Against Nozick, the chapter enlists Berkeley's esse est percipi to explain Mal's choice: a perceived world is real, and Inception's shared dreams pass Berkeley's intersubjective test in ways private dreams cannot (Cobb apologizes to Arthur for being shot; dream acts carry waking consequences). It concludes that reality becomes what we choose to believe — Cobb's final refusal to watch the top, like the cave prisoners rejecting release, is the power of choice.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 22 "The Kick—Back to ‘Reality’" — Richardson and McWilliams read Inception as an 'existential heist film' by diving through four layers of meaning. At the layer of reality they use Descartes's dream skepticism and wax argument, Hume on belief as custom and cause-effect, and Goffman on being shocked between frames to argue the film makes touch — the fall that wakes, pain ('pain is in the mind'), Saito's wrong-textured polyester carpet, the broken totems (Cobb's top, Arthur's loaded die, Ariadne's holed chess piece) — the only semi-trustworthy sense, while Mal, who locks her totem in the dollhouse safe and picks the dream, replays the cave prisoner who chooses the shadows. The car-chase layer ('downwards is the only way forwards'), Saito's 'old man filled with regrets' limbo, and the pharmacy dreamers who 'come to be woken up' are read through existentialism (Beckett's Waiting for Godot, Jaspers on loneliness and nothingness) and Peirce on the continuity of consciousness, with Cobb cast as the ideological existentialist who chooses action and reality where Cypher in The Matrix and Vanilla Sky's David face the same choice. The chapter then treats the film's reflexivity — the team as screenwriter/producer/director, the Escher-esque Penrose stairs, cross-cut dream time à la Peckinpah — as a lesson in film theory, and finally reaches phenomenology: Cobb's angry projection of Mal shows the dream world displaying his subjective meanings, against Arthur's calm, orderly hotel mindscape.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 23 "12 The Shadow Realities of Indiana Jones" — Matthew Crippen and Matthew Dixon read the franchise's caves through Plato's allegory: in Crusade, stand-ins for God (the Cross of Coronado, the Grail, with the decoy chalices as shadows of a representation) appear underground, while Indy's self-realizations with his father occur at sunlit cave mouths, inching from shadow toward the Good. They fuse this with newer, active accounts of truth — James's 'truth happens to an idea' realized in the leap from the lion's head, Dewey on poetry as revelation, and Heidegger's aletheia as unconcealment — while Nietzsche's critique shows Platonic fictions can still be life-enhancing. The father and son 'shadow' one another (with Oedipal overtones through Elsa) until Henry Sr. relinquishes the Grail to save 'Indiana,' his path out of the cave.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 18 "Over Four Thousand Words to Say No" — Spanakos asks whether Stark's assembling, disassembling, and reassembling of the Avengers and his unseen-hand management of Civil War make him the Republic's philosopher guardian, and answers no. Tony fits the surface profile — the gold-souled ruler of Socrates' noble lie, the elite training, indifference to money, the technê of an MIT engineer who envisions the future — but he lacks epistêmê: he never climbs from the cave's shadows to grasp the forms of justice and the good, and his appetites (womanizing in The Ultimates, 'Demon in a Bottle') show a soul where passion is not ruled by reason. His puppet mastery is reactive problem-solving guided by each situation, not philosophy, and reading him as a philosopher king is our failure to read The Republic meditatively, as Ortega y Gasset urged.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 31 "Live From New York" — Perez sorts SNL's realities using Plato's cave and Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation: Kate McKinnon's Bieber Calvin Klein ad is a first-phase reflection, Natalie Portman's raps a masking second phase, Ferrell's commodified Bush a second-order copy, and Maya Rudolph's Donatella Versace a third-phase simulacrum with no reality behind it that Versace herself protested. The Church Lady's 2016 Update appearance and the Palin-meets-Palin and Hillary-at-the-bar sketches show characters substituting for the real, while the May 2018 cold open where the real Stormy Daniels tells Baldwin's Trump 'a storm's a-comin',' live-tweeted by @nbcsnl, achieves Baudrillard's hyperreality where fiction and reality are abolished as distinct. Studio 8H becomes a Plato's cave viewers willingly re-enter each Saturday to glimpse the real through simulation.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 37 "Notes" — Uses the holodeck as a working model for the ancient claim that everyday reality is appearance: Plato's cave shadows, maya in Hindu and Buddhist thought, and Bostrom's simulation argument (his ancestor simulations mirrored in Data and Geordi's endless Holmes holoprograms) converge with quantum "holographic universe" speculation to suggest our universe may be a cosmic holoprogram with limit conditions like light speed as processing boundaries. Moriarty seizing the Enterprise in "Ship in a Bottle", Vic Fontaine, and the EMH dramatize self-aware programs confronting their code, and the chapter argues our "free will" may be similarly bounded - Data-as-Holmes must stay in character, and Picard "can't transcend the script" any more than his NPCs can. Picard's closing admission that our reality may be "an elaborate simulation running inside a little device" delivers the skeptical upshot, alongside the ethical question of whether self-aware holograms deserve rights.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 35 "22. Unmasking the World and Its Heroes" — Claims the Superman-vs-Batman debate misses the point: both heroes are cave-escapers who must first see beyond appearances—Bruce renouncing vengeance on Joe Chill and then shaking Gotham from apathy (the ferries refusing the Joker's detonators), Clark learning from Jonathan and Jor-El that his powers are not for touchdowns but to lead humanity out by example. Masks serve the Socratic warning of the Apology that the just man must act privately to survive—Jonathan Kent dies keeping Clark's secret—yet risk becoming their own trap, from Smallville's Red Kryptonite ring to Batman's sonar surveillance that Lucius Fox calls too much power for one person. The chapter closes on Socratic ignorance and Man of Steel's genesis chambers: a hero, like Socrates, knows his wisdom is worth nothing, and anyone who chooses can be one.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Johnson-Moxley tests Perez's lasso of truth - which makes people face truths about themselves, like being dragged from Plato's cave - against four ethical touchstones: Kantian duty (truth-telling as a perfect duty, respect for autonomy), utilitarianism, virtue ethics, and care ethics. Cases drive the argument: binding Ares so he sees his apocalypse annihilates what he rules, freeing Vanessa from Dr. Psycho's false memories only with her permission, and lashing two warlords into 'twins of pain' to end bloodshed. She concludes via Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity that compelling truth is justified only to restore someone's rational self-direction, never paternalistically, with Gandhi's satyagraha ('truth-force') as the model of active, compassionate truth-telling.
- **X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse**, ch. 7 "X-Men and Philosophy" — This block finishes Davis's essay (Xavier's 'good nonsense' rules vs. Magneto/Dennett/Hobbes evolutionary morality) then runs several more. Robichaud's 'Professor X Wants You' weighs whether Storm should join the X-Men or Brotherhood using Nozick's experience machine (Rogue vs. 'Eugor') for well-being and Dworkin's civil-disobedience tiers for when violent resistance is permissible. Housel's 'X-Women' reads Jean Grey, Rachel Summers, Scarlet Witch, Storm, Mystique, Rogue, and Kitty through Sartre's 'existence precedes essence,' bad faith, Ortega's project, and Baudrillard. McWilliams uses Singer's speciesism and human-rights declarations to ask if mutants deserve moral consideration and whether torture/experimentation on them can be justified. Darowski reads Deadpool's fourth-wall breaks as postmodern metafiction raising Plato's-cave ontological questions.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 24 "Hoop Dreams, Blacktop Realities" — Bernard Jackson Jr. argues that basketball is an institution where black manhood is socially constructed (leaning on Naomi Zack's feminist point that gender identity is imposed by social designation), and that love among black players is essential to that construction while toughness is equivocal - the 'soft' label stuck to the gentlemanly David Robinson even as the Pistons walked off without congratulating the Bulls. Reading the documentary Hoop Dreams, he shows Arthur Agee and William Gates being used as commodities by recruiters, Coach Pingatore, and family expectations, invoking Marx on exploitation and 'use value' (Spike Lee's Nike-camp speech) and Kant's demand that persons be treated as ends, never merely as means. He likens William Gates's return to Chicago's Cabrini-Green as a minister to Plato's enlightened prisoner going back down into the cave.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy and Non-Philosophy of Potato Salad" — Scribner uses Ginsberg's 'Howl for Carl Solomon'—and Solomon's throwing potato salad at a Dada lecture—to ask whether the Beats' performative acts count as philosophy at all. He argues philosophy is constituted by self-contestation, its relation to a 'non-philosophy' of madness and raw experience, reading Solomon's silence and Ginsberg's poetic mediation through Foucault's 'Madness and Civilization' and Derrida's rebuttal in 'Cogito and the History of Madness.' Ginsberg-to-Solomon is made analogous to philosophy-to-the-Beats: a betraying translator who nonetheless must give the mute event voice, grounded in Plato's failure to banish the poets from the Republic.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 8 "Raising Arizona as an American Comedy" — Gilmore reads Raising Arizona as a classical comedy (bad-beginning-to-good-ending) about the American 'optative mood' of self-creation, using Hi McDunnough's outlaw-to-family arc and his name-as-height-metaphor to figure Emerson's aspirational American self. He deploys Plato's two kinds of cave-laughter to distinguish the film's 'tender,' welcoming comedy (Hi and Ed, Gale and Evelle) from mocking ridicule, and frames Hi's need to abandon outlaw identity via Heidegger's Augenblick and Badiou's 'event' sparked in Ed's mug-shot flash. Nietzsche on dreams-as-origin-of-metaphysics grounds the film's dream/reality tension, and Hi's over-identification with the outlaw universal is glossed as Sartrean bad faith.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 21 "From “Impassioned Morality” to “Bloodless Agnosticism” A Philosophy of David Cronenberg through the Burroughs" — Jones Irwin analyzes Cronenberg's adaptations of Burroughs's Naked Lunch and Ballard's Crash, arguing that while all three share an aesthetic of body horror and a Nietzschean perspectivist experimentalism, Burroughs and Ballard hold an 'impassioned moralism' (Crash as cautionary tale, Marcuse's one-dimensional man, an ethics of complicity and responsibility) that Cronenberg replaces with 'bloodless agnosticism.' Cronenberg aestheticizes Burroughs's wife-killing and reads Crash literally, using Plato's appearance/reality (cave) distinction to show he strips out the sociopolitical and moral frame the writers intended.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 18 "7. The Art of Playing Along with Dancing Little People" — Luzecky and Elsby argue that Twin Peaks is genuine art because, against Plato's condemnation of mimetic art as confusing copies to be exiled, it fulfills Aristotle's Poetics: art's essential function is dramatic reversal, surprising and transfixing us (Dougie's absurd casino win, the dancing Man from Another Place). Drawing on Gadamer's 'Spiel' (play/game) and Ingarden's schematized, incomplete artworks, they contend the work of art exists only as an ongoing rhythmic 'to and fro' between image and viewer—so we complete the Red Room scene by participating in it, moving it from potentiality to actuality.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 22 "The Matrix, the Cave, and the Cogito" — Conard argues that The Matrix alludes to Plato's cave (the pod-bound humans mistaking the program for reality, Neo's painful ascent) and to Descartes' dream argument and evil-genius doubt (the singular consciousness generating the Matrix), but betrays their spirit by rejecting transcendence and the a priori. Because the film is 'Christianity without God'—Neo can only remake the shadow-world of the Matrix, not touch ultimate reality—it grounds knowledge in a subjective gut feeling ('being the One is just like being in love') rather than Descartes' intellectual intuition of God or Plato's rational grasp of the Forms, leaving no answer to whether life outside the Matrix is itself another illusion.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 28 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — McFarland reads Soderbergh's Solaris as a meditation on recollection, recognition, and repetition, grounding it in Platonic recollection (the Phaedo, the cave, and the Symposium's love as desire) and Augustine's Confessions, where memory strains toward an elusive beloved-as-God, the 'cruel miracle' of present absence. When Solaris materializes Rheya, Chris Kelvin first jettisons the 'bad copy' but then, tempted by Snow, embraces Deleuze's endless degraded repetition of copies to erase his guilt over her suicide. Against this, Gibarian voices a Kierkegaardian call (Repetition, Either/Or) that there are 'only choices'; McFarland faults Chris, like Odysseus choosing Kalypso's island, for choosing the deathless eternal present over the human world of forward-moving choice.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — LaRocca argues Burton's 'Ed Wood' (1994) is a metafilm that, via Baudrillard's simulacra and Plato's cave/dialectic, transforms how we watch Wood's 'bad' films. He casts Wood as a cave-dweller and naive literalist who conflates representation with reality ('film equals life,' 'that was perfect'), while Burton is the Platonic dialectician who posits two worlds and provokes thought. He distinguishes two interacting metafilm types—biographical simulacrum (a hyperreal Ed Wood with no original, per Baudrillard's 'artificial resurrection') and mimetic reenactment (loyal remakes of Wood's films)—so that Martin Landau's Lugosi and Parker-as-Fuller's non-acting reveal the emotional 'affect without illusion' latent in Wood's work.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 21 "The Work of Art in the Age of Embedded Journalism Fiction versus Depiction in Zero Dark Thirty" — Evans argues that Kathryn Bigelow's Zero Dark Thirty fails morally and epistemically because its immersive 'boots-on-the-ground' realism traps the viewer inside Maya's single point of view, so we can never see the CIA torture program's lunacy the way an outside witness would. Drawing on Wittgenstein's Tractatus claim that the subject is a limit of the world (the eye that cannot see itself), she shows how the film effaces its own privileged viewpoint to pass off a partial view as impartial reality. Against this she sets a Platonic point that genuine reality is glimpsed only through fiction that ironically juxtaposes contrasting viewpoints, citing scenes like the SEALs' banter and Maya's final weeping where the film briefly becomes true art. The 'depiction is not endorsement' defense collapses because the narrative logic still credits torture with finding bin Laden.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 18 "16_LaRocca_Chapter_015.html" — Dan Geva re-reads Dziga Vertov's The Man with the Movie Camera as a coherent philosophy of documentary he calls 'praxis' or 'cine-seeing the invisible,' distilling ten 'diktats' (Unplayed Cinema, Life-Caught-Unawares, the interval theory of montage, etc.). He argues Vertov, like Plato, Marx, Nietzsche and Freud, privileges hidden depths over surface appearance, and reads the dialectical move from 'film fact' to 'film thing' as a Hegelian synthesis rather than a paradox. Crucially he aligns Vertov's Kino-Eye truth with Heidegger's notion of truth as aletheia (a partial unconcealment) rather than correspondence, tying the camera's revelation of the invisible to Heidegger's meditation on technology and seeing.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 22 "12. A Cave of His Own Making" — Golden reinterprets Plato's Allegory of the Cave to argue Chuck enslaves himself in a 'cave of his own making'—his hypochondriacal electromagnetic hypersensitivity—to keep Jimmy accountable and to exact vengeance for Jimmy's unpunished childhood thefts. Using Aristotle's De Anima psychology and the function argument, he places Chuck's imagination (phantasia) below reason: Chuck retains the rationality to serve clients like Mesa Verde and to detect Jimmy's document fraud, but sinks below the Golden Mean into the vices of meanness (short of kindness) and cowardice (short of courage) toward his brother. He adds Kierkegaard's Repetition: Chuck is stuck in backward-looking 'recollection' of vengeance and cannot make the forward, committed 'repetition' of simply being Jimmy's brother.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 9 "2. Socrates’s City and Seldon’s Galaxy" — Goldberg maps Plato's Republic onto Asimov's Foundation Trilogy: Socrates's three-class city (Guardians, Auxiliaries, Producers ruling by knowledge of the Forms) parallels Seldon's galaxy (Second Foundationers, First Foundationers, and everyone else, ruling by the abstract mathematics of psychohistory), with the tyrannical Thrasymachus paralleling the Mule. He shows the Prime Radiant functions as Plato's Allegory of the Cave, and that both Guardians and Second Foundationers govern through 'noble lies' (the metals myth; the Encyclopedia sham and the Second Foundation's fake destruction), then questions whether those lies are truly noble given doubts about objective truth.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 9 "1. A Man for All Seasonings" — Shaffer uses Brillat-Savarin's distinction between direct and reflective taste and Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' to argue gastronomic expertise is only the acquired ability to describe tastes richly, not a superior sense. He then casts Bourdain as a culinary Socrates who, like the freed prisoner in Plato's allegory of the cave, returns to lead provincial eaters out of the darkness of narrow experience toward cultural tolerance.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 14 "Stephen King and the Art of Horror" — Littmann stages a mock trial of King's horror using classical aesthetics: Plato prosecutes, condemning fiction as lies that misrepresent gods, afterlife, and paternal authority (Carrie's mother, Jack Torrance, the Loser's Club disobeying elders) and corrupt morals through spectacle. Aristotle counters that Poetics-style poetry is 'more philosophical than history' and that tragedy's catharsis purges pity and fear, which King echoes in Danse Macabre's claim that horror lances real terrors via Danny Torrance, Paul Sheldon, and Louis Creed. Hume's 'Of Tragedy' explains why we enjoy fictional suffering (Pennywise, Annie Wilkes) we would hate in life; Littmann finally revises Hume, arguing horror's pleasure is the spur to imagination rather than mere appreciation of artistic skill.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 27 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Baron, a new father, weighs whether to let his son Maxwell consume violent popular media (from Halloween to SpongeBob, Grand Theft Auto, and Schindler's List) by testing three hypotheses. He uses Plato's Republic warning against exposing the young to stories they can't interpret for the 'causal hypothesis'; Aristotle's Poetics on learning pleasure from painful images for the 'edification hypothesis'; and Aristotle's account of tragic catharsis (homeopathic vs allopathic purging) for the 'catharsis hypothesis,' concluding that context matters more than ratings and that fathers watching alongside their children are the decisive influence.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 8 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Porn journalist Gram Ponante's foreword riffs on Plato's Allegory of the Cave, casting porn as the shadows on the cave wall and the viewer as both prisoner and fire. He argues that unlike the manipulated prisoners, the porn viewer actively projects meaning onto a deliberately thin surface — forgiving porn its fake 'MILF' and 'schoolgirl' labels because the images 'become what we want them to be.' Porn is 'a cave to be filled in,' and adding plot or realism only breaks the fantasy by making the images less available for projection.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 31 "GARDENING" — Cotton reads the grower image in Plato's Phaedrus—the wise gardener who sows seed in proper soil for a slow harvest rather than the frivolous 'gardens of Adonis'—as Plato's model of philosophical education as natural growth. The educator plants logoi (discourse) in a 'proper soul,' where it must be cultivated by the learner's own reflection and eventually reproduces itself in others, against Thrasymachus's vessel model of pouring knowledge in. She connects this to the Republic's cave, the Apology's gadfly, and the Symposium/Theaetetus images of pregnancy and midwifery, then argues Plato's own aporetic, contradiction-laden dialogues and the corpus as a whole act as the wise grower, teaching readers to become 'gardeners of their own souls.'
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 25 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Thorsby reads 'getting high' as a rupture of ordinary, unreflective consciousness and asks why cannabis use grows fastest in the affluent capitalist West. He pairs Plato's allegory of the cave—ordinary consciousness as prisoners mistaking shadows for reality—with Marx's account of alienation and commodity fetishism, in which workers are estranged from the products of their labor and see value as inhering in things rather than in human labor. Drawing on Fromm's 'having vs. being,' he argues that cannabis offers a momentary escape from and critique of this alienated consciousness, though it cannot cure it.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 18 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Ken Burak describes teaching yoga in his philosophy class — a 'three wheels' exercise moving from the true self behind our masks to the Upanishadic identity of Atman and Brahman ('Thou Art That') — to give students embodied access to the universal/particular problem. He reads Western philosophy from Plato's Phaedo (Socrates seeking death as liberation of soul from body) through Descartes' doubt as a 2500-year practice of pratyahara (sense-withdrawal), one limb mistaken for the whole journey, and asks what asana and this long retreat could each bring the other.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 30 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — J. Lenore Wright reads the Quest through the Western journey-narrative, both outward (Plato's climb out of the cave, Augustine's conversion) and inward (Descartes's methodological doubt turning toward the cogito). Frodo's leaving the Shire and freely accepting the Ring dramatizes the outward journey and the limits of freedom, while the wounding-and-healing of Sam, Merry, and Pippin marks an existential journey toward the Nietzschean charge to 'become who you are.' Wright contrasts the Yea-saying hobbits, transformed into resilient masters, with Nay-sayers Smeagol and Saruman locked in inauthentic self-pity, and argues Tolkien's ordinary pilgrims show that binding oneself to the good makes ordinary life extraordinary.
- **Comics as Philosophy**, ch. 6 "index" — This composite chapter argues philosophy through several comics. Jeremy Barris pairs Plato's dialogues with Amazing Spider-Man, using the allegory of the cave, the Forms, and Platonic love/eros to show that Spider-Man's bodily beauty, awkwardness, and self-trivializing irony draw readers toward goodness the way Plato says lust for beautiful bodies leads the soul upward to truth. Iain Thomson reads Moore and Gibbons's Watchmen as a 'deconstruction of the hero,' running Rorschach, Ozymandias and Dr. Manhattan through Nietzsche's Ubermensch and 'do not throw away the hero in your soul,' Heidegger's authentic 'choosing one's hero' and the uncanny, Kierkegaard's knight of faith, and Baudrillard's idea that an extreme realization destroys its own idea. Laura and Paul Canis read Daniel Clowes's Ghost World through Sartre's existentialism: Enid's post-high-school 'three o'clock' limbo enacts thrownness, abandonment, radical freedom and the flight from it into bad faith, contrasting Enid's authentic self-creation with Rebecca's settled conformity. Aldo Regalado's essay treats Tarzan, Superman, Captain America and the Black Panther as responses to modernity and race.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 6 "NOTES" — William Irwin's introduction argues philosophy must engage popular culture rather than fear it as Plato feared Homer and the poets. He invokes Plato's allegory of the cave to make the case that the philosopher who has left the cave must return and 'learn to see the shadows again'—use The Simpsons, The Matrix and Seinfeld as the vernacular through which prisoners can be led out—and answers Adorno-style culture-industry worries that mass entertainment is mere opiate. He closes by echoing Aristotle's serious treatment of the popular art (tragedy) of his day as warrant for treating today's pop culture philosophically.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 9 "NOTES" — Irwin asks 'what is popular culture?', rejecting Noel Carroll's 'mass art' accessibility criterion (using the Sex Pistols, Slipknot and the Beatles as counterexamples of inaccessible-yet-popular art) and Walter Benjamin's aura/mechanical-reproduction account, settling on popular culture as 'artifacts and subjects of mass interest and appreciation.' He rebuts Adorno's and Zizek's culture-industry charge that pop culture (e.g. The Matrix, The X-Files) ideologically ensnares audiences, and again deploys Plato's cave and the returning prisoner—citing Socrates meeting interlocutors where they are—to justify using pop culture as a bridge to philosophy while warning against 'abuse' (studying pop culture as philosophy).
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 4 "2. Twilight Zone as Philosophy 101" — Marinucci uses The Twilight Zone as a triple introduction to philosophy, the show, and the handbook, arguing that philosophy is defined not by necessary-and-sufficient conditions but by Wittgensteinian family resemblance and salient features (curiosity, depth, abstraction, controversy) learned through MacIntyre-style immersion in a practice. She reads episodes as thought experiments: the amnesiac astronaut in 'Where Is Everybody?' and living-doll/robot episodes echo Plato's cave and Descartes's Method of Doubt about appearance versus reality, Nagel's 'what is it like to be a bat?' frames the problem of other minds, and episodes like 'The Shelter' and 'It's a Good Life' dramatize the tension between egoism and altruism and social conformity, including feminist gaslighting in 'Twenty Two.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 44 "41. Blade Runner as Philosophy What Does It Mean to Be Human" — Shanahan argues Blade Runner is philosophical despite Ridley Scott's denial, using the replicants (Roy Batty, Rachael, Leon) as defamiliarizing 'mirrors' for the human condition. He shows the Nexus-6 replicants satisfy Descartes' two criteria for a thinking soul (linguistic flexibility, novel problem-solving) while human characters like Deckard prove as cold and empathy-deficient as the machines, collapsing the human/replicant distinction the Voight-Kampff test presumes. He then reads Rachael's implanted memories through Locke's memory theory of personal identity, Roy's 'tears in rain' death through Epicurean worries about finitude, and frames the whole via Plato's Cave line 'they are like us' — the replicants model our own concerns with memory, death, and the meaning of a temporally bounded life.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 51 "48. The Matrix as Philosophy Understanding Knowledge, Belief, Choice, and Reality" — Perez reads the Matrix trilogy as a sustained argument about how choosing what to believe and 'know' shapes the reality we live in. He opens with Descartes' dream problem and cogito, contrasting Descartes' foundationalism with Rorty's anti-foundationalism to explain Cypher's choice to reject reality for the Matrix's certitude, and uses Searle's brute vs. institutional facts (the cookies, the steak, 'there is no spoon') to show social reality is constructed. Against the fatalism of the Oracle, Architect, and Merovingian, he argues nearly every character makes free choices, and resolves the tension via Hume's compatibilism — liberty requires necessity, and choices gain meaning only in response to causality — while noting agent-causation objections (Reid, O'Connor, Rowe) that make Neo's 'Because I choose to' significant. Gettier's justified-true-belief critique and Plato's Cave frame the knowledge and enlightenment themes.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 68 "64. George Carlin as Philosopher It’s All Bullshit. Is It Bad for Ya" — Engels reads Carlin's insistence that 'it's all bullshit, and it's bad for ya' as a defense of truth over comforting illusion, mapping his bits onto Plato's Allegory of the Cave (Carlin dragging audiences up from shadows like 'prostitution is immoral' or 'the American Dream' to expose deeper essences), Nozick's Experience Machine (Carlin's sun-worship chosen because it is real, not a pleasing fiction), and Clifford/Beauvoir on the ethics of belief and the 'serious world.' Bits on rights, the sanctity of life, homelessness/'houselessness,' and 'proud to be an American' show Carlin arguing that false beliefs breed complacency and harm, so there are moral reasons to prefer truth.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 83 "78. The Witness as Philosophy How Knowledge Is Constructed" — Cuddy asks what epistemology Blow built into The Witness's frustrating puzzles and its windmill videos (Burke, Feynman, Moriarty, Spira, Gangaji). He rejects the sophistic/Protagorean 'knowledge depends on the observer' reading (most puzzles have objective, inductive-and-deductive solutions, e.g. the yellow-glass bunker) and the strict scientific realism of the Burke video defended by Putnam's no-miracles argument. Using Plato's cave and the aporia of Socrates' Meno (the puzzle's 'ah-ha' epiphanies), and Kuhn's incommensurable paradigm shifts (the game's 'hard left turns' forcing players to overhaul their understanding), he concludes the game argues that true knowledge is attainable, individually and collectively, though reached by a nonlinear, paradigm-shifting route rather than pure realism or relativism.

### Deontology

Deontology is the family of ethical theories holding that the rightness of an action depends on its conformity to moral duties or rules, not merely on its consequences. Its most influential form is Immanuel Kant's, which grounds duty in the categorical imperative and insists that persons be treated as ends in themselves and never merely as means. Deontology responds to the intuition that some acts, such as lying or killing the innocent, are wrong even when they would produce good results, thereby setting itself against consequentialist views that judge actions solely by their outcomes.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 32 "The Moral Sophistication of Buffy the Vampire Slayer" — Greene and Yuen reconstruct seven moral principles from Buffy's conduct — slay those who typically harm humans, never harm humans (Faith's accidental killing of the Mayor's henchman), spare the defenseless and the controllable (chip'd Spike, caged Oz) — and note that blackmailing Spike and roughing up demons would violate Kant's Formula of Humanity if the patients were rational persons, exposing the show's human/non-human moral hierarchy and its animal-rights parallel. 'The Gift' dramatizes deontology (Buffy refuses to kill Ben) against consequentialism (Giles strangles him), and the chapter ranks BtVS above after-school-special, culpable-clown, and faux-realist TV morality because it supports its stands by appeal to general moral principles while keeping Aristotelian habituation and real-life moral complexity in view.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 33 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Bassham and Bagget observe that amid the film's unscriptural brutality Jesus never resists — he stops Peter's sword, heals Malchus's ear, and climbs back up for a second scourging — and ask whether this nonviolence can be rationally grounded without theological premises. They reject four classic readings of 'resist not evil' (Catholic counels-of-perfection, Schweitzer's interim ethics, Luther's penitential ethic, Tolstoy's absolute pacifism, noting Jesus himself used force against the money-changers) in favor of a hyperbole-plus-implicit-qualifier reading; then they show act utilitarianism licenses atrocities, rule utilitarianism at best yields an unpalatable absolute pacifism, and Kantian single-principle deontology preserves a right of self-defense Jesus's ethic calls us to lay aside — closing with a 'character model' of the Passion (duty vs freedom vs character) on which nonviolence is becoming the kind of person for whom violence is no longer an option, justified ultimately only by the cross.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 93 "I’m a Lover, Not a Fighter!" — Turns to Kantian nonconsequentialism: persons must be treated as ends in themselves and never merely as means, from duty rather than consequences, with negative duties (not harming) stronger than positive duties (aiding) — so Reed Richards may not kill a pedestrian for organs to heal Doctor Doom's victims, though a utilitarian would require it. Since neither becoming Spider-Man nor refusing to violates any negative duty, being a superhero is supererogatory: 'with great power comes great responsibility' is at most a duty not to misuse power, and precisely because heroes don't have to do what they do — as Clark Kent's Superman II choice shows — their choosing it is what makes them praiseworthy.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 94 "I Fought the Law and the Law Won" — Argues that Batman's warrantless raids, intimidation and evidence-free arrests violate negative duties that bind everyone regardless of role, so producing good (the utilitarian reply) cannot justify them, and superpowers earn no legal exemptions that we would deny police. When Spider-Man evades NYPD warrants, the chapter applies Socrates' argument in Plato's Crito that citizens owe the law their obedience even when wrongly accused, though it concedes that keeping a secret identity safe from villains who would torture or kill loved ones can override the duty to submit, a move consistent with non-Kantian nonconsequentialism since Kant could not abide any lie.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 95 "But It’s Just a White Lie!" — Asks whether superheroes may deceive the people they love, testing Kant's absolute duty not to lie against resolvable conflicts of negative duties: Peter may deceive Aunt May only because telling her would seriously harm her. But the chapter rejects the paternalistic silence Clark keeps from Lois and Peter from MJ, arguing that assuming the women cannot keep secrets or would crumble under worry fails to treat them with the respect owed to persons, so superheroes owe their loved ones the truth about who they are.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 129 "Keeping Secrets" — Takes up the objection that secret identities require the deception superheroes condemn, and answers that skillful deception within a legitimate context — quarterback fakes, a painter's perspective tricks — is acceptable, while even a lie bad in itself can be morally right or obligatory when needed to prevent great harm to the innocent. So Spider-Man's secrecy about being Peter Parker is justified, even praiseworthy, because a slipped secret would hand his enemies leverage over Aunt May and his friends.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 20 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Tedesco dissects what the double-0 'license to kill' could actually mean, ruling out self-defense and mere on-the-job killing and concluding that Bond is a state-sanctioned assassin who earned his status through two assassinations in Casino Royale. He tests that status against Kant's categorical imperative - persons as ends in themselves, though Kant also defended capital punishment as respecting the murderer's choice - and against consequentialism, which vindicates Bond's elimination of Kananga but stumbles on the surgeon's organ-harvesting dilemma. Because ordinary morality mixes duty-based and consequence-based intuitions, the chapter leaves Bond's moral status genuinely open and links it to live policy debates on assassination and torture after 9/11, including Britain's Intelligence Services Act that leaves room for a real-life double-0 agent.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 28 "So, Case Closed – Right" — White asks why Batman never simply kills the Joker despite the graveyard he keeps filling, framing the question with Foot's and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant-surgeon variant. Utilitarianism says kill one to save many; deontology says the agent-relative 'do not kill' — but the Batman case differs from the classic dilemmas because the Joker himself endangers his victims, Batman cannot be certain he will kill again (the foggy-track variant), and killing him would amount to the Minority Report-style prepunishment of a crime not yet committed. White, a self-described strict deontologist, concedes the case is genuinely hard and leaves the means-versus-ends debate open.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 41 "It’s Not That Simple" — Donal O'Mathuna uses 24 to run the torture debate: the ticking bomb scenario (Syed Ali's nuclear bomb, Miles pressing to torture Audrey) dramatizes the utilitarian case for forward-looking interrogational torture, while Jack slicing off the Russian consul's finger and Morris's broken guilt show torture as a deontological violation that destroys character on both sides and usually fails to extract truth. Against the show's sanitized, banal presentation (Agent Burke as the "kindly torturer"), he sets Abu Ghraib, the systematic training of torturers, and the metastatic spread of torture programs once permitted. Fiction can open the ethical question, he concludes, but must not be mistaken for the reality of torture.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 30 "Walking the Tightrope" — Louis Melancon weighs the Fleet leadership's secrets and lies: Adama's 'blind squirrel' lie about Earth, classifying the fact that Cylons look human, Roslin's faked death of the baby Hera, and Tom Zarek's secret collaboration courts on New Caprica. Democratic duty is framed as a deontological obligation of transparency grounded in the governed's trust, while the leadership repeatedly defaults to consequentialist wartime exceptions. The chapter proposes a rule-of-thumb: secrecy is justified only to hide specific information from an external threat like the Cylons, never to protect the government from its own citizens, and each violation erodes the trust on which Colonial democracy's 'soul' depends.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 16 "“I’ve Never Been Good at Good-byes”" — Lee treats DS9's Cardassian Occupation as a case of transitional justice like post-Holocaust and post-apartheid reckonings, asking whether Odo, security chief on Terok Nor, was a collaborator. Applying Kant's deontology — the good will, both formulations of the categorical imperative, illustrated by Kai Opaka's Kendra Valley betrayal, Quark's smuggling in 'Little Green Men', and Sisko's fraud in 'In the Pale Moonlight' — he judges Odo's letting three innocent Bajorans die in 'Things Past' as negligence, but his years-long cover-up as using the victims merely as means to protect his reputation, and hence genuine collaboration, as was his neglect of duty under the Link's pull in 'Behind the Lines.' Kant's imperfect duty of beneficence then redeems Odo's final departure from Kira: returning to cure and educate the Founders in 'What You Leave Behind' is a moral duty owed to rational beings.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 32 "The Lesson and Legacy of Din, Nayru, and Farore" — Horn argues the three Triforce pieces are morally neutral: by Kant's Groundwork, only the good will that acts from duty (Link never rescues Zelda for a reward) is good without qualification, so courage, wisdom, and power can each serve evil, and the Triforce would have corrupted Zelda or Link too if fortune had dealt it otherwise. Plato's Ring of Gyges and the Glaucon-Socrates debate explain Ganondorf: he chose to lust for power, and his wealth, status, and fear-based honor are hollow because justice is good for its own sake and his soul is out of balance (which is why the Triforce split at his touch in Ocarina of Time). Aristotle's doctrine of the mean then defines proper use: Link's courage between cowardice and rashness (getting the map, compass, and weapon before the boss), Zelda's internalized prudence, and Ganondorf's power in insatiable excess.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 31 "As Nasty as I Wanna Be" — Greene asks whether Maguire's Elphaba is really wicked, first clearing away her reputation (she adopts the 'Wicked Witch' name because 'it liberates you from convention,' echoing Glaucon's challenge in the Republic about the just person with an unjust reputation and vice versa) and then her nature (the midwife-biting birth, green skin, and witchcraft establish no vampire-like evil essence, since Glinda and Nor are good witches). Following Hume's view that morality is not found in the world but in our assessments, he treats wickedness as a matter of performing actions we judge evil, and weighs Elphaba's life under both headings: good intentions with horrific outcomes (the bees that kill the chef, the icicle that kills Manek, Sarima's family executions) and bad intentions with none (her two failed attempts on Madame Morrible). The verdict is deliberately suspended: if she is wicked at all, it can only be through the consequences of her actions.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 40 "Lester’s Duties and Capabilities" — Maguire asks whether the Royals did wrong by trying to hit in the late innings of Jon Lester's May 2008 no-hitter, working through Kant's distinction between perfect duties (always binding—playing hard, honoring the codified rules) and imperfect duties (praiseworthy obligations that admit exceptions—respecting the unwritten convention against bunting for a hit in a blowout). Sympathy for Lester's cancer recovery must not enter the calculation, since Jim Abbott's 1993 no-hitter shows the duty must universalize; bunting would be 'bush league' rather than wrong, a lapse in imperfect duty. He extends the analysis to Francona's pitch counts and warns that wanting Ellsbury to bunt against a Yankees no-hitter would treat the pitcher as a mere means to fan pride.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 22 "World Death Rate Holding Steady At 100 Percent" — Dan Miori, a palliative-care physician assistant, uses Onion medical stories — 'Loved Ones Recall Local Man's Cowardly Battle With Cancer,' the 'Vehicular Manslaughter Doctor,' animal hoarder Tricia McCory's 'I'm A Diseased And Deformed Animal Lover,' and the Terry Schiavo American Voices — to survey how end-of-life decisions actually get made. He runs each dilemma through Mill's consequentialism, Kant's deontology, and Aristotle's virtue ethics (with Monty Python's Philosopher's Song as running gag), then through Beauchamp and Childress's four principles of medical ethics, showing that McCory's kindness to dying animals fails autonomy and nonmaleficence because kindness can be cruel. The chapter closes by restoring 'euthanasia' to its Greek meaning of 'good death,' arguing that accepting the 100 percent death rate means planning ahead with living wills and honest bad-news delivery rather than dying tube-filled in an ICU.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 23 "Allons-y into the Starry Heavens" — Smith reads the Doctor–Rose tragedy through Kantian deontology: shaped by Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's virtue ethics into a good will, both must still choose duty over inclination, so in 'Parting of the Ways' and the Battle of Canary Wharf in 'Doomsday' they each act from the categorical imperative — sacrificing their love to save humanity — because love, as Kant warns, impels partiality. Even in 'Journey's End' the Doctor sends Rose to Pete's World with the meta-crisis Doctor for the greater good, ending alone under Kant's starry heavens and the moral law within.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 26 "Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign" — Lewis defends the Cybermen: using the 'Genesis of the Daleks' dilemma he shows the Doctor reasons like a Kantian duty ethicist — refusing to kill innocent proto-Daleks whatever the consequences — rather than a utilitarian, and that performing bad actions does not make an agent evil. After the Mondas, Lumic, and Morrison origins establish that Cybermen seek to cure pain and death, he argues the Doctor's 'good to strive for but bad to achieve' argument in 'Age of Steel' is invalid, and that upgrading would be morally acceptable — an applied-ethics fix — if the Cybermen obtained informed consent and respected human autonomy instead of forcing conversions.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 23 "You Control Your Urges—They Do Not Control You" — Waller and McAlear first rebut the amoral reading: Dexter does feel (he sobs over Rita, loves Deb, misses Harry) and does control his urges through the Code, so morality applies to him, and the Dark Passenger is merely everyone's socially unacceptable desires - the very thing that gives rise to moral codes. They then test the three theories: Aristotelian virtue ethics mostly fails because murder admits no mean and Harry's Code teaches killer's skills rather than virtues (though its 'don't kill innocents' dispositions are genuine virtues); utilitarianism fails even in rule-utilitarian form - via the organ-harvesting doctor and Harry's own utilitarian guilt over Laura Moser's death - because Dexter kills because the Code requires it, not because it maximizes happiness. What fits is dark deontology: like Kant's argument that murderers consent to their own execution out of respect for their rationality, Dexter kills only killers, acts from duty rather than enjoyment, and treats 'don't get caught' as a condition for the possibility of his true imperative.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 25 "De-Deontologizing Dexter" — Sultan Ahmed argues Dexter is not really a Kantian deontologist: the urge to kill came first (the teenage animal killings, and his brother Rudy/Brian, who developed the same dark desire without Harry and rationalized it differently), and Harry's Code is a post-hoc rationalization built on top of that desire. Drawing on psychological research (Joshua Greene, Jonathan Haidt) that deontological judgment tends to be emotional rationalization rather than moral reasoning, he reads Dexter's killings as serving emotional needs - the need to control the helplessness of the shipping-container trauma and the Ernest Becker-style need to belong, seen in his bonding with Miguel, Rita, and the kids. Even Dexter's refusals to kill Ellen Wolf or the bound Tony Tucci are framed as feelings and standards, not a sense of moral duty.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 24 "Wrapping Up the Case" — Don Fallis organizes the whole canon as a casebook in the epistemology of deception: why characters deceive (concealing crimes like Dr. Roylott's speckled band, committing them like John Clay's Red-Headed League tunnel, Holmes's own smoke-rocket trick on Irene Adler and his faked death at the Reichenbach Falls), how they deceive (Bell and Whaley's hide-the-truth versus show-the-false, unpacked through disguises as masking, repackaging, dazzling, mimicking, inventing and decoying), and how deception is detected, by microexpressions avant la lettre or by inconsistency, as in 'The Problem of Thor Bridge'. Along the way he sorts lying from false implicature (Inspector Baynes's 'I didn't say so'), lies of omission and bald-faced lies, invokes Kant's absolute ban on lying and Augustine's taxonomy of lies, and asks whether Holmes's belief in Moriarty's web, where the absence of evidence counts as evidence, is rational inference or self-deception.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 24 "Psych and Philosophy" — Rocha argues Kant is not the absolutist of legend: in 'On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy' Kant denies only a right to lie - Gus could be held responsible if his lie to Shawn's pursuing murderer goes wrong - and in The Metaphysics of Morals Kant openly leaves questions like polite untruths unanswered, to be judged by agents in their concrete circumstances. The deeper ground is Kant's duty to oneself: lying shows disrespect for the honest communication through which social beings sharpen their rationality, and so 'throws away and annihilates' the liar's dignity, which is why Uncle Jack's gold-hunting lies in 'The Greatest Adventure in the History of Basic Cable' are beyond rescue.
