He weighs deontology (torture treats persons as mere means) and virtue ethics (it degrades torturers like Agent Burke) against the utilitarian case, and shows the show itself refutes the argument: torture didn't get Fayed's bombs, innocents like Audrey Raines get caught, torturers are ruined, and Shue himself recanted - so the sanitized ticking-bomb fantasy misrepresents real, degrading torture.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 24 "NOTES" — Becky Vartabedian uses W. D. Ross's agent-specific ethics of prima facie duties to evaluate Michael's betrayal at the dock. She lays out Ross's six duties—fidelity, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, noninjury—and argues Michael's role as Walt's father makes beneficence his 'actual duty,' overriding fidelity and noninjury to Jack, Kate, and Sawyer. Because overridden duties do not vanish, Michael incurs guilt and owes amends (he is also implicated in the deaths of Libby and Ana Lucia), which Ross calls the 'moral risk' of choosing between competing prima facie duties; Locke's refusal to push the button is read as a duty of self-improvement whose rightness still depends on the intervening facts.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 20 "Pragmatist Ethics with John Dewey, Horton, and the Lorax" — Alexander contrasts Dewey's reflective, character-centered ethics with utilitarianism and Kantian deontology using the Lorax and Horton. The Once-ler is cast as the shortsighted 'utilitarian' maximizing Thneed happiness while the Lorax, urging us to 'stop and think' about the whole ecosystem, is really a Deweyan practicing reflective morality and deliberation as 'dramatic rehearsal.' Horton's conscientious care for the Whos illustrates Dewey's 'Who Factor' and growth of character rather than cold rule-following, showing morality as the ongoing education of desire toward inclusive, shared ends.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 24 "MOTHERHOOD" — Kevin and Janet Elliott argue that letting infants 'cry it out' (as advocated by Ferber and Weissbluth) is ethically problematic because all three major ethical theories – utilitarianism, deontology, and virtue ethics – condemn causing a child extended distress absent overriding reasons, with virtue ethics' compassion making the strongest case. They rebut claims that the crying causes little suffering and that co-sleeping is unsafe or ruins parental sleep, concluding that co-sleeping (historically near-universal) is often the ethically preferable alternative while stressing that the right choice varies by family and child.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 12 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Dylan Ryder (a working porn star) and Dave Monroe argue that being a porn performer does not necessarily lower the prudential quality of one's life, against the common-sense view (fed by films like Boogie Nights) that porn stars are damaged, coerced, or degraded. They reject Aristotle's claim that virtue is necessary for eudaimonia and, citing Kant's deontology and utilitarianism as theories that sever welfare from morality, distinguish moral value from subjective wellbeing. Deploying the 'Happy Slave' thought experiment and Ron Amundson's disability-welfare research, they contend outsiders' pity reflects social stigma, not the performer's own first-personal welfare judgment.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 26 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Gavrielides argues that going along with the Santa custom (leaving cookies, filling stockings, providing 'evidence') genuinely is lying, but that it is not wrong. She tests three ethical frameworks: a Kantian deontological analysis (with the 'murderer at the door' case) makes the lie at best 'wrong but permissible,' failing to capture parents' intuition of innocence; a Millian utilitarian analysis reduces character to a mere tool for good action; only virtue ethics, grounded in Plato's Republic account of edifying storytelling and Aristotelian character formation, captures why Santa stories are good — they cultivate kindness, charity, and self-reflection, and the myth is self-destructing as children's critical thought naturally dismantles it.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 12 "Who is Who" — This chapter tests the Doctor's ethics against consequentialism and Kantian/Nagelian deontology, arguing both fail because his alien longevity and time-travelling relation to consequences resist algorithmic moral judgment ('School Reunion,' 'Attack of the Cybermen'). It proposes instead de Beauvoir's 'ethics of ambiguity' rooted in Romanticism and Sartrean radical freedom and bad faith (the student anecdote; Turlough refusing the Enlightenment diamond), casting the Doctor as a Promethean figure who liberates companions into risky self-perfection.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 28 "So, Case Closed – Right" — Mark White asks why Batman doesn't kill the Joker, using the question to contrast utilitarianism (kill one to save the Joker's future victims) with deontology (killing is wrong regardless of consequences), and Batman's own agent-centered refusal. He runs Foot and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant surgeon case, then modifies them: the Joker is the guilty one who created the danger, his future victims are uncertain, and killing him would be 'prepunishment' for crimes not yet committed. White, a self-described deontologist, concludes the case is genuinely hard and admits great good might have come from killing the Joker, using comics as thought experiments about killing to prevent future killing.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 29 "“Who watches the watchmen ”" — J. Robert Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as an apparent consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) who sacrifices millions of New Yorkers for the greater good, and Rorschach as an apparent deontologist ('I shall not compromise'), then argues neither is true to his stated theory. Utilitarianism is critiqued through Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ever ends' (the infinite future defeats the calculus) and its trouble grounding rights, while Rorschach's hypocritical, dichotomous, disrespect-for-persons stance is shown to be fascism, not Kant's categorical imperative (universalization and treating persons as ends). Loftis contends the deeper target is authoritarianism itself: the corrupt superheroes show that ethical theories are rationalizations of power, so no one should be entrusted with too much of it.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 41 "It’s Not That Simple" — O'Mathuna uses 24's Jack Bauer to stage the ethics of torture through the "ticking bomb" argument. He frames it with deontology (torture treats persons as mere means), utilitarianism (Shue's ticking-bomb calculus, Mike Novick's "a few may die to save millions"), and virtue ethics (what torture does to Jack and Agent Burke). Marshalling the UN Convention, evidence that torture usually fails (Jack endures Chinese torture; Fayed is tricked, not broken), and its spread to innocents like Audrey Raines, he concludes the sanitized fictional case misrepresents torture's real degradation.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 11 "9. The Handmaid’s Tale as Philosophy Autonomy and Reproductive Freedom" — Robison-Greene argues that Gilead's core wrong is denying women autonomy, reducing them from Kantian moral agents to moral patients — walking incubators. She uses Frankfurt's theory of personhood (second-order desires and volitions about what we care about) to show how Gilead dismantles a woman's will by restricting first-order options, language, and critical thinking, so Offred's Scrabble tiles and forbidden reading become acts of reclaimed autonomy. She situates the Sons of Jacob's 'feminine function' ideology in Plato's Republic classes, Aristotle's natural slaves and History of Animals, Aquinas's natural-law subordination of women, and Malebranche's brain-fiber claims, contrasting Beauvoir's complicity of women and framing forced reproduction as the deontology-versus-consequentialism clash over whether species survival could ever justify treating women as mere means.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 81 "76. The Last of Us as Moral Philosophy Teleological Particularism and Why Joel Is Not a Villain" — Horn takes The Last of Us as moral philosophy, arguing Joel is read as a villain only because players assume consequentialism or deontology. On Bentham/Mill's utilitarianism Joel fails to maximize utility by killing many to save Ellie; on Kant's categorical imperative his lying, stealing and killing are always impermissible. Horn instead defends 'teleological particularism' — an agent acts rightly when acting in conformity with a role, roles being socially constructed and variable — so Joel's role as Ellie's surrogate father (mirrored in his carrying her out as he carried Sarah, and the 'Future Days' lyric) obligates him to put her above humanity. On this view Joel's refusal to let the Fireflies kill Ellie, and his final lie, are morally permissible, not villainous.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 13 "4. The Good of the Doctor" — The chapter distinguishes aesthetic 'good' (taste, beauty of the Daleks) from ethical 'good,' then tests the Doctor against the major moral theories: utilitarianism (rejected when Sarah Jane urges exterminating the Daleks in 'Genesis of the Daleks'), Kantian duty ethics (the Doctor's 'never met anyone who wasn't important' and attempts to save Davros and the Master), virtue ethics (the Eleventh Doctor guarding Christmas in 'The Time of the Doctor'), and feminist care ethics. Concluding that none quite fits because the Doctor values non-rational beings and feels compassion, the author proposes the Doctor follows Wolterstorff's 'ethic of need'—justice as meeting the needs of all—consistent with 'getting in the thick of things' as a flâneur.

### Possible Worlds

Possible worlds are complete alternative ways things might have been, used in logic and metaphysics to analyze claims about necessity and possibility: a statement is necessary if it holds in all possible worlds and possible if it holds in at least one. David Lewis defended the striking doctrine of modal realism, on which these worlds are not mere abstractions or fictions but concrete realities as fully existent as our own, spatiotemporally isolated from us. Though few accept Lewis's full realism, possible-worlds talk has become an indispensable tool across philosophy of language, modality, and counterfactual reasoning.

- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 79 "So, Is Dumbledore Gay" — Gendler tests whether fictional truth works like historical truth and finds it fails: whereas a biographer discovers facts about the one actual world, a storyteller chooses among infinitely many imaginary worlds - David Lewis's point that 'every way that a world could possibly be is a way that some world is' - so storytelling mixes creation with discovery. She distinguishes the 'primary truths' stated on the Potter novels' 4,100 pages (discounting trivial inconsistencies like Percy's badge color and Moaning Myrtle's S-bend versus U-bend) from unstated 'secondary truths' like Hermione having ten fingers, rejects a maximal inclusiveness principle that would import every actual-world fact into the story, and closes with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics advice to seek only the exactness a subject allows.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 119 "The DC Comics Multiverse" — Recounts how DC resolved its Silver Age continuity mess: rather than treat Jay Garrick's adventures as a fiction-within-a-fiction, Flash #123 has Barry Allen cross into Earth-2 and meet Garrick — and one cannot meet a merely fictional character — so the multiverse is born. As alternative histories multiplied and heroes routinely world-hopped, the only correction strategy left was postulating yet another world, setting up 1985's Crisis.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 120 "Crisis on Infinite Earths The Story Unfolds" — Summarizes Crisis: Krona's forbidden experiment splits one universe into a multiverse plus an antimatter universe whose Anti-Monitor devours worlds; the Monitor self-sacrifices to pocket five Earths; heroes and villains travel to the dawn of time, where the Spectre's intervention leaves a single positive-matter universe. The aftermath — Superman of Earth-2 mourning a Lois who "never existed," three Supermen on one Earth — sets up the two metaphysical conjectures, time travel and multiverse, to be examined.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 122 "More Things in Heaven and Earth" — Surveys real multiverse arguments: the Everett-Wheeler many-worlds reading of quantum mechanics, fine-tuning explained by every possible initial condition existing somewhere rather than by God, and David Lewis's modal realism, on which every way the world could have been is a causally isolated world — it was possible to write a shorter chapter because in some world Hanley did. Tegmark's physics multiverses round out the menu before the question: does any of this fit Crisis?
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 123 "A Multiversity" — Rules out Lewis's modal realism for the DC multiverse (DC worlds interact; Lewis's are causally isolated) and standard branching many-worlds too, then proposes "hypertime," a second time dimension that makes sense of a traveler arriving in another timeline's "1984." Since Crisis speaks of the multiverse becoming one "at the dawn of time" — something that cannot happen in plain time or hypertime — Hanley posits a six-dimensional cosmos with "supertime" and superhistories.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 125 "Identity in Crisis" — Poses the persistence problem through Superman-1 and Superman-2: are they strictly identical? Perdurantism — persons as four-dimensional space-time worms made of temporal parts — makes them distinct worms with no parts in common, so Superman meeting his counterpart is no stranger than you meeting a friend; endurantism, with wholly present strict identity, could identify them across timelines but balks at the impossibility of Superman meeting himself.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 20 "Poker and Philosophy" — Northcott loses his first casino tournament to a fluky inside straight and mines the bad beat for philosophy of science: objective odds collapse into knowledge-relative probabilities (a card-tracking magician would assign different numbers to the very same draw), Laplacean determinism versus quantum chance bears on whether decision theory presupposes free will, and bad-beat counterfactuals — 'I'd have won the tournament but for that hand' — get David Lewis's possible-worlds closeness analysis and Hume's counterfactual account of causation, with no settled verdict. Even game theory cannot deliver a perfect system: a Nash-equilibrium strategy is only optimal against other optimal players, so the mindless all-in 'Stupidus' beats it. Conclusion: no can't-lose system exists, and poker will never be a game for robots.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 19 "Putting Together the Triforce" — Duncan and Gee study the Nintendo NSider forum threads where fans build Zelda timelines, showing that their marshaling of evidence (Ganon's trident, whether the Master Sword is 'legendary' because of an earlier hero or its sage creators, Hyrule's geography as a marker of time) mirrors scientific argumentation. Using Latour and Woolgar's Laboratory Life, they argue that what 'counts' as evidence, even down to excluding the BS Zelda and CD-i games as non-canon, is socially constructed within a community of practice, not value-free data. David Lewis's plurality of worlds supplies the metaphysics for the split-timeline debate after Ocarina of Time, and the chapter concludes that knowledge in general, in labs and in fandoms alike, is constructed through tools, discourse, and interaction.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 17 "The Loneliest Witch" — Auxier gives three theories of why water melts the Wicked Witch, one for each register of Oz: as dream (Bergson's account of dreams as memory explains the fire/water effect-swap), as Baum's fairytale (Susanne Langer's presentational symbols make dryness-wickedness versus water-as-life the tale's moral physics), and as Gregory Maguire's possible world, where the philosophy of language takes over. He narrates Frege's sense/reference distinction—mayor of the Munchkins—to explain how fiction can support truth and falsity ('Dorothy melts the Witch' true, 'Dorothy tried to melt her' false), then deploys Putnam's Twin Earth thought experiment: 'water' in Oz is XYZ while Kansas water is H2O, so Elphaba's word 'water' does not mean what Dorothy's does, and meanings just aren't in the head. Elphaba—the unique being straddling two worlds, killed by H2O she cannot name and terrified by dreams of oceans—is offered as an even stronger argument for Putnam's semantic externalism than Twin Earth's molecule-for-molecule doppelgangers.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 20 "Getting to Oz" — Auxier uses the Wizard's demand that Dorothy kill the Witch to split 'ought' from 'can'—ethics from the metaphysics and logic of possibility—and then asks whether Oz is a genuinely possible world. He explains David Lewis's modal realism (every genuine possibility actual in its own causally isolated world) through counterfactuals about which network aired the film, dissolves the silver-versus-ruby slippers conflict by assigning book-Oz and film-Oz to different possible worlds, and argues that since no flat contradiction can be eked out of the Oz stories, Lewis is committed to Oz's being real—though Maguire's inter-world travel and Elphaba's hybrid, soul-less trans-world identity (her counterpart in our world being, playfully, Dorothy) stretch Lewis's 'counterparts' doctrine to its limit. Peirce supplies the closing caution, with Boole, that logic is a set of norms for how we can and ought to think rather than a proven mirror of other worlds, so believing in Oz's full reality remains permissible fun rather than an obligation.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 20 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Auxier tests Pullman's many-worlds premise, setting Asriel's coin-toss explanation and the Barnard-Stokes hypothesis against Book III's claim that unchosen possibilities are 'snuffed out like candles,' then measures the trilogy against David Lewis's causally independent possible worlds, which forbid the subtle knife's transworld travel and leave the chill Lyra feels at the thought of 'another Lyra' in Will's Oxford as an unresolved transworld-identity puzzle. Compiling fourteen kinds of conscious beings from humans and dæmons to specters and the Abyss itself, he argues Pullman's cosmology is panpsychist and aesthetic rather than moral or epistemic, ordered by what the alethiometer, the knife, and the spyglass can and cannot do, with the alethiometer submitting to the knife and love alone able to break it, as Will's love for his mother and for Lyra does twice. Peirce's agapicism, evolution by creative love alongside chance and mechanical necessity, supplies the closest philosophical analogue to Pullman's 'Matter loved Dust.'
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 24 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Finley puts Pullman's parallel worlds beside philosophers' possible worlds: the twin Oxfords sharing Simon Parslow's scratched initials invite the inference that Lyra's world has its own Madagascar, while modal realists like Lewis ('out there going on') take possible worlds to really exist and more skeptical theorists treat them as convenient fictions like 'in the story.' She contrasts their origins, quantum splitting at the level of elementary particles versus eternal logical possibility, explains why the indexical 'actual world' is one we can never leave, and argues that Lewis's underdetermination of fiction means the books describe not one possible world but vast numbers differing in unmentioned details like the population of alternate Madagascar. Lewis's counterpart theory then resolves Lyra's chill at 'perhaps there was a Lyra': the counterpart in Will's Oxford could never be her, only someone remarkably like her.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 13 "Which World Am I In" — Juan Ferret tells the story from inside the game: Admetus the Human Mage, chased through Alterac Valley by an Undead Rogue, works through Zeno's paradox of motion, the convergence of infinite series, and whether space and time are discrete, coached by a bodiless voice that turns out to be his player. The voice's revelations — 'You are my creation,' autorun, polymorph, Blink — force the free-will-versus-determinism question from the character's side, since every action is controlled from above. Reference frames, Heisenberg's uncertainty, EPR entanglement, and hidden nods to David Lewis ('Siwel Divad' on possible worlds) and many-worlds theory leave the mage wondering which world, server, or parallel universe he really inhabits.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 32 "Too Big a Byte to Chew" — Kylie Prymus uses a slain Orc to stage the metaphysics of Azeroth: whether the 'dead' Orc is anything more than electrons obeying code (Democritus's atomism), and why explaining Ironforge's empty Tuesday mornings forces us to 'go meta' just as Aristotle's Metaphysics went beyond his Physics. The problem of other minds gets a WoW twist: without nameplates we would sort NPC from PC by the argument from analogy, the same imperfect tool we use offline for pain, coma patients, and animal minds. David Lewis's plurality of worlds becomes concrete through servers — 'the gates could be open' is true for the Uther player because on Medivh they opened on January 23rd — and she concludes that the real world is no better defined than Azeroth.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 41 "Where in the World(s) Are We" — Ablondi asks whether fans' 'if only' claims—'If Bob Stanley had struck out Mookie Wilson, the Sox would have won in 1986,' 'if Pesky had hurried his relay in 1946'—can be true when they lack truthmakers in the actual world. He presents David Lewis's modal realism and counterpart theory as the standard solution, then objects: a Fisk counterpart with a different body, birthday and nickname, or a Red Sox made of 1986 Mets counterparts, is not recognizably Fisk or the Red Sox, and nobody cares about a Lonborg counterpart who won Game Seven. He concludes counterfactuals need some other explanation and that we should savor the actual Foulke-to-Mientkiewicz final out of 2004 instead.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 11 "The Good Gossip" — Borge weighs Jimmy Sirrel's claim that the best team always wins and the rest is gossip against Alex Ferguson insisting his side played better in a 1–4 defeat to Liverpool, framing the dispute as football Nominalism (only particular matches and results exist) versus football Platonism (an ideal way of playing exists over and above results). He rejects the Platonic ideal as metaphysically impossible—two perfect teams could never both score on every chance while conceding nothing, and style comparisons like catenaccio versus Brazil 1970 collapse without appeal to results—and instead uses possible-worlds counterfactuals: a team can be 'really' best yet unlucky when it creates objective scoring opportunities, like John Terry's slipped 2008 Champions League penalty or Spain's wrongly disallowed golden goal against South Korea in 2002, that go in across the closest possible worlds. Since Liverpool's deeply unfair 2005 comeback in Istanbul is celebrated as a classic, football is fiction and drama rather than a fairness-measuring contest, and the resulting what-if moaning is the good gossip that makes barstool debate worthwhile.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 12 "We Wouldn’t Be Here Without Time Travel" — Worley distinguishes logical from empirical possibility (Leonardo's round-square in 'City of Death') and shows that time-travel paradoxes — Leela's self-caused antibodies, the unauthored 'Blink' Easter egg, the Master's Toclafane — can be handled with Zeno-style analysis of contradiction and David Lewis's distinction between external and personal time, under which travelers instantiate rather than rewrite history ('The Visitation', 'The Time Meddler'). He then reads 'Turn Left' and the Doctor's 'alternative time' in 'Pyramids of Mars' through Leibniz's possible worlds and Lewis's actualism about parallel universes, concluding that in 'City of Death' time travel is essential to life on Earth existing at all.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 18 "Halo as a Catalyst for a Buddhism Videogame" — Luke Cuddy uses Halo 3 checkpoints and emulator save states—two mutually exclusive Flood-fight outcomes both in some sense true—to make David Lewis's possible worlds and modal truth concrete, with Leibniz as the doctrine's ancestor. Halo's infinite lives make players genuinely angry, and the chapter argues this is upaya territory: like the father in the Lotus Sutra's parable of the burning house, the game promises mastery (the goat-, deer-, and ox-carts) to lure players toward something greater outside it. Master Chief becomes a Bodhisattva whose avatar slides between extension of self and other, provoking the 'who am I?' crisis that reveals the ego as empty at the ultimate level of the Two-Fold Truth, while the Dalai Lama's enemies-as-teachers turns the seven-year-old who pwns you into practice in the first two Noble Truths' suffering and anger.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 8 "Education never ends Watson. It is a series of lessons with the greatest for" — J. Solomon Johnson asks whether Holmes's conclusions are knowledge or luck, walking through justified true belief with a Holmesian Gettier case (Watson rightly believing the killer was a former ship hand for the wrong reason), Moore's proof that knowledge entails belief, and Russell's stopped clock as an unsafe belief. BBC Sherlock's fake Vermeer and the 2009 film's 'resurrected' Lord Blackwood illustrate beliefs that fail safety or sensitivity across nearby possible worlds, while 'The Stock-Broker's Clerk' shows Holmes's observation of the scorched slippers making his belief sensitive. The verdict: Holmes is justified by the track record of his own expert methods, a professional billiards player rather than a beginner's-luck fluke, though real-world imitators could never rule out enough alternatives to match him.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 92 "Alternate Realities" — Reads the Bureau's adjustments as producing alternate realities — Ed Fletcher's boss as 'a different Douglas. A different version!' — and takes déjà vu, Dick's 'manifold of partially actualized realities,' and Ragle Gumm's haunting sense of having been inside a building he has only seen as a model in Time Out of Joint as clues that variables were reprogrammed in our past. Dick's late speculation converges, the chapter notes, with David Lewis's view that possible worlds are as real as ours, and with Hawking and Mlodinow's M-Theory multiverse.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 163 "Preparatory Human Beings" — The counter-tendency gathers Dick's empowering temporalities. 'The Golden Man' presents Cris Johnson, a golden-haired mutant with virtually no frontal cortex, who survives a random-firing gun by 'pre-thinking' a panorama of possible futures - Homo superior as superhuman beast, by instinct rather than intelligence. In Now Wait for Last Year, General Molinari uses the drug JJ-180 to trip sideways into parallel presents and recruit healthy duplicates of himself, virtually overcoming mortality with 'a dynasty consisting of himself'. And in The Man in the High Castle, Abendsen's The Grasshopper Lies Heavy, Frank Frink's handwrought jewelry and Tagomi's meditative slip all point toward an alternate present - ours - where the Allies won, making art and the I Ching oracles of resistance to totalitarian domination.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 164 "On the Advantage and Disadvantage of Eternity for Life" — The essay's close presents Dick's own 'wicked thought' from 'If You Find This World Bad, You Should See Some of the Others': a plurality of universes arranged laterally to linear time, 'ten thousand bodies of God' hung like suits, including one where Germany and Japan won World War II. It asks whether lateral change might explain schizophrenic experience and whether eternity, in Dick's phrase being 'free from and somehow out of and above time', is supertemporality - occupying multiple time sequences at will. Like Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, Dick's multiverse is a test rather than a doctrine: those crushed by an aimless universe remain merely human, while those who can affirm endless strife or tap parallel presents are virtually superhuman, resisting time's supposedly inexorable march.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 167 "Reality" — Taking Dick's 'What is reality?' as its theme, this section distinguishes The Man in the High Castle's alternate world from sham worlds like Time Out of Joint's fake 1950s: the alternate history is as real as ours, its inhabitants no more able to escape into a realer reality than we are, even when Tagomi briefly glimpses our Embarcadero. It introduces Leibniz's possible worlds and David Lewis's modal realism - every consistent way things might have been really exists, and calling only our world 'actual' is mere 'world chauvinism', like a New Yorker denying London exists. Because Dick's characters dismiss worlds like ours as unreal as readily as we dismiss theirs, the symmetry suggests our world has no exclusive title to the label 'real'.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 168 "Determinism" — Citing Dick's 1976 'soap-bubble' reality interview, this section observes that Lewis's many worlds, each complete in all detail at all times, are deterministic in Laplace's sense - history on rails. Three considerations tell against determinism in our world: our experience of free choice, which grounds praise and blame; quantum indeterminacy, where a nucleus splits when it splits; and objective chance and coincidence - Zangara's near-miss, two wheat grains touching in a granary, Churchill's silence at the crucial meeting tipping the premiership from Halifax, who would likely have negotiated with Hitler. Simons grants that hinge events deviate history by mere inches, but rejects Dick's hint, and Lewis's theory, that all the possible worlds are equally real: only our world is real.
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 12 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Westfall asks whether the Larry we watch is a character or the man himself, since George Costanza was based on Larry yet Curb-Larry insists 'I'm George' and takes Jason Alexander's roast of George personally in 'The Car Salesman.' Sorting the season-seven 'Seinfeld' reunion into three realities—Real, Curb, and Seinfeld—he shows Jason Alexander playing himself playing George while George says Larry's 'pretty, pretty, pretty good' inside a fiction where Larry David does not exist, leaving Larry 'real in fewer ways' than his castmates. The chapter concludes that we can adore and despise Larry at the same moment only because the show makes us treat a non-existent character as real, capped by Larry's catastrophic attempt to play George himself ('There were two Darrens on Bewitched').
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 21 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — David Morgan separates the franchise's two kinds of time travel. Forward travel is physically respectable: special-relativistic time dilation (Taylor's six months against nearly 700 Earth years implies 99.99997 percent of light speed) and gravitational dilation near black holes, confirmed daily by muon lifetimes and GPS satellite corrections. Backward travel, as when Cornelius, Zira, and Milo flee the doomsday blast to 1973, invites the Grandfather Paradox - Hasslein killing the apes would erase the future they came from - but the films resolve it through a closed causal loop in which Hasslein's killings set Caesar's rebellion in motion. Morgan then reads the Aldo-versus-Caesar continuity clash between Escape and Conquest through Hasslein's freeway-of-time speech as a multiple-timelines model aligned with the Many Worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics, which also lets fans file the Burton and Rise reboots as parallel-universe futures.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 24 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Burkett uses Fry's accidental incest in 'Roswell that Ends Well' - protecting Enos only to cause his death and then becoming his own grandfather via Mildred - to examine backwards time travel through David Lewis's Grandfather Paradox. Killing one's grandfather is shown to be logically impossible (it makes Enos both dead and alive in 1947, so every would-be assassin fails for ordinary reasons like a jammed rifle), while becoming your own grandfather is a consistent causal loop, and branching timelines merely kill a man who is no one's grandfather. The 'paradox-correcting' time spheres of Bender's Big Score fail on Hermes's stolen body, and Bender's year-long loop would spawn infinitely many duplicates were it not for the Globetrotters' Doom Field - so backwards time travel is bizarre but logically possible.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 14 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Sharon Kaye stages a fourteenth-century debate over a contradiction: Jesus truthfully prophesied that the Antichrist will come, yet the Antichrist remains free not to. Peter Aureoli denies bivalence for statements about the future, Thomas Bradwardine has God swap among infinite possible-world 'movies,' and Ockham's follower John of Mirecourt concludes that Jesus simply lied - each solution self-defeating or heretical. Using Ockham's Razor and her comic fantasy of seducing the Antichrist, Kaye argues the unsolvable prophecy problem helped discredit prophetic religion, ushered in theological determinism via Luther and Calvin, and opened a secular age.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 19 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Montoya asks whether Prismo, Adventure Time's wish-granting stand-in for God, produced the best possible world when he restored Ooo over Farmworld. After explaining Leibniz's answer to the problem of evil—that an all-good, all-knowing God permits some evil because every possible world contains some, and ours contains the least—the chapter compares Farmworld (no Lich, but Finn becomes the Ice King, Jake mutates into the Lich, Marceline dies ancient and insane) with Ooo, where the same characters flourish as heroes. Prismo, no omnibenevolent deity, remakes Ooo out of friendship with Jake, and Farmworld's horrors vindicate the Leibnizian point that wishing one evil out of existence can unleash far worse.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 25 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Through a hot-tub dialogue in Prismo's Time Room, the chapter walks Jake through the main theories of time: McTaggart's A-theory versus B-theory, plus presentism, the growing block, eternalism and four-dimensionalism, illustrated with the mirror-Finn dream, Farmworld Finn, Jake's unchangeable croak dream, and the Ancient Psychic Tandem War Elephant as a thing stretched across past, present and future selves. Booko's description of the multiverse becomes a springboard for David Lewis's possible-worlds realism and Everett's many-worlds reading of Prismo's 'alternate wish worlds'. Finally, quotes from McTaggart and Bergson delivered as Finn's Glasses of Nerdicon rant argue that time resists spatial and scientific analysis and must be lived, which the authors tie to relativity, black-hole cosmology and Prismo's Time Room as the one dimension outside time.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 11 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Christopher Ketcham's mock lost episode 'Charlie Gets Beatified' - in which Frank fakes a water-into-wine miracle with red food dye so the Gang can monetize Charlie's canonization - frames a genuine exercise in medieval modal metaphysics. Aristotle's definition of contingency, on which opposites can occur only at different times, is set against Duns Scotus's view that something can be otherwise at the very moment it acts, so that God's immutable foreknowledge coexists with a will 'endowed with something of his own freedom'. The chapter spells out necessity, contingency, and impossibility in possible-worlds terms (a gang needs at least two members in every world; Frank is impossible in Season One) and reads 'Gun Fever Too: Still Hot' as empirical confirmation of Scotus and Olivi: the Gang holds opposite positions within a single episode, proving real contingency and free will.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 17 "6. Weeping Angels and Many Worlds" — Sutton argues the causal loops of 'Blink' and 'The Angels Take Manhattan' need not destroy libertarian free will: the Doctor's claim that a known future is 'written in stone' conflates ordinary foreknowledge, which leaves agents free to make the knower wrong, with infallible knowledge that only exists because the act occurs. Adapting Hugh Everett's many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics to free choices, he shows how branching timelines let the Doctor read Melody Malone, decline to break River's wrist, and still close the loop—some parallel Doctor does what the book records—while Aristotle's future contingents in De Interpretatione secure the indeterminacy of what 'will' happen. Answering the objection that branch-splitting is really fatalism, he appeals to the subjective viewpoint (what matters is 'my me'), explains how Kathy and Billy's messages in 'Blink' reach Sally on at least one branch, and solves why the Doctor is always so lucky: we follow the one branch where he survives.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 19 "8. Could the Doctor Have Avoided Trenzalore" — Pigliucci treats the two Trenzalore timelines of 'The Name of the Doctor' and 'The Time of the Doctor' as allohistory—an if-then counterfactual in Livy's tradition about Alexander the Great—and argues Everettian many-worlds quantum mechanics best explains how the Time Lords' one decision (granting or withholding a new regeneration cycle) can go both ways across parallel worlds. Rejecting contra-causal free will as a theological leftover, he prefers the cognitive scientist's 'volition' and defends compatibilism: the split stems from ordinary quantum-random interaction during deliberation, not magic, so the Doctor's choices are real without violating physics. Distinguishing fate from free will via Oedipus and the Doctor's 'Destiny Trap,' he concludes the Doctor was fated to make his last stand on Trenzalore as a fixed point in time, while the outcome of the siege depended on a genuine choice that, as David Deutsch puts it, thickened the stack of universes where good things happen.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 18 "7. Who Should Have Won the Battle of Wits" — Greene observes that the Battle of Wits never really happened - Westley implied the iocane was in one goblet but poisoned both - so he constructs a 'near possible world' (crediting David Lewis's realist take on possible worlds) in which a fair contest occurs between the same two men. Vizzini's verbal 'deduction' is specious, he is hopeless at reading people (every 'inconceivable!' marks an underestimate), and his hubris and compulsive trickery make him predictable, while Westley reads character expertly, from Inigo's oath on his father's soul to Fezzik's sportsmanship. Greene concludes that in the majority of possible worlds the Man in Black wins a fair battle, and cheated in ours only because his real goals were getting the knife from Buttercup's throat and seeing Vizzini dead.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 36 "22. How to Solve the Contradictions in Deadpool Killustrated" — Because Deadpool Killustrated has him kill the real Captain Ahab, Ishmael both dies at Deadpool's hands and survives the Pequod's sinking in Moby-Dick, making the comic a depiction of something logically impossible in Hume's sense that contradictions cannot even be imagined. The chapter canvasses the escape routes: Matravers's claim that reading requires understanding rather than imagining, Gendler's aspect-imagining (Ahab as 'inspiration of Marvel heroes' rather than Melville's creation), Lewis's modal realism - defining the possible as what happens in some possible world, with the Killustrated Ahab a counterpart of Moby-Dick's and 'chunking' for contradictions - and finally Graham Priest's dialetheism and impossible worlds for stories like 'Wade's Impossible Day' with its square circle.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 28 "16. How Close Is That World to Our World" — Brett Coppenger treats the show as a nearby possible world identical to ours until the 1930s, then uses Gettier-style cases — Joe Blake forming justified true beliefs while driving through Alvin Goldman's Barn Façade County — to show such beliefs can still fail to be knowledge. Robert Nozick's truth-tracking conditions, defined via what happens in the closest possible worlds, handle the barns but generate 'abominable conjunctions' (knowing Jones killed the Crown Prince while not knowing the Crown Prince was killed), and the chapter closes on the thought that the large stock of shared knowledge is exactly what makes that dystopia feel only a few big events from our world.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 29 "17. When Worlds Diverge" — Ananya Chattoraj tests David Lewis's modal realism — possible worlds as real, spatiotemporally and causally isolated, each actual to its own inhabitants — against Tagomi's journeys: the TV Tagomi's silent bench appearance leaves his world a genuine Lewisian possible world where 'actual' just means 'where we live.' But the novel's Tagomi talks with the policeman, a passerby, and a coffee-shop patron, creating two-way spatial and causal relations that break Lewis's isolation criteria, so the book's two realities are better seen as 'island worlds' of one larger world with Tagomi as the bridge.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 24 "13. The Essence of Dogbert" — Knuths asks whether Dogbert is essentially a dog and only accidentally white, importing Aristotle's Metaphysics distinction between essential and accidental properties and its modern modal gloss: essences are what an object has in all possible worlds, with David Lewis's concrete-constructionist reading noted against the standard view of worlds as abstract sets of propositions. The puzzle is that Dogbert's 2014 stint as CEO, combined with his canine essence, would prove dogs can be CEOs, threatening absurd conclusions about the real world unless we choose an ontology of fiction. Three candidates are weighed without a verdict: possibilism (Adams discovered a possible world), Meinongianism (Dogbert has being without existence, at the cost of square circles), and creationism (Dogbert is Adams's abstract artifact, troubled by the Not-Adams duplicate-creator case).
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 15 "5. Who’d Rick Kill Or, Who Killed Rick" — Framing Rick's massacre of the Council of Ricks in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption' as a crime-scene investigation, the chapter asks whether killing qualitatively identical Ricks is murder or suicide. It contrasts Leibniz's abstractionism (possible worlds as mere descriptions, pictured as the Palace of Fates in the Theodicy, allowing transworld identity via essential properties) with David Lewis's concretism/modal realism (all worlds really exist but are causally isolated, with world-bound individuals and counterpart theory instead of transworld identity). The show, it argues, is a modified concretism: portals let people interact across worlds, so Rick C-137 murdered distinct cosmic doppelgangers, not himself, as the interdimensional cable channels of 'Rixty Minutes' confirm.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 16 "6. Truth in a Multiverse" — Expanding outward from Rick's garage to define a 'world' as everything spatiotemporally connected, the chapter explains truth via the correspondence theory (claims are true when they match actual events, like the 2016 election) and the coherence theory (for truths like googol arithmetic that correspond to nothing). It argues that in Rick and Morty's world possible worlds are not abstract tools but real alternate timelines: Beth really could have been a human doctor and Jerry really could have been on DiCaprio's yacht, as 'Rixty Minutes' shows, and the Cronenberg timeline's brave Jerry proves a non-weenie Jerry is possible. Yet infinite timelines may still miss possibilities (Jerry's favorite even number), so abstract possible worlds keep a role, with David Lewis the lone real-world philosopher who took them as actually existing.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 30 "17. Who Is “Rick” Anyway" — Starting from the mangled sentence 'Rick is the Rickest Rick who ever Ricked', the chapter asks what the name 'Rick' refers to in a multiverse. It contrasts Saul Kripke's view, names rigidly designate the same person across imagined counterfactuals, which would absurdly make the Council of Ricks one many-located Rick, with David Lewis's counterpart theory, each possibility a real world of world-bound duplicates. The show sides with Lewis: the Council says 'Rick C-137', C-137 works like a distinguishing last name, and Morty's 'I eat breakfast twenty yards away from my own rotting corpse' in 'Rixty Minutes' is true only because the corpse belongs to a Morty just like him. The chapter ends by noting Lewis never handled inter-reality travel, so which Summer C-137 Morty now refers to remains open.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 14 "5. Getting Time Travel Right" — Duncan Gale asks whether Endgame 'gets time travel right,' using David Lewis's 'The Paradoxes of Time Travel' to explain personal time versus external time (Steve and Nebula meeting their past selves), causal loops (Tony quoting the saying about money and time back to Howard, who seemingly hears it first), and the grandfather paradox (Rhodey's baby-Thanos plan, which the existence of Nebula proves the Avengers would always fail to carry out). He traces Marvel's branching-timeline rule from Marvel Two-In-One #50 through the Ancient One's warning that removing a stone splits reality, and argues the film's moral is that the Avengers refuse quick resets and dutifully return the stones, while Thanos would shred the universe and rebuild a 'grateful' one. The chapter closes with Ivan Karamazov's challenge about building the edifice of human happiness on a tortured child's tears, which Thanos would accept and the Avengers refuse.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 16 "7. Something Strange about Time Travel" — Rhys Woodward asks how MCU time travel can be coherent when future Captain America fights past Captain America and future Nebula kills past Nebula, apparent contradictions a frozen Steve Rogers by contrast does not even count as time travel. He lays out David Lewis's view that a time traveler simply cannot do what would generate a logical contradiction, then argues the MCU is more permissive and proposes that Avengers time travel jumps not through one timeline but to alternate worlds, reading the Ancient One's 'branching' when a stone is removed as an allusion to the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics cued by the quantum realm of the Ant-Man films. On this multiverse reading past Nebula belongs to a different world history than future Nebula, so the murder does not erase the killer, and the apparent plot holes dissolve into deliberate clues.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 23 "All Joking Aside, This Is a Modal Muddle" — Sam Cowling and Chris Ragg ask whether Batman could have been the Joker, using the Indiscernibility of Identicals and the Necessity of Identity over possible worlds to argue that if 'Batman' is a name of a merely possible individual, he could not have been identical to the Joker. The 'Robin argument' (many people have been Robin) pushes back that 'Batman' might be a disguised description, and the authors then treat Batman and the Joker as abstract fictional characters whose modal properties are stipulated by their authors. On that view the Elseworlds tale Batman: Two-Faces, where the two are literally one Jekyll-and-Hyde person, shows Batman could have been the Joker after all.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 23 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Mackonis shows Sheldon is wrong about being wrong: Stuart's tomato counterexample ('it's very wrong to say it's a suspension bridge') refutes his claim that wrongness admits no gradation, and closeness to truth is cashed out with possible-worlds similarity — vegetable theory sits one small alteration from actuality, echoing Sheldon's own many-worlds refusal to dance in any of them. The Raj exchange ('So you were wrong' / 'I didn't say that') motivates many-valued logics in which degrees of truth let both be partly right, while the 'Cooper-Wrongness Paradox' argues that if Sheldon always knew when he was wrong, he could never know that he was wrong. Hume's problem of induction then shows his post-Toby confidence in his other beliefs can never be inductively verified, only sometimes falsified, and his French-sprinkled 'victory' over an exhausted Stuart is sheer logical fallacy.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 11 "The Plurality of Worlds to Come" — Horn tests BioShock Infinite's lighthouse multiverse against the metaphysics of modality: actualism versus possibilism, transworld identity versus counterpart theory, and the Arnauld-Leibniz dispute over whether punishment for Wounded Knee requires that the Booker who did it be identical to the Booker who could have refrained. Applying the essentialism menu (anti-, super-, moderate) he argues superessentialism forces world-boundedness, so the game, whose worlds are concrete yet traversable through Elizabeth's tears, best fits a possibilist counterpart-theoretic model: Booker/Comstock split at the baptism, Anna/Elizabeth across the severed finger, and the Luteces as counterparts existing in every world. He ends by suggesting the always-a-lighthouse-man-city refrain makes the series' recurring figures necessary beings, a structural echo of God.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 12 "Final Thoughts" — Squires and McBain argue the ending wrongly necessitates that Booker's baptism must produce Comstock in every possible world, cashing out the necessity in possible-world terms and quoting William James on determinism's closed future. Against this 'God of necessity' they defend a traditional omniscient, omnipresent (panentheist) God whose foreknowledge does not determine choices, citing the justice requirement for free will and the biblical case of Hezekiah's prayer adding twenty years as proof the future stays open. Read this way, Booker never had to become a racist zealot, and the game's shockingly limited ending unfairly reinforces the stereotype that deep religious devotion necessarily leads to extremism.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 79 "So, Is Dumbledore Gay" — The chapter argues the historian's model fails for fiction: by David Lewis's point that 'every way that a world could possibly be is a way that some world is,' there are endlessly many Harry Schmotter and Harry Plotter worlds, so the storyteller must decide rather than discover which one is the world of Harry Potter. Gendler distinguishes primary truths (the 4,100 pages, minus inconsistencies like the silver versus scarlet prefect badge and the S-bend versus U-bend) from secondary truths (Hermione has ten fingers; Cedric Diggory does not play for the Red Sox), shows the 'maximal inclusiveness principle' proves too much, and closes with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics advice that exactness must fit the subject matter, so secondary truths need only rules of thumb.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 80 "Closing Speculations Genre" — Weighing the four criteria against 'Dumbledore is gay,' the chapter finds it no primary truth but arguably suggested by the text, Dumbledore's confession that Grindelwald's ideas 'inflamed' him and the absence of any heterosexual interest. It sets the anti-intentionalist view held by Wimsatt, Beardsley, Gadamer, Barthes, Foucault, and Derrida, that language is a social creation so texts must speak for themselves and there are as many Potter worlds as readers, against E. D. Hirsch's intentionalism and Rowling's own claim 'He is my character,' concluding that most fans rightly accept her announcement as an oral appendix alongside all her interview backstories.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Luck argues backward time travel is nearly useless for a hero: after the grandfather paradox (Hiro hearing of Kaito's murder only because Kaito died), he shows Lewis's linear time travel makes Hiro necessarily fail to save Kaito, Charlie, or Isaac, yet cannot explain Hiro meeting Ando two days after a five-week absence or New York being spared. Branching time travel, where each trip into the past spawns an alternate universe, fits Volume 1 coherently by building a Heroes multiverse of Hiro-1 through Hiro-4 and explaining Future Hiro's subway appearance as a 'brute fact' copied into branching universes. The price of coherence is that Hiro only ever saves other universes' New Yorks, never his own.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 30 "Notes" — Leuenberger argues that a LEGO MOC is a surprisingly faithful model of David Lewis's Humean supervenience: the world is just a vast mosaic of local matters of particular fact — homogeneous, arbitrarily recombinable atomic bricks (fundamental properties at space-time points) with no necessary connections, Hume's 'greater denier', versus gunky Play-Doh or jigsaw pieces. Ockham's Razor motivates the view (while also able to cut against a divine master builder, whom Lewis's world lacks, though LEGO-world builders likewise stand outside their creations), and Lewis's concrete possible worlds make every build a replica rather than a creation, answered to the 'incredulous stare' by quantitative parsimony. Four-dimensionally stacked creations model change as variation along temporal parts, while the causation objection — nothing in one LEGO creation brings about the next — marks the fundamental Humean/non-Humean divide.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 9 "None of It Matters Anyway, Then, Does It" — Devlin applies David Lewis's analysis of time travel (external versus personal time) to seasons 5 and 6: Faraday's 'whatever happened, happened' expresses an eternalist four-dimensional block universe in which Sayid's shooting of young Ben and Faraday's death at Eloise's hands were always part of the past. He reads the flash-sideways as initially exploring a branching-universe model in which Jughead's detonation actualizes an alternative 2004 time line. Lewis's tools then dissolve the puzzles: the Hurley-Miles 'we already had this conversation' exchange, baby and adult Miles as one person spread like a time-worm, the Faraday-kills-Eloise grandfather paradox, and the Locke-Richard compass causal loop, whose point of origin the show leaves unresolved.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 11 "NOTES" — Barnbaum treats the season 6 flash-sideways as counterfactual conditionals and evaluates them with David Lewis's possible-worlds semantics: in the closest possible world where James Ford's parents were still conned but he never became a grifter, Sawyer plausibly becomes a cop, whereas a world in which Jack fathers a child with Juliet demands too many extra changes to count as close to ours. She pairs this with Rawls's veil of ignorance - applied to dividing the crash survivors' water, where Jack's life-saving skill could justify unequal shares - as another famous hypothetical thought experiment whose conclusion rests on what people would agree to in the Original Position.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 38 "Notes" — Sorts out Spock-Prime, bearded Mirror-Spock, and Abrams's Spock-2 using David Lewis's modal realism, counterparts, and Humean supervenience: identity is not directly perceived but judged from adjacent similar instances, as with Hume's natural properties. The refit Enterprise versus the Enterprise-A, plus the thought experiment of downloading the old ship's computer into the new one, carry a Ship-of-Theseus-style analysis of whether swapped cells and Spock's katra-separated death and Genesis resurrection preserve identity. Mirror-Spock turns out to be a worldmate within one enlarged world (Kirk's crossover in "Mirror, Mirror" makes the universes spatiotemporally continuous), not a transworld duplicate, and Spock-Prime and Spock-2 are like two highways overlapping until Nero's arrival in 2233 makes them diverge - two similar individuals formed by different successes and failures, never identical.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 25 "Notes" — Jones takes Beard's 'tip our caps to the rascal pulling the strings' seriously and reconstructs Bostrom's simulation trilemma without the math: humanity goes extinct before simulating ancestors, advanced civilizations decline to run them, or we are almost certainly simulated. He then brings in David Lewis's modal realism to argue the different Teds - happily married in Kansas, the coach we watch, the rage-monster Led Tasso - are real possible people, and concludes that even if we are simulations our consciousness is real and meaningful: ancestor-simulations are the future tipping its caps to us.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 17 "NOTES" — Delfino and Sheahan assume that past-changing time travel is possible and find two flaws in The Terminator: the 'Bad Timing Problem,' where instantaneous 'time compression' (the rusted-nail thought experiment) means Reese entering the time machine after the T-101 is either too late or unnecessary, and the 'Who-Is-Your-Daddy? Problem,' where John must already exist to send Kyle back to father him - a vicious circle. Testing the two-timelines repair, they show it buys two different John Connors (a personal-identity problem), infinitely multiplying timelines, or a parallel-universes reading in which humanity both wins and loses. They conclude the story flirts with incoherence yet defend metaphysical imagination, with Kant's epigraph on our addiction to metaphysics and Aristotle's definition of wisdom as knowledge of deepest causes.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 25 "14. The Science of Alternate Realities" — Morgan unpacks the science behind the 'fifth dimension': higher spatial dimensions as in the portal of 'Little Girl Lost,' Einstein's time as a fourth dimension with time-dilation travel ('A Kind of a Stopwatch'), and the grandfather paradox, which 'Back There' handles inconsistently (some events change, others cannot) while 'No Time Like the Past' gets right: past events are eternally true. Quantum many-worlds fits 'The Parallel,' where Major Gaines slips into a nearly identical reality, and infinite universes would make every possibility actual. But the cosmological multiverse, he argues with Popper's falsifiability criterion, is untestable and hence not science, remaining a dimension of mind and imagination.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Xhignesse defends The Wheel of Time against the charge that it merely derives from Tolkien, using philosophy of literature to argue that stories are necessarily incomplete and rest on 'background' and a defeasible Reality Assumption (drawing on David Lewis's 'Truth in Fiction'). He argues that because our world lies in WoT's background and Jordan deliberately laced The Eye of the World with Lord of the Rings allusions (Trollocs, Padan Fain as Gollum, Rand as Arthur), the events of LotR are literally true in WoT's distant past, making Jordan's mytho-poetic project a fictional-mythology-within-a-fictional-mythology rather than lazy imitation. He also deploys Baxandall on influence and Walton/Friend on genre's standard versus contra-standard properties to show influence enables originality.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 18 "The Fiction of Truth in Fiction Some Reflections on Semantics and eXistenZ" — Graham Stevens uses eXistenZ to attack David Lewis's possible-world semantics for truth in fiction. Lewis analyzes 'according to the fiction f, p' as truth in the world(s) where the story is told as known fact; but eXistenZ's nested game-within-a-game ending, where even the characters cannot tell whether 'we are still in the game,' deliberately has no determinate world in which its events are fact. Stevens concludes fictions need not correspond to complete determinate worlds and proposes a stringent view: nothing is true in a fiction unless the fiction explicitly asserts it.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 15 "Some Paradoxes of Time Travel in The Terminator and 12 Monkeys" — Devlin uses The Terminator and 12 Monkeys to work through time-travel paradoxes with David Lewis's framework. He resolves the personal-identity paradox of the two James Coles at the airport via Lewis's distinction between personal and external time, and treats the grandfather paradox differently for each film: 12 Monkeys holds a possibilist growing-universe model in which the fixed past cannot be changed (Cole cannot kill his younger self), while The Terminator adopts a branching-universe model allowing the past to change into an alternate timeline. He closes on the causal loop of the Army of the 12 Monkeys message, which lacks an origin unless uncaused causes are allowed.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 12 "We Wouldn’t Be Here Without Time Travel" — Peter Worley finishes the Doctor's "wibbly-wobbly" speech from "Blink" by distinguishing empirical from logical possibility (via a fictional chat with Leonardo about a round-square) and asking whether time travel is coherent. Using "The Edge of Destruction," "The Aztecs," "The Visitation," and "Turn Left," he deploys David Lewis's external-versus-personal time distinction and Lewis's rule that a time traveler's acts must be the very events that made history, then treats the Doctor and Lewis as "actualists" about possible worlds to dissolve grandfather-style paradoxes and time loops.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 38 "The Odd Thought of Doctor Who" — Gregory Kalyniuk maps Leibniz's monadology onto Doctor Who. The Doctor's identity across regenerations is a thinking monad whose individual concept holds necessary predicates while appurtenant body-monads are replaced; the Time Lords play Leibniz's God overseeing pre-established harmony and permitting evil in the best world (refusing to stop the Daleks in 'Genesis'). The dimensionally transcendental TARDIS illustrates the identity of indiscernibles, the Matrix is a Leibnizian mill of confused perceptions (with the Master as Descartes's evil demon), and the incompossible Valeyard of 'Trial of a Time Lord' is read via Leibniz's Theodicy pyramid and Borges's forking paths.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 9 "None of It Matters Anyway, Then, Does It" — William J. Devlin applies David Lewis's distinction between external time and the traveler's personal time to Lost's season 5-6 time jumps, showing how Faraday's eternalist 'whatever happened, happened' (Chang's unbreakable rules) contrasts with the branching-universe model that Faraday later embraces with 'we're the variables.' Lewis's account resolves specific puzzles: why baby Miles and adult Miles can coexist without violating the indiscernibility of identicals, whether Faraday could kill his mother Eloise (the grandfather paradox), and the uncaused causal loop of the compass Locke and Richard pass between 1954 and 2007.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 11 "NOTES" — Deborah R. Barnbaum reads season 6's flash-sideways as a set of counterfactual conditionals ('if Sawyer weren't a con man, then he would have been a cop') and uses David Lewis's possible-worlds semantics and his ordered similarity priorities to judge which are plausible. She argues Sawyer-as-cop is a 'closest world' change of one fact while Jack-and-Juliet-with-a-son changes too much to be true, and she pairs this with Rawls's veil of ignorance and A Theory of Justice as a parallel counterfactual thought experiment governing how the castaways should ration scarce water and medicine.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 25 "14. The Science of Alternate Realities" — Morgan surveys the physics and philosophy behind the show's 'fifth dimension': higher spatial dimensions and parallel universes ('Little Girl Lost'), time as Einstein's fourth dimension and relativistic time dilation ('A Kind of a Stopwatch'), the Grandfather Paradox and the self-consistency of time travel ('Back There,' 'No Time Like the Past'), the Many Worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics ('The Parallel'), and the cosmological multiverse. He closes with Popper's falsification criterion, arguing that unobservable other universes may be, like the show itself, forever 'a dimension of mind.'
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 19 "Ur 88,416" — Auxier reconstructs the metaphysics of King's Tower across Ur and 11/22/63, treating imagination as a power that defies present time to reach the 'nowhen.' He maps King's multiverse onto Everett's many-worlds and Brian Greene's quantum/quilted multiverses, then extracts three 'laws of Dark Tower dynamics': the obduracy of the past (resistance proportional to how much the future would change), the conservation of harmony (time-strings converging like sympathetic guitar strings on an ideal order), and the danse macabre. He shows the 'reset' Jake believes in is really the creation of new Ur strings, dismantles Al Templeton's meat-buying and epistemic-radiation theories via thermodynamics, and closes with Kant's three functions of imagination to argue time travel is a 'plausible impossible' symbol we can imagine but never actually enact.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 31 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Holdier asks how the many rival Elizabeth Bennets (Austen's, P.D. James's Death Comes to Pemberley, Grahame-Smith's zombie killer) can share an identity. He rejects the Cartesian cogito for ignoring circumstance and adopts Paul Ricoeur's ipse/idem distinction: the three Elizabeths may share the same ipse (moment-to-moment self and personality) while their different worlds produce distinct idem (narrative) identities. He then applies David Lewis's possible-world semantics and modal realism, arguing each Elizabeth is 'world-bound' and the others are her equally real 'counterparts,' sufficiently similar to be compared across worlds without being identical, so 'Elizabeth Bennet' can name both a single ipse and many idem narratives.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 29 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Downes argues, against a Cartesian confidence in self-knowledge, that climbers do not have reliable access to their own internal states while climbing. Drawing on Nisbett and Wilson's sock experiment and dual-process 'new unconscious' psychology, he shows self-reports are often post-hoc confabulations: climbers who declare a wobbler 'felt easy,' claim to be 'not strong enough' on moves they later top-rope easily, or unknowingly dab or stand on the rope. He recommends leaning on external 'scaffolding' (partners, chalk marks, guidebooks) and the 'you're only as good as your last problem' rule to temper dangerous self-assessments, since overrating ability sits in a deceptively close possible world.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 15 "Who is Who" — The time-travel chapter grounds Doctor Who's paradoxes in Parmenides and Zeno on the impossibility of change and Aristotle on the logical necessity of past and future statements ('You can't rewrite history!' in 'The Aztecs'), then deploys determinism, David Lewis on the paradoxes of time travel, and the consistency/autonomy principles ('Father's Day,' the Reapers). It uses Leibniz's possible worlds and the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics to read 'Inferno' and 'Turn Left,' arguing quantum indeterminacy and entanglement make the Doctor's 'wibbly-wobbly, timey-wimey' theory of fixed points and flux coherent.
- **Comics as Philosophy**, ch. 5 "index" — This composite chapter opens with the volume's Introduction and then runs several essays. Jeff McLaughlin's 'What If?' reads DC's Crisis on Infinite Earths and Marvel's What If? series as literal illustrations of Leibniz's possible-worlds metaphysics: the multiverse of Earth-1, Earth-2 and the 3,000 doomed universes dramatizes counterfactuals and Leibniz's Theodicy argument (via the principle of sufficient reason) that God actualizes only the best of infinitely many possible worlds, with Descartes invoked on why a perfect God permits imperfection. Amy Kiste Nyberg's essay analyzes the 1954 Senate hearings on EC horror comics (Gaines's 'The Orphan') as an applied-ethics clash between publishers' free expression and protecting children, explicitly deploying Mill's On Liberty and harm principle to argue why the child-audience framing defeats the anti-censorship case. Stanford Carpenter's piece treats the Black Captain America (Truth: Red, White, and Black) as an epistemology-of-authorship problem.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 24 "22. Rick & Morty as Philosophy Nihilism in the Multiverse" — The chapter argues that Rick Sanchez's nihilism is built on cultural relativism plus the metaphysical fact of a multiverse. It reads Rick's mockery of racist alien snakes and the Gazorpazorp matriarchy through Montaigne's essay on cannibals to establish cultural relativism, and treats the microverse 'battery' society through Marx's base/superstructure and Foucault's docile bodies to argue all social values are constructed for the rulers. Rick's dimension-hopping (the Cronenberg episode, the Vat of Acid) literalizes David Lewis's modal realism and Leibniz's possible worlds, so that no action matters because a counterpart always does the opposite; his resulting hedonism and Birdperson's 'Wubba lubba dub dub' reveal Rick as a depressed near-Camusian who cannot live his own absurdist creed.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 97 "91. Deadpool’s Killogy as Philosophy The Metaphysics of a Homicidal Journey Through Possible Worlds" — Manninen argues that Cullen Bunn's Deadpool 'Killogy' is best read through David Lewis's genuine modal realism and counterpart theory: when Deadpool enters the Nexus of All Realities and finds piles of distinct Spider-Man corpses, he discovers other worlds are concrete and their inhabitants are counterparts, not identical selves, refuting Plantinga's actualist transworld identity. Framing Deadpool as an anti-Sisyphean 'hero' who tries to end the Absurd (the Continuity) by killing everyone rather than affirming it as Camus's Sisyphus does, the chapter supplements Lewis with Thomasson's artifact theory of fiction to handle the literary characters of the Ideaverse.

### The Culture Industry

The culture industry is a concept developed by Theodor Adorno, with Max Horkheimer, to describe how mass-produced entertainment—film, popular music, radio, and the like—is manufactured on industrial and commercial lines much like any other commodity. On their account this standardized, profit-driven culture promotes conformity and passivity, offering the appearance of choice while delivering more of the same and dulling audiences' capacity for critical thought. Rather than liberating, popular culture thus helps reconcile people to an unjust social order. The idea was central to the Frankfurt School's critique of modern capitalism and mass media.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 113 "Unknown" — Invoking Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry, the chapter asks whether The Matrix is itself part of the capitalist dream-world it tells us to wake up from, then uses Marx's theory of surplus value to show the film fails as Marxist critique: it never displays exploitation because the Matrix looks hip, with 'really good noodles', steady work, and club nights—humanity is paid exactly what it is worth. Had the Matrix been shot in black and white and the Nebuchadnezzar in color, the revolutionary wake-up call, like Dorothy leaving Kansas for Oz, would actually have registered.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 19 "No Love (for Hip Hop), No problem" — Taylor starts from his own lack of passion for hip hop as a black man and the "Eminem enigma" of the respected white rapper to ask whether hip hop belongs to black people by nature, using Dre's sellout dilemma in Brown Sugar to examine the communitarian language of roots, authenticity, and alienation. Following Cornel West's "racialist reasoning", he argues classical racialism is false, and that even critical racialism - races as socially constructed groups - plus the survival, duty, and cultural-preservation arguments (hip hop as "the black CNN", the ecosystem argument for reclaiming hip hop from the culture industry) fail to obligate blacks to embrace it, so no love for hip hop, no problem.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 7 "Does Johnny Rotten Still Hate Pink Floyd" — Reisch argues that Johnny Rotten's 'I hate Pink Floyd' T-shirt was a provocation aimed at the band everyone loved, since Pink Floyd was the exception to late-1970s corporate blandness rather than a symptom of it. Tracing the band from Syd Barrett's disintegration (the ever-changing 'Have You Got It Yet?', his unrecognizable 1975 walk-in at the Wish You Were Here sessions) through the Dark Side triumph and the Waters/Gilmour split, he contends that Pink Floyd 'was punk long before the Ramones and the Sex Pistols.' Where punk used two-minute power chords, Pink Floyd meticulously sharpened an ax to grind: 'Have a Cigar' and 'Welcome to the Machine' dissect the industry machine that cages and commodifies artists, and the whole project attacks the inauthenticity, alienation, and tragedy of modern life.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 16 "The Eclipse of Musical Alienation" — Macan uses Adorno to measure Pink Floyd's career-long confrontation with alienation: after 'Echoes' fused metaphysical loneliness ('I am you and what I see is me') with an explicitly Marxist account of capitalist atomization and commodification, the early epics 'Interstellar Overdrive,' 'Careful with that Axe, Eugene,' 'Set the Controls,' and 'Echoes' unknowingly resurrected Stravinsky's primitivism, their LSD-shaped structures (dechronization, depersonalization, dynamization) modeling the ego's dissolution and reintegration through climactic 'breakthrough' passages of maximum alienation, just as Schoenberg's twelve-tone music 'points out the ills of society' by musically modeling them. Against Adorno's 'On Popular Music,' he argues the early Floyd audience sought challenge rather than reassurance, but that from Dark Side onward the increasingly conventional music, polished by producer Bob Ezrin on The Wall, began 'hearing for the listener,' so Waters's plainspoken social critique lost its transgressive force. The Adornian moral is that you cannot critique alienation through music that is no longer itself alienating.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 12 "Springsteen’s Revolution" — Anderson and Anderson open with the Che Guevara t-shirt problem and Marcuse's one-dimensional man: the system assimilates protest, so internal critique (Springsteen on the cover of Rolling Stone, its Chevrolet calendar, the Eagles sold at Wal-Mart, Adorno's verdict on co-opted popular music) is a sop to Cerberus. Against this they set Springsteen's own account of his music as 'a very long conversation with my audience' — a transactional public service — and argue he survives the co-optation charge as a 'Socratic revolutionary' who, like Socrates refusing to leave Athens, works from within: listening without obeying ('I liked the old Bruce better'), refusing to ride the Born to Run wave, turning to Guthrie and Seeger, and drawing no hard conclusions, only opening spaces of reflection ('Born in the U.S.A.', 'Radio Nowhere', 'Long Walk Home'). Revolution is just another form of work — practice, sweat, and the personal job of 'growin' up.'
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 45 "32 - Dreamers in the Night [ ]" — This fan story stages the fanfiction debate inside the fleet: Roslin recites the 'Scorpion School' line, Adorno's mass culture mindlessly absorbed and Benjamin's fear that reproduction destroys an artwork's aura, while aide Billy Keikeya counters with Henry Jenkins, arguing fanfiction is culture repairing myths owned by corporations and that the zine writers build real community. Baltar, secretly a fan himself, needles Number Six by calling the Cylons 'a fanfiction of the human brain,' and her insistence that there should be one singular truth of the show mirrors her fundamentalist monotheism. Adama and Roslin conclude the fan writers are harmless, even healing, leaving creativity and communal play on the human side of the human-Cylon divide.
