- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 28 "Tools Like Us" — Arnold coins 'podcrastination' — the voluntary suspension of engagement with reality — and tests podcasting against two poles: Adorno's consciousness industry, under which plugging into an administered device is a 'cyborgian opiate' that deepens our thrall (CBS's listener-programmed KYOU station is still 'administrated'), and Postman's warning that 'we are tools of our tools'. The chapter's spine is Enzensberger's 1970 socialist media theory: podcasting fulfills his eight emancipatory criteria — decentralized programming, each receiver a potential transmitter, interaction, feedback, mobilization, political learning, self-organization — and could coordinate 'smart mobs' like the text-messaging crowds that toppled Estrada at Manila's EDSA plaza. Yet the media's potential is betrayed as much as realized — the Abu Ghraib photos and the 'Macaca' video circulated without catalyzing change — so the prediction is that the podcast will be squandered rather than co-opted: the iPod 'is not going to further a cyborg manifesto. It's only going to create a cyborg lament.'
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 29 "Unity in Diversity" — Lombardo asks whether the podcast, born as an unsanctioned side effect users reinvented out of the iPod (as hip hop reinvented the turntable before corporate co-option made it the hegemonic form), can be a public-sphere institution. Following Habermas's Structural Transformation — coffeehouses, salons, and a subscription-financed press later corrupted by advertising into 'the soft compulsion of constant consumption-training' — and Dewey's call in The Public and Its Problems for institutions people actually participate in, he argues podcasts resemble the liberal-era press: resistant to advertising (readily fast-forwarded or deleted), enthusiast- and subscriber-funded, and open to marginal voices like a 'gun-owning, gay Texan' commentator that gatekept mass media would never air. But most Web 2.0 talk merely supplements advertising with consumerist pseudo-debate, so podcasts must link their fragmented diversity into a broader conversation of public relevance to become a socially transformative public sphere rather than 150,000 isolated niches.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 18 "Go Slowly" — Wittkower frames In Rainbows' pay-what-you-want release with Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry: music is expressive communication awkwardly trapped in commodity form — even 'Happy Birthday' has an owner until 2030 — and digital distribution is finally tearing that frame down. He then applies Rawls's justice as fairness to music distribution: the first principle now supports everyone's liberty to listen, rip, and share, because viable alternative models mean restricting listeners can no longer be justified as necessary to artists; and the difference principle, with the sadists-objection to utilitarian aggregation, shows that how benefits are distributed among persons matters, which he extends to racial wealth gaps and the affirmative-action dilemma. His conclusion is that we must 'go slowly': listeners' rights to their culture outweigh labels' legitimate profit expectations, the way emancipation outweighed plantation business models, and labels must adapt into service providers rather than gatekeepers.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 24 "The Dalek Within" — Comparing the Doctor's hesitation at the Dalek hatchery in 'Genesis of the Daleks' with the half-human Doctor's instant genocide in 'Journey's End', the authors argue the Daleks are mirrors of us: their survival-driven wars enact Hobbes's state of nature, while their industrial 'extermination' embodies Arendt's banality of evil and Weber's iron cage of instrumental rationality. Drawing on Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry and Foucault's disciplinary institutions — modern techniques that mold the inner life as Davros's genetic engineering molds the Kaleds — they conclude the Dalek tendency is a human possibility, so we cannot exterminate the Daleks without indicting ourselves.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 63 "Chapter 09 - Matt Damon Is a Vast Sinister Conspiracy" — Argues that 'Matt Damon' is an industrially manufactured person — a simulacrum sustained by executives, marketers, and gossip media that exploits instincts once used to judge trustworthy tribemates. Reading David Norris's tie-choosing specialists in The Adjustment Bureau, Tyrell's 'More human than human,' and the novels The Simulacra and Time Out of Joint, it claims Dick's paranoid fantasy is true: manufactured fake realities keep us docile, distracted, and consuming so we never notice we would rather be lying on a rock in the warm sun.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 180 "Chapter 33 - “The Gun”" — Benjamin Stevens reads 'The Gun' - a mindless automated weapon still defending a dead community - as an early statement of Dick's fear that in the Cold War military-industrial complex our very capacities for thought, will and free action may have been objectified into products of a mechanized system that no longer serves us. He brings Dick into dialogue with Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry (we are industrially 'produced' as consumers, turned into the carbon-based equivalent of plastic), Walter Benjamin's loss of aura under mechanical reproduction, Hannah Arendt's worry that Sputnik signals an unwise desire to escape our earthliness, and Heidegger's broadened question concerning technology as social control. Like Plato, Dick insists the unexamined life is not worth living: the best life cannot be lived inside a culture that has, without our informed consent, made us artificial.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 84 "Mad Men" — Auxier argues rock periodically cleanses itself of commercial packaging, citing Hall and Oates versus Johnny Rotten and Culture Club versus Kurt Cobain as each era's corrective upheaval. The Madison Avenue 'Mad Men' sell kids sanitized three-minute morsels like Herman's Hermits, but the kids' own bottled energy finds ground anyway, and once they 'get their ya-yas out' the packaged pop stops working. The Stones enter as the real rhythm that arrives when something has to be put 'under the whip.'
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 11 "Girls and Philosophy" — Frost argues that critics who call Girls unwatchable because Hannah steals the hotel housekeeper's tip and the characters are unlikeable are watching television the wrong way. Using Adorno's 'How to Look at Television,' he shows how mainstream standardized shows (Friends and its copies) pre-digest viewing, how Sex and the City exemplifies Adorno's ideological 'fake-realism,' and how hidden messages of adjustment work through audience identification - none of which Girls permits with its raw sex scenes, Hannah's unglamorous body, and Jessa's non-judged promiscuity. Because identification with Hannah, Marnie, and Jessa (the diary-reading, the request to Laird for heroin) is impossible, Girls escapes the culture industry and exercises the viewer's critical faculties toward the Kantian autonomy and emancipation Adorno demands - which is also why role-model feminist criticism (Catherine Scott's) misses the point.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 31 "16. European Intellectuals Follow Charlie Brown!" — The chapter traces how European intellectuals legitimized Peanuts: Eco read the strip as mass culture whose repeated patterns expose a microcosm of the human condition (children warped by industrial civilization, Lucy as contemporary values incarnate), while Bassano di Tufillo finds 'sociable individualism' and, via Bateson and aboriginal spirituality, an ecological vision granting animals, trees, and school buildings equal dignity. It then applies Heidegger's distinction between calculative and reflective thinking to management: Lucy's rigid direction of the Christmas play ('You've got to have respect for your director!') is calculative leadership that treats people as resources, while Charlie Brown's refusal of the All-Stars sponsor - which would have expelled girls and Snoopy - models the authentic, reflective organization that values dignity and diversity over results.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 34 "18. Psycho-Politics in a Burnout Society" — Pagnoni Berns and Aguilar read the show through Byung-Chul Han's philosophy: in the transparency society everyone stacks their life online - Krista is transparent to Elliot because her password is Dylan and her birthday, while he stays opaque - and psycho-politics replaces Foucauldian punishment with seduction, a digital panopticon (Operation Berenstain, Minister Zhang) whose inmates voluntarily build it. Elliot's attention deficits, Tyrell's breakdown over Sharon Knowles's corpse, and Gideon's fatigue embody the burnout society's neuronal violence, and even fsociety reproduces the systemic coercion it fights, leaving 'real life' only outside the system.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 35 "19. Please Tell Me You’re Seeing This Too" — Ehrnberger argues Mr. Robot hooks us like a Trojan horse: Todorov's 'ambiguity of the fantastic' - the irresolvable hesitation over whether Elliot's world is real or imagined - makes his unreliable narration endlessly rewatchable, which is how a mainstream network show smuggles in Adorno's critique of the very culture industry that airs it. Adorno explains the sedation Elliot decries ('we wanna be sedated') and why enlightenment reverts to mythology - meritocracy, consumerism, digital connection as modern myths we no longer recognize as myths - while Ehrenberg's 'illness of responsibility' explains why freed people retreat into the comfort of those myths rather than bear freedom's weight.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 32 "19. Looking Like Number 12" — Busk argues 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' disturbs because it dramatizes Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry: standardized cultural products manufacture conformist subjects, and Marilyn's forced Transformation into Number 8 — complete with 'Instant Smile' — is the literal industrial production of a person with the capacity for critical resistance stripped out. 'The After Hours' extends the point, with mannequin Marsha as the culture-industry subject reduced to a plastic prop granted brief prearranged 'free time,' and he ends on Adorno's residual hope: the very existence of these failed protesters, like the theory itself, proves some subjectivity survives the system.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 24 "Indiscernibles and Autonomous Viewers “Time to Write my Own Fucking Story”" — The Forests ask whether Westworld is self-referential modernist art or 'meta-kitsch,' reading the park's dueling productions (Sizemore's clichéd narratives versus Ford's ambitions, with Cullen's corporate meddling mirroring HBO's pressure on Nolan and Joy) through Kant's relocation of aesthetic judgment to the subjective, Greenberg's avant-garde/kitsch divide, Adorno's contrast of liberating autonomous art with standardized heteronomous commodity culture, and Danto's Brillo Box problem of indiscernibles. Guests mistaking Teddy for a fellow guest and actors' 'reverse-reveries' show that host/guest indiscernibility mirrors the show's own indiscernibility from formulaic prestige TV. Their conclusion: the series counts as art rather than entertainment only for 'autonomous viewers' alert to its self-referential critique, the viewer-side counterpart of Dolores's 'when I discover who I am, I'll be free.'
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 10 "1. Free Falling into Postmodernism" — Sewell reads Petty's 1976 debut through Jameson's postmodernism: Petty's music is a cut-and-paste amalgam of 1960s jangle, 1970s heartland rock and punk attitude whose pastiche dissolves the high/low art distinction as aesthetic production merges with commodity production, which is exactly why it feels timeless. He then applies Butler's performativity to Petty's "cool," arguing the persona was learned and performed so incessantly that Petty and his audience came to experience it as innate. Finally Baudrillard's hyperreal and simulacra frame the conclusion that there never was a "real" Petty, only copies of copies, yet if the perceived sincerity feels real and empowering, it is real enough.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 24 "12. When Money Shouldn’t Be King" — Berkey reconstructs Petty's two industry battles, the bankruptcy gambit to void the contract sold along with Shelter Records and the month-long standoff against MCA's $9.98 superstar pricing, then reads The Last DJ as Petty's considered position on the business of music. He argues Petty rejected subjectivism about music's value: because listeners can be mistaken about the value of their own enjoyment, a formal argument shows executives like "Joe" who program only what profits act wrongly, even if consumers willingly pay. "Money Becomes King" completes the critique, showing how profit-focus degrades the fan's quasi-religious concert experience and corrodes Johnny's motivation to make valuable music at all.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 45 "32 - Dreamers in the Night [ ]" — This fan-fiction interlude dramatizes the fandom debate aboard Galactica: Roslin voices the Frankfurt School view (a 'Scorpion School' of Adorno and Benjamin - mass culture as mindless absorption, reproduction destroying the artwork's aura), while aide Billy cites Henry Jenkins and Textual Poachers to defend fanzines as participatory culture repairing corporate ownership of myth, and a fan meeting wins the President over as community-building. Baltar and inner Number Six extend the argument: Six demands 'the singular truth of the show' against fan rewriting, and Baltar answers that the Cylons are themselves a fanfiction of the human brain - twelve unoriginal faces. Starbuck is revealed as the anonymous fanfic writer.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 13 "Resistance" — Reading Fifteen Million Merits through Marx, the chapter treats Bing's world of endless pedaling, Wraith Babes, and Hot Shot as a commodity society in which people themselves carry use and exchange values — Oliver the 'lemon,' Glee deemed 'quite worthless,' Abi's unsellable papier-mache penguin discarded as detritus. Marx's commodity fetish explains the universalized pricing in merits, and Lukacs-style reification shows things commanding people (Cuppliance compelling compliance). Adorno's culture industry explains why all the shows share one form and why Bing's glass-shard rebellion is absorbed as just another commodity, while Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man supplies the hope that reason, love (Bing's love for Abi as something 'real'), and switching off the media can still seed resistance.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 36 "The Real World" — Written as a choose-your-own-adventure whose branches mirror Bandersnatch's, the chapter treats you, the Netflix viewer, as the external force Stefan suspects: Libet-style readiness-potential neuroscience suggests conscious choice is an after-the-fact story, and compatibilist rescues (Frankfurt's second-order desires, Fischer's guidance control) founder on the 'BundyBot' argument that programmed desires are not freedom. Everett's many-worlds interpretation supplies the multiverse of 'one reality for each possible course of action,' and David Lewis's fixed-past block universe answers the grandfather paradox raised by Stefan's mirror-trip to die on the 8:45 train with his mother. Aristotle does double duty: the Poetics explains why Bandersnatch rightly limits your options (Sartrean absolute freedom would make a crappy story), and the Nicomachean Ethics on voluntary action pins moral responsibility for Stefan's murders on the viewer rather than the coerced Stefan. Adorno's culture industry asks whether Tuckersoft's 'hit factory' - and Black Mirror itself - can produce genuine art, while Kierkegaard's dread of irreversible choice is overturned by an episode that always lets you go back and try again.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 38 "Things Worth Believing" — Butterfield stages the Frankfurt School critique of her own Disney love: Marx's three alienations (from work, from others, from species-being) explain the Seven Dwarfs' 'dig dig dig' and the FastPass-scheduled vacation that converts leisure into consumption, while Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man diagnoses the parks' engineered euphoria and 'false needs' as a 'comfortable, smooth, reasonable, democratic unfreedom' that blunts protest — with Adorno adding that consumers see through the advertising and buy anyway. Against the critic, she argues a Disney trip done right can challenge alienation by reviving play, family togetherness, and childlike belief in 'things worth believing.'
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 32 "19. Looking Like Number 12" — Busk explains why 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' is so disturbing despite having no monsters: through Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry, standardized cultural products manufacture conformist subjects whose critical capacities and powers of resistance atrophy until difference itself looks pathological, as with Marilyn's doctors diagnosing her refusal. 'The After Hours' extends the diagnosis, with mannequin Marsha as the subject reduced to an industrial prop granted brief furloughs of 'free time.' Yet the very existence of Marilyn's and Marsha's doomed protests, like Adorno and Horkheimer's own theory, shows some subjectivity survives the production line.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 24 "Indiscernibles and Autonomous Viewers “Time to Write my Own Fucking Story”" — Forest and Beckley-Forest ask whether Westworld is self-referential 'high art' or 'meta-kitsch,' tracing aesthetic modernism from Kant's subjective turn through Greenberg's avant-garde/kitsch split and Adorno's autonomous versus heteronomous art. They read Sizemore's clichéd Western narratives and the park's stock characters as commodified kitsch that mirrors the show's own corporate constraints under HBO, and use Danto's Brillo Box problem of indiscernibles to argue that host/guest and entertainment/art distinctions lie in the viewer's reflection. Dolores's line 'when I discover who I am, I'll be free' models the Adorno-style liberation available to an alert viewer.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 20 "The Politics of Mad Science in The Fly and Dead Ringers" — R. Barton Palmer reads The Fly and Dead Ringers as a diptych on 'mad science' descended from Stevenson's Jekyll and Hyde rather than Frankenstein, in which the scientist turns the investigative gaze on himself and self-destructs. He grounds this in the Frankfurt School critique of Enlightenment (Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment, Bacon's domination of nature, Marcuse's Eros and Civilization): Brundle's telepod and the Mantle twins' surgery expose the failure of Baconian objectivity and rationalization, with monstrousness emerging from within the divided self.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 19 "Film Noir and the Frankfurt School America as Wasteland in Edgar Ulmer's Detour" — Cantor argues that Ulmer's Detour deconstructs the American dream in a manner that closely parallels the Frankfurt school's culture critique. Al Roberts's westward journey toward success collapses into crime and doom, dramatizing Horkheimer and Adorno's claim in 'The Culture Industry' that Hollywood sells the masses an illusory lottery of hope (Haskell's horse 'Paradisical,' Sue's failed stardom) to reconcile them to capitalism. Cantor ties Roberts's disgust at jukebox music and his 'jazzing up' of Brahms directly to Adorno's polemics against mechanical reproduction and Benjamin's loss of the artwork's aura. He finally suggests both Ulmer and the émigré Marxists project a European elitist alienation onto an America they picture as an empty wasteland.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 19 "The Dialectic of Enlightenment in Metropolis" — Abrams reads Fritz Lang's Metropolis as anticipating Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment by two decades. He maps the film's arc—from the Christian mythology of the catacombs, through Joh's technototalitarian rational city and the human-machine fusion of Rotwang's false Maria, back into ancient myth (the M-Machine as Moloch, the whore of Babylon, the Tower of Babel)—onto their thesis that Enlightenment reason turns totalitarian and reverts to mythology and madness. He ties reason's self-destruction to Nietzsche's will to power and contrasts the descent into 'absolute madness' with Hegel's progress toward absolute mind.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 21 "Disenchantment and Rebellion in Alphaville" — Woolfolk reads Godard's Alphaville as an imagination of spiritual disaster: the Alpha 60 computer's reduction of time to divisible units suppresses the Bergsonian durée and fundamental self, and the city's architecture of 'nonplaces' embodies Weber's disenchantment and the Frankfurt School's culture-industry critique. Following Charles Taylor, he argues disenchantment opens a new heroic framework of facing an indifferent universe with lucidity, in which Lemmy Caution—a postmodern pastiche of noir dandies—rebels through an aestheticized eroticism and Éluard's surrealist poetry, achieving a Weberian 'this-worldly salvation' of art and love that succeeds where Orwell's Julia and Huxley's Savage fail.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — Olson argues Burton's signature saturated-versus-drab color palette in 'The Nightmare Before Christmas' and 'Corpse Bride' operates as a marketing strategy that commodifies childhood, conditioning children as future consumers who associate the films' colors with a utopian fantasy world to be bought back. She reads Jack's craving for the color of Christmas Town ('I want it for my own') through Lacan's objet petit a and through bell hooks's 'commodification of difference' (the Other consumed while its meaning is stripped away), and treats the Disney/Burton fairy-tale film as a Fordist commodity whose color palette—echoed on store shelves—drives product loyalty and nostalgic desire.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 17 "On Experience and Illumination Werner Herzog’s Dialectical Relationship with Society" — Stefanie Baumann reads Herzog's attack on the 'accountant's truth' of the Minnesota Declaration alongside Horkheimer and Adorno's critical theory, arguing that the cult of facts reifies perception, creates norms, and serves the 'administered world' via the culture industry. She contends Herzog's films (Lessons of Darkness, Fata Morgana, Aguirre, The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser) resist this not by escaping society but by dialectically mediating singular, uncategorizable outsiders through the historically developed social order — Kaspar Hauser's 'obstinate otherness' exposing the social violence of enforced assimilation, a subversive constellation rather than an explicit political message.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 12 "3 Lawsuits, Master Narratives, and Artistic Commodification" — Mitchell examines Young's Geffen-era lawsuit (sued in 1983 for "uncharacteristic" music like Trans and Everybody's Rockin') and the competing rebel/misunderstood-artist/lost-in-the-video-era narratives around it. Using Heilbroner on capitalism's commodification of rebellious art and Mark Fisher's "capitalist realism" and pre-corporation of dissent (Cobain as spectacle), he argues that Young himself actively authored the "rocker-turned-folkie" and anti-commercial persona, so that even his gestures of resistance to the music business were absorbed as marketable integrity.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 24 "The Dalek Within" — Ed Webb and Mark Wardecker contrast the Fourth Doctor's refusal to abort the Daleks in "Genesis of the Daleks" with his half-human self's genocide in "Journey's End" to ask whether a genocidal species should be exterminated. Reading Daleks as Nazis and Hobbesian survivalists in a lawless state of nature, they argue their real horror is Arendt's banality of evil, bureaucratic order-following, and that Foucault's disciplinary institutions and the Frankfurt School's culture industry show humans can be "made" Dalek-like. Their moral: we must not exterminate the Dalek but guard against the Dalek within, since it took the Doctor's added humanity to commit the genocide.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 42 "The Doctor Dances" — Alexander Bertland uses Vico, Cassirer, and Horkheimer and Adorno to argue Doctor Who refuses to simply side with science over myth. Vico shows myth as world-constructing ritual that binds community and carries moral wisdom ('Snakedance's' Snakedance defeats the Mara; 'Meglos' shows myth's danger), while Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment argues science is itself a limiting, mythical framework: the Doctor's insistence that 'fixed points' in time cannot be changed ('The Fires of Pompeii,' 'The Waters of Mars') reflects his own self-constructed scientific paradigm, not real necessity. The Doctor lives well by humbly balancing myth and science.
- **Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy**, ch. 6 "Screaming for Change" — Opening chapter that reframes punk not as fashion, genre, or subculture but as a philosophy, using Gramsci's hegemony as the analytic lens. It traces punk's history (Sex Pistols, the Clash, hardcore, NOFX, Bad Religion) and argues the movement's real target is the hegemonic mainstream that co-opts and commodifies dissent (Green Day/Offspring signing to majors as 'selling out'). Marx's alienation of the industrial worker is invoked to explain the dole-queue discontent that birthed British punk, positioning punk style and sound as surface manifestations of an underlying oppositional ideology.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 17 "8. Between Cynicism and Faith" — Buhlert contrasts the Apple TV+ series' reverent treatment of religion (the sincere anti-science faith of Synnax, the elaborate Luminism whose 'walking the spiral' ritual seems to vindicate that clones lack souls) with Asimov's cynical originals, where religion is Marx's 'opium of the people'. She shows the fake religion of Scientism in 'The Mayors' and the hypocritical Askonian elders in 'The Traders' treat faith as an instrument of control, situates this within Golden Age SF (Leiber's Gather, Darkness!, de Camp's Lest Darkness Fall) and its techno-optimism, and speculates on why the showrunners omitted Scientism.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 9 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Gerald Erion reads The Daily Show through Neil Postman's Amusing Ourselves to Death, arguing that Stewart's opening headline mockery of hurricane 'reporters in canoes,' 'Senior Correspondents,' and graphics packages like 'Mess O'Potamia' targets not the day's events but television's own entertainment bias, which renders even serious news trivial. He treats Stewart's Crossfire plea to 'stop hurting America,' the Jim Cramer 'Brawl Street' interview, and the Rally to Restore Sanity's '24-hour politico pundit perpetual panic conflictinator' as Postman-style critiques that a medium built to amuse cannot carry rational public discourse.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 32 "19. Looking Like Number 12" — Busk reads 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' through Horkheimer and Adorno's 'culture industry' and a philosophical account of subjectivity as active, critical agency. Marilyn's forced 'Transformation' into a standardized model (with banned books, 'Instant Smile,' and 'super soccer') dramatizes how commodified mass culture produces conformist, mannequin-like subjects who cannot resist—linking it to 'The After Hours,' where Marsha is literally a department-store mannequin. Yet Marilyn's and Marsha's very existence, like Adorno's theory, is a faint hopeful sign that critical subjectivity survives.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 12 "Gertrude McFuzz Should’ve Read Marx, or Sneetches of the World Unite" — Jacob Held uses the Once-ler, Pontoffel Pock, the Sneetches, and Gertrude McFuzz to explain Marx's theory of alienation. The Once-ler is the capitalist owning the means of Thneed production; Pontoffel Pock's dull pickle-works job shows labor severed from the worker's essence as a free, conscious producer (an idea Held traces to Hegel on self-expression through work). The Sneetches buying stars from Sylvester McMonkey McBean and Gertrude popping pill-berries dramatize how alienated people chase belonging through consumption, which Held elaborates via Fromm's 'having vs being' and Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry, concluding the fault lies not in the characters but in a society that denies self-realization through labor.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 25 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Wear traces the espresso aesthetic from the idealized, egalitarian Italian caffè—which he reads as an 'aestheticized Marxist' image of identical shots for businessman and street sweeper—to its dilution under neoliberal consumer choice, epitomized by the endless-customization L.A. Story 'half-caf twist of lemon' scene. He invokes Kant's Critique of Judgement and the sublime to argue that flavor and taste-judgment are neglected aesthetic faculties, and enlists the Frankfurt School (Adorno, Benjamin, Marcuse) and Bourdieu's cultural capital to explain how the market absorbs the espresso's beauty. He concludes that a single humble shot, as a memorial to the vast exploited labor chain behind it, is a truer aesthetic object than a branded frappuccino.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 16 "The Fall of the House of Ulmer Europe vs. America in the Gothic Vision of The Black Cat" — Cantor reads Edgar Ulmer's The Black Cat (1934) as a European emigre's Gothic allegory of Europe vs. America, with Karloff's architect Poelzig and Lugosi's psychiatrist Werdegast as mirror-image 'living dead' fixated on the horrors of World War I. He connects Poelzig's modernist house-over-Fort-Marmaros to a Freudian map of ego and id and to the war-driven rise of psychoanalysis, and reads the naive, unconscious American honeymooners against the cultured but nihilistic Europeans. He explicitly links the film's high-culture/pop-culture opposition to Heidegger's vision of Europe squeezed between a leveling America and Russia and to the Frankfurt School critique of American mass entertainment.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 21 "Kitsch and Camp and Things That Go Bump in the Night; or, Sontag and Adorno at the (Horror) Movies" — Johnston uses his childhood TV horror host Sir Graves Ghastly to distinguish kitsch from camp in the horror genre. Drawing on Greenberg's 'Avant-garde and Kitsch' and Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry, he argues that the Universal Horror sequels, Jaws, and most slasher films are kitsch: nonchallenging, formulaic variations that pacify consumers, while autonomous works like Carpenter's They Live or Craven's Scream interrogate the genre. Via Sontag's 'Notes on Camp' and Isherwood's making-fun-of versus making-fun-out-of, he sorts They Live, Scream, I Know What You Did Last Summer, and Scary Movie into deliberate camp, naive camp, and mere kitsch.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 6 "NOTES" — William Irwin's introduction argues philosophy must engage popular culture rather than fear it as Plato feared Homer and the poets. He invokes Plato's allegory of the cave to make the case that the philosopher who has left the cave must return and 'learn to see the shadows again'—use The Simpsons, The Matrix and Seinfeld as the vernacular through which prisoners can be led out—and answers Adorno-style culture-industry worries that mass entertainment is mere opiate. He closes by echoing Aristotle's serious treatment of the popular art (tragedy) of his day as warrant for treating today's pop culture philosophically.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 9 "NOTES" — Irwin asks 'what is popular culture?', rejecting Noel Carroll's 'mass art' accessibility criterion (using the Sex Pistols, Slipknot and the Beatles as counterexamples of inaccessible-yet-popular art) and Walter Benjamin's aura/mechanical-reproduction account, settling on popular culture as 'artifacts and subjects of mass interest and appreciation.' He rebuts Adorno's and Zizek's culture-industry charge that pop culture (e.g. The Matrix, The X-Files) ideologically ensnares audiences, and again deploys Plato's cave and the returning prisoner—citing Socrates meeting interlocutors where they are—to justify using pop culture as a bridge to philosophy while warning against 'abuse' (studying pop culture as philosophy).
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 13 "NOTES" — Richard Shusterman defends the entertainment value of popular art from a pragmatist ('meliorist') stance, tracing entertainment's genealogy through Plato, Aristotle, Montaigne, Kant, Hegel, Nietzsche, Heidegger and Adorno—whose 'culture industry' opposes pleasure to cognition. Using rap (KRS-One's 'Edutainment', Public Enemy, Ice-T) and T.S. Eliot's 'superior amusement,' he argues knowledge and enjoyment are compatible. He rejects Hannah Arendt's contrast of imperishable art vs. life-serving entertainment, and critiques G.E. Moore's Principia Ethica 'method of absolute isolation' for intrinsic value, replacing it with a Deweyan transactional account in which even intrinsic values are relational and temporal.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — South reads Batman, Batgirl, and Catwoman comics through J. M. Bernstein's Adorno-derived account of the 'damaged life' lived under Weberian rationalization and the disenchantment of the world. The Joker's 'one bad day' in The Killing Joke embodies 'affective skepticism'—the split between rational universal norms and agent-specific motivation—while the debate between moral internalism and externalism (which he ties to Kant-style abstract justification) expresses the hurt of a disenchanted world where justifying and motivating reasons no longer converge. Barbara Gordon's 'because I can,' Bruce Wayne's vow, and Selina Kyle's turn toward 'basic human dignity' exemplify Bernstein's 'fugitive ethics,' fragile promises that restore authority outside juridico-legal channels and produce genuine happiness in damaged lives.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 23 "21. Black Mirror as Philosophy A Dark Reflection of Human Nature" — The chapter asks whether Black Mirror condemns technology or human nature, and argues for the latter: the 'black mirror' reflects the viewer's character. It tests and rejects the reading of the show as depicting Bostrom-style existential risk or superintelligence (via 'Metalhead' and 'San Junipero') and rejects that Clark and Chalmers's extended-mind coupling (the 'grain' in 'The Entire History of You,' 'Arkangel,' 'Crocodile') destroys human identity. Drawing on Frankfurt School critique—Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry, Marcuse's one-dimensional man—and Plato's and Aristotle's natural-versus-artificial distinction, it concludes technology is an agency-less imitation that magnifies preexisting human vices, and closes with Benjamin's reproducibility thesis and Bandersnatch's interactivity to suggest the show can prompt viewers to confront their own darkness.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 43 "40. Deadpool as Philosophy Using Humor to Rebel Against the System" — Brake argues that Deadpool advances an implicit thesis about humor as a threefold vehicle of liberation, testing it against Horkheimer and Adorno's Frankfurt School charge that the culture industry produces interchangeable, aesthetically impoverished pop-culture 'trash' (the formulaic MCU) that pacifies workers, and Marcuse's warning that revolutionary material gets absorbed as just another commodity. Following Kathryn Tanner's rejoinder that consumers can creatively repurpose pop culture, he shows Wade Wilson's self-mocking, fourth-wall-breaking humor achieving personal liberation from tragedy (invoking Freud on humor as the ego's assertion of invulnerability), liberation from the oppressive Mutant Factory by exposing Ajax/Francis's vulnerability and asserting his own autonomy, and a partial liberation from superhero genre tropes, while conceding humor's reactionary tendency to reinforce the status quo since Deadpool ultimately reproduces the genre and hands Disney its money.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 84 "79. Cyberpunk 2077 as Philosophy Balancing the (Mystical) Ghost in the (Transhuman) Machine" — Lay reads Cyberpunk 2077's transhuman Night City against the enhancement debate. Using the Ship of Theseus, Parfit's continuity plus fission/fusion (V and Johnny 'fusing,' the Delamain AIs) and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind, he argues enhancement neither destroys personal identity (which Parfit says doesn't matter) nor dehumanizes users — it may be the purest expression of Clark's cyborg humanity. The real danger is corporate exploitation of bodies, explained via Adorno's culture industry and Arendt's banality of evil. Buddhist nonattachment (Nagarjuna's emptiness, echoed by a Schopenhauer shard) grounds each ending's pacification-versus-attachment theme, but Lay corrects it with Weil's critique of power and Buber's I-Thou, concluding the game urges transcending the boundary between 'me' and 'you' through mystical interpersonal relation.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 7 "Welcome Aboard the TARDIS—It’s Bigger on the Inside" — The author argues that Doctor Who functions as a 'great educator' that shapes viewers' reality and their conception of the good life, framing our birth into the world as being 'thrown' into a new environment we must assimilate. He applies Hegel's historical dialectic to the Doctor-versus-Daleks conflict, treating the Doctor (wisdom, liberty, compassion) and the Daleks (obedience, hatred, conquest) as opposing theses whose ongoing struggle synthesizes the wider universe's fear of the Daleks. Drawing on Carroll and Danesi, he claims pop culture like Doctor Who validates experience and creates collective structures of meaning, and that our chosen first Doctor becomes the interpretive framework through which we judge every later one.

### Bad Faith

Bad faith is Sartre's term for the self-deception by which we flee from our own freedom, pretending to be fixed things rather than the free beings we are. A person in bad faith might treat their social role, past, or circumstances as an unchangeable essence in order to disown the responsibility of choosing. Sartre illustrates it with figures like the waiter overplaying his role, showing how we lie to ourselves to escape the anxiety of radical freedom.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 88 "Popping a Bitter Pill Existential Authenticity in The Matrix and Nausea" — The chapter frames Neo's red/blue choice as the existential choice between authenticity - honest awareness of a condition without inherent purpose or design - and inauthenticity, named as Sartre's bad faith, Camus's intellectual suicide, and Heidegger's 'levelling down of all possibilities'. It notes the irony that although existentialists praise authenticity, their literary portraits make authentic characters anxious, alienated, and near-mad while the inauthentic remain tranquil - raising the possibility that ignorance is bliss and the blue pill is wiser - before promising an argument, via The Matrix and Sartre's Nausea, for the red pill.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 91 "Unknown" — The chapter concedes authenticity's costs - the truths of death, suffering, and meaninglessness are hard to stomach, and inauthenticity is the social norm that makes the authentic person feel alienated and even mad (Roquentin's 'crazy loon category', The Matrix's 'hardware' people who fight unplugging) - but argues the red pill still wins. Inauthenticity never eradicates anxiety (the 'splinter in the mind'), only misattributes it to mundane causes like jobs and cars, and it costs freedom and genuinely informed choice; authenticity ends the flight from being and yields a serenity Roquentin finds when existence becomes 'a perfect free gift'.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 22 "The Dangers of Hedonism" — Sander Lee reads A Midsummer Night's Sex Comedy as Allen's warning against hedonism, tracing that ethos to empiricist thought from Hobbes and Locke through Bentham's utilitarianism to American pragmatism, embodied in Leopold Sturgis, an Ayer-style positivist philosopher who denies everything unprovable yet dies of passion with Dulcy and is deified by Andrew's spirit ball as pagan 'pure essence'. Using Sartre's Nausea, the chapter shows Andrew and Ariel's attempt to recreate their lost 'perfect moment' by the brook failing on every count, proving such moments inauthentic fantasies that ignore freedom, responsibility, and the passage of time. Through Bazin's Nietzschean reading of Renoir (Apollonian order versus Dionysian impulse), it argues that unlike Isaac Davis in Manhattan, the film's characters end more committed to hedonism than they began, with no character left qualified to condemn it.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 25 "Hope" — Jill Gordon reads Another Woman as a film about self-knowledge structured by Socrates' self-seeing eye from Plato's Alcibiades I: just as an eye sees itself only in another eye, the emotionally walled-off philosophy professor Marion Post finally sees her own repression by overhearing the 'other woman' Hope's therapy through a vent. Each of her relationships, with husband Ken, brother Paul, renounced lover Larry, stepdaughter Laura, and friend Claire, mirrors back truths ('she stands above people and evaluates them') that her self-deception refuses until her dream stages her own analysis and the final session describes her own life exactly. Counting the irrecoverable cost of her chances (Larry, the aborted child), the chapter closes with Rilke's 'Archaic Torso of Apollo', 'You must change your life', as the command Marion finally obeys, yielding a hard-won and still hopeful transformation.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 14 "Sick of Love" — Krein and Levin read Dylan's portraits of fallen socialites in "Like a Rolling Stone," "Just Like a Woman," and "To Ramona" as critiques of bad faith - characters who hide from freedom and responsibility in consumerist status games, in Sartre's sense that existence precedes essence. But Beauvoir's Second Sex exposes the cost: the women Dylan praises ("Girl from the North Country," "One More Cup of Coffee") are praised precisely for staying in immanent, pastoral passivity, denied the transcendence that for Beauvoir constitutes full humanity. Borrowing Benjamin's and Buck-Morss's notion of modern "dreamworlds," they finally read Dylan's pastoral utopias as a counter-dreamworld spun after the collapse of the mass-utopian promise of consumer happiness.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 8 "“Life’s a Piece of Shit” The Question of Heroism" — Argues Life of Brian is heretical rather than blasphemous: it never mocks Jesus or belief in God but ridicules gullible, smug believing — the Sermon on the Mount crowd mishearing 'blessed are the cheesemakers,' the sandal schism — a critique the chapter aligns with Hume on the appetite for the marvelous and on anthropomorphism. It reads Brian's window sermon ('You're all individuals... think for yourselves') as Kant's Sapere aude and as an existentialist, possibly Christian, humanism. Against the charge of nihilism, it places Brian squarely in Camus's absurd universe (the pointless crucifixion finale and 'Always Look on the Bright Side of Life') and asks whether Brian is an absurd hero like Sisyphus, Meursault, or Dr. Rieux; he is not — he never scorns his fate — so the chapter proposes 'absurd decent guy': Brian lives sincerely, without waiting for miracles, and humor rather than revolt is the counterweight to absurdity.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 21 "A Nietzschean Conclusion" — Slowik argues the Pythons have a positive existentialist message: Kafka's bureaucratic insanity, where ordinary people beat helplessly against irrational rules, recurs in the 'Cheese Shop' and 'Dead Parrot' sketches, and Camus's Sisyphus lives on in the monotonous lives of Palin's city stockbroker and the accountant who dreams of lion taming — repetition without Sisyphus's defiance. The core claim is that Python endorses individual-centered existentialism: Brian's 'You've got to think for yourselves. You're all individuals!' is the troupe's rare direct statement of Sartre's 'existence precedes essence', confirmed by Cleese's and Palin's interviews about resisting those who tell you how to behave, a theme the chapter extends through Nietzsche's critique of moral tradition and organized Christianity. Sartrean bad faith explains Python's stereotyped characters — the aggressive policeman, the pepperpots, and Mr. Praline insisting 'I am not a loony!' while demanding a fish license for his halibut — while Arthur Pewtey's meek 'Right. Right.' and Ron Obvious's physical limits raise nature/nurture objections to Sartrean freedom. The 'Nietzschean Conclusion' is that Monty Python itself exemplifies will to power as 'giving style' to one's character, constantly overcoming its own formulas rather than repeating what succeeded.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 33 "The Viewer and the Look" — Meyer and Schneider use the mockumentary camera of The Office (British and American versions) as Sartre's Look: Pam caught gazing at Jim and Karen in "The Merger" stages shame at being fixed as an object by the Other, while David Brent's bragging over his Inside Paper cover is pride as bad faith, an attempt to control the Other's gaze that requires denying the employee's freedom. Dwight and Angela's furtive affair and the Michael-Jan speakerphone call in "Cocktails" illustrate Foucault's panopticon: the mere possibility of the camera makes characters police themselves. The viewer, positioned behind the lens, becomes complicit in the objectifying Look that constitutes the show's comedy of embarrassment.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 15 "Bad Faith" — Lee reads the 'Breakdown' episode of Alfred Hitchcock Presents existentially: when the executive Callou coldly fires Humka and hangs up on his despair, he treats a person as a thing, Buber's 'I-It' pseudo-listening where Humka sought an 'I-Thou' dialogue with the godlike source of authority in his world. Heidegger's account of inauthenticity explains the mask of rational control behind which Callou hides, and Sartre's bad faith names the self-deception by which he pretends his godlike management of others is justifiable. Paralyzed and taken for a corpse after a car crash, Callou can be saved only when rational strategy fails and he finally weeps: the single tear reveals his caring nature, Jessie addresses him person-to-person, and, vulnerable before God and others, he becomes an authentic self, Hitchcock's pointed moral for bosses who give an employee the sack.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 11 "The Avatar Unparalleled Opportunities" — Cuddy asks how gamers relate to BSG videogame avatars — as an extension of the ego or a disposable other — using Freud's id/ego/superego to cast the avatar as a socially safe venue for reconciling forbidden desires (piloting a Cylon Raider) with the superego's demands. Against Rehak's claim that gamers simply drop the avatar when losing, he enlists Sartre: blaming the game or 'cheating' opponents is bad faith, a denial of the freedom to create one's own essence, with Lee's '33' debate about responsibility for the Olympic Carrier and Baltar's vacillation as in-show parallels. Sartre's facticity bounds the freedom — hard missions are fixed facts to deal with — so the gamer, like Adama's fleet, must take responsibility within limits.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 13 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Fairweather casts the campaign against Pullman's books as Socrates's trial rerun (impiety plus corrupting the young) and asks whether legally protected speech can still be morally wrong, weighing Mill's On Liberty point that children lack the 'maturity of their faculties' against the charge that Pullman's 'killing God' rhetoric inflicts spiritual violence on young believers, by his own image of intercision. The answer comes through Nietzsche's Three Metamorphoses: Asriel, Will, and Lyra play the lion that slays the great 'thou shalt' of the Authority, but the lion's destruction is only the possibility of freedom, since full freedom is Nietzsche's child creating its own values rather than lapsing into nihilism or Sartrean bad faith. Pullman's Republic of Heaven, with its virtues of courage, compassion, love, kindness, and curiosity held in community, is a social ideal rather than a radically Nietzschean one, so the charge of corrupting young readers is deflated.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 30 "Are These World Series Champions Really Our Red Sox" — Lee casts pre-2004 fandom as a Kierkegaardian leap of faith ('We Believe') and the Curse of the Bambino as Schopenhauer's irrational deterministic will, with the 1918–2004 cycle of spring hope and October collapse as Camus's Sisyphus. But he argues fans are really existentialists: blaming losses on fate or the Curse is Sartrean bad faith that evades responsibility, since fans did hold Bill Buckner (1986 error) and Grady Little (leaving a spent Pedro in during 2003 ALCS Game 7) individually accountable. The 2004 and 2007 champions remain 'our' Red Sox because we freely choose to care about the team's journey, not because it has a fixed essence; a coda borrows Russell's point about ambiguous reference for the word 'Yankee,' and Andy Wasif's appendix runs Yankees-as-evil through relativism, objectivism and subjectivism.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 42 "Refereeing in the World" — Crowe uses Sartre to explain why refereeing is existentially anguished: in the moment of decision — Grosso's fall over Neill's outstretched legs at the 2006 World Cup — the referee is radically free and solely responsible, and that anguish drives the six familiar referee types into bad faith. The stickler hides behind the letter of Law 12 as Sartre's student hid behind ethical formulas, the ditherer repeats the woman who leaves her hand inert on her date's, the poseur and frustrated player over-act the café waiter's role, and the postman and tough guy play the 'champion of sincerity' who treats character as fixed. The ideal is the authentic referee 'refereeing in the world' — Collina disallowing his own awarded goal at San Siro and explaining why to Inter — who owns his contingency: 'This is what I have chosen.'
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 20 "“Howzat!” Prometheus Is a Fast Bowler" — Decker argues the Doctor's morality resists formula — his motives are private, his timey-wimey perspective complicates consequentialist calculation, and the 'Genesis of the Daleks' child hypothetical breaks rule theories like Kant's and Mill's — so he reads it as an 'ethics of ambiguity' fusing Romanticism (Shelley's imagination, the infinite glimpsed in cups of tea and small beautiful events, Romantic-Gothic divided consciousness) with Sartrean existentialism. Via Sartre's WWII student, bad faith, and Beauvoir's 'adventurer' contrasted with the sub-man and the serious man, he casts the Doctor as a Gallifreyan Prometheus whose gifts of freedom are both dreadful and delightful.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 36 "Bad or Bad Faith" — Rebecca Steiner Goldner reads the show through Sartre's Being and Nothingness: Dexter's watching is the Look that crystallizes his victims into a fixed essence - Matt Chambers can never again reinvent himself in a new town - and the kill room stages the demanded shame and confession ('Look at what you did!'), echoing Sartre's caught peeping-Tom. She then argues Dexter's belief that he was born a killer, that his Dark Passenger leaves him no choice, is itself bad faith: existence precedes essence, and by Sartre's account even the reformed thief remains responsible for his past, as with Jeremy Downs and Dr. Meridian. We viewers root for Dexter because we see the freedom he denies - and love him because he never makes the authentic choice to abandon his murderous project.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 53 "What Does A Scanner See" — The chapter answers Arctor's question with Sartre: the gambler cannot observe his way out of deciding again, because consciousness is a nothingness with no determinate essence to be observed, so a scanner used to find yourself 'sees nothing', and Fred watching his own footage is bad faith, hiding from freedom behind presumed facts about himself. Butler then flips the bleakness into Sartre's optimism, reading Dick's 'I myself, I am not a character in this novel: I am the novel' as the author freely remaking his life through the book, his first written without amphetamines, after the break-in he suspected he had staged himself.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 54 "Phil Chews the Fat" — The chapter closes on VALIS's opening gambit, 'I am Horselover Fat, and I am writing this in the third person to gain much-needed objectivity', and Dick's proliferating self-theories (vitamin C overdose, alien telepathy, past lives, Gnostic revelation) across VALIS, Radio Free Albemuth and the Exegesis. Butler weighs the bad-faith reading, that Dick was nailing down a determinate identity to escape the responsibility to choose, against Dick's own android-human essays, in which the authentic human acts spontaneously and throws off masks, concluding that Dick's refusal to settle on any one theory of himself was his playful, Sartrean way of knowing he is not an android.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 15 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Rood unpacks Klosterman's 'This Is Emo' thesis that no woman will ever satisfy him: women love Lloyd Dobler rather than John Cusack, and everyone measures real relationships against Hollywood fake love (Coldplay songs, the Woody Allen Personality Type) until, as Klosterman puts it, real people actively trying to live like fake people are no less fake. He reads this through Sartre's cafe waiter and Butler's gender performativity to argue identity is learned performance, and through Plato's cave updated to a reclining-seat movie theater where we mistake projected shadows for real love. The deepest diagnosis is Baudrillard's hyperreal, glossed as a social-constructionist rerun of Kant's Copernican revolution, against which Rood's own objection lands: Klosterman covertly assumes a pure unmediated self that cannot exist, so the answer to fake love is not escape from mediation but self-control within it.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 25 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Robert Tally Jr. reads The Graveyard Book as 'spectral existentialism': Bod's climax, 'I'm Nobody Owens. That's who I am,' is Sartre's existence precedes essence made literal, a self made rather than found, and the climactic claiming of the name enacts the self-ownership of the nursery-rhyme pauper 'who nobody owns.' Heidegger supplies the uncanny not-at-home-ness (unheimlich) of the graveyard, which Tally, citing Foucault's 'Of Other Spaces,' calls a heterotopia, while Silas the vampire embodies Lukacs's transcendental homelessness and Kierkegaardian anxiety is transmuted by Bod into the spectral gift of Fear he wields on his bullies. The identity-leeching ghouls named after the Duke of Westminster and the 33rd President are the avatars of bad faith, and the Jacks' attempt to dodge the prophecy fulfills it like Oedipus's, showing that Bod's fate, too, is self-made.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 13 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Argues Heisenberg is not an alter ego but Walt finally escaping the Prufrock-like bad faith of his pre-cancer life: the pork-pie-hat persona acknowledges the absurd, owns his freedom and responsibility, and so achieves the authenticity Camus and Sartre demand. Walt becomes Camus's Sisyphus - rebelling against death, social norms, and Skyler, owning his rock with silent joy - citing the fulminated-mercury showdown with Tuco in 'Crazy Handful of Nothin'', running down Gus's dealers in 'Half Measures', and confessing to Skyler in 'No Mas'. The chapter closes that, like Sisyphus, we must imagine Walt happy.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 26 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Round argues the real horror of The Walking Dead is humanity itself, read through existentialism: walkers cannot choose, so the humans who attack, torture, and steal from each other are the true 'zombie Other.' She traces Rick's self-made, revisable moral code — from law-enforcer to 'You kill? You die' to killing Dexter — as authentic situation-based morality, paralleled with Kierkegaard's Abraham and with Abraham Ford's confession 'I did what I wanted to do' set against Eugene's bad-faith 'I did what I had to do.' Suicides like Jim, Jacqui, and Carol embody existential angst before an absurd world, the Governor's Woodbury is an Adorno-style inauthentic hierarchy that manipulates its people, and Rick's 'WE ARE THE WALKING DEAD!' speech uses facticity to insist the group admit what they have already become.
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 18 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Zanelotti takes up the charge that Larry is a self-hating Jew, from whistling Wagner to 'The End,' where learning he is a gentile turns him into a churchgoing enthusiast who sings 'Go Tell It on the Mountain' and gives Richard Lewis his kidney. Sartre's bad faith diagnoses both poles: Larry denying his facticity by imagining he can simply shed his Jewish past and re-adopt it at will, and critics who demand he live up to an 'authentic' Jewish essence; Marx's false consciousness, meanwhile, explains the self-hating baldy who buys into the haired agenda. Using Ronald de Sousa's rejection of the 'Just Joking Defense'—we are accountable for laughter because we let ourselves become people who cannot restrain it—the chapter argues the show sets a comic frame that mocks bad faith rather than Judaism. Its deeper target, via Nietzsche's death of God, is the overenthusiastic meaning we manufacture when faith is 'curbed,' which is why Larry ridicules only public displays of religion, not belief itself.
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 26 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Reads Larry as a textbook existentialist: his agonizing over trivia ('Doctor?... Pharmacist?') instantiates Heideggerian anxiety and Sartrean anguish, because every choice, even yanking his 5 wood out of a casket in 'The 5 Wood,' proclaims an image of how everyone ought to live. Since existence precedes essence there is no fixed human nature for Larry to appeal to; he must author his values alone, which the chapter says also makes him an optimist ('I'm not an inventor, but I'm an improver'). Larry dispels others' bad faith when he tells Susie she obviously can share the brownie recipe in 'The Benadryl Brownie,' and his baldness crusade, firing the toupee-wearing chef Phil Dunlap in 'The Grand Opening,' is a demand for authenticity about one's facticity. The 'Larry David Stare' is analyzed through Sartre's Look: the squinter tries to inspect another consciousness empirically and necessarily fails, since the other's freedom can never be objectified.
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 27 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Grants that Larry looks like the Romantic ideal of the authentic self, Rousseau's amour de soi turned into candid self-expression, but argues his authenticity collapses into egoism: petty commandments about chicken skewers and beach jackets, one-strike firings like the toupee-wearing chef, and ceaseless sincerity tests. Through Sartre's categories Larry is bad faith in both directions, the 'cowardly bastard': he denies transcendence ('I can't help it') and hides behind fabricated personas, faking concern over a sick dog and exaggerating his Jewishness to the kidney consortium. Charles Taylor's The Ethics of Authenticity supplies the verdict that self-creation needs 'pre-existing horizons of significance,' so Larry's 'anything goes' authenticity is really moral relativism and justified self-interest, with Ayn Rand's virtue of selfishness as its unwanted philosophical ally. The chapter closes that only a relational authenticity, like the African ideal of ubuntu, could redeem Larry, and he lacks it, so 'maybe authenticity isn't for everyone.'
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 23 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Robison-Greene reads the returning soldiers through Camus and Sartre. War reveals the absurd - Jimmy's Argonne story of the German soldier who would not die even in a hopeless situation strips life of inherent value - and Van Alden's fervent Christianity is the escapist response to absurdity, bad faith that denies his own desires. Jimmy and Richard are trapped in bad faith over facticity and transcendence, Richard pinned by 'the look' of a community that only sees his ruined face ('Hell is other people'); neither fully becomes an absurd hero like Meursault, since Richard still craves meaningful ties, but Jimmy finally embraces the absurd at the War Memorial, arranging his own death with the calm of a man who 'died in the trenches, years back.'
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 26 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Robison-Greene applies Beauvoir to the show's women. Powerful men are the One and women (like Chalky's community under the Klan) are made the inessential Other, and Beauvoir's apparatus - bad faith, the 'appeal' free beings must make to one another, and the happiness that lets women be complicit in their own oppression - frames Lucy, Gillian, and Margaret. Lucy happily performs the role her men write for her, Gillian is so consumed by the fact of her rape that even her apparent freedom keeps her the object of male desire ('just the loneliest person on earth'), while Margaret - Temperance Leaguer, advocate for women's reproductive health, and finally the woman who shuts the door on Nucky's cash - comes closest to making the appeal and to freedom.
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 12 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter uses Sartre to diagnose Barney's fixed persona of suits, womanizing, and Bro Code worship as bad faith: having freely chosen to become the suited businessman who stole Shannon, Barney now acts as if those are his only options, denying his radical freedom. Hardy maps Sartre's own examples onto the show - Wendy the Waitress play-acting a stereotypical waitress, the woman who ignores the knee-touch, Barney tuning out criticism with 'I'm awesome' - and reads emotions, via Sartre's Sketch for a Theory of the Emotions, as magical transformations of the world like Marshall's 'best burger' quest and the Bob Barker paternity story. Barney's love for Robin and his secret reunion of Marshall and Lily are the moments he breaks out of bad faith and chooses freely against his persona.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 16 "The Devil and Philosophy" — James McLachlan splits the Satans of history into 'the Rebel' of Romanticism (Blake, Shelley's turn to Prometheus, the sexy vampires of film) and 'the Asshole' who wants to be God. Using Sartre's 'hell is other people' and the desire to be a complete being, he reads Dracula, Scarface's Tony Montana, and Bond villains as figures who cannot endure the otherness of real persons. With Bohme and especially Schelling's two wills - self-assertion and love of others - he argues evil is a positive, perverted order of pure egoism, and that not even Satan can achieve the total asshole-ness he wants, because selfhood exists only in relation to others.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 19 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Elizabeth Butterfield reads The Devil's Advocate through Sartre: Kevin Lomax's 'You set me up!' excuse - after defending the guilty Gettys and Cullen and abandoning MaryAnn - is textbook bad faith, a lie to himself about his own free choices. Milton the Devil plays existentialist, insisting 'I'm no puppeteer... I only set the stage. You pull your own strings,' until Kevin admits his vanity, his drive to win, motivated every choice. Radical freedom entails radical responsibility, and Kevin's final suicide is his last free act, chosen to keep coming out on top, while free will remains the one limit the Devil cannot breach.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 10 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Talia Morag reads Brody's colliding roles - Marine, congressman, father, Muslim, follower of Abu Nazir - and Carrie's unstable ones (CIA agent, bipolar patient, lover) through Korsgaard's notion of practical identities, whose contradictory obligations (kill and not kill) demand reconciliation. Following Kierkegaard's advice to rethink labels like 'Christian', Brody reinterprets his suicide tape as acting 'as a Marine' against domestic enemies - a rationalizing move the chapter treats as bordering on bad faith - while Dana's phone call in 'Marine One' reasserts the father identity and stops the bombing. Carrie's 'Q&A' re-description of Brody as a good man and future hero shows identities are constructed through choices, Sartre's point that we are not summaries of our past.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 17 "Girls and Philosophy" — Archibald reads Jessa as Girls' quintessential existentialist: her unbothered abortion ('I'm offended by all the supposed to's'), her 'I am a junkie' honesty, and her refusal to blame her rough past (Sartrean facticity) enact existence precedes essence and Camus's embrace of the absurd. Kierkegaard's 'the crowd is untruth' and 'leveling' explain her contempt for rehab group conformity, while her panic marriage to Thomas-John after Katherine's motherly intervention is diagnosed as bad faith and angst. Her assisting the dying Beadie's suicide attempt - and calling 911 when Beadie recants - becomes the chapter's closing confrontation with Camus's one serious philosophical question, answered by living 'without appeal.'
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 19 "Girls and Philosophy" — Crossley reads the millennials of Girls through Sartre's anguish: Hannah, cut off financially in the pilot, is 'condemned to be free' in a recession that owes her nothing, and Marnie's firing from the gallery ('I don't know what I want... I wish someone would tell me') confronts her with facticity and the terror of self-determination. Marnie's flight into wishing for a moral dictator and her later choice to sing map the bad faith/authenticity distinction, as does Hannah swapping her hoarder-story reading for a pretentious piece on death to please Ray. Even Jessa's total rejection of the 'supposed to's' is outed as its own bad faith, and the ad-agency arc shows twenty-first-century authenticity is inevitably compromised by the need to eat.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 20 "Girls and Philosophy" — Van Loon explains the q-tip scene ('On All Fours') as Kierkegaardian anxiety made flesh: freed by her parents and facing the e-book deadline, Hannah confronts the infinity of possibilities and, like Sartre's vertigo over the cliff, shoves the q-tip into her ear - embracing all possibilities at once and relapsing into bad faith by becoming a victim of fate. Each girl handles freedom differently: Shoshanna remains in an innocence prior to freedom, Jessa jokes her way out of seriousness, Marnie denies her anxiety. Against these, the Season Two FaceTime call to Adam models Kierkegaard's leap of faith and the 'knight of faith' - surrendering, making oneself vulnerable, and accepting that anxiety will return.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 27 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Pardi argues Jobs lived philosophically as an existentialist: the 'Steve Jobs Roll Your Own Calculator Construction Set' anecdote shows design by touch and intuition rather than master plans, every detail of a product mattered because it belongs to a life narrative of 'making a ding in the universe,' and he avoided both Kierkegaard's despair (the gap between actual and possible self) and Sartrean bad faith—quoted from Being and Nothingness—by never lying to himself about his products, calling faulty work 'shit' and redoing it. Against him stands Bill Gates the pragmatist, whose utilitarian Windows-for-every-desk business and 'rationality only goes so far' humility embody William James's pragmatic method, while Jobs's Zune taunt ('we made the iPod for ourselves') shows the existentialist refusing to compromise authenticity for market share.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 11 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Hoyt argues the show's core lesson is dropping the little lies we tell ourselves: Bennett calls his crush on Daya 'love' to excuse framing Mendez, Pornstache is a man performing a blustering guard (Sartrean bad faith), and Larry and Polly's 'love just happened' dodges responsibility for betrayal. Piper's arc (the Colt 45 scene in '40 Oz. of Furlough') shows the payoff of authenticity, while Healy's Safe Place is a fantasy that cannot will a change of worldview. Using Wittgenstein's aspect-seeing from Philosophical Investigations, he shows how characters and viewers miss ethically significant meanings, like Taystee's shower 'compliment' as intimidation and Piper's convenient blindness to Soso's humanity when selling her for a blanket.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 24 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Walker contrasts Pennsatucky's Christian fundamentalism with Piper's secular humanism (Kurtz's six features) in their 'Fool Me Once' confrontation. With no God, Sartre's existence precedes essence makes Piper condemned to create her own meaning: owning her crime to her mother and confessing the Pennsatucky prank, while Red and Vee play Sartre's cafe waiter, reducing themselves to chef and dealer, and Pennsatucky's 'defender of the unborn' persona is de Beauvoir's sub-man sheltering behind ready-made values. Marx's opium-of-the-people analogy explains why comforting, unverifiable belief can block the authentic, responsible pursuit of a meaningful life.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 26 "10. We’re Not Free to Save Lee" — Bowman uses Telltale's Walking Dead videogame, where Lee always dies no matter what the player does, to stage the free will versus determinism debate. Laplace's demon grounds the determinist pole (the game's outcome is fixed like set particles), while Sartre's radical freedom and bad faith explain the player who says "I thought I could save both" at Hershel's farm rather than owning her choice. The chapter resolves the tension with fatalism or soft determinism - a compatibilist itinerary where Lee's death is a fixed benchmark but the player's choices in between define the character - and extends Bostrom's simulation hypothesis to ask whether we are Lee-like players inside someone else's game.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 25 "11. Louis C.K.’s No-Bullshit Philosophy" — Marie Snyder uses Sartre's existentialism to unpack Louis's Conan monologue about the 'forever empty': with God gone we are condemned to be free, thrown into a world with no ready-made purpose and alone with our choices - which explains both the cellphone distraction economy and the Live in Portland bit that 'even if you're with someone, you're alone.' Authenticity means ruthlessly honest self-awareness and owning every choice with no excuses - Sartre's waiter example, the claim that there is no cowardly temperament, and Louis's refusal to let 'a flaw in the human male' excuse the tits bit or porn masturbation. Since in choosing for ourselves we choose for all humanity, Snyder pairs Sartre's universalized responsibility with Louis's 'act in a way that, if everybody acted that way, things would work out,' and reads intimate others, as in the Sartre-Beauvoir open relationship, as mirrors that reflect us back to ourselves against the connectionless 'we're just cummers' porn culture. Bad faith - self-deception, distraction, blame - is the fallenness Louis keeps diagnosing in his audiences and confessing in himself.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 26 "12. Confronting the “Forever Empty”" — Argues that Louis's 2013 Conan 'forever empty' confession—welcoming the sadness of listening to Bruce Springsteen alone in his car instead of texting—is an exemplary case of existentialist authenticity: Heideggerian anxiety discloses the nothingness beneath our projects, and Sartre's radical freedom, facticity, and bad faith explain why texting while driving and other distractions are escapes from self-creation. It then contrasts Eddie in Louie's 'Eddie' episode, whose suicide plan is a bad-faith loss of care and passion, with the 'Late Show' trilogy, where Janet exposes Louie's bad faith over the Letterman audition and he ends by shouting 'I did it!' at the Ed Sullivan Theater after Tardigan's scam.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 19 "9. When Jumpin’ Jack Flash Met Ziggy Stardust" — Auxier reads the 1973 Jagger-Bowie intimacy and rivalry ethically: Keith Richards's portrait of Mick's envy frames Kierkegaard's Either/Or warning against the aesthetic life and the Kantian morality-duty wedding Bowie fled, against Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity, which demands that one own one's freely chosen hollowing-out without appeal to any authority. Beauvoir's bad faith and authenticity then explain the outcome - Bowie beat Jagger by killing Ziggy, firing the Spiders, and finally making his very death a persona ('authentically Bowie'), while Jagger, forever only the Stones' singer, can respond only in bad faith, because 'hell is other people': each glimpsed the faker in the other.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 16 "7. Being for Red" — Courtland Lewis asks who Darrow is—Red, Gold, hybrid, savior—and surveys theories of the self: Plato's immortal soul ruling the body, Descartes's cogito as thinking thing, and Hume's denial that introspection ever reveals more than a stream of perceptions (we never experience a soul, only thinking). Freud's id-ego-superego offers a secular soul, but Sartre carries the chapter: Darrow is being-for-itself, perpetually projecting what he is not, tortured by the Look of others—Eo seeing a savior, Mustang holding him at gunpoint, Roque's betrayed friendship—and prone to bad faith through 'guardrails' like the Vale, excuses about Eo and Uncle Narol, and pining for Mustang instead of owning his choice. Since existence precedes essence, Darrow is nothing but the sum of his free choices, and to live otherwise is to choose slavery.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 16 "5. Guilty of Being a Dwarf" — Engels runs Tyrion's arc through Sartre's existentialism: his facticity as a dwarf makes everyone from Catelyn to Tywin presume his guilt, while 'Never forget what you are, wear it like armor' states the Sartrean authenticity of owning facticity while freely choosing one's essence. Catelyn's dagger accusation, the comic confession at the Eyrie, the wildfire ship at Blackwater, and the trial outburst ('I am guilty of a far more monstrous crime: the crime of being a dwarf') show him choosing rather than being defined; the murders of Shae and Tywin dramatize the slide into bad faith - embracing the 'monster' essence others assigned - before his choice to join Daenerys resumes the burden of self-creation.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 33 "18. No End to Philosophy" — Four vignettes pin philosophical problems to Peanuts' marginal characters: Camus's absurd - caring beings condemned to an uncaring universe - is answered by Sally's School Building, which grows a heart and drops bricks on her enemies; the 95472 kids motivate a tour of personal identity (same soul, same body, memory) through the Ship of Theseus; Pigpen's dirt raises Sartre's bad faith (facticity, transcendence, being-for-others) - we prize his authenticity over cleanliness - and Aristotle's golden mean, which moderates cleanliness while crediting his curiosity as a virtue; and finally the ontology of fictional characters asks whether the Kite-Eating Tree and Red Baron really exist inside the fiction and whether The Peanuts Movie's changed Charlie Brown counts as canon.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 24 "13. Weapon X Machina" — Cole Bowman argues Deadpool is the Marvel Universe's deus ex machina: phenomenologically alienated from a body he treats as a prop (cutting off his own hand to escape Colossus's manacle and flipping the silver behemoth the bird), he can step outside the causal chain the way Leibniz's Primary Truths says any genuinely free agent in a created order must. Sartre supplies the engine—radical freedom against determinism, with She-Hulk's shallow fourth-wall gags (killing the already-dead Porcupine) as bad faith by contrast and Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe as the extreme exercise of freedom against his creators and fans. Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy account of the deus ex machina replacing metaphysical consolation frames this new kind of inside-the-story god, who complicates plots rather than conveniently fixing them.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 18 "8.
