He then surveys infinite-universe speculation, quantum Many Worlds, and multiverse cosmology as readings of 'The Parallel,' where Major Gaines slips into a near-identical reality, before closing with Popper: since no experiment could in principle falsify the existence of other universes, the multiverse is unfalsifiable — a dimension of mind, not science.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 27 "15. The Twists and Turns of Second Chances" — Karavitis sorts TZ episodes into three types — nostalgia ('The Sixteen-Millimeter Shrine,' 'Walking Distance,' 'The Incredible World of Horace Ford'), time travel ('Back There,' 'No Time Like the Past'), and second chances ('Mr. Bevis,' 'A Game of Pool,' 'Printer's Devil') — to argue that the past is unalterable and that only moving forward, knowing yourself well enough to use it, earns a do-over. Kierkegaard's Either/Or supplies the philosophy: Rocky Valentine's wish-fulfilling Hell and Jesse Cardiff's eternity in the pool hall embody the aesthetic stage's repetitive despair, while Douglas Winter's renunciation of his Devil's contract in 'Printer's Devil' shows the transition to the ethical stage of taking responsibility for one's actions.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 14 "5. Getting Time Travel Right" — Duncan Gale asks whether Endgame 'gets time travel right,' using David Lewis's 'The Paradoxes of Time Travel' to explain personal time versus external time (Steve and Nebula meeting their past selves), causal loops (Tony quoting the saying about money and time back to Howard, who seemingly hears it first), and the grandfather paradox (Rhodey's baby-Thanos plan, which the existence of Nebula proves the Avengers would always fail to carry out). He traces Marvel's branching-timeline rule from Marvel Two-In-One #50 through the Ancient One's warning that removing a stone splits reality, and argues the film's moral is that the Avengers refuse quick resets and dutifully return the stones, while Thanos would shred the universe and rebuild a 'grateful' one. The chapter closes with Ivan Karamazov's challenge about building the edifice of human happiness on a tortured child's tears, which Thanos would accept and the Avengers refuse.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 15 "6. Nebula’s Time Travel Paradox" — Charlene Esby defends Endgame against the charge that Nebula killing her past self is a plot hole. She reconstructs the grandfather paradox from Nathaniel Schachner's 'Ancestral Voices,' explains how conceiving time as a fourth dimension makes travel conceivable, and deploys Aristotle's Physics (time as the number of change and rest) and the De Interpretatione sea-battle problem, where the past is necessary but the future contingent on present choices, to argue the Avengers' victory depends on free choices made now, which is why the Ancient One releases the Time Stone only on Banner's promise. The resolution is Hulk's subjective-timeline point: once traveled to, the past becomes the traveler's present, so present Nebula kills past Nebula in a shared present rather than negating her own future, just as Thanos from the past arrives alive in a present where he already died.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 16 "7. Something Strange about Time Travel" — Rhys Woodward asks how MCU time travel can be coherent when future Captain America fights past Captain America and future Nebula kills past Nebula, apparent contradictions a frozen Steve Rogers by contrast does not even count as time travel. He lays out David Lewis's view that a time traveler simply cannot do what would generate a logical contradiction, then argues the MCU is more permissive and proposes that Avengers time travel jumps not through one timeline but to alternate worlds, reading the Ancient One's 'branching' when a stone is removed as an allusion to the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics cued by the quantum realm of the Ant-Man films. On this multiverse reading past Nebula belongs to a different world history than future Nebula, so the murder does not erase the killer, and the apparent plot holes dissolve into deliberate clues.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 24 "Time to End" — Jones uses Kang to walk through the physics and metaphysics of time travel: Einstein's twin paradox (Quicksilver aging one year while Wanda's clock runs twenty), Gödel's spinning universe and van Stockum's cylinder yielding closed timelike curves, Thorne's wormhole time machine, and Hawking's Chronology Protection Conjecture against energy-stealing paradox loops. Applied to the comics, Prime Kang's purge of his flawed selves, Immortus's Forever Crystal, and Iron Lad's murder of his future self all confirm the fixed-timeline view: attempts to change the past only prune variants or create transient branches that snap back, so Kang can never un-become Kang. The Avengers end up as the Marvel Universe's Chronology Protection Agency, enforcing the rule that even where time travel exists, the past cannot be rewritten.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 9 "“One Can’t Believe Impossible Things”" — Laas runs BioShock Infinite through the free will debate: since the game posits Everett's many-worlds, every Booker is pinned by constants (the coin always landing heads, the always-recruited Bookers) and lacks alternate possibilities, which the incompatibilist would read as destroying responsibility. He answers with Frankfurt's counterexamples, modeling Jack's Little Sister choice under the hidden 'would you kindly' trigger with Atlas's prior-sign intervention as a Frankfurt case where one is responsible though one could not have done otherwise. The drowning ending then implies a 'transworld moral responsibility' in which every counterpart Booker is answerable for all Bookers, a secular massa damnata that the chapter finally challenges with Kant's 'ought implies can'.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 36 "The Real World" — Written as a choose-your-own-adventure whose branches mirror Bandersnatch's, the chapter treats you, the Netflix viewer, as the external force Stefan suspects: Libet-style readiness-potential neuroscience suggests conscious choice is an after-the-fact story, and compatibilist rescues (Frankfurt's second-order desires, Fischer's guidance control) founder on the 'BundyBot' argument that programmed desires are not freedom. Everett's many-worlds interpretation supplies the multiverse of 'one reality for each possible course of action,' and David Lewis's fixed-past block universe answers the grandfather paradox raised by Stefan's mirror-trip to die on the 8:45 train with his mother. Aristotle does double duty: the Poetics explains why Bandersnatch rightly limits your options (Sartrean absolute freedom would make a crappy story), and the Nicomachean Ethics on voluntary action pins moral responsibility for Stefan's murders on the viewer rather than the coerced Stefan. Adorno's culture industry asks whether Tuckersoft's 'hit factory' - and Black Mirror itself - can produce genuine art, while Kierkegaard's dread of irreversible choice is overturned by an episode that always lets you go back and try again.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 19 "We’ve Run Out of Time… or Have We" — The chapter argues that the film's multiverse, where sorcerers 'harness energy drawn from other dimensions,' is best modeled on the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics, walking through Tegmark's Level I-III multiverses, Schrodinger's cat, the double-slit experiment, and the measurement problem (Copenhagen, von Neumann-Wigner's mind-caused collapse, and Everett's branching) to show that interpreting the formalism is philosophy rather than physics. It defends many-worlds against the objections of counterintuition and Ockham's razor, and suggests that Strange trapping Dormammu in a time loop works like a quantum experiment, with branching worlds dissolving the grandfather paradox.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 29 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Kind uses John Stewart's Justice League arc, thrown into the future by Chronos, meeting his son Warhawk, and hiding it from Hawkgirl while dating Vixen, to stage fatalism: Pike and Taylor's arguments that a foreknown future, whether God's or a time traveler's, cannot be otherwise. Time travel itself forces a choice between presentism and eternalism, since Warhawk must 'exist now, already, in the future' for GL and Batman to visit him, and Smart's tenseless four-dimensionalism, with GL a series of timeslices and 'now' as subjective as 'here,' dissolves the fatalist worry by banishing tensed facts. The chapter lands on GL's battlefield advice to his son: 'Plant your feet,' owning a fate you cannot escape.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 35 "NOTES" — The section defends fixed time from the Prisoner of Azkaban episode, where later-Harry casts the stag Patronus that saved earlier-Harry and nothing about the past changes, against Hermione's warnings that wizards have killed their past selves, which the author recasts as travel between possible timelines. A special-relativity argument that there is no absolute present supports fixed time, and the cascade of lucky coincidences from brewing Polyjuice in Moaning Myrtle's bathroom through Felix Felicis, Malfoy Manor, and the Shrieking Shack finally suggests that some providential guide, rather than dumb luck, steered events toward the prophecy's fulfillment.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Luck argues backward time travel is nearly useless for a hero: after the grandfather paradox (Hiro hearing of Kaito's murder only because Kaito died), he shows Lewis's linear time travel makes Hiro necessarily fail to save Kaito, Charlie, or Isaac, yet cannot explain Hiro meeting Ando two days after a five-week absence or New York being spared. Branching time travel, where each trip into the past spawns an alternate universe, fits Volume 1 coherently by building a Heroes multiverse of Hiro-1 through Hiro-4 and explaining Future Hiro's subway appearance as a 'brute fact' copied into branching universes. The price of coherence is that Hiro only ever saves other universes' New Yorks, never his own.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 20 "NOTES" — Faraci asks why Hiro may prevent the nuclear future ('save the cheerleader') but comes to agree it would be wrong to save Kaito from the past ('we cannot play God'). Using thought experiments (a variant where Hiro learns of his father's death in the future) he isolates the past/future asymmetry as the candidate morally relevant factor, then tests justifications: Aquinas's natural law fails because observing the past would be equally 'unnatural,' and a duty to keep the timeline intact would also forbid changing the future, which is just as 'settled' to a time traveler. Since every theory of where Hiro's 'present' lies fails or collapses into subjectivity, he concludes there is no good reason to treat altering the past differently from altering the future, while demonstrating how normative ethics evaluates moral intuitions.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 8 "NOTES" — Davies defends Lost's convoluted plotting using Aristotle's Poetics, arguing the show works as a tragicomic epic that keeps closure and relevance even with Juliet's pre-crash storyline, genre mixing (Hurley's golf course beside Sayid's captivity), and shifting characters like Ben. He then uses the 'We have to go back' flash-forward to lay out McTaggart's two conceptions of time, eternalism versus presentism, and argues the flash-forward pushes viewers toward fatalism about Jack's already-fixed meeting with Kate near LAX. Finally he contends the past cannot be changed - Hurley in 2007 cannot undo his 1977 stay in the Dharma Initiative, since contradictions would entail everything - so viewers enjoy the time-travel plot by 'shielding' its mutually contradictory time lines.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 9 "None of It Matters Anyway, Then, Does It" — Devlin applies David Lewis's analysis of time travel (external versus personal time) to seasons 5 and 6: Faraday's 'whatever happened, happened' expresses an eternalist four-dimensional block universe in which Sayid's shooting of young Ben and Faraday's death at Eloise's hands were always part of the past. He reads the flash-sideways as initially exploring a branching-universe model in which Jughead's detonation actualizes an alternative 2004 time line. Lewis's tools then dissolve the puzzles: the Hurley-Miles 'we already had this conversation' exchange, baby and adult Miles as one person spread like a time-worm, the Faraday-kills-Eloise grandfather paradox, and the Locke-Richard compass causal loop, whose point of origin the show leaves unresolved.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 10 "NOTES" — Pierce argues that Lost's time travel runs on a fixed-time model in which nothing that happened can be undone, so the live question is ethical: Kate insists saving young Ben is still obligatory and Sayid remains responsible for shooting him, while Jack's plan to detonate Jughead at the Swan shows that trying to change the past can cause the very evil it targets, the Incident. Using Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity - future-tense truths made true by our own free choices - he shows that 'whatever happened, happened' does not abolish moral responsibility, applying the point to the Man in Black's causal-loop manipulation of Locke, Richard, and Ben. Desmond's consciousness travel in 'The Constant' is treated as the exception requiring hyper-time or alternate realities, and Pierce concludes that morality in time travel is simply ordinary morality, with Kate offering the most balanced view of the characters' choices.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 20 "The End" — Berghofer uses the Rebels episode 'A World Between Worlds' to ask whether Ezra changed the past when he pulled Ahsoka out of her duel with Vader, arguing that past-changing time travel breeds contradiction: the grandfather paradox looms over his attempt to save Kanan ('if he is taken out of this moment, you all die'), and on the Lewis-style consistent model Ezra caused but never changed the past. He surveys presentism, eternalism, and the growing block to locate Star Wars' metaphysics of time — Ezra's travel rules out presentism, and the Mortis god's 'the future, by its nature, can be changed' fits a growing block with an open future. Anakin's tragedy of acting to prevent prophesied events and thereby causing them frames the whole analysis.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 17 "NOTES" — Delfino and Sheahan assume that past-changing time travel is possible and find two flaws in The Terminator: the 'Bad Timing Problem,' where instantaneous 'time compression' (the rusted-nail thought experiment) means Reese entering the time machine after the T-101 is either too late or unnecessary, and the 'Who-Is-Your-Daddy? Problem,' where John must already exist to send Kyle back to father him - a vicious circle. Testing the two-timelines repair, they show it buys two different John Connors (a personal-identity problem), infinitely multiplying timelines, or a parallel-universes reading in which humanity both wins and loses. They conclude the story flirts with incoherence yet defend metaphysical imagination, with Kant's epigraph on our addiction to metaphysics and Aristotle's definition of wisdom as knowledge of deepest causes.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — Leiber develops three themes of the resistance: the time-travel paradoxes (Skynet's own mission proves the T-101 must fail, and future John has no need to send Reese), the moral status of machines, and the inevitability of smart weapons. La Mettrie's Man a Machine and Turing's 1950 test ground the claim that the T-101 who asks to be lowered into the molten steel is a rights-bearing person committing suicide, not a broken appliance - 'human chauvinism' says otherwise. Then, via Laplace's determinism, Einstein's conserved space-time, and his father Fritz Leiber's 'Law of Conservation of Reality,' he argues the continuum resists change, so 'Judgment Day is inevitable' is a scientist's claim about conserved mass-energy-time rather than a prophecy - with Augustine's puzzle about time framing why the future seems to protect the past.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Miller reconciles Kyle's 'no fate but what we make' with Sarah's 'you're dead already': eternalism (defended by the special-relativity argument Hilary Putnam made famous) makes 2029 as real as 1994, so Judgment Day cannot be changed, and the grandfather paradox - using Caesar's unalterable assassination as the model - blocks the T-101 from preventing its own existence. She then tests growing-block, presentist, meta-time, and branching-timeline (McCall-style) models against T2 and T3, asking whether any lets Sarah's attack on Cyberdyne legitimately delay Judgment Day. The conclusion works under every model: even on a fixed four-dimensional block, Judgment Day happens because of what humans do, not independently of them, so fixed fate and making our own future turn out to be compatible.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 9 "1. Lost in Time" — Rard argues that the suspended-animation heist of 'The Rip Van Winkle Caper' is not time travel, using David Lewis's definition (a discrepancy between the duration of the journey and the time between departure and arrival). 'Last Flight' illustrates a consistent causal loop: in 1959 Terry Decker learns he saved Mackaye in 1917, which motivates him to go back and do it, with nothing changed. 'No Time Like the Past' enacts Lewis's response to the grandfather paradox: Paul Driscoll's attempts to kill Hitler and warn Hiroshima are thwarted by mundane coincidences, and at Homeville he always was the one who caused the schoolhouse fire he tried to prevent.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 25 "14. The Science of Alternate Realities" — Morgan unpacks the science behind the 'fifth dimension': higher spatial dimensions as in the portal of 'Little Girl Lost,' Einstein's time as a fourth dimension with time-dilation travel ('A Kind of a Stopwatch'), and the grandfather paradox, which 'Back There' handles inconsistently (some events change, others cannot) while 'No Time Like the Past' gets right: past events are eternally true. Quantum many-worlds fits 'The Parallel,' where Major Gaines slips into a nearly identical reality, and infinite universes would make every possibility actual. But the cosmological multiverse, he argues with Popper's falsifiability criterion, is untestable and hence not science, remaining a dimension of mind and imagination.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 27 "15. The Twists and Turns of Second Chances" — Karavitis sorts episodes into three types to show that the past is dead and only moving forward counts: nostalgia ('The Sixteen-Millimeter Shrine,' 'A Stop at Willoughby,' 'Walking Distance'), time travel ('Back There,' 'No Time Like the Past,' where every attempt to fix history fails), and granted second chances ('A Nice Place to Visit,' 'A Game of Pool,' 'Printer's Devil'). Kierkegaard's Either/Or supplies the philosophy: Rocky Valentine's wish-factory and Jesse Cardiff's poolhall limbo depict the aesthetic stage's despair, while Douglas Winter taking responsibility for his pact shows the ethical stage. Second chances succeed only for those who, in Kierkegaard's words, live life forwards.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 7 "An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science Fiction Film" — Sanders's editorial introduction surveys the twelve essays, arguing that science fiction film and philosophy are thematically interdependent, and previews each film's problem: Deckard's possible replicant status in Blade Runner, Biderman's existential reading of Quaid in Total Recall, his own paranoia interpretation of Invasion of the Body Snatchers, McMahon's Heideggerian being-toward-death in Frankenstein. He raises critical objections of his own, e.g. that the 'Deckard is an android' inference is logically invalid and that equating computer rationality with value-free computability (2001, Colossus) cannot yield normative judgment.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 15 "Some Paradoxes of Time Travel in The Terminator and 12 Monkeys" — Devlin uses The Terminator and 12 Monkeys to work through time-travel paradoxes with David Lewis's framework. He resolves the personal-identity paradox of the two James Coles at the airport via Lewis's distinction between personal and external time, and treats the grandfather paradox differently for each film: 12 Monkeys holds a possibilist growing-universe model in which the fixed past cannot be changed (Cole cannot kill his younger self), while The Terminator adopts a branching-universe model allowing the past to change into an alternate timeline. He closes on the causal loop of the Army of the 12 Monkeys message, which lacks an origin unless uncaused causes are allowed.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 12 "We Wouldn’t Be Here Without Time Travel" — Peter Worley finishes the Doctor's "wibbly-wobbly" speech from "Blink" by distinguishing empirical from logical possibility (via a fictional chat with Leonardo about a round-square) and asking whether time travel is coherent. Using "The Edge of Destruction," "The Aztecs," "The Visitation," and "Turn Left," he deploys David Lewis's external-versus-personal time distinction and Lewis's rule that a time traveler's acts must be the very events that made history, then treats the Doctor and Lewis as "actualists" about possible worlds to dissolve grandfather-style paradoxes and time loops.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 13 "The Daleks Can Stop the Pyramids from Being Built!" — Philip Goff asks whether Daleks could travel back and stop the pyramids being built, arguing the answer turns on one's theory of time. He shows presentism forbids travel to a non-existent past and eternalism permits travel but forbids changing a static block, then defends the growing-block theory (past and present real, future not) as a middle way that lets time travelers genuinely alter history. He works out how a new pyramid-less history advances at the same rate as the present, never overwriting it, and distinguishes concrete from abstract past existence to keep historical records true.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 14 "Prognosis" — William Eaton reconstructs the Doctor's "Blink" philosophy of time using David Lewis's four-dimensionalism. He shows how Lewis's external/personal-time distinction explains the Doctor meeting his own regenerations and reversed causation (a black eye before the punch), and how "Blink" hinges on a closed causal chain (the DVD Easter-egg transcript that authors itself). He rehearses the Grandfather/Bilking paradox and Lewis's "can" equivocation solution, then places the Doctor alongside Horwich and Ismael, arguing the Doctor goes furthest by holding closed causal chains actually exist.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 19 "Time Travel and Fixed Time" — Pierce uses Harry Potter's prophecies to analyze destiny, fixed time, and freedom. Distinguishing Trelawney's fraudulent fortune-telling from her two genuine prophecies, he classifies kinds of prophecy (fallible, infallible, self-fulfilling) and, drawing on Aristotle's sea-battle problem and Alexander of Aphrodisias, argues Voldemort's choice of Harry rather than the prophecy itself made it true. He then sorts compatibilist and libertarian readings of Rowling's denial of destiny, argues her time travel (saving Buckbeak) implies a fixed view of time consistent with relativity, and suggests the improbable luck fulfilling prophecies hints at providential guidance.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 8 "NOTES" — Richard Davies uses Aristotle's Poetics (the principles of closure, relevance, and the unities of place and time) to defend Lost's tangled narrative as an epic rather than a broken tragedy, arguing that flashbacks, flash-forwards like Jack's 'We have to go back,' and multi-season arcs such as Juliet's remain within Aristotelian bounds. He then imports McTaggart's contrast between eternalism and presentism to explain why a flash-forward is philosophically unsettling, and argues that changing the past (as season 5's time travel invites) generates a logical contradiction from which anything follows, so viewers must 'shield' Hurley's 1977 experiences to keep enjoying the plot.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 9 "None of It Matters Anyway, Then, Does It" — William J. Devlin applies David Lewis's distinction between external time and the traveler's personal time to Lost's season 5-6 time jumps, showing how Faraday's eternalist 'whatever happened, happened' (Chang's unbreakable rules) contrasts with the branching-universe model that Faraday later embraces with 'we're the variables.' Lewis's account resolves specific puzzles: why baby Miles and adult Miles can coexist without violating the indiscernibility of identicals, whether Faraday could kill his mother Eloise (the grandfather paradox), and the uncaused causal loop of the compass Locke and Richard pass between 1954 and 2007.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 10 "NOTES" — Jeremy Pierce argues that Lost mostly assumes fixed (eternalist) time and moves from its metaphysics to its ethics: even if 'whatever happened, happened,' ordinary morality still applies, so Sayid's shooting young Ben is wrong regardless of his good intentions and Jack is responsible for detonating Jughead even though he causes the very Incident he meant to prevent. Invoking Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity, Pierce holds that foreknowledge (the Man in Black's manipulation, Desmond's course-corrected saving of Charlie) does not erase free choice, concluding via Kate that morality in time travel is 'simply morality, period.'
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 9 "1. Lost in Time" — Rard uses David Lewis's definition of time travel—a discrepancy between the duration of the journey and the gap between departure and arrival—to show that 'The Rip Van Winkle Caper' suspended-animation heist is NOT time travel, while 'Last Flight' (Terry returning to save Mackaye) is, complete with a self-consistent causal loop. She then applies Lewis's argument that mundane events always thwart attempts to change the past to 'No Time Like the Past,' where Paul Driscoll is repeatedly distracted from killing Hitler and even accidentally causes the schoolhouse fire he meant to prevent, illustrating that the past is unalterable but interactable.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 25 "14. The Science of Alternate Realities" — Morgan surveys the physics and philosophy behind the show's 'fifth dimension': higher spatial dimensions and parallel universes ('Little Girl Lost'), time as Einstein's fourth dimension and relativistic time dilation ('A Kind of a Stopwatch'), the Grandfather Paradox and the self-consistency of time travel ('Back There,' 'No Time Like the Past'), the Many Worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics ('The Parallel'), and the cosmological multiverse. He closes with Popper's falsification criterion, arguing that unobservable other universes may be, like the show itself, forever 'a dimension of mind.'
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 16 "What Happens to the Present When It Becomes the Past" — Daniels asks whether the airline passengers in The Langoliers are truly time travelers and what theory of time their dead, tasteless past implies. Using David Lewis's distinction between 'personal time' and 'external time,' he shows the discrepancy between the characters' day-long journey and the few hours that elapse in the present qualifies them as genuine time travelers despite the deserted world. He then rules out presentism (incompatible with time travel via the 'nowhere problem') and eternalism (which denies any privileged present), arguing the vibrant, 'oomph'-laden moving now the characters race to rejoin fits the moving spotlight theory, while the langoliers merely consume the world's contents, not spacetime itself.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 18 "Time Belongs to the Tower" — Auxier frames King as 'Tolkien meets Poe' and reads the Dark Tower's temporalization through the literary and psychological experience of time. Drawing on Susanne Langer's 'virtual present' and Sartre's psychology of imagination, he argues readers surrender their real present to a novel's suspended time, which he links to William James's 'will to believe' rather than mere suspension of disbelief. He uses Kant's distinction between amazement (seeing the seemingly impossible) and admiration (accepting it) to explain the psychological cost time travelers like Jake Epping and Wesley Smith should pay, faulting King for keeping ordinary heroes sane while displacing the strain onto insane 'gatekeepers,' and concludes the Tower is 'real' as the way each person binds possibility to their own lived past, present, and future.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 19 "Ur 88,416" — Auxier reconstructs the metaphysics of King's Tower across Ur and 11/22/63, treating imagination as a power that defies present time to reach the 'nowhen.' He maps King's multiverse onto Everett's many-worlds and Brian Greene's quantum/quilted multiverses, then extracts three 'laws of Dark Tower dynamics': the obduracy of the past (resistance proportional to how much the future would change), the conservation of harmony (time-strings converging like sympathetic guitar strings on an ideal order), and the danse macabre. He shows the 'reset' Jake believes in is really the creation of new Ur strings, dismantles Al Templeton's meat-buying and epistemic-radiation theories via thermodynamics, and closes with Kant's three functions of imagination to argue time travel is a 'plausible impossible' symbol we can imagine but never actually enact.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 15 "Who is Who" — The time-travel chapter grounds Doctor Who's paradoxes in Parmenides and Zeno on the impossibility of change and Aristotle on the logical necessity of past and future statements ('You can't rewrite history!' in 'The Aztecs'), then deploys determinism, David Lewis on the paradoxes of time travel, and the consistency/autonomy principles ('Father's Day,' the Reapers). It uses Leibniz's possible worlds and the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics to read 'Inferno' and 'Turn Left,' arguing quantum indeterminacy and entanglement make the Doctor's 'wibbly-wobbly, timey-wimey' theory of fixed points and flux coherent.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 19 "Time Travel and Fixed Time" — Jeremy Pierce analyzes prophecy and destiny in Harry Potter, distinguishing fallible from infallible prophecies and cataloguing how a Seer might access a fixed or open future (raising Aristotle's sea-battle problem about future truths). He argues Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are not merely likely guesses and considers self-fulfilling readings (via Alexander of Aphrodisias and Oedipus), which he rejects since the prophecy did not force Voldemort's choice. Reading Rowling's denial of 'destiny' against her fixed-time treatment of time travel and the improbable luck that fulfills the prophecy, he suggests the story fits a fixed future guided by providence better than libertarian openness or sheer coincidence.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 9 "7. Doctor Who as Philosophy Four-Dimensionalism and Time Travel" — Decker asks what the universe must be like if Doctor Who's time travel were real, using David Lewis's distinction between personal and external time and the TARDIS as a Wellsian (not Thornian) time machine traversing a 'hypertime' vortex. After surveying the arrows of time and paradoxes like the bootstrap paradox ('Day of the Daleks') and the grandfather paradox (imagined via Tegan's grandfather), and rejecting Deutsch-Lockwood's Many-Worlds and growing-block solutions, he argues the Whoniverse fits 'Four-Dimensional Realism'/eternalism, quoting the Twelfth Doctor that time's passage is an illusion of 'still pictures.' He then confronts 4DR's threat to free will and moral responsibility, finding compatibilism and 'fixed points' inadequate given eternalism's succession-not-production of events.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 20 "18. Russian Doll as Philosophy Life Is Like a Box of Timelines" — The chapter treats Russian Doll's time loops (Season One) and time portals (Season Two) as vehicles for the metaphysics of time, comparing them to Groundhog Day and canvassing presentism, eternalism, and the growing-block theory. It argues the show is committed to a Parfit-style 'multiple timelines' solution to the problem of whether looped characters are numerically identical, and rejects a Berkeleyan idealist alternative. Its climax reads Nadia through Camus's Myth of Sisyphus: unable to change significant past events, she becomes an 'absurd hero' who embraces her family and lot in life, smiling in the mirror, so Season Two's lesson (echoing Nietzsche's eternal recurrence) is that meaning comes from owning one's circumstances.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 60 "57. Tenet as Philosophy Fatalism Isn’t an Excuse to Do Nothing" — The chapter reads Nolan's Tenet as an argument for metaphysical fatalism set in a block-universe (eternalism), using the Sator Square, the palindromic 'ten,' and Neil's refrain 'what's happened, happened' as evidence that every event, including the Protagonist's and Kat's, was fated and unchangeable. It deploys David Lewis's solution to the grandfather paradox and reverse causation (Feynman/Wheeler positrons) to show the future cannot kill its ancestors, then argues fatalism entails no libertarian free will, rejecting Frankfurt's compatibilist second-order-desires account and citing van Inwagen that indeterministic acts are no freer. Via a back-tracking counterfactual it concludes fatalism is still no excuse to do nothing, because different action would have yielded a different (annihilated) world.

### Falsificationism

Falsificationism is Karl Popper's proposal that what distinguishes genuine science from pseudoscience is not verifiability but falsifiability: a theory is scientific only if it forbids something and can in principle be refuted by observation. Popper rejected the idea that we confirm theories by piling up supporting instances, arguing instead that we can never prove a universal law true but can decisively show it false. On this account science advances through bold conjectures exposed to severe testing, with theories provisionally accepted only so long as they survive sincere attempts to refute them.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 16 "Pals" — Madeline Muntersbjorn uses Season Four's Initiative-versus-Scoobies conflict to dissolve the Science Wars: Professor Walsh's secret, unfalsifiable Project 314 makes her Karl Popper's bad scientist, while Buffy's gang embodies Feyerabend's pluralism and Peirce-and-James pragmatism — Buffyverse rules are probabilistic rather than deterministic, and the gang welcomes anyone willing to ask questions and do research. Her three ideals — pluralism, pragmatism, pals — culminate in 'Primeval,' where the combo-Buffy enjoining spell (Willow's spirit, Xander's heart, Giles's mind, Buffy's hand) literally enacts James's meliorism: the world may be saved if each agent does their level best, together. Walsh dies alone because she has no pals; Buffy saves the world 'a lot' because she does.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 19 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Steele starts from Orwell's worry that laypeople accept scientific consensus as unreflectively as tribesmen accept witch-doctors — sharpened by Lysenko and Nazi 'racial science' — and answers it with Popper's critical rationalism: since Hume's problem of induction bars proof from instances, we can only provisionally prefer theories that survive severe attempts at falsification, so trusting experts is reasonable exactly when their community tests rather than defends its theories. Kuhn's paradigms explain why dissident alternatives like Atkins talk past the dominant school (Atkins and Agatston are cardiologists, not dieticians), and the 2002–2004 studies showing improved lipids on more fat figure as the kind of surprise that precedes paradigm change. His verdict: neither trusting nor resisting experts is foolish; 'human knowledge is too important to be left to experts.'
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 7 "Bullshit and Philosophy" — 'The Year in Bullshit' catalogues the fraud climate surrounding the book's success: James Frey's fabricated memoir A Million Little Pieces exposed on Oprah, the wholly invented author J.T. Leroy, product placement and paid word-of-mouth advertising blurring the line between ads and ordinary conversation, and scientific fraud in pharmaceutical and federal research. It invokes Karl Popper's claim that science deserves respect precisely because it falsifies its own claims, presenting headlines about fabricated results as that ideal fading. Frank Rich's verdict that 'such distinctions have long since washed away in much of our public life' supplies the chapter's explanation of the book's appeal as cultural despair.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 94 "Combatting the Two Kinds of Bullshit" — Douglas argues that 'universal standards bullshit' — the assumption that evidence must meet one threshold before it counts as scientific — comes from textbook schooling and has no warrant: there is no such standard, and we shouldn't want one. She shows how it distorts debate on all sides, from Bush administration uncertainty claims to Michael Gough's Popper-inspired insistence that climate models cannot be tested, and argues that whether evidence suffices always depends on the risks of error — the gas-gauge warning versus the bomb in your car. Genuine politicization (suppressing evidence, firing researchers) must be condemned, but deciding how much uncertainty is acceptable is an ineliminably political and ethical judgment.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 9 "Is Monk’s Certainty Justified" — Rauhut tests Monk's method against two models of discovery: Holmes-style eliminatism, modeled on Popper's falsification via reductio ad absurdum, and CSI-style confirmationism in the mold of Hempel and Carnap (Gil Grissom letting evidence speak). Monk fits neither — in 'Mr. Monk and the Astronaut' he refuses to eliminate the alibi-solid Steve Wagner, and in 'Mr. Monk Falls in Love' he ignores a hatpin, a motive, and a confession pointing at Leyla. Instead Monk is an 'epiphanist': he registers every anomaly (the secretary hired from a Lamaze-class ad in 'Mr. Monk Fights City Hall', Crawford's odd phrasing 'No, she wouldn't be drinking now'), suddenly sees the one theory explaining all of them, and only afterwards manufactures shareable evidence for others. His absolute certainty, the chapter argues, rests on a metaphysical faith that only the true theory can explain every anomaly — a Leibnizian 'best of all possible ordered worlds' — the same obsession with order that makes him notice anomalies at all, though it makes him epistemically irresponsible by ordinary standards that weigh alternative hypotheses and simplicity.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 8 "Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New ‘Intelligent Falling’ Theory" — Ruiz uses Onion stories—'Jesus Answers Half The Prayers At Area Roulette Table,' 'God Answers Prayers Of Paralyzed Little Boy,' 'Christianity Celebrates One Billionth Unanswered Prayer'—to argue that belief in God lacks rational justification. Following Hume's empiricism (all ideas trace to sense perception), methodological naturalism, and Ockham's Razor, he shows that feelings of God's presence, scriptural circularity, and answered prayers (riddled with selection bias) all fail as evidence, and the prayer hypothesis is unfalsifiable—a theory that explains any outcome, like the brain tumor thanking God for its surviving surgery, is supported by no evidence. He closes by dismantling Paley's watchmaker design argument through the infinite regress ('who designed God?') and by treating 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' as the reductio of design reasoning.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 26 "The Future of Sandy Cheeks" — Wilson González-Espada assesses Sandy Cheeks as a portrait of the scientist: she explodes the 'Draw a Scientist' stereotype — female, socially popular, working in an open treedome that mirrors peer review — yet the show muddles the nature of science, calling inventions 'experiments' and a clipboard of math 'science'. The chapter applies Popper's falsifiability to SpongeBob's one-sided evidence that Squidward is a true friend and Newton's principle of parsimony to Sandy's ghost scare, then closes with Aldo Leopold's land ethic, reading 'Jellyfish Hunter' and 'SpongeBob's Last Stand' as environmental parables about habitat and overexploitation.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 32 "Our Best Bet" — Terjesen argues Mycroft surpasses Sherlock because he truly grasps Hume's Problem of Induction: Sherlock's celebrated eliminations (the three key possibilities for Cadogan West in 'The Bruce-Partington Plans') and his newspaper-ad tests are inductive, Popperian conjecture-testing that can never confirm anything, while Goodman's 'grue' shows the same evidence always supports rival explanations. Watson's failed attempt in 'How Watson Learned the Trick,' the amateur reasoner's wrong solution in 'The Lost Special,' and Holmes's own 'Norbury' failure in 'The Yellow Face' prove that a correct method guarantees nothing. Mycroft, who 'would rather be considered wrong than take the trouble to prove himself right,' implicitly embraces Reichenbach's pragmatic justification — induction is simply our best bet — and therefore hunts longer for the facts that do not fit, acting only when England's fate is at stake.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 103 "Circles within Circles" — Applies Imre Lakatos's 'degenerating research programs' — geocentric astronomy surviving by adding epicycles — to conspiracy theories like Pentagon 'truthers' who must keep patching their account to explain debris, eyewitnesses, and phone calls. But David Coady's rejoinder, voiced through Lies, Inc. where the 'cranks' who doubted Whale's Mouth were right, and the makeshift excuses for Saddam's WMD, show the official story can be the degenerating program, so rejecting conspiracy theories out of hand leaves you easily manipulated.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 127 "Philip K. Dick and Philosophy" — The section argues Precrime needs no evidence of an actual murder, attempt, or plot because pre-criminals are charged with future-murder, which, unlike plots that fizzle or attempts that bungle, always succeeds absent intervention. Using Anderton's demonstration of Witwer's caught ball, it distinguishes a person's NA-future (if not arrested) from the A-future (if arrested), concluding that what happens after an arrest cannot falsify an NA-prediction, since the prediction only ever described the uninterfered-with path.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 15 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Cooke defends his three-year lawful-evil wizard campaign against religious and secular critics by dismantling each style of argument. The propaganda charge fails because D&D rulebooks present no 'attitudes for export' about the real world; the puzzle of imaginative resistance dissolves once Can'tian and Won'tian readings are rejected for a 'Hardian' view that some things are merely hard to imagine, undercutting Dadlez's explanation of the Romulan spy's angry opponents; and the Werther-effect-style empirical case against D&D collapses on the data like parallel panics over jazz, video games, and pornography. The remaining character-warping objection—the Platonic and Aristotelian habituation worry that enjoying evil play mistrains the sentiments Hume warned about—turns unfalsifiable in the way repressed-desire claims do, leaving a firm moral gap between imagining evil and doing it.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 15 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Bernard Rollin reads Dr. Zaius's tribunal as 'scientific ideology' in action - 'human see, human do' refuses to believe its own eyes, just as bishops refused to look through Galileo's telescope. He traces the ideology from Newton's 'hypotheses non fingo' through logical positivism's verifiability criterion (which validates the Hasslein Curve prediction while rendering 'there are intelligent beings in Heaven' meaningless) and Wittgenstein's point that 'killing is wrong' is not a fact of the universe, to the 'science is value-free' dogma that left animal pain untested and untreated - as he documents from his own campaign: the empty analgesic literature search, the 1985 federal legislation, and the pain physiologist whose dog research refutes his own denial. Zira's neurosurgery on mute humans repeats what Descartes's beast-machine doctrine licensed, and IASP's language requirement for pain collapses into a Cratylus-grade confusion of necessary and sufficient conditions ('You can't step into the same river once').
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 21 "Psych and Philosophy" — Mahon and Ceballos read the pilot through the big-lie principle credited to Hitler and Goebbels: the truth - hyper-observation plus a photographic memory - is too mundane to be believed, so only the biggest possible lie, 'I am a psychic,' saves Shawn from jail, exploiting the reverse psychology by which hearers assume no liar would say something so implausible. The lie's durability is then explained with Karl Popper's falsifiability criterion: like horoscopes and psychoanalysis, Shawn's psychic claim is unfalsifiable, so the ex-con's finger-counting 'tests' in 'Woman Seeking Dead Husband' can confirm it but never refute it - a virtue for a liar, and precisely what makes a claim unscientific. Finally the chapter shifts blame to the victims: like Madoff investors who 'kind of saw it coming,' the SBPD is self-deceived, complicit in a lie it half knows is a lie because the gift horse keeps closing cases.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 33 "Psych and Philosophy" — Courtney Neal explains that Santa Barbara believes Shawn is psychic because pseudoscience offers easier, more appealing explanations than the truth: in the pilot, 'he's psychic' beats 'he's the killer' as a narrative that fits the facts, and psychic claims are worded so they cannot be disproved. She shows how Shawn's real observational deductions are packaged through cold reading (the comic-convention scene in 'Shawn vs. the Red Phantom'), Robert Cialdini's social-influence principles of liking, social proof, and commitment/consistency, and the self-fulfilling prophecy of his reputation - so even Lassiter's skepticism cannot dislodge a belief the city keeps confirming.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 40 "Psych and Philosophy" — This chapter is a skeptical debunking tour of real-life 'psycho psychics' - Babylonian astrologers, the Delphi oracle that set Socrates testing the claim he was wisest, Nostradamus's hindsight-friendly quatrains, Blavatsky, Cayce, spoon-bender Uri Geller, and Sylvia Browne's failed Shawn Hornbeck prediction - arguing that no repeatable, peer-reviewed evidence of ESP has ever existed and that figures like cold-reading psychic detective Peter Hurkos thrive on gullibility. It ties to Psych through Gus's credulity about UFOs and werewolves and the real police practice of consulting psychic detectives that Shawn's con parodies, while Houdini's congressional testimony and James Randi's Million Dollar Challenge model the evidence-demanding skepticism the show's fake psychic gets away from.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 35 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Peter Stone applies Dawkins's memetics and Dennett's Breaking the Spell to the rise of 'Hallelujah' from the troubled release of Various Positions to ubiquity via John Cale, Jeff Buckley, Shrek, and Rufus Wainwright. On Dennett's account religious memes thrive through hyperactive agency detection, doctrines rendered unfalsifiable and thus immune to evidence, and 'belief in belief' - and 'Hallelujah' is religiously ambiguous enough, from David and Bathsheba to Buckley's 'hallelujah of the orgasm,' to be as religious as any singer or congregation wants it to be, whether as Rabbi Kagan's hymn of the heretic or the Holy Trinity Church's 'Amazing Grace' lyric swap. Machiavelli's maxim that fortune governs half the outcome frames the song's lucky trajectory, and its carefully engineered ambiguity makes it a set of very 'happy memes' likely to keep replicating.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 9 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Karavitis argues Finn's 'Finn-losophy' is a metaphysics that prefers magic over Princess Bubblegum's science, and that this choice shapes his ethics: magic is the 'easy way out' requiring no understanding (Jake's stretching, the Glasses of Nerdicon), while science demands observation, experiment, and falsifiable ideas—'reality is the ultimate spell-checker.' Because magic promises instant gratification, Finn rushes into danger ('Wizard,' 'Donny,' the Goblin Kingdom) behind an inflexible hero code, and his altruism misfires, as the never-ending prize-winning battles of the 'Mystery Train' episode illustrate. The chapter concludes that your view of how the world works—magical or scientific—determines whether you can grow ethically at all.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 26 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Russ Hamer takes Mac's 'Science Is a Liar Sometimes' defense - Aristotle, Galileo, and Newton each proved his predecessor 'a bitch' - and his claim that believing in evolution takes as much faith as belief in God, and answers with philosophy of science. Popper's falsificationism explains why Mac's 'I won't change my mind... regardless of the facts' is the essence of the non-scientific: only theories risking precise, falsifiable predictions (Einstein's light deflection) count as science, unlike vague astrology or Charlie's cherry-picked evidence that the Waitress will love him. Kuhn's distinction of normal and revolutionary science explains why past failures never discredited science - falsifications within a paradigm are tuning, and the Gang's group-configuration trials in 'The Gang Solves the Gas Crisis' are normal science at its best - so revisability is science's strength, not a reason to fear looking like a science bitch.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 38 "18. Gruesome Walkers" — Yuen turns the walkers into a lesson on Hume's problem of induction: the pre-apocalyptic belief that the dead do not rise was justified by all past experience until Rick wakes to a world where they do, and Rick's distrust of Alexandria repeats the same inductive move from Woodbury, Terminus, and Grady - useful, Hume says, since custom compels us, but never knowledge. Russell's chicken illustrates the fatal surprise, and Goodman's grue (the pun of the title) shows the outbreak could be a future-swinging regularity like the seventeen-year cicadas, undermining even Jenner's experimental science. Popper's falsificationism is offered as the rescue - Shane's reanimation falsifies the "walkers make walkers" theory, leaving the "everyone is infected" theory corroborated but never known.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 18 "8. Is It a Fact that Facts Don’t Matter" — Steele distinguishes facts as mind-independent reality from facts as expert-certified statements to show that Kellyanne Conway's alternative facts and Adams's own slogans trade on this ambiguity, and that Adams performatively contradicts himself every time he insists his predictions are true and matter. Analyzing the cognitive-dissonance hallucinations of Trump-is-Hitler and then Trump-is-incompetent, he argues that on Adams's own account brute facts proved irresistible, and that such belief revision is rational Popperian conjecture and refutation, plus the conservative strategy of saving fundamental theories (Coulomb's law) and dropping minor ones when the fuse blows. Against the claim that humans are irrational he recalls Aristotle's Rhetoric as persuasion's legitimate complement to the Prior Analytics, and leans on Percival to show propaganda fits a rational-reader model, citing the slow, fact-driven shift on gay marriage.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 27 "15. Bias Is Rational!" — Percival, whose Myth of the Closed Mind Adams cites, rebuts the Moist Robot Hypothesis that visual, emotional, repetitive anchors make us ninety-percent irrational. Against Kahneman's fast-and-dumb System 1 he sets Gigerenzer's ecological rationality (the gaze-angle heuristic that catches fly balls, the recognition heuristic that lets ignorant German students beat Americans on Detroit versus Milwaukee), then goes further with Popper's critical rationalism: babies as little scientists conjecturing and refuting, experience always theory-laden (the duck-rabbit), and Newton's boy on the seashore facing an infinite but navigable ocean of error elimination. The Stoic insight that all emotion is thoughtful and all thought emotional (the falling-tiles misperception that flips anger to relief) shows feelings track beliefs, so a free battle of the biases, not fact-free affirmation in the lineage of Le Bon and Pavlovian conditioning, is how rationality actually works.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 28 "16. Why Scott Adams Is Stupid" — Miori audits Adams's science talk through epistemology: warrant for belief, empiricism versus rationalism, Wittgenstein's demand for unambiguous clarity, and Clifford's epistemic responsibility, that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence, which condemns sampling television news while blogging on climate science. Popper's falsifiability, learned from Einstein's willingness to be refuted against Freud's confirmation-seeking, exposes Adams's double standard in waving confirmation bias at critics while crediting his own predictions, and Feyerabend's epistemological anarchism is the view Adams most resembles, except that Feyerabend took responsibility and retracted. Cipolla's Basic Laws of Human Stupidity (the stupid person causes losses to both self and others) frames the closing charge: Adams suggests and retreats, sells product, and shirks the epistemic duty that experts in climate science and medicine shoulder.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 25 "14. The Science of Alternate Realities" — Morgan explains what a dimension is mathematically (hypercubes, with 'Little Girl Lost' as a portal into the fourth spatial dimension) and then time as the fourth dimension in Einstein's relativity, using time dilation and the Grandfather Paradox to contrast 'Back There,' which inconsistently lets Corrigan alter some outcomes of Lincoln's assassination, with 'No Time Like the Past,' where Driscoll fails exactly as an eternally fixed past requires. He then surveys infinite-universe speculation, quantum Many Worlds, and multiverse cosmology as readings of 'The Parallel,' where Major Gaines slips into a near-identical reality, before closing with Popper: since no experiment could in principle falsify the existence of other universes, the multiverse is unfalsifiable — a dimension of mind, not science.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 15 "The Lasting Legacy of Logic" — Treats Carroll the Oxford logician as a teacher hiding five lessons in Wonderland: watch your assumptions (the King infers the Knave's guilt from an unsigned letter), know what your words mean (Humpty Dumpty on 'glory'), don't confuse categories (the King's 'Nobody' and the Hatter's personified Time), don't switch subjects and predicates ('I mean what I say' versus 'I say what I mean'), and don't confuse necessary with sufficient conditions (Alice's Ada and Mabel arguments, with a hammer-and-egg illustration). David S. Brown grounds the lessons in Hume on causes discoverable only by experience, Aristotle's law of non-contradiction and categories, the Marx Brothers' 'Either he's dead or my watch has stopped', and Popper's point that a successful prediction cannot prove a hypothesis, only a failed one can refute it.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 18 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Jones explains the Leonard–Leslie breakup ('Tell me, Leonard, how would we raise the children?') as a genuine clash of research commitments: string theory with its demanded extra dimensions versus Leslie's loop quantum gravity. Along the way he uses Popper's falsifiability and Kuhn's paradigms — the 1998 dark-energy discovery as falsification at work, Sheldon's alien-parasite hypothesis as paradigm-protecting refusal to accept that Amy is aroused by Zack — and the Dirac-to-Anderson antimatter story alongside Sheldon's North Pole monopole expedition to weigh theoretical against experimental science. Leonard emerges as the Feynman-style skeptic ('At best you can say, hey, my idea has internal logical consistency'), which is exactly what Leslie cannot forgive.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 28 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Pigliucci reads the 'Evolution, Schmevolution' series (Helms's Dayton, Tennessee reenactment-town piece, Stewart's panel with ID proponent Dembski and the scrotum question) as one of the best media treatments of the creation-evolution controversy. Popper's falsificationism marks intelligent design as non-science, since Dembski's designer works outside testable law and miracles are, as Larson says, unrepeatable and unfalsifiable, while Stewart's bad-design jokes about the scrotum and Mayr's 99.99% extinction figure replay the problem of evil. A compressed tour of rationalism (Plato to Descartes's radical doubt) versus Hume's empiricism explains why science yields tentative conclusions, and the chapter ends that resolving the controversy, like Aristotle's eudaimonia, is a lifelong personal project.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 18 "Of Science, Sorcery, and Philosophy" — The chapter reads Strange's conversion from neurosurgeon to sorcerer as a Kuhnian paradigm shift: his medical materialism is 'normal science' puzzle-solving that keeps resisting anomalies (Pangborn's impossible recovery, the astral projection, the multiverse tour) until Kamar-Taj offers a rival paradigm with its own exemplars, which he can only adopt by learning 'knowledge how' through tedious practice. It explains incommensurability through Strange's inability to rationally persuade his old medical colleagues, then contrasts Kuhn with Popper's falsificationism, Feyerabend's 'anything goes' anarchism (sorcery once looked as disreputable as early heliocentrism), and Lakatos's progressive versus degenerating research programs to ask whether sorcery could count as a science in Strange's world.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 15 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Cooke defends his three-year campaign of a lawful evil wizard (Oraximon, who magic-missiled an innkeeper and hid the bodies in a rope trick) against religious and secular critics. The epistemic charge fails because rulebooks are invitations to imagine, not assertions, and the Smurfs-as-Krishna example shows an 'attitude for export' needs authorial evidence D&D lacks; Hume's twin claims about the impropriety of imaginatively endorsing flawed sentiments are dismantled by splitting Can'tians from Won'tians over Gendler's stories and defending a 'Hardian' view on which resistance is just difficulty, making imaginative resistance a chimera. The causal charge fails on the evidence (the Werther effect and its video-game and jazz cousins are post hoc plus confirmation bias), the character-warping charge risks the unfalsifiability of the repressed-desire diagnosis, and Plato's ban on the arts — enforced via the noble lie — would be the price if imagining were as bad as doing.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 22 "NOTES" — Asks how to tell genuine science from pseudoscience using Chandra Suresh's rejected Activating Evolution theory, Sheldrake's morphic fields, alchemy, and Behe's intelligent design. Kuhn's picture of normal science, anomalies, and revolutions explains why Suresh would need a full-blown crisis in evolutionary theory — such as people actually flying — before the community accepts him, and why time rather than mockery settles a theory's fate. Ockham's razor condemns the unnecessary organizing principles in both Sheldrake's and Suresh's theories, and intelligent design is exposed as bad method because, like creationism, it was devised to protect a prior commitment from disconfirming fossil and cosmological evidence.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Addey analyzes the show's web of coincidences - Sawyer and Boone crossing paths in the Australian police station, Jack meeting Desmond in the hatch - and distinguishes genuine coincidence from divine providence, fatalism, and determinism. She applies Jung's theory of synchronicity to Locke's walkabout conviction that he was 'meant' to reach the island, then uses the birthday paradox, the law of truly large numbers, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability to show why viewers and conspiracy theorists overestimate the improbability of such connections. Finally she evaluates Jacob's candidacy experiment as flawed social science: the candidates' circumstantial ignorance, maintained by the Others' deceptions, undermines the free and morally responsible choices Jacob claims to be testing, which is why the curious Hurley deserved to become protector.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 13 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Dueck takes Stan's closing pluralism in 'Super Best Friends'—all religions have something valuable to teach, as the interfaith superheroes' combined powers defeat Blaine—and tests it against Hick's pluralism, exclusivism, and Rahner's inclusivist 'anonymous Christians', using 'Go God Go's warring atheist factions to show exclusivity is unavoidable even without God. Hume's miracle argument explains why Jesus's look-away water-into-wine trick convinces no one in the episode: testimony can never outweigh the laws of nature, so supernatural evidence resists natural evaluation. Popper's falsificationism warns that watering doctrines down to make religions compatible (the rabbit-pope of 'Fantastic Easter Special') leaves nothing to test, while James's will to believe and Plantinga's defense of exclusivism ground the conclusion that faith can be rationally justifiable where evidence runs out—beware the Blainetologists, but do not surrender ways of life that define us.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 25 "14. The Science of Alternate Realities" — Morgan unpacks the science behind the 'fifth dimension': higher spatial dimensions as in the portal of 'Little Girl Lost,' Einstein's time as a fourth dimension with time-dilation travel ('A Kind of a Stopwatch'), and the grandfather paradox, which 'Back There' handles inconsistently (some events change, others cannot) while 'No Time Like the Past' gets right: past events are eternally true. Quantum many-worlds fits 'The Parallel,' where Major Gaines slips into a nearly identical reality, and infinite universes would make every possibility actual. But the cosmological multiverse, he argues with Popper's falsifiability criterion, is untestable and hence not science, remaining a dimension of mind and imagination.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 8 "Sherlock's Reasoning Toolbox" — Pigliucci shows that Holmes's celebrated 'deduction' is really a mix of induction and abduction, contrasting Aristotelian syllogism and Cartesian rationalism (with its failed Cartesian circle) against the fallibility of real investigation. He walks through Hume's problem of induction (Russell's inductivist chicken), the Mill-Whewell 'great induction debate,' and Popper's falsificationism—qualified by the Neptune/Uranus episode where scientists shielded Newton. Using 'Thor Bridge' and 'The Three Students,' he concludes Holmes is a pragmatic scientist wielding a whole toolbox, since there is no single scientific method.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 22 "12. Raven Seldon Predicts Disaster" — Malloy argues psychohistory rests on induction and therefore inherits Hume's problem of induction: Seldon generalizes from Trantor's past to predict the Empire's fall, but nothing guarantees the future will resemble the past, and the Mule's unprecedented rise shows there is no deductive guarantee (the future-unlike-past idea is not self-contradictory). He tests Popper's falsificationism, under which psychohistory is science because it makes falsifiable predictions and can never be confirmed, then notes Popper leaves hypothesis-origin and post-failure revision inductive, and finally offers Reichenbach's pragmatic 'vindication' of induction, likening it to Hardin making do with the only tools at hand in a Seldon Crisis.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 24 "14. Beyond Loyalty and Disloyalty" — Bartolo Alegre uses Seldon's trial claim that 'scientific truth is beyond loyalty and disloyalty' to ask whether even formal sciences like logic can be biased. Against Bogdanov's and Lenin's Marxist idea of a 'proletarian logic,' he shows that logical principles (non-contradiction, explosion) have been revised by paraconsistent logicians on purely mathematical grounds, using Hardin's symbolic-logic decoding of the Anacreon message and Orwell's doublethink as illustrations. Drawing on Popper's rejection of uninformative contradictions, Kuhn's sociological account of scientific change, and Lakatos's rational reconstruction, he argues science transcends individual scientists' loyalties only through a diverse, competing community of experts, as when Hummin's loyalty to humanity pushed Seldon to make psychohistory practical.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Briony Addey defines coincidence and distinguishes three theories the castaways might invoke to say events are 'meant to be' — divine providence, fatalism, and determinism — using Locke's belief in his walkabout destiny and Eloise Hawking's 'the universe course corrects' as fatalist cases. She introduces Jung's synchronicity and collective unconscious as an acausal explanation of meaningful coincidence, then debunks our intuitions with the birthday paradox, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability, before criticizing Jacob's deception 'experiment' on the candidates for failing standards of informed consent and culpable versus non-culpable ignorance.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 28 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Pigliucci uses the 'Evolution, Schmevolution' series and the Dover trial to argue that intelligent design is not science because it is unfalsifiable and invokes supernatural causation. He cites Popper's falsificationism (and Popper's recantation about Darwinism), contrasts Descartes's rationalism with Hume's empiricism to characterize science as a tentative blend of the two, flags Feyerabend's 'anything goes' as an irrational view of knowledge, invokes Aristotle's eudaimonia to argue meaning in life is a personal work in progress, and turns Dembski's theistic-evolution concession into a Pyrrhic victory via the problem of evil ('argument from bad design').
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 25 "14. The Science of Alternate Realities" — Morgan surveys the physics and philosophy behind the show's 'fifth dimension': higher spatial dimensions and parallel universes ('Little Girl Lost'), time as Einstein's fourth dimension and relativistic time dilation ('A Kind of a Stopwatch'), the Grandfather Paradox and the self-consistency of time travel ('Back There,' 'No Time Like the Past'), the Many Worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics ('The Parallel'), and the cosmological multiverse. He closes with Popper's falsification criterion, arguing that unobservable other universes may be, like the show itself, forever 'a dimension of mind.'

### Immortality and the Soul

Questions of immortality and the soul concern whether some part of a person, often called the soul or mind, survives bodily death, and what such survival would consist in. Dualist traditions, from Plato onward, treat the soul as a distinct immaterial substance capable of existing apart from the body, while materialists deny any such separable entity and tie personal existence to the living organism. The topic bears on religious hopes for an afterlife, on debates about personal identity over time, and on what it would even mean for the same person to persist beyond death.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 60 "Unknown" — This section catalogues the film's Christian typology, noting it was released on Easter weekend: Neo is the messianic 'One' (an anagram, and Greek for 'new'), Choi calls him 'my own personal Jesus Christ', Thomas Anderson means doubting Thomas and 'Son of man', his pod escape is a virgin birth, his hosing-down rescue a baptism, the Agents' temptation parallels the desert, and Trinity's kiss raises the genuinely dead Neo to a glorified body that flies - transfiguration and ascension included. Cypher is Judas/Lucifer, Zion the heavenly city, and the Nebuchadnezzar's plate cites Mark 3:11's 'You are the Son of God'.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 80 "Unknown" — The chapter presents the subway confrontation as the film's turning point: defying the crew's iron rule that one runs from Agents, and Cypher's 'realistic' sneering, Neo freely accepts death to save Morpheus, overcoming the fundamental fear that grounds the Matrix's power in both worlds. The Oracle's 'next life' prophecy is then fulfilled to the letter when Trinity - 'I'm not afraid anymore... you can't be dead. Because I love you' - refuses to believe in death, and Neo returns in his next life as the One.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 81 "Unknown" — The chapter argues the third postulate must be a this-worldly immortality: since no single lifetime suffices to realize the Highest Good, Kant himself (in Universal Natural History) imagined the soul reborn over and over as it climbs the ladder of human perfection, and Mahayana Buddhism's bodhisattva - who chooses to remain on the wheel of rebirth to enlighten all beings - matches the monkish boy 'Potential' and the Oracle's hints. The One accordingly appears in three incarnations: the earlier liberator who freed the first rebels, Neo's second life, and the third life glimpsed at the film's end.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 24 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Bill Davis asks why Arwen would 'choose a mortal life' with Aragorn and why wise elves and men call death a gift. The Ringwraiths show that existence can be worse than death - undead kings whose frustrated nature is perpetual torment - while Socrates in the Apology, Lucretius, Sartre, and Camus supply reasons not to fear annihilation, and the elves' endless life raises Boethius's and Bernard Williams's problem of boring immortality (Camus's Sisyphus, Wowbagger the Infinitely Prolonged). He concludes that Arwen and Aragorn, uncommonly wise and loving, accept death as Ilúvatar's gift: she prefers a finite life of deep love, and they trust the old stories of a world 'remade' beyond the circles of Arda.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 10 "The Failure of Our Attempts at Meaning" — Conard argues that Allen's films converge on one position: life is inherently meaningless because nothing in the universe is permanent, so only something eternal (God) could ground value — and God is a self-deception ('tradition is the illusion of permanence' in Deconstructing Harry; Rabbi Ben's 'blind faith' in Crimes and Misdemeanors). He traces the impermanence argument from Mickey Sachs's mortality panic in Hannah and Her Sisters and young Alvy's dread of the expanding universe in Annie Hall, to Lloyd's 'temporary convulsion' speech in September, Sandy Bates's 'Ozymandias Melancholia' in Stardust Memories, and Louis Levy's suicide. Since real value would require permanence, Conard concludes, Allen's characters' attempts at meaning through romance (Peter's 'I have to sleep alone tonight' in September) and art (Renata's failed faith in posterity in Interiors) are merely distractions and self-deceptions we need 'like we need the air'.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 12 "From Knowledge to Faith" — Lawler reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Kant's problem of the Highest Good: Judah's unpunished murder of Dolores shows a world where the wicked prosper and the good (Cliff, the blind Ben) suffer, the scandal Job complains of, while Levy's suicide shows that a bare existentialist 'yes' to life fails without love. Kant's 'I had to deny knowledge to make room for faith' is applied to the film's two visions: the deterministic, dog-eat-dog world of science and Adam Smith's economic egoism (with Hobbes's war of all against all) is only appearance, not reality. Kant's gallows example shows Judah could have discovered authentic freedom by respecting Dolores's dignity rather than seeing 'the black eyes of an insect', and the postulates of freedom, God, and immortality ground Ben's not-really-blind faith — so it is Judah who is truly blind.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 11 "Philosophical Conceptions of the Soul" — Scott Sehon opens his chapter by cataloguing how central souls are to the plot: Harry, Sirius, and Dudley narrowly escape dementors while Barty Crouch Jr. does not, and Voldemort's Horcruxes split his soul into eight parts that must all be destroyed before he can die. He sets up the guiding question of what the soul is in Rowling's world, where souls generally survive bodily death, and announces a survey of philosophical accounts to test whether her picture is plausible.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 18 "The Dementor’s Kiss" — Argues materialism is straightforwardly false within the Potter universe, using Hermione's claim that a sword through the body leaves the soul untouched, and then taxonomizes the forms surviving souls take: Nearly Headless Nick's explanation that ghosts are imprints of wizards who refused to 'go on', Voldemort's bodiless state as 'less than the meanest ghost' after his curse rebounded on baby Harry, the graveyard echo in Goblet of Fire where Cedric and Harry's parents emerge 'more solid' than ghosts, and the Resurrection Stone in Deathly Hallows returning Sirius, Lupin, and his parents as 'neither ghost nor truly flesh'.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 20 "A Plausible View" — Reconstructs Slughorn's lesson to young Tom Riddle, that murder rips the soul and the torn piece can be hidden in a Horcrux, an act 'against nature', and argues that because Voldemort's intellect and magical powers remain intact while his capacity to charm gives way to rule by fear and his body becomes snake-like, Rowling's soul must be the sentimental one: our humanity, love, and moral conscience. On this view the soul is damaged by supreme evil and can be repaired only through remorse, which is exactly what Harry urges on Voldemort ('be a man... try for some remorse') before the final killing curse rebounds.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 21 "NOTES" — Steps outside the fiction to ask whether Rowling's hybrid soul theory is actually plausible, answering probably not: neuroscience shows no brain events lacking physical cause, mind-body interaction remains the classic obstacle for any dualism, and it is doubly implausible that an immaterial substance would be responsible only for our deepest emotions and conscience. The differing physical powers of ghosts, Resurrection Stone shades, and Horcrux-souls make the metaphysics even harder, though the chapter concedes that a fictional soul picture that vividly dramatizes what we care about needs no truth to make a terrific story.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 133 "The Integrity Objection" — Draws Voldemort's inversion in full: each Horcrux rips and destabilizes his soul (Hermione notes only excruciating remorse could reunite it, a pain that could destroy him), his attempt on baby Harry leaves him disembodied vapor parasitic on others' blood and limbs, in stark contrast to the feasting, affection, and romance of Harry's circle. The Godric's Hollow inscription 'the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death' and Hermione's claim that the soul survives whatever happens to the body ground the contrast between Voldemort's unmourned, mundane death and the honored, grieved dead - Dobby, Fred, Lupin, Tonks, Colin Creevey.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 141 "Reap a Destiny" — Reads the King's Cross limbo through Heidegger's counsel to choose a hero from the past and gain insight through dialogue with them: Dumbledore appears not as a king of that place but as the humble penitent, confessing his youthful hunger for glory, and the way-station evokes purgatory.
