Ed Crane, the barber who kills Big Dave, is an absurd Camusian figure who finds preexecution peace in 'seeing it whole', making the film an existentialized meditation on unknowability and meaninglessness.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Sanders coins 'sunshine noir' for Miami Vice as postmodern neo-noir, defining postmodernism via antirealism, skepticism about knowledge, and enigmas of personal identity, anticipated by Nietzsche's perspectivism. He analyzes three episodes: 'Heart of Darkness', where undercover agent Artie Rollins is consumed by his fantasy self (mirroring Crockett's Sonny Burnett) and hangs himself; 'Shadow in the Dark', where Crockett adopts the burglar's mind-set (Dilthey's Verstehen) in a dreamlike, glass-imagery structure that undermines the realist camera; and 'Lend Me an Ear', where the surveillance expert Duddy, echoing The Conversation, collapses into paranoid moral solipsism.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 11 "Picturing Paranoia Interpreting Invasion of the Body Snatchers" — Sanders rejects the standard Cold War-allegory and feminist readings of Invasion of the Body Snatchers and argues the film is best understood as film noir dramatizing paranoia. He shows that the mechanics of pod duplication are riddled with incoherence (multiple duplicates, location, timing, matching), then reads the frame story as evidence that Miles's whole account is a delusional psychosis. Dr. Hill's acceptance of the wild story on flimsy evidence violates Hume's maxim that a rational person proportions belief to evidence, making the film an ironic meditation on the philosophical significance of paranoia and lost humanity.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 5 "Sherlock Holmes as Epistemologist" — Baggett reconstructs Holmes's detective practice as an expansive epistemology built on observation, background knowledge, and abductive inference-to-the-best-explanation, using cases like 'The Blue Carbuncle' hat and the 'eliminate the impossible' maxim. He argues Holmes's boldness in drawing inferences is intellectual courage rather than hubris, invoking William James on the risk of losing truth by excessive caution. He then tests Holmes against feminist epistemologists who fault his cult of cold objectivity and mistrust of women (the Mary Morstan and Irene Adler episodes), concluding Holmes is partly vindicated by his imagination, intuition, and passion but still too fragmented between reason and emotion.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 15 "(Still) Fighting the Power Public Space and the Unspeakable Privacy of the Other in Do the Right Thing" — Finnegan reads Do the Right Thing as a dramatization of philosophical skepticism and the 'problem of other minds,' using Wittgenstein's private-language argument, Austin's speech acts, and Cavell to argue that racism is not an epistemic failure to 'know' the Other but an ethical refusal to acknowledge. She shows Lee's split cinematic style (naturalistic interiority for the Italian Americans, alienating canted wide-angle shots for Radio Raheem and the black characters) enacts what being 'othered' looks like, while the Racial Slur Montage stages words as perlocutionary acts and Arendt's 'space of appearances' explains the black characters' exclusion. Mookie's thrown trash can and Sal's Wall of Fame register powerlessness rather than resolution.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Murray and Schuler argue that Kubrick's unifying vision is a dogmatic skepticism - the 'banality of the good' - in which good characters (Dax, Alice, Alex's parents) are flat and helpless while the wicked have sass, and irony rules. Drawing on Hume's essay 'The Sceptic' and Marx's dissertation on Epicurus's swerving atom, they read Kubrick as a 'rebel without a cause' whose skeptical tropes of cosmic insignificance, present pleasure, and the veneer over the ape (Dr. Strangelove, The Killing, 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) accommodate rather than comprehend capitalist modernity. They contend Kubrick's Sartrean 'make your own meaning' answer is a false door, since projecting value either really transforms the world (refuting the claim it is indifferent) or projects nothing at all.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — The editors' introduction surveys the volume and frames Soderbergh as a maker of 'philosophical cinema' whose films engage epistemology, metaphysics, and ethics. It previews the essays' claims: that sex, lies, and videotape and Schizopolis stage epistemological questions of truth, evidence, and skepticism; that The Underneath and The Limey use Bergson's durée to explore time and self-understanding; that Traffic tests Kant's ethics against Sartrean individual decision; and that Solaris recasts memory and authenticity via Augustine and Baudrillard's simulacra. It positions Soderbergh within Indiewood filmmaking after Welles as a self-reflexive artist.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Rodriguez-Ruiz argues that Schizopolis and sex, lies, and videotape function as everyday 'thought experiments' about knowledge, contrasting them with Descartes's evil-genius and dream arguments and Dretske's disguised-zebra case. Fletcher must literally become his wife's lover's double to know she is cheating, and Ann pieces together John's affair from a stray earring, dramatizing how high the bar for knowledge of others is and how much depends on lucky accident. The trashcan-music scene stages the problem of induction and Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp. Soderbergh's boss's 'confirm nor deny' speech and Lester's preventable death show the films endorse a moderate skepticism that still affirms nature and power as real, rejecting full relativism and dogmatism.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 23 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Sanders reads Soderbergh's HBO series K Street as a paranoid meditation on appearance and reality set in a Washington lobbying firm, where James Carville and Mary Matalin play fictionalized versions of themselves and the reclusive owner Richard Bergstrom manipulates everyone from afar while endlessly rewatching Mildred Pierce. Through three unresolved mysteries and a 'house of mirrors' structure, the show dramatizes the characters' skepticism about their capacity to know reality and Bergstrom's moral solipsism. Sanders argues Soderbergh's run-and-gun docudrama form itself enacts the epistemic uncertainty, leaving the text radically underdetermined about whether Bergstrom is a con man, a pawn, or a phantom-chasing paranoid.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 16 "“All in War with Time” Medium as Meditation in Sherman’s March" — Rhu reads Ross McElwee's Sherman's March—ostensibly a documentary about Sherman's Civil War campaign but really about a heartbroken filmmaker's search for love amid Cold War nuclear dread—through Walker Percy's The Last Gentleman and Stanley Cavell's The World Viewed. He shows how the film enacts Cavell's ontology of film (viewing the world "from behind the self," movies as reliefs from private fantasy) and the dialogue between perfectionism and skepticism Cavell draws from Emerson's "Experience" and Nietzsche and Kierkegaard. McElwee's deliberately unpolished, self-conscious "personal documentary"—stumbling on the riverbank, leaving in his own second thoughts—turns the war film into a meditation on consciousness, mediation, and being "all in war with Time."
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 4 "02_LaRocca_Chapter_001.html" — Cavell argues that photography's power expresses the mind's fall into skepticism about the external world, reading film as 'a moving image of skepticism' since we see things present to us that are not actually before us. Interpreting Capra's Mr. Deeds Goes to Town, he treats Gary Cooper's Deeds defending his 'fidgetiness' as thinking as a popular-cinema reenactment of Descartes's cogito: after Emerson, who says we can no longer say 'I think, I am' for ourselves, the proof of existence shifts from the mind's self-certainty to the live body's visible restlessness caught by the camera. He links the fidgeting body to Heidegger's das Man and Nietzsche's last man, and invokes Wittgenstein and Emerson on our being 'away' from the world.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 6 "Spinning Tops and Brains in Vats" — This bundle of essays reads Memento and Inception as epistemology. Knepp uses Peirce's icon/index/symbol triad and Plato's Phaedrus critique of writing to show Leonard Shelby's tattoos and Polaroids give a false illusion of permanent truth (he tattoos Teddy as 'John G.' on purpose). Hoffman uses Kierkegaard's subjective truth to contrast Leonard, who lies to himself while pretending to gather objective 'facts', with Cobb, who takes a Kierkegaardian leap of faith and walks away from the spinning totem to embrace his children. Watson runs the Cartesian/Pyrrhonist dream argument against Inception's totems, arguing beliefs can be valuable via intellectual virtue even if unverifiable, and Lindenmuth pits Nozick's experience machine against Cobb's choice of real children over the dream-shade of Mal to argue reality matters more than pleasure.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "Doomed to Be Perceived" — Paula Smithka uses the Vashta Nerada and Weeping Angels to examine perception and the reality of unobservables. She sets Berkeley's "to be is to be perceived" against Locke's hidden substance and Hume's empiricist skepticism (and Paley's design argument), then distinguishes direct from indirect perceptual evidence, using the shadows, skeletal remains, and Neptune's discovery to frame scientific realism versus van Fraassen's antirealism. The Weeping Angels invert Berkeley, existing only when unperceived and turning to stone when observed, so for them to be is NOT to be perceived.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 11 "How to do Philosophy" — Johnson uses Stephen Colbert's coinages to refute relativism and gut-thinking. 'My Truth' represents individual relativism and 'Wikiality' cultural relativism, both of which Johnson rejects via the correspondence theory of truth and counterexamples like slavery and Nazi Germany. 'Truthiness' is intuitionism, which Johnson attacks using Locke's critique of 'enthusiasts' who reason in a circle, and he argues that appeals to 'a right to my opinion' reveal indifference to truth. Following Socrates, he concludes we should defend beliefs with argument and admit ignorance rather than trust the gut.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" — Jacoby uses Stan Marsh as the embodiment of W. K. Clifford's ethics of belief, that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence. Stan debunks TV psychic John Edward, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the one making extraordinary claims. Jacoby distinguishes evidential from prudential reasons, presents and criticizes Pascal's Wager (using 'Cartmanland' and the problem of undeserved suffering), and argues via Clifford that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken the mind and, as Stan tells Edward, slow 'the progress of all mankind.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 14 "Skepticism Outside the Matrix" — Lawrence uses The Matrix to raise Cartesian skepticism: Neo's deception dramatizes Descartes's dream argument and evil demon, the computer-run Matrix being a technological version of the demon. He argues even Morpheus cannot be certain he has truly awakened ('the Matrix within the Matrix'), so the only certainty is Descartes's cogito. Drawing on Russell's 'Appearance and Reality,' he then argues that even setting aside Matrix scenarios, naive realism fails, since a chair's color, texture, solidity and shape are all perception-relative, leaving the external world's nature deeply uncertain.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 20 "10. Memories Are Made of This" — Nisley reads two episodes through Hume's skepticism about the continued existence of objects and selves, which rests on memory, resemblance, and imagination rather than proof. In 'And When the Sky Was Opened,' three spacemen (Forbes, Harrington, Gart) progressively vanish as memory and corroborating testimony fail, dramatizing Hume's point that belief in continued existence needs more than force and vivacity of ideas. In 'The Trouble with Templeton,' Booth's dead wife Laura reappears but behaves unlike his memories, showing the imagination 'feigns' continuity; both episodes undermine memory as the foundation of rational belief.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 14 "Neither Here, nor There, nor Anywhere" — Randall Auxier reads Green Eggs and Ham as a primer in Peircean pragmatism. The contrarian 'C' illustrates how thinking only begins when a problem interrupts action, and Peirce's distinction between 'genuine doubt' and settled belief-as-habit explains why C clings to 'I do not like them' without ever trying them. Auxier runs C's stubbornness through Peirce's four methods of fixing belief (Authority, A Priori, Tenacity, Science), arguing C relies on tenacity, and likens Sam-I-Am to Saint Monica pestering Augustine into genuine doubt, so that even after C eats the eggs he only knows they settled belief in one context.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 15 "McElligot’s Pool Epistemology (with Fish!)" — Ron Novy uses Marco's faith that unseen fish swim in McElligot's Pool to survey theories of knowledge as justified true belief. The farmer's empiricism and Marco's inference from a book frame a tour through Descartes's evil-genius doubt and skepticism, Locke's primary/secondary qualities (indirect realism), Berkeley's idealism ('to be is to be perceived'), and rationalist a priori knowledge, before turning to feminist epistemology (Schott, Kant's 'intuitions without concepts are blind,' Nietzsche on perspectival seeing) and Quine's naturalized epistemology to argue knowers are situated and the pool may indeed be 'bigger than you or I know.'
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 22 "Chapter 10 Mark Twain’s Serious Humor and That Peculiar Institution" — Kramer argues, against Davenport, that Twain can be simultaneously serious and funny, using humor to attack the 'spirit of seriousness'—the dogmatic certitude and epistemic closure Sartre and Beauvoir describe—rather than sincerity itself. Drawing on Schopenhauer's account of seriousness and Beauvoir's remark that the mystified slave takes his condition as natural, Kramer shows Twain's satire of Christianity ('Little Bessie,' 'Letters from the Earth,' the anti-adultery commandment, the Philippines massacre) exposing the incongruity between professed omnibenevolence and real suffering. Like Democritus the 'laughing philosopher' and a Socratic ironist, Twain undermines complacent certainty without offering dogmatic Truth in its place.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 23 "Chapter 11 Socratic Irony in Twain’s Skeptical Religious Jeremiads" — Jacquette demands a precise definition of Twain's much-invoked irony, adopting Vlastos's/Quintilian's formula that irony says the contrary of what is meant while letting the real meaning be recovered. He classifies Twain's irony as local vs. global and comic vs. sober (tragic/historical): 'Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc' is globally ironic (falsely presented as de Conte's eyewitness manuscript), while the relic-mocking passages of 'The Innocents Abroad' (St. Luke's Madonna, kegs of true-cross nails, three skulls of John the Baptist) are local comic irony. Jacquette concludes Twain's irony is distinctively Socratic: like Socrates interpreting the Delphic oracle, Twain makes a moral and epistemic virtue of ridiculing experts who claim to know what no one can know about God, sin, and the afterlife.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 11 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Jurgensen and Southworth apply Hume's argument against miracles to the virgin birth, treating it as a claimed violation of the natural law that virgins do not conceive. They attack the credibility of the only witnesses, Matthew and Luke, noting their third-hand sources (Mark, Q, L/M), their contradiction over whether Mary and Joseph were married, and the mistranslation of Isaiah's ambiguous 'almah' as the Greek 'parthenos' (literal virgin). Invoking Hume's four defects of miracle testimony and his maxim that no testimony suffices unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the event, they conclude a rational person must reject the Christmas miracle.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 27 "GARDENING" — O'Brien reads Voltaire's closing injunction in Candide, 'we must cultivate our garden,' through David Hume to argue that gardening is therapy—a retreat from metaphysics and religion into the tranquility of common life. Hume rejects belief in miracles and religious 'enthusiasm' not by logic but by recalling everyday reasoning (a melon seed, not a miracle, explains melons in the greenhouse), and the gardener is the sophisticated artisan-reasoner attuned to nature's regularities. Gardening inculcates Humean virtues (industry, patience, balancing action, pleasure and indolence) and Haybron's attunement/engagement/endorsement, yielding Epicurean ataraxia; the Sisyphean gardener (Camus) fighting slugs, and Wittgenstein taking up gardening as a cure, illustrate the point.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 14 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Roche's 'Seeing Snakes' attacks the psychedelicist claim (William James on nitrous oxide, Huxley's 'reducing valve,' Leary) that drugs including cannabis reveal reality-as-it-is. He deploys Russell's line that we 'can make no distinction between the man who eats little and sees heaven and the man who drinks much and sees snakes,' and a reliabilist demand that knowledge have a source proven reliable over independently verifiable cases, to argue drug 'revelations' are indistinguishable from delusion. Foucault is cited that drugs have 'nothing to do with truth and falsity,' and Nietzsche's Dionysian veil-of-Maya passage is used as an example of the mystical rhetoric he debunks.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 21 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Kakko's 'Hallucinatory Terror' uses Fitz Hugh Ludlow's 1857 The Hasheesh Eater to ask 'How can these things be?' — the ontological status of hallucinations that neither exist nor fail to exist. He traces Ludlow's own reading from Locke's empiricism through Hume's skeptical worry that all perception may be hallucinatory with no verifiable external object, to Kant's Copernican turn: the phenomenal/noumenal distinction, synthetic a priori judgments, and space and time as pure forms of intuition. Kant's framework lets Kakko recast Ludlow's 'virtual change of worlds' as a literal, non-metaphorical restructuring of the intuitions conditioning experience.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 27 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Penrose subjects the 'soft drug / hard drug' distinction to conceptual analysis, arguing that—unlike genuinely graded soft-vs-hard eggs—it tracks no single real spectrum. He tests three candidate bases: phenomenological intensity of the high (incoherent, since 'comparable amounts' and interpersonal 'highness' can't be measured), addictiveness (fails, since the traditional distinction counts non-addictive LSD as 'hard'), and dangerousness (Nutt's Lancet study ranks cannabis as more dangerous than some 'hard' drugs, and the distinction trades on illicitly excluding legal alcohol and nicotine). He concludes drugs vary along many distinct property-lines, so the traditional binary is simply false.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 29 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Downes argues, against a Cartesian confidence in self-knowledge, that climbers do not have reliable access to their own internal states while climbing. Drawing on Nisbett and Wilson's sock experiment and dual-process 'new unconscious' psychology, he shows self-reports are often post-hoc confabulations: climbers who declare a wobbler 'felt easy,' claim to be 'not strong enough' on moves they later top-rope easily, or unknowingly dab or stand on the rope. He recommends leaning on external 'scaffolding' (partners, chalk marks, guidebooks) and the 'you're only as good as your last problem' rule to temper dangerous self-assessments, since overrating ability sits in a deceptively close possible world.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 14 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — David Robles's 'The Seeker' argues that declining trust in Western absolutist religion drives people toward yoga as an experiential, self-directed spirituality. His central move is that Patanjali's Yoga Sutras rank direct perception above testimony and scripture — mirroring the scientific method — so yoga functions as a 'spiritual science' harmonious with empiricism, whereas established religion rests on second-hand revelation. He distinguishes 'spiritual' (personal, inspiration-based) from 'religious' (culturally binding dogma) and casts the American 'seeker' as building a better, results-oriented, pragmatic spirituality.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 16 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Steve Jacobson's 'Standing on Your Head' asks whether an educated Westerner can reasonably believe 'yoga theory' (chakras, prana, kundalini, koshas) given that science has superseded ancient theories. He raises a 'standard objection' from the superior predictive power of science (invoking Hume's problem of induction), rejects weak replies, but argues via the epistemology of testimony that people with weak scientific grounds and strong critical testimony can rationally accept yoga theory. He concludes that even if no part of it is credible, abandoning it would leave yoga intact — 'yoga with fewer illusions.'
- **Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low**, ch. 23 "BLUES" — Jesse Steinberg argues that doubt — a pervasive blues theme (B. B. King's 'nobody loves me but my momma,' Otis Spann's 'another mule kickin' in my stall,' Buddy Guy's 'I Smell a Rat') — supports Descartes's external-world skepticism, since knowledge would require ruling out the dreaming hypothesis. Against the 'I don't care' hedonistic reply he deploys Nozick's experience machine to show we value authentic reality over mere pleasant appearance, and he rejects contextualism as a solution. Endorsing Socrates' examined life, he settles for strong justification rather than certainty, reading Charley Patton's 'can't tell my future, can't tell my past' as the blues' honest coping with irreducible doubt.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 8 "Horror and the Idea of Everyday Life On Skeptical Threats in Psycho and The Birds" — Philip J. Nickel argues horror has an epistemological value structurally parallel to philosophical skepticism: it maliciously rips away the tacit 'cognitive trust' backing our everyday actions. In The Birds, the diner 'symposium' where Mrs. Bundy's confident science that birds cannot coordinate an attack is refuted moments later dramatizes a paranoid scenario we cannot rationally rule out. In Psycho, Marion Crane's isolation and misplaced trust in the seemingly normal Norman Bates enacts the skeptical premise that the ordinary person you rely on could murder you. Like Hume returning to backgammon, viewers can only resume everyday life, which Nickel says horror exposes as a necessary but insecure construction.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 8 "2. The Matrix" — Rowlands reads The Matrix as a vivid staging of Cartesian skepticism: Neo's pod-world is Descartes's dream and evil-demon conjectures (AI plays the demon) plus the modern brain-in-a-vat, showing we cannot be certain the external world exists. He uses the 'there is no air/muscles' and 'twin buildings' variant of Putnam's Twin Earth to argue we cannot even be certain which thoughts we think. The Hume-Nietzsche bundle critique undermines even the cogito, and the spoon-bending boy ('there is no spoon') illustrates Berkeley's idealism as the endpoint of skepticism about the physical world.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 14 "Skepticism Outside the Matrix" — Matt Lawrence uses The Matrix to stage the skeptical problem, running Descartes's dream argument and evil-demon method of doubt (the Matrix as a technological demon) and even a 'Matrix within the Matrix' to show Morpheus cannot know he is awake. Descartes's cogito supplies the one certainty that survives radical deception. Lawrence then draws on Russell's analysis of the red chair to argue against naive realism: color, texture, solidity, and shape are appearances, so even setting aside the Matrix we cannot know the world in itself.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 25 "23. The X-Files as Philosophy Navigating the “Truth Out There”" — The chapter argues that Darin Morgan's X-Files episodes philosophize by critiquing the show's own 'the truth is out there' mantra from within. Through the conflicting hypnosis testimonies and identical camera blocking in 'Jose Chung's From Outer Space,' Morgan cinematically stages Nietzsche's perspectivism and the claim that 'truth is as subjective as reality'; through Clyde Bruckman and the doomed Ansel of 'Quagmire,' he mounts an anti-Socratic case that relentlessly pursuing truth (as Mulder does) is not worth the ruin it brings. Kowalski then rebuts Morgan using Descartes's cogito and inference-to-the-best-explanation to defend objective truth against radical skepticism, arguing subjectivism about truth is self-refuting.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 52 "49. A Serious Man as Philosophy The Elusiveness of Moral Knowledge" — Biderman reads the Coens' A Serious Man through Beauvoir's figure of the 'serious man' (from The Ethics of Ambiguity), the man who craves a single absolute value and blinds himself to moral complexity: physics professor Larry Gopnik, beset by divorce, a bribing student Clive, and Sy Ableman's death, seeks moral knowledge that would let him be such a man. The chapter argues Larry's quest fails across cognitivist, noncognitivist, and pluralist accounts of moral knowledge, showing moral knowledge to be elusive if not impossible. The film's Kafkaesque fables (the Dibbuk, the Goy's Teeth, Rabbi Nachtner's 'L'olam ha-ba', Schrodinger's cat, and the Binding of Isaac in Caravaggio's painting) all stage the absurd collapse of interpretation, echoing the Book of Job, which Maimonides read as a parable rather than history.

### The Will to Believe

The will to believe is William James's argument that in certain cases we are entitled to adopt a belief on faith, before the evidence is conclusive, when the choice is genuine, momentous, and cannot be settled by intellect alone. James responded to the demand that we withhold assent until proof arrives, contending that some truths—especially moral and religious ones—only become available to those willing to commit in advance. Refusing to decide, he noted, is itself a choice with consequences, so passionate belief can be legitimate rather than a lapse in reason.

- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 13 "Who Should Be Committed" — Thomas Senor argues that rooting for the perennially losing Cubs is rationally and morally on a par with religious commitment: genuine fandom, like faith, is loyalty that survives repeated disappointment (distinguished from the zealot's 'my team right or wrong' via the Portland Trailblazers' 'Jailblazers' era). Since beliefs and fan loyalties are not under direct voluntary control, he rereads Pascal's wager not as choosing to believe but as cultivating belief indirectly: attending Mass the way moving to Chicago and following the Cubs daily can make you a fan. The believer's epistemic optimism toward religious experience and the devout's second-order hope in dark times mirror the Cubs fan's springtime optimism, so neither Cubs fans nor the religious should be committed.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 39 "21b" — A paired metaphysics debate on whether superstition helps performance. Steven Streeter argues yes: baseball's mystery-rich outcomes breed ritual (Sparky Anderson refusing to step on foul lines, Wade Boggs's chicken, Nomar Garciaparra's glove taps), whose invisible forces — like black holes — can be inferred from their measurable effects on attention, preparation, and focus, with William James's belief-makes-reality as the capstone. Neil Feit counters no: on the counterfactual account of helping, a player cured of superstition would perform the same since his athletic ability is untouched, routines that aid concentration need involve no magical belief, and the burden of proof lies with the believer.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 28 "“A New Hope”" — Long stages William Clifford's ethics of belief against William James's will to believe, with Luke Skywalker as James's exemplar. Clifford's shipowner story condemns faith as 'wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone,' which would convict Luke of immorality when he switches off his targeting computer and trusts the Force; James replies that where a choice is intellectually undecidable and a genuine option - live, forced, and momentous, like Luke's turn to the Jedi life or Obi-Wan's response to Leia's hologram - pragmatic faith is justified and even salvific. Faith can create truths: Han flying into the asteroid field, Luke's unjustified belief that there is good in Vader bringing Anakin back, the author's faith in his students, and Martin Luther King Jr.'s dream - all illustrating 'a new hope.'
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 15 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Steven Lovell reads the Green Witch's enchantment in The Silver Chair (the sun is only a copy of the lamp, Aslan only a bigger cat, Narnia a children's tale) as Lewis's staging of the Freudian critique of religion, and answers that similarity cannot tell copy from original, that the genetic fallacy vitiates arguing from a belief's origin, and that Aslan is 'not safe,' so Christianity is hardly wish-fulfillment (Augustine's restless heart and Pascal's God-shaped hole point the other way). Puddleglum's stamping out the fire and vow to live 'as like a Narnian as I can even if there isn't any Narnia' is defended through Pascal's Wager and James's 'The Will to Believe': the reality of Narnia is a live, forced, and momentous option that may legitimately be decided on passional grounds.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 11 "Poker and Philosophy" — Ventimiglia mines No-Limit Hold'em for seven lessons philosophers also teach: we lack certain knowledge (Descartes' cogito is the famous quest for certainty, but philosophy's own history of disagreement proves uncertainty is the human condition), and like William James against Clifford we must still believe and act without the nuts — waiting for pocket aces while the blinds eat you alive is no strategy. Risking everything echoes Thoreau's escape from lives of quiet desperation, trusting hunches over arithmetic follows Thoreau and Peirce's sentimentalism, and the Darwin-and-Spencer competition of tournament poker hides a deeper cooperative social contract: get caught cheating and you are out of the game. It closes with Plato's four classic virtues from the Republic — wisdom, courage, moderation, and the justice of a balanced soul — as the perfection of a poker player.
- **The Beatles and Philosophy - Nothing You Can Think that Can't Be Thunk**, ch. 12 "CHAPTER 4 “A REVELATION TO BEHOLD”" — Argues that the Beatles' devotion to rock and roll was a literal religious phenomenon rather than loose metaphor: Lennon's first hearing of Elvis is analyzed as a William James-style conversion, the Radio Luxembourg broadcasts were treated 'like scripture,' Hamburg was a 'baptism by fire,' and Epstein's new suits at the Cavern were announced as 'a revelation.' Drawing on James's Varieties of Religious Experience and Pragmatism, the chapter reads Beatlemania's screaming crowds as collective ecstatic ritual and the 'toppermost of the poppermost' chant as the will-to-believe making its own truth, in the way James says truth 'happens' to an idea. Aristotle's four causes supply the metaphysical frame — the 'magic' of Liverpool and the sacred quality fans reported are formal-final causation against the material-efficient causation of disenchanted modernity — while the band's double irony ('tarrying with the negative,' after Hegel) let them hold skepticism inside belief, as in Lennon's 'flaming pie' origin parody and the 'more popular than Jesus' episode.
- **The Beatles and Philosophy - Nothing You Can Think that Can't Be Thunk**, ch. 13 "CHAPTER 5 “AN EXTREME SENSE OF DESTINY”" — Reads Bob Dylan's 'extreme sense of destiny' as lived Aristotelian final causation: Dylan's passivity about fame ('It happened like anything else happens'), his 'Jack Fate' persona, and the odyssey of 'goin' home' all treat his future self as the telos drawing him forward rather than his past pushing him. William James's Will to Believe ('faith creates its own verification') explains the self-fulfilling portents Dylan found in Gorgeous George's wink, his felt succession to Woody Guthrie, and his premonition of Joan Baez, while the chapter insists this destiny is not fatalism since Dylan could have ignored the signs and 'gone off another way.' It closes by taking Dylan at his word that 'Bobby Zimmerman' died when his namesake was killed in a 1961 motorcycle crash — a Jungian synchronicity that seals the shamanic death-and-rebirth 'transfiguration' Dylan claims for himself, where Heraclitus's river captures that the old self cannot be recovered.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 12 "Introduction" — Frames Part II's epistemology chapters. Jacoby's chapter uses Stan Marsh debunking TV psychic John Edward, holistic healers, and Mormon belief to teach the ethics of belief against Pascal's wager; Lawrence's uses The Matrix to pose the skeptical problem and Descartes' response; Silverman's uses Adama's lie about Earth in Battlestar Galactica to raise the Gettier problem and the Clifford–James dispute over believing without sufficient evidence.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Silverman uses Adama's 'true lie' about Earth to motivate the Gettier problem: Starbuck's belief that Earth exists is true and justified by Adama's testimony, yet because that testimony is a lie, her justified true belief is not knowledge — just as Helo's true belief that the woman before him is 'Sharon' rests on mistaking Boomer for Athena. Goldman's reliabilism then questions whether sight, memory, and testimony are reliable belief-formers in a world of humanoid Cylons, weighing Hume's suspicion of testimony against Plantinga's defense of it. Finally Clifford's evidentialism is set against James's will to believe: the Colonials' forced, momentous choice to seek Earth shows that in an uncertain world pragmatic belief can be reasonable — 'so say we all.'
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 15 "Tough and Tender, The Dead Keep Truckin’" — Gary Ciocco traces a line from Emerson and James through Kerouac, Ginsberg, and Neal Cassady to the Grateful Dead: Emerson's nonconformist 'infinitude of man' and James's 'live options' and religious appetite for being 'more fully alive' become, in the Beats, the project of living life itself as art ('the only people for me are the mad ones'). He argues the Beats splintered because each chased an atomistic, individual epiphany — Kerouac swinging wholesale from tender- to tough-minded temperament — while the Dead turned the same Jamesian hunger into a shared communal religious experience, a 'kindler, gentler' scene that better achieves Aristotle's eudaimonia. Cassady, muse of On the Road and driver of the Pranksters' bus, literally connects the two movements, but the Dead's unity-in-diversity made them the evolution, not the echo, of the Beats.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 21 "Back from the Edge" — McKenna and Pratt use McDermott's 'Promethean self' and meliorism to answer the riddle of Nebraska's closer 'Reason to Believe': among the dead dog, the deserted bride and the groom left at the altar, 'still at the end of every hard earned day people find some reason to believe.' They trace Springsteen's shift from escape songs ('Born to Run,' 'Thunder Road') to life at the edge ('Badlands,' 'Darkness on the Edge of Town,' and the two midnight drivers of 'State Trooper' and 'Open All Night'), arguing meaning is made by cutting and connecting relations at the margins. Belief without evidence of salvation is legitimate hope but illegitimate certainty; the reason to believe is Jamesian meliorism — making things 'not perfect, simply better.'
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 6 "Ex Astris, Scientia GEORGE A REISCH" — The editors' introduction takes Starfleet Academy's motto 'Ex Astris, Scientia' as its frame: Picard handing cadet Wesley Crusher a book by William James shows officers need philosophy, not just ship operations, and the starry-heavens motif runs from Thales and Plato's cave through Kant's 'moral law within and starry heavens above.' It surveys the book's Trek dilemmas (Picard and Dathon's alien language, Data's emotion chip, Khan's vengeance, Riker's Q powers) as 2,500-year-old philosophical problems, and argues Trek's optimism — Picard's 'the acquisition of wealth is no longer the driving force' — restates Aristotle's claim that all humans by nature desire to know. Like philosophy from Socrates on, Trek is presented as 'an entertaining, edifying preparation' for living by one's ideals, a life-education primer sealed with Roddenberry's advice to 'slip in a heavy idea or two.'
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 22 "“Something to Believe In”" — Reads Worf's crisis over the clone 'second coming' of Kahless in 'Rightful Heir' as a live, forced, and momentous option in William James's sense, where 'faith creates its own verification.' Peirce's methods of fixing belief — tenacity, authority, and science — explain why Worf cannot accept Koroth's pious fraud once Gowron's DNA test exposes the clone, while Data's own 'leap of faith' in believing he is more than a machine supplies the Jamesian model of believing without evidence. Worf's compromise — telling the Klingon people the truth but installing Kahless-the-clone as spiritual emperor because 'the words are more important than the man' — is offered as pragmatist truth: what works while staying answerable to hard facts.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 10 "“Trip Around the Sun”" — Phil Oliver pairs Buffett with William James: both hold that philosophy is 'not a technical matter' but each person's sense of what life deeply means, had in non-verbal moments of elevation as much as argued in words. The chapter's core is James's 'moral holiday' — a morally legitimate respite from care and struggle — naturalized in Buffett's 'License to Chill' and 'Trip Around the Sun' ('it's good to know it's out of my control'), joined by James's lightness about error from 'The Will to Believe' and Russell's and Dawkins's responses to cosmic annihilation. Against those who hear mere hedonism, Oliver insists Jamesian holidays are care-free but never care-less: like Thoreau's 'live deliberately' echoed in 'Growing Older But Not Up,' they renew us for the return to work, and James's ambivalence about alcohol in The Varieties of Religious Experience mirrors the risk of Buffett's frozen concoctions.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 15 "Wishing and Dogmatism" — Matthew Pierlott argues Colbert the satirist conflates two things his character, Stephen, merges: truthiness (trusting gut and heart over external authorities like dictionaries) and bullshit in Frankfurt's exact sense - speech indifferent to truth, which Pierlott finds in Hillary Clinton's dismissal of economists on the gas-tax holiday and likens to Steve Careill's habitual pleasantries versus Jon Stewart's honesty and Stephen's lies. He defends gut and heart as evidence-bearing tools - knowing a candidate's 'heart' from character evidence (the Westmoreland Ten Commandments interview), gut intuitions as unconsciously processed experience, and choosing which of the two Cheneys (1994 quagmire prophet or 2003 liberators booster) to trust - so in an information-saturated democracy truthiness is a necessary part of any orientation toward truth. The real enemy is dogmatism, the 'Dark Side of Truthiness' that cuts off future evidence, while wishful thinking kept modest (optimism that people are honest) can even be beneficial, a Jamesian willing-to-believe.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 14 "Questioning the Question" — Hartung takes Ross's snapping reply to Armitage's repeated 'Why are you helping me?' in Armitage the Third: Poly-Matrix as a misreading: she wants a practical reason for his choice, not theoretical evidence, and since no evidence can prove an android is a person, William James's 'Will to Believe' applies — Ross's belief in her moral standing is a live, forced, and momentous genuine option (suspending judgment means she is scrapped, and losing her means losing a possible life together), so his passions may legitimately decide. He contrasts this with evidentialist cases where suspending judgment is right (the shuttle company skipping inspection; Dr. Asakura's silicon-based-life hypothesis) and with Pascal's Wager, reading Mars's church-empty, hedonistic culture of sex-tourism Seconds as one that denies genuine options and so kills Thirds. The attached original screenplay 'Eye Am,' a sequel to Magnetic Rose, extends the theme as salvage officer Nadine Beckner is lured by the AI Eva/Sam impersonating her dead husband Heintz, with Schrodinger-style observer-affected reality deciding which version becomes real.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 21 "Do You Believe It" — Patrick Tiernan argues that Fenway fandom is a genuine religion: William James's four marks of mystical experience (ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity) map onto memories of Buckner's error and Dave Roberts's steal, and Peter Berger's 'signals of transcendence' structure the rituals of Truck Day, the hopes of spring training, the damnation of Bucky Dent and Johnny Damon, and the humor of 'Cowboy Up.' He roots the Curse of the Bambino in New England's Puritan-Calvinist legacy of persecution and original sin (Frazee's sale of Ruth), then deploys Hume's account of superstition from 'Of Superstition and Enthusiasm' to deflate the exorcism rituals fans actually performed, from a Sox hat on Everest to dredging for Ruth's piano, as post hoc fallacies. Even so, the rituals reveal the human need for religious practice, and Maslow's peak experience renders the 2004 comeback a brush with the sacred, so the Faithful believe because they have to.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 35 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Hamer tests sanity against truth using Kierkegaard's asylum anecdote - the escapee intoning 'Boom, the earth is round' proves his insanity precisely by resting it on objective fact - and applies it to 'Insane in the Mainframe,' where Fry, wrongly committed to a robot asylum, is only released once he subjectively believes he is a robot, and to 'The Sting,' where comatose Leela's plan to keep Fry's corpse under her mattress to 'prove I'm not insane' fails the same traitorous way. Pure objectivity cannot certify sanity and pure subjectivity licenses lunacy, so the chapter brings in James's 'The Will to Believe': some beliefs must be held first before their evidence can even count. Fry, who abandons his robot belief the moment his knife-nick bleeds human blood, models the justified believer who pursues the objective truth subjectively.
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 24 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter compares Barney's 'True story' pronouncements with William James's pragmatism, using James's squirrel anecdote and the 'Zoo or False' monkey-mugging to ask when an evidentially undecidable dispute becomes a live practical question. Like James's pragmatic cases for free will and religious comfort, Barney's monkey story and the twenty-eight-year-old 'with some sun damage' are beliefs made true by their practical (mostly entertainment) value, then replaced like outdated theories when new evidence arrives, as James's consistency requirement demands. The divergence: the Barney Stinson (BS) theory of truth is self-serving, engineering unverifiable stories others cannot disprove, while James weighs what works for everyone's experience.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 19 "8. I Will Never Doubt Again" — Watson and Guidry-Grimes ask whether Buttercup was rational to accept the evidence that Westley was dead, and whether Westley's Fire Swamp optimism and Inigo's twenty-year hunt for the six-fingered man are wishful thinking or something better. After laying out the evidentialist tradition (Descartes's rule of evidence, Hume's 'a wise man proportions his belief to the evidence,' Clifford's condemnations), they use Adrienne Martin's account of hope as 'endorsed desire plus uncertainty' to argue that value-shaped belief can be rational when it sustains well-being and character. Their conclusion expands rationality beyond evidence-tracking: hope, unlike wishful thinking, takes evidence seriously while balancing it against what makes a life good, which is why Buttercup's despair on the wedding night, not her earlier resignation, is the real failure.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 27 "16. You Made Me First" — The chapter argues that origin stories fix character: Batman, forged by watching his parents murdered (and in Burton's film by the Joker himself - 'You made me first'), is trapped by a past that sets his trajectory, since as Schopenhauer said we can do what we will but cannot will what we will. Kal-El's origin is instead an act of hope - his parents launch him into the universe believing the wildly unlikely - which the chapter reads through William James's will-to-believe, the same faith Bruce needs to jump the chasm unroped in The Dark Knight Rises. Because the past causes the future and 'I can do whatever I want' is not free will, Bruce can never escape his tragedy, while Superman's hopeful origin lets him believe, and make us believe, that we might yet fly.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 27 "13. Linus’s Wager" — The chapter stages a three-way debate over whether Linus may believe in the Great Pumpkin without evidence. Clifford's ethics of belief (the ship-owner whose wishful thinking sinks his ship) condemns Linus's sincerity-based wager; Pascal's Wager endorses it (forgoing one night of trick-or-treating costs nothing if the Pumpkin is fake and wins toys if he is real) but assumes a doxastic voluntarism we lack, since no one can make themselves believe for even a million-dollar reward. William James's 'The Will to Believe' gets the final word: if Linus's option is live, forced, and momentous with no decisive evidence either way, his leap of faith - like loving without guarantees - is morally justified whenever life would be greatly impoverished without it.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 29 "16. I Should Have Known It" — Watkins reads the later albums Mojo and Hypnotic Eye ("Power Drunk," "Burnt Out Town," "Playing Dumb," "Shadow People") through Clifford's ethics of belief: the powerful suppress their doubts like the unseaworthy shipowner and come to sincerely believe their own lies, while the overpowered hide behind the cliche that everyone is entitled to an opinion. Because belief formation is a doing inseparable from action, there is a moral obligation to hold beliefs to evidentiary standards, we should have known, and James's will-to-believe and fideist appeals (Tertullian, Pascal, Kierkegaard) offer no license for self-serving faith. Facing the evidence in front of us is the first step to telling the power-drunk it is the last time they are going to hurt us.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 13 "5. Greatness or Nothingness" — Courtland Lewis uses KISS's career gambles to compare theories of decision-making. After Tolstoy's twig-over-the-dragon allegory of mortal life, he tests W.K. Clifford's shipowner (never act without sufficient evidence) against KISS's counter-evidence bet on the Alive! live album, models the choice with Pascal's Wager, and uses the Prisoner's Dilemma to explain the flop of the four 1978 solo albums. He then argues William James's pragmatism — beliefs as rules for action, the living, forced, and momentous option that 'KISS is the best' — best explains why acting on the band's self-created narrative was authentic, with Nietzsche completing the picture: greatness requires leaping, living dangerously, tightrope-walking toward self-defined success.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 29 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Malloy examines Walter's incorrigible leaps — Bunny kidnapped herself on no evidence, the toe is a fake ('I can get you a toe by three o'clock'), the Big Lebowski can walk — through Clifford's ethics of belief (the ship-owner who sinks his passengers) and James's 'Will to Believe' reply with its living, forced, and momentous genuine options, applied to Walter's 'dabbled' pacifism and his preference for Nazism's ethos over nihilism's nothing. Walter's conversion to Judaism for Cynthia raises whether practice can will belief, tested via Pascal's wager and James's objection, and the verdict borrows Bernard Williams: we cannot choose beliefs, but Walter's reckless policy of dismissing counterevidence makes him 'not just an asshole, he is also wrong'.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 12 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Johnson uses 'Go God Go's' future of 2546—where Dawkins-style atheism has become a warring religion and otter scientists intone 'Oh my Science!'—to ask whether science and religion genuinely conflict and whether New Atheism is itself a faith. Applying abduction and the four criteria of adequacy, he argues the embellished-story hypothesis beats miracle claims about Jesus (whose legend grew Gospel by Gospel), Sathya Sai Baba, Joseph Smith, and Xenu, that Mr(s). Garrison's 'you can't disprove God' and the show's sarcasm commit an appeal to ignorance, and that Stan's water-into-wine scene with Jesus shows how easily people are fooled. He allows Kuhnian theory change in science but rejects James's will-to-believe for existence claims—the moon whale Willzyx needs evidence—and concludes Parker and Stone are unfair to Dawkins: ending religion would not end violence, but it would remove the easiest justification for it, and some answers are simply true even when unknown.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 13 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Dueck takes Stan's closing pluralism in 'Super Best Friends'—all religions have something valuable to teach, as the interfaith superheroes' combined powers defeat Blaine—and tests it against Hick's pluralism, exclusivism, and Rahner's inclusivist 'anonymous Christians', using 'Go God Go's warring atheist factions to show exclusivity is unavoidable even without God. Hume's miracle argument explains why Jesus's look-away water-into-wine trick convinces no one in the episode: testimony can never outweigh the laws of nature, so supernatural evidence resists natural evaluation. Popper's falsificationism warns that watering doctrines down to make religions compatible (the rabbit-pope of 'Fantastic Easter Special') leaves nothing to test, while James's will to believe and Plantinga's defense of exclusivism ground the conclusion that faith can be rationally justifiable where evidence runs out—beware the Blainetologists, but do not surrender ways of life that define us.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 27 "16. You Made Me First" — Starting from the Joker's 'You made me' / Batman's 'You made me first' exchange in Tim Burton's Batman, the chapter argues origin stories fix character: Bruce's witnessed trauma destines him to darkness (and we expect his death to match), while Kal-El is sent to Earth as an act of hope that the chapter reads through William James's will-to-believe—belief itself makes success possible, like Bruce's ropeless leap in The Dark Knight Rises. Against 'I can do whatever I want' free will it deploys Schopenhauer's 'we can do what we will, but we cannot will what we will': Bruce cannot will away his vengeance, and Red Son's Soviet-raised Superman shows biology and upbringing determining who Clark becomes. Superman still wins because his origin story permits the hope that Bruce's cannot.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 11 "Notes" — Baggett sets W. K. Clifford's evidentialism (the negligent shipowner; believing on insufficient evidence is a 'sin against mankind') against William James's precursive faith, which permits believing ahead of the evidence when an option is forced, live, momentous, and evidentially undecided. He applies this to Sam's taping over the Dubai Air logo as social-coordination faith, Richmond's belief that it can finally beat Everton, romantic risk-taking like Roy and Keeley's, and the marriage of belief with hard work (Ted's practice tirade, Nate's False Nine), ending with James and Pascal on how evidential ambiguity about God makes a passional step of faith rational.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica to explore knowledge as justified true belief. Adama's 'true lie' about knowing Earth's location makes Starbuck's belief in Earth a Gettier case, a justified true belief resting on false justification. He tests Adama's testimony against Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for spotting Cylons; memory deceives Boomer and Tigh) and Hume's skepticism about testimony versus Plantinga's defense of it. Finally, against Clifford's evidentialism he deploys William James's 'will to believe,' arguing that faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice that gives the Colonials purpose.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 18 "Time Belongs to the Tower" — Auxier frames King as 'Tolkien meets Poe' and reads the Dark Tower's temporalization through the literary and psychological experience of time. Drawing on Susanne Langer's 'virtual present' and Sartre's psychology of imagination, he argues readers surrender their real present to a novel's suspended time, which he links to William James's 'will to believe' rather than mere suspension of disbelief. He uses Kant's distinction between amazement (seeing the seemingly impossible) and admiration (accepting it) to explain the psychological cost time travelers like Jake Epping and Wesley Smith should pay, faulting King for keeping ordinary heroes sane while displacing the strain onto insane 'gatekeepers,' and concludes the Tower is 'real' as the way each person binds possibility to their own lived past, present, and future.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 6 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — In this Foreword, John Rousmaniere argues that sailing's 'numinous' moments — like his own experience of stillness on a becalmed ketch mid-Atlantic, when the skipper cut the engine and the crew felt suspended between sky and sea — are paths to genuine philosophical truths, not embarrassing flights of fancy. He enlists William James's 'Varieties of Religious Experience' and James's nautical metaphor for free will (the passenger who volunteers to take the helm) to argue that such mystical feelings can 'team up' with reason rather than opposing it. He insists mystery and craft must work together: piety is no substitute for seamanship (Shelley drowned in an unseaworthy boat), yet competence and numinous experience nurture each other.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 25 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Johnson argues that the Santa Claus lie is immoral and should be abandoned, giving three reasons: it is deceptive lying (Kant's absolute prohibition is too strong, but the lie lacks life-saving justification and functions as a Platonic 'noble lie' no more noble than a cult leader's); Santa robs parents of credit and warps children's moral development and trust, illustrated by anguished 'finding out' stories and Virginia O'Hanlon's letter; and it damages credulity, invoking Clifford's 'Ethics of Belief' against belief on insufficient evidence while James's 'Will to Believe' cannot rescue Santa since evidence against him is overwhelming. He recommends revealing the truth early, even via a Socratic-Method questioning game.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 14 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Roche's 'Seeing Snakes' attacks the psychedelicist claim (William James on nitrous oxide, Huxley's 'reducing valve,' Leary) that drugs including cannabis reveal reality-as-it-is. He deploys Russell's line that we 'can make no distinction between the man who eats little and sees heaven and the man who drinks much and sees snakes,' and a reliabilist demand that knowledge have a source proven reliable over independently verifiable cases, to argue drug 'revelations' are indistinguishable from delusion. Foucault is cited that drugs have 'nothing to do with truth and falsity,' and Nietzsche's Dionysian veil-of-Maya passage is used as an example of the mystical rhetoric he debunks.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 20 "NOTES" — Hare treats mass photography—from the daguerreotype through digital cameras, Abu Ghraib snapshots, and diagnostic imaging—as making everyone a practicing epistemologist caught between two folk tenets: the photo as mirror of reality and as manipulation of reality. Defending photography as a genuine causal 'mode of seeing' (a prosthetic like telescopes), he proposes 'flexible realism,' adjusting Dewey's warranted assertibility and virtue-epistemology standards to context, and invokes William James's defense of beneficial 'overbeliefs' when National Geographic images strengthen confidence in one's own culture. Reading the Fallujah lead-pipe photo debate between editors Sullivan and Kushner, he uses Quine's recalcitrant-experience and web-of-belief holism—extended by Morton White's 'holistic pragmatism'—to show moral, epistemic, sensory, and emotional claims are tested together, and frames photography's democratization via Walter Benjamin's mechanical reproduction and loss of aura.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Eric Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica's Adama, who lies that he knows Earth's location, to run the Gettier problem: Starbuck's true belief that Earth exists rests on a false justification (that Adama knows), so it is justified-true-belief without being knowledge. He tests testimony via Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for telling Cylons from humans) and the Hume/Locke/Plantinga debate over testimony's epistemic role. He closes with James's 'will to believe': faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice where agnosticism forfeits meaning, so belief without certainty can be reasonable.

### Possible Worlds

Possible worlds are complete alternative ways things might have been, used in logic and metaphysics to analyze claims about necessity and possibility: a statement is necessary if it holds in all possible worlds and possible if it holds in at least one. David Lewis defended the striking doctrine of modal realism, on which these worlds are not mere abstractions or fictions but concrete realities as fully existent as our own, spatiotemporally isolated from us. Though few accept Lewis's full realism, possible-worlds talk has become an indispensable tool across philosophy of language, modality, and counterfactual reasoning.

- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 79 "So, Is Dumbledore Gay" — Gendler tests whether fictional truth works like historical truth and finds it fails: whereas a biographer discovers facts about the one actual world, a storyteller chooses among infinitely many imaginary worlds - David Lewis's point that 'every way that a world could possibly be is a way that some world is' - so storytelling mixes creation with discovery. She distinguishes the 'primary truths' stated on the Potter novels' 4,100 pages (discounting trivial inconsistencies like Percy's badge color and Moaning Myrtle's S-bend versus U-bend) from unstated 'secondary truths' like Hermione having ten fingers, rejects a maximal inclusiveness principle that would import every actual-world fact into the story, and closes with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics advice to seek only the exactness a subject allows.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 119 "The DC Comics Multiverse" — Recounts how DC resolved its Silver Age continuity mess: rather than treat Jay Garrick's adventures as a fiction-within-a-fiction, Flash #123 has Barry Allen cross into Earth-2 and meet Garrick — and one cannot meet a merely fictional character — so the multiverse is born. As alternative histories multiplied and heroes routinely world-hopped, the only correction strategy left was postulating yet another world, setting up 1985's Crisis.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 120 "Crisis on Infinite Earths The Story Unfolds" — Summarizes Crisis: Krona's forbidden experiment splits one universe into a multiverse plus an antimatter universe whose Anti-Monitor devours worlds; the Monitor self-sacrifices to pocket five Earths; heroes and villains travel to the dawn of time, where the Spectre's intervention leaves a single positive-matter universe. The aftermath — Superman of Earth-2 mourning a Lois who "never existed," three Supermen on one Earth — sets up the two metaphysical conjectures, time travel and multiverse, to be examined.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 122 "More Things in Heaven and Earth" — Surveys real multiverse arguments: the Everett-Wheeler many-worlds reading of quantum mechanics, fine-tuning explained by every possible initial condition existing somewhere rather than by God, and David Lewis's modal realism, on which every way the world could have been is a causally isolated world — it was possible to write a shorter chapter because in some world Hanley did. Tegmark's physics multiverses round out the menu before the question: does any of this fit Crisis?
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 123 "A Multiversity" — Rules out Lewis's modal realism for the DC multiverse (DC worlds interact; Lewis's are causally isolated) and standard branching many-worlds too, then proposes "hypertime," a second time dimension that makes sense of a traveler arriving in another timeline's "1984." Since Crisis speaks of the multiverse becoming one "at the dawn of time" — something that cannot happen in plain time or hypertime — Hanley posits a six-dimensional cosmos with "supertime" and superhistories.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 125 "Identity in Crisis" — Poses the persistence problem through Superman-1 and Superman-2: are they strictly identical? Perdurantism — persons as four-dimensional space-time worms made of temporal parts — makes them distinct worms with no parts in common, so Superman meeting his counterpart is no stranger than you meeting a friend; endurantism, with wholly present strict identity, could identify them across timelines but balks at the impossibility of Superman meeting himself.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 20 "Poker and Philosophy" — Northcott loses his first casino tournament to a fluky inside straight and mines the bad beat for philosophy of science: objective odds collapse into knowledge-relative probabilities (a card-tracking magician would assign different numbers to the very same draw), Laplacean determinism versus quantum chance bears on whether decision theory presupposes free will, and bad-beat counterfactuals — 'I'd have won the tournament but for that hand' — get David Lewis's possible-worlds closeness analysis and Hume's counterfactual account of causation, with no settled verdict. Even game theory cannot deliver a perfect system: a Nash-equilibrium strategy is only optimal against other optimal players, so the mindless all-in 'Stupidus' beats it. Conclusion: no can't-lose system exists, and poker will never be a game for robots.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 19 "Putting Together the Triforce" — Duncan and Gee study the Nintendo NSider forum threads where fans build Zelda timelines, showing that their marshaling of evidence (Ganon's trident, whether the Master Sword is 'legendary' because of an earlier hero or its sage creators, Hyrule's geography as a marker of time) mirrors scientific argumentation. Using Latour and Woolgar's Laboratory Life, they argue that what 'counts' as evidence, even down to excluding the BS Zelda and CD-i games as non-canon, is socially constructed within a community of practice, not value-free data. David Lewis's plurality of worlds supplies the metaphysics for the split-timeline debate after Ocarina of Time, and the chapter concludes that knowledge in general, in labs and in fandoms alike, is constructed through tools, discourse, and interaction.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 17 "The Loneliest Witch" — Auxier gives three theories of why water melts the Wicked Witch, one for each register of Oz: as dream (Bergson's account of dreams as memory explains the fire/water effect-swap), as Baum's fairytale (Susanne Langer's presentational symbols make dryness-wickedness versus water-as-life the tale's moral physics), and as Gregory Maguire's possible world, where the philosophy of language takes over. He narrates Frege's sense/reference distinction—mayor of the Munchkins—to explain how fiction can support truth and falsity ('Dorothy melts the Witch' true, 'Dorothy tried to melt her' false), then deploys Putnam's Twin Earth thought experiment: 'water' in Oz is XYZ while Kansas water is H2O, so Elphaba's word 'water' does not mean what Dorothy's does, and meanings just aren't in the head. Elphaba—the unique being straddling two worlds, killed by H2O she cannot name and terrified by dreams of oceans—is offered as an even stronger argument for Putnam's semantic externalism than Twin Earth's molecule-for-molecule doppelgangers.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 20 "Getting to Oz" — Auxier uses the Wizard's demand that Dorothy kill the Witch to split 'ought' from 'can'—ethics from the metaphysics and logic of possibility—and then asks whether Oz is a genuinely possible world. He explains David Lewis's modal realism (every genuine possibility actual in its own causally isolated world) through counterfactuals about which network aired the film, dissolves the silver-versus-ruby slippers conflict by assigning book-Oz and film-Oz to different possible worlds, and argues that since no flat contradiction can be eked out of the Oz stories, Lewis is committed to Oz's being real—though Maguire's inter-world travel and Elphaba's hybrid, soul-less trans-world identity (her counterpart in our world being, playfully, Dorothy) stretch Lewis's 'counterparts' doctrine to its limit. Peirce supplies the closing caution, with Boole, that logic is a set of norms for how we can and ought to think rather than a proven mirror of other worlds, so believing in Oz's full reality remains permissible fun rather than an obligation.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 20 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Auxier tests Pullman's many-worlds premise, setting Asriel's coin-toss explanation and the Barnard-Stokes hypothesis against Book III's claim that unchosen possibilities are 'snuffed out like candles,' then measures the trilogy against David Lewis's causally independent possible worlds, which forbid the subtle knife's transworld travel and leave the chill Lyra feels at the thought of 'another Lyra' in Will's Oxford as an unresolved transworld-identity puzzle. Compiling fourteen kinds of conscious beings from humans and dæmons to specters and the Abyss itself, he argues Pullman's cosmology is panpsychist and aesthetic rather than moral or epistemic, ordered by what the alethiometer, the knife, and the spyglass can and cannot do, with the alethiometer submitting to the knife and love alone able to break it, as Will's love for his mother and for Lyra does twice. Peirce's agapicism, evolution by creative love alongside chance and mechanical necessity, supplies the closest philosophical analogue to Pullman's 'Matter loved Dust.'
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 24 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Finley puts Pullman's parallel worlds beside philosophers' possible worlds: the twin Oxfords sharing Simon Parslow's scratched initials invite the inference that Lyra's world has its own Madagascar, while modal realists like Lewis ('out there going on') take possible worlds to really exist and more skeptical theorists treat them as convenient fictions like 'in the story.' She contrasts their origins, quantum splitting at the level of elementary particles versus eternal logical possibility, explains why the indexical 'actual world' is one we can never leave, and argues that Lewis's underdetermination of fiction means the books describe not one possible world but vast numbers differing in unmentioned details like the population of alternate Madagascar. Lewis's counterpart theory then resolves Lyra's chill at 'perhaps there was a Lyra': the counterpart in Will's Oxford could never be her, only someone remarkably like her.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 13 "Which World Am I In" — Juan Ferret tells the story from inside the game: Admetus the Human Mage, chased through Alterac Valley by an Undead Rogue, works through Zeno's paradox of motion, the convergence of infinite series, and whether space and time are discrete, coached by a bodiless voice that turns out to be his player. The voice's revelations — 'You are my creation,' autorun, polymorph, Blink — force the free-will-versus-determinism question from the character's side, since every action is controlled from above. Reference frames, Heisenberg's uncertainty, EPR entanglement, and hidden nods to David Lewis ('Siwel Divad' on possible worlds) and many-worlds theory leave the mage wondering which world, server, or parallel universe he really inhabits.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 32 "Too Big a Byte to Chew" — Kylie Prymus uses a slain Orc to stage the metaphysics of Azeroth: whether the 'dead' Orc is anything more than electrons obeying code (Democritus's atomism), and why explaining Ironforge's empty Tuesday mornings forces us to 'go meta' just as Aristotle's Metaphysics went beyond his Physics. The problem of other minds gets a WoW twist: without nameplates we would sort NPC from PC by the argument from analogy, the same imperfect tool we use offline for pain, coma patients, and animal minds. David Lewis's plurality of worlds becomes concrete through servers — 'the gates could be open' is true for the Uther player because on Medivh they opened on January 23rd — and she concludes that the real world is no better defined than Azeroth.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 41 "Where in the World(s) Are We" — Ablondi asks whether fans' 'if only' claims—'If Bob Stanley had struck out Mookie Wilson, the Sox would have won in 1986,' 'if Pesky had hurried his relay in 1946'—can be true when they lack truthmakers in the actual world. He presents David Lewis's modal realism and counterpart theory as the standard solution, then objects: a Fisk counterpart with a different body, birthday and nickname, or a Red Sox made of 1986 Mets counterparts, is not recognizably Fisk or the Red Sox, and nobody cares about a Lonborg counterpart who won Game Seven. He concludes counterfactuals need some other explanation and that we should savor the actual Foulke-to-Mientkiewicz final out of 2004 instead.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 11 "The Good Gossip" — Borge weighs Jimmy Sirrel's claim that the best team always wins and the rest is gossip against Alex Ferguson insisting his side played better in a 1–4 defeat to Liverpool, framing the dispute as football Nominalism (only particular matches and results exist) versus football Platonism (an ideal way of playing exists over and above results). He rejects the Platonic ideal as metaphysically impossible—two perfect teams could never both score on every chance while conceding nothing, and style comparisons like catenaccio versus Brazil 1970 collapse without appeal to results—and instead uses possible-worlds counterfactuals: a team can be 'really' best yet unlucky when it creates objective scoring opportunities, like John Terry's slipped 2008 Champions League penalty or Spain's wrongly disallowed golden goal against South Korea in 2002, that go in across the closest possible worlds. Since Liverpool's deeply unfair 2005 comeback in Istanbul is celebrated as a classic, football is fiction and drama rather than a fairness-measuring contest, and the resulting what-if moaning is the good gossip that makes barstool debate worthwhile.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 12 "We Wouldn’t Be Here Without Time Travel" — Worley distinguishes logical from empirical possibility (Leonardo's round-square in 'City of Death') and shows that time-travel paradoxes — Leela's self-caused antibodies, the unauthored 'Blink' Easter egg, the Master's Toclafane — can be handled with Zeno-style analysis of contradiction and David Lewis's distinction between external and personal time, under which travelers instantiate rather than rewrite history ('The Visitation', 'The Time Meddler'). He then reads 'Turn Left' and the Doctor's 'alternative time' in 'Pyramids of Mars' through Leibniz's possible worlds and Lewis's actualism about parallel universes, concluding that in 'City of Death' time travel is essential to life on Earth existing at all.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 18 "Halo as a Catalyst for a Buddhism Videogame" — Luke Cuddy uses Halo 3 checkpoints and emulator save states—two mutually exclusive Flood-fight outcomes both in some sense true—to make David Lewis's possible worlds and modal truth concrete, with Leibniz as the doctrine's ancestor. Halo's infinite lives make players genuinely angry, and the chapter argues this is upaya territory: like the father in the Lotus Sutra's parable of the burning house, the game promises mastery (the goat-, deer-, and ox-carts) to lure players toward something greater outside it. Master Chief becomes a Bodhisattva whose avatar slides between extension of self and other, provoking the 'who am I?' crisis that reveals the ego as empty at the ultimate level of the Two-Fold Truth, while the Dalai Lama's enemies-as-teachers turns the seven-year-old who pwns you into practice in the first two Noble Truths' suffering and anger.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 8 "Education never ends Watson. It is a series of lessons with the greatest for" — J. Solomon Johnson asks whether Holmes's conclusions are knowledge or luck, walking through justified true belief with a Holmesian Gettier case (Watson rightly believing the killer was a former ship hand for the wrong reason), Moore's proof that knowledge entails belief, and Russell's stopped clock as an unsafe belief. BBC Sherlock's fake Vermeer and the 2009 film's 'resurrected' Lord Blackwood illustrate beliefs that fail safety or sensitivity across nearby possible worlds, while 'The Stock-Broker's Clerk' shows Holmes's observation of the scorched slippers making his belief sensitive. The verdict: Holmes is justified by the track record of his own expert methods, a professional billiards player rather than a beginner's-luck fluke, though real-world imitators could never rule out enough alternatives to match him.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 92 "Alternate Realities" — Reads the Bureau's adjustments as producing alternate realities — Ed Fletcher's boss as 'a different Douglas. A different version!' — and takes déjà vu, Dick's 'manifold of partially actualized realities,' and Ragle Gumm's haunting sense of having been inside a building he has only seen as a model in Time Out of Joint as clues that variables were reprogrammed in our past. Dick's late speculation converges, the chapter notes, with David Lewis's view that possible worlds are as real as ours, and with Hawking and Mlodinow's M-Theory multiverse.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 163 "Preparatory Human Beings" — The counter-tendency gathers Dick's empowering temporalities. 'The Golden Man' presents Cris Johnson, a golden-haired mutant with virtually no frontal cortex, who survives a random-firing gun by 'pre-thinking' a panorama of possible futures - Homo superior as superhuman beast, by instinct rather than intelligence. In Now Wait for Last Year, General Molinari uses the drug JJ-180 to trip sideways into parallel presents and recruit healthy duplicates of himself, virtually overcoming mortality with 'a dynasty consisting of himself'. And in The Man in the High Castle, Abendsen's The Grasshopper Lies Heavy, Frank Frink's handwrought jewelry and Tagomi's meditative slip all point toward an alternate present - ours - where the Allies won, making art and the I Ching oracles of resistance to totalitarian domination.
- **Philip K.
