- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 41 "It’s Not That Simple" — Donal O'Mathuna uses 24's Jack Bauer to dissect the ethics of torture, centering on Henry Shue's utilitarian 'ticking bomb' argument that torturing the bomber to save thousands is justified. He weighs deontology (torture treats persons as mere means) and virtue ethics (it degrades torturers like Agent Burke) against the utilitarian case, and shows the show itself refutes the argument: torture didn't get Fayed's bombs, innocents like Audrey Raines get caught, torturers are ruined, and Shue himself recanted - so the sanitized ticking-bomb fantasy misrepresents real, degrading torture.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 15 "6. In a Mirror Is Our Image" — Karavitis arranges thirteen Twilight Zone android/machine episodes on a moral spectrum from simple machines ('The Brain Center at Whipple's,' 'Steel') to indistinguishable androids ('The Lonely,' 'I Sing the Body Electric,' 'The Lateness of the Hour') to fully synthetic humans ('The Trade-Ins'). Using personhood, moral-agent/moral-patient distinctions, Aristotle's and Kant's views on animals, Singer and Regan on degrees not kinds, and Locke's memory theory of identity, he argues that if body-swapped Holts remain persons then scratch-built androids are persons too—so the destroyed androids were murdered, and evil is treating persons as disposable objects.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 18 "9. Machines Who Care" — Weiss examines 'robots that care' through 'The Lonely' and 'I Sing the Body Electric,' invoking Sherry Turkle's 'relational artifacts' and current debates (PARO, Alexa, Coeckelbergh, the Sparrows) about outsourcing companionship and care to machines. He notes Alicia becomes a relational artifact the moment she weeps, and that both she and the electric grandma are gendered, boxed, assembly-line products designed to fill human loneliness that a consumer culture itself produced. The essay asks whether we want a society where care and love are purchased off an assembly line—fable or nightmare.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 23 "12. The Twilight Zone on Our Doorstep" — Jones argues the Twilight Zone is not really 'somewhere else': Serling's narration insists on a remote realm, but episodes like 'The Hitch-Hiker' and 'Eye of the Beholder' take place in recognizable America. He claims the show performs a 'double distancing'—framing mundane, uncomfortable truths (we're selfish, easily manipulated, not special, mortal) as strange by locating them elsewhere and delivering them via impossible catalysts (gremlins, the Devil). 'The Shelter,' with no supernatural cause and a Cold War fallout-shelter premise Kennedy actually urged, breaks the pattern, forcing viewers to see that the Twilight Zone is the room they sit in.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 25 "It’s Not Personal . . . It’s Just Bizzyneuss Business Ethics, the Company, and Its Stakeholders" — Pierlott frames the shareholder-versus-stakeholder debate (Friedman versus Freeman) using Aristotle's function argument to ask what makes a 'good' company, then judges business relationships by Kant's humanity formula. McBean's manipulation of the Sneetches and the digital-TV cases show consumers used merely as means; McGurk's cavalier overworking of Sneelock in If I Ran the Circus and Maitland's sweatshop defense are answered with Marx's account of labor exploitation and Aristotle's voluntary-versus-mixed actions; the Once-ler's Lorax devastation shows firms externalizing environmental costs when profit is maximized at any value unprotected by law.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 26 "Speaking for Business, Speaking for Trees Business and Environment in The Lorax" — The Klaassens read The Lorax as a joint business-and-environmental-ethics text organized around three questions the Thneed provokes: do we consume too much (invoking Thoreau's 'simplify' and DesJardins on practical, ethical, and environmental over-consumption), must business grow (Daly's distinction between quantitative growth and qualitative development), and why the Once-ler ignores sustainability (the Brundtland definition and Daly's rules for natural capital). The Lorax's self-appointment as one who 'speaks for the trees' is tied to Christopher Stone's argument that natural objects should have legal standing through guardians, like corporations or incompetents.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 6 "“Sometimes Dead Is Better”" — Katherine Allen reads Pet Sematary and The Tommyknockers as bioconservative fables staging the transhumanism debate: Louis's resurrected, 'fundamentally wrong' cat Church and cannibal son Gage, and Bobbi's tooth-shedding 'New Improved' becoming, dramatize Kass, McKibben and Fukuyama's warning that erasing our limits erases our humanity. Against them she sets Nick Bostrom's 'Fable of the Dragon-Tyrant,' in which death is an unquestioned evil we should slay, and Bernard Williams's worry about the tedium of immortality. King's insistence that 'sometimes dead is better,' and that forbidden knowledge (the Micmac ground, the buried ship) works like an addiction, sides with the deathist view that mortality and finitude give life its meaning.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 25 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Olson and Taliaferro examine the ethics of secrets in Austen, refining Sissela Bok's definition so that a secret conceals what convention would normally make public. They argue secrets in Austen are usually corrosive (Wickham and Lydia's elopement endangering the Bennets, Brandon's silence about Willoughby harming Marianne, Lucy Steele's engagement binding Elinor) yet can be virtuous, as when Darcy secretly funds Lydia's marriage to avoid self-aggrandizement. They propose an 'ideal observer' standpoint (an all-knowing, impartial, affective narrator) for judging when a secret is honorable, and argue the Emma-Miss Bates incident is not a failure to keep a secret but a genuine vice of contempt Austen condemns.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 29 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Riter analyzes Pride and Prejudice and Zombies as mashup literature, arguing the form requires readers to know the source while denying its prestige, so Austen must be both 'dead' and 'alive.' She uses Roland Barthes's 'The Death of the Author' to explain how the loss of Austen's authorial authority opens her text to reinterpretation and legally permits Grahame-Smith's rewriting. But she argues Grahame-Smith actually attacks a caricatured 'living Jane' of popular culture (the saintly, class-obsessed romance writer) rather than the historically complex Austen, noting his inconsistency in celebrating the class-conscious zombie-slayer Lady Catherine while mocking Mrs. Bennet for the same class focus.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 19 "Chapter 8 The Noble Art of Lying" — James Edwin Mahon reconstructs Twain's two essays on lying ('On the Decay of the Art of Lying' and 'My First Lie') into a philosophy of lying. Twain holds that everyone lies constantly, that lying need not be spoken or deceptive (the 'silent lie,' nondeceptive polite lies, acts as lies, and 'modified' lies/palters), and that the gravest lies are the 'silent National Lies' such as the collective silence that slavery was not unjust. Mahon shows Twain's ethics of lying is broadly utilitarian and Rossian: guided by nonmaleficence and beneficence, an injurious truth is no better than an injurious lie, and self-sacrificing lies that help others are virtuous, so lying should be practiced as a cultivated art.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 27 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Baron, a new father, weighs whether to let his son Maxwell consume violent popular media (from Halloween to SpongeBob, Grand Theft Auto, and Schindler's List) by testing three hypotheses. He uses Plato's Republic warning against exposing the young to stories they can't interpret for the 'causal hypothesis'; Aristotle's Poetics on learning pleasure from painful images for the 'edification hypothesis'; and Aristotle's account of tragic catharsis (homeopathic vs allopathic purging) for the 'catharsis hypothesis,' concluding that context matters more than ratings and that fathers watching alongside their children are the decisive influence.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 22 "MOTHERHOOD" — Chris Mulford, a nurse and lactation consultant, analyzes infant feeding as an ethical question of rights, duties, and responsibilities, drawing on a feminist ethic of care and the claim that women learn empathy through caregiving (linked to oxytocin's role in birth and nursing). She argues that the right at stake is the mother-child dyad's 'protection from interference' with breastfeeding, that no mother is saddled with a solitary duty to breastfeed, and that the duty toward breastfeeding falls on the whole community; she frames the mother's dependency on 'the kindness of strangers' via A Streetcar Named Desire and the innate 'breast crawl.'
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 27 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Parker interviews Stumptown's director of operations Matt Lounsbury, probing for a single underlying value that unifies the roaster's ethics and aesthetics. Lounsbury insists quality—'how good the coffee can be'—is the gravitational center that pulls ethical behavior (record-breaking direct-trade prices, building washing stations in Rwanda, full health care for baristas, the Meet the Producers program) into orbit, while Parker suspects a deeper commitment to community and justice. The exchange enacts the book's recurring ethics/aesthetics entanglement: whenever asked about one, Lounsbury 'slips into' the other, framing direct trade as a win-win-win business model rather than idealism.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 29 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Bramucci and Mulholland use Kenyan smallholder farmers—Lucy Wanja, David Gachigi, Henry Maina, who earn $0.02–$0.10 per pound for coffee sold north for $12—to argue that fair-trade certification, while an improvement, secures only a 'minimum' wage and leaves growers trapped by mills, middlemen, and depressed global prices. They advance direct trade (Intelligentsia, Stumptown, and the author's own Safi Coffee, which makes farmers shareholders and pays up to twenty-fold more) as a more genuinely just alternative that invests in producers' long-term capacity. The ethical claim is that 'fair' as a sticker falls short of real equity, and that consumers' smug conscience is only earned by paying beyond the fair-trade minimum.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 30 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Kirkwood argues that caffeine is uncontroversially a performance-enhancing drug—boosting memory, reaction time, endurance—and that by WADA's own three-part test (performance-enhancing, potentially harmful, against the spirit of sport) coffee should count as doping, yet never has. He dismantles the standard anti-doping arguments as applied to coffee: the cheating/unfairness charge is circular and dissolves when everyone may use it; the 'unnaturalness' argument commits a non sequitur (umbrellas are unnatural too, and chewed coffee beans seem natural); and the harm test fails because the positive threshold sits at a mere 20-ounce serving, far below caffeinism. His conclusion is that coffee escapes the 'doping' label not through moral reasoning but through public acceptance—the emotive word 'drug' is withheld from the substance everyone uses.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 31 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Aleman, an ethnobotanist, asks 'Is coffee green?' and unpacks the many senses of 'green' (raw bean, naïve, money, and ecologically friendly) before weighing coffee's growth, organic and shade-grown methods, fair trade, globalization, and value chain. She judges coffee greenest at the source (shade-grown farms preserve migrating-bird habitat) but least green in the fossil-fueled journey from Global South farm to Global North cup, invoking Vandana Shiva's claim that 'drinking coffee is a political act' and Rigoberta Menchú on coffee and indigenous survival. She concludes the answer is partly subjective—withholding final judgment while resolving to keep drinking fair-trade, organic, shade-grown, single-source coffee—and warns of the cognitive dissonance, mirroring oil dependence, between judging coffee ungreen and drinking it anyway.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 24 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Geist, a conservation biologist, argues from physiology (elastin-digesting enzymes, B12 need), athletics (one-legged balancing for stalking, precision throwing), and the herbivore-like pattern of human speciation that humans evolved as hunters — a 'carnivorous herbivore.' He contends morality itself was born from hunting: because tools-as-weapons (clubs, spears) let an aggressor kill without retaliation, escaping natural selection's check, early humans had to invent social taboos distinguishing right from wrong. He contrasts Neanderthal 'rodeo' close-quarters spearing with Cro-Magnon distance throwing, linking spear-tracking to endurance running, language, and art — concluding that questioning hunting's morality questions our humanity.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 25 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Duerr surveys the worldwide 'Master/Mistress of Animals' figure (Artemis, the /Kaggen of the Bushmen, the Huaulu Lord of the Forest) as a mythic sanction against over-hunting, arguing that the near-universal guilt hunters feel over killing sentient, human-like game reflects a real moral dilemma. She invokes Singer's utilitarian claim that painlessly killing non-self-conscious animals whose deaths are compensated by replacement 'may not be wrong,' reading the mythic 'solutions' (denial, propitiation, taking only what you need, restoring bones so game is reborn) as a folk 'hunting code of ethics' that manages the wrong of ending a life without starting another.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 21 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Darci Doll treats celebrity sex tapes (Pamela Anderson/Tommy Lee, Paris Hilton, Kim Kardashian, Colin Farrell) as a cautionary tale about privately recorded porn. She argues taping is defensible only with informed adult consent and agreed terms of distribution, then analyzes the appeal — celebrity obsession, voyeurism, and the fantasy of 'having sex with' a star — and the motives for release, including career boosts. Against these she sets the risks of theft, accident, and betrayal by a jilted ex, plus the 'sexting' problem among minors, concluding that because release is essentially irreversible, a sexually positive culture must protect trust rather than assume amateur tapes are safe from a market.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 10 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — The editors' introduction argues that fashion, despite philosophers' contempt for it, raises serious questions in aesthetics, ethics, identity, and political philosophy. It surveys the volume's contributors: fashionability as an expert-plus-masses property (Prinz/Farennikova), Zangwill's alienation thesis, Russell on 'cool' as aesthetic virtue, the objectification of women through Barbie play and sweatshops, and Singer's demand (via the drowning-child argument) that spare money go to poverty relief rather than trendy clothes. It uses concrete cases — Ugg boots, the National Airlines 'Fly me' campaign, Tommie Smith and John Carlos's 1968 Olympic salute, foot binding — to show fashion carries the zeitgeist and can both liberate and enslave.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 12 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Farennikova and Prinz ask what makes something fashionable, arguing through thought experiments (Calvin Klein jeans, khakis, Robinson Crusoe's leather jacket, the accidental thrift-store punk, Gang Green, the mod couple) that four conditions must hold: many people wear the look, recognized experts endorse it, wearers intend to conform, and they regard it as having aesthetic value. They distinguish being fashionable from being merely popular or 'cool,' show fashionability is relative to group and to time, and note fashion must change to serve its signaling purpose — the Amish are 'intentionally unfashionable.'
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 25 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Pierlott examines sweatshops in the garment industry through the lens of ancient Cynicism (Antisthenes, the Stoics' Zeno of Citium and his thieving slave), using the Cynic critique of fashion-driven consumption to strip legitimacy from the demand that feeds sweatshops. He rebuts the 'inevitability argument' (comparing it to excusing the Holocaust as inevitable) and the free-choice defense using Aristotle's category of 'mixed' action — sweated workers' consent is coerced by desperate alternatives — and argues, via Adam Smith on the undervaluing of labor, that giant retailers like Wal-Mart distort natural labor prices. He stresses that sweatshops overwhelmingly exploit young women, tying objectification of women as fashion consumers to their oppression as producers.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 26 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Cassidy, through an interior monologue of a shopper eyeing Indonesian-made sandals, weighs individual responsibility for consumerism. She contrasts Singer's drowning-child duty to relieve suffering with Pogge's 'you break it, you buy it' claim that the Global North caused Southern poverty, then uses Scheffler's 'restricted' common-sense responsibility and Cannon's butterfly-effect virtues (replacing the American Dream's acquisitiveness with interconnectedness). Adapting Claudia Card, she distinguishes three senses of responsibility — credit (backward-looking blame), management (of one's lifestyle), and care-taking — and, invoking Noddings's ethics of care, argues that since globalization's impact is uncertain we should shift from assigning blame to caring *about* distant workers, buying less out of boredom-driven habit.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 15 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Scott Aiken argues the conservative 'War on Christmas' pushed by Gibson and O'Reilly is illusory on both fronts: cultural Christianity has already won, and keeping nativity scenes out of public schools protects minority rights under the Establishment Clause rather than persecuting the majority. He then mounts a separate attack, claiming both Christmas myths are bad on their merits – the nativity (star that leads wise men, vanishing Magi, Joseph's pointless genealogy) promotes mere credulity rather than tested faith, while the Santa myth glorifies a slave-owning surveiller who makes goodness merely instrumental. He adds that teaching the false Santa story undercuts parents' testimonial authority to teach the gospel as true.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 17 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Mark Mercer argues that a now largely secular Christmas can help build a liberal, rather than communitarian, multicultural society. He distinguishes liberal multiculturalism, which prizes each individual's flourishing and rests on respect, equality and decency, from communitarian multiculturalism, which treats cultural groups as basic units and breeds identity politics and envy. He detaches Christmas from its Christian origins – trees, lights and Santa now embodying good will and generosity rather than doctrine – and against those who would ban public displays or say only 'Season's Greetings', contends that a shared secular Christmas is one of the few common holidays that can bind citizens of a diverse society together.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 13 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — In this memoir (book Chapter 1, 'A Cannabis Odyssey'), Harvard psychiatrist Lester Grinspoon recounts how his 1967 review of the anti-marijuana literature convinced him he had been 'brainwashed' by a fear-based 'cannabis catechism,' coining 'cannabinophobia' and likening it to the 'madness of crowds.' He argues from personal use — hearing Sgt. Pepper for the first time, quitting psychoanalysis after 'stoned' self-critiques — that beyond recreation and medicine there is a third category, 'enhancement.' The piece is autobiographical drug-policy advocacy rather than the application of a specific named philosopher.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 18 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Taliaferro and Le Gall's 'The Great Escape' weighs four philosophical objections to cannabis-induced altered states — falsehood (Plato's ban on poetry/theatre in the Republic), distortion of reason (Euripides' Bacchae, James on nitrous oxide), undermining of agency (the Sirens, De Quincey's opium), and loss of self-determination (the Stoic Epictetus on freedom) — then surveys Jewish, Christian and Islamic treatments of wine, coffee and hashish. They rebut the objections using Aristotle's cathartic defense of theatre and Locke's imagination-based account of freedom, concluding that if cannabis is no worse than wine the philosophical and religious case against it is not decisive.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 22 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Holt and Kaufman's 'Marijuana and Creativity' surveys creativity research (Guilford's divergent thinking — fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration) and US drug law (Anslinger, 'Reefer Madness,' Schedule I) to test the popular belief, held via figures like Cheech and Chong, Bob Marley and Willie Nelson, that cannabis boosts creativity. Controlled THC-vs-placebo biscuit studies show no benefit — placebo groups who merely believed they were high scored higher, while actual THC reduced fluency and flexibility. They explain the persistent belief through placebo/expectancy effects, spurious correlation, and salience bias, concluding any drug–creativity link is 'manufactured in the drug user's mind.'
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 26 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Tahko surveys the empirical evidence on cannabis from the standpoint of the individual and of society, concluding that its health harms (respiratory illness, mild cognitive impairment, possible dependence, weak links to psychosis) pale beside those of alcohol and tobacco. He argues the gravest costs—legal risk, social isolation, contaminated black-market supply—are consequences of prohibition itself, not the drug. Endorsing public-health experts, he recommends abandoning elimination-based policy for a harm-reduction approach modeled on the Dutch coffee-shop system and Portuguese decriminalization.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 27 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Penrose subjects the 'soft drug / hard drug' distinction to conceptual analysis, arguing that—unlike genuinely graded soft-vs-hard eggs—it tracks no single real spectrum. He tests three candidate bases: phenomenological intensity of the high (incoherent, since 'comparable amounts' and interpersonal 'highness' can't be measured), addictiveness (fails, since the traditional distinction counts non-addictive LSD as 'hard'), and dangerousness (Nutt's Lancet study ranks cannabis as more dangerous than some 'hard' drugs, and the distinction trades on illicitly excluding legal alcohol and nicotine). He concludes drugs vary along many distinct property-lines, so the traditional binary is simply false.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 30 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Earleywine dissects the moral versus practical arguments over prohibition, attacking legal moralism—the drug-czar claim (Bennett, Wilson) that use is wrong simply because it is immoral—as circular, and noting that the law does not criminalize every immoral act (broken contracts, lying). He shows purported moral arguments collapse into utilitarian harm estimates that the data undercut, since use rates are essentially orthogonal to policy across Amsterdam, Australia, Portugal, and US states. He then weighs anti-prohibition rights arguments (religion, privacy in Ravin, property via Szasz, self-determination) and closes on proportionality: owning a harmless plant merits no punishment.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 10 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Schmid's editorial introduction reads climbing through Tejada-Flores' 'Games Climbers Play,' arguing that each climbing game (bouldering, trad, expedition) has its own rules and that climbing ethically means respecting the rules of the game one plays, with 'better style' meaning voluntarily adopting more restrictive rules. Invoking Russell on the value of philosophy and Mallory's 'because it's there,' he surveys the volume's essays and their applied-ethical questions about risk, free soloing, hold manufacturing, and environmental impact. The piece is a map of the book's terrain rather than an argument for one doctrine, previewing Krein's Stoic freedom, Treanor's Aristotelian virtue, Levey's Hegel, and Swan's Zen.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 15 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Heidi Howkins Lockwood examines the 'asymmetry thesis'—that a climber's gratuitous risk is less acceptable than an astronaut's necessary risk—and argues its two standard defenses fail: the Rule of Rescue is neither necessary (free soloists need no rescue yet are condemned) nor sufficient (Hornbein and Unsoeld's risky Everest traverse was praised because it succeeded), and the argument from compassion collapses into circularity. She then shows the intuition is really driven by external background assumptions, especially gender inequality: the media vilified climber-mother Alison Hargreaves while lauding astronaut-mother Christa McAuliffe, because ambition-for-profit violates the 'traditionally female' role of service. She concedes a limited, defensible version tied to the assumption that seeking risk as a mere end (rather than an ineliminable means) is irresponsible.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 18 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Pam Sailors distinguishes two kinds of high-altitude climber: the goal-oriented 'summiteer,' who pursues the summit at all costs for self-affirmation and may neglect others, and the process-oriented 'mountaineer,' who seeks relationship with the mountain, attains self-transcendence, and feels moral responsibility for comrades. Drawing on J. S. Russell and Jonathan Simon, and on cases like the 2006 abandonment of David Sharp versus Dan Mazur giving up his summit to save Lincoln Hall, she argues both types find value in dangerous sport but that the mountaineer—exhibiting courage, compassion, and care—is the morally better person. She backs this with Reinhold Messner, Ed Viesturs, and Sherpa judgment that mountains are not conquered but simply allow, or do not allow, us to climb them.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 19 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Philip Ebert and Simon Robertson defend the self-sufficiency thesis (S): other things being equal, the more self-sufficiently a mountaineering objective is achieved, the better the achievement. Ranking Hermann Buhl's solo, free, alpine-style first ascent of Nanga Parbat above a hypothetical roped-team version and far above a guided, oxygen-and-porter Everest ascent, they argue self-sufficiency (alpine over siege, solo over team, free over aid) is good because it is more committing and adventurous and is partly constitutive of mountaineering itself. They handle objections about foolhardiness (Lafaille on Makalu), incomparable routes (Lhotse South Face), teamwork, and blind climber Erik Weihenmayer via an 'other things being equal' clause, and conclude self-sufficiency acts as a catalyst raising the subjective difficulty and thus the value of every other mountaineering good.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 24 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Ramsey applies the methods of practical/applied ethics to the taboo of hold manufacturing ('chipping'), using Peter Singer's drowning-child argument as his model of following an argument to its uncomfortable conclusion. He builds a syllogism: since climbers accept modifying rock (removing loose rock, vegetation) to make routes climbable, and hold manufacturing is another such modification, manufacturing is sometimes acceptable. He dismantles four common objections (safety, environment, harming future climbers, slippery slope) to argue the near-universal condemnation of chipping is an unjustified bias inconsistent with climbers' actual practices, like the chiseled Jardine Traverse on The Nose.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 31 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Miori, a palliative-care physician assistant and clinical bioethicist, separates personal ethics, professional ethics, and bioethics, then evaluates tattooing through Beauchamp and Childress's principles—especially autonomy (intention, understanding, freedom from outside influence) weighed against risk versus benefit. He concludes tattooing is bioethically fine because safer pigments and market forces reduced its disease risks and because autonomy makes 'to ink or not' the patient's own call, echoing a Millian liberty that one's choice not harming others is 'none of your beeswax.' He ends by defending the memorial tattoo as therapeutic 'memory remodeling' that gluing a positive event in place with pain can make good for you.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 32 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Woods asks whether the claim 'tattooing is immoral' can be defended, taking Adolf Loos's 1908 'Ornament and Crime' (tattooed free men are latent criminals or degenerate aristocrats) as his provocation. He rejects Loos's equation of tattooing with murder, since tattooing is voluntary and self-regarding, but resists the liberal 'sovereign self' reply drawn from Mill's On Liberty by arguing autonomy and the body are relational, not absolute, so a person's self-regarding choices remain open to reasoned challenge and even regulation. He proposes regret evidence in informed consent and an age-25 minimum, concluding tattooing is a matter of both taste and morality.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 26 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Abby Thompson, a somatic psychologist, sets Raja yoga metaphysics (five koshas, a blissful true self distinct from the ego, nadis and chakras as energy flow) beside clinical psychology's brain-chemistry, DSM model, arguing the two paradigms are complementary. Using warrior II and camel pose plus the neuroscience maxim 'neurons that fire together wire together,' she shows how yoga trains self-regulation, distinguishes constructive discomfort from injurious pain, and can serve as complementary therapy — with instructors bearing therapist-like responsibility for the emotional vulnerability and transference that arise on the mat.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 12 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Emily Langan uses focus-group data from 75 self-described ideologically conservative, mostly Christian young men to argue that flirting is a site of moral decision-making, opening with Hitch's 'right broom' line to show these men reject its libido-driven premise. She reports three shared themes—flirting is not about sex but about honesty of motive, timing within a relationship's stages, and reciprocity ('it has to be a two-way street')—and three tensions (healthy vs. harmful, superficial vs. serious, overt vs. covert), drawing on courtship-stage and flirting-style research to show that, contrary to the stereotype that only women agonize over relationships, conservative men wrestle with being 'risqué yet respectable.'
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 17 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Kristie Miller asks whether any dating behavior—dating a sibling, a gorilla, or a blow-up doll—is genuinely 'taboo' in the prudential (self-interested, utility-maximizing) rather than ethical sense, using decision theory's notion of maximizing expected utility. She sorts behaviors labeled 'pathological' into merely conventionally pathological, pseudo-pathological (e.g., polyandry explained by resource scarcity and childrearing), and genuinely pathological (arising from malfunctioning evolved mate-selection modules like symmetry or MHC-odor detection). Because inclusive fitness and utility diverge, and using future-selves discounting and weakness of will (the stable partner vs. the bad-boy biker), she concludes that in some circumstances even dating a sibling or a gorilla can be the utility-maximizing, and thus rational, choice.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 18 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Anne Barnhill uses John Cusack's boom-box serenade in Say Anything, his poolside pleading in The Sure Thing, and Andy Bernard's 'Take a Chance on Me' serenade in The Office to defend 'prospective boundary violation'—violating a boundary that would not exist in a closer relationship in order to create that relationship. She rejects the Kantian reading of Korsgaard and Hill that treating people as ends forbids all non-rational manipulation, arguing instead that such charming pushiness is 'faking it till you make it,' which works via Aristotle's habituation whereby feelings catch up with actions. She then sets four rules (no harm, not too much closer too fast, genuinely wanting the relationship, and that the other would plausibly want it) to separate appropriate from wrong boundary violations.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 19 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Kyla Reid and Tinashe Dune attack the bestselling dating manual The Rules by Fein and Schneider, focusing on Rule 4 (never go Dutch—let the man pay) and Rule 12 (dump him if he gives no romantic gift like jewelry). They line up 'Rules Girls' against sex workers offering a paid 'girlfriend experience' and 'professional girlfriends'/gold diggers, arguing that all three approach relationships in a systematic, 'business-like' way that packages and markets the woman as a product, measures her worth by what the man spends, and treats gifts like performance bonuses. Because monogamy, public recognition, and belief in the relationship cannot make it authentic, they conclude The Rules obstruct genuine intimacy and that everyone should be more critical of dating conventions about who pays and what gifts mean.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 7 "Introduction" — Thomas Fahy's editorial introduction frames the volume by comparing horror to his skydiving experience: both offer the thrill of confronting danger within a promise of safety. He organizes the collection's essays around morality, identity, cultural history, and aesthetics, previewing how each contributor yokes a pop-culture horror text to a philosopher (Nickel's skeptical reading of Psycho/The Birds, Morris on Kant and torture-horror, his own Hobbes reading of In Cold Blood, Lutz's Marx and Land of the Dead). He argues horror's 'play,' hybridity, and repetition let it raise questions about fear, suffering, justice, and the human capacity for violence.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 13 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Theodore Schick treats the Rings of Power as an allegory-free meditation on externalized 'potency,' applying it to emerging genetics, nanotechnology, and robotics. He contrasts the Council of Elrond's choice to destroy the Ring with Boromir's wish to wield it, and with Bill Joy's call to relinquish dangerous research versus Drexler's promise that nanotech could end poverty and disease. Schick argues our situation differs from Middle-earth because the knowledge cannot be un-forged, so grassroots social taming, not destruction of a single artifact, is the realistic response to knowledge-enabled mass destruction.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 41 "It’s Not That Simple" — O'Mathuna uses 24's Jack Bauer to stage the ethics of torture through the "ticking bomb" argument. He frames it with deontology (torture treats persons as mere means), utilitarianism (Shue's ticking-bomb calculus, Mike Novick's "a few may die to save millions"), and virtue ethics (what torture does to Jack and Agent Burke). Marshalling the UN Convention, evidence that torture usually fails (Jack endures Chinese torture; Fayed is tricked, not broken), and its spread to innocents like Audrey Raines, he concludes the sanitized fictional case misrepresents torture's real degradation.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 17 "15. Grey’s Anatomy as Philosophy Ethical Ambiguity in Shades of Grey" — The chapter argues that Meredith Grey embodies Simone de Beauvoir's existentialist ethics from The Ethics of Ambiguity, rejecting the childlike 'spirit of seriousness' that treats moral rules as absolute. Through episodes where Meredith stabilizes a bomb inside a patient's chest, coaches a death-row inmate to induce his own brain death, switches an Alzheimer's-trial placebo for Adele, and commits insurance fraud to treat an immigrant child, it shows her breaking institutional protocol to positively will the freedom of others while owning her choices. It contrasts her authentic embrace of moral ambiguity and risk against Shepherd's, Bailey's, and Webber's rule-bound seriousness or self-interest, framing medical dilemmas as an ambiguous moral realm where no single correct answer exists.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 47 "44. Gattaca as Philosophy Genoism and Justice" — Grinnell argues Gattaca depicts a society built on 'intrinsic genoism' and diagnoses it with Rawls's justice as fairness. He adapts Appiah's distinction between racialism and intrinsic vs. extrinsic racism to genoism, showing that Valids like Josef, Anton, and Eugene treat In-valids like Vincent as inferior simply for being In-valid, discounting all counterevidence. Using Janet Radcliffe Richards's 'separate spheres' argument he shows the caste system is either superfluous or unjust, and via Kitcher's 'life theme' he argues nearly everyone — Vincent, Irene, Anton, Eugene — suffers a low quality of life from having their theme thrust upon them. He concludes that Rawls's veil of ignorance and difference principle would dismantle the separate spheres and give everyone a fair, autonomy-respecting shot at their chosen life.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 48 "45. A.I. Artificial Intelligence as Philosophy Machine Consciousness and Intelligence" — Gamez uses Spielberg/Kubrick's A.I. to separate three things the film conflates: intelligence, consciousness, and emotion. He argues intelligence is a functional property (David could pass a Turing test but a skilled interrogator would spot him), whereas consciousness is a physical property that cannot be inferred from David's human-like behavior — only a mathematical theory mapping physical to conscious states could tell whether David really experiences the love, fear, and pain that drive our empathy in the Flesh Fair. He insists the ethics of destroying mechas should hinge on their consciousness, not their intelligence, and connects David's engineered, irreversible imprinting-love to Lorenz's ethology and Damasio/James theories of emotion, and his eerie early behavior to Mori's uncanny valley.

### Ockham's Razor

Ockham's Razor is the methodological principle that, among competing explanations, one should not multiply entities or assumptions beyond necessity, so that the simpler account is to be preferred when it explains the evidence equally well. Named for the fourteenth-century logician William of Ockham, who favored parsimony in his rejection of superfluous metaphysical posits, it functions as a rule of theoretical economy rather than a proof of truth. It responds to the temptation to explain phenomena by inventing unobserved causes, urging that explanatory machinery be justified by what it actually accounts for.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 23 "Erotic Love and Friendship" — Maps Aristotle's three levels of friendship onto Buffy's three boyfriends: Riley is a utility friendship chosen for the rational goal of a 'normal' boyfriend (echoed by Warren's robot April and the Buffybot, which prove programmed perfection cannot be loved), Spike is a pleasure friendship driven by passion and danger that Buffy ends in 'As You Were,' and Angel is a complete friendship where each values the other for his own sake despite the gypsy curse. This lets the authors solve Aristotle's love paradox (is erotic love chosen or does it choose us?) by adding Augustine's and William of Ockham's third power of the soul, the will: an arational faculty that values the other as an end in himself, neither rationally chosen nor irrationally caused.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 28 "The Meta-Fear of Fear" — Noel Carroll traces Halloween's Undead imagery to the Celtic Samhain and its Catholic absorption into All Hallows' Eve, then asks the paradox: why do we take pleasure in images of the death that, as Heidegger says, is the deep source of Angst we spend our lives denying? He examines Ernest Jones's Freudian analysis - the vampire as wish-fulfillment disguising an incestuous desire, horror as the price the super-ego exacts - and rejects it as theoretically expensive, invoking the demand for simpler, more economical explanation. His own hypothesis is the 'meta-fear of fear': adolescent viewers (and aging ones) use horror films and the holiday's zombie costumes to test and master fear itself, with parody and Bergson's laughter as companion devices of emotional control - a folk remedy that needs no unconscious to work.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 27 "Emergentism Now Can Scotty Beam Us Up" — Tests three theories of mind against Spock's katra transfer in The Wrath of Khan and The Search for Spock and his mind melds with Kirk, the Horta, and Rock people. Descartes's divisibility argument backs the dualism the katra assumes, but the argument from parsimony (Ockham's razor), the problem of mental causation, and the conservation of energy weigh against it; Churchland's eliminative materialism plays by science's rules but runs into Nagel's 'what it is like' objection, dramatized by Geordi failing to describe anger to Data without circularity. The author lands, cautiously, on Searle-style emergentism — mind as an emergent, irreducible feature of neural complexity, as when Nomad and V'Ger exceed their programming — while conceding Kim's charge that it may be dualism in disguise.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 20 "Zelda Is a Communication Game!" — Johnson argues that because Zelda has no single authorial vision (teams, outside developers, cryptic Aonuma interviews), the timeline is a 'communication game' fans play together. Interpretation follows the hermeneutic circle of Heidegger and Gadamer (parts inform the whole, as when Wind Waker's references to Ganon's earlier attacks make sense of the series), faces Leibnizian underdetermination since infinitely many theories fit the games, and uses Ockham's razor, whose failures (the y=2x formula) show that simplicity is relative to a community's training, as in Wittgenstein's pupil who suddenly counts '1,004, 1,008'. Hence Miyamoto's own claim that Zelda is a communication game: designers supply puzzle pieces, and the fan community creates the meaning.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 9 "Is Monk’s Certainty Justified" — Rauhut tests Monk's method against two models of discovery: Holmes-style eliminatism, modeled on Popper's falsification via reductio ad absurdum, and CSI-style confirmationism in the mold of Hempel and Carnap (Gil Grissom letting evidence speak). Monk fits neither — in 'Mr. Monk and the Astronaut' he refuses to eliminate the alibi-solid Steve Wagner, and in 'Mr. Monk Falls in Love' he ignores a hatpin, a motive, and a confession pointing at Leyla. Instead Monk is an 'epiphanist': he registers every anomaly (the secretary hired from a Lamaze-class ad in 'Mr. Monk Fights City Hall', Crawford's odd phrasing 'No, she wouldn't be drinking now'), suddenly sees the one theory explaining all of them, and only afterwards manufactures shareable evidence for others. His absolute certainty, the chapter argues, rests on a metaphysical faith that only the true theory can explain every anomaly — a Leibnizian 'best of all possible ordered worlds' — the same obsession with order that makes him notice anomalies at all, though it makes him epistemically irresponsible by ordinary standards that weigh alternative hypotheses and simplicity.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 8 "Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New ‘Intelligent Falling’ Theory" — Ruiz uses Onion stories—'Jesus Answers Half The Prayers At Area Roulette Table,' 'God Answers Prayers Of Paralyzed Little Boy,' 'Christianity Celebrates One Billionth Unanswered Prayer'—to argue that belief in God lacks rational justification. Following Hume's empiricism (all ideas trace to sense perception), methodological naturalism, and Ockham's Razor, he shows that feelings of God's presence, scriptural circularity, and answered prayers (riddled with selection bias) all fail as evidence, and the prayer hypothesis is unfalsifiable—a theory that explains any outcome, like the brain tumor thanking God for its surviving surgery, is supported by no evidence. He closes by dismantling Paley's watchmaker design argument through the infinite regress ('who designed God?') and by treating 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' as the reductio of design reasoning.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 28 "Get Serious" — David Kyle Johnson takes Nietzsche's suggestion that God is slowly dying and reads The Onion's religion stories — the faith healer who loses a patient during a routine miracle, Kansas fundamentalists lobbying to overturn the Second Law of Thermodynamics, and 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' — as evidence of secularization. He splits blind faith (irrational belief despite evidence, as with Bush's 'Blind-Faith-Based Initiatives') from genuine faith as belief without sufficient evidence, arguing religion does science badly whenever it shields creationism from falsification. But science rests on unproven assumptions too, he shows via Hume's problem of induction, Descartes' skeptical problem, and Wittgenstein's charge that naming a 'strong nuclear force' explains no more than God pushing things down. Ockham's razor then decides for atheism — an unexplained universe is simpler than God plus a universe — though William James's will to believe leaves a door open for faith where evidence is impossible, qualified by Clifford's warning that beliefs likely to harm others are never permissible.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 26 "The Future of Sandy Cheeks" — Wilson González-Espada assesses Sandy Cheeks as a portrait of the scientist: she explodes the 'Draw a Scientist' stereotype — female, socially popular, working in an open treedome that mirrors peer review — yet the show muddles the nature of science, calling inventions 'experiments' and a clipboard of math 'science'. The chapter applies Popper's falsifiability to SpongeBob's one-sided evidence that Squidward is a true friend and Newton's principle of parsimony to Sandy's ghost scare, then closes with Aldo Leopold's land ethic, reading 'Jellyfish Hunter' and 'SpongeBob's Last Stand' as environmental parables about habitat and overexploitation.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 13 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Don Fallis proposes deception rather than language as the personhood test: following Dennett, a deceiver must be a second-order intentional system who can want someone else to have a false belief, as when General Thade lies to Senator Sandar about Ari's kidnapping, Zira and Cornelius feign muteness before the Presidential Commission, and Caesar fakes his own electrocution in Conquest. The roles' reversal makes this a test for the films' mute humans too, while Descartes's beast machines, Wittgenstein on dogs that cannot simulate pain, and Lloyd Morgan's canon voice the skeptical reading of fake alarm calls and Koko's 'Cat did it.' Against them Fallis invokes Occam's Razor over Hare, Call and Tomasello's food-competition experiments: apes track who sees what, but they fail the misinformed false-belief version, so real apes may not be 'sneaky enough to be people.'
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 11 "Psych and Philosophy" — Jones argues that Shawn's 'psychic' act is really hypersensory perception (HSP) - noticing cat fur, fine print, blood spatter - feeding inference to the best explanation (IBE), the natural abductive method Sherlock Holmes mislabels deduction, with Clever Hans and Ilga Kirks as real-world parallels. Applying IBE with Ockham's Razor to the two hypotheses 'he's psychic' versus 'he's hyper-observant,' she concludes the natural explanation should win for everyone: Lassiter's skepticism tracks the evidence, Gus knows better despite believing in ghosts, and Chief Vick shouldn't buy the supernatural story either. Juliet's belief survives only through background supernatural beliefs, a psychic-friendly culture, and ignoring the clues Gus feeds Shawn, which the chapter diagnoses as the same public misunderstanding of the scope and limits of science that keeps most Americans believing in ESP.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 15 "Psych and Philosophy" — Guidry-Grimes treats Chief Vick's hiring of Shawn as a genuine problem in applied ethics rather than a joke: the Psi hypothesis fails Ockham's Razor and no controlled study supports paranormal ability, yet Vick - unlike viewers who know Shawn is a fraud - must weigh her obligations to victims, the department, and taxpayers on the evidence she has. The chapter argues that hiring Shawn is ethically defensible given his record of solving over fifty unsolvable cases, but it catalogues the costs: false hope for distraught families (Marc Klaas's resentment of psychic tipsters), damage to Lassiter's morale, wasted resources, and the fragile public trust bound up with taxpayer money. The conclusion is a compromise: Vick is ethically required to use every tool in the arsenal, including a successful 'psychic,' only in desperate high-stakes cases where the victim's family does not object, and otherwise merely permitted.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 14 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Sharon Kaye stages a fourteenth-century debate over a contradiction: Jesus truthfully prophesied that the Antichrist will come, yet the Antichrist remains free not to. Peter Aureoli denies bivalence for statements about the future, Thomas Bradwardine has God swap among infinite possible-world 'movies,' and Ockham's follower John of Mirecourt concludes that Jesus simply lied - each solution self-defeating or heretical. Using Ockham's Razor and her comic fantasy of seducing the Antichrist, Kaye argues the unsolvable prophecy problem helped discredit prophetic religion, ushered in theological determinism via Luther and Calvin, and opened a secular age.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 15 "6. The PowerPoint Conspiracy Theory" — In a sustained deadpan parody, Ketcham builds a conspiracy out of Ockham's Razor: William of Ockham's minimalist principle explains PowerPoint's big-type bullet points, but the slide deck (secretly engineered by DARPA with Microsoft, exported via Siberia to Putin) becomes a weapon that breeds stupidity, conditions Trump to tweet-length simplicities like fake news and crooked, and finally rigs him, not the voting machines. The chapter also wields the Razor correctly, insisting that a minimalist explanation must still be good and complete, as when little Jill's one bullet point tells us too little. Testing moral realism, Kant's absolute prohibition on lying, and utilitarianism's greatest happiness against the conspiracy's missing facts, it concludes we lack the information to render any moral verdict, which is exactly what the conspiracy-minded minimalists want.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 17 "7. Scott Adams’s Joy of Logic" — Bilsker turns Adams's Joy of Work catalogue of irrational co-workers into a critical-thinking syllabus: faulty analogy (from dogs fetching sticks to potatoes dancing, and Francis Bacon's body-politic passage praising war as exercise), huge-pants faulty causation, the Reinhart-Rogoff debt paper that drove austerity policy on mere correlation until Herndon, Ash, and Pollin exposed it, complex and objectionable cause, the overapplication of Occam's Razor to moon-landing hoaxes, misplaced authority, begging the question, and egocentric biases like I Am the World. He then contrasts the classroom view that confirmation bias is an unconscious background program with Win Bigly's claim that bias is the operating system itself, worrying about the implication that reasoning with anyone is futile, and concludes that Adams overstates how incapable we are of overcoming our biases.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 19 "We’ve Run Out of Time… or Have We" — The chapter argues that the film's multiverse, where sorcerers 'harness energy drawn from other dimensions,' is best modeled on the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics, walking through Tegmark's Level I-III multiverses, Schrodinger's cat, the double-slit experiment, and the measurement problem (Copenhagen, von Neumann-Wigner's mind-caused collapse, and Everett's branching) to show that interpreting the formalism is philosophy rather than physics. It defends many-worlds against the objections of counterintuition and Ockham's razor, and suggests that Strange trapping Dormammu in a time loop works like a quantum experiment, with branching worlds dissolving the grandfather paradox.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 22 "NOTES" — Asks how to tell genuine science from pseudoscience using Chandra Suresh's rejected Activating Evolution theory, Sheldrake's morphic fields, alchemy, and Behe's intelligent design. Kuhn's picture of normal science, anomalies, and revolutions explains why Suresh would need a full-blown crisis in evolutionary theory — such as people actually flying — before the community accepts him, and why time rather than mockery settles a theory's fate. Ockham's razor condemns the unnecessary organizing principles in both Sheldrake's and Suresh's theories, and intelligent design is exposed as bad method because, like creationism, it was devised to protect a prior commitment from disconfirming fossil and cosmological evidence.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 21 "10 Fact, Truth, and Evidence A Lesson from Dr. Tyree" — Dean Kowalski stages an imagined dialogue between Indy and William E. Tyree — Harrison Ford's real Ripon College philosophy professor, whom Ford's own script rewrite placed 'right down the hall' — to show that 'archaeology is the search for fact, not truth' is self-defeating if truth is correspondence with reality. Tyree's epistemology primer (principles of evidence, inductive generalization, hypothesis testing like Indy's Sankara-stone glow prediction, and Ockham's Razor) explains Indy's resistance to the God hypothesis despite witnessing the Ark, the Grail's instant healing of Henry Sr., and the invisible bridge he crossed on guesswork rather than knowledge. The resolution: Indy practices methodological naturalism, keeping deeper truths out of archaeology, without being committed to metaphysical naturalism.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 30 "Notes" — Leuenberger argues that a LEGO MOC is a surprisingly faithful model of David Lewis's Humean supervenience: the world is just a vast mosaic of local matters of particular fact — homogeneous, arbitrarily recombinable atomic bricks (fundamental properties at space-time points) with no necessary connections, Hume's 'greater denier', versus gunky Play-Doh or jigsaw pieces. Ockham's Razor motivates the view (while also able to cut against a divine master builder, whom Lewis's world lacks, though LEGO-world builders likewise stand outside their creations), and Lewis's concrete possible worlds make every build a replica rather than a creation, answered to the 'incredulous stare' by quantitative parsimony. Four-dimensionally stacked creations model change as variation along temporal parts, while the causation objection — nothing in one LEGO creation brings about the next — marks the fundamental Humean/non-Humean divide.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 20 "Zelda Is a Communication Game!" — Carl Matthew Johnson argues that the split-timeline versus linear-timeline fan war, settled by Eiji Aonuma's 2006 Nintendo Dream interview, is really a hermeneutic meta-game fans play on top of Zelda. He applies the Heidegger-Gadamer hermeneutic circle — the Ganon references in Wind Waker make sense only from knowledge of the whole series, while gossip-stone text about Kaepora Gaebora feeds back into the whole — then uses Leibniz's curve-fitting problem to show timeline evidence underdetermines any single interpretation. Ockham's razor and Wittgenstein's counting-by-twos rule-following example reveal that simplicity is community-relative, culminating in Miyamoto's 2007 claim that Zelda was designed from the start as a 'communication game' among players.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 20 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Curry argues that angels like Anna and Castiel can reasonably be atheists, because a higher perspective confers no epistemic advantage about God: Anna admits only four angels have seen him and the rest 'take it on faith.' Aquinas's cosmological argument, illustrated by the endless causal chain behind the Impala, yields at most an uncaused first cause rather than an omnipotent, omnibenevolent one, and Paley's design argument, an Impala in the desert implies a designer, is undermined by Darwinian natural selection, which Castiel himself witnessed ('Don't step on that fish'). The free-will theodicy fails against natural evils like famine and childhood cancer, and the principle of parsimony tells angels to expect a natural explanation for their own existence, so Uriel's 'There is no will. No wrath. No God.' turns out to be rational.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 29 "NOTES" — Richard Brown uses the title 'The Terminator' itself to run the debate over definite descriptions: Russell's theory of descriptions makes 'The Terminator can't be bargained with' false (there are many T-101s, and no real-life Terminator at all), while Strawson insists Kyle's utterance genuinely refers to the machine at the door. Donnellan's referential/attributive distinction is staged through Lieutenant Traxler's 'The phone book killer has no pity' — true of whoever fits the description, or of the very Terminator Sarah has in mind — and Kripke's arguments from 'Russell English,' anaphora, and indirect quotation are weighed against Devitt's pronoun-of-laziness and reference-borrowing replies. The chapter sides with Grice's modified Ockham's razor: descriptions are not semantically ambiguous, so the title is literally false but apt, since Cameron referentially means the T-101.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 26 "When Life Gives You Chlamydia" — Andrew Zimmerman Jones explains Veronica's casework as inductive reasoning: Occam's razor dispatches Meryl's 'space laser' speculation and identifies Gia's stalker via the simplest explanation (the stalker drove off in the pick-up), while Keith's refusal to accept Abel Koontz's confession shows the razor's limits — Sheriff Lamb's laziness being Sidney Brenner's 'Occam's broom,' whisking inconvenient facts like Lilly's body temperature under the rug. Distinguishing Aristotle's particulars-to-universal induction from deduction, the chapter teaches the probability fallacy through the Mercer evidence (clippers, cologne, and GHB make it likely the rapist owns them, not that their owner is the rapist — the same confusion fueling suspicion of PCH-ers) and catalogues the fallacies — false dilemma, false cause, ad hominem, appeal to emotion — that Veronica's jealousy-driven reasoning commits in the Sully case. The chlamydia diagnosis revealing Cassidy raped her is the final lesson: new evidence overturns even well-confirmed conclusions, so certainty is a sucker's bet.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 21 "19_LaRocca_Chapter_018.html" — Rick Altman dismantles four and a half 'fallacies' that let film theory ignore sound: the historical fallacy (sound as a late add-on), the ontological fallacy (image alone is cinema), the reproductive fallacy (recording reproduces rather than represents sound), the nominalist fallacy, and the half-fallacy of indexicality. In the nominalist section he explicitly frames the dispute over whether the 'same' sound heard from different seats shares a real identity as the medieval realism-versus-nominalism debate, casting Plato and Augustine as the realists and William of Ockham as the nominalist, and warning that ultra-nominalism about sound jeopardizes shared understanding. He uses Peirce's index/icon/symbol distinction to argue electronics has desacralized cinema's indexicality.

### The Question Concerning Technology

In his reflections on technology, Heidegger argues that its essence is not any particular machine or tool but a mode of disclosure he calls "enframing," in which everything shows up as a stockpile of resources to be ordered and exploited. Modern technology thus reveals nature and even human beings as mere "standing-reserve," narrowing our sense of what things are. Heidegger warns that this way of seeing is dangerous because it threatens to conceal other, richer relations to the world, yet he suggests that recognizing it may also open a path toward a freer relationship with technology.

- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 19 "Only a Jedi Can Save Us Forgetting and Recollecting" — Abrams reads the saga through Heidegger's philosophy of technology: the lightsaber Luke learns to feel as an extension of his body is the authentic 'ready-to-hand,' while the Death Star - a massive mechanical eye that enfames Alderaan on its viewscreen before destroying it - embodies the 'present-at-hand' gaze of enframing that converts nature into standing reserve (clone and droid armies, stormtrooper armor). Yoda on Dagobah is perfect attunement, an authentic being-in-the-world who is 'at home' with being, and the Force parallels Heidegger's being: everywhere, easily forgotten. Anakin's slide - slave of Watto, severed hand replaced by cybernetics, final encasement in Vader's armor - is progressive enframing and forgetting of his own being, and Luke's 'the name of your true self... you've only forgotten' is the recollection of being by which the Jedi, not a god, saves us.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 15 "U2 and Philosophy" — Thomson uses U2's self-declared postmodern phase to define postmodernity itself: a sensitivity to poetic polysemy against modernity's fantasies of total control (Heidegger's reduction of everything to optimizable resource), Lyotard's incredulity toward metanarratives - defended against the self-refutation charge and narrowed to the dying metanarratives of unity and emancipation - and the Marx-Nietzsche-Freud hermeneutics of suspicion that fragmented the subject, with Kierkegaard and early Heidegger as the resisters. Derrida's 9/11 analysis of autoimmunity and hauntology is read into 'Peace on Earth' and the sorrows that 'learned to swim' in 'Until the End of the World'. The payoff is a polysemic reading of 'Even Better than the Real Thing': risky as a seeming hymn to Baudrillard's simulacra, addressed to a live audience it celebrates a communal love 'even better' than personal love - Diotima's ladder generalized - making the postmodern U2 continuous with the 'Christ-ian' U2 of universal love, sealed by 'One'.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 25 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Zani reads the Q-branch scene through Heidegger's 'The Question Concerning Technology': technology as technê, a revealing and bringing-forth that turns dangerous when it reduces the world to standing-reserve and turns people into stockpilists, as with Goldfinger, who kills Jill Masterson over gold and cannot let anything he does not own exist. Bond's villains (Drax declaring 'What he doesn't own he doesn't want' before shooting pheasants for sport; Grant's garrote watch) use technology as domination and amusement, whereas Bond uses it defensively and refuses to be owned by it - hurling the ATAC off the cliff with 'That's détente' and preferring the lighter to the match 'until they go wrong'. The repeated match-and-lighter password exchange in From Russia with Love encapsulates the films' Heideggerian moral: a free relation to technology that uses tools when needed and lets them recede, rather than becoming what one controls.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 26 "James Bond and Philosophy" — McKinney argues that '007' is a technological construction distinct from the human James Bond: drawing on Dewey's broad view of technology as technique (the shaken martini as technological artifact), Heidegger's account of naming as revealing and enframing, and Don Ihde's technological embodiment (the party-game hand axe that is art, paperweight, or tool depending on perception). Film dialogue shows the naming at work: Moneypenny calls him 'James' but announces '007 is here' to M; Goldfinger greets '007' and is corrected with 'My name is James Bond'; M threatens '008 can replace you' and, in Die Another Day, declares 'You are no use to anyone now' while rescinding his status. The chapter closes with the Kantian point that persons must be treated as ends in themselves, yet the designation '007' constitutes Bond as precisely a replaceable means to MI6's ends.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 9 "iPod" — Raven reads design history as a pendulum between 'Beauty Waves' (Art Nouveau's sinuous decoration, 1960s psychedelia) and 'Truth Waves' (Art Deco functionalism, Le Corbusier's 'machine for living'), poles he grounds in Berkeley's 'esse est percipi' idealism versus metaphysical realism. The late-1990s blobject -- the iMac, the New Beetle, the MACH3 razor -- begins merging the waves through computer-aided design, and the iPod, launched five weeks after 9/11 and named for Kubrick's pod ('Open the pod bay door, Hal'), is the 'minimalist blobject' or 'squircle' where the merger completes. Reading the moment through Heidegger's claim that technology transforms human existence 'in its innermost recesses' and through Freud's pleasure versus reality principles, he argues the Iraq War sealed the reality principle into consumer design: 'our iPods now have edges.'
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 16 "Thinking Inside the Pod" — Condella reads the opening of Saturday Night Fever -- Tony Manero strutting to 'Stayin' Alive' while delivering a can of paint -- as the iPod condition in miniature: music that alters rather than captures reality, now dial-up-able for workouts ('Eye of the Tiger'), bus rides, and grocery runs. Through Heidegger he argues the iPod is calculative thinking incarnate, annihilating the time, silence, and solitude meditative thinking requires (the shower as last refuge), and deepening technological homelessness by flattening every place into whatever soundtrack we choose -- the Rhine dammed into a 'gigantic gasoline station,' the iPod pushing us 'pretty far down' in Plato's Cave, its very possibility prepared by Descartes's thinking thing. Yet his wife's yoga instructor chanting on a Bronx bus shows the iPod can also open meditative space, so what Heidegger demands is not Luddism but Gelassenheit, a free relationship to technology.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 22 "The Verdict" — Turner runs an ethical audit of iPod use through Levinas's face-to-face: sharing one iPod with his wife forces 'musical justice' negotiations (veto power over a Motörhead cut, gnashing through Bette Midler), his toddler son's listening requires vigilance, and illegal downloading fails Levinas's test that morality begins by ceding 'my place in the sun' to the Other — hence Radiohead's pay-what-you-want release as the Levinasian move, and iPod cafés where strangers DJ for each other while language preserves alterity. Heidegger supplies the counterweight: the shuffle's 'openness to mystery' versus calculative mastery that reduces The Who's Tommy to the 'Pinball Wizard' riff and silences all non-digital media, just as Kant's conditions of possible experience (space, time) would silence things outside them. Derrida's point that categories contain traces of what they exclude illuminates unclassifiable marginal works — bluegrass Pink Floyd, San Francisco Symphony plays Metallica — and the verdict closes with Hölderlin's 'where danger is, grows the saving power also', exiting Plato's cave by thinking the iPod's ethics at all.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 7 "Where Pink Floyd Ends and Radiohead Begins" — Reisch asks whether Radiohead is the Pink Floyd of the twenty-first century and answers that the comparison misleads: where Barrett-era Floyd used electronics to escape into psychedelic fantasy, Radiohead's apparent space-rock is phenomenological, giving voice to pre-reflective experience of technological modern life. He reads 'No Surprises' (Yorke singing with his head in a filling glass sphere) as a study in the political infantilization of commuters, and OK Computer's car crash ('Airbag'), 'Let Down', and 'Lucky' as registering the feel of a fragile, technology-saturated world. Quoting Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man and Chomsky on manufactured consent, he argues we can see no alternative to the technologically rational system, and then, against Descartes' priority of the isolated 'I', invokes Heidegger's Being-in-the-world and Merleau-Ponty's embodied subject to suggest that our deepening immersion in technology may be changing the self itself — the truth the collapsing pedestrians of the 'Just' video cannot face.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 26 "At Ease" — Adam Koehler reads Kid A's disfigured, barely intelligible vocals through Heidegger's account of how enabling technology withdraws into an invisible backdrop of everydayness: Pablo Honey hides its studio machinery behind "natural" rock, but Kid A — the cycled voice of "Everything in Its Right Place," the unintelligible vocoded "Kid A," "How to Disappear Completely" — forces the artifice itself into view, and with it the withdrawn world technology ordinarily conceals. The song is beautiful, he argues, because its willful failure to communicate feels human, enacting the anxiety of living in an information age that traps as much as it connects; John Mayer's lyric-clearing acoustic cover misses the point, since making sense now means risking not making sense, and the album's demand is that we listen to, and understand, everything withdrawn in the background.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 27 "If You Think that You’re Strong Enough . ." — Matthew Lampert argues that Radiohead's stock theme of "alienation" is exactly Heideggerian inauthenticity: das Man's platitudes made audible in "Fitter Happier," the falling into the world's "uninhibited hustle" of "Ripcord" and "Let Down," and the tranquility that hides both the problem and any exit. He traces the band's arc from the punk-romantic fix of "Anyone Can Play Guitar" (choose and win yourself, form a band) to a deeper diagnosis on The Bends and OK Computer, where Heidegger's Ge-stell and standing-reserve show that in a technological framework only further technological solutions to technological alienation are available. Following "Why Poets?" and Holderlin's question, he concludes that Kid A makes Radiohead the poets in a desolate time: by risking disappearance itself ("How to Disappear Completely," "Idioteque") and singing alienation in its fullness rather than offering false hope, they stare into the abyss where "the more brightly do the ways into the saving power begin to shine."
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 25 "The Sacrificial Lamb" — Argues Astro Boy re-enacts the sacrificial logic of the atomic age: Atomu is the nuclear-powered copy of the dead Tobio, born from Dr. Tenma's refusal to accept mortality, and his repeated self-sacrifice for humans who discard him (as in 'Save the Classmate,' where the rescued boys' parents still want him removed) shows him functioning as Heidegger's 'standing-reserve' — an object valued only as stored power, with humans themselves next in line. Drawing on Plato's Republic anxiety over originals and copies, Adorno and Horkheimer's dialectic of enlightenment, and Rey Chow's account of mimesis as the sign left by sacrifice, the chapter reads the series as mourning an innocence that became impossible after Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 18 "Only an Ortiz Can Save Us Heidegger’s Revelation of Being" — James Pontuso reads Red Sox history through Heidegger: technology that turns the world into 'standing reserve' breeds the anxious 'everydayness' of the mediocre Pinky Higgins teams, while the run of near-misses from 1967 through Bucky Dent in 1978 and Buckner in 1986 threw fans into an authentic encounter with tragedy, mortality and the mystery of Being that the Yankees' free-agent 'technology of power' could never teach. Fenway Park, quirky and continuous with the pre-Hitler past, serves as 'home' in Heidegger's homeless age, and the literati's tragic framing of the team (language as the house of Being) made its fate a matter of existential weight rather than mere sport. David Ortiz's 2004 ALCS heroics then function as Heidegger's longed-for revelation of Being, the answer to 'only a god can save us,' after which fans have lived through all three states: everydayness, tragic anxiety, and wonder.
- **Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_**, ch. 4 "index" — Six essays on friendship in the Facebook age. Tedesco asks whether the low-demand 'Facebook friendship' can reconcile the utilitarian demand for impartiality (Mill, Railton, Kagan) with the partiality of real friends, and concludes Facebook ties are only supplementary to relationships built elsewhere. Hamington surveys a hundred users and argues in Noddings's care-ethics terms that Facebook's information transfer makes caring possible (knowledge of the concrete other is necessary for care), though it also makes dropping a student over one racist comment effortless. Bloor reads Facebook through Heidegger's technological nihilism and the anonymous 'one', warning that speed of exchange erodes Aristotle's few deep, morally formative friendships, while Briggle's farewell letter to Facebook judges the site by Ivan Illich's convivial-tool criteria and Cuonzo recasts pokes and virtual gifts as efficient successors to primate grooming; Lattimore applies Bakhtin's 'excess of seeing' to how viewers 'consummate' other users' self-presentations.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 21 "The Test of Humanity" — Reads the Butlerian Jihad through Heidegger's philosophy of technology: technology is not a device but a way of 'enframing' the world as a standing-reserve, so the Harkonnens see Arrakis, the Fremen, and even Mentat Piter as mere resources, while the Fremen's maker hooks and ecological terraforming show tools absorbed into a lived practice that shapes their users in turn. Paul's prescience becomes the ultimate tool—perfect advice that puts his life on autopilot through Dune Messiah—so Leto II's breeding of Siona-gene humans invisible to oracles completes the Jihad's lesson: self-determination and 'living judgments,' not optimization, are what the Gom Jabbar's test of humanity is for.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 26 "Straining the Limits of Machine and Man" — Reads Peart's ambivalence about technology through Heidegger's techne as revealing and Marx's account of the worker: 'Working Man''s no-time-for-living day, '2112''s priests whose 'great computers' smash the protagonist's guitar, 'Manhattan Project''s Oppenheimer problem, and 'Test for Echo''s 'video vertigo.' Against Ellul-style autonomous technology the chapter insists Peart believes we still control our machines, and it ends with Rush mastering its own studio gear — and the motorcycle of Ghost Rider as the machine that carries Peart through grief.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 18 "The Lung-less, All-Penetrating Masterful World-Silence" — The section reads Do Androids Dream through Heidegger's 'The Question Concerning Technology': mood organs, empathy boxes, Buster Friendly and catalog-bought animals alienate humans from the world, each other and themselves until only the 'silence of the world' remains, which Isidore theorizes as the inevitable kipple-ization of the universe. Byron's 'Darkness' and Nietzsche's parable of the clever beasts frame Deckard's drive into the dead desert after his last retirement, where he confronts a universe of dead stones that perceive and remember nothing.
- **Philip K.
