The virtuous poet wins all nine Muses by wooing their mother Mnemosyne — tapping the collective memory of the race with gratitude and discipline — which explains why Springsteen, unlike the prideful Dylan who lost the Muses, retains moral authority; the philosophers, needless to say, are just jealous of the bar.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 9 "Where Do We Go from Here" — David Kyle Johnson argues that Colbert's gut-thinking persona (the Harriet Miers 'I know her heart' bit, 'that's my right' on the Panama Canal) satirizes a real and widespread vice, and he refutes the philosophies behind it. Individual and moral relativism collapse into self-contradiction and absurdity ('Lincoln was not assassinated' would be 'true for' someone; Hitler could not be condemned), while gut-justification is what Locke called 'enthusiasm' - a belief that is 'its own proof,' circular like the prophet whose revelation needs no burning bush. Following Jamie Whyte, he dismantles the 'right to my opinion' (running example: the friend who insists on a grassy-knoll shooter despite the melon-head evidence): there is no epistemic or moral right to undefended belief, and no right to intellectual comfort. Against this he holds up Socrates, wisest because he alone admitted ignorance, and insists philosophy and politics progress only through argument, so truthiness is never an acceptable substitute.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 20 "Colbert Is (the Tragedy and Comedy of) America, and So Are We" — Ralkowski asks whether Colbert is America's Socrates, comparing Colbert's ironic interviews (Caitlin Flanagan on feminism, Harvey Mansfield on manliness, Howard Dean's superdelegates, the ABC Stephanopoulos-Gibson debate) to Socrates' definitional refutations of Euthyphro and the Athenian elite. Like Socrates in Plato's cave allegory, Colbert is a shadow on the wall undermining truthiness from within, yet both fail: audiences laugh, guests collect the campaign-donation 'Colbert Bump,' and nothing changes, making America the self-satisfied one who is ignorant of its ignorance. Through Nehamas's contrast of Socratic and Platonic irony and the Symposium's demand that the greatest work read as both tragedy and comedy, the chapter concludes Colbert may be America's Plato — condemning and laughing at us like a Sisyphean liberator who knows we will not leave the cave.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 7 "World of Warcraft and Philosophy" — The editors' introduction, framed as an in-game quest log ('Read a Philosophy Book,' reward: +21 Intellect), argues that WoW is a profound cultural phenomenon that deserves philosophy because the world is virtual but the people, guilds, and Blizzard developers behind it are real. It models philosophizing on Socrates' claim that he knew he did not know, inviting readers to honestly examine the guiding principles they already rely on when playing and living. Chapters can be tackled in any order like a quest log, and the goal is a more open mind about gamer life rather than final answers.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 17 "Alone into the Desert" — Audits Duniverse lives by Socrates's standard—the condition of the soul over wealth and power, with justice, courage, temperance, and wisdom—finding Baron Harkonnen utterly wanting, 'Leto the Just' compromised by forgery and concubinage, Paul unjust in his myth-making holy war (though Plato's Republic would smile on ruling myths), and the Fremen admirable in temperance and courage but fatally sure of themselves where Socrates prized knowing that you do not know. Aristotle's function argument and golden mean follow: Paul's first worm-ride is courage between rashness and cowardice, but Paul's and Leto II's extreme, humanity-saving selflessness has no excess to moderate and so breaks the doctrine of the mean. The author concludes Socrates is too harsh and Aristotle closer, yet even he fails: sometimes the best life requires extreme virtue and even injustice, as with the two Atreides emperors.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 7 "Know Thyself" — George Reisch's introduction frames the volume with Martha Stout's claim that one in twenty-five people is a conscience-free sociopath who hides in plain sight, arguing that we viewers do the hiding work for them just as Deb, LaGuerta and Batista's assumptions shield Dexter. It presents Dexter's incessant inner questioning as the show's philosophical hook and previews the book's competing verdicts on Harry's Code: monster, Kantian-style model actor, utilitarian good, aesthete, or superhero. It ends by inverting Socrates: normally we point 'know thyself' inward, but the real epistemic danger is the sociopath next door, so our skepticism should aim at the guy in forensics - unless we are ourselves among the one-in-twenty-five, in which case Socrates' injunction to self-examination was spot on.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 27 "Secret Revealed . . . I Wonder" — Robert Vuckovich reads 'The Secret Box' through Plato's Theaetetus — wonder as the birth of philosophy, with Patrick playing Socratic midwife to SpongeBob's desire to know — and Hobbes's diagnosis of curiosity as 'a lust of the mind' that obsesses and torments until satisfied. SpongeBob's masked break-in turns epistemic desire into what Cicero condemns as 'knavery that wears the mask of wisdom', nearly destroying the friendship, while the Charmides ideal of self-knowledge as temperance is exactly what he lacks. The episode ends like a Platonic dialogue in aporia: SpongeBob peeks but does not search, learns nothing, and Patrick still guards the secret.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 179 "Chapter 32 - “The Exit Door Leads In”" — Eric Beck reads 'The Exit Door Leads In' as a modernized Platonic dialogue: like Oedipus before the Sphinx, the average salesman Bob Bibleman wins mandatory university admission by answering a computerized waiter's riddle, staging the Delphic 'Know Thyself' against Plato's Gorgias ideal of self-mastery, while Plato's Socrates in Charmides disclaims healthy self-knowledge. When Bibleman's terminal spills classified engine schematics, he decides not on universal principle but on what he thinks the authorities want; his honest answer that he would have handed them over anyway gets him expelled for failing a test he could not read, a double bind showing self-knowledge is contingent and situational. Dick thus revises knowing oneself as negotiation of the state's expectations rather than discovery of an essence, though the ending - Bibleman paying the computer after deciding not to - leaves open that he may one day rebel and need re-education.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 10 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Vannatta explains why Seinfeld reruns now fall flat through Klosterman's neologism 'unironically': since about 1991 irony has become the invisible background of American comedy, a pervasive detachment that David Foster Wallace named and that Jedediah Purdy's For Common Things attacks as the gap between phenomenon and essence. Against Purdy's ironist (Seinfeld's Jerry, mastered by irony, believing in nothing but his own interests), the chapter sets Kierkegaard's Socrates, whose 'infinite absolute negativity' and confessing ignorance serve a truth he cannot define, and asks whether Klosterman, probing the gap between Bono's rehearsed car-ride persona and his inner self, is master of irony or mastered by it. The answer places Chuck midway between the two jailed ironists, Socrates and the Seinfeld finale: like Socrates he knows his own ignorance and serves the undefined idea of self-understanding, but only through pop-culture resemblance (KISS where Jerry used Superman), unable to master irony any more than he can bite his own teeth.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 13 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Curko and Greguric read Klosterman's glam-rock fandom as a problem of identity and masks: Nietzsche's Apollonian-Dionysian split casts Chuck as a self-controlled Apollonian writing about Dionysian excess in Guns N' Roses, Motley Crue, and Whitesnake, while Descartes's remark that actors wear masks to hide their shame introduces the tribute band Paradise City, a 'real copy' whose members would have no personalities left if they fully succeeded. The authors extend the mask question to Facebook and online avatars, where media saturation makes us 'copies without the original' and identity stops being self-same. They end by crowning Klosterman a modern Socrates of 'Know thyself' and a Stoic exemplar: admire your heroes like Satriani but do not steal their identities, control what you can (never your reputation or your time of death), and keep daring the endless search for self-knowledge.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 26 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Daniel Wanless reads Jeopardy! through the Meno: contestants can formulate the right question only because the answer is already given, just as Socrates answers Meno's paradox by claiming that all inquiry is recollection of truths the immortal soul already holds - latent knowledge that explains how Ken Jennings buzzes in before he consciously knows the response. A priori logical ability (the slave boy's doubled square, the law of non-contradiction applied to which of three cities is southernmost) guides the search for answers, while Final Jeopardy!'s blind wagering embodies Kierkegaard's 'life is only understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards.' Socrates would bet it all, Wanless concludes, because the unexamined life is not worth living: his whole life was preparation for the ultimate Final Jeopardy!, lived in the form of a question.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 30 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Mills-Knutsen reads the Brain Spawn - floating brains whose pain at others' thoughts drives them to dumb life down and finally to hoard all knowledge in the Infosphere ('The Day the Earth Stood Stupid,' 'The Why of Fry') - as Futurama's funhouse mirror of the West's distrust of intellectuals, from Pandora and Eve to Frankenstein and comic-book evil geniuses. Fry, the delta-brainwave-lacking hero made stupid by doing 'the nasty in the pasty,' stabs the Big Brain with Bonfire of the Vanities and later banishes the Brains to another dimension, just as Athens executed Socrates. A close reading of Plato's Apology - Socrates's feigned ignorance exposing everyone else's, his demand of free meals in lieu of exile, and his prophecy of even more annoying successors - maps onto the Big Brain's snobbery and onto universities (Wernstrom's tenure scam in 'A Big Piece of Garbage,' Amy's doctorate in 'That Darn Katz!') as society's way of paying intellectuals to stay out of the way.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 20 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Christopher Lauer argues Cohen's lyrics seduce through Socratic irony as Kierkegaard analyzes it in The Concept of Irony: ostentatious self-concealment that makes hearers aware of the gap between words and intentions, building 'personality' and promising intimacy. Songs like 'Closing Time,' 'Everybody Knows,' and 'Democracy' oscillate between cynical third-person verdicts and sudden second-person address, offering a hidden sincerity only to withdraw it - an erotic improvement on Plato's Socrates that dissolves its own ironic distance. 'Hallelujah' and 'Anthem' make the program explicit, treating brokenness as the space in which love develops, while 'Tower of Song' shows the bleak side: irony collapsing into pure cynicism, the singer speaking sweetly from the Tower long after all promises of genuine intimacy have been disavowed.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 36 "22. The Dao of Master Westley" — Doll tests each character against the Dao: Confucius's identification of the Dao with tradition and ritual fails because Florinese tradition is exactly what enables Humperdinck's murder and war plans, so she turns to Laozi's De and wu-wei, diagnosing Vizzini's fatal overconfidence (he lacked Socratic knowledge of his own ignorance), Humperdinck's paranoia, and Buttercup's passivity as failures to sense when to act and when to refrain. Westley emerges as Zhuangzi's ideal - like Cook Ting the butcher, mastering skills until instinct suffices: adapting through the Fire Swamp, treating Vizzini's death as 'an appropriate death', yet sparing Inigo and Fezzik because killing them would be against nature, which is why the giant and the Spaniard accept him as their sage.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 21 "8. Should Jane Get to Be Bored" — Daniel Addison defends Louie's 'you don't get to be bored' admonishment of Jane in 'Country Drive' against Mathew Remski's charge that it transfers adult anxiety, pointing to Louis's Conan 'forever empty' monologue and reddit advice as proof that Louis insists on facing despair rather than fleeing it. The real aim, he argues, is Socratic: Louis wants Jane and the plane-complaining generation brought to aporia, the perplexity Plato's Socrates induces in the Meno's slave boy so that, no longer thinking he knows, he 'would be glad to find out.' Aristotle grounds the optimism - every human by nature desires to know, philosophy begins in wonder, and our deepest happiness lies in contemplating - so Louis's 'everything's amazing' tirade is a demand that we become philosophical rather than 'kinda satisfied' consumers. Boredom, on this reading, is failed wonder, and Louie is playing Socrates to his daughter.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 35 "22. Unmasking the World and Its Heroes" — Mapping both heroes onto Plato's cave, the chapter argues each must first see past shadows: Bruce abandons revenge on Joe Chill to change Gotham's whole idea of justice, its citizens climb out of apathy when the Dark Knight ferries refuse the Joker's detonators, and Clark needs Jonathan Kent ('It's not to score touchdowns') and Jor-El to learn what his powers are for. Socrates' Apology supplies the mask's rationale - the just man must lead a private life to survive, so secret identities protect loved ones from Luthor's kryptonite stabbing and FBI kidnapping - and Plato's warning that the returned cave-escapee would be killed explains why the heroes must lead by hope rather than force. The oracle story's lesson that wisdom is knowing that you know nothing grounds the close: anyone can be a hero, as Batman tells Gordon about the coat around a boy's shoulders.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 12 "3. The Only Chapter in This Book You Need to Read!" — Writing as two bickering versions of himself from different universes, Karavitis reads Deadpool Kills Deadpool as showing that the multiverse of Deadpools is the delusion of a single narcissist: the alternate 'Pools' are mirror-image projections of himself (Lacan's mirror stage), his self-love is Rousseau's pathological amour propre rather than healthy amour de soi, and his claim to be the progenitor of all reality is solipsism—hence there is no fourth wall. Freud, Fromm, and Marcuse supply rival diagnoses of that narcissism, from arrested development to proto-fascist willfulness to authentic rebellion against social control through unconscious conformity. A closing twist argues philosophers who claim sole access to truth are the same solipsistic narcissists, which would make Socrates, who never claimed a final answer, the only true philosopher.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 32 "19. Deadpool Can’t Know Fear" — Borrowing Socrates' definition of courage as remaining steadfast in the face of danger and choosing death above dishonor, the chapter argues that Deadpool's healing factor removes his risk of death, so he cannot experience the fear of helpless annihilation, cannot display courage, and is not an anti-hero but 'post-heroic.' Worse, mapping Luttwak's post-heroic warfare of drones and ballistic missiles onto his invulnerability, the chapter shows how fighting Deadpool drags opponents like the ULTIMATUM contract army and Crossbones into a trap where they can never test his courage and are stripped of their role as defenders, becoming mere targets. It closes that having a little fear and the chance to overcome it might be better than being unable to die.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 13 "4. Scoundrels, the Lot of Us" — Karavitis finds a Hegelian dialectic in the three-panel Dilbert strip (thesis, antithesis, synthesis) delivered through irony, then tests that irony against philosophy: Socrates' feigned-ignorance questioning that leaves interlocutors in aporia, Hegel's complaint that irony is vanity withdrawing from objective reality, and Kierkegaard's dissertation on the concept of irony plus Either/Or, where irony is the bridge from the aesthetic to the ethical life. The punchline is that after nearly three decades of Dilbert the white-collar workplace has not changed, so readers who feel superior to their bosses and co-workers have taken the vain, narcissistic, aesthetic reading Hegel warned against, making the joke a scoundrelly way of avoiding responsibility. A Leo Strauss aside casts Adams as an esoteric writer whose irony preserves him from the powerful.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 14 "5. The Serious Point of Scott’s Humor" — Guerra and Barkman argue that Dilbert's humor is doing serious philosophical work: strips like the Pointy-Haired Boss's scheme to strip app users of free will, rebranded by Dilbert as marketing, distill manipulative corporate practice to its absurd essential core, and humor serves as a logical tool that, when it preserves the target's integrity rather than straw-manning it, exposes the equivocation in earnest arguments about getting something from nothing. They ground the practice in Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, where wittiness is the virtuous mean between the vices of buffoonery and boorishness, read Adams's catalogue of failures and his luck-first, passion-is-bullshit account of success as a Socratic acknowledgment of ignorance that deflates the American Dream, and treat Win Bigly's persuasion lessons (visuals, repetition, intentional mistakes, the Hitler counterexample) as further proof that Adams has the virtue of wit.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 15 "6. No Wisdom to Offer You" — Distinguishes public intellectuals like Chomsky, who deliver their own conclusions, from public philosophers who get audiences thinking for themselves, and argues Schumer is the latter. Her memoir claim that she has 'no wisdom to offer' is set beside the Socratic ignorance of Plato's Apology, where wisdom is worth nothing. Sketches like 'Football Town Nights', whose coach condemns rape only to praise violent domination, and 'The Trial of Bill Cosby' withhold conclusions and force viewers to work out for themselves the links between football and rape culture, or between un-conflicted entertainment and justice.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 21 "9. A Rose by Any Other Brand" — Callis treats Gilead's rise as a marketing campaign, reading it through Thom Braun's philosophy of branding built on Heraclitus (brands as false stability amid flux, the 'hidden connection' of the 'Balm in Gilead' hymn), Socratic questioning that Gilead forbids its citizens, Plato's brand-as-becoming, and Aristotle's four causes (the Sons of Jacob as efficient cause, the subjugation of women as the brand's function). She argues the brand was doomed because its core premise—that women exist to breed—is false, so Waterford's quip that love is 'lust with a good marketing campaign' foreshadows its Shakespearean collapse. The resistance works the other way: handmaids reclaiming their real names ('My name is June—and I will survive') is what breaks the brand.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 18 "7. Rick and Morty as Socratic Television" — The chapter argues Harmon and Roiland write the show as Socratic dialogue: in 'Mortynight Run' Morty's confident moral position (saving Fart from Krombopulos Michael is right) is dismantled until Morty himself pulls the trigger, leaving him in aporia; in 'Auto Erotic Assimilation' Summer's faith in freedom is razed by Unity's happy paternalist hive and the nipple-shaped race war it unleashes; and 'Look Who's Purging Now' refuses to choose between liberalism and conservatism when the post-purge town instantly re-founds the Festival. Like Socrates in Plato's Meno, the show's goal is not to teach lessons but to reduce viewers to confusion, because doing philosophy begins there.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 12 "3. Wonder and Philosophy as a Way Home" — Nathan and Leilani Mueller argue the theme song's 'neighborly day in this beautywood' makes beauty a transcendental leading to wisdom, as in Plato's Symposium ascent to loving the beautiful itself and Aquinas's convertibility of truth, goodness, and beauty. Reading Rogers's questioning of batteries and boxes (episode 1655) through the Meno's genuine curiosity and Pierre Hadot's account of philosophy as a way of life, they tour the show's three philosophical spaces: the domestic living room, the community visit (blind saxophonist Eric Kloss), and Make-Believe as thought experiment.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 13 "4. The Gently Socratic Inquiry of Fred Rogers" — Ben Lukey and Steve Bein, veterans of p4c Hawai'i, argue Rogers ran a 'gently Socratic' community of inquiry on television: unlike Socrates the public gadfly who made asses of interlocutors, Rogers created intellectual safety, treating Daniel Striped Tiger's 'What does assassination mean?' (after MLK's murder) and the Officer Clemmons kiddie-pool scene as philosophy with children. Using Dr. Tom Jackson's Good Thinker's Toolkit to show children are philosophers, they defend 'little p philosophy' as activity over 'Big P Philosophy' as content, casting Rogers and Socrates as midwives rather than lecturers.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 37 "21. You Gotta Be Bad if You Wanna Be Good" — Shearer argues the show dismantles ethical dualism, the good/evil binary that sorts people wholly into the Good Place or the Bad Place and that underwrites real-world 'us versus them' thinking. Following Aristotle, being good is a learnable skill like reading or an instrument, acquired by practice and unlearning, not a fixed nature. Following Socrates in the Apology, progress begins with admitting you do not know, and the chapter shows that the characters who self-generate that admission, Eleanor confessing and Michael realizing he loves the humans, grow the most, while Jason's moral neutrality exposes a case the Good Place/Bad Place binary cannot classify at all.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 43 "30. Socratic Superheroism" — Stages a dialogue between Socrates and Nebula to build a four-part scorecard of 'Socratic Heroism' — question all assumptions, intellectual humility (Socrates before the Delphic oracle: 'I am very conscious that I am not wise at all'), improve society without ever doing injustice, and courage unto death (the gadfly of the Apology) — then scores Thanos 0 for 4: 'I am incapable of error' and 'reality can be whatever I want' are the very opposites of humility and of objective, heavenly truth. It nominates Doctor Strange as the MCU's Socratic hero, whose humbling at Kamar-Taj, willingness to hand over the Time Stone against the obvious choice, and trust in the one winning future among 14,000,605 pass the tests.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 16 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Barad maps fifth-century Athens onto contemporary America to cast Stewart as a Socratic reformer confronting modern sophists, advertisers, pundits and media figures who make weaker arguments appear stronger without caring about truth, exemplified by Ed Helms admitting network stories are pre-written from 'conventional wisdom' and Ann Coulter's conformity-peddling. She details the shared method: flattering the 'expert', feigned ignorance, and layer-by-layer questioning that traps targets like Rumsfeld ('It may not seem like much, but for this administration it's a huge policy shift') in contradiction, with Socratic irony doing the work of Stewart's awestruck deadpan and mute astonished reactions to Bush clips. Against Bill O'Reilly's 'stoned slacker' charge she cites the Annenberg finding that the show's young audience is better informed, and weighs Ken Tucker's 'monkey' question through the Crossfire 'I'm not going to be your monkey' exchange, concluding that, like Socrates facing trial and execution, Stewart uses irony as means and truth as end.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 34 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Decker asks whether the 'Stephen Colbert' persona is the ironist of the Romantics and Rorty: the precise inverse of Socrates, who was declared wisest by the Delphic oracle precisely because he knew he knew nothing. Through Schlegel's Romantic irony, Hegel's complaint that the ironist abdicates responsibility, Kierkegaard's reading of Socrates as standing ironically above every relationship, and Rorty's ironist with her radically doubtable 'final vocabulary', he reads Colbert's self-redescription, Rally to Restore Sanity and/or Fear, and Super PAC stunt as exposing the contingency of political selves. Yet truthiness at its worst is dangerous subjectivism, and the chapter ends with Colbert breaking persona before Congress ('I like talking about people who have no power') as the non-ironic face that keeps the irony honest.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 10 "The Sorcerer Socratic" — Timm argues Strange follows Socrates' path from arrogance to Socratic heroism: the hand injury forces intellectual humility (the Oracle-at-Delphi moment), the Ancient One's keyhole metaphor and astral-form lesson ('to show you just how much you don't know') enact the Socratic method of questioning the supposedly wise, and the astral projection is literally the examined life — Socrates' unexamined life not worth living. Strange's commitment to protecting humanity from interdimensional evil parallels the gadfly who risks death to improve Athens, his refusal to do injustice even under pressure echoes the Crito, and his repeated willingness to die for others (facing Dormammu, holding the Shambler back) completes the Socratic Hero profile.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 11 "We Can All Be Socratics Supreme" — Pape uses the Ancient One's keyhole metaphor to argue that all knowledge is partial and biased: Bacon's confident scientific method ('human knowledge and human power meet in one') is itself just a useful belief, while Socratic awareness of one's ignorance — knowing that you have blind spots, even if you cannot see them — is the real wisdom. She reads the film's running gags as bias lessons (the 'Mister Doctor' exchange, Strange mistaking the wifi password 'Shamballa' for a mantra, the noble-savage prejudice) and feminist critiques of impartiality as itself partial. The whitewashing controversy around Tilda Swinton's Ancient One — weighed against the Fu Manchu stereotype of the 1963 comics and Iron Man 3's Mandarin-as-Trevor-Slattery subversion — shows how filmmakers can confront the biases they cannot simply remove.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 20 "Knock and the Door Will Be Opened… Eventually" — The chapter reads Strange pounding on Kamar-Taj's door as Kierkegaard's passionate collision with 'that which thought cannot think': the materialist surgeon hits the unknown as a frontier, takes offense at the Ancient One's talk of healing through belief, and can only proceed by surrendering intellectual control ('I control it by surrendering control?'). It applies Kierkegaard's two teachers from Philosophical Fragments: Pangborn is healed the Socratic way, recollecting a power already within him, while the Ancient One's astral knock-out and eviction of Strange acts like the god as teacher, forcing him to discover that he is untruth, until faith becomes 'controlling magic by surrendering to it.'
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 17 "Alone into the Desert" — Has Socrates and Aristotle rate the good life in the Duniverse: the Baron fails every Socratic virtue (breaking his promise to Yueh, intemperance, betrayal), Duke Leto is 'Leto the Just' yet forges certificates and plans adultery, Paul's theocratic myth-making is unjust despite his temperance and courage, and the Fremen are brave and temperate but fatally unquestioning, lacking the Socratic awareness of ignorance that would have saved them from manipulation. Aristotle's function argument, his doctrine of the mean (Paul's worm-riding as courage between rashness and cowardice), and his external goods are then applied, but the author finally breaks with both philosophers: Paul's and Leto II's extreme selflessness admits no mean, their unjust oppression can still be right, and such extreme self-sacrifice may be the best life of all.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 23 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Abraham Schwab turns Ygritte's 'You know nothing, Jon Snow' into a theory of epistemic humility: Jon misreads wildling courtship norms, Sam's dragonglass shatters on wight Small Paul, Lord Mormont assumes Mance fights like a southern king and pays for it at the Fist of First Men, while Arya's accurate self-knowledge keeps her alive. Formalizing with justified true belief - Sam's lucky dagger thrust is not knowledge, and the Watch's warranted belief that the dead Othor was harmless justifies falsity - he uses Lysa's letter, which sent Ned to King's Landing on a lie, to ask what justification is: Descartes's absolute certainty is too strict, reliabilism vindicates testimony ('dark wings, dark words'), so that only Sansa need witness Ned's beheading for the Starks to know it, and between Melisandre's circular dogma about Azor Ahai and total skepticism, moderate skepticism best governs belief - a humility the south lacked about the Horn of Winter.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 37 "21. You Gotta Be Bad if You Wanna Be Good" — Argues that no one can improve without first admitting they are bad: the rigid Good Place/Bad Place binary is ethical dualism whose cracks show in Mindy St. Claire's Medium Place and Jason, a naive moral neutral who fits neither side. Socrates' Apology supplies the method — wisdom is knowing what you do not know, so self-aware fault-finding precedes growth — while Aristotle's account of virtue as learned by practice, like an instrument, grounds the claim that goodness can be acquired even in the afterlife, though unlearning old habits is harder. Eleanor's trash storm, Tahani's failed party, and Chidi's theory-practice gap mark each character's admissions of error, and the worst offenders, Eleanor and Michael, improve most because they confess unprompted.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 74 "Harry’s Cloak, the Ring of Gyges, and the Temptations of Power" — The chapter reads Tom Riddle as Plato's unfit ruler: from the orphanage ('I can make them hurt if I want to') he violates Kant's dictum never to use persons merely as means, treating even his 'friends' as followers, killing Lily despite Snape's devotion, and splitting his soul for Horcruxes. Dumbledore, offered the Ministry repeatedly yet refusing because 'power was my weakness and my temptation,' has the Socratic self-knowledge that he cannot be trusted with power, and that self-awareness, not flawless virtue, is what keeps him from Grindelwald's and Voldemort's path and makes him the series' nearest philosopher-ruler.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 28 "NOTES" — Reads the show's eclipse icon against Plato's sun of the good — goodness has become hard to discern — and tests four theories of evil on the characters: Socrates' claim that no one errs knowingly is half-confirmed since villains like Angela and Nathan always take themselves to be doing right; Aristotle's akrasia and vice as an excess or deficiency of disposition fit Sylar's blood-scrawled 'Forgive me' apartment and his uncontrolled hunger; and Nietzsche's Übermensch and pre-Christian master morality raise the uncomfortable question of why Sylar preying on inferiors is not heroic like Achilles. The chapter's endorsed answer is Gilligan's ethics of care: the heroes are good because they care — Matt for Molly and Daphne, Bennet for Claire — while evil is the absence of care, though Bennet's authoritarian, family-only care shows that care itself must be both widened and restrained.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 8 "a2.xhtml" — Bassham reads The Hobbit as a story of moral growth: the comfort-loving Bilbo who trembles like jelly at the dwarves' plans grows into the hobbit who volunteers to carry the Ring to Mordor. Growth in wisdom comes from Socratic self-examination (learning how little one knows) and from broadened experience of the wide world; growth in virtue comes either from sudden conversion (Thorin's Scrooge-like deathbed repentance) or, as Aristotle taught, from slow habituation - Bilbo's repeated courageous and generous acts (sparing Gollum, returning the elf-keys, giving up the Arkenstone) build lasting character. Seneca's view that hardship strengthens supplies the framework for why Bilbo's trials on the road ennobled rather than broke him.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 8 "Notes" — Argues that Underwood's fourth-wall asides are the show's device for dramatizing the Platonic being-versus-seeming distinction: his public performances (reassuring Blythe over the leaked education bill, the confessional letter typed on the Underwood typewriter to destroy Walker, goading the President into appointing a special prosecutor) are contradicted point by point by what he tells the camera. The chapter reads Frank as a Ring of Gyges success story — the show so far teaches it is better to be the bad guy who seems good — while Socrates' examined life from the Apology and Crito shows Frank never asks why he wants power, and his cockiness is the opposite of Socratic ignorance. It closes with the Gorgias' contrast of Sophistic rhetoric (producing belief, not knowledge) and Machiavelli's advice to feign, casting Frank as the manipulator of opinion Socrates called a tyrant's politics.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 8 "Notes" — Gray argues Frank's fourth-wall asides dramatize Plato's being-versus-seeming distinction: the camera confidences reveal the true motive behind the public performance, as in the Blythe education-bill martyrdom gambit, the deliberately failed persuasion of Walker over the special prosecutor, and the seduction letter typed on the Underwood typewriter. The chapter reads Frank as winning the Ring of Gyges bet — enjoying adultery, corruption, and murder while seeming good — exactly the outcome the Republic sets out to refute. Against this it sets Socrates' examined life and Apology profession of ignorance: Frank pursues power without asking to what end, and his mastery of rhetoric over knowledge makes him the Sophist of the Gorgias rather than Plato's true politician, with Machiavelli's dissembling prince as his model.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 22 "If Not on the Island of Ethical Subjectivism, Then Where" — George Wrisley uses Lost as a testing ground against ethical subjectivism and cultural relativism: the disagreement over Sayid shooting young Ben (monster or innocent child?) motivates relativism, but the Argument from Disagreement fails for the same reason Locke and Mr. Eko's button dispute does not change what will actually happen if it goes unpushed. Simple subjectivism makes every judge infallible (the Man in Black could declare his murders right) and dissolves genuine disagreement between Jacob and his brother over killing their 'mother,' while cultural relativism makes the Dharma Initiative's torture of Sayid 'right' and would have ruled Martin Luther King Jr. wrong. He concludes that Lost's ambiguous cases - Michael's murder of Ana Lucia and Libby, Ben killing Jacob, Jack extorting Ben on the operating table - invite viewers to seek objective grounds Socratically, questioning their own moral judgments with further 'why's.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 12 "And Now, Deep Thoughts…" — Reynolds places comedy on a spectrum from philosophy to satire to smart-assery and argues SNL mostly sits at the silly end: Gumby, Mr. Robinson, Hermione's cleavage, and Hobbit Office are parody with an absurd twist but no constructive target, unlike genuine satire such as Mr. Bill. He develops the comparison through Aristophanes' Clouds, whose caricature of Socrates at the Thinkery helped send him to his death, and through the 'Playboy Philosophy' sketch with Belushi as Socrates. Socrates himself emerges as a satirist: the oracle of Delphi, his claim to know only that he knows nothing, and his elenchus that unmasks the supposedly wise are read as comedy in the service of seriousness, before the chapter concedes SNL's absurdism is philosophical mainly in mocking an absurd world.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 9 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Kirby reads the 'Imaginationland' trilogy as a satire of post-9/11 America interpreted through Ulrich Beck's world risk society: the Pentagon generals, still thinking in Cold War categories like 'Project X' and Chinese imagination portals, embody Beck's denial response and end up voting to nuke Imaginationland, while Cartman's Rambo-style self-interest embodies the apathetic response. Socrates' practice of demanding definitions frames the chapter's question of what terrorism actually is (via Hoffman's five criteria), and Socratic ignorance about what one does not know is contrasted with the worse condition of not being able to know what you do not know. Kyle's courtroom speech that imaginary beings like Luke Skywalker and Santa are 'realer' than most real people, and Butters' creative power to imagine Santa back to life, point to Beck's cosmopolitan 'transformation': imagination and cross-border cooperation as the way out of risk panic.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 35 "22. Unmasking the World and Its Heroes" — Claims the Superman-vs-Batman debate misses the point: both heroes are cave-escapers who must first see beyond appearances—Bruce renouncing vengeance on Joe Chill and then shaking Gotham from apathy (the ferries refusing the Joker's detonators), Clark learning from Jonathan and Jor-El that his powers are not for touchdowns but to lead humanity out by example. Masks serve the Socratic warning of the Apology that the just man must act privately to survive—Jonathan Kent dies keeping Clark's secret—yet risk becoming their own trap, from Smallville's Red Kryptonite ring to Batman's sonar surveillance that Lucius Fox calls too much power for one person. The chapter closes on Socratic ignorance and Man of Steel's genesis chambers: a hero, like Socrates, knows his wisdom is worth nothing, and anyone who chooses can be one.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Gilmore reads Unforgiven as Socratic wisdom done in images — the recognition that we do not know what we really want. He analyzes the opening montage (shadowed windows, the cut prostitute) as Freud's Primal Scene, the audience forced to interpret sex and violence without adequate concepts, which he calls the primal scene of philosophy itself. Drawing on Huizinga's Homo Ludens and Leone's Once Upon a Time in the West, he frames the gunslinger as a 'Bad Man at play' for mortal stakes, free of the repressions civilization demands. William Munny's banal Christianized 'goodness' versus the terrifying Bad Man that drink releases dramatizes Thoreau's 'quiet desperation' and a godless world where deserving is irrelevant.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 7 "The Last Supper Game" — This editor's introduction frames Bourdain as a modern philosopher by playing a variation on his 'Last Meal' game and choosing Bourdain as the ideal dinner companion. It argues that Bourdain's professed humility about how little he knows ('realizing how small I am, and unwise') echoes Socratic ignorance and the love of wisdom, and previews the volume's questions about happiness, authenticity, taste, and freedom.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 23 "Chapter 11 Socratic Irony in Twain’s Skeptical Religious Jeremiads" — Jacquette demands a precise definition of Twain's much-invoked irony, adopting Vlastos's/Quintilian's formula that irony says the contrary of what is meant while letting the real meaning be recovered. He classifies Twain's irony as local vs. global and comic vs. sober (tragic/historical): 'Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc' is globally ironic (falsely presented as de Conte's eyewitness manuscript), while the relic-mocking passages of 'The Innocents Abroad' (St. Luke's Madonna, kegs of true-cross nails, three skulls of John the Baptist) are local comic irony. Jacquette concludes Twain's irony is distinctively Socratic: like Socrates interpreting the Delphic oracle, Twain makes a moral and epistemic virtue of ridiculing experts who claim to know what no one can know about God, sin, and the afterlife.

### Epistemic Injustice

Epistemic injustice, a concept named by Miranda Fricker, is a wrong done to someone specifically in their capacity as a knower. She distinguished two main forms: testimonial injustice, in which prejudice leads a hearer to give a speaker's word less credibility than it deserves, and hermeneutical injustice, in which gaps in a society's shared interpretive resources leave some group unable to make sense of their own experiences. The idea shows that unfairness can operate not only in the distribution of goods but in whose knowledge and understanding are recognized.

- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 36 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Jason Davis opens with Sammy Davis Jr. thanking the white producers for the best film ever made on black-white relations, and their cluelessness, to show that white privilege rests on an epistemology of ignorance, paralleled by the human enjoyment of ape slavery in Conquest. He reads the ape castes through the ontology of race: the films first stage race as biological realism and essentialism (warrior gorillas, chimpanzee scientists, orangutan priests), but Battle for the Planet of the Apes shows biology is not destiny, and human genetics (race accounts for about 0.012 percent of human variation) discredits biological racial realism altogether. Via Charles Mills's social ontology of race and Kwame Anthony Appiah's racial skepticism, the chapter treats ape racism as a mirror of anti-miscegenation-era America whose racial categories are social constructs, down to the dropped ape-human hybrid child.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 39 "Psych and Philosophy" — Mona Rocha asks whether Psych is sexist given Shawn's eighth-grade-girl caricature of Juliet in 'Spellingg Bee' and the secret knowledge kept from the show's women, then argues it is not: the women's inferior epistemic position is a byproduct of the con, not misogynist gatekeeping, because Shawn works collaboratively and non-hierarchically, shares credit (solving Lassiter's Back Bay Killer case for him in 'From the Earth to Starbucks'), gives the Chief the glory in 'There Might Be Blood,' and confronts the oilrig chauvinist outright. The contrast is The Mentalist, where Patrick Jane's withholding of deductions from Lisbon - going behind her back in 'Red Hair and Silver Tape' and getting evidence thrown out in 'Blood Money' - enacts patriarchal paternalism that undermines female leadership.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 20 "9. Not Knowing Serial Killers with Hannibal Lecktor" — Davis reads Manhunter's Lecktor through agnotology - Robert Proctor's study of how ignorance is made - arguing that Lecktor runs a 'knowing game' with Will Graham, strategically withholding what he knows (the Pilgrim's lunar cycle, his fan mail from the Tooth Fairy) so that Graham must do his own dangerous 'field work' and risk becoming killer or bait, a playbook he delivers as an invented Rumsfeldian riff on known knowns and unknown unknowns. The same lens then exposes the real world: the FBI's post-Silence serial-killer panic (Jenkins's evidence that the BSU's statistics were false, capped by the USS Iowa profiling fiasco) as institutional ignorance-making that inflated the FBI's power, and Egger's 'less-dead' - marginalized victims like Kendall Francois's Poughkeepsie sex workers whom media footprints render invisible, 'the missing missing' - as the human cost of our fascination with a killer who never existed.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 19 "8. Brienne and the Struggle for Recognition" — Giladi reads Brienne as a challenge to the Westerosi recognition order: winning the melee at Renly's camp and requesting the Kingsguard, she embodies knightly virtue in a society that deems it naturally male, and the crowd's bewildered, muted applause is a recognition injustice that withholds the social conditions of her self-confidence and authenticity. He analyzes Jaime's mockery in 'The Prince of Winterfell' - sexualizing her as 'boring as you are ugly' where he would never treat Barristan Selmy so - as stripping Brienne of her status as a conversational peer and equal rational enquirer, while the attempted gang-rape by Locke's men in 'Walk of Punishment' shows the violent backlash her struggle for recognition provokes.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 25 "14. Five Stereotypes that Sustain Grape Zones" — Explains 'grape', Schumer's grey area between rape and consent, through Miranda Fricker's hermeneutical gaps: bundles of stereotypes about the stranger rapist, the chaste victim, the resisting victim, the racialized 'barbarian rapist', and the unrapeable strong-ass woman leave holes in shared knowledge, so non-stereotypical rapes go unrecognized and unprosecuted. The 'Football Town Nights' players' excuses and the Leather Special's fat-but-brave monologue ridicule these schemas, while Brock Turner's lenient sentence versus Brian Banks's imprisonment shows how intersecting racist and sexist biases protect white rapists and discredit victims. The chapter concludes that debunking the five stereotypes shrinks the grape zones.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 23 "11. What about the Men" — Jones argues that Nick is coerced as surely as June—ordered by Serena, married off to Eden, unable to refuse without Gilead's punishments—so calling his unwilling sex rape should be uncontroversial. Yet he then argues the 'what about the men?' question itself is inappropriate: because politics and film are male-dominated (19 percent women in Congress, 4.1 percent of top films directed by women), women's lived experience rarely gets center stage, and male readers instinctively bend such rare texts back toward themselves. Pieixoto's flirty, fact-obsessed keynote is the model of this failure, and the challenge for male viewers is to listen to what the show says about women's experience—including #MeToo-era sexual violence—without making it about men.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 26 "The Proud Disabled Person as Counterstory" — Argues Toph Beifong is not a pejorative Supercrip stereotype but a Proud Disabled Person counterstory, using Hilde Lindemann's account of master narratives and identity: the BOD and IIH narratives (better-off-dead, irrationally happy) and the Supercrip all presume disability means suffering, while Toph's grumpiness, depth, and central role defy them. Her blindness is disability gain rather than tragedy, since being unsighted led her to learn earthbending from the original teachers, the badgermoles, and to immerse herself in seismic-sense bending full-time. Drawing on Elizabeth Barnes and Miranda Fricker's hermeneutical injustice, the chapter claims disability pride gives disabled viewers permission to celebrate themselves, and shows Toph driving the plot (inventing metalbending, training Aang in 'Bitter Work') instead of teaching non-disabled characters a moral lesson.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 27 "The Buck Stops Here" — Argues Earth King Kuei is genuinely responsible for Ba Sing Se's fall because he willfully maintained ignorance of the war and of his own capital's poverty so he could enjoy royal privilege (doting on the bear Bosco while never having left his palace). Using Charles Mills, Miranda Fricker, and Shannon Sullivan on epistemic ignorance, it reads the city's ringed walls as architecture that hides refugees from elites, and the Dai Li's brainwashing of Jet and Joo Dee as a state-fostered 'there is no war in Ba Sing Se' knowledge/ignorance. The chapter's target is our tendency to blame the scheming Long Feng and absolve the 'childlike' king: the buck stops with the powerful man whose privilege depended on not knowing.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 26 "The Proud Disabled Person as Counterstory" — Argues that Toph Beifong is not the harmful 'Supercrip' stereotype (an exceptional individual who overcomes disability through talent and grit, which blames ordinary disabled people for their disadvantage) but a 'Proud Disabled Person' counterstory. Her blindness is a disability gain: it led her to learn earthbending from the badgermoles, the original earthbenders, and to live immersed in bending as her constant way of navigating the world, deepening her mastery. Using Hilde Lindemann's master narratives and counterstories and Elizabeth Barnes's mere-difference view, the chapter shows Toph fits neither the 'better off dead' nor the 'irrationally happy' stereotype: she is grumpy, nuanced (adapting her teaching of Aang in 'Bitter Work'), and a central driver of the plot rather than a moral prop. Fricker's hermeneutical injustice explains why disabled viewers struggle to make sense of flourishing with a disability, and why Toph's portrait gives them permission to celebrate it.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 27 "The Buck Stops Here" — Argues that Earth King Kuei, not Grand Secretariat Long Feng, bears the real responsibility for Ba Sing Se's fall, because he willfully maintained ignorance of the war and of his own capital's poverty so he could enjoy palace privilege, playing with his bear Bosco and never once riding the monorail among his people. The city's ring walls work as architectural exclusion that keeps the lower ring's refugees out of elite sight, while the Dai Li's brainwashing ('there is no war in Ba Sing Se', Jet's reconditioning at Lake Laogai) actively manufactures the ignorance the King depends on. Drawing on Charles Mills's epistemology of ignorance and Fricker and Medina's work, the chapter reads Kuei's 'I can't believe I never knew' as epistemic ignorance retained because knowing would cost him his lifestyle, so the buck stops with the seemingly childlike king rather than the arch-villain behind the throne.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 26 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Almassi grades the Dude as a halfway feminist ally: he divests from the Big Lebowski's patriarchal achiever-masculinity ('that and a pair of testicles'), respects Maude's conception project without paternalism (O'Neill's Kantian line between love and respect), and defends pacifist Smokey — yet his pacifism has stalled into passivity that King's active nonviolence would reject, he leaves Bunny's objectification unchallenged while 'Mr. Treehorn treats objects like women', and he only belatedly gives Maude the credibility Fricker's testimonial justice demands ('why don't you fucking listen occasionally?'). Using bell hooks's feminist masculinity and Larry May's progressive male standpoint, the chapter leaves the Dude five pins up with a spare still to pick up.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 13 "4 “What Would You Have Wakanda Do about It ” Black Panther, Global Justice, and African Philosophy" — Hobden argues Wakanda's isolationist 'us vs. them' politics is Western rather than African in spirit: Ramonda's branding of Killmonger as a 'charlatan' enacts Fricker's testimonial injustice and echoes the colonial epistemicide that dismissed African knowledge, while African philosophers (Etieyibo, Eze, Menkiti) derive cosmopolitan duties from ubuntu ('I am because we are') and Igbo proverbs like 'the right hand washes the left,' which welcome the stranger as a bearer of knowledge. She finds it striking that an isiXhosa-speaking Wakanda shows no trace of ubuntu, and reads T'Challa's UN speech as a Western-style aid relationship ('what would you like us to do about it?') rather than genuine recognition of shared humanity.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 26 "15 Wakandan Resources The Epistemological Reality of Black Panther’s Fiction" — Ruby Komic treats Black Panther as an 'epistemic resource' in Gaile Pohlhaus's sense: because of its majority-Black creative team the film supplies audiences with narrative tools that answer to real Black experience, against Anthony Mackie's charge that the film's Black-only hiring is itself racist. The chapter reads the film's plural representations - the T'Challa/Killmonger ideological tension, Nakia's 'No, I save my country' defiance of Okoye's institutional loyalty, Okoye throwing away her wig, Black viewers rooting for the 'villain' - as the kind of nuanced material that remedies decades of stereotypical representation. Following Miranda Fricker, it concludes that the historic scarcity of such resources is an epistemic injustice against Black knowers, and that Black Panther is a partial act of epistemic justice.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 11 "We Can All Be Socratics Supreme" — Pape uses the Ancient One's keyhole metaphor to argue that all knowledge is partial and biased: Bacon's confident scientific method ('human knowledge and human power meet in one') is itself just a useful belief, while Socratic awareness of one's ignorance — knowing that you have blind spots, even if you cannot see them — is the real wisdom. She reads the film's running gags as bias lessons (the 'Mister Doctor' exchange, Strange mistaking the wifi password 'Shamballa' for a mantra, the noble-savage prejudice) and feminist critiques of impartiality as itself partial. The whitewashing controversy around Tilda Swinton's Ancient One — weighed against the Fu Manchu stereotype of the 1963 comics and Iron Man 3's Mandarin-as-Trevor-Slattery subversion — shows how filmmakers can confront the biases they cannot simply remove.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Sergio Uruena argues the Brotherhood of Steel converts preservation into monopoly: Scribe Yearling buys prewar books as sacred relics, squads seize a settlement's water-purification rigs, and Knight Titus dies on a mission to recover 'a fucking toaster' - read through Langdon Winner's 'Do Artifacts Have Politics?' and Feenberg's contrast between authoritarian and democratic rationalizations of technology. Fricker's epistemic injustice does the central work: 'Blind Betrayal' makes Danse's testimony inadmissible once his synth identity is known (testimonial injustice), while hoarding diagnostic terminals, schematics, and archives strips wastelanders of the interpretive devices through which they understand their world (hermeneutical injustice, extended via Ihde's hermeneutic mediation of technology). Jasanoff's co-production explains how this gatekeeping builds social order itself - Maximus is trained into obedience alongside repair, with access tiered even inside the Brotherhood - against the Followers of the Apocalypse's open archives, closing the parallel between locked bunkers and Silicon Valley's gated source code.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Phillipson uses Thom Merrilin the gleeman in the Amazon series to illustrate standpoint epistemology, arguing (via Heidi Grasswick) that Thom's socially marginal position as a wandering artist grants him epistemic privilege: he understands the murdered Aiel and empathizes with Mat looting a corpse where settled Andorans only fear and judge. She then presses the limits of the theory through Thom's failures, his inability to convey his knowledge to his channeling nephew Owyn, his killing of the Darkfriend innkeeper Dana, and his mistaken diagnosis of Mat, drawing on Bat-Ami Bar On's critique that valorizing marginality for its own sake and grounding privilege in mere distance from a social center is problematic, since Darkfriends are the most marginal of all.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 8 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Marinucci's editorial introduction surveys the volume, framing Austen's six novels as a body of work with philosophical value across love/marriage, morality/virtue, wealth/class, concepts, and zombie mashups. It previews each contributor's thesis: Bufacchi reading Anne Elliot and the Bennets through Fricker's epistemic injustice, Dougherty aligning Austen's ideal marriage with Aristotelian complete friendship, Lindenmuth pairing Austen with Nietzsche on marital happiness, and Bane's Marxist reading of the 1940 Pride and Prejudice film. It argues Austen is an 'accidental philosopher' whose insight into social relations, especially women's vulnerability, carries philosophical weight.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 10 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Bufacchi applies Fricker's testimonial and hermeneutical epistemic injustice to Austen's heroines, arguing women like Anne Elliot ('only Anne,' her word carrying no weight) and Elizabeth Bennet are denied credibility as knowers, while Mr. Collins's certainty that a woman's 'no' means 'yes' shows men's epistemic arrogance. He layers in Young's structural injustice to explain the Bennet women's economic vulnerability under entailment, then extends Fricker with his own 'Perpetuating Force of Epistemic Injustice': Emma Woodhouse, herself a victim, becomes a perpetrator by silencing Harriet Smith's love for the farmer Robert Martin, showing how the oppressed reproduce the injustice on those below them.

### Ecofeminism

Ecofeminism examines the connection between the domination of women and the domination of nature, arguing that both stem from a shared logic of hierarchy and dualism that ranks culture over nature, reason over emotion, and man over woman. The Australian philosopher Val Plumwood, among its leading theorists, criticized the way Western thought treats nature as a passive, valueless background to human activity. The view seeks to dismantle these interlocking structures of oppression and to recover a relational understanding of humans as embedded in the natural world.

- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 30 "Mirror, Mirror" — Sailors convicts Dorothy of being the stereotypical female of Baum's and Fleming's versions, disowning responsibility for killing both witches and living to please others, then contrasts her with Elphaba of Wicked as a feminist hero who leaves home, protects Animals, and mixes 'hot' male and 'cold' female anger into a single fury. She reads Elphaba's indeterminate gender through Marilyn Frye's point that easily identifiable groups are the easiest to oppress, through de Beauvoir's 'One is not born, but becomes a woman' and Mill's line that the 'nature of women' is an eminently artificial thing. Singer's liberation logic, together with the Wollstonecraft-Taylor 'Vindication of the Rights of Brutes' episode and the ecofeminist link between the oppression of women and animals, is applied to Elphaba's Animal-rights activism and her position as 'neither man nor beast,' before the Witch's mirror recognition of Dorothy forces the author to soften her verdict.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 23 "The Onion’s New Environmental Ethic" — Matthew Altman reads Onion environmental satire as a staged escape from anthropocentrism: 'New, Delicious Species Discovered' and 'Beauty Of National Forest Enjoyed By Logger' expose that even appreciating nature is just valuing it for us, while the mascara-testing lab rabbit and 'Funny Monkey Tested On' make Singer's speciesism charge vivid against factory farming and animal experiments. He then widens the argument to a biocentric concern for species and ecosystems via 'Stuffed-Animal Biodiversity Rising' and 'Consumer-Product Diversity Now Exceeds Biodiversity,' and to ecofeminism via 'Raped Environment Led Polluters On,' where the forest as flirtatious woman links domination of nature to sexism and victim-blaming. Global stories like the Bush 'national air conditioner' piece show Western overconsumption displacing blame onto Third World overpopulation, and 'I'm Doing My Inconsequential Part' satirizes the self-satisfaction of green consumerism itself — leaving the measure of the Onion's philosophical importance as how dangerous it is.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 34 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Jeff Ewing reads Victor's science through ecofeminist and Marxist critiques: M. Waldman's promise to 'penetrate into the recesses of nature' and 'show how she works in her hiding-places' exemplifies exactly what Val Plumwood condemns - male knowers wringing secrets from a nature pictured as a passive female slave - and Victor studies natural elements 'in their death, not in their life' as raw material for power. Marx and Engels supply the parallel diagnosis: capitalism biases science and technology toward profit, turning tools and knowledge into means of domination rather than human flourishing, just as Victor's knowledge serves only his glory and kills everyone he loves. The chapter concludes that we breed Frankenstein's monsters whenever science treats nature, workers, women, and othered peoples as mere instruments, and only replacing those social relations frees science from power and profit.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 28 "15. Red Harvest in Roanoke" — Reads Roanoke through ecocriticism and ecofeminism: the culture-nature dualism collapses as the urban Millers' wooded retreat turns predatory (rain of teeth, pig-men); the Butcher's backstory - a colonial woman starved by men whose blood-sacrifice pact makes the land flourish - aligns women and Nature as co-exploited by patriarchy, with Shelby's 'irrational' warnings ignored and Lee's maternal fury a force of nature; the animalizing of victims (pig-headed roasting, the Polks' barn-raised children, Matt's tryst with the Witch of the Wood) dissolves the human/animal hierarchy; and the media crew's attempt to package wilderness for ratings ends with Nature striking back at Agnes in the woods.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 17 "Questioning Our Attitudes, Sokka‐style" — The chapter sets Kant's view that animals are mere things owed only indirect duties against Korsgaard's pathocentrism, on which animals matter for their own sakes because they can mind how they are treated. Sokka's arc from shouting 'Dinner!' at Momo to bonding with the saber-tooth moose lion cub Foo Foo Cuddlypoops, and his aborted vow of vegetarianism in 'Bitter Work,' models empathy-driven reassessment of meat, while his sparing Momo for Aang's sake is exactly Kant's indirect duty. Aang's harm-free fun, otter penguin sledding and riding hog monkeys 'because that's what makes it fun,' shows that even non-cruel use of animals demands justification, with the unagi firefighting as a case that might pass the test.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 22 "11 Beastly Boys The Racial-Sexual Politics of Meat" — Huerter reads M'Baku's 'I'm kidding. We are vegetarians' punchline through Carol Adams's sexual politics of meat and bell hooks's plantation patriarchy: since colonial meat-eating signified masculine mastery over nature (Plumwood's reason/nature dualism) while enslaved people were fed plant foods and cast as edible themselves, audiences primed by the racist cannibal trope expect M'Baku to be a savage, so his refusal of flesh turns the colonizer's gaze back on itself. Killmonger, by contrast, embodies the Black patriarchy produced by the American military-industrial complex ('He's one of ours'), a plantation patriarch whose hypermasculine conquest — killing Linda, burning the Herb garden, his defiant 'death was better than bondage' exit — replays colonial violence even in liberation's name, against which M'Baku's warrior-but-vegetarian politics marks a moral asymmetry.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 26 "Tilting at Windmills" — Reads Protogen through Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment: like Odysseus tied to the mast while his sailors take the wax, Dresden's team had empathy surgically removed ('we modified our science team to remove ethical restraints'), Mao weeps at Julie's protomolecule corpse yet calls her death 'lucky', and Strickland experiments on Katoa and Mei Meng — self-made monsters serving the Baconian dream of conquering nature (New Atlantis, witch-trial language of 'penetrating her holes and corners'). Via Maria Mies and Carolyn Merchant's ecofeminism, it traces this domination of nature to pastoralist castration and the control of women's reproduction, culminating in Marco's theft of Filip and 'She left us. She left us both' — Naomi cast as nature to be mastered. Against them, Holden's childhood on the family farm, a cooperative 'let grow and make grow' world, is why Avasarala cannot play him and why he withholds broadcasts at Ilus: he is a knight who wants everyone to grow and speak for themselves, not to conquer.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 13 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — Jason Blahuta reads The Spirits Within as staging the debate between General Hein's anthropocentric, domination-of-nature outlook (traced to the Genesis tradition and thinkers like Bacon and Descartes) and Aki's Gaia-hypothesis and ecofeminist view of nature as a self-regulating whole. Hein's repeated firings of the Zeus Cannon, which injure rather than kill the Phantoms and doom New York, dramatize what happens when we meddle with a self-regulating Gaia, while the chapter's survey of intrinsic-value versus enlightened-self-interest accounts of nature's worth ends with Lovelock's bleak verdict that humanity has become a tumor inside Gaia and must choose to be a benign or a malignant one.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Kolb reads the whole franchise through Carol Gilligan's ethics of care and the ecofeminism of Ariel Salleh and Mary Mellor: Max begins as a caregiver in an egalitarian marriage, Toecutter's gang and the Citadel embody toxic masculinity, and Aunty Entity shows women can administer patriarchal capitalism too. In Fury Road, 'We are not things,' the milking mothers, and water branded as Aqua Cola literalize Salleh's claim that capitalist patriarchy treats women and nature as resources. The Vuvalini, the Keeper of the Seeds, Max washing in mother's milk, and his voluntary blood transfusion to Furiosa enact the ethic of care as the film's saving alternative to domination.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Quick applies Cary Wolfe's humaninized/animalized humans and Carol Adams's animalized women to the Citadel: Max is hunted, caged, and muzzled as an unnamed 'it', War Pups serve like littermates, and the milking mothers produce Adams's 'feminized protein' while the 'breeders' are groomed like show animals. Following Val Plumwood's ecofeminist critique of the masculinity that conquers mother nature — and Joe's branding of water as Aqua Cola — the chapter reads Furiosa's return to the Citadel as an ecofeminist revolution in which 'We are not things' restores women, men like Nux and Max, and nature itself from property to personhood.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 11 "Landscapes of Gendered Violence Male Love and Anxiety on the Railroad" — Collins analyzes the railroad in Tycoon and both versions of 3:10 to Yuma, drawing on feminist critics (Irigaray, Bordo, Grosz, Haraway, Merchant) who expose a masculinist 'panoramic' epistemology coding mind as male and passive nature/landscape as female. She argues trains destabilize rather than confirm this mastery: in Tycoon, Johnny Munroe conflates conquering the feminized Andean landscape with dominating his wife Maura, yet the bridge and train fail; in the 2007 Yuma, the railroad's promise of masculine legitimacy is sustained only by 'cruel optimism' and male homosocial love between Dan Evans and Ben Wade, over anxieties about racial Others (Apache, Chinese laborers).
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 31 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Aleman, an ethnobotanist, asks 'Is coffee green?' and unpacks the many senses of 'green' (raw bean, naïve, money, and ecologically friendly) before weighing coffee's growth, organic and shade-grown methods, fair trade, globalization, and value chain. She judges coffee greenest at the source (shade-grown farms preserve migrating-bird habitat) but least green in the fossil-fueled journey from Global South farm to Global North cup, invoking Vandana Shiva's claim that 'drinking coffee is a political act' and Rigoberta Menchú on coffee and indigenous survival. She concludes the answer is partly subjective—withholding final judgment while resolving to keep drinking fair-trade, organic, shade-grown, single-source coffee—and warns of the cognitive dissonance, mirroring oil dependence, between judging coffee ungreen and drinking it anyway.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 16 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Cerulli narrates his path from vegan to deer hunter, arguing that the same ethic — the intent to 'do no harm,' rooted in compassion, ahimsa, and feminist critiques of domination — underlies both vegetarianism and his hunting. Confronting the animal deaths hidden behind organic agriculture (farmer Joey 'plugging' deer and smoke-bombing woodchucks), he invokes Carol Adams's 'absent referent' to explain why he had to face the killing directly. Shooting and butchering a buck himself, guided by his Buddhist friend Richard, becomes an act of integrity and refusal of 'forgetfulness.'
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 33 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Merskin takes an ecofeminist view (Karen Warren's linkage of the domination of women and nature) of women who hunt, testing Marti Kheel's 'happy/holistic/holy' hunter typology against online interviews with female hunters and finding their motivations mirror men's. She surveys how hunting became a male-coded rite of separation from the mother—drawing on Freud's 'instinctive urge'—and how hunting media (Traditional Bowhunter) juxtapose women, animals, weapons, and sexual conquest as objects of male predation. Invoking Artemis/Diana and Mary Zeiss Stange's 'woman the hunter,' she argues women who hunt expose aggression as a human, not merely male, trait.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 31 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Megan Burke reads yoga's asanas through Vandana Shiva's 'Earth democracy,' arguing that poses named for other creatures (frog, camel, tree, sun salutation) shift the yogi's perspective and dissolve the sense of separation from nature that underwrites environmental destruction. 'Becoming-frog' yields non-human knowledge and, via the Vedic vasudhaiva kutumbakam (the Earth family) that both Shiva and Iyengar invoke, an ethic of care extending off the mat — casting yoga as a political, green practice that heals an anthropocentric, dominating relationship with the environment.
- **Comics as Philosophy**, ch. 7 "index" — This file bundles three essays. Kevin de Laplante reads Paul Chadwick's Concrete story 'Stay Tuned for Pearl Harbor', treating Concrete's angry monologue about oil companies and overpopulation as enlightened anthropocentrism, while Maureen's silent reverie of merging her body with root systems and being 'raped' by bulldozers dramatizes Arne Naess's deep-ecological expanded self and an ecofeminist link between the oppression of nature-as-female and of women; the utilitarianism of Bentham and Mill and Leopold's 'think like a mountain' land ethic frame the anthropocentrism/nonanthropocentrism debate. Pierre Skilling reads The Adventures of Tintin through Montesquieu's and Aristotle's typologies of government, casting Marshal Kurvi-Tasch's Borduria as Arendt-style totalitarianism (a secret police as true executive, a bid for world domination) against the legitimate monarchy of King Muskar XII, whose Syldavian sceptre works as a check on royal power. Terry Kading argues that 9/11 collapsed the superhero genre's binary of good versus evil into reality: bin Laden's 'monomaniacs' act as supervillains with a murky agenda, yet Spider-Man, Captain America and Superman comics concede no real superhero can rescue us, leaving only ordinary heroism and the compromised politics of national security.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 37 "34. The Lord of the Rings as Philosophy Environmental Enchantment and Resistance in Peter Jackson and J.R.R. T" — Whitmire and Henderson read Peter Jackson's LotR films as environmental philosophy, arguing they use fantasy to recover a sense of nature's wonder and model a plurality of caring, non-instrumentalizing ways of inhabiting the land (Hobbits' gardens, the Rohirrim and their horses, the Elves of Lorien, the Ents of Fangorn) against the extractive, insatiable devastation of Saruman's Isengard and Sauron's Mordor. They explicitly deploy Leopold's Land Ethic ('the conqueror role is eventually self-defeating') to condemn Saruman's clear-cutting and dam-building, and Val Plumwood's ecofeminist notion of 'backgrounding' to explain why holding trees and mountains in visual focus is itself an argument. Thoreau's Maine Woods passage on the living pine grounds their claim that a tree is more than lumber, and the film's resistance (the Ents tearing out the dam, the White Tree's bloom) is read as a call to active ecological hope.

### Anthropocentrism

Anthropocentrism is the view that human beings are the central or most significant entities in the world, and that value or moral standing belongs primarily or exclusively to them. In environmental philosophy the term often carries a critical edge, naming the assumption that nature matters only insofar as it serves human interests. Critics argue that this outlook licenses exploitation of the nonhuman world, while defenders distinguish a chauvinistic version from a more modest claim that humans can only evaluate the world from a human standpoint.

- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 26 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Andrew Light identifies a distinctive environmental theme he calls 'green time': Tom Bombadil and the ents embody nature's long rhythms and are largely indifferent to the War of the Ring - Tom would simply mislay the Ring, and the ents march to war only after Saruman strips Fangorn. Against readings that make elves or dwarves stand-ins for nature, he argues the text lets nature speak for itself, from a collective, ecosystemic perspective: the ents, 'made of the bones of the earth', decline with their forests and lost the entwives to the tilled land. Deploying Wittgenstein's point that we could not understand a talking lion, he concludes that Tolkien's personified nature trains us in the long view and humility needed for problems like global warming.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 16 "Restoring Balance to the Force" — Cooke uncovers an environmental ethic in Star Wars: after surveying anthropocentric resource-management views and Singer's anti-speciesism (Luke blithely shooting womprats, the Geonosian arena's abused beasts), she builds the chapter on Holmes Rolston III's claims that organisms and ecosystems have intrinsic value and that value is systemic and holistic. The 'living Force' - life creates it, midi-chlorians live symbiotically in all cells - makes Jedi training a discipline of respecting nature, exemplified by Yoda's mud hut on Dagobah and the self-sufficient Gungan and Ewok eco-communities that defeat droid armies and stormtroopers. Restoring balance to the Force therefore means restoring symbiotic balance between human culture and the natural world, which the chapter links to Leopold-style land-ethic holism of the biotic community.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 18 "The Legend Has Come True. The Wind Has Come Back" — Haas opposes two princesses of Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind: Kushana of Tolmekia, whose 'whatever it takes' survivalism (invading Pejite, resurrecting a God-Warrior) is consequentialism pursued to its limit, and Nausicaa, whose attention to each act — befriending the biting fox-squirrel, staying her sword over her father's killer because vengeance would doom the Valley — restricts means, not just ends. The reductio comes from Pejite, whose torture of a baby Ohmu to bait a stampede on the Valley is exactly what strict outcome-maximization requires; against this, Kant's demand to treat beings as ends in themselves explains Nausicaa's 'mysterious power' of empathy. Because she respects the jungle and the sentient Ohmu rather than viewing nature anthropocentrically as a plague to burn, she discovers the plants are purifying the war-poisoned earth — the knowledge that saves everyone and proves Kushana's conquering approach self-defeating even on its own terms.
