- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 25 "De-Deontologizing Dexter" — Sultan Ahmed argues Dexter is not really a Kantian deontologist: the urge to kill came first (the teenage animal killings, and his brother Rudy/Brian, who developed the same dark desire without Harry and rationalized it differently), and Harry's Code is a post-hoc rationalization built on top of that desire. Drawing on psychological research (Joshua Greene, Jonathan Haidt) that deontological judgment tends to be emotional rationalization rather than moral reasoning, he reads Dexter's killings as serving emotional needs - the need to control the helplessness of the shipping-container trauma and the Ernest Becker-style need to belong, seen in his bonding with Miguel, Rita, and the kids. Even Dexter's refusals to kill Ellen Wolf or the bound Tony Tucci are framed as feelings and standards, not a sense of moral duty.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 24 "Wrapping Up the Case" — Don Fallis organizes the whole canon as a casebook in the epistemology of deception: why characters deceive (concealing crimes like Dr. Roylott's speckled band, committing them like John Clay's Red-Headed League tunnel, Holmes's own smoke-rocket trick on Irene Adler and his faked death at the Reichenbach Falls), how they deceive (Bell and Whaley's hide-the-truth versus show-the-false, unpacked through disguises as masking, repackaging, dazzling, mimicking, inventing and decoying), and how deception is detected, by microexpressions avant la lettre or by inconsistency, as in 'The Problem of Thor Bridge'. Along the way he sorts lying from false implicature (Inspector Baynes's 'I didn't say so'), lies of omission and bald-faced lies, invokes Kant's absolute ban on lying and Augustine's taxonomy of lies, and asks whether Holmes's belief in Moriarty's web, where the absence of evidence counts as evidence, is rational inference or self-deception.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 24 "Psych and Philosophy" — Rocha argues Kant is not the absolutist of legend: in 'On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy' Kant denies only a right to lie - Gus could be held responsible if his lie to Shawn's pursuing murderer goes wrong - and in The Metaphysics of Morals Kant openly leaves questions like polite untruths unanswered, to be judged by agents in their concrete circumstances. The deeper ground is Kant's duty to oneself: lying shows disrespect for the honest communication through which social beings sharpen their rationality, and so 'throws away and annihilates' the liar's dignity, which is why Uncle Jack's gold-hunting lies in 'The Greatest Adventure in the History of Basic Cable' are beyond rescue. On Rocha's reading even Kant could endorse the one lie to rule them all - claiming to be psychic - because it respects rationality and human life in a society that irrationally esteems the supernatural, while Shawn's Gus-alias gags and bunny fabrications remain immoral.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 26 "Psych and Philosophy" — The Bock brothers ask whether Shawn's fake-psychic lie is morally permissible, testing it against Augustine's and Kant's absolute prohibitions on lying, Nietzsche's claim that all language is metaphorical (the 'Lights, Camera . . . Homicidio' acting-as-lying scene), and Machiavelli's ends-justify-the-means deception from The Prince. Using Sissela Bok's three-question test they contrast justified police undercover work - Juliet infiltrating the sorority in 'Scary Sherry' and the roller derby team in 'Talk Derby to Me' - with Shawn's ruse, which fails because it protects Shawn's own interests rather than others. They end by weighing Sorensen's bald-faced lies (Shawn's 'I know you know I'm not telling the truth') and conclude Chief Vick's genuine belief shows these are real, indefensible lies.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 19 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — James Edwin Mahon sorts the show's plots by the gap between deed and motive: Patti Nyholm helps save Marjorie Garnett's liver in 'In Sickness' purely to leverage her firm, Lockhart Gardner sues Chumhum in 'Great Firewall' for the mercenary reason Alicia laments, and the Demorys bribe a juror in 'Fixed' out of altruism. Working through Mill's exchange with Llewellyn Davies and Kant's shopkeeper, he argues motives can be good or bad but never right or wrong, and that no good motive makes a wrong action right - Kant denied even a philanthropic right to lie. Hence Alicia's persuading Shen Yuan to lie about his torture, however compassionate, was wrong.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 32 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Nicole Pramik asks whether the demons of Brandon Mull's Fablehaven can be taught morality, using Kant's deontology as the measuring stick. Seth's kindness to Graulas looks dutiful and universalizable, and Graulas at first seems a rational agent respecting the categorical imperative - until healed, he betrays Seth, demolishes the preserve's treaty, and declares himself 'pure, deliberate evil' who used Seth as a mere means. Nagi Luna never even tries, and the Sphinx who models her is himself a serial user of persons, so the chapter concludes that rational demons remain impervious to the moral law: you can lead a demon out of Zzyzx, but you cannot make it good.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 20 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Christophe Porot and Charles Taliaferro ask whether Homeland's pervasive hypocrisy and deceit can be justified, starting from Walden's cover-up of the drone strike and Brody's heroic persona hiding a terrorist plot. Machiavelli's Prince supplies the case that political relationships with allies (Saul's 'Us and Them' speech to Carrie) require hypocrisy, while the Smith-inspired 'honest politicking' model - trading openly on self-interest, as with Carrie blackmailing al Sahrani - fails because politics should secure the public good, though la Rochefoucauld's 'homage vice pays virtue' explains Saul extorting the judge into doing right. Weighing Kant's unconditional duty not to lie (Carrie's fatal lie to Lynne Reed) against consequentialism, the chapter lands on the Walzer Dirty Hands view: some acts stay wrong yet necessary, and honest agents accept the guilt.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 31 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Robert Arp uses Saul's interrogation of Afsal Hamid (sleep-deprivation via cold, strobe lights, heavy metal) and the good cop/bad cop dynamics of Brody's 'Q&A' interrogation to examine deception in interrogations, including the nine-step Reid technique and its role in false confessions documented by the Innocence Project. He then tests the routine practice of lying to sources against three frameworks: Kant's absolute duty not to lie, Mill-inspired rule utilitarianism, which permits lies when telling truth regularly harms but lets interrogation exceptions serve the greater good, and Aristotle's virtue theory, on which habitual lying makes the agent vicious. Saul's lie about Hamid's family shows why the utilitarian exception dominates in the war on terror.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 32 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Dona Cayetana and Nathan Everson argue that 'enhanced interrogation techniques' is a euphemism - with Zizek and Badiou they show relabeling torture as what the West does while 'torture' is what Muslims do conceals identity between the acts, as 'Blind Spot''s safe-house interrogation of Hamid demonstrates. Utilitarianism justifies Saul's fatiguing of Hamid by its results, while the Kantian view that persons must never be mere means condemns it categorically; the chapter contends the show's framing nudges viewers to accept torture as a necessary evil. Carrie's gendered role as Zizek's 'new face of torture' - a pretty white woman whose desirability and perceived vulnerability become interrogation tools, from sex with Brody to 'You broke my heart' - feminizes and normalizes the spectacle.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 34 "Homeland and Philosophy" — John Fitzpatrick asks whether anything goes in war, using the FBI's killing of two innocents in the mosque and the ensuing official lie, plus Walden's strike on Issa's school. Truman's Hiroshima utilitarianism (saving lives overall) meets Anscombe's deontology - 'to choose to kill the innocent as a means to their ends is always murder' - before Rawls's social contract supplies a middle path: rules rational parties would agree to behind a veil of ignorance ('we won't kill your children if you don't kill ours'), which condemns both Nazir and Walden since neither faces an 'extreme crisis' like 1940 Britain. Brody's turn is itself Rawlsian: what breaks him is the unfairness of killing children as collateral damage.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 35 "Homeland and Philosophy" — William Rodriguez traces terrorism's evolving meaning from the Jacobins' state Terror through anarchist 'propaganda by deed' (Nechayev, Bakunin) to non-state groups, then tests whether Abu Nazir's campaign, grounded in bin Laden's 1998 fatwa grievances and the greater/lesser jihad distinction, can be morally justified. On a utilitarian defense terrorism could be last-resort self-defense against a collectively guilty population, but the just war criteria of competent authority, right intention, last resort, discrimination, and proportionality all fail for al-Qaeda, since civilians killed on 9/11 were neither combatants nor guilty. Deontologically, targeting civilians violates the right to life and human dignity, so Nazir's attacks on innocents are murder, however real the grievances.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 22 "Girls and Philosophy" — Sirvent and Avery take Shoshanna's Listen, Ladies! advice book to ask whether rules can govern romance, contrasting Kantian rule-duty ethics (Ray's dating rules that are 'not commandments') with Bentham-Mill utilitarian calculation (Jessa's 'depends on the virgin'). Kierkegaard and Nietzsche - extended through Žižek's Lacanian 'Big Other' of God, Duty, or Utility - show such impersonal systems let us dodge responsibility: Jessa plays Kierkegaard's aesthete escaping boredom, while Hannah's 'just to be an asshole' boss seduction and the Marnie-Elijah hookup express ressentiment and self-hatred. Their positive proposal is Aristotelian virtue ethics - becoming a certain kind of person - completed by Butler's Undoing Gender: to be ethical you must risk being 'undone by each other,' as Adam demands of Hannah ('You don't wanna know me').
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 10 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter juxtaposes the 1992 no-knock raid in which 84-year-old paraplegic Annie Rae Dixon was shot in her bed with Raylan's pilot-episode ultimatum to Tommy Bucks, arguing both deaths count as 'justified' only because aggressive proactive policing manufactured the lethal encounter. It catalogues Raylan's tactics - provoking draws, kidnapping the cartel chief's niece and Dickie Bennett, the lucky-sniper standoff at the Bennett compound - and asks whether we want our police to be judge, jury, and executioner. On the deontological approach Raylan's routine lawbreaking cannot be justified whatever the results, and even on the consequentialist approach the war-on-drugs data (soaring murder rates in targeted neighborhoods, mass incarceration) suggest proactive policing fails on its own terms.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 19 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter maps the Raylan-Boyd rivalry onto two ethical theories: Raylan is a Kant-style deontologist who does his duty (tracking Tommy Bucks to Miami, weighing duty to the law against duty to Arlo, giving every opponent the choice to walk away), while Boyd is a Mill-style consequentialist maximizing good for himself and Ava, whose vigilante church and revenge plots follow from outcomes rather than rules. Their season-one team-up against Bo Crowder and the Miami shooters is read as contractarianism, two moral agents cooperating toward a right. Each man's choices become his undoing - Raylan's damsel-saving affairs, Mags's family loyalty, Dewey's impulsiveness - which the chapter takes as the show's thesis that what we do results in who we are.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 12 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Jordan asks what makes Dracula obey his rules (no entry without an invitation, native soil, garlic, the crucifix) when he obeys no morality: self-imposed Kantian moral rules and a vampire-cabal enforcing Hohfeldian duties both fail because the Count's self-interest is too strong, so the rules must be natural law set by God or nature. He then uses Wesley Hohfeld's jural relations (duty, claim, liberty, power, immunity, liability, disability) to analyze Dracula's rule over his brides, servants, and victims - Lucy's lost consent shifting power and letting the Count through her door - concluding that only this legal-relations analysis plus natural law explains both Dracula's restraints and his apparent violations of physics like defying gravity and commanding the weather.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 19 "8. Lie Is So Unmusical a Word" — Neal pits Kant's absolute prohibition on lying against Violet's scheme after Sybil's death: the Dowager pressures Dr. Clarkson to 'review the evidence' until he tells Cora and Robert that surgery could not have saved their daughter, reuniting the marriage his honest second opinion had broken. Working through the Categorical Imperative, the murderer-at-the-door case, and Kant's essay 'On a Supposed Right to Lie Because of Philanthropic Concerns,' the chapter asks whether Clarkson actually lied ('Lie is so unmusical a word'). It concludes that his rational, carefully planned, dignity-respecting lie to save the family meets the criteria for a Kantian exception, so the rule against lying still holds while this particular lie is morally permitted.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 15 "5. Office Hours Are for Patients" — Alloy argues that the psychiatric code of ethics - confidentiality with Franklyn ('It would be unethical to approach a patient'), the formal boundaries Lecter scrupulously observes once Will becomes an official patient, and even the oath-violating concealment of Will's encephalitis with Dr. Sutcliffe - is the closest Hannibal can come to friendship, because professional rules artificially manufacture the trust that friends enjoy organically. Working through informed consent, placebo deception, paternalism, and psychiatry's extraordinary power to declare patients incompetent to exercise autonomy at all, he shows the Will-Hannibal relationship cycling through four stages between professional ethics and friendship - 'Office hours are for patients. My kitchen is always open to friends' - while never achieving either, since every display of trust is a manipulation and the power asymmetry never disappears.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 15 "Walker Bite. Let’s Just Do What’s Right" — Devlin and Cooper present Dale as the show's Kantian deontologist: he acts from duty regardless of consequences, applying the humanity formula - treat people always as ends, never merely as means - when he blocks the execution of Randall in 'Judge, Jury, Executioner' and refuses to let the group do consequentialist math about abandoning the search for Sophia. Shane, the Governor, and the Termites serve as the consequentialist foils who treat Otis, the prison residents, and their victims as mere means to survival. The chapter argues Dale dies with his humanity and dignity intact, and that the series' recurring drama is a three-sided battle between his deontology, the survivors' consequentialism, and Rick's eventual virtue ethics.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 17 "4. Lie or Die" — Hawkes uses Rick's bar confrontation with Dave and Tony in 2.8 'Nebraska' to ask when lying is right, after defining lying through the Governor's white flag at the National Guard camp and Eugene's false cure claim. He rejects moral relativism - the Claimers' rules, Terminus's 'butcher or cattle', the Governor's 'we will do the only thing' - because it forbids criticizing rapists and cannibals and erases moral progress, then finds utilitarianism shaky given Eugene's unforeseen deadly consequences and Rick's refusal to hand Michonne to the Governor at 'Arrow on the Doorpost.' He defends a duty-based deontology in which the duty to protect the farm overrides the duty not to lie, and closes with Robert Kirkman's own lie about an alien invasion that got The Walking Dead published.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 18 "8. Saints and Superheroes" — Malloy uses the two heroes to explain supererogation - Urmson's "Saints and Heroes" puzzle of acts that are praiseworthy but not obligatory, like Batman rushing into burning buildings while Jimmy Olsen is under no duty to follow. Against the utilitarian and deontological denials that anything goes beyond duty (Singer's argument that Clark Kent's designer glasses are money he owes to charity, and Susan Wolf's Loving and Rational Saints whose lives, like Batman's broken retirements in The Dark Knight Returns and Batman Beyond, leave no room for anything worth living), he adopts Raz's view that a duty can be overridden by the moral reason of grave personal risk. Hence Batman's nightly risk-taking is a genuinely heroic choice, while Superman's powers make saving others morally required - so Batman is more truly a hero and Superman "just a good person with the powers of a living god."
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 24 "13. Time to Choose" — Goldberg and Gavaler read the heroes' first-year comics (The Superman Chronicles, The Batman Chronicles) as rival moral codes: Superman is a "super consequentialist" out to benefit mankind - reforming the Blakely Mine owner, demolishing slums, buying back swindled stock - while Batman is a "dark deontologist" whose vengeance oath makes consequences irrelevant, waiting out the Joker's murders of Claridge, Wilde, and Judge Drake because catching the villain, not saving victims, is his duty. Mill's utilitarianism frames Superman's consequentialism and Kant's Groundwork - intentions over outcomes, the batarang blocked by invisible glass leaving Batman's morality untouched - frames Batman's, with moral luck the battleground: deontology shrugs it off, but Superman's powers let him smooth luck over too. On the opening dilemma, Superman defuses the bomb while Batman chases the villain, so the authors judge Superman's code superior because Batman's can let hundreds die without moral failure.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 35 "21. Stannis—Knight of Faith or Tragic Hero" — Devlin asks whether Stannis, who burns Shireen to save his army, is Kierkegaard's knight of faith or merely a tragic hero. Stannis's duty-obsessed deontology - knighting Davos while cutting off his fingertips, striking 'beloved brother' from a letter as a lie - is Kantian, and the Shireen dilemma looks like Abraham's teleological suspension of the ethical; yet because Stannis always calculates and justifies ('Faith? In a real war, the side with the greater number wins nine times out of ten'), he never makes the leap on the strength of the absurd, and Davos ends up following Kant's own verdict on Abraham: 'If he commands you to burn children, your lord is evil.' He is therefore a tragic hero in the line of Agamemnon and Jephthah, rationally comprehensible and fittingly undone by Brienne's 'do your duty.'
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 22 "9. I Hate Reasons!" — The chapter uses Lucy's worst lectures - birds don't fly south, the wearing-down of the Earth, the telephone-pole tree, piano-career statistics she admits she made up - to catalog adult critical-thinking failures: motivated reasoning, fallacious appeals to authority, suppressed evidence, post hoc, and appeal to superstition, with the kindergarten cast letting us laugh at our own practices without defensiveness. It then argues, with Kant and W.K. Clifford, that we owe each other more than not lying: we owe others assertions backed by evidence, since Lucy's fabricated numbers could crush Schroeder's dream of a musical career just as vaccine misinformation costs society herd immunity. Lucy's vice is a want of intellectual honesty and humility - she wants to know things, but wants to know them now.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 18 "8. How Shitty Can a Hero Be" — Corey Horn maps the Deadpool movie onto Joseph Campbell's monomyth—ordinary world, call to adventure (the cancer diagnosis), refusal of the recruiter's offer, acceptance, and the ordeal of hunting Ajax—then asks whether a mercenary chasing reward can be a hero at all. MacIntyre's chess example distinguishes instrumental from intrinsic rewards of a practice, and Kant splits motivation into duty versus self-interested motives; since Wade hunts Ajax to recover his face and Vanessa, both thinkers would deny his journey is moral. Still, MacIntyre's allowance for migrating from instrumental to intrinsic motivation leaves Deadpool a hero-in-progress, already promising Colossus he will consider joining the X-Men.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 25 "15. Iron Kant or Captain Kant" — Bosma and Barkman run both heroes' positions on the Superhuman Registration Act and the Sokovia Accords through Kant's deontology. Iron Man's maxim 'I should obey the government' looks universalizable, but it collapses once Cap's critique of the atomic bombings shows an unjust order (killing innocent civilians, or a Doctor Doom takeover) must be refused, and the humanity formulation condemns registration for treating heroes as mere means to the government's ends. Cap's own maxims - fight for freedom and justice, obey only a just government - universalize cleanly, so the chapter awards the deontological duel to Captain America.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 8 "Keep a Little Soul" — Section introduction to the ethics chapters, framed by Petty’s October 2017 death: it argues his real achievement was working to be timeless — the shelved 1982 outtake “Keep a Little Soul” sounding native in 2018 — and that he “lived what he believed,” chasing dreams despite guaranteed heartache, refusing to explain his songs, and standing up to record-company executives. It closes by describing Petty’s political thought as “a deontology that puts duty to the fans first,” invokes Nietzsche as appreciating the gesture of turning the volume up rather than snoozing through the Reagan years, and sketches the volume’s five philosophical “buds”: epistemology, aesthetics, ontology, and two ethics chapters on the outcast and heartbroken as redeemable antiheroes of the everyday.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 28 "15. Chidi’s Indecision" — Vannatta argues Chidi's indecision exposes the shared flaw of the Big Three theories, Kantian deontology, Bentham and Mill's consequentialism, and Aristotle's virtue ethics of the golden mean: their rationalism pretends moral conflict can be eliminated by applying the correct rule, when Chidi's trolley terror shows moral situations are experienced as genuinely uncertain. Dewey's 'Three Independent Factors in Morals', the Good of desire, the Right of duty, and the Virtuous of communal praise, legitimizes that felt uncertainty and explains Eleanor's talent for finding option C between binary dilemmas. The chapter concludes that the show's real, unspoken moral theory is care ethics: partiality, relationship maintenance, and moral growth through the experience of being cared for, as Eleanor learns from Chidi's friendship rather than his lectures.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 9 "1. Rights and Wrongs of Reversing the Snap" — Philip Mouch weighs consequences against rights to ask whether the Avengers were wrong to undo the Snap in Endgame. He imagines a survivor whose returned spouse finds her remarried, cataloguing displaced families, food shortages, and political turmoil, and argues these harms, however real, are outweighed by restoring the lives Thanos took. The deeper problem is Bruce Banner's wager with the Ancient One: removing the Time Stone dooms a branch reality on a 1-in-14,000,605 chance, gambling innocent lives without their consent, which resembles Thanos's non-consensual sacrifice of Gamora rather than the noble self-sacrifice of Hawkeye and Black Widow on Vormir. He concludes that two wrongs do not make a right: even for a noble end, risking countless lives tramples the rights of others.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 19 "9. With Infinite Power Comes No Responsibility" — James Hart casts Tony Stark as a consequentialist and Steve Rogers as a deontologist, then argues Endgame's infinite stakes destroy Tony's morality through Nick Bostrom's 'infinitarian paralysis': in an infinite multiverse every act leaves the balance of happy and sad lives unchanged, as an infinite Stark orphanage rearranged Hilbert's-Hotel style shows, and even genocide becomes permissible so long as infinitely many remain alive. Tony's attempted fixes each fail: the causal approach collapses because reversing the Snap has infinite butterfly effects, expected value (credited to Frank Jackson) runs into Pascal's Mugging and an 'infinitarian trance' demanding suicidal bets on any chance of infinite value, and Bostrom's 'infinity shades' that filter tiny probabilities would blind Tony to the one-in-a-trillion time-heist chance he should take. The chapter concludes there is no consequentialist way to say when wagering lives on infinite stakes is ethical, and Iron Man should let Captain America lead.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 9 "1. Is Perry Mason a Good Guy" — Muyskens asks whether Mason is genuinely good, noting his spotless record may be pure resultant luck: he never knows when he takes a case whether the client is innocent, as 'The Case of the Velvet Claws' shows when Eva Belter lies, tampers with the will, and even confesses to murder yet turns out to have missed. Using Kant's good will and Nagel's four types of moral luck (circumstantial, constitutive, resultant, causal), she argues outcomes alone cannot make Mason praiseworthy, then reads 'The Case of the Deadly Verdict' (his only loss, where he keeps investigating out of faith in Janice Barton) and 'The Case of the Terrified Typist' (where he engineers a mistrial for a guilty client) as proof that his commitment to justice, not his win record, is what makes him a good guy.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 10 "2. A Paragon of Righteous Virtue" — Allinson reads Gardner's novels, especially The Case of the Blonde Bonanza, as philosophy disguised as pulp: Mason acts from curiosity, compassion, and justice rather than utility, a 'pure Kantian or ancient Confucian' deontologist whose loyalty to clients ('erase ATTORNEY AT LAW from the door') functions as his own Categorical Imperative. The chapter's crux is the perjury dilemma of the Blonde Bonanza: Mrs. Winlock's offered false testimony would free Dianne Alder, which Mason twice refuses yet curses ('To hell with it'), showing that the plot's deus ex machina dissolves but never solves the ethical dilemma, while George Winlock's truth-telling-at-any-cost mirrors Kant's prohibition on lying even to the Gestapo. Socrates's better-to-suffer-evil, Plato's Meno reversal, Aristotle's rhetoric, Confucian and Hebrew filial piety in Dianne's character, and Rawls's justice as fairness all serve as lenses on Mason's virtues.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 10 "Olympic Tetherball A Final Lesson on Moral Frailty" — The chapter asks whether Kenneth the page is a Kantian rule absolutist who never makes exceptions, or an Aristotelian 'contextual absolutist' who sees that the right act depends on circumstances, as when he runs the Hill Witch ruse to scare Tracy into eating well. Jack's lifeboat hypothetical and rigged-elevator test bounce off Kenneth's refusal to believe in hypothetical situations, but Jack's gift of illegal cable exposes Kenneth's moral frailty when he enjoys the stolen channels. It concludes that Kenneth's gullibility, trust, and loyalty make his simple moral vision both admirable and easily corrupted, and that the real lesson is facing our failures with resolve rather than shame.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 7 "Special Order 937—Crew Expendable" — Reads Weyland-Yutani as 'greed is good' cost-benefit reasoning embodied by Ash, Mother, and Burke (Gordon Gekko's Wall Street speech transplanted into space), and asks who can be held accountable when every employee fills only a narrow role and scapegoats absorb blame. It then weighs Kantian deontology - Bishop's inviolable no-harm rules, the absolute wrongness of killing crew for profit - against utilitarian reasoning: Ripley's quarantine refusal to save the many, Parker's refusal to flame the alien holding Lambert, and the uncomfortable thought that acquiring the Xenomorph might genuinely benefit billions.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 19 "What if Hama Was Wrong" — Gregory argues bloodbending necessarily uses persons as mere means because it overrides the victim's will regardless of their actual consent, unlike buying tea from Zuko but like Azula's deception of Long Feng, and so violates Kant's Formula of Humanity in every offensive use. Katara's bloodbending of Hama in self-defense is permissible because she stops Hama's wrong rather than using her toward any end, and even a hypothetical consensual 'cooperative model' cannot redeem the practice, since the sheer power it grants and its corrupting effects on practitioners (Noatak and Tarrlok in LoK) justify Katara's ban.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 19 "What if Hama Was Wrong" — Gregory argues bloodbending necessarily violates Kant's Formula of Humanity: controlling the water in another body 'enforcing your own will over theirs,' as Hama puts it, uses a person as a mere means because the bender's maxim ignores the victim's actual consent, even when a victim happens to consent, as in the Ozai medical-experiment analogy. Katara's vengeful bloodbending of Yon Rha in 'The Southern Raiders' is therefore impermissible, while her restraint of Hama uses no one as a means at all since it only halts a rights violation. Even if a cooperative, consent-based bloodbending were possible, Katara's Republic City ban is defensible, because the standing power to override wills corrupts practitioners, as Noatak's and Tarrlok's downward spiral in LoK shows.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 8 "Ethicists Assemble!" — White casts the 'Avengers Prime' as three living ethical systems: Tony Stark is the utilitarian who, during Civil War and the registration crisis, bets on outcomes he alone claims to foresee (stopping the Crimson Dynamo's heart, enlisting the Thunderbolts, exiling the Hulk); Captain America is the deontologist who refuses registration on principle ('we maintained the principles we swore to defend... you sold your principles') and rejects the Punisher and the Negative Zone prison regardless of consequences; Thor is the virtue ethicist who condemns Iron Man not by utility or duty but for violating loyalty, trust, and friendship in cloning him, and who refuses the Twilight Sword because using it would make him 'the same demon'. The chapter argues all three frameworks still demand judgment and conviction, which the heroes share.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 20 "And the war Rages on" — Robichaud runs the Kree-Skrull War (Avengers #89–97) through Michael Walzer's just war theory: the Avengers' defense of Earth against Ronan's Plan Atavus is justified self-defense meeting proportionality and last resort, while Ronan's preventive 'devolve humanity' war fails for lack of evidence and exhausted diplomacy. The Skrulls' shape-shifting trick that gets Mar-Vell to build the Omni-Wave Projector might squeak through on consequentialist grounds, but the emperor's threat to make Captain Marvel watch the Scarlet Witch and Quicksilver die counts as torture—and is impermissible on the Kantian ground that it treats a person merely as a means, whatever the consequences. The point is that even a cosmic comic war displays the real moral complexity of military ethics.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 21 "“This is the Kind of Thing that is Going to Bite US in the Butt”" — Melançon pictures Avengers ethics as Hawkeye's arrow sliding along a line from deontological duty toward consequentialist results, focusing on secrets and lies: Doctor Strange's deception—disguising his Sanctum Sanctorum as a coffee shop to shelter the underground New Avengers after Civil War—is tested against Michael Walzer's 'supreme emergency', the wartime exception (Allied bombing of Germany, the ticking time bomb) that permits violating your own values so they can survive. Strange keeps sliding—possessed by a demon against the Hulk—until the Eye of Agamotto strips him of his title, showing emergencies must stay rare and the agent 'worthy of surviving'. Steve Rogers's secret black-ops Secret Avengers repeat the danger: unlike democratic intelligence agencies, they have zero oversight or accountability, so the WikiLeaks-style leak of their informant dealings threatens the reputation of the whole Avengers enterprise.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 10 "So, Case Closed-Right" — Mark D. White asks why Batman refuses to kill the Joker even after the Joker murdered Jason Todd, paralyzed Barbara Gordon, and killed Sarah Essen. Framing the refusal as deontological rather than utilitarian, he runs the case through Foot and Thomson's trolley problem and transplant case, arguing the classics disanalogize because the Joker himself creates the danger and because 'do not kill' is an agent-specific rule rather than an agent-neutral one. He extends the analysis to prepunishment via Philip K. Dick's Minority Report, and concedes that even a self-described strict deontologist can conclude Batman maybe should have killed the Joker years ago.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 18 "Batman Forever" — Randall Jensen examines the boyhood promise Bruce made after his parents' murder ('I swear by the spirits of my parents... to avenge their deaths by spending the rest of my life warring on all criminals') and argues it is a backward-looking, deontological moral reason that consequentialism cannot accommodate. He then asks whether a promise to the dead can bind at all, weighing Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us against Aristotle's and Thomas Nagel's postmortem and unexperienced harms, concluding Bruce wrongs the living people Thomas and Martha Wayne were if he breaks it. From The Dark Knight Returns to Kingdom Come, Batman emerges as a man who can never fully keep the promise yet cannot live without it.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 30 "Walking the Tightrope" — Melancon weighs the Fleet leadership's secrets and lies: Adama's false claim to know the way to Earth, concealing that Cylons look human, Roslin faking Hera's death and hiding the baby, and Zarek's secret collaboration courts on New Caprica. He argues that keeping secrets from the Cylons can be justified by the state's duty to protect, but the leadership repeatedly deceives the governed themselves, discarding the transparency democratic legitimacy requires. Deontological duty to the governed keeps losing to consequentialist reasoning, and the chapter asks what happens to Colonial democracy's 'soul' when trust between government and governed erodes.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 25 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Fallis uses Sheldon — a lousy liar with an elaborate theory of lying — to probe the philosophy of lying: Kant's absolute prohibition (even 'out of frivolity'), Bok's presumption against deceit, Plato's noble lies reserved for philosopher kings, and Nietzsche's self-deceiving overmen, whose counsel explains the 'un-unravelable webs' of fake Facebook and blog evidence for the imaginary cousin Leopold Houston. Ryle's knowing-how versus knowing-that split explains how Sheldon can state the rules ('casually, no rapid breathing') yet botch the performance, while the Bazinga! pranks and the insincere courtroom apology break the Augustinian definition that lying requires intent to deceive. Grice's norms of conversation then ground the author's own definition — lying as intending to violate the norm against saying what you believe false — until a hypothetical, convention-oblivious liar like Kripke forces him to concede a counterexample and admit he was wrong.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 29 "“King of space, right here!”" — The chapter asks whether Robert Daly wrongs the USS Callister NPCs even if they are 'merely' sentient code: his theft of co-workers' DNA violates a fundamental right to privacy, and Kant's focus on the will shows his in-game intentions aim at real people — he logs in solely to strangle James's NPC and make him confess to being pathetic, wanting to harm the actual James. Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the second indictment: because hyperrealistic VR blurs game and life, Daly's daily practice of cruelty habituates vice and makes cruelty part of who he is, unlike clearly fictional violence such as Mortal Kombat. Merleau-Ponty's intentionality links avatar actions to the self, so the chapter ends by asking what our own intentions in games like The Sims or Grand Theft Auto reveal about our character.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 23 "The Bill Comes Due" — The chapter uses Michael Walzer's Problem of Dirty Hands to weigh the Ancient One's secret lifelong use of forbidden dark magic against Kaecilius's summoning of Dormammu, arguing that only she faces a genuine dirty-hands dilemma because her end (defending Earth) is good while his is not. It asks why dark magic is forbidden at all and answers with rule-utilitarian reasoning that has taken on a deontological life of its own, then invokes Kant's murderer-at-the-door essay to argue, with Mordo's 'the bill comes due,' that whoever does wrong for good ends bears responsibility for the downstream consequences—and that Strange's willingness to break Kamar-Taj's rules while accepting the cost is what makes him a hero.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 19 "8. Lie Is So Unmusical a Word" — Neal weighs Dr. Clarkson's coached retraction, that surgery would not have saved Sybil after all, engineered by Violet with 'Lie is so unmusical a word' to end Cora's blame of Robert and reunite the grieving couple, against Kant's absolute prohibition on lying in his moral works and in 'On a Supposed Right to Lie.' She lays out Kant's reasoning that lying destroys the trust, dignity, and rights that make rules binding, with the murderer-at-the-door case as the classic objection, then argues Clarkson's lie approaches an exception because it is rational, carefully deliberated, and aimed at preserving the Crawleys' dignity and the household itself rather than personal gain. The chapter concludes that the Kantian rule still holds generally, but this particular lie, for this particular moral reason, can be excused.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 26 "14. Things Can Happen that Nobody Could Imagine Only a Few Years Ago" — Donna Marie Smith reads the series through Hegel's philosophy of history: the Crawleys' world is a clash of opposing forces - Lord Grantham's traditionalism against Matthew's and Branson's modernization, Violet's fear of electricity against Sybil's and Rose's embrace of the new - and this very conflict drives progress toward greater freedom. She uses Hegel's Elements of the Philosophy of Right both to explain the entail and primogeniture that bar Mary from inheriting (the law preserves the 'house' over the immediate family, which Hegel calls an infringement of the freedom of property) and to frame Robert's refusal to challenge it as duty to his social standing outweighing personal wishes. WWI, which Hegel experienced through Napoleon's occupation of Jena, is presented as a 'march toward freedom' that breaks down class barriers and finally pushes Robert to accept change on the estate: 'Let's give it a go and see what the future brings.'
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 28 "16. Female Integrity in Times of Change" — Melanie Abbott tests Bernard Williams's account of integrity - publicly and consistently standing up for the beliefs that make you you - merged with Kant's claim that only a good will is good without limitation, against five Crawley women across three generations. Sybil elopes with the socialist chauffeur Branson and never wavers in her egalitarian convictions, Edith's secrecy about her baby fails Williams's openness condition, Mary grows from custom-bound heiress into an estate manager who stands up to Robert over selling land, Cora chafes at the voice she surrendered as an American heiress, and even Violet eventually bends. The chapter's guiding question is how much truth and openness integrity requires, and it credits 'the Sybil effect' with spreading proper integrity through the whole family.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 12 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Don Fallis starts from Joffrey's lie about Arya and the butcher boy Mycah - which costs Mycah's life and Sansa's direwolf Lady's - to dissect lying versus other deception in Westeros: Catelyn accusing Tyrion is not lying because she believes it, Ned's coerced confession at the Great Sept is a real lie (Austin's duress excuse fails, as Thomas More's counterexample shows), and Ned's silence about Joffrey's parentage before the dying Robert is deception by withholding that he himself mistakes for lying. He asks whether lying is morally worse than misleading - Kant and Chisholm say yes, Williams and Scanlon no - testing breach of invited trust (Mirri Maz Duur's 'only death may pay for life'), responsibility-shifting to the audience ('That was a lie you told yourself'), and preserved autonomy (Kant's Groundwork, Mill's On Liberty). Finally, is it worse to lie to a king? Consequentialism explains the danger of misleading the powerful, oaths of fealty and divine right suggest a special duty, but Locke's demolition of divine right (seconded by Monty Python) leaves only the punishment, not the wrongdoing, greater.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 28 "15. Chidi’s Indecision" — Surveys the 'Big Three' through the show: Kantian deontology (Chidi's boots lie, Tahani's mere-means charity), Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism (Jason's alligator frame-up, the trolley simulation), and Aristotle's golden mean (courage between Jason's rashness and Chidi's paralyzed deficiency), arguing their shared rationalism cannot accommodate the real uncertainty Chidi feels. John Dewey's 'Three Independent Factors in Morals' — the Good, the Right, and the Virtuous as irreducible — explains why Chidi sees only binaries while Eleanor finds 'option C' and imagines the Medium Place. The chapter concludes the show's unstated moral theory is care ethics: relational selves, justified partiality toward friends, and moral growth through the experience of being cared for, as when Chidi models care rather than lecturing it.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 22 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Tallman and Southworth set the Hippocratic Oath against the Green Lantern oath in Soranik Natu, a Korugarian surgeon who must either stop healing mid-battle or disobey the Book of Oa. They survey the options, with Wonder Woman discarding vows for consequences, Isamot Kol letting the Corps trump his vow to Qalyra, Dr. Mid-Nite always putting patients first, and Dick Grayson going by context, then argue through Hursthouse that Natu, who treats both oaths as absolute, is in an irresolvable dilemma of her own making, more like the double-betrothed man than Williams's tragic Jim and the twenty Indians. Their verdict is that she should turn in the ring, a cautionary tale for real military medics whose oaths also collide.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 84 "How Revealing Are Our Choices" — The chapter builds on Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics account of choice (prohairesis) as 'deliberative desire' for things within our power and a better test of character than actions, then distinguishes three senses of choice. Internal-choice is Draco deciding but failing to kill Dumbledore; act-choice is Dumbledore's poor youthful choices; and motive-choice is captured by Kant's two shopkeepers who both refuse to cheat customers, one from fear of jail and one from honesty, so that only knowing the motive reveals the choice's moral worth.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 10 "NOTES" — Miles asks whether extraordinary power generates extraordinary obligations, testing Spider-Man's 'with great power comes great responsibility' against Claude the invisible thief and the heroes' reluctance. He uses Singer's principle of minimal obligation (Micah diverting the train from the infant; Claire's negligible risk in burning-building rescues; Hiro teleporting across distance) and Kant's perfect/imperfect obligation distinction (Niki choosing between saving Monica and mothering Micah; Noah Bennet lying to protect Claire) before deploying Fishkin's three 'explosion' objections: too many endangered people, too many capable heroes, and too many repeated rescues dilute obligation. He concludes the heroes went beyond the call of duty in saving New York, so saving the world could legitimately be their paid job, like lifeguards or soldiers.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 17 "Notes" — Uses Sartre's play Dirty Hands and Walzer's 'Political Action: The Problem of Dirty Hands' to ask whether Frank's willingness to do the 'necessary thing' — from the opening mercy-killing of the dog to the Season 3 drone strike — could ever count in favor of an Underwood presidency, with utilitarians (nothing wrong with dirty hands) and absolutists like the bishop ('Love God, and love each other. Period.') dissolving the problem from opposite sides. Walzer's later 'supreme emergency' standard and threshold deontology frame the Jordan Valley staring contest with Petrov and the resulting deal as the one case where Frank's capability might genuinely matter, while Heather Dunbar's reluctance (her refusal of Stamper's offer of Claire's diary, then her reversal) tests the ideal of a leader both capable of and averse to dirtying her hands. The verdict: Frank's only advantage over Dunbar is his capacity for dirty hands, and even that fails because he lacks the scruples to keep them clean when it is not necessary.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 13 "4 Raiders of the Lost Kant Indy Meets the Categorical Imperative" — Mia Wood tests Raiders against Kant's categorical imperative: Belloq's maxim of taking whatever he wants cannot be universalized without destroying property itself, and he repeatedly uses persons as mere means — deceiving the Hovitos about the Golden Idol, preying on Dietrich's fears, and treating Marion as a possession to be seduced with wine and a white dress. Indy fails too: his affair with the sixteen-year-old Marion ('It was wrong and you knew it'), leaving her bound and gagged to pursue the Ark, and Kant's absolutist ban on lying is probed through Katanga's noble lie to Dietrich. The first film's shadowy cinematography visualizes this moral ambiguity — Indy starts as merely one more 'raider' and only gradually redeems himself across the sequels.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 13 "Notes" — Robson argues that The Man Upstairs' real moral flaw is neither stinginess toward Finn nor mere instruction-following, both of which he defends, but 'rule worship': treating LEGO construction instructions — rules with at best conventional status like chess or etiquette rules — as sacrosanct commandments to be followed for their own sake. The contrast is with Kant, who does claim absolute status for central moral rules such as the prohibition on lying, and with the moral/conventional distinction from psychologists like Kelly and Stich that The Man cannot grasp. Emmet's rule-following differs because it serves goals like fitting in, and the flaw scales from office Micromanagers and Velma Staplebot to Inspector Javert and the mafioso, showing how misdirected rule worship becomes genuinely vicious.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 32 "The Lesson and Legacy of Din, Nayru, and Farore" — Charles Joshua Horn asks whether power belongs beside wisdom and courage in the Triforce. Kant's good will shows all three pieces are morally neutral — Link and Zelda act from duty rather than reward, so courage and wisdom could be misused just as easily as Ganondorf misuses power. Plato's Ring of Gyges shows power does not automatically corrupt (Ganondorf chose to steal the Triforce for the Gerudo), and Socrates's answer to Glaucon explains why Ganondorf's ill-gotten wealth and honor leave him morally bankrupt. Aristotle's doctrine of the mean then gives the goddesses' intended use: Link's courage sits between cowardice and rashness (he gathers map, compass, and weapon before the boss room), Zelda's wisdom is really prudence, and Ganondorf's vice is power in excess.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 24 "NOTES" — Becky Vartabedian applies W. D. Ross's agent-specific ethic of prima facie duties to Michael: at the dock his actual duty of beneficence toward the kidnapped Walt overrides fidelity and noninjury to Jack, Kate, and Sawyer, but does not erase his responsibility for Ana Lucia's and Libby's murders. Because Ross requires amends rather than giving a blank check, the chapter asks whether Michael's spying as 'Kevin Johnson' aboard the Kahana - culminating in giving Jin time to escape the bomb - repairs his wrongs, or whether Walt's rejection and Michael's exile from the closing church scene show he failed to make things right on the terms of those he wronged.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 20 "“The Wrong Direction”" — Barkman builds a definition of lying (communicating what one believes false while hiding that fact, with intent to hurt or disrespect, which distinguishes mere deception and parts ways with Aquinas's blanket ban) and applies it to five advertising worries, from bags of chips designed to invite false inference to the Belle Jolie 'promise' no one actually believes and the Israeli Tourism ad that omits danger. Persuasion is legitimate because rational souls are equals to be treated as ends (Aristotle's justice), but manipulation (ads aimed at preschoolers that use children to pressure parents) and fear-preying coercion (Clearasil on insecure teenagers, nylons to unmarried women like Rachel Menken) treat people as means, while government must regulate factually (FDA 'smoking kills' labels) without overriding adult choice. Responsibility is then distributed across producer, agency, media, public, and state, and Don was indeed 'looking in the wrong direction' in this sense: being able to talk anyone into anything does not mean he should.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 11 "The Office and Philosophy" — Weighs the morality of Jim and Pam's workplace flirting (while Pam is engaged to Roy) using three ethical frameworks: act utilitarianism has them tot up their own happiness against effects on co-workers' morale and Dunder-Mifflin's bottom line; rule utilitarianism models HR's blanket anti-dating policies and asks whether Jim and Pam could justify an exception without destroying the rule (the Hawaiian shirt day analogy); deontology searches for duties against office romance (favoritism in evaluation, distraction from duties) and finds none once harassment is set aside, concluding that in the absence of a deontological prohibition, Jim and Pam may keep flirting until 5 p.m.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 11 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — White analyzes Spider-Man's public unmasking in Civil War as a familiar ethical choice between the right and the good. Peter's promise to Tony Stark and obedience to the Superhuman Registration Act are deontological duties, explicated through Kant's test of universalizing the maxim of promise-breaking, while his worry for Aunt May and MJ pulls him toward consequentialist reasoning whose uncertainty, complexity, and incommensurability the chapter details. Aunt May's 'some things are worth the risk' speech tips Peter toward principle, but the Kingpin's sniper shoots her anyway, and Peter's hellish aftermath — ending in the Mephisto deal of 'One More Day' — shows both the tragedy of doing the right thing and the argument that when consequences are unknowable one should simply do what is right.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 10 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Takes Tig's misplaced revenge on Laroy—which kills Veronica Pope and triggers Damon Pope's burning of Tig's daughter and Opie's prison murder—together with the club's unconditional convoy rescue in 'To Be, Act 1' to ask whether loyalty is a virtue. It tests three accounts: the Aristotelian view (via Ladd's 'loyal Nazi is a contradiction') that only the virtuous can be loyal, which would deny that SAMCRO members can be loyal at all; the Humean view that loyalty is bigoted partiality; and the Kantian point that only the good will is unconditionally good, so loyalty can serve any wrongdoing. The chapter defends Ewin's line that loyalty is good in itself but issues in right action only joined with virtue, while the Stahl frame-up of Opie and Donna's death show the dark enforcement side—'rats deserve to die, end of story.'
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 27 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Defends South Park's anti-paternalism on both consequentialist and deontological grounds. 'Major Boobage' shows the futility of Gerald's cat ban meant to stop kids 'cheesing' — Kenny still gets high and Gerald himself relapses — while 'Medicinal Fried Chicken' shows how the KFC prohibition births a violent black market, with Cartman's $85 snack pushing him into the Colonel's Scarface-style drug war. On the deontological side, Mill's 'over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign', Locke's self-ownership, and Kantian respect for rational agents (via Nozick's inviolability, and the authors' autarchy-versus-autonomy distinction) ground the claim that coercion is wrong even when benevolent: 'Butt Out' has Kyle and Stan tell Rob Reiner that forcing others to quit smoking is fascism, while Big Tobacco's Kevin Harris wins their approval simply by informing and letting people choose.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 22 "“Rebellions Are Built on Hope!”" — Eberl asks whether Galen Erso, who knowingly resumed work on the Death Star while planting its exhaust-port flaw, is culpable for the deaths on Jedha, Scarif, and Alderaan. A utilitarian defense (his flaw net-saved the galaxy, per the negative-responsibility principle applied to the Death Star II 'Clerks' debate) founders on moral luck — everything depended on Luke's impossible shot — while Bernard Williams's integrity objection, via the chemist 'George' case, condemns his betrayal of conscience. The chapter finally deploys Thomistic tools for cooperation with evil: because Galen's contribution was mediate and remote (Tarkin ordered the firing, the gunners pulled the triggers, Leia's defiance provoked Alderaan's destruction) and the weapon would have been built without him, his collusion is justified by the reasonable hope — the 'new hope' — of the Death Star's destruction.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 18 "8. Saints and Superheroes" — Alloy uses supererogation — Urmson's saints-and-heroes puzzle — to separate the heroes: utilitarianism (via Singer's Famine, Affluence, and Morality, where even Clark's novelty glasses are stolen from charity) and deontology both erase acts that are good but not required, and Susan Wolf's moral saints show where that lands — a Bruce Wayne with no hobbies, friends, or life, like Astro City's Samaritan. Alloy's own Raz-style fix (requirements overridden by moral permitting reasons) yields the verdict: Batman risks his life by choice and so is a true hero, while Superman, facing no real danger, merely does what his powers make morally required — 'a good person with the powers of a living god'.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 24 "13. Time to Choose" — Goldberg and Gavaler read Superman's first-year Action Comics adventures (reforming the Blakely Mine owner, demolishing slums, buying back swindled stock) as consequentialism on Millian lines, and Batman's Detective Comics year (letting the Joker's victims die while 'the time isn't ripe', the batarang deflected by invisible glass) as a dark, vengeance-based cousin of Kant's duty ethics. Moral luck is the pivot — deontology ignores it, consequentialism is hostage to it — but Superman's powers cancel luck, and in the opening Luthor/Joker two-bomb scenario Superman defuses while Batman chases the villain, so the chapter rules Superman's 'super consequentialism' the superior code.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 17 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Browning shows that 'Jus in Bello' is built from Romero's Night of the Living Dead: the besieged police station is a 'survival space' (a form he traces to Matheson's I Am Legend), Henricksen takes Ben's role and Nancy Barbra's, and the massed possessed townspeople mirror the shuffling zombie horde. Inside that space the show stages a clash of values, Ruby's utilitarian spell requiring Nancy's heart against Dean's absolute refusal to kill an innocent ('your choice is not a choice'), resolved by the rock-salt-and-exorcism plan that kills no one. The survival space works as a proving ground for its occupants' values, and the ending, where Lilith slaughters Nancy anyway, indicts the heroes' scruples and asks what the body count says about the viewers who enjoyed it.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 34 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Yuen argues cannibalism is not automatically wrong: both utilitarian and Kantian frameworks permit eating the already-dead in a genuine survival situation like the Andes crash of Alive, since corpses lose no happiness and lack the rational nature owed dignity. But Chris's hunters in 'Fear the Hunters' become moral monsters because they kill to eat (murdering their own children, amputating and eating the still-living Dale to prolong his terror), which neither maximizes utility nor treats persons as ends, and Chris's 'we had no choice' excuse fails because starving is not a license to murder when one could befriend other survivors, eat walkers, or starve. Rick's execution of the hunters is then defended on Kantian grounds of deserved punishment: applying Chris's own maxim ('if Dale was good as a steak, so is Chris') as a universal law.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 24 "Notes" — Kowalski applies Kant's ethics to the Aes Sedai Three Oaths in the Amazon series, arguing that because the Oath Rod makes sisters physically unable to lie, 'ought implies can' means they get no moral credit for truth-telling, like praising water for freezing. He examines acting from duty versus according to duty (few Aes Sedai accept the Oaths for the right reason; Moiraine may be the exception), and the universal-law formulation against lying promises. He then presses Kant's absolutism through Moiraine's careful literal truths to the Whitecloak Valda ('I have a sister in Whitebridge'), arguing that Kant's own 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' and Schopenhauer's self-defense objection show WoT can talk back to Kant about conflicting duties.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 25 "Notes" — Bein uses the 'kill baby Hitler' time-machine puzzle and the question of whether Moiraine and Lan should still the Dragon Reborn to probe the Aes Sedai's mysterious ethics. He argues they are not Kantian deontologists (the Three Oaths are loose plot-device rules Moiraine games with ambiguous innuendo, and Kant forbids treating the ferryman as mere means) and are bad consequentialists at best (they cannot lightning-bolt Valda or Hitler who are not Darkfriends). He proposes they are closest to Buddhist ethics: wise compassion good in itself (Tam sitting with dying Tigraine regardless of outcome), and reads the flexible Oaths through upaya (skillful means) and a WoT-adapted Eightfold Path, making them less pacifist nuns than violence-reducing Shaolin nuns.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 21 "Notes" — White reconstructs the 'Sacrifice' storyline - Maxwell Lord mind-controlling Superman, telling lasso-bound Wonder Woman 'Kill me,' and her snapping his neck - and asks whether it was right. He argues Wonder Woman reasons as a threshold deontologist: her usual respect for life holds until the certain cost of letting Lord live (he would wield Superman to kill again) crosses the threshold where the consequentialist body-count argument takes over, and she was justified, so she would do it again. The contrast with Batman's refusal to kill the Joker shows his refusal is virtue-ethical self-definition ('I won't become them'), while Diana, regretting the necessity but feeling no remorse, is an Amazon warrior for whom lethal protection of lives is sometimes exactly the job.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 23 "Notes" — Barkman and Tokbergenova defend 'just torture': Wonder Woman's lasso interrogations of Captain Nazi, the double agent Marcia in the 1970s pilot (saving the Brooklyn Navy Yard's 70,000 workers), and the terrorist Nikos Aegeus are ticking-bomb cases of the sort Henry Shue concedes, and the authors answer Luban's slippery-slope objection with absolute limits (never the innocent or the family) and Dershowitz-style torture warrants. Citing Aristotle's Rhetoric that coerced testimony is often false, they propose trained professional torturers, and conclude that since the right thing is not always the ideal thing, torture should be legalized, rare, and conducted openly - as Wonder Woman models.
- **X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse**, ch. 6 "X-Men and Philosophy" — Four-plus essays. White defends Jean Grey's altruistic suicide in the Dark Phoenix Saga through Kant's categorical imperative (both formulas) and the confl icting-duty case of the rabid-dog letter, ranking deontology over utilitarian and virtue readings. Kavadlo reads the X-Men as existential literature, tying Sartre's bad faith and anti-Semitism and Camus's Sisyphus to the mutants' Jewish/Holocaust roots and never-ending serial struggle. Burnett uses Mister Sinister, Sentinels, and eugenics to trace bioethics through Spencer's evolutionary ethics and Galton. Dunn casts Layla Miller as Bacon's 'knowledge is power' against Aristotle's contemplative ideal. The Davis 'Magneto, Mutation, and Morality' essay begins here, opening the evolutionary-ethics question of Xavier vs. Magneto.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 11 "To Hack or Not to Hack" — Kennedy asks how a great player like Kareem (the NBA's career foul leader) can be excellent while fouling so much, and answers that deontology (Kant's categorical imperative) and utilitarianism (Mill's greatest-happiness principle) can condemn dangerous 'goon' fouling but cannot explain why the legal Hack-a-Shaq strategy still feels 'clownish.' Invoking Shaq's self-nickname 'the Big Aristotle,' he argues Aristotelian virtue ethics fits better: the excellent player, like the person of good character, perceives the situation rightly and fouls (or risks a foul) at the right time in the right way, so excellence is a habit of seeing well rather than rule-following.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 15 "5. Albert Among the Chowder-Head Yokels and Blithering Hayseeds" — The Phillipses argue that abrasive forensic agent Albert Rosenfield is a model Kantian: his refusal to lie to spare Truman's feelings follows the formula of universal law, and his insistence that Truman be punished for the assault treats Truman as an autonomous end. They run Gordon Cole's manipulative lying through the universalizability test (it fails, unlike wanting pie), distinguish hypothetical from categorical imperatives via Cooper's rebuff of Audrey, and read Albert's 'I love you, Sheriff Truman' and Gandhi/King nonviolence as respect for persons as ends in themselves—duty done for the right reason.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Berger uses Harold Becker's The Onion Field to challenge Kant's moral idealism. Kant held that any rational being can deduce categorical imperatives and that conscience necessarily convicts the guilty and vindicates the innocent. Yet the killers Powell and Smith feel no guilt for murdering Kant-admiring cop Ian Campbell (Smith calls guilt a trick 'rich white guys dreamed up'), while the innocent, blameless Hettinger is destroyed by shame, thievery, and near-suicide. Berger weighs Schopenhauer's 'evil genius' objection and the sociopathy explanation, concluding Hettinger's guilt is a doomed attempt to preserve moral meaning.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 13 "Sherlock Holmes and the Ethics of Hyperspecialization" — Costello and Bassham critique Holmes's 'brain-attic' theory from 'A Study in Scarlet'—that the mind has fixed capacity and should hold only vocationally useful knowledge. Cognitive science (interference and schema theory) and the sociology of social/cultural capital show useless knowledge is often useful, as when Holmes trades boxing lore or reads cultural cues. They then argue for a duty of self-improvement grounded in consequentialism, Kantian and Rossian deontology, and virtue ethics (Aristotle, Aquinas, MacIntyre) plus Socratic care of the soul, concluding that Holmes—an omnivorous reader who quotes Goethe and Hafiz—doesn't practice what he preaches and took specialization too far.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 18 "The Dialectic of King and X in Do the Right Thing" — Silberstein reads Do the Right Thing as staging the ideological dialectic between Martin Luther King Jr.'s absolute nonviolence and Malcolm X's defense of retaliatory self-defense, both grounded in a theologically informed natural-law view of rights (King's Christian imago dei, X's Islamic tradition). He argues King mixes a deontological ethic (violence is always wrong) with a Gandhian consequentialist claim that violence begets violence, while X frames a race war as a just holy war. The film's Radio Raheem (LOVE/HATE knuckles), Buggin' Out's boycott of Sal's Wall of Fame, the Racial Slur Montage, and Mookie throwing the trash can dramatize whether ends justify means; the closing Sal-Mookie money exchange reframes racism as symptom of a deeper capitalist greed both King and X came to critique.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 26 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Biderman and Devlin use Traffic's four intertwined characters to test Kantian moral absolutism, applying the three formulations of the categorical imperative: Helena's decision to have witness Eduardo Ruiz murdered fails universalization, while Javier's whistleblowing on General Salazar (motivated only by duty, refusing reward) passes the autonomy formula. They argue Kant handles these cleanly but strains on DEA agent Montel's revenge (treating Carlos as a means) and outright fails on drug-czar Robert Wakefield's conflict between two absolute duties, to nation and to his addicted daughter. Following Sartre's critique that the categorical imperative is too abstract for concrete dilemmas, they show Soderbergh siding with existentialist choice as Robert invents his own law and quits to save his daughter.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 16 "The Duty of Reason Kantian Ethics in High Noon" — Evans argues that Marshal Will Kane in High Noon is Kant's ideal moral agent, acting from duty and a good will rather than from consequences. He shows the townsfolk, Kane's friends, Harvey Pell, Helen Ramirez, and Amy all reasoning consequentially or heteronomously (the mayor privileging the town's finances, Mildred lying about Sam per Kant's essay on the supposed right to lie), while Frank Miller's revenge is a maxim that cannot be universalized. Kane's maxim of standing against lawlessness regardless of cost satisfies all three formulations of the categorical imperative—universal law, humanity as an end, and autonomy—making him a member of the kingdom of ends and contrasting Kant with Mill's utilitarianism.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 18 "The Cost of the Code Ethical Consequences in High Noon and The Ox-Bow Incident" — Ken Hada reads High Noon and The Ox-Bow Incident through Nussbaum's neo-Aristotelian critique of Kantian duty. Will Kane's absolute, self-sacrificing return to face Frank Miller and Major Tetley's honor-bound insistence on hanging the accused both exemplify the Kantian categorical imperative applied without regard to consequences. The essay argues that the films themselves undermine this code: Kane's triumph brings no joy and Tetley's rigid 'reason' masks self-interest and produces the lynching of three innocent men. Following Nussbaum, it holds that attention to particulars, emotion, and social context—embodied by Davies in Ox-Bow—yields more just moral perception than blind allegiance to an absolute rule.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 20 "No Country for Old Men The Decline of Ethics and the West(ern)" — William J. Devlin argues that No Country for Old Men deconstructs the western's three ingredients (moral hero, comprehensible villain, redemptive showdown) and collapses the genre into Nietzschean nihilism. Where Shane's courage is legible through Aristotelian virtue-ethics and Kantian deontology, Sheriff Bell grows old and afraid, walking away rather than confronting evil. Anton Chigurh perverts deontology—killing on 'principle' and because he 'gave his word'—while his coin flips invoke Nagel's moral luck to disclaim responsibility, so the good/bad polarity dissolves and, as Ellis says, 'you can't stop what's comin'.'
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 21 "The Northwestern McCabe and Mrs. Miller" — Deborah Knight and George McKnight read Altman's McCabe and Mrs. Miller as an 'end-of-genre' western in the ironic mode, using Frye's Aristotle-derived mythos to map the classic western's binary oppositions (hero/villain, community/wilderness, virgin/whore) and then show the film collapsing them. Against Nussbaum's and Booth's ethical criticism, which extols works that make us 'finely aware and richly responsible,' they argue irony is itself a moral stance of detached scrutiny: McCabe is no hero but a vulgar, unimaginative businessman crushed by the Harrison Shaughnessy company and shot in the back in the snow while the town obliviously saves its burning church, dramatizing the implosion of the western's moral vision.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 19 "10 Listening with Neil’s Vulnerable Voice and the Ethics of Care" — Jostedt argues that Young's raw, high "dental" singing voice (contrasted with Dylan's nasal sneer) invites empathetic "listening-with" rather than the detached individualism of Kant's deontology or Mill's utilitarianism. Drawing on Gilligan's In a Different Voice, Jane Addams and the ethics of care's emphasis on relatedness, he shows how songs like "Ohio," "Stringman," "Cortez the Killer" and the album Trans (evoking his son's cerebral palsy) make listeners feel with the downtrodden and disabled.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 23 "Allons-y into the Starry Heavens" — Donna Marie Smith uses the Doctor and Rose's separation in "Doomsday" and "Journey's End" to explicate Kantian deontology. After framing the Doctor's virtues via Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and distinguishing eros, philia, and agape (with Reinette illustrating chivalrous self-sacrifice), she argues that Kant's categorical imperative and the duty-versus-inclination conflict explain why the Doctor and Rose Kant be together: their love pulls toward partiality while duty to save humanity is what they ought to do, so acting for the greater good is precisely what forces their parting.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 26 "Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign" — Courtland Lewis argues the Cybermen are not evil but altruistic, distinguishing utilitarianism (right equals good consequences) from Kantian duty-ethics (right can diverge from good), using the Doctor's "Genesis of the Daleks" dilemma about killing a future dictator. He reads the Cybermen as "Cybertarians" who genuinely aim to cure human pain and death, and attacks the Doctor's "Age of Steel" argument that it is good to strive for but bad to achieve a pain-free deathless life. He proposes that Cybermen's real fault is violating autonomy through forced upgrades, and that respecting informed consent (a medical-ethics ad campaign) would make upgrading morally acceptable.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 18 "8. Which Brother Is the Good One" — Browning contrasts the brothers' ethics: Dean is a consequentialist who judges hunts by outcomes ('the ends justify the means,' killing werewolf Madison or faith-healer Roy for the greater good), while Sam is a deontologist who treats lying, stealing, and killing as wrong in themselves. Tracking episodes like 'Bloodlust,' 'Croatoan,' and 'Fresh Blood,' he argues the murder-versus-kill distinction and the blurring line between human and monster show Dean's darker consequentialism is better suited to the Hunter's war, though both are driven to do good.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 19 "9. God the Programmer Is Dead" — De Vries defines a 'monster' in Supernatural as one who breaks the social contract, then argues Sam and Dean are deontologists loyal to a rigid duty—but a 'social contract of two' (family) that produces double standards toward Cas and Jack. She contrasts the angels' box-checking utilitarianism and Hobbesian collapse without God, Hell's contractual capitalist democracy, and Chuck as a controlling 'programmer God' whose perfection cannot tolerate imperfection; Jack's hands-off deity and Chuck's Nietzschean death-of-God let humanity write its own moral code.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 8 "1. Scamming for Fun" — Clipsham distinguishes Jimmy and Kim's 'scamming for fun' (deceiving Ken over rare tequila in 'Switch', or a montage of pointless cons in 'Marco') from the 'scheming for benefits' of Mike, Gus, and Chuck, who lie only to secure a specific end. Using Kant's prohibition on treating people merely as means, he argues that scheming for a benefit is more disrespectful than scamming for its own sake, because the latter treats a mark as an unwitting player in a game rather than a tool. He also rejects the worry that fun-scamming corrupts character, noting Jimmy was already dishonest and that Gus and Lalo's worst vices have no root in playful deception.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 31 "20. Why Is Breaking Skateboarders’ Legs Wrong" — The chapter uses three characters to test three single-value moral theories: Chuck as a Kantian deontologist whose rigid loyalty to the categorical imperative and the 'sacred' law destroys his bond with Jimmy; Jimmy as a Mill-style consequentialist whose ends-justify-means scams (Sandpiper, the squat-cobbler film) let him decide what counts as good outcomes and cost him integrity, invoking Bernard Williams; and Mike as a Scanlonian contractualist who honors even immoral agreements like the Tuco hit. Through cases like the 'murderer at the door,' it argues each theory alone leads people to do wrong, so a moral life must combine outcomes, rules, and contracts.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 33 "21. Finding the Good in Nacho" — The chapter uses Kant to argue that Nacho Varga, though a genuinely bad drug dealer, can perform morally worthy acts in isolated moments. Because Kant locates morality in the rational will and intention rather than accomplishment, it treats Nacho's attempts on the Salamancas and his desire to leave the game as evidence of active moral reasoning, while conceding his motives are muddied by self-interest and love for his father (the shopkeeper example warns against acts done for loved ones). Its clean case is the phone call in 'Something Unforgivable,' where Nacho risks everything to plead for Lalo's near-innocent staff, doing the right thing purely because it is right.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 26 "15. Morality and Manipulation" — Kahn frames the Foundation series around personal autonomy, using Mill's image of humans as a growing tree rather than a machine 'built after a model' to condemn both coercion and manipulation. He shows Hari Seldon as a paradoxical champion of autonomy who nonetheless deceives his own followers about the fraudulent Encyclopedia Galactica and secretly forecloses their freedom of action via the Seldon Plan and Second Foundation—echoing the Mule's mind-control of Han Pritcher. He reads Salvor Hardin's maxim ('never let your sense of morals prevent you from doing what is right') as consequentialism that maximizes galaxy-wide autonomy, contrasts it with the deontology exemplified by Gaia/Bliss (who refuse to manipulate Trevize) and critics like Toran Darell and Branno, and leaves the reader to judge as Bliss urges Pelorat to think for himself.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 27 "16.
