White defends Jean Grey's altruistic suicide in the Dark Phoenix Saga through Kant's categorical imperative (both formulas) and the confl icting-duty case of the rabid-dog letter, ranking deontology over utilitarian and virtue readings. Kavadlo reads the X-Men as existential literature, tying Sartre's bad faith and anti-Semitism and Camus's Sisyphus to the mutants' Jewish/Holocaust roots and never-ending serial struggle. Burnett uses Mister Sinister, Sentinels, and eugenics to trace bioethics through Spencer's evolutionary ethics and Galton. Dunn casts Layla Miller as Bacon's 'knowledge is power' against Aristotle's contemplative ideal. The Davis 'Magneto, Mutation, and Morality' essay begins here, opening the evolutionary-ethics question of Xavier vs. Magneto.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Koepsell reads The Ice Storm as an existentialist masterpiece dramatizing Sartre's Being and Nothingness in Nixon's America. He maps Paul's Fantastic Four 'negative space/void' monologue onto Sartrean no-thing-ness and the tension between being-in-itself, being-for-itself and being-for-others, arguing the alienated, bourgeois Hoods and Carvers live inauthentically in bad faith, objectifying one another. Mikey's joyous reveling in the ice storm before his electrocution is a fleeting authentic immersion in existence (like Roquentin in Nausea), and the closing embraces—Wendy hugging Sandy, a weeping Ben meeting Paul—show characters momentarily overcoming alienation and freely remaking their essence.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 18 "John Clellon Holmes and Existentialism" — Charters recounts how John Clellon Holmes—who coined the framing question 'How are we to live?' and prompted Kerouac's 'beat generation' label—was steeped in existentialism, reading Sartre, Camus, and Kierkegaard in the postwar New York scene. She argues his novel 'Go' is an existentialist text: its beat characters (modeled on Kerouac, Ginsberg, Cassady) enact freedom, self-transcendence, and the refusal of nihilism, saying 'no' in order to say 'yes' as in Camus's 'The Rebel.' Holmes ultimately rejected Sartre's atheist existentialism for a Kierkegaardian, faith-based one, valuing 'the evidence of soul' and reading Kerouac's characters as fleeing the absurd toward spiritual conviction.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Jennifer McMahon reads Walt Kowalski of Gran Torino as Camus's rebel by pairing the film with The Plague. Against the absurd—the feeling that arises when reason's demand for order meets a world that disappoints—Camus rejects plain and 'philosophical' suicide (including religious faith) in favor of revolt, embodied by Dr. Rieux fighting the plague and echoing Nietzsche's life-affirming 'yes.' Walt, like Rieux, acts lucidly and courageously against a threat (Spider's gang) that authorities and the priest Janovich cannot remedy. McMahon defends Walt's engineered death as revolt not suicide via the doctrine of double effect: he intends the community's deliverance and Thao's future, not escape, dying in cruciform sacrifice as an ordinary man who becomes an existential hero.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 11 "No Country for Old Men The Coens’ Tragic Western" — Gilmore reads No Country for Old Men as the Coens' tragic Western, casting Llewelyn Moss as an Oedipus-like hero whose competence-plus-hubris (wounding the antelope, going back to the dying man) triggers his ruin, per Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and the Delphic 'know thyself.' Anton Chigurh is a Nietzschean force beyond good and evil whose coin-toss rule preserves invulnerability by subordinating desire to chance, an amoral Dionysian wildness the essay ties to Thoreau's 'in Wildness is the preservation of the world' and Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian balance from The Birth of Tragedy. Heraclitus's 'geometrical mean' models the hunter-to-prey structure (Chigurh:humans::Moss:antelope), and Bell's fatalism and closing dream of carrying fire voice a Greek-tragic 'you reap what you sow.'
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 24 "“What Kind of Man Are You ” The Coen Brothers and Existentialist Role Playing" — Gaughran argues the Coens presuppose an absurd, valueless world (announced by Blood Simple's 'you're on your own' voice-over) in which characters must, per Sartre's 'existence precedes essence,' invent a self by adopting a style. He surveys the hats of Miller's Crossing, Everett's Dapper Dan dandyism in O Brother read through Camus's The Rebel, and Ed Crane of The Man Who Wasn't There as a Meursault-like figure who forges an identity through violence. Against Camus, murder and suicide are illegitimate revolts, and Sisyphus—not the nihilistic killers—stands as the true absurd hero who never resolves the tension between mind and indifferent world.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 25 "Being the Barber Kierkegaardian Despair in The Man Who Wasn’t There" — Hoffman maps Ed Crane's arc onto Kierkegaard's typology of despair from The Sickness unto Death. Early Ed, the passive barber who defines himself by profession and possessions, embodies despair as a lack of infinitude and possibility—the finitized 'mass man.' Through blackmail, killing Big Dave, and his failed attempt to manage Birdy, he becomes a man of immediacy with reflection, then shifts to 'despair over the eternal,' sensing finite things cannot satisfy. Hoffman concludes Ed ends not free of despair but as Kierkegaard's self of 'inclosing reserve'—withdrawn, watching himself, craving a confidant—having never made the leap of faith that alone escapes despair.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 26 "Thinking beyond the Failed Community Blood Simple and The Man Who Wasn’t There" — Palmer reads Blood Simple and The Man Who Wasn't There as a diptych re-composing James M. Cain's The Postman Always Rings Twice and Double Indemnity, whose core theme is a failed community where self-interest poisons human bonds. Blood Simple dramatizes the Cainian problem—Visser and the others destroyed by instrumentalization and fatal miscommunication—while The Man Who Wasn't There, framed by Camus's The Stranger and Sartre's Nausea, stages its utopian solution. Ed's Sartrean disgust at hair and physicality drives his dry-cleaning scheme; like Meursault he kills and is condemned for the wrong crime, but unlike Cain's solipsistic heroes he ends yearning for communion with Doris beyond the grave, imagining the restoration of the lost community.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 26 "13. Reason and Catharsis" — Elsby and Luzecky argue that we compulsively rationalize Twin Peaks (tulpas, pale-horse omens, Diane-as-tulpa) the way we abstract concepts to tame the contradictory sensible world (Plato's long-and-short finger), but Lynch—especially in Part 8—deliberately thwarts this, exposing what Nietzsche in Twilight of the Idols calls the post-Socratic tyranny of rationality. They offer an alternative reading of Aristotelian catharsis (via Trela): because the fictional world is not ours, we can experience its irrationality and absurdity, emotions purged of their tie to reality, as freedom rather than the existential despair the absurd would cause in our own world.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 33 "19. A Pataphysical Cherry Pie" — Pagnoni Berns, Aguilar, and Veteri argue Twin Peaks stages metaphysics—a dual reality of a physical world and an unknowable superimposed one—drawing on Descartes' dualism and Gustav Fechner's animistic day/night double aspect (souls of plants, the Log Lady's log). They then claim its real philosophy is Alfred Jarry's pataphysics, the science of imaginary solutions to real problems: Cooper solves crimes not by deduction but by absurd means—smelling trees, throwing rocks at a bottle while naming suspects, reading dreams—superimposing another plane on ours (echoing Baudrillard), so Twin Peaks is 'metaphysics with humor.'
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 7 "Introduction" — Mark Conard's introduction opens with thumbnail plots of Double Indemnity, The Maltese Falcon, and Out of the Past to ask what noir has to do with philosophy, then frames the definitional problem (genre, style, cycle, or mood) as itself a philosophical question about essence. It surveys the volume's thirteen essays, noting that French existentialism was contemporaneous with classic noir (1941-58, Maltese Falcon to Touch of Evil) and shares its themes of moral ambiguity, reason versus passion, and pessimism even without direct influence. It previews the arguments to come, including Nietzsche's death of God as a lens on noir, neo-noir realism, Aristotelian tragedy and catharsis, and Schopenhauer's parallels in Ride the Pink Horse.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 15 "Film Noir and the Meaning of Life" — Steven Sanders uses film noir to motivate philosophical reflection on the meaning of life, reading its pessimistic sensibility (Touch of Evil, Detour, Out of the Past, D.O.A., Vertigo) as the presupposition that life is meaningless per se. He runs through Schopenhauer's pessimistic arguments from the vanity and transience of existence, Nagel's rebuttal that our not mattering in a million years does not stop things mattering now, and the tension between Sartrean existentialist freedom and noir's Freudian fatalism of the inescapable past. He then lays out three models of meaninglessness (Baier's worthlessness and purposelessness, Camus/Nagel's absurdity met with irony), reading noir protagonists as ironists, before rejecting the noir view that life must be meaningless and arguing that meaning is a matter of degree, requiring realizable projects of positive value.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 16 "The Horizon of Disenchantment Film Noir, Camus, and the Vicissitudes of Descent" — Alan Woolfolk reads noir through Weber's disenchanted world and Charles Taylor's cultural horizons, arguing the noir protagonist can neither resist the darkness like Conrad's Marlow nor fully embrace it like Coppola's Willard, remaining trapped between times in an ethically irrational universe. He contrasts Camus, who counters disenchantment with an ethic of honesty grounded in a Rousseauian benign nature (The Stranger's Meursault) and with the Baudelairean dandy as aesthetic model, against noir protagonists (Neff, Marlowe, the Swede, Scottie Ferguson) whose 'banked fires' fail and who lose self-possession. Drawing on Freud's id as 'a cauldron full of seething excitations,' he argues the femme fatale drags the protagonist downward into the timeless unconscious where anything is possible (Noah Cross's incest in Chinatown, the radioactive box in Kiss Me Deadly, Body Heat's Ned Racine), and reads noir as backward- and downward-looking through Palmer/Bakhtin's chronotope.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — Editor Jerold Abrams argues Kubrick's whole filmography forms a coherent 'cinematic existentialism' in which a free subject stands against a cold, uncaring world, synthesized with strands of Stoicism and pragmatism. He surveys the volume's essays as variations on this theme: Camus' absurd in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove, Nietzschean flux in Full Metal Jacket, Heideggerian being-toward-death and authenticity in Paths of Glory, and Nietzsche's overman as the Star Child in 2001. The essay ties specific films (the ape's femur, HAL, Humbert, the Overlook) to the claim that each Kubrick subject must invent its own meaning in a meaningless universe.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 10 "Understanding the Enemy The Dialogue of Fear in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove Elizabeth F. Cooke" — Cooke reads Kubrick's Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove through Camus' absurdism, arguing that facing fear and meaninglessness is a task each person must do alone. In Fear and Desire the detached Lieutenant is Camus' lucid 'stranger,' while mad Sidney and death-seeking Mac fail by fleeing into fantasy or false hope; the interchangeable soldiers and doubled enemy general dramatize the sheer contingency of which side one is on. In Dr. Strangelove the individual is dissolved into insane institutions (Ripper, Strangelove, the Doomsday Machine, the War Room round table), so that Sartrean bad faith becomes systemic and no one can face the absurd honestly.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 18 "Rebel without a Cause Stanley Kubrick and the Banality of the Good Patrick Murray and Jeanne Schuler" — Murray and Schuler argue Kubrick's unifying sensibility is a dogmatic Hellenistic-style skepticism (via Hume's 'The Sceptic' and Seneca) that yields 'the banality of the good': in a world of cosmic futility and near-state-of-nature human nature, decent characters like Dax are helpless while the wicked (Barry Lyndon, Alex, Quilty) have vitality. They read Kubrick's Playboy remarks on human insignificance as Humean size/duration tropes, and diagnose his Sartrean 'create your own meaning' answer as a self-refuting false philosophy. Using Marx's critique of Hegel's accommodation to capitalism, they contend Kubrick's skepticism and irony merely reflect the 'bourgeois horizon' rather than comprehending it, ending in present-pleasure hedonism ('fuck' as the last word of Eyes Wide Shut).
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 22 "The Shape of Man The Absurd and Barry Lyndon Chris P. Pliatska" — Pliatska reads Barry Lyndon through Camus's Sisyphus and, chiefly, Nagel's distinction between conventional absurdity (a discrepancy between aspiration and reality, like the mechanical digger wasp Sphex) and philosophical absurdity (the collision of participant and external viewpoints). He argues Kubrick's painterly tableaux, slow reverse zooms, and the detached narrator force viewers from identification into an external, sub specie historiae perspective, exposing Barry's ambitions as conventionally absurd. That recognition then turns back on the audience as the inescapable philosophical absurdity of the human condition, though Pliatska finds Kubrick's tone more lamenting than Nagel's ironic equanimity.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — McMahon argues After Hours uses dark comedy to reveal the existential truth that anyone, at any moment, is vulnerable to absurdity. She sets Sartre's account (absurdity as the contingency of existence, fled via bad faith) beside Camus' (absurdity as a feeling born of the clash between human need for order and the world's silence), then maps Paul Hackett's nightmarish SoHo night onto Sartre's Nausea (the ordinary Roquentin overwhelmed by objects and people) and No Exit ('hell is other people'), where others become the mechanism that discloses the absurd. She contends comedy, like horror, exploits our fascination with grim spectacle, and that laughing at absurdity—rather than horrific spectacle—lets audiences acknowledge and manage existential anxiety and still live well.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Palmer casts the protagonists of The Jericho Mile and Thief as 'outsiders' in Colin Wilson's sense—men 'awakened to chaos'—read through Camus's Myth of Sisyphus. Rain Murphy, running endless meaningless laps and hurling away the timer, is Mann's Sisyphus: his fate belongs to him, the struggle itself filling his heart. Thief's Frank, who 'gets to where nothin' means nothin',' shreds his dream-collage and destroys everything rather than be owned by Leo, enacting the absurd hero's scorn for a Hobbesian 'war of all against all' where law lacks connection to justice.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Abrams argues that neo-noir differs from classic noir by replacing the search for an external villain in the city with the detective's search for his own divided self, structured through time (past, present, future noir). He reads Angel Heart and The Ninth Gate as theological past-noir, Blade Runner and Minority Report as high-tech future-noir where amnesia and precognition fracture identity, and Memento, The Bourne Identity, and Fight Club as present-noir where the sleuth must reconstruct himself from bodily clues; Leonard Shelby becomes a 'Sisyphus of memory' whose total self-consciousness recedes indefinitely.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Spicer argues that the noir antihero embodies existentialism's darker side (alienation, contingency, dread), and that neo-noir intensifies this via European neo-modernism. In Point Blank, Boorman renders Walker's revenge as possibly a dying hallucination, using repetition, doubling, and drained color so that the story becomes an existentialist meditation on desire, faulty memory, and fragile identity. In Memento, Nolan's reverse-chronology 'Mobius strip' structure and Teddy's claim that memories are subjective interpretations leave Leonard's identity in tatters, ending both films on profound existential ambiguity.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Palmer situates The Man Who Wasn't There within New Hollywood's self-conscious 'metagenericism', distinguishing Collins's 'eclectic irony' from the 'new sincerity' that seeks a genre's 'missing harmony'. The Coens revive James M. Cain's noir (Double Indemnity, Postman) but historicize it in 1949, layering the Heisenberg uncertainty principle voiced by the lawyer Riedenschneider ('there is no what happened', 'the more you look, the less you know') onto the plot. Ed Crane, the barber who kills Big Dave, is an absurd Camusian figure who finds preexecution peace in 'seeing it whole', making the film an existentialized meditation on unknowability and meaninglessness.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 21 "Disenchantment and Rebellion in Alphaville" — Woolfolk reads Godard's Alphaville as an imagination of spiritual disaster: the Alpha 60 computer's reduction of time to divisible units suppresses the Bergsonian durée and fundamental self, and the city's architecture of 'nonplaces' embodies Weber's disenchantment and the Frankfurt School's culture-industry critique. Following Charles Taylor, he argues disenchantment opens a new heroic framework of facing an indifferent universe with lucidity, in which Lemmy Caution—a postmodern pastiche of noir dandies—rebels through an aestheticized eroticism and Éluard's surrealist poetry, achieving a Weberian 'this-worldly salvation' of art and love that succeeds where Orwell's Julia and Huxley's Savage fail.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Abrams's editorial introduction argues that Kubrick's whole filmography forms a coherent cinematic existentialism in which the isolated self stands against a cold, uncaring world. It threads the individual Kubrick films through named philosophers - Camus's absurd in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove, Nietzsche's flux and Overman in Full Metal Jacket and 2001, Heidegger's thrownness and being-toward-death in Paths of Glory, Kant's marriage-morality in Eyes Wide Shut - and notes Kubrick blends this existentialism with Stoicism (The Killing) and pragmatism. It frames each contributor's essay as reading one film through that lens.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Cooke reads Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove as studies of how we face Camus's absurd. In Fear and Desire the detached Lieutenant is Camus's lucid 'stranger,' while Sidney goes mad and Mac chooses a suicidal assassination as false meaning; each faces death alone, so it is not tragedy. In Dr. Strangelove the individual is dissolved into insane institutions - Ripper, Bat Guano, the War Room round table - so no one can face the absurd lucidly; Cooke uses Sartre's bad faith to name how men become mere representatives of their institutions, and contrasts both films with Descartes's and Plato's method of certainty.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Murray and Schuler argue that Kubrick's unifying vision is a dogmatic skepticism - the 'banality of the good' - in which good characters (Dax, Alice, Alex's parents) are flat and helpless while the wicked have sass, and irony rules. Drawing on Hume's essay 'The Sceptic' and Marx's dissertation on Epicurus's swerving atom, they read Kubrick as a 'rebel without a cause' whose skeptical tropes of cosmic insignificance, present pleasure, and the veneer over the ape (Dr. Strangelove, The Killing, 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) accommodate rather than comprehend capitalist modernity. They contend Kubrick's Sartrean 'make your own meaning' answer is a false door, since projecting value either really transforms the world (refuting the claim it is indifferent) or projects nothing at all.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Pliatska reads Barry Lyndon through Thomas Nagel's essay 'The Absurd' (built on Camus's Sisyphus), distinguishing conventional absurdity (a discrepancy between aspiration and reality, like the mechanical digger wasp Sphex) from philosophical absurdity (the collision of the engaged participant perspective with the detached external one). He argues Kubrick's three signature devices—the painterly aesthetic that renders eighteenth-century rituals AS rituals, the slow reverse zoom that literally moves from close-up participant view to overwhelming long-shot external view, and the ironic omniscient narrator—make viewers see Barry's conventional absurdity and then confront their own inescapable philosophical absurdity. He notes Kubrick laments this predicament pessimistically where Nagel counsels irony.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 19 "“Back Off to What ” The Search for Meaning in The Wild Bunch" — Richard Gaughran reads Peckinpah's The Wild Bunch as an existentialist western set in 1913, a world 'unhinged' by Nietzsche's death of God where no a priori values remain. Pike Bishop's code of loyalty ('when you side with a man you stay with him') keeps failing—he abandons Crazy Lee, Sykes, and Angel—showing, in Sartrean terms, that only action, not talk or intention, creates meaning. Dutch's question 'Back off to what?' opens onto the abyss; the Bunch's final suicidal march to rescue Angel is read as a Camusian act of revolt that fashions authentic meaning where none was given, saying 'Let's go!' rather than surrendering to the deathward drift.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 11 "3. The Nasty Bits" — Calef asks how Bourdain could find disgusting foods (cobra heart, blood soup, warthog anus) delicious, using Korsmeyer's taxonomy of disgust and the 'paradox of aversion.' He argues their appeal comes from Aristotelian learning-through-representation, Burke's and Bullough's sublime experienced at psychical distance, and Kristeva's 'abject' — foods that remind us of death and mortality let Bourdain transcend and disarm it by eating them appreciatively.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 7 "Dare to Enter the Zone" — Hooke and Rivera's editors' introduction argues that The Twilight Zone dramatizes the Nietzschean disappointment of the epigraph from Twilight of the Idols—that we seek great human beings and find only 'the apes of their ideal.' They cast Rod Serling as a reincarnated Socrates, a gadfly whose episodes ('Time Enough at Last,' 'The Hunt,' the eternal-youth trade-in) stage the gap between our ideals of love, justice, and truth and the treacherous, self-deluding creatures we actually are, so that viewers laugh at absurd twist endings because we are the species most deserving to be laughed at.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 19 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Seitz gives an existential-phenomenological meditation on hunting's essence, leaning on Ortega y Gasset's Meditations on Hunting: 'one does not hunt in order to kill; on the contrary, one kills in order to have hunted.' Using his daughter Sabina's squirrel-versus-grouse reasoning and his own pronghorn stalks, he argues meat is the 'sign' but not the essence, and (via Heidegger) that hunting is 'a mode of revealing.' Contrasting Marx and Heidegger on technology with Ortega's claim that hunting 'cannot progress,' he frames the hunter as 'natural/prehistoric man' annihilating historical time — a vanishing figure in a climate-changed, thirsty future.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 7 "1. Frankenstein" — Using the De Niro monster of Branagh's Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, Rowlands argues absurdity arises from a clash between the view of ourselves from the inside (a locus of meaning) and from the outside (sub specie aeternitatis, insignificant). The monster is assembled from second-hand parts and thrown into a hostile world he did not choose, just as we are stitched together by genes and environment we did not choose (Sartre/Heidegger thrownness). He develops Camus's Myth of Sisyphus, arguing the horror is futility not difficulty, to frame the problem of the meaning of life that underlies every deep philosophical problem.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 20 "18. Russian Doll as Philosophy Life Is Like a Box of Timelines" — The chapter treats Russian Doll's time loops (Season One) and time portals (Season Two) as vehicles for the metaphysics of time, comparing them to Groundhog Day and canvassing presentism, eternalism, and the growing-block theory. It argues the show is committed to a Parfit-style 'multiple timelines' solution to the problem of whether looped characters are numerically identical, and rejects a Berkeleyan idealist alternative. Its climax reads Nadia through Camus's Myth of Sisyphus: unable to change significant past events, she becomes an 'absurd hero' who embraces her family and lot in life, smiling in the mirror, so Season Two's lesson (echoing Nietzsche's eternal recurrence) is that meaning comes from owning one's circumstances.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 24 "22. Rick & Morty as Philosophy Nihilism in the Multiverse" — The chapter argues that Rick Sanchez's nihilism is built on cultural relativism plus the metaphysical fact of a multiverse. It reads Rick's mockery of racist alien snakes and the Gazorpazorp matriarchy through Montaigne's essay on cannibals to establish cultural relativism, and treats the microverse 'battery' society through Marx's base/superstructure and Foucault's docile bodies to argue all social values are constructed for the rulers. Rick's dimension-hopping (the Cronenberg episode, the Vat of Acid) literalizes David Lewis's modal realism and Leibniz's possible worlds, so that no action matters because a counterpart always does the opposite; his resulting hedonism and Birdperson's 'Wubba lubba dub dub' reveal Rick as a depressed near-Camusian who cannot live his own absurdist creed.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 52 "49. A Serious Man as Philosophy The Elusiveness of Moral Knowledge" — Biderman reads the Coens' A Serious Man through Beauvoir's figure of the 'serious man' (from The Ethics of Ambiguity), the man who craves a single absolute value and blinds himself to moral complexity: physics professor Larry Gopnik, beset by divorce, a bribing student Clive, and Sy Ableman's death, seeks moral knowledge that would let him be such a man. The chapter argues Larry's quest fails across cognitivist, noncognitivist, and pluralist accounts of moral knowledge, showing moral knowledge to be elusive if not impossible. The film's Kafkaesque fables (the Dibbuk, the Goy's Teeth, Rabbi Nachtner's 'L'olam ha-ba', Schrodinger's cat, and the Binding of Isaac in Caravaggio's painting) all stage the absurd collapse of interpretation, echoing the Book of Job, which Maimonides read as a parable rather than history.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 54 "51. Magnolia As Philosophy Meaning and Coincidence" — Engelen interprets Paul Thomas Anderson's Magnolia as a meditation on sense-making and Camus's notion of the absurd: the film's raining frogs and the interlocking coincidences (Sydney Barringer's death, the narrator's insistence that 'this cannot be one of those things') stage our compulsion to find meaning colliding with a universe that yields none. He reads characters' struggles with trauma and regret through Epictetus's Stoic dichotomy of control and Jung's synchronicity, and the 'Wise Up' sing-along as a call to accept what cannot be changed. The chapter endorses Camus's third response to the absurd—neither denial nor suicide but defiant acceptance—linking it to Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and Nagel's take on life's meaning.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 82 "77. Journey as Philosophy Meaning, Connection, and the Sublime" — Hamer argues Journey works through the interplay of connection, the sublime and meaning. The wordless multiplayer bond with an unnameable stranger before vast vistas dramatizes emotional connection where the ancestors' greed failed. The looming mountain and immense dunes evoke the sublime, read through Burke's pleasurable terror and Kant's mathematical and dynamical sublime (imagination overwhelmed while reason comprehends; feeling power over a nature that cannot harm the deathless player, then rebirth surpassing the sublime into joy). The cyclical return to the start recasts the game as Camus's Myth of Sisyphus: a meaningless repeated ascent that players nonetheless replay, so we must imagine the Traveler — and ourselves — happy to make the beautiful repetition our own.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 95 "89. The Joker as Philosopher Killing Jokes" — Brake reads Moore and Bolland's The Killing Joke as staging Camus's absurd: the Joker tortures Commissioner Gordon to prove the world is random and unjust ('one bad day') and that reason, tied to continuous memory, should be abandoned for a fragmented 'multiple choice' self. Drawing on Nietzsche's wave-like unstable self (via Morrison's 'super-sane' Joker) and Foucault on how madness haunts modern reason, the chapter argues Batman and Gordon also flirt with madness, while questioning whether the Joker, seeking revenge, has really embraced the absurd or is more rational than he admits.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 97 "91. Deadpool’s Killogy as Philosophy The Metaphysics of a Homicidal Journey Through Possible Worlds" — Manninen argues that Cullen Bunn's Deadpool 'Killogy' is best read through David Lewis's genuine modal realism and counterpart theory: when Deadpool enters the Nexus of All Realities and finds piles of distinct Spider-Man corpses, he discovers other worlds are concrete and their inhabitants are counterparts, not identical selves, refuting Plantinga's actualist transworld identity. Framing Deadpool as an anti-Sisyphean 'hero' who tries to end the Absurd (the Continuity) by killing everyone rather than affirming it as Camus's Sisyphus does, the chapter supplements Lewis with Thomasson's artifact theory of fiction to handle the literary characters of the Ideaverse.

### The Myth of Sisyphus

In The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus takes the figure condemned by the gods to roll a boulder eternally uphill only to watch it fall as the emblem of the absurd human condition. Rather than despair, he argues that Sisyphus can be imagined happy: by consciously embracing his fate without illusion or hope of reward, he wrests a kind of freedom and dignity from a meaningless task. The essay is Camus's answer to what he calls the only serious philosophical problem, whether life is worth living, and it concludes that one can affirm life precisely in the face of its lack of ultimate meaning.

- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 24 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Bill Davis asks why Arwen would 'choose a mortal life' with Aragorn and why wise elves and men call death a gift. The Ringwraiths show that existence can be worse than death - undead kings whose frustrated nature is perpetual torment - while Socrates in the Apology, Lucretius, Sartre, and Camus supply reasons not to fear annihilation, and the elves' endless life raises Boethius's and Bernard Williams's problem of boring immortality (Camus's Sisyphus, Wowbagger the Infinitely Prolonged). He concludes that Arwen and Aragorn, uncommonly wise and loving, accept death as Ilúvatar's gift: she prefers a finite life of deep love, and they trust the old stories of a world 'remade' beyond the circles of Arda.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 8 "“Life’s a Piece of Shit” The Question of Heroism" — Argues Life of Brian is heretical rather than blasphemous: it never mocks Jesus or belief in God but ridicules gullible, smug believing — the Sermon on the Mount crowd mishearing 'blessed are the cheesemakers,' the sandal schism — a critique the chapter aligns with Hume on the appetite for the marvelous and on anthropomorphism. It reads Brian's window sermon ('You're all individuals... think for yourselves') as Kant's Sapere aude and as an existentialist, possibly Christian, humanism. Against the charge of nihilism, it places Brian squarely in Camus's absurd universe (the pointless crucifixion finale and 'Always Look on the Bright Side of Life') and asks whether Brian is an absurd hero like Sisyphus, Meursault, or Dr. Rieux; he is not — he never scorns his fate — so the chapter proposes 'absurd decent guy': Brian lives sincerely, without waiting for miracles, and humor rather than revolt is the counterweight to absurdity.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 21 "A Nietzschean Conclusion" — Slowik argues the Pythons have a positive existentialist message: Kafka's bureaucratic insanity, where ordinary people beat helplessly against irrational rules, recurs in the 'Cheese Shop' and 'Dead Parrot' sketches, and Camus's Sisyphus lives on in the monotonous lives of Palin's city stockbroker and the accountant who dreams of lion taming — repetition without Sisyphus's defiance. The core claim is that Python endorses individual-centered existentialism: Brian's 'You've got to think for yourselves. You're all individuals!' is the troupe's rare direct statement of Sartre's 'existence precedes essence', confirmed by Cleese's and Palin's interviews about resisting those who tell you how to behave, a theme the chapter extends through Nietzsche's critique of moral tradition and organized Christianity. Sartrean bad faith explains Python's stereotyped characters — the aggressive policeman, the pepperpots, and Mr. Praline insisting 'I am not a loony!' while demanding a fish license for his halibut — while Arthur Pewtey's meek 'Right. Right.' and Ron Obvious's physical limits raise nature/nurture objections to Sartrean freedom. The 'Nietzschean Conclusion' is that Monty Python itself exemplifies will to power as 'giving style' to one's character, constantly overcoming its own formulas rather than repeating what succeeded.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 29 "“The Cheese Shop,” Episode 33, Monty Python’s Flying Circus, “Salad Days”" — This is Hardcastle's full talk: analytic philosophy's two revolts map onto Python clips, beginning with the logical positivists' revolt against metaphysics, whose cornerstone verifiability criterion self-destructs because it cannot verify itself. The positivist collapse hands philosophy to Quine's semantic holism — statements face experience 'not individually but only as a corporate body' — which the Dead Parrot sketch enacts as Praline the verificationist checking experiences against the shopkeeper-holist who preserves 'pining for the fjords' by adjusting other statements, and again in the Black Knight, who maintains 'None shall pass' through the loss of every limb. Holism's darker consequence, that no shared axioms are guaranteed so reason cannot found society, appears in the 'Argument Clinic' and in 'Nudge Nudge' as two men effectively speaking different languages in different worlds, while the witch-burning logic illustrates empirically bad human reasoning. The Cheese Shop sketch crowns the continental side — Mr. Mousebender an existentialist hero choosing cheese in an unfeeling world, Mr. Wensleydale the burden of life returning negative answers like Sisyphus's rock — and the Bruces' Philosophers Song is declared the best history of philosophy because it is sung.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 15 "Poker and Philosophy" — Vernezze uses Dostoevsky to make gambling existential: Notes from Underground's insistence that will trumps reason ('what do I care for the laws of nature and arithmetic?') and The Gambler's portrait of the calculating gambler — who loses like everyone else and worships money with a 'German' soul — prefigure existentialism's three traits: lost confidence in reason, despair as part of the human condition, and the willed overcoming of absurdity (Camus' Sisyphus happy, Sartre's condemned freedom). Dostoevsky's own roulette addiction fuels the reading, with Amarillo Slim and Brunson's side bets as heirs. The Cincinnati Kid's climax clinches it: Lancey Howard 'making the wrong move at the right time' by chasing a straight flush proves poker's essence lies beyond reason — a truly Dostoevskean activity.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 15 "Would You Help Me to Carry the Stone" — Weinstein argues critics who call Waters a gloomy misanthrope misread him: he is an existentialist whose work maps point for point onto Camus's absurd, the human demand for unity endlessly frustrated. Waters's imagery tracks Camus's: the sun (Plato's cave symbol of the good, and the light Sisyphus loved on earth) against the eclipsed moon of death and madness; the stone we secrete through failed communication ('the bad blood slows and turns to stone' in 'Dogs,' 'would you help me to carry the stone' in The Wall) against Sisyphus's rock; and Pink's Trial, condemned for 'showing feelings of an almost human nature,' replaying Meursault's condemnation for failing to cry at his mother's funeral. Since the institutions of home, school, military, and the music industry's machine block every genuine encounter, Waters's persistence in making art that mostly fails to communicate is itself the absurd revolt, so with Camus one must imagine Sisyphus happy, and Weinstein imagines Waters happy too.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 28 "Resignation and Exploration—I’ll Climb the Hill in My Own Way" — Steven Gimbel asks how to live with the 'pink' malaise of Waters's lyrics and tests five options: capitulation (Marx's four alienations via 'In the Flesh?', 'Have a Cigar', and 'Dogs'), medication ('Comfortably Numb' and the Prozac-ad mother as one of the 'neuro-chemically well-adjusted sheep'), re-creation of childhood (Nietzsche's child playing 'between the fences of past and future' against memory's 'it was' in 'Remember a Day'), and emancipation through LSD or romanticized madness ('See Emily Play', 'Brain Damage'), with Syd Barrett's vacant eyes as the fatal counterexample. What survives is Camus's Sisyphus — fully conscious of his futility yet 'superior to his fate', imagined happy — joined to 'Fearless''s 'I'll climb that hill in my own way' and the mutual care of 'Pigs on the Wing', closing on Socrates' unexamined life: the answer lies in the searching itself, so living pink means living.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 25 "Driftin’ Off to a Foreign Land" — Dick explains how 'Straight Time' makes us see Charlie's cycle of drudgery through Sartre's The Imaginary: the title is a Sartrean sign that welds prison time, rendering-factory time and straight-and-narrow time into one image of endless oppression, and Bruce's first-person characterization works like Dana Carvey impersonating Jimmy Stewart — consciousness overlooks discrepancies until we recognize 'our' Charlie. Against the escape fantasy of 'Thunder Road,' Camus's Sisyphus frames Charlie as swapping rocks (prison, factory, his uncle's car-theft heist) while the hill remains and 'there is no top of the hill.' Springsteen's answer to the absurd is to climb alongside his characters in empathetic brotherly love.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 38 "Embracing Death" — David Vessey argues the humanoid Cylons' resurrection denies them the 'successful death' that makes a life meaningful: like Greek heroes governed by moira or Socrates drinking the hemlock, mortals must be able to see life as a completed whole that death can crown, with how one lived shaping what death means. Cylon deaths (dying out of range of a resurrection ship, D'Anna being boxed) are always failures or shames, and their religion carries no after-death stakes, unlike Socrates' philosophical preparation for death. Camus's Sisyphus shows agency and the option of suicide remain necessary for meaning, while Plato's Symposium model of immortality through children is the only one left to the Cylons, via mortal human-Cylon babies like Hera.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 13 "Why I Can Play Zelda for Four Hours Straight" — Fellela reads Link's endless drudgery (slashing grass for rupees, collecting bottles, leaving the final Ganon fight at a 'permanent pause') through existentialism: Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' is dramatized in Ocarina of Time's opening, where Link must acquire sword, fairy, and skills to make himself the hero, and Nietzsche's 'God is dead' call to become gods is answered by Link restoring meaning to a hostile Hyrule. Camus' Sisyphus figures the repetitive world-saving quest as an absurd hero's owned task, and Frankl's logotherapy (meaning as the tension between what one is and what one should become) explains why humiliating menial tasks, in camp or in laundromats or in Zelda, become bearable and even meaningful. Link's fixed options even illustrate Frankl's point that freedom is the stance we take toward conditions, not freedom from them.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 21 "How to Misunderstand Politics Completely" — Melançon argues Radiohead's real politics lie not in the overt content of Hail to the Thief but in a Camusian movement from absurdity to revolt: 'Exit Music'''s violent shift from Romeo's tender 'you' to the distorted 'we hope that you choke' enacts revolt against imposed rules and wisdom, while the android of 'Fitter Happier' ('a pig in a cage on antibiotics') and the wished-for alien of 'Subterranean Homesick Alien' dramatize absurd life under others' dictates. Following The Myth of Sisyphus and The Rebel — 'I revolt, therefore we are' — he shows how the songs' 'I' becomes a collective 'we' ('Karma Police', 'Lucky', 'Dollars and Cents') whose revolt, like Sisyphus's conscious walk back down the mountain, affirms life without ever justifying murder. Merleau-Ponty's philosophy of expression then explains why the songs are political anyway: artists express a still-unspoken 'fever' (it took years before 'Nude' could be said), creating a public and a common world — politics as unveiling rather than governing, down to 'Electioneering'''s admission that the band too campaigns for our vote.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 29 "A Large Rock Saved My Life" — Lindsey Fiorelli reads OK Computer as Camus's absurd universe: "Subterranean Homesick Alien" and "Fitter Happier" portray a technological world drained of meaning, where to belong you must become a robotic "pig in a cage on antibiotics" and "Let Down" offers only the "emptiest of feelings." She stresses that Camus demands revolt, not escape — Sisyphus and Meursault embrace the absurd and thereby become happy — whereas Yorke's lyrics keep longing to flee (spaceships, growing wings, the resigned "No Surprises"). Yet the music itself embraces the technology the lyrics curse, and this, she concludes, is Radiohead's real Camusian move: like Camus writing novels about an alienating world, they carve Sisyphus's rock — modern technology, synthesizers and computers — into new and marvelous sounds, overcoming alienation by working within it.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 20 "Colbert Is (the Tragedy and Comedy of) America, and So Are We" — Ralkowski asks whether Colbert is America's Socrates, comparing Colbert's ironic interviews (Caitlin Flanagan on feminism, Harvey Mansfield on manliness, Howard Dean's superdelegates, the ABC Stephanopoulos-Gibson debate) to Socrates' definitional refutations of Euthyphro and the Athenian elite. Like Socrates in Plato's cave allegory, Colbert is a shadow on the wall undermining truthiness from within, yet both fail: audiences laugh, guests collect the campaign-donation 'Colbert Bump,' and nothing changes, making America the self-satisfied one who is ignorant of its ignorance. Through Nehamas's contrast of Socratic and Platonic irony and the Symposium's demand that the greatest work read as both tragedy and comedy, the chapter concludes Colbert may be America's Plato — condemning and laughing at us like a Sisyphean liberator who knows we will not leave the cave.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 6 "Mr. Monk Meets Alexander the Great" — Wittkower argues that Monk's daily, unwinnable war on dirt and disorder is Camus's happy Sisyphus made concrete: Monk vacuums ceilings, touches lampposts, and solves murders knowing the dirt and the murderers will always return ('There's never hope... Hope. I hate hope's guts' in 'Mr. Monk Can't See a Thing'), yet he still finds enough satisfaction to take up the wipe again. Reading Ecclesiastes' vanity alongside the uncaring wasp of the opening, the chapter claims Monk shows us how to live wisely without resignation in an absurd world that does not care. He is paired with Diogenes the Cynic, whose barrel, raw onions, and midday lantern mirror Monk's pot-pie-Tuesdays and his refusal to overlook what everyone else ignores; like Diogenes telling Alexander the Great 'get out of my sun,' Monk lives by his own ideals no matter how society judges him. The essay closes that, like Camus addressing the Dominican monks, we should refuse to 'be reasonable' about evil and disorder and keep struggling without hope, wipe in hand.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 18 "Here’s What Happened" — Kane, a catalog librarian, argues that Monk's detecting mirrors library cataloging. Monk 'collocates' — identical boxes on one wall, a row of matching Trudy photos on another — and reasons user-first, exactly as Cutter's rule says to choose the entry a library's users will look under first: in 'Mr. Monk and the Bad Girlfriend' he sees the suspect with no alibi must be innocent because a killer who hides in the bathroom already has an alibi secured. Like the invisible cataloger, Monk imposes the order others see without knowing someone arranged it, and both face Sisyphus's rock: Monk's control ends at his apartment door ('Mr. Monk Makes the Playoffs' tailgate chaos), and Universal Bibliographic Control — one standard for describing every work ever created — will never stay at the top of the hill. The Cutter-versus-Dewey rivalry parallels Monk versus Harold Krenshaw, the flashy thunder-stealer who gets famous first, and the chapter ends by pronouncing Monk a natural-born cataloger.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 30 "Are These World Series Champions Really Our Red Sox" — Lee casts pre-2004 fandom as a Kierkegaardian leap of faith ('We Believe') and the Curse of the Bambino as Schopenhauer's irrational deterministic will, with the 1918–2004 cycle of spring hope and October collapse as Camus's Sisyphus. But he argues fans are really existentialists: blaming losses on fate or the Curse is Sartrean bad faith that evades responsibility, since fans did hold Bill Buckner (1986 error) and Grady Little (leaving a spent Pedro in during 2003 ALCS Game 7) individually accountable. The 2004 and 2007 champions remain 'our' Red Sox because we freely choose to care about the team's journey, not because it has a fixed essence; a coda borrows Russell's point about ambiguous reference for the word 'Yankee,' and Andy Wasif's appendix runs Yankees-as-evil through relativism, objectivism and subjectivism.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 11 "The Stoic Warrior" — Jeff Sharpless imagines a Spartan mourning Kurt-051 and asking what his abduction, augmentation, and endless war mean, concluding his life is absurd in Camus's sense: bred as an instrument by the very humanity he is celebrated for saving. Camus's Sisyphus supplies one answer—meaning in the defiant moment of turning back down the hill, which recasts Master Chief's 'I need a weapon' as either hollow absurdity or quiet revolt. Epictetus supplies the alternative: distinguish what is up to us from what is not, withhold assent from impressions like 'we are all going to die,' and the Chief's silence becomes Stoic tranquility—though the chapter concedes Stoicism risks minimizing the injustice done to the Spartan children.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 13 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Argues Heisenberg is not an alter ego but Walt finally escaping the Prufrock-like bad faith of his pre-cancer life: the pork-pie-hat persona acknowledges the absurd, owns his freedom and responsibility, and so achieves the authenticity Camus and Sartre demand. Walt becomes Camus's Sisyphus - rebelling against death, social norms, and Skyler, owning his rock with silent joy - citing the fulminated-mercury showdown with Tuco in 'Crazy Handful of Nothin'', running down Gus's dealers in 'Half Measures', and confessing to Skyler in 'No Mas'. The chapter closes that, like Sisyphus, we must imagine Walt happy.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 23 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Rachel Robison-Greene reads the survivors through Camus: walkers are mere digger wasps, living tedious, meaningless loops without the consciousness that would make it agonizing, but the living - Morgan longing for the real Jenny back, Andrea losing Amy - face the absurd confrontation between human longing and an indifferent universe, just like Oran in Camus's The Plague. Of Camus's options, suicide (Jacqui and Dr. Jenner staying in the exploding CDC) and religion ('GOD FORGIVE US' on the farmhouse wall) are escapist, so she offers the absurd hero: Sisyphus with his rock, Rieux with his plague, matched by Rick hunting Atlanta for his family, Merle's self-preservation, and Daryl fighting uphill with an arrow in his side. Against Nagel's ironic alternative, she argues we cheer Rick when he alone will shoot Sophia in Hershel's barn because his subjective commitments stay noble even with no objective meaning behind them.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 11 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Crosby takes Bunk's 'misdemeanor homicide' exchange about Marlo as the show's thesis that post-industrial capitalism makes human lives worth less, season by season devaluing beat cops, longshoremen, would-be reformers, the schoolkids of Season Four, and finally the journalists meant to sound the alarm. She deploys Foucault's Discipline and Punish to explain how institutions train docile participants and then require their regular sacrifice to keep operating, so that Simon's 'indifferent gods' of Greek tragedy are now postmodern institutions whose lightning bolts hit everyone in the 'hood. She ends with Camus's Sisyphus: Simon's call to commit to a righteous cause you probably will not win is the only response that offers human dignity, because 'this ain't Aruba... this America, man.'
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 16 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Lewis argues that Futurama's answer to the fear of being forgotten - Zoidberg thriving on negative attention, Bender's billion-cubit statue and the Shrimpkins' forced worship both failing - is to become existentially intertwined with others through friendship, love, and family. Bender's arc in 'A Pharaoh to Remember' is read through Camus's Sisyphus: life itself is meaningless, but our freedom lets us fill it with meaning, which Bender finds not in monuments or worship but in seeing others remember him. Fry's devotion in 'Godfellas' and 'Jurassic Bark' (Seymour waiting outside Panucci's forever), Bender's Big Score, the holophonor opera of 'The Devil's Hands Are Idle Playthings,' and Yancey naming his son after Fry in 'The Luck of the Fryish' show remembrance surviving inside the people we have shaped, including the viewers.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 12 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Agust Magnusson argues that Cohen's 'crack in everything' credo from 'Anthem' is an existentialist celebration of brokenness against a culture demanding an unattainable perfect offering. He reads 'Waiting for the Miracle' alongside Camus's Sisyphus - the narrator stops waiting for a transcendent Answer and accepts the absurd, while 'The Future' and 'Democracy' dramatize both the fright of relativism and its resolution in humanistic hope. Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling then explains 'Hallelujah': Abraham's leap beyond the ethical into the religious models a resignation in which broken Hallelujahs are still worth singing, and The Sickness unto Death shows despair overcome by letting go of the ego so that suffering begets compassion and love.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 16 "Girls and Philosophy" — Blessing and Wezowiczi test theories of life's meaning on the two narcissists of Girls: Hannah, whose purpose-driven pursuit of being a writer (manufacturing experiences, ignoring her father's medical procedure) shows that goal achievement alone collapses into Taylor's and Camus's Sisyphus problem, and Jessa, whose 'life addict' desire-satisfaction illustrates the Nietzschean live-in-the-moment view the authors find reckless and irresponsible. Using Wielenberg's excrement-eater and the subjectivist/objectivist debate, they land on Susan Wolf's 'loving objects that are worthy of love,' then argue via Socrates's examined life and Sartre's bad faith that neither Hannah's phony narrative nor Jessa's protective persona counts as authentic, examined living.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 34 "Dracula and Philosophy" — In imaginary letters, Meursault of Camus's The Stranger describes his meaning-free life, his trial that condemned his refusal to perform feelings, and his death-row move from indifference to acceptance of the absurd, then inducts Dracula into Camus's gallery of absurd heroes beside Don Juan, Don Quixote, and Sisyphus - those who reject suicide, reject help from higher powers, and accept life's absurdity. Dracula accepts the first two traits but categorically rejects despairing acceptance, claiming love and conquest instead. An appendix lets Sisyphus himself grumble that Camus finding happiness in boulder-pushing is the real absurdity.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 13 "2. Maybe Jenner Was Right" — Cowan uses Jenner's suicide in the exploding CDC (1.6 'TS-19') to pose Camus's question 'Why should I not commit suicide?', and rejects Jenner's despair the Camusian way: Michonne in 4.9 'After' - slaying her own walker look-alike and then her two pet walkers - is his Sisyphus in revolt, unlike Gareth, whose revolt lacks the respect for human dignity that makes Sisyphus happy. He then objects that Camus never explains why human life has intrinsic dignity in a godless universe, noting that Sartrean authenticity could equally license the Governor's Woodbury experiments or Gareth's cannibalism, and turns to Hershel's providential hope as the religious alternative. Following Plantinga, he argues belief in God can be properly basic through a sensus divinitatis - Hershel seeing God's hand in 2.4 'Cherokee Rose' and the tornado-spared barn of 5.10 'Them' - so if God exists, Jenner was not right.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 16 "6. The Absurdity of the Luggage" — Kempner reads the Luggage - the sapient, homicidal pearwood chest that pursues Rincewind from The Color of Magic through The Light Fantastic and Interesting Times - as the embodiment of Camus's absurd: the 'divorce' between our demand that the world make sense and a world that does not care. Rincewind, who dreams of a rational, scientifically ordered universe while the Disc sails on a turtle and the gods smash atheists' windows, is cast as Sisyphus, and the trolls who 'suffer from philosophy' and freeze solid show where the futile quest for order ends. When Rincewind finally says 'Come on' to the huddled Luggage and readers come to love what once terrified them, the chapter performs Camus's acceptance of the absurd as freedom.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 20 "8. Laughing in the Face of the Absurd" — Argues that watching Beth die on the platform is Sarah's existential awakening — the absurd realization that "it is no longer true that everyone has their own face" — analyzed through Camus's absurd (the impossible and the contradictory), Sartre's nausea at inhuman humans, and Beauvoir's "subman" who never wakes from the mechanical life. Sarah must repeatedly witness "her own" death (Beth, Katja, Jennifer, the Helsinki clones), which robs death and life of settled meaning, yet she refuses nihilism: exercising the radical freedom Sartre says grounds all values, she fights Dyad on behalf of everyone's freedom, implicitly choosing it for all humanity. Like Camus's Sisyphus, whose rock is his thing, her struggle is her thing — and the Season Two clone dance party is her laughing in the face of the absurd.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 17 "8. Living for More" — Kevin McCain separates meaning of life—why humans exist at all, with no creator-God found in Gold nihilism ('the Golds have no God'), the Obsidians' manufactured Norse religion, or the Reds' Vale and Old Man—from meaning in life, following Susan Wolf's distinction. After rejecting supernaturalism and pessimistic naturalism (Nero's universe that 'does not notice us,' met by Karnus's Camus-like defiant pride and Thomas Nagel's ironic stance), he rejects Richard Taylor's subjectivism via the Sisyphus story: Karnus and the Boneriders enjoy their cruelty, but enjoying it does not make their lives meaningful. Wolf's objectivism wins—a meaningful life is actively and lovingly engaged in projects of worth—which is exactly Darrow's living for more, contrasted with the Jackal's loveless, self-loathing pursuit of mattering.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 12 "1. Charlie’s Eternal Quest for the Little Red-Haired Girl" — The chapter reads Charlie Brown's lifelong, unconsummated longing for the never-seen Little Red-Haired Girl as a quest narrative without closure: like Beckett's Vladimir and Estragon he cannot act, and like Camus's Sisyphus he is an absurd hero whose dignity lies in persisting (the 2,120 lunch hours, the losing team, the pulled football) without reward. Using Lacan's account of desire - the wish for the Other's recognition, suspended between the demand for need and the demand for love - it argues Schulz keeps her invisible (except one 1998 silhouette) precisely so Charlie's desire stays in permanent suspension, like a Hitchcock MacGuffin. The closing section attacks The Peanuts Movie (2015) for betraying this existential vision: by showing the girl, rewarding Charlie with a kiss, and swapping Sisyphean defiance for 'believe in yourself' truisms, it delivers Sisyphus from his rock and so kills what made him admirable.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 13 "2. 3eanuts and the Existential Schulz" — The chapter introduces existentialism and reads Peanuts through it: Charlie Brown's defeats expose the 'groundlessness' of value, and the 3eanuts web project (deleting each strip's final gag panel) restores the despair that punchlines normally defuse. It explains Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' and the ideal of authenticity versus passively inhabiting roles, Heidegger's care and Dasein (even in despair there is an inner place where it happens), and Camus's absurd and Sisyphus revolting against a fate he cannot change. Lucy's hillside sermon ('WELL, LIVE IN IT, THEN!') and the final image of Charlie running at the football figure his revolt: he keeps kicking because in that moment a world without boxes exists in him.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 21 "10. Always a Pallbearer, Never the Corpse" — Heidi Samuelson argues Deadpool is Camus's absurd hero improved: his origin and his survival of impossible dismemberments embody the absurd as 'disproportion between intention and reality', and facing Camus's one real philosophical problem—suicide—he tries to die via the Hulk to join mistress Death yet must live on, rejecting both actual and 'philosophical' suicide (dogma). His mercenary sense of purpose, jokes in the face of oblivion, and compassion for Blind Al, Weasel, deaf Hawkeye, and Evan exemplify Camus's revolt, freedom, and passion. Sisyphus is the model: like him, Deadpool owns his rock—the healing factor and the killing—and is happy, laughing where Sisyphus is silent.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 12 "2. A Death Worth Living" — Argues that dying in the Murder House or the Hotel Cortez removes death's usual harms - Ben Harmon can reunite with his ghost family and keep counseling patients, and Liz Taylor's chosen death brings reunion with Tristan plus open-ended projects protecting the hotel - but then poses Bernard Williams's boredom problem: finite projects run out over eternity and replacing them would make you a different person. Richard Taylor's Sisyphus and the Hotel's contented Laundress supply the answer that repetitive tasks embraced as meaningful can sustain even an immortal afterlife.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 27 "14. The Absurdity at the Heart of Horror" — Uses Camus's Myth of Sisyphus to argue that AHS's deepest horror is absurdity - the human quest for meaning in a meaningless universe: the Harmons' doomed attempts to protect each other in the Murder House mirror Sisyphus's futile push, Dr. Arden's experiments on aliens who mock him ('Arden you quack who would make a better duck?') show comprehension of the universe is beyond reach, the Countess's bored immortality and Ma Petite's casual murder stage the confrontation between human longing and a universe that cannot care, and the answer to 'why do bad things happen to good people?' is simply: 'because they do. There is no reason.'
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 19 "9. A Human Fighting the Gods" — Luzecky and Elsby argue gods cannot be heroes: Thor's strength, Hulk's rage and Tony's godlike intellect stand outside humanity, whereas Erskine's serum amplified Cap's nascent human goodness (as it exposed the Red Skull's badness), making him the best human rather than a superhuman. Reading Cap through Camus's absurd - the paradox of beings who strive for universality while stuck in particularity - they show him refusing both nihilistic reduction (Alexander Pierce's helicarriers in Winter Soldier) and Nietzsche's flight to 'other worlds' that hates this one. When Loki commands the crowd to kneel, the refusal Cap embodies is Sisyphus's defiant persistence, which is why he, and not the gods, is the Avengers' greatest hero.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 22 "11. Dilbert’s Absurd World" — Christian contrasts Camus's absurdity, the futile collision between our demand for meaning and a silent world whose only exits are suicide, a leap of faith, or Sisyphean revolt (an active defiance he takes partly from Nietzsche's rejection of resignation), with Adams's office absurdities. In Dilbert the absurd is contained and epistemic rather than pervasive and metaphysical: the battery-dead LED request, Dadaist mission statements, Catbert's evil HR policies, Wally's self-congratulatory Wally Reports, and Alice's harpoon all trace to people being idiots about different things, and could be fixed by honest credit and realizable plans. Dilbert's Business Dorky acceptance therefore looks Camusian but is not: it is recognition minus revolt, bewildered amusement where revolt and reform remain genuinely available.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 25 "14. Of Course It Sucks—It’s Work" — Wible stages three theories of work against Dilbert strips: the Greek view of Plato and Aristotle that labor is freedom-sapping and leisure is the civilized ideal, Marx's capitalist critique in which workers become objects and machines (Wally gives off no human vibe, and robots are coming for the engineers), and Desjardins's human-fulfillment model built on Schumacher's creativity, challenge, development, honesty, and beauty, with Wells Fargo's fake accounts showing how jobs that force lying corrupt character. He endorses instead a Kantian middle ground anchored in Norman Bowie's moral minimum: never treating workers as mere means, so the CEO making intern Asok drink industrial sludge on stage is a violation of respect for persons, not just bad management. Sisyphus supplies the image of pointless labor, though even he might be redeemed if he loved the rock.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 17 "8. Sexistentialism" — Reads Schumer through Camus's absurd: Trainwreck's gender-reversed commitment-phobe and the sketch where friends kill themselves rather than accept a compliment expose the futility of finding meaning in patriarchal gender scripts. Browning argues that advocating change against so systemic a sexism is a Sisyphean task, and that the film's romantic-comedy ending is 'existential' because Amy freely chooses commitment and owns the absurdity rather than escaping it. The chapter ends by asking whether Schumer's jokes are a battle cry whose very pointlessness might be the point.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 28 "16. Death Becomes Her" — Hendrik Kempt reads Drag Race's pervasive death imagery - death-drops, the 'lip sync for your life,' mirror messages, the 'Death Becomes Her' runway - through the philosophy of death. Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' and Stoic self-possession (Ru's 'pay them bitches no mind,' Violet Chachki enduring a tiny corset) explain why elimination, like death, gives no ground for worry once it arrives, while Socrates' 'philosophy is training for death' makes the show a workout video for dying - Socrates even dying fussing over a rooster like a drag mother to Miss Fame. Heidegger's thrownness and being-toward-death set up Sartre's radically free, future-oriented self - so voluntary exits like BenDeLaCreme's self-elimination and Charlie Hides's listless lip-sync betray one's own plans - and Camus's Sisyphus makes Chi Chi DeVayne and Roxxxy Andrews's doomed All Stars returns models of 'acceptance without resignation.' The closing weighs transhumanism's promise of conquered death against a DragCon-forever thought experiment, concluding with Ru's roast eulogy for Lady Bunny that love and irreverence, not immortal life, are the point.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 18 "7. Eleanor and the Meaning of Afterlife" — Yang frames Eleanor's predicament as a dilemma: a finite life seems drained of value by its ending, while an immortal one collapses into boredom or into the disconnection of the 802 memory-wiped reboots. Camus's Sisyphus and Richard Taylor's desire-fulfillment view prove inadequate, so he adopts Susan Wolf's account of meaning as loving what deserves to be loved, which Eleanor's study of moral philosophy, her friendships, and her romance with Chidi satisfy even without God or eternity. John Martin Fischer's narrative approach then redeems the reboots as self-contained episodes, and Eleanor's note to herself in Scanlon's book shows memory wipes need not sever the story of a life.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 10 "2. What Does Life Mean after the Snap" — This chapter reads four post-Snap Avengers as existentialist answers to how life keeps meaning after catastrophe. Tony Stark embodies Sartre's existence precedes essence, defining himself through free choice up to his final 'I am Iron Man' snap that erases Thanos and his army; the merged Professor Hulk lives Camus's Sisyphus, embracing the absurd and concluding 'all is well' after watching his own past rage; Captain America lives Levinas's ethics of the Other, from refusing to abandon brainwashed Bucky in Civil War to wielding Mjolnir to save Thor; and Ronin-era Hawkeye enacts Nietzschean nihilism until Black Widow's Vormir sacrifice, read through Zarathustra's burning in one's own flame, restores his meaning. The authors conclude Marvel's answer is affirmation: courage to affirm freedom, the Other, and life itself against Thanos as personification of genocide, climate change, and war.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 25 "One Must Imagine Ripley Happy" — Reads Ripley-8 through Camus's Myth of Sisyphus: discovering the room of failed clones confronts her with the absurd gap between her longing to be Ellen Ripley and the world's answer that she is lab-grown Number 8. Of Camus's three responses she refuses physical suicide (declining Call's knife - 'What makes you think I would let you do that?') and philosophical suicide (mocking the auton's programmed crossing herself in the chapel), instead living in revolt - 'I rebel--therefore we exist' - shared with Call, so that her serial extermination of Xenomorphs across four films becomes Sisyphean toil, and one must imagine Ripley happy.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 22 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Brown and Fosl read the twin Lebowskis as America's post-1960s despair: the Big Lebowski is Kierkegaard's failed Caesar who despairs because he cannot rid himself of the self that did not become Caesar (a fake achiever living on an allowance), while the Dude is the failed leftist whose revolutions collapsed. Against nihilism Walter pulverizes with Nietzschean will, Kierkegaard prescribes the leap of faith, and Camus revolt — but the Dude offers a distinctly American answer, abiding repetition: rolling balls frame after frame like Camus's happy Sisyphus, repeating phrases and roles (Butlerian performativity) so that re-creating himself is his victory over meaninglessness, with No Country for Old Men as the dark twin where nihilism may be winning.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 44 "The Death of Death" — Reading Black Mirror's deaths through Bandersnatch's train ending, Be Right Back's AshBot, and San Junipero, the chapter uses Heidegger's presence-at-hand (Stefan's absent mother and rabbit remain present as possibilities he can act on) and Derrida's différance (the meaning of life and death is endlessly deferred as technology scrambles the presence/absence binary - Martha's simulated Ash, Liam's Grain deletions, Chris's guilt-haunted fiancée). A central section frames the whole debate as transhumanism - Kurzweil's three bridges to the posthuman against Fukuyama's warning that self-directed evolution replaces God - before Camus resolves the question of meaning: Kelly and Yorkie, like Sisyphus, create meaning by choosing their fate in a VR heaven that objectively matters nothing. Freud's Eros/Thanatos drives and Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' close the chapter's question of whether to extend, hasten, or simply accept mortality.
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 9 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — William Irwin reads the Ozzy-era catalog as unwitting British existentialism: "Johnny Blade", "Paranoid", and "Wheels of Confusion" voice Camus's absurd, the mismatch between our desires and a world where life has no meaning and "hell is other people" explains why Iron Man, saved yet treated as a mindless thing, plans vengeance. The chapter argues the band moves from despair toward freedom and self-creation: "Supernaut" and "Under the Sun" reject religion in the spirit of Nietzsche's death of God, "Cornucopia" depicts bad-faith conformity to plastic suburban lives, and "Children of the Grave" plus Sabbath's own music-making exemplify the claim that artistic creativity is the proper response to pain, with the fan invited to sculpt himself into an authentic individual Sisyphus-style.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 4 "Death Gives Meaning to Life" — Lee reads Strange's car crash as Heideggerian angst and the Call of conscience that ends his 'ontic' life of treating patients as reputation-building problems, forcing a choice between authenticity and a mask. Kaecilius and Dormammu embody the inauthentic flight from death (Kaecilius going 'beyond good and evil' Nietzsche-style), while the Ancient One's confession — drawing on the Dark Dimension only until Strange could replace her, then stretching one moment into a thousand to watch the snow — models accepting mortality. Dormammu's torment in Strange's time loop is compared to Camus's Sisyphus, supporting the thesis that without an ending life is endless repetition, so 'death gives meaning to life.'
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 18 "7. Eleanor and the Meaning of Afterlife" — Builds a dilemma from 'Existential Crisis': Michael's prospective retirement (via Todd May's Death) makes finitude look meaning-destroying, while the humans' endless existence — 802 reboots, Mindy St. Claire's eternal Cannonball Run II in the Medium Place — threatens boredom and disconnection from past selves. Testing God-free answers, it runs through Camus's Sisyphus, Richard Taylor's desire-fulfillment view, Susan Wolf's requirement that we love what deserves to be loved (Eleanor's philosophy study, friendship with Tahani, romance with Chidi), and John Martin Fischer on free authorship and narrative order (Eleanor's note to herself in What We Owe to Each Other). Conclusion: Eleanor and friends can lead meaningful lives even if damned and repeatedly rebooted.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 16 "6 The Absurd Hero Indiana Jones, God, and Sisyphus" — Justin Fetterman takes the Big Bang Theory objection seriously — Indy is superfluous in Raiders and loses nearly every artifact he chases — diagnosing him first with Kierkegaard's despair of possibility from The Sickness Unto Death, where each failure only convinces him success lies just ahead. But Indy refuses Kierkegaard's leap of faith even after witnessing Shiva's Sankara Stones and the Ark, since multiple gods' demonstrations cancel any single revelation, and Kierkegaard demands faith without comprehension. The chapter then re-reads him through Camus: like Sisyphus he repeats near-identical quests (Raiders and Crusade both have him lead the Nazis to a Judeo-Christian relic that destroys them), and his value lies in 'the most living' and the struggle itself, making him an absurd hero rather than a failed believer.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 13 "Why I Can Play Zelda for Four Hours Straight" — Toni Fellela gives an existentialist reading of Zelda, confessing she leaves Ocarina of Time and Twilight Princess permanently paused before the final Ganon fight because the meaning lies in the process of becoming, not the ending. Sartre's existence precedes essence structures Link's growth from a swordless Kokiri boy collecting equipment into the hero; Nietzsche's death of God ('we must become gods') fits Link restoring meaning to a godless Hyrule, while Camus's Sisyphus dignifies the repetitive drudge work of slashing grass for rupees. Viktor Frankl's logotherapy anchors the chapter's payoff: even the most mundane tasks — in a camp or a laundromat or Hyrule Field — become bearable and meaningful when connected to a future goal, which is why the author can play for four hours straight.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Kohoutek tests Max against two models of heroism: Joseph Campbell's 'hero with a thousand faces' and Camus's absurd hero from The Myth of Sisyphus. Max never completes the Campbellian cycle — no apotheosis, no decisive victory, no return and reintegration — because the refinery tribe and the Waiting Ones mythologize him from outside (as Messiah, as Captain Walker) while he himself returns each film to the same desert. Like Sisyphus, for whom 'the whole being is exerted toward accomplishing nothing,' Max helps people build pockets of civilization he is always shut out of, making his heroism absurd rather than archetypal.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 32 "Getting the Joke" — Gray reads Jack Handey's Deep Thoughts and Fuzzy Memories as packaged existentialism: Sartre's existence precedes essence grounds Handey's responsibility for self-made meaning ('if you're robbing a bank and your pants fall down... life is funny'), Camus's absurd and Sisyphus's happy perseverance match 'sometimes I think the world has gone completely mad. And then I think, Aw, who cares?', and Beauvoir's ruts of inferiority warn against the ease of 'just sitting there' wanting money. Heidegger's authenticity and mortality appear in the parachute-swimming gag, dying laughing rather than in dread. The chapter also explains why the deadpan delivery over serene stream imagery makes morbidity funny, and worries that Handey's 'truth is... unreal' anticipated post-truth politics.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 23 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Rachel Robison-Greene applies Camus's absurdity to the series: walkers, like digger wasps, live meaningless loops without the self-reflective consciousness that 'poisons' experience, while survivors like Morgan longing for Jenny and Andrea for fishing trips with her father embody the clash between human longing and an indifferent universe, exactly as in Camus's The Plague at Oran. Suicide (Jacqui and Jenner as the CDC explodes) and religious consolation are escapist responses—the latter 'philosophical suicide'—so the authentic path is the absurd hero: Rick searching Atlanta for his family, Daryl fighting uphill with an arrow in his side, the Vatos group caring for abandoned elders. Weighing Nagel's objection that absurdity arises from our clashing subjective and objective perspectives, she concludes we cheer Rick shooting Sophia in the barn because subjective commitment stays noble even where objective meaning is nowhere to be found.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete.
