Following Kathryn Tanner's rejoinder that consumers can creatively repurpose pop culture, he shows Wade Wilson's self-mocking, fourth-wall-breaking humor achieving personal liberation from tragedy (invoking Freud on humor as the ego's assertion of invulnerability), liberation from the oppressive Mutant Factory by exposing Ajax/Francis's vulnerability and asserting his own autonomy, and a partial liberation from superhero genre tropes, while conceding humor's reactionary tendency to reinforce the status quo since Deadpool ultimately reproduces the genre and hands Disney its money.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 84 "79. Cyberpunk 2077 as Philosophy Balancing the (Mystical) Ghost in the (Transhuman) Machine" — Lay reads Cyberpunk 2077's transhuman Night City against the enhancement debate. Using the Ship of Theseus, Parfit's continuity plus fission/fusion (V and Johnny 'fusing,' the Delamain AIs) and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind, he argues enhancement neither destroys personal identity (which Parfit says doesn't matter) nor dehumanizes users — it may be the purest expression of Clark's cyborg humanity. The real danger is corporate exploitation of bodies, explained via Adorno's culture industry and Arendt's banality of evil. Buddhist nonattachment (Nagarjuna's emptiness, echoed by a Schopenhauer shard) grounds each ending's pacification-versus-attachment theme, but Lay corrects it with Weil's critique of power and Buber's I-Thou, concluding the game urges transcending the boundary between 'me' and 'you' through mystical interpersonal relation.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 7 "Welcome Aboard the TARDIS—It’s Bigger on the Inside" — The author argues that Doctor Who functions as a 'great educator' that shapes viewers' reality and their conception of the good life, framing our birth into the world as being 'thrown' into a new environment we must assimilate. He applies Hegel's historical dialectic to the Doctor-versus-Daleks conflict, treating the Doctor (wisdom, liberty, compassion) and the Daleks (obedience, hatred, conquest) as opposing theses whose ongoing struggle synthesizes the wider universe's fear of the Daleks. Drawing on Carroll and Danesi, he claims pop culture like Doctor Who validates experience and creates collective structures of meaning, and that our chosen first Doctor becomes the interpretive framework through which we judge every later one.

### One-Dimensional Man

In One-Dimensional Man, Herbert Marcuse argued that advanced industrial society pacifies and absorbs dissent by satisfying material desires and manufacturing new ones through consumption and technology. The "one-dimensional" person is one whose critical, oppositional, and imaginative capacities have been flattened, so that thought and behavior no longer reach beyond the existing system to envision genuine alternatives. Even apparent freedoms and comforts, Marcuse suggested, serve to integrate individuals more deeply into the status quo. A member of the Frankfurt School, he offered the book as a critique of how affluent capitalism neutralizes radical possibility.

- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 11 "Forgetting the Love We Bring" — John Drabinski argues that the Deadhead parking lot is an 'occasional community' offering real hope against modernity's managed, one-dimensional life. Starting from his own Amherst-to-Worcester commuter routine read through Wittgenstein's forms of life — a community of nodding strangers at the same mini-marts — he stages Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man and Bauman's managed death as the deadening background against which such moments crack open. Where the commuter's community stays merely occasional, the parking lot's saturated friendship and shared undergoing (com-passion, good trip and bad, frat guy comforting and comforted) converts occasion into a genuine alternative ethos, drawing on Heidegger's sense of ethos as dwelling place — an everyday miracle of conversion he says we need now more than ever.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 12 "Springsteen’s Revolution" — Anderson and Anderson open with the Che Guevara t-shirt problem and Marcuse's one-dimensional man: the system assimilates protest, so internal critique (Springsteen on the cover of Rolling Stone, its Chevrolet calendar, the Eagles sold at Wal-Mart, Adorno's verdict on co-opted popular music) is a sop to Cerberus. Against this they set Springsteen's own account of his music as 'a very long conversation with my audience' — a transactional public service — and argue he survives the co-optation charge as a 'Socratic revolutionary' who, like Socrates refusing to leave Athens, works from within: listening without obeying ('I liked the old Bruce better'), refusing to ride the Born to Run wave, turning to Guthrie and Seeger, and drawing no hard conclusions, only opening spaces of reflection ('Born in the U.S.A.', 'Radio Nowhere', 'Long Walk Home'). Revolution is just another form of work — practice, sweat, and the personal job of 'growin' up.'
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 7 "Where Pink Floyd Ends and Radiohead Begins" — Reisch asks whether Radiohead is the Pink Floyd of the twenty-first century and answers that the comparison misleads: where Barrett-era Floyd used electronics to escape into psychedelic fantasy, Radiohead's apparent space-rock is phenomenological, giving voice to pre-reflective experience of technological modern life. He reads 'No Surprises' (Yorke singing with his head in a filling glass sphere) as a study in the political infantilization of commuters, and OK Computer's car crash ('Airbag'), 'Let Down', and 'Lucky' as registering the feel of a fragile, technology-saturated world. Quoting Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man and Chomsky on manufactured consent, he argues we can see no alternative to the technologically rational system, and then, against Descartes' priority of the isolated 'I', invokes Heidegger's Being-in-the-world and Merleau-Ponty's embodied subject to suggest that our deepening immersion in technology may be changing the self itself — the truth the collapsing pedestrians of the 'Just' video cannot face.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 17 "But Does Political Satire Promote Democratic Values" — Michael Tiboris and Kory Schaff answer their title question affirmatively: Colbert's satire promotes democratic values by practicing Foucault's parrhesia - fearless speech that speaks the truth freely, functions as criticism of interlocutor and self, and flows from moral duty - unlike bumper-sticker assertion, since it enters risky dialogue and invites being refuted. Against this stands a corporate-consolidated media ('monopoly of meaning' from GE, Viacom, News Corp, Time-Warner) whose framing, slanting, and spinning - McCain's 'transcendental' war, the Obama-dresses-like-Ahmadinejad story, WMD as Word of the Year - exemplify Marcuse's one-dimensional thought absorbing oppositional language ('clean bomb,' 'harmless fall-out'). The WØRD models parrhesiastic critique by speaking media's own language while the bullet points undercut it ('Definitions will greet us as liberators'), exposing how politicians and pundits merely appear truthful and teaching viewers their own duty of critical assessment.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 11 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter argues coal made Boyd Crowder possible: company scrip, Bloody Harlan's union-busting terror, black lung (Boyd's would-be assassin takes the bridge job because mining ruined his lungs), and Black Pike's mountaintop removal leave Harlan no viable work outside the mines, so crime is the rational alternative. It reads this through Hegel's 'rabble' from the Philosophy of Right - civil society is never wealthy enough to prevent an excess of poverty, and the rabble loses the honor of self-support - plus Marcuse's affluent-society critique of an existence that 'violently defends its own servitude'. Boyd's outlawry, which sets its own code above mere criminality, is a rebellion against being pushed into the rabble, and Hegel's remedy of emigration explains why leaving Harlan is the only escape, though the coal train hauls coal out while the people stay.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 12 "3. The Only Chapter in This Book You Need to Read!" — Writing as two bickering versions of himself from different universes, Karavitis reads Deadpool Kills Deadpool as showing that the multiverse of Deadpools is the delusion of a single narcissist: the alternate 'Pools' are mirror-image projections of himself (Lacan's mirror stage), his self-love is Rousseau's pathological amour propre rather than healthy amour de soi, and his claim to be the progenitor of all reality is solipsism—hence there is no fourth wall. Freud, Fromm, and Marcuse supply rival diagnoses of that narcissism, from arrested development to proto-fascist willfulness to authentic rebellion against social control through unconscious conformity. A closing twist argues philosophers who claim sole access to truth are the same solipsistic narcissists, which would make Socrates, who never claimed a final answer, the only true philosopher.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 13 "Resistance" — Reading Fifteen Million Merits through Marx, the chapter treats Bing's world of endless pedaling, Wraith Babes, and Hot Shot as a commodity society in which people themselves carry use and exchange values — Oliver the 'lemon,' Glee deemed 'quite worthless,' Abi's unsellable papier-mache penguin discarded as detritus. Marx's commodity fetish explains the universalized pricing in merits, and Lukacs-style reification shows things commanding people (Cuppliance compelling compliance). Adorno's culture industry explains why all the shows share one form and why Bing's glass-shard rebellion is absorbed as just another commodity, while Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man supplies the hope that reason, love (Bing's love for Abi as something 'real'), and switching off the media can still seed resistance.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 38 "Things Worth Believing" — Butterfield stages the Frankfurt School critique of her own Disney love: Marx's three alienations (from work, from others, from species-being) explain the Seven Dwarfs' 'dig dig dig' and the FastPass-scheduled vacation that converts leisure into consumption, while Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man diagnoses the parks' engineered euphoria and 'false needs' as a 'comfortable, smooth, reasonable, democratic unfreedom' that blunts protest — with Adorno adding that consumers see through the advertising and buy anyway. Against the critic, she argues a Disney trip done right can challenge alienation by reviving play, family togetherness, and childlike belief in 'things worth believing.'
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 16 "Television and Existential Awakening" — Jaarsma argues Mad Men dramatizes an existential rather than Kantian-enlightenment model of advertising: Don's 'freedom from fear' pitch ('Whatever you are doing is okay. You are okay') sells escape from the anxiety of real choice, which is precisely Sartrean bad faith and what de Beauvoir calls the stagnant 'happiness' of women rewarded for being the other. Betty on her psychiatrist's couch, Peggy measured by Joan's paper-bag mirror and the Playtex bullet-bra silhouette, and the closeted Salvatore all internalize the dominant values Marcuse describes, finding meaning in conformity to the objectifying gaze ('bras are for men; women want to see themselves the way men see them'). Rachel Menken, who refuses to 'put on an apron' and calls out the contingency of gendered embodiment, models authenticity as choosing to choose, and the chapter closes with the hope that television itself can occasion the viewer's existential awakening.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 24 "Indiscernibles and Autonomous Viewers “Time to Write my Own Fucking Story”" — Forest and Beckley-Forest ask whether Westworld is self-referential 'high art' or 'meta-kitsch,' tracing aesthetic modernism from Kant's subjective turn through Greenberg's avant-garde/kitsch split and Adorno's autonomous versus heteronomous art. They read Sizemore's clichéd Western narratives and the park's stock characters as commodified kitsch that mirrors the show's own corporate constraints under HBO, and use Danto's Brillo Box problem of indiscernibles to argue that host/guest and entertainment/art distinctions lie in the viewer's reflection. Dolores's line 'when I discover who I am, I'll be free' models the Adorno-style liberation available to an alert viewer.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Zietsma reads Hulk and Taking Woodstock as antiwar films that subvert the hegemonic culture of heroic violence, fitting Lackey's category of universal (Gandhian/early-Christian) pacifism. He argues both films disturb their genre's expected narrative and demasculinize the hero: Elliot the gay nonviolent hero and the transgender vet Vilma, and a weeping Hulk who is rescued by Betty and finally gives up his power rather than kill David Banner. He reads the bathroom-mirror 'Puny human' scene as an inverted Lacanian mirror stage unmasking America's violent militarism, framing the Vietnam War and war on terror as violence that only begets more violence.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 27 "William Burroughs as Philosopher From Beat Morality to Third Worldism to Continental Theory" — Jones Irwin makes the case for 'Burroughs as philosopher,' tracing an 'impassioned moralism' and antihumanism (human as adjective, not noun) that separates him from other Beats and postmodernists. He links Burroughs's critique of alienation to Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man and to Sartrean existentialism and bad faith ('there are no victims, just accomplices'), and reads the Beats' 'third force' Third Worldism via Freire, Fanon's Wretched of the Earth, and Paz. Close readings of Naked Lunch's 'Bradley the Buyer' and the sex-and-death delirium of 'AJ's Annual Party' connect Burroughs to Artaud's body without organs, Bataille's Sadean tradition, and Derrida's deconstruction of embodiment and 'distance touching.'
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 20 "The Politics of Mad Science in The Fly and Dead Ringers" — R. Barton Palmer reads The Fly and Dead Ringers as a diptych on 'mad science' descended from Stevenson's Jekyll and Hyde rather than Frankenstein, in which the scientist turns the investigative gaze on himself and self-destructs. He grounds this in the Frankfurt School critique of Enlightenment (Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment, Bacon's domination of nature, Marcuse's Eros and Civilization): Brundle's telepod and the Mantle twins' surgery expose the failure of Baconian objectivity and rationalization, with monstrousness emerging from within the divided self.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 21 "From “Impassioned Morality” to “Bloodless Agnosticism” A Philosophy of David Cronenberg through the Burroughs" — Jones Irwin analyzes Cronenberg's adaptations of Burroughs's Naked Lunch and Ballard's Crash, arguing that while all three share an aesthetic of body horror and a Nietzschean perspectivist experimentalism, Burroughs and Ballard hold an 'impassioned moralism' (Crash as cautionary tale, Marcuse's one-dimensional man, an ethics of complicity and responsibility) that Cronenberg replaces with 'bloodless agnosticism.' Cronenberg aestheticizes Burroughs's wife-killing and reads Crash literally, using Plato's appearance/reality (cave) distinction to show he strips out the sociopolitical and moral frame the writers intended.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 9 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Gerald Erion reads The Daily Show through Neil Postman's Amusing Ourselves to Death, arguing that Stewart's opening headline mockery of hurricane 'reporters in canoes,' 'Senior Correspondents,' and graphics packages like 'Mess O'Potamia' targets not the day's events but television's own entertainment bias, which renders even serious news trivial. He treats Stewart's Crossfire plea to 'stop hurting America,' the Jim Cramer 'Brawl Street' interview, and the Rally to Restore Sanity's '24-hour politico pundit perpetual panic conflictinator' as Postman-style critiques that a medium built to amuse cannot carry rational public discourse.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 32 "19. Looking Like Number 12" — Busk reads 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' through Horkheimer and Adorno's 'culture industry' and a philosophical account of subjectivity as active, critical agency. Marilyn's forced 'Transformation' into a standardized model (with banned books, 'Instant Smile,' and 'super soccer') dramatizes how commodified mass culture produces conformist, mannequin-like subjects who cannot resist—linking it to 'The After Hours,' where Marsha is literally a department-store mannequin. Yet Marilyn's and Marsha's very existence, like Adorno's theory, is a faint hopeful sign that critical subjectivity survives.

Following Kathryn Tanner's rejoinder that consumers can creatively repurpose pop culture, he shows Wade Wilson's self-mocking, fourth-wall-breaking humor achieving personal liberation from tragedy (invoking Freud on humor as the ego's assertion of invulnerability), liberation from the oppressive Mutant Factory by exposing Ajax/Francis's vulnerability and asserting his own autonomy, and a partial liberation from superhero genre tropes, while conceding humor's reactionary tendency to reinforce the status quo since Deadpool ultimately reproduces the genre and hands Disney its money.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 71 "67. Hari Kondabolu as Philosopher Enacting a Philosophy of Liberation" — Heppard frames Kondabolu—who resists the 'political comic' label—as enacting Enrique Dussel's 'philosophy of liberation' and Marcuse's aesthetics of liberation: comedy as 'barbarian philosophy' spoken from the periphery. Kondabolu's Swiftian 'eat the rich' health-care proposal, his 'White Chocolate Joke,' 'Feminist Dick Joke,' Columbus/Joe DiMaggio bit, and Bobby Jindal takedown rupture the audience's identification with white supremacy, patriarchy, and liberal hypocrisy (negative freedom) while his absurd alternatives exercise the 'radical imagination' (positive freedom). Heppard concludes that although comedians are not revolutionaries, the revolution must be funny.

### The Idols of the Mind

The Idols of the Mind are Francis Bacon's classification, set out in his Novum Organum (1620), of the systematic errors that distort human understanding and obstruct genuine knowledge of nature. He named four: the Idols of the Tribe, rooted in human nature itself; the Idols of the Cave, arising from an individual's particular temperament and upbringing; the Idols of the Marketplace, caused by the ambiguities and misuse of language; and the Idols of the Theater, inherited uncritically from received philosophies and dogmas. Bacon urged that recognizing and purging these idols was a necessary preparation for his new inductive, experimental method.

- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 20 "The Politics of Mad Science in The Fly and Dead Ringers" — R. Barton Palmer reads The Fly and Dead Ringers as a diptych on 'mad science' descended from Stevenson's Jekyll and Hyde rather than Frankenstein, in which the scientist turns the investigative gaze on himself and self-destructs. He grounds this in the Frankfurt School critique of Enlightenment (Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment, Bacon's domination of nature, Marcuse's Eros and Civilization): Brundle's telepod and the Mantle twins' surgery expose the failure of Baconian objectivity and rationalization, with monstrousness emerging from within the divided self.

### The Problem of Evil

The problem of evil is the challenge of reconciling the existence of a God who is all-powerful, all-knowing, and wholly good with the reality of suffering and wrongdoing in the world. In its logical form it alleges an outright contradiction between such a God and any evil at all, while its evidential form argues that the sheer amount and distribution of suffering makes God's existence unlikely. Responses, known as theodicies, appeal to free will, soul-making, or the limits of human understanding to explain why a good God might permit evil.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 26 "Against Fascism" — Neal King argues the Buffyverse is proto-fascist: Buffy kills demons and vampires on sight within a race-like hierarchy, tempered only by an Augustinian split between natural and moral evil (soulless vampires cannot choose otherwise; soul-bearing humans like Faith, Willow, and Warren can repent), she derives authority from an ancient calling rather than democracy, and the graduation battle of 'Graduation Day, Part Two' stages citizenship forged in mass combat. He imagines a fascist Buffyverse of 'brownskirt' death squads and concludes only the show's secrecy prevents full fascism, finally recommending that the racism be dropped but the ritual sacrifice of evildoers kept — with Willow's flaying of Warren as the model.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 29 "No Big Win" — Reads sacrifice, salvation, and redemption in the Buffyverse as secular myth: vampires manifest the shadow-side of the human (Liam's resentment becomes Angelus, William's repressed romanticism becomes Spike's rebellion), and the contrast between soulless Spike's genuine moral growth through love of Buffy and human Xander's arrested development shows redemption is measured by 'what have you done with what you've been given.' The Purpose of Evil section argues good and evil must stay in balance because without evil there is no free choice and hence no redemption, and Angel's 'no big win' epiphany — no grand plan, only lessening suffering one kindness at a time — locates life's meaning in the journey of becoming rather than final victory.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 21 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Scott Davison asks whether Tolkien's world is Manichean - two equal forces of Good and Evil - and answers no: the Ring is not 'altogether evil' in itself but animated by Sauron's infused will, and nothing, not even Sauron, is totally evil, since 'nothing is evil in the beginning'. Developing Augustine's account, he shows evil as parasitic privation - Ringwraiths wear robes 'to give shape to their nothingness', the Eye is 'a window into nothing' - and traces evil to inordinate desire: Sam stays content with his garden while Boromir, Saruman, Denethor, and Sauron reach for more than their place allows. Evil unmakes itself (Saruman dies by Wormtongue's knife), and because goodness is the world's default, there is always hope of overcoming it.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 28 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Thomas Hibbs reads the Quest's ending as providential: the Ring is destroyed against Frodo's own will at the Cracks of Doom, through Gollum, exactly as Gandalf hinted when he said Bilbo was 'meant' to find the Ring, 'and not by its maker'. Providence first appears as chance - Bilbo's arrival, Aragorn's landing at the Pelennor, Gandalf 'sent back' until his task is done - and is discerned only in hindsight as the epic's dramatic unity. Against the worry that providence cancels freedom, he uses Kant on duty and dignity (Frodo's 'I will take the Ring', Sam's 'I must see it through', set against Denethor ruling his 'own end'), while noting Tolkien rejects Kant's autonomy/heteronomy split, and with Augustine he treats evil as parasitic, able only to mar itself ('Oft evil will shall evil mar').
- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 33 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Uses the show to argue the problem of evil is evidential rather than logical, and tests each theodicy against Sopranos cases: evil as natural-law by-product (Junior's and Jackie's cancers), punishment for sin (Carmela's cancer scare, Ralph telling Father Phil his hospitalized son is God's payback in 'Whoever Did This'), God's higher morality (rejected as meaningless as 'a triangle with four sides'), long-run goods (Artie's restaurant fire), and character-building (rejected with Melfi's 'How many people have to die for your personal growth?'). The free-will defense also fails - God could have given us Meadow-like dispositions - and Tony's 'You're born to this shit' versus Melfi's insistence on genuine choice dramatizes the debate. The chapter ends with Tony as the Old Testament Yahweh writ small: a jealous, vengeful, tribal ruler whose appeal is no more mysterious than His.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 12 "From Knowledge to Faith" — Lawler reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Kant's problem of the Highest Good: Judah's unpunished murder of Dolores shows a world where the wicked prosper and the good (Cliff, the blind Ben) suffer, the scandal Job complains of, while Levy's suicide shows that a bare existentialist 'yes' to life fails without love. Kant's 'I had to deny knowledge to make room for faith' is applied to the film's two visions: the deterministic, dog-eat-dog world of science and Adam Smith's economic egoism (with Hobbes's war of all against all) is only appearance, not reality. Kant's gallows example shows Judah could have discovered authentic freedom by respecting Dolores's dignity rather than seeing 'the black eyes of an insect', and the postulates of freedom, God, and immortality ground Ben's not-really-blind faith — so it is Judah who is truly blind.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 24 "The End Is It All Darkness" — John Pappas reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Glaucon's ring of Gyges in Plato's Republic: Judah Rosenthal's wealth and prestige are his invisibility ring, and when his mistress Dolores threatens exposure he 'pushes the button', has his gangster brother Jack murder her, and gets away with it. Against Socrates' claim that injustice corrodes the harmonious soul and that virtue is its own reward, the film, unlike Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment, lets the murderer and the 'yutz' Lester prosper while honest Clifford loses everything; Bergson's theory of the comic explains why Lester is invisible to himself, and Rousseau's reverie about what he would do with the ring marks Clifford as the one man who might use it decently. Aunt May's post-Holocaust atheism, 'might makes right' with nothing 'handed down in stone', supplies the argument from evil that releases Judah, leaving only the qualified hope that it is 'not all darkness'.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 26 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Dallas Willard defends the film's excess of violence as its whole point: it visualizes human evil as beyond the remedies of education, law, or counseling (the route Plato and Aristotle tried), with Satan — the androgynous figure carrying the smug dwarf through the scourging crowd — explaining why only Christ's non-resistant embrace of the cross can break evil's grip. Against the passive reading of 'the Passion,' he argues Jesus 'played' his judges, deliberately laying down his life to inaugurate the kingdom of God. The argument leans on the hidden God (deus absconditus): God stays hidden, contra Sartre's 'no nature' self-creation and closer to Pico della Mirandola, so that we can freely make ourselves, which is also why demanding 'more evidence' misses what belief in God requires.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 29 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Paul Moser answers the objection that an all-loving God could not plan His Son's torture by arguing the cross is God's scandalous self-giving love: Jesus is no mere moral guru but the unique atoning sacrifice (the mad/Satanic/Son-of-God trilemma, 'he who delivered me to you has the greater sin'), and the crucifixion is God's grand reversal where self-giving love defeats death. He attacks the 'nice god' of natural theology as domesticating idolatry — God hides His plans from 'the wise and the intelligent' — and holds that we know God not by philosophical evidence but through Gethsemane-style filial obedience ('not my will but yours'), noting that Gibson himself appears in the film driving a nail, casting all of us as the crucifiers whom God forgives.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 15 "The Fate of Evil after the Overthrow of the Empire" — Brown treats Luke's 'Is the Dark Side stronger?' as the problem of evil: distinguishing natural evils (the wampa, bigger fish) from moral evils (Tarkin destroying Alderaan), he surveys the Platonic craftsman working recalcitrant matter and the Manichean dualism of two gods - the Emperor as would-be 'evil incarnate' - before giving Augustine's answer. On Augustine's free-will defense, no creature is inherently evil; the origin of each moral evil is the creature's own pride and free choice, so Anakin, not the Emperor's seduction, is responsible for his turn ('I'm a Jedi. I know I'm better than this'). The chapter ends on whether evil can ever be finally defeated, arguing the Jedi prophecies of 'balance' fit a world where evil is a permanent possibility that heroism needs.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 32 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Frames the problem of pain with Hume's Dialogues (Demea and Philo) and reconstructs Lewis's answer as played out on Aslan: pain is God's megaphone that rouses Edmund on the Witch's frozen sledge and strips Eustace's dragon skin in the transforming embrace. Suffering also reveals hidden strengths, as when Aslan's pursuit goads Shasta into unexpected courage, modeled on Augustine's reading of the binding of Isaac as teaching Abraham, not God, what Abraham could endure. Aravis's claw wounds are treated as retributive punishment, tear for tear, exactly proportioned to the drugged slave's whipping, which the chapter defends via Lewis's retributivist theory against purely deterrent punishment. Because divine goodness aims at making creatures good rather than merely happy, Aslan can be both good and terrible, 'not a tame lion', since free will cannot be coerced into perfection.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 36 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Observes that only Talking Animals enter Aslan's country when Narnia ends in The Last Battle, then critically examines Lewis's case against wider animal salvation: derivative immortality through human love (Sarah Smith's train of beasts in The Great Divorce), compensation of animal pain in an afterlife, Lewis's follow-Descartes claim that most animals are sentient but not conscious enough to feel pain or have a surviving 'self'. The chapter argues each point fails: the physiological evidence shows animals suffer, resurrection or God-given souls remain possible (Strawberry's transformation into a winged Talking horse), and a compensatory hereafter is still the most promising answer to why a loving God permits the fawn's miserable death. Aquinas's rational-creature hierarchy frames the Talking/Dumb divide, and the Hindu-Buddhist rebirth theodicy is considered and rejected as unbiblical.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 17 "Prayer (A Euphemism for Butt-Kissing and Begging)" — Argues the Pythons' religious gags perform philosophy's preliminary job of challenging doctrine: the 'every sperm is sacred' family makes God a voyeur of contraception, the Life of Brian stoning (rocks flying each time anyone utters 'Jehovah') shows blasphemy law run absurd, and 'Christmas in Heaven' exposes heavenly reward as material compensation. Deploying Socrates and Plato — the Republic's ban on portraying pettiful gods, the Apology on why the virtuous need not fear death, and above all the Euthyphro — the chapter reads the witch-weighing and the Holy Hand Grenade as the ancient problem whether acts are just because God sanctions them, and the chaplain's toadying prayer against God's own 'don't grovel' as proof that sacrifice and prayer are bargaining a perfect being has no need of. The upshot is not atheism but the Socratic verdict that the mobs punishing blasphemy, not the mocked, are the real blasphemers.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 8 "U2 and Philosophy" — Wrathall's introduction argues U2 is philosophically interesting because its enormous popularity holds up a mirror to what 'we' care about (by Nietzsche's test of how a culture stands toward life) and because the band publicly wrestles with the contradictions of the technological-global economy: unprecedented freedom of choice paired with loss of rooted identity, and distant suffering ('Crumbs from Your Table') that we feel both powerless to fix and responsible for. Its showcase reading treats 'Miracle Drug' as a musical theodicy: Bono's plea 'God, I need your help tonight' is answered by the Edge's guitar and by the Matthew 25:35 refrain, so science and medicine count as works of Christian charity. The piece then frames the volume's essays: Plato's ascent of love in the early songs, Kierkegaardian despair after Achtung Baby, Bono's search for authentic identity, the simulacra of 'Even Better than the Real Thing', being-toward-death in the apocalyptic songs, and the Plato-versus-Aristotle quarrel over music's emotional power.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 17 "U2 and Philosophy" — Merrick sets XTC's 'Dear God' - being 'just struck' that no loving, all-powerful God rules this world - against U2's laments ('Wake Up Dead Man', 'Peace on Earth', '40') and Bono's reading of the Psalms as the blues shouted at God: both share outrage, but U2 adds yearning for the redemption promised in 'the story about eternity' plus Jubilee 2000-style action against debt and AIDS. He then argues the atheistic reaction to evil cannot be reason-producing, since neither divine design nor unguided evolution would give us a faculty that 'just sees' atheism from evil, any more than one that just sees there is no plant life on Mars. If God instead made us so that outrage at evil can trigger conviction that he will make all right, U2's reaction - 'Grace makes beauty out of ugly things' - can be as reasonable as visual perception.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 21 "Introduction" — Frames Part IV's philosophy of religion chapters. Johnson's chapter sets Cartman's million-dollar theme park against God's goodness, with South Park characters giving answers echoing Calvin, Hick, and Job; Gallagher's uses Rose's 'I just know' on Lost and Aquinas' distinctions between knowledge, opinion, and faith to argue that faith is not knowledge; and Eberl and Vines' uses Battlestar Galactica's Cylon monotheism versus Colonial religion and atheism to ask whether God can be proven, whether evil disproves him, and whether life is meaningful without God.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 22 "Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy" — Johnson turns 'Cartmanland' into a survey of answers to the problem of evil: Kyle's hemorrhoid-versus-Cartman's-wealth argument is the logical problem of moral evil; the story of Job fails because Job's continued belief does not rebut the evidence; Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' mirrors Calvin's and Edwards' God-glorifying answer; and Stan's 'Cartman is totally miserable' restores Kyle's faith via second-order goods. The free will defense (via Augustine) handles moral evil but not natural evil, so the chapter closes with John Hick's soul-making theodicy — mirrored by South Park's Jesus saying life is about overcoming problems and growing — before conceding the evidential problem of evil still stands.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 24 "“You Have to Believe in Something”" — Eberl and Vines use Battlestar Galactica to weigh theism against atheism: Baltar's scientific rationalism meets Aquinas' five ways (the universe's ordered structure demands an unmoved, uncaused cause), Six's faith faces the problem of evil answered through Augustine on the perverse will and John Hick's soul-making (Starbuck's mother, 'your life is a testament to pain'), while Hume's faulty-architect analogy presses the atheist case. The chapter concludes with Russell's 'A Free Man's Worship': even in a Godless universe the Colonials find meaning in comradeship and humanity's survival — 'the gods shall lift those who lift each other.'
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 12 "A Proper Answer" — Tallon takes Psycho as a case study in the problem of evil: after Hume's Epicurean challenge, Marion's shower murder and Norman's shattered psyche exemplify Marilyn McCord Adams's 'horrendous evils,' whose grotesque disproportion between any crime and its fate threatens to destroy the positive meaning of a life. The free will defense (Plantinga, Augustine) fails because Marion's death is bad luck rather than punished choice, and Hick's soul-making theodicy fails because evil here shatters character rather than building it. Carroll's definition of monsters is revised so that monsters are beings of severe disorder and disproportion, which Norman, Dracula, and Hitler all display, and Swinburne's Principle of Honesty offers the closest answer: God allows horrors because systematically preventing them would deceive us about the truth that evil is the privation of proper order, inherently grotesque and disordered.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 19 "Encore" — Randall Auxier adopts 'I trust Phil' — Phil Lesh the bass player who hears the whole sound — as his epistemic principle for asking whether death is to be dreaded, staging the essay around interview riffs with Deadheads Dale, Robbie, and Cory. Socrates in the Phaedo and the Buddha's Four Noble Truths converge on welcoming death — samsara is the 'Samsonite Scenario', bad luggage your own wishing keeps repacking — while Hume's Dialogues make God's power, goodness, and evil an inconsistent triad, so immortality is 'not that cool'. Kant's postulates (God, freedom, immortality) and categorical imperative prove too rule-bound for creative life; Whitehead's self-creativity and 'objective immortality of the past' supply the real bass line: even God cannot unmake what you have played, and the properly Grateful response is gratitude for the chance to add your riff to the Acid Test.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 6 "Introduction" — The editors' introduction opens with Socrates on trial for corrupting the youth of Athens and quips that on stage before the youth of Athens, Georgia, Cash could claim he was only asking "What is truth?" It frames Cash as Kris Kristofferson's "walking contradiction" whose paradoxes generate the book's questions: how evil fits a world rated by a benevolent God, where the enduring "I" hides while Cash insisted he was always changing, and what makes a law unjust. It also presents the Man in Black as social critic lobbying officials at San Quentin and Folsom for prison reform and raising money for reservation schools, before welcoming readers with the 1969 Arthur, Illinois concert where hippies and Amish rubbed shoulders.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 27 "Redemption" — Stephen Bilynskyj tests John Hick's soul-making theodicy—that God allows suffering because virtues like courage, temperance, and compassion need pain to form—against Cash's life and songs. Using Aristotle on habituation by pleasure and pain (Cash's first amphetamine euphoria and the ostrich-attack painkillers as missed occasions for temperance) and Aquinas on innate aptitude and divinely infused virtue, he argues virtue can form without suffering (by genes or miracle), so soul-making alone cannot justify evil, as Cash himself implies about his mother's grief after Jack's death. Cash instead locates redemption in Christ's suffering ('Redemption,' 'Why Me, Lord?'), while the intervention by his son John Carter shows pain still occasioning real growth in temperance.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 28 "“A Boy Named Sue” A Cashian Theodicy" — Jamie Carlin Watson reads Cash's Christian worldview as Augustinian: evil is not a positive substance but a privation or corruption of good (contra the monism Leibniz risks and the Manichean dualism Augustine rejected), so humans alone bear blame for moral evil through freely corrupting good things—'Cocaine Blues,' 'The Wall,' the Folsom prisoner who admits he 'had it coming,' and the divided self of 'The Beast in Me' echoing Romans 7. Natural evil, as in 'Guess Things Happen That Way' and the flood of 'Five Feet High and Rising' (Cash's mother's 'blessing' of rich river dirt), serves punishment or greater goods. 'A Boy Named Sue' dramatizes the residual tension: the father's get-tough-or-die theodicy convinces neither Sue nor us that the sheer amount of evil is justified.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 29 "Christmas in Jamaica" — David Werther frames Jack Cash's saw death—which Cash told Nick Tosches he considered murder—and the 1982 armed robbery at Cinnamon Hill as tests of Epicurus's old questions (quoted via Hume): could a good, powerful God have prevented these evils? Distinguishing the evidential from the logical problem, he answers the logical problem with Plantinga's libertarian free will: not even God could ensure Cash freely 'walked the line' with Vivian, since guaranteeing fidelity would eliminate freedom. He rebuts the compatibilist counterobjection by arguing, with Aquinas, that nothing can be the cause of its own nature, and argues heaven can still fulfill Johnny and June's hope of meeting 'on the far side banks of the Jordan' even if the redeemed can no longer act wrongly.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 23 "Moments of Redemption" — Ventimiglia sets Augustine's three answers to the problem of evil (free will, the toddler-at-the-doctor 'greater good,' evil as privation) against Nebraska's title track, where mass murderer Charlie Starkweather's 'I guess there's just a meanness in this world' makes Augustine's metaphysical gymnastics look like sophistry. 'Atlantic City' and 'Johnny 99' show free will compromised by debts, job loss and winners-and-losers, and Springsteen neither glorifies nor explains evil away. What Bruce and Augustine share is the yearning for redemption: Plato's Symposium pictures Eros — poor, barefoot, homeless, a hunger for the beautiful — and Springsteen answers that hunger with temporary moments of deliverance ('meet me tonight in Atlantic City') rather than guaranteed salvation.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 21 "Death on Veridian III" — Uses the holodeck to re-run the problem of evil: if a safe, painless simulated world like Barclay's fantasy life in 'Hollow Pursuits' is available, why is the painful real one better? Against Hume's Dialogues complaint that a benevolent God should have cut the pain, and Leibniz's best-of-all-possible-worlds optimism, the authors stack Whitehead's 'major beauty' of intensity, Aristotle's tragic magnitude, Swinburne's good of serious responsibility, and Hick's soul-making, reading Moriarty's imprisonment in 'Ship in a Bottle,' Q's humbling in 'Déjà Q,' and Kirk leaving the Nexus because 'nothing here matters' as evidence that intensity, responsibility, and character growth exist only in the real world. Kirk's death on Veridian III in Generations supplies the cautionary counterweight: the real world's goods cost real suffering.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 34 "Rescuing Princess Zelda" — Collins runs the problem of evil in Hyrule: Mackie's logical problem (an all-good, all-powerful God inconsistent with Ganondorf's evil) partially dissolves because nothing in the games says the three goddesses are omnipotent or omniscient, and Plantinga's free will defense, plus the best-of-all-possible-worlds idea, shows the Triforce is itself a free-will device, since a wish-granter that could grant any desire cannot limit evil without undoing itself. A 'game-making theodicy' modeled on Hick's soul-making theodicy explains why evil must be excessive and randomly distributed (else players would never strive to grow), and why the goddesses therefore provided a chosen hero: Link, unlike anyone on Earth, is the divine answer to excessive evil, divinely marked to reclaim the Triforce and rescue Zelda.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 19 "Roll Credits" — Dunn contrasts Baum's book, where evil is wonderfully 'small'—Dorothy melts the Witch in a fit of righteous anger at a stolen Silver Shoe, and personal plus social virtues (kindness repaid by the field-mice Queen) reliably conquer it—with the 1939 film, which smuggles back the 'heartaches and nightmares' Baum banished and resolves the Witch only by an accidental stroke of luck. He sorts Oz's harms into moral evils (the Witch's enslavements, the Wizard's frauds) and natural evils (the cyclone, the Deadly Poppy Field), cites Hume's catalogue of the world's ills, and observes that Baum needs neither Kant's postulate of God and a future life to join virtue with happiness nor John Hick's 'vale of soul-making' theodicy—Oz simply delivers the reward. Dorothy's abundant virtue at age five rebukes Aristotle (children, he says, cannot be virtuous or happy) and instead embodies Rousseau's Emile, natural goodness uncorrupted by civilization, while Chesterton's Doctrine of Conditional Joy and Tolkien's insistence on serious, non-technological magic frame the Old-World Christian outlook that Baum's demystified American fairy tale—and the movie's ending—quietly betray.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 24 "Thinking in Rainbows" — Jason Lee reads Hail to the Thief as a metaphysics of evil anchored in blurred boundaries between self and other: the "radiohead" conceit (Descartes' inert matter vs. thinking souls, Bowie's Thomas Newton) makes the sentient android of "Paranoid Android" the emblem of a self porous to signals and control, while "Where I End and You Begin" ("I will eat you alive") locates evil in the feared Other, glossed through Heidegger's das Nichts (evil as lack, not a thing) and Foucault's account of Enlightenment reason classing unreason as inhuman. He hears "Sit Down. Stand Up." as Auschwitz ("the raindrops could be gas") and "Go to Sleep" via The Wicker Man's human sacrifice, then argues The Most Gigantic Lying Mouth of All Time and Yorke's turn to Friends of the Earth and pay-what-you-want In Rainbows show philosophy is no longer sovereign: discourse with the Other is "responsibility, the call to respond ethically" — you have not been paying attention, so act before it's too late.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 12 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Robison measures Pullman's Authority against the three attributes that make the Christian God worthy of worship and finds it fails all three: the suffering of intercision victims like Tony Makarios and the Authority's delegation to the malevolent Metatron defeat omnibenevolence, because unlike with the real God we know no free-will theodicy applies, since the Authority simply does not care; his ignorance of Lyra's destiny (which witches and the Consistorial Court learn long before he does) defeats omniscience; and his demented weeping in the crystal litter before dissolving in open air defeats omnipotence. Since the Authority never created the universe and lied about being its creator, he is not God at all, so Pullman's plot never refutes the God of the philosophers. What the books do establish, she argues, is a powerful attack on organized religion: the Magisterium's suppression of Dust research and harming of children mirror real religious institutions' punishment of Galileo, resistance to evolution, and persecution of dissenters.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 25 "Red Sox Future" — Peter Kreeft argues that the classic pre-2004 Red Sox fan's philosophy is 'Primitive Mysticism' across all eight divisions of philosophy: certainty comes by mystical intuition (fans 'just know' Murphy's Law will strike, as with Dent in 1978 and Buckner in 1986), Parmenides's identity puzzles frame the post-championship identity crisis, free will only chooses among fated tortures, and the greatest good is humiliating the Yankees in Manichean fashion. He opposes Hegel's rational philosophy of history ('the real is the rational') with a history written by 'an insane, drunken, demon-possessed leprechaun,' and inverts the problem of evil: eighty-six years of systematically improbable suffering is probable evidence for a God whose design is a test of faith rather than a refutation of Him. The 2004 title's new rational-optimist 'Enlightenment' identity now threatens to erase the lovable old mysticism, leaving the fan unsure whether to mourn or rejoice.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 8 "Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New ‘Intelligent Falling’ Theory" — Ruiz uses Onion stories—'Jesus Answers Half The Prayers At Area Roulette Table,' 'God Answers Prayers Of Paralyzed Little Boy,' 'Christianity Celebrates One Billionth Unanswered Prayer'—to argue that belief in God lacks rational justification. Following Hume's empiricism (all ideas trace to sense perception), methodological naturalism, and Ockham's Razor, he shows that feelings of God's presence, scriptural circularity, and answered prayers (riddled with selection bias) all fail as evidence, and the prayer hypothesis is unfalsifiable—a theory that explains any outcome, like the brain tumor thanking God for its surviving surgery, is supported by no evidence. He closes by dismantling Paley's watchmaker design argument through the infinite regress ('who designed God?') and by treating 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' as the reductio of design reasoning.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 13 "Jesus Delays Second Coming Because Of Offensive Article" — Littmann runs Hume's Dialogues argument from evil through Onion headlines: 'God Answers Prayers Of Paralyzed Little Boy' (Timmy Yu's resounding no), 'God Outdoes Terrorists Yet Again,' 'God Wastes Miracle On Running Catch In Outfield,' and 'God Cites Moving In Mysterious Ways As Motive In Killing Of 3,000 Papua New Guineans.' He dispatches the theodicies one by one: limiting God's power or goodness (as Mill's lesser deity would) abandons the God of the tradition; the free will defense fails because police rightly restrain gunmen and no human freedom explains hurricanes; soul-building is pointless for a being who could implant compassion innately or stage fake evils; the 'no best possible world' dodge would excuse the reporter who watches a man burn; and the mystery defense makes reason useless. He concludes no all-knowing, all-good, all-powerful God exists, while insisting readers think it through for themselves.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 30 "Voltaire Lives" — Douglas Ficek traces The Onion's God stories — 'Lord Under Investigation For Failure To Provide,' God refusing to heal paralyzed little Timmy Yu, and 'God Cites Moving In Mysterious Ways' — back through Voltaire's Candide to Leibniz's theodicy, the 'best of all possible worlds' doctrine that Dr. Pangloss keeps reciting through hanging, slavery, and syphilis until Candide concludes we must cultivate our garden. The chapter's sharpest claim is that theodicy works by victim-blaming: Jerry Falwell's 9/11 rant earned the headline-only 'Jerry Falwell: Is That Guy A Dick Or What?' because he excused God by blaming secular Americans, just as Pastor Ellsworth blames heathen tsunami victims. Following theologian Dorothee Soelle, Ficek names this 'theological sadism,' and offers the Bible-drop missionaries of 'Poverty-Stricken Africans Receive Desperately Needed Bibles' as a modern Pangloss who mistakes moral obliviousness for grace.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 18 "The Emergence of Good from Evil" — Uses David Lynch's film—Baron Harkonnen as evil personified, Paul's prophetic dreams as biblical revelation, 'the sleeper must awaken'—to stage the problem of evil: if God is omnipotent, omniscient, and wholly good, why do Harkonnens and man-eating worms exist? It lays out the free will defense, J.L. Mackie's objection that God could have created beings who always freely choose good, and the moral/natural evil distinction (Feyd's poisoned blade versus the worm destroying the spice crawler), then extracts the film's own alternative theodicy: good is defined against evil, since the Fremen's dormant 'goodness' awakens only in the struggle Paul leads against their enslavers. The chapter ends with John Hick's soul-making thought that spiritual growth comes through response to challenges, while conceding the evidential problem of evil's sheer quantity.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 151 "What Happens in Carthage Stays in Carthage" — The section likens Augustine's adolescence in Carthage — the Las Vegas of his day — to a rolling-stone youth of sex and sin, noting that Jagger was actually the more responsible teen, enrolling at the London School of Economics. Its key move: in the song's catalog of atrocities the Devil only watches ('I watched with glee') and never causes, so if Lucifer is not the guilty party, the evil must be human — exactly the question Augustine's Confessions was written to answer.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 152 "(I Can’t Get No) Satisfaction . . . Or the Satisfaction that I Ought To" — Augustine's theory of evil is explained through a concert-photography analogy: a dark photo of a brightly lit stage contains no real darkness, just a camera lacking proper exposure, fixable with editing. Likewise, evil is not an entity or polar opposite of good but a privation — something missing the 'good-making' features it ought to have — so no Devil is needed to explain the darkness in the world or in us.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 153 "Who’s to Blame" — The section turns to Augustine's pear theft, where 'it was the sin that sweetened' the act: evil is chosen for the thrill of the forbidden, not forced by any demonic power. It names this 'moral impotence' — knowing the right yet willingly choosing the wrong, as with a missed curfew — an instinct no era has cured. The background vocals' 'Who? Who?' and Jagger's 'I'll tell you one time, you're to blame' thus land the blame for history's catastrophes squarely on 'you and me'.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 156 "Just as Every Cop Is a Criminal, and All the Sinners Saints" — This section lays out Augustine's journey from the Manichean two-gods heresy, through reading Plato, to the view of evil as an 'absence' rather than a force. Its core is the dilemma of Confessions 7.3: if God is wholly good, who sowed the 'seed of bitterness' — the wicked will — into us, and who made the devil? Augustine's answer runs through original sin (the pride of Adam and Eve, demons as fallen angels) and an awkward compromise on which humans are free yet constrained by predestination, so that evil becomes necessary — and confession itself a good.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 159 "But What’s Puzzling You Is the Nature of My Game" — The section situates the song after the 1967 Redlands Bust and amid 1968's collapses — Paris riots, Vietnam, Bobby Kennedy's assassination, which forced the lyric change from 'Who killed Kennedy?' to 'Who killed the Kennedys?' the night before a recording session. Against both Augustine and Bulgakov, it argues Jagger's Devil is far more human and unpredestined: by demanding we 'guess my name', the song fingers us as Satan, tracing the world's malice to our own impulses rather than any divinely scripted plan.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 160 "I Tell You One Time, You’re to Blame" — The closing section follows the song's aftermath through Godard's session film — Brian Jones inaudible in his booth as a Dylanesque draft turns into a 'rocking samba' — to Jones's death, the Altamont killing (shown by Gimme Shelter to have happened during 'Under My Thumb', not 'Sympathy'), and the end of Mick and Marianne. Its verdict: Augustine's narrow, predestined free will leaves humanity out of the picture, while Jagger's human Devil puts responsibility back on us — a world without the Stones would be less enlightened about evil, and their song 'demands more of us, perhaps, than Augustine's Confessions'.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 162 "It’s Just that Demon Life Has Got Me in Its Sway" — Reads "Sympathy for the Devil" through Saint Augustine's Confessions rather than only through Bulgakov's Master and Margarita, which supposedly inspired the lyrics. Augustine's stolen pears and his confession that he loved evil "solely because it was evil" show him needing "the companionship of others sinning," which the chapter pairs with the song's "Who killed the Kennedys?... It was you and me" and with Lee Harvey Oswald's refusal to have acted alone. But the paths split: Jagger's Devil makes evil real and ours, while for Augustine evil has no positive existence at all.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 163 "It’s Only Rock’n’Roll, But I Complicate It" — Casts Augustine as the first Christian rock artist — a rebellious, sex-obsessed convert who, like Plato, ranked the body below the soul — and explains his privation doctrine: "evil has no positive nature; but the loss of good has received the name 'evil.'" Evil is "a swerving of the will which is turned toward lower things," so free will is crucial: God permits evil because virtues like courage could not exist in a world without it. The chapter closes with the constellation of opposites (soul/body, pride/humility, temporal/eternal) Augustine says we must live through to approach philosophical truth.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 164 "I Shouted Out, Who Killed Meredith Hunter" — Takes the refrain "what's puzzling you is the nature of my game" to mean the song presents the Devil as a real, personal force present at the crucifixion, the Russian Revolution, World War II and the Kennedy assassinations — not the mere lack of goodness Augustine allows. It cites Richards's 2002 remark, on the heels of 9/11, that confronting evil puts him "out of a job," and reads "Sweet Neo Con" as Jagger still indicting ideology. Against Augustine's weak-willed sinner, "every cop is a criminal" locates evil in human strength and resolve — with Godard's Eve Democracy answering "Yes" to "Is the Devil God in exile?"
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 165 "Under Our Thumb" — Corrects the popular error that Meredith Hunter was killed while "Sympathy for the Devil" played: eyewitnesses and the Gimme Shelter footage show the murder happened during "Under My Thumb" at the Altamont free concert of December 6, 1969. It surveys the assigning of blame — Rolling Stone captioning Jagger's picture "Is Mick responsible for the killing?", Norma Coates blaming the era's burden on the counterculture — and concludes Jagger sides against Augustine's privation view: Hunter did not die "at the hands of a bunch of privations," since the evil the band saw was an in-your-face reality.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 166 "A Wild Murder Couldn’t Drag Me Away" — Draws Augustine and Jagger together as brothers who fell far before finding restraint: Augustine's many conflicting wills must collapse into one good will by actually choosing, and his Manichean past taught him some truths must be performed or willed, like his "grant me chastity — just not yet." The chapter reads Gimme Shelter as likewise double — harrowing documentary or joyous concert footage, forced to choose — and argues the post-Altamont Stones had to make "Sympathy for the Devil" a performative force for understanding evil rather than a scapegoat, then stayed in the flesh, confronting good and evil through the blues.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 167 "Chapter 21 - Lucifer Rising and Falling" — Opens Dan Dinello's chapter with Richards's 1971 "Everybody's Lucifer" and sets up its two rival accounts of evil: the Christian Satan enshrined by Augustine — Lucifer expelled for prideful disobedience, seducing God's weak-willed children into sin — and the moral authorities of the 1960s (press, police, clergy) who cast the Stones as "Satan's Jesters" luring youth astray. The Stones answered with a nineteenth-century Romantic Lucifer, the rebellious angel fighting moral repression, blaming the mob of hypocritical authorities for the world's horrors.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 169 "From Satyrs to Martyrs" — Shows how Augustine forged the machinery of Christian evil — sex as sin, the invention of Original Sin, The City of God's mandate to compel heretics, and the goat-god Pan as Satan's visual model — then maps it onto the 1960s persecution of the Stones: press mockery, police drug busts, Bill Wyman hauled into court as a "shaggy monster." The persecution backfired, making the Stones martyrs and pushing Jagger toward the self-embraced "Lucifers of Rock" image of "Paint It, Black" and the Their Satanic Majesties Request cover.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 172 "The Devil Is My Name" — Reports Jagger's own genealogy of the song — "an old idea of Baudelaire's," Bulgakov's Master and Margarita (given to him by Marianne Faithfull), and his Lucifer Rising conversations with Kenneth Anger — and follows its studio metamorphosis from country dirge to voodoo samba under Godard's camera. The finished recording, whose working title was "The Devil is My Name," builds into a celebration of humanity's hatred and hypocrisy from the crucifixion through the Blitzkrieg to the Kennedys (pluralized when RFK was shot on June 5, 1968, during the sessions), putting humanity on trial by the devil rather than the other way around.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 10 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Sets Walt's 'There's nothing but chemistry here' materialism - the missing 0.111958 percent of the human body that Gretchen calls the soul - against Augustine's Confessions, arguing both men want redemption without giving up their sins: 'give me chastity, but not yet.' It maps Augustine's problem of evil (evil as corruption of the will toward self-destruction) onto Walt's pros-and-cons list over killing Krazy-8 and his 'no-rough-stuff-type deal' fantasy after Tuco. Werner Heisenberg's uncertainty principle then turns chemistry's laws into tendencies, opening room for free choice inside a materialist world - so Walt's remission in 'Over' saves the body, while only changed choices, which he keeps deferring, could save the man.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 18 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Sirvent and Baker take Van Alden's 'strong providential theology' - 'his fate rests in God's hands' at the burned Agent Clarkson's bedside - as a live version of the problem of evil, traced through Augustine and Aquinas to Calvin's all-determining divine omnipotence. The Arminian free-will escape leaves God like a parent watching a child run into traffic, and the 'mysterious ways' reply makes God's moral vocabulary so alien that a God who burns his beloved is 'one-sided' and unworshipable - the same theology that lets Van Alden shift blame for Lucy's pregnancy onto a 'charge from God' before drowning Sebso as 'the judgment of the wicked.' They close with Nucky's God, an inner impetus toward good that asks rather than coerces, and with process theology's persuading God, while Gyp Rosetti's Easter rant at the crucifix shows what believing in the omnipotent alternative costs.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 26 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Oschman reads 'Godfellas' as an answer to the problem of evil: Bender, made god of the Shrimpkins, destroys them by meddling too much, and the God Entity explains 'if you do too much, people get dependent. And if you do nothing, they lose hope.' After testing the contrast response (pain makes Slurm sweet) and the Free Will Defense (which covers moral evils like the returning garbage ball of 'A Big Piece of Garbage' but not natural evils or the taste of anchovies), the chapter adopts John Hick's soul-making theodicy: God's epistemic distance - compared to Fry's obsession after tasting super Slurm - keeps creatures uncompelled so they can grow into free moral agents. Fry's slow evolution from delivery boy to 'slightly less lazy slob' is soul-making, and 'The Late Philip J. Fry' wryly confirms life's purpose is 'probably some hogwash about the human spirit.'
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 40 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Trip McCrossin casts the creature as a modern Job: repeatedly and unreasonably mistreated by the De Laceys, the rustic whose child he saved, and Victor despite his benevolence, he cries 'This was then the reward of my benevolence!' - but unlike Job he loses faith, because his problem of evil is secular, justifying not 'the Ways of God to Man' but 'the Ways of Man to monsters.' The chapter traces the problem from Job and Paradise Lost through Bayle's defense of faith over reason and the Optimists' 'best of all possible worlds,' whose credibility drowned with the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, setting Rousseau against Voltaire: Rousseau's Emile ('All is good leaving the hands of the author of things') demands that we make evil intelligible through self-knowledge, while Candide counsels tending our garden. The creature embodies Rousseau's line - 'I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend' - yet ends in self-abhorring remorse over Victor's death, leaving open whether self-knowledge can ever answer unreasonable suffering.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 8 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Jeremy Proulx reads Ender through F.W.J. Schelling's account of evil as a real, positive force rather than Augustine's mere privation of good: Ender's kicks to Stilson and Bonzo, his killing of the Giant in the mind game, and his 'I destroy them' confession all display the 'contraction into the self' Schelling thinks haunts every moral agent. He argues Graff deliberately isolates Ender to force this dark ground to the surface, and that Valentine's 'welcome to the human race' and the hive-queen's forgiveness teach Ender that evil, though never excusable, can be understood and atoned for - his fate also shows freedom tainted by a necessity we neither choose nor control.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 10 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Robert Arp's introduction opens with Halloween culture and his own seminarian past to ask whether belief in the Devil can survive scrutiny. He lays out a 'just deserts' argument - Hitler, Stalin, and Mao died unpunished while Job, Socrates, and Thomas More died unrewarded, so God, the Devil, Heaven, and Hell must exist to balance the scales - and then answers it with Freud's projection critique (religion as wishful thinking for comfort and moral control) and with the neuroscience tying the mind to a dying brain, which undermines the soul that Hell would punish. The chapter frames the whole book's project: testing devil-belief with arguments and evidence rather than taking it on authority.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 35 "The Devil and Philosophy" — A.G. Holdier pits Augustine against Star Wars: South Park's pay-per-view Satan-Jesus boxing match and the Force's balanced light and dark sides picture God and the Devil as equals, but Augustine - drawing on his Manichaean past and Zoroastrianism's Ahura Mazda versus Angra Mainyu - shows this is really two-gods worship, not monotheism. For Augustine the Devil is a derivative creature, created good and freely fallen, and evil is not a positive force but a privation, an absence of God like cold or darkness, so Vader's corruption and redemption both hang on free choice. Mordred's rebellion against Arthur gives the right picture: the Dark Side can never win because it is only diminished goodness.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 37 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Ray Bossert reads Tolkien's Silmarillion through Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy: elves, being artists, understand Melkor not as tempter but as bad artist, from his rebellious solo in the Music of the Ainur to his botched sub-creations - orcs bred from kidnapped elves - and his covetous collecting of the silmarils. Boethius supplies the machinery: evil seeks a good by unnatural means and only approximates it, wickedness debases its practitioner into a beast, God's foreknowledge embraces free choices without causing them, and Providence is a spinning disc at whose center alone one is steady - so Melkor's rebellion leaves him less free, dragged around the rim. Tolkien's contrast between art (for beauty) and magic (for control) explains why the Devil can only mimic creation, never make anything real.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 41 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Thomas Ward reconstructs C.S. Lewis's argument from The Problem of Pain that either demons exist or God doesn't. The free will defense, credited to Augustine, covers the evil humans freely do - freedom being required for love, as the rubber-ducky world shows - but John Perry's baby bat eaten by cockroaches and William Rowe's burned fawn are natural evils no human is responsible for. Given the not-crazy assumptions that God exists and is never morally responsible for evil, something non-human, personal, and wicked must bear that responsibility: hence demons, who like us misused their freedom, stretching the free will defense to cover every evil whatsoever.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 65 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Olli Pitkänen maps the Satanist spectrum beyond the Devil-worship of films like The Mother of Tears: LaVey's atheistic, morally subjectivist Church of Satan; the Nietzschean Übermensch cult of the Order of Nine Angles with its initiatory violence; the chaos-gnostic Temple of the Black Light (whose ideal, he says, is the Joker in The Dark Knight); and Finland's Star of Azazel, theistic Satanists whose theosophical moral realism makes Satan a presenter of choices rather than a willer of evil. On that last reading Vader destroying Palpatine and Sauron perishing with the One Ring show evil as human projection, and even Jesus counts as 'satanic' in the rebel-against-dogma sense.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 7 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Robert Arp's introduction explains that Homeland's jihadist material (Nazir, Hamid, Brody, 9/11) drew him in and previews the book's philosophizing with a sample argument: whether morality needs God. He argues jihadists ground ethics in Allah's commands, but since faith defies rational proof, competing conceptions of God conflict, and scripture (Abraham and Isaac, the Flood, the Egyptian firstborn, the genocide commands in 1 Samuel and Hosea) has God commanding atrocities, either the terrorists' God is evil or morality is better grounded in reason without God. The dilemma he poses - a good God would not command 9/11, so the command conception or God's goodness must go - is the Euthyphro structure applied to terrorism.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 28 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Trip McCrossin reads Carrie's 'I missed something once before... everyone's not me' as the modern, secular problem of evil: as Susan Neiman argues, unreasonable suffering threatens reason itself, and the Rousseau-Voltaire split defines the responses. Carrie takes Rousseau's side - 'All is good leaving the hands of the author of things' degenerates in human hands, so evil is intelligible and redemption possible, the chance at redemption she offers Brody and even Nazir - against Voltaire's Candide-style tending of the garden. The finale deepens this with Boethius's Consolation: Carrie's 'I believe one of the reasons I was put on this Earth was for our paths to cross' fuses fate with providence, and she accepts Brody's execution as a redemptive end 'more so if he dies'.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 19 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Montoya asks whether Prismo, Adventure Time's wish-granting stand-in for God, produced the best possible world when he restored Ooo over Farmworld. After explaining Leibniz's answer to the problem of evil—that an all-good, all-knowing God permits some evil because every possible world contains some, and ours contains the least—the chapter compares Farmworld (no Lich, but Finn becomes the Ice King, Jake mutates into the Lich, Marceline dies ancient and insane) with Ooo, where the same characters flourish as heroes. Prismo, no omnibenevolent deity, remakes Ooo out of friendship with Jake, and Farmworld's horrors vindicate the Leibnizian point that wishing one evil out of existence can unleash far worse.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 23 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — White argues Apple's 'Think Different' commercial packages together two distinct character traits: genuine independence, in Rand's sense of judging from the facts of reality (thirteen-year-old Jobs confronting his pastor with the problem of evil via the Biafran children—'Does God know about this?'—rejecting dogma at Stanford, killing the iPod's screen, bending Corning to make gorilla glass on schedule), and pseudo-independence that asserts the primacy of consciousness over reality (refusing to bathe because his diet 'prevented' odor, treating cancer with fruit juice, NeXT's impossible eighteen-month promise). Using Binswanger's 'fallacy of false integration' (the surgeon-and-murderer 'cutter' example), he charges the ad with merging the traits into one folder, so Jobs should instead be praised without qualification for his independence and blamed without qualification for his pseudo-independence.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 15 "6. Tris’s Compassion and the Problem of Evil" — McCrossin reads Tris's whole arc as a struggle with the problem of evil, both the theological version from Job and the modern secular one Susan Neiman describes, in which unreasonable suffering threatens trust in human reason. He casts Tris as cut from Rousseau's mold - her insistence on making the evils of Jeanine, Marcus, and Evelyn intelligible - against Voltaire's Candide refusal to rationalize suffering, and treats the faction system as Rousseau's social-contract strategy for containing the inclination to evil while Tris herself plays a wartime Emile. The key is Tobias's lesson that selflessness and bravery are not that different: selflessness enables the courage that compassion motivates, from pressing her forehead to Jeanine's gun in the fear landscape to taking Caleb's place at the weapons lab, so that the trilogy ends with Tobias's 'we mend each other.'
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 31 "18. Wondering What It’s All For" — Trip McCrossin reads Lord Grantham's 'we've dreamed a dream' as an echo of Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 2 and follows the war story line - Matthew and William missing before Amiens, William's slow death, Mr. Lang's shell shock, Mrs. Patmore's nephew Archie shot for cowardice - to show how obscure war's causes and realities remain to those who have not lived them. The Dowager Countess's 'we don't always get our just deserts' as Matthew dies under his car, and the stretcher-bearer's 'it comes down to luck,' raise the problem of evil from the Book of Job: good and bad fortune fall without premonition or meaning. Against complacency about war's inevitability, the chapter argues that since class and traffic harms can be reduced, warfare's can be too - we should 'band together as Daniel,' interpret the wars a few dream up, and not allow them to come to be.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 14 "4. Acts of God" — McCrossin reads Lecter's parable of the church collapses - 'It must feel good to God - He does it all the time, and are we not made in His image?' - as Lecter's solution to the problem of evil in both its theological (Job) and secular (Neiman) forms: a malevolent deity of the kind de Sade's Saint-Fond describes, doing God's work becomes Lecter's justification, and killing feels good because 'if one does what God does enough times, one will become as God is'. Following Neiman, he sets Rousseau's tradition (evil must be made intelligible - 'All is well leaving the hands of the author of things') against Voltaire's Candide refusal of theodicy, showing that Will and Starling live in Rousseau's camp except when facing Lecter himself, and that the Hannibal/Hannibal Rising revelation that Mischa's murder 'happened' to him radically revises his earlier claim that 'we don't invent our natures', with Starling's reason finally making 'a place for Mischa' in Lecter and Starling together.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 16 "6. The Psychiatrist as Sociopathic God" — Hassert takes Lecter's 'First principles, Clarice' at its Aristotelian word - nature is revealed through capacities and action, as an acorn's telos is not pumpkins and a kitten will never be a Great Dane - to explain Lecter's psychiatry: he reads each patient's essence and potential, prescribing Mason Verger's face-peeling so appearance finally matches essence, and force-raising Will toward equality so that Aristotelian perfect friendship between the alike-in-virtue (which Franklyn's flattery can never reach) might become possible.
