Finally, contrasting Russell's meaning-amid-a-godless-cosmos with religious faith, they argue atheism need not entail nihilism and that survival and human solidarity give the Colonials common ground.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 48 "Reap a Destiny" — Jonathan and Jerry Walls read Harry Potter's Deathly Hallows through the question of death and afterlife. Harry's willing death-march models Heidegger's authenticity and being-toward-death, while Voldemort's terror of death makes him inauthentic. At King's Cross the maimed Voldemort-soul embodies William James's 'sow a character, reap a destiny': having refused remorse, he has become evil beyond repair, whereas the repentant Dumbledore has grown. Against Heidegger's atheism, Rowling's Christian resurrection imagery, backed by Locke on memory-identity, Kant, and Pascal, makes our character-forming choices infinitely consequential.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 49 "House and the Life of Reason" — Henry Jacoby argues that despite House's line that we are 'selfish, base animals crawling across the Earth,' House lives a meaningful life. Rejecting God-, soul-, and afterlife-based meaning (House's Euthyphro-style objections and his '97 Seconds' near-death experiment), Jacoby locates meaning in the Socratic examined life and Aristotle's life of reason as humanity's proper function. House's relentless curiosity and puzzle-solving, tied to action and to saving lives, exemplify reason governing desire and yield eudaimonia - so 'doing things changes things,' and House, however miserable he seems, leads the examined, meaningful life.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 6 "Part Five D Is for Destiny" — This editor's introduction (Sharon Kaye) frames the whole volume by recounting a childhood memory of being lost at a carnival and using it to argue that the show taps a philosophical fear of being cut off from everything we know, forcing the viewer to confront questions like 'Why am I here?' and 'Does my life matter?' It organizes the nineteen essays under the acronym F.O.U.N.D. (Fortune/metaphysics, Origin/epistemology, Unity/social-political, Necessity/ethics, Destiny/religion), presenting Lost's plane-crash premise as an occasion for asking the meaning-of-life and fate-versus-free-will questions the survivors face.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 15 "NOTES" — Jeremy Barris argues that Lost dramatizes the structure of life itself, using Heidegger's claim that the inquirer's own being is the clue to all questions and his notion of 'thrownness' to read the castaways' accidental arrival as a mirror of our own bewildering birth into circumstances we did not make. He reframes the show's central puzzle as 'the question of life after birth,' contends against Sartre and Camus that life is neither fully sensible nor fully absurd but a half-understood riddle, and invokes Wittgenstein's On Certainty to show that total doubt is impossible because understanding senselessness presupposes understanding something.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 27 "NOTES" — Brett Chandler Patterson reads Lost alongside C. S. Lewis's Chronicles of Narnia as myth rather than allegory, arguing both use a fantasy world of second chances to stage redemption in community. He aligns the castaways' violent arrival on the island with the Pevensie children's magical passage into Narnia and Edmund's betrayal-and-forgiveness arc, using the island's life-and-death setting to force existential commitment. Emmanuel Levinas's ethics of responsibility to the face of the Other and H. Richard Niebuhr's relational theology are invoked to argue that healing and faith come not individually but in communion with others.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 28 "NOTES" — Daniel B. Gallagher uses Thomas Aquinas on the knowledge of God to read the characters' searches for meaning on Lost. Aquinas's 'approaching Peter' image—recognizing a human without yet knowing it is Peter—models how everyone confusedly knows God as the object of happiness while mistaking finite goods (Jack's curing, Kate's deception, Jin's job, Charlie's brother) for the ultimate good, paralleled with the castaways staring at the unidentifiable Smoke Monster. Gallagher then applies Aquinas's sin of acedia (spiritual sloth that deems the good unattainable) to Desmond's fear over Penny and Charlie's despair before Rose tells him faith is never impossible, tying the desire for happiness to Augustine's restless heart.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 27 "15. The Twists and Turns of Second Chances" — Karavitis groups twist-ending episodes into nostalgia, time-travel, and second-chance types and reads them through Kierkegaard's Either/Or distinction between the aesthetic and ethical modes of life. Living aesthetically—chasing present gratification—leads to despair, as in 'A Nice Place to Visit' (Rocky's boring 'heaven' is Hell) and 'A Game of Pool' (Jesse wins only an eternity in Limbo). Living ethically—taking responsibility and moving forward—earns a real second chance, as when 'Printer's Devil' editor Winter reclaims his soul; life must be understood backward but lived forward.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 3 "Introduction" — Jacob Held defends the philosophy-and-popular-culture project against snobbery and argues that King's horror is genuine philosophy because it forces readers to confront finitude, meaning, and their deepest values. He reads King's own account of 'existential horror' through Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian pairing, casting the horror tale as a Dionysian crack in an Apollonian order that ends by restoring equilibrium, and frames doing this fun, relatable work as its own eudaimonia poised between nihilism and Aristotelian flourishing. Using Lovecraft's Cthulhu and King's Desperation/The Regulators (Tak), he claims horror shakes us into reaffirming the values that orient us and so bridges abstract academic philosophy and lived experience.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 6 "“Sometimes Dead Is Better”" — Katherine Allen reads Pet Sematary and The Tommyknockers as bioconservative fables staging the transhumanism debate: Louis's resurrected, 'fundamentally wrong' cat Church and cannibal son Gage, and Bobbi's tooth-shedding 'New Improved' becoming, dramatize Kass, McKibben and Fukuyama's warning that erasing our limits erases our humanity. Against them she sets Nick Bostrom's 'Fable of the Dragon-Tyrant,' in which death is an unquestioned evil we should slay, and Bernard Williams's worry about the tedium of immortality. King's insistence that 'sometimes dead is better,' and that forbidden knowledge (the Micmac ground, the buried ship) works like an addiction, sides with the deathist view that mortality and finitude give life its meaning.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 15 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Barnwell argues that fatherhood can constitute the ultimate meaning of a man's life, answering the paradox that a meaningful life 'all about the kids' seems not to be about the father by noting fatherly acts are still the father's own freely chosen activities. He confronts Camus's Myth of Sisyphus – the worry that childrearing is endless pointless rock-pushing across generations – by insisting children, unlike rocks, have intrinsic value, and invokes the Sartrean existentialist idea that choosing an activity confers value on it (illustrated by his buying oatmeal for 'Sally').
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 30 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Morgan asks when it is wrong for fathers to impose their ideals on children, arguing that forcing activities (like violin practice) risks alienation because meaningful pursuits must be embraced 'from the inside.' Using Robert Noggle's Rawls-derived hierarchy of goods (basic, pre-primary, primary, secondary, specialized), he grants fathers may guide toward universal goods but rejects Noggle's claim that parents may impose a full religious worldview, favoring David Archard's weaker right to 'guide family life' while respecting the child's growing capacity to choose – permitting compelled practice of talents only in light of the child's emerging identity.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 6 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — In this Foreword, John Rousmaniere argues that sailing's 'numinous' moments — like his own experience of stillness on a becalmed ketch mid-Atlantic, when the skipper cut the engine and the crew felt suspended between sky and sea — are paths to genuine philosophical truths, not embarrassing flights of fancy. He enlists William James's 'Varieties of Religious Experience' and James's nautical metaphor for free will (the passenger who volunteers to take the helm) to argue that such mystical feelings can 'team up' with reason rather than opposing it. He insists mystery and craft must work together: piety is no substitute for seamanship (Shelley drowned in an unseaworthy boat), yet competence and numinous experience nurture each other.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 10 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Jack Stillwaggon recounts his 1965 voyage as a seventeen-year-old crewing the replica HMS Bounty from New York to Florida — fires aboard, thirty-five-foot seas, seasickness, a crewman nearly left to die — and asks why modern people abandon comfort to court danger and discomfort. His answer is that we face the sea to prove something to ourselves about our worth and abilities: like the paratrooper who stays under fire or the soldier earning his 'red badge of courage,' the survived ordeal becomes a cherished high point that adds meaning to an otherwise 'silly' comfortable existence, leaving him more at peace and expecting more of himself thereafter.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 13 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Richard Hutch develops a phenomenology of 'moral presence' — an assertion of human integrity in the face of despair when nothing else can be done — from the autobiographies of solo ocean sailors. He identifies three pathways: technical finesse (Robin Knox-Johnston, whose 'God helps those who help themselves' pragmatism Hutch reads as the Taoist wu-wei, action through non-action), cosmic quest (Bernard Moitessier's mystical communion, slingshot instead of radio), and personal test (Kay Cottee's epiphany near Cape Horn, transforming terror into fascination via Otto's mysterium tremendum et fascinans). He frames sailing as tragic-comic drama with technology as a deus ex machina, arguing that doing nothing is often the zenith of value.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 19 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Nicholas Hayes describes the Chicago-to-Mackinac race, cataloguing its boats (passenger trains, Model Ts, booster rockets, retreads), its nights (darkest, stormy, breathless, velvet, brightest), and its sailor-types (tweener, superhero, teammate, yogi, minister, salt) to build toward a claim about an 'awareness shift.' He argues that far from land and its electric lights, sailors slip into a place where the emotional self meets 'the most real and primitive world' and confronts a new relationship with time, culminating on the 'day of hope' in the realization that one controls nothing but oneself and owns nothing but one's time — 'Everything is now' — a transcendence he loosely likens to skepticism and enlightenment themes.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 27 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Hilaire Belloc's essay 'The Channel,' serving as the volume's literary epilogue, argues that the 'glamour in the mind' and 'freshness of beginnings' our ancestors knew can be recovered by using the body simply and hardly — best of all by sailing a small boat under twenty-five feet across the Channel. Narrating his own first crossing from the Goodwins to Calais, drifting on the ebb and waiting for the flood, he presents sailing as the 'old drama by which the soul of a healthy man is kept alive,' teaching terror, salvation, exultation, and repose as lived realities rather than mere words. He closes by withholding the tale of the stormy return, imploring readers not to hear of it but to sail it themselves.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 30 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Tallman offers a naturalistic (atheist) justification for celebrating Christmas, arguing first that the holiday's date and rituals (December 25 solstice, Christmas trees, Odin-derived Santa) predate and are not exclusively Christian, so non-believers may find their own meaning in them. Drawing on George Santayana's and Steven Cahn's 'religious naturalism,' she argues rituals and moral communities give meaning without supernatural belief, so atheists engaging even overtly religious rites (like Westerners doing Hindu-rooted yoga) are not being disingenuous. She locates a secular 'spirit of Christmas' — giving, love, community — in It's a Wonderful Life, where humans, not God, save George Bailey, and closes on a Venn-diagram overlap of Christian and naturalist Christmases.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 36 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Arp frames a dialogue between two ex-seminarians who once got matching cross tattoos: Bill, who added more Christian ink, and Rick, who now regrets his cross as an atheist secular humanist. Bill defends God via Aquinas's combined proof from motion and causation—tracing the tattoo artist and even the Big Bang back to an unmoved mover / uncaused cause—and the 'three Ms' of mind, meaning, and morality, gesturing toward Paley-style design. Rick counters with a self-sustaining infinite series, the interaction problem between a supernatural God and nature, and the charge that God is a comforting fiction, so morality and meaning are humanly made rather than divinely guaranteed.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 6 "Introduction" — Rowlands introduces the 'sci-phi' project: science fiction confronts us with the alien 'other' as a mirror in which we understand ourselves, so lowbrow sci-fi films like The Matrix, Total Recall and Starship Troopers make abstract philosophy concrete. He argues philosophy is doing rather than knowing, invoking Fishburne's 'know the path vs walk the path' line and Nietzsche's dictum that one repays a teacher poorly by remaining a pupil. He mentions his own earlier 'fyborg' thesis that human cognition is embedded in the wider informational environment, prefiguring the extended mind.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 7 "1. Frankenstein" — Using the De Niro monster of Branagh's Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, Rowlands argues absurdity arises from a clash between the view of ourselves from the inside (a locus of meaning) and from the outside (sub specie aeternitatis, insignificant). The monster is assembled from second-hand parts and thrown into a hostile world he did not choose, just as we are stitched together by genes and environment we did not choose (Sartre/Heidegger thrownness). He develops Camus's Myth of Sisyphus, arguing the horror is futility not difficulty, to frame the problem of the meaning of life that underlies every deep philosophical problem.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 15 "9. Blade Runner" — Using Blade Runner's replicants ('I want more life, fucker!') and Roy's dying soliloquy, Rowlands asks how death can harm the one who dies. He states the Epicurean argument (while we live death is not yet; when dead there is no one to harm) and answers via harms of deprivation, illustrated by Tyrell's imagined brain damage. Drawing on Wittgenstein (death as the limit of life) and Heidegger's being-towards-death/being-towards-a-future, he distinguishes weak (non-conceptual) from strong (conceptual) possession of a future, arguing death harms more those with more invested. Linear time and the ultimate horizon of death are what let a life have meaning at all.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 31 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — John Davenport argues The Lord of the Rings is religious not as Christian allegory but as an epic fairy tale in Tolkien's sense from 'On Fairy-stories,' delivering 'eucatastrophe,' the sudden joyous turn that, like Kierkegaard's faith in a salvation beyond our own power, hints at eschatological hope. Using Sir Gawain and the Green Knight as Tolkien's model for Frodo (both accept an impossible burden, both fail and bear a scar of mortality), he identifies the destruction of the Ring via Gollum, Eowyn's healing, and the sapling of Nimloth as eucatastrophic 'turns.' Davenport concludes the veiled religious message is that evil cannot stand forever, yet deliverance requires our sacrifice and faith beyond rational hope that 'day shall come again.'
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 24 "“You Have to Believe in Something”" — Jason Eberl and Jennifer Vines use Battlestar Galactica's Baltar (skeptic) and Caprica Six/Roslin (believers) to debate God's existence, presenting Aquinas's five ways (unmoved mover, uncaused cause, governance) against a self-explaining big bang, and noting Baltar's self-serving faith resembles Pascal's Wager. They raise the problem of evil, answering with Augustine's free-will account of moral evil and Hick's soul-making theodicy (via Hume's faulty-architect analogy) for natural evil. Writing as a theist and an atheist, they argue meaning survives without God in human solidarity ('the gods shall lift those who lift each other'), and that faith and reason can share common ground.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 48 "Reap a Destiny" — The Walls brothers read Harry Potter's confrontation with death through Heidegger's authenticity and being-toward-death: Harry's calm march to the Forbidden Forest and Colin Creevey's sacrifice exemplify accepting mortality, while Voldemort's terror of death makes him inauthentic. The King's Cross scene lets Dumbledore be Harry's Heideggerian hero from the past; via William James's "sow a thought … reap a destiny," Aristotle, Locke on memory-identity, and Kant on the afterlife, they argue our choices forge a character — and Voldemort's refusal of remorse seals his ruin.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 49 "House and the Life of Reason" — Jacoby argues that despite House calling us "selfish, base animals," House lives Socrates' examined life and Aristotle's life of reason. He dismisses God-given meaning using the Euthyphro dilemma and rejects the soul and afterlife (the "97 Seconds" self-experiment), insisting "our actions here are all that matters." Meaning must be both subjective and objective; House's puzzle-solving realizes humanity's rational function, tied to action and virtue, and — per Aristotle — yields eudaimonia, so his life is meaningful even when it doesn't feel that way to him.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 6 "4. Star Trek The Next Generation as Philosophy Gene Roddenberry’s Argument for Humanism" — Decker reads Star Trek: The Next Generation as Roddenberry's argument for secular humanism, using Corliss Lamont's ten propositions to frame a naturalistic, this-worldly ethic embodied by a militantly secular Enterprise crew. The recurring antagonist Q dramatizes tests of virtue and the Ring-of-Gyges question of power without consequences, while 'Who Watches the Watchers' and 'Devil's Due' stage humanist critiques of religion: Picard refuses to become a god to the Mintakans and dismantles Ardra's 'god of the gaps' con by showing the Ventaxians saved themselves. Decker invokes Hume's proportioning belief to evidence, Bacon's idols of the mind, and the Euthyphro to argue morality needs no divine command, framing Roddenberry's 'agonism' and the professional social ethics behind the Federation.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 44 "41. Blade Runner as Philosophy What Does It Mean to Be Human" — Shanahan argues Blade Runner is philosophical despite Ridley Scott's denial, using the replicants (Roy Batty, Rachael, Leon) as defamiliarizing 'mirrors' for the human condition. He shows the Nexus-6 replicants satisfy Descartes' two criteria for a thinking soul (linguistic flexibility, novel problem-solving) while human characters like Deckard prove as cold and empathy-deficient as the machines, collapsing the human/replicant distinction the Voight-Kampff test presumes. He then reads Rachael's implanted memories through Locke's memory theory of personal identity, Roy's 'tears in rain' death through Epicurean worries about finitude, and frames the whole via Plato's Cave line 'they are like us' — the replicants model our own concerns with memory, death, and the meaning of a temporally bounded life.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 54 "51. Magnolia As Philosophy Meaning and Coincidence" — Engelen interprets Paul Thomas Anderson's Magnolia as a meditation on sense-making and Camus's notion of the absurd: the film's raining frogs and the interlocking coincidences (Sydney Barringer's death, the narrator's insistence that 'this cannot be one of those things') stage our compulsion to find meaning colliding with a universe that yields none. He reads characters' struggles with trauma and regret through Epictetus's Stoic dichotomy of control and Jung's synchronicity, and the 'Wise Up' sing-along as a call to accept what cannot be changed. The chapter endorses Camus's third response to the absurd—neither denial nor suicide but defiant acceptance—linking it to Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and Nagel's take on life's meaning.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 57 "54. The Man from Earth as Philosophy The Desirability of Immortality" — Berk brings The Man from Earth—about John Oldman, a 14,000-year-old non-aging man—into dialogue with Bernard Williams's 'The Makropulos Case,' which argues immortality must become boring and identity-destroying (the dilemma of exhausted versus radically changed categorical desires). Against these 'immortality curmudgeons,' the chapter argues John's mild boredom, enduring loves, friendships, and pursuit of knowledge show an immortal life can stay worth living, invoking Fischer's 'repeatable pleasures.' It also engages Nussbaum's 'Mortal Immortals' and Beauvoir's All Men Are Mortal (the miserable Fosca), which tie courage and love to finitude and sacrifice, noting John is only 'medically' rather than 'genuinely' immortal and so can still make sacrifices.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 63 "60. Little Women as Philosophy Death or Marriage and the Meaning of Life" — The chapter tests Susan Wolf's 'fitting fulfillment' theory (meaning as subjective attraction meeting objective attractiveness) against Greta Gerwig's Little Women, arguing the March sisters and most historical women are ill-fitted to it. Jo is forced to make her writing 'mercenary and commercial' and marries; Amy abandons painting and marries Laurie because 'marriage is an economic proposition'; Marmee, Hannah, and Mrs. Hummel live from duty and self-sacrifice without joy. Invoking Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but becomes a woman' and Imposter Syndrome, it concludes fulfillment is indicative but not necessary for meaning, urging a purely objective theory that can value women's lives 'appropriately appreciated at least in principle.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 70 "66. Marc Maron as Philosopher Comedy, Therapy, and Identification" — Kapica argues Maron's 'WTF' philosophy—both indignation and liberation—turns Kenneth Burke's rhetorical theory of identification and 'consubstantiality' into comedic catharsis, treating stand-up as therapy. He reads Maron's opening move from 'What is the meaning of life?' to 'How am I being used?' through Richard Taylor and Camus's Sisyphus: in 2009, a broke and failing Maron is Sisyphus, and WTF is his license to invent meaning. Via his cold-sore and sobriety bits and his WTF podcast interviews (Seinfeld, Gallagher), Maron makes his audience a surrogate therapist, using performed vulnerability to bind them into an 'acting-together' that Kapica claims genuinely saved Maron's life.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 82 "77. Journey as Philosophy Meaning, Connection, and the Sublime" — Hamer argues Journey works through the interplay of connection, the sublime and meaning. The wordless multiplayer bond with an unnameable stranger before vast vistas dramatizes emotional connection where the ancestors' greed failed. The looming mountain and immense dunes evoke the sublime, read through Burke's pleasurable terror and Kant's mathematical and dynamical sublime (imagination overwhelmed while reason comprehends; feeling power over a nature that cannot harm the deathless player, then rebirth surpassing the sublime into joy). The cyclical return to the start recasts the game as Camus's Myth of Sisyphus: a meaningless repeated ascent that players nonetheless replay, so we must imagine the Traveler — and ourselves — happy to make the beautiful repetition our own.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 16 "6. Religion, Loss, and Afterlife" — The chapter asks whether Doctor Who is a religion, testing it against Hopfe's and Ninian Smart's criteria and concluding it is best understood as a Humanist-and-religious 'philosophy'—sacred and 'holy' (Otto) but lacking a genuine transcendent 'unseen.' On loss, it uses Kierkegaard's 'aesthetic life' and 'rotation method' to explain why we fear endings and regenerations, urging viewers to root life in lasting meaning rather than fleeting pleasure. On death, it deploys Socrates in the Apology and Phaedo and Aristotle on courage (Jabe, Harriet Jones, Donna sacrificing themselves) to argue death is nothing to fear, and reads the Matrix and Nethersphere as the show's two Socratic afterlife options.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 18 "Epilogue" — The closing essay exhorts readers to 'approach life as the Doctor'—engaged, compassionate, and critically thinking—insisting each person is important and that fandom passion, even when fractious, expresses the Doctor's engaged life (invoking Voltaire on free expression). Using 'Father's Day' and 'The Day of the Doctor,' it argues we cannot change the past but must seize the present, and ties 'truth' and 'trust' to a shared root to claim a meaningful life requires trusting oneself and others rather than merely proving oneself right. It affirms that wisdom is lived truth, that being wrong is how we mature, and that courage is doing what must be done while afraid.

### General mentions

- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 30 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — This companion piece profiles philosophers who actually practiced law or rhetoric: the sophists Thrasymachus and Protagoras (whose 'man is the measure' relativism was rhetoric for hire and whom Plato and Aristotle despised), Demosthenes, Cicero - called 'the closest thing to a Philosopher King any society has ever seen' - Plutarch with his virtue-and-vice maxims, Cordoba's jurist Averroes, legal-team veteran Francis Bacon, natural-law theorist of war Hugo Grotius, law-degree holders Descartes and Leibniz, Montesquieu of the separation of powers, Bentham (panopticon architect whose utilitarianism lets ends justify means like waterboarding), and legal positivists Hart and Dworkin. Its running joke is that the lawyer-sophist connection is as old as philosophy itself, which is precisely the stereotype The Good Wife plays against.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 27 "Shooting with Confidence" — Kevin Kinghorn asks why practice stars like Kentucky's Josh Carrier suddenly choke in games and argues, via Bernard Williams's 'Deciding to Believe', that a player cannot simply choose to believe her next shot will go in: beliefs aim at truth, so a belief known to be self-chosen would not be a belief at all, any more than a mapmaker could 'choose' where to put Florida. Instead, desire and fear shape belief indirectly - Francis Bacon's 'whatever a man wishes were true, that he more readily believes' explains Larry Bird's unshakeable confidence, while fear of being the goat (Fred Brown's 1982 pass, Chris Webber's timeout) sabotages the underconfident. The practical strategies are to stockpile evidence of success through goals and visualization, or to remove the feared consequences of missing, as Rick Pitino did by publicly promising Kenny Walker he would stay a Knick as long as he kept shooting.

## Alvin Goldman

*b. 1938 · 12 chapters in the corpus.*

Alvin Goldman (b. 1938) is an American philosopher who has been a central figure in epistemology and the philosophy of mind. He is a leading proponent of reliabilism, the view that a belief counts as knowledge when it is produced by a reliable, truth-conducive process, offered as one response to the Gettier problem. Goldman also helped found social epistemology, the systematic study of how social practices and institutions bear on the acquisition of knowledge, and contributed to debates on simulation theory in the understanding of other minds.

### The Gettier Problem

The Gettier problem, named for Edmund Gettier's brief 1963 paper, challenges the long-standing definition of knowledge as justified true belief. Gettier presented cases in which a person holds a belief that is both true and justified yet intuitively fails to count as knowledge, because the belief is true only by luck—its justification and its truth are connected in the wrong way. The problem prompted decades of work in epistemology attempting to add a fourth condition or reformulate the analysis so as to rule out such accidentally true justified beliefs.

- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 13 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Kevin Kinghorn uses virtue epistemology (Sosa, Code) to solve the puzzle of why Uncle Andrew alone hears only roaring when Aslan sings Narnia into being: he fails all four intellectual virtues. He does not value truth for its own sake (unlike Frank the Cabby), indulges wishful thinking (like Edmund defending the Witch for Turkish Delight, or imagining Jadis fancies him), lets fear dictate belief (terror of the animals he has vivisected), and lacks Socratic self-knowledge, which the dragonized Eustace painfully acquires. A closing reading of Prince Caspian has each character's ability to see Aslan track their earlier trust in Lucy's testimony: sin blinds, and faith produces its own authenticating evidence.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 12 "Introduction" — Frames Part II's epistemology chapters. Jacoby's chapter uses Stan Marsh debunking TV psychic John Edward, holistic healers, and Mormon belief to teach the ethics of belief against Pascal's wager; Lawrence's uses The Matrix to pose the skeptical problem and Descartes' response; Silverman's uses Adama's lie about Earth in Battlestar Galactica to raise the Gettier problem and the Clifford–James dispute over believing without sufficient evidence.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Silverman uses Adama's 'true lie' about Earth to motivate the Gettier problem: Starbuck's belief that Earth exists is true and justified by Adama's testimony, yet because that testimony is a lie, her justified true belief is not knowledge — just as Helo's true belief that the woman before him is 'Sharon' rests on mistaking Boomer for Athena. Goldman's reliabilism then questions whether sight, memory, and testimony are reliable belief-formers in a world of humanoid Cylons, weighing Hume's suspicion of testimony against Plantinga's defense of it. Finally Clifford's evidentialism is set against James's will to believe: the Colonials' forced, momentous choice to seek Earth shows that in an uncertain world pragmatic belief can be reasonable — 'so say we all.'
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 8 "Education never ends Watson. It is a series of lessons with the greatest for" — J. Solomon Johnson asks whether Holmes's conclusions are knowledge or luck, walking through justified true belief with a Holmesian Gettier case (Watson rightly believing the killer was a former ship hand for the wrong reason), Moore's proof that knowledge entails belief, and Russell's stopped clock as an unsafe belief. BBC Sherlock's fake Vermeer and the 2009 film's 'resurrected' Lord Blackwood illustrate beliefs that fail safety or sensitivity across nearby possible worlds, while 'The Stock-Broker's Clerk' shows Holmes's observation of the scorched slippers making his belief sensitive. The verdict: Holmes is justified by the track record of his own expert methods, a professional billiards player rather than a beginner's-luck fluke, though real-world imitators could never rule out enough alternatives to match him.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 14 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Richard Greene asks what, if anything, walkers know. Rick's optimistic feeling that Lori and Carl survived turns out true, yet is not knowledge - true belief is necessary but insufficient, the gap Gettier cases exploit - and since walkers can never weigh evidence or think about their thoughts, only externalist, reliability-based accounts of knowledge can count them as knowers. Walker behavior defeats Jenner's 'mindless instinct' line: Jenny turning the handle of her old house, the little girl walker retrieving her teddy bear, a walker smashing the department store window with a rock, and the horde seeing through Rick and Glenn's gut disguise once rain washes the scent away. Zombie knowledge is real but limited to simple things recalled from the person's past, the more complex the task the less likely they know it.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 20 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Robert Arp argues that Jeopardy! contestants display only declarative memory - the mere recalling level of Bloom's Taxonomy, which trained apes like Koko and Kanzi can approximate - rather than genuine smarts. Working through the Theaetetus analysis of knowledge as justified true belief, with the correspondence theory of truth and Aristotle's demand for explanation and evidence, he shows that a lucky Final Jeopardy! guess ('What is tree pulp?') is a true belief that falls short of knowledge because it is true only by accident. Real knowledge lives at the analysis, synthesis, and especially evaluation levels - constructing and critiquing arguments - though he concedes many contestants can probably do this off-stage, so it would be a fallacy of hasty conclusion to insist they all ain't smart.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 14 "Psych and Philosophy" — The Senors use Psych to separate true belief from knowledge: Shawn's hunch that Shabby the sea lion was murdered is true but shabbily evidenced, and his justified, true belief that a Clayton family member sabotaged the plane fails to be knowledge when the killer turns out to be a son-in-law he had no reason to think existed - a textbook Gettier case from 'He Dead.' They then weigh the two main theories of justification, evidentialism (with its base rates and prior probabilities) and reliabilism, and both vindicate the careful, methodical work of Lassiter and Juliet while Shawn's trigger-happy belief-forming habit strikes out twice. Shawn is redeemed only as an evidence-generator whose disregard for priors takes 'impossible' suspects like a murdered sea lion seriously, so that pairing his talents with the detectives' rigor yields the complete detective.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 28 "Psych and Philosophy" — Ronda Bowen argues that because Shawn delivers true conclusions under a false justification (psychic power), the SBPD's beliefs are Gettier-style justified true beliefs rather than knowledge, using Plato's Theaetetus (perception and true judgment fail as definitions) as the frame and Gettier's Smith/Jones and Ford/Brown cases to model episodes like 'Spellingg Bee,' where the police infer Miklous's guilt from Shawn's staged psychic demonstration. John Hawthorne's lottery propositions explain why Lassiter's 'Shawn isn't a psychic' certainty can never be fully justified, and the chapter closes on internalism versus externalism and the reliability of testimony, concluding the detectives become internally justified only when they re-derive Shawn's conclusions through their own reasoning.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 30 "Psych and Philosophy" — Courtland Lewis replays Plato's Theaetetus with Shawn and Henry to show that perception and true judgment fail as accounts of knowledge, then recasts both Gettier cases with Psych material: Chief Vick's justified-but-lucky belief about the chief-of-police job, and Juliet's disjunction 'Shawn is a psychic or Gus is in Mazatlan.' Since justified true belief is not knowledge, he argues Shawn's trained senses fit reliabilism - distinguished from lucky predictors like Leonard Koppett and probed through Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp against Gus's super sniffer - and closes by combining reliabilist-foundationalism (Alston's two levels of knowledge), coherence theory, and Klein's infinitism into Shawn's observe-eliminate-conclude method.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 13 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter turns Raylan's claim that shooting Tommy Bucks was 'justified' into a question of epistemic justification, expounding Plato's Meno definition of knowledge as justified true belief, Gettier's 1963 counterexamples (rebuilt with Boyd truly but luckily predicting that a marshal will be arrested), and the repairs of Goldman's no-false-causal-link condition and Harman's inference to the best explanation. It then grades the show's reasoners: Raylan knows the Crowes rather than Boyd killed Wade Messer, Boyd knows Cassie milks the revival snakes' venom, Art Mullen does not yet know Raylan helped Winona return the evidence-room money, and gut-feeling victims like Ellen May do not know what they saw. Against Humean skepticism about cause and effect it defends inductive, detective-style knowledge - Raylan can know who done it without courtroom proof.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 7 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Using 'Flowers for Charlie', where a placebo pill convinces two scientists and even the Waitress that Charlie has become a genius, the chapter asks what actually makes something philosophy. Sounding smart is not philosophy: big words, the Sokal-style hoax paper submitted to a leading journal, and the 'Guru Effect' of credulous admirers all fail, yet Charlie's pronouncements turn out true by sheer luck - which is exactly Edmund Gettier's problem of epistemic luck illustrated with the broken-clock example. Since we can never verify our premises or our reasoning, the chapter sides with Aristotle's response to Plato's theory of forms that we can never determine what a thing is, only what it is not, and concludes the show is philosophical precisely because the Gang is the exact antithesis of reality, truth, and right action.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 21 "10. Does Bates Know Who Raped Anna" — The Nisleys ask whether Bates's belief that Green raped Anna counts as knowledge. His belief is true, and Plato's Theaetetus defines knowledge as justified true belief, but Mrs. Hughes's false testimony, Anna's denials, and mere observed flirting mean Bates's reasons are defective: his belief could be true by coincidence, a Gettier-style failure in which truth is not earned by justification. The chapter also examines testimony - a reliable testifier like Mrs. Hughes would normally confer justification, but she deliberately lies - and concludes with Anna's own verdict that Bates 'might have suspected, but he did not know.'
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 28 "16. Getting at the Truth" — The chapter sets out the Platonic justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge with Discworld examples—Archchancellor Ridcully as a fallible authority, the physics of thaum particles as coherentist justification—before constructing a Discworld Gettier case in which a young wizard sees a fake level-seven wizard killed and truly but accidentally reports that 'a level seven wizard was killed.' It then tests the standard repairs, applying Nozick's truth-tracking function and Goldman's causation function to a case where a man blames the notorious Reacher Gilt for a theft actually committed by the dwarf he bumped into, and argues that neither truth-tracking nor specificity makes the problem go away. The upshot is that Discworlders, used to expecting to be wrong, may let go of false 'knowledge' more easily than our confidently wrong Roundworld.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 28 "16. How Close Is That World to Our World" — Brett Coppenger treats the show as a nearby possible world identical to ours until the 1930s, then uses Gettier-style cases — Joe Blake forming justified true beliefs while driving through Alvin Goldman's Barn Façade County — to show such beliefs can still fail to be knowledge. Robert Nozick's truth-tracking conditions, defined via what happens in the closest possible worlds, handle the barns but generate 'abominable conjunctions' (knowing Jones killed the Crown Prince while not knowing the Crown Prince was killed), and the chapter closes on the thought that the large stock of shared knowledge is exactly what makes that dystopia feel only a few big events from our world.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 24 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Builds the justified-true-belief account of knowledge from Bluth cases (Tobias's belief in his own acting lacks justification, Michael's belief that he crashed the car under Lucille's manipulation lacks truth), then shows the writers smuggling Gettier cases into the show: George Sr. 'knows for a fact' the government has no case via Cindi Lightballoon's blind faith, Buster forms the true belief that Oscar is his father from George Sr. disguised as Oscar, and Michael's disbelief of Maggie Lizer is luckily true despite the swapped pregnancy bodysuit. The chapter closes by surveying fixes: demanding certainty, Russell's no-false-premises condition, and Goldman-style causal theories of knowing.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 30 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — In the method of ordinary language philosophy (Wittgenstein, Austin, Ryle), Stern and Wilkinson defend the Dude's retort to Jesus as no misuse of 'opinion': knowledge is justified true belief, undermined by Gettier-style epistemic luck, and opinions are beliefs supported only by subjective justification — like the taste of White Russians, Locke's secondary qualities — rather than public evidence. Jesus's claim that he and Liam will 'fuck you up' is a prediction that could in principle be publicly justified, but with no available evidence it is an unsupported opinion; Donny's gut-feeling Raiders pick shows opinions need not concern 'matters of opinion', and it is stubborn Walter who is truly 'opinionated'.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 21 "10. Does Bates Know Who Raped Anna" — The Nisleys ask whether Bates's conviction that Mr. Green raped Anna counts as knowledge, starting from the Theaetetus's definition of knowledge as justified true belief. Bates's belief is true, but his evidential position is compromised: Mrs. Hughes, though genuinely reliable, gives him false testimony pointing to a stranger, Anna denies it was Green, and his own grounds (Green's flirting and Green's admission that he left the concert) are too weak, so the truth of his belief is largely coincidental, exactly the Gettier predicament that true belief is not sufficient for knowledge. The chapter applies reliabilist reasoning about testimony to conclude that Bates 'might have suspected, but he did not know.'
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 23 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Abraham Schwab turns Ygritte's 'You know nothing, Jon Snow' into a theory of epistemic humility: Jon misreads wildling courtship norms, Sam's dragonglass shatters on wight Small Paul, Lord Mormont assumes Mance fights like a southern king and pays for it at the Fist of First Men, while Arya's accurate self-knowledge keeps her alive. Formalizing with justified true belief - Sam's lucky dagger thrust is not knowledge, and the Watch's warranted belief that the dead Othor was harmless justifies falsity - he uses Lysa's letter, which sent Ned to King's Landing on a lie, to ask what justification is: Descartes's absolute certainty is too strict, reliabilism vindicates testimony ('dark wings, dark words'), so that only Sansa need witness Ned's beheading for the Starks to know it, and between Melisandre's circular dogma about Azor Ahai and total skepticism, moderate skepticism best governs belief - a humility the south lacked about the Horn of Winter.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 14 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Richard Greene surveys zombie types, from the radio-using corpse of Return of the Living Dead to White Zombie's servants, to fix walkers as the standard zombie worth asking what they know. Against Dr. Jenner's 'mindless instinct' verdict he cites the little girl walker retrieving her teddy bear, Jenny working her former home's doorknob, walkers breaking a shop window with a rock, and their sniffing out Rick and Glenn's gut disguise as evidence of genuine beliefs. He argues that zombie knowledge, which cannot involve weighing evidence, supports externalist, reliability-based accounts of knowledge over internalist ones, and that walkers know only simple things recalled from past experience—the more complex the task, the less likely they know it.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 13 "“Freaks of Nature” Extrasensory Perception and the Paranormal in the Films of David Cronenberg" — Keith Allen uses Stereo, Scanners, and The Dead Zone to explore the philosophy of ESP: telepathy and precognition challenge C. D. Broad's 'basic limiting principles' about causation (action at a distance, backward causation, changing the future). He asks whether ESP has the phenomenal 'tang' of genuine perception (Hume on force/vivacity; Nagel's 'what it is like'), and uses BonJour's reliable-clairvoyant Norman case plus Gettier to argue about internalist justification and knowledge, asking whether Johnny Smith needs reasons to trust his precognitive visions.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica to explore knowledge as justified true belief. Adama's 'true lie' about knowing Earth's location makes Starbuck's belief in Earth a Gettier case, a justified true belief resting on false justification. He tests Adama's testimony against Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for spotting Cylons; memory deceives Boomer and Tigh) and Hume's skepticism about testimony versus Plantinga's defense of it. Finally, against Clifford's evidentialism he deploys William James's 'will to believe,' arguing that faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice that gives the Colonials purpose.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Eric Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica's Adama, who lies that he knows Earth's location, to run the Gettier problem: Starbuck's true belief that Earth exists rests on a false justification (that Adama knows), so it is justified-true-belief without being knowledge. He tests testimony via Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for telling Cylons from humans) and the Hume/Locke/Plantinga debate over testimony's epistemic role. He closes with James's 'will to believe': faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice where agnosticism forfeits meaning, so belief without certainty can be reasonable.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 51 "48. The Matrix as Philosophy Understanding Knowledge, Belief, Choice, and Reality" — Perez reads the Matrix trilogy as a sustained argument about how choosing what to believe and 'know' shapes the reality we live in. He opens with Descartes' dream problem and cogito, contrasting Descartes' foundationalism with Rorty's anti-foundationalism to explain Cypher's choice to reject reality for the Matrix's certitude, and uses Searle's brute vs. institutional facts (the cookies, the steak, 'there is no spoon') to show social reality is constructed. Against the fatalism of the Oracle, Architect, and Merovingian, he argues nearly every character makes free choices, and resolves the tension via Hume's compatibilism — liberty requires necessity, and choices gain meaning only in response to causality — while noting agent-causation objections (Reid, O'Connor, Rowe) that make Neo's 'Because I choose to' significant. Gettier's justified-true-belief critique and Plato's Cave frame the knowledge and enlightenment themes.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 61 "58. Tom Sawyer as Philosopher Lying and Deception on the Mississippi" — The chapter treats Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer novels as applied epistemology, arguing lying is far broader and more varied than spoken falsehood. Using Augustine's intent-to-deceive definition it analyzes Tom whitewashing the fence, the blood oath about Injun Joe's murder, Huck's 'sacrifice lie' about smallpox, and disguises as 'showing the false' (mimicking, inventing, decoying) versus 'hiding the truth' (masking, repackaging, dazzling). It invokes Gettier's method of counterexamples as a parallel to Twain showing the traditional definition of lying is too narrow, and links Tom's gaslighting of Aunt Sally and evolutionary/self-deception to modern fake news and deepfakes.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 17 "7. Knowledge, Space, and Time" — The chapter uses the TARDIS to defend a 'block universe' theory of spacetime over Presentism (since the Doctor visits past and future), then turns to epistemology, distinguishing belief from knowledge and 'belief in' the Doctor from 'belief that' he exists. It re-stages Gettier's justified-true-belief counterexample as picking the Doctor's next companion by a blue jean jacket, surveys Descartes's Cogito foundationalism, Hume's induction, and Reid's direct perception, and endorses Alston's reliabilist two-level foundationalism plus Klein's infinitism. It argues the Doctor's benefit-of-the-doubt toward non-rational creatures fits a reliabilist 'lower level' of knowledge and an imaginative, engaged, virtuous (Zagzebski) search for truth.

### Reliabilism

Reliabilism is a family of theories in epistemology, associated especially with Alvin Goldman, that ground the justification or knowledge-status of a belief in the reliability of the process that produced it. On this view a belief counts as justified when it is formed by a process—such as accurate perception or sound reasoning—that tends to yield true beliefs, rather than by any evidence the believer can consciously cite. Reliabilism arose partly as a response to Gettier-style cases and shifts the focus of epistemic evaluation from internal reasons to the truth-conducive workings of belief-forming mechanisms.

- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Silverman uses Adama's 'true lie' about Earth to motivate the Gettier problem: Starbuck's belief that Earth exists is true and justified by Adama's testimony, yet because that testimony is a lie, her justified true belief is not knowledge — just as Helo's true belief that the woman before him is 'Sharon' rests on mistaking Boomer for Athena. Goldman's reliabilism then questions whether sight, memory, and testimony are reliable belief-formers in a world of humanoid Cylons, weighing Hume's suspicion of testimony against Plantinga's defense of it. Finally Clifford's evidentialism is set against James's will to believe: the Colonials' forced, momentous choice to seek Earth shows that in an uncertain world pragmatic belief can be reasonable — 'so say we all.'
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 13 "More than a Feeling" — Rachel Robison-Greene asks whether Dexter's rule to 'be sure' actually gives him knowledge of his victims' guilt. Distinguishing Cartesian certainty - skeptical hypotheses about deceiving senses, dreams and evil demons, echoing The Matrix - from mere felt certainty, she tests the belief-truth-justification analysis of knowledge traced to Plato against the show: LaGuerta's witness theory fails on belief, Deb's conviction that Neil Perry is the Ice Truck Killer fails on truth, and Astor's accusation of Dexter fails on justification. Neither strong internalism (Dexter straps down Jamie Jaworski without knowing how the murder was done), weak internalism, coherence theory (his false but coherent case against Jonathan Farrow), nor reliabilism (his spidey-sense is explicitly not sufficient by his own admission) captures his practice, so his 'certainty' is just a feeling - and the people on his table may include ones he does not know to be guilty.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 8 "Education never ends Watson. It is a series of lessons with the greatest for" — J. Solomon Johnson asks whether Holmes's conclusions are knowledge or luck, walking through justified true belief with a Holmesian Gettier case (Watson rightly believing the killer was a former ship hand for the wrong reason), Moore's proof that knowledge entails belief, and Russell's stopped clock as an unsafe belief. BBC Sherlock's fake Vermeer and the 2009 film's 'resurrected' Lord Blackwood illustrate beliefs that fail safety or sensitivity across nearby possible worlds, while 'The Stock-Broker's Clerk' shows Holmes's observation of the scorched slippers making his belief sensitive. The verdict: Holmes is justified by the track record of his own expert methods, a professional billiards player rather than a beginner's-luck fluke, though real-world imitators could never rule out enough alternatives to match him.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 128 "Philip K. Dick and Philosophy" — This section rebuilds the evidential case for the precogs from their verified early track record, which was free of errors of commission (predicting murders that never happened) and omission (missing murders that did). The still-zero present-murder rate rules out omissions, and cases like Howard Marks, caught mid-attempt, form a random and representative sample of the precogs' predictions showing commissions have not crept in, since arrest-timing delays correlate with nothing systematic about guilt.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 129 "Philip K. Dick and Philosophy" — The section concedes that Precrime techs erred in the Anne Lively case, failing to notice that some previsions showed ripples moving toward the shore and others away. But it argues this is only the general problem of interpreting any evidence, from confessions to forensics to eyewitness reports, and that human fallibility does not imply unreliability, any more than fallible traditional policing meant murders should go uninvestigated.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 14 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Richard Greene asks what, if anything, walkers know. Rick's optimistic feeling that Lori and Carl survived turns out true, yet is not knowledge - true belief is necessary but insufficient, the gap Gettier cases exploit - and since walkers can never weigh evidence or think about their thoughts, only externalist, reliability-based accounts of knowledge can count them as knowers. Walker behavior defeats Jenner's 'mindless instinct' line: Jenny turning the handle of her old house, the little girl walker retrieving her teddy bear, a walker smashing the department store window with a rock, and the horde seeing through Rick and Glenn's gut disguise once rain washes the scent away. Zombie knowledge is real but limited to simple things recalled from the person's past, the more complex the task the less likely they know it.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 14 "Psych and Philosophy" — The Senors use Psych to separate true belief from knowledge: Shawn's hunch that Shabby the sea lion was murdered is true but shabbily evidenced, and his justified, true belief that a Clayton family member sabotaged the plane fails to be knowledge when the killer turns out to be a son-in-law he had no reason to think existed - a textbook Gettier case from 'He Dead.' They then weigh the two main theories of justification, evidentialism (with its base rates and prior probabilities) and reliabilism, and both vindicate the careful, methodical work of Lassiter and Juliet while Shawn's trigger-happy belief-forming habit strikes out twice. Shawn is redeemed only as an evidence-generator whose disregard for priors takes 'impossible' suspects like a murdered sea lion seriously, so that pairing his talents with the detectives' rigor yields the complete detective.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 28 "Psych and Philosophy" — Ronda Bowen argues that because Shawn delivers true conclusions under a false justification (psychic power), the SBPD's beliefs are Gettier-style justified true beliefs rather than knowledge, using Plato's Theaetetus (perception and true judgment fail as definitions) as the frame and Gettier's Smith/Jones and Ford/Brown cases to model episodes like 'Spellingg Bee,' where the police infer Miklous's guilt from Shawn's staged psychic demonstration. John Hawthorne's lottery propositions explain why Lassiter's 'Shawn isn't a psychic' certainty can never be fully justified, and the chapter closes on internalism versus externalism and the reliability of testimony, concluding the detectives become internally justified only when they re-derive Shawn's conclusions through their own reasoning.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 30 "Psych and Philosophy" — Courtland Lewis replays Plato's Theaetetus with Shawn and Henry to show that perception and true judgment fail as accounts of knowledge, then recasts both Gettier cases with Psych material: Chief Vick's justified-but-lucky belief about the chief-of-police job, and Juliet's disjunction 'Shawn is a psychic or Gus is in Mazatlan.' Since justified true belief is not knowledge, he argues Shawn's trained senses fit reliabilism - distinguished from lucky predictors like Leonard Koppett and probed through Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp against Gus's super sniffer - and closes by combining reliabilist-foundationalism (Alston's two levels of knowledge), coherence theory, and Klein's infinitism into Shawn's observe-eliminate-conclude method.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 24 "The Devil and Philosophy" — John Karavitis (with tongue-in-cheek co-author 'Lucifer') treats The Ninth Gate as an epistemology case study, sorting the characters' beliefs about the Devil - true-believer Balkan, skeptic book-dealer Corso, the occult-tourist Order of the Silver Serpent - and testing them against Plato's Theaetetus definitions of knowledge as perception, true belief, and justified true belief. Balkan's justification is only an internally coherent web of book-learned beliefs, while Corso's external evidence (engravings signed 'LCF,' his journey's experiences) is weighed by the general reliability of his sources. Descartes' dreaming and the deceiving demon then leave the viewer skeptical that the Devil ever appeared at all.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 20 "9. How the Doctor Knows" — Smithka argues the Doctor is a reliabilist about knowledge rather than a Cartesian strong foundationalist: using 'Amy's Choice,' 'The Beast Below' (the glass of water, the engine room, Amy's inference that the Star Whale came willingly), 'Silence in the Library' (the chicken-leg experiment implicating the Vashta Nerada), and Davros's Dalek trials in 'Genesis of the Daleks,' she shows him trusting perception in the right causal chain and reasoning inductively and abductively—Peirce's inference to the best explanation—instead of demanding Cartesian certainty. Against Descartes's dream and evil-genius skepticism, updated as Putnam-style brain-in-a-vat scenarios via the Dream Crabs of 'Last Christmas' and the Dream Lord's two-worlds game, she deploys Goldman's three criteria for perceptual knowledge: justification is packed into reliable belief-forming processes, and doubt is warranted only in known abnormal contexts like funhouses or Dream Lord games.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 21 "10. Does Bates Know Who Raped Anna" — The Nisleys ask whether Bates's belief that Green raped Anna counts as knowledge. His belief is true, and Plato's Theaetetus defines knowledge as justified true belief, but Mrs. Hughes's false testimony, Anna's denials, and mere observed flirting mean Bates's reasons are defective: his belief could be true by coincidence, a Gettier-style failure in which truth is not earned by justification. The chapter also examines testimony - a reliable testifier like Mrs. Hughes would normally confer justification, but she deliberately lies - and concludes with Anna's own verdict that Bates 'might have suspected, but he did not know.'
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 14 "4. Special Epistemic Agent Dale Cooper" — A chapter-length epistemology tutorial delivered as Cooper's tapes to Diane, applying the justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge to his investigation. An Invitation to Love example (Chet's Ouija board actually guided by Jade's ghost) distinguishes internalist justification from externalist/reliabilist justification — a belief formed by a truth-conducive process can be justified even when the believer lacks reasons — and Cooper then earns internal justification by treating his dreams and visions as a hypothesis that yields testable predictions: "sometimes her arms bend back" matches Albert's autopsy, and the Giant's three pronouncements (man in a smiling bag, the owls are not what they seem, without chemicals he points) are confirmed by Jacques' hanging body bag, Major Briggs' deep-space transmission, and MIKE emerging off his haloperidol. The chapter cautions against confirming vague prophecies like bunny-shaped clouds, concluding Cooper becomes a truly "Special Epistemic Agent."
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 9 "A Strange Ending" — Manninen applies virtue epistemology — built on Aristotle's virtue ethics and golden mean — to the four students of the Ancient One, asking not what they knew of the mystic arts but how they knew it. Strange's photographic memory exemplifies reliabilist epistemic ability, while Montmarquet's responsibilist virtues (impartiality, intellectual courage) are measured against Pangborn's self-serving magic, Kaecilius's courage without impartiality, and Mordo's epistemic rigidity and blind deference to authority ('no more questions'), each a vice of excess or deficiency. The Book of Cagliostro frames Wong's 'no knowledge in Kamar-Taj is forbidden, only certain practices,' and Strange emerges closest to the balanced intellectual character, though Aristotle demands consistency, not a single virtuous act.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 21 "10. Does Bates Know Who Raped Anna" — The Nisleys ask whether Bates's conviction that Mr. Green raped Anna counts as knowledge, starting from the Theaetetus's definition of knowledge as justified true belief. Bates's belief is true, but his evidential position is compromised: Mrs. Hughes, though genuinely reliable, gives him false testimony pointing to a stranger, Anna denies it was Green, and his own grounds (Green's flirting and Green's admission that he left the concert) are too weak, so the truth of his belief is largely coincidental, exactly the Gettier predicament that true belief is not sufficient for knowledge. The chapter applies reliabilist reasoning about testimony to conclude that Bates 'might have suspected, but he did not know.'
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 23 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Abraham Schwab turns Ygritte's 'You know nothing, Jon Snow' into a theory of epistemic humility: Jon misreads wildling courtship norms, Sam's dragonglass shatters on wight Small Paul, Lord Mormont assumes Mance fights like a southern king and pays for it at the Fist of First Men, while Arya's accurate self-knowledge keeps her alive. Formalizing with justified true belief - Sam's lucky dagger thrust is not knowledge, and the Watch's warranted belief that the dead Othor was harmless justifies falsity - he uses Lysa's letter, which sent Ned to King's Landing on a lie, to ask what justification is: Descartes's absolute certainty is too strict, reliabilism vindicates testimony ('dark wings, dark words'), so that only Sansa need witness Ned's beheading for the Starks to know it, and between Melisandre's circular dogma about Azor Ahai and total skepticism, moderate skepticism best governs belief - a humility the south lacked about the Horn of Winter.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 14 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Richard Greene surveys zombie types, from the radio-using corpse of Return of the Living Dead to White Zombie's servants, to fix walkers as the standard zombie worth asking what they know. Against Dr. Jenner's 'mindless instinct' verdict he cites the little girl walker retrieving her teddy bear, Jenny working her former home's doorknob, walkers breaking a shop window with a rock, and their sniffing out Rick and Glenn's gut disguise as evidence of genuine beliefs. He argues that zombie knowledge, which cannot involve weighing evidence, supports externalist, reliability-based accounts of knowledge over internalist ones, and that walkers know only simple things recalled from past experience—the more complex the task, the less likely they know it.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 13 "“Freaks of Nature” Extrasensory Perception and the Paranormal in the Films of David Cronenberg" — Keith Allen uses Stereo, Scanners, and The Dead Zone to explore the philosophy of ESP: telepathy and precognition challenge C. D. Broad's 'basic limiting principles' about causation (action at a distance, backward causation, changing the future). He asks whether ESP has the phenomenal 'tang' of genuine perception (Hume on force/vivacity; Nagel's 'what it is like'), and uses BonJour's reliable-clairvoyant Norman case plus Gettier to argue about internalist justification and knowledge, asking whether Johnny Smith needs reasons to trust his precognitive visions.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 14 "4. Special Epistemic Agent Dale Cooper" — Written as Cooper's dictations to Diane, Rard uses the justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge and the internalism/externalism debate to ask whether Cooper is justified in trusting dreams and visions in a world with supernatural forces. Through the Invitation to Love Ouija-board example she shows how a reliable but unrecognized source yields externally justified belief (reliabilism); Cooper then earns internal justification the way one tests a hypothesis—treating the giant's predictions ('man in a smiling bag', 'the owls are not what they seem', 'without chemicals he points') as testable predictions that come true, making him a 'special epistemic agent.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica to explore knowledge as justified true belief. Adama's 'true lie' about knowing Earth's location makes Starbuck's belief in Earth a Gettier case, a justified true belief resting on false justification. He tests Adama's testimony against Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for spotting Cylons; memory deceives Boomer and Tigh) and Hume's skepticism about testimony versus Plantinga's defense of it. Finally, against Clifford's evidentialism he deploys William James's 'will to believe,' arguing that faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice that gives the Colonials purpose.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 14 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Roche's 'Seeing Snakes' attacks the psychedelicist claim (William James on nitrous oxide, Huxley's 'reducing valve,' Leary) that drugs including cannabis reveal reality-as-it-is. He deploys Russell's line that we 'can make no distinction between the man who eats little and sees heaven and the man who drinks much and sees snakes,' and a reliabilist demand that knowledge have a source proven reliable over independently verifiable cases, to argue drug 'revelations' are indistinguishable from delusion. Foucault is cited that drugs have 'nothing to do with truth and falsity,' and Nietzsche's Dionysian veil-of-Maya passage is used as an example of the mystical rhetoric he debunks.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Eric Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica's Adama, who lies that he knows Earth's location, to run the Gettier problem: Starbuck's true belief that Earth exists rests on a false justification (that Adama knows), so it is justified-true-belief without being knowledge. He tests testimony via Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for telling Cylons from humans) and the Hume/Locke/Plantinga debate over testimony's epistemic role. He closes with James's 'will to believe': faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice where agnosticism forfeits meaning, so belief without certainty can be reasonable.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 17 "7. Knowledge, Space, and Time" — The chapter uses the TARDIS to defend a 'block universe' theory of spacetime over Presentism (since the Doctor visits past and future), then turns to epistemology, distinguishing belief from knowledge and 'belief in' the Doctor from 'belief that' he exists. It re-stages Gettier's justified-true-belief counterexample as picking the Doctor's next companion by a blue jean jacket, surveys Descartes's Cogito foundationalism, Hume's induction, and Reid's direct perception, and endorses Alston's reliabilist two-level foundationalism plus Klein's infinitism. It argues the Doctor's benefit-of-the-doubt toward non-rational creatures fits a reliabilist 'lower level' of knowledge and an imaginative, engaged, virtuous (Zagzebski) search for truth.

### The Will to Believe

The will to believe is William James's argument that in certain cases we are entitled to adopt a belief on faith, before the evidence is conclusive, when the choice is genuine, momentous, and cannot be settled by intellect alone. James responded to the demand that we withhold assent until proof arrives, contending that some truths—especially moral and religious ones—only become available to those willing to commit in advance. Refusing to decide, he noted, is itself a choice with consequences, so passionate belief can be legitimate rather than a lapse in reason.

- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 13 "Who Should Be Committed" — Thomas Senor argues that rooting for the perennially losing Cubs is rationally and morally on a par with religious commitment: genuine fandom, like faith, is loyalty that survives repeated disappointment (distinguished from the zealot's 'my team right or wrong' via the Portland Trailblazers' 'Jailblazers' era). Since beliefs and fan loyalties are not under direct voluntary control, he rereads Pascal's wager not as choosing to believe but as cultivating belief indirectly: attending Mass the way moving to Chicago and following the Cubs daily can make you a fan. The believer's epistemic optimism toward religious experience and the devout's second-order hope in dark times mirror the Cubs fan's springtime optimism, so neither Cubs fans nor the religious should be committed.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 39 "21b" — A paired metaphysics debate on whether superstition helps performance. Steven Streeter argues yes: baseball's mystery-rich outcomes breed ritual (Sparky Anderson refusing to step on foul lines, Wade Boggs's chicken, Nomar Garciaparra's glove taps), whose invisible forces — like black holes — can be inferred from their measurable effects on attention, preparation, and focus, with William James's belief-makes-reality as the capstone. Neil Feit counters no: on the counterfactual account of helping, a player cured of superstition would perform the same since his athletic ability is untouched, routines that aid concentration need involve no magical belief, and the burden of proof lies with the believer.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 28 "“A New Hope”" — Long stages William Clifford's ethics of belief against William James's will to believe, with Luke Skywalker as James's exemplar. Clifford's shipowner story condemns faith as 'wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone,' which would convict Luke of immorality when he switches off his targeting computer and trusts the Force; James replies that where a choice is intellectually undecidable and a genuine option - live, forced, and momentous, like Luke's turn to the Jedi life or Obi-Wan's response to Leia's hologram - pragmatic faith is justified and even salvific. Faith can create truths: Han flying into the asteroid field, Luke's unjustified belief that there is good in Vader bringing Anakin back, the author's faith in his students, and Martin Luther King Jr.'s dream - all illustrating 'a new hope.'
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 15 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Steven Lovell reads the Green Witch's enchantment in The Silver Chair (the sun is only a copy of the lamp, Aslan only a bigger cat, Narnia a children's tale) as Lewis's staging of the Freudian critique of religion, and answers that similarity cannot tell copy from original, that the genetic fallacy vitiates arguing from a belief's origin, and that Aslan is 'not safe,' so Christianity is hardly wish-fulfillment (Augustine's restless heart and Pascal's God-shaped hole point the other way). Puddleglum's stamping out the fire and vow to live 'as like a Narnian as I can even if there isn't any Narnia' is defended through Pascal's Wager and James's 'The Will to Believe': the reality of Narnia is a live, forced, and momentous option that may legitimately be decided on passional grounds.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 11 "Poker and Philosophy" — Ventimiglia mines No-Limit Hold'em for seven lessons philosophers also teach: we lack certain knowledge (Descartes' cogito is the famous quest for certainty, but philosophy's own history of disagreement proves uncertainty is the human condition), and like William James against Clifford we must still believe and act without the nuts — waiting for pocket aces while the blinds eat you alive is no strategy. Risking everything echoes Thoreau's escape from lives of quiet desperation, trusting hunches over arithmetic follows Thoreau and Peirce's sentimentalism, and the Darwin-and-Spencer competition of tournament poker hides a deeper cooperative social contract: get caught cheating and you are out of the game. It closes with Plato's four classic virtues from the Republic — wisdom, courage, moderation, and the justice of a balanced soul — as the perfection of a poker player.
- **The Beatles and Philosophy - Nothing You Can Think that Can't Be Thunk**, ch. 12 "CHAPTER 4 “A REVELATION TO BEHOLD”" — Argues that the Beatles' devotion to rock and roll was a literal religious phenomenon rather than loose metaphor: Lennon's first hearing of Elvis is analyzed as a William James-style conversion, the Radio Luxembourg broadcasts were treated 'like scripture,' Hamburg was a 'baptism by fire,' and Epstein's new suits at the Cavern were announced as 'a revelation.' Drawing on James's Varieties of Religious Experience and Pragmatism, the chapter reads Beatlemania's screaming crowds as collective ecstatic ritual and the 'toppermost of the poppermost' chant as the will-to-believe making its own truth, in the way James says truth 'happens' to an idea. Aristotle's four causes supply the metaphysical frame — the 'magic' of Liverpool and the sacred quality fans reported are formal-final causation against the material-efficient causation of disenchanted modernity — while the band's double irony ('tarrying with the negative,' after Hegel) let them hold skepticism inside belief, as in Lennon's 'flaming pie' origin parody and the 'more popular than Jesus' episode.
- **The Beatles and Philosophy - Nothing You Can Think that Can't Be Thunk**, ch. 13 "CHAPTER 5 “AN EXTREME SENSE OF DESTINY”" — Reads Bob Dylan's 'extreme sense of destiny' as lived Aristotelian final causation: Dylan's passivity about fame ('It happened like anything else happens'), his 'Jack Fate' persona, and the odyssey of 'goin' home' all treat his future self as the telos drawing him forward rather than his past pushing him. William James's Will to Believe ('faith creates its own verification') explains the self-fulfilling portents Dylan found in Gorgeous George's wink, his felt succession to Woody Guthrie, and his premonition of Joan Baez, while the chapter insists this destiny is not fatalism since Dylan could have ignored the signs and 'gone off another way.' It closes by taking Dylan at his word that 'Bobby Zimmerman' died when his namesake was killed in a 1961 motorcycle crash — a Jungian synchronicity that seals the shamanic death-and-rebirth 'transfiguration' Dylan claims for himself, where Heraclitus's river captures that the old self cannot be recovered.
