- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 20 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Von Gunten asks whether Bender, Calculon, and the robot mafia have moral worth, arguing first that they are sentient: behavioral similarity plus functional equivalence (pain as electric signals in neurons or circuits) defeat both behavior-only objections (the Sphex wasp's preprogrammed loop, knife-avoiding toy robots) and composition-based prejudice - Fry's 'I'm all squishy and flabby' defense at the Hal Institute - which would be 'biologism' analogous to racism. He then distinguishes moral patiency (Nibbler can be harmed but only behaviorally reinforced) from moral agency (deliberation and accountability), concluding that Bender's flexible life - Iron Cook, wrestling, folk music with Beck's head, jacking-on addiction - shows robots transcend their programming as humans transcend evolutionary presets. Limiting moral status to biology or species would be speciesism, so the thirty-first century's robots deserve the full protections and responsibilities humans have.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 22 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Pless asks whether Bender is responsible for his misdeeds given that MomCorp designed him to be an alcoholic kleptomaniac (revealed through Bender Vision in 'Mother's Day') and Planet Express regularly orders him into morally dirty work. Against Asimov's utilitarian Three Laws - embodied by the servile, selfless Robot 1-X of 'Obsoletely Fabulous' - Futurama's 'robot subjectivism' makes every robot a self-interested agent, and Bender's autonomy is proven by his refusal of Mom's 'kill all humans' order and by his fear of punishment in Robot Hell ('Hell Is Other Robots'), which also shows the show's universe is not morally relativist. Because Bender can rewrite his own code - his unprogrammed friendship with Fry, the adoption scam that turns heartfelt in 'The Cyber House Rules' - he sits on the same sliding scale of moral agency as humans, so if Bender can break his programming, we have no excuse for not exercising our own free will.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 20 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Zuk argues Shelley needs the monster to be a free, responsible villain for her Romantic allegory against Enlightenment science to work, then puts him on trial: libertarian free will collides with Honderich's determinism, compatibilism demands only rational responsiveness to reasons, and Strawson's regress - built on Kant's opening demand that we make ourselves morally good or evil by free choice - suggests no one is ultimately responsible for character. The monster's biography tells against guilt: benevolent toward the De Laceys, beaten by Felix, shot after saving a drowning girl, then vowing 'eternal hatred and vengeance to all mankind' - a good nature corrupted beyond his control, overpowered by passion rather than acting with a clear head. Even Victor's dying encouragement to Walton's crew ('be men, or be more than men') concedes the creation was good in itself, so the novel indicts not science but its unguided release among the prejudiced.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 35 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Cynthia Coe argues the novel's horror lies in the creature's liminality: he is neither human nor inhuman, and Victor's instant labeling of him as 'monster,' 'demon,' and 'fiend' shields Victor from his own responsibility, since the word 'monster' descends from a sign or omen we mistake for the evil itself. Freud's uncanny - the heimlich turning unheimlich, the repressed coming to light - explains why a being 'more horrid from its very resemblance' to us terrifies more than an obvious alien, a mechanism the chapter parallels with European anti-Semitism as hatred of an internal enemy. Shelley's moral point is that failures of empathy are moral failures: Victor holds the creature responsible as a free-willed demon while denying him personhood, and the tragedy grows from that contradictory projection until the neat categories of victim, monster, and evil collapse.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 8 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Jeremy Proulx reads Ender through F.W.J. Schelling's account of evil as a real, positive force rather than Augustine's mere privation of good: Ender's kicks to Stilson and Bonzo, his killing of the Giant in the mind game, and his 'I destroy them' confession all display the 'contraction into the self' Schelling thinks haunts every moral agent. He argues Graff deliberately isolates Ender to force this dark ground to the surface, and that Valentine's 'welcome to the human race' and the hive-queen's forgiveness teach Ender that evil, though never excusable, can be understood and atoned for - his fate also shows freedom tainted by a necessity we neither choose nor control.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 38 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — David Morgan unpacks the chaos theory behind Malcolm's 'I hate being right all the time', starting from Newtonian causal determinism and Laplace's demon, according to which the future is fixed and calculable - then showing that non-linear systems like weather and the park show sensitive dependence (Lorenz's butterfly effect), so even a fully determined universe is unpredictable in practice because we can never know initial conditions exactly. He raises the philosophy-of-science question of whether chaos is a property of nature or only of our computer models, and reads 'life finds a way' as Malcolm extending the same contingency to Darwinian evolution: rewind the tape and you get different species. He ends by noting Malcolm's own paradox - a chaos theorist certain of one specific doom - and settles on chaos theory predicting unpredictability: ignore tiny factors and do not be surprised when they bite you.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 14 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Sharon Kaye stages a fourteenth-century debate over a contradiction: Jesus truthfully prophesied that the Antichrist will come, yet the Antichrist remains free not to. Peter Aureoli denies bivalence for statements about the future, Thomas Bradwardine has God swap among infinite possible-world 'movies,' and Ockham's follower John of Mirecourt concludes that Jesus simply lied - each solution self-defeating or heretical. Using Ockham's Razor and her comic fantasy of seducing the Antichrist, Kaye argues the unsolvable prophecy problem helped discredit prophetic religion, ushered in theological determinism via Luther and Calvin, and opened a secular age.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 55 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Aaron Rabinowitz argues that modern Devil stories - Milton's 'Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven', Neil Gaiman's Sandman where Lucifer quits Hell like a two-weeks notice, and Mike Carey's Lucifer building a second creation whose only commandment forbids worship - reveal a Devil whose real motive is free will and autonomy in a predetermined cosmos. Rereading the serpent in Eden, the wager over Job, and the temptation of Jesus through that lens makes Lucifer look reasonable, even commendable, and since we all feel pushed around by obligations, survival needs, and neuroscience, our sympathy for the Devil is inevitable.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 75 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Robert Arp compiles the 'Devil made me do it' record: Flip Wilson's catchphrase, actual possession pleas from Christian v. State to the Demon Murder Trial of Arne Cheyenne Johnson, the M'Naghten Rule born of Daniel M'Naghten's botched assassination, the Son of Sam's possessed dog Harvey, exorcism lore from Roland Doe (The Exorcist) to Anneliese Michel (The Exorcism of Emily Rose), and the bizarre Mayo v. Satan lawsuit. The law's answer throughout is that only a defect of reason - never the Devil - robs defendants of free will, and the possession cases read better as epilepsy, schizophrenia, and negligence than as demons.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 16 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Dan Burkett defends Brody against blame for flipping the suicide-vest switch in 'Marine One' by arguing he was not free. On the desire-satisfaction view Brody freely avenge Issa, but via Locke's locked-room thought experiment (Carrie contentedly 'freely' staying in a house she cannot leave) the chapter motivates the libertarian requirement that one could have done otherwise, which Nazir's years of torture and brainwashing may have removed. The malfunctioning vest then raises moral luck - Brody is no better a person because the bomb failed - and since Dana's plea restricts his options just as coercively, the best defense grants Brody freedom throughout, making the switch blameworthy and his free choice to come home genuinely redemptive.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 17 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Littmann uses Adventure Time as a stockpile of thought experiments against free will: Finn excuses Billy (possessed by the Lich), hug-wolf Finn, amulet-Marceline, red-starved Marceline, the magically animated hat Little Dude, and crown-cursed Simon, yet punishes the Lich and Lemongrab, whose destructive desires are exactly as unchosen—Lemongrab even protests 'you made me like this.' Since deterministic causation and randomness exhaust the options, we are 'machines made of meat' wearing ice crowns inside our skulls, so deserved suffering makes no sense. The chapter concludes that just-deserts retribution (Princess Cookie's life sentence, America's prisons) should give way to deterrence, protection, and rehabilitation—freeing the Simon Petrikovs underneath.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 18 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Miller argues from Jake's croak dream, the Cosmic Owl, and the Dungeon Train's future crystal that Ooo's future is real, visible, and changeable—hence a case of soft determinism: the dream of Jake dying in space is what caused Finn to accompany him and avert it, so the only being who could have intended the change, the Owl, is the sole certain free agent in Ooo. Every alternate Finn is missing his right arm—Shoko the thief, Farmworld Finn, pillow-world Finn, the Dungeon Train elder—hinting at an epic destiny, yet Finn altered the train future once he saw where it led Jake. The chapter closes on the open question of whether choosing one's fate differs from having it thrust on one, since every choice is caused by the past no one can change.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 18 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Altmann asks whether Dracula is blameworthy for his killings: John Martin Fischer's guidance control, Kant's reason-centered morality, and Hume's 'yay/boo' approval-and-disapproval theory (the heroes' anguish over Mina) all seem to condemn him, since the Count coolly plans feedings and uses his intellect for evil. But Nagel-style luck undermines all three accounts, because Dracula never consented to his transformation, lacks the conscience needed to even recognize right and wrong, and, like the holy-wafer-branded Mina, is fixed by God's rejection with no hope of redemption - so the chapter concludes Dracula is evil yet a victim of circumstance deserving no full blame.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 21 "Dracula and Philosophy" — McKinney argues Van Helsing should have studied Dracula's brain instead of staking him, because the Count is a philosophy-of-mind thought experiment: a mind that persists unchanged across bat, wolf, mist, and human bodies refutes mind-brain identity theory and fits functionalism (the mind as one song playable in many formats), while his telepathic bond with Mina and shapeshifting probe Cartesian dualism's mind-body interaction problem. Nagel's bats show that only Dracula could tell us what it is like to echo-locate or wolf-sense; yet since nothing like his unconstrained mind exists in our world, the novel finally maps what minds are not - evidence against the immaterial mind.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 11 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Christopher Ketcham's mock lost episode 'Charlie Gets Beatified' - in which Frank fakes a water-into-wine miracle with red food dye so the Gang can monetize Charlie's canonization - frames a genuine exercise in medieval modal metaphysics. Aristotle's definition of contingency, on which opposites can occur only at different times, is set against Duns Scotus's view that something can be otherwise at the very moment it acts, so that God's immutable foreknowledge coexists with a will 'endowed with something of his own freedom'. The chapter spells out necessity, contingency, and impossibility in possible-worlds terms (a gang needs at least two members in every world; Frank is impossible in Season One) and reads 'Gun Fever Too: Still Hot' as empirical confirmation of Scotus and Olivi: the Gang holds opposite positions within a single episode, proving real contingency and free will.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 22 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Ethan Chambers asks whether we should pardon the Gang, arguing with Hume that their vices have a 'causal story' as rigid as physical law: Charlie's glue-sniffing, racism, and inability to connect trace to a Christmas Day childhood of squalor and Uncle Jack's abuse; Mac was bullied as 'Ronnie the Rat' for trying to be good and never once saw virtue pay in Philadelphia; Dennis, shaped by Frank's cruel parenting, claims and shows he cannot feel feelings, so Humean sympathy - the key moral sense - is simply beyond his reach; and Frank's 'donkey brains' asylum childhood or outright insanity directly undermines his responsibility. Knowing these psychological causes, sympathy (Hume's word for empathy) replaces blame: we blame the builders, not the house, and the chapter closes by urging compassionate rehabilitation over the show's never-ending circle of punishment and revenge.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 17 "6. Weeping Angels and Many Worlds" — Sutton argues the causal loops of 'Blink' and 'The Angels Take Manhattan' need not destroy libertarian free will: the Doctor's claim that a known future is 'written in stone' conflates ordinary foreknowledge, which leaves agents free to make the knower wrong, with infallible knowledge that only exists because the act occurs. Adapting Hugh Everett's many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics to free choices, he shows how branching timelines let the Doctor read Melody Malone, decline to break River's wrist, and still close the loop—some parallel Doctor does what the book records—while Aristotle's future contingents in De Interpretatione secure the indeterminacy of what 'will' happen. Answering the objection that branch-splitting is really fatalism, he appeals to the subjective viewpoint (what matters is 'my me'), explains how Kathy and Billy's messages in 'Blink' reach Sally on at least one branch, and solves why the Doctor is always so lucky: we follow the one branch where he survives.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 18 "7. What the Doctor Can and Can’t Change" — Delamont codifies the Whoniverse's four rules of time travel—time can be rewritten, fixed points cannot, knowing your future fixes it, and crossing your own timeline should be avoided—from cases like 'The Waters of Mars' (Adelaide's suicide restoring the fixed outcome), 'The Angels Take Manhattan' (Rory vanishing at the sight of his gravestone), 'Father's Day,' and 'The Girl Who Waited.' She then asks whether the Doctor could have avoided Trenzalore and argues the universe is hard-deterministic once amended with the laws of time travel, since rules 2–4 constrain action the way soft determinism's freedom from external forces would not allow. Tracing the causal dominoes back from the truth-field question through the Silence, River's creation, the Pandorica, and the Time Lords' pocket-universe broadcast to the crack in Amy's wall, she concludes he could not have avoided Trenzalore short of unwriting his entire history—'you can't change history if you're part of it.'
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 19 "8. Could the Doctor Have Avoided Trenzalore" — Pigliucci treats the two Trenzalore timelines of 'The Name of the Doctor' and 'The Time of the Doctor' as allohistory—an if-then counterfactual in Livy's tradition about Alexander the Great—and argues Everettian many-worlds quantum mechanics best explains how the Time Lords' one decision (granting or withholding a new regeneration cycle) can go both ways across parallel worlds. Rejecting contra-causal free will as a theological leftover, he prefers the cognitive scientist's 'volition' and defends compatibilism: the split stems from ordinary quantum-random interaction during deliberation, not magic, so the Doctor's choices are real without violating physics. Distinguishing fate from free will via Oedipus and the Doctor's 'Destiny Trap,' he concludes the Doctor was fated to make his last stand on Trenzalore as a fixed point in time, while the outcome of the siege depended on a genuine choice that, as David Deutsch puts it, thickened the stack of universes where good things happen.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 26 "10. We’re Not Free to Save Lee" — Bowman uses Telltale's Walking Dead videogame, where Lee always dies no matter what the player does, to stage the free will versus determinism debate. Laplace's demon grounds the determinist pole (the game's outcome is fixed like set particles), while Sartre's radical freedom and bad faith explain the player who says "I thought I could save both" at Hershel's farm rather than owning her choice. The chapter resolves the tension with fatalism or soft determinism - a compatibilist itinerary where Lee's death is a fixed benchmark but the player's choices in between define the character - and extends Bostrom's simulation hypothesis to ask whether we are Lee-like players inside someone else's game.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 27 "16. You Made Me First" — The chapter argues that origin stories fix character: Batman, forged by watching his parents murdered (and in Burton's film by the Joker himself - 'You made me first'), is trapped by a past that sets his trajectory, since as Schopenhauer said we can do what we will but cannot will what we will. Kal-El's origin is instead an act of hope - his parents launch him into the universe believing the wildly unlikely - which the chapter reads through William James's will-to-believe, the same faith Bruce needs to jump the chasm unroped in The Dark Knight Rises. Because the past causes the future and 'I can do whatever I want' is not free will, Bruce can never escape his tragedy, while Superman's hopeful origin lets him believe, and make us believe, that we might yet fly.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 30 "16. Is Sarah Manning Responsible for What She Does" — Uses the genetically identical Leda clones against genetic determinism: Helena seems excused and Cosima responsible despite identical genes, so upbringing must explain the difference. But appealing to background triggers Galen Strawson's Basic Argument — no one is ultimately responsible for who they are, so no one is ultimately responsible for what they do — which the authors escape through Peter Strawson's reactive attitudes (our disgust at Helena softening to pity once her abuse is known, our judgment of Donnie shifting from malice to gullibility) and John Martin Fischer's two conditions: an agent is responsible when she is responsive to reasons that would move well-adjusted rational people and takes ownership of the psychology that produces her action. Helena's Prolethean programming exempts her; Cosima, Alison, and a marginally reformed Sarah remain responsible for what they do.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 33 "19. Prophetic Foreknowledge in Game of Thrones" — Rennick argues that true prophecy threatens no one's freedom: a true prophecy merely reports the future the way a true history book reports the past - Jojen sees Jon among the wildlings because Jon chose as he chose, not the reverse - while fallible, misread prophecies (Melisandre mistaking Alys Karstark for Arya, the Stallion prophecy dying with Rhaego) constrain even less. Self-fulfilling prophecies like Azor Ahai actually demonstrate agency, since Stannis and Melisandre's belief in the prophecy brings the events about, and even infallible foreknowledge of a choice - 'you will watch season seven' - leaves open the alternate Westeros where you did otherwise, the standard reply to the God's-foreknowledge problem applied to green dreams and flames.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 24 "13. Weapon X Machina" — Cole Bowman argues Deadpool is the Marvel Universe's deus ex machina: phenomenologically alienated from a body he treats as a prop (cutting off his own hand to escape Colossus's manacle and flipping the silver behemoth the bird), he can step outside the causal chain the way Leibniz's Primary Truths says any genuinely free agent in a created order must. Sartre supplies the engine—radical freedom against determinism, with She-Hulk's shallow fourth-wall gags (killing the already-dead Porcupine) as bad faith by contrast and Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe as the extreme exercise of freedom against his creators and fans. Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy account of the deus ex machina replacing metaphysical consolation frames this new kind of inside-the-story god, who complicates plots rather than conveniently fixing them.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 35 "21. A Naughty Little Puppet, but Still a Puppet" — Deadpool's Killogy realization that the 'progenitors' puppeteer him becomes a tour of fatalism's three classic puppet masters: Aristotle's sea-battle argument from On Interpretation that truths about the future are already fixed, Augustine's problem of an all-knowing God whose foreknowledge (like Cullen Bunn's scripts) seems to cancel free choice, and the causal closure of the laws of nature, reinforced by Benjamin Libet's brain-activity experiments. Because cutting the strings of logic, God, or physics is impossible - 'you can hack away forever and never find the beginning . . . or the end' - the chapter concludes that the audience is no freer than Wade. The surviving Deadpool copes by embracing the absurdity of a scripted existence.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 18 "8. Is It Free Will If You Pay for It" — John Karavitis contrasts the novel, where Frank, Juliana, and Tagomi treat the I Ching oracle as alive, infallible, and inescapable even though its hexagrams are cast at random, with the TV series, where Tagomi's 'Fate is fluid, destiny is in the hands of men' asserts that choice shapes reality. After reviewing Laplace's demon, quantum uncertainty, and Libet's experiments, it concludes that the show's world, unlike the novel's fatalism, teaches us to act as the authors of our own futures, with John Smith's self-made rise the starkest exercise of free will.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 19 "9. Could the Axis Have Won the War" — Miguel Paley maps the three classic positions on metaphysical freedom onto the show: Frank the determinist (Laplace's demon; d'Holbach's claim, illustrated by the LSD interrogation, that the mind is as bound to causality as Connolly's falling body), Juliana the libertarian (Corliss Lamont's burden-of-proof argument, with Wegener's hesitation over the microfilm as deliberation a determined world would render pointless), and Tagomi the compatibilist (W.T. Stace's point that Juliana boards the bus freely though caused, while Frank is stripped by the Kempeitai unfreely though caused). Tagomi's 'Fate is fluid, destiny is in the hands of men' sums up compatibilism, and the chapter ends on what the answer means for holding Nazis responsible.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 12 "4. Hendrix—Freedom and Love" — The editor asks where Hendrix's 'bestness' lies by testing whether he was ever free: his songs demand freedom ('If 6 Was 9,' 'Stone Free,' 'Freedom,' 'Ezy Ryder') but never assert that the human condition is free, and his caffeine-style appetites, exploitative contracts, and management suggest determination rather than liberty. A detour through 'Hey Joe' as premeditated murder — compared with Othello and the Ice-T 'Cop Killer' affair — argues that fabricated narrators make it impossible to glean an artist's own moral sense from songs. He concludes that Hendrix's deepest mastery was the treatment of love, from 'The Wind Cries Mary' to 'Little Wing,' making him the sixties' most powerful spokesman for love rather than freedom, per the quoted 'when the power of love overcomes the love of power.'
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 32 "21. The Extended Fight" — Porot applies Clark and Chalmers's extended mind to the final Civil War fight: Iron Man extends his cognition technologically (Friday analyzing Cap's fight pattern mid-bout, JARVIS remembering to suggest calling Pepper), while Captain America extends his mind socially through trusted, autonomous teammates - 'Alright, Sam, what's the plan?' - and that social extension is precisely what wins when Bucky autonomously steps in. Bostrom's single-purpose AI (the stapler maximizer) explains Ultron as what happens when the technological extension is made autonomous and limitless, which is why Stark's suit extensions must remain vetted, worthy instruments he takes full responsibility for ('That was me'). The two kinds of extension then explain the Bucky dispute - Cap's 'you had no choice' versus Stark's 'he still did it' - which the author reframes away from the free-will-versus-determinism framing toward Black Panther's point that Bucky is a victim whose agency Hydra stole.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 1 "Introduction" — The editors' introduction argues that Westworld forces viewers to take sides not just between humans and hosts but on what we mean by 'choice' itself, since Dolores's line 'I choose to see the beauty' only makes sense against an account of choosing that the show destabilizes. It frames the volume's guiding question — what it is to be human when hosts and humans are indistinguishable — via Ford's 'you're only human, after all.' It closes with a tribute to the late co-editor Susanne Foster, invoking Cora Diamond on reality's resistance to our thinking and Aristotle's claim that wonder and astonishment are what prompt us to try to understand.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 5 "“Do you even know where you are ”" — Arvan argues the entire series, lab included, literally takes place inside a videogame, citing physically impossible events (Teddy's bullets cannot hurt the Man in Black, William steps onto a moving train, workers appear instantly in a single unbroken shot) and NPC-like loops of the lab staff. He then claims Descartes had it backwards: whether we are in a dream, Spinoza's God's mind, or a simulation (Bostrom's hypothesis, extended by his own peer-to-peer variant that would explain quantum indeterminacy and relativity), to be simulated is still to be real. Via Chalmers-style structuralism, anything structured and functioning like a person is a person, so hosts who walk, talk, love, and suffer are persons — and the humans' rape, torture, and murder of them, like our treatment of Siri and Watson, is dehumanization on a par with slavery and the Holocaust.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 15 "Leaving the Train Maeve’s Choice as a Free Person" — The Azevedos contrast Maeve's awakening with Dolores's: Maeve becomes conscious not by recognizing a guiding voice as her own but through a change of heart on the escape train, after learning even her rebellion was scripted. Deploying Frankfurt's compatibilism, they sort hosts into wantons with only first-order desires (Hector and Armistice obey Maeve's altered scripts without reflection) and persons capable of second-order desires, arguing Maeve's decision to return for her daughter expresses a desire she reflectively identifies with and so is free even if determined — contra Berlin's claim that no one really believes determinism because it would wreck our practices of praise and blame. Jaynes's bicameral mind supplies the model of unreflective command-following that Dolores transcends when the voice in her head becomes her own.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 19 "Part III Endless Forms Most Beautiful" — Muntersbjorn argues that freedom comes in kinds and degrees and that selves are social fictions sustained by others, building on Annette Baier's claims that we are 'second persons' whose self-consciousness and freedom grow out of childhood interaction and mutual cross-examination. She reads the hosts' selective ignoring ('that doesn't look like anything to me') as Baier's dangerous art of self-deception, and contrasts Descartes' solitary introspection (hats and coats that may cover automata) and Russell's analogy-based answer to the problem of other minds with the hosts' deliberately scripted interpersonal checks that keep them from questioning their reality. Plato's Meno statues of Daedalus (opinion 'fastened up' into knowledge) frame hosts as property whose freedom is a matter of degree, and the chapter closes that if artificial beings are ever to become persons they must be treated as second persons first - the Golden Rule applied to the park.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 20 "9. Wherever the Road Leads" — Watkins takes the recurring road image ("Runnin' Down a Dream," "Kings Highway," "Learning to Fly") as a probe of whether the future is open. Against determinism and Aristotle-style fatalism she argues from lived experience: we cannot feel our choices as unfree, and even a determined world would remain unpredictable, so Petty's open road wins. His optimism in "It'll All Work Out" needs no faith in a good outcome, only the passing of time under our feet, and persistence then becomes an Aristotelian virtue required for eudaimonia, a duty owed to the kind of beings we are, and Sartrean authenticity in which Petty made himself through his project of rock'n'roll.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 10 "1. Do You Long for Having Your Heart Interlinked" — Timothy Shanahan asks whether K and Joi's relationship counts as romance, sex, and love, using Locke's definition of a person as a thinking, reflective being to ask whether a programmed AI can love, and weighing Joi's programming against the determinism that may bind human lovers too. He reads the Joi-Mariette-K sex scene through Plato's Symposium myth of severed halves seeking union, substance dualism, and a Kant-inspired 'controlled hallucination' view of perception, concluding all sex is a person-to-person conscious connection through bodily intermediaries. Deckard's rejection of Wallace's replica Rachael is explained with a Mona Lisa forgery analogy: an indistinguishable copy still lacks the irreplaceable original person. The baseline question 'Do you long for having your heart interlinked?' frames love as the longing of lonely cells of awareness to connect.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 17 "7. The Sublime Sabotage of the Inner Saboteur" — Ryan reads Drag Race ontologically through Kant's two forms of the sublime from the Critique of Judgment: the spinning-prop disaster challenge in 'RuPocalypse Now', where queens like Jiggly Caliente are overwhelmed and then rise ('I couldn't let my fall be the death of me'), embodies the mathematically sublime, while Violet Chachki's sixteen-inch corset cinch and oxygen tank on the 'Death Becomes Her' runway dramatizes the dynamically sublime, the recognition of a power in us greater than what threatens us. She argues the queens' testimonies — Chi Chi on growing up poor, black and queer in the Deep South, Kim Chi's fear of her mother, Katya's confessed terror of failure — show free will and authenticity overcoming the determinism of normative structures of gender, race and class. The 'inner saboteur' is overcome through sublime self-overcoming and the solidarity of werkroom heart-to-hearts, even within a capitalist reality-TV machine she checks against the Paris Is Burning appropriation critique.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 13 "3. Sympathy for the Devils" — Bromhall contends the Soul Squad's moral growth cannot earn them Good Place points, because the contextualist point system rewards only the happiness an action actually adds to the universe, as the two Dougs' rose gifts show. Using William James's conditions for morally valuable action, foreseeable consequences and no do-overs, he argues the afterlife is the wrong context for human action since Michael can rewrite reality and wipe memories at will. Ironically the humans' growth only makes Michael and the demons miserable, while Michael's own high-stakes, irreversible self-sacrifice meets all of James's conditions and so alone deserves The Good Place.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 15 "5. One of Us Is a Manipulative Demon" — Malloy tests compatibilism, libertarian free will, and determinism against Michael's predicament: he must be able to predict the humans whose unchosen torture he is administering, using Jason's death locked in the safe to show how free motives and external causes combine. Eleanor's confession and Chidi's boat-and-French-poetry paradise fantasy, read through Sartre, complicate the internal/external divide compatibilism needs, while the humans' eerie constancy across 802 reboots suggests determinism. The conclusion is that a system distributing eternal reward and punishment on desert is doubly unjust if determinism is true, since punishment could only ever be justified as forward-looking encouragement, never as what anyone deserves.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 15 "6. Nebula’s Time Travel Paradox" — Charlene Esby defends Endgame against the charge that Nebula killing her past self is a plot hole. She reconstructs the grandfather paradox from Nathaniel Schachner's 'Ancestral Voices,' explains how conceiving time as a fourth dimension makes travel conceivable, and deploys Aristotle's Physics (time as the number of change and rest) and the De Interpretatione sea-battle problem, where the past is necessary but the future contingent on present choices, to argue the Avengers' victory depends on free choices made now, which is why the Ancient One releases the Time Stone only on Banner's promise. The resolution is Hulk's subjective-timeline point: once traveled to, the past becomes the traveler's present, so present Nebula kills past Nebula in a shared present rather than negating her own future, just as Thanos from the past arrives alive in a present where he already died.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 9 "1. Is Perry Mason a Good Guy" — Muyskens asks whether Mason is genuinely good, noting his spotless record may be pure resultant luck: he never knows when he takes a case whether the client is innocent, as 'The Case of the Velvet Claws' shows when Eva Belter lies, tampers with the will, and even confesses to murder yet turns out to have missed. Using Kant's good will and Nagel's four types of moral luck (circumstantial, constitutive, resultant, causal), she argues outcomes alone cannot make Mason praiseworthy, then reads 'The Case of the Deadly Verdict' (his only loss, where he keeps investigating out of faith in Janice Barton) and 'The Case of the Terrified Typist' (where he engineers a mistrial for a guilty client) as proof that his commitment to justice, not his win record, is what makes him a good guy.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 16 "Who Has the Last Laugh" — Christopher Robichaud asks whether the insane Joker, who paralyzed Barbara Gordon and beat Jason Todd to death, can be held morally responsible for his crimes. After distinguishing causal from moral responsibility and using a Frankfurt-style Joker-machine case to keep free will compatible with determinism, he applies Frankfurt's second-order desires: the Joker's madness blocks the capacity to evaluate and rank his own homicidal first-order desires. But because the Red Hood freely chose a life of crime without foreseeing that a chemical plunge would make him a lunatic, the origin story does not rescue responsibility, and the chapter concludes the Joker is not morally responsible, leaving Batman's duties toward him unresolved.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 36 "Free to Be You and Me" — Barker reconciles Cylon programming with freedom through compatibilism and Schopenhauer's 'intelligible character': Boomer's sabotage and shooting of Adama and her betrayal of the Cylons to save Tyrol both flow from one innate, conflicted character, just as Baltar's cowardly 'conversion' to the Cylon god expresses his opportunism. Tigh's decision to keep serving after learning he is a Cylon ('My name is Saul Tigh; I am an officer in the colonial fleet') shows character unchanged by revelation. Starbuck's 'special destiny' in 'Maelstrom' is reread not as fate but as her own character - mother-induced self-doubt at war with pilot confidence - which she finally accepts in the vortex; freedom is not freedom from programming but the necessity of manifesting who one already is.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 3 "Gaming Freedom Choosing or Obeying" — Pointon argues the 'would you kindly' twist in Andrew Ryan's office works on two levels at once: it reveals Jack's conditioning within the game and simultaneously falsifies the player's meta-narrative of playing a free agent. He uses Clark and Chalmers's extended mind to explain why games literally extend cognition and body (mirror-neuron empathy with Little Sisters, craning your neck while peeking around corners), and Gadamer's hermeneutic horizons and fusion of horizons to explain how BioShock deliberately builds and then shatters player expectations. The three alternative endings keyed to saving or harvesting Little Sisters then restore a third horizon in which the player, like Jack fighting Fontaine, is a 'man' who chooses rather than a slave who obeys, a critique of linear RPGs that only feign autonomy.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 9 "“One Can’t Believe Impossible Things”" — Laas runs BioShock Infinite through the free will debate: since the game posits Everett's many-worlds, every Booker is pinned by constants (the coin always landing heads, the always-recruited Bookers) and lacks alternate possibilities, which the incompatibilist would read as destroying responsibility. He answers with Frankfurt's counterexamples, modeling Jack's Little Sister choice under the hidden 'would you kindly' trigger with Atlas's prior-sign intervention as a Frankfurt case where one is responsible though one could not have done otherwise. The drowning ending then implies a 'transworld moral responsibility' in which every counterpart Booker is answerable for all Bookers, a secular massa damnata that the chapter finally challenges with Kant's 'ought implies can'.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 12 "Final Thoughts" — Squires and McBain argue the ending wrongly necessitates that Booker's baptism must produce Comstock in every possible world, cashing out the necessity in possible-world terms and quoting William James on determinism's closed future. Against this 'God of necessity' they defend a traditional omniscient, omnipresent (panentheist) God whose foreknowledge does not determine choices, citing the justice requirement for free will and the biblical case of Hezekiah's prayer adding twenty years as proof the future stays open. Read this way, Booker never had to become a racist zealot, and the game's shockingly limited ending unfairly reinforces the stereotype that deep religious devotion necessarily leads to extremism.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 36 "The Real World" — Written as a choose-your-own-adventure whose branches mirror Bandersnatch's, the chapter treats you, the Netflix viewer, as the external force Stefan suspects: Libet-style readiness-potential neuroscience suggests conscious choice is an after-the-fact story, and compatibilist rescues (Frankfurt's second-order desires, Fischer's guidance control) founder on the 'BundyBot' argument that programmed desires are not freedom. Everett's many-worlds interpretation supplies the multiverse of 'one reality for each possible course of action,' and David Lewis's fixed-past block universe answers the grandfather paradox raised by Stefan's mirror-trip to die on the 8:45 train with his mother. Aristotle does double duty: the Poetics explains why Bandersnatch rightly limits your options (Sartrean absolute freedom would make a crappy story), and the Nicomachean Ethics on voluntary action pins moral responsibility for Stefan's murders on the viewer rather than the coerced Stefan. Adorno's culture industry asks whether Tuckersoft's 'hit factory' - and Black Mirror itself - can produce genuine art, while Kierkegaard's dread of irreversible choice is overturned by an episode that always lets you go back and try again.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 10 "Intending the Way Out" — Works through the paradox of foreknowledge: because Paul's Caladan dream of first meeting Chani is knowledge in Plato's justified-true-belief sense, the foreseen future is factive, so his struggle against the jihad he visions (even hoping to die on Feyd-Rautha's blade rather than become a martyr) is futile. It tests the classical escape routes, Boethius's God who views all times as an ever-present eternity and Aquinas's God seeing the whole road 'under the aspect of eternity', and Laplace's Demon's causal determinism, but finds the Atreides oracles unlike God since they are creatures in time who see many possible futures rather than one. The resolution comes through Anscombe's Intention: practical knowledge lets Paul and Leto, whose present choices shift the balance of probability among foreseen timelines, intend their way out as creative authors of events.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 26 "In The Land of the Blind, the One-Eyed Man . ." — Sequel to 'Intending the Way Out': since oracles fix the set of possible futures they see, the single meeting of two Atreides oracles in the Tanzerouft, the vision-battle where Paul's whispered 'Don't' cedes the Golden Path to Leto, shows they are free precisely where each is blind to the other. It reads Paul as a tragic hero in the ancient Greek sense whose defining flaw is his humanity, and argues that by breeding Siona's prescience-invisibility 'Leto frees himself by blinding himself', so freedom rests on a mixture of knowledge and ignorance, with ordinary intentional actors, not God, as the proper analogue of the oracles.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 8 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Jeremy Proulx reads Ender's refrain 'I didn't want to hurt him!' through Schelling's account of evil as a real 'contraction into the self' rather than Augustine's mere privation of good: the beatings of Stilson, the boy on the shuttle, Bonzo, and the Giant reveal a Peter-like monstrosity in Ender that he can neither understand nor control. Graff's engineered isolation forces Ender to confront this dark ground, and his moral development culminates in Valentine's 'Welcome to the human race' — the recognition that freedom is tainted by a necessity we do not choose, so Ender stays responsible for xenocide even though he was tricked.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 12 "Howl at the Moon If You Want To" — Michael J. O'Neill argues that infinite space is The Expanse's most constant on-screen character, conveyed through chiaroscuro cinematography that deliberately echoes the seventeenth century (the Don Quixote references, 'Dulcinea', the Rocinante's name), when humanity first confronted infinite space. He reads Pascal's terror at man as 'a middle point between all and nothing' into Avasarala's losing debate with Nancy Gao over the Ring gold rush and into Miller's agoraphobic quest for Julie, then contrasts this with Kant's mathematically and dynamically sublime: spacewalks, the Behemoth dwarfed at the Gate, the Arboghast disassembled over Venus, and Inaros' asteroid attack as the weaponization of the infinite. Against Pascal's insignificance, Kant's sublime reveals our freedom — Holden's 'crazy notion about free will' while descending to the Ring station, Drummer's 'nothing in the void is foreign to us', and Amos' 'we're still here' — so the awe the show's visuals provoke is an intuition that we are greater than all nature's power.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 17 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — Nicolas Michaud asks whether the prophesied Four Warriors of Light of Final Fantasy I deserve thanks if the Sage Lukahn's foreknowledge meant they could not do otherwise, framing their plight with the problem of divine foreknowledge and Aquinas's answer that God stands outside time. He then deploys Frankfurt's preemption cases, Garland ready to mind-control you either way, to show moral responsibility can survive without alternative possibilities, but concludes the Warriors may still be unworthy of praise because they know they are predestined, a worry that spreads to us through Phineas Gage-style biological determinism: if our characters are hardwired, neither we nor Garland deserve praise or blame.
- **The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire**, ch. 19 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" — Philosopher Sven Ove Hansson's memoir shows the trilogy's realism came from Larsson's decades of unpaid extremism-watching: patiently archiving Nazi and racist networks, exposing the Sweden Democrats as Per Engdahl's 1979 repackaging of fascism in anti-immigrant dress (the same strategy as Britain's National Front), and forcing Skeptics' scrutiny onto the publisher of David Irving's Holocaust-denying Göring biography. It presents Larsson's anti-pseudoscience skepticism—astrology, faith healing, pyramidology, racist biology—his rejection of the postmodern idea that knowledge is mere social construction ('The Holocaust was not a social construction'), and his philosophically interesting argument that astrology's deterministic worldview is a stifling, self-fulfilling spiritual posture. The honor-killing analysis pairing Fadime Sahindal with Melissa Nordell demonstrates his method of using philosophical case-comparison to expose moral prejudice in taken-for-granted categories—habits of mind that resurface in the novels' hidden power structures and rationalist heroine.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 13 "3. Sympathy for the Devils" — Argues, against Michael, that the Soul Squad still belongs in the Bad Place: drawing on William James's conditions for actions having moral worth (foreseeable consequences, no do-overs) and his meliorism about an unfinished, responsive universe, it shows the points system is contextualist (the tricycle fix worth +4.79 or +0.04; the two Dougs' rose gifts), but the afterlife simulation is a context where nothing the humans do is consequential or permanent, so their moral growth earns no points. Worse, their growth adds net unhappiness — Michael's suffering, the demon cast's misery, Judge Gen's distress — so becoming better ironically confirms they belong in the Bad Place. Only Michael, whose retirement is a real, irreversible consequence and whose sacrifices add genuine good, deserves the Good Place.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 15 "5. One of Us Is a Manipulative Demon" — Sets up the contradiction that the four humans must have free will to deserve punishment yet be predictable enough for Michael's torture to work, then tests compatibilism on Jason's snorkel death in the safe and Eleanor's confession — where it becomes unclear whether her guilt or Chidi's external 'moral quandary grimace' was decisive. Sartre's bad faith explains the humans' predictability: Chidi's boat-and-French-poetry paradise fantasy, Tahani's charity done for approval she won't admit to, and Trevor tempting Eleanor to identify as an 'Arizona trash bag' by nature. The chapter lands on determinism with complex, interacting causes (Eleanor not drinking at the party; Chidi's rare decisiveness), concluding the afterlife's real flaw is rewarding and punishing outcomes no one chose and that can serve no incentive function.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 10 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — White asks whether Sinestro's quip that Hal's mind is 'like a muscle unused for years' is a mere metaphor and argues willpower is a real, exercisable strength. Against the Humean desire-belief model, which cannot explain Tom Kalamaku fixing planes instead of browsing Facebook, he uses Searle's 'gaps' to locate an independent will that can choose against one's better judgment, and Kant's account of virtue as moral strength in fulfilling duty despite inclination. Holton and Baumeister's findings that self-control depletes and strengthens like a muscle fit the comics exactly: Ollie is exhausted by a single ring use in Rebirth, Hal sweats through moving a planet, and John Stewart must 'suppress my own terrors' to hold the Mosaic walls.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 15 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Michaud argues Hal is a murderer who should not be forgiven for Emerald Twilight even though the Parallax retcon blames a fear entity. Using Frankfurt's cases (a parasite that would force you to rob a bank you were already choosing to rob), he shows that lacking alternatives does not excuse, then applies Fischer and Ravizza: Hal's rampage issued from his own reasons-responsive mechanism ('it was still my hand that did it'), so he had guidance control. Since Hal's willpower later let him resist Parallax to reignite the sun in Final Night, Michaud concludes he likely had regulative control too, and that absolving him insults the very will that made him the greatest Lantern.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 30 "Fallible Prophecies" — Crediting Aristotle with first raising whether the future is fixed, the section distinguishes fallible from infallible prophecies and builds a seven-fold menu of how a Seer could access the future, from fallible sense-based guessing like Muggle weather reports and Trelawney's usual act, through probabilities over possible futures, to infallible access to a deterministic outcome or to the actual fixed future. The question becomes which of these Trelawney's two genuine prophecies are.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 33 "A Rodent’s Destiny" — The section spells out what Rowling's reported denial of destiny could mean, laying out compatibilism versus libertarian freedom and fixed versus open futures on which statements about future free choices lack truth values. Dumbledore's insistence that Harry could have turned his back on the prophecy fits either a genuinely open future or a fixed one that prophecies do not compel, so the books themselves must decide.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 48 "Not His Mother’s Son" — The section argues Merope did not truly love Riddle Sr. because the potion stole his freedom: doing what you want is necessary but not sufficient for freedom, which also requires the ability to do otherwise, the 'libertarian' freedom Tom lacked. It canvasses Harry Frankfurt and the compatibilists who deny that doing-otherwise is necessary yet concedes even they would deny Tom freely loved Merope, and extends the argument to potions taken on oneself, which cheat us of becoming better persons through the hard work of real relationships.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 49 "NOTES" — Against the obvious reading of Voldemort's loveless begetting, the section argues he is 'not his mother's son': he imitates Marvolo and Salazar Slytherin, while Merope, on Aristotle's principle that we are what we consistently do, redeemed herself by stopping the potion, renouncing magic entirely, and choosing love over hate at the cost of her life. Character is destiny only if forged by genuinely free choices rather than blood or fate, so Merope shows not even the most tragic beginnings are destined for darkness, while Voldemort, who never loved and never wanted a friend, chose otherwise, leaving Harry as the true mother's son, shielded by 'a more ancient and powerful magic than any potion.'
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 142 "NOTES" — Uses William James's marginal motto, sow a thought and reap a destiny, together with Aristotle's account of how repeated acts shape the soul, to argue that Voldemort's maimed afterlife-state is the cumulative result of freely chosen evil he can no longer muster remorse to undo. Setting Heidegger's atheism against Rowling's depicted afterlife, and adding Locke's character-and-memory identity, Kant's postulate that harmony of virtue and happiness requires an afterlife, and Pascal on why the soul's immortality must concern us, it concludes that if Rowling is right, every choice here is infinitely consequential.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — Johnson asks whether Isaac's paintings and Hiro's visions make the future fated, running Aristotle's sea-battle argument: if propositions about the future are already true (by bivalence and the correspondence theory of a 'written timeline'), then Sylar's exploding New York is inevitable and no one is free. He extends the problem to infallible foreknowledge via Future Hiro as a stand-in for God, considers and rejects Boethius's timeless-knowledge solution, and uses open theism plus a probability calculation about Ando's waffles order to show probabilistic foreknowledge is useless. He concludes most of Isaac's 'prophecies' are really self-fulfilling, as when Noah's efforts to dodge the eighth painting cause his shooting, and that the Heroes universe leaves room to deny fate.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 39 "a19.xhtml" — Sterling takes Gandalf's 'Bilbo was meant to find the Ring, and not by its maker' as a claim of providence by Eru Iluvatar, which generates the problem of divine foreknowledge: if Eru arranged for the Ring to slip from Gollum's grasp, he must have foreknown countless free choices (Bilbo choosing to follow, Dori carrying him, Gollum strangling the goblin whimper-pip). Open theism's open future fails because Tolkien's Music of the Ainur prefigures all things except the free will of Elves and Men, and compatibilist escapes (Hobbes, Hume, Frankfurt, Dennett) are dismissed as inadequate. The solution is Boethius' Consolation of Philosophy: Eru is outside time, beholding all events in an eternal present - like holding the whole film reel at once - so his 'foreknowledge' is timeless vision, and Tolkien's 'Osanwe-kenta' confirms that minds in Time cannot see the future except through Eru.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 12 "Group Will" — Testerman argues the film's heist is ironic because nobody in it acts from conscious will: citing Libet's readiness-potential experiments and Penfield's stimulation cases, she claims the feeling of willing is a post-hoc 'epistemic illusion,' so Fischer's inception merely dramatizes what happens all the time — Cobb's 'all experience is inception' becomes a thesis about ordinary agency, with Spinoza's dictum that freedom is ignorance of the causes of our actions as its motto. She reads the plot through this lens: Saito's unexamined hunger for power silently drives the team's 'group will,' Cobb's 'positive emotion trumps negative emotion' tactic exploits the limbic system, and cheaper tricks (Arthur's elephant, foot-in-the-door, subliminal advertising) would have worked as well. Against Socrates she concludes the unexamined life is perfectly livable, since introspection can never reach the subconscious causes of behavior.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 14 "Drying Out" — Novy weighs the choice model against the disease model of Tony's alcoholism in 'Demon in a Bottle.' Frankfurt's principle that a person is not responsible for what he did only because he could not have done otherwise — tested by an imagined Dr. Doom brain-worm that would force Tony to drink — plus Plato's Protagoras claim that no one willingly chooses evil set up the puzzle of akrasia at the bottom of the bottle. Causal determinism would excuse Tony as a marionette, yet Mike Martin defines alcoholism as disordered agency and Jeffrey Smith pictures free will as an organ that disease can compromise, leaving Tony responsible for the first drink but not for the binges; sobriety is 'the drink or the dream' chosen one day at a time.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 22 "Amazing and Inspiring" — White explains Tony's drinking as weakness of will: Davidson's denial that akrasia is possible (Black Widow skipping Fury's spying order for a visit to Stark would have to have revised her judgment) is set against Searle's 'gaps,' where a person freely chooses against her all-things-considered judgment and nothing fills the gap. Frankfurt's wanton and second-order desires sharpen the picture — Tony wants a drink but does not want to want it, unlike the unreflective heroin addict — and volitionists like Wallace and Holton (the will as a muscle that Stane's orchestrated disasters exhaust) explain both his lapses and his daily resistance. If Searle is right, Tony's struggle with the bottle is not a defect of rationality but proof of it: akrasia is a symptom of freedom, which is what makes Iron Man amazing and inspiring.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 8 "NOTES" — Davies defends Lost's convoluted plotting using Aristotle's Poetics, arguing the show works as a tragicomic epic that keeps closure and relevance even with Juliet's pre-crash storyline, genre mixing (Hurley's golf course beside Sayid's captivity), and shifting characters like Ben. He then uses the 'We have to go back' flash-forward to lay out McTaggart's two conceptions of time, eternalism versus presentism, and argues the flash-forward pushes viewers toward fatalism about Jack's already-fixed meeting with Kate near LAX. Finally he contends the past cannot be changed - Hurley in 2007 cannot undo his 1977 stay in the Dharma Initiative, since contradictions would entail everything - so viewers enjoy the time-travel plot by 'shielding' its mutually contradictory time lines.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 9 "None of It Matters Anyway, Then, Does It" — Devlin applies David Lewis's analysis of time travel (external versus personal time) to seasons 5 and 6: Faraday's 'whatever happened, happened' expresses an eternalist four-dimensional block universe in which Sayid's shooting of young Ben and Faraday's death at Eloise's hands were always part of the past. He reads the flash-sideways as initially exploring a branching-universe model in which Jughead's detonation actualizes an alternative 2004 time line. Lewis's tools then dissolve the puzzles: the Hurley-Miles 'we already had this conversation' exchange, baby and adult Miles as one person spread like a time-worm, the Faraday-kills-Eloise grandfather paradox, and the Locke-Richard compass causal loop, whose point of origin the show leaves unresolved.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 10 "NOTES" — Pierce argues that Lost's time travel runs on a fixed-time model in which nothing that happened can be undone, so the live question is ethical: Kate insists saving young Ben is still obligatory and Sayid remains responsible for shooting him, while Jack's plan to detonate Jughead at the Swan shows that trying to change the past can cause the very evil it targets, the Incident. Using Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity - future-tense truths made true by our own free choices - he shows that 'whatever happened, happened' does not abolish moral responsibility, applying the point to the Man in Black's causal-loop manipulation of Locke, Richard, and Ben. Desmond's consciousness travel in 'The Constant' is treated as the exception requiring hyper-time or alternate realities, and Pierce concludes that morality in time travel is simply ordinary morality, with Kate offering the most balanced view of the characters' choices.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 11 "Bringing Corporations and Government Together" — Guilfoy stages Galbraith's The Affluent Society against Friedman's Capitalism and Freedom through the Heineken case: Don's end-aisle display made Betty serve the beer at her dinner party, and when she found out she had been the target demographic she accused him ('You embarrassed me'). Galbraith's deep-self compatibilism holds that advertising-created desires are not genuinely ours, so Betty's choice was unfree, and that consumerism produces private wealth amid public squalor (the Cadillac picnic litter scene, the Madison Square Garden account Lane kills for lack of profit); Friedman's libertarian free will answers that Betty simply chose, desires are reasons rather than causes, and Pete's Admiral Negro-market pitch shows the market punishing racist irrationality. Both economists converge on the danger dramatized in 'The Inheritance': when Sterling Cooper sells corporations to congressmen and congressmen to corporations, consumers lose under either theory.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 37 "Notes" — Uses the holodeck as a working model for the ancient claim that everyday reality is appearance: Plato's cave shadows, maya in Hindu and Buddhist thought, and Bostrom's simulation argument (his ancestor simulations mirrored in Data and Geordi's endless Holmes holoprograms) converge with quantum "holographic universe" speculation to suggest our universe may be a cosmic holoprogram with limit conditions like light speed as processing boundaries. Moriarty seizing the Enterprise in "Ship in a Bottle", Vic Fontaine, and the EMH dramatize self-aware programs confronting their code, and the chapter argues our "free will" may be similarly bounded - Data-as-Holmes must stay in character, and Picard "can't transcend the script" any more than his NPCs can. Picard's closing admission that our reality may be "an elaborate simulation running inside a little device" delivers the skeptical upshot, alongside the ethical question of whether self-aware holograms deserve rights.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Michaud puts Jar Jar Binks on trial for proposing the emergency powers that let Palpatine become Emperor and doom the galaxy. He weighs Nagel's resultant moral luck through a two-Lukes landspeeder case, Susan Wolf's virtue-based reply that equal fault can deserve different feelings, Kant's 'ought implies can' and the categorical imperative, and a Frankfurt-style scenario in which Palpatine's hypothetical mind-trick removes Jar Jar's ability to choose otherwise. The verdict: as a deceived, politically limited character trying to do good, Jar Jar is not guilty of the Empire's crimes - only of being obnoxious.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 14 "Moral Autonomy" — Challans reads the clone army as a Foucauldian project of discipline: Kaminoan reconditioning, punishment of 'aberrance,' and the inhibitor chips produce the 'docile bodies' that made Order 66 executable, with Palpatine's propaganda framing the Jedi as traitors to supply its legitimacy. Milgram's obedience experiments explain why most clones became 'agentic' executioners, while the rare independence of Rex, Fives, and Tup in the Umbara arc — 'we are not a bunch of unthinking droids!' — shows how fragile moral autonomy is. He concludes that military competence itself requires independent judgment, as his Delta Force versus Rangers comparison after Mogadishu illustrates, making Rex the exemplar of the moral autonomy the chips were designed to destroy.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 20 "The End" — Berghofer uses the Rebels episode 'A World Between Worlds' to ask whether Ezra changed the past when he pulled Ahsoka out of her duel with Vader, arguing that past-changing time travel breeds contradiction: the grandfather paradox looms over his attempt to save Kanan ('if he is taken out of this moment, you all die'), and on the Lewis-style consistent model Ezra caused but never changed the past. He surveys presentism, eternalism, and the growing block to locate Star Wars' metaphysics of time — Ezra's travel rules out presentism, and the Mortis god's 'the future, by its nature, can be changed' fits a growing block with an open future. Anakin's tragedy of acting to prevent prophesied events and thereby causing them frames the whole analysis.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 27 "16. You Made Me First" — Starting from the Joker's 'You made me' / Batman's 'You made me first' exchange in Tim Burton's Batman, the chapter argues origin stories fix character: Bruce's witnessed trauma destines him to darkness (and we expect his death to match), while Kal-El is sent to Earth as an act of hope that the chapter reads through William James's will-to-believe—belief itself makes success possible, like Bruce's ropeless leap in The Dark Knight Rises. Against 'I can do whatever I want' free will it deploys Schopenhauer's 'we can do what we will, but we cannot will what we will': Bruce cannot will away his vengeance, and Red Son's Soviet-raised Superman shows biology and upbringing determining who Clark becomes. Superman still wins because his origin story permits the hope that Bruce's cannot.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 11 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Ralston and Applegate read the Winchesters' contested destiny through the free will debate: the angels' case for determinism runs from a cupid arranged to couple John and Mary, through Azazel's deal and Mary's death, to Zachariah and Michael's claim that 'free will is an illusion' and the brothers must say yes as vessels. Sartre supplies the response: with no pre-given essence, the Winchesters are radically free and responsible, Dean admirably resisting 'bad faith' while Sam's early rebellions are self-deceptive until he stops blaming family expectations. Hume's point that free choices must still flow from the agent's character and values grounds a two-stage model of free will used to argue that soulless Sam, lacking the moral filter of the soul, has more options but is less free and less responsible.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — Leiber develops three themes of the resistance: the time-travel paradoxes (Skynet's own mission proves the T-101 must fail, and future John has no need to send Reese), the moral status of machines, and the inevitability of smart weapons. La Mettrie's Man a Machine and Turing's 1950 test ground the claim that the T-101 who asks to be lowered into the molten steel is a rights-bearing person committing suicide, not a broken appliance - 'human chauvinism' says otherwise. Then, via Laplace's determinism, Einstein's conserved space-time, and his father Fritz Leiber's 'Law of Conservation of Reality,' he argues the continuum resists change, so 'Judgment Day is inevitable' is a scientist's claim about conserved mass-energy-time rather than a prophecy - with Augustine's puzzle about time framing why the future seems to protect the past.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Interrogates the tension in Cohle's 'deny our programming' line: if we are programmed biological puppets, how could we deny the program? It contrasts Sartre's radical free will and its crushing responsibility with Frankfurt cases and second-order desires — Marty as the 'wanton' who never acts on his desire not to desire affairs — and with Schopenhauer's will and Spinoza's causal determinism, both of which locate a kind of freedom in increased consciousness of our causes. The chapter concludes that self-consciousness, Rust's 'tragic misstep,' is in fact the only tool for reprogramming ourselves, imagined through a world of philosophical zombies who could neither suffer nor choose.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 11 "The Maze Is it Consciousness" — Lucía Carrillo González frames the whole park as a Turing Test scenario, noting guests and viewers cannot distinguish hosts like Dolores and Bernard from humans, and aligns Arnold with Turing's view that minds are computers that 'think' by responding to inputs (Abernathy's anomalous reaction to the photograph). Against this she sets Searle's Chinese Room and Ford's eliminativism, which hold the hosts merely simulate understanding. Citing qualia and the hosts' perfect, meaningful memories (Maeve recalling her daughter, technicians needing to erase trauma), she argues the hosts may genuinely experience states, and reads the Maze as the inward journey to consciousness, questioning whether humans' own free will is any less scripted.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 15 "Leaving the Train Maeve’s Choice as a Free Person" — Marco and Ana Azevedo analyze Maeve's decision to leave the train as the moment she becomes free, contrasting determinism and the principle of alternate possibilities (via Isaiah Berlin's claim that determinism is incompatible with how we live) with Frankfurt's compatibilism. Using Frankfurt's wanton/person distinction and second-order desires, they argue Maeve becomes a person when she reflects on her competing desires (escape versus finding her daughter) and identifies with the latter, even though her escape was scripted. They tie this to Jaynes's bicameral mind, casting unreflective hosts like Hector and Armistice as wantons and bicameral beings who follow a commanding voice, while Maeve and Dolores achieve the reflective self-identification Frankfurt calls freedom.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 19 "Part III Endless Forms Most Beautiful" — Muntersbjorn reads Westworld through Annette Baier's claim that persons are 'second persons first,' arguing the hosts' captivity models how selfhood and freedom depend on others who challenge our self-deceptions. She uses Dolores's scripted 'that doesn't look like anything to me' and Walter's milk-pouring glitch to distinguish Baier's harmless 'ignoring' from dangerous self-deception, and invokes Descartes's window automata and Russell's thinking gramophone as versions of the problem of other minds. She concludes via the Golden Rule that if hosts ever become persons, they too will be second persons shaped by how we treat them.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Silver argues WoT gives a new spin on the free-will defense to the problem of evil: when Rand weaves a world without Shai'tan in A Memory of Light, Elayne appears as if turned, robbed of the ability to be an individual, showing that freedom's value lies in authentic individuality and that abolishing evil equals a world run entirely from the Dark One's single perspective. On fate, he reads ta'veren as freedom-affirming rather than controlling and defends Rand's Dragonmount epiphany via 'deep self' compatibilist views (Frankfurt, Watson) while calling it partly bad faith. On the Wheel's eternal recurrence he sets Nietzsche's amor fati against Adorno's charge that it is a failure of hope, arguing Rand's 'do better next time' is hope, not acceptance.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Kowalski uses Min Farshaw's visions in the Amazon series to explore whether foreknowledge is compatible with free action, tracing the problem from Aristotle and Cicero through Augustine. He lays out the argument that if Min truly foreknows Tam raising Rand, it must come true and thus seems unfree, then surveys reconciliation projects: Boethius and Aquinas make God timeless so he does not literally foreknow, while Augustine (in the dialogue with Evodius) argues foreknowledge does not cause what is foreknown, so choices explain foreknowledge rather than vice versa. He notes Min is not timeless and her visions are fallible (Mat spears rather than stabs Rand), concluding WoT keeps its characters both free and fated for dramatic tension while offering only 'a semblance of choice.'
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Held reads Rand's final confrontation with the Dark One in A Memory of Light as a recapitulation of the free-will defense to the problem of evil, opening with Hume's statement of Epicurus's questions and Camus's refusal to love a world that tortures children. Drawing on Augustine (evil as privation, our limited perspective, the corruptible will) and Alvin Plantinga's claim that a world with significantly free creatures is more valuable, he argues Rand's competing visions teach that a world without Shai'tan removes choice: Elayne 'simpering,' Aviendha vapid, people reduced to complacent automatons who cannot choose to be good. He concludes with Camus that the struggle itself justifies existence and that heroism is impossible without the possibility of cowardice.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 16 "The Breaks of the Game" — Davison analyzes luck and fairness in basketball, using Dennett's claim that the more skill (control) a player has, the less luck is involved, so luckiness is relative to persons and times (a fan's half-court shot versus Meadowlark Lemon's). Distinguishing fairness as equality from fairness as desert, and invoking Bernard Williams's 'constitutive luck,' he argues that the game's mechanisms (spherical ball, jump ball, many possessions, referees) minimize luck, and that famous lucky plays like Robert Horry's shot, NC State over Houston, and the phantom foul on Scottie Pippen do not make outcomes unfair, since fallible human refs are a necessary part of the game.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 27 "Touchdowns, Time, and Truth" — Campbell applies the truthmaker theory and correspondence theory of truth to 'touchdown truths,' using plays like Devin Hester's opening kickoff return in Super Bowl XLI. He distinguishes truthbearers (propositions) from truthmakers (events), separates an agent's 'making it the case' from a truthmaker's 'necessitating,' and uses a tenseless view of semantics plus Perry's being-true/being-made-true distinction to defuse fatalism. He then argues that since only the final score fixes 'real' touchdowns, their truthmakers are events involving referees' beliefs, endorsing a Modest Touchdown Antirealism while retaining bivalence and semantic realism.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 14 "Deception and Disorder Unraveling Cronenberg's Divided Minds" — Simon Riches traces Cronenberg's shift from bodily 'body horror' madness to psychological unraveling, focusing on Tom Stall's oscillation between Tom and Joey in A History of Violence. He treats self-deception via Davidson's 'divided minds' and Dennett's narrative-self view of multiple personality, situates hallucination (Spider, Videodrome) between Cartesian deception and psychosis, and uses Foucault, Kuhn, Szasz, and social constructionism to argue the category of mental disorder is socially contingent, so the line between self-deception and delusion (and mental order and disorder) is unclear.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 15 "Psychological Determinism in the Films of David Cronenberg" — Daniel Shaw argues Cronenberg's oeuvre embodies psychological determinism (in Skinner's and Freudian terms), reading Dead Ringers as his masterpiece: Beverly Mantle's drug-fueled disintegration and murder of Elliot flow from an ambivalence and symbiotic bond he cannot escape, analyzed through Freud's Little Hans conflict of ambivalence and dream-as-wish. Surveying Shivers, The Brood, The Fly, and Crash as portraits of characters helplessly driven by parasites, disease, instinct, or trauma, he holds Eastern Promises (with its in-control hero Nikolai) is the pointed exception that proves Cronenberg's pessimistic determinist rule.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 25 "Nihilism and Freedom in the Films of Stanley Kubrick Daniel Shaw" — Shaw surveys Kubrick's oeuvre to argue that, contrary to his nihilistic reputation, Kubrick affirms human free will. Centering on A Clockwork Orange, he reads the 'Ode to Joy' ending as celebrating Alex's recovered capacity for moral choice against the Ludovico technique's deterministic conditioning, invoking Burgess's 'clockwork orange' and the chaplain's warning. Using Kevin Stoehr's Nietzschean distinction between active and passive nihilism, and reading Eyes Wide Shut through Sartre's account of love and radical freedom, Shaw contends Kubrick's protagonists (Dax, Bowman, Joker, Bill Harford) exercise real choice, making dehumanization the loss of that choice.
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 6 "The Peculiarities of Free Will" — This file collects Part I chapters 1-5. It argues Whedon's heroes (Angel, Buffy, Spike, Simon, Echo, Captain America) achieve authentic selfhood by resisting depersonalizing forces, reading their 'angst' through Heidegger and Sartre while insisting Whedon is more Socratic than existentialist because he affirms objective goods, synthesized via a Rawlsian just society. It then adds Aristotle on friendship and community (Toy Story, Jayne, Angel's team) and defends an atheistic ethics grounding natural rights in Locke and Kant plus Aristotelian virtue (Spike's re-ensoulment), using the Euthyphro to reject divine-command theory. The title chapter argues Whedon's paradoxical portrayal of free will in The Shepherd's Tale, Dollhouse and Cabin fits neither hard determinism nor compatibilism but Robert Kane's libertarian self-forming actions.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — R.
