Barton Palmer situates Scorsese as a 'saint of cinema' whose Emersonian transcendentalism—the 'influx of light and power' breaking through the material everyday—pervades even his commercial films, focusing on Bringing Out the Dead against Casino and Taxi Driver. He traces the Bressonian 'decisive moment' and Schrader's Calvinist-Jansenist reading of predestination and grace (Ace Rothstein's inexplicable survival in Casino, the elect/damned divide of Taxi Driver and Hardcore), where Travis Bickle remains 'God's lonely man' beyond redemption. Palmer argues Scorsese departs from Schrader's bleak limited atonement: Frank Pierce earns communal grace through willed effort, releasing Mary's father, asking forgiveness, and ending in a Pieta embrace that affirms redemption is attainable within the material world.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 24 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Shaw asks whether Kubrick's worldview is nihilistic by tracking the free-will-versus-determinism question across his films, arguing (against Vincent Canby) that A Clockwork Orange celebrates rather than condemns Alex's recovered capacity for moral choice: the state's Ludovico conditioning, which makes him retch at sex and violence, is more monstrous than Alex because it destroys the free will that grounds human meaning. Invoking Kevin Stoehr's distinction between Nietzsche's passive and active nihilism, Shaw claims Kubrick highlights the negative to point beyond it. He surveys the oeuvre—Dax, Bowman, Barry, Wendy, Joker, Bill Harford as choosing agents—and reads Eyes Wide Shut through Sartre's Being and Nothingness on the contradiction of wanting the beloved's freely-given yet secure love.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 23 "Minority Report, Molinism, and the Viability of Precrime" — Kowalski defends the conceptual coherence of Minority Report's Precrime by dissolving the freedom-vs-foreknowledge worry: the precogs' prevision of Howard Marks knifing his wife shows only that 'necessarily, if it is foreknown, it happens,' not that the act happens necessarily, so contingency and free choice survive (Anderton's rolling-ball demo and Agatha's 'You can choose!'). He recasts the precogs' power as Luis de Molina's knowledge of the conditional future (middle knowledge)—Agatha narrating the life Sean never lived—invoking Aristotle, Augustine, Boethius, Aquinas, and Ockham on the problem, and finally rejects Spielberg's shut-it-down stance as a fallacious slippery-slope argument.
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 6 "The Peculiarities of Free Will" — This file collects Part I's chapters, arguing the Whedonverse embodies serious philosophy. It reads Angel, Buffy, Simon Tam, Echo, and the Avengers through Heidegger's inauthenticity/angst and Sartre's existentialism (Dr. Horrible and the Operative as inauthentic 'monsters'), then adds Rawls and Aristotle to claim some authentic lives are better led, using Gyges's ring (in 'Gone' and 'In the Dark') and Aristotelian friendship (Team Angel, Serenity's crew) as touchstones. It defends an atheistic moral realism via Kant on personhood and Locke's natural rights (Mal insisting Saffron is 'no one's property'), and closes on free will: reading The Shepherd's Tale, Dollhouse, and The Cabin in the Woods against d'Holbach's hard determinism, Flamson's compatibilism, and Robert Kane's libertarian self-forming actions (Connor's choice in 'Inside Out').
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 8 "Conclusion" — The concluding chapter argues that Joss Whedon 'does philosophy' through the Whedonverse, building on Mulhall, Wartenberg and Shaw's hierarchy of filmic philosophizing. It reads Angel's 'Deep Down' and 'Epiphany' speeches as endorsing that kindness is a self-standing good regardless of God, framing sacrifices by Simon (for River), Cordy (for Angel) and Buffy (for Dawn) as a cinematic thought experiment refuting the claim that ethics is incoherent without God. It reads Connor as exemplifying Kane's libertarian free will (Darla and faux-Cordelia 'stir up' quantum indeterminacy), Angel/Angelus as a years-long test of memory-continuity personal identity against Parfit's Neo-Lockean view, and 'The Cabin in the Woods' plus Dollhouse's 'Man on the Street' as endorsing a Noddings-style ethics of care and Whedon's religious non-realism, with Angel offered as a Socrates-like moral exemplar.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 14 "Prognosis" — William Eaton reconstructs the Doctor's "Blink" philosophy of time using David Lewis's four-dimensionalism. He shows how Lewis's external/personal-time distinction explains the Doctor meeting his own regenerations and reversed causation (a black eye before the punch), and how "Blink" hinges on a closed causal chain (the DVD Easter-egg transcript that authors itself). He rehearses the Grandfather/Bilking paradox and Lewis's "can" equivocation solution, then places the Doctor alongside Horwich and Ismael, arguing the Doctor goes furthest by holding closed causal chains actually exist.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 10 "2. The Winchesters’ Revolt Against the Divine Plan" — Steele argues the Winchesters' fifteen-season revolt against Chuck's authored 'divine plan' stages the free-will-versus-determinism debate: Chuck writes their lives yet Sam shooting God shows the plan can be surprised, leaving 'free will in the details' as compatibilism. She frames the cosmic contest of angels, demons, and Chuck as Nietzsche's competing wills to power, but concludes Supernatural finally rejects Nietzsche for Rousseau, championing individual free will and a General Will where Sam and Dean rebuild Heaven to match their own choices.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 23 "12. Finally Free" — McCrossin argues Supernatural is a rare popular treatment of the theological (not merely secular) problem of evil, with Dean's rant echoing Job and the Book of John's Lazarus (why does God let good people suffer, and why withhold guidance?). Tracing the four showrunner 'eras' as a theodicy incubator, he reads Cas's consolation—life is an obstacle course whose obstacles Chuck may have designed but whose race 'we' ran—through Kant on freedom under determinism, concluding the show's novel theodicy is that meaning comes from being the storytellers of our own lives once Chuck stops writing them.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 18 "9. The Prequel versus Free Will" — Frim argues that Better Call Saul, precisely because it is a prequel, illustrates Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason—every event, including Walt's meth empire or Jimmy's burner-phone hustle, has a causal 'because' stretching infinitely back—and thus a deterministic universe. He dismantles the appeal to Heisenberg/quantum indeterminacy (randomness is not free choice) and refutes three myths: that determinism is boring (the causal 'Story One' is far more gripping than the free-will 'Story Two'), amoral (murder is wrong for its effects; we can keep 'suffering' and drop 'guilt'), and mindless (Nacho's ordered mind versus Tuco's drug-addled one shows minds function well or badly). He enlists Socrates' 'no one goes willingly toward the bad' to recast wrongdoing as disordered reasoning.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 30 "19. Can We Blame Jimmy for Being Jimmy" — The chapter runs Thomas Nagel's 'Moral Luck' argument on Jimmy, cataloguing his constitutive, circumstantial, causal-deterministic, and outcome luck (the con-man 'wolves and sheep' encounter, the Chicago sunroof children, the missed 1.6 million) to suggest we cannot fairly blame him. It then rebuts Nagel with a poker-and-wager analogy: since 'wagering on freedom weakly dominates' wagering on fatalism, we should treat character as cultivable through virtue theory's habits. It concludes that because nobody prevented Jimmy from changing and he has the resourcefulness to do so, his moral decline was unnecessary and blameworthy.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 6 "In the Wrong Hands, It’s a Weapon—in the Right Hands, Deliverance" — The editors' introduction frames Foundation's central conceit, psychohistory, as a vehicle for the question of determinism: if the chain of events from the founding of Rome to the reader's own hands was fixed by preceding causes, only a predictor's lack of information stands between us and perfect foresight. It uses Gibbon's Decline and Fall (Asimov's model) to raise whether the fall of empires must happen as it does, and previews the volume's further questions about obligations to future generations, science versus religion, and the ethics of deception and robot programming.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 12 "4. Demons, Game Shows, and Baguettes" — Wenmackers traces psychohistory's scientific lineage from Newtonian determinism through Laplace's demon, arguing Foundation stays within nineteenth-century limits by predicting only probabilities. She uses Newcomb's Paradox to capture the unease of living under a predicted Seldon Plan, Poincare's chaos and the three-body problem to show determinism need not mean predictability, and Poincare's baguette-fraud tale plus Quetelet's social physics and statistical mechanics to explain psychohistory's core assumption that mobs of billions behave lawfully even when individuals do not. She suggests Seldon's science was in some sense historically inevitable.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 33 "21. A Foundation-al Lesson on Free Will and Determinism" — Simpson argues Asimov balances determinism and free will through probabilistic psychohistory and reads the Mule—an unpredictable mutant—as an Epicurean 'swerve' meant to break the plan's apparent determinism, though he shows randomness no more secures freedom than determinism (the free-will dilemma). Turning to compatibilism, he uses Han Pritcher's mental 'Conversion' by the Mule to defeat classical hypothetical analyses and Gary Watson's valuational account, since Pritcher still does what he 'wants.' He builds on Frankfurt's rejection of alternative possibilities and Susan Wolf's requirement of responsiveness to the True and the Good, contrasting the manipulated Lord Stettin with Second-Foundationer Lady Callia, to give an account of free agency that would have let Asimov grant his characters agency in a deterministic universe without needing the Mule.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 22 "Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy" — Johnson uses 'Cartmanland' to lay out the problem of evil: Kyle loses his faith when the wicked Cartman gains perfect happiness, giving a logical problem-of-moral-evil argument against God. Johnson shows why the story of Job and Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' fail, then explains the greater-good and free-will defenses (invoking Augustine that only free acts are good) and the residual problem of natural evils like Kyle's hemorrhoid. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by South Park's Jesus, that God permits both moral and natural evil so we develop character, while noting the surviving evidential problem of evil's sheer amount.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 8 "NOTES" — Richard Davies uses Aristotle's Poetics (the principles of closure, relevance, and the unities of place and time) to defend Lost's tangled narrative as an epic rather than a broken tragedy, arguing that flashbacks, flash-forwards like Jack's 'We have to go back,' and multi-season arcs such as Juliet's remain within Aristotelian bounds. He then imports McTaggart's contrast between eternalism and presentism to explain why a flash-forward is philosophically unsettling, and argues that changing the past (as season 5's time travel invites) generates a logical contradiction from which anything follows, so viewers must 'shield' Hurley's 1977 experiences to keep enjoying the plot.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 10 "NOTES" — Jeremy Pierce argues that Lost mostly assumes fixed (eternalist) time and moves from its metaphysics to its ethics: even if 'whatever happened, happened,' ordinary morality still applies, so Sayid's shooting young Ben is wrong regardless of his good intentions and Jack is responsible for detonating Jughead even though he causes the very Incident he meant to prevent. Invoking Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity, Pierce holds that foreknowledge (the Man in Black's manipulation, Desmond's course-corrected saving of Charlie) does not erase free choice, concluding via Kate that morality in time travel is 'simply morality, period.'
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 9 "1. Lost in Time" — Rard uses David Lewis's definition of time travel—a discrepancy between the duration of the journey and the gap between departure and arrival—to show that 'The Rip Van Winkle Caper' suspended-animation heist is NOT time travel, while 'Last Flight' (Terry returning to save Mackaye) is, complete with a self-consistent causal loop. She then applies Lewis's argument that mundane events always thwart attempts to change the past to 'No Time Like the Past,' where Paul Driscoll is repeatedly distracted from killing Hitler and even accidentally causes the schoolhouse fire he meant to prevent, illustrating that the past is unalterable but interactable.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "Notes on Foreknowledge, Truthmaking, and Counterfactuals from The Dead Zone" — Manninen uses Johnny Smith's clairvoyance in The Dead Zone to probe how knowledge of the future is possible without fatalism, focusing on the truth condition of knowledge and truthmaker theory rather than the Gettier-vexed justification condition. Reviving Aristotle's sea-battle problem from De Interpretatione, he argues that if Johnny's statement 'Stillson will start a nuclear war' has a truthmaker the future seems fixed, foreclosing deliberation. He resolves this via Luis de Molina's middle (counterfactual) knowledge: Johnny knows only that IF Chuck attends the party or IF Stillson becomes president, THEN disaster follows, so by blocking the antecedent (keeping Stillson from office) he can avert the linked future while the general problem of divine foreknowledge and free will remains.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 26 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Dromm and Salter analyze Persuasion by distinguishing persuasion (rational, argument-based belief change), influence (nonrational, resting on a person's charisma or status, as Lady Russell has over the Elliots), and 'overpersuasion.' Against Captain Wentworth's view that persuadability is a vice and firmness of mind a virtue (his hazelnut analogy, Louisa Musgrove's fatal fall from the Cobb), they adapt Mill's On Liberty: just as free discussion lets a society exchange error for truth and gain confidence in true beliefs, a persuadable person is happier and epistemically better off. They add that Anne broke the engagement from a sense of duty, not fickleness, and it is her own persuasion that finally reunites her with Wentworth.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 21 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Ilundáin-Agurruza, Gagliardini Graça, and Jáuregui-Olaiz chart sailing's aesthetic facets — sublime, tempestuous, graceful, existential. They deploy Kant's analysis of the sublime as the balance between the imagination's failure before the ocean's immensity/power and the pleasure of meeting it through skill and reason (Ilundáin sailing in thirty-knot gusts on the point of balance between fear and joy). Dewey's notion of 'an experience' anchors sailing's transformative, self-revealing potential, terrifying storms included (Jáuregui's Snowgoose ordeal mistaking a bordello's red light for a harbor). Closing with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, they argue freedom is 'relative' and earned: we cannot change the wind but adjust the sails, gaining restrained autonomy by cultivating skill within constraint.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 26 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Tamar Rudavsky and Nathaniel Rudavsky-Brody trace how the dangerous sea drove philosophers to grapple with fate, foreknowledge, and freedom. Aristotle's sea-battle example in On Interpretation defends an indeterminate future to salvage human freedom against fortune-telling (Diagoras the atheist mocking the votive paintings). Maimonides, mourning his brother David who drowned on the India passage, asks in the Guide why a just man drowns, and answers with Aristotle that the shipwreck is chance while divine providence attaches only to the human intellect's choice to board. Finally Nietzsche makes the open sea and Columbus his image for abandoning Christian morality — 'the sea, our sea, lies open again,' the death of God, Zarathustra's summons to daring venturers to sail uncharted waters and forge a trans-valuation of values.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 24 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Felipe Carvalho frames a friend 'Toby's' worry – tattoos are forever, so should one be impulsive or cautious? – as a problem about bodily freedom versus irreversible change. He rejects the hedonist position (seize the day, regret is just part of freedom) as too simple and the Millian position (drawing on Mill's On Liberty argument that one cannot freely alienate one's freedom, as in selling oneself into slavery) as too precautionary, noting his friend's happy irreversible ear surgery. He proposes a 'middle path' learned from the tattoo community: a complex interplay of motif, the tattooist-as-artist, and the body-as-canvas that lets permanence guide more principled choices – so no 'I Love Becky' tattoos.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 25 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Heaps uses the loaded question a stranger asks a tattooed person ('aren't you afraid of being stuck with it?') to raise the freedom-versus-determinism problem, then rejects Kant's Critique of Practical Reason solution of an 'alternate nature' of rational autonomy because it quarantines free choice from the physical act of being inked. He argues instead for an 'embodied freedom' that rests on but is not determined by biology, illustrated by deciding, saving for, sitting through, and healing a tattoo. He closes with Socrates' 'know thyself' and 'the unexamined life is not worth living,' making self-examination the way to develop the effective willingness that real freedom requires.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 28 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Decker reads Ray Bradbury's 'The Illustrated Man' (William Phelps, whose witch-inked tattoo of murdering his wife Lisabeth becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy) and 'The Illustrated Woman' (Emma and Willy Fleet's shared delusion of an invisible masterpiece) to ask whether 'the body is our fate.' He aligns Phelps's predetermined tattoo with Alvin Goldman's 'Book of Life' thought experiment about foreknowledge and lost free will, and with Foucault's claim that power socially constructs docile bodies. Against this fatalism he sets George Herbert Mead's creative social self, 'taking the attitude of the other,' arguing tattooing is a plural renegotiation of identity rather than a fixed inscription.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 16 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Vargas argues that a psychopathic serial killer can be profoundly evil yet not morally responsible. Reviewing the clinical literature (Hare, the moral/conventional rule distinction, the 'mrah'/harm thought experiment), he holds that psychopaths are blind to moral rules and so, since blame requires understanding wrongdoing, cannot be blamed — the appropriate response is quarantine rather than resentment. He then separates evil from responsibility: to be evil is to desire others' harm for its own sake, and such evil, like being a jerk, need not be something one is responsible for, which is why psychopathic killers can be genuinely evil though not blameworthy.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 26 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Deal compares fictional Dexter Morgan with real killer John Wayne Gacy to explore whether serial killers are morally responsible, working through moral agency, free will, determinism, and Dennett's compatibilism (from Freedom Evolves). He argues moral responsibility requires intentional choice and the capacity to know right from wrong, which the delusional self-narratives of Dexter (the 'Dark Passenger') and the denying Gacy call into question. Drawing on experimental philosophy (Knobe and Nichols) and cognitive 'frames,' he shows our verdicts hinge on emotion: the 'abused child' frame makes Dexter sympathetic while the 'murderous psychopath' frame condemns Gacy, so how a killer's story is framed drives our attribution of responsibility.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 19 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — J. Neil Otte contrasts Patanjali's 'weak' dualism — in which prakriti and purusha are revealed as united in samadhi — with Descartes' 'deep' dualism of irreconcilable mind and body, whose interaction problem (Princess Elisabeth's objection, the pineal gland) it never solved. He traces La Mettrie's materialist 'Man a Machine,' Wittgenstein on public meaning, and neuroscience (Penfield, out-of-body proprioception experiments) to argue mind depends on brain, and that yoga's 'interdependence' of mind and body fits modern science better than either Cartesian dualism or eliminative materialism — so yoga's critics will come around.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 9 "3. Terminator I & II" — Rowlands uses the Terminator cyborg to pose the mind-body problem: how the inside view (consciousness, intentionality) meshes with the outside view (neurons firing). He rejects dualism because it only says what mind is not and cannot explain mind-body interaction (no mass, so no momentum/energy transfer), and because it would make intelligent-machine sci-fi impossible. He argues for materialism, then distinguishes 'nerd' symbol-crunching AI (Schank's restaurant scripts, Deep Blue) from 'jock' neural-network, embodied designs as the route to building an intelligent Terminator that can flexibly respond like Arnie mugging the biker.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 11 "5. Minority Report" — Rowlands uses Minority Report's precogs (a truncated Laplace's demon) to argue the film is about determinism: to certainly foresee a murder the future must be fixed by the past, distinct from predestination. He runs the dilemma of determinism, using Cruise's choice not to shoot Leo Crow: if actions are caused they are inevitable and unfree; if uncaused (indeterminism) they are merely random, citing Libet/Kornhuber experiments and the involuntary-arm-twitch example. He rejects Hume's compatibilism (freedom is doing as you please) because genuine freedom requires 'pleasing as you please,' and rejects agent-causation theory as reviving dualism's problems.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 21 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Scott Davison argues that The Lord of the Rings rejects the Manichean view of evil as an independent force equal to good and instead dramatizes Augustine's view that evil is a privation, parasitic on goodness. The Ring is not evil metal but Sauron's power working through it, the Ringwraiths wear robes to give shape to their nothingness, and Sauron himself is a corrupted will, not the source of all evil. Following Augustine's 'inordinate desire,' Davison locates the root of evil in the free choice to want more than one's fair share, illustrated by Boromir, Saruman, and Sauron's wish to usurp Iluvatar, and contrasted with Sam's contented 'plain hobbit-sense.'
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 28 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Thomas Hibbs argues that Tolkien dramatizes providence as chance that brings good out of evil, chiefly through Gollum, whose theft and fall at the Cracks of Doom completes the Quest that Frodo, having claimed the Ring, could not. Providence presupposes real freedom and duty: Hibbs compares Gandalf's counsel to do what is in us for the years we are set with Kant on freely accepting duty, while distinguishing Tolkien's enchanted, morally saturated cosmos from Kant's opposition of autonomy and nature. Following Augustine's privation view of evil (echoing the volume's earlier essay), he reads Saruman's self-destruction and Sauron's blind self-projection as evil marring itself, met fittingly by wonder, joy, and gratitude at events like Gandalf's return.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 15 "Who is Who" — The time-travel chapter grounds Doctor Who's paradoxes in Parmenides and Zeno on the impossibility of change and Aristotle on the logical necessity of past and future statements ('You can't rewrite history!' in 'The Aztecs'), then deploys determinism, David Lewis on the paradoxes of time travel, and the consistency/autonomy principles ('Father's Day,' the Reapers). It uses Leibniz's possible worlds and the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics to read 'Inferno' and 'Turn Left,' arguing quantum indeterminacy and entanglement make the Doctor's 'wibbly-wobbly, timey-wimey' theory of fixed points and flux coherent.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 19 "Time Travel and Fixed Time" — Jeremy Pierce analyzes prophecy and destiny in Harry Potter, distinguishing fallible from infallible prophecies and cataloguing how a Seer might access a fixed or open future (raising Aristotle's sea-battle problem about future truths). He argues Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are not merely likely guesses and considers self-fulfilling readings (via Alexander of Aphrodisias and Oedipus), which he rejects since the prophecy did not force Voldemort's choice. Reading Rowling's denial of 'destiny' against her fixed-time treatment of time travel and the improbable luck that fulfills the prophecy, he suggests the story fits a fixed future guided by providence better than libertarian openness or sheer coincidence.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 22 "Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy" — David Kyle Johnson frames Kyle's loss of faith in 'Cartmanland' (Cartman's undeserved happiness plus Kyle's hemorrhoid) as the logical and evidential problem of evil, then tests South Park's answers against real theodicies. He rejects the Book of Job answer and Chef/Edwards/Calvin's 'God benefits from our suffering,' examines greater-good and Augustine's free-will defense (only free acts are good), and notes the free-will defense fails for natural evil. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by the show's Jesus ('life is about overcoming problems'), as covering both moral and natural evil, while conceding the sheer amount of evil still fuels the evidential problem.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 34 "Determinism and the Dark Knight" — Hart uses Heidegger's Being and Time to explain Batman beyond the free-will/determinism binary. Dasein is a "thrown-project" always being-toward-death; Alfred's world of trays and clocks illustrates the interpretive horizon of a chosen life. Witnessing his parents' murder confronts Bruce Wayne with Angst and his own finitude, and — as in Miller's Year One, where a bat crashes through the window and he decides "I shall become a bat" — he authentically chooses his crime-fighting mission rather than being mechanically driven by trauma or vengeance.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 9 "7. Doctor Who as Philosophy Four-Dimensionalism and Time Travel" — Decker asks what the universe must be like if Doctor Who's time travel were real, using David Lewis's distinction between personal and external time and the TARDIS as a Wellsian (not Thornian) time machine traversing a 'hypertime' vortex. After surveying the arrows of time and paradoxes like the bootstrap paradox ('Day of the Daleks') and the grandfather paradox (imagined via Tegan's grandfather), and rejecting Deutsch-Lockwood's Many-Worlds and growing-block solutions, he argues the Whoniverse fits 'Four-Dimensional Realism'/eternalism, quoting the Twelfth Doctor that time's passage is an illusion of 'still pictures.' He then confronts 4DR's threat to free will and moral responsibility, finding compatibilism and 'fixed points' inadequate given eternalism's succession-not-production of events.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 13 "11. Futurama as Philosophy Wisdom from the Ignorance of a Delivery Boy" — Lewis surveys how Futurama's satire raises philosophical questions without taking sides. 'Zoidberg's Freedom Lesson' pits Mill's harm principle and free speech against Feinberg's offense principle; the mutants' and robots' oppression is read through Foucault's disciplinary normalcy and Locke's and Rawls's social contracts (state of nature, veil of ignorance). 'The Problem with Popplers' stages Bentham's utilitarianism, a might-makes-right food-chain view, and an intelligence criterion that commits Singer's 'speciesism,' with sentimentality winning. 'The Late Philip J. Fry' and 'Free Will Hunting' dramatize determinism, Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, and Sartre's existentialist free will, while 'Godfellas' and 'A Clockwork Origin' probe the problem of evil, fine-tuning, and Occam's razor.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 51 "48. The Matrix as Philosophy Understanding Knowledge, Belief, Choice, and Reality" — Perez reads the Matrix trilogy as a sustained argument about how choosing what to believe and 'know' shapes the reality we live in. He opens with Descartes' dream problem and cogito, contrasting Descartes' foundationalism with Rorty's anti-foundationalism to explain Cypher's choice to reject reality for the Matrix's certitude, and uses Searle's brute vs. institutional facts (the cookies, the steak, 'there is no spoon') to show social reality is constructed. Against the fatalism of the Oracle, Architect, and Merovingian, he argues nearly every character makes free choices, and resolves the tension via Hume's compatibilism — liberty requires necessity, and choices gain meaning only in response to causality — while noting agent-causation objections (Reid, O'Connor, Rowe) that make Neo's 'Because I choose to' significant. Gettier's justified-true-belief critique and Plato's Cave frame the knowledge and enlightenment themes.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 60 "57. Tenet as Philosophy Fatalism Isn’t an Excuse to Do Nothing" — The chapter reads Nolan's Tenet as an argument for metaphysical fatalism set in a block-universe (eternalism), using the Sator Square, the palindromic 'ten,' and Neil's refrain 'what's happened, happened' as evidence that every event, including the Protagonist's and Kat's, was fated and unchangeable. It deploys David Lewis's solution to the grandfather paradox and reverse causation (Feynman/Wheeler positrons) to show the future cannot kill its ancestors, then argues fatalism entails no libertarian free will, rejecting Frankfurt's compatibilist second-order-desires account and citing van Inwagen that indeterministic acts are no freer. Via a back-tracking counterfactual it concludes fatalism is still no excuse to do nothing, because different action would have yielded a different (annihilated) world.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 91 "86. God of War as Philosophy Prophecy, Fate, and Freedom" — Horn argues that the God of War series dramatizes theological fatalism—the apparent conflict between foreknowledge (the Oracle, Fates, Norns, Giants) and libertarian freedom—as Kratos, Zeus, and Kronos bring about the very fates they flee. He tests Boethius/Aquinas's timeless-eternity solution (rejected because the games' seers act in time), Molina's middle knowledge (rejected because none of the beings are provident), and Ockham's counterfactual power over the past (the only one workable across both arcs). He concludes the Greek Trilogy depicts a deterministic universe with fixed fate, while the Norse Duology, via the fallible Open-Theism-style Norns and Faye's 'possible path' mural, shows fate is malleable when Kratos changes himself and 'opens his heart.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 94 "88. Watchmen as Philosophy Illustrating Time and Free Will" — Goldberg and Gavaler argue that Moore and Gibbons's Watchmen operationalizes eternalism (McTaggart's B-series) both through its rigid 3x3 grid and mirror-symmetric layouts and through Doctor Manhattan, who narrates all moments as simultaneously present ('nothing ever ends'). Because eternalism means no one could have done otherwise, libertarian free will is ruled out, and the chapter argues the operative view is compatibilism rather than determinism, using Frankfurt's rejection of the principle of alternative possibilities and Dennett's Luther example to read Doctor Manhattan's hesitant killing of Rorschach as free action he could not have done otherwise.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 10 "2. The Dangers of Being the Doctor" — The chapter weighs the Doctor's ethic of interference against the Time Lords' non-interference, using determinism and the 'butterfly effect' (Martha in 'The Shakespeare Code') to concede when disengaged observation is prudent, while insisting that non-interference fails to protect human dignity. Drawing on Terrence Des Pres's account of dignity as 'inward resistance,' and real-world dissidents Adam Michnik and Václav Havel's 'power of the powerless,' it reads 'Rosa,' 'The Woman Who Fell to Earth,' and the people of Le Chambon as models of dignified, communal resistance to wrongdoing. Citing Iris Young, it argues everyone bears moral responsibility to engage rather than remain a detached, complicit 'objective observer.'

### Personal Identity

Personal identity concerns what makes someone the same person over time despite change, and what the self fundamentally is. Philosophers have offered competing criteria: the body or brain, continuity of memory and psychology, or the persistence of an immaterial soul. Locke's memory-based view, Hume's bundle theory that finds no enduring self behind experiences, and later refinements have all sought to say why the child and the adult, or the person before and after profound change, count as one and the same. The question matters for responsibility, anticipation, survival, and the concern we have for our own futures.

- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 23 "Inauthenticity and Fascism" — David Detmer treats Zelig, the mock-documentary 'chameleon man' who turns black, Chinese, fat, or a Nazi depending on his company, as a stark dramatization of personal identity and the existentialist critique of inauthenticity. After rejecting the memory, bodily-continuity, and immaterial-soul criteria of identity, the chapter takes the existentialist line, quoting Heidegger on Dasein's selfhood, that a self is its choices, projects, and commitments, so Zelig's chameleonism is self-estrangement motivated by fear and the craving to be liked. Politically, the chapter draws Allen's lesson that genocides happen not because millions go mad but because millions passively conform, made literal by Zelig appearing at a Hitler rally, and supports it with Asch's conformity experiments and Milgram's obedience studies.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 19 "Horcruxes" — Uses Lupin's account of the Dementor's Kiss, whose victims like Barty Crouch Jr. go on existing as empty shells without memory or self, to eliminate the leading views of the soul: the soul cannot be the source of life, of sentience, or even of Cartesian higher thought, since the soulless victim may still sense and think dimly. The chapter compares the Kiss's aftermath to severe dementia or to Lockhart after his backfired memory charm, raising the question of whether the person rather than just the body survives.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 23 "Mind-Body Distinctions" — Eric Saidel launches his chapter from a puzzle: why would Sirius, outside for the first time in months, celebrate by chasing his tail in Order of the Phoenix? He asks whether an Animagus is a man in a dog's body, a dog in a man's body, or a third thing, and extends the question to Pettigrew, Rita Skeeter, McGonagall, werewolf Lupin, boggarts, and Polyjuice transformations such as Barty Crouch Jr.'s eerily effective impersonation of Moody.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 24 "Whose Reasons" — Tests the Cartesian division of the transformed Padfoot into mind plus body across four possible combinations and rejects them all: Sirius's human body cannot plausibly slip 'into non-being' during transformation (against McGonagall's quip), yet a Sirius-mind cannot explain tail-chasing and a dog-mind cannot explain Padfoot standing on his hind legs to embrace Harry at King's Cross. Mind-body dualism thus fails as an account of what the transformed person is.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 27 "NOTES" — Concludes that transformed persons are unified mind-body wholes rather than pilot-and-ship pairings, enlisting Descartes himself, who insisted he is 'not only lodged in my body, like a pilot in his ship' but compounded with it into a single whole. The evidence is textual: Polyjuiced Harry naturally 'thunders' with Runcorn's powerful frame while acting for Harry's reasons, Luna recognizes Harry through Barny Weasley's facial expression, and Crouch-as-Moody makes sense as an indivisible embodiment, so Padfoot is neither man nor dog but a third kind of being, a man-dog.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 111 "“A Swirling, Silvery Mass”" — Opens Amy Kind's Pensieve chapter: the basin lets you offload memories like data from a hard drive, gain distance from obsessions, and, as Dumbledore tells Harry, spot patterns and links when reviewing them from outside. Its real intrigue is philosophical: if thoughts can be extracted from the mind, tampered with, stored elsewhere, shared, and discarded, then the boundaries of mind, memory, and self are up for grabs - and memory-based accounts of personal identity, on which philosophers have modeled our continuing existence, come under pressure.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 132 "The Inversion of Voldemort" — Distinguishes remorse from mere regret through Voldemort's cold 'I regret it' after ordering Nagini to kill Snape: remorse requires owning one's act, and at the final duel Harry addresses him as 'Tom Riddle' and demands he 'try for some remorse' - the death-to-self Riddle cannot perform. Dumbledore's remorse over the cursed Resurrection Stone ring and his arranged death, and Harry's voluntary death that destroys the Horcrux within him and restores his whole soul, exemplify dying to the past self for renewal, while Harry's renunciation of his temper toward Ron and Hermione and his love for Ginny mark his continuous moral regeneration.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 134 "The Fantasy Objection" — Takes up the integrity objection from psychoanalyst Melanie Klein: renouncing one's past self ('Bad Charles' versus 'New Charlie') risks self-deception, since the reformed person remains the self-same wrongdoer, as the alcoholic who stays sober for decades still knows himself to be. Taliaferro concedes the regeneration model can be abused but insists renewal requires a death-like renunciation, illustrated negatively by Snape, who loves Lily, feels remorse for the 'Mudblood' insult and for giving Voldemort the prophecy, yet cannot confess or release his resentment, and so remains unintegrated.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 142 "NOTES" — Argues via William James's 'sow a thought... reap a destiny' and Aristotle's account of how repeated action incrementally shapes the soul that Voldemort's flayed remnant is a character fully forged by choices, stuck with itself forever - a postmortem fate Heidegger's atheism cannot frame but Rowling's afterlife can. The section weighs Locke's memory-and-character account of identity, Kant's postulate that harmony of virtue and happiness requires an afterlife, and Pascal on why the immortality question must govern how we live, and ends asking whether Voldemort's evil is ignorance, as Plato held, or a cultivated appetite that only vice can satisfy.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 111 "Chapter 17 - Questions of Identity Is the Hulk the Same Person as Bruce Banner" — Frames the chapter with a San Francisco criminal trial in which Bruce Banner's lawyer argues the Hulk — a large green figure — literally was not the same individual who now stands small and pale before the judge. Ruling requires criteria for "continuity of personal identity over time": what makes you the same person today as ten years ago, applied here to whether Banner should answer for the Hulk's rampage.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 112 "The Hulk’s Bodily Identity" — Tests the everyday bodily criterion of identity: the Hulk's body contains far more atoms than Banner's, but since all our cells turnover anyway — the "Stan Lee Schooner" has every part replaced yet stays the same boat, the Ship of Theseus problem — and the organ-donor case of "Herb Trimpe" shows a body with greater physical continuity to Kinghorn than to its owner, bodily continuity cannot be what personal identity consists in.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 113 "The Mental Realm of the Hulk" — Applies Locke's memory theory: the shape-shifting Martian Manhunter and the irradiated Fantastic Four stay the same people through mental continuity, and the early comics' Banner-minded Hulk meets Locke's criterion — but the later "Hulk smash!" Hulk, who recognizes Betty Ross yet lacks Banner's memories, fails it. The chapter then breaks the criterion itself with Reid's brave-officer objection (the general both is and is not the flogged boy), Alzheimer's and Doc Ock's amnesia attack on Spider-Man, and the circularity of distinguishing genuine from false memory (the deluded fan who "remembers" starring in Adventures of Superman).
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 114 "A Causal Account of the Hulk’s Identity" — Proposes that the Hulk is Banner because Banner "Hulks out" — the monster state develops causally from Banner's body and mind through radiation, danger and anger, rather than one person being swapped for another. But a mad scientist's cloning accident that splits Banner into two simultaneous rampaging Hulks breaks the account, since both would be causally derived from Bruce yet could not both be the one person — the fission-style counterexample that afflicts every theory so far.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 115 "Is There No Way to Tell" — Presents Derek Parfit's challenge to the whole enterprise: just as there need be no answer to whether a repaired machine is "the same" machine, Parfit's divided-brain case — each half housed in a new body — suggests a person can "survive as two different people without implying that I am these people," so identity questions may lack answers. Kinghorn resists the leap: difficulty finding the truth does not show there is none.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 116 "The Hulk’s Relational Identity" — Defends a relational account: a person's identity persists through continuing relationships with others (like a marriage or a corporation), against our post-Enlightenment fixation on private attributes. Objections — severed relationships, the castaway, others' biased projections — are answered by positing a God who relates to every person without distortion and guarantees each identity, and who, since divine power cannot do the logically impossible, could not make Banner identical with two numerically distinct Hulks at once.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 117 "What Should We Conclude" — Renders the verdict in the Banner trial: Bruce is the Hulk, because their relationships continue — when David Banner phones to say Betty Ross will be eliminated, Bruce forms the protective intention the Hulk then executes by destroying the three mutant poodles, and Betty, David and General Ross all relate to the Hulk as Bruce. Physical, mental and causal indicators are mere cues to the deeper continuity of relationships that constitutes who someone is.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 125 "Identity in Crisis" — Poses the persistence problem through Superman-1 and Superman-2: are they strictly identical? Perdurantism — persons as four-dimensional space-time worms made of temporal parts — makes them distinct worms with no parts in common, so Superman meeting his counterpart is no stranger than you meeting a friend; endurantism, with wholly present strict identity, could identify them across timelines but balks at the impossibility of Superman meeting himself.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 126 "Endurantist Past-Changing" — Chases the endurantist bullet: if one thing can differ across timelines, one and the same timeline can exist differently in different hyperhistories, letting Joe's murder of Wolfman make 1984 "not the way he remembers it." Yet even this yields only switching, not the dynamic change Crisis dramatizes, so the six-dimensional cosmos stands; Hanley closes with Wolfman's own secret plot device for bringing back the killed Barry Allen Flash.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 128 "Dual Identities" — Lists the classic hero/normal identity pairs (Batman/Bruce Wayne, Spider-Man/Peter Parker, plus Woody Allen's joke alias) and separates costume as role-transition — the Fantastic Four's public uniforms, doctors' scrubs, Bob's garage shirt — from costume as tool, Batman's fear-theater aimed at "a superstitious and cowardly lot" and the female heroes' calculated "gawk factor." What most superheroes do is the distinct third thing, masking: personas from the Latin for mask, keeping Peter's Spider-Man and Matt Murdock's Daredevil secret in both directions.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 28 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Uses Narnia's magical transformations to probe personal identity, starting with the qualitative/numerical identity distinction illustrated by the look-alike twins Shasta and Corin in The Horse and His Boy. Aristotle's essential/accidental properties frame the question of what Eustace can lose and remain Eustace, including turning into a dragon, and Rabadash into a donkey, showing persons are not identical to their bodies. Descartes's soul argument and Locke's memory theory are tested and rejected, the latter because it cannot handle Rilian's enchanted amnesia, Shasta's forgotten infancy, or Susan's disowned memories without circularity. The chapter defends instead a first-person-perspective theory on which a person is constituted by, not identical to, a body, illustrated by the repeatedly repaired Dawn Treader and by the heroes surviving death in The Last Battle as restored points of view.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 21 "“Nobody’s Bob Dylan”" — Vernezze and Lulewicz take Dylan's 1964 Halloween quip "I got my Bob Dylan mask on" as an entry into personal identity, testing each theory against his life: the bodily view (Zimmerman to Dylan) survives cell turnover but stumbles on brain-transplant cases; Locke's memory theory handles them but faces Reid's brave-officer regress and Alzheimer's cases, and Dylan's reincarnation lyrics ("Shelter from the Storm," "I and I") ignore memory altogether. The Christian soul view of the gospel albums ("When He Returns," "Gotta Serve Somebody") follows Descartes and Plato but cannot justify the swirl-to-filling inference that souls exist. The chapter ends sympathetic to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist no-self: Dylan's "I is another," his name as fabrication, and the cover album Self Portrait all deny a fixed self-created essence.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 8 "Dead People" — William Larkin uses Romero's films - Karen Cooper devouring her father in Night of the Living Dead, Roger begging Peter to shoot him in Dawn, Riley's 'Those people are all dead' in Land - to argue that persons are res corporealis, bodily continuers, rather than Descartes's res cogitans. Our terror of becoming a zombie ourselves and our grief at recognized neighbors in the horde reveal that deep down we think persons survive as corpses, so bodily continuity suffices for identity while psychological continuity is unnecessary. The Locke-style body-switching intuition (prince and cobbler) that supports the psychological approach is dismissed as theoretically biased data compared to what good zombie fiction draws out of us.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 9 "Zombies and Us" — Hamish Thompson asks why we kill zombies with so few qualms and whether zombification releases us from obligations to the person who was, testing brain-death criteria, altered-identity and self-defense justifications against Shaun of the Dead (Shaun's mother and Ed), Day of the Dead's Bub, White Zombie, and Invasion of the Body Snatchers. He borrows Hume's bundle theory - the self as a fiction, a bundle of perceptions rather than an essence - and Parfit's degrees of psychological continuity to dissolve the sharp alive/dead and same-person/other-person dichotomies that make zombie-killing easy. The payoff is that we are already partly zombie (Shaun's checkout line, Ed on the sofa, the author's all-night gaming), differing only in our capacity for brief autonomous, goal-directed choices like Shaun's three-plan montage.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 30 "Oh Yes, There Will Be Blood" — Rachel Robison asks why blood, of all substances, carries metaphysical powers in vampire lore - Elizabeth Bathory's youth-giving baths, Dracula's control over Mina once she drinks his blood, Sookie's bond with Bill in True Blood. Her explanation is historical: the ancient cardiocentric view (Aristotle, Empedocles, Chrysippus placing the rational center in the heart and making blood its product) plus Galenic humorism and bloodletting made blood the carrier of the self, so drinking someone's blood plausibly transmits bits of their personal identity, knowledge, and even domination over one's free will. She then tests the show's synthetic 'True Blood': either some essential property of blood (or of the act of drinking it) carries the power, or the legend is parasitic on our lingering habit of locating emotion and character in the heart ('hot blooded') - either way the myth stays credible because our metaphors of blood never died.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 18 "Be Slow to Judge" — Southworth tests Locke's memory theory on Wolverine: the Cassandra Nova/Xavier mind-swap shows identity follows mind, not body, and Wolverine's serial memory wipes (Team X, Weapon X, Apocalypse's brainwashing) mean that on Locke's connected-memory view several different people have inhabited his body — with House of M's total recall suddenly loading him with responsibility for all their deeds. Jamie Madrox's duplicates then carry Parfit's objection that shared memories cannot suffice for sameness of person, pushing toward physical continuity and the chapter's deflationary moral: be slow to judge who deserves blame.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 19 "Identities, Selves, and Others" — Patterson uses Thornhill's being mistaken for the fictitious George Kaplan to test theories of personal identity: the body theory fails a CIA thought experiment in which a Kaplan double is slowly rebuilt from Thornhill's own replaced cells; Locke's memory theory fails on amnesia scenarios and circularity, since one cannot have memories of a self unless one already has a self; and Parfit's psychological continuity survives, with Thornhill drifting along a 'Psychological Spectrum' toward 'one hundred percent Kaplan' as he plays the spy. The chapter then turns existentialist: with Sartre, no essential nature fixes who Thornhill is, so he is totally responsible for the self his choices create, from 'Expedient Exaggerations' to risking death on Mount Rushmore. Charles Taylor's claim that a self exists only in dialogue with a community explains why Eve and others literally help make Thornhill into the person he becomes.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 17 "Was Jerry Garcia the Soul of the Grateful Dead" — John Uglietta asks what made the Grateful Dead the Grateful Dead when they swapped five keyboardists yet stopped being themselves the moment Jerry Garcia died, prompting the rename to The Dead. Testing Aristotle's essential versus accidental properties, Peter French's structural account of group identity (the Yankees, the Glenn Miller Orchestra), same-stuff theories via a VW bus rebuilt piece by piece from its old parts — a Ship of Theseus puzzle — and Locke's memory theory applied to Phil Lesh's liver (but feared brain) transplant, he proposes that the band's essence was a group spirit born of members 'surrendering their own little trip'. The soul of the Dead was bigger than Jerry but smaller than the whole band, and its loss at his death was something the survivors could recognize but not replace.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 20 "Absolutely Curtains" — Michael Patton retells the Ship of Theseus (his 'Trump Princess' rebuilt part-by-part from spares, then duplicated from the salvaged parts) to ask whether Pink Floyd survived its upheavals: Bob Klose's pre-Piper exit, Syd Barrett's 1968 dismissal ('No, fuck it, let's not bother' on the drive to Southampton), Rick Wright's firing during The Wall, and Roger Waters's 1985 lawsuit to stop Gilmour and Mason using the name. Roster, stylistic ('Lucifer Sam' versus 'Money'), legal, and nominal criteria each fail, so he proposes an 'Officeholder View' of identity in which constituencies decide sameness — as when UFO Club's Joe Boyd saw a different Syd at the June 1967 show, while the author's locked-in brother Josh (like Bauby in The Diving Bell and the Butterfly) remained the same son and brother to his family. Parfit's claim that survival tracks memory and personality rather than body underwrites the 'death of a thousand cuts' scenario: the band's criteria, not Syd's own, ended the life of the person 'Syd Barrett', and he didn't get a vote.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 6 "Introduction" — The editors' introduction opens with Socrates on trial for corrupting the youth of Athens and quips that on stage before the youth of Athens, Georgia, Cash could claim he was only asking "What is truth?" It frames Cash as Kris Kristofferson's "walking contradiction" whose paradoxes generate the book's questions: how evil fits a world rated by a benevolent God, where the enduring "I" hides while Cash insisted he was always changing, and what makes a law unjust. It also presents the Man in Black as social critic lobbying officials at San Quentin and Folsom for prison reform and raising money for reservation schools, before welcoming readers with the 1969 Arthur, Illinois concert where hippies and Amish rubbed shoulders.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 8 "Authentic Cash" — Butler rehearses how the Johnny Cash persona was socially manufactured: Sam Phillips coined the name "Johnny Cash" for its rebellious marketing value, "Folsom Prison Blues" narrates a prison term Cash never served (and borrowed from Jimmie Rodgers and Gordon Jenkins), and the Man in Black image began as an accident of black shirts at a Memphis church performance. Against Jung's persona-as-mask and Dr. Phil's "authentic core self," and armed with George Herbert Mead's social theory of the self, he argues authenticity is not fidelity to a hidden inner essence but active engagement with the social processes shaping one's identity, the way paper money gains "cash value" through use. Cash invested the imposed persona with value by sincerely living it (for example, writing "Man in Black" to give the black clothes his own meaning), so the construct became genuinely his identity.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 9 "A Modest Conclusion" — Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro stage the diachronic-versus-episodic debate about the self (Galen Strawson's episodic view included) against Leigh Edwards's "no single Johnny Cash": the hotel-room-wrecking addict and the Billy Graham touring Christian do not fit one biography. They argue the private J.R. was a third option: on stage he becomes wholly absorbed in story characters (the Folsom narrator, the man who shot a man in Reno) while a self not defined by time slips in and out of the persona, evidenced by his account of gradually shedding "Johnny Cash" after shows. Johnny Cash the public quilt is compared to the Ship of Theseus, every original piece of J.R. replaced yet still owned by him, and the modest conclusion is that J.R., like anyone making a free choice, stood above the timeline of instants and could inhabit both the episodes and the grand narrative.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 26 "Memories Are Made of This" — Randall Jensen asks whether Cash's hope of reunion with the dead ('Meet Me in Heaven,' 'If We Never Meet Again This Side of Heaven') is even coherent, using the 'One Piece at a Time' Cadillac and a hypothetical 1954 Plymouth to retell the Ship of Theseus puzzle about identity through part replacement. He canvasses Platonic dualism from the Phaedo (Cash is his soul, the body a rusty cage), the materialist hope that God can reassemble a resurrected body despite dispersed matter, and the psychological-continuity view that persons are 'made of memories,' ending on the duplication problem: if God made two heavenly bodies both carrying Cash's memories, which one would be Cash?
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 19 "Case the Promised Land" — Herstein reads 'Thunder Road' as an event, not an object: the screen door slam and Mary's waving dress form a single event that language can only serially narrate, and Whitehead's event ontology (with Ricoeur's Time and Narrative on how we discover and rewrite ourselves in stories, and Emerson's 'monstrous corpse' of memory from 'Self Reliance') explains why the Seanachie's tale creates a world rather than describing one. His own autobiographical turn — first hearing the song while stuck in a dead-end life, then at the 1980 Los Angeles 'Factory' performance watching Springsteen's voice resolve two warring rhythms by adding a third — shows narrative running backwards, retelling and redeeming the past, which is why the burnt-out Chevrolets are already behind the dirty hood. The solo-harmonica version strips away porch, vision, and redemption to desolation, yet the conclusion is freedom: because the events of the world await our creative retelling, you are the Seanachie of your own life, and 'maybe I am that young, after all.'
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 9 "Retelling Our Stories" — Milsky uses Ricoeur and MacIntyre's narrative theory of personal identity to read the two Sharons: Boomer's fabricated human backstory suffers a 'factual disruption' when she shoots Adama, while Athena's 'disruption of belief' comes from falling in love with Helo. He argues such disruptions — also suffered by humans like Starbuck (recovered memories of abuse in 'Maelstrom'), Roslin (coming to believe she is Pythia's dying leader), and Helo — need not destroy identity, since narratives can be retold, as the Final Four do in 'Crossroads, Part 2' with Tigh's 'My name is Saul Tigh' speech. Third-party narratives (Six disowning Athena, the crew refusing to see Boomer as Boomer) show identity is partly socially constructed and can become self-fulfilling prophecy, with Boomer's blackouts resembling dissociative identity disorder.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 10 "Frak-tured Finality" — Booth argues that the 'Resistance' webisodes fracture BSG's narrative across television and Internet, forcing viewers to actively construct the story — Jammer's execution in 'Collaborators' and Duck's suicide bombing only make full sense if you pieced the webisodes together — and that this viewer-side fragmentation mirrors the characters' fractured identities. Drawing on Foucault's constructed self, Deleuze and Guattari's 'schizophrenia,' Goffman's performed roles, and Haraway's cyborg, he reads Baltar's 'Am I a Cylon?', Boomer's amnesia in 'Water,' Hera's human-Cylon hybridity, and Tigh's choice in 'Crossroads' to actively construct who he will be. The payoff: there is no central location for the self, the narrative, or Cylonhood — each becomes whole only through active construction.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 14 "“Sometimes You Just Have to Bow to the Absurd”" — Eberl weighs genetic enhancement and cloning through Trek's test cases: Julian Bashir's parents' enhancement leaves him feeling 'a fraud' ('You used to be my father. Now, you're my architect'), the Moab IV 'Masterpiece Society' breeds out 'the unknown, self-discovery, things that make life worth living', and the Jem'Hadar show desire itself engineered for control. He argues the right to an open future constrains designing children (B'Elanna's wish to de-Klingonize her baby, Worf pressuring Alexander), defends genetic treatment while rejecting genetic determinism, and uses Kass and Rovane with Picard and Shinzon, the Mariposa clones, and Trip's clone Sim to show clones are numerically distinct persons. Against Malik's Augments quoting Nietzsche — 'mankind is something to be surpassed' — the chapter argues the Übermensch demands self-mastery through philosophy, not eugenic engineering, tracing eugenics from Plato's Guardian breeding scheme through Buck v. Bell to modern prenatal selection.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 26 "“I Feel Exactly What You Feel”" — Runs Star Trek's transporter and android stories as thought experiments on personal identity: the body theory (Kirk rejecting android Korby — 'Dr. Korby was never here' — and Picard telling the resurrected Rishon Uxbridge 'you do not exist'), the brain theory ('Spock's Brain,' Bashir refusing to replace half of Vedek Bareil's brain), and Locke's memory theory as vindicated by the Trill (Lela Dax's 'a person is but the sum of their memories,' the 'Dax' extradition hearing over Curzon's crimes). Riker's transporter double in 'Second Chances' and the Tuvix fusion then break the memory theory through fission and fusion, prompting Parfit's move that psychological continuity, not numerical identity, is what matters in survival. Memory erasure in 'Dagger of the Mind' and Kurn's rebranding after the failed Mauk-to'Vor in 'Sons of Mogh' count as death if we are our memories.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 17 "Solutions to the Problem The youth whose destiny it is to lead Hyrule to the" — Robison asks how Link stays the same person through Ocarina of Time's child/adult switches, Twilight Princess's wolf form, and Wind Waker's consciousness-projection into seagulls and mages. Physical-continuity views fail because Link's body changes or is left behind; Locke's memory-based psychological continuity fails because adult Link's past hasn't happened yet when he travels back. After a Ship of Theseus variant (Ganon reassembling Tetra's sunken planks) she proposes that in Zelda's stipulative metaphysics, destiny, the goddess-given roles of courage, wisdom, and power, is the necessary and sufficient condition of identity, fitting videogame universes whose metaphysics are fixed by designers.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 14 "Epilog-Rolling" — Patton turns the Tin Woodman's backstory—the enchanted axe that costs Nick Chopper his legs, arms, torso and heart, then his head, each replaced by the tinsmith—into a cyborg thought experiment about how much of a person can be swapped out before the person is gone. After a framing nod to Plato's Republic on censoring frightening tales (his father's ban on 'mental violence' fantasy), he brings in Derek Parfit: the R-relation, the 'My Division' brain-split, and the Branch-Line teletransportation case are mapped onto the Woodman (including a hypothetical straw-bodied second Nick) to argue that survival gets different answers from first-person and third-person perspectives. The closing wildcat episode, where the tinned Woodman neatly decapitates a wildcat to save a field mouse, is offered as textual evidence that the tin head failed to preserve moral consistency—so the original Nick Chopper is gone for good, and the Scarecrow's shared brain explains why the two friends later refuse to part.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 20 "Getting to Oz" — Auxier uses the Wizard's demand that Dorothy kill the Witch to split 'ought' from 'can'—ethics from the metaphysics and logic of possibility—and then asks whether Oz is a genuinely possible world. He explains David Lewis's modal realism (every genuine possibility actual in its own causally isolated world) through counterfactuals about which network aired the film, dissolves the silver-versus-ruby slippers conflict by assigning book-Oz and film-Oz to different possible worlds, and argues that since no flat contradiction can be eked out of the Oz stories, Lewis is committed to Oz's being real—though Maguire's inter-world travel and Elphaba's hybrid, soul-less trans-world identity (her counterpart in our world being, playfully, Dorothy) stretch Lewis's 'counterparts' doctrine to its limit. Peirce supplies the closing caution, with Boole, that logic is a set of norms for how we can and ought to think rather than a proven mirror of other worlds, so believing in Oz's full reality remains permissible fun rather than an obligation.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 28 "You Can Go Home Again" — Fortune stages the movie as a morality play between two conceptions of personhood: the Wizard is an atomist, a self-sufficient ball from the Chuck E. Cheese ball pit who is the same humbug in Omaha or Oz and who reduces heart, brains, and courage to a testimonial, a diploma, and a medal, while Dorothy is a relationalist, a pineapple chunk that belongs on one particular pizza, a person constituted by her web of relations to home. 'There's no place like home' is therefore the relationalist's slogan, an acceptance of home for everything it is, good and bad, with Toto's fate still unresolved under Miss Gulch's law. He closes by suggesting the film's delayed television-era triumph is existential nostalgia: modern, rootless, ear-budded Americans keep watching because the relationalist country it mourns is 'what's in our blood.'
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 7 "Transformers and Philosophy" — The editors' introduction frames the volume around First Contact with a robotic civilization: citing SETI's Seth Shostak, they argue aliens are more likely to be AI machines than little green men, with the Autobot-Decepticon civil war catching humans in between on a moral as well as physical plane. They pose the book's questions about Optimus Prime and Megatron: whether Transformers have moral status and minds despite passing the Turing Test, whether they have souls and are capable of Platonic or erotic love, and what makes Optimus the same being whether robot or vehicle. Probing Transformer nature, they conclude, is really probing human nature, since Transformers are our own creations.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 13 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Spicher argues that when Bumblebee trades his beat-up 1976 Camaro for a shiny 2007 model only his appearance changes (an accidental change), never his identity, because transforming is part of a Transformer's essence like a human wearing a mask. Locke's memory continuity and Thomson's bodily criterion each fail - the embryo, coma, and corpse problems, plus the thought experiment of Megatron's memories transplanted into another body - so he defends an Aristotelian composite of form and matter in which the Spark is the soul-like form organizing the machine body, preserving identity through transformation as form guides matter toward actuality.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 11 "19" — Four 'Phase Five' puzzle essays. Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro use Secret Wars to test omnipotence: the Beyonder, Doom, and Galactus cannot do the logically impossible (no spherical cubes, no stone too heavy to lift), two omnipotent beings collide, and a truly omnipotent being has no desires - so villains can never climb to the top they crave. Matthewson and Wall use Frankfurt cases and reasons-responsive source compatibilism to explain why Eddie Brock is responsible for Venom's villainy (he voluntarily bonded and endorses the symbiote's adjusted psychology) while Anne Weying, horrified by what the symbiote made her do, bears only minimal blame. Pickavance reconstructs the Ship of Theseus with Sandman's 'mansand': combining part exchange with materialism lets Norman Osborn reassemble a duplicate Sandman from his scattered remains, and since neither principle nor soul-dualism comes free, personal identity through material change remains unsolved. Loader argues Brainiac's reinvention as a 'facts and logic' computer embodies disembodied Cartesian AI, so the frame problem (Dennett's exploding robots) and embodied cognition (Clark's Tetris, Dreyfus) suggest his detachment from body and world would make him less, not more, intelligent than the humans he scorns.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 9 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — The editors' introduction argues that His Dark Materials is philosophy-rich rather than a mere children's fantasy: its metaphysics of parallel worlds, dæmons, angels, armored bears, and mulefa poses genuine epistemic questions and ethical dilemmas. It frames the volume around the controversy over whether exposing children to Pullman's anti-religious vision is spiritual violence or an education in thinking for oneself like Lyra. It also sets up the trilogy's alternative afterlife, where Lyra frees the dead from the drab land of the dead to dissolve into Dust, and flags dæmons as puzzles of personal identity and soul-body interaction.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 25 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Harris and Baer use the Boatman scene ('Pan is me... we'd die') to test criteria of personal identity against the trilogy: Lyra and Will's inference to a thinking third part, the ghost, reenacts Descartes's dualist reasoning about mind-body distinctness, Iorek's lack of a ghost exemplifies the same-body criterion, and Pantalaimon's instant shape-shifting favors the psychological criterion, spelled out through Locke's prince-and-cobbler memory thought experiment and Parfit's psychological connectedness and continuity. They ask whether Lee Scoresby's dissolution into conscious atoms that reunite with Hester's counts as genuine survival, best accommodated by Locke's consciousness criterion or a panpsychist matter criterion, with Chalmers cited as the contemporary defender of conscious matter. The chapter closes with individuation, whether Lyra and Pan are one person or two, applied to a Primal Fear-style multiple-personality murder trial, the hypothetical of Pan killing someone while Lyra is innocent, and living wills in persistent vegetative states.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 18 "Coda" — Gimbel asks what makes a band remain the same band over time: Led Zeppelin survived replacing drummer John Bonham with his son Jason, yet Page and Jones insist no singer could replace Robert Plant. Working through Plutarch's Ship of Theseus, Aristotle's essential properties, and Locke's continuity account of identity, he uses Peter French's distinction between aggregates (groups defined by membership) and conglomerates (defined by role structure) to argue a band is a conglomerate. The twist is that a reunion would be a monument like Theseus's preserved ship rather than a working vessel: Plant is an Aristotelian essential of what Zeppelin was, while Jason Bonham's family link supplies the reverence and facsimile-fidelity a monument needs.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 16 "Mr. Monk Is Mr. Monk" — Malloy runs the classic theories of personal identity through Monk episodes. Bodily (really brain) identity fails when 'the Monk' — the reckless medicated alter of 'Mr. Monk Takes His Medicine' — shares Monk's body and brain yet is not held responsible, and Stanley Tucci's method actor in 'Mr. Monk and the Actor' shows that copying Monk's looks and behavior does not transfer identity. Locke's memory theory breaks on the amnesia of 'Mr. Monk Bumps His Head' (Monk becomes roofer 'Jerry') and the blackout in 'Mr. Monk and the Rapper,' and Reid's brave-officer paradox yields contradiction once recovered Monk remembers being both Monk and Jerry. Hume's bundle theory — 'I never can catch myself,' the self as theatre of successive perceptions — grounds psychological continuity's graded identity, but then cult-swayed Monk in 'Mr. Monk Joins a Cult' might count as a different person, making his deprogramming a kind of murder; the chapter closes by rejecting Reid and Butler's 'simple and unassayable' escape, insisting a philosopher, like a detective, must keep theorizing how Monk stays Monk.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 13 "Is Everybody Disembodied (or, Have We Always Been Posthuman Beings )" — Stevens uses the film's closing voice-over 'I am Tetsuo' in Otomo's Akira to run the classic identity-and-mind problems: Heraclitus's river and Plutarch's Ship of Theseus ask whether the grotesquely transformed, Akira-absorbed Tetsuo is still the same person, while Descartes's cogito — riffed as 'cogito ergo Tetsuo' — Turing's Test, and Searle's Chinese Room test whether a voice that seems to think proves a thinker behind it (syntax is not yet shown sufficient for semantics, though Edwin Hutchins's distributed cognition reads the Room from the inside out). Weighing embodiment (Pinker's brain-makes-mind, Dennett's self as a 'center of narrative gravity') against disembodiment (Akira levelling Neo-Tokyo from nothing but cryogenically stored remains; Tetsuo's matter teleportation), he concludes through the problem of representation — every utterance is re-presented, as in Augustine's guilty tears over Dido — that we always treat semblances of thinkers as thinkers, so we may have always been decentered, re-presented, posthuman beings no different from Tetsuo and Akira.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 8 "Dead People" — William Larkin pits Descartes's res cogitans (the person as psychological continuum, reinforced by Locke's prince-and-cobbler body-switch) against a res corporealis view in which bodily continuity suffices for identity, using Romero's Dead films as intuition pumps. The terror of Roger's 'I don't want to be walking around like that' and Rain's request in Resident Evil only makes sense if we think it would be us rising as zombies, and the tragedy of Karen Cooper devouring her father or Johnny menaging Barbara only lands if the same person persists. Against the 'just dead flesh' scientists and the mall-memory reading of Dawn, he argues zombie psychology is merely residual instinct, so our fear and pity reveal we really believe persons survive as corpses, hence as bodies, not as minds.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 9 "Zombies and Us" — Hamish Thompson asks what could justify killing zombies, canvassing self-defense, total-brain-death criteria, and release from obligations to a radically altered person, using Shaun of the Dead's mother-killing, Bub's trained shooting in Day of the Dead, White Zombie's piano-playing heroine, and the pod-people substitutions of Invasion of the Body Snatchers. He deploys Hume's bundle theory of the self as a fiction of succeeding perceptions and Parfit's graded psychological continuity (with Locke's prince/cobbler case) to argue identity comes in degrees, so zombie termination is never as clean as the genre pretends. The chapter ends by turning the lens around: Shaun's checkout-line beepers and Ed's sofa-and-video-game existence suggest ordinary lives differ from zombiehood only by intermittent acts of imaginative self-direction.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 30 "Oh Yes, There Will Be Blood" — Rachel Robison asks why mythology — from Elizabeth Bathory's blood baths to Dracula's control over Mina once she drinks his blood, and True Blood's Sookie sensing and desiring Bill and then Eric — credits blood with immortality, youth, erotic compulsion, and shared knowledge, including the vampire's dark inversion of the Eucharist. Her answer runs through the history of philosophy and medicine: Aristotle, Empedocles, and Chrysippus located rationality in the heart and made blood its product, while Galen's humoral theory and bloodletting treated blood as the carrier of health, temperament, and identity — so blood naturally reads as the vehicle of personal identity, free will, and even knowledge, explaining how drinking it could transmit a maker's self to Sookie or Mina. She then asks whether the synthetic 'True Blood' of HBO's show could carry the same powers, concluding it works only if some property is shared with real blood or if the power attaches to the act of drinking what is taken as blood.
